card_text: This page focuses on how rising rental rates are the primary driver pushing core consumer price index inflation higher. It features a single line chart titled "Rental rates driving core CPI higher," which plots the three-month annualized percentage change in inflation from January 2003 through early 2006. The vertical axis ranges from 0.0% to 3.5%, and the horizontal axis tracks the years. The chart compares two metrics: CPI excluding energy, shown as a dashed orange line, and CPI excluding energy and rents, shown as a solid green line. While the two series closely track each other for most of the period between 2003 and late 2005, fluctuating cyclically between troughs near 0.5% and peaks above 3.0%, they diverge sharply in 2006. By the end of the observed period, the CPI excluding energy measure climbs toward 3.0%, while the index excluding both energy and rents remains flatter, hovering around 2.25%. This divergence visually demonstrates that when rental rates are factored out, core inflation pressures appear significantly more subdued. The data is sourced from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and MacData, and the page concludes with contact information for Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of JPMorgan Private Bank.

This page features a commentary by Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of JPMorgan Private Bank, arguing that larger countries in the Middle East and Southeast Asia generally struggle to provide the same level of wealth to their citizens compared to smaller ones. He warns that the stark economic divisions in these regions could spark instability and regional crises in the future, which would have broader global implications for OECD military spending, risk premia, and the value of the US dollar. 

The argument is supported by a scatter plot titled "Population and per capita GDP in the Middle East and Southeast Asia," which uses actual or estimated 2006 data from the International Monetary Fund. The chart plots population in millions on the x-axis against per capita GDP in 2006 dollars on the y-axis, illustrating a clear inverse relationship. Smaller nations boast the highest per capita GDP, with the United Arab Emirates exceeding $30,000, followed closely by Kuwait, Singapore, and Hong Kong. In contrast, highly populated countries cluster at the bottom right with extremely low per capita wealth; Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Indonesia, which all have populations over 140 million, have per capita GDPs of $2,000 or less. Mid-population nations like South Korea, Taiwan, and Saudi Arabia occupy a middle ground with per capita GDPs ranging between $15,000 and $20,000. Meanwhile, numerous other countries with smaller populations, such as Libya, Malaysia, Thailand, Iran, Vietnam, and the Philippines, reside in the lower-left quadrant with low per capita wealth, reinforcing the stark divide between the region's wealthy few and its highly populated, less affluent nations.

This page examines "The Pickens Energy Plan" following an interview with T. Boone Pickens regarding his proposal for the expanded use of wind and natural gas to reduce U.S. reliance on foreign oil. The core of Pickens’ argument is that spending $700 billion annually on Middle Eastern oil subjects the United States to unacceptable geopolitical and economic risks. 

The first chart on the page, titled "World energy consumption as a % of GDP," shows annual historical averages from 1970 through 2007, along with a 2008 estimate assuming a $130 oil price. The chart illustrates that global energy spending peaked near 7% of GDP in the early 1980s, fell to under 2% by the late 1990s, and has surged back up toward 4.5% in 2008, confirming that the world is spending more on energy than at almost any time in the prior 40 years. 

The discussion addresses the concept of peak oil, with current global production running at 84.5 million barrels per day (bpd). While some industry forecasts estimate peak production at around 95 million bpd within the next decade, Pickens argues that depletion rates in major fields like Saudi Arabia's Ghawar, as well as in Mexico, Russia, and the North Sea, are closer to 6% than 3%, meaning new production is merely replacing lost output. A footnote cites ConocoPhillips CEO Jim Mulva and France Total CEO Christophe de Margerie, who both stated in 2007 that a level of 100 million bpd is unlikely to ever be reached. 

Addressing U.S. domestic supply, Pickens supports drilling in the Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) and the Alaska National Wildlife Reserve (ANWR) but cautions that low extraction rates of 30% to 35% will yield only 10 to 15 billion barrels of actually recoverable oil, far below the combined 28 billion barrels of estimated reserves. 

The second chart, titled "The supply curve is steep, and the marginal barrel sets the price," illustrates North American Marginal Oil/Gas Costs for 2007. The chart plots the marginal cost of production in dollars per barrel of oil equivalent ($/boe), ranging from $20 to over $80, against cumulative production in thousands of barrels of oil equivalent per day (kboepd), up to 22,000. It shows a highly inelastic, steep curve at the upper end of cumulative production, indicating that the final barrels of supply are very expensive to extract and ultimately set the market price. The author notes that while adding just 1 to 2 million bpd of supply could significantly lower the marginal cost of oil—explaining why oil prices were expected to fall after reaching the mid-$140s—such measures do not provide the 20- to 40-year structural solution needed to counter declining global reserves.

This page, authored by Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of JPMorgan Private Bank, presents two charts illustrating positive macroeconomic trends: fair domestic equity valuations and the widespread benefits of globalization. 

The first chart, titled "For a low inflation period, price-to-earnings multiples are fair," plots the S&P 500 operating price-to-earnings ratio against the core Consumer Price Index percent change over four quarters from 1955 through 2007. The scatter plot reveals a clear historical relationship where lower inflation rates support higher P/E multiples, represented by a downward-sloping trend curve. A marker labeled "Today" shows the position at the time of publication sitting directly on this trend line, with core CPI inflation at approximately 2% and the operating P/E ratio around 16, suggesting that equity valuations are fair and aligned with historical norms for a low-inflation environment. 

The second chart, titled "Reaping the benefits of globalization: a more balanced world," uses International Monetary Fund data from 1982 to 2006 to show how global economic growth has become more synchronized and widespread. The chart compares two trends: the number of countries experiencing strong economic growth versus those experiencing stagnant growth. The blue line, representing nations with annual growth rates above 4%, has risen significantly from around 40 countries in the early 1980s to nearly 110 countries by 2006. Meanwhile, the orange line, representing nations with growth rates below 1%, has declined from a peak of over 50 countries in the early 1980s to fewer than 10 countries by 2006. This dramatic divergence highlights the stabilizing and uplifting effect of globalization, which has successfully transitioned a vast majority of countries into higher-growth tiers. The page concludes with contact details for Michael Cembalest at JPMorgan Private Bank in New York.

This page, published by Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer at JPMorgan Private Bank, illustrates the dramatic expansion of global trade integration through two charts tracking the rise of regional trade agreements and the decline of average applied tariff rates from the late 20th century into the early 2000s. 

The first chart, titled Growth in Regional Trade Agreements, covers the period from 1958 to 2004. It utilizes a dual-axis format, with the left vertical axis measuring the annual number of new agreements on a scale of 0 to 30 and the right vertical axis tracking the cumulative total of agreements on a scale of 0 to 300. The blue bars show that new agreements remained consistently low—typically fewer than five per year—until around 1990. Following 1990, a dramatic acceleration occurred, with new agreements peaking above 25 per year in the early 2000s. Consequently, the orange line tracking cumulative agreements shows an exponential rise, surging from fewer than 50 agreements in 1990 to nearly 300 by 2004. This data is sourced from World Trade Organization and World Bank 2005 Global Economic Prospects data.

The second chart, titled Trends in average applied tariff rates, spans from 1988 to 2003 and displays the steady dismantling of global trade barriers. It also uses a dual-axis format: the left vertical axis measures the average tariff rate for developing countries on a scale of 5% to 30%, while the right vertical axis measures the tariff rate for high-income OECD nations on a scale of 2% to 10%. The blue line reveals that average applied tariffs in developing countries plummeted from nearly 30% in 1988 to roughly 11% by 2003. Concurrently, the green line shows that average applied tariffs in high-income OECD nations fell from approximately 9% in 1988 to about 3.5% by 2003. This data is compiled from United Nations Trade Analysis and Information Systems (TRAINS), World Trade Organization, and various Trade Policy Review Country Reports. Together, these charts document a historical shift toward globalized, liberalized trade characterized by fewer regulatory barriers and more interconnected regional markets.

This page examines the "Pickens Plan" proposed by T. Boone Pickens, situating it within the context of the United States' lack of a coherent energy policy and its heavy reliance on foreign oil. The author outlines Pickens' core strategy, which suggests that the 20% of domestic electricity currently generated by natural gas could instead be met by wind power, thereby freeing up natural gas to be diverted for automotive use. According to the plan, this transition would reduce reliance on foreign oil, decrease carbon emissions, create jobs, and serve as a bridge to future technologies like electric vehicles and biofuels. 

To assess the feasibility of this plan, the text references a 2005 Stanford University study by Cristina Archer and Mark Jacobson. This global study of over 8,000 stations estimated that annual global wind power reached 72 terawatts in 2000, vastly exceeding the global electricity demand of approximately 2 terawatts. The authors posit that capturing just 10% of this wind power—even after factoring in a 30% power efficiency limit—could fulfill global electricity needs, equivalent to the output of 2,000 standard nuclear power plants. 

This potential is illustrated by a geographic plot titled "Map of U.S. wind speed," which maps wind classes at an 80-meter height across seven categories. The categories range from Class 1 (less than 5.9 meters per second) represented by light blue dots, up to Class 7 (greater than or equal to 9.4 meters per second) represented by black dots. The map displays a dense concentration of high-velocity winds, defined as Class 3 or higher, stretching along both coasts and through a massive central corridor from Texas up to the Dakotas. This spatial distribution supports Pickens’ assertion that the United States is the "Saudi Arabia of wind." Ultimately, the page concludes that the primary challenge for wind energy is not resource abundance or kinetic energy sufficiency, but rather the economic cost of harnessing it.

This page discusses the crucial role of transmission infrastructure and technology in scaling up wind energy, addressing the physical and logistical limitations of moving power over long distances. Highlighting estimates by T. Boone Pickens, the author notes that implementing widespread wind power will require massive investment, including $1 trillion for wind farms and $200 billion for transmission lines. 

To illustrate wind farm efficiency, a bar chart in the top left from the Department of Energy shows wind farm productivity peaking outside the Heartland region. It breaks down productivity from 0% to 45% across five regions—Heartland, Texas, California, Northwest, and Mountain—by the date of plant construction, ranging from pre-1998 to 2006. The data demonstrates that newer installations, especially those from 2006, show significantly higher productivity, often reaching 35% to 40% in regions like Texas, the Northwest, and the Mountain area. 

To address transmission losses, a bottom-left chart sourced from ABB Power Systems demonstrates how Direct Current technology overcomes the distance limitations inherent in Alternating Current lines. The chart plots power capacity in megawatts against distance in kilometers up to 1,000 kilometers. A red dotted line representing a 400 kilovolt AC line shows power carrying capacity plunging rapidly from roughly 1,200 megawatts near the source to under 500 megawatts at 400 kilometers, and close to zero by 600 kilometers. In contrast, a blue solid line representing a 320 kilovolt DC line maintains a steady capacity of around 1,100 to 1,200 megawatts over the entire 1,000-kilometer distance. 

The text elaborates on the potential of High Voltage Direct Current technology, citing an ABB project in China designed to carry 6,400 megawatts of power over 2,000 kilometers on an 800 kilovolt line. This technology allows generation to be placed in optimal remote locations, such as deserts or oceans, rather than near population centers where they face local opposition. Concepts for Europe involve connecting offshore wind, Scandinavian hydro, and Northern African solar—including a proposed $60 billion Sahara solar project producing 100,000 megawatts. On the policy side, the author notes that the Energy Policy Act of 2005 grants the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission the authority to override state objections to designate national transmission corridors, indicating that federal eminent domain may be vital for national energy planning.

Finally, the page addresses the dilemma of baseload versus peaking capacity. Because wind is intermittent, natural gas is expected to remain essential for meeting peak demands, as gas plants operate only 21% of the time compared to coal at 70% and nuclear at 90%. To make wind reliable, grids must link diverse geographic regions to smooth out local wind disparities. Achieving the goals of the Pickens Plan would demand a five- to six-fold increase in high-voltage line construction, requiring approximately 40,000 miles of new HVDC connections.

This page discusses the growth, policy dependencies, and structural challenges of wind power in the United States. The author argues that while the United States has significant absolute wind capacity at around 17,000 megawatts, second only to Germany, it lags far behind Europe and India when wind is measured as a percentage of total electricity generation. This is illustrated in a horizontal bar chart titled "U.S. wind power contribution lags Europe," which projects wind generation at the end of 2007 as a percentage of electricity consumption. Denmark leads the chart at over 20%, followed by Spain, Portugal, Ireland, and Germany, while the United States sits near the bottom at under 2%, just behind Sweden and Italy, and ahead of only France, Australia, Canada, Norway, China, Japan, Brazil, and the global total. 

A primary reason for this lagging adoption is inconsistent congressional support for the Production Tax Credit. Wind power relies heavily on these subsidies, which cover 25% to 30% of a project's total cost, or roughly $20 to $25 per megawatt hour. The visual evidence of this policy dependency is shown in a bar chart titled "Wind capacity additions grind to a halt without subsidies," which tracks annual U.S. capacity additions in megawatts from 1990 to 2007. The chart highlights three distinct drops in 2000, 2002, and 2004 when Congress allowed the tax credits to lapse, demonstrating how capacity growth dramatically stalls without a stable regulatory environment, before climbing back near 5,000 megawatts in 2007 under renewed subsidies. At the time of writing in August 2008, the author notes that credits are set to expire in December 2008, with renewal delayed by political gridlock over offshore drilling. This uncertainty threatens the approximately 225,000 megawatts of wind projects currently in planning stages, a volume thirteen times the existing base.

The page also addresses emerging cost and efficiency challenges. A scatter plot titled "Wind project costs rising" tracks individual and average online project costs in 2007 dollars per kilowatt from 1982 to 2007. A red polynomial trend line illustrates that while average costs fell steadily from over $4,000 per kilowatt in the early 1980s to a low of approximately $1,300 per kilowatt between 2000 and 2002, they have since risen back toward $2,000 per kilowatt due to the increasing cost of turbine materials and energy inputs. Finally, the author points out that wind turbine technology is maturing, with capacity factors cresting at around 35% in most regions outside the Heartland. Consequently, the author concludes that achieving broader wind energy targets will require building significantly more wind farms rather than relying on future turbine efficiency breakthroughs.

This page features a chart titled "There is a disconnect between oil prices and unsold supply," authored by Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer at JPMorgan Private Bank. The chart compares the historical spot price of oil with the volume of floating unsold oil inventory from 1992 through mid-2008, using data current as of May 23, 2008. 

The left-hand axis tracks the oil spot rate in US dollars, ranging from 0 to 140, which is represented by an orange dashed line. This series shows that oil prices remained relatively low and stable, fluctuating between $15 and $30 per barrel throughout the 1990s, before beginning a steep and continuous rise starting around 2002 that carried the price toward $130 per barrel by 2008. 

The right-hand axis measures floating unsold oil inventory in thousands of tons, ranging from 0 to 6,000, depicted by a solid blue line. During the 1990s, this unsold inventory was highly volatile but frequently elevated, often hovering between 2,000 and 5,000 thousand tons. However, from 2002 through 2006, this inventory fell to near-zero levels. It experienced only a minor increase to around 1,000 to 1,500 thousand tons by 2008. 

The core observation of this page is the distinct lack of correlation between skyrocketing oil prices and unsold global inventory in the years leading up to 2008. Despite historic price increases, there was no massive buildup of unsold oil stored at sea, pointing to a fundamental disconnect between market pricing and physical unsold supply.

This page examines public debates surrounding wind power and analyzes the feasibility of natural gas-powered vehicles, highlighting the trade-offs of the Pickens Plan. In the first section, the author addresses emotional objections to wind energy, such as aesthetic concerns and bird fatalities. To contextualize the debate over bird deaths, a horizontal bar chart titled "Birds have a lot more to worry about than wind farms... and the analysis excludes global warming" shows the percent composition of bird fatalities by source. The chart reveals that wind turbines account for less than 1 per 10,000 fatalities, making them a negligible threat compared to buildings and windows, which cause 5,500 per 10,000 fatalities (or 55% of the total). Other major contributors include cats and other sources at 1,000 per 10,000 each, high-tension lines at 800, and vehicles and pesticides at 700 each. The author points out that major environmental groups, like the Audubon Society and the Sierra Club, support wind power because fossil-fuel-driven climate change is a far greater threat to wildlife. The author also touches on local controversies, such as aesthetic opposition to the Cape Wind project in Nantucket Bay and media efforts to find opposition to wind farms in Sweetwater, Texas, arguing that these localized concerns must be balanced against national interests and the massive financial and geopolitical costs of foreign oil dependence, citing the five-hundred-billion-dollar cost of the war in Iraq.

The second half of the page shifts to natural gas, noting that technological improvements like deep-water and horizontal drilling in places like the Barnett Shale have unexpectedly boosted natural gas supplies by nine percent since early 2007, and by fifteen percent in Texas. Despite this supply boom, the author questions the viability of transitioning the transportation sector to natural gas vehicles, as proposed in the Pickens Plan. The concern is that natural gas reserves may not be abundant enough to support both widespread automotive conversion and the power sector's massive, growing demand. This dynamic is illustrated in a line chart showing US natural gas consumption by sector in trillions of cubic feet from 1990 to 2007. The chart shows that electricity generators have steadily increased their natural gas consumption from around three trillion cubic feet in 1990 to nearly seven trillion cubic feet in 2007, rivaling the industrial sector, which fell from over eight trillion to around six and a half trillion cubic feet. Meanwhile, residential use remained flat near five trillion, commercial use was stable near three trillion, and vehicle fuel usage remained virtually non-existent at the bottom of the chart. The author concludes that pushing natural gas for vehicle fuel runs directly counter to the electricity sector's deep and growing reliance on the resource as it shifts away from coal and nuclear power due to regulatory and operational challenges.

This page discusses the feasibility, benefits, and drawbacks of Natural Gas Vehicles (NGVs) as well as the limitations of bio-ethanol as an alternative energy source. The author examines both liquid and compressed natural gas (LNG/CNG) systems, noting there were currently 130,000 such vehicles in the United States and several million worldwide. It highlights the Honda Civic GX as a prominent CNG model, praised by the EPA as the cleanest combustion engine on Earth with a fuel efficiency of 32 miles per gasoline gallon equivalent. Other manufacturers like John Deere, Cummins Westport, GM, Volkswagen, Fiat, and Peugeot are noted for their contributions to natural gas engines for passenger and commercial vehicles. While natural gas cars carry a premium of $4,000 to $5,000 over gasoline cars and suffer from reduced trunk space and halved driving ranges, they offer fuel cost savings of 25% to 50% per energy unit, despite historical natural gas price volatility between $8 and $13 per million British thermal units.

To address the lack of refueling infrastructure—noting there are only 1,600 CNG stations compared to over 200,000 gasoline stations—the page features a map titled "Compressed natural gas: all that's left to build is retail distribution." Sourced from the Energy Information Administration, this map illustrates the vast, nationwide coverage of interstate pipelines, intrastate pipelines, and compressor stations across the United States. The graphic argues that since a dense pipeline backbone already covers almost every metropolitan and major suburban community, expanding the system requires only retail-level distribution. This could be achieved via $400,000 service station retrofits or $3,500 home-refueling units like the "Phill." The text notes that public figure T. Boone Pickens recommends prioritizing centrally-fueled fleets, such as government vehicles and long-haul trucks, for early conversion.

The second half of the page critiques bio-ethanol. The author questions its viability, pointing out that its Energy Returned on Energy Invested (EROEI) is barely above 1.0, even using the USDA's positive estimate of 1.2, which is significantly lower than that of fossil fuels, solar, or wind. The text details the scientific challenges of cellulosic ethanol, explaining the difficulty in replicating the highly complex termite enzymes and DNA code required to break down cellulose. Ultimately, the author warns that allocating 33% of U.S. corn production to ethanol triggers severe side effects, specifically food price inflation and wheat crop displacement, despite a 2007 Department of Energy initiative investing $375 million to make cellulosic ethanol competitive within five years.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" by Michael Cembalest presents a stark visual representation of the escalating 2008 financial crisis through two primary charts tracking Federal Reserve interventions and long-term systemic leverage in the United States, followed by a glossary of key financial acronyms. 

The first chart, titled "Chart 1: Sum of all Federal Reserve Liquidity Facilities Outstanding," shows the total billions of dollars in credit extended across various emergency programs from July 2007 through October 1, 2008. The data series aggregates the Term Auction Facility, Discount Window, Primary Dealer Credit Facility, Asset Backed Commercial Paper Money Market Fund Liquidity Facility, emergency loans, Maiden Lane LLC (the Bear Stearns facility), Term Securities Lending Facility, Foreign Term Auction Facility, and Open Market Operations Collateral. The chart highlights that initial intervention efforts, which held steady at around $500 billion from April to July 2008, ultimately failed to contain the crisis, as emphasized by an arrow pointing to this period with the caption, "This didn't work." Immediately following this plateau, outstanding liquidity facilities spiked vertically, skyrocketing to over $1.2 trillion. 

The second chart, titled "Chart 2: U.S. total debt as a percentage of GDP," presents the broader historical context of the crisis by showing the accumulation of all consumer, government, and corporate debt as a percentage of nominal GDP from 1952 to early 2008. The line graph illustrates a relatively stable level of debt of around 130% to 170% of GDP from the 1950s until the early 1980s. However, starting around 1982, the nation embarked on a massive, uninterrupted borrowing cycle. Total debt as a percentage of GDP surged past 220% by the late 1980s, continued its upward trajectory through the 1990s, and accelerated sharply after 2002 to peak near 350% of GDP by 2007.

To help readers navigate the rapidly shifting regulatory and corporate landscape of the crisis, the bottom of the page defines several essential "Acronyms of the week." These include GSE (Government Sponsored Enterprise), REIT (Real Estate Investment Trust), SIPC (Securities Investor Protection Corporation), PWC (PricewaterhouseCoopers), FSA (Financial Services Authority in the U.K.), AIG (American International Group), GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles), and DIP financing, which is defined as Debtor in Possession Financing where monies are advanced at structurally senior levels to other debt and equity claims.

This page from the publication addresses widespread concern regarding massive derivative exposures at large financial institutions like J.P. Morgan during the 2008 financial crisis. Author Michael Cembalest aims to demystify how trillions of dollars in gross "notional exposure" are whittled down to much smaller reported net risk figures. 

The text outlines a three-step reduction process. First, banks utilize bilateral netting via ISDA agreements to offset mutual obligations with individual counterparties. Second, they convert massive notional contract sizes into mark-to-market exposure, which reflects only the actual fluctuating value at risk. Third, banks eliminate positions that are collateralized by counterparties using cash, Treasuries, and agency securities. 

To illustrate the nature of these derivatives, the page features a pie chart titled "Notional amount of derivatives held by U.S. commercial banks in Q2 2008: heavy emphasis on rates and FX." Based on data from the OCC’s Quarterly Report on Bank Trading and Derivatives Activities, the chart shows that the overwhelming majority of derivative holdings are interest rate contracts, followed by foreign exchange, with much smaller slivers dedicated to credit derivatives, equity, and commodity/other contracts. The text supports this by stating that 80% of J.P. Morgan's derivative contracts are linked to interest rates and 9% to foreign exchange, while for the top 25 commercial banks, interest rates and foreign exchange make up 90% of all derivative contracts. 

Through these adjustments, J.P. Morgan's massive Q2 2008 gross notional derivatives exposure of $91 trillion is reduced to a reported exposure of $109 billion. When factoring in an additional $21 billion of collateral that is not cash or Treasuries, the uncollateralized derivatives exposure drops to approximately $88 billion. This represents just 0.12% of the original gross notional amount and accounts for 6% of the bank's total assets, which is small compared to its $540 billion in loans and $120 billion in securities. The author concludes by noting that this remaining $88 billion in exposure is diversified across 18,000 counterparties, including foreign governments, sovereign wealth funds, institutional investors, endowments, and corporations, rather than being concentrated solely among peer banks and brokers.

This page, titled "Tarp shooter," critiques the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) bill, arguing that its prospects for success are mixed due to two primary shortcomings. First, the bill fails to address the critical need for fresh bank capital to absorb losses and protect creditors. Second, the policy process failed to adequately engage the American public regarding the severe risks to their well-being if an effective solution is not executed. The text suggests that prior banking crises were successfully resolved through public sector equity injections and highlights alternative proposals from former FDIC Chairman William Isaac and Nobel Prize-winning economist Edmund Phelps of Columbia University. Current estimates suggest that between $400 billion and $600 billion in public capital additions is required to restore bank capital adequacy to pre-crisis levels.

To illustrate the mounting pressure on the financial system, the page features two charts. Chart 1 displays the sum of all outstanding Federal Reserve liquidity facilities in billions of dollars from July 2007 through October 2008. This total includes a wide array of interventions, such as the Term Auction Facility, Discount Window, Primary Dealer Credit Facility, Asset-Backed Commercial Paper Money Market Fund Liquidity Facility, emergency loans, Maiden Lane LLC (the Bear Stearns facility), and foreign term auction facilities. The chart shows that outstanding liquidity hovered below $200 billion until late 2007, then climbed to a plateau of around $600 billion by mid-2008. An arrow points to this flat period with the annotation "This didn't work," after which the line spikes vertically, surpassing $1.2 trillion by October 2008. 

Chart 2 presents unused corporate commitments from all national commercial banks in trillions of dollars from 1992 through 2007. These commitments include commercial lines of credit, overdraft facilities, and retail credit plans. The data shows a steady climb from approximately $0.7 trillion in 1992 to $1.6 trillion in 2000, followed by a brief plateau and a subsequent rapid acceleration to a peak of nearly $2.4 trillion in late 2006, before starting a slight decline. This visual emphasizes the massive volume of potential off-balance-sheet credit liabilities that commercial banks faced as the credit crisis began to unfold.

This page continues a discussion on the commercial viability of alternative fuels, focusing on the limitations of hydrogen and the potential of synthetic fuels before concluding with an analysis of natural gas and wind power. 

The text begins by detailing the inefficiency of hydrogen fuel cells, noting that skeptics predict a hydrogen car would travel only half the distance of an electric car using the same electricity input. The author cites various energy experts and initiatives, such as the federal FreedomCAR initiative and the CAFÉ fuel standards, highlighting the high cost and transport dangers of hydrogen. As an alternative, the page explores synthetic fuels produced via the Fisher-Tropsch process, which uses wind power to create hydrogen via electrolysis and combines it with carbon monoxide captured from coal plant exhaust. While this process is carbon-neutral and avoids the need to redesign internal combustion engines, its primary hurdles remain cost and scale.

To illustrate how technology costs fall as they scale, the page includes a log-log chart from the UC Berkeley Energy Research Group titled "Renewables need scale and time to succeed." The vertical axis measures capital cost in 2004 USD per Watt (ranging from 1 to 100), and the horizontal axis measures cumulative installed capacity in Megawatts (ranging from 1 to 100,000). The chart traces the declining cost trajectories of five technologies: Ethanol (1978–1996), Solar Thermal (1985–1991), Solar PV (1975–2003), PV Inverters (1995–2002), and Wind Power (1981–2001). Each line demonstrates a steep downward learning curve, showing that as cumulative capacity expands, capital costs dramatically decrease.

In the "Concluding Thoughts" section, the author addresses recent natural gas discoveries, such as the Marcellus Black Shale in Ohio, which is estimated to contain 225 trillion cubic feet. Despite falling extraction costs below $5 per mm BTU and projected natural gas prices of $7, the author argues that natural gas reserves are insufficient to support both electricity generation and a massive fleet of compressed natural gas (CNG) vehicles. To achieve the energy transition championed by T. Boone Pickens, wind power must be deployed to displace natural gas in the power sector. 

This argument is supported by a bar chart titled "Annual U.S. Natural gas production (trillion cubic feet per year)," which displays U.S. gas production from 1990 to a forecasted 2008. The vertical axis ranges from 0 to 28 trillion cubic feet. While annual U.S. production has historically remained flat between 18 and 20 trillion cubic feet, a prominent orange block is stacked on top of the 2008 forecast bar to represent the additional supply needed to replace gasoline for trucks and buses. This visual emphasizes that without the contribution of wind power to free up gas supplies, U.S. natural gas production would have to increase by 25 percent to supply the 39 billion gallons of gasoline equivalent needed annually for heavy transportation.

This page examines the systemic failures and underwriting mistakes that fueled the 2007–2008 financial crisis, focusing specifically on counterparty credit risk and the flaw of ratings-based collateral triggers. The author first highlights how insurance bought from major monoline and private mortgage insurers—including XL, AMBAC, MBIA, Radian, Genworth, and PMI—turned out to be worth a fraction of its value. This discrepancy led to "commutations," in which distressed insurers repurchased their liabilities at deep discounts. For example, Merrill Lynch accepted a $500 million settlement on $2.5 billion in hedging gains owed by XL Insurance, and MBIA terminated $5 billion in contracts with no payment. Additionally, government-sponsored enterprises Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac incurred massive counterparty risks from these insurers, with Freddie Mac reporting $65 billion of exposure to insurers that lost 95% of their market value. 

To illustrate this industry collapse, a line chart titled "Selected insurers' stock price performance" displays the stock prices of AMBAC, MBIA, Radian, and PMI from January 2007 to October 2008. The chart demonstrates a near-total wipeout of equity value across all four entities, with AMBAC's stock falling from a peak of nearly $90 and MBIA falling from around $70 down to the single digits by late 2008, while Radian and PMI collapsed from peaks of around $60 and $50 respectively.

The text then shifts to the structural dangers of ratings-based collateral triggers, using American International Group as a primary example. Many protection buyers only required AIG to post collateral if its credit rating was downgraded. This loophole allowed AIG's capital markets subsidiary, AIGFP, to amass $440 billion in insured claims without posting collateral. When downgrades finally occurred, the sudden demands for tens of billions of dollars in collateral led to AIG’s collapse, necessitating an $85 billion government loan and an additional $38 billion liquidity facility. 

A second line chart, "American International Group (AIG): the ratings trigger for collateral lagged the markets," plots AIG's stock price on the left axis against its inverted five-year credit default swap spread in basis points on the right axis from June 2007 to August 2008. The chart shows AIG's stock price steadily declining from over $70 to under $20, while its CDS spreads widened drastically to over 2,000 basis points. Despite these severe market indicators of distress, rating agencies left AIG's rating at AA- for almost the entire period, only downgrading it to A- in August 2008. This visualization reinforces the author's argument that credit rating downgrades lagged far behind actual market deterioration, meaning the collateral triggers were tripped only after it was already impossible for AIG to raise the funds publicly.

This page from the publication analyzes the global economic outlook as the world heads into 2009, arguing that a rapid deceleration is underway with similarities to the severe recessions of 1973–1975 and 1981–1982. The author details widespread economic deterioration, noting that U.S. consumer spending is failing to respond to lower oil prices, business investment in equipment and software has collapsed alongside the ISM new orders index to its lowest level since 1980, and 58% of residential mortgages modified in the first quarter of 2008 have already re-defaulted. Globally, Chinese economic growth is tracking at 5% with negative year-over-year export growth for the first time in seven years, the Baltic Freight Index has plunged 95%, and Germany’s Bundesbank expects the nation's worst recession since 1948. The author points to the GSE conservatorship and other regulatory decisions as the catalysts that unleashed a global credit market collapse. 

The primary structural difference of this recession compared to prior episodes is the potential contraction of household and corporate debt. In previous downturns, debt levels actually increased relative to GDP to help mitigate economic pain. An accompanying line chart, titled "U.S. household & corporate debt around recessions: an increase seems unlikely this time," plots debt as a percentage of nominal GDP from 1952 to 2007, showing a rise from roughly 70% to nearly 250%. Barbells on the line represent the six-month periods before and after recessions, showing that debt consistently increased during past downturns. However, because total debt has tripled since 1952, the author poses a question mark for the current recession, suggesting that a further debt expansion is unlikely and could make this downturn worse than its predecessors.

A major impediment to credit expansion is the shutdown of securitized capital markets, which formerly served as a dominant source of credit. A second chart, titled "Asset backed securities: from $240 billion per quarter to zero," tracks the total quarterly supply of these securities in billions of dollars from 2000 to 2008. The stacked area chart breaks down the supply by categories, including Home Equity (Subprime), Commercial Real Estate, Autos, Credit Cards, Student Loans, Non-U.S. Residential Mortgages, and Equipment. The supply peaked near $270 billion per quarter in 2006 before plummeting to a mere $424 million by late 2008. The author observes that even excluding subprime mortgage assets, the economy must absorb a $50 billion per quarter shortfall in auto, credit card, and student loan financing. Because the share of credit creation handled by traditional banks fell from two-thirds in 1980 to only one-third by 2007, this securitization freeze has broad systemic consequences, leaving corporate draws on pre-committed bank credit lines as the only remaining area of active lending.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" analysis examines the global government response to credit collapse and deflation risks, focusing on the unprecedented interventions of the U.S. Federal Reserve and the incoming Obama administration's fiscal plans. The author argues that central banks and treasuries are aggressively leaning into the wind with trillions in financing, asset purchases, and deposit guarantees to offset the decline in private sector activity. 

A key visual highlights the massive growth of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet, showing that from a starting point close to zero in August 2007, the Fed's ownership or financing of private sector assets surged to $1.945 trillion by late 2008. A detailed breakdown in the chart lists the components of these outstanding liquidity facilities, which include $448 billion in the Term Auction Facility, $312 billion in the Commercial Paper Funding Facility, $191 billion in the Term Securities Lending Facility, and $634 billion in other Federal Reserve assets, among several other smaller facilities. 

To measure whether the Fed is providing sufficient liquidity, a second chart tracks the change in the monetary base as a percentage of total outstanding debt from 1919 to 2009. This chart illustrates a historic spike in late 2008, reaching nearly 2.5% following the November 25, 2008 announcement regarding asset-backed and mortgage-backed securities. This surge is significantly higher than the levels seen during the Great Depression and dwarfs the peaks seen during Japan’s quantitative easing experiments in the 1990s and in 2002, signaling that the Fed is taking an aggressive, "gloves off" approach to prevent deflation.

The author assesses whether these monetary interventions are working, noting mixed results. While prime money market funds, Libor, and commercial paper markets have shown some improvement because the government has stepped in as a marginal buyer, the transmission of lower mortgage rates to home sales remains blocked. A scatter plot comparing the Mortgage Refinancing Index to the Fannie Mae 30-year current coupon rate from 2000 through November 2008 shows that refinancing activity, marked by orange squares for post-September 2008 readings, has begun to rise but is still lagging behind historical curves. The author attributes this muted response to tighter underwriting criteria and collapsing home values.

Turning to fiscal policy, the publication notes that the incoming Obama administration is planning a peacetime-record deficit in the neighborhood of 8% to 9% of GDP, which is comparable only to deficits run during World War II and surpasses the 6% peaks of the 1970s and 1980s. Addressing critics of large budget deficits, the author argues that aggressive fiscal expansion is a proven tool to combat depression. Supporting this, the text cites the historical precedent of Franklin D. Roosevelt's administration, where loosening fiscal policy helped lower non-farm unemployment from 31% to 11% prior to the start of World War II, whereas a premature tightening of fiscal policy in 1937 triggered a secondary recession.

This page analyzes the historical patterns of equity markets and corporate profits during recessions to determine tactical portfolio weightings heading into 2009. The author argues that asset prices historically bottom well before the broader economy does, specifically finding that the S&P 500 has bottomed anywhere from one to seven quarters prior to peak unemployment, with a historical average of about three quarters. This is illustrated in a bar chart detailing the quarters before peak unemployment that the S&P bottomed during major postwar recession years, showing two quarters in 1958 and 1960, five in 1970, three in 1974, one in 1982, seven in 1990, and three in 2001.

Addressing corporate profits, the author notes that large-cap earnings have already dropped by 23% as of the third quarter of 2008, matching typical deep recession drawdowns. A line chart depicting the maximum drawdown of S&P 500 EPS from 1940 to 2006 contextually highlights this current 23% decline, with J.P. Morgan forecasting a total peak-to-trough earnings drop of roughly 30% to about $65 per share in 2009. 

Despite these historical precursors suggesting a market bottom might be near, J.P. Morgan advises an underweight position on equities heading into 2009, asserting that this recession features unprecedented hurdles. These include vast unrealized bank losses and the uncertain efficacy of extraordinary government interventions. Consequently, the firm is preserving cash and fixed-income reserves at 32% to 42% in balanced portfolios. Regarding specific equity allocations, they are underweighting Europe relative to the United States, maintaining an underweight stance on small-cap stocks relative to large-cap, staying close to neutral on growth versus value, and avoiding Asian equities.

To mitigate downside risks, the firm recommends strategies that "sell" high volatility. This approach is illustrated by a line chart showing 12-month S&P 500 implied volatility from 1994 through late 2008, which depicts volatility spiking to nearly 45% by November 2008. Additionally, the page references economist Nouriel Roubini of New York University, who projects ultimate industry credit losses closer to $2 trillion compared to the $1 trillion recognized by late 2008. To illustrate the banking sector's distress, the author points to Wachovia, which had already booked losses equal to 332% of its June 2007 tangible book value, and warns that peak default rates on credit cards, Alt-A, and jumbo mortgages have not yet been reached.

This page argues for the necessity of targeted, goods-and-services-based fiscal stimulus to combat the economic downturn, while addressing the critical question of whether governments can afford such massive interventions. 

The first chart, titled "1930 – 1950: validating fiscal stimulus rather than contradicting it," plots the U.S. budget surplus or deficit as a percentage of nominal GDP against the nonfarm unemployment rate. It illustrates that premature fiscal tightening caused the sharp 1937–1938 recession, pushing unemployment back over 15%, whereas the massive deficit spending of World War II successfully drove unemployment down to near zero. The author uses this historical data to argue that fiscal stimulus works when sustained, contrary to critics who point to Japan as a failure of stimulus, which the author counters was actually a case of inaction.

To illustrate the long-term benefits of productive public spending, a second chart titled "The benefits of an infrastructure boom have historical precedent" displays the rolling 10-year percentage change in nonfarm productivity from 1957 to 2007. It highlights a massive productivity peak of over 35% in the late 1950s and early 1960s following the creation of the Interstate Highway System. The author notes that this system, despite making up only 1% of the nation's road network, carried 23% of the traffic and accounted for a quarter of U.S. productivity growth by reducing freight costs, commuting times, and accident-related losses. For 2009, the author suggests modern equivalents in energy efficiency, such as building insulation, HVAC upgrades, LED office lighting, and high-voltage direct current lines linked to the Pickens Plan. The text stresses that stimulus must involve direct purchases of goods and services rather than asset purchases or tax rebates, pointing out that banks and individuals are currently in a hoarding mode, as evidenced by a $40 billion T-bill auction that was four times oversubscribed at a 0% rate.

Addressing whether governments can afford these rescue packages, a third chart titled "Total banking sector liabilities as a % of government debt" shows that bank liabilities are dangerously large compared to public debt in several countries. While the U.S. ratio is relatively modest, the United Kingdom's bank assets are ten times the size of its government, and liabilities in Iceland and Switzerland are off the charts, with Iceland exceeding 3,500% and Switzerland surpassing 3,000%. 

These extreme imbalances are causing significant political tension within Europe. The text discusses how Germany, which maintains a combined budget and current account surplus of 7% of GDP, rejected Italy's proposal for "Eurozone bonds" and resisted French pressure to spend more. Additionally, the German finance minister criticized the United Kingdom's value-added tax cuts. Consequently, yield differentials between Italian and German government bonds have widened back to levels not seen since May 1997, two years before the launch of the Euro.

This page discusses the 2009 outlook across hedge funds, commercial real estate, and commodities following the disruptions of 2008. 

The author begins by analyzing hedge fund gating, arguing that while halting redemptions prevents forced asset sales when there is no bid, it ultimately delays the price discovery needed for an economic recovery. A chart titled Capital Protection Comparison: Hedge Funds vs. Stock/Bond Portfolio illustrates index performance drawdown percentages from 1990 to late 2008, comparing the HFRI Fund Weighted Composite Index with a benchmark of 60 percent S&P 500 and 40 percent Lehman Aggregate Bond Index. While the hedge fund index historically maintained much milder drawdowns, both series plummeted in 2008, with the HFRI dropping near 20 percent and the 60/40 benchmark falling roughly 24 percent. Despite this, potential silver linings are noted for surviving hedge funds, such as statistical arbitrage strategies recovering in 2008 and opportunities to buy deeply oversold subprime mortgages and leveraged loans.

Turning to commercial real estate, the outlook for 2009 is presented as highly challenging. A chart titled Tight Connection Between Unemployment and Office Vacancy Rates plots the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate on the left axis (ranging from 3.5 percent to 8.0 percent) against the national office vacancy rate on the right axis (ranging from 6 percent to 18 percent) from 1984 to 2008. The close tracking of these two lines indicates that rising unemployment will drive up vacancy rates. This cyclical trouble is compounded by the collapse of the commercial mortgage-backed securities market, which accounted for 30 percent of outstanding commercial real estate debt and 42 percent of recent issuance by the end of 2007. Lending terms from 2001 to 2007 became highly lenient, with interest-only loans rising from under 5 percent to more than 50 percent of the market, loan-to-value ratios exceeding 100 percent, and equity subordination levels collapsing. Special servicers are underprepared to modify these loans, and insurance companies cannot easily provide refinancing due to their own investment portfolio issues.

Finally, the page reviews the outlook for commodities following a dramatic market turn. A chart titled Commodity Collapse: Globalization Thesis Hits the Wall displays the Reuters/Jefferies CRB Commodity Price Index from 1973 through late 2008. The index shows a massive spike peaking near 450 in mid-2008 before experiencing a severe drop back toward the 200 level by December. The author reflects on the prior commodity rally, which was driven by pension fund allocations and an eight-fold increase in over-the-counter energy derivative contracts over three years. While long-term growth in China and India has merit, the positive thesis became fully priced in. Decades of underinvestment in industrial metals and agricultural commodities created temporary supply shortages and price spikes, which are now reversing as industry capital spending rises.

This page discusses the investment outlook for credit markets, municipal bonds, private equity, and hedge funds during the late-2008 financial crisis. 

Regarding credit, J.P. Morgan advises against avoiding the market entirely, arguing that default expectations currently priced into the market are significantly worse than the worst historical defaults. This point is supported by a table titled "Credit markets are pricing in some terrible outcomes," which compares current implied default rates to the worst observed historical default rates. For investment-grade corporates, the current implied default rate is 14% (assuming a 20% recovery rate) compared to a worst observed rate of 3% during the five-year period starting in 1981. For high-yield bonds, the current implied rate is 55% compared to a historical worst of 34%. For leveraged loans, the implied rate is 70% (assuming a 60% recovery rate) compared to a historical worst of 23% from 1999 to 2003. For super senior AAA CMBS, the implied rate is 70% (the level needed to bring current loan losses to 30%) compared to a historical worst of 32% for the 1986 commercial real estate vintage year. Consequently, J.P. Morgan maintains a half-weight to credit and has added exposure to investment-grade corporate bonds, which they expect to be well-bid as U.S. pension plans buy them to hedge liabilities under the Pension Protection Act of 2006.

In anticipation of a modest increase in Federal tax rates, J.P. Morgan has reduced exposure to diversified hedge funds and increased exposure to municipal bonds. They note that nearly half of municipal bonds are no longer wrapped by monoline insurers like AMBAC and MBIA, which heightens the importance of independent security selection over relying on bond insurer ratings. 

The outlook for private equity is analyzed across three distinct segments. While deals from 2001 to 2005 performed well, transactions from 2006 and 2007 are heavily burdened by excessive debt. LBO sponsors are actively trying to engineer "coercive" debt exchanges to avoid Chapter 11 bankruptcy. J.P. Morgan highlights a recent attempt by Cerberus to convince bondholders to accept a principal writedown on GMAC debt to transition it into a Bank Holding Company, which has struggled with low participation. They point out that typical recent debt exchanges only reduce company leverage marginally—such as from 14x to 12.7x EBITDA—which fails to resolve the structural issues of over-leveraged companies. However, they maintain a 5% to 7% portfolio weight to private equity, finding opportunity in less-leveraged transactions, growth equity, and distressed debt.

Finally, the outlook for hedge funds is described as highly challenged. Unlike the 2001–2002 bear market where hedge funds successfully preserved capital, hedge funds in 2008 merely tracked the falling stock-bond proxy. This underperformance, coupled with client liquidity needs, has led to massive capital outflows that could erase one-third of the industry's assets, estimated at $400 billion. The sector’s future is further clouded by tighter prime brokerage terms, regulatory uncertainty over short-selling rules, over-reliance on leverage for illiquid positions, and widespread redemption suspensions among major funds.

Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Global Wealth Management, opens this page of the 2009 market outlook by analyzing commodities and macro risks. He argues that current oil prices in the $40s and $50s present an investment opportunity, as they align with marginal production costs, correcting the irrational $140 peak seen earlier in 2008. For gold, Cembalest notes potential near-term downward pressure from deflation fears and potential selling by the Swiss National Bank to repay its $54 billion swap line to the Federal Reserve, which was utilized to buy distressed assets from UBS. However, he maintains that gold remains a viable long-term hedge against today's monetary expansion. 

Addressing broader economic anxieties, Cembalest rejects extreme client-forwarded research predicting societal collapse by 2010 but cautions that investors must be compensated for taking on the risks of aggressive fiscal and monetary expansions. He estimates that U.S. Treasury borrowing needs will double from $1 trillion in 2008 to $2 trillion in 2009 to cover refinancing and deficit spending. Furthermore, he points out the unorthodox nature of the Federal Reserve hinting at issuing its own notes to fund asset purchases. 

These widening deficits arrive just as entitlement spending is set to change trajectory in three to four years. A chart titled "Federal spending projections for Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid" illustrates this dilemma. Plotting the percentage of nominal GDP from 1962 projected out to 2042, the chart shows the combined cost of Medicaid, Medicare, and Social Security rising from under 10% of GDP in the early 2000s to approximately 20% by 2042, driven primarily by Medicare and Medicaid. Cembalest emphasizes that this shift will eventually force difficult political decisions, including tax hikes, spending cuts, or entitlement reductions.

Looking forward into 2009, Cembalest expects a final wave of forced selling and downward revisions to corporate profit expectations to establish solid market entry points. This historical cycle of long-term performance is depicted in a chart titled "U.S. large cap returns, annualized 10-year moving average since 1881." This line chart tracks the 10-year moving average of stock returns, which historically swings between a peak of nearly 20% and a trough of around -5%. At the end of 2008, the moving average is shown plunging toward zero, a generational low comparable to the bottoms of the 1930s and 1970s. Cembalest advises that while historical recessions show that risk-taking should increase before the economic smoke clears, investors must remain cautious given the unprecedented public sector interventions. He concludes with a note on the legacy of former Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, contrasting Greenspan’s push for financial deregulation with the resistance of his predecessor, Paul Volcker.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" publication, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the depth of the 2008 financial crisis by comparing current economic indicators to historical recessions, particularly those in 1974 and 1981–1982, while also examining how government intervention has shaped credit spreads. 

The first set of charts illustrates that a severe lack of credit has dragged economic indicators down to levels as bad as the 1981–1982 recession. The Conference Board Consumer Confidence index plunged toward a level of 35, matching historical lows. Concurrently, the ISM Manufacturing Index dropped below 40, approaching the worst levels of the early 1980s. Housing starts fell below an annualized rate of 750,000 units, marking a historical low that sits far below any level recorded since 1959. Quarter-over-quarter consumption growth also experienced a sharp contraction, diving well below negative 4%. 

The second set of charts highlights key structural differences between the current crisis and those of 1974 and 1982, showing that the macroeconomic backdrop in 2008 contains some relative strengths. Core inflation is significantly lower, standing at roughly 2% compared to approximately 10% in 1974 and 8% in 1982. Unit labor costs are also subdued at around 1%, whereas they exceeded 8% in the earlier periods. Non-farm productivity remains positive at roughly 1.5%, contrasting with the negative productivity growth observed in 1974 and 1982. Additionally, inventory valuation adjustments as a percentage of corporate profits are under 5%, indicating higher overall earnings quality than in 1974, when high inflation forced adjustments to near 40%. 

The final set of charts demonstrates how the cost of credit reflects the presence of government guarantees. In markets receiving direct government support, shorter-term rates remained anchored. In the high-grade commercial paper market, 1-day spreads stayed relatively low, while 30-day and 90-day spreads spiked to over 350 and 400 basis points. A similar pattern occurred in Dollar LIBOR, where overnight rates stayed low while 30-day and 90-day spreads surged above 300 basis points. In contrast, credit sectors lacking direct government support experienced extreme stress: par equivalent loan CDS spreads skyrocketed from under 300 basis points to nearly 1,475 basis points, and high-yield corporate bond spreads, measured by the JPMorgan Domestic High Yield Index, spiked from 600 basis points to around 2,000 basis points.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market presents nine historical charts, labeled Exhibits 2a through 2i, to illustrate the thesis that equity market inflection points are rarely visible when they occur and typically happen well before a recession officially ends. Each chart depicts a specific U.S. recessionary period, tracking the S&P Total Return Index using data from Ibbotson. In every chart, the horizontal axis spans from 18 months before to 18 months after the numeric bottom of the index, which is set at time zero and marked by a vertical black line. The shaded grey regions represent the official recessionary periods.

The first chart covers the July 1953 to May 1954 recession, showing the S&P Total Return Index bottoming in August 1953, shortly after the recession began, and embarking on a clear upward trend. The second chart, for the August 1957 to April 1958 recession, displays the index bottoming in December 1957, roughly halfway through the downturn, before rising steadily. In the third chart, representing the April 1960 to February 1961 recession, the market bottomed in October 1960, a few months prior to the end of the recession. The fourth chart depicts the December 1969 to November 1970 recession, with the market bottoming in June 1970 and recovering thereafter. The fifth chart shows the November 1973 to March 1975 recession, where the market bottomed in September 1974. The sixth chart showcases the brief January 1980 to July 1980 recession, showing the market bottoming very early in March 1980. The seventh chart, covering the July 1981 to November 1982 recession, shows the market bottoming in July 1982, several months before the recession concluded. The eighth chart, for the July 1990 to March 1991 recession, shows a bottom in October 1990. Finally, the ninth chart displays the March 2001 to November 2001 recession, where the index bottomed in September 2001, though this instance is unique as the market experienced subsequent volatility and further declines after the official recession ended.

Collectively, these charts demonstrate that in nearly all cases, the equity market established its bottom and began to recover while the economy was still contracting. This visual evidence supports the broader argument that investors who wait for clear economic recoveries to emerge often miss the earliest and most robust stages of a market rebound.

This page discusses two distinct topics: a historical analysis of Japan's policy response to deflation and an outlook on investing in municipal bonds. 

In the first section, the author argues that Japan's economic policy response to deflation risks between 1985 and 2002 was not the aggressive "big bang" intervention that many believe it was. On the monetary side, Japan's monetary expansion relative to total debt was minimal during the 1990s and peaked well below the levels of the Federal Reserve. On the fiscal side, actual net stimulus was only 1.5 percent of GDP spread over a five-year period. Two bar charts, sourced from research by Adam S. Posen, illustrate Japan's conservative fiscal position relative to other major economies. 

The first chart, titled "Size of government relative to GDP," measures the percentage of government size from 1970 to 1995. It shows France with the largest government relative to GDP at roughly 56 percent, followed by Germany at 46 percent, Canada and the United Kingdom both at 40 percent, the United States at 32 percent, and Japan with the lowest share at approximately 28 percent. The second chart, titled "Counter-cyclical fiscal stabilization," measures the beta coefficient of spending to GDP to show how much governments spend when the private sector is in distress. Here, the United States ranks highest with a coefficient of nearly 0.6, followed by Canada at 0.4, the United Kingdom at 0.25, and Japan in fourth place at approximately 0.21. Germany and France rank lowest at roughly 0.13 and nearly 0.0, respectively. The author concludes that Japan represents an example of policy inaction rather than a failure of fiscal and monetary stimulus.

The second section of the page provides strategic guidelines for investing in municipal bonds in the post-monoline era, drawing conclusions from J.P. Morgan's asset management division. The publication highlights that municipal default rates are historically very low. Fitch reports cumulative default rates of less than 0.25 percent for tax-supported and traditional revenue bonds, and 0.60 percent for hospital-related healthcare. To avoid the rare defaults that do occur, the authors advise staying away from non-hospital healthcare, industrial revenue bonds, and local multi-family housing, which have much higher historical default rates of 17 percent, 15 percent, and 6 percent, respectively. State general obligation bonds are noted as particularly secure due to strong institutional oversight and the fact that 49 out of 50 states have constitutional requirements for balanced budgets. 

Looking forward, the publication forecasts that states will face significant recessionary challenges over the next two years, with estimated budget gaps of $50 billion to $75 billion. To bridge these gaps, states are expected to cut expenditures and raise taxes or fees, aided by rainy day funds that reached an aggregate of 11.5 percent of expenditures in 2006. For revenue bonds, the authors emphasize focusing on "essential purpose" facilities such as water, sewer, mass transit, and electricity. They advise avoiding optional-use projects like new toll roads or sports stadiums, and suggest taking a cautious approach to university and airport bonds. Reflecting these defensive guidelines, J.P. Morgan's largest municipal mutual funds hold 18 to 19 percent in pre-refunded municipals backed by the U.S. Treasury, 23 to 36 percent in state-level general obligation bonds, and 18 to 25 percent in high-quality essential service revenue bonds.

This page introduces the primary author of the publication, Michael Cembalest, alongside the key members of the J.P. Morgan Wealth Management Investment Strategy Team. A portrait of Michael Cembalest, the Chief Investment Officer and Global Head of Investment Strategy, is featured at the top of the page. The accompanying text outlines his responsibilities in managing over $600 billion in client assets and his role on the J.P. Morgan Asset and Wealth Management Investment Committee, which oversees $900 billion in assets. His biography also details his 22-year career history at J.P. Morgan and his educational background at Tufts University and the Columbia School of International Affairs. 

Below this introduction, the page features headshots and brief professional biographies for six key members of the Investment Strategy Team. Jack Caffrey is profiled as the lead for equity strategy, responsible for portfolio recommendations and equity-linked derivatives structures. Richard Madigan is introduced as the head of international investment strategy, managing the $4.5 billion Global Access portfolios. Anthony D. Werley is highlighted for his role in portfolio construction, policy, and model portfolios. Ivan Leung is presented as the chief investment strategist for Asia, based out of the region. Stuart Schweitzer is profiled as the global markets strategist responsible for economic and financial market analysis, noting his past experience at the Federal Reserve. Lastly, Stephen Mitchell is introduced as the chief investment strategist for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, based in London.

This page of the commentary analyzes the severe global economic downturn during the Great Recession, noting that several key metrics have hit their worst post-war levels. The author highlights collapsing U.S. residential investment and consumer spending, alongside falling manufacturing orders and automotive purchase surveys. Internationally, Chinese electricity production and industrial profits, as well as Japanese industrial production, are showing severe weakness. The commentary points out a major systemic issue in the housing sector: 45 percent of mortgages modified in the first quarter of 2008 had already reverted to delinquency. The author argues that because bank capital levels of around 8 percent are not equipped for a recession of this depth, the economy faces a clash between deflationary forces and aggressive monetary and fiscal stimulus, the likes of which have not been tested in eighty years. 

To support these observations, the page features two charts. The first, titled "Consumer spending since 1960," tracks the five-month annualized percentage rate of U.S. nominal consumer spending. While historical growth usually stayed well above zero—even during recessions marked by grey vertical bars—the red line plunges sharply to around negative 4.5 percent at the end of 2008, indicating an unprecedented drop in consumer activity. The second chart is titled "U.S. household & corporate debt around recessions: an increase seems unlikely this time." This chart plots combined household and corporate debt as a percentage of nominal GDP from 1952 through 2007, with barbells representing the periods six months before and after recessions. The debt-to-GDP ratio shows a persistent upward trend from about 50 percent in 1952 to nearly 270 percent by late 2007. A question mark at the end of the trendline underscores the author’s expectation that, unlike in past recessions, an increase in corporate and household borrowing will not cushion this economic contraction. Finally, the text notes that while commercial paper issuance increased by 300 billion dollars since mid-October, this expansion was entirely driven by the Federal Reserve's Commercial Paper Funding Facility purchasing the issuance.

This page presents three charts representing key global and domestic economic indicators during the depths of the Great Recession in late 2008 and early 2009. Together, these charts highlight a severe contraction in global manufacturing and services, a collapse in global trade, and the extent to which expansionary monetary policy cushioned the decline of domestic leading indicators.

The first chart, titled J.P. Morgan Global PMI Index – New Orders, tracks index levels for manufacturing and services from 2000 through January 2009 against a neutral expansionary threshold of 50. In the second half of 2008, both sectors plummeted to historic lows. Manufacturing new orders fell sharply from around 50 down to a trough of approximately 27, while services dropped from above 50 to around 35 before ticking back up to just above 40 in January 2009. This chart uses data from J.P. Morgan Securities Inc. as of January 31, 2009.

The second chart, titled Baltic Dry Index, measures the price of moving major raw materials by sea, serving as a real-time proxy for global trade activity. Tracking the index from January 2008 through January 2009, the chart illustrates an unprecedented collapse. The index peaked near 11,500 in May 2008 and subsequently plummeted to near 1,000 by late 2008, demonstrating a near-total freeze in global maritime commerce before leveling off with a minor uptick in early 2009. This chart is based on Bloomberg data as of February 4, 2009.

The final chart, titled Leading Economic Index, displays the index level using 2004 as a base year equal to 100, comparing the metric with and without the M2 money supply component from December 2006 to December 2008. While the standard index containing M2 declined from around 105 to 99, the series representing the index without M2 diverged dramatically in late 2008, plunging to about 95. This visual comparison illustrates that massive liquidity injections and money supply expansions by central banks were masking the full severity of the underlying economic deterioration. This chart features data from The Conference Board as of December 31, 2008.

This page of the commentary introduces the Financial Stability Plan and contextualizes the ongoing global economic downturn, which the author describes as a synchronized global collapse. The central argument is that central bankers, regulators, and politicians are grappling with an unprecedented economic contraction across manufacturing, employment, consumption, investment, and sentiment in both developed and developing markets, with many indicators breaching historic lows from 1974 and 1982.

To visually demonstrate the breadth of this downturn, the page features a "Worst in Show" graphic composed of thirty small line charts tracking various economic indicators. Sourced from Bloomberg, J.P. Morgan Securities, and the OECD, these charts are color-coded by the starting decade of their historical data, and each shows a sharp, near-vertical downward plunge ending in a red dot to mark its current historic low. 

The indicators starting from 1940, outlined in blue, include GAAP earnings, municipal deficits, ISM orders, the ISM survey, housing starts, consumer spending, equipment and software investment, payrolls, Germany leading indicators, and the probability of finding a job. The indicators starting in 1960, outlined in green, cover OECD deficits as a percentage of GDP, new home sales, Germany new orders, home prices, consumer confidence, Korea exports, restaurant sales, and OECD leading indicators. The indicators tracking data since 1980, outlined in orange, comprise US auto sales, Japan auto sales, France industrial production, India industrial production, Japan business confidence, small business optimism, and Brazil industrial production. Lastly, the indicators beginning in 1990, outlined in purple, depict the shipping order book relative to the total fleet, European PMI, Russia exports, China electricity production, and sales to or within China. Collectively, these charts illustrate a synchronized collapse across diverse global regions and sectors.

Following this graphic, the commentary pivots to the US Treasury's Financial Stability Plan. The author notes a major surprise in the policy's design: the absence of an "Aggregator Bank" and the instead-planned emergence of a "Public-Private Partnership." This represents a shift away from the government directly setting a fair value—positioned between market value and par value—to purchase distressed assets directly from banks.

This page discusses the fiscal sustainability of New York State's government finances relative to other U.S. states and outlines strategic implications for municipal bond investors. 

Two scatter plots illustrate New York's outlier status in taxing and spending. The first chart, titled "Escape From New York," plots personal state and local sales, property, and income taxes per capita against total government spending per capita using 2006 data. It reveals that New York is an extreme outlier, with per capita spending near $12,000 and personal taxes of approximately $4,900 per capita. For comparison, Connecticut has high personal taxes of about $4,700 but lower spending around $9,000, while Wyoming matches New York's high spending levels of roughly $11,500 but boasts lower personal taxes around $3,600. The second chart, "Escape From New York, II," plots corporate income taxes per capita against total spending per capita. Once again, New York is a significant outlier, combining its nearly $12,000 in per capita spending with corporate taxes around $470 per capita. Only New Hampshire exceeds New York in corporate tax burden at roughly $430 per capita, though its per capita spending is much lower, near $7,000. Most other states cluster below $200 per capita in corporate taxes and under $9,000 in total spending.

The text asks what these high burdens mean for investors in New York municipals. The author explains that while immediate solvency is not threatened because the state budget was successfully balanced, the bloated nature of New York's finances could eventually become unsustainable. The publication expresses a general preference for diversified national municipal bond portfolios over state-specific ones, noting that 75% of their managed municipal assets reside in national strategies. However, because transitioning out of a New York portfolio is currently expensive due to wide bid-offer spreads, defensive measures have been taken within New York-specific managed accounts. Specifically, about 25% of these portfolios are held in pre-refunded bonds backed by U.S. Treasuries, and another 50% are invested in essential service revenue bonds, such as water and sewer, which are legally protected and prioritized for payment immediately after the issuer's operating expenses under Chapter 9 bankruptcy rules.

This page features commentary by Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Global Wealth Management, who compares the public scrutiny over a potential U.S. auto industry bridge loan to the federal rescue of AIG. 

The first chart, titled "Auto sales adjusted by number of households," shows seasonally adjusted annual auto sales deflated by the number of households from 1976 to late 2008, using 1976 as a base year. The data reveals a highly cyclical trend, with sales peaking near 18 million units in 1986, dipping below 10 million in the early 1990s, and stabilizing between 10 and 14 million during the late 1990s and early 2000s. By late 2008, sales collapsed sharply to nearly 7 million units, highlighting the severity of the economic downturn. 

The second chart, titled "Bigger <> Better: Big 3 domestic car sales as % of total U.S. car sales," tracks the combined market share of General Motors, Ford, and Chrysler from 1994 to late 2008. The visual shows a persistent downward trend, with the Big 3's market share dropping from approximately 65% in 1994 to below 30% by the end of 2008. A prominent upward spike to nearly 60% around 2005 is noted as an outlier resulting from a Chrysler incentive program.

In the text, Cembalest questions why there is so much hand-wringing over the auto bailout while the government's $152 billion support for AIG has faced little public rejection. He notes that the U.S. Treasury initially justified the AIG funds as collateral for capital markets contracts written against residential mortgage-backed securities and European corporate loans, arguing taxpayer risk was low. However, with the onset of the global recession and new investment losses in AIG's securities lending operations, Cembalest warns it is unclear how much of the $152 billion is now at risk of direct loss.
