He concludes that any auto industry bailout should be evaluated on the same playing field as the AIG bailout, which ultimately served to rescue downstream brokerage firms and European bank counterparties.

This page examines the double-edged sword of massive government economic stimulus, warning of both the fiscal burden of skyrocketing public debt and the severe political dangers of failing to contain high unemployment. 

To illustrate the long-term financial consequences of stimulus, the author provides a chart titled Japan: Nikkei vs. Debt to GDP, tracking data from 1988 to 2002. The chart compares the Nikkei 225 Index on the left axis against Japan's Gross Government Debt to GDP ratio on the right axis. The visual shows that while Japanese equities experienced several brief, sharp rallies of up to 40 percent, the overall trajectory of the Nikkei 225 was a massive long-term decline from an index level above 270 in late 1989 down to roughly 80 by 2002. During this exact period, Japan's government debt to GDP ratio escalated dramatically from around 60 percent in 1990 to over 150 percent by 2002, demonstrating how prolonged government stimulus can saddle an economy with soaring debt.

The author then transitions to the existential risks of failing to intervene during economic crises, arguing that unchecked unemployment can lead to disastrous political shifts. While the United States turned to Franklin D. Roosevelt during the Great Depression when non-farm unemployment reached 28 percent, other nations experienced far darker outcomes. This dynamic is illustrated in a chart titled German unemployment and Reichstag seats, by party, which covers the Weimar Republic era from 1922 to 1934. The chart displays the German unemployment rate as a green shaded area, which spiked to approximately 30 percent in the early 1930s. Red bars show the percentage of Reichstag seats won by the totalitarian National Socialist Party, demonstrating a direct correlation where their electoral success rose alongside unemployment, surging to nearly 40 percent in 1932 and 1933. Conversely, blue bars representing liberal parties, specifically the German Democratic Party and the German People's Party, show their share of Reichstag seats collapsing from about 15 percent in 1924 to just 2 percent by 1933. 

The page concludes with a note on credit provisioning. The author highlights the ISI Group's cumulative provisioning estimates for 2009 and 2010 as reasonable but not unassailable. These estimates include loss rates of 15 percent to 20 percent on credit cards, 10 percent to 20 percent on residential construction, 2.5 percent to 5.0 percent on residential first liens, 7.5 percent to 15.0 percent on residential second liens, 3.5 percent to 6.0 percent on commercial and industrial loans, and 3 percent on commercial real estate.

In this commentary, the author provides a stark update on global economic indicators through a visual metaphor termed the "Periodic table of economic elements." The main argument is that despite unprecedented policy responses—such as bank stress tests, recapitalizations, global fiscal and monetary stimulus, pending mortgage servicer safe harbor legislation (H.R. 1106), and the implementation of TALF and PPP programs—significant downside risks remain for equity prices. The author advises that portfolios remain heavily underweight in equities, noting that the global economy is undergoing a painful but necessary transition to reduce corporate and household debt levels, which do not need to exceed 250 percent of GDP to sustain survival.

The central visual is a color-coded grid containing 35 individual line charts, each tracking a different economic metric. A red dot positioned at the bottom right of every single chart symbolizes that the metric has collapsed to historic or multi-decade lows. The charts are categorized by the start date of their data series. The earliest data, beginning in 1940 and outlined in blue, displays historic drops in GAAP earnings, municipal deficits, ISM orders, S&P dividends, and capacity utilization. Indicators beginning in 1950, outlined in brown, include housing starts, consumer spending, the probability of finding a job, homeowner vacancy rates, and Japanese industrial production. Data starting in 1960, shown with green borders, captures dramatic declines in equipment and software investment, payrolls, German leading indicators and new orders, OECD deficits as a percentage of GDP, new home sales, home prices, consumer confidence, South Korean exports, and restaurant sales. Metrics starting in 1980, bordered in orange, show plunges in OECD leading indicators, bank construction loans as a percentage of total assets, US and Japanese auto sales, industrial production in France, India, and Brazil, Japanese business confidence, small business optimism, and the shipping order book relative to the total fleet. Finally, data from 1990 onward, outlined in purple, reveals severe contractions in architectural billings, European PMI, Russian exports, Chinese electricity production, and sales to and within China. Six of these charts—specifically S&P dividends, capacity utilization, architectural billings, homeowner vacancy rates, Japanese industrial production, and bank construction loans—are new additions to this "worst-ever" compilation, underscoring the widespread and synchronized nature of the global downturn across multiple regions and sectors.

This page analyzes the capitalization of major United States banks amidst ongoing financial stress and evaluates the early success of China's economic stimulus program. 

The author begins by asserting that the U.S. economy is performing worse than the Federal Reserve's stress test base case, suggesting that the first quarter of 2009 may represent the high-water mark for bank earnings before further stress emerges later in the year. To illustrate bank health, a scatter plot titled "Large cap bank provision and capitalization, Q1 vs Q4" compares loan loss reserves as a percentage of end-of-period loans against tangible common equity (TCE) as a percentage of risk-weighted assets. The chart tracks individual institutions—including Citigroup, Wells Fargo, PNC, US Bancorp, Bank of America, BB&T, SunTrust, and JPMorgan Chase—showing changes from the fourth quarter of 2008 to the first quarter of 2009. For instance, Citigroup is positioned with very low TCE but high loan loss reserves near 4.5%, while JPMorgan Chase occupies a stronger position with TCE above 6.5%. Footnotes add that the U.S. Treasury is reportedly considering a "World Cup format" to group banks into four categories, from Group A (strong enough to repay TARP) to Group D (unable to operate independently).

Addressing toxic assets, the commentary notes that adverse housing scenarios are heavily priced into debt securities, where many AAA-rated assets trade at steep discounts, offering potential unleveraged returns of 10% to 15%. This environment underpins the government’s Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility (TALF) and Public-Private Investment Program (PPIP) initiatives, which encourage leveraged buying of these distressed securities.

The second half of the page focuses on China, arguing that its aggressive economic stimulus is starting to yield real demand. While skyrocketing loan growth reflects government policy, genuine economic recovery is indicated by improvements in industrial value added, housing prices, imports, electricity output, and retail sales. This economic momentum is supported by three charts tracking data from the late 1990s through early 2009: RMB Loan Growth, which shows year-over-year change spiking toward 30%; Industrial Value Added, showing a recovery trend from a low of around 5% in late 2008; and China Auto Sales, where the three-month moving average year-over-year change has sharply rebounded from negative territory back toward positive growth. Given China's low debt-to-GDP ratio of just 18%, the author notes that the country is uniquely positioned to afford such stimulus, prompting JP Morgan to shift portfolio allocations away from the United States and Europe in favor of Asia ex-Japan.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan evaluates the state of the U.S. banking sector, housing market, and corporate earnings, arguing that while central bank actions have successfully postponed a systemic collapse, substantial risks remain. J.P. Morgan remains ten percent underweight on equities, preferring credit markets, because sustainable equity market gains require higher-quality earnings than those recently preannounced by Wells Fargo. Cembalest observes that the future of the banking sector is closely tied to the housing market, where he expects an additional fifteen percent national decline in home prices. He highlights that seven hundred fifty billion dollars in Option ARMs are deteriorating rapidly, with sixty percent of these loans concentrated in California and ten percent in Florida. Globally, financial institutions have lost approximately one trillion dollars in capital and raised a matching amount, but economists like Nouriel Roubini and organizations like the IMF expect remaining writedowns to equal the losses already taken.

The commentary features three detailed charts analyzing the mortgage and foreclosure landscape using data up to March 2009. The first chart, titled "60+ day delinquencies by loan type," plots delinquency rates from 1999 to 2009 as a percentage of the remaining loan balance. It shows that delinquencies across all categories remained flat and low until spiking dramatically around 2007. By early 2009, Subprime delinquencies rose to nearly forty percent, Option ARMs reached approximately twenty-five percent, Alt-A surpassed fifteen percent, HELOCs climbed toward ten percent, and Prime Jumbo loans rose to around five percent. The second chart, "Recovery values by loan type," plots the percentage of loan value recovered upon default over the same 1999 to 2009 period. While recovery rates historically hovered between seventy and ninety percent, they fell precipitously after 2007, dropping to between twenty percent and fifty percent by early 2009 for all major loan types, including Prime Jumbo, Alt-A, Option ARM, Subprime, and HELOC. The third chart, "Another foreclosure wave in the pipeline," tracks monthly metrics from September 2006 to March 2009. The solid line representing Notices of Default, measured on the left axis, climbs to a historic peak of nearly one hundred thirty thousand notices. Meanwhile, the dashed line representing the percentage of these notices moving to auction, measured on the right axis, reaches a cycle high of seventy-four percent, indicating that foreclosure mitigation efforts have failed to stop loans from progressing to auction.

Cembalest applies these housing market insights to analyze Wells Fargo and the upcoming government bank stress tests. He notes that Wells Fargo's provisions and charge-offs are thirty to forty percent below expectations, which is highly concerning given its outsized risk exposures. Specifically, Wells Fargo holds the largest commercial real estate portfolio at one hundred forty-two billion dollars, the largest Option ARM portfolio at ninety-three billion dollars net of writedowns, one hundred twenty-nine billion dollars in second liens, and fifteen billion dollars in off-balance sheet CDO exposure. Despite these massive exposures, the bank’s loan loss reserves and capital adequacy rank in line with or lower than peer banks, raising the question of whether its provisioning policies are sufficiently conservative. Cembalest concludes that while some banks might withstand scrutiny, the results of the upcoming bank stress tests may not pass muster for institutions like Wells Fargo.

This page highlights J.P. Morgan's cautious investment stance and outlines the potential opportunities and risks in structured credit markets during the 2009 financial crisis. 

The author begins by defending a modest underweight of approximately 10% to public equities, favoring allocations to credit, cash, and commodities instead. Key macro concerns include rising savings and unemployment rates, historic lows in bond recovery rates since December (15 cents on the dollar for secured and 9 cents for unsecured), and low volume during the recent market rally. An accompanying chart, titled "Incorporating the reality of a shallow recovery: earnings expectations are zero," plots S&P 500 forward EPS growth from 1985 through early 2009, illustrating a sharp drop from pre-crisis peaks to nearly 0% by 2009, a level not seen since the recessions of 1975 and 1981.

The publication then evaluates the risks and rewards of investing through the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility (TALF) and the Public-Private Investment Program (PPIP). While many structured credit securities have fallen from par pricing yielding Libor plus 0.25% down to 45 cents on the dollar, the risk-return dynamics of TALF-funded credit card and auto loan securities appear highly favorable. The downside cases for these assets are extreme, appearing to model a 15% unemployment rate. Two bar charts show potential internal rates of return (IRR) for these programs. For credit cards, the IRR is 14.0% in the Base Case (Exit at Par), 22.9% in the Upside Case (Exit at 102), and negative 33.5% in the Downside Case (Exit below 94). For auto loans, the IRR is 38.4% in the Base Case, 43.4% in the Upside Case, and 7.4% in the Downside Case (Exit below 91). An adjacent table, titled "Indicative CMBS pool: Effective loan purchase price as a percentage of original investment," lists ten commercial real estate deals. Notable entries include the NYC Park Avenue Office at 27%, the NYC Midtown Office (Ground Lease) at 15%, and the Boston CBD Office at 31%, contributing to a Trust aggregate purchase price of just 25% of the original investment.

The page concludes with a discussion of creditor battles and bankruptcy remoteness, focusing on the recent bankruptcy filing of General Growth Properties (GGP), a major real estate investment trust. Although lenders typically require borrowers to place assets in supposedly "bankruptcy-remote" Special Purpose Entities (SPEs) to protect CMBS debt, several of GGP’s property-specific SPEs filed for bankruptcy alongside the parent company. While GGP maintains these SPE filings were merely procedural and not intended to consolidate assets into the parent company, the author warns that this situation represents a serious challenge to the assumed safety of secured, separate structures.

This page analyzes the roots of the 2007 credit crunch, arguing that the disruption was primarily caused by the collapse of the securitized loan markets rather than a contraction in traditional bank lending, which remained remarkably stable. The author emphasizes that any future regulatory or legislative efforts must recognize this distinction. 

To illustrate the composition of the credit market, a horizontal bar chart titled "Where loans come from (trillions, as of June 2007)" divides the $24 trillion in outstanding private sector loans. Securitized loans, or structured credit purchased by capital market investors, represented the largest portion at $10 trillion, followed by traditional bank loans at $8.5 trillion and bond markets representing the remainder of the total. 

The stability of traditional bank credit is supported by a line chart titled "Total bank credit to individuals and companies." The chart tracks outstanding credit in billions from December 2003 to December 2008, showing a steady rise from $6,000 billion to over $9,000 billion. Even after the marked "onset of credit crisis" in late 2007, when outstanding credit stood at approximately $8,500 billion, bank credit continued to expand rather than shrink, defying typical recessionary trends.

To counter claims that this stability is merely an illusion caused by banks rolling over pre-existing obligations, the page includes a line chart titled "Commercial & industrial loans made under prior commitments." Measuring these loans as a percentage of total commercial lending from late 2003 to late 2008, the chart shows that prior commitments fluctuated between roughly 74% and 84%. By late 2008, the percentage fell below 75%, proving that commitments were no higher than they were during the preceding bull market. 

Finally, a line chart titled "Borrowing rates on newly issued commercial & industrial loans" displays the average interest rate on new business loans from December 2003 to December 2008. Rates peaked near 7.0% in late 2006 and early 2007 but dropped sharply to below 3.0% by late 2008. This downward trend demonstrates that despite underwriting mistakes and an ongoing recession, banks continued to channel credit to the broader economy at an increasingly lower cost. All charts utilize data from the Federal Reserve Board, the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, and Standard & Poor's.

This page, titled "The Source of that Giant Sucking Sound," analyzes why credit appeared so scarce during the 2008 financial crisis. Michael Cembalest argues that the credit crunch was primarily caused by the sudden collapse of the securitized loan markets—often referred to as shadow banking—rather than a contraction of lending by traditional banks. Securitization emerged in the early 1990s as investors sought higher yields, allowing pools of loans to act as alternative lending sources. The traditional banking sector simply could not expand enough to replace this shadow market, which had grown to be larger than the banking system itself.

The page features four charts that illustrate the dramatic rise and subsequent collapse of this shadow credit system. The first chart, showing the growth of consumer credit by lender from 1990 to 2008, tracks total credit climbing to over $2.5 trillion. The stacked area data series includes commercial banks, finance companies, credit unions, savings institutions, and nonfinancial businesses. It highlights that the vast majority of credit growth after 2000 was driven by pools of securitized assets, while traditional bank lending grew very little in real terms.

The second chart, which details asset-backed securitized quarterly loan issuance from 2000 to 2009, demonstrates the suddenness of the 2008 collapse. Issuance peaked at nearly $300 billion per quarter around 2006, with significant contributions from subprime mortgages, commercial real estate, auto loans, credit cards, and student loans. By 2009, this total quarterly issuance had plummeted to a mere $17 billion, almost completely cutting off credit to these sectors.

The third chart tracks outstanding asset-backed commercial paper from December 2000 to December 2008. It shows outstanding paper steadily climbing from around $600 billion in 2000 to a peak of nearly $1.2 trillion in mid-2007, followed by a sharp retrenchment back down toward $700 billion by late 2008.

The fourth chart displays collateralized loan obligation issuance from 2001 to 2009 in billions of dollars. This bar chart shows that diversified pools of corporate loans peaked at $564 billion in 2006 and $525 billion in 2007, before falling sharply to $239 billion in 2008 and collapsing to just $88 billion in 2009.

Cembalest concludes that tight credit conditions are the direct result of the wholesale departure of these securitized loan buyers. However, he notes that this pain was not felt equally across all sectors. Citing the April 2009 Empire State Manufacturing Survey, he points out that fewer than ten percent of manufacturers surveyed reported that credit difficulties had adversely affected their production or sales, suggesting that general sales weakness, rather than financing hurdles, was their primary challenge.

This page of the commentary focuses on the health of the credit markets, the ongoing efforts by the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and Treasury to revive the securitized loan market, and warnings against counterproductive legislation such as mortgage cramdowns. Michael Cembalest argues that altering bankruptcy rules to permit judicial modification of primary residence mortgages—an idea historically resisted to encourage capital flow—would ultimately increase the cost and reduce the availability of bank credit. This argument is contextualized against a backdrop where the U.S. faces a projected 12% deficit in 2009, putting public debt on a path to 70% of GDP, a ratio not seen since World War II. 

An accompanying bar chart, titled "Change in credit outstanding, June 2007 – December 2008," uses Federal Reserve Flow of Funds data to demonstrate that banks have continued to lend despite contracting securitization markets. The chart shows that while bank loans grew by roughly $800 billion over this period, securitized loans excluding Government-Sponsored Enterprises contracted by nearly $300 billion. The author projects that without new issuance, these non-GSE securitized loan balances will continue to shrink by $50 billion to $100 billion per quarter as existing loans mature, highlighting that while short-term policy interventions and fiscal stimulus provide immediate relief, their long-term costs remain an open and critical question.

This page explores the structural drivers behind the credit crisis, focusing on the post-World War II American borrowing spree and the inherent vulnerability of non-dedicated investors in securitized loans. 

The author first highlights the massive expansion of household debt with a chart titled "Household debt service as % of disposable income," sourced from Bridgewater Associates. The chart traces this percentage from 1919 to 2007, showing a historical peak of over 16% in the mid-1930s, followed by a sharp drop to nearly 3% by the early 1950s, and a subsequent steady, decades-long rise back to approximately 14% by 2007. The author argues that this rise reflects the general public's excessive risk appetite, poor balance sheet management, and inadequate savings, refuting the simple explanation that banks merely acted as an enabling machine.

The analysis then shifts to the transience of investors in securitized loans, calling this non-dedicated buyer base the system's biggest Achilles heel. When the Federal Funds rate fell to 1% in the summer of 2003, many investors turned to enhanced income funds to chase yield, buying AAA- and AA-rated securitized loan tranches at narrow spreads of 0.20% to 0.45% over Libor. A chart titled "The rise and fall of Enhanced Income mutual funds," using Bloomberg data up to April 2009, illustrates the rapid boom and bust of these vehicles. Luxembourg-based enhanced income funds saw assets under management surge from near zero in 2004 to a peak of nearly $70 billion in mid-2007, before plummeting back to near zero by early 2009. U.S.-based enhanced income funds followed a similar but smaller trajectory, peaking near $18 billion before declining to under $10 billion. Major asset managers involved in these onshore and offshore markets included J.P. Morgan, Legg Mason, Oppenheimer, HSBC, BlackRock, and Fidelity.

Finally, the author details the connection between securities lenders and hedge funds, noting that securities lending assets expanded dramatically from 4% of GDP in 1998 to 18% of GDP in 2007. In this system, pension funds lent stocks to short-selling hedge funds in exchange for cash collateral, which securities lenders then reinvested to capture a spread. This mechanism collapsed when losses on securitized loans prompted pension funds to pull back on lending, while shrinking hedge fund assets simultaneously reduced demand. This double-whammy forced securities lending portfolios to slash their holdings of asset-backed commercial paper by $400 billion between 2007 and 2008.

This page explores why the securitized loan markets collapsed during the 2007 financial crisis, identifying a web of interconnected participants as having shared blame. A central hub-and-spoke diagram illustrates the complex ecosystem surrounding securitized loans, linking them to investors, rating agencies, broker-dealers, banks, law firms, the SEC, FASB, individual borrowers, corporate borrowers, and independent loan originators. 

The author highlights poor underwriting by rating agencies as a key point of failure, explaining that these agencies underestimated the loss protection needed for AAA-rated loan tranches due to a lack of empirical history on newer collateral types. At the same time, investor apathy grew as buyers accepted lower yields alongside weakening protections. In the commercial mortgage-backed securities market, which financed about 40% of real estate activity from 2003 to 2007, loan-to-value ratios rose above 100%, debt service coverage fell below 1.0x, and interest-only loans climbed from 10% to 50% by 2007. Laxity was also present in securitized home equity loans; for example, GMAC and Refco saw reduced-documentation borrowers rise from under 3% of their securitized second-lien pools to 60% by 2007.

To explain how market participants were lulled into a false sense of security, the author includes a line chart tracking loan delinquency rates by loan type from 1988 through 2006, using Federal Reserve Board data. The chart plots delinquency percentages for agricultural loans, C&I loans, consumer loans, residential real estate loans, lease loans, consumer credit loans, and commercial real estate loans. Nearly all categories experienced a long-term decline, with agricultural delinquencies dropping from around 11% in 1988 to under 2% by 2006, and other categories clustering at historic lows of 1% to 4% in 2006. This trend encouraged the belief that the benign credit cycle would continue indefinitely. When the recession began in 2007, unprepared investors fled the securitized markets, whereas traditional banks were better positioned to weather the storm due to their loan loss reserves and direct borrower relationships. The page concludes by acknowledging the role of borrowers, lender liability, predatory lending, and inadequate disclosures in the wider credit crisis.

This page analyzes the collapse in demand for securitized loans during the financial crisis, focusing on the roles of non-bank entities such as hedge funds, structured investment vehicles, and broker-dealers. The author argues that the credit collapse was driven not by traditional commercial banks, which maintained steady exposure, but by these alternative financial participants who suddenly abandoned the market.

At the top left of the page, a line chart titled Decline in hedge fund AUM affects securities lending tracks hedge fund assets under management in billions of dollars from 1990 through early 2009. The data reveals a dramatic climb from near-zero in the early 1990s to a peak of nearly 1.9 trillion dollars in late 2007, followed by a precipitous decline to around 1.4 trillion dollars by early 2009. This drop in asset volume directly reduced the capital available for securities lending.

The text describes structured investment vehicles, or SIVs, as highly leveraged, unregulated entities operating without central bank access or stable depositors. These SIVs experienced an unwind of 350 billion to 400 billion dollars. A pie chart titled SIV portfolio assets: red indicates securitized loans shows that, as of 2007, the vast majority of SIV holdings consisted of securitized debt. While financial assets made up 41.6 percent and corporate assets accounted for a mere 0.2 percent, the red-colored securitized sectors dominated the portfolio. These included RMBS prime at 21.3 percent, CDOs at 13.2 percent, CMBS at 7.6 percent, ABS at 7.2 percent, student loans at 4.6 percent, home equity/subprime loans at 2.0 percent, and CDOs of ABS at 0.3 percent. 

The final resting place for many securitized loans was the balance sheets of large broker-dealers who could no longer sell them. Between 2004 and 2007, the securities holdings of major broker-dealers grew three to four times faster than those of the largest US banks, with broker-dealer leverage peaking at 25x to 30x in June 2007. A line chart titled Broker-Dealer marketable securities accounts vs. banks indexes securities holdings from late 2004 to late 2008. It highlights a massive spike and subsequent collapse for major investment firms. Lehman Brothers peaked above an index value of 220 in mid-2007 before plunging toward zero, while Merrill Lynch peaked near 190, UBS near 180, and Morgan Stanley near 170 before all collapsed dramatically. Combined, securities holdings at Merrill, Lehman, and Morgan Stanley declined by 1.4 trillion dollars from June 2007 to December 2008. In stark contrast, the index for the top ten largest US banks by assets showed continuous, stable growth throughout the entire period, reaching an index level of roughly 170 by the end of 2008.

The author concludes that traditional banks remained resilient and stayed the course during the crisis. Finally, the page notes that legislative proposals to resolve repayment issues on primary mortgages, consumer credit, and small business loans are gaining support.

This page features commentary from Michael Cembalest regarding the massive scale of the global policy response to the 2008 financial crisis, using the metaphor of ancient "Sun God" worshippers to argue that recent positive economic indicators are the direct, expected result of unprecedented government intervention rather than an organic recovery. While acknowledging real signs of economic stabilization—such as rebounding regional manufacturing surveys, rising consumer goods purchases, and a record-low 2.1% growth in employment costs—the author emphasizes that this "healing" has been purchased with trillions of dollars in stimulus, guarantees, and asset purchases. 

To illustrate the current economic stabilization, the page includes two top-level charts. The first, "JPMorgan Global Purchasing Managers' Index: orders to inventory," plots the seasonally adjusted ratio from 1998 through early 2009, showing a steep plunge to a low of approximately 0.65 in late 2008, followed by a sharp rebound back toward a more normal level of nearly 0.9 by early 2009. The second chart, "Interbank counterparty risk spread," measures the 3-month Libor-OIS spread in basis points from December 2007 to March 2009. It depicts a massive spike that peaked near 350 basis points in late 2008 before dramatically falling back to around 75 basis points by March 2009, signaling a return to near-normalcy in interbank lending. 

The core of the author’s argument is visualized in a large bubble chart at the bottom, titled "Public sector response to recessions: a new zip code." This chart compares the policy response of the current recession against nine historical recessions dating back to 1953. The x-axis measures fiscal stimulus as the growth in the U.S. Treasury debt-to-GDP ratio, the y-axis measures monetary stimulus as the growth in the monetary base, and the bubble sizes represent the reduction in the Fed Funds Rate. While all historical recessions cluster tightly in the bottom-left corner—with fiscal stimulus under 10% and monetary growth below 50%—the current response, labeled "Sun god 2008-??", is of an entirely different magnitude. The projection for 2009 shows monetary stimulus exceeding 100% and fiscal stimulus at roughly 15%. The projection for 2010, which includes an additional $1.25 trillion in Treasury, agency, and mortgage-backed securities purchases, climbs to approximately 250% monetary growth and nearly 25% fiscal growth. 

The text highlights that the active U.S. stimulus of $2.7 trillion does not account for an additional $7 to $10 trillion in undrawn capacity, and notes that stimulus measures in Europe and Japan have reached roughly 15% of GDP. Ultimately, the author warns that while these interventions have successfully spurred immediate economic payback, markets will eventually have to confront the severe long-term costs associated with this unprecedented global rescue mission.

In this market commentary, the author argues against the theory of a V-shaped economic recovery, pointing out critical issues with both "earnings quality" and "income quality" in the United States. While market excitement has grown around companies beating their first-quarter S&P earnings estimates, the author explains that this profitability is built on unsustainable expense-slashing rather than top-line growth. 

This dynamic is visualized in the first chart, titled "Earnings quality: earnings beat, revenues don't," which shows net positive surprises as a percentage of the total across various sectors. The chart displays two series: blue bars for earnings per share (EPS) and orange bars for revenue. While EPS surprises are strongly positive across almost all sectors—reaching over 60% in financials and health care—revenue surprises are deeply negative across almost every sector, falling to around negative 40% in industrials and nearly negative 60% in materials and telecom. 

The author also highlights headwinds for the U.S. consumer, including surging notices of default, declining credit card issuance, and a heavy reliance on government transfers. This shift is depicted in the second chart, "Income quality: government transfer payments as % of personal income," which plots the percentage of personal income derived from government transfers from 1960 through April 2009. The line shows a steady long-term climb from around 6% in 1960 to a dramatic spike of over 16% by early 2009. Given these unsustainable dynamics, the author predicts that household savings rates must rise significantly and maintains an underweight position on equities.

In the final section on fixed income, the author discusses how investors are searching for yield, noting a shift of over $40 billion out of T-bill funds into higher-yielding credit. The author provides a outlook on several fixed-income sectors. For U.S. Treasuries, despite a projected 30% to 40% increase in publicly held debt, the author expects yields to remain range-bound in the near term due to the Federal Reserve's $300 billion purchase program, though they advise avoiding the long end of the curve. For Agency debt, the author warns that rising losses have discouraged foreign central banks, causing foreign purchases of Agencies to plunge from positive $50 billion per quarter to net sales of $100 billion to $150 billion. High-quality investment-grade corporate bonds yielding 6% to 7% are deemed fairly priced, though their rally is likely finished. Lastly, short-duration asset-backed securities are highlighted as attractive, especially with Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility (TALF) leverage, which makes 2009 originations look cheap compared to older vintages.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication provides a comprehensive analysis of global fixed-income opportunities as of mid-May 2009, focusing on the relationship between pre-tax yields and maturity across various credit sectors. 

The primary visual is the "Global Fixed Income Monitor" scatter plot. The vertical axis measures pre-tax yield from 1% to 8%, while the horizontal axis tracks maturity from 1 to 14 years. A detailed legend categorizes the data points into subprime, convertibles, high yield, trust preferreds, leveraged loans, commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS), Build America Bonds, municipals (distinguished as squares), sovereign bonds, asset-backed securities (ABS), investment-grade corporates, U.S. agencies, and U.S. Treasuries. Low-risk assets like U.S. Treasuries and agencies anchor the bottom of the plot under 3%, while high-yield corporate names such as Tyson, HCA, Motorola, Sally Beauty, AutoNation, and Altria yield between 7% and 8%. 

The accompanying commentary details several key structural observations. First, high-quality sovereign debt is trading in line with high-quality corporates; for instance, Mexico’s yield is only 40 basis points wider than Italy's. To make municipal bonds comparable for taxable U.S. investors, their yields are grossed up assuming a combined 40% federal, state, and local tax rate. The text highlights "Build America Bonds" as a newly introduced taxable instrument successfully attracting non-traditional municipal buyers such as foundations and non-U.S. investors. Additionally, the author observes a notable rally in BB-rated bond yields, which fell from 16% to 11.5% since November. High-yield and leveraged loans featured on the chart are generally short-term issues where refinancing is highly probable due to strong balance sheet cash. 

The analysis also covers bank trust preferreds, which are plotted using both final maturity (ranging from 40 to 60 years) and call dates (2 to 4 years), and convertible bonds, which have their embedded call options factored into the displayed yields to show their total value. For higher-yielding assets between 8% and 18%, the author warns that yield-to-maturity should not be taken literally due to substantial default, restructuring, and extension risks. Defensive corporate names with inelastic demand, like Tenet and HCA hospitals or Qwest telecom, trade tighter than highly cyclical, discretionary spenders. Lastly, while the monitor includes senior AAA-rated CMBS and subprime tranches, it explicitly excludes distressed sovereign issuers such as Pakistan, Ecuador, and Argentina.

This page focuses on the fixed income market, specifically addressing the steeper yield curve of municipal bonds, the credit risks of monoline insurers, and the controversial corporate restructuring of MBIA. 

A prominent chart titled "Global Fixed Income Monitor" plots the pre-tax yields of various global debt instruments against their maturities, which range from one to over fourteen years. The visual highlights a dramatic dispersion of yields across different asset classes during this period. High-yield corporate issuers and distressed sovereign debts are scattered near the top of the chart, with Michaels yielding around 17.5% at a four-year maturity, and Sealy and Venezuela both yielding near 17%. Other notable high-yield entries include Cooper at approximately 16.5% and Atlas Pipe at 17%. Structured finance products also show elevated yields, with the Subprime ABX 06-2 AAA index plotted near 14.5% yield at a four-year maturity. Numerous other corporate issuers, such as US Steel, Sirius, Calpine, and Harrahs, are shown yielding between 12% and 15%, demonstrating the pervasive high-yield environment of mid-2009.

In the commentary, the author discusses the municipal bond market, pointing out that because the municipal yield curve is steeper than Treasury and corporate curves, investors must take on credit risk to beat after-tax municipal yields, particularly at the short end. The publication recommends that investors diversify municipal holdings by state and focus heavily on General Obligation bonds, pre-refunded bonds, and essential service revenue bonds. 

The text transitions into a critique of monoline insurers like AMBAC and MBIA, noting that market participants no longer value their insurance wrappers; in fact, some wrapped bonds trade wider than unwrapped ones. The author highlights MBIA’s controversial restructuring in February 2009, described as an "amoeba undergoing mitosis." MBIA split itself by establishing a new subsidiary, the National Public Finance Guarantee Corp, which inherited MBIA's municipal insurance liabilities and was capitalized using cash from the parent company's balance sheet. This move, apparently supported by the New York Insurance Commissioner, designed a preference for municipal bondholders at the expense of structured credit holders like banks and hedge funds, leading to accusations of fraudulent conveyance. The author compares this to a failed 1990s rehabilitation strategy by Executive Life that was eventually struck down by the California Appellate Courts.

Finally, the page outlines upcoming federal legislative responses to this monoline crisis. The House Financial Services Committee is noted to be reviewing the draft "Municipal Bond Insurance Enhancement Act," which would have the Federal Government reinsure $50 billion of bonds annually from 2011 to 2015 to give the monoline industry time to rebuild. Other draft bills under consideration include liquidity facilities for municipal money market funds, increased oversight of monolines, and the "Municipal Bond Fairness Act," which aims to force rating agencies to adjust their municipal rating standards.

This publication reviews J.P. Morgan’s "Reflation Nation" investment strategies implemented over the prior winter, following the tripling of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet and fiscal deficit. The author points to early signs of a global production rebound, illustrated in a line chart showing the JPMorgan Global Purchasing Managers’ Index ratio of orders to inventory from January 1998 to May 2009. The seasonally adjusted ratio shows a dramatic V-shaped recovery, plunging from a high point in early 2008 down to a historical low of 0.6 in late 2008, before surging back to a normal level of over 1.2 by mid-2009. 

In discussing banking sector health, the author highlights the Fed's Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP). He notes that the program relies on new capital raising for only 17% of bank solvency goals, with the remaining 83% dependent on pre-provision income. The author warns that this reliance poses a risk, as declining mortgage refinancing and slowing credit demand may hurt pre-provision income, especially with realized credit card and Alt-A loan losses tracking the Fed's adverse scenario.

The publication provides updates on specific reflation investments, beginning with oil. After recommending client sales in mid-2008 when WTI spot prices peaked above $140, the firm recommended adding oil exposure once prices fell below $40 in late 2008 and early 2009. A line chart of WTI spot prices from May 2008 to May 2009 tracks this trajectory, marking the peak sell recommendation and the subsequent purchases of oil structures, ETFs, and exploration and production equities—specifically Newfield, Plains Exploration, and Pioneer Resources. An inset chart of daily execution levels on structured oil notes shows exact buying periods clustered between November 2008 and March 2009.

Finally, the author details currency strategies in a chart tracking dollars per euro from January 2008 to May 2009. In the summer of 2008, when the euro traded near $1.55, J.P. Morgan added long-dollar hedges. As the global crisis intensified and dollar demand surged, they unwound these positions at two specific points, labeled Exit 1 (between $1.25 and $1.27) and Exit 2 (between $1.30 and $1.32). The author subsequently recommended shorting the dollar against commodity currencies and the Chinese RMB, predicting that the dollar must eventually decline further to resolve long-term consumption and savings imbalances between the East and the West.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market commentary addresses the dilemma of when and how to transition back to normal portfolio investing during a period of extreme monetary expansion and compromised public finances. To illustrate the firm’s positioning, the author presents a visual titled Portfolio Risk Speedometer, which is designed as an analog speedometer scale from zero to 160 miles per hour. A red needle points to roughly 45 miles per hour, indicating J.P. Morgan’s cautious stance within the Nitrous Oxide Boost zone. This zone represents a market supported by historic monetary and fiscal expansion that mitigates insolvency risks but introduces long-term instability, fiscal unwind risks, and impending higher taxes, while notes highlight that China can likely rescue its own region but not the entire global economy. 

To the left of this position, the speedometer’s lowest range from zero to 40 miles per hour is marked Gasket Failure, warning of a Roubini Apocalypse scenario characterized by stalled credit, failed stimulus, rapid consumer deleveraging, and another major growth collapse. To the right of the current needle, from 80 to 120 miles per hour, sits The U-Turn, denoting signs of a classic economic bottom, such as rising manufacturing orders, a bounce in world trade, and active technology initial public offerings, offset by weak housing and consumer spending. Higher still, the Valuation Hazard Removed zone from 120 to 140 miles per hour notes that valuations have returned to their 1950 to 1990 historical averages and points to consensus estimates of 30 percent S&P 500 earnings growth in 2010. The highest range, Driving Blind on Technicals from 140 to 160 miles per hour, argues that historical trends following a decade of zero-percent equity returns support aggressively adding risk. A footnote cautions that the widely cited mountain of cash on the sidelines is largely an illusion created by a one-trillion-dollar expansion in Treasury bill issuance rather than a true signal of sidelined investment capital.

Beneath the speedometer graphic, the text discusses private equity and energy markets. In secondary private equity, a severe liquidity squeeze is forcing over-leveraged sellers—such as endowments, pension funds, family offices, and distressed financial firms like American International Group and Lehman Brothers—to accept steep discounts. Transactions are taking place at 50 percent of December 2008 net asset values, allowing J.P. Morgan's manager to buy companies with manageable debt of 3.5 times EBITDA at cheap 1980s-era valuation multiples of 5.0 times. In the oil and gas sector, the author describes a similar distressed-seller landscape. After advising clients to sell when oil peaked above 130 dollars per barrel in 2008, the firm began buying again when oil fell below 40 dollars and natural gas collapsed from 13 dollars to 3 dollars. This dramatic decline led to insolvency for many energy companies, as exemplified by the financial struggles of Chesapeake Energy and Quicksilver Resources. Consequently, the firm is now working with partners to acquire assets directly from these distressed exploration and production companies.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest analyzes early signs of a global recovery from the first-quarter deep freeze, a phenomenon he terms boulder economics, while warning about the unprecedented financial costs of engineering this rebound. To highlight the thawing economic activity, the page features three charts. The first, detailing monthly high-yield new issuance in billions from May 2006 to May 2009, shows a massive surge in issuance for May 2009 that approaches twenty-five billion dollars, marking its highest point since the credit bull market. The second chart, tracking a global car sales rebound indexed to June 2007, shows sales surging past an index level of 160 in China and recovering to over 110 in Germany and Brazil by March 2009, even as the Euro Area and Japan remain depressed. The third chart, showing weekly Manhattan apartment activity from June 2008 to June 2009, tracks volatile new listings alongside a modest rebound in signed contracts, which clawed back toward two hundred after bottoming out in late 2008 following price cuts of twenty-five to thirty percent.

Cembalest cautions that government interventions, such as Germany's cash-for-clunkers program, carry massive taxpayer costs—at least three and a half billion dollars in Germany's case—and merely pull forward future demand. To contextualize the scale of this intervention, a fourth chart compares current monetary and fiscal policy against the 1970s. While today's spare capacity, measured by the cumulative output gap, is twice as large as in the 1970s, the current monetary base expansion is already four times larger and growing, and the fiscal expansion, measured by trough-to-peak public debt to GDP, is nine times larger. Although money multipliers are not yet picking up, the author warns that this coordinated avalanche of stimulus is akin to the giant boulder at the start of Raiders of the Lost Ark, with rising commodity prices and Treasury yields suggesting the risks are closing in. 

Finally, the discussion turns to domestic fiscal policy, specifically proposals to fund the healthcare bill by limiting itemized deductions for taxpayers earning over two hundred and fifty thousand dollars. Cembalest characterizes this as a stealth tax hike that would be equivalent to an additional three and a half to four and a half percent federal tax rate increase for residents of high-tax states like New York and California, coming on top of scheduled federal tax rate increases to thirty-nine point six percent by 2011.

This page analyzes investment opportunities in agriculture and credit markets while outlining a hypothetical three-step exit strategy for the Federal Reserve. 

The discussion on agricultural prices introduces the concept of Peak Soil, driven by steady declines in crop yield improvements cited by the World Bank, irreversible soil salinization documented by the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization, low wheat and corn inventories, biofuel-driven supply pressures, and a connection between rising temperatures and falling crop yields. This latter point references research by David B. Lobell of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and Christopher Field of the Carnegie Institution. Despite these long-term constraints, a collapse in leveraged risk positions caused agricultural prices to drop fifty percent from their early 2008 peak. J.P. Morgan added agricultural exposure in mid-April 2009, citing growing per capita meat and cereal consumption in China, though they note that government price controls could cap upside potential. 

This agricultural thesis is illustrated by three charts. The first, S&P GSCI Agricultural Index Excess Return, tracks index levels from May 2007 to May 2009, highlighting a peak above one hundred in early 2008, a drop below fifty-five, and a circled April entry point when the index level was around fifty-five. The other two charts plot historical data from January 1970 to January 2005, showing the inverse relationship between stocks-to-use ratios and real prices. The Wheat stocks-to-use chart shows ratios ranging from fifteen to thirty-three percent against real wheat prices indexed to January 1970, and the Corn stocks-to-use chart shows ratios from ten to forty-five percent against indexed real corn prices. Both include USDA estimates for the 2008/2009 and 2009/2010 crop years.

In credit markets, the author explains that J.P. Morgan began buying high-grade and convertible bonds in December 2008, anticipating that Federal Reserve credit facilities would boost performance. They now expect fewer capital gains because investment-grade bonds have reached fair value at six and a half percent all-in yields. New investments in leveraged loan funds are being curtailed now that first-lien prices are in the mid-eighty-dollar range. 

This credit discussion is supported by two charts. The High Grade Bond Spread to Treasury chart, spanning June 2008 to April 2009, shows spreads peaking near six hundred basis points in December 2008, where green dots mark J.P. Morgan’s buying program, before narrowing to around three hundred fifty basis points by April 2009 as fair value was reached. The Merrill Lynch Convertible Bond Index chart tracks total returns from June 2008 to June 2009, marking two distinct investment dates in late 2008 when the index level fell below seventy, followed by a recovery to around eighty by June 2009.

Finally, the page outlines a three-step Federal Reserve exit strategy. Step one is to delay action due to massive excess capacity and deflationary risks. Step two is to allow maturing lending facilities to unwind—such as the Primary Dealer Credit Facility, Term Auction Facility, Term Securities Lending Facility, Asset-Backed Commercial Paper Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility, Commercial Paper Funding Facility, and foreign currency swap lines—noting that these facilities have already shrunk in aggregate from one point seven trillion dollars to eight hundred fifty billion dollars. Step three is for the Fed to sell its American International Group securities portfolio to the Treasury and force a disposition of AIG business lines.

This page analyzes the historical resilience of entrepreneurship during downturns, reviews recent U.S. retail sales trends, and introduces factors influencing corporate profit recovery. 

The first section discusses the concept of creative destruction, citing a Kauffman Foundation study showing that more than 50% of Fortune 500 companies were founded during recessions or bear markets dating back to the 1700s. This is illustrated by a bar chart titled "Number of Fortune 500 companies founded (by decade)" spanning from the 1700s to the 2000s, which displays consistent entrepreneurial activity across centuries, peaking with over 45 companies founded in both the 1900s and 1980s. The author argues that startup growth is the primary driver of employment, presenting a second chart titled "Job creation, with and without startups (millions)" from 1977 to 2005. This chart compares steady startup job creation, which consistently hovers around 3 million jobs annually, against net job creation for the economy absent startups, which frequently drops into negative territory, falling as low as negative 4.5 million during recessions. The author warns that policy changes regarding unionization, healthcare, H-1B visas, and corporate taxation could severely threaten this crucial source of job creation.

In the market update, the author notes that while U.S. economic data has stopped falling, areas tied to the consumer, such as housing and credit card losses, remain under intense pressure, highlighting California's recent foreclosure moratorium. To demonstrate how economic charts can be misread, the author provides two charts on retail sales. The first, "Retail sales, QoQ change, seasonally adjusted, annualized" from 1992 to 2008, shows a sharp, positive-looking rebound toward 0% following a historic plunge of nearly 25% in late 2008. The second chart, "Retail sales, billions" from 2000 to 2009, contextualizes this rebound by showing that absolute sales remain mired at around $335 billion, down significantly from their peak near $375 billion. The author predicts this will stand as the weakest retail sales response to a mega-stimulus ever recorded. 

The page concludes with a discussion on corporate profits, explaining that labor costs dominate 60% to 70% of corporate expenses. The author observes that falling unit labor costs have historically translated into rising profits, except during the high-inflation period of the late 1970s. Looking ahead, the author forecasts a near-term production bounce due to business over-retrenchment and suggests that if businesses do not immediately restaff to meet rising demand, unit labor costs will fall, leading to higher corporate profits.

This page discusses the extreme shock of the 2008–2009 financial crisis, termed "Disasteroids," and the subsequent unprecedented global policy response. The author explains that businesses aggressively slashed inventories and labor in anticipation of a severe economic downturn. This initial collapse is illustrated by two charts: one showing U.S. steel inventories plunging to a 20-year low of less than 4,000 thousand tonnes by early 2009, and another showing year-over-year growth in hours worked per employee plummeting in both the United States and Germany, with Germany dropping past negative 4 percent by early 2009. 

In response, the OECD and G-20 nations launched what the author calls the "Strategic Deflation Initiative"—a massive fiscal and monetary rescue effort. The IMF reported G-20 fiscal deficits of 6.6 percent in 2009 and 6.5 percent in 2010. Furthermore, total asset purchases, capital injections, and financial guarantees in advanced G-20 countries reached a staggering 50 percent of GDP, though only 5.3 percent of this was funded upfront. In the United States, this massive federal stimulus was heavily needed to offset an estimated $110 billion to $210 billion drag from state-level tax increases and spending cuts.

This extraordinary policy intervention sparked a sharp cyclical rebound in mid-2009, described as the "nitrous oxide" phase of the cycle. North American auto production was projected to rise by nearly 50 percent in the second half of 2009 compared to the first half, aided by "Cash for Clunkers" programs, and companies like U.S. Steel began recalling workers. The recovery was particularly intense in Asia, fueled by a tripling of government-sponsored bank lending in China. This regional boom is depicted in two additional charts: Chinese steel production showcases a sharp V-shaped recovery, surging from a late-2008 low of around 35,000 thousand tonnes back up to nearly 45,000 thousand tonnes by April 2009. Similarly, a chart of emerging Asia's electronics industrial production growth shows a dramatic rebound from a trough of nearly negative 70 percent to an almost vertical spike reaching approximately 100 percent annualized growth. 

Despite the immediate relief, the author ends with strong warnings. Chinese corporate profits are heavily tied to their own rising stock portfolios, which artificially inflates P/E ratios. Furthermore, the massive credit expansion risks creating long-term debt problems, reminiscent of the $600 billion to $800 billion in non-performing Chinese bank loans from previous cycles, while the Congressional Budget Office's long-term U.S. budget outlook points to serious fiscal challenges ahead.

This page focuses on the efficiency, economics, and viability of electric vehicles, specifically examining plug-in hybrid electric vehicle conversion kits. Michael Cembalest highlights testing data from the Idaho National Laboratory’s Advanced Vehicle Testing Area, which evaluated Hymotion 5 kWh conversion kits that transform standard Toyota Prius hybrids into plug-in hybrids. 

The central visual is a data table outlining nine different testing cycles based on various driving conditions. It tracks urban miles, highway miles, miles driven before recharging, electricity used in kilowatt-hours, gallons of gasoline consumed, and the resulting miles per gallon. The data demonstrates that mileage is highest under urban driving conditions with frequent recharges; Cycle 1, which featured 600 urban miles and recharges every 10 miles, yielded 117.6 MPG, whereas Cycle 3, with the same mileage but recharges every 40 miles, dropped to 84.2 MPG. Longer commutes significantly reduce mileage, and driving behavior plays a major role, as shown by comparing Cycle 4's aggressive driving (64.3 MPG) with Cycle 5's more moderate driving (99.8 MPG) over the same 300-urban/300-highway mile course. Additionally, cold weather can reduce fuel economy by up to 20 MPG, and when factoring in electricity costs of 10 cents per kilowatt-hour, the true "effective" mileage of the converted vehicles ranges from 49 to 67 MPG.

Cembalest notes that with gasoline priced at $3 per gallon, the high cost of the Hymotion conversion kit results in an unattractive payback period of over ten years, indicating that industry scale is necessary to lower battery costs. Despite this, he observes that decades of research are finally yielding improvements in lithium-ion battery technology, which will be vital for reducing fossil fuel dependence. 

In terms of broader energy policy, Cembalest highlights a notable shift in the United Kingdom. He details how the U.K. Minister for Energy and Climate Change and the Labor party, alongside Greenpeace co-founder Patrick Moore, have grown increasingly supportive of nuclear power as a necessary complement to renewable technologies like tidal, solar, wave, and wind energy. Finally, a footnote clarifies the technical distinctions between parallel and series plug-in hybrids and notes Toyota's plan to lease 500 plug-in hybrid cars by the end of 2009.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s financial commentary publication addresses investor questions concerning non-agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS), California municipal bonds, and debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing. 

The first section discusses why anyone would invest in non-agency MBS, explaining that managers concentrate on fixed-rate jumbo and Alt-A securities to generate stable returns primarily through current income. A table titled "How bad can it get?" contrasts conservative manager projections against actual June 2009 performance metrics for defaults and losses. For Prime Jumbo, the manager models a severe 20% to 30% default rate and a 60% to 70% loss upon default, far worse than the June 2009 actuals of 5% defaults and 46% losses. For Alt-A, the manager projects 60% to 65% defaults and 70% losses compared to the actual 22% defaults and 60% losses. For Subprime, the manager assumes an extreme 95% to 100% default rate and an 80% loss, compared to actuals of 40% and 74%. Despite these adverse assumptions, the publication estimates 10% to 14% returns on recent purchases and plans to deploy these investments before the fall, anticipating the launch of the $40 billion Public-Private Investment Program (PPIP).

The next section explains J.P. Morgan's decision to maintain a massive underweight position in California municipal bonds—holding only 2% in state general obligation bonds compared to a 15% weight in national indices. The author attributes this stance to California's high tax rates, volatile capital-gains-dependent revenue, and a structural spending problem. This spending growth is illustrated in a bar chart titled "California: Annual population plus inflation growth vs. annual spending growth, 1991 - 2009," which compares the three gubernatorial administrations of Pete Wilson, Gray Davis, and Arnold Schwarzenegger. Under all three administrations, spending growth consistently outstripped the combined rate of population growth and inflation, with spending growth hovering around 5% to 6.5% while population plus inflation growth remained lower, between roughly 3.8% and 5%. The text highlights rising state employment costs, such as the state paying 100% of healthcare costs for retired workers, and critiques California's energy policy, noting that its ambitious 33% renewable energy target contrasts sharply with a current renewable output of just 4%, posing a risk of electricity shortages by 2011.

The final section explores how U.S. courts protect debtor-in-possession (DIP) lenders. The author notes that the best DIP lending opportunities exist where suppliers and customers have a vested interest in the company’s survival, and that because these are post-petition loans, they bypass the pre-petition legal uncertainties seen in bankruptcies like Chrysler and General Growth Properties. A stacked bar chart titled "Pro-forma capital structure of a bankrupt company" displays the progression of a company's capital structure through pre-petition, Chapter 11, and exit phases. The pre-petition stack consists of equity (E), senior notes (S), term loans (T), and a revolving line of credit (R). During Chapter 11, equity is wiped out, and a DIP loan (D) is introduced at the top of the stack, illustrating how DIP lenders are legally permitted to "prime" (or jump ahead of) pre-petition creditors, including revolving credit and term loans. At exit, the structure reorganizes into equity, term loans, and exit loans (X).

This J.P. Morgan commentary analyzes U.S. corporate earnings for the second quarter of 2009 and the critical role of China in the global economic recovery. In the market update, the author uses Eaton Corporation as a prime example of the disconnect between company performance and stock reactions during this period. Despite a 30% year-over-year drop in revenue, a 90% decline in profit, and multiple guidance cuts, Eaton's stock rallied because its earnings per share of $0.23 beat heavily reduced analyst expectations of $0.15. This beat was largely driven by severe cost-cutting measures, including a 10% workforce reduction, suspended pension contributions, and a negative tax rate. The commentary attributes the broader market rally to rekindled animal spirits, high short-term productivity from labor cuts, and positive stimulus feedback loops, pointing to a global auto production rebound and Japan's record quarterly jump in industrial production and exports.

A key visual on the page is a bar chart tracking year-over-year earnings growth for companies that beat analyst second-quarter 2009 expectations. The chart, sourced from Bloomberg, counts the number of companies across growth bins ranging from under negative 100% to over positive 100% for both the S&P 500 and the Russell 1000. It visually demonstrates that many companies beating analyst expectations actually experienced negative year-over-year growth, particularly concentrated in the negative 30% to 49% and negative 50% to 99% ranges. An inset table shows that with 31% of S&P 500 companies and 37% of Russell 1000 companies reporting to date, 72% and 75% respectively beat estimates. Despite this high beat rate, the author expresses low conviction in the long-term sustainability of results driven by severe expense cuts, opting to cap long equity allocations in Balanced portfolios at 35% to 38%.

The discussion then shifts to China's economic resilience during a period of weak exports. The author notes China's explosive domestic loan growth, its overseas acquisitions like the bid for Argentine oil and gas company YPF, and its capital spending on railways and coal, which is boosting the broader ASEAN region. China is also aggressively hoarding industrial commodities to sustain domestic infrastructure and commercial property development without driving up global commodity prices. A detailed footnote elaborates on China's ongoing purchase of U.S. debt, noting that China continues to buy about $230 billion in Treasuries every 12 months, though roughly 75% of this buying has shifted to short-term T-bills while buying of Agency paper has ceased. The author poses a critical forward-looking concern, noting that while Chinese buying has helped finance almost the entire fiscal year 2009 U.S. deficit, these trends must continue to prevent bond market disruptions when financing the upcoming deficit of over $1.5 trillion.

This page analyzes the leverage and valuation multiples of the 2006–07 private equity vintage, exploring how capital markets value the debt and equity of these leveraged buyout companies during the global recession. 

An initial bar chart, titled "Distribution of purchase price to cash flow multiples," illustrates that the vast majority of the analyzed buyout portfolio was purchased at historically high multiples. Specifically, the portfolio is highly concentrated in the 8x to 10x tier (at nearly 30%) and the 10x to 12x tier (at over 30%), with very little exposure below 8x. A corresponding footnote cites S&P LCD data showing LBO total debt-to-EBITDA levels rising from 4.1x in 2001 to 6.2x in 2007. A brief informational box defines cash flow conventions and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) as the standard metric to compare buyout companies.

The text questions what debt markets reveal about the equity value of these companies. The author argues that while loan and bond prices reflect credit risk, they are also heavily influenced by technical, non-fundamental market factors. These exogenous pressures include structured credit liquidations, the repricing of loose covenants, a collapse in Libor that reduced the cash flow benefit of floating-rate loans, and reduced prime broker leverage. Consequently, broad indices are not perfect barometers for LBO survival risk. This point is supported by a line chart tracking "High yield and leveraged loan performance" from July 2008 to July 2009, comparing the price indices of the S&P/LSTA Leveraged Loan 100 Index and the Merrill Lynch High Yield Index. Both indices fell sharply in late 2008, bottoming near 50 to 60, before staging a partial recovery by mid-2009.

To address this, the report tracks 250 plus tranches of bonds and loans issued by 43 composite LBO companies. A bar chart showing the "Price distribution of LBO Composite debt" as of August 18, 2009, breaks down bonds and loans by the percent of the portfolio across price intervals. Loans are heavily concentrated at discounted levels between 75 and 90, while bonds show a wider distribution, including a spike of over 20% priced above par. Despite the recent market rebound, a substantial amount of the composite debt remains priced below par, which the author states implies a significant decline in LBO equity values. 

The page concludes on a more optimistic note, indicating that while equity values have dropped and earnings have declined, most of these 43 companies still have "breathing room" because their debt maturity profiles delay immediate repayment obligations, giving management time to execute operational recoveries.

This page discusses a resurgence in active management, provides a global market update following the 2009 stimulus measures, and highlights growing concerns regarding weak corporate revenue and pricing power. 

The author begins by asserting that active equity management and hedge funds are staging a recovery after a dry spell. While institutional investors like the Illinois State Board of Investments and the retirement systems of San Francisco, Hawaii, and Rhode Island reduced active management in favor of index-based strategies in 2008, J.P. Morgan did the opposite by halving its exchange-traded fund allocation and returning to active managers. This rotation generated a year-to-date global equity manager alpha of approximately 2.7 percent, led by U.S. large-cap and Asia ex-Japan managers. Furthermore, J.P. Morgan's hedge fund platform outperformed the S&P 500, the MSCI World, and the HFRI Fund of Funds indices through June, boosted by equity and credit relative value, leveraged loans, and diversified multi-strategy funds.

Focusing on the broader economy, the author observes that massive global stimulus drove first-order benefits and lifted equity markets starting in March 2009. This trend is captured in a multi-line spaghetti chart titled "Global Hail Mary stimulus pays off in Q2," which plots various indicators indexed to 100 as of December 31, 2007, spanning December 2007 through June 2009. The chart reveals a steep collective decline for nearly all indicators into late 2008 or early 2009, followed by a noticeable second-quarter recovery. An accompanying sidebar notes that these diverse global economic indicators include Japan Exports, UK Manufacturing PMI, ISM Manufacturing New Orders, German Business Expectations, Brazil Retail Sales of Construction Materials, Turkey Consumer Confidence, Japan Industrial Production, France Industrial Production, U.S. Small Business Optimism, Japan Small Business Confidence, China Electricity Production, Taiwan Exports, J.P. Morgan Global Manufacturing PMI, Taiwan Industrial Production, Eurozone Manufacturing PMI, Japan Capacity Utilization, South Africa Steel Production, Denmark Business Confidence, and South Korea Real GDP.

Despite this recovery, the author raises open questions about unsustainable second-order effects. In China, capital formation drives 88 percent of growth, and a 56 percent expansion in shipping capacity threatens an already oversupplied industry. Footnotes highlight that even internal Chinese voices, such as articles in Caijing and warnings from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, are questioning this reckless investment in excess capacity. Furthermore, the author notes that while 75 percent of S&P and Russell 1000 companies beat earnings estimates, this rally was not driven by short-covering—as short interest actually increased—but rather by investor frustration with zero cash returns and aggressive corporate cost-cutting. 

The author warns that revenue must improve soon, presenting a weak outlook supported by two historical charts from the National Federation of Independent Business spanning January 1973 to January 2009. The first chart, showing the percentage of firms reporting higher sales this quarter over last, illustrates a plunge to an unprecedented low of nearly negative 40 percent in early 2009. The second chart, measuring the percentage of firms that have increased prices over the last three months, similarly depicts a historic drop to nearly negative 30 percent, underscoring severe deflationary pressures and a lack of pricing power among small businesses.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, published during the post-crisis period in 2009, argues that while global manufacturing and employment indicators are rebounding, the recovery is uniquely and precariously dependent on an unprecedented volume of monetary and fiscal stimulus. J.P. Morgan’s Global Manufacturing PMI index, incorporating data from 24 countries, demonstrates that the global manufacturing decline has ended, with the index sharply recovering from its late 2008 low of nearly 30 back toward 50 by mid-2009. This improvement is mirrored in labor markets, as shown in a chart of PMI employment sub-indices for the United States, Japan, and the Euro area. All three regions saw employment indices bottom out near 30 in late 2008 before showing a sharp upward hook by July 2009, with the U.S. and Japan leading the rebound. Similarly, a chart of Euro area coincident and U.S. leading indicators shows both metrics turning upward by mid-2009, with the U.S. leading indicators index rising from a low of about 83 back toward 90. 

However, the author emphasizes that this recovery is heavily artificial. A bar chart titled "Stimulus applied per unit improvement in the ISM" measures monetary and fiscal expansion as a percentage of GDP divided by ISM recovery points. In all ten previous recessionary rebounds dating back to 1952, this ratio rarely exceeded 0.2, and many recoveries required virtually no stimulus. In contrast, the 2008–2009 cycle shows a staggering ratio of approximately 1.5, illustrating that the current recovery requires massive "stimulus firepower" compared to any prior period. This pattern of high-cost growth is repeated internationally. A line chart tracking Chinese loan growth per unit of real GDP improvement shows the ratio spiking from its historical range of 1.0 to 2.5 up to an unprecedented high of over 4.0 by early 2009, indicating that China is requiring massive credit expansion to generate economic growth. 

To illustrate the sheer scale of global intervention, the author cites several policy and corporate examples. GM sales in China surged 78% year-over-year due to domestic small-car incentives and rural subsidies, while Switzerland and Hong Kong saw monetary base growth exceed 100%. Meanwhile, countries like Brazil, Russia, and Malaysia implemented fiscal stimulus packages representing 8% to 10% of their GDP. Looking ahead, the author forecasts that while the U.S. ISM survey should continue to rise over the next year, the massive amount of monetary and fiscal expansion already set in motion means this historically high ratio of stimulus-to-improvement is unlikely to change.

This page serves as an introduction to a special edition focused on China’s role in the global economy, summarizing discussions from J.P. Morgan's Aspen Client Insights Series. The main text introduces interviews with Ronnie Chan, Chairman of Hang Lung Group, and Lee Kuan Yew, the former Prime Minister of Singapore. A sidebar profiles Mr. Chan, highlighting his leadership of Hang Lung Group, which has planned a five-billion-dollar investment in eighteen commercial complexes in mainland China, and his active role in international conferences and cultural restoration projects.

The primary argument presented is that China's current economic resurgence is not an aggressive expansion but rather a return to its historical position on the world stage. To support this, a bar chart titled "The 20th century was a growth anomaly for China" displays China's share of world GDP from the year 1 to 2003. According to Angus Maddison's historical statistics, China consistently accounted for 25% to 30% of global GDP from the year 1000 through 1820. Its share precipitously declined during the 20th century, bottoming out below 5% between 1950 and 1980, before beginning a modest recovery toward 15% by 2003. 

The text also addresses international anxieties regarding China's rising military power, noting that while neighbors like Japan and South Korea view its rise warily, Chinese military spending remains only a fraction of U.S. levels. This dynamics is illustrated by two additional charts utilizing data from the Stockholm International Peace Institute. The first, "Chinese military spending (constant 2005 dollars)," is a dual-axis chart showing that between 1989 and 2007, Chinese military spending grew from approximately $12 billion to over $60 billion, while per capita military spending rose from $10 to nearly $50. Despite this growth, a second chart titled "Global distribution of military expenditure" for the year 2007 shows that China accounted for only about 5% of global military spending, compared to the United States, which dominated with approximately 43% of the world total.

This page evaluates the financial health and refinancing challenges of highly leveraged, private-equity-backed companies during the 2009 recessionary period. The author begins by highlighting the LBO Composite debt maturity schedule, which demonstrates that very little debt matures between 2009 and 2012; instead, the vast majority—nearly 90 percent—is pushed out to 2013 and beyond. While Standard & Poor’s reports that half of all defaulting companies in 2009 were owned by private equity sponsors, J.P. Morgan’s own Composite tells a more resilient story: as of March 31, 2009, all but one company was in compliance with its debt covenants and interest obligations, with the single outlier successfully restructuring via sponsor equity and a debt-for-equity exchange. 

The broader macroeconomic backdrop also shows signs of an industrial rebound that could support earnings. This recovery is illustrated by the J.P. Morgan Global Purchasing Managers Index, which tracks orders, output, employment, and inventories across 24 countries. This index bottomed out near 30 in late 2008 but has since staged a sharp, V-shaped recovery back toward 50 by mid-2009. This trend is mirrored in a chart mapping positive earnings revisions against the ISM Manufacturing Index from December 2005 to July 2009. The two series track closely: both bottomed in late 2008, with the ISM index dropping to approximately 32 and upward earnings revisions falling to 20 percent, before both rebounded significantly by July 2009, with ISM climbing back toward 45 and revisions reaching nearly 50 percent. 

Despite these positive short-term signals, LBO managers face a daunting refinancing wall starting in 2013, as an average of $160 billion in leveraged loans will mature annually from 2013 to 2015. The historical funding vehicle for these loans, the Collateralized Loan Obligation market, is currently insufficient to support this volume. A chart of Global CLO funded issuance by year shows that issuance peaked near $140 billion in 2006 and $135 billion in 2007, fell to about $30 billion in 2008, and collapsed to under $10 billion in 2009. To navigate this dry spell, sponsor-backed companies are increasingly turning to the high-yield bond market to buy time, even at the cost of higher interest rates.
