Specifically, sponsor companies have issued $16.6 billion of high-yield bonds in 2009, with notable issuers including HCA, Harrah’s, US Oncology, Toys “R” Us, Nielsen, and Univision.

This page evaluates the potential return of capital for 2006–2007 vintage leveraged buyout investments by analyzing three core components: earnings growth, exit multiples, and debt paydown. 

The author begins by noting that credit market access has improved, driven by approximately $25 billion in year-to-date inflows into high-yield bond funds, primarily sourced from money market funds. This trend is supported by an accompanying line chart depicting high-yield mutual fund weekly flows on a four-week rolling average from 1993 to 2008, which highlights a highly volatile history of inflows and outflows that recently stabilized and ticked upward. Additionally, LBO companies are securing more time through $14 billion in restructured "amend-to-extend" loan agreements and discounted debt repurchases, which are supported by tax law changes deferring cancellation-of-debt income.

The first part of the analysis focuses on earnings. The LBO Composite EBITDA fell by 21% from the first quarter of 2008 to the first quarter of 2009, matching the 21.9% decline in the S&P 500. This performance was better than expected given that the Composite's concentration in consumer discretionary is nearly 2.5 times higher than that of the S&P 500. A bar chart of the portfolio sector breakdown as of March 2009 illustrates this concentration, showing the LBO Composite with over 20% exposure in consumer discretionary compared to under 10% for the S&P 500, while being significantly under-allocated to energy and telecom. To project future earnings, the author's model assumes the EBITDA decline carries through 2009, followed by 8% growth in 2010 and 5% thereafter. This recovery assumption is compared to historical S&P Industrials Index EBITDA growth, which averaged 7.2% from 1967 to 2008.

The second part examines exit multiples, assuming exit valuations will be 1x to 2x lower than entry multiples based on historical sector averages, with exits occurring six years from the initial investment. The author observes that exit multiples have shown signs of holding up, citing a semiconductor IPO priced at 12.5x EBITDA and a median purchase multiple of 8.5x EBITDA for the ten largest strategic US M&A transactions year-to-date. However, a key risk remains for large-cap transactions, which are less likely to find strategic buyers and must rely more heavily on public IPO markets for exit strategies. 

Finally, the third part addresses debt paydown. While LBO sponsors typically use excess cash flow to pay down 35% to 45% of debt within the first five to six years of an LBO, the author warns that current pressures on cash flows will limit this paydown capability within their valuation model.

This page of the J.P. Morgan report explores the historical origins and economic trajectory of China's ascent, arguing that the severe societal traumas of the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution created a collective willingness to accept Deng Xiaoping's market reforms starting in the late 1970s. The author provides four charts illustrating different dimensions of this rapid economic transition. 

The first chart, titled "China's trade openness begins with Deng reforms," plots total trade as a percentage of GDP from 1952 to 2007. It shows trade to nominal and real GDP remaining flat and low, mostly under 20%, until the Deng reforms began, after which both measures climbed dramatically to reach nearly 70% of GDP by 2007. 

The second chart, "China's catch-up the fastest so far," compares per capita GDP trajectories across a 15-year horizon starting from when each respective nation’s per capita GDP equaled Japan's in 1950. Tracking Japan, China, Taiwan, South Korea, and India, the data illustrates that China's growth from 1994 to 2007 was the steepest of all, rising from roughly 2,500 to over 8,000 USD in just 13 years, outstripping the catch-up speeds of its regional peers.

The lower half of the page focuses on domestic restructuring and the privatization of the Chinese economy. The third chart, "Entrepreneur explosion," displays the number of enterprises by ownership type in millions from 1992 to 2006. It illustrates a massive shift toward private ownership, with the total number of enterprises rising toward 10 million, increasingly dominated by private firms while the share of state-owned and collective enterprises shrank. 

Complementing this transition is the fourth chart, "Government subsidies to loss-making SOEs," which tracks absolute subsidies in billions of RMB on the left axis and as a percentage of government expenditures on the right axis from 1985 to 2006. Government subsidies peaked in 1989 and 1990 at nearly 60 billion RMB, representing about 20% of the government's budget. By 2006, these subsidies fell to under 20 billion RMB, representing nearly 0% of total government expenditures. 

The narrative concludes by highlighting how a combination of inexpensive labor and heavy foreign direct investment helped China climb the high-tech export chain, positioning it to rival or surpass the United States as a trading partner for nations ranging from Japan to Brazil. Footnotes add further context, citing a 30-to-40 million death toll from the Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution, detailing Deng Xiaoping's critical 1978 meeting with Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew, and noting that while subsidies to loss-making state-owned enterprises have been cut, profitable state enterprises still benefit from subsidized credit that artificially inflates their profitability.

This page explores the dynamics of China's economic recovery, arguing that while indicators are rebounding sharply, generating GDP growth has required an unprecedented amount of stimulus. This reliance on credit and capital formation to drive expansion is deflationary in a world already burdened with excess capacity, though it serves immediate job creation goals. For example, Chinese shipbuilding has risen 50% year-to-date despite a massive capacity glut. Despite potential asset bubbles, the author asserts that these investments will yield long-term productivity benefits, comparing China's current infrastructure push to the electrification of American farms in the 1930s or the development of the U.S. Interstate Highway System in the 1950s. A primary focus is China's massive railway expansion, which aims to reverse a nearly 50-year stagnation in per-capita rail kilometers. Significant productivity opportunities also exist in the agricultural sector, where Chinese corn yields remain far below U.S. and European levels.

Four charts support these observations. The first line chart, "Chinese loan growth per unit improvement in real GDP," plots the ratio of loan growth to real GDP from June 1998 to December 2008. The ratio historically fluctuated between 0.5 and 2.5 but spiked sharply to over 4.0 by late 2008, illustrating the massive credit injection needed to support recent growth. Below this, a stacked bar chart titled "Capital formation contribution to GDP growing..." details the components of China's GDP growth rate from 2000 through the first half of 2009, divided into consumption, capital formation, and net trade. In the first half of 2009, net trade became a major drag at -2.9%, while capital formation contributed a dominant 6.2% and consumption contributed 3.8%. 

To the right, a line chart of the "Global operating rate," measured in standard deviations from the 1991–2007 average, shows the rate plummeting to nearly -5 standard deviations by 2009. This highlights that China's capital expansion is occurring precisely when global capacity utilization is at an extreme low. Finally, a column chart titled "Fixed asset investment by industry" displays the year-over-year percentage change of cumulative fixed asset investment from January to June. Railway transport stands out as the dominant recipient of investment, growing by more than 120%, while other sectors—including coal, electricity and heat, oil and natural gas, non-metal products, ferrous metals, and non-ferrous metals—grew at more moderate rates ranging between 20% and 50%.

This page analyzes the significant commodity demand generated by China's rapid economic growth and urbanization, alongside the geopolitical strategies China employs to secure these natural resources. The author notes that China's ongoing transition is highly commodity-intensive, making it the primary global user of key metals like aluminum, copper, zinc, and nickel, with recent price surges reflecting heavy stockpiling.

To contextualize this demand, the page features two charts. The first, titled Chinese urbanization trends, plots urbanization as a percentage of total population from 1960 to 2005. It shows that while China's urban population has grown steadily to around 40 percent by 2005, it remains far below the levels of the United States at around 80 percent, Japan, South Korea, and other high-income OECD nations, indicating substantial potential for future growth. The second chart, titled China's share of world commodity usage, tracks the percentage of global total consumption from 1960 to 2020, with estimates extending beyond 2009. This visual shows a sharp upward spike beginning in the late 1990s, with China's share of aluminum, copper, zinc, and nickel rising from under 10 percent to between 30 and 40 percent by 2009, and projected to reach up to 45 percent by 2020. In contrast, crude oil usage is growing at a slower but steady rate, projected to reach about 15 percent of the world total by 2020.

The text highlights that despite this massive total consumption, China's per capita commodity demand is still relatively small, meaning demand could jump dramatically as incomes rise. Additionally, while China produces many of its own commodities, its net import demand remains high, particularly for cotton, soybeans, and copper. Crucially, the International Energy Agency projects that Chinese net oil imports will surge from 3.5 million barrels per day to 13.0 million barrels per day by 2030.

To secure these resources, China has aggressively expanded its presence in Africa, a strategy illustrated in the third chart, titled Trade with Africa. This chart measures trade value in billions of U.S. dollars from 1980 to 2007. It shows that while U.S. trade with Africa historically dominated and spiked to nearly 80 billion dollars by 2007, Chinese trade, which was virtually nonexistent before 2000, surged exponentially over the following seven years to nearly equal the U.S. volume by 2007.

The author discusses how Chinese companies are securing access by building critical African infrastructure, such as roads, hospitals, airports, and fiber optic networks, and exporting many of China's 2.5 million annual engineering graduates to work on these projects. This strategy is aided by Beijing's policy of noninterference with domestic affairs, which contrasts sharply with the United States' insistence on democratic reforms before providing aid. A commentator named Ronnie is quoted arguing that the U.S. is unwise to impose these democratic preconditions, noting that a middle class must exist before democratic ideals can take root, and concluding that China's pragmatic approach is far better suited to securing critical commodities in resource-scarce regions.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s publication, Eye on the Market, highlights the severity of the 2009 recession through capital spending and employment data. In the introductory notes, the author mentions leveraging research by Emmanuel Saez, Joel Slemrod, Matthew Eichner, and Todd Sinai to compute base erosion effects from higher tax rates, noting that these effects reduce taxable income and capital gains by 3.5% to 5.0% in J.P. Morgan's models. Under the section titled Capital spending and employment severities in recessions, two scatter charts compare the current recession against every other recession since 1953. The first chart, plotting business capital spending declines against GDP declines, shows that the current recession has experienced an unusually steep capital spending decline of approximately 18% on a GDP decline of nearly 4%, falling well below the historical trendline. The second chart compares private employment declines to GDP declines, showing that the current recession is a severe outlier here as well, with private sector employment plummeting by about 5.5% compared to historical recessions with similar GDP contractions. Finally, the page provides a glossary of common financial and government acronyms—such as OMB, CBO, LBO, BEA, DIP, SOE, FHA, FNMA, and VAT—alongside contact information for Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Global Wealth Management.

This page, titled "Challenges for the 21st century" from J.P. Morgan's special edition on China, addresses the long-term economic, geopolitical, and structural headwinds facing the nation. The author argues that China is confronting a crossroads defined by declining U.S. consumer debt, a significant domestic demographic shift toward middle age over the coming decade, rising tensions over U.S. protectionism, global pressure regarding carbon emissions, and ongoing questions regarding relations with Taiwan. 

A central focus of the commentary is the challenging business environment in China. The author notes that foreign clients frequently experience issues with contract law, where agreements are often subjected to unilateral renegotiation during market volatility. Prominent figures Ronnie Chan and Lee Kuan Yew suggest that foreign entities must simply adapt to this unique Chinese business style, which carries heightened risks when dealing with state-owned enterprises like Rio Tinto.

This business environment is further illustrated by a bar chart titled "China ranks high on one measure of corruption," which utilizes 2008 data from Transparency International. The chart displays the percentage of respondents who report frequent corrupt practices across twenty-two nations. It categorizes corruption into three series: bribery to high-ranking politicians, bribery to low-level public officials to speed things up, and the use of personal and familiar relationships on public contracting. Russia and Mexico lead the index, with Russia showing more than fifty percent of respondents reporting low-level bribery. China ranks fourth overall, with around thirty percent of respondents reporting the use of personal relationships and nearly thirty percent reporting bribery to low-level officials. In contrast, Western nations like the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada show these practices occurring at rates well under ten percent. Lee Kuan Yew comments that while corruption and reliance on personal connections might eventually constrain growth, it has not yet discouraged foreign direct investment. He predicts that Hong Kong will remain the primary hub for dispute resolution unless the mainland adopts a consistent rule of law, which could allow Beijing and Shanghai to displace Hong Kong and Singapore.

The page also addresses mutual protectionism and espionage. While China has expressed disappointment over blocked acquisitions in the West—such as 3Com, Unocal, and Maytag—the author highlights that the Chinese Ministry of Commerce similarly blocked Coca-Cola's proposed acquisition of domestic juice manufacturer Huiyuan Juice Group to protect domestic competitors. A sidebar text box focuses on the severe threat of industrial espionage, noting that China-related espionage cases handled by the FBI in Silicon Valley are rising by twenty to thirty percent annually, and German and Canadian companies lose billions of dollars monthly to Chinese espionage.

In the footnotes, the author captures additional political forecasts. Lee Kuan Yew argues that the U.S. administration's anti-free-trade stance effectively gives China an eight-year free reign to solidify its relationships across Asia, Latin America, and Africa. On Taiwan, Minister Lee believes President Hu Jintao is realistic that reunification will not happen during his term, though recent four-billion-dollar procurements of Taiwanese goods by the Chinese government and Lenovo indicate improving bilateral relations.

This page analyzes the temporary boost provided by global government stimulus and warns of the potential economic drop-off as these programs fade. The main argument is that while global GDP growth is tracking at 4% to 5% for the third quarter of 2009, led by a 12% expansion in Asia during the second quarter, this recovery is highly stimulus-dependent. 

A dual-axis line chart titled "Since the recession began, growth has been stimulus-dependent" supports this point. The chart maps data from 2007 through projections for 2011. The left axis measures the contribution of fiscal stimulus to GDP growth, peaking at a JPMorgan estimate of 4% in the third quarter of 2009 before sharply declining toward zero in 2010. The right axis tracks the annualized quarter-over-quarter percentage change in real GDP, which fell to nearly negative 7% in early 2009 before rebounding sharply alongside the surge in stimulus. This correlation suggests that improving economic data may be artificial compared to prior cycles that recovered organically.

To demonstrate what happens when government support is withdrawn, the author examines the housing and automotive sectors through two smaller charts. The first, titled "Before and after: California New Home Tax Credit and monthly building permits issued," displays monthly building permits in California from January 2007 to July 2009. The chart illustrates a multi-year decline from 8,000 permits to under 2,000, interrupted by a temporary red-highlighted bump in early 2009 due to the state tax credit. Once the credit expired, July building permits fell by 29%. 

The second sectoral chart, "Before and after: Cash for Clunkers and Edmunds' car buying intent," plots an index of vehicle purchase intent from June to late August 2009, where January 31, 2009, equals 100. The index spiked dramatically from under 140 to nearly 240 when the "Cash for Clunkers" program started on July 27, peaked again when extended on August 6, and then collapsed back toward 120 as the program ended on August 24. A similar trend is noted in Germany, where the 7-billion-dollar Abwrackprämie program recently ran out of funds. Additionally, the author notes that solvency issues at the Federal Housing Administration, driven by a tight 2% capital cushion and low 3.5% down-payment requirements, could lead to a tightening of mortgage credit reminiscent of the Fannie Mae crisis.

The page concludes by addressing fiscal exit strategies and critiquing the U.S. Administration's proposal to close the deficit by taxing the wealthy. The author calculates that the annual income taxed at the highest two marginal rates, including capital gains, totals only about 1.5 trillion dollars. This amount is insufficient to close the Office of Management and Budget's 9-trillion-dollar, 10-year deficit. Consequently, the author predicts that spending cuts, higher middle-class taxes, value-added taxes, and permanently higher debt burdens are inevitable. This fiscal dilemma is not unique to the United States; similar deficit-debt dynamics are expected to challenge the United Kingdom, Spain, and Japan.

This page discusses two primary financial topics: S&P 500 profit expectations paired with the global industrial production cycle, and a critique of the popular narrative that U.S. consumer de-leveraging is well underway. 

In the first section, the author argues that stronger-than-expected first- and second-quarter profits in 2009 were driven by corporate cost controls and robust demand from emerging markets where government stimulus spurred a faster recovery. A table titled "Recovery of Peak-to-Trough Industrial Production decline, through August 2009" lists dozens of countries to demonstrate the vast geographical divergence in economic recovery. It shows that countries like the United Kingdom, Sweden, and Canada had experienced zero recovery in industrial production, and the United States had recovered only ten percent. Meanwhile, Germany recovered nineteen percent, and emerging powerhouses like China and India had surged well past their previous peaks, standing at recoveries of 156 percent and 176 percent, respectively. 

To support the notion that corporate earnings might continue to surprise on the upside, the page includes two charts. The first, "Are Q3 earnings expectations too low?", plots quarterly 2009 S&P 500 EPS expectations from late 2008 through late 2009. It marks actual Q1 earnings at twelve dollars and eighty-three cents and Q2 at sixteen dollars, juxtaposed against depressed estimates for Q3 at fourteen dollars and eighty-three cents and Q4 at sixteen dollars and sixty-two cents. The second chart, "Rebound in FirstCall earnings revisions," plots the thirteen-week average of upward revisions divided by total revisions from 1990 to 2009. This line shows a sharp rebound from its post-crisis bottom of twenty percent up to nearly fifty percent, signaling that corporate profit revisions are turning more positive.

The second section of the page tackles what the author labels the myth of U.S. consumer de-leveraging. Responding to media commentary about contracting consumer credit and low mortgage interest obligations, the author points out that total household debt relative to disposable income has barely decreased from its pre-crisis peak. The chart "Limited signs of de-leveraging so far" plots mortgage and consumer debt balances as a percentage of disposable income from 1959 through 2008. The visual shows a decades-long upward trend, climbing from under fifty percent in the late 1950s to a peak of roughly 120 percent around 2008, with almost no visible downward slope at the end of the series. The text notes that while low interest rates and loan modifications have reduced the immediate cost of servicing this debt, the underlying principal balances remain largely unpaid. To get a truer sense of household leverage, the author suggests examining debt service coverage using organic disposable income that excludes unsustainable government transfer payments, setting up a deeper analysis on the following page.

This page details an analysis of Brazil’s macroeconomic landscape, banking sector, and commodity-driven equity markets, emphasizing both structural improvements and the heavy role of government stimulus. The author notes that Brazil has undergone a dramatic shift since the mid-1990s, with its budget deficits now reversed relative to the United States, stable public debt trajectories, low unemployment, and rising consumer confidence. However, a key driver of this resilience has been aggressive state intervention. 

To illustrate this, the first chart, titled "Brazil's publicly-owned banks doing the heavy lifting," plots the year-over-year percentage change in bank lending from January 2003 to January 2009. The chart reveals a stark divergence following the 2008 global financial crisis: while private sector bank lending collapsed from its peak of nearly 40% growth in early 2008 down to about 15% by early 2009, public sector bank lending (comprising state-owned entities like Banco do Brasil, Caixa Economica, and BNDES) surged dramatically from around 20% to over 40% growth. Additionally, the government supported this credit expansion by cutting reserve requirements by 40% for top banks.

Regarding valuations, Brazilian equities trade at roughly 18 times 2010 earnings. While reasonable for an emerging market with 20% earnings growth, the author highlights that the MSCI Brazil Country Index is highly concentrated, with Petrobras and Vale/CVRD accounting for 42% of its weight. 

The outlook for Petrobras is clouded by aggressive production expectations and severe geological challenges. Although massive sub-salt reserves exist, the market prices in 10% to 12% production growth, which is significantly higher than the company's historical 4.7% growth rate from 2001 to 2009. Petrobras also repeatedly missed its two-year forward targets by 6% to 13% between 2004 and 2007. Footnotes describe the extreme difficulty of sub-salt drilling 2 to 3 kilometers below the water's surface and another 3 to 4 kilometers under rock and sand, comparing these deepwater Lower Tertiary projects to a moon landing due to low permeability, massive tar pockets, and high pressure/temperature differentials.

The second major index constituent, Vale/CVRD, is highly exposed to Chinese iron ore demand, which shows signs of weakening. This trend is illustrated in the second chart, "Iron ore supply/demand worsening with Chinese stock building," which spans June 2006 to June 2009. The chart utilizes two axes: the left axis measures China's iron ore inventory in ten thousand tons, and the right axis measures the China iron ore spot price in RMB per metric ton. The blue area depicting inventory shows a steady climb from approximately 4,000 ten thousand tons in 2006 to over 7,000 by mid-2009. This massive stockpiling has coincided with a sharp drop in the spot price (represented by a brown line) from its peak near 1,450 RMB in early 2008 down to around 725 RMB in mid-2009.

In terms of portfolio positioning, J.P. Morgan maintains a modest 2% to 4% allocation to Brazilian equities within non-US portfolios, alongside holdings of outright Reais and World Bank bonds denominated in Reais. The author cautions that while the global stimulus train has provided an enjoyable ride, rising concerns among international policymakers, such as South Korean officials warning of the need to rein in emergency stimulus to avoid asset bubbles, suggest the eventual end of this cycle may be difficult. The author metaphorically concludes with a reference to the Kris Kristofferson song, "Please Don’t Tell Me How the Story Ends."

This page addresses the challenges of consumer de-leveraging, the impact of recent credit card legislation, and the performance of defensive equity strategies implemented during the market lows of early 2009. 

The first section argues that despite discussions of consumer de-leveraging, debt service obligations remain near historical peaks. An accompanying line chart, titled "Even on a debt service basis, not far from the peak," tracks mortgage and consumer debt payments as a percentage of disposable income (minus government transfers) from 1977 to 2009. The chart displays two series. The lower series, "Interest payments only," shows a steady rise from 7% in 1977 to peaks near 10% in 1989 and 2007, hovering around 9% in 2009. The upper series, "Interest payments plus 1.5% annual amortization of mortgage and consumer balances," shows a more pronounced upward trend, peaking near 13% around 2007–2008 and remaining near 12% in 2009. Cembalest warns that leverage and spending could fall further due to the Credit Card Accountability, Responsibility, and Disclosure Act. By restricting banks from using risk-based pricing on non-delinquent accounts, the law makes it difficult to manage unsecured credit risk, where recoveries average only 15 to 18 cents on the dollar. This regulatory constraint is expected to prompt banks to tighten credit eligibility and raise rates for all customers.

The second part of the page evaluates the structured equity strategies utilized in client portfolios in early 2009, which capped upside returns in exchange for downside protection amidst fears of bank nationalizations. A line chart titled "Spring 2009: a good time to be sellers of volatility" plots the 1-year forward implied volatility of S&P 500 options from October 2007 to October 2009. A red box highlights the spring of 2009, when implied volatility remained elevated between 33% and 42%. Cembalest notes that selling volatility in this high-risk environment offered strong compensation for giving up upside. However, following a subsequent 40% to 50% rally in global equities through September 2009, many of these investments have hit their caps. As a result, portfolios with a high concentration of capped investments no longer have adequate exposure to equity market gains and may require rebalancing to restore target allocations, even though the defensive posture was appropriate under previous market conditions.

This page addresses the sluggish macroeconomic recovery in Europe following the 2008 financial crisis and answers why investors might still want to own European equities despite weak domestic fundamentals. The author argues that while Europe's domestic economic rebound is the weakest among major regions, European corporations are highly insulated because they have aggressively diversified their revenue streams outside of the continent. 

To demonstrate the weakness of the European domestic recovery, the page features three tables detailing the recovery of peak-to-trough declines across retail sales, industrial production, and employment. In retail sales, Germany is at 0% recovery, France is at 5%, and Spain and Italy are at 16%, though the United Kingdom stands out as an exception at 89%. In industrial production, the United Kingdom, Sweden, and Ireland are all at 0% recovery, Spain is at 3%, and Germany and France are at 21% and 23%, respectively. In employment, nearly all listed European nations, including France, Spain, Sweden, the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Norway, show 0% recovery, with Germany being the sole major exception at 77%.

Two charts further illustrate Europe's structural headwinds. The first chart, showing Euro area government debt as a percentage of nominal GDP, tracks a steep rise from approximately 66% in 2007 to estimated levels reaching nearly 95% by 2012. The second chart compares unit labor costs in Germany, the United States, and Japan from 2002 to 2009. While Japan's unit labor costs fell to an estimated 92.4 by the first quarter of 2009, Germany's costs spiked rapidly to 106.3 by the second quarter of 2009, close behind the United States at 108.8, which pressures German corporate profit margins.

The author outlines additional long-term challenges for the region, including demographic issues—such as European birth rates dropping to 1.5 children per woman, well below the replacement rate of 2.1, led by France at 2.0 and Italy lagging at 1.3—and rising energy vulnerability. The European Union currently imports 50% of its total energy needs, a figure projected to rise to 70% by 2030, compared to the United States which imports only 30%. 

Despite these severe domestic headwinds, the author finds a compelling reason to hold European equities: corporate revenue diversification. Over the decade preceding 2009, the percentage of revenues earned by European companies outside of Europe rose significantly from 27% to 40%. The author notes that while exposure to North America was less beneficial during this cycle, increased exposure to high-growth emerging economies has successfully cushioned European corporate earnings from the region's weak domestic recovery.

This page examines the disconnect between local economic struggles in Europe and the performance of European equities, which are increasingly supported by global exposure, particularly to emerging markets. The discussion highlights that emerging market economies now represent between 35% and 50% of total world output, making stock baskets with high emerging market exposure an attractive recommendation. 

The first chart, titled "Revenue exposure of European companies," tracks the percent of total revenues from 1997 to 2009, demonstrating that European corporate revenue from emerging markets steadily rose from 12% in 1997 to nearly 24% by 2009, overtaking exposure to North America, which fell from a peak of 21% in 2003 to around 16% in 2009. The adjacent chart, "% of Global GDP represented by EM economies" from 1980 to 2008, contrasts two calculation methods: when computed with market exchange rates, the emerging market share of global GDP stands at approximately 35% in 2008, but when computed using purchasing power parity exchange rates to adjust for currency interventions, the share exceeds 50%. 

Spain is presented as a key example of this phenomenon, noting that despite having perhaps the worst domestic housing and fiscal conditions in Europe, Spanish equities have outperformed benchmarks in Europe, the United States, and Japan. This outperformance is driven by Spain's five largest companies on the IBEX index—Santander, Telefonica, BBVA, Iberdrola, and Repsol—which constitute 70% of the index's market capitalization and generate between one-third and two-thirds of their revenues outside Europe, a result of massive outward direct investment that grew from 3% of GDP in the 1990s to 44% by 2007.

Finally, the page reviews overall European equity valuations, noting that while they currently appear close to long-term historical averages, they rarely stay there for long. The chart "Price/Earnings ratios in 'fair' territory" shows that the price-to-one-year-forward earnings ratio for the MSCI Europe ex-UK index has rebounded from its late-2008 lows of under 10 to near its 20-year average of roughly 14. A companion chart, "Same for Price/Book," tracks the price-to-book ratio for the same index from 1980 to 2009. It shows the metric plunged from over 3.0 in 2007 to near 1.5 in 2009, with a separate "ex-financials" series tracking slightly higher, highlighting the deep discount on financial sector book values during the crisis period.

This page analyzes European bank recapitalization needs, historical equity market bottoms relative to corporate earnings declines, and the viability of the ambitious DESERTEC solar energy initiative. 

The author begins by noting that European banks require EUR 27 billion to raise core Tier 1 capital ratios to 8 percent, plus an additional EUR 28 billion to repay government equity injections. Once this recapitalization is complete, banks will likely begin selling off non-performing loans, opening up a massive EUR 500 billion opportunity set where distressed debt managers are already acquiring loan pools at less than 50 cents on the Euro. 

To evaluate the timing of equity market recoveries, a chart titled "When do asset prices bottom? Peak-to-trough decline in European earnings" tracks historical European earnings downturns from 1969 to 2008. The chart's vertical axis measures peak-to-trough earnings declines from 0 percent down to negative 50 percent, and vertical black lines indicate the historical bottoms for MSCI European equities. The visual data clearly demonstrates that equity markets consistently bottom out before or precisely at the absolute trough of an earnings decline. Because of this historical trend, the firm maintains a position in European equities slightly below long-term targets, viewing the substantial macroeconomic headwinds as already priced in after a 57 percent market decline. 

The lower portion of the page evaluates the DESERTEC project, which aims to install concentrated solar power stations across 17,000 square kilometers in the Sahara to transmit electricity to Europe, covering 15 percent of its power needs. Though backed by major industrial and financial giants like Munich Re, ABB, E.ON, Siemens, and Deutsche Bank, the project faces steep hurdles. The author outlines key logistical and economic challenges, including the Sahara’s brutal temperature swings from 60 degrees Celsius to negative 10 degrees Celsius in a single day, an astronomical project cost of EUR 400 to 500 billion, and significant security and expropriation risks in North Africa. 

Furthermore, because CSP plants do not generate power when the sun is not shining, they possess lower capacity factors, requiring 1.5 to 3.0 gigawatts of solar capacity to displace just 1 gigawatt of coal. CSP estimates also run 12 to 15 cents per kilowatt-hour, making it 30 to 40 percent more expensive than coal or natural gas, even when assuming a carbon tax of 30 dollars per ton. Despite these formidable obstacles, the author notes that concentrated solar power is a proven, emissions-free technology already operating in locations like Spain, California, and Australia. The technology remains highly relevant to the European Union, where a potential six-meter rise in sea level threatens to submerge major coastal cities like Barcelona, Venice, Amsterdam, London, Stockholm, and Lisbon. The author concludes on a hopeful note, pointing out that as renewable technology capacity doubles, costs historically fall by 10 to 15 percent, suggesting that desert solar costs could eventually converge with traditional fossil fuels.

In this J.P. Morgan commentary, Michael Cembalest analyzes upcoming third-quarter corporate earnings and addresses a correction regarding U.S. household leverage. Regarding earnings, Cembalest outlines several reasons to expect results to meet or exceed expectations: strong corporate operating leverage with expenses reduced by 88 cents for every dollar of revenue decline, peak U.S. stimulus growth, strong Chinese loan growth of 30 percent to 35 percent, high cash balances fueling mergers and acquisitions, and an imminent PC upgrade cycle. This upgrade cycle is depicted in a line chart showing the PC installed base by operating system from 1998 to 2008. The chart highlights that older operating systems, specifically Windows XP, still dominated the installed base at around 60 percent to 70 percent in 2008 despite peaking near 80 percent in 2006, indicating significant pent-up demand for upgrades.

In the second part of the page, Cembalest responds to a question from CEO Jamie Dimon regarding whether U.S. household leverage would decrease significantly if adjusted for future defaults on delinquent mortgage and consumer loans, which total 900 billion dollars and 145 billion dollars, respectively. Cembalest asserts that the reduction would be less substantial than expected. A second chart plots mortgage and consumer debt balances as a percentage of disposable income from 1959 to 2008. The chart shows that even under the extreme assumption that all 1.0 trillion dollars of delinquent loans are fully repudiated rather than restructured, household leverage would only drop from its peak of roughly 125 percent to approximately 115 percent, as represented by two distinct dots on the chart. Cembalest notes that such massive repudiation would additionally trigger concerns over bank capital ratios, suggesting that the actual outcome will likely fall somewhere between these two data points as loans are modified.

This page focuses on a third-quarter earnings update and analyzes the massive global market rally that began in March 2009, placing it in historical context. The author argues that while the 67% global market rally since the March lows feels unusually rapid, it is fundamentally consistent with prior economic cycles where equity markets bottomed and began to rebound well before visible improvements in employment, delinquencies, defaults, or corporate earnings. 

The update begins with an overview of third-quarter corporate performance, noting that with 19% of companies reporting, 82% are beating earnings forecasts and 68% are beating revenue estimates. General Electric is highlighted as a key bellwether; its industrial cash flow has returned to trend, though its GE Capital division saw earnings decline 93% year-over-year. Beyond earnings, the author expresses caution about the broader economy. He notes that while there are minor improvements in jobless claims, small business conditions remain poor, and nearly 60% of the decline in continuing unemployment claims is merely due to individuals exhausting their benefits. Furthermore, the U.S. housing outlook remains troubled, as pending foreclosures are expected to overshadow recent improvements in home prices.

To prove that stock markets routinely bottom before the economy recovers, the page presents several historical comparisons. A chart on the left, titled "Peak-to-trough decline in European earnings vs. the equity market troughs," displays historical earnings declines from 1969 to 2008. It illustrates that MSCI European equities bottomed in March 2009 and rose approximately 50% even as corporate earnings continued to decline. Beside this, a table titled "Equity market bottom to recession end" lists historical U.S. recessions, showing how many months before the end of a recession the S&P 500 bottomed, alongside the resulting rally. For instance, in the July 1953 to May 1954 recession, the market bottomed 9 months before the end, resulting in a 29% rally. For the recession spanning December 2007 to July 2009, the market bottomed 4 months prior to the end of the recession, yielding a 46% rally. 

The bottom of the page features three comparative charts analyzing the relationship between bank stock prices and cumulative bank failures during major financial crises. Each chart tracks the bank index level against cumulative bank failures, marking the point at which bank stocks bottomed. In the chart for "The Great Depression: 1929 to 1934," the Dow Jones Industrial Average bottomed when cumulative bank failures reached 48% of the cycle's total. In the "Savings and Loan Crisis: 1988 to 1994" chart, the S&P 500 Bank Index bottomed when cumulative bank failures stood at 63%. Finally, in the "Financial crisis: 2008 to present" chart, the S&P 500 Bank Index bottomed when cumulative bank failures were at only 34% of the eventual total. This indicates that bank stocks in the 2008-2009 cycle bottomed even earlier in the failure cycle than they did during the Great Depression or the Savings and Loan crisis.

This page analyzes global economic developments, focusing on massive credit expansion in China, the growth of the United States monetary base, and the expansion of the global government safety net through deposit guarantees. 

The author compares the economic situation in China to a monumental, yet uncertain event, highlighting a surge in year-over-year loan growth to 35% that is driving gross domestic product growth back toward 9%. However, almost all of these loans are directed toward public-sector entities rather than the private sector. The accompanying line chart, titled "Chinese loan growth," shows year-over-year percentage change from 1998 through 2008, illustrating a steep spike in late 2008 and 2009 that approaches 35% after years of hovering between 10% and 25%. This credit boom is fueling a 130% rise in the Shenzhen equity market, an 84% year-over-year increase in passenger car sales, and a 44% increase in residential floor space sold, with home sales values rising 73% year-over-year. The author warns that household incomes do not support these housing prices and notes that China’s reliance on capital investment to drive growth is unprecedented—even compared to the industrial eras of Korea, Germany, and Japan—with capital formation representing close to 50% of GDP and its debt-to-GDP ratio exceeding 100%.

Next, the page addresses the rapid expansion of the U.S. monetary base. The chart titled "Explosion of U.S. monetary base" tracks Federal Reserve purchases of Treasury, Agency debt, and mortgage-backed securities in billions of dollars from September 2008 through March 2010. The line rises sharply from near zero in late 2008 to over $1.2 trillion in late 2009, with estimated future data points indicating purchases reaching up to $1.75 trillion by March 2010. Although there is no current evidence of this expansion leaking into broader monetary aggregates like M2, the author cautions that easy money may bypass traditional goods and services and go directly into financial asset speculation.

Finally, the discussion turns to the expanded global government safety net, referencing massive asset protection schemes provided to financial institutions like Citigroup, Bank of America, RBS, and Lloyds. The author notes that the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation now guarantees 84% of all bank deposits, which creates substantial taxpayer risk and distorts bank incentives. An accompanying table, "Expanded bank deposit insurance," outlines previous versus new guarantees across several countries and currencies. Notable changes include the United States increasing its deposit guarantee from $100,000 to $250,000; the United Kingdom rising from £35,000 to £50,000; Germany from €20,000 to €50,000; and Ireland and Denmark moving from €20,000 and 300,000 DKK respectively to unlimited guarantees. The text also mentions that the Chinese government guarantees over $600 billion of Asset Management Company bonds, specifically those of DongFang, Cinda, Huarong, and Great Wall, further demonstrating the scale of state-backed financial guarantees.

In this analysis, the author discusses portfolio strategy during the 2009 market recovery, focusing on credit market dynamics and the mounting fiscal challenges of the public sector. For their Balanced portfolios, the managers maintained an equity allocation of 30% to 38% while actively purchasing credit, which they determined offered the best risk-adjusted returns. High-yield bond spreads rallied much faster in this cycle than in previous ones. This phenomenon is highlighted in three historical charts comparing credit spreads to cumulative defaults across three cycles: 1987 to 1993, 1999 to 2004, and 2006 to 2009. In the first cycle, cumulative high-yield issuer defaults stood at 55% of the cycle's total at the time spreads peaked. In the second cycle, defaults reached 76% at the spread peak. In the 2006 to 2009 cycle, however, spreads peaked when cumulative defaults were at just 42%, showing that the high-yield market anticipated the recovery far earlier than in the past. 

A similar pattern of rapid recovery ahead of deteriorating fundamentals is shown in the commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) market. A chart tracking the AAA CMBS spread alongside 60-day-plus delinquency rates from 2006 to 2009 demonstrates that AAA spreads surged toward 1,400 basis points in early 2009 and then fell sharply. This peak occurred well before the commercial real estate delinquency rate finished its climb, which steadily rose from near 0% to approximately 3.5% by late 2009. While this early pricing-in can look like normal market anticipation, the author attributes much of this financial market recovery to unprecedented public sector intervention, which they dub the "Four Horsemen" due to its long-term impact on public finances.

The final section explores the looming fiscal challenges facing OECD countries, particularly the United States and the Euro area, due to these rescue efforts. A chart titled "U.S. and European debt: the end of an era" tracks gross government debt as a percentage of GDP from 1991 through 2008, with estimates extending to 2012. The data shows U.S. debt climbing from around 60% of GDP in 2007 to an estimated peak near 100% by 2012, while Euro area debt is projected to rise from roughly 66% to 90% over the same period. The author warns that exiting these heavy debt burdens will be exceptionally difficult. Unlike post-war debt recoveries, which were easier to manage because expenditures could be cut and debt was domestically owned, modern debt is heavily driven by entitlements and funded by foreign investors. Though U.S. banks could theoretically absorb up to $1 trillion in incremental demand by increasing their Treasury and Agency holdings from 13% to 22% of assets, the author notes this would inevitably displace other productive assets on bank balance sheets.

This page of the publication explores the value and dynamics of network effects, focusing on how Skype might leverage them as it transitions to cellular networks. The author notes that Skype, previously limited to PC-to-PC calls, has moved to mobile; when it launched on the iPhone, it reached one million downloads in just two days, a rapid expansion bolstered by AT&T’s decision to allow Skype on its 3G network. 

To explain network effects, the text compares different digital business models. It argues that search engines benefit heavily from network effects, where more searches help Google improve its results, whereas email services do not naturally become better for the next user just because more people use them. This is visualized in two charts. The first, "Online search engines," displays search engine volume from Experian Hitwise and StatCounter, showing Google's commanding lead at approximately 70% to 80% market share, followed distantly by Yahoo! at 10% to 15%, and Bing, Ask, and AOL with negligible shares. The second chart, "U.S. web email service usage," shows unique visitors from December 2008 to July 2009. Yahoo! Mail leads with over 100 million unique visitors, followed by Hotmail at around 45 million, Gmail at roughly 35 million, and AOL declining to about 30 million. This demonstrates that while email services lack strong network effects, legacy players can still maintain large, competitive user bases.

The author further analyzes hardware and software applications to show that dominant players must couple network effects with continuous innovation to survive. Two additional charts support this. The "Rich Internet Application software" chart shows Adobe Flash installed on over 90% of computers, compared to Sun Java at around 70% and Microsoft Silverlight at roughly 25%. The "Portable Music Players" chart shows Apple iPod dominating the market with over 70% share in the first quarter of 2008, while competitors like ScanDisk Sansa, Microsoft Zune, and Creative Zen struggle at 10% or less. 

Ultimately, the author poses an open question for Skype: can its current network effect advantage be coupled with enough innovation and differentiation to ward off challengers? Footnotes reinforce this inquiry by citing marketing research concluding that network effects will not shield market leaders indefinitely from competitors with superior products, and that quality ultimately wins out over first-mover advantages.

This page explores the dynamics of network effects, focusing on how they can establish dominant market leaders but do not guarantee permanent dominance. The author uses examples from video sharing, online movie retailing, social networking, and internet browsers to demonstrate that industry leaders can be displaced by fast-following competitors or because of technical and strategic shortcomings. 

A bar chart titled Video sharing displays monthly visitors in millions as of October 2009. It illustrates YouTube's absolute dominance, showing it leading with approximately 80 million monthly visitors, while competitors like Metacafe, tv.com, Dailymotion, MySpace Video, Truveo, Veoh, and Yahoo! Video all languish well below the 20 million visitor mark. The text notes that Google Video, despite launching a month before YouTube, only achieved a 4 percent market share and chose to acquire YouTube rather than continue competing.

Beside it, a bar chart titled Online movie retailing compares annual revenues in millions for 2007. It shows Netflix dominating with approximately 1,200 million dollars in annual revenue compared to Blockbuster's roughly 550 million dollars, highlighting how Netflix overcame Blockbuster's substantial head start and established customer base in movie rentals.

Underneath, a bar chart titled Social networking tracks unique U.S. monthly visitors in millions, comparing October 2008 against September 2009. The chart visualizes Facebook's rapid ascension, surging from roughly 50 million visitors in 2008 to nearly 125 million by late 2009. In doing so, Facebook overtook MySpace, which slipped slightly from around 55 million to 53 million. Other networks like Twitter, Classmates, and LinkedIn remain much smaller, staying below 25 million monthly visitors.

The final line chart, titled Internet Browsers, tracks percentage market share from 1994 to 2009. It traces the dramatic rise and fall of various web browsers over fifteen years. Mosaic began with nearly 100 percent market share in 1994 but vanished by 1996. Netscape quickly peaked near 80 percent around 1995 before collapsing to near zero by 2002. Internet Explorer climbed from near zero in 1995 to a peak of around 95 percent in the early 2000s, but fell back to roughly 65 percent by 2009 as Mozilla/Firefox climbed to about 20 percent and newer entrants like Safari and Google Chrome began to capture market share. 

The accompanying commentary explains the browser wars as a cautionary tale of disappearing network effects. Mosaic fell after key staff departed to form Netscape. Netscape, in turn, lost its dominance to Microsoft's Internet Explorer. While Microsoft benefited from its operating system dominance, Netscape's decline was also driven by technical issues—such as slow cache loading, installation difficulties, and crash-prone software—which persisted too long and caused the company to lose its subscriber base.

This J.P. Morgan research report discusses investment strategies for non-performing loans (NPLs) in the United States and Europe, followed by an optimistic macroeconomic outlook based on key financial indicators. 

The first section highlights a strategy of purchasing U.S. NPL portfolios made available through bank failures and FDIC restructurings, contrasted against a European strategy of purchasing NPLs directly from going-concern banks due to the rarity of European bank failures. This is supported by two charts. The first, a line graph titled "Number of failed U.S. banks 2008 to present," shows the cumulative number of failed banks rising sharply from near zero in early 2008 to over 120 by October 2009. The second visual is a bar chart titled "Non-performing loans - Select European countries," which compares 4Q 2008 to 2Q 2009 in billions of Euros. It shows double-digit percentage increases in NPLs across all four featured nations: the UK rose 46 percent to roughly 140 billion Euros; Spain rose 49 percent to around 45 billion Euros; Germany surged 71 percent to approximately 18 billion Euros; and Portugal increased 42 percent to about 12 billion Euros. Footnotes supplement these findings, highlighting that while over 120 U.S. banks failed by late 2009, over 1,600 failed during the Savings and Loan Crisis, and Europe's banking landscape comprises fewer but significantly larger institutions on average.

The second section provides a market outlook focused on the "Usual Suspects" normally associated with rising asset prices. Following a brief anecdote about former Louisiana Governor Huey Long, the author evaluates eight key economic areas. Global manufacturing orders are high relative to inventories, paired with a spike in U.S. vendor delivery delays. U.S. employment metrics show positive momentum, with declining jobless claims and stronger demand in ISM surveys. Inventories have experienced their largest collapse in 60 years, which typically signals a future growth contribution from inventory replenishment. Equity valuations are noted as reasonable relative to future earnings and inflation, listed at 12.8 times earnings in Europe and 15.3 times in the United States. A "Wall of Cash" is building, as over 400 billion dollars has exited U.S. money market funds, and corporate balance-sheet cash has hit a 50-year high. Sovereign Wealth Funds are increasingly active, with the 280-billion-dollar China Investment Corporation and Abu Dhabi's Mubadala deploying capital globally. Additionally, the housing market shows signs of early stabilization through declining inventories and rising pending home sales. Finally, S&P 500 corporate earnings are performing strongly, with 84 percent of reporting companies beating earnings estimates and 58 percent beating revenue estimates.

This page analyzes macroeconomic, equity, and housing trends to argue that despite some seemingly positive recovery signals, investors should remain cautious rather than increasing portfolio risk. The author emphasizes that recent positive corporate earnings are merely beating exceptionally low expectations, the housing market faces a massive wave of impending foreclosures, and overall economic growth remains overly dependent on unprecedented government stimulus.

The top portion of the page features eight charts tracking global economic indicators. The JPM Global Manufacturing PMI chart shows a sharp plunge in late 2008 down toward the 35 level before starting a recovery. Similarly, the ISM Manufacturing Employment index tracks a steep decline to nearly 25 in early 2009, followed by a partial rebound. Real business inventories, represented quarter-over-quarter on an annualized rate from 1947 to 2007, demonstrate highly volatile cycles of destocking and restocking. Looking at equity valuations, the 12-month forward P/E chart comparing the US and Europe from 1987 to 2008 shows both regions contracting dramatically from their late 1990s peaks, with valuations falling into the 10 to 13 range by 2008.

Additional charts highlight market liquidity, asset allocation, and housing inventories. Money market funds are shown rising rapidly from 1999 to peak past $3.3 trillion by late 2008. The China Investment Corporation’s asset allocation is depicted in a pie chart showing a highly liquid posture, with 87% held in cash and only 13% in non-cash assets. In the US housing market, the housing inventory chart tracks existing home inventory peaking near 4.5 million units around 2007 before turning down, while new home inventory peaked earlier and fell to around 0.3 million units by 2009. The S&P 500 third-quarter 2009 "beats" chart shows that while roughly 75% of companies beat earnings-per-share estimates, only about 60% managed to beat revenue expectations.

The lower half of the page details the specific headwinds facing the market. A chart on S&P 500 quarterly EPS estimates shows that the third-quarter 2009 estimate of $16.41 is an improvement from the $14.72 expected at the beginning of the reporting cycle, while the forecast for the third quarter of 2010 jumps to $19.90. To counter this optimism, the chart on pending foreclosures for securitized non-agency mortgages shows a dramatic rise in distress from 2005 to 2009, with loans 60 or more days delinquent soaring toward 25%, loans in the foreclosure process rising past 10%, and bank-owned properties ticking upward. The author warns that this "pig-in-the-python" problem of $1 trillion in delinquent mortgages has yet to fully impact home prices.

In the final section, titled "The gospels according to Paul," the author discusses the future of the US dollar. Noting that prominent economists Paul Samuelson and Paul Volcker have warned of a rough ride ahead for the currency, the author advises keeping portfolios tilted toward non-dollar bonds and non-dollar proxies. The Federal Reserve's trade-weighted US dollar index is highlighted as being only 5% to 7% above its all-time post-gold standard low set in 2008. An extensive footnote references a commentary by Samuelson, in which he heavily criticizes various political and economic figures, including John McCain, Alan Greenspan, Milton Friedman, Friedrich Von Hayek, and the Reagan and Bush administrations, while predicting a massive run against the US dollar within the next decade.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, "Eye on the Market," focuses on the efficacy, pitfalls, and historical precedents of fiscal stimulus and government spending, with a specific case study on New Orleans and Hurricane Katrina. Cembalest argues that while prolonged deficits are depressing, certain federally funded projects have historical track records of reaping massive rewards. 

To support this, the page features three charts illustrating successful public investments. The first line chart, titled "Percent of farms with electricity" (sourced from the Rural Electrification Administration), shows a steady increase in electrified farms from just over 10% in 1935 to nearly 45% by 1945. The second chart, a bar graph titled "Interstate highway benefits (bn, 1995$)" from the American Highway Users Alliance, compares the direct costs of the interstate system (well under $500 billion) against its massive benefits, which exceed $2 trillion. These benefits are subdivided into lower product prices, time savings and operating costs, and reduced fatalities, injuries, and accidents. The third line chart, titled "Thermal efficiency - Power gen facilities" (sourced from Chubu Electric Power Company), tracks power generation efficiency from 1970 to 2010. It shows efficiency stepping up from 40% to nearly 60%, with a sharp rise highlighted after the establishment of the Department of Energy’s Advanced Turbine Systems Project in the early 1990s, leading up to General Electric's H-System Turbine.

Cembalest transitions to the critical concept of preventive spending, using Hurricane Katrina as a prime example of missed opportunities. He notes that while the government spent or allocated $120 billion for relief and reconstruction, the Army Corps of Engineers could have conducted detailed subsurface exploration beneath flood walls for just $10 million. Spacing testing intervals too far apart to save money led to faulty extrapolations and the subsequent canal wall failures that caused 80% of the damage. 

Additionally, the author uses New Orleans to illustrate the post-disaster pitfalls of government stimulus. Although the influx of government funding kept New Orleans unemployment 2% below the national average and limited job losses to less than 1% (compared to 4% nationally), the execution was highly inefficient. One year after the emergency, 50% of government contracts were still being awarded non-competitively, and years later, 30% to 50% of homes in Orleans and St. Bernard parishes remained vacant or blighted. Cembalest concludes with a warning for global policymakers in the U.S., China, and Brazil: for stimulus-driven growth to remain affordable over the long term, productivity must keep pace with this newly created extra capacity.

This page, written by Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Global Wealth Management, analyzes the dynamics of Statistical Arbitrage investing during and after the 2007 financial market dislocation. The author explains how extreme underperformance of cheap stocks drove forced selling, but ultimately cleared the field of crowded competition, allowing disciplined managers with updated risk models to thrive.

The first chart, titled "Out (under)-performance of the cheapest stocks, 1962-2007," illustrates the five-day relative performance of the cheapest versus most expensive stock deciles based on price-to-free-cash-flow (represented by blue squares) and price-to-book (represented by red diamonds). The vertical axis tracks relative performance from negative six percent to positive one percent across a timeline spanning 1961 to 2007. The data shows that the severe underperformance in 2007, where relative performance dipped to negative three percent to negative five percent, was an extremely rare event only seen on a handful of occasions over the preceding forty-five years.

The second chart, titled "Market value of 15 institutional quant managers," tracks the total long market value in billions of dollars for these managers from the second quarter of 2007 through the second quarter of 2009. The vertical axis ranges from zero to 350 billion dollars. The bar chart shows a steep and steady decline from a peak of over 300 billion dollars in the second quarter of 2007 down to a low of approximately 120 billion dollars in the first quarter of 2009, demonstrating the massive outflows and de-leveraging that occurred across the industry.

The accompanying text explains how these major outflows and the resulting smaller, de-leveraged Statistical Arbitrage universe reduced competitive overlap and lowered cross-fund correlations. The J.P. Morgan manager adapted by dialing down leverage and revising risk models to account for competitor redemptions and crowd behavior, which enabled quicker exit decisions and the avoidance of crowded trades. Consequently, while the broader hedge fund industry faced severe redemptions in 2008 and early 2009, this manager’s Statistical Arbitrage strategy performed exceptionally well on both an absolute and risk-adjusted basis. In contrast, the author notes that many other managers across the industry continued to struggle in 2009 due to a market rally led by lower-quality stocks, particularly after late August of that year.

This page of the publication, written by Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest, discusses the investment implications of the ongoing healthcare reform debates, focusing primarily on early-stage healthcare and biotechnology. Cembalest notes that J.P. Morgan's active equity managers are generally overweight healthcare—specifically favoring health care equipment and life sciences—while remaining underweight large-cap pharmaceutical companies.

The commentary examines the pending healthcare bill's potential impact on early-stage investments and biologics. Despite proposals designed to foster bio-generic competition and curtail patent defenses through the creation of FDA pathways and bans on reverse patents, the author highlights several positives for biotech. These include a potential twelve-year data exclusivity period instead of the five to seven years initially proposed, the absence of return-limiting mechanisms like those in the 1993-1994 Clinton health plan, and a Senate negotiation that reduced the proposed medical device tax from forty billion dollars to twenty billion dollars over ten years. 

With patent expirations threatening thirty percent of global large-cap pharma revenues by 2011, major firms like Roche, Abbott, and Wyeth are acquiring biotech assets, supported by a reopened high-grade and high-yield debt market. The author identifies opportunities in drug development for Hepatitis C, oncology, and Alzheimer’s, especially given a seventy percent reduction in industry venture capital fundraising between 2004 and 2007, which has made the investment field less crowded.

A dedicated informational callout box defines biologics as medicines utilizing living tissue rather than inert chemicals, tracking their rise since the 1982 approval of recombinant human insulin. The box notes that biologics accounted for a quarter of U.S. and European drug approvals between 2003 and 2006, with sales growing three to four times faster than traditional drugs. Highlighting top-selling therapies like Avastin, Rituxan, Humira, Enbrel, and Lantus, the publication cites an EvaluatePharma forecast that seven of the top ten drugs globally will be biologics by 2014, up from five in 2008 and just one in 2000. It also mentions the successful Talecris IPO, which returned twenty-three times Cerberus' investment.

In conclusion, the author expects Senate and conference deliberations to delay the bill's passage until early 2010. While components like taxes on high-end Cadillac plans and bundled fees aim to control unit costs, the bill's primary effect will be to expand coverage and raise overall costs. Nonetheless, Cembalest concludes that today's legislation does not seem to stifle R&D incentives in the way the 1993-1994 Clinton plan did, nor does a UK-style regulatory body like the National Institute for Clinical Excellence—which rejects expensive treatments based on quality-adjusted life years—appear to be on the immediate horizon for the United States.

This page of the publication addresses the U.S. labor market and the historical composition of presidential cabinets, arguing that the Obama administration represents a stark departure from the traditional balance of public and private sector experience. To evaluate how the administration views job creation, the author analyzed the prior private sector backgrounds of 432 cabinet members across nine key economic and domestic departments since 1900. 

A central bar chart titled "Cabinet Appointments: Prior Private Sector Experience, 1900-2009" illustrates this historical trend. Across most of the twentieth century, cabinet members with private sector experience routinely made up 30% to nearly 60% of these positions. For example, Eisenhower’s cabinet peaked at around 57%, Reagan’s was at 56%, and both George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush maintained levels over 50%. Even the prior lows, such as Kennedy at 30% and Carter at 32%, far exceed the Obama administration, which sits as a dramatic outlier at under 10%. 

The author explains that this lack of private sector representation reflects a broader contemporary cynicism toward business leaders following the colossal mismanagement of major financial and automotive firms during the 2008 financial crisis. This skepticism is highlighted by quotes from Congressman Barney Frank and a deputy of Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner, both of whom argue that the government, rather than the private sector executives who "got us into this mess," must lead the way out. Footnotes further contextualize the discussion by noting that the probability of finding a job and the Conference Board's Help Wanted Index have reached their lowest levels in 60 years.

This page examines recent developments in commercial real estate securitization (CMBS) markets and the historical performance dynamics of statistical arbitrage investing. 

In the first section, the author highlights a small but significant reopening of the CMBS market, citing Developers Diversified Realty’s $400 million borrowing at a 5% all-in cost. This transaction is notable given that overall securitization collapsed from $500 billion per quarter in 2007 to just $50 billion by September 2009. Although this deal features strict constraints—such as a 52% maximum loan-to-value ratio, conservative cap rates, and a high-quality retail portfolio leased to tenants like Wal-Mart, Home Depot, and Lowe’s—it establishes a benchmark for new cash buyers targeting 9-10% equity returns and validates J.P. Morgan’s early 2009 CMBS investments.

The second section explores statistical arbitrage, addressing why a major multi-strategy manager on J.P. Morgan's platform continues to allocate about 25% of its capital to the strategy despite historical turmoil. The author reviews the lead-up to the August 2007 "quant squeeze," explaining how the strategy's early success attracted massive capital, which compressed returns and led managers to utilize up to 10x leverage. When Bear Stearns' subprime mortgage hedge funds collapsed in July 2007, forced de-leveraging and overlapping portfolio holdings triggered a rapid unwind of statistical arbitrage positions, causing severe performance declines and fund liquidations. 

Two charts illustrate these market dynamics leading up to the 2007 crisis. The first chart, showing annualized six-month rolling returns for statistical arbitrage from 1990 through July 2007, reveals a clear downward trend in performance from historical peaks above 20% in the 1990s down to the single digits by the mid-2000s. The second chart depicts the massive surge in assets under management (AUM) for Equity Market Neutral and Long/Short strategies from 1995 to 2007. According to this chart, combined AUM skyrocketed from less than $20 billion in 1995 to approximately $160 billion in 2007, with Long/Short strategies comprising the vast majority of the capital, illustrating how crowded the quant space had become just before the collapse.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues for the crucial role of the private sector and profit motives in driving medical innovation, particularly in biotechnology and gene therapies. He contrasts the high cost of traditional palliative cancer care—which can reach up to one million dollars per month—with the potential of permanent cures from emerging immunotherapies that train the body to fight disease recurrence. To illustrate this, the page features a visual comparison of two PET scans tracking outpatient results over fourteen months for a patient with Stage IV metastatic melanoma treated with an oncology vaccine developed by Gradalis at the Mary Crowley Cancer Research Center. The first scan displays multiple active cancer areas marked by red circles, while the subsequent scan shows a complete response with biopsy-negative results, where the entire post-surgery care for this now cancer-free patient cost less than fifty thousand dollars. 

Cembalest emphasizes that while the National Cancer Institute has spent one hundred and five billion dollars since 1970 without changing advanced cancer survival rates, the private biotech industry is uniquely positioned to achieve breakthroughs despite the high rate of failure and the decades required to develop gene therapies. He cites Tufts University data showing that seventy-five percent of drugs approved worldwide between 2005 and 2007 were introduced in the United States, illustrating the country's massive lead in pharmaceutical and biological innovation. Ultimately, he expresses skepticism toward legislative efforts to hold down healthcare costs without addressing consumption, asserting that trusting the private sector to develop these cost-saving, life-improving therapies is the most viable path forward.

This page examines the landscape of the private sector in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, analyzing the scale of corporate losses, the limitations of public sector employment in solving job crises, and the historic magnitude of the ongoing policy stimulus. 

The first chart, titled "Companies that lost more than their book value," plots the ratio of total losses to 2007 tangible book value on the y-axis (ranging from 0 to 13) against total absolute losses in billions on the x-axis (ranging from $0 to $150 billion). It shows that several major institutions suffered losses that far exceeded their book values. E*Trade stands out with a loss ratio of nearly 12 times its book value, while IKB Bank, Ford, and Freddie Mac experienced loss ratios between 9 and 11. In absolute terms, government-sponsored enterprises Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac experienced massive total losses of approximately $135 billion and $110 billion, respectively. Other notable firms plotted include RBS, GM, Ambac, Wachovia, Citigroup, and AIG. In accompanying footnotes, the author notes that while public sector HUD mandates in 1996 "lit the fuse" by requiring Fannie and Freddie to purchase lower-income loans, the private sector ultimately drove the crisis by underwriting the vast majority of subprime and Alt-A loans with reckless abandon.

The discussion then turns to employment, supported by a chart titled "Public sector employment % of nonfarm payrolls" spanning 1945 to 2005. The chart demonstrates that public sector employment has historically ranged from a low of around 15% to a peak of 19% during the deficit spending of the 1970s, returning to roughly 17% by 2005. The author argues that the public sector cannot be the solution to unemployment, particularly given that state and local employees represent 12% of the U.S. workforce but account for a staggering 64% of all unfunded pension liabilities. 

Regarding job creation policies, the author addresses a proposed hiring tax credit, citing Princeton economist Alan Blinder's warning that such programs are highly susceptible to corporate abuse and gaming. Instead, the author highlights the critical role of entrepreneurship, noting that firms under five years old accounted for all net job creation in the U.S. between 1980 and 2005. A survey by the National Federation of Small Business reveals that small enterprises are primarily hindered by poor sales, high taxes, and regulation, whereas lack of credit was cited by only 4% of respondents.

The final chart compares the "Sum of all fiscal and monetary stimulus in prior post-WWII recessions" against the "Current fiscal and monetary stimulus," both measured as a percentage of nominal GDP. While the combined stimulus of nine previous recessions from 1953 to 2001 amounted to less than 10% of GDP, the current stimulus program from 2007 onward dwarfs this history, reaching nearly 35% of nominal GDP. The author concludes with the open warning that any future policy debate must be weighed against the immense cost of paying for the historic volume of stimulus already in motion.

This page addresses alternative energy as a replacement for coal and the current financial health of U.S. municipalities. It starts by discussing the announced shutdown of fifteen coal plants by Exelon and Progress Energy over the next ten years, which will eliminate 2,500 megawatts of generation capacity. The author questions whether renewable energy can fill this gap, highlighting that while solar and wind are projected to grow by 15% to 30% annually, they face hurdles. In the solar sector, Chinese polysilicon expansion has driven panel prices down by 60%, pushing solar capacity toward cost competitiveness with natural gas, though many producers still prefer Europe's regulatory certainty and long-term contracts. Wind is even closer to competing with natural gas, aided by federal tax credits. Biofuels, specifically Brazilian ethanol utilizing efficient sugar cane, also present strong alternative opportunities. However, because renewables (excluding hydro) account for only 4% of U.S. electricity generation, and the shuttered coal capacity represents roughly 15% of all existing U.S. wind and solar power, the author predicts a substantial ongoing need for natural gas. 

The analysis then transitions to U.S. municipal credit quality. While municipal bonds have rallied as investors flee zero-percent cash yields, the underlying credit fundamentals of states are weak. The author warns that state deficits only look stable because of a temporary $170 billion federal stimulus injection. Once these federal transfers run out in 2010, municipalities will face a very difficult year in 2011, likely leading to tax hikes and spending cuts. 

This financial distress is supported by two line charts from the Bureau of Economic Analysis. The first chart, "State government receipts & expenditures" from 1989 to 2009, shows a massive divergence. While the line representing total receipts minus expenditures hovers near zero, the line representing receipts excluding federal transfers minus expenditures plunges severely starting in the late 1990s, reaching a deficit of over $600 billion by 2009. This highlights the heavy reliance of state budgets on federal aid. The second chart, "Total benefits per full-time employee" from 1998 to 2008, illustrates that benefit costs for state and local government employees have risen much faster than those in the private industry, climbing from around $8,000 in 1998 to over $15,000 in 2008, compared to private benefits which slowly rose from approximately $6,000 to just under $10,000.

This page analyzes the European economic and corporate earnings outlook, comparing it to the United States and highlighting how labor market policies distort official economic data. The main argument is that while European corporate earnings are improving, this recovery is driven by cost-cutting and emerging-market demand rather than local economic strength. This trend is supported by an expected recovery in European earnings, projected to rise from their 2008 peak of $169 to $117 in 2010 and $141 in 2011, even as domestic industrial activity remains subdued.

The first chart, titled "Euro industrial production & manufacturing survey," tracks data from 1997 to 2009.
