For the overall S&P 500, roughly 80% of companies beat EPS estimates and over 60% beat sales estimates. The information technology sector performed exceptionally well, with around 90% beating EPS and 80% beating sales estimates, whereas telecom lagged, with beats under 40%. This broad outperformance has led analysts to revise earnings expectations upward, as depicted in the dual-axis chart, "Forward S&P 500 earnings estimates on the rise." This chart shows 2010 earnings per share estimates rising from $78 in January to around $81 in May, while 2011 estimates rose from $94 to over $100 during the same period.

Although U.S. equities trade at a reasonable 14.5 P/E multiple, the author expresses caution regarding the future impact of monetary and fiscal stimulus withdrawal. Furthermore, the commentary maintains a bearish outlook on housing, which remained a drag on first-quarter GDP. The author notes that housing-related topics—including Fannie Mae, OFHEO, speculative buying, Alt-A loans, and rising household debt-to-income ratios—will be examined in a future publication.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest warns that investors risk making major portfolio allocation errors if they focus solely on rising corporate profits while ignoring broader structural imbalances in the global financial system. To illustrate this point, the top of the page displays three line charts tracking S&P 500 12-month trailing earnings per share (EPS) prior to historical market downturns. The first chart, showing the period before the savings and loan collapse, shows trailing EPS rising from around $16 in 1985 to nearly $26 by 1989. The second chart, tracking the period before the dot-com crash, shows EPS climbing from $25 in 1994 to roughly $55 by 2000. The third chart, leading up to the global financial crisis, shows EPS rising from $45 in 2002 to over $90 by 2006. In all three historical episodes, severe equity market corrections occurred while corporate profits were still actively expanding. 

Cembalest notes that current cyclical indicators are positive, pointing to strong U.S. payroll figures, high U.S. productivity and profit margins, a 5% increase in German factory orders, and rising manufacturing surveys in Spain, Ireland, and Italy. However, he asserts that structural problems will limit these cyclical improvements, making many sell-side forecasts for 2010 equity returns too optimistic. J.P. Morgan Private Banking expects 2010 U.S. equity returns of only +7% to +9% with high volatility, prompting them to keep equity allocations in their Balanced Portfolios restricted to 35% to 40% while holding substantial positions in commodities, credit, and low-net-exposure hedge funds. 

The bottom left bar chart, titled "2010 S&P 500 projections: too high in a world of pervasive public sector problems," displays year-end forecasts from major financial institutions. J.P. Morgan Private Banking’s cautious projection of 1,175 to 1,225 sits at the lower end of the range, comparable to Citi at 1,175 and Morgan Stanley at 1,200. This stands in contrast to higher projections from Goldman Sachs at 1,250, Credit Suisse at 1,270, and a cluster of firms at 1,300—including Bank of America, HSBC, and UBS—with Deutsche Bank posting the highest projection at 1,375. The bottom right line chart, "Global rebound still on track for now," plots the J.P. Morgan Global PMI output index from 2000 to 2010 for manufacturing and services. The visual illustrates a sharp recovery for both sectors from their post-2008 recessionary lows of under 35 and 40, respectively, back up to expansionary levels above 50 by mid-2010.

This page from the publication addresses the spreading European sovereign debt crisis, focusing specifically on the structural challenges of Greece's fiscal adjustment. The author argues that pursuing austerity alone is an unproven and extraordinarily difficult path. To support this, the author points to the falling prices of Greek government bonds maturing in March 2012, which indicates that financial markets do not believe Greece can deliver on its austerity promises. Given the historical precedents, the commentary suggests that achieving these targets would be nothing short of a miracle. 

To visualize this challenge, the page features a three-dimensional bubble chart titled "2010 Greece Fiscal Adjustment: No Man's Land." The chart compares various historical national fiscal adjustments across three axes: annual fiscal adjustment percentage on the vertical axis (ranging from 0.5% to 2.5%), GDP growth percentage on the horizontal axis (ranging from 0% to 3%), and currency devaluation percentage on the depth axis (ranging from 20% to 100%). Additionally, the color of each bubble represents the size of the country's tradables sector relative to GDP at the start of the period: red indicates a small sector of under 45%, yellow represents a moderate sector of 45% to 75%, and blue denotes a large sector of over 75%.

The visual data highlights Greece's projected 2010–2014 adjustment as a red bubble isolated in "No Man's Land" at the upper left. This position reflects an extremely demanding annual fiscal adjustment of 2.5% combined with 0% GDP growth and 0% devaluation. The chart contrasts this with historical precedents to show how other nations achieved high adjustments. For example, countries like Mexico (1981–1988) and Brazil (1982–1990)—both red bubbles added to this version of the chart—achieved high annual adjustments of roughly 2.3% and 1.8% respectively, but did so with massive devaluations of over 60%. Denmark (1982–1986) completed a high adjustment of about 2.4% with the help of devaluation and a larger tradables sector. Other nations that undertook fiscal adjustments without high devaluation either had the cushion of a large tradables sector, such as Ireland (1981–1989) and Belgium (1983–1990), or settled for much smaller annual adjustments under 1.5%, such as the United Kingdom, Spain, Italy, France, and the Netherlands. Ultimately, the chart demonstrates that Greece's combination of zero devaluation, zero growth, a small tradables sector, and an aggressive 2.5% annual fiscal adjustment target has no historical parallel, reinforcing the author's skepticism.

This page from Michael Cembalest summarizes J.P. Morgan's core portfolio positions, which remain unchanged from previous months. The investment strategy recommends underweighting European equities overall while selectively holding long positions in mid-cap German exporters. It also advises underweighting or shorting the Euro against long positions in Asian currencies, while holding little to no fixed income exposure to Portugal, Greece, Ireland, and Spain. The recommended portfolio equity weight is 35-40%, featuring a significant overweight to US large-cap equities with downside protection on European equities, alongside an S&P 500 forecast of 1175 to 1225 for 2010. Furthermore, the strategy outlines a gradual reduction of credit investments made in 2009, holding gold with plans to hedge against falling prices starting between $1,250 and $1,300, a $90 price target for oil, and a shift into merger arbitrage hedge funds given that corporate cash is high and both the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank are expected to remain on hold. 

The page also features an illustration from the German fairy tale "Die Geschichte vom fliegenden Robert" (The Story of Flying Robert) from Heinrich Hoffman’s Struwwelpeter, depicting a boy being blown away in a storm with an umbrella over a landscape with a church. Below this, Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest asks clients to share any first- or second-hand experience with pediatric scoliosis surgery. Finally, a notes section provides details for conference call replays and defines key economic acronyms.

This page analyzes the sudden political and economic shifts within the Eurozone following the decision to bail out Greece. The author highlights the profound turnabout by the European Central Bank, which previously adhered to a strict no-bailout policy. This policy shift triggered immediate political backlash in Germany, causing Chancellor Angela Merkel’s CDU party to suffer a severe electoral defeat in its largest state. A line chart titled "CDU electoral results in North Rhine Westphalia" tracks the percentage of the popular vote from 1947 to 2010, demonstrating that the CDU's support plummeted to a historic low of approximately 34% in 2010. Critics in German political and media circles expressed deep concern that this bailout would permanently undermine the long-term stability and credibility of the euro. 

The author transitions to discussing the severe economic austerity measures that European nations must now face, noting that succeeding with austerity without currency devaluation is historically rare. While some forward-looking manufacturing indicators show promise, actual GDP recovery remains fragile, particularly in Southern Europe. The line chart titled "Euro manufacturing PMI" from December 2009 to April 2010 highlights this divergence; while manufacturing indexes in Germany and France rose strongly—with Germany climbing past 60—Greece’s PMI fell below 45. This weakness is mirrored in the "European GDP recovery" index chart (indexed to Q4 2006 = 100), which shows that while Germany and France have stabilized, GDP levels in Ireland collapsed below 93 by late 2009, with Spain and Greece also languishing near the bottom.

Germany’s economic engine remains heavily reliant on trade, though this exposes the country to regional instability. A line chart titled "Germany trade exports" from 2004 to 2009 illustrates a volatile path where exports peaked near 90 billion EUR in 2008 before plunging to nearly 55 billion EUR and staging a partial recovery toward 70 billion EUR by late 2009. The accompanying pie chart, "Germany export destinations," shows that the Eurozone accounts for by far the largest share of Germany's exports at 43.3%, followed by other European nations at 24.4%, Asia at 9.4%, and the United States at 6.7%. This heavy concentration means that German economic prosperity is deeply intertwined with the fiscal health of its Eurozone partners.

Finally, the page reviews global labor markets through an "Employment PMI" bar chart, which categorizes countries into Eurozone and non-Eurozone economies. Non-Eurozone nations such as the United States, Sweden, and Switzerland occupy the highest end of the employment index (above the neutral 50 mark), while Eurozone nations are clustered at the lower end. Germany and Austria hover near the 50 mark, while France, Italy, Ireland, Spain, and Greece lag significantly behind, remaining in contraction territory. The author poses the open question of whether the European Monetary Union can survive in the long term without addressing these stark competitiveness differentials through deep structural reform, warning that failure to do so could result in permanent fiscal transfer mechanisms.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication analyzes the European sovereign debt crisis, focusing on whether the massive joint European and IMF rescue package—referred to as "the Kitchen Sink"—is large enough and politically feasible. Author Michael Cembalest, alongside Dr. Jacob Frenkel, argues that contagion risks remain high across peripheral Europe because, even where sovereign debt appears manageable, private sector debt is heavily elevated and likely to migrate to government balance sheets during austerity-driven deflations. 

The first chart on the top left displays total country debt as a percentage of GDP for the fourth quarter of 2009 across Greece, Ireland, Portugal, and Spain, broken down by government, households, and non-financial firms. It demonstrates that while Greece's sovereign debt is the highest at 114% of GDP, Ireland and Portugal face massive private liabilities, with Irish households holding debt at 122% of GDP and Portuguese non-financial firms at 142% of GDP. 

The second chart, on the top right, compares the 860 billion Euros in approved and announced packages against gross financing needs (maturities and deficits) from 2010 to 2013. The data reveals that the 860 billion Euro package is sufficient to cover the 2010–2012 financing needs of Greece, Ireland, Portugal, and Spain, which total 745 billion Euros. However, if 2013 needs of 167 billion Euros and Italy’s massive 2010–2013 financing needs of 892 billion Euros are factored in, the total gross financing need escalates to 1.805 trillion Euros. The author notes that Italy’s risks are lower due to its low primary deficit and high domestic ownership of its debt, suggesting the package buys enough time for fiscal adjustments.

An open question is whether the 440 billion Euro Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) mechanism will be approved by member parliaments. The third chart on the bottom left illustrates potential German contributions as a percentage of GDP under various participation scenarios. If non-EMU members do not participate and troubled nations cannot contribute, the financial burden falls on core nations like Germany, France, and the Benelux countries. Under this scenario, Germany's potential share—comprising the EU SPV, bilateral aid to Greece, IMF contributions, and other facilities—could approach 8% of GDP. The chart places this in historical context, showing it exceeds both the annual cost of German unification since 1991 (around 4% of GDP) and peak Versailles reparations paid in 1929 (around 3% of GDP).

Finally, a table on the bottom right details the specific initiatives of the rescue plan and their intended results. It outlines the 440 billion Euro Eurozone government-backed loan guarantees, the 60 billion Euro EU Balance of Payments facility, and the 220 to 250 billion Euros from the IMF, all designed to allow sovereign issuance at reasonable rates. It also lists the monetary policy tools intended to ease funding conditions and stabilize markets, including the ECB's uncapped three- and six-month repo lines with relaxed collateral rules, the expansion of the Federal Reserve's US dollar swap lines to the ECB, and secondary market bond purchases by the ECB.

This J.P. Morgan report focuses on the market and portfolio outlook, explaining why the firm is not reducing portfolio risk despite concerns over public sector problems. The author argues that their balanced portfolio proxy has maintained return volatility below ten percent—comparable to a traditional portfolio with sixty percent fixed income—by utilizing credit, commodities, currencies, hedge funds, and principal-protected equity investments rather than a heavy bond allocation. While the firm remains constructive on the United States corporate profit outlook, it warns against over-weighting this view, predicting single-digit returns for developed market equities due to the friction of private sector profits co-existing with significant public sector problems. 

To support the constructive profit outlook, the page features five charts. The first, detailing trailing twelve-month S&P 500 earnings from 2000 to 2010, argues against a double-dip recession in corporate profits. It shows that both reported and operating earnings are recovering strongly toward eighty dollars per share, with top-down and bottom-up estimates projected to near ninety dollars. The second chart compares actual year-over-year corporate profit growth to a model forecast from 1993 to 2010, highlighting a year-over-year growth rate of 30.6 percent in the fourth quarter of 2009 and a projected model peak of 37.7 percent in the third quarter of 2010. The third chart displays pre-tax margins to show how high operating leverage is supporting these profits. Comparing fourth-quarter 2009 margins to incremental margins versus the fourth quarter of 2008, the chart shows massive incremental margin gains, particularly in economically sensitive sectors like commodities, capital goods, technology, and consumer durables, where incremental margins spiked past one hundred percent. 

The fourth chart compares various Wall Street firms' 2010 S&P 500 projections to argue that most forecasts are too high. It places J.P. Morgan Private Bank’s relatively conservative forecast of 1,175 to 1,225 toward the lower end of the spectrum, alongside Citi at 1,175, Morgan Stanley at 1,200, and Barclays at 1,210. This is contrasted with much higher projections from other institutions, such as Goldman Sachs at 1,250, Credit Suisse at 1,270, Bank of America and HSBC at 1,300, UBS at 1,350, and Deutsche Bank leading the consensus at 1,375. Finally, the fifth chart tracks the J.P. Morgan Global PMI output index from 2000 to 2010 to show that the global economic rebound is still on track. Both the manufacturing and services series demonstrate sharp V-shaped recoveries from their 2008 and 2009 lows, with manufacturing rebounding to near sixty and services rising to around fifty-five by 2010.

This publication from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market focuses on the market and portfolio outlook, specifically analyzing how the massive global stimulus programs of 2009 have led to costly consequences that are weighing down markets in 2010. The author introduces the concept of Leaner Pastures, reflecting on their previous Outlook where they used bovine anatomy to convey the risks of a recovery driven by government support. To illustrate these risks, the page features a diagram of an ox with several sections highlighted in red, representing the specific areas of stimulus and policy that are now dragging on the global economy.

Four key pressure points are detailed alongside the ox graphic. First, the historic 2009 stimulus in China has forced aggressive tightening measures in 2010, such as loan quotas and higher mortgage down-payments; however, with national property prices up 12.8 percent in April and money supply growth on track to exceed 20 percent, further tightening is expected, which is negatively impacting Asian equity markets. Second, the relaxation of European Central Bank collateral rules exposed structural vulnerabilities in European credit markets, particularly regarding Greece. The author notes that European banks are three to four times larger relative to GDP than their U.S. counterparts and hold six to eight times more of their own sovereign debt, creating a precarious web that the International Monetary Fund and European taxpayers are now beginning to dismantle. Third, historically high peacetime deficits in the United States are expected to lead to post-midterm-election tax hikes, such as carbon or value-added taxes, because entitlement spending is projected to devour 70 percent of government expenditures by 2015. Similarly, the United Kingdom is undergoing a post-election debate that may see capital gains tax rates surge from 18 percent to between 40 percent and 50 percent. Finally, government guarantees and bank bailouts in the United States, United Kingdom, and Europe have triggered severe regulatory backlash.

A yellow sidebar titled Strings Attached lists these regulatory consequences, noting that they could slash pre-provision bank earnings by 20 percent to 30 percent if fully enacted. The listed measures include too-big-to-fail taxes, derivatives restrictions, limits on Federal Reserve and FDIC independence, higher capital and liquidity ratios, financial transactions taxes, credit card interest caps, debit card interchange fee regulations, restrictions on hedge funds and proprietary trading, narrowed Federal preemption of state laws, securitization retention rules, and the segregation of bank swap desks. Ultimately, the author warns that these market-dampening consequences are the logical result of the previous year's massive stimulus actions.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market argues that contagion risks for Italy are subdued in the near term compared to other peripheral European nations, despite Italy's massive economy. The author contrasts Italy with Spain, Portugal, Ireland, and Greece to explain why Italy is not as immediate of a crisis flashpoint. Four key arguments are presented, each supported by a chart. First, Italy has a much smaller budget deficit problem than its peers, with a 2009 primary deficit under one percent compared to Greece's nine percent. Second, while Italy and Greece share the highest gross sovereign debt-to-GDP ratios in Europe, Italy benefits from high domestic ownership of its debt, with domestic residents holding forty-five percent compared to twenty-five percent in Greece and fourteen percent in Ireland. Third, Italy relies far less on foreign capital, holding a modest three percent current account deficit compared to nine to twelve percent for Portugal and Greece. Finally, Italy's banking sector is exceptionally well-funded, possessing a low reliance on wholesale funding markets and the lowest borrowing from the European Central Bank across Europe.

Four charts illustrate these arguments. The first, depicting gross financing needs versus approved and announced packages in billions of Euros, shows that approved and announced packages of eight hundred sixty billion Euros easily cover the seven hundred forty-five billion Euros in financing needs for Greece, Ireland, Portugal, and Spain from 2010 to 2012, plus their 2013 needs of one hundred sixty-seven billion Euros. However, it does not cover Italy's independent financing needs of eight hundred ninety-two billion Euros for 2010 to 2013, bringing total regional needs to one thousand eight hundred five billion Euros. 

The second chart, displaying gross sovereign debt as a percentage of GDP from 1992 to 2010, plots debt percentages for Italy, Greece, France, Portugal, Ireland, Germany, and Spain. Italy and Greece consistently top the chart, climbing toward one hundred twenty percent of GDP by 2010, whereas nations like Ireland and Spain started much lower but have risen sharply. 

The third chart, tracking the current account balance as a percentage of GDP, shows Italy's current account deficit remaining relatively stable near negative three percent from 1992 to 2010, while Greece and Portugal plunged into deep deficits of ten to fifteen percent in the late 2000s. 

The fourth chart, detailing total borrowing from the European Central Bank as a percentage of bank assets, compares peak and current borrowing across ten European countries. Italy, highlighted by a red arrow, shows the lowest ECB borrowing at roughly one percent of bank assets for both peak and current periods, while Ireland and Greece peak at nearly twelve percent.

While Italy's short-term outlook is relatively stable, the author raises longer-term, structural concerns. Specifically, Italy has a large shadow economy, second only to Greece in Europe, which may weigh on long-run growth, productivity, and per capita development.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer at J.P. Morgan Private Banking, analyzes Italy’s structural economic vulnerabilities, comparing them to Greece, while evaluating the Eurozone's debt crisis response and highlighting Asia as a more promising destination for investment due to its strong consumption growth.

The top portion of the page presents three visuals demonstrating Italy's relative underperformance compared to its European peers. A line chart displaying World Bank Governance Indicators from 2008 shows percent ranks for various nations across six categories: accountability, political stability, government effectiveness, regulatory quality, rule of law, and corruption. Across almost all measures, Italy and Greece score far lower than Germany, the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Spain, and Portugal, trailing in the 50th to 70th percentile range while nations like Germany and the UK sit in the 80s and 90s. Accompanying tables focus on R&D expenditure and business scale. The first table shows annualized R&D expenditure as a percentage of GDP, revealing that Italy sits at the bottom of the list at 1.10%, far below Sweden’s 3.89%, Germany’s 2.48%, and the EU-27 average of 1.84%. The second table, displaying average firm size by number of people, shows that Italy's average firm size is uniquely tiny at 2.7 people, compared to Germany’s 11.4, the UK's 10.6, and Spain's 4.4. 

Cembalest argues these structural features—such as low R&D, small scale, and concentration in low-cost textile sectors—explain Italy’s lagging growth rate. While Italy is currently experiencing a cyclical bounce in industrial production alongside the rest of the Euro area, its low growth combined with high government debt raises persistent long-term challenges. However, J.P. Morgan does not view Italy as a weak link that will require additions to the EUR 750 billion bilateral/IMF bailout package. Regarding Eurozone policy, the author notes political friction in Germany, including FDP head Frank Schaeffler stepping down, but predicts that the European Stabilization Mechanism legislation will pass both the Bundestag and Bundesrat with a simple majority.

Looking globally, Cembalest advises investing in regions with growing incomes, sustainable debt levels, and favorable terms of trade, specifically pointing to Asia. To illustrate the shifting tides of global wealth, a chart plots annualized auto sales as a percentage of the population from 2000 to 2010. The chart compares total World sales on the left-hand scale with World ex-China sales on the right-hand scale. The post-2008 recovery period shows a stark divergence: while the world excluding China struggled to recover from its drop down to the 0.6% level, the global total rebounded sharply back toward 0.85%, underscoring China's leading role in driving modern global consumer demand.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" publication reviews portfolio strategies from late 2009 and analyzes global macroeconomic pressures, specifically focusing on U.S. public debt and the divergent currency needs within the Eurozone. 

The author begins by evaluating portfolio decisions made in late 2009 to navigate the post-stimulus uncertainty of 2010. Balanced Portfolios kept equity weights defensive at 35% to 40%, favoring U.S. large- and mid-caps while remaining underweight in Europe. Exposure to Asia was trimmed due to concern over inflation and soaring property prices, with Beijing property prices already falling 25% in some areas. While active equity positions underweighted European financials and favored Germany, high allocations to hedge funds (17% to 22%) and credit instruments like high-yield and leveraged loans generated positive returns. These gains helped offset missed opportunities in gold and long-duration Treasuries. 

Addressing whether the United States might inflate away its public debt, the author notes that while this strategy worked after World War II—reducing debt-to-GDP from 108% in 1946 to 58% after a decade of 4.4% inflation—it is far riskier today. This is because the average maturity of public debt is much shorter now (4.3 years versus 9 years in 1946) and is no longer held 100% domestically. Consequently, the author expects the Federal Reserve to normalize its balance sheet over five years and recommends selling gold at modestly higher levels.

The final section examines the Eurozone crisis through a concept called "EURashomon," which analyzes the exchange rate needed for individual countries to resolve external imbalances without domestic deflation. This analysis is illustrated in a bar chart titled "Equilibrium Euro by country: solvency without deflation," which plots the implied USD/EUR exchange rate for various nations against a historical December 2009 baseline of approximately $1.45 and a current level of approximately $1.25. The chart reveals massive disparities in the equilibrium exchange rate required by each member state: Germany sits highest at roughly $1.85, followed by Ireland at $1.20, France at $1.05, Italy at $0.95, Spain at $0.60, and both Portugal and Greece at around $0.30. Because German inflation concerns make an extremely weak Euro politically and economically implausible, the author concludes that peripheral nations cannot rely on currency devaluation. Instead, highly indebted countries like Spain, Greece, and Portugal will be forced to rely on painful austerity measures to carry the burden.

This page focuses on the economic challenges of European integration, federal regulation of the financial sector, and state-level legislative threats to New York's financial industry.

The author begins by discussing the Eurozone crisis, quoting former European Commission President Romano Prodi, who argued that the dissolution of the Euro is the only alternative to greater coordination of economic policies. The author warns that this crisis-driven push toward federalism creates significant risks, noting that European capital markets and merger activity had fallen 17% year-to-date, whereas activity in the United States and Asia had risen by 53% and 68%, respectively.

To illustrate the underlying economic imbalances within Europe, a line chart titled "Something's rotten near Denmark: Current account deficit, % of GDP" tracks OECD data from 1975 to 2008. The chart plots two distinct series: one line for France, Germany, and the United Kingdom, and another for Greece, Italy, Ireland, Portugal, and Spain. A vertical dashed line marks 1999, the year the Euro exchange rate was fixed. Before 1999, both groups experienced cyclical fluctuations but stayed mostly between a positive 2% and negative 4% of GDP. After the Euro was fixed, a massive divergence occurred. The France, Germany, and United Kingdom group maintained a stable surplus fluctuating between 1% and 2% of GDP. Conversely, the Greece, Italy, Ireland, Portugal, and Spain cohort experienced a continuous, steep plunge in their current account balance, declining from roughly negative 2% of GDP in 1999 to nearly negative 8% by 2008.

The text then transitions to post-crisis financial reform, detailing goals such as ending "too big to fail," establishing a systemic risk regulator, requiring securitization originators to retain risk, and increasing derivative oversight. The author highlights tension over regulatory overreach, citing former Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker’s opposition to Section 716, which would force banks to push swaps activities into separate holding companies.

The discussion of excessive regulation culminates in a dedicated section on New York State, titled "Das Eigene Nest Beschmutzen" (To Soil One's Own Nest). Summarizing a report by the Public Policy Institute of New York, the author criticizes state politicians for failing to protect their primary industry. The text highlights that New York's legislature is considering 94 bills targeting financial services, which could cost the industry up to $12 billion annually. Using Bureau of Economic Analysis multipliers, the text notes that the financial sector accounts for $187 billion of New York's $318 billion economy, generates 39% of state wage income, and pays 40% of all personal income taxes. The author warns that these punitive measures, combined with the rising popularity of telecommuting, risk driving the industry out of state. This threat is particularly acute given that New York has the second highest per capita state debt in the nation behind New Jersey, with state spending having grown 20% faster than personal income and 30% faster than inflation from 1999 to 2010.

The page begins with a brief introduction to a broader series on rising Chinese consumption and global investment opportunities. It highlights China’s resilient consumption growth amid global recessions, driven by urbanization and rising wages, and contrasts historical ideology using quotes from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping alongside an image of Chinese yuan banknotes. However, the primary focus of this page is a detailed commentary on the Gulf of Mexico oil disaster and the feasibility of replacing offshore oil with alternative energy.

The author examines whether US offshore oil production—which accounts for thirty percent of total US production—could be phased out in favor of alternative energy powering electric vehicles. To illustrate the scale of this challenge, the page features a stacked bar chart titled "Incremental MW by alternative energy source needed to replace all U.S. federal and state offshore oil production powering vehicles." The vertical axis measures capacity in megawatts up to 140,000, and the horizontal axis shows five alternative energy sources: hydro, solar, wind, biomass, and geothermal. Each bar shows the current installed capacity in blue and the required incremental capacity in dark brown. Hydro has the highest current installed capacity at approximately 78,000 megawatts but still requires about 52,000 megawatts of incremental capacity. Solar has almost no installed capacity on this scale and requires roughly 110,000 megawatts of incremental capacity. Wind has about 26,000 megawatts installed and needs another 76,000 megawatts. Biomass needs roughly 33,000 megawatts of incremental capacity on top of 13,000 megawatts installed, and geothermal requires about 25,000 megawatts of incremental capacity over its small 3,000 megawatt base. 

The accompanying analysis explains that matching the pure energy output of offshore oil would require a fifteen-fold increase in wind power. Even when accounting for the higher efficiency of electric cars, which reduces the required expansion to a quadrupling of wind capacity, the physical and logistical hurdles remain immense. This quadrupling would require 7,000 square miles of new wind farms, an area nearly the size of New Jersey, calculated at a rate of 60 acres per megawatt. Additionally, the transition would bring a host of complex issues, including high upfront capital costs, the need for upgraded high-voltage direct current transmission lines, grid instability, eminent domain battles, backup natural gas facilities for wind intermittency, lithium battery supply constraints, and political resistance. 

The page concludes with data from the Energy Information Administration and other sources, noting that annual US offshore oil production stands at 683 million barrels, seventy-three percent of which is used to power vehicles. The author argues that while the US must reduce its reliance on offshore and imported oil, the nation desperately needs an open, honest discussion about the massive sacrifices and costs involved in making that transition.

This publication, authored by Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer at J.P. Morgan Private Banking, addresses the politically motivated discrepancies in congressional discussions regarding the actualized costs of the financial crisis interventions. Cembalest argues that while the public debate focused heavily on the supposed high costs of the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), the estimated costs have actually tumbled, the Federal Reserve's Maiden Lane facilities are in the black, and emergency credit facilities have been nearly entirely repaid. Meanwhile, the potentially massive losses from Government-Sponsored Enterprises (GSEs) like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have generated comparatively little introspection.

To support this, a bar chart titled Potential losses, TARP vs GSEs compares the low May 2010 U.S. Treasury Department estimate for TARP losses—which registers well under $150 billion across its HAMP, Autos, and AIG components—against several much larger private and public sector estimates for GSE losses. These GSE loss projections span from Roubini Associates' $250 billion estimate in late 2008 to Bridgewater's peak estimate of $806 billion in April 2009, alongside high projections from the Congressional Budget Office, Wallison/AEI, and Laurie Goodman. A footnote explains that the TARP costs exclude $16.7 billion in offsetting gains, while some GSE losses will be absorbed by putbacks, private mortgage insurers, and fee income rather than direct Treasury contributions.

Two line charts illustrate the recovery of emergency interventions. The first, detailing Maiden Lane I, II, and III facilities from July 2008 to April 2010, shows that net portfolio holdings recovered and consistently exceeded the principal loan amount from early 2009 onward, proving the facilities are profitable. The second chart tracks the Federal Reserve's emergency credit facilities, which skyrocketed from near zero in late 2007 to a peak of nearly $2.0 trillion in late 2008, before steadily declining back to negligible levels by April 2010. By that point, 86 percent of the remaining minimal balance was concentrated in FX Swaps, AIG, and TALF, with all other emergency facility loans fully repaid with interest.

In the concluding section, titled Odds and Ends, Cembalest highlights several global market developments. He notes that the Standard and Poor's deliberate approach to the Financial Sector Reform Bill has minimized downgrade risks to major banks like Citigroup, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo. He comments on the fragility of global markets, pointing out that European banks have struggled with funding, as exemplified by Spain's BBVA being unable to renew $1 billion in commercial paper and Libor rates rising despite the Fed's ECB lending program. Finally, he outlines two geopolitical opportunities and risks: South Korea's forward price-to-earnings multiple dropping below 10x, making it an attractive entry point if conflict is avoided, and the strategic leverage China holds over U.S. foreign policy toward North Korea due to its massive $800 billion holdings in U.S. Treasuries.

This page focuses on Chinese consumer spending patterns and the operational realities for global investors seeking to target this rapidly growing market. The author argues that as Chinese consumers accumulate wealth, their desires extend beyond automobiles into prestige, luxury, and home goods, though foreign companies face unique cultural and regulatory hurdles.

The page features two charts illustrating these purchasing dynamics. The first chart, titled "What Chinese people buy when they get wealthier," uses a consumption index across wealth categories from poor to affluent. It shows a rapid surge in automobile purchases, which peaks near an index value of 105 for affluent consumers, followed by steady rises in prestige and luxury goods and home decoration. The second chart, titled "Chinese luxury purchases: survey results," presents brand preferences from a sample of 627 major city shoppers. It highlights Louis Vuitton as the clear leader at approximately 33%, followed by Gucci at 26%, with Chanel, Prada, Hugo Boss, Ferragamo, Armani, and Dior clustering between 7% and 8%, and Burberry and Max Mara trailing.

The text emphasizes that reaching affluent Chinese consumers requires expanding far beyond the eastern seaboard hubs of Shanghai and Beijing. A map visual titled "Number of locations with significant affluent populations expected to expand dramatically" contrasts dot maps from 2010 and 2020, illustrating a massive projected spread of affluent populations inland. Reaching 70% of middle and affluent class consumers required only 70 locations in 2005, but requires 240 locations today.

The author notes that foreign brands do not always have an advantage due to consumer ethnocentrism, which is particularly strong among older, male, and rural demographics. Advertisements by McDonald's, KFC, Toyota, and Nike, such as a LeBron James commercial, have previously offended consumers and provoked boycotts. However, in Western China, some foreign brands are so highly trusted that consumers mistake them for domestic brands.

Finally, the page outlines the operational challenges of doing business in China. While an April 2010 American Chamber of Commerce survey showed that 71% of U.S. companies were profitable and 91% were optimistic about their five-year outlook, they still face significant hurdles. These include inconsistent intellectual property enforcement, licensing issues, market access limitations, stricter regulatory standards, and China's Indigenous Innovation Policy favoring local companies. The author concludes that doing business in China remains highly complex, drawing historical parallels to Marco Polo, 18th-century Britain, and modern corporations like Google.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer at J.P. Morgan Private Banking, addresses the Deepwater Horizon Gulf of Mexico oil spill by placing it in the context of global oil production and other societal failure rates. Citing data from Gavekal Securities, Cembalest notes that between 1978 and 2009, the ratio of barrels of oil spilled to total barrels produced was 1 in 30,000. When factoring in the 2010 Gulf incident, with an estimated four million barrels released, the ratio drops to 1 in 25,000. 

To evaluate these figures, Cembalest presents an "index of unwelcome events" comparing various industrial, medical, and consumer safety failure rates. The table shows that high-probability failures include salmonella contamination in chickens at 1 in 7 (sourced from Consumer Reports) and medical prescription errors at 1 in 9 (from Baylor Medical Center and Brigham & Women’s Hospital). Moderate failure rates include the U.S. bridge collapse rate from 1966 to 2005 at 1 in 400 (Texas Transportation Institute and U.S. Highway Administration) and the 2001 recall rate for Firestone Wilderness AT tires at 1 in 5,000. On the lower-probability end of the spectrum, the table lists pacemaker malfunction fatalities at 1 in 43,000, contaminated blood transfusions resulting in Hepatitis C at 1 in 2 million, and fatal airline accidents per departure from 1990 to 2007 at 1 in 4.5 million. 

Ultimately, Cembalest finds this comparative exercise unconvincing. He argues that while the statistical hazard ratio for oil extraction appears better than many other failure rates, oil spills have unique, long-lasting environmental and community impacts that do not compare easily to bridge collapses, medical errors, or tire failures. He also highlights the lack of reliable data regarding nuclear power risks. Concluding with a historical perspective, Cembalest notes that the rise of fossil fuels and electricity since 1850 helped drive U.S. life expectancy from 39.5 to 77.4 years. However, because these productivity gains come with the risk of severe failures, he raises open questions about the long-term impacts of the BP spill on future energy supplies, offshore drilling, and broader energy policies, emphasizing that transitioning away from offshore drilling offers no easy answers.

This page addresses the fiscal challenges of California, arguing that while the state is politically polarized and fiscally undisciplined, it is not insolvent. The author contrasts California’s situation with Greece, noting that California’s budget gap of $22 billion on a $1.6 trillion state GNP requires only 10% of the relative spending cuts or tax hikes that Greece needs. To illustrate the legislative gridlock, a line chart titled "Party polarization at an all-time high" tracks the degree of partisanship in Congressional roll calls from 1879 to 2009. The chart reveals that polarization in both the House and the Senate has climbed steadily since the mid-20th century, returning to historic, post-Reconstruction highs near 0.9 for the House and 0.8 for the Senate by 2009. 

A second chart, "California: Annual population plus inflation growth vs. annual spending growth, 1991 - 2009," compares the combined rate of population growth and inflation (represented by blue bars) against actual spending growth (represented by brown bars) across three state administrations: Pete Wilson, Gray Davis, and Arnold Schwarzenegger. Under all three administrations, spending growth outpaced the combined rate of population and inflation growth, with annual spending increases averaging between 5% and 6.5%, while population plus inflation remained lower, between 3.5% and 5%. 

The text highlights several structural factors driving this spending imbalance, including the state paying 100% of healthcare costs for retired state workers, state and local employment rising 33% faster than population growth since 1990, and public salaries being roughly 44% higher than private-sector equivalents. Furthermore, a highly concentrated tax base where 1% of Californians paid 81% of capital gains taxes in 2007 exacerbates the risk of recessions. Unfunded liabilities were also compounded by retroactive pension increases in 1999 under Governor Davis. 

Looking forward, the author warns that if California attempts to finance its gap too heavily through revenue anticipation notes, rating agencies may downgrade its credit to BBB- or lower. However, J.P. Morgan does not anticipate severe defaults on general obligation or essential service revenue bonds. The author advises clients—especially residents of high-tax states like New York, New Jersey, and California—to hold national portfolios of municipal bonds. Consequently, J.P. Morgan maintains its California municipal bond exposure at 5% to 10% below the state’s 16% weight in national benchmarks, noting that the state’s yields, which are 100 basis points higher than top-tier states like Virginia and Georgia, accurately reflect its credit risks.

In this commentary, J.P. Morgan’s Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest argues that buying Chinese equities is a poor way to monetize the country’s economic growth, advising investors to look elsewhere to capture the rise of the Chinese consumer. To support this claim, the page features two scatter plot charts comparing cumulative and annualized equity market performance against nominal GDP growth for a wide range of emerging and developed nations, with data source credit to the International Monetary Fund and Bloomberg as of May 24, 2010. 

The first chart, titled "Equity markets vs. GDP growth - Q4 2007 to the present," plots cumulative USD equity market performance on the vertical axis (from -70% to 30%) against cumulative nominal USD GDP growth on the horizontal axis (from -10% to 70%). China, circled in red at the bottom right, is a stark outlier, showing the highest cumulative nominal GDP growth at approximately 60%, yet suffering nearly the worst cumulative equity market returns at roughly -50%. The second chart, titled "Equity markets vs. GDP growth - 2003 to the present," displays annualized metrics. It plots annualized USD equity market performance on the vertical axis (0% to 45%) against annualized nominal USD GDP growth on the horizontal axis (0% to 25%). Once again, China sits circled in red near the bottom right, registering a robust annualized nominal GDP growth of around 20%, but yielding an annualized equity market performance of only about 8%, which is among the lowest on the chart.

A third visual, a pie chart titled "Chinese stock market breakdown by sector," explains this disconnect using Shanghai Composite Index data from FactSet. The chart reveals that the index is heavily dominated by financials at 32.3% and energy at 21.9%, followed by industrials at 16.8% and materials at 9.9%. In contrast, sectors tied to modern entrepreneurial growth and direct consumption represent minor fractions: consumer discretionary is 5.9%, utilities is 4.0%, consumer staples is 3.2%, health care is 2.9%, information technology is 2.3%, and telecommunications is a mere 0.8%. Cembalest points out that these dominant financial and energy sectors are primarily state-owned enterprises with objectives other than profitability, making the public market function more like a liquidity casino reflective of monetary stimulus rather than corporate profit trends.

The text details the systemic capital allocation issues within China, noting that Chinese banks primarily channel capital to state-owned enterprises, which represent only 5% of all enterprises but receive 75% of all bank loans. Meanwhile, small and medium-sized enterprises received less than 5% of the loans extended in 2009, forcing entrepreneurs to look offshore for growth capital. Consequently, Cembalest suggests that an effective China consumer strategy should target private companies through growth equity investments. 

The page concludes with a historical anecdote about a 1978 meeting between Singapore’s former Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew and Deng Xiaoping, which inspired the designation of Xiamen, Shantou, Zhuhai, and Shenzhen as Special Economic Zones to kickstart China's market-oriented reforms. Looking forward, Cembalest predicts that despite current financial market adjustments related to the withdrawal of stimulus, overheating property prices, and wage pressures, the long-term trajectory of rising per capita wealth and consumption in China remains secure.

This page from the publication expresses a cautious outlook on global equity markets, expecting single-digit returns for 2010 amid 20% volatility. The author refutes two widely held market assumptions.

First, the author challenges the view that European sovereign debt auctions are going well. While 43 billion euros of debt was issued in May and June 2010, this was heavily supported by the European Central Bank through repo lending and 51 billion euros in debt purchases. To illustrate, a table titled "ECB support for sovereign debt issuance" details sovereign debt issued, repo funding from the ECB, and ECB debt purchases for five countries. Italy issued 21.7 billion euros of debt with 3.9 billion in repo funding, while Spain issued 14.0 billion with 14.0 billion in repo funding, indicating Spanish banks are funding the buying behind the scenes. Ireland and Portugal issued small amounts (3.3 billion and 3.9 billion respectively) but relied on massive repo funding (14.5 billion and 23.3 billion) and ECB debt purchases, joining Greece (which had no debt issued and negative 5.4 billion in repo funding) as effective wards of the state.

An adjacent line chart, "Banking system reliance on short term funding," tracks the funding gap as a percentage of assets from 1998 to 2010. It shows that while the United States successfully reduced its funding gap to zero percent after the 2008 financial crisis, Europe's banking system remains highly reliant on short-term funding, with its gap hovering unchanged near 20% to 25%, mimicking 2007 levels.

Second, the author refutes the claim that the S&P 500 is exceptionally cheap at an 11.5 times price-to-earnings multiple based on consensus 2011 earnings estimates of 95 dollars. The author argues that analysts are historically prone to overestimating earnings. A bar chart titled "Beginning of year vs. End of year earnings estimates" shows the percentage change in the S&P 500 universe from 1986 to 2010. In most years, estimates decline significantly by year-end, with notable drops exceeding 15% to 20% during downturns, though recoveries like 2004 to 2007 saw upward revisions. If earnings instead hit 85 dollars, representing a historically consistent 11% miss, the resulting 12.9 times price-to-earnings multiple would be reasonable but not exceptionally cheap. A final line chart, "Percent of S&P 500 stocks with mean analyst rating of 'Sell' or 'Hold/Sell'" from 1996 to 2010, demonstrates a persistent optimistic bias, with negative ratings rarely exceeding 10% of stocks, even after the enactment of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s financial commentary addresses two main themes: China’s currency policy and the emerging limits of low interest rates to stimulate risk-taking, a phenomenon the author terms "zerophobia."

The first section analyzes the People's Bank of China’s announcement regarding the resumption of a crawling peg for the renminbi (RMB). The author argues that this policy change, likely driven by G-20 political considerations, is minor, pointing out that an expected 3% annual appreciation is far lower than the appreciation rate seen from 2005 to 2008. A more aggressive currency appreciation is deemed unlikely due to slowing domestic growth and a shrinking trade surplus, which dropped from 11% of GDP in 2007 to 3% in the first quarter of 2010. 

To contextualize this, two charts are presented at the top. The first, "Chinese reserve accumulation: unprecedented," compares China's reserve accumulation as a percentage of GDP from 1990 to 2009 against historical periods for Germany and Japan from 1955 to 1975. While Germany and Japan both peaked at or below 2% of GDP, China's reserve accumulation surged exponentially to approximately 12% by year 21, demonstrating a lack of historical parallel. The adjacent chart, "Chinese renminbi spot price," tracks the exchange rate against the U.S. dollar from late 2004 through early 2010. It shows a 2.0% one-time appreciation in August 2005, followed by a 5.7% annualized appreciation trend that leveled off flatly around 6.83 per dollar starting in late 2008.

The second section questions the assumption that low interest rates will indefinitely drive investors into riskier assets. While a Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco study by Glenn D. Rudebusch suggests that economic conditions warrant keeping interest rates at zero until 2012—with a theoretical target rate of -2.9%—the author cautions that persistently low rates might instead induce risk aversion. 

Two bottom charts support this discussion. The left chart, "Funds rate rule adjusted for unconventional policy," displays the historical and projected Fed funds rate from 2002 to 2012. It contrasts the actual Fed's target rate (which dropped to 0% in 2009) with two theoretical alternatives: a "suggested target rate from simple rule" that plummets to nearly -4% in 2009 before rising, and a "suggested target rate taking into account unconventional policy" that sits near -2% in 2010. The right chart, "Flows into global equity and bond funds," displays average monthly flows in billions of dollars up to May 2010, comparing the last 12 months against 2010 year-to-date (YTD). It reveals that monthly equity flows plunged from over $4 billion to nearly zero YTD, while monthly credit flows declined from roughly $16 billion to around $12 billion YTD. This decline in asset flows suggests that investors are already showing signs of "zerophobia."

Finally, the author predicts that if these economic conditions prompt a second round of quantitative easing (QE2) by the Federal Reserve, it would heighten concerns about monetary stability. Under such circumstances, gold is identified as the primary beneficiary. Because of the global necessity for easy monetary policy and the low opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets, J.P. Morgan has removed its price targets for gold, anticipating further upward price momentum.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses China's rising labor costs and analyzes whether they pose a significant threat to Chinese profit margins or U.S. inflation. He argues that while the era of negative unit labor cost growth from 1991 to 2004 has concluded, rising wages are unlikely to disrupt the global economy immediately. This is because labor compensation represents only about 14% of the value of goods and services produced in China, compared to roughly 66% in the United States. Cembalest forecasts that low single-digit unit labor cost growth will continue as the Chinese economy gradually shifts its focus from production to domestic consumption. 

To illustrate historical productivity trends, the page presents a line chart titled "China labor productivity - manufacturing & construction," which tracks the year-over-year percentage change in productivity from 1981 to 2009. The data reveals highly volatile but consistently strong productivity gains, peaking near 35% in 1993, dipping briefly into negative territory around 1989, and finishing at a lower but positive single-digit rate in 2009.

A second scatter plot, titled "China: Labor is a much smaller % of goods and services than in the U.S.," compares forty-two distinct Chinese economic sectors against the United States average. The vertical axis measures labor compensation per unit of output from 0% to 70%, while the horizontal axis shows each sector's size as a percentage of total output from 0% to 8%. A benchmark line near the top highlights the United States average across all sectors at approximately 66%. Below this line, the Chinese sectors are plotted and color-coded into services, energy, and manufacturing. The chart highlights that while service-oriented sectors have higher labor components—such as agriculture at a 5.5% sector size with 55% labor compensation, and education and social organizations at roughly 40% labor compensation—almost all manufacturing and energy sectors are clustered at the bottom of the chart with labor components below 10%. This concentration demonstrates that there is considerable room for Chinese labor costs to rise before U.S. import prices or corporate profits are substantially affected.

In his concluding remarks, Cembalest provides a forecast regarding foreign exchange, stating that J.P. Morgan views the recent Renminbi announcement as primarily political. He expresses skepticism that annual RMB appreciation will exceed 3% to 4%, though he notes that the move supports J.P. Morgan's existing positions in other Asian currencies funded against the Euro.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest, analyzes the state of the United States housing market recovery and details the strategic benefits of investing in diversified portfolios of macro hedge funds. 

Addressing the housing market, Cembalest critiques the common 2009 argument that record-high theoretical affordability would automatically trigger a sharp housing rebound. He argues that this perspective is fundamentally flawed because standard metrics, such as the National Association of Realtors Home Affordability Index, assume a constant twenty percent down payment. In reality, tighter post-crisis underwriting standards and higher down-payment requirements for many borrowers have completely offset the benefits of lower home prices and lower mortgage rates. Consequently, despite more than one trillion dollars in Federal Reserve mortgage and agency purchases, FHA refinancing, homebuyer tax credits, and modification programs, the actual housing recovery has remained highly tepid, and J.P. Morgan does not see a true recovery on the immediate horizon.

Two charts illustrate this divergence between theoretical affordability and actual performance. The first chart plots theoretical home affordability from 1981 through 2009, showing the index of renters' ability to qualify for a starter home mortgage spiking to near-historic highs of approximately 180 by 2009. The adjacent chart tracking actual housing indexes from 2000 to 2010 shows a weak recovery. In this chart, the Case-Shiller 20-city composite, the FHFA house price index, and the NAR median sales price of existing homes sold all illustrate a sharp decline from their mid-2000s peaks, with the NAR median price flattening out near an index value of 125 and the Case-Shiller composite remaining depressed near 140.

In the second section, Cembalest outlines J.P. Morgan’s tactical shift toward macro hedge funds within their twenty percent overall hedge fund allocation for balanced portfolios. Shifting exposure to macro funds is intended to capitalize on ongoing market volatility and a rally in credit. Historically, macro hedge funds have outperformed a standard sixty-forty World Equity and Fixed Income blend with lower volatility over multi-year periods starting in 1990, 1995, and 2000. 

To address the risks inherent in individual, concentrated macro hedge funds, J.P. Morgan advocates for commingling five or more funds. Two scatter plots using data from Hedge Fund Research Inc. demonstrate the effectiveness of this diversification. The chart showing the five-year performance of individual macro funds reveals an extremely wide dispersion, with annualized volatility ranging from under ten percent to over seventy percent, and annualized returns spanning from negative twenty percent to over thirty percent. In contrast, the chart showing portfolios of five randomly selected macro funds demonstrates a dramatic collapse in dispersion risk, with the data points tightly clustered together, showing steady annualized returns of five to fifteen percent and annualized volatility tightly bound between five and fifteen percent. This collapse in risk is noted to be more pronounced in macro strategies than in other hedge fund styles such as long-short, distressed, merger arbitrage, or statistical arbitrage.

Michael Cembalest argues that mediocre U.S. economic data is insufficient because the economy’s "return on stimulus" remains disappointingly weak. He asserts that the current recovery is historically unique due to the unprecedented fiscal costs required to emerge from the prior recession, and that industrial production increases are translating poorly into broader GDP growth. 

This historical perspective is demonstrated in Figure 1, titled "Recoveries used to bloom on their own," which compares recoveries from 1952 through 2010. The chart tracks the increase in the ISM manufacturing survey in points (represented by blue bars) alongside the increase in the Federal Debt-to-GDP ratio as a percentage (represented by red bars). While previous recoveries achieved significant ISM gains with little to no increase in federal debt, the 2008–2010 recovery—projected through the end of 2010—exhibits a massive surge in Federal Debt-to-GDP of roughly 16% alongside an ISM gain of about 20 points.

Figure 2, titled "Lower follow-through from production to growth in Q1 2010," is a scatter plot of non-annualized quarterly data from 1948 to 2010 mapping industrial production growth on the horizontal axis against GDP growth on the vertical axis. The chart highlights the outlier status of Q1 2010, where a robust industrial production growth rate of over 6% translated to a meager GDP growth rate of just about 1%. 

To achieve economic escape velocity and support a positive outlook for equities, Cembalest notes that the market requires a combination of consistent U.S. capital spending and consumption gains, U.S. payroll gains closer to 200,000 per month, credible European bank stress tests, and easier monetary policy in China. He emphasizes that standard metrics like inflation, productivity, and P/E multiples are no longer enough to evaluate this cycle. Instead, investors must watch complex systemic risks, including European wholesale funding issues, China's record money supply expansion, and the unresolved U.S. mortgage delinquency pipeline.

The roots of these systemic issues are tied to the previous credit boom, illustrated in Figure 3, "Non-agency securitization quadruples." This line graph tracks total quarterly issuance in billions of dollars from 2000 to 2007, encompassing subprime mortgages, HELOCs, Alt-A, option ARMs, and commercial real estate. Issuance grew from roughly $100 billion in 2000 to nearly $450 billion at its peak in late 2005 and early 2006, a trend that led to deteriorating underwriting standards and subsequent widespread credit aversion.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Private Banking, addresses the challenges of investing during a historic period of monetary and fiscal experimentation, focusing on European banking risks, analyst earnings optimism, and opportunities in credit markets. 

Cembalest first points out that Europe's wholesale funding risks remain unchanged since the start of the financial crisis, with 3.3 trillion Euros of wholesale debt outstanding, half of which is set to mature within two years. While he hopes European Central Bank policy and stress tests will reassure investors, J.P. Morgan remains underweight on Europe until valuations cheapen relative to the U.S. and Asia. Meanwhile, Chinese equities show signs of bottoming out, as some companies in Shenzhen and Shanghai are trading more cheaply than in Hong Kong, reversing their typical onshore premium and suggesting that Asia's decline in risk appetite may be nearing an end.

This divergence in banking system stability is illustrated in Figure 9, which plots the funding gap as a percentage of assets for both Europe and the U.S. from 1998 through 2010. The chart shows that while Europe's reliance on short-term funding remains stubbornly high at roughly 23% to 25% in 2010, the U.S. banking system has dramatically reduced its vulnerability, with its funding gap plunging from a 2008 peak of over 15% down to nearly 0% by 2010.

To navigate the equity landscape, the author advises caution regarding corporate earnings forecasts. Figure 10 displays the percentage change in S&P 500 universe earnings estimates from the beginning to the end of each year from 1986 to 2010. The bar chart demonstrates a strong historical bias toward over-optimism, as analysts revised their estimates downward in the vast majority of years, with particularly severe downward revisions exceeding 20% during the recessions of 2001 and 2008. Because of this trend, J.P. Morgan discounts consensus estimates, valuing current equity holdings at 12.5x to 13x expected 2010 earnings.

Given these equity valuations, portfolios are increasingly relying on alternative investments, particularly credit. In credit markets, first-lien exposures in commercial property, residential property, and high-yield corporations offer yields between 6% and 11%. Cembalest highlights newly underwritten mezzanine loans to commercial property owners as an attractive, albeit higher-risk, opportunity. These loans now require owners to contribute 30% to 35% equity, rely on conservative loan-to-value ratios that incorporate 40% to 50% property price declines, and offer cash pay yields of 11% to 13%. Cembalest concludes that if markets continue to trend sideways over the next few years, credit investments may offer the best risk-adjusted returns.

This page provides a market and merger and acquisitions (M&A) update, focusing on the upcoming European bank stress tests and broader macroeconomic indicators. The author examines the impending European bank stress tests, comparing estimated European capital needs of 80 billion EUR against an existing equity base of over 1 trillion EUR. To illustrate that these stress tests should conceptually be less demanding than past US exercises, a bar chart titled "On paper, stress tests should be less stressful for Europe" compares the U.S. SCAP in May 2009 with the European stress test. The chart shows that while the US had 523 billion in existing equity and required 75 billion in capital, Europe boasts 1,014 billion in existing equity against an estimated capital requirement of 81 billion. Despite this favorable math, the author poses critical questions about the adequacy of European loss assumptions, particularly for German Landesbanken and Spanish Cajas, and queries whether the adverse scenario GDP assumptions—which are only 3 percent below EU Commission forecasts—are too optimistic.

Transitioning to the macroeconomic outlook, the author notes that while U.S. corporate profits remain strong, industry GDP forecasts for the remainder of 2010 are being revised downward due to a slowdown in spending, housing, and labor beginning in June. A line chart titled "Capital spending leads employment" demonstrates that business spending has historically been a reliable leading indicator of employment over the last 50 years. The chart plots year-over-year percentage changes from 1955 to 2010, pairing business equipment and software spending on the left-hand axis, ranging from negative 20 percent to positive 25 percent, against seasonally adjusted non-farm payrolls on the right-hand axis, ranging from negative 5 percent to positive 5 percent.

Due to muted expectations for growth and equity returns, J.P. Morgan is shifting allocations away from directional equities toward credit and hedge funds, specifically favoring merger arbitrage strategies. This shift is supported by high corporate cash balances and rising transaction activity. A final dual-axis chart, "Rising M&A premiums and transaction volumes," tracks data from 2000 to 2010, plotting the average transaction premium as a percentage on the left-hand scale, ranging from 10 percent to 35 percent, and the number of deals in thousands on the right-hand scale, ranging from 4.0 to 9.0. This visual shows that recent average premiums have spiked above 30 percent, buoyed by notable deals involving companies such as Aon and Hewitt, United Financial and LSB-Smithtown, Carlyle and NBTY, Johnson & Johnson and Micrus Endovascular, Tyco Electronics and ADC, Honam Petrochemicals and Titan, and TPG and Healthscope.

In this publication, Michael Cembalest examines the policy and regulatory lessons of the May 6, 2010 Flash Crash, framing the event as a prompt for necessary adjustments to electronic and high-frequency trading (HFT) systems. He outlines several positive developments that may result from the crash, beginning with the introduction of stock-specific circuit breakers. Cembalest notes that while Asia and Europe have long used daily bands and temporary trading halts, the U.S. has been slow to adopt them, only recently launching a pilot program of 10% circuit breakers that has already been triggered on stocks like Citigroup, Anadarko, and the Washington Post Company. Additionally, the Securities and Exchange Commission is considering restricting HFTs from having unfiltered, naked access to exchanges.

The author also argues for a more balanced discussion regarding HFTs, challenging the industry claim that high-frequency trading represents pure liquidity. Pointing to a Tabb Group survey where 73% of participants felt the market structure was not orderly, Cembalest suggests HFTs should be required to register as broker-dealers. Finally, he advocates for proposals that force HFTs to act more like traditional floor specialists, who were historically obligated to maintain fair and orderly markets. 

To illustrate how HFT activity has distorted the market, a line chart titled "HFTs driving order cancellations higher" displays the ratio of cancelled to executed orders from 2002 through 2009. Utilizing NASDAQ ITCH data provided by Knight Capital Group, the chart shows this ratio climbing from around 11 in 2002 to a peak of nearly 33 by late 2009. This trend underscores Cembalest's point that today's ratio of 30 cancelled orders to every one executed represents a 97% cancellation rate, reflecting "opportunistic liquidity" rather than stable, traditional market depth.

This page focuses on the critical importance of performing deep, granular historical analysis to identify systemic vulnerabilities and financial bubbles before they collapse. Michael Cembalest argues that "getting into the weeds" of global markets reveals structural imbalances that high-level indicators often miss, illustrating this point across five separate historical episodes.

The first visual, Figure 4, titled "Loss protection for AAA CMBS investors," shows the percentage of protection afforded to AAA commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) from 1995 to 2008. The chart illustrates how subordinate "Below AAA" protection steadily eroded over time, shrinking from approximately 35% in 1995 to nearly 10% by 2007 and 2008, which left senior investors far more exposed to losses than in previous cycles.

Figure 5, "Flightless birds, circa 1999," focuses on the late 1990s tech bubble by tracking Cisco, EMC, Oracle, and Qualcomm. This dual-axis chart compares the flat average of analysts' long-term earnings per share (EPS) forecasts, which hovered around 30% to 35%, against the skyrocketing aggregate market capitalization of these four companies, which surged tenfold from under $100 billion in 1995 to nearly $1 trillion by 2000. This stark divergence left massive equity value vulnerable to even minor disappointments. 

Figure 6, "Signs of stress - Korea, Thailand & Indonesia," uses a three-country average from 1990 to 1997 to show how the 1998 Asian Financial Crisis could have been anticipated. The chart plots a rise in bank lending to the private sector from roughly 45% to over 70% of GDP and a dramatic spike in short-term debt from 100% to nearly 160% of foreign exchange reserves, contrasted against volatile inward foreign direct investment as a percentage of the current account deficit. 

Figure 7, "Mexican exchange rate peg and consumption," analyzes the mid-1990s Mexican Peso crisis. It highlights that while the exchange rate peg initially appeared stable, it unleashed a massive consumption boom, with year-over-year consumption growth averaging around 5% between 1989 and 1993 compared to just 1% in the pre-peg years of 1981 to 1988. Because this consumption boom was not backed by rising productivity, it led to a balance of payments crisis. Cembalest uses this example to voice suspicions regarding modern Eurozone nations, warning that a consumption boom paired with rising labor costs and a currency peg often yields a bad outcome for countries like Greece, Spain, Portugal, and Ireland.

Finally, Figure 8, "Commercial property boom a consequence of 1981 bill," details the millions of square feet of US commercial real estate from 1980 to 1990. The chart shows how the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981, which permitted passive tax deductions against active income, caused net new supply to skyrocket to nearly 140 million square feet by 1985, far outpacing the actual increase in occupied space. This tax-shelter-driven oversupply precipitated the Savings and Loan (S&L) crisis and a subsequent recession, which was only corrected after the Tax Reform Act of 1986 removed those incentives and caused supply to plunge.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication critiques the European bank stress test results issued by the Committee of European Bank Supervisors, characterizing them as grade inflation. Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest argues that the reported total capital shortfall of 3.5 billion euros is absurdly low compared to market expectations of 60 to 90 billion euros. To illustrate this point, the page features a small regional map highlighting the tiny country of Andorra nestled between France and Spain, reflecting Cembalest's opening joke that 3.5 billion euros sounded like a shortfall for Andorra alone rather than all of Europe. 

Cembalest outlines several flaws in the methodology, noting that the tests failed to apply a realistically dark economic outlook. Specifically, the adverse case gross domestic product growth was set at only 0.8 percent below contemporary levels, a contrast to the 2009 U.S. stress tests that assumed Great Depression-era losses two to three times higher than the European assumptions. Furthermore, the 560 billion euros in assumed adverse-case losses were conveniently offset by an identical amount of projected pre-provision income, which Cembalest views as overly optimistic for a region undergoing fiscal austerity. Additionally, sovereign stress was only applied to trading books rather than the larger hold-to-maturity portfolios, and private sector default reporting utilized an odd percent-of-a-percent metric that obscured actual risk. Cembalest suspects the tests were designed to minimize capital needs to avoid triggering the European Financial Stability Facility borrowing mechanism. While modest signs of receding financial fear are visible through debt issuance in Greece, Spain, Portugal, Germany, and by the Spanish bank BBVA, Cembalest warns that Europe’s recovery remains uneven, with strong German growth driven by exports rather than local consumption. Consequently, J.P. Morgan maintains its portfolio barbell strategy focused on U.S. and Asian equities.

Expanding on the analysis, European Private Bank Strategist Cesar Perez discusses the systemic liquidity challenges facing European banks. Despite a temporary easing of near-term pressures due to the G-20 softening Basel 3 requirements under ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet, Perez warns that European banks grew their balance sheets over the prior decade by relying less on stable deposits and more on wholesale funding. He explains that replacing this funding will require costlier customer deposits, deleveraging, or issuing long-term debt at higher spreads, all of which will depress the banking sector's return on equity for years to come. Perez references upcoming data visualizations regarding the shift away from deposits and the redemption profile of European bank debt, noting that 2010 and 2011 maturities must be refinanced in a new, far less receptive market environment.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer at J.P. Morgan Private Banking, discusses managing downside risk in venture capital portfolios, focusing heavily on late-stage biotech investing and global venture capital dynamics. 

To illustrate how J.P. Morgan approaches biotechnology venture capital, the author outlines the extreme risks of early-stage drug development. Even Phase 1 clinical trials suffer an 80% failure rate. By prioritizing later-stage investments, such as Phase 3 clinical trials, investors can significantly lower the incidence of failure, aligning better with risk-return goals despite lower corresponding expected returns. 

This risk-reduction strategy is illustrated in a chart titled "Improving the odds in VC investing," sourced from the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America. The graphic depicts a pipeline starting with 5,000 to 10,000 compounds in the drug discovery phase, which takes three to six years. This pool narrows to 250 compounds during the preclinical phase and further shrinks to just five compounds entering Phase 1, Phase 2, and Phase 3 clinical trials, a process spanning six to seven years. Ultimately, after a regulatory review period lasting half a year to two years, only one FDA-approved drug reaches large-scale manufacturing. A list on the page highlights J.P. Morgan's specific medical areas of interest, which include advanced medical devices like digital imaging and ingestible cameras, treatments for neurodegenerative illnesses like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, cancer vaccines and leukemia therapies, cryosurgery, and therapies for macular degeneration and neuromuscular conditions.

Beyond biotechnology, Cembalest notes that J.P. Morgan is active in other VC sectors, citing a successful pre-IPO investment in alternative energy where entering at a later stage—once proof of concept was established but prior to expansion—yielded returns several times the invested capital. When evaluating venture investments outside the United States, the firm seeks specific indicators of a healthy ecosystem: a high ratio of R&D to GDP, deep pools of scientific talent near academic hubs, supportive government seeding programs, a strong track record of IPO monetization, a local shortage of VC capital, and discounted private valuations relative to public peers.

Since robust public IPO markets are vital for monetizing venture investments, a final chart titles "Average monthly IPO issuance" in billions of USD (using Bloomberg data) compares regional IPO volumes across three critical periods: the pre-crisis years (January 2000 to August 2008), the financial crisis nadir (September 2008 to June 2009), and the subsequent recovery (July 2009 to July 2010). In the pre-crisis years, average monthly IPO volumes averaged 5.1 billion USD in the United States, 4.4 billion USD in Western Europe, and 2.9 billion USD in Developed Asia Pacific.
