To establish the scale of this shift, chart c7 tracks the post-war share of total world GDP on a purchasing power parity basis from 1950 to 2008. It highlights a dramatic rise for Asia ex-Japan, which surged from roughly 10% in 1950 to over 33% by 2008, while the United States and Europe both declined from their mid-century peaks of nearly 30% down to around 20% each. 

This rapid expansion has brought rising headline and core inflation across Asia and Latin America, which the author notes is primarily driven by food prices. Chart c8, detailing Brazilian inflation through 2010, shows that headline annualized three-month inflation spiked over 8%, while headline inflation excluding food hovered much lower, around 3%. Similarly, chart c9 shows that Chinese YoY inflation is food-driven, with food inflation peaking over 20% in late 2007 and rising again past 10% in late 2010, while overall CPI remained near 5% and non-food inflation stayed extremely low. 

The report suggests that China's traditional inflation controls, like bank reserve requirements and Central Bank bill issuances, may be losing their edge. This is illustrated in chart c10, which tracks frequent overheating in Chinese residential property markets via a highly volatile average daily sales metric for Shanghai, Beijing, and Shenzhen from 2009 through late 2010. Because of China’s immense influence on other emerging economies—often acting like a "tractor beam"—chart c11 traces the tightening correlation of 14 EM countries to China’s YoY GDP growth from 1991 to 2009. The correlation coefficients, once scattered and occasionally negative in the 1990s, consolidated into a tight positive band between 40% and 80% by 2009. Chart c12 visualizes how Chinese monetary policy functions on a grand scale, plotting foreign exchange reserves alongside sterilization efforts (central bank bills and bank reserve requirements) in billions of USD from 2003 to 2009. Both lines rose in lockstep from near-zero to nearly $2.5 trillion, showing how China actively accumulates reserves to prevent exchange rate appreciation while simultaneously implementing sterilization to manage domestic liquidity.

Looking forward, the publication expects emerging market central banks to cool their economies successfully, allowing robust growth to continue. Chart c13 illustrates that private sector annualized bank credit growth in emerging markets (ex-China) remained healthy around 6% in 2008, contrasting sharply with developed markets, which plummeted from nearly 10% in 2006 to flatlining near 0% in 2008. This credit expansion has supported jobs; chart c14 shows quarter-over-quarter quarterly employment growth for the emerging world remaining resiliently positive and recovering to roughly 3% by 2010, whereas the developed world experienced a deep contraction down to nearly -3% in 2009. 

The author asserts that if emerging markets overdo their monetary tightening, most have ample fiscal room to apply additional stimulus. This cushion is highlighted in chart c15, which compares 2010 fiscal deficits as a percentage of GDP. Brazil (around -2%), Developed Asia (~-3%), and EM Asia (~-4%) boast much smaller deficits than Europe (~-6%), Japan (~-8%), and the United States (~-10%). Despite risks of capital misallocation and high credit growth in China, the report concludes with a positive view, noting that J.P. Morgan continues to hold positions in Asian currencies, funded against G3 currencies, because they remain fundamentally undervalued.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Outlook report focuses on investment portfolios and explains why the firm is comfortable holding a 35% to 45% allocation to equities in balanced and growth portfolios. The central argument is that equity markets are pricing in a high level of pessimism, making valuations quite attractive. 

The first chart, (c26), displays forward P/E equity multiples from 2003 to 2010, illustrating that multiples for the United States, Europe, and Emerging Markets have converged into a cheap 10x to 13x range. Chart (c27) shows the P/E ratio of the top decile of growth stocks relative to the market from 1978 to 2010, indicating that growth stocks are pricing in significant pessimism, with their relative valuation hovering near a historic low of 1.3x. Chart (c28) tracks mega-tech stocks—including Microsoft, IBM, Apple, Intel, Hewlett-Packard, Cisco, Oracle, Google, Qualcomm, and Corning—revealing a massive divergence between 2000 and 2010. While collective cash and equivalents soared past $200 billion, their average P/E multiples plummeted from over 60x to approximately 15x.

The report highlights the United States as their largest regional equity allocation, noting that US profit growth is resilient because S&P 500 revenues are heavily tied to global rather than domestic expansion. Chart (c29) shows that from 1996 to 2010, average S&P 500 core revenue growth of over 6.0% and World GDP growth of nearly 6.0% outpaced US GDP and final sales, which grew closer to 5.0%. This global dependency is mirrored in chart (c30), which shows US corporate profits from the rest of the world rising steadily since 1948 to nearly 3.0% of GDP by 2010. Additionally, chart (c31) shows that S&P 500 earnings are diversified across end-markets, with Business taking 21%, Consumer Staples 18%, Energy & Commodities 17%, Financials 16%, and Medical and Consumer Discretionary at 14% each. Within this space, the authors prefer large-cap over small-cap stocks, favoring growth sectors like technology and healthcare.

Looking ahead to 2011, the report forecasts roughly 10% returns for the S&P 500, driven by 8% to 10% earnings growth and a 2% stock buyback yield. However, the authors express caution regarding long-term multiple expansion due to structural profit drivers. Chart (c32) displays US profit drivers from 1947 to 2010, showing that while corporate sales as a percentage of GDP have fallen to a 50-year low of around 47%, profit margins remain high because labor costs as a percentage of sales have plummeted to roughly 61%. Because corporate earnings are so heavily reliant on these suppressed real wages, the firm is reluctant to forecast much higher valuation multiples.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2011 Outlook focuses on identifying global private equity opportunities across low-growth, high-growth, and high-usage environments. 

In low-growth Europe, high borrowing levels and shrinking financial institutions—specifically citing RBS, Hypo Real Estate, WestLB, and HSH Nordbank—are creating opportunities in distressed assets. The author notes that senior-secured bank loans have recently been purchased at roughly 65 cents on the dollar, equivalent to 50% of traditional loan-to-value, while non-performing residential mortgages have traded as low as 35 cents of face value. 

In high-growth Brazil, private equity penetration remains low but is expanding, represented by Brazil securing 18% of all emerging market private equity fundraising in 2009. Visualizing this environment, chart c44 displays the Economist Intelligence Unit's Private Equity Attractiveness Index from 2006 to 2010, where Chile leads with a score of approximately 75, while Brazil has steadily risen to reach about 65, placing it ahead of Mexico, Colombia, Peru, Costa Rica, and Argentina. An accompanying EIU scorecard lists positive Brazilian attributes such as favorable tax treatments, venture capital fund formation laws, and corporate governance standards, countered by negatives like weak judicial strength, perceived corruption, and weak intellectual property protections. Chart c45 underscores the public-to-private market disconnect in Brazil, illustrating that while services, transports, and telecoms (excluding financials) account for nearly 50% of Brazil's GDP, they make up only 15% of the commodity-heavy Bovespa index, revealing a substantial opportunity for private capital to target consumer-focused sectors.

The final section explores investing where digital usage is high, focusing on the global explosion in bandwidth demand. With OECD broadband users rising from 15% of the total population in 2006 to 25% in 2010, the infrastructure is now in place to support massive growth in electronic content and mobile e-commerce. Chart c46 projects mobile data traffic growth from 2009 to 2014, showing an exponential climb from near zero to roughly 3.5 million Terabytes per month by 2014. Chart c47 details the projected composition of this 2014 mobile traffic, showing that by application, Video heavily dominates over P2P, Gaming, VoIP, and other uses. By device type, smartphones, netbooks, and tablets make up the vast majority of the traffic compared to traditional broadband. Lastly, chart c48 outlines historical U.S. cable industry infrastructure expenditures from 2000 to 2009, showing that investment peaked at roughly $16 billion in 2001, fell to a low of approximately $10 billion in 2003, and subsequently recovered to over $14 billion by 2009, reinforcing the scale of physical network upgrades supporting this digital transition.

This page serves as a reference and index section for the Outlook 2011 publication. It begins by defining key financial and economic acronyms used throughout the report, including Emerging Markets (EM), International Monetary Fund (IMF), European Monetary Union (EMU), Value-Added Tax (VAT), quantitative easing (QE), and several others. The main portion of the page is dedicated to a comprehensive listing of data sources for the charts, numbered from c1 to c57, and tables, labeled t1. These sources encompass a wide array of global financial institutions, research entities, and government agencies, such as J.P. Morgan Securities, Bloomberg, the Bureau of Economic Analysis, the Federal Reserve, the OECD, and various international central banks and statistical offices. The page concludes with standard legal disclaimers clarifying that the content represents general market commentary rather than formal research.

This page contains biographies and portrait photographs for three key members of the J.P. Morgan Investment Strategy Team. The featured individuals are Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer and Head of Investment Strategy of global private banking; Stuart Schweitzer, global markets strategist for J.P. Morgan Private Bank and J.P. Morgan Asset Management; and Richard Madigan, Chief Investment Officer and Head of the Investment Team managing the Global Access Portfolios and Access Funds. Each entry details the individual's role, professional responsibilities, history within the firm, public commentary engagements, and educational background.

On this page of the J.P. Morgan 2011 Outlook, the investment team discusses opportunities in US commercial real estate and hedge funds. After pulling back from commercial real estate in 2007, they are reinvesting, particularly in capital-scarce areas such as commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) rollovers, mezzanine lending, and distressed real estate. The authors argue that commercial overbuilding during the recent credit boom was much less severe than in past cycles, such as the mid-1980s and the late 1990s. 

This observation is supported by three charts. Chart 38, titled "New office supply, Private fixed investment in office, Percent GDP," displays historical data from 1959 to 2007. It shows that private fixed investment in offices peaked during the mid-1980s "Tax boom" at nearly 1.0% of GDP and during the late 1990s "Tech boom" at around 0.7%, whereas the late 2000s "Credit boom" peaked much lower, around 0.5% of GDP. Chart 39, "New retail center supply, Private fixed investment in retail, Percent GDP," covers the same historical span, illustrating that retail investment peaked near 0.28% of GDP in the late 1980s and again in the early 2000s before falling to around 0.12% by 2007. Chart 40, "Evolution in capital structures," provides an illustrative example comparing capital stacks. In the 2007 Pre-Credit Crisis Scenario with a hypothetical $100 valuation, the stack consisted of 75% Senior Debt ($75), 10% B-Note/Mezzanine ($10), and 15% Equity ($15). In the 2010 Post-Credit Crisis Scenario, which assumes a 30% decline in valuations to $70, the restructured stack shows Senior Debt at 50% ($35), Mezzanine at 30% ($21), and Equity at 20% ($14). The authors note that while CB Richard Ellis forecasts office vacancy rates to peak in the second quarter of 2011, real estate asset prices are poised to rise before fundamentals improve.

Moving to hedge funds, the authors express optimism regarding merger and acquisition (M&A) activity and macro hedge funds, but caution that high stock correlation makes stock-picking strategies difficult. Chart 41, "Rising M&A premiums and transaction volumes," tracks the average premium on the left axis (ranging from 10% to 35%) and the number of deals on the right axis (ranging from 4.0 to 9.0 thousand) from 2000 to 2010. While deal volume fell sharply after 2007, average premiums remained relatively high, ending 2010 near 30%. Chart 42, "Tough environment for stock picking, Median pairwise correlation," shows median pairwise correlation for the S&P 500 and the MSCI World ex-US from 2007 to 2010. The S&P 500 pairwise correlation spiked dramatically from around 15% in 2007 to over 50% by 2010, while the MSCI World ex-US rose from around 12% to 25%. Finally, Chart 43, "Company specific drivers of stock performance, Unexplained alpha," charts unexplained alpha from 1950 to 2010 on a scale of 0 to 30. It shows that while high levels of unexplained alpha in the late 1990s and early 2000s made stock picking easier, the level collapsed toward historic lows near 3% by 2010, indicating a much harder environment for long-short investing styles like statistical arbitrage. Consequently, the authors suggest focusing stock selection outside the United States where correlations are lower.

This page explores the deep-seated cultural and social divisions within Europe that complicate the path toward European Federalism and fiscal integration. The author argues that while European Monetary Union countries share similar levels of individualism and self-expression, they differ dramatically on a traditional-versus-secular value spectrum. These cultural divides must be addressed as European leaders confront regional austerity and coordinate fiscal transfers.

The primary visual is a global cultural map based on World Values Surveys by Professors Ron Inglehart and Christian Welzel. It plots country data across two synthesized axes: a horizontal axis representing Survival versus Self-Expression Values, and a vertical axis representing Traditional versus Secular/Rational Values, ranging from negative 2.0 to positive 2.0. Distinct cultural regions are highlighted, including Protestant Europe, Catholic Europe, Ex-Communist nations, English-speaking countries, Latin America, South Asia, Africa, and Confucian societies. 

The chart demonstrates that while European nations like Germany, Italy, Spain, France, Belgium, Portugal, and Greece cluster tightly on the horizontal self-expression axis, they are highly fractured vertically. For example, the cultural distance between Catholic Spain and Protestant Germany is exceptionally large—surpassing the overall cultural variance found within regions like Latin America or East Asia, and dwarfng domestic differences such as those between college-educated and non-college-educated citizens. Quotes from the authors emphasize that national identity remains the single most powerful predictor of personal values, far outweighing demographic factors like income, education, occupation, gender, or sub-national region.

A supporting line chart in the bottom right tracks periphery unemployment, weighted by population, for Greece, Ireland, Spain, and Portugal from 1970 to 2010. The metric shows a cyclical climb from under 3% in 1970 to a peak near 14% in 1985, followed by a decline to around 8% in the mid-2000s, and a subsequent sharp spike back to 14% by 2010. The author concludes that reconciling these persistent cultural divides will be essential to overcoming record periphery unemployment and bolstering public support for the European Union, which has fell to some of its lowest levels since 1973.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Outlook 2011 focuses on commodity investments and the long-term outlook for the US dollar. The central argument is that while emerging market demand continues to grow rapidly and command a larger share of the world's resources, investors should choose commodities based on scarcity and structural supply constraints rather than short-term momentum. The author highlights copper, oil, gold, platinum, and palladium as preferred holdings, often using structures with downside protection, while remaining cautious on commodities with ample supply.

To illustrate emerging market resource demand, chart c49 shows the rising share of global consumption for key industrial metals from 1995 to 2010. Over this fifteen-year period, emerging market consumption of copper and zinc surged from around 30% to over 60%, while aluminum and nickel usage climbed from roughly 25% to near 50%. The structural backdrop for these commodities is detailed in the commodity supply grid in table c50, which categorizes assets by their supply tightness. Copper, lead, zinc, gold, platinum, and palladium are classified as having tightly constrained supply. Meanwhile, commodities like crude oil, coal, nickel, silver, cocoa, wheat, corn, cotton, and soybeans face potential intermittent disruptions, whereas sugar, coffee, natural gas, and aluminum show no major structural constraints. 

This supply-demand dynamic is further supported by chart c52, which plots production shortfalls and surpluses as the trend growth in demand minus ten-year production. Nickel, copper, oil, tin, zinc, and lead all show clear structural shortfalls, led by nickel at over 2% and copper near 1.5%. Conversely, aluminum exhibits a substantial supply surplus of nearly 1.5%. For oil, as shown in the price chart c51, prices recovered from their 2009 lows near $40 per barrel to hover around $80 per barrel by late 2010. The text predicts that oil spare capacity will continue to decline because non-OPEC production losses and growing demand will outpace new OPEC supply. Production gains in Iraq are critical to offsetting accelerating declines in Mexico, Norway, and the United Kingdom, and despite potential gains of 6 million barrels per day from enhanced recovery techniques by 2030, a massive production gap remains. 

On precious metals, the report predicts that gold's volatile upward trajectory will continue, with prices expected to end 2011 higher. This forecast is supported by low central bank gold holdings in emerging markets—which account for less than 5% of their total reserves—along with a surge in private-sector gold imports in China and the introduction of China's first Qualified Domestic Institutional Investor gold fund. To underscore how underinvested the market remains, the author notes that the total market capitalization of gold exchange-traded funds is roughly equal to that of Verizon. 

Finally, the page addresses the future of the US dollar. While the dollar currently dominates foreign exchange transactions, accounting for 85% of transactions compared to 39% for the Euro, 19% for the Yen, 13% for Sterling, and just 0.3% for the Chinese Renminbi, the author draws a historical parallel to the British Pound's loss of reserve currency status in the 20th century. Just as Commonwealth countries held sterling reserves out of mercenary self-interest until the 1967 devaluation forced their hand, emerging market central banks today have a similar relationship with the US dollar. Ultimately, J.P. Morgan expects that the tide of history will favor higher valuations for Asian currencies relative to both the US dollar and the Euro. This trend is reinforced by the massive domestic demand in Asia, noted in a footnote, where Chinese consumption of appliances and cars is up 40% to 80% since 2008, hotel construction is growing by 1,000 properties per year, and electrification is expanding rapidly across Pakistan, India, and Indonesia.

This page provides professional biographies for three of J.P. Morgan's regional chief investment strategists, alongside a list of "Eye on the Market Special Editions" published in 2010. 

The biographies begin with Ivan Leung, the Chief Investment Strategist for Asia, who is responsible for setting regional investment strategy and managing discretionary portfolios. He holds degrees from the University of Toronto and the Schulich School of Business. Next is Cesar Pérez, the Chief Investment Strategist for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. He has seventeen years of experience in investment management, including previous roles at Credit Suisse Asset Management, M&G Investments, and J.P. Morgan. The final biography is for Phil Guarco, the Chief Investment Strategist for Latin America, who previously served as a senior credit officer for Latin American financial institutions at Moody’s and holds degrees from Grinnell College and Johns Hopkins University. Headshots accompany each of the three profiles.

The bottom portion of the page lists six special editions of the publication from 2010. These include "A Don Quixote Thanksgiving" from November 18, which analyzes strains in Europe's peripheral regions; "From Nehru to Now" from October 26, which examines India's economy; "Are JGBs the Short of a Lifetime?" from August 23, focusing on Japanese sovereign debt; "5 Best things about the flash crash" from July 13; "Northern Star" from June 1, which explores Chinese consumption; and "The Sick Men of Europe" from February 11, which details the challenges confronting the European Monetary Union.

This page warns of the systemic dangers of a policy mistake or a sudden rise in interest rates, arguing that abnormally low rates are masking unsustainable debt levels across major economies and sectors. The author highlights an "OK-as-long-as-rates-dont-rise" paradigm affecting countries like Japan, Italy, and the United States, as well as households in the US and real estate in Hong Kong. Low debt servicing costs are currently sustained only by low interest rates and short average debt maturities of around four years in the US and Japan. To emphasize the danger of ignoring these structural risks, the text notes a historical parallel from a highly optimistic March 8, 1987, Los Angeles Times article that praised plentiful liquidity and low equity valuations shortly before the 1987 stock market crash.

Four charts and a prominent text callout box support this argument. The first chart, showing world growth driven by low budget deficit countries from 2010 to 2015 projections, illustrates that world GDP growth is powered heavily by surplus countries, low-deficit countries, and other emerging economies, while high-deficit nations pose significant fiscal risks despite their contribution. 

The second chart tracks US household debt and debt service ratio as a percentage of disposable income from 1980 to 2010. It shows that household debt peaked around 130% of disposable income before declining to 118% by 2010. Meanwhile, the household debt service ratio fell from approximately 14% to 11.5% during this period, a drop the author attributes more to lower interest rates and defaults than to actual debt reduction. 

The third chart traces Hong Kong housing affordability, measured as the monthly mortgage installment relative to median household income, from 1994 to 2010. Affordability spiked to extremely unaffordable levels over 100% in 1997, dropped to a highly affordable low of around 20% in 2003, and rose back to approximately 40% in 2010. The author argues this level is only perceived as normal because mortgage rates are exceptionally low at 2.5% in an economy growing at 9%. 

The fourth chart presents a rate sensitivity analysis of Japanese interest expense as a percentage of tax revenue. Using 2009 data as a baseline where interest expenses consumed slightly over 20% of tax revenue, the model projects that a 100-basis-point rate increase would push interest expenses to nearly 40% of tax revenues, a 150-basis-point increase would drive it to almost 50%, and a 200-basis-point hike would raise it to nearly 60%, rendering Japan's fiscal accounts virtually inoperable. 

Finally, a callout box documents Ben Bernanke’s shifting perspective on central banking limits. In 2002, Bernanke asserted that under a fiat money system, the government has a technology called the printing press that allows it to produce US dollars at no cost to prevent deflation. By 2009, however, Bernanke warned that due to the retirement of the baby-boom generation, rising medical costs, and elevated debt-to-GDP ratios, the US would not be able to continue borrowing indefinitely to meet these demands.

This page highlights the profound impact of Brazil's commodity abundance and its ongoing domestic consumer revolution. With commodities representing roughly two-thirds of its total exports, Brazil is uniquely positioned to supply the intensive resource demands of emerging giants like China and India. 

A series of charts illustrates Brazil’s natural resource advantages. The first chart, detailing the availability of arable land in millions of hectares, reveals that Brazil possesses the world's largest reserve of non-cultivated arable land at nearly 300 million hectares, dwarfing the potential of other nations such as the United States, Russia, and China. A second chart displays 2009 oil reserves in billions of barrels under different scenarios; while Brazil's conventional reserves without sub-salt are modest, the "official" sub-salt projections lift its reserves past 100 billion barrels, and the "best" sub-salt scenario suggests reserves could top 200 billion barrels, positioning Brazil just behind Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. A third chart tracks Brazil's trade with China from 1980 to 2008, showing a dramatic, near-vertical surge in both imports and exports to nearly $30 billion by the end of the period.

The second half of the page focuses on the rise of 50 million Brazilian consumers, driven by sound monetary policies, the commodity boom, and targeted social welfare. Six supporting charts and tables detail this socioeconomic transformation. A chart tracking social classes from 2003 to 2014 projects that the middle class will grow from about 65 million to nearly 100 million people, while the lower and bottom classes steadily shrink. Despite this consumption boom, a chart of consumer credit as a percentage of household income shows that Brazil's credit penetration remains very low at approximately 25%, compared to over 170% in the United Kingdom and over 135% in the United States, signaling massive runway for credit-led growth. This is complemented by a historical chart of private consumption, which depicts strong real annual growth rates peaking between 6% and 8% in the late 2000s. 

Further evidence of Brazil's development is found in a chart showing school enrollment for children aged 7 to 14 climbing steadily from 80% in 1992 to nearly 98% in 2006, alongside a poverty chart showing the poverty rate halving from nearly 30% in 2001 to around 15% in 2009. Finally, a table ranks Brazil as one of the world's largest consumer markets across several key sectors, placing second globally for wall and floor tiles and cosmetics, third for mobile phones, fourth for chocolate, fifth for soft drinks, vehicles, and computers, and eighth for education.

This page focuses on Brazil’s historic economic transformation, its emerging opportunities in private equity, and its transition from a volatile emerging market to a stable global economic power. The author highlights that by the end of the decade, Brazil will likely overtake Britain and France to become the world's fifth-largest economy. 

An introductory section notes how financial markets panicked during Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s 2002 presidential campaign, causing the return on one-year exposure to Brazil risk to skyrocket. This is illustrated in the first chart, "Brazil sovereign credit risk," which plots the country's one-year CDS spread from 1998 to 2008. The spread spiked dramatically to 40% when Lula was elected in 2002 before quickly plummeting back below 10% as public policies remained stable. 

The report outlines a broader, steady transformation across Latin America away from state-led development and toward lower inflation, smaller fiscal deficits, privatization, and central bank independence. This regional shift is supported by four charts. The first, "Latin America inflation," shows year-over-year percent change from 1995 to 2011, noting that while inflation ranged from 200% to 700% between 1991 and 1994, it fell from 45% in 1995 to steady single digits by the late 1990s. The "Latin America fiscal balance" chart shows the regional deficit recovering from a low of nearly -35% of GDP in 1989 to near 0% by 2009. The "Difference in real GDP growth" chart comparing Latin America minus the U.S. from 1990 to 2010 displays volatile relative growth that fluctuated between -4% and +4%, ending with a strong positive differential in 2010. The fourth chart, "Latin America reserves ex gold," tracks reserves in billions of USD from 1985 to 2009, highlighting a sharp, upward trajectory starting around 2003 that pushed total reserves to nearly $600 billion by 2009.

While Lula often gets credit for these achievements, the text emphasizes that President Cardoso (1995–2003) laid the groundwork by committing to a primary budget surplus and reducing reliance on foreign debt, which ultimately helped Brazil achieve an investment-grade rating in 2008. This domestic stability is depicted in four final charts tracking metrics from 1998 to 2010. "Government interest payments" as a percent of GDP declined from an 8% peak in 2002 to roughly 5.5% in 2010. Concurrently, "Gross foreign debt" fell from 40% of GDP in 2002 to under 15% in 2010. "International reserves" rose exponentially from around $50 billion in 2002 to approximately $300 billion by 2010. Lastly, the "Fiscal deficit/surplus" chart shows a consistently positive primary balance hovering between 2% and 4% of GDP alongside a nominal balance that improved from -6% of GDP in 1998 to roughly -2% in 2010. A concluding footnote elaborates on the pitfalls of Brazil's former state-led growth model, citing historical examples such as pre-1989 computer market protectionism that created a six-year technology gap with the United States.

This analysis outlines the primary risks facing investors in Brazilian financial markets, categorized into short-term inflation, medium-term reliance on "hot money" portfolio flows, and long-term structural impediments to growth. 

In the short term, inflation is being driven primarily by food prices, which represent twenty-three percent of the local consumption basket. Compounded by secularly low unemployment and high capacity utilization, this inflationary pressure led Brazil to raise policy rates by two percent in 2010 and implement an entry tax on the Brazilian Real. The accompanying chart, "Brazilian inflation fueled by food," tracks the three-month annualized percentage change from 2007 through 2010, highlighting a significant divergence where headline inflation spikes above eight percent in late 2010 while the headline ex-food rate remains stable near four percent.

The medium-term risk lies in how Brazilian consumption is financed. The market has shifted away from stable foreign direct investment toward volatile portfolio inflows. The chart "How consumption is financed" measures these dynamics as a percentage of GDP from 2008 to 2010. In 2008, foreign direct investment dominated at over three percent of GDP while portfolio inflows were negligible; by 2010, this reversed, with portfolio inflows rising near three percent of GDP and foreign direct investment dropping below two percent. This shift exposes the Real to sharp depreciation or forces higher interest rates to keep foreign investors from fleeing.

In the long term, structural impediments continue to restrict growth and productivity. Capital formation remains remarkably low, as demonstrated by the fact that only thirteen percent of Brazil's roads are paved. The line chart "Brazil: Fixed capital formation lags" compares capital formation as a percent of GDP from 1999 to 2009 across major emerging markets, showing Brazil flatlining below twenty percent, well behind Russia, India, and China, the latter of which neared fifty percent. 

This lack of infrastructure investment stems from high mandated government expenditures, particularly social security and pensions, which have earmarked over eighty percent of spending since the 1988 Constitution was established after the military dictatorship. The "Government consumption" chart shows this structural jump, where consumption doubled from roughly ten percent of GDP prior to 1980 to twenty percent by 2004. Consequently, when balancing budgets, the government is forced to cut infrastructure or raise taxes. This has given Brazil the largest tax burden in Latin America by a wide margin, as shown in the final chart, where Brazil's tax burden climbed above thirty-five percent of GDP by 2005, while all other Latin American nations clustered between ten and twenty-five percent. A footnote highlights that Brazil's social security spending stands at 11.7 percent of GDP, a ratio comparable to older nations like Finland, Sweden, and Germany, despite Brazil having a much younger population.

This page discusses the intersection of declining agricultural productivity and extreme global weather patterns. The author highlights a report from Science magazine showing that the growth rate in major crop yields in the industrialized world fell by half between the 1961–1990 and 1990–2007 periods. This trend is supported by USDA research indicating agricultural productivity grew by only 0.9% per year from 2000 to 2007, making global food supplies highly vulnerable to rising demand and weather shocks. 

To address whether recent extreme weather events are part of an ongoing trend or random occurrences, the author consults Richard Seager of the Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory. The discussion focuses on two primary weather phenomena: severe flooding and extreme freezing. Heavy flooding in Australia and droughts in Kansas are linked to a powerful La Niña cycle, which is characterized by cold tropical sea surface temperatures forcing heavy rainfall westward. This ocean-atmosphere interaction is illustrated in the left-hand set of charts, titled "Sea surface temperature differentials, Nino 3.4 region," which plots Celsius deviations from the mean temperature between 1950 and 2012. Spanning four multi-decade panels with a scale of -2 to 3 degrees Celsius, these charts visually depict the cyclical alternation between warm El Niño phases (shown in red) and cold La Niña phases (shown in blue), highlighting the significant La Niña dip that occurred around 2010. 

Severe winter weather across the Northern Hemisphere is explained by a drop in the pressure differential between the Lisbon/Azores high-pressure system and the Icelandic low-pressure system. When this differential declines, the polar jet stream migrates southward, bringing arctic temperatures to North America and Northwestern Europe. This phenomenon is tracked in the right-hand set of charts, titled "North Atlantic Oscillation index (atmospheric pressure differentials), 3 month rolling average," which covers 1950 to 2012 with a scale of -2 to 2. These charts show a highly negative NAO Index reading during the winters leading up to 2011, visible as deep downward-pointing spikes. All meteorological data is sourced from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication analyzes the investment landscape in Brazil, focusing on public and private equity opportunities. The author highlights immediate drivers of domestic growth, such as infrastructure demands from rising vehicle purchases, urban migration, hosting the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics, and developing challenging deepwater sub-salt oil fields, such as the Tupi field by Petrobras. Despite Lula's massive Growth Acceleration Program, which initially dedicated $250 billion and was later renewed for $880 billion, the victory of Dilma Rousseff has ushered in government spending cuts that threaten infrastructure funding. Furthermore, private sector participation remains low compared to other Latin American nations, and recent tragic mudslides costing an estimated $1.2 billion have redirected funds toward emergency flood management. 

In public equity, Brazilian price-to-earnings multiples are modestly higher than their historical ten-year average but remain supported by solid fundamentals. While the Bovespa index yielded an annual return of 18% over five years compared to 13% for emerging markets, public markets are constrained by extreme sector concentration and a small overall exchange size. A line chart depicting the twelve-month forward P/E multiple from 1996 to 2010 shows multiples for Brazil and "Brazil ex Petrobras" fluctuating between roughly 5.0 and 15.0, ending 2010 around 11.0 to 13.0. The extreme concentration is illustrated by a pie chart showing that just eight companies—Petrobras, Vale, Itau Unibanco, Ambev, Bradesco, Banco do Brasil, Santander, and OGX—account for more than half of the BM&FBOVESPA's total market value. A comparative line chart tracking stock performance from 2004 to 2010 (indexed to 100 in January 2005) highlights Bovespa's volatile ride, showing it peaked near 450 in late 2007, fell sharply to around 150 during the 2008 financial crisis, and rebounded to over 400 by late 2010, significantly outperforming both the broader EM Index and the S&P 500.

These public market limitations, paired with high local interest rates, create a highly fertile ground for private equity. Smaller companies face borrowing rates as high as 29% in Reais, while larger firms pay in the mid-teens, and subsidized BNDES financing is limited to preferred sectors at 6% to 7%. This dynamic forces companies to seek equity financing instead of debt. Moreover, while the public Bovespa index is dominated by a few massive resource and financial firms, the real economy is highly diversified. This structural disconnect is illustrated in a final bar chart demonstrating that services, transport, and telecommunications (excluding financials) comprise a massive 50% of Brazilian GDP but account for only about 11% of the Bovespa index. Consequently, private equity investors have robust opportunities in control transactions, co-investments, and minority growth positions among thousands of underrepresented private companies.

Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer at J.P. Morgan, argues that the U.S. municipal bond market is highly diverse and that Illinois is a extreme fiscal outlier rather than a representative example of state financial management. Contrasting the municipal market with the uniform vulnerabilities seen in 2007 broker-dealer balance sheets or peripheral European sovereign debt, the author emphasizes that state-level fiscal health varies dramatically. Because of this fragmentation, J.P. Morgan continues to recommend nationally diversified municipal bond portfolios over concentrated, state-specific strategies.

The primary visual support is a scatter plot titled "Illinois: in a league of its own," which maps major U.S. states based on their leverage and structural deficits. The vertical axis measures leverage, defined as 2009 general obligation debt plus underfunded pension liabilities (excluding other post-employment benefits) as a multiple of state revenues, ranging from 0.0x to 4.5x. The horizontal axis measures the structural deficit, defined as the projected fiscal year 2012 budget gap as a percentage of fiscal year 2011 expenditures, ranging from zero to fifty percent. The chart's background transitions from green in the lower-left (healthier fiscal standing) to yellow and then deep red in the upper-right (severe fiscal distress). 

The data includes states with general obligation debt and unfunded pension obligations exceeding fifteen billion dollars. Illinois stands isolated in the extreme upper-right red zone of the chart, with leverage exceeding 4.0x and a structural budget gap of roughly forty-five percent of expenditures. The author notes that this data does not account for subsequent increases in Illinois's personal and corporate income tax rates, nor does it include other post-employment benefits, an area where Illinois holds one of the largest estimated unfunded obligations in the nation. 

In contrast to Illinois, other fiscally strained states exhibit less extreme combinations of these two metrics. For instance, New Jersey shows a high budget gap of nearly thirty-seven percent but with leverage under 3.0x, while Oregon has leverage around 3.2x but a smaller budget gap of twenty-five percent. Most other analyzed states—such as California, Texas, New York, Pennsylvania, and Georgia—cluster safely in the lower-left and middle sections of the graph, showing leverage under 3.0x and budget gaps well below thirty-five percent.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication analyzed the "madness of crowds" across several investment sectors: European bank non-performing loans (NPLs), US bank consolidation, and US commercial property. 

The first section discusses European bank NPLs as a prime target for bargain-hunting. European banks rely heavily on wholesale funding rather than stable deposits, resulting in high loan-to-customer deposit ratios. Tightening regulations under Basel III and ECB rules mean banks must shrink their balance sheets and shed non-core assets. The author highlights Europe as the epicenter for distressed investing in 2011, noting that one manager purchased commercial real estate NPLs in Germany and the UK at just 36 cents on the dollar. An accompanying bar chart, "G-3 banking sector loan to deposit ratios," illustrates this vulnerability. It compares Western Europe, the United States, and Japan, displaying both median and weighted average ratios. Western Europe shows a much higher weighted average ratio of approximately 1.5 and a median of 1.3, compared to the US and Japan, where both metrics hover much lower, between 0.7 and 0.8.

The second section addresses US bank consolidation, noting that while the credit crisis and recession paused the decades-long shrinking of US banks, the consolidation trend is re-emerging. Target banks are commanding high acquisition premiums ranging from 1.5 to 2.5 times tangible book value, as seen with NewAlliance Bancshares, Danvers Bancorp, and Legacy. Despite historical research over the past 30 years showing that bank mergers do not typically add value to acquiring shareholders, the herd instinct drives larger banks to continue buying smaller ones, with mergers in the final four months of 2010 already matching the total for the prior year. A dual-axis line chart titled "Consolidation in the U.S. banking industry" tracks the number of mergers per year from 1980 to 2008. The chart displays data from multiple studies—including FRB, FDIC, and Capital IQ/S&P—showing a peak of over 600 mergers per year in the late 1990s, followed by a steady decline to under 200 by 2008. A separate series for public, non-distressed sales, plotted on the right-hand axis, shows volume fluctuating between 40 and 100 sales annually during the 2000s.

The final section compares direct real estate investing to publicly traded Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs). The author argues that retail "yield mania" has crowded the REIT market, making them more expensive than direct property acquisitions, with REIT dividends dropping below historical averages compared to corporate bonds, Treasuries, and TIPS. Direct investing is presented as offering modestly better value. A supporting line chart shows the "U.S. commercial real estate public market premium," comparing REIT premiums to private market valuations from February 1994 to October 2010. Two data series from Green Street Advisors and J.P. Morgan Investment Management depict highly volatile premium levels. After plunging to historic lows of negative 40% to 50% during the 2008 financial crisis, the premium rebounded sharply by late 2010, trading positive in the 10% to 20% range, indicating that public REITs are indeed expensive relative to private property values.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, authored by Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest, focuses on two main topics: a looming recovery in subsea internet infrastructure demand and the combustible socioeconomic situation in Egypt.

In the section titled The internet mania, version 2.0, Cembalest explains that the previous decade's internet bubble collapsed because technology and user behavior did not develop quickly enough, leaving a massive amount of unlit subsea fiber. He forecasts that over the next three to four years, demand will finally catch up, presenting new investment opportunities in infrastructure. This is supported by a line chart titled Existing cable capacity continues to diminish, which tracks the percentage of potential capacity in use from 2002 to 2013 (projected) for Trans-Atlantic and Trans-Pacific routes. Both series remained flat below twenty percent until 2007, after which they rise sharply, with Trans-Pacific capacity projected to approach nearly ninety-five percent and Trans-Atlantic capacity reaching roughly eighty-five percent by 2013.

The second half of the page, titled Egypt: a year of living dangerously, addresses the political and economic instability in the country. Despite official IMF-reported unemployment of nine percent, youth unemployment is near twenty-eight percent, and forty-four percent of Egypt's population survives on less than two dollars a day. The situation is exacerbated by low literacy, high labor rigidity, and extreme sensitivity to food prices. For instance, Egypt's tomato crop collapsed from forty tons per acre in 2009 to fifteen tons in 2010. These issues are illustrated in an accompanying table comparing Middle East and North Africa nations across indicators such as youth unemployment, labor rigidity, food as a percentage of CPI, poverty index, corruption rank, and adult literacy. Egypt stands out with a food-to-CPI ratio of forty-five percent, a poverty index of twenty-three point four percent, a corruption rank of 111, and adult literacy of just sixty-six point four percent, which is significantly worse than peers like Qatar, the UAE, or Kuwait.

Cembalest compares the current Egyptian situation to historical events in Indonesia in 1965 and 1998, where political upheaval preceded major economic growth inflection points. This historical context is displayed in two line charts titled The Years of Living Dangerously (Indonesia), Real GDP in constant dollars, trillions. The first chart covers 1950 to 1974, marking when Suharto replaced Sukarno after violent protests in the mid-1960s, triggering a rise in GDP from about zero point zero five trillion dollars to nearly zero point twenty-five trillion dollars. The second chart covers 1971 to 2003, highlighting Suharto’s resignation amid violent protests in 1998, after which Indonesian GDP fell briefly before resuming a strong upward trajectory toward one trillion dollars. Cembalest poses the open question of whether Egypt will experience a similarly positive economic turnaround after its political transitions.

At the bottom of the page is a list of academic citations detailing the historical lack of shareholder value created through US bank mergers, referencing articles from publications such as the Journal of Performance Management, Antitrust Bulletin, and the Journal of Economic Perspectives.

This page analyzes the economic dynamics within the European Monetary Union and evaluates the structural recovery of the structured credit market following the 2005–2007 bubble. 

In the first section, the author examines the relationship between France and Germany, referencing Charles De Gaulle’s famous metaphor that Europe is run by France as the coachman and Germany as the horse. Two charts illustrate the widening economic divergence between the two nations. The first chart, "Widening French/German export gap," plots the ratio of France's real exports of goods and services divided by Germany's from 1970 through approximately 2008. The ratio peaked near 60% in the mid-1990s before steadily declining to around 43% by 2008, demonstrating Germany's growing export dominance. The second chart, "Manufacturing unit labor costs: Vive la difference!", indexes labor costs from December 1998 to December 2010. It shows France's manufacturing unit labor costs rising to an index level of 104 in late 2008 before finishing near 98 in late 2010. In contrast, Germany's labor costs fell to 88 by late 2006, spiked to about 94 in late 2008, and dropped back to 88 by the end of 2010, highlighting Germany's superior cost competitiveness. The author argues that Germany has chosen to support the Eurozone by accepting sustained financial transfers to the periphery, which keeps France's political influence intact. In response to these dynamics, J.P. Morgan is seeking investment opportunities in oversold European healthcare, consumer staples, financials, and bank sales of non-performing loans.

The second half of the page addresses structured credit, arguing that underwriting standards have returned to healthier levels after the excesses of the pre-crisis era. The author notes that during the 2005–2007 credit bubble, investor protection cushions were precariously thin. This is illustrated in the chart "Property decline cushions return to sanity," which tracks AAA commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) subordination adjusted for loan-to-value (LTV) ratios from 2001 to 2011. Subordination levels fell from 30% in 2001 to a mere 5% in 2007—meaning a minor 5% drop in property values would expose AAA tranches to losses—before recovering to 35% in 2010 and settling around 28% in 2011. A parallel improvement is shown in the collateralized loan obligation (CLO) market in the chart "Pre-crisis vs. post-crisis CLO subordination levels." This bar chart compares AAA CLO subordination percentages, showing that pre-crisis protection levels of 25% have been replaced by post-crisis levels ranging between 30% and 45% throughout 2010 and early 2011. Due to these significantly improved risk buffers, the author states that J.P. Morgan is actively investing in structured credit across both new issue and secondary markets.

This analysis examines the tension between a strong global economic recovery and rising geopolitical and policy risks, themed around the "Ides of March." The author observes that global manufacturing surveys show an expanding economy, particularly in the developed world, driven by "zero cost of money" policies. This recovery is illustrated by two top charts. The first, "Manufacturing surveys: the G-3 takes center stage," tracks seasonally adjusted indexes from 2006 to 2011 for developed markets, emerging market Asia, and Latin America. All three regions bottomed out dramatically in early 2009—with developed markets plunging to near 30—before recovering by early 2011 to expansionary territory between 50 and 58. The second chart, "Cost of money = zero," tracks inflation-adjusted policy rates from 1981 to 2011, showing that developed market real policy rates dropped below zero percent by 2010, while emerging market rates hovered around one to three percent. 

Despite this economic momentum, the author warns that 2011 likely marks the end of the "free money train," ushering in higher market volatility. Consequently, the publication projects a year-end S&P 500 range of 1350 to 1375, which is lower than the median consensus forecast of 1425. To navigate this volatility, preferred portfolio allocations include large-cap US growth equity, private lending to real estate and mid-sized corporates, merger arbitrage, and distressed European bank loans.

A major portion of the page is dedicated to Middle Eastern geopolitics, particularly brewing instability in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia's oil-rich Eastern Province. While noting upcoming "Days of Rage" and localized Shi'a protests in Qatif, the author argues that Saudi Arabia is unlikely to experience the same revolutionary combustion seen in Egypt. This is attributed to a generous domestic entitlement system and highly pervasive policing. 

To contrast the two nations, a table presents rankings out of 110 countries from the 2010 Legatum Prosperity Index. The data shows that Saudi Arabia and Egypt are vastly different on economic and institutional trust metrics; Saudi Arabia ranks highly on business and government corruption (7th versus Egypt's 48th), perceived job availability (8th versus 85th), and the environment for entrepreneurs (16th versus 109th). However, they are highly similar in their lack of social and political liberties, with both countries ranking near the bottom for political rights (Saudi Arabia at 102nd, Egypt at 93rd), personal freedom (103rd versus 109th), and the separation of powers (106th versus 82nd). 

Finally, the author highlights that Saudi stability is vital to global energy markets, as investors rely on Saudi Arabia to offset oil export declines from Libya and Algeria. A chart titled "Saudi Arabia spare capacity" tracks thousands of barrels per day from 1999 to 2010. It shows spare capacity fluctuating wildly, dropping below 1,000 thousand barrels per day around 2003 to 2004, but rebounding strongly to nearly 3,000 thousand barrels per day by 2009 due to lower domestic production and capacity additions from the Khurais and Shaybah fields.

This page opens with an announcement of an upcoming J.P. Morgan conference call featuring Vali Nasr, a professor of international politics and Senior Advisor to the U.S. State Department, to discuss the geopolitical risks building in the Arab world and South Asia. Michael Cembalest explains that while the global recovery was deepening as of early March 2011, it is colliding with complex headwinds. These include political upheaval across the Arab world, fiscal crises in the European Monetary Union, and monetary tightening in Asia. Cembalest argues that removing the massive central bank stimulus—which has already driven up commodity prices—will be highly disruptive and non-linear.

The page features two data tables. The first, titled "Global Recovery in the Works" and sourced from Bridgewater Associates, measures the percentage of countries growing faster than they were three months prior, comparing March 3, 2011, to November 2010. The data shows a sharp acceleration in momentum: the global figure jumped from 38% to 79%, the Developed World surged from 17% to 83%, Asia climbed from 50% to 88%, and Central & Eastern Europe rose from 25% to 75%, while Latin America remained flat at 60%. 

The second table, "The Ides of March," outlines a packed calendar of geopolitical and macroeconomic flashpoints for March 2011. Key events include protests in Qatif, Saudi Arabia, on March 3; the Irish Parliament reconvening on March 9 to revisit its EU/IMF bailout; Moody’s downgrading Spain's credit rating to Aa2 on March 10; Saudi Arabia's "Days of Rage" scheduled for March 11; a Eurozone summit on March 11; a Federal Reserve FOMC meeting on March 15; and central bank meetings throughout the month across nations like Brazil, Mexico, Norway, India, Taiwan, and Korea.

Despite a global manufacturing and services rebound, high profit margins, and low price-to-earnings multiples in developed markets, Cembalest advises holding less equity risk than usual. He recommends that investors complement equities with macro, merger arbitrage, and credit hedge funds, diversified commodity exposure, and private lending opportunities, such as buying distressed European bank loans or collateralized commercial property loans. 

This cautious stance on monetary policy is visually illustrated by an intricate black-and-white etching titled "Figure 1: Printing Press," which served as the cover art for the 2011 Eye on the Market. The illustration depicts a sprawling, industrial machine room where workers assemble crates of capital created by central banks since January 2008 to buy government debt and manipulate exchange rates. The crates are labeled with currency amounts and their relative size to national GDP, including $1.1 trillion (8.1% of GDP) for the United States, ¥15.1 trillion (3.3% of GDP) for Japan, HK$ 879 billion (53.8% of GDP) for Hong Kong, NT$ 3.6 trillion (29.1% of GDP) for Taiwan, CHF 191 billion (35.6% of GDP) for Switzerland, B2.4 trillion (21.3% of GDP) for Thailand, and R$ 150 billion (3.8% of GDP) for Brazil.

This page features a highly detailed, color-coded map titled "Religious Composition of the Core Areas of the Middle East," reprinted from the Columbia University Gulf2000 Project and originally created by M. Izady in 2006. The map provides a comprehensive geographic overview of the diverse religious sects across the Middle East, parts of North Africa, the Caucasus, and Central Asia, including nations such as Turkey, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Iran, Syria, Yemen, and Oman. 

The primary focus of the visual data is the distribution of different Islamic denominations. Sunnism is represented in light green, showing its dominance across Turkey, Egypt, Syria, Jordan, northern Iraq, and large portions of Afghanistan and Pakistan. Shiism, shown in dark green, is concentrated heavily in Iran, southern Iraq, Azerbaijan, and portions of Yemen, with notable pockets in Lebanon and eastern Saudi Arabia. Wahhabism, represented in a pale cream color, is the prominent sect in the central interior of Saudi Arabia and Qatar, accompanied by a specific map remark noting that only Wahhabism is allowed to be publicly confessed and practiced in Saudi Arabia. Ibadism, shown in yellow-green, is located almost exclusively in Oman. The map also distinguishes regions with mixed Sunni and Shiite populations, as well as areas of mixed Shiite and Wahhabi populations. 

In addition to Islamic sects, the map highlights other religious groups in the region, including Christianity in blue—visible in Cyprus, Armenia, Georgia, and localized parts of Egypt, Syria, and Lebanon—and Judaism in orange, centered in Israel. Red squares mark Shi'a holy cities, such as Karbala, Najaf, Qom, and Mashhad, while black boxes highlight Najaf and Qom as major Shi'a centers of religious learning. Uninhabited and sparsely populated desert regions are represented in white and light tan, respectively. There are no market forecasts or financial predictions on this page, which serves strictly as a demographic and geopolitical reference.

This analysis focuses on the unfolding sovereign solvency crises in Europe, specifically addressing the situations in Greece, Portugal, Ireland, and Spain. The commentary notes that while markets are increasingly factoring these risks into bond and equity prices—which helps prepare investor portfolios for potential debt restructurings—significant uncertainty remains regarding how European banks account for sovereign debt. The upcoming European Union summits present a major hurdle, as debtors and creditors remain deeply divided on the path forward. This tension is underscored by a quote from outgoing Bundesbank President Axel Weber, who warns that strong German import demand cannot fix the structural flaws of debtor nations, making painful domestic adjustments inevitable.

To illustrate the market's pricing of these crises, a chart titled "Price for benchmark government bonds" tracks bond values in Euros across maturity dates ranging from 2012 to 2020. The chart reveals deep discounts, with Spanish bonds sliding from approximately €98 down to €93, Portuguese bonds dropping from €95 to €81, Irish bonds declining from €83 to €74, and Greek bonds trading at the deepest discount, falling from about €80 down to €68. These market pressures set the stage for the March Summit meetings, which are summarized in a comparison table of conflicting demands. Debtor nations are seeking maturity extensions on the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF), lower borrowing rates, EFSF secondary market debt purchases, increased EFSF capacity, and senior bank loan haircuts. In contrast, creditor nations are demanding binding debt reduction plans, EU Commission monitoring of competitiveness with fines for imbalances, constitutional sovereign debt limits, and tax harmonization.

The regional economic strain has also depressed European equity valuations relative to the United States, as shown in two valuation charts. The "Europe cheap to US: price to earnings" chart tracks the ratio of Europe's 10-year trailing P/E to that of the US from 1998 to 2010. This ratio peaked near 1.15 in late 2007 before falling to approximately 0.80 by 2010. Similarly, the "Europe cheap to US: price to book" chart shows the relative price-to-book ratio dropping from a high of nearly 0.90 in late 2006 to around 0.73 by early 2011, signaling that European equities have become historically cheap.

The final segment highlights Ireland's fiscal distress through a bar chart and commentary titled "Ireland: The Road to Serfdom." The chart tracks Irish national debt as a percentage of GNP, showing a dramatic surge from roughly 20% in 2007 to over 110% in 2010, with projections reaching roughly 130% by 2012. This debt spiral was driven by the 2008 recession and subsequent bank debt guarantees, followed by sequential recapitalizations of Anglo Irish and Nationwide banks in 2009 and 2010 alongside mounting entitlement deficits. The author argues that Ireland’s decision to safeguard the broader European banking system by recapitalizing its own banks—under heavy pressure from the EU to protect senior creditors—has left the nation heavily burdened. While Ireland represents a small fraction of the global economy, its unresolved structural issues loom as a highly symbolic threat to the stability of the European Monetary Union.

This page of commentary analyzes global oil market dynamics, inventory buffers, and the vulnerability of various economies to potential supply disruptions and price shocks. The author argues that while commercial oil inventories are at the high end of their historical ranges, logistical bottlenecks and political hurdles complicate their use. Specifically, US commercial inventories are concentrated in the Midwest where they cannot be easily transported to offset rising prices elsewhere, and there remains significant resistance to releasing the government's Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR). Furthermore, although global economic growth has become structurally less oil-intensive since 1980, rising US retail gasoline prices are absorbing a growing share of consumer earnings, threatening to trigger demand destruction. 

These arguments are supported by six charts. The first, titled "Commercial and government oil inventories" from 1992 to 2010, plots days of consumption on the y-axis against time. It shows United States and OECD commercial inventories fluctuating in a relatively stable range of 45 to 65 days, whereas the series for the United States with its Strategic Petroleum Reserve demonstrates a much larger buffer, dropping to a low near 70 days in the early 2000s before climbing back to nearly 100 days by 2010. 

The regional mismatch is highlighted in the second chart, "Commercial oil inventories by region" from 1981 to 2011, which plots millions of barrels. The Gulf Coast holds the largest share, fluctuating between 140 and 180 million barrels, while the Midwest has steadily increased to nearly 100 million barrels by 2011. In contrast, the West Coast, East Coast, and Rocky Mountain regions have remained flat or declined, highlighting the difficulty of transporting reserves to the areas that need them most. 

The third chart, "Oil intensity declining worldwide," tracks billions of barrels of oil consumed per unit of GDP from 1980 to 2010. It shows a persistent decline across all regions: non-OECD intensity fell from about 3.3 to 0.7, the world average fell from 2.1 to 0.5, and OECD intensity dropped from 1.8 to roughly 0.4. Despite this structural improvement, the fourth chart, "US retail gas prices as a share of average hourly earnings," shows that fuel costs still heavily impact household budgets. This metric rose from a low of 9% in the late 1990s to a sharp peak of over 21% in 2008, before dropping and climbing back up to approximately 17% in late 2010. 

To assess the broader macroeconomic fallout of these trends, the fifth chart, "Two views on the impact of an oil price shock," compares projected percentage declines in GDP across various countries using models from Bridgewater on the vertical axis and the ISI Group on the horizontal axis. Open and trade-dependent Asian economies face the deepest projected downturns, with Singapore suffering a GDP decline of around 1.3% under Bridgewater's model and 0.8% under ISI's, followed closely by Taiwan, Thailand, and South Korea. Conversely, net oil exporters such as Canada, Mexico, Malaysia, and Argentina are projected to experience neutral to slightly positive GDP impacts. 

The final chart, "Saudi Arabia spare capacity vs potential supply loss," displays Saudi spare capacity in thousands of barrels per day from 1999 to 2010 alongside combined Libyan and Algerian exports. Although Saudi spare capacity has historically been volatile, reaching a low of 500,000 barrels per day in 2003, it recovered to over 3 million barrels per day by 2010. This level is shown to be sufficient to absorb a total shutdown of exports from both Libya and Algeria, which combined represent just under 2 million barrels per day, underlining the market's heavy reliance on Saudi Arabia to stabilize global supply.

This page provides a detailed update on the unfolding nuclear crisis at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station in Japan following the devastating earthquake and tsunami. The central argument is that the rapid deterioration of the situation was likely triggered by the catastrophic failure of back-up power systems. Specifically, the fuel storage tanks supplying the backup generators were located directly on the beach rather than underground, leading them to be washed away by the tsunami. This loss of electricity crippled the cooling systems, sparking a chain reaction of hydrogen explosions, structural damage, and the dangerous exposure of active and spent fuel rods. In contrast, the nearby Fukushima Daini reactors, situated ten miles away, avoided this fate and achieved a normal cold shutdown because their emergency power sources remained intact.

To illustrate the physical impact, the page features a before-and-after aerial photograph of the Fukushima Daiichi plant, with arrows indicating where the beachfront fuel storage tanks were swept away while neighboring structures just inland survived.

Below this image is a comprehensive table compiled by the Japan Atomic Industrial Forum outlining the status of units one through six at the plant. The table reveals critical damage across the facilities. Units one, two, and three, which were active and underwent automatic shutdown during the quake, all suffer from damaged cores and non-functional cooling systems. Seawater injections are continuously being attempted on units one and three to cool the reactors, while containment vessel damage is suspected in units two and three. The physical integrity of the buildings is also heavily compromised, with units one, three, and four classified as severely damaged due to hydrogen explosions. While units four, five, and six were already shut down for maintenance before the disaster, they present their own severe hazards. Unit four's spent fuel pool has low water levels with suspected fuel rod damage, and units five and six are experiencing rising pool temperatures. The table notes that radiation levels at the station's border reached 646.2 microsieverts per hour, and details the active safety protocols, including a twenty-kilometer evacuation zone and shelter-in-place orders for residents within twenty to thirty kilometers of the plant.

The author emphasizes that the exposure of uranium and plutonium rods to the air significantly increases the likelihood of a meltdown, highlighting the critical nature of ongoing efforts to stabilize the spent fuel pools. The analysis points to the failure of backup power as the root cause of the entire disaster, leaving open questions about the long-term containment integrity of the damaged reactors.

This page introduces a series of key charts representing critical trends driving global financial markets, framing the macro-environment as mostly positive for the United States and China, while noting challenges elsewhere. 

In the United States, the author argues that global disturbances are occurring against a strong backdrop of corporate health, unlike the recessionary environment of 2001. Corporate cash flow and S&P 500 net income are on the rise, supported by cyclically low debt ratios. This financial strength is fueling stock buybacks, corporate mergers, and a 13% year-over-year increase in non-financial dividends in the final quarter of 2010. The author expects private-sector job growth to average around 200,000 per month. Supporting this positive outlook, Dallas Fed President Richard Fisher is cited declaring the recovery self-sustaining and calling for an end to monetary accommodation after June, while Cleveland Fed President Sandra Pianalto points to a virtuous cycle of growth. This optimistic view is further backed by strong capital spending and manufacturing surveys, recovering from 2009 when capital spending fell to depreciation levels.

Two charts illustrate the financial strength of US corporates. The first chart, "S&P 500 ex-financial net income vs. free cash flow," plots billions of dollars from March 1999 through late 2010. It shows both metrics recovering sharply from their 2009 lows, with free cash flow peaking near $180 billion and consistently running ahead of net income, which reached approximately $140 billion. The second chart, "S&P 500 ex-financials net debt/equity ratios," tracks corporate leverage from 1999 to 2010. This ratio peaked near 110% in 2002 but has since declined significantly, bottoming out at around 72% in late 2010, illustrating that non-financial corporate debt is at its lowest cyclical point in a decade.

Following a brief transition noting future investment reviews regarding expanding global bandwidth infrastructure, the focus shifts to China. The author highlights the risks of the "Bretton Woods II" system, where Asian nations accumulate foreign exchange reserves and redeploy them into Western assets. This system is threatened by rising inflation, with emerging market headline inflation reaching 6.0% year-over-year in February 2011. China's easy monetary policy has driven spikes in real estate prices, prompting the government to aggressively build social housing to cool the private market. The official target is to complete 36 million social housing units by 2015 to satisfy 20% of urban households, though the author questions if local governments—who must provide free land and bear construction costs—have the incentives to meet this goal. 

The accompanying chart, "Government spending on social housing designed to cool overheated housing market," displays completed housing units in millions from 1999 through estimates to 2015. Commercial housing completions, shown in blue, rise steadily from roughly 2 million units in 1999 to more than 10 million units by 2015. Social housing completions, depicted in brown, remain negligible for over a decade before a massive projected spike to roughly 10 million units in 2011 and 2012, before leveling off to around 4 million completed units annually through 2015.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, titled "Direct radiation comparisons," provides a highly detailed visual guide comparing various sources of radiation exposure in millisieverts per year (mSv/year). Reprinted with permission from Professor Rama Hoelzstein of Aalborg University at Copenhagen, the graphic is designed to put the March 2011 radiation levels in Tokyo following the Fukushima disaster into global and medical context.

The central element of the page is a logarithmic chart spanning from 0.05 to over 100.0 mSv/year. It traces a time series of Tokyo's radiation levels from March 15th to March 21st, 2011, plotted in orange. This timeline shows a brief peak of 14 mSv/year on March 15th at 10:37 AM, followed by another peak of 9 mSv/year later that evening, before steadily declining and stabilizing mostly between 0.7 and 2.0 mSv/year over the subsequent days. This is contrasted against Tokyo's typical natural background level, which is below 0.5 mSv/year.

To contextualize these spikes, the chart plots numerous benchmark reference points. At the extreme high end, natural radioactive hot springs in Ramsar, Iran, produce 260 mSv/year, and Kerala, India, sits at approximately 30 mSv/year. Heavy smoking of 1.5 packs a day adds an additional 30.0 mSv/year of exposure. Occupational limits are also highlighted, showing the annual limits for nuclear workers and airline workers clustering around the 10.0 to 20.0 mSv/year range, while common medical procedures range from a full body CT scan at around 10.0 mSv/year to a mammogram at just under 2.0 mSv/year. Geographic baseline levels for various world cities are plotted, showcasing higher natural background radiation in high-altitude or geologically unique places like Denver, Colorado, and Guarapari, Brazil, compared to lower baseline cities like New York, San Francisco, and Tokyo's typical natural baseline.

On the right-hand side, a stacked vertical bar chart illustrates the average accumulated radiation per person in a single year, which totals 6.2 mSv, alongside the normal background sources of 2.4 mSv/year. The breakdown reveals that natural radon is the single largest source of exposure at 42%, followed by terrestrial background radiation at 16%, cosmic radiation at 13%, and medical radiation at 10%. Consumer products make up 3%, occupational exposure represents 2%, and nuclear fallout or nuclear accidents account for less than 1% of the average person's annual radiation exposure. Footnotes at the bottom list a variety of scientific sources, including the New England Journal of Medicine, the Health Physics Society, and the National Academy of Sciences, among others.

This page examines how long-term improvements in energy efficiency—specifically computations per kilowatt-hour—have acted as a crucial and underappreciated force enabling the proliferation of mobile computing devices. The author points out that while public attention typically focuses on the growing raw power of semiconductors, the steady increase in computations per kilowatt-hour allows mobile devices to perform far more work without requiring larger batteries. 

The featured chart plots computations per kilowatt-hour on a logarithmic scale from one to ten quadrillion over a timeline spanning 1940 to 2010. It shows an extraordinarily consistent exponential upward trend, with computations per kilowatt-hour doubling approximately every eighteen months, representing an average doubling time of 1.57 years from 1946 to 2009. The regression analysis of eighty data points yields an adjusted R-squared of 0.983, modeled by the formula where computations per kilowatt-hour equals the exponential of 0.4401939 times the year minus 849.1617. 

The chart traces this historical trajectory through specific milestone machines. It begins with early vacuum-tube computers like the Eniac, Univac I, EDVAC, and Univac II in the 1940s and 1950s, before moving to transistorized systems such as the SDS 920 and Univac III in the 1960s. It then transitions to mini and supercomputers like the DEC PDP-11/20, Cray 1 supercomputer, and the Altair 8800 in the 1970s. The trajectory advances through the personal computer boom with the Apple IIe, Commodore 64, IBM PC, IBM PC-XT, IBM PC-AT, and Macintosh 128k in the 1980s, and continues through desktop and mobile devices including Compaq Deskpros, Dell Optiplex and Dimension systems, Gateway P3s, SiCortex servers, and late-2000s laptops. This visualization and the accompanying data are based on a 2010 study by Koomey and colleagues titled "Implications of historical trends in the electrical efficiency of computing," published in the IEEE Annals of the History of Computing.

This page analyzes investment opportunities arising from the post-crisis landscapes in Japan and Europe, while also assessing the environmental fallout of the Fukushima nuclear disaster. 

Regarding investment strategies, the author identifies opportunities in Japan as reconstruction costs approach five percent of the nation's GDP. Key sectors positioned to benefit include companies involved in the production of industrial metals like iron ore, copper, steel, and aluminum, construction machinery sales, residential and commercial property rebuilding, and non-nuclear energy providers such as liquefied natural gas and coal producers. In Europe, the focus shifts to bank de-leveraging and the contraction of the shadow banking system, which has been accelerated by Basel III regulations and a ninety-six percent decline in new collateralized loan obligation origination since 2006. With banks pledging approximately one trillion Euros in asset sales, distressed residential and commercial property loans, along with discounted senior-secured corporate loans, present attractive opportunities, particularly as capital remains scarce to refinance two hundred seventy billion Euros of high-yield debt maturing through 2015.

The appendix details the ongoing nuclear crisis in Japan, where emergency cooling measures have failed to utilize normal closed-loop heat exchangers, forcing operators to spray water using diesel pumps. This process has generated vast amounts of radioactive runoff, leading Tokyo Electric Power to release more than ten thousand tonnes of contaminated water containing Cesium-137 and Iodine-131 into the ocean. Chief Cabinet Secretary Yukio Edano warned of a major impact on the ocean and predicted it could take months to halt the leaks. 

The author expresses skepticism toward sanguine media reports that downplay risks to marine life by assuming the ocean will dilute the radiation. This critique is supported by two comparative maps of the Japanese coast displaying Cesium-137 concentrations measured in becquerels per cubic meter. The April 2005 baseline map shows minimal radioactivity, ranging between one and ten becquerels per cubic meter. In contrast, the map from late March 2011 reveals highly elevated coastal radiation levels reaching between one hundred thousand and ten million becquerels per cubic meter, with offshore concentrations three hundred miles out remaining at one thousand to ten thousand becquerels per cubic meter. Although the International Atomic Energy Agency highlights that offshore concentrations are three to four orders of magnitude lower than those on the immediate coast, the author emphasizes that these offshore levels are still three to four times higher than normal.

This page from J.P.
