This page examines the risks and structural limitations of sovereign debt investing, particularly during crises, and argues that investors must demand substantial premiums because official sector credit facilities often fail to prevent severe market declines. The author contrasts corporate credit—where lenders have enforceable mechanisms like sharing clauses, trustees, and subordination agreements to ensure equal treatment—with sovereign debt, where such remedies are rarely used because they are nearly impossible to enforce. Even standard provisions like "pari-passu" clauses are shown to have little practical meaning, despite a rare historical exception in 2000 when a hedge fund successfully used New York and Belgian courts to force Peru to fully pay its loans.

To support the argument that official aid packages do not halt market declines, the page presents four historical case studies showing debt price trajectories following major international bailouts. The first chart, depicting Argentine sovereign debt prices from 1998 to 2004, shows that despite a December 2000 promise of $40 billion in aid from banks, the IMF, the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB), and Spain, debt prices plummeted from around 90 to below 30 by 2002. The second chart focuses on Mexico's Brady Bond debt from late 1993 to early 1995. Even after the United States and Canada established a permanent $6.7 billion credit line in April 1994, debt prices continued to slide; it was only after a $20 billion Exchange Stabilization Fund was created in February 1995 that prices bottomed around 50 and eventually stabilized.

The third chart illustrates Russia's GKO sovereign debt in 1998. It highlights overly optimistic statements from Stanley Fischer of the IMF in January 1998 when prices were near 80, followed by a fleeting rally to around 70 in July 1998 when a $22.6 billion IMF-led loan package was announced. Ultimately, the market collapsed, dragging prices down toward 40. The final chart details Indonesian sovereign debt from 1996 to 1998. Even as the IMF praised cabinet negotiations and prepared to resume lending under a $40 billion package in April 1998, sovereign debt prices fell from their historical levels near par (100) to a low around 60. Collectively, these examples show that while 50% to 70% currency devaluations eventually helped Mexico and Indonesia stabilize and recover, the declines in Argentina and Russia were permanent, reinforcing the necessity for high yields to justify sovereign risk.

This page from the publication, titled Appendix A: The pain in Spain, and a history of European austerity and social unrest, analyzes the compounding economic misery in Spain and the historical link between fiscal austerity and social instability across Europe. The author argues that Spain is approaching the socioeconomic limits of austerity within a currency union, given its staggering 23 percent overall unemployment, over 40 percent youth unemployment, and looming deficit adjustments. 

To illustrate Spain's severe economic contraction, the page presents six charts. Chart c73 displays the Spanish services activity Purchasing Managers Index from 2000 to 2011, showing a steep drop from over 60 down to a low near 30 in 2008, before hovering weakly between 40 and 50. Chart c74 tracks the Spanish unemployment rate from 1983 to 2011, showing that after falling to under 10 percent in 2007, unemployment surged back up near its historical 1994 peak of 22 percent. Chart c75 tracks Spanish industrial production index from 2007 to 2011, showing a drop from 100 down to approximately 75 by 2009, with no recovery through late 2011. Chart c76 displays cement consumption in millions of tons from 1973 to 2008, highlighting a massive property-led boom that peaked near 55 million tons in 2007 before collapsing below 20 million tons. Chart c77 shows Spanish retail sales from 2003 to 2011, depicting a steady decline from an index peak of 113 in 2007 to below 90 by 2011. The only bright spot is shown in chart c78, which tracks Spanish exports as a year-over-year percent change from 2000 to 2011; exports crashed to negative 14 percent in 2009 but staged a sharp double-digit recovery, stabilizing around 8 percent growth by 2011.

The commentary then shifts to the broader historical consequences of European austerity, drawing on a Centre for Economic Policy Research study by Ponticelli and Voth covering 32 European countries from 1919 to 2008. Chart c79, titled Austerity and unrest in Europe, 1919 - 2008, plots the average number of annual incidents per country across three measures of instability: demonstrations, riots, and general strikes. For each measure, five colored bars represent different fiscal policies, ranging from expenditure increases to progressively larger expenditure reductions of over 1 percent, 2 percent, 3 percent, and 5 percent. The data reveals a clear escalating pattern of unrest: as budget cuts deepen, demonstrations rise from about 0.5 per year during spending increases to nearly 1.5 per year during cuts exceeding 5 percent. Similarly, riots surge from nearly zero to over 1.0 per year, and general strikes increase to roughly 0.3 per year. The study finds that this relationship holds true regardless of ethnic fragmentation, inflation, mass media penetration, or institutional quality, though higher starting levels of government debt worsen the unrest.

Ultimately, the author questions whether Europe can sustain political and social cohesion along its current path. The text points to rising systemic tensions and a perceived democratic deficit at the EU level, highlighted by Germany's Constitutional Court. The author cites a highly critical comment by Christian Noyer, head of the Bank of France, who argued that credit rating agencies should downgrade Britain instead of France because Britain has higher deficits, comparable debt, higher inflation, lower growth, and slumping credit. The author concludes that such statements demonstrate the fracturing limits of European solidarity in an era of declining growth and intense budgetary pressure.

This analysis focuses on "Das Kapitulation," referring to Germany’s acceptance of aggressive monetary expansion by the European Central Bank (ECB) through its long-term refinancing operations (LTRO). The author argues that by printing money and lending it to European banks for three years, the ECB is effectively replacing lost global capital to ease sovereign and banking pressures, slow the EU recession, and aid deleveraging. However, the author warns that winning this "balance sheet expansion race" may not be desirable, pointing to Japan’s historical central bank expansion which failed to stave off low growth and asset deflation. 

The first chart, "Central bank balance sheets" as a percent of GDP from 2007 to late 2011, visualizes this expansion. While the United States and United Kingdom balance sheets represent roughly 15% to 20% of their respective GDPs, the ECB's balance sheet is shown rising sharply. With the current level plus the February LTRO (estimated at twice the net December LTRO), the ECB's balance sheet is projected to reach approximately 30% of GDP, surpassing Japan's level of around 28% of GDP.

The immediate relief from this monetary injection is illustrated in the sovereign yield curves for Italy and Spain, comparing November 29, 2011, with January 24, 2012. For Italy, the short-term rates collapsed dramatically, with 3-month yields falling from nearly 6% to under 2%, and 2-year yields dropping from over 7% to around 4%. Spain’s yield curve shows a similar shift: its 3-month yield fell from over 4% to approximately 1.5%, while its 2-year yield decreased from over 5.5% to about 3.5%. This shift makes the combined €225 billion in 2012 financing needs for Spain and Italy look far more manageable, especially with "engineered" demand from domestic champion banks and continuous ECB bond purchases.

A supporting table, "Table 1: Crisis management, by any means necessary," highlights additional policy shifts aiding this stabilization. Key initiatives include the relaxation of ECB collateral lending rules, efforts by finance ministers Schauble and Baroin to water down certain Basel III standards, and a directive allowing EU banks to cover a €115 billion capital shortfall through earnings rather than dilutive rights offerings. Other measures feature the dilution of Maastricht 2.0 deficit constraints, the proposed creation of a European rating agency, treating EBA stress tests and mark-to-market valuations for sovereign bonds as a one-time event, and halving the bank reserve requirement ratios from 2% to 1%.

This page from the publication analyzes the low levels of stock dispersion in the US market alongside the deepening financial crisis and capital flight in Europe. 

In the first section, the author highlights that 2011 was a year of "slim pickings" for active stock pickers. A table titled "Stock dispersion in 2011: slim pickins" outlines the dispersion of calendar year stock returns by sector. For the S&P 500 overall, the 2011 dispersion was just 23%, far below the 20-year average of 34% and close to the 20-year minimum of 21%. Technology stood at 26% dispersion compared to its historical average of 46%, and Utilities fell to 14%. The accompanying line chart, "Stock dispersion and active equity management," tracks the relationship between S&P 500 stock dispersion and the percentage of Large Cap Core managers beating their benchmark from 1991 to 2011. The chart shows a strong positive correlation, revealing that as stock dispersion collapsed toward its lows in 2011, the share of active managers beating their benchmark plummeted to around 20%.

The second half of the page focus on "strange days" in Europe, where the author argues that the European Central Bank (ECB) is the only force keeping Spain and Italy in the Eurozone. A line chart titled "A proxy for intra-European capital flight" shows the year-over-year percentage changes of M2 money supply from 2003 to 2011, comparing the Core (Germany, France, Netherlands, and Finland) against the Periphery (Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece, and Spain). While Core M2 growth rose to around 5% by late 2011, Periphery M2 imploded to roughly -3%, indicating massive capital flight out of southern Europe. 

To offset this, the ECB has expanded its balance sheet aggressively, represented metaphorically by Gustave Doré’s 1875 watercolor "Scene from Gargantua." The area chart "ECB support to European banks and sovereigns" shows that total ECB support approached 1 trillion EUR by late 2011. This support was increasingly driven by repos to periphery banks and Purchases of Periphery Bonds (SMP), while repo funding to core banks shrank. 

Finally, the chart "Holdings of government bonds by Euro area banks" reveals that despite this intervention, commercial banks are not buying sovereign debt. Following the first longer-term refinancing operation in late 2008, bank holdings of government bonds had surged from 1.2 trillion EUR to over 1.4 trillion EUR. However, by late 2011, holdings had reversed course, dropping from a peak near 1.6 trillion EUR to roughly 1.45 trillion EUR. The author poses the open question of whether the ECB's massive intervention is buying valuable time for Spain and Italy to reform, or if it is simply shifting private sector losses onto the public balance sheet.

This J.P. Morgan report presents a playful metaphorical "medical check-up" on the United States economy in early 2012, treating the nation as a patient residing at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. The analysis observes that, similar to the early months of 2011, the country's economic expansion is gathering momentum. Positive signs include improving job prospects, rising consumer confidence, decreasing delinquency rates, expanding credit flow, and elevated activity in vehicle sales, rail, and freight. However, the author notes a potential vulnerability: the increased inclination to spend appears driven by lower savings rates rather than rising earned income. 

Nine charts support this diagnosis. A chart on vehicle sales shows a rebound from a recession low of 9 million seasonally adjusted annual rate units in 2009 back up to around 14 million by early 2012. Loan growth has also turned around, with year-over-year commercial and industrial loans and small business lending both recovering from deep declines of negative 25% in 2009 to solid positive territory by late 2011, with commercial and industrial loans exceeding 10% growth. Concurrently, credit card and mortgage delinquency rates are improving; 90-plus day delinquent credit cards fell from a peak near 3.0% in late 2009 to around 1.7% by late 2011, while the share of always-current mortgages transitioning to delinquent non-agency mortgages fell from a peak of 2.0% to about 1.0%.

In the labor market, the four-week moving average of initial jobless claims steadily declined from nearly 675,000 in early 2009 to approximately 375,000 by early 2012. A payroll chart reveals a stark divergence in the recovery: while total payrolls excluding construction, government, and finance climbed back from 94 million up to nearly 98 million, employment within those three cyclical sectors remained flat near 35 million. 

Logistics and trade indicators show a strong parallel recovery. An index of railroad and trucking stocks indicates substantial rebounds from their 2009 lows, with railroads in particular surging from around 300 to nearly 800. In manufacturing, the ISM index for both new orders and export orders rebounded from sub-30 contraction levels in late 2008 to sit comfortably in the mid-50s by early 2012. The economy-wide ISM service sector survey shows a similar trajectory, recovering from under 40 to above 55. Finally, year-over-year growth in US retail chain store sales recovered from a decline of nearly 2% in late 2008 to steady positive territory fluctuating between 1% and 4% by early 2012.

The page concludes with a humorous prescription list addressing the nation's structural physical health challenges. These include a prescription of Xenical for weight loss, noting that the US is the world's most obese country with 34% of adults affected; Lipitor for cholesterol, noting that cholesterol-reducing agents are the most common prescription medication in the country, taken by 11.4% of the population; and antibiotics like Zithromax, noting that the US ranks in the top five countries globally for per capita antibiotic prescriptions.

This page presents an economic checkup on the United States, framing the country as a medical patient suffering from structural dependencies. The patient is diagnosed with several key addictions, including ultra-loose monetary policy via free money from the Federal Reserve, cheap labor to pad corporate bottom lines, government transfers to households, imported energy, and a heavy reliance on a single company, Apple. If inflation rises, the analysis suggests the patient will face the uncomfortable remedy of monetary tightening. On energy, despite progress in refined petroleum exports, the US remains highly reliant on imports for crude oil, importing eight to nine million barrels per day, alongside heavy imports of natural gas, electricity, and uranium oxide.

To support these observations, the page features six charts. The first chart, tracking market expectations of future policy rates from January 2012 to January 2015, shows that market-implied expectations for interest rates fell significantly between October 2011 and January 2012, shifting downward toward the Federal Reserve's median expectation of keeping rates near zero percent. 

The second chart measures labor costs as a percentage of corporate sales from 1947 to 2010. Historically fluctuating between 62 percent and nearly 70 percent, this ratio plummeted after 2003, bottoming out near 61 percent by 2010, illustrating how suppressed wage growth has subsidized corporate profit margins. 

The third chart highlights net energy imports as a percentage of total primary energy supply from 1960 to 2010, encompassing fossil fuels, nuclear, hydro, and other renewables. Imports rose from around 6 percent in 1960 to a peak of nearly 28 percent in the mid-2000s, before retracing to roughly 22 percent by 2010. 

The fourth chart monitors government transfers to households as a percentage of disposable income from 1960 to 2010. This dependency metric rose from under 7 percent in 1960 to hover around 15 percent for decades, before spiking sharply to over 20 percent following the 2008 financial crisis. 

The final two charts focus on the distorting impact of Apple on corporate earnings. One chart compares S&P 500 year-over-year earnings growth by quarter in 2011 with and without Apple. In the fourth quarter of 2011, overall S&P 500 earnings growth was roughly 4.5 percent with Apple, but was virtually flat at 0 percent without it. This concentration of growth is further emphasized in a final chart comparing S&P 500 tech earnings per share indexed to December 31, 2010. With Apple, tech earnings per share rose to an index value of approximately 107 by December 2011, whereas without Apple, tech earnings per share actually contracted, falling to an index value of approximately 97.

This page presents a fiscal health check-up for the United States, creatively framed as a medical diagnosis for a patient residing at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. Author Michael Cembalest argues that the nation's long-term economic prognosis is concerning because it attempts to combine a European welfare state with a libertarian tax policy. 

The centerpiece visual is a chart detailing US long-term debt scenarios, plotting net debt to GDP as a percentage from 2004 to projected levels in 2022. The chart compares four trajectories. The CBO Baseline, which assumes tax rates return to 2001 levels, the AMT exemption is no longer indexed to inflation, and scheduled Medicare and Budget Control Act cuts proceed, is the only scenario where debt-to-GDP declines, dropping from around 74 percent in 2012 to approximately 60 percent by 2022. In contrast, the Realistic Case—which extends income tax cuts, indexes the AMT, and avoids Medicare cuts—projects net debt rising to nearly 90 percent of GDP. The CBO Alternative Case, which also shelves automatic Budget Control Act cuts and extends various tax incentives, pushes debt past 95 percent of GDP by 2022. The chart also indicates that the administration's Tax the Rich proposals, while helpful, would only modestly reduce these alternative trajectories, leaving the overall debt burden on an unsustainable upward path.

To contextualize the spending dynamics, two smaller line charts display spending as a percentage of GDP from 1972 to 2022. The mandatory spending and interest costs chart shows a steady climb from under 9 percent in 1972 to a projected high of over 16 percent by 2022 under the baseline case. Conversely, the discretionary spending chart shows a dramatic decline from its peak of around 10 percent of GDP in the late 1970s down to a projected 40-year low of under 6 percent by 2022. 

Cembalest highlights that since discretionary spending is already slated to fall to historic lows, stabilizing the debt will require politically difficult choices, such as broad tax increases, entitlement cuts, or ending the deductibility of state, local, and mortgage interest taxes. He also discusses monetary policy, pointing out that since Operation Twist began in October 2011, the Federal Reserve has effectively monetized 90 percent of all 20-year and 30-year Treasury issuance. While current demand for US Treasuries remains strong—supported by Asian and Middle Eastern central banks, deposit-heavy US commercial banks, and pension buyers—Cembalest cautions that this favorable demand environment is a recessive gene that could mutate without warning if structural deficit issues are not addressed.

This page presents a diagnostic assessment of the United States housing and consumer sectors, framed as a medical check-up for the country. The author argues that while historic affordability and significant pent-up demand favor a housing recovery, several headwinds persist. These include the overhang of shadow inventory, widespread negative equity, and tighter mortgage credit, as seen in average prime mortgage FICO scores rising from 725 to 775. Despite these challenges, the analysis suggests new home sales and housing starts have bottomed, and a rebound in durable goods purchases is likely.

The first chart, tracking pent-up demand through household formation versus trend in millions of households from 1990 to 2010, shows a severe deficit starting in 2006. This metric bottomed near negative 1.5 million households around 2008 before rebounding sharply to nearly 1 million by late 2011, signaling substantial deferred demand.

The second chart displays the housing affordability index from 1995 to 2011, which measures the ratio of median family income to the amount necessary to purchase a median-priced home with a twenty percent down payment. After falling to a low near 100 in 2006, the index surged to a historic high near 200 by late 2011, indicating that housing has become highly affordable.

The third chart illustrates the shadow housing inventory from 2003 to 2011, with total units rising from approximately 3 million to a peak of over 8 million in 2010 before stabilizing. The stacked area chart breaks this down into existing inventory, loans ninety-plus days delinquent, foreclosures, bank-owned real estate, and current but underwater mortgages, illustrating the massive pool of distressed properties weighing on the market.

The fourth chart shows mortgages with negative equity as a percentage of non-agency mortgages from 2005 to 2011. This rate spiked from near zero percent in 2006 to approximately sixty percent by 2009, remaining elevated at that level through 2011.

The fifth chart compares year-over-year home price percentage changes, highlighting the difference between all sales and those excluding distressed sales. In formerly hot market states like California, Florida, Arizona, and Nevada, overall sales fell around six and a half percent, while excluding distressed sales narrowed the decline to about two and a half percent. In other large states like Texas, New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Virginia, Massachusetts, Georgia, North Carolina, Washington, and Maryland, excluding distressed sales brought price growth to zero percent. For the entire United States, excluding distressed sales reduced the price decline from four and a half percent to just one and a half percent, demonstrating that the core market is stabilizing once distressed sales are stripped out.

The final chart shows personal consumption of durable goods as a percentage of gross domestic product from 1947 to 2011. Cyclical declines pushed this ratio down to a fifty-year low of roughly seven and a half percent by 2011, leading the author to project that durable goods purchases are poised to rise.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest discusses the potential outcomes and limitations of a proposed Greece debt restructuring deal. He argues that while the deal would not provide a clean slate for Greece and will likely lead to further economic contraction due to severe austerity measures, it succeeds in ring-fencing the Eurozone by shifting Greek debt from private investors to official institutions. Because Greece represents only a small fraction of Eurozone GDP and population, its domestic economic struggles present minimal direct risk to overall European growth, especially since foreign private investment has already largely fled the country.

To illustrate this shift in debt ownership, the page features a multi-part comparative data layout. The first table shows the current composition of Greek government debt, totaling 162% of GDP. At this stage, private owners hold the largest share at 68% of GDP, followed by official lenders like the IMF, EU, and European Financial Stability Facility at 34%, the European Central Bank at 22%, Greek banks at 21%, and Greek social security funds at 14%. After accounting for transition assumptions, including a 60% haircut on face value and varying levels of participation, a second table projects the debt composition for 2013. Under these projections, the total debt drops to between 135% and 145% of GDP depending on holdout scenarios, while the share held by the IMF, EU, and EFSF rises dramatically to 94% of GDP. Meanwhile, private ownership falls to 36% of GDP, and the European Central Bank’s direct holdings drop to zero. 

The decline in foreign private exposure is further documented in a line chart showing the foreign private sector investment position in Greece from 2002 to 2011. The series illustrates a steady rise from about 75 billion Euros in 2002 to a peak of nearly 280 billion Euros around 2008, followed by a sharp collapse back to approximately 75 billion Euros by 2011, indicating that most private capital had already exited the country prior to the deal. 

An explanatory box breaks down the assumed uses of the new 130 billion Euro IMF and EU funding package. This includes 30 billion Euros for bondholder incentives, 30 billion Euros for bank recapitalization costs, 35 billion Euros to finance upcoming interest payments, and another 35 billion Euros for Greece to buy back its bonds from the European Central Bank at cost. The author notes that these allocations highlight the complicated and interconnected nature of the rescue package, which requires Greece, led by Prime Minister Lucas Papademos, to implement deeply unpopular reforms such as minimum wage cuts and public sector layoffs under the supervision of the Troika.

This page presents a Q1 medical check-up metaphor for the United States, analyzing its political polarization, economic activity, and market opportunities, particularly within the technology sector. The author diagnoses the US with a psychiatric evaluation of multiple personality disorder, driven by extreme political polarization and a lack of compromise. He also notes a warning regarding the European Central Bank, which faces potential systemic risk from one hundred seventy billion dollars in exposure to Greece. Despite weakening corporate earnings growth at the end of 2011, the author advises maintaining a regional overweight to US equities, supported by resilient economic momentum and exceptionally healthy corporate balance sheets. He highlights technology stocks as especially attractive due to strong cash generation and reasonable valuations, while advising investors to watch upcoming spring labor reports for signs of continued economic improvement.

Five charts illustrate these political and financial dynamics. The first chart, depicting Congressional polarization from 1879 to 2010, shows the degree of partisanship based on Congressional roll calls. The distance between the parties in both the House and the Senate fell to its lowest levels between 1930 and 1950, hovering between thirty and forty percent. Since then, polarization has steadily climbed, reaching historic highs by 2010 at nearly ninety percent for the House and eighty percent for the Senate. 

The second chart tracks S&P 500 consensus earnings-per-share estimates in USD from January 2009 to January 2012. The 2011 estimate rose steadily to settle near ninety-six dollars. However, the estimates for 2012 and 2013 show downward revisions in late 2011, with 2012 estimates dropping from a peak of around one hundred twelve dollars to one hundred eight dollars, and 2013 estimates sliding from one hundred twenty-five dollars to approximately one hundred twenty-one dollars, illustrating the late-year weakening in earnings expectations.

The third chart compares the forward price-to-earnings multiples of the S&P 500 and the S&P 500 Tech Index from 1995 to 2010. During the dot-com bubble around 2000, the technology index traded at a massive premium, with its multiple peaking near seventy while the broader S&P 500 peaked around twenty-five. Over the subsequent decade, this premium completely evaporated, and by 2010, both series converged at a multiple of roughly thirteen to fifteen, showing that tech stocks no longer carry a valuation premium.

The fourth chart explains this tech sector attractiveness by comparing cash flow and capital expenditure from 1994 to 2010. Capital expenditure as a percentage of operating income peaked at nearly sixty-five percent in 2001 and fell to around twenty percent by 2010. Meanwhile, the free cash flow margin as a percentage of sales climbed from near zero in 2002 to over twenty percent in 2010.

The final chart tracks US corporate cash balances as a ratio of cash and equivalents to tangible assets from 1952 to 2010. This cash ratio bottomed out near five percent around 1980 but has since risen consistently, accelerating through the 2000s to reach more than thirteen percent by 2010, signaling a multi-decade high in corporate liquidity.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication analyzes the broader structural challenges in the Eurozone, questioning what a potential "Greece deal" can realistically achieve and emphasizing that the core issue has shifted from sovereign liquidity to fundamental economic growth and structural imbalances.

The first section examines whether Spain and Italy can achieve economic growth following a temporary rally in credit spreads. A chart on the left details Italian and Spanish ten-year government bond yields from 2005 to early 2012. It reveals that after years of staying below 5.0%, yields for both countries spiked dramatically starting in late 2010, with Italy’s yield peaking near 7.5% and Spain’s surpassing 6.5% in late 2011. Although yields moderated slightly by early 2012, they remained historically high. The adjacent chart of seasonally adjusted manufacturing PMI surveys from 2005 to 2012 illustrates why growth remains a concern. Using the 50-level mark to separate expansion from contraction, the chart shows that while both Italy and Spain rebounded from their 2008–2009 recession lows of around 30 to briefly expand in 2010, both manufacturing sectors fell back into contraction by early 2012, with Italy around 45 and Spain dropping even lower.

The second section addresses the political and structural constraints within the Eurozone, focusing on France and peripheral nations. The bottom-left chart, titled "Could Hollande cope with a 3% deficit constraint?", tracks the French budget deficit as a percentage of GDP from 1980 to 2010. It shows that France has rarely stayed within the proposed "Maastricht 2.0 ceinture de chasteté" (chastity belt) of a 3% deficit. French deficits plummeted to nearly -7.5% of GDP around 2009, highlighting the severe fiscal tightening François Hollande would have to navigate to meet these new rules. 

To the right, a final chart demonstrates how the creation of the Euro ushered in massive private-sector imbalances. It compares the current account deficits as a percentage of GDP for two groups from 1975 to 2008: a core group (France, Germany, and the United Kingdom) and a peripheral group (Greece, Italy, Ireland, Portugal, and Spain). Before the Euro exchange rates were fixed around 1999, both groups tracked closely together, fluctuating between -2% and 2% of GDP. Following the monetary union, however, a massive divergence occurred: while the core group maintained a balanced current account, the peripheral nations sank into a collective current account deficit of nearly -7% of GDP by 2008.

At the bottom, the page defines key terminology relevant to the ongoing sovereign debt negotiations, including the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA), Credit Default Swaps (CDS), Collective Action Clauses (CAC), and Private Sector Involvement (PSI).

Michael Cembalest comments on oil markets, Iran, and energy policy by quoting a press release from House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi. In the press release, Pelosi blames Wall Street speculators and oil companies for high gasoline prices while praising the Obama administration's efforts to expand domestic energy resources. Avoiding direct political commentary, Cembalest instead presents four charts to highlight the economic and scientific realities behind US oil imports, OPEC spare capacity, retail gasoline pricing, and speculative activity.

The first chart plots US net imports of crude oil in millions of barrels per day from 1920 to 2010, posing the question of how much of a dent rising domestic production from shale and deepwater Gulf wells has actually made. The data shows that while net imports have ticked down from their mid-2000s peak of over 10 million barrels per day, they remained high at around 9 million barrels per day in 2010, illustrating that substantial import dependency persists.

The second chart displays the OPEC crude oil utilization rate as a percentage from 1980 to 2010. Cembalest observes that Iran accounts for 3% to 4% of global oil exports. If Iranian exports were offline, OPEC's utilization rate would approach 98%, indicating a highly sensitive global oil market with almost no safety margin. 

The third chart tracks Brent crude oil prices in USD per barrel against the US average for all grades of retail gasoline in USD per gallon from 1994 to 2010. The chart demonstrates a near-perfect historical correlation between the two, revealing that retail gasoline prices are not artificially detached or out of whack but are instead tightly bound to the price of international crude.

The fourth chart examines the debasement of cash and speculative oil contracts from 1999 to 2010 to show the impact of aggressive monetary expansion on investor appetite for real assets. It plots aggregate central bank balance sheets for Japan, the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Switzerland as a percentage of aggregate GDP alongside net WTI crude oil non-commercial contracts outstanding. As central bank balance sheets ballooned from around 12% of GDP in 2007 to over 24% by 2011, speculative net non-commercial contracts outstanding surged in tandem, peaking near 250,000 contracts.

In this analysis, the author evaluates the impact of the European Central Bank’s first unlimited bank lending program, LTRO #1, arguing that while its long-term effect on European economies remains an open question, it has acted as a powerful stabilizing force for global equity markets. The intervention has successfully reopened bank debt markets, lowered sovereign spreads, and prompted well-bid bond auctions, though Italy and Spain remain in recession and are only a fraction of the way toward meeting their 2012 funding goals. The author suggests that Germany has effectively capitulated to prevent worst-case outcomes by potentially allowing the European Stability Mechanism and European Financial Stability Facility to run in parallel, and posits that further LTRO interventions remain an open possibility.

This stabilizing market reaction is illustrated in a chart titled MSCI World Equities, which plots the index level from July 1 through February 24. The chart highlights a dramatic drop in market turbulence following the December 21 LTRO announcement, with average weekly volatility falling from a pre-LTRO level of 27% to a post-LTRO level of 10% as the index recovered from its autumn lows of roughly 1,070 to reach 1,300 by late February. 

A second narrative focuses on how cheap equities had become by late 2011 amid exaggerated macro risks and massive sidelined cash balances. This valuation extreme is depicted in a long-term chart titled Real S&P 500 earnings yield, which measures the S&P 500 earnings yield minus core CPI from 1956 through early 2012. The chart features two critical milestones: a peak yield near 7% on September 30, 2011, which marked a period of extreme cheapness, and a slightly lower but still historically high yield of approximately 5.5% on February 28, 2012. 

The author concludes that central banks intervened to avert a systemic collapse, and while some fear a future inflation tax, current excess manufacturing and labor capacity are still high enough that central bankers are unlikely to tighten policy soon. Key entities discussed include the European Central Bank, the European Stability Mechanism, the European Financial Stability Facility, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Empirical Research Partners, and nations facing financial or political transition, including Germany, Spain, Italy, Ireland, and Greece.

This page analyzes the shift in market valuations following Europe's retreat from immediate sovereign default risks in early 2012. The author argues that valuations have shifted from catastrophic to simply inexpensive, supporting continued equity exposure. This valuation trend is illustrated in a chart of S&P 500 price-to-earnings multiples from 1960 to 2012, which shows trailing P/E multiples rising from 12 to 14 since late 2011, with forward P/Es rising from 10 to approximately 12. To highlight broader economic conditions, a line chart titled "Weakness in US ex. auto consumer demand" plots three-month rolling, quarter-on-quarter annualized growth from 2007 to 2012. This chart compares overall consumer spending with spending excluding autos, showing a clear divergence where spending excluding automobiles dipped near zero percent by early 2012, signaling underlying consumer fragility. 

The discussion then focuses heavily on Europe as the primary catalyst for the market rally, though it remains a structural vulnerability. Despite political tensions—specifically Bundesbank head Jens Weidmann expressing concerns to ECB head Mario Draghi about permanent ECB financing and declining collateral standards, and former ECB member Stark calling the balance sheet shocking—the author views Weidmann as a paper tiger who will ultimately fail to change ECB policy. 

To visualize the scale of the ECB's intervention, a chart designed by Chief Economist Michael Vaknin titled "The ECB: financing a rush for the exits" measures the periphery balance of payments excluding ECB support in billions of euros from 2003 to 2015. Historical blue bars show a massive deficit drop reaching nearly negative 350 billion euros in 2011, with red triangles highlighting the massive scale of emergency ECB lending to periphery banks that financed these capital outflows. Projections through 2015, shown as yellow bars, assume a gradual closure of the current account deficit but indicate that significant ECB financing will still be required in the interim to handle maturing foreign debt positions. 

Finally, a stacked bar chart titled "Bank funding: ECB still a small component" analyzes Italian and Spanish banking sector liabilities using data from Bridgewater Associates. The chart demonstrates that despite the focus on emergency central bank lending, the ECB portion remains a very small component at the top of overall liabilities. Instead, local interbank markets and especially retail deposits, which account for roughly 50% to 60% of total liabilities, remain the dominant funding sources for both Italian and Spanish banks.

This page analyzes the state of the economic recovery in the United States, focusing on the tension between positive labor market signals and the unprecedented scale of the federal budget deficit supporting the rebound. The author argues that despite seasonal adjustments and underlying weaknesses, US job markets and consumer spending are gradually improving. While the Federal Reserve is expected to keep stimulus in place to sustain a 2.25% GDP growth rate, the recovery's sustainability is questioned due to the massive primary budget deficit. 

The first visual is a table titled "The importance of the US consumer," which highlights components of GDP in billions of USD as of the fourth quarter of 2010. It underscores that US households are the largest economic force globally, showing US private consumption at 10,417 billion USD, which is larger than the total private consumption of Europe (9,670 billion USD) or Asia (8,231 billion USD, with China at 1,969 billion USD and Japan at 3,501 billion USD). Additional US figures include investment of 1,818 billion USD, government spending of 3,020 billion USD, and net exports at negative 500 billion USD. 

The second visual is a line chart titled "In past cycles, claims were a great market signal," plotting continuing claims as a percentage of the labor force from 1967 to 2012. The chart demonstrates that in the prior three business cycles, when continuing claims fell through a 2.2% threshold (indicated by arrows in 1982, 1993, and 2003), it marked an ideal time to add risk to investment portfolios. The chart indicates that the US recently crossed through this 2.2% barrier again in early 2012, signaling the potential for a self-sustaining business cycle. 

However, the author contrasts this optimistic signal with a third visual, a line chart titled "Paging Dick Cheney: Do Deficits Matter?" which tracks the seasonally adjusted primary budget deficit (excluding interest) as a percentage of GDP from 1954 to 2012. This chart reveals that during previous recoveries where jobless claims crossed the 2.2% threshold, the deficit was comparatively mild. In contrast, the current recovery is supported by an extraordinary deficit that dipped to nearly negative 10% of GDP around 2009–2010 and remains deeply negative. 

The author poses the open question of when this primary deficit will begin to constrain financial markets, suggesting it will only matter when treasury bond demand falters or when the economic cost of closing the deficit becomes too high. Footnotes on the page elaborate on labor market distortions analyzed by Chief Economist Michael Vaknin, noting that adjusted payroll growth remains positive but weak. The footnotes also address the rigor of the Fed's US bank stress tests, which simulated losses worse than those in 2008 and comparable to the Great Depression, concluding that US financial institutions are on much firmer footing than their European counterparts.

In this commentary, J.P. Morgan's Chief Investment Officer, Michael Cembalest, outlines the firm's moderate investment approach in a market characterized by exaggerated risks, high levels of sidelined cash, and cheap corporate earnings. Rather than taking extreme positions, the firm splits the difference by keeping equity allocations slightly below normal levels, holding about 35 percent public and private equity in its Balanced portfolio alongside a 22 percent allocation to hedge funds, with the remainder in credit and commodities. Cembalest defends this middle-ground stance against both hyper-optimistic and hyper-pessimistic clients who foresee economic Armageddon.

To illustrate the unprecedented policy environment supporting this market, the first chart, titled "Not on my watch," plots the aggregate balance sheets of the central banks of Japan, the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Switzerland as a percentage of aggregate GDP from 1999 through early 2012. The chart shows that aggregate balance sheets hovered between 10 percent and 13 percent of GDP for nearly a decade before skyrocketing after the 2008 financial crisis, peaking at nearly 28 percent in early 2012. This spike includes quantitative easing programs from the Bank of Japan (valued at 37 trillion yen) and the Bank of England (valued at 50 billion pounds), alongside the European Central Bank's Long-Term Refinancing Operations (LTRO).

This massive liquidity injection has fueled what Cembalest describes as a different kind of stock market rally, analyzed in the second chart, "Goldilocks indeed: a different kind of stock market rally." This chart tracks the 1,000-day cumulative price returns for both the S&P 500 (in blue) and gold (in red) during historical periods when the S&P 500 gained over 75 percent, comparing the mid-1980s, the late 1990s, and the rally leading into 2012. Historically, during major stock market booms, gold returns were flat or negative, dropping to around negative 20 percent in the late 1990s. In the post-2009 rally, however, both the S&P 500 and gold have risen dramatically, with gold returning a positive 20 percent to 40 percent. This simultaneous rise indicates that while investors are enthusiastic about stock gains, they remain highly concerned about the risks of the central bank solution.

Looking ahead, Cembalest notes that while the global economy faces structural headwinds like retrenching household balance sheets, large public deficits, and weak labor and housing markets, central bank money-printing is designed to facilitate a gradual healing process rather than a destructive liquidation crisis. He is pessimistic about Peripheral Europe, predicting that cyclically-adjusted current account deficits reveal lingering competitiveness gaps that will require years of painful deflationary austerity to resolve. Ultimately, the author advocates for a balanced, "all things in moderation" portfolio strategy, remaining neutral between declaring a new bull market and predicting central bank failure.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s commentary discusses the fundamental role of energy in global economic growth and the investment dynamics of publicly tradable energy stocks. The author argues that despite fierce debates over fossil fuel externalities, the global economy will remain carbon-driven for the foreseeable future because oil and natural gas are too central to be easily disintermediated. A footnote highlights the limitations of renewable energy, citing Spain’s recent regulatory proposals to halt solar construction to save costs, and noting that profitable US solar and wind projects often rely on heavy subsidies and contracts priced two to three times above wholesale power rates. 

To support the link between energy and economic progress, the page features two historical charts. The first, US primary energy consumption by source, plotted in quadrillion BTUs from 1805 to 2010, shows how US energy consumption grew to nearly 100 quadrillion BTUs. Coal dominated the 19th century, while petroleum and natural gas grew rapidly to dominate the 20th century, with renewables representing only a small fraction of the total. Side-by-side with this is a chart of US per capita GDP in real constant thousands of dollars from 1800 to 2000. It shows an accelerating upward climb from near-zero to approximately $30,000 per capita, illustrating how rising living standards historically mirrored rising primary energy consumption.

The discussion then shifts to the investment performance of publicly tradable energy stocks. The author notes that after underperforming from 1980 to 2000, energy equities rebounded in the 2000s due to rising non-OECD growth, higher crude prices, and declining spare capacity. However, energy stocks remain highly volatile—the second highest behind financials—and face constraints such as capital expenditures that are 50% higher than the market average relative to depreciation. Furthermore, rising replacement costs for oil, potential environmental liabilities, and political risks like windfall profit taxes restrict returns on equity. 

These dynamics are illustrated in two additional charts. The relative performance of the Energy sector chart shows the two-year rolling relative return of energy stocks against the top 1500 US stocks by market capitalization from 1971 to 2008. This volatile history shows massive outperformance spikes of over 50% in the late 1970s and mid-2000s, contrasted with steep underperformance of down to negative 50% during the 1980s and 1990s. The final chart, Global oil consumption, tracks demand in million barrels per day from 1965 to 2010 across three segments. OECD consumption peaked near 48 million barrels per day in 2005 before falling to around 45 million barrels per day by 2010. Conversely, Non-OECD consumption climbed continuously from under 10 million barrels per day in 1965 to over 40 million barrels per day in 2010, nearly catching up to OECD levels. A separate line for the Asia-Pacific region excluding China shows much slower growth, rising from 5 million to about 18 million barrels per day over the same period, highlighting that China has been the primary driver of expanding global oil demand.

This page of the publication, titled "Reservoir Digs: on energy investing and private equity," analyzes global oil consumption, inventory dynamics, valuation metrics, and the performance and volatility of various energy sub-sectors. The author argues that while non-OECD oil consumption is rising, oil intensity is declining globally. If energy efficiency improves and countries in the Middle East and Asia reduce domestic gasoline subsidies, global oil demand could drop by one to two million barrels per day. Such a demand drop, given tight global supplies, could push oil prices down to eighty-five to ninety dollars per barrel, which is currently where equity markets seem to forecast long-term oil prices.

To support these arguments, the page presents several charts. The first chart, titled "Oil intensity declining worldwide," plots billions of barrels per real GDP in constant 2000 USD trillions from 1980 to 2010. It shows that non-OECD oil intensity has steadily declined from approximately 0.27% in 1980 to 0.17% in 2010. Meanwhile, the world average declined from about 0.13% to 0.08%, and OECD intensity dropped from 0.08% to 0.05%. The second chart, "Global oil inventories to build (modestly) in 2012," measures days of demand from 2000 to 2012. It shows days of demand peaking near fifty-seven days in 2002, dropping to about thirty-seven days in 2011, and forecasting a modest recovery to around forty-two days in late 2012.

The text goes on to explain that energy valuations are historically inexpensive because the market is hesitant to assume oil prices will remain sustainably above one hundred dollars per barrel. To illustrate this, a third chart shows the S&P 500 Energy sector's enterprise value to trailing twelve-month EBITDA from January 1993 to late 2011. This multiple peaked near ten in the late 1990s and early 2000s, crashed to under four in late 2008, and recovered to approximately six by late 2011. 

A fourth chart details the "Total return of S&P 500 Energy sub-industries" from 2002 to 2012, indexed to one hundred starting on January 1, 2002. This chart tracks exploration and production (E&P), equipment and services, refining, drilling, and integrated majors. E&P performed the best, peaking near five hundred fifty in 2008 and ending near four hundred fifty in 2012. In contrast, drilling and integrated majors underperformed, with drilling ending near one hundred fifty and integrated majors finishing near two hundred fifty.

Finally, the fifth chart shows the "Average annual stock price volatility of S&P 500 industries" from March 2002 to March 2012. It ranks various industries by their average annual volatility percentage. The energy equipment, services, and drilling industry is the most volatile of all S&P industries, topping the chart at nearly thirty-seven percent volatility. In contrast, the integrated oils and E&P sub-sector sits in the middle of the pack at approximately twenty-four percent volatility, falling below sectors like diversified financials, metals and mining, and semiconductors, but remaining well above low-volatility consumer sectors like food products, which sits near sixteen percent.

This page, titled "Reservoir Digs: on energy investing and private equity," discusses US natural gas dynamics, the potential for export markets, and enhanced oil recovery (EOR) techniques. The text highlights a recent transaction in the Permian Basin where a manager purchased gas-heavy shale fields with 31 million barrels of proven reserves with plans to shift the mix toward an even split of 50% oil and 50% dry gas to capitalize on the current oil-gas price discrepancy. US natural gas spot prices sit around $2.25 per mcf, down from a peak of $13 in 2008, driven by a severe supply glut. While European gas prices are five to six times higher, US exports are hindered by high shipping costs and a lack of LNG terminals. Domestically, gas continues to displace coal, with natural gas's electricity generation share rising by 10% since 1997, and an expected 30 GW of coal capacity projected to go offline by 2017. Additionally, the author addresses fracking risks, suggesting that standard safeguards will eventually be established and that natural gas's environmental footprint is minor compared to coal mining.

The second half of the page covers EOR techniques, pointing out that while some scientists believe recovery factors can double or triple, realistic post-tertiary recovery levels are closer to 45% to 50%. This is accompanied by a table detailing potential oil recovery efficiencies of original oil in place. Under primary methods, recovery ranges from 5% for liquid and rock expansion to 60% for water influx. Secondary methods, such as gas re-injection and water flooding, can achieve up to 70% efficiency, while tertiary methods, including thermal, miscible, and chemical processes, can reach up to 80%. 

A multi-decade line chart illustrates the real-world application of these methods at Shell's Denver Unit in West Texas, the world's largest CO2 injection project. Plotting production in barrels per day on a logarithmic scale from 1,000 to over 1,000,000 from 1938 to 1998, the chart shows that oil production declined following its primary and secondary water injection phases. However, the introduction of tertiary CO2 injection stabilized oil production, creating a marked EOR wedge of incremental oil. In 2010, the project produced 31,500 barrels of oil per day, with 26,000 barrels representing incremental gains from CO2 injection. The author notes that even a minor 1% increase in global recovery factors would yield nearly 90 billion barrels of oil, representing about three years of global production.

This page of the publication, titled "Reservoir Digs: on energy investing and private equity," examines the hurdles of investing in energy infrastructure, specifically focusing on pipelines, equipment, and the oil services sector. 

The author starts by explaining that while pipelines are economically attractive—costing around four times cash flow to build and selling for eight to ten times once operational—navigating the regulatory approval process is exceptionally difficult. This is illustrated by a pipeline project submitted to Canada's National Energy Board and the North Dakota Public Service Commission. The application includes strict environmental constraints, such as halting construction if an endangered whooping crane from the Aransas Wood Buffalo Population is spotted within one mile, or halting work near sharp-tailed grouse and nesting piping plovers during specific dates and times. Despite these hurdles, the author notes that natural gas pipeline development is highly established. 

To illustrate this, a map of the US Natural Gas Pipeline Network from the Energy Information Administration in 2009 is provided, displaying the extensive web of interstate and intrastate pipelines spanning the country. The 80 miles planned for this new project would represent just a 0.026 percent addition to the existing 305,000 miles of pipelines in the US.

To the right of the map, a line chart titled "Rig count supportive of oil services" displays the number of rotary rigs from February 1999 to late 2011, sourced from Bloomberg and Baker Hughes. The chart plots two data series: the World Oil and Gas rotary rig count and the US Oil and Gas rotary rig count. Both series show a general upward trend that peaked in late 2008, with the world count near 3,500 and the US count near 2,000. Both series fell sharply during the global financial crisis before recovering steadily by late 2011, with the world count approaching 3,500 and the US count returning to nearly 2,000.

Under the heading "Equipment and oil services: some diamonds in the rough, but riskier than you might think," the commentary details how the equipment and services sector is highly volatile and sensitive to commodity prices, despite rising global rig counts. The author makes a distinction between production, midstream, and exploration services, noting that production and midstream services sustain demand even when new drilling halts. However, public companies like Exterran, Tetra, and Helix have historically underperformed. 

The text highlights a private equity play where a J.P. Morgan manager invested in a competitor to Exterran specializing in high-powered natural gas compression services. Because dry gas prices are low, operators prefer to lease rather than buy this equipment to handle the massive volume of shale gas being produced. This specialized company enjoys operating margins above 50 percent by avoiding lower-margin fabrication and marketing businesses, though the author cautions that navigating the industry's inherent cyclicality remains essential for long-term success.

This page, titled "Appendix B: natural gas fracking and seismic risks," is part of a broader commentary on energy investing and private equity. Author Michael Cembalest discusses key insights from a session with scientists at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory regarding the seismic and environmental risks of hydraulic fracturing. The primary argument is that the actual process of hydraulic fracturing creates extremely small microearthquakes that are generally harmless, while the larger, more noticeable seismic events are instead linked to the subsequent re-injection of used fracking fluids into disposal wells. The text highlights occurrences of larger quakes in states like Ohio, Texas, Colorado, Arkansas, and Oklahoma—the latter of which experienced a 5.7 magnitude earthquake—and points out that operators can choose less risky locations for fluid disposal, as demonstrated by Pennsylvania trucking its wastewater to Ohio. Additionally, the author notes that managing reservoir pressure and slowing re-injection flow rates, as seen in experiments in Rangely, California, can reduce seismic activity. Regarding groundwater safety, the page explains that fracking takes place 4,000 to 8,500 feet below the surface, separated from drinking water aquifers (which lie above 850 feet) by half a mile of rock. Thus, the real risk to groundwater stems from wellbore cement failures or surface spills during transport and storage, rather than subterranean migration. 

An accompanying bar chart, "C. Distribution of Magnitudes of Microseismic Events," illustrates the minor scale of direct fracking-induced tremors. The chart plots the cumulative number of microseismic events on a logarithmic vertical axis from 1 to 10,000 against Richter scale magnitudes on the horizontal axis ranging from -3.6 to -1.4. The data shows that the vast majority of these events are tiny, with cumulative counts exceeding 1,000 for magnitudes around -3.6 and dropping sharply to single digits as the magnitude approaches -1.4, reinforcing the point that these events are negligible without sensitive monitoring equipment. Sources cited at the bottom include publications from the National Energy Technology Laboratory, the University of Texas at Austin, and the Worldwatch Institute.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the difficulty of predicting when economic and monetary imbalances will trigger market corrections. He draws historical parallels, comparing the current serene S&P 500 rally to similarly calm periods in March 1987 and November 1928, both of which occurred shortly before historic market crashes. While noting that post-2007 economies have resolved many imbalances, he cautions that markets are often caught unaware, citing how the August 2011 market drop was triggered by a US credit downgrade rather than European debt issues. 

Despite these structural risks, institutional optimism has reached a new post-recession peak, alongside a rise in corporate insider selling. Cembalest observes that current equity valuations are not overly demanding, as illustrated by two valuation charts. The first chart, "Real S&P 500 earnings yield," displays the earnings yield less core CPI from 1973 to 2012, showing that the current real yield is healthy at around 5% compared to negative levels seen in the late 1970s and 2000. The second chart, "S&P 500 price to earnings multiple," tracks the price to next twelve months operating EPS from 1985 to 2012, showing that the current multiple of approximately 13x is far below its peak of over 24 during the tech bubble. 

To sustain the current rally, Cembalest notes that strong earnings growth is required, highlighting that Apple alone offset 40% of the decline in estimated S&P earnings for the year. In the chart "Global earnings revisions vs. global equities" from 2008 to 2012, the ratio of upgrades minus downgrades (left axis) is plotted against the MSCI World Index (right axis). The visual indicates that while global negative revisions have slowed, Q4 2012 S&P 500 earnings expectations remain ambitiously high at 16% year-over-year growth. This keeps J.P. Morgan from holding maximum-risk portfolios, particularly due to ongoing economic concerns in China and Europe.

Lastly, the page addresses how government policy transmission channels can have unintended consequences. Cembalest argues that the collapse of Fannie Mae underwriting standards was driven by federal mandates rather than purely private action. The chart "A look back at the origins of the housing crisis" traces annual loan volume metrics from 1980 to 2007. It shows that HUD affordable lending targets, measured on the right axis under FHEFSSA legislation, grew from about 30% in the early 1990s to over 55% by 2007. Accompanying this regulatory push, the share of FHA and Fannie Mae home purchase volumes with a loan-to-value (LTV) or combined LTV ratio of 97% or greater, measured on the left axis, ballooned from nearly 0% in the early 1990s to almost 35% by 2007. The author concludes that this government-mandated underwriting corrosion paved the way for private sector banks to aggressively issue bad loans, emphasizing that observers must acknowledge the impact of the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) alongside other policy tools like the Portfolio Rebalancing Channel.

This page analyzes US fiscal trends at the state and local levels, investor fund flows, and equity valuations, particularly within the banking sector. The author argues that state and local governments are making meaningful efforts to address fiscal issues, unlike the federal government, with over 40 states reducing pension liabilities through measures like higher employee contributions and raised retirement ages. Furthermore, concerns over municipal bond defaults are highly exaggerated. To support this, the text notes that from 1970 through 2011, only 71 out of 17,700 Moody’s-rated municipal issuers defaulted, boasting a 65% average recovery rate compared to just 49% for corporate senior unsecured bonds. 

A pair of charts illustrates public revenues and investor behavior. The first chart, "State and local tax revenue," displays the year-over-year percentage change of a four-quarter moving average from 2004 to 2011. It shows that state tax collections have recovered strongly, rising for seven consecutive quarters to positive territory around 5% to 10% by 2011, after bottoming near negative 10% in 2009. Meanwhile, local tax collections remain stagnant near 0% due to depressed home prices. Despite this improving economic backdrop, investors have defensively favored bonds over equities. The second chart, "US mutual fund flows," tracks cumulative flows in billions of USD from 2007 to 2012. It shows a dramatic divergence: bond fund inflows rose steadily to nearly $1 trillion by 2012, while equity flows steadily declined to around negative $250 billion.

The author contends that this shift away from equities is not driven by high valuations. The third chart, "S&P 500 ex-bubble price to earnings multiple," plots the price to next-twelve-months operating EPS from 1985 to 2012. A martini glass icon is placed over the 1998 to 2001 tech bubble peak, when multiples spiked above 24x. Excluding this bubble period, the current P/E multiple sits in the middle of its historical 25-year range at approximately 13x. 

Finally, the author highlights opportunities in US bank stocks, noting they have low capital adequacy concerns compared to European peers and do not rely on wholesale funding. This point is illustrated by the fourth chart, "US bank price to book ratio," which maps Datastream and Morgan Stanley indices from 1969 to 2010. The chart demonstrates that bank valuations have plummeted from their late-1990s peaks of over 4.0x book value down to historic lows near 1.0x, making them look highly attractive to long-term investors.

This page presents a Q&A-style analysis of United States debt dynamics, comparing historical post-World War II debt reduction strategies against modern entitlement challenges and the growing fiscal burden of state and local pension systems. The author uses the metaphor of the 1951 science fiction novel The Day of the Triffids to argue that seemingly benign economic scenarios can lead to severe, unforeseen consequences. To illustrate how hindsight can blind policymakers, a footnote highlights a 2007 article by Austan Goolsbee, former Chairman of the Council of Economic Advisors, who praised the rise of subprime lending just prior to the financial crisis. 

The primary historical argument focuses on how the United States managed to reduce its net debt from 80 percent of GDP in 1950 to 46 percent by 1960. A table titled "1950's debt reduction was based on growth, not austerity" tracks annual indicators from 1950 to 1960. It reveals that the absolute level of nominal net debt remained relatively flat, rising from $219 billion to $237 billion at a compound annual growth rate of just 0.8 percent. Instead of austerity, the debt-to-GDP ratio was reduced by robust economic expansion, with nominal GDP growing at a compound annual rate of 6.6 percent (4.3 percent in real terms) from $273 billion to $519 billion. During this period, government outlays and receipts as a percentage of GDP stayed balanced, generally fluctuating between 14 percent and 21 percent. The author cautions that the unique tailwinds of the 1950s—such as the creation of the interstate highway system, the rebuilding of Europe and Japan, and a lack of severe entitlement liabilities—cannot easily be replicated today, leaving the nation vulnerable to long-term debt burdens without a new productivity boom.

The focus then shifts to state and local governments, where more than $1 trillion in unfunded pension and healthcare (OPEB) liabilities were recognized over the prior decade. An area chart titled "As reported unfunded state pension and OPEB liabilities" displays the growth of these obligations from 2001 to 2009. Unfunded liabilities were negligible in 2001 but climbed steadily, with pension obligations forming the base and OPEB liabilities stacking on top to exceed a combined $1.2 trillion by 2009. 

The author warns that even these official figures may be significant underestimates because they rely on overly optimistic investment return assumptions. A bar chart titled "State and local unfunded pension liabilities under different portfolio return assumptions" illustrates this sensitivity. If state and local pension funds achieve an average 8 percent return, their unfunded liabilities remain around $0.7 trillion. However, if return assumptions are lowered to reflect more conservative market realities, the liabilities scale up dramatically, rising to approximately $1.6 trillion at a 6 percent return, over $2.2 trillion at a 5 percent return, and nearly $3.0 trillion at a 4 percent return. The page concludes that under-risking these pension funds poses a severe systemic threat to state and local government stability.

This page analyzes the potential severity of US fiscal tightening scheduled for 2013 and explores the debate over whether the government should pursue austerity or continued stimulus. The author questions how tight fiscal policy will get, noting that while current law dictates a massive shift, Congress is likely to delay or "punt" these adjustments. 

The first chart, titled "Wide range of outcomes for 2013 austerity," traces the annual change in the cyclically-adjusted federal deficit as a percentage of potential GDP from 1963 to 2013. Historically, values above zero represent fiscal stimulus and values below represent fiscal drag. For 2013, the chart illustrates two distinct scenarios: if current laws are allowed to expire, the fiscal drag would be severe, approaching a 4% reduction in GDP. However, if Congress punts, the drag is estimated to be limited to about 1% of GDP. An accompanying table outlines the specific policies driving this potential fiscal drag. The largest components are the expiration of middle-income Bush tax cuts, which would create a drag equal to 0.9% of potential GDP, followed by the Alternative Minimum Tax at 0.8%, the Payroll Tax Cut at 0.6%, discretionary sequester automatic cuts at 0.4%, and Bush tax cuts for high incomes at 0.3%. Other factors include emergency unemployment compensation and the Affordable Care Act, each contributing a 0.2% drag.

The author discusses the political and academic context of this decision, noting that Congress will likely attempt to limit 2013 austerity to under 1% of GDP. Advocates for this approach can point to a March 2012 paper by economists Larry Summers and Brad DeLong, who argue against tightening fiscal policy when interest rates are near zero. They claim that tightening could permanently damage human capital, labor productivity, and overall trend growth.

To support the case for continued stimulus, advocates often point to two historical trends shown in the charts at the bottom of the page. The bottom-left chart, "Rising Federal debt? No problem for Treasury markets," plots the US debt-to-GDP ratio alongside the 10-year Treasury yield from 2004 to late 2012. It shows that even as federal debt surged from roughly 35% of GDP in 2007 to over 75% in 2012, the 10-year Treasury yield fell steadily from around 4.8% to under 2.0%. The bottom-right chart, "Rising Fed balance sheet? No problem for inflation," compares the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet as a percentage of GDP against year-over-year Core CPI. It demonstrates that while the Fed's balance sheet ballooned from 6% of GDP to nearly 20% between 2008 and 2012, Core CPI remained stable and low, generally hovering between 1.0% and 2.5%, and recently coming in below 2%. 

While the author agrees these charts show amazing trends, he concludes with a warning. He cautions that no one knows how long these dynamics can be sustained, suggesting that fiscal constraints pose a far greater threat than monetary ones, and metaphorically compares the looming danger of rising federal debt to the sci-fi threat of giant man-eating plants in "The Day of the Triffids."

This page analyzes escalating economic and market distress in Spain, arguing that despite interventions by the European Central Bank to buy or finance sovereign debt, Spanish credit risks and equity markets are deteriorating. The author maintains a firm underweight position on European equities relative to the United States, pointing to several worrying trends visualized across five charts and one performance table.

The first chart, tracking Spanish bank holdings of Spanish government bonds in billions of Euros, reveals a sharp upward trend, rising from around 100 billion in 2009 to over 220 billion in early 2012. This sovereign reliance is mirrored in the second chart, which shows ECB lending as a percentage of Spanish banks' total liabilities skyrocketing from under 2% in late 2011 to nearly 10% in early 2012. As a consequence of these funding pressures, Spain's credit spreads—measured via 5-year credit default swaps in basis points—surged back up toward 500 basis points in early 2012 after briefly easing in the winter.

The short-lived impact of central bank liquidity is further illustrated in a total return equity index chart comparing the US, Italy, and Spain from October 2011 to April 2012. While the US equity index steadily climbed from a baseline of 100 to nearly 130, Italian and Spanish equities collapsed after initial LTRO-fueled bounces, with Spain dropping below its starting index level to around 90 by April 2012.

Another critical point of concern is Spain's domestic economy, depicted in a dual-axis chart comparing Spanish unemployment with non-performing loans from 1999 to 2011. While unemployment rocketed from under 10% to approximately 23% and non-performing corporate loans surged to over 10% of gross loan balances, consumer and residential delinquencies remained curiously flat. The author urges skepticism toward this seemingly resilient residential data, noting that markets are pricing in these risks by discounting Spanish banks; BBVA and Santander trade at less than 1.0 times tangible book value, domestically-focused Cajas trade around 0.5 times, and Caixabank recently acquired Civica at approximately 0.35 times book value.

Finally, a performance table underscores the decision to remain underweight in Europe. Comparing total returns through mid-April, the table shows the S&P 500 consistently outperforming European equities, with the S&P 500 delivering 15.1% in 2010, 2.1% in 2011, and 9.6% in 2012, compared to MSCI Europe in USD terms which returned 4.4%, -10.3%, and 5.5% over the same periods.

This page introduces a planetary perspective on the global economy, focusing specifically on Sub-Saharan Africa and the potential of social investing to address its deep-seated challenges. The author argues that economic progress on the continent is severely hindered by unresolved health and human services crises, pointing out that basic diseases like diarrhea remain the leading cause of death for children under five in many African nations. While most regions of the world have experienced dramatic growth in post-war real per capita incomes, Sub-Saharan Africa has suffered from prolonged stagnation. 

This economic disparity is illustrated in a line chart titled "Africa in context," which plots real per capita GDP in thousands of constant dollars from 1950 to 2010. The chart compares various global regions, showing Sub-Saharan Africa at the very bottom, represented by a flat red line that barely rises above the $1,000 level over the sixty-year period. In stark contrast, developed economies show significant upward trajectories, led by the United States with an indicated level of $31,000, Japan at $22,000, and Western Europe at $21,000. Intermediate paths of varying growth are shown for Eastern Europe, the East Asia Tigers, Latin America, the Middle East, China, the Caribbean, India, and Developing Asia, all of which visually outpace the flatline of Sub-Saharan Africa. The data for this visual is sourced from Angus Maddison at the University of Groningen.

Despite these grim historical trends, the author highlights notable health successes that can be built upon, including a 30 percent reduction in African malaria deaths over the prior decade due to investments in drugs, bed nets, and spraying. Another success story is the Meningitis Vaccine Project, which delivered a vaccine costing just 50 cents per dose to nearly 20 million people during the 2010-2011 epidemic season. Looking ahead, the continent is expected to benefit from improved distribution infrastructure established by GAVI, the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization. To address the fundamental challenge that pharmaceutical companies lack commercial incentives to develop products for impoverished populations, the author proposes social investing. This strategy involves providing capital to a social investment fund, which then provides low-cost capital to drug companies in exchange for commitments to sell treatments at low cost to global health agencies.

This page analyzes several skyrocketing economic and market trends, balancing signs of real estate affordability and strong corporate earnings against a highly challenging fiscal outlook. 

The first section focuses on the real estate market and consumer behavior. The chart "Percent of MSA's where buying is cheaper than renting" tracks the percentage of Metropolitan Statistical Areas from 2000 to 2012. Historically flat below 15% for much of the decade, this metric skyrocketed to nearly 50% by 2012, indicating a dramatic shift toward housing affordability. Beside this, the chart "Housing crash has sidelined household cash" plots residential investment alongside household cash balances as percentages of GDP from 1985 to 2010. Following the housing crash, residential investment plummeted from its peak of over 10% in 2005 to under 4% by 2010. Simultaneously, sidelined household cash balances skyrocketed from roughly 3% of GDP to over 10%, indicating that consumers have pulled capital out of housing and into cash.

The next section examines corporate profits, which continue to rise. Early in the reporting quarter, 86% of companies were beating revenue estimates and 77% were beating earnings estimates. The chart "S&P 500 Operating earnings per share" uses a log scale to show rolling four-quarter sum operating earnings from 1988 to 2012, indicating that earnings are climbing toward high estimates for 2012 and 2013. However, the author cautions that analyst expectations for 2013 profit margins are unsustainably high. This is illustrated in the chart "Profit margin expectations for 2013," which shows the percentage of the top 1500 US stocks expecting year-over-year net margin increases. While the historical norm from 1970 to 2012 generally fluctuated between 30% and 65%, and the 2012 estimate sits at roughly 40%, the 2013 estimate skyrockets to an unprecedented level near 90%. The author predicts these profit margin expectations will likely have to be adjusted downward.

The final section addresses the United States' fiscal challenges, which the author describes as the "biggest fly in the ointment." The chart "Fiscal deficits" displays the first six months of the fiscal year as an inverted percentage of annualized GDP from 1955 to 2010. It shows that deficits have run historically deep and remain extremely elevated (around -5% of annualized GDP on the inverted scale) even three years into the economic recovery. Lastly, the chart "Scheduled austerity for 2013" measures the change in the cyclically-adjusted federal deficit as a percentage of potential GDP from 1963 to 2013. Assuming "current law" is maintained, the 2013 estimate projects a massive fiscal drag of nearly -4% of potential GDP, which would represent the sharpest scheduled policy contraction in fifty years. While the author doubts that such severe austerity will actually be fully implemented, the scheduled fiscal drag presents a major headwind, and the commentary notes that bull markets generally do not thrive until these types of fiscal issues are resolved.

The page begins by discussing the structure of social investing in African health. Under this model, if a medical treatment is successful, the drug company returns capital to the fund along with a low single-digit return. If the treatment fails, the company does not have to pay it back.
