To protect investors, philanthropic organizations and governments act as a safety net, absorbing the first 20 percent of loss and 50 percent of subsequent losses, which caps an investor’s principal loss at 40 percent. The author argues that this model creates more leverage and accountability than outright grants.

The author then transitions to the topic of how commercial enterprises are valued, presenting this question through the eyes of an alien observer. The text briefly reviews various historical economic systems, including Soviet Bolshevism, the Latin American Import Substitution model, the Nehru-Gandhi Central Planning model, pre-war Fascism in Europe, and Maoist Collectivism, concluding that these alternatives yielded stagnant per capita incomes compared to capitalism. 

To address current valuations, a line chart illustrates price-to-trailing earnings multiples for the S&P 500 and the German DAX from 1954 through early 2012. The chart shows that multiples, which historically peaked near 30x in the late 1990s and bottomed near 5x in the late 1970s due to rampant inflation, are currently near the lower end of their historical ranges. The author notes that because the low valuations of the 1970s were driven by inflation, an inflation-adjusted view would make current valuations look even cheaper.

This point is supported by a comprehensive table titled Valuation snapshot as of April 20, 2012, which covers forward price-to-earnings, forward earnings per share, dividend yield, return on equity, and market capitalization across several nations and regions. The United States has a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 12.5, forward earnings per share of 10.9, a dividend yield of 2.2 percent, and a return on equity of 15.4 percent, with a market cap of 13.57 trillion dollars. Europe overall is priced at a lower forward price-to-earnings ratio of 9.7, with France at 9.4, Germany at 9.7, Spain at 8.4, and Italy at 7.8. In Asia, China has a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 9.0 and a return on equity of 16.9 percent, while India sits at a multiple of 13.1. Japan shows a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 12.4, but its return on equity is extremely low at 4.6 percent, which the author attributes to long-standing structural issues rather than the recent tsunami. In Latin America, Mexico stands out with a higher forward price-to-earnings multiple of 15.4 and forward earnings per share growth of 28.2 percent. 

The author concludes with a positive assessment of the United States corporate earnings pulse. With one-third of companies by market capitalization having reported, 83 percent have beaten expectations, and overall earnings have exceeded estimates by 5 percent. This performance sits within the typical 4 percent to 9 percent range observed since March 2009. Furthermore, on a global scale, corporate earnings revisions have finally halted their forty-week downward trend.

This page analyzes global macroeconomic imbalances and their impact on equity valuations, presenting the perspective that massive debt levels across OECD nations represent a major headwind for the Western world. Although stock valuations appear cheap relative to history, the author explains that the sheer volume of household, corporate, and government debt—which nearly quadrupled in real terms between 1980 and 2010—depresses growth and valuation multiples. While central banks have injected historic amounts of liquidity to ease the de-leveraging process, boosting assets like gold and occasionally equities, real economic growth remains subdued. The author references the Rogoff thesis, noting that high debt levels typically drag on future growth, and warns that governments may address deficits through private sector taxation rather than spending cuts. Ultimately, the author advises investors to exercise caution rather than panic when structuring portfolios, as current low equity valuations likely price in much of this negative outlook.

The page features five charts to illustrate these points. The first, located at the top left, displays S&P 500 actual versus estimated earnings per share, excluding financials, from September 2008 to March 2012. This bar chart shows that the percentage by which actual earnings exceeded estimates peaked near ten percent in late 2009 and early 2010 before declining to a more modest four percent by March 2012. Adjacent to this, a chart on global earnings revisions tracking the number of upgrades minus downgrades over total revisions from 2008 to 2012 highlights a deep plunge to negative zero-point-six in late 2008, a strong rebound to positive zero-point-three in 2010, and a return to net negative territory during 2011.

Two middle charts focus on OECD non-financial sector debt from 1980 to 2010, utilizing data from a Bank for International Settlements paper by Stephen G. Cecchetti, M. S. Mohanty, and Fabrizio Zampolli. The left chart displays debt as a percentage of GDP for eighteen OECD economies, showing total debt rising from roughly one hundred seventy percent in 1980 to over three hundred percent by 2010, driven by gains in government, corporate, and household debt. The right chart displays real debt levels deflated by consumer prices, indexed to one hundred in 1980. This chart illustrates a massive climb in real total debt to over five hundred by 2010, with real government debt showing a particularly sharp spike after 2008.

The final chart at the bottom right details cumulative mutual fund net flows in billions of US dollars from 2007 to 2012. It visualizes the stark divergence in asset allocation as investors shunned equities in favor of fixed income. US bond funds received the most significant inflows, accumulating nearly one trillion dollars by 2012, while global bond funds grew to approximately seven hundred billion dollars. Conversely, US equity funds experienced severe cumulative outflows, dropping to negative three hundred fifty billion dollars, while global equity funds remained relatively flat, finishing slightly below zero.

This page addresses the sovereign debt crisis in Southern Europe, exploring why a region that represents only 6% of global GDP dominates global financial discussions. The author argues that Southern Europe’s threat lies in transmission risk and its disproportionate share of global sovereign and bank debt, meaning a crisis there heavily impacts the broader leveraged financial system. 

The page features a table evaluating global disruption risks for 2012–2013 across lower, medium, and high-risk categories. Lower-risk regions include emerging Asia, commodity-producing nations, Latin America, India, and China, with China representing 12% of world GDP and 11% of world trade. Medium-risk regions include Japan (holding 21% of world net sovereign debt), the United States (holding 23% of world GDP and 34% of net sovereign debt), non-Euro European countries, and Northern European nations like Germany, France, the Netherlands, and Belgium. High-risk areas are the southern "Eurovirus" countries—Spain, Italy, Portugal, Ireland, and Greece—which collectively hold 10% of world net sovereign debt and 9% of global bank debt despite only producing 6% of global GDP. 

To illustrate these regional risks, the text notes that Spain's official central and regional debt is reported at 68% of GDP, but J.P. Morgan estimates the true "fully-loaded" figure to be closer to 85% of GDP once bank restructuring, loan write-downs, and government guarantees are factored in. Furthermore, unlike Japan, whose massive debt is 93% domestically owned, Southern Europe relies heavily on volatile cross-border capital, necessitating dramatic intervention from the European Central Bank.

A line chart on the page, titled "Germany: decline in orders from within the Euro area," tracks seasonally adjusted industrial new orders from 2003 to 2012 to show the tangible transmission risk to Northern Europe. The chart compares two data series: orders from outside the Euro area and orders from within. While German orders from outside the Euro area recovered strongly after the 2008 financial crisis, rising back up to an index value of nearly 140 by 2012, orders from within the Euro area collapsed significantly starting in 2011, dropping down to an index value of around 90. 

In terms of political and economic outlooks, the author describes the French and German economies as stagnant, noting that economic strain in France has bolstered support for the National Front, while the Netherlands struggles with the newly agreed-upon fiscal compact. Ultimately, the author poses an open question: Germany must soon decide if, how, and when it will finance European fiscal integration to preserve the Euro. The author concludes that global markets might manage to bypass a collapse in Europe's periphery, but only if the ECB continues printing money and the IMF expands its financial firewall.

This page analyzes US equity valuation methods, specifically examining how the Graham-Dodd and Robert Shiller price-to-earnings (P/E) models function and questioning their underlying assumptions. The author addresses client concerns that S&P 500 earnings appear historically expensive when using these smoothed, ten-year backward-looking valuation tools. He questions two inherent assumptions in these models: first, how best to compare multiples across time when inflation has been so different, and second, what the implications are of using the last ten years as a proxy for the future. He points out that P/E multiples are historically lower during high-inflation periods, such as the 1970s, because earnings streams are worth less and inventory replacement costs render income statements less reliable. To resolve this, he suggests adjusting for inflation by inverting the P/E ratio into a real earnings yield, which demonstrates that current valuations are actually not as expensive as traditional backward-looking metrics suggest.

The analysis is supported by four charts. Chart I, titled "S&P 500 Price-to-10 year average reported earnings," presents J.P. Morgan's version of the Graham-Dodd model from 1901 to 2011. Measured as a multiple from 0x to 35x, the line trends upward toward 25x to 30x in the final years, pushing it near the "Expensive" threshold, with historical lows below 10x designated as "Cheap." Chart II displays the same S&P 500 Price-to-10 year average reported earnings but overlays the Shiller P/E ratio alongside the Graham-Dodd version. The two series track each other closely over the 110-year period, with both showing elevated levels above 20x by 2011.

To adjust for varying inflation regimes, Chart III shows the "Nominal S&P 500 10-year trailing earnings yield" from 1945 to 2011, measured in percent from 2% to 10%. On this chart, high yields represent "Cheap" valuations and low yields indicate "Expensive" ones; the nominal yield sits at roughly 4.5% near 2011, down from its peak of nearly 10% in the early 1980s. Chart IV, titled "Real S&P 500 10-year trailing earnings yield," subtracts headline CPI inflation from the earnings yield, showing data from 1945 to 2011 with a vertical axis ranging from -2% to 5%. In this real-yield view, the valuation near 2011 sits around a positive 2% real yield, which is well above the "Expensive" lows of the late 1990s and the negative real yields of the mid-1970s. 

Ultimately, the author concludes that the historical perspective on equity valuations changes dramatically when accounting for how inflation affects required equity returns. The page references methodology from Empirical Research Partners and sources data from Robert J. Shiller and Standard & Poor’s.

Michael Cembalest introduces the theme of human resilience in the face of self-inflicted catastrophes, contrasting Stephen Hawking's pessimistic warnings about potential alien colonizers with a more hopeful view of humanity's capacity to rebound. However, he warns that while capitalism is resilient, it remains highly mistake-prone. He specifically points to policy-driven errors, such as US affordable housing policies and the structural imbalances of the Eurozone, as key contributors to the global recession. 

To demonstrate historical resilience, the page features two charts. The first, titled Post Civil War recovery in Confederate farm income, tracks an index where 100 equals the year 1859. The index shows a severe decline during the war to around 85 by 1866, followed by a sharp recovery peaking above 104 by 1870, and ultimately ending near 106 in 1880. The second chart, Post World War II recovery in the Axis Powers, highlights the rapid post-war rebounds of Japan and Germany. On the left axis, Japan's industrial production index drops from approximately 180 in 1944 to a low of 40 in 1946, before steadily recovering to cross 200 by 1956. On the right axis, German exports rise dramatically from near zero in 1948 to over 7,000 million dollars by 1956.

The bottom half of the page features a long-term chart of the Dow Jones Industrial Average from May 1896 to April 2012 on a logarithmic price scale. The chart categorizes the market into alternating periods of sideways, volatile channels highlighted in red, and structural bull markets highlighted in blue. The first red period, spanning from 1896 to the late 1940s, represents an under-regulated era of frequent recessions, bank failures, and the Great Depression. This was followed by a blue secular bull market driven by post-war prosperity, a productivity boom, and the rebuilding of the Axis Powers. The subsequent red period, from the late 1960s to the early 1980s, is labeled as a mess of Vietnam, Nixon, OPEC, and high inflation. The second major blue bull market was set in motion in the early 1980s when Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker destroyed inflation, causing interest rates to tumble. The final period leading to 2012 is shaded red, capturing the inflation and bursting of the credit, housing, and European debt bubbles. Cembalest poses the question of where the market goes next, predicting that it might take longer than some expect to exit the current sideways, volatile channel. He advises investors to see the markets realistically rather than wishing for a premature bull market.

This page highlights positive US economic recovery signals alongside a discussion on policy, corporate cash, and global market dynamics. Five charts support this analysis. The first chart, tracking US small business optimism from 2000 to 2012, shows the index recovering from a recessionary low of around 81 in 2009 up to approximately 95 by 2012. The second chart, measuring US job openings in millions, shows a rise from a trough of 2.5 million in 2009 to nearly 3.5 million. The third chart shows recovering railroad carloads (excluding coal, as a four-week moving average in thousands of railcars), which bounced back to around 170,000 cars from a low of 130,000 in 2009. The fourth chart displays upbeat sales surveys for airlines, trucking companies, and homebuilders from 1998 to 2012, with airlines and trucking showing sharp post-crisis rebounds, while homebuilders experience a more modest uptick. The final chart illustrates corporate cash and equivalents as a percentage of tangible assets from 1952 to 2012, showing that corporate cash has accumulated to a multi-decade high of nearly 14%.

Michael Cembalest poses the question of what policy mix could unleash these mountains of corporate cash. He doubts that further Federal Reserve intervention, such as a third round of quantitative easing, would be effective given that interest rates are already at zero and the 10-year Treasury yield is below 2%. Instead, he advocates for an aggressive, pro-growth agenda modeled after the 1950s under President Eisenhower. He points out that from 1950 to 1960, the US federal debt fell from 80% to 46% of GDP through real GDP growth of over 4%, rather than inflation or austerity. During this period, federal expenditures remained near 17% of GDP, tax burdens on small businesses were eased, wage and price controls were eliminated, and private sector employment reached a post-war peak of 86%.

In his market wrap-up, Cembalest notes the fragile interdependence of global growth, where China, Europe, and the US are highly reliant on one another. He highlights an unusual market anomaly in the US: 98% of the S&P 500’s cumulative 27% return since January 2010 occurred either during corporate earnings seasons or immediately following quantitative easing programs, while the market remained flat the rest of the time. Given these conditions, he advises investors to take modestly less risk, favoring allocations to distressed residential and commercial real estate, long-term energy projects, and private lending. The publication concludes that the best public and private equity opportunities reside in the US and the Pacific Rim, excluding China and Japan.

This J.P. Morgan Eye on the Market publication analyzes the escalating Eurozone debt crisis, framing it around the Icarus factor where the foundational vision of the single currency faces a dramatic downfall. The author critiques the policy responses of the IMF, EU, and ECB, particularly regarding Greece, and includes an image of Jacob Pieter Gowys 1650 painting, The Fall of Icarus, to symbolize the faltering Euro project. 

The discussion focuses on several key European nations: Greece, France, Spain, and Germany. For Greece, the author outlines a grim scenario of deep GDP decline, youth unemployment exceeding 50 percent, and political radicalization. He argues that Greek debt relief efforts have left the country in a debtors prison, as 70 to 80 percent of bailout funds were merely round-tripped to pay off foreign bondholders and facilitate capital flight. This argument is supported by a line chart titled Greeces debtors prison, which plots post-restructuring debt-to-GDP percentages from 2009 projected to 2020. It compares Greeces projected trajectory against historical benchmarks like Mexicos 1990 post-restructuring debt, which remained steady around 40 to 50 percent, and Argentinas 2001 post-restructuring debt, which hovered around 80 percent. In contrast, the J.P. Morgan central scenario for Greece projects debt-to-GDP to remain stubbornly high, peaking over 170 percent and ending near 170 percent in 2020, while the IMF/ECB/EU baseline shows it declining to only about 125 percent by 2020.

Turning to France, the commentary explores whether the newly elected socialist president, Francois Hollande, will be constrained by financial markets despite a political legacy of heavy state intervention. A bar chart titled Frances twin deficits may constrain Hollande tracks the countrys current account and budget balance as a percent of GDP from 1960 to 2010. The budget deficit, shown in brown bars, has been persistently negative since the late 1970s, plunging to around -8 percent of GDP by 2010, while the current account, shown in blue bars, has also fallen into negative territory, approaching -2 percent of GDP. The author suggests these large twin deficits will limit Hollandes ability to deviate far from fiscal discipline.

For Spain, the author notes that while the recapitalization of Bankia, the nations third-largest bank, is positive, much more capital will be required as sovereign debt nears 90 percent of GDP. He warns that ECB firewall funds could run dry by the end of 2012, and the ECBs decision to declare seniority over Greek bondholders poses risks for Spanish debt holders. Lastly, the piece posits that Germany, being in strong economic health, may tolerate higher inflation to support the struggling Southern European nations and avoid a collapse similar to the Exchange Rate Mechanism crisis of the early 1990s.

This page features introductory commentary from the author followed by a satirical fifteen-panel comic strip titled "Waiting for Godot, 2012," illustrating the policy paralysis of the Eurozone debt crisis. 

In the introduction, the author outlines his current allocation of time, analyzing economic data showing stable but weak US recoveries at around two percent, slowing growth in China down to seven to eight percent, and a challenging environment in Europe. He monitors high US corporate margins with slowing profit growth and reviews favored investment areas such as distressed US real estate, oil and gas, high yield, Asian private equity, US tech stocks, and European bank loan sales. He notes that due to Europe's 38.6 percent equity underperformance compared to the US since the onset of the EU crisis in November 2009, he feels stuck in a state of suspended animation.

The visual focus of the page is the comic strip set at a bar in Madrid or Milan, featuring the characters Vladimir and Estragon. Through their dialogue, they critique the systemic gridlock of the European sovereign debt crisis. They debate whether the European Central Bank can resume buying Spanish bonds, mocking the recurring resignations of German officials from the ECB. The characters discuss the shortcomings of European deposit guarantees compared to the US FDIC, prompting savers to flee to Deutsche Bank. They further analyze the feasibility of joint Eurobonds, noting they are legally obstructed by Maastricht Article 125—which they joke is an anagram for "Chasm Trait"—and the 2011 German Federal Constitutional Court ruling against unquantifiable financial treaty risks. 

The dialogue also highlights the limitations of global rescue efforts, noting that the IMF’s entire global capacity of 360 billion has been proposed solely for Europe, jokingly justified because a European runs the institution. They outline the political resistance from Finland, Austria, Netherlands, and Germany—humorously acronymized as "FANG"—to using the EU Stabilization Fund for direct bank recapitalization. Ultimately, the characters lament the ten trillion dollars of outstanding peripheral European debt, concluding that "nothing is to be done." They end by mocking EU bank stress tests, pointing out that supposedly safe institutions like Dexia and BFA-Bankia were nationalized shortly after passing, which they ironically categorize as mere exceptions, just like Greece.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s market commentary addresses the modern "German Question": whether Germany will use its accumulated wealth to save the Eurozone from collapse and what the financial cost of doing so would be. Historically, the "German Question" referred to geopolitical conflicts that coincided with Germany's economic power outpacing its neighbors. This historical trend is illustrated by three charts plotting German GDP growth relative to its neighbors prior to major conflicts. The first chart, covering 1850 to 1871, shows German GDP relative to France rising from an index of 100 to nearly 120 before the Franco-Prussian War. The second chart shows German GDP relative to France and England rising from an index of 100 in 1890 to roughly 135 by 1911, just before World War I. The third chart shows German GDP relative to France and England rising from 100 in 1924 to over 160 by 1942, before World War II. 

In the modern context, authors Michael Cembalest and Michael Vaknin estimate that backstopping the European periphery for five years (from 2012 to 2016) would cost Germany approximately 1 trillion Euros. This calculation assumes Germany bears the cost alone, without French or IMF aid, and without relying on ECB asset dumping or inflationary solutions. 

A detailed table breaks down the estimated funding requirements for five peripheral nations over this five-year period, measured in billions of Euros. For Portugal, public capital account support is estimated at 26, private capital at -46, and current account at -6, leading to a balance of payments deficit of 26 and total support of 52. For Ireland, public capital support of 45, private capital of 0, and current account of -1 result in a balance of payments surplus of 44 and a total support of 1. Italy requires 166 in public capital support, with private capital at -168 and current account at -106, yielding a balance of payments deficit of 107 and total support of 273. Greece’s public capital support is 43, private capital is 0, and current account is -90, yielding a balance of payments deficit of 47 and total support of 90. Spain requires the largest amount of aid, with public capital support of 305, private capital at -479, and current account at -111, leading to a balance of payments deficit of 284 and total support of 589. Across the entire periphery, the total public capital support of 584, combined with a balance of payments support of 420, brings the total required support to 1.005 trillion Euros.

These calculations rely on several key assumptions. It is assumed that there is no more official support from the Troika (comprising the EU, IMF, and ECB), and that proceeds are used to fund fiscal and balance of payments deficits over five years. The authors assume foreign investors will withdraw 60% of their accumulated investments made from the Euro's inception to its peak in 2009, though capital flight is projected at zero for Greece and Ireland. Additionally, the authors project gradual current account improvements as import demand remains depressed, and they explicitly note that their 1 trillion Euro estimate excludes potential bank recapitalization costs, which could ultimately make the final figure much larger.

This page analyzes the viability of a proposed one-trillion-Euro five-year fix to preserve the Eurozone, arguing that the decision is fundamentally political because Germany does not have the fiscal capacity to absorb such a debt burden. To contextualize this massive sum, the author compares it to the historical costs of German reunification. A bar chart titled Cost of German unification, and saving the Euro (for now) measures various historical estimates of German unification costs from 1991 onward in billions of Euros, ranging from roughly 600 billion to nearly 1.6 trillion Euros. This is shown alongside J.P. Morgan Asset Management's estimate of one trillion Euros to save Europe. A corresponding line chart, German gross general government debt as a percentage of GDP from 1991 to 2016, illustrates how Germany's debt rose from under 40 percent in 1991 to approximately 80 percent in 2011. The chart projects that adding the estimated one-trillion-Euro cost would force Germany’s debt-to-GDP ratio past the 100 percent threshold, peaking near 115 percent.

The commentary then shifts to market dynamics and capital flight, introducing two distinct visual interpretations of a bull run. The first chart, Running of the bulls, part 1, tracks foreign private sector investment positions as a percentage of GDP from 1999 to 2011 for Greece, Italy, Spain, and Portugal. It illustrates a stark decline in foreign private investment across the European periphery beginning around 2009, with Greece falling toward 50 percent and Portugal dropping from a peak of nearly 270 percent to around 225 percent, while Spain and Italy also show notable downward trends. 

The second chart, Running of the bulls, part 2, captures Wall Street's reaction to these events, plotting the S&P 500 index level from December 2011 to May 2012. It overlay's index performance with S&P 500 year-end target revisions from major investment banks. During the first quarter of 2012, strategists at Credit Suisse, UBS, Citi, HSBC, and Bank of America raised their targets, anticipating that the European Central Bank's liquidity auctions would resolve the sovereign debt crisis. Meanwhile, Deutsche Bank, J.P. Morgan Securities, Barclays, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley kept their forecasts unchanged. The author notes that this rally proved to be temporary, as the ECB's auctions would likely only support Spanish and Italian government debt through the end of 2012.

In conclusion, the author remains highly skeptical of European equities, which have underperformed US markets by 36 percent over the preceding three years. Pointing out that a summit between François Hollande and Angela Merkel yielded minimal concrete results, the author notes that potential systemic solutions—such as jointly guaranteed Euro T-bills, a pan-European deposit guarantee program, ESM direct bank capitalization licenses, or expanded IMF rescue programs—remain entirely speculative. The page advises extreme caution and recommends maintaining an underweight allocation to European assets.

This page consists of a multi-panel satirical comic strip exploring the cyclical and contradictory arguments surrounding the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis, followed by a concluding commentary on the structural limitations of the European monetary union. 

The comic strip features a conversation between two silhouetted figures who critique the policy responses and proposed solutions of the era. They begin by debating whether the European Central Bank can buy more Spanish bonds or continue lending to European banks to purchase sovereign debt, noting that credit spreads are widening and foreign interbank funding is fleeing. The dialogue pokes fun at political figures and events, referencing Nicolas Sarkozy’s premature declaration that the crisis was over and depicting a dream where the artist Christo wraps a giant plastic austerity belt around France before François Hollande can stop him. 

The conversation then shifts to the feasibility of Eurobonds. The figures debate how Eurobonds would disproportionately bind Germany to debt three times its own size, especially since German debt already exceeds 80% of GDP. They mock Mario Monti’s support for Eurobonds and highlight a critical structural flaw: the European Union lacks a federal taxation system, noting that while 66% of US taxes are paid to Washington, D.C., only 2% of European taxes are earmarked for EU-level activities. They also target Jean-Claude Trichet's assertion that there was no design flaw in the Euro, and contrast this with Giulio Tremonti's claim that Eurobonds would have prevented the crisis altogether. The absurdity of proposed solutions is highlighted by the European Redemption Fund, which would require Italy to run a 4% primary surplus for 25 consecutive years and implement constitutional debt brakes that would have been breached 70% of the time since Italian unification in 1861. The comic ends in a loop, with the characters returning to their original, flawed idea of ECB-to-bank lending before concluding that they cannot go on like this.

At the bottom of the page, a commentary block poses the open question of how long this crisis can continue, pointing out that Spain’s situation looks particularly terrible. The author argues that a decisive new policy option is desperately needed but expresses deep skepticism that one will emerge. To provide historical context, the author cites an influential 1949 paper from the US Quarterly Journal of Economics regarding how the United States survived the Great Depression. The paper highlights that unilateral regional transfers by the US Treasury—functioning essentially as gifts or capital movements—were critical in enabling weaker American districts to maintain consumption and growth levels. The author implies that without similar federal fiscal transfer mechanisms, the European monetary union remains fundamentally vulnerable.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market publication focuses on the unresolved tension between strong corporate fundamentals—referred to as "The Whale"—and severe, persistent macroeconomic imbalances—referred to as "The Squid." The author argues in favor of maintaining an underweight position in equities, predicting that global macroeconomic imbalances will continue to weigh down the market despite historically high corporate cash balances, low equity valuations, and rising profits. 

The tension is illustrated by two side-by-side charts. The first, titled "The Squid: Tentacles of macroeconomic imbalances," spans 1980 to 2010 and depicts rising systemic risks across several measures, including OECD government debt to GDP, China's capital spending to GDP, the US fiscal deficit, Spanish reliance on foreign capital, the periphery-less-Germany unemployment rate gap, and the Germany-less-Italy industrial production gap. These metrics show a sharp, collective rise in global structural imbalances over the decades. Opposite this is "The Whale: The cheapness of corporate profits and piles of cash" chart, which tracks the S&P earnings yield, economy-wide profits to GDP, and corporate cash to tangible assets from 1985 to 2012. This chart demonstrates that corporate health remains highly robust, with profits and cash piles hovering near multi-decade highs.

A third chart, "Another Prague Spring," plots the Global Composite Purchasing Manager's Index (PMI) from 2007 to 2012 on a scale of 35 to 60, with 50 representing the threshold for expansion. Shaded regions mark periods of monetary stimulus, showing that global economic activity tends to fade immediately after central bank support ends. The author uses the term "Prague Spring" as a metaphor for springtime economic data that melts away by summer, noting this disappointing pattern occurred in 2010, 2011, and 2012, which repeatedly leads to renewed market expectations for further stimulus. 

Finally, the author justifies a heavy analytical focus on Europe by noting that around one-third of all OECD banking system assets are held by banks in distress, which is defined as having credit spreads wider than 3%. Because the vast majority of these distressed banks are European, the author warns that the region's debt crisis remains a critical threat to global portfolios.

In this commentary from J.P. Morgan, author Michael Cembalest discusses the economic prospects of Greece leaving the Eurozone, drawing a direct comparison to Argentina's landmark default and currency devaluation in late 2001. Addressing critics who argued that Greece should not be compared to Argentina or that a Euro exit would be catastrophic, the author contends that while leaving the Euro would cause short-term pain, it ultimately offers Greece its only viable path to economic recovery. He admits that Argentina's post-devaluation recovery was aided by rising soybean prices and that its official figures underreport inflation by about half. However, he argues that the broader trajectory of a sharp short-term shock followed by a substantial recovery—which he terms the economic morning after—is highly typical. He notes that similar patterns of post-devaluation recovery occurred in the United Kingdom after 1992, Southeast Asia after 1998, and Iceland after 2009. While acknowledging that Greece would likely recover more slowly due to the structural damage from Eurozone membership and austerity, the author argues that a Greek exit, combined with IMF-supported structural adjustment lending rather than bailouts aimed at French and German banks, represents Greece's only real hope.

To support this thesis, the page displays fifteen individual charts documenting Argentina's economic indicators before and after its late 2001 devaluation, which is marked on each chart by a vertical dotted line. The first chart, showing the peso overnight interbank interest rate, illustrates a massive, brief spike to nearly 90 percent at the end of 2001, which rapidly normalized to under 10 percent by 2003. The second chart depicts year-over-year inflation spiking to approximately 40 percent immediately after devaluation before subsiding to a stable range of 5 to 10 percent. The third chart shows that while real GDP growth bottomed out at a severe contraction of negative 15 percent at the end of 2001, it quickly rebounded to sustained positive growth rates of 8 to 10 percent between 2003 and 2006.

The second row of charts examines broader economic and social impacts. Real GDP per capita fell from over 8,000 pesos down to a trough of 6,500 pesos in 2002 before recovering back to nearly 8,000 pesos by 2005. The current account balance experienced a massive positive shift, moving from a pre-crisis deficit of roughly 3 to 5 percent of GDP into a substantial surplus that peaked near 10 percent of GDP in 2002. Gross investment as a percent of GDP plunged to a low of 11 percent in 2002 but steadily climbed back to 22 percent by 2005. Concurrently, the poverty index, measuring the percentage of the population living below 1.25 dollars a day, spiked from around 4 percent up to 12 percent in 2002, but then fell back to approximately 5 percent by late 2003.

The third row highlights inequality, labor, and market performance. Inequality, measured by the Gini coefficient, peaked at over 54 percent in 2002 before declining toward 48 percent in 2003. The unemployment rate peaked at over 20 percent in 2002 and declined steadily to about 12 percent by 2005. The Merval equity index, measured in US dollars, crashed to a low near 100 in 2002 before rising dramatically to nearly 700 by 2005. Industrial production fell below an index value of 90 in 2002 but surged to over 130 by late 2004.

The fourth row focus on domestic confidence and fiscal metrics. Real wages fell from an index level of 100 down to 85 post-devaluation, representing a steep drop in purchasing power, but rebounded to over 115 by 2005. Corporate Chapter 11 filings spiked to nearly 190 in 2002 and subsequently fell to historical lows under 50 by 2005. Consumer confidence plummeted to a trough of about 32 before recovering to pre-crisis levels near 55. Finally, the public sector fiscal balance turned positive; the primary balance rose from zero to a surplus of 4 percent of GDP, while the headline balance, including cash interest payments, improved from a deficit of nearly 4 percent of GDP to a surplus of over 1 percent of GDP by 2004.

This page, titled "A postscript on Beijing" under the theme of "What could go right in the world," examines China's modern geopolitical outlook through the lens of its historical relationship with the West during the nineteenth century. Drawing on insights from Henry Kissinger, the text argues that China's current political consciousness is heavily shaped by the trauma of the Opium Wars, which led to widespread addiction, massive silver outflows, and the eventual collapse of the Qing Dynasty—events that are still deeply remembered in China today. 

The historical impact is illustrated by two line charts spanning the early-to-mid 1800s. The first chart, "Opium imported into China," tracks the number of chests imported from 1801 to 1857. It highlights a key marker in 1836 for the "Re-instatement of Imperial opium ban" when imports hovered around 30,000 chests, which was followed by a brief decline and then a steep, volatile rise to nearly 80,000 chests by the late 1850s. The second chart, "Chinese silver outflows to England and India," displays a five-year rolling average in millions of silver dollars from 1818 to 1854. A marker around 1820 highlights when the Chinese balance of payments shifted from surplus to deficit, showing outflows escalating from under five million to over 25 million silver dollars by the early 1850s. Both charts source data from Man-houng Lin's Harvard University Asia Center publication, "China Upside Down."

Transitioning to modern relations, the page outlines Kissinger's advice that the West must understand China's unique perspective on global energy security, North Korea, climate change, currency, and trade. Despite ideological tension—exemplified by a footnote citing former US official Aaron Friedberg's assertion that the ultimate US strategy should be to hasten a peaceful revolution to replace China's authoritarian state—Kissinger contends that conflict is not inevitable. Because both nations are deeply integrated and have immense economic stakes to protect, they are highly incentivized to maintain the status quo. The author concludes that if Kissinger's constructive view holds true, a stable and cooperative US-China relationship could serve as a major positive surprise against prevailing negative global expectations. The page concludes with a list of historical and research sources, alongside standard economic abbreviations.

This page examines the challenges faced by non-investment grade companies when they are forced to seek alternative financing options, termed Plan C, after traditional bank loans and public bond markets become inaccessible. The author argues that while high-yield bond spreads rallied back sharply after spiking during the 2008 recession, aggregate indices hide a highly fragmented market. 

To illustrate the high-yield landscape, the author presents two initial charts. The first, US High Yield Spreads, traces the spread to worst in basis points from 1987 to 2011. This line chart highlights a massive spike during the 2008 recession, when spreads quintupled to nearly 2,000 basis points, before retreating back below 800 basis points. The second chart, the J.P. Morgan US High Yield Index, displays the distribution of spreads across companies as of June 6, 2012. It plots the spread to worst in basis points on the horizontal axis against the number of companies on the vertical axis. The chart marks a current index spread to worst of 709 basis points with a dashed line, showing a wide, right-skewed dispersion where some companies enjoy low spreads under 450 basis points while a long tail of riskier borrowers faces spreads exceeding 1,550 basis points.

The text explains that this dispersion is driven by structural shifts that have curtailed credit access for small and medium-sized firms. Two additional charts support this point. The chart showing US CLO Quarterly Gross Issuance in billions of USD from 2000 to 2012 demonstrates that collateralized loan obligations—previously a massive driver of demand—shrank from a peak of over $30 billion per quarter in 2006 and 2007 to near-zero during the financial crisis, with only a marginal recovery by 2012. Consequently, smaller firms have been locked out of public debt issuance. This is confirmed by the adjacent line chart, Debt Issuance by Mid-Market Firms (defined as companies with an EBITDA of $50 million or less), which plots the quarterly number of deals from 1997 to 2012. The volume of deals crashed from peak levels of roughly 110 to 120 deals per quarter down to fewer than 20 deals in 2009, remaining severely depressed through 2012.

As a result, smaller firms must resort to private credit markets, such as mezzanine lending. The author notes that since 2009, private lending has offered highly attractive terms for investors, including substantial equity subordination of 30% to 40% below mezzanine debt, cash coupons of 10% to 12%, discounts to par, and pro-forma debt service coverage of 2.4x to 2.7x. The author concludes by posing a question about companies and countries, like Spain, that have even larger problems and are forced to seek rescue or growth financing, setting up a transition to a discussion on the opportunities within rescue financing markets.

This page analyzes the deep-seated macroeconomic challenges facing Europe and the United States, focusing on unrealistic European fiscal policy proposals and banking insolvency risks alongside sluggish American economic growth. 

The author strongly criticizes the "European Redemption Fund" proposal drafted by German economic advisors, which would require Eurozone countries to target a sixty percent debt-to-GDP ratio over twenty-five years. For Italy, this plan would necessitate a primary surplus of four percent annually for twenty-five years, a requirement the author calls ridiculous and historically unprecedented. An accompanying line chart of Italy's primary fiscal balance as a percentage of GDP from 1960 to 2010 illustrates this skepticism, showing that Italy's balance was deeply negative for decades—dropping to nearly negative seven percent in the mid-1970s—and only briefly crossed the proposed four percent threshold in the late 1990s due to tax collection spikes rather than spending cuts. This policy discussion is framed by another line chart showing the percentage of OECD banking system assets in distressed banks, defined as those with credit spreads exceeding three percent. This systemic distress metric peaked near twenty percent during the 2008 financial crisis and surged past forty percent in late 2011, underscoring the extreme fragility of the banking sector.

The commentary asserts that the money from the European Central Bank’s rescue operations has largely been exhausted. A data table outlines what Spanish and Italian banks did with their December 2011 to February 2012 Long-Term Refinancing Operation funding. Out of one hundred ninety-five billion Euros in LTRO funding, Spanish banks allocated one hundred two billion Euros to purchase government bonds and loans, leaving only twenty billion Euros remaining. Italian banks received one hundred fourteen billion Euros but spent seventy-three billion Euros on government bonds and seventy-one billion Euros combined on other bonds and interbank liabilities, leaving them with a deficit of forty-eight billion Euros. 

Further complicating the European outlook is the solvency crisis of Bankia, Spain's third-largest bank, which is detailed in a timeline sidebar. The timeline traces Bankia's rapid decline from receiving a clean bill of health in July 2010 to its three-billion-Euro IPO in July 2011, followed by a series of massive capital shortfalls. By May 2012, the Spanish government converted four point five billion Euros of preferred shares to equity and announced that another nineteen billion Euros was needed to cover provisions, sending Bankia shares down seventy-two percent from their IPO price. The author expresses doubt that Germany has the financial capacity or political will to resolve these banking crises, given its own eighty percent debt-to-GDP ratio.

In the United States, a disappointing payroll report has dampened hopes that American growth will stabilize global markets. Economists are actively revising 2012 US GDP growth forecasts down toward two percent. Weakening disposable income is expected to keep business capital spending subdued. While falling gasoline prices and lower debt service costs provide a temporary cushion for consumer cash flow, the author concludes that the US economy still lacks the momentum to achieve escape velocity.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market highlights the high stakes of the upcoming European Union summit, explaining why European financial health remains critical for global markets. The author points out that one-third of all OECD banks are in distress and notes that Europe accounts for 15% of S&P 500 revenues, 23% of S&P industrial revenues, and roughly 30% of technology revenues. Highlighting this global exposure, the text mentions that major companies like Procter & Gamble, Texas Instruments, Starbucks, FedEx, and Adobe have lowered their earnings guidance due to European headwinds. 

While the EU summit aims to address bank recapitalization, Greek repayment terms, and deposit guarantees, Germany is constrained by national debt exceeding 80% of GDP. At the same time, the periphery economies of Italy, Spain, Greece, and Portugal are contracting at an annualized pace of 2% to 5%. This distress is visualized in a line chart titled "Spanish and Greek unemployment," which tracks unemployment rates from 1985 to 2012. The chart reveals that after 2008, unemployment rates in both Spain and Greece skyrocketed, rapidly climbing past 20% by 2012. 

To illustrate the political risks of such severe joblessness, the author presents a historical comparison chart titled "Unemployment and the end of liberal capitalism, 1930's," which plots German unemployment alongside Reichstag seats by party from 1922 to 1934. The chart shows that when German unemployment—shaded in red—surged past 20% and peaked near 30% during the Great Depression, the Reichstag seats held by the totalitarian National Socialists spiked dramatically. Concurrently, representation for liberal democratic parties collapsed. The author warns that a failure to improve the current European jobs crisis risks boosting fringe political parties in the periphery today.

The commentary also criticizes the EU Economic and Monetary Committee’s proposed Rating Agency Reform draft, which seeks to make rating agencies legally liable for methodological errors and mandates that financial institutions rely on internal ratings instead. The author views this as a counterproductive attempt to silence dissenting analytical opinions, satirically comparing the move to the Roman Inquisition's historic silencing of Galileo Galilei. 

Ultimately, the author argues that the Eurozone's challenges extend far beyond a sovereign debt or banking crisis, pointing to fundamental incompatibilities within the single currency union. To demonstrate the scale of the problem, the text notes that Spanish banks are borrowing over €300 billion from the European Central Bank, yet this massive sum represents only 12% of their total liabilities. Additionally, a footnote highlights that of the €410 billion in Greek rescue packages over the preceding two years, an estimated €15 billion actually reached the real Greek economy, with the rest spent to protect private and official creditors. The page concludes that despite years of painful austerity, the cyclically-adjusted current account deficits of the periphery countries are barely changed from three years prior, indicating that Europe still has a long road to recovery.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan evaluates the Federal Reserve's efforts to jumpstart US growth amidst a broader global economic slowdown and a long-term US budget impasse. He argues that with 10-year interest rates already down to 1.6%, the Fed's quantitative easing tools may have lost their potency, raising the question of what else can jumpstart economic growth, confidence, and corporate cash deployment. 

The first chart, titled "Another Prague Spring (PS)," displays the Global Composite Purchasing Manager's Index from 2007 through mid-2012, where a level above 50 indicates expansion. Shaded grey areas indicate periods of monetary stimulus, and peaks labeled "PS" in 2010, 2011, and 2012 demonstrate recurring temporary upturns followed by subsequent slowdowns, confirming a pattern of weakening global momentum. 

The second chart, titled "Earnings still outperforming the economy," plots the ratio of two-year earnings growth to two-year nominal GDP growth from 1952 onward. The chart highlights that corporate profits have been outrunning GDP growth by the widest margin in decades, with recent peaks reaching ratios of 14.3x and 5.4x, which are significantly higher than the historical average peaks of 2.1x and 4.2x. 

The bottom half of the page introduces J.P. Morgan's "Squid vs Whale" framework to illustrate today's macroeconomic risks alongside corporate valuations and cash piles. The first of these, "The Squid: Tentacles of macroeconomic imbalances," charts diverse risks from 1980 to 2010, tracking the US fiscal deficit, China's capital spending to GDP, OECD government debt to GDP, Spanish reliance on foreign capital, the industrial production gap between Germany and Italy, and the unemployment rate gap between the periphery and Germany. These lines intertwine to show escalating systemic pressures. In contrast, "The Whale: The cheapness of corporate profits and piles of cash" maps data from 1985 to 2012, demonstrating historically high levels of economy-wide profits to GDP, corporate cash relative to tangible assets, and S&P earnings yields. Together, these charts suggest that while the macroeconomic "squid" represents massive imbalances, the corporate "whale" represents highly profitable companies sitting on protective, cheap piles of cash. 

The author concludes with a fiscal policy focus, stating that the US cannot indefinitely sustain a libertarian tax policy alongside a Scandinavian welfare state. Pointing to the Bowles-Simpson plan as a potential bipartisan template to close this gap, Cembalest raises the open question of how realistic it is to expect such a budget compromise to be passed following the 2012 Presidential election.

This page, titled "Appendix: Presidential Politics, 2012," argues that the 2012 US Presidential election between Barack Obama and Mitt Romney represents a modern anomaly due to the historically low level of prior high-level public service experience held by the candidates. Combined, Obama and Romney possessed only 12 years of high-level experience—reflecting Obama's single term in the US Senate and Romney's single term as Governor of Massachusetts.

To illustrate this trend, the page features a line chart titled "US Presidential Elections: prior years of high level public sector experience of both candidates combined, 1912-2012." The chart plots combined years of prior experience on the vertical axis, ranging from 0 to 60, against election years on the horizontal axis. It tracks two metrics: Category 1 (represented by a green line), which counts years served as a Governor, US Senator, US Representative, Vice President, or President; and Category 1 plus Category 2 (represented by a brown line), which adds major military leadership roles, Supreme Court justices, and Cabinet posts. 

The chart reveals that the combined experience in 2012 plummeted to 12 years, a depth not seen since 1952 and 1924. The author points out that although the 1952 election between Dwight Eisenhower and Adlai Stevenson appears low on the chart, both candidates possessed significant uncounted public sector heft, such as Eisenhower's high-level military staff roles under Generals Fox Connor, George Moseley, and Douglas MacArthur, and Stevenson’s wartime roles in the State and Navy departments. Thus, to find a truly comparable historical low, one must look back to the 1924 election between Calvin Coolidge and John W. Davis, where combined experience fell below 10 years. For context, the chart shows that combined candidate experience peaked in 1996 at 50 years, with other high points occurring in 1964 and 2004. 

The author reflects that this shift away from experienced candidates is unsurprising given that public confidence in major institutions like banks, Congress, and the Federal Reserve is near multi-decade lows. However, the commentary poses a cautionary open question: do politicians who have never wielded substantial power underestimate the consequences of being wrong? The author warns that it is easy to be overly certain about policy choices when one has never had to navigate a public policy failure of their own making. 

Finally, a footnote explains why state legislative experience was excluded from the calculations, pointing to the 20th-century shift in power from state capitals to the federal government. To support this, the author references the Brennan Center for Justice at the NYU School of Law, which famously characterized the New York State legislature as the most dysfunctional and least deliberative legislative body in the nation.

This page presents a mid-year self-assessment of the major market, economic, and investment views published in J.P. Morgan’s 2012 Outlook. The assessment is structured as a scorecard using a color-graded system where green indicates a correct call, yellow indicates a mixed or partially correct result, and red represents an incorrect prediction. 

The author outlines several correct calls that received green grades. The view that OECD private sector economies would have to make it on their own was validated as fiscal stimulus ended and the European Central Bank balance sheet grew by 620 billion Euros, with Spanish banks requiring significant financial support. The firm’s regional equity positioning was highly successful: the US was their largest position and gained 9 percent, Asia ex-Japan was the next largest and rose 7.9 percent, while underweighted regions like Europe and Japan lagged, gaining just 1.1 percent and 2.5 percent, respectively. The outlook’s optimism on US corporate profits was also accurate, correctly predicting that S&P earnings growth would slow down to 10 percent from the 20 to 30 percent gains of previous years. In Europe, sovereign risk calls were precise. The author correctly anticipated that markets would remain skeptical of Italian solvency, where the gross domestic product contracted at a 2 percent pace, and that Spain would be the focal point of the European Union crisis, experiencing a recession, capital flight, and a 19.5 percent equity market decline.

Mixed results, graded in yellow, include the prediction regarding German resistance to commingled risks. While Germany resisted Eurobonds and joint deposit guarantees, the potential for the European Stability Mechanism to directly recapitalize European banks introduced an unexpected level of burden-sharing. Additionally, the forecast for US economic growth was slightly too optimistic, predicting 2.25 percent gross domestic product growth and 200,000 monthly payroll gains; actual gross domestic product growth was 1.9 percent in the first quarter and estimated at 1.5 percent in the second quarter, while monthly payrolls averaged 150,000 to 159,000. 

Two primary views were graded red. First, the expectation that the US economy would remain more resilient than Europe and Asia failed in June when US manufacturing, new orders, and export orders collapsed to their weakest levels since 2009. Second, the author's nervousness regarding long-duration US government bonds was incorrect. Despite an 8 percent deficit and a troubling long-term fiscal outlook, heavy buying from foreign central banks and the Federal Reserve—which purchased 66 percent of all Treasury issuance in 2011—maintained strong demand and kept bond yields low.

This page presents a tabular self-assessment of J.P. Morgan’s 2012 market, economic, and investment views, using color-coded columns to evaluate how each outlook has performed so far in the year. The evaluation covers ten specific predictions, highlighting successful calls in green, mixed outcomes in yellow, underperforming views in red, and long-term views as "N.A." for those requiring more time to evaluate.

The evaluation begins with China, where the outlook is designated as mixed (yellow). While headline and core inflation fell, the RMB stopped appreciating (declining 1.1% compared to a 5% rise in 2011), and Chinese consumption as a share of GDP reached its highest level since the late 1990s, the authors admit they did not anticipate the severity of the economic slowdown, which has settled into 6% to 7% growth. 

Several equity-related calls are highlighted in green as successful. The broad recommendation to put capital to work in equities has borne fruit, with the MSCI World Equity Index up 5.8% and the firm's preferred strategy of MSCI World ex-Europe up 7.6%. Technology stocks have also outperformed, with the S&P 500 Info Tech sector rising 12.8% compared to a 9% gain for the broader S&P 500. Large-cap multinationals have done well, evidenced by a 10.7% return for the Morgan Stanley Multinational Nifty Fifty Index. However, the call to focus on high-dividend equity income stocks is marked as yellow, as the S&P Dividend Aristocrats Index rose 8.4% year-to-date, slightly underperforming the broader S&P 500. 

For credit and valuations, the prediction that equity valuations would remain low is marked green; the MSCI World trailing P/E ratio fluctuated between 13x and 15x, ending at 14x amid macro imbalances and stagnant labor compensation. Finding value in distressed loans from over-leveraged European banks, real estate, and private mezzanine debt is categorized as "N.A." due to the long-term nature of these assets. Meanwhile, the positive view on high-yield and leveraged loans is marked green, supported by the Barclays High Yield Index gaining 7.9% and the S&P/LSTA Leveraged Loan Index rising 4.8%, fueled by zero-interest-rate Federal Reserve policies.

The lowest-performing call on the page is the firm’s belief in macro hedge funds, marked in red. The HFRI Macro Hedge Fund Index rose only 1% through May, underperforming the broader HFRI Fund Weighted Composite at 1.6%. The text notes that macro managers missed the long-duration bond rally, were whipsawed by the Japanese Yen, and failed to generate gains in oil or gold. Lastly, the outlook on gold is marked yellow as a highly volatile "wild ride." Gold began the year at $1,563, peaked near $1,800 in February, and subsequently retraced its gains to end up near its starting point at $1,584.

The author provides a self-assessment of J.P. Morgan's 2012 market and economic views, noting that while their outlook on Europe was appropriately bearish, their US economic outlook was overly optimistic. Despite subpar US economic data, US equities have been stabilized by resilient corporate profits and significant liquidity. This disconnect is illustrated in a scatter plot titled "US equity performance relative to change in Economic Surprise index." This chart plots the six-month change of the S&P 500 against the six-month change of the Citigroup US Economic Surprise Index with data since 2003. A highlighted data point from June 29, 2012, shows that even with a significant negative reading on the surprise index of around negative 75, the S&P 500 experienced a positive return of roughly 15 percent, defying historical trends where negative economic surprises usually correlate with negative equity returns.

The underlying liquidity supporting US markets is detailed in three additional charts. The first, "US commercial bank excess deposits," tracks deposits and loans in trillions of dollars from 2000 to 2012. It shows that deposits and loans grew in tandem until 2008, after which deposits surged to nearly 8.5 trillion dollars while loans flattened out near 7 trillion dollars, creating a massive gap of excess liquidity. The second chart, "Foreign exchange reserves," displays the growth of reserves in trillions of dollars from 1970 to 2012, showcasing a dramatic divergence where emerging market reserves surged to nearly 8 trillion dollars while Japan's reserves remained flat around 1 trillion dollars. The third chart, "US corporate cash balances," plots cash and equivalents as a percentage of tangible assets from 1952 to 2012. It reveals that after dropping to a multi-decade low of around 5 percent in the late 1990s, corporate cash balances steadily rebuilt to nearly 10 percent by 2012, further highlighting the abundance of corporate liquidity.

Turning to Europe, the author analyzes the June EU summit, which initially pleased markets by permitting the European Stability Mechanism to directly recapitalize banks and purchase periphery bonds to stabilize yields. This marked a shift for German Chancellor Angela Merkel, who dropped her previous objections under pressure from Spain, Italy, and France. However, the author cautions that the positive market reaction is highly conditional, listing five major conditions that could derail progress. These include whether the European Stability Mechanism is fully ratified by all governments, whether it actually recapitalizes banks rather than just lending to them, whether any Eurozone members reject the recapitalizations, whether potential losses discourage future investment (as occurred in Ireland where the National Reserve Pension Fund lost 80 percent on its bank recaps), and whether the German Constitutional Court objects.

Ultimately, the author remains cautious, citing a pattern where prior summits have consistently disappointed markets once the initial hype cleared. The underlying issue in the Eurozone is viewed as an external imbalance between the private sector economies of the core and periphery nations, with sovereign and banking crises being mere symptoms. A key negative indicator highlighted is that loan creation in Italy has turned negative for the first time in twenty years, which poses a severe threat to a country that already has the lowest growth rate in the OECD next to Japan. The author concludes by stating that they are waiting for subsequent private sector credit, growth, and employment data before revising their bearish stance on Europe.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s commentary for J.P. Morgan Asset Management focuses on the geopolitical tensions of the June 2012 European Union summit, examining whether monetary unions are ultimately forged or fractured by politically strong-arming Germany—the nation expected to fund the Euro’s survival. 

To illustrate these dynamics, the page features a stylized map of Europe titled "June 2012 EU Summit Maneuvers." The map utilizes colorful arrows and symbols to trace how different nations positioned themselves during the negotiations, pointing to an isolated Germany at the center of the conflict. 

According to the author's detailed key of the summit's maneuvers, France and Italy coordinated to force German concessions. French President François Hollande threatened to let the summit fail and withhold support for his own growth compact unless Germany eased its austerity demands. Meanwhile, Italian Prime Minister Mario Monti defected from Germany's camp to join Hollande, threatening to collapse the talks and place the blame entirely on German Chancellor Angela Merkel. Spain, suffering from a severely weakened economy and banking sector, allied with Italy to push for European Union purchases of sovereign bonds with minimal conditions. 

This coordinated pressure left Germany isolated, forcing it to retreat from its strict European Stability Mechanism lending stance in exchange for vague commitments regarding region-wide banking oversight by the European Central Bank. This concession provoked significant domestic backlash for Merkel, including public criticism from German economists and the German President, alongside reluctance from France to cede its own banking authority to an EU regulator. Germany’s fiscally conservative allies, including Austria, Finland, and the Netherlands, were also dealt a blow by these concessions, despite high voting thresholds designed to protect their interests.

The commentary details the positions of several other European nations. Ireland viewed itself as a major winner of the Franco-Italian push, hoping the EU would directly recapitalize Allied Irish Bank and the Bank of Ireland with 15 billion Euros, which represents about 10 percent of Irish GNP, to prevent its debt-to-GNP ratio from spiking above 140 percent. Great Britain remained on the political sidelines in what the author calls "Splendid Isolation" after vetoing the fiscal compact, a position the author views as beneficial given the EMU's ongoing crises. Switzerland saw its monetary neutrality heavily challenged by capital fleeing the Periphery, forcing the Swiss National Bank's foreign exchange reserves to grow by an extraordinary 40 percent of GDP since 2009. Finally, Poland expressed a desire to join the Eurozone but is waiting for Germany to resolve the crisis and for peripheral nations to adhere to strict fiscal rules.

In terms of the broader economic outlook, the author concludes that while Germany remains motivated to prevent sovereign and banking failures in the Periphery, the exact form of future assistance remains highly uncertain. Because a clear road map is unlikely to emerge, the markets will have to rely on private sector recoveries in the United States and China, further monetary stimulus, and lower oil prices to support growth in the second half of the year.

This page presents J.P. Morgan's "Report card charts" as part of a self-assessment of global economic, market, and investment views in mid-2012. It features nine distinct charts covering global macroeconomic trends, equity valuations, monetary policy, and sovereign debt. 

The first chart tracks central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP from early 2011 through mid-2012. It highlights a massive expansion by the European Central Bank, which surged from around 20% of GDP to over 31% before tapering slightly, while the United Kingdom's balance sheet rose steadily to about 25%, Japan's hovered near 30%, and the United States Federal Reserve remained comparatively flat around 19%. The second chart displays global manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index surveys from 2010 to 2012, showing the Euro area falling deeply into contractionary territory below 50 to reach nearly 45 by late 2011, while the US remained expansionary above 52 and Asia hovered near the 50 line. The third chart details US annualized real GDP growth from 2010 through the second quarter of 2012, illustrating a deceleration from a peak of nearly 4% in late 2011 down to an estimated 1.5% in mid-2012.

Market-specific performance is addressed in the next set of charts. Chart four displays regional equity total returns in USD for the first half of 2012, highlighting the US as the strongest performer, peaking above 13% before settling near 8% in July, while European equities performed poorly, dropping to negative 7% in mid-2012 before a modest recovery. Chart five reveals a steady year-over-year deceleration in trailing four-quarter S&P 500 operating earnings per share growth, falling from over 40% in late 2010 to just over 10% by early 2012. Chart six tracks Italian 10-year government bond yields, which experienced extreme volatility, plummeting from over 7.25% in January down to under 5% in March, before climbing back over 6% by mid-year.

The final row of charts explores broader global indicators. Chart seven shows the contribution of equipment and software spending to US real GDP growth from 2005 to 2011, noting its recovery from a deep low of negative 2% in 2009 back to a positive contribution of around 1% in 2011. Chart eight focuses on China, tracking a simultaneous decline in both the reserve requirement ratio, which fell from 21.5% to 20.5% by early 2012, and year-over-year headline inflation, which cooled from over 6% in mid-2011 down to approximately 3% by early 2012. Chart nine graphs the MSCI World trailing price-to-earnings multiple from 1995 to 2011, illustrating that the global equity valuation multiple sat at a historically low level of around 14 by late 2011, far below the dot-com bubble peak near 30. A key of acronyms defines OECD, ECB, RMB, MSCI, HFRI, EU, and ESM.

This page of J.P. Morgan's publication analyzes why US equity markets have remained resilient despite weak global economic indicators, arguing that the primary driver of corporate profit margins in the current recovery is depressed labor compensation. Michael Cembalest notes that while economic data in the US, China, and Europe has been sluggish, US equities have risen 7% and Asia ex-Japan has risen 5%. He characterises the weak US recovery as a lion in winter struggling to maintain a 2% growth rate, though corporate profits have managed to outpace overall GDP. 

To illustrate this weak economic growth, the chart titled US real GDP growth following post-war recessions plots the index of GDP growth, starting at 100 at the GDP trough, over 16 quarters. The current recovery line sits at the very bottom of all historical post-war recoveries, barely reaching an index value of 108 after 12 quarters. 

Despite this tepid growth, corporate earnings have significantly outperformed the broader economy, as shown in a chart tracing the ratio of 2-year earnings growth to 2-year nominal GDP growth from 1952 onwards. Historically, the peak of this ratio averaged 2.1x in the mid-20th century and 4.2x from the late 1980s onward. However, in the current period, the ratio surged to an unprecedented peak of 14.3x before settling at 5.4x, demonstrating that profit growth has disconnected from nominal GDP growth.

The source of these fat profit margins is explored by comparing the current corporate profit cycle against the average of the past five US recoveries (1958, 1974, 1982, 1990, and 2001). Both charts track the changes in sales, labor compensation, and corporate profits in billions of 2005 dollars over 13 quarters following a profit trough. In past recoveries, sales growth rose to approximately $900 billion, and labor compensation grew steadily to about $400 billion, while corporate profits saw the smallest increase, peaking around $300 billion. In the current US recovery, the pattern is reversed. Corporate profits have skyrocketed to roughly $800 billion, far exceeding sales growth of about $600 billion. Meanwhile, labor compensation fell sharply at the start of the recovery and has remained nearly flat, barely climbing above zero by quarter 13.

Cembalest observes that while weak labor compensation has driven the profits boom and margins may remain high for a while, the resulting weak consumer spending, reliance on large government transfers, and political acrimony will likely suppress P/E multiples. He indicates that any acceleration in labor compensation would be positive, but nominal average hourly earnings and the employment cost index remain low, growing at just 2% year-over-year. For a more optimistic outlook, Cembalest argues that US real GDP growth needs to rise above 2.5%.

This page analyzes three key economic and market issues: the components of US manufacturing costs, the downward revision of corporate profit expectations, and the generational conflict underlying two distinct "fiscal cliffs" in the United States. 

To address US manufacturing margins, the first chart measures labor and energy intensity across multiple sectors as a share of total expenses. It illustrates that labor costs overwhelmingly dwarf energy costs in every category, including foods, machinery, technology, semiconductors, autos, papers, chemicals, plastics, metals, and iron and steel. Across all manufacturing sectors combined, labor represents approximately 20% of total expenses, while energy costs comprise less than 5%. The author cautions that while cheap natural gas is beneficial, its impact on margins is limited by this low expense share, suggesting investors should temper their enthusiasm.

The discussion then turns to US corporate profits. S&P 500 operating earnings per share estimates from August 2010 to April 2012 show that analyst projections have dropped significantly. Estimates for Q2 2012 fell from a peak near $27.50 down to approximately $25.50, representing a low hurdle of just 0.9% year-over-year growth (or 0% as expected by some analysts). Meanwhile, Q4 2012 estimates also declined from roughly $30.00 to $28.50, though they still represent a much tougher hurdle of 16.3% year-over-year growth. The author notes that US equities have historically risen 28% cumulatively since January 2010, driven almost entirely by earnings reporting seasons (13%) and quantitative easing announcements by the Fed and ECB (13.5%), while the remaining periods accounted for only 1.5% of gains.

Finally, the author contrasts two competing "fiscal cliffs." The first fiscal cliff is depicted in a chart showing the change in cyclically-adjusted federal deficit as a percentage of potential GDP from 1963 to 2013. While prior decades saw alternating periods of fiscal stimulus and fiscal drag, the 2013 estimate assuming current law projects an unprecedented fiscal drag of nearly -4% of GDP. Avoiding this immediate cliff, however, leads directly to the second fiscal cliff: escalating national debt. The final chart displays net debt to GDP on an inverted scale from 2004 to 2022, emphasizing the visual downward trajectory of rising debt. Under the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) Alternative Case, net debt to GDP plunges toward 90% by 2022, whereas the CBO Baseline and Post-Budget Control Act (BCA) cases project stabilization around 60%. The author poses the open question of whether the US can continue to escape market consequences for its escalating debt burden, concluding that completely avoiding the immediate austerity of the first cliff simply passes a massive, generational burden to future posterities.

This page from the publication addresses two primary topics: a historical analysis of how the United States successfully reduced its post-World War II debt during the 1950s, and the accelerating credit contraction within the Eurozone, referred to as the European Credit Divorce. 

In the first section, the author dispels common misconceptions about the US post-war economic recovery, arguing that the reduction of debt was not driven by government spending cuts, radical tax hikes, or engineered negative interest rates. Instead, the author credits a strong competitive advantage over recovering war-torn nations and pro-business policies, such as the Eisenhower administration's elimination of price controls and the introduction of Subchapter S legislation to avoid double-taxation on small businesses. A supporting historical table covering the years 1950 through 1960 shows that while absolute net debt remained relatively flat—increasing only slightly from $219 billion to $237 billion, representing a 0.8% compound annual growth rate—the ratio of net debt to GDP was nearly halved, dropping from 80% to 46%. This reduction was driven by robust real GDP growth, which expanded at a compound annual rate of 4.3% (growing from $273 billion to $415 billion in 1950 USD). The table also illustrates that government outlays as a percentage of GDP actually increased slightly over the decade from 16% to 18%, while receipts hovered between 14% and 19%, and average real 10-year interest rates remained positive in most years, ending at 2.7% in 1960. Highlighting that the private sector accounted for a post-war peak of 86% of total employment during this era, the author raises the open question of how the modern US will successfully address its current 80% net-debt-to-GDP ratio without these same pro-business conditions. This section also includes a brief philosophical detour noting that US filmmakers have historically harbored an anti-capitalist bias, often depicting corporations as villainous despite benefiting from the wealth generated by capitalism.

The second section focuses on the unraveling of European monetary integration. The author notes that Eurozone banks and international lenders are rapidly pulling back their credit exposure to the European Periphery, leaving the European Central Bank to act as a stop-gap financier to prevent a depression. Two charts illustrate this capital flight. The first chart, titled "Flight of the Bumblebee," plots cross-border lending within the Eurozone in trillions of USD on the left axis alongside non-Eurozone lending to the Periphery on the right axis from 2004 to 2011. Both metrics show a steep decline after peaking around 2007–2008: Eurozone cross-border lending fell from nearly $6.5 trillion to $4.5 trillion, and non-Eurozone lending to the Periphery dropped from around $1.0 trillion to $0.6 trillion. The second chart, titled "Peripheral sovereign and financial debt," uses a stacked area format to depict the cumulative growth of peripheral debt in trillions of Euros from 2002 to 2011. It shows that total outstanding debt—split between sovereign and financial obligations—grew from roughly 3 trillion Euros in 2002 to nearly 7 trillion Euros in 2011, with both components expanding significantly. The author concludes with the warning that until economic conditions and structural reforms improve in the Periphery, there remain serious unresolved questions about how the European Central Bank and the European Union will secure the funding needed to refinance this massive pool of maturing debt that private investors no longer wish to hold.
