This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication, written by Michael Cembalest, explores the cognitive effects of aging and retirement. Drawing on a study by Fabrizio Mazzonna and Franco Peracchi from the Munich Center for the Economics of Aging, the commentary highlights how mental faculties tend to decline after age 50, but notes that staying employed and understanding gender-based cognitive trends can offer valuable insights for aging individuals. 

The page features two sets of charts illustrating these trends across five cognitive dimensions—orientation, immediate recall, delayed recall, fluency, and numeracy—plotted against ages ranging from 50 to 70. The first set of charts, which compares average test scores by gender, shows that women consistently outperform men in orientation, immediate recall, delayed recall, and fluency throughout the entire age range. Numeracy is the only category where men maintain a distinct and steady lead over women. 

The second set of charts compares test scores based on employment status, contrasting retired individuals with those who remain employed. Across all five cognitive categories, employed individuals maintain significantly higher average scores than retired individuals of the same age. The downward trends across both chart sets emphasize the overall decline in cognitive performance after age 50, but the persistent gap between the employed and retired cohorts leads Cembalest to conclude that continuing to work is highly beneficial for preserving cognitive health, particularly when coupled with a zero-interest-rate environment.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" explores the burgeoning investment opportunities within Big Data, detailing how a massive expansion in connected devices, internet bandwidth, and corporate databases has set the stage for a technological transformation. The author points to the proliferation of 30 million sensor nodes growing at 30 percent annually, alongside massive healthcare and corporate ERP databases, such as the 71 billion credit and debit transactions recorded in the United States in 2011. 

To illustrate the technical drivers of this shift, the page features two charts plotted on logarithmic scales to emphasize their exponential progress. The first chart, "Cost of a gigabyte of storage," shows the dramatic decline in per-unit storage costs from 1980 to 2008. Over this period, indicative retail prices compiled from manufacturers like VR Data Corp., Percom, Western Digital, Seagate, Maxtor, Quantum, Fujitsu, and Hitachi collapsed from $1,000,000 per gigabyte to nearly $0.01. The second chart, "Processing power," tracks transistor count per processor from 1971 to 2011 using data from Intel, AMD, Sony, IBM, and Sun Microsystems. The visual illustrates a climb from roughly 1,000 transistors per processor to nearly 10 billion. A practical real-world example notes that a 32 GB camera chip today weighs half a gram and costs under $100, making it millions of times lighter and 30,000 times cheaper than equivalent technology from 30 years prior. 

The bottom half of the page details a variety of existing and emerging Big Data products and services categorized across four sectors: Government, Healthcare, Pharmaceutical, and Automotive. In government, applications include tax and Medicare fraud prevention, military satellite and signal intercept analysis, and municipal smartphone-based toll and pothole tracking. In healthcare, the page highlights that the digitization of medical records, supported by $20 billion in funding from the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, helped drive US hospital electronic record adoption from 16 percent in 2009 to 35 percent in 2011. Other medical applications include clinical decision support systems and remote patient monitoring. The pharmaceutical section notes that faster data analysis could speed up clinical drug evaluations or identify adverse drug effects earlier, citing Vioxx as an example of a drug that might have been pulled from the market sooner. Finally, the automotive sector utilizes data to integrate traffic, accident, and maintenance statuses—highlighting manufacturers like GM and BMW—and compiles cellular signals to analyze traffic patterns for fuel and emission savings.

This page explores the expanding investment opportunities and practical applications of Big Data across multiple economic sectors, emphasizing the technical shift toward managing unstructured information. In retailing, Big Data is leveraged through RFID tracking of shopping carts and geo-targeted ads to counter online margin pressures, which have caused retailers' share of consumer goods operating profits to drop from over 50% in 1999 to 30% today. In financial services, firms use satellite imagery to price real estate risk, while Nilson estimates that debit and credit card purchases will make up 67% of transactions by 2015, up from a baseline where cash and checks accounted for 84% in 1990. Telecommunications companies use social media connections to predict customer churn, aerospace and defense sectors deploy complex modeling to manage supply chains, and utilities apply route optimization to reduce delivery costs.

To explain how Big Data functions, the text notes that most newly aggregated data is unstructured—consisting of social media feeds, video, and machine data—requiring specialized databases like Hadoop, Splunk, and NoSQL rather than traditional relational databases. The author highlights a severe shortage of machine learning expertise, citing Carnegie Mellon observations on the supply-demand imbalance in the field. 

Two graphics illustrate these trends. A stacked bar chart titled "Unstructured data takes over" displays worldwide total archived capacity in exabytes from 2008 to a 2015 estimate, categorized by E-mail, Relational databases, and Unstructured data. The chart reveals an exponential surge in archived capacity, rising from under 50 exabytes in 2008 to over 300 exabytes in 2015, with unstructured data accounting for nearly the entire expansion and reaching roughly 270 exabytes. The second graphic is a disease network visualization from the MIT Senseable City Lab Health Infoscape project and GE. Analyzing 217 million medical records, this colorful cluster diagram maps co-occurring health conditions, visually connecting nodes such as depression, tobacco abuse, diabetes, and chest pain to help human operators recognize hidden public health patterns.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest analyzes the divergence between strong stock performance and mediocre economic growth, specifically focusing on how US equity markets rose thirteen percent in 2012 despite lackluster economic data. He argues that corporate profits are outstripping broader economic indicators due to structural differences—such as the S&P 500 being more heavily weighted toward manufacturing than the overall US economy—and a historic fifty-year low in labor compensation, which bolsters profit margins at the expense of general economic growth. Cembalest also expresses nervousness regarding the ongoing European economic situation, promising a more detailed exploration of the European experiment in early September.

The page features two charts to support these observations. The first chart, titled "Global equities and global growth, 1970-2012," is a scatter plot mapping annualized first-half global GDP growth on the horizontal axis against global equity returns through August 1st on the vertical axis. A highlighted area titled "Box: Low growth and positive equity returns" shows that while positive equity returns typically align with three to six percent global GDP growth, years like 2012 stand out by generating positive stock returns of over ten percent despite global GDP growth hovering under two percent. 

The second chart, titled "Earnings still outperforming the economy," plots the ratio of two-year earnings growth to two-year nominal GDP growth from 1952 through 2012. This ratio line illustrates how corporate earnings have historically outpaced nominal GDP, with the average peak ratio doubling from an early historical norm of 2.1x to a later average peak of 4.2x. The data shows a massive spike to 14.3x following the 2008 financial crisis, with the ratio recently resting at 4.0x. The page concludes with a glossary of acronyms relevant to the broader economic discussion, including the Economic Cycle Research Institute, Bureau of Labor Statistics, European Central Bank, Bank of England, and various monetary policy programs like quantitative easing, long-term refinancing operations, and the securities markets program.

This J.P. Morgan commentary analyzes the surprising 13 percent year-to-date rally in US equity markets in 2012 despite weak economic indicators and falling earnings forecasts. The author argues that Bronze is the new Gold, meaning investor expectations are so low that mediocre, slightly better-than-recessionary economic news can trigger massive positive market reactions, largely because investors anticipate central bank intervention rather than an organic private-sector recovery. 

The page features two charts illustrating these trends. The first, a line chart titled Global economy very reliant on monetary stimulus, tracks the Global PMI survey, which measures manufacturing activity and sentiment on a scale from 35 to 60, from 2007 to 2012. Shaded areas on the chart mark four distinct periods of major monetary easing: Fed QE1 and BoE QE1 in 2009; Fed QE2 and BoE QE2 in late 2010; Fed Twist, BoE QE3 and QE4, and the ECB LTRO in late 2011; and Fed Twist 2, BoE QE5, the ECB rate cut, and SMP hints in mid-2012. This visual underlines how global economic sentiment peaks have consistently been driven by coordinated central bank actions. 

The second chart, titled Instances when payroll gains resulted in same-day S&P 500 gains of greater than 2 percent (1966-2012), is a bar chart depicting normalized payroll job gains in thousands across historical instances. It places the August 3, 2012 payroll announcement, where 160,000 jobs were created (normalized to 163,000 on the chart and shown in red), in historical context. Historically, 2 percent rallies on payroll days typically occurred alongside massive gains, such as 427,000 jobs on August 3, 1984, or 351,000 jobs on December 7, 1973. The 2012 figure of 163,000 is near the absolute bottom of historical catalysts, surpassed in weakness only by anomalous days in 1999 during the height of the dot-com bubble featuring stocks like Global Crossing, JDS Uniphase, and theGlobe.com, and July 5, 2002, when market fears of a terrorist attack overshadowed payroll data. 

Looking forward, the author disagrees with the Economic Cycle Research Institute's prediction that the US is already in a recession, instead forecasting stable but mediocre growth with payrolls averaging around 150,000 and GDP growth at roughly 2 percent. The author notes that the durability of this trend relies heavily on the upcoming election and the resolution of the fiscal cliff. Markets are currently pricing in a successful negotiation that will reduce the projected 4.5 percent tax drag on GDP down to 1.5 percent. Finally, the author points out that massive cash reserves held overseas by large tech, pharma, and industrial firms are driving an increase in buybacks and mergers and acquisitions, while the prospect of unlimited bond purchases by the European Central Bank to absorb sovereign and bank debt exposure continues to provide a tailwind to equities.

In this analysis, the author discusses how global equity markets have managed to rise about ten percent in 2012 despite disappointing global GDP growth and weak leading manufacturing indicators. This unusual divergence is attributed to robust corporate profits in the second quarter, low starting price-to-earnings multiples, anticipation of a negotiated resolution to the United States fiscal cliff, and aggressive monetary easing. Most importantly, the rally has been fueled by the actions and statements of the European Central Bank under President Mario Draghi, who committed to preserving the Eurozone by intervening in bond markets.

The disconnect between market performance and economic reality is supported by three charts. The first, titled "Global equity returns vs GDP growth, 1970-2012," plots annual global equity returns on a vertical axis from negative forty-five percent to positive forty-five percent against annual global GDP growth on a horizontal axis from negative two percent to six percent. A highlighted box captures years with low growth and positive equity returns, showcasing 2012 with an annualized first-half GDP growth of approximately one and a half percent alongside a global equity return of nearly ten percent. The second chart, "New global manufacturing orders, slowing down again," displays a global manufacturing index from 1998 to 2012 where a reading above fifty represents expansion. This line shows that after recovering to nearly sixty in 2010, the momentum has faded, with the index slipping back below the critical fifty threshold in 2012.

The third chart, "The European Creosote Bank?", compares central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP from 2008 through mid-2012, with projections into 2013. It tracks the Federal Reserve, the Bank of England, the Bank of Japan, and the European Central Bank. While the United States balance sheet sits at roughly twenty percent of GDP and the United Kingdom stands at twenty-five percent, the European Central Bank's line has risen rapidly to over thirty percent. A prominent red dot projects that an additional one-trillion-Euro expansion would push the European Central Bank's balance sheet past forty percent of GDP, exceeding Japan's thirty percent level. 

The author compares this massive balance sheet expansion to the fictional, overeating character Mr. Creosote, warning of potentially messy long-term consequences. While central bank debt purchases temporarily postpone defaults and lower short-term yields, the author raises open questions about how this will ultimately play out. European stocks trade at a substantial discount to those in the United States; since January 2010, the S&P returned thirty-three percent, compared to just one and a half percent for the MSCI Europe index and a negative fourteen percent return for European Monetary Union nations.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market examines the consequences, risks, and massive capital shifts associated with the European Central Bank’s debt monetization strategies during the European debt crisis. The analysis begins by highlighting how US equities have dramatically outperformed European equities. A chart illustrating European stock valuation discounts to the US shows European stocks trading near historical lows, approaching a thirty-five percent discount by 2012 when measured on a composite basis of price-to-earnings, price-to-book, and price-to-dividend ratios. Accompanying this, a chart of cumulative US dollar returns from January 2008 to August 2012 demonstrates that the S&P 500, which recovered to near its starting cumulative level, vastly outperformed the MSCI European Union index, which sat near sixty, and the MSCI Europe Monetary Union index, which lagged around fifty.

The author poses the open question of what risks and costs are associated with the ECB's debt monetization policies, turning to Germany as a primary case study. While German wage gains and housing prices show signs of life, overall core inflation remains low. Three supporting charts tracking German economic metrics from 1999 to 2011 illustrate this dynamic: wage inflation in industry and construction has risen to between three and four percent year-over-year; annual house price growth has rebounded sharply from negative territory in the mid-2000s to over four percent; yet core inflation remains stable and well below the target, fluctuating around one point two percent.

The text warns of potential losses at the ECB, explaining that central banks can hide losses or offset them through seigniorage, which is the spread between the yield on purchased bonds and their zero-percent cost of capital. However, the author forecasts that the ECB may ultimately have to orchestrate a Paris Club style debt restructuring rather than executing a clean exit strategy. This intervention is deemed necessary to counter a massive capital flight from southern Europe, which the author dramatically compares to historic mass migrations. A bottom-left chart shows that cumulative ECB lending to periphery banks rose in near-perfect lockstep with net capital and trade outflows from the Periphery, with both cumulative metrics reaching approximately eight hundred and sixty billion Euros by mid-2012. Lastly, a final chart tracking foreign private investment outflows as a percentage of GDP shows the severity of this capital flight, with cumulative outflows peaking at over one hundred and sixty percent for Portugal, around one hundred and twenty percent for Spain, roughly eighty percent for Greece, and a minor, late-stage spike for Italy, illustrating the systemic vulnerability of the European periphery.

This page focuses on the cheapness of technology and cyclical stocks and reflects on the disconnect between weak global economic indicators and strong market performance in 2012. The author argues that the death of equities theme is misplaced, advocating for equities as a cornerstone for portfolios seeking to beat inflation. Within the US market, technology is highlighted as a preferred sector due to earnings doubling since 2007 despite a halved price-to-earnings multiple, high cash flow yields, and rising productivity.

To illustrate these points, four charts are presented. The first chart, titled Technology stock valuations, displays data from 2003 to 2012. It plots the sector's price-to-earnings multiple on the left axis, ranging from 10 to 55, against cash flow yield in percent on the right axis, ranging from 5 to 15 percent. The chart shows the P/E multiple falling from around 50 in 2003 to roughly 15 in 2012, while the cash flow yield climbed from about 5 percent to over 10 percent during the same period. The second chart, titled Technology sector productivity and capital efficiency, tracks return on equity on the left axis, from 10 to 35 percent, and sales per employee in thousands of US dollars on the right axis, from 300 to 900, between 2003 and 2012. Both lines trend steadily upward, showing sales per employee rising from around 400 thousand to over 800 thousand dollars, and return on equity increasing from below 15 percent to nearly 30 percent.

The third chart, Cyclicals trading very cheaply vs. Defensives, plots the ratio of cyclicals to defensives trailing P/E from 1974 to 2010 on a scale from 0.4 to 1.8. The chart reveals that cyclicals are trading at one of their largest discounts in decades, with the ratio dipping to around 0.8 by 2010. The fourth chart, titled Remembrance of things past: negative returns on cash, displays the ex-post real return on US Treasury bills from 1934 to 2011 on a scale from negative 10 percent to positive 10 percent. This chart highlights that real returns have been negative for 45 consecutive months, a trend with no end in sight, particularly following a speech by Woodford.

The text goes on to characterize 2012 as a strange year, noting that while economic worries were justified, global equity markets rose 13 percent. The author lists several signs of economic weakness, including weakening global manufacturing indicators; sharp export slowdowns in China, South Korea, and Taiwan, with China potentially growing at only 6 percent; stagnant European growth of around 0 percent with peripheral recessions; weak US jobs reports; slowing US capital spending; industrial fatigue in Brazil from a strong currency; a lack of political clarity from the upcoming US election; and slowing corporate profit growth. Despite these headwinds, the author concludes that massive global liquidity and continued monetary stimulus have driven equity markets to outperform expectations, rewarding investors who looked past economic weakness to take advantage of low equity valuations.

This page examines central bank balance sheet expansion and the massive volume of sidelined global cash that is beginning to flow into riskier assets. The central argument is that the European Central Bank's announcement to further expand its balance sheet—dubbed "Das Kapitulation" because German resistance to debt monetization has effectively collapsed—is a deliberate effort to delay restructurings and preserve the Euro. This monetary easing mirrors earlier strategies by the U.S. Federal Reserve to debase cash and compel investment in higher-risk assets, a dynamic that is starting to draw down a historic "wall of cash" that has earned negative real returns for four years. 

Several visual aids illustrate this environment of massive liquidity and cautious investor positioning. A top-right chart tracks central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP from 2008 to 2013, showing a dramatic spike for the European Central Bank following a one-trillion-euro injection, which pushed the ECB balance sheet past thirty percent of GDP, exceeding the UK's twenty-five percent and the US Federal Reserve’s fifteen to twenty percent range, while matching Japan’s elevated levels.

A trio of middle charts details the "wall of cash." The first shows foreign exchange reserves in trillions of USD from 1970 to 2010, showing emerging markets' reserves skyrocketing to over eight trillion dollars, vastly outpacing Japan’s stable level of around one trillion dollars. The second chart illustrates U.S. commercial bank deposits and loans from 2000 to 2012, highlighting a massive divergence after 2008 where deposits surged past eight trillion dollars while outstanding loans flatlined below seven trillion dollars. The third chart details U.S. cash balances from 1960 to 2008, displaying elevated levels for both corporate cash-to-assets, which rose toward eight percent, and household cash-to-GDP, which peaked near eleven percent.

At the bottom of the page, the author connects these cash dynamics to asset markets. A chart on U.S. mutual fund net flows from 2006 to 2011 highlights the extreme caution of retail investors, showing cumulative inflows into bonds climbing over one trillion dollars while equity mutual funds suffered outflows of nearly four hundred billion dollars. The final chart demonstrates that the S&P 500 rise was driven entirely by multiple expansion rather than corporate fundamentals. Over the course of the year, consensus earnings-per-share estimates for the S&P 500 steadily declined from over one hundred six dollars to under one hundred three dollars, yet the price-to-earnings multiple expanded from roughly 12.2 times to nearly 14.0 times, indicating that rising stock prices were a reflection of multiple expansion rather than improving earnings.

This commentary by Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management focuses on the sovereign debt challenges in Europe, specifically Spain, and presents a quantitative critique of using tax hikes on high earners to solve the United States budget deficit. Cembalest begins by questioning the European Central Bank's ability to easily isolate and support Spain and Italy. He warns that the ECB's strategy of shortening the maturity of Italian and Spanish debt may only delay a larger crisis for three years. 

To illustrate Spain’s severe economic imbalances, the page features a multi-line chart titled "Spanish Armada runs aground, again," alongside a painting by Philip James de Loutherbourg depicting the historical defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588. The chart plots several economic indicators from 1980 to 2010. It shows that following the Euro's inception in 1999, Spain's unit labor costs relative to Germany rose steadily, and its reliance on foreign capital, measured by Net International Investment Position as a percentage of GDP, deteriorated sharply into deep negative territory. Following the 2007 financial crisis, Spain experienced dramatic spikes in its unemployment rate, bankruptcies per quarter, and non-performing loans as a percentage of total lending, while German industrial production significantly outpaced Spanish production.

In the second half of the page, Cembalest discusses "The 71% solution," a thought experiment exploring how high top marginal federal income tax rates would need to rise to reduce the US budget deficit to 3% of GDP by 2020 under the Congressional Budget Office's Alternative Case scenario, assuming taxing the wealthy is the sole mechanism. His calculations reveal that the top marginal rate would have to reach 71%, with the second highest bracket at 57%. When combined with state, local, and payroll taxes, total income tax rates would near 80% in states like New York and California. Cembalest argues this demonstrates that taxing the rich alone is mathematically insufficient to solve the deficit. Instead, he suggests the US will ultimately require broader tax reform affecting the middle class, larger spending cuts, or debt monetization by the Federal Reserve. He notes that trying to grow out of the deficit would require an unrealistic average real GDP growth of 8.6% per year through 2020, far exceeding the projected 2.9%. In a footnote, he addresses historical comparisons, pointing out that while statutory marginal rates exceeded 80% in the 1950s, they only applied to individuals ten times wealthier in inflation-adjusted terms than today's top bracket, and effective tax rates were much lower due to abundant deductions. He concludes by stating that CBO tables suggest the US tax system has actually become substantially more progressive since 1979.

This page examines the progressivity of the US tax system over time across different income brackets, alongside an appendix detailing the underlying assumptions used by the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) in its fiscal projections. 

Two tables using CBO data compare effective federal tax rates from 1979 to 2009 across five quintiles (Low, Second, Middle, Fourth, High) and the Top 1%. The first table, detailing the Average Effective Federal Income Tax rate, illustrates that the bottom two quintiles have increasingly negative effective income tax rates due to transfers and tax credits. Specifically, the Low quintile's effective rate dropped from 0.0% in 1979 to -9.3% in 2009, while the Second quintile went from 4.0% to -2.6%. Middle-income taxpayers saw their rate fall from 7.4% to 1.3%. For the highest earners, the Top 1% rate dropped from 22.7% in 1979 to 21.0% in 2009, after peaking at 24.3% in 1999. 

The second table covers the Average Effective Federal Total Tax rate, which includes payroll and other federal taxes. It shows that overall tax burdens fell across all brackets over the thirty-year span. The Low quintile's total effective rate fell from 7.5% to 1.0%, the Middle quintile's rate dropped from 18.9% to 11.1%, the High quintile's rate declined from 27.1% to 23.2%, and the Top 1% saw their rate fall from 35.1% to 28.9%. 

An appendix outlines the CBO’s Alternative Case assumptions for top tax bracket analysis, which deviates from legislated baselines to reflect realistic political outcomes. The Alternative Case assumes that all tax cuts are extended with no changes to capital gains and dividend rates. It assumes that the post-2011 payroll tax holiday—which temporarily reduced the Social Security withholding rate from 6.2% to 4.2% under the Tax Relief Act of 2010—will expire. The Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) exemption is assumed to continue to be indexed to inflation, preventing more taxpayers from falling into this tax bracket. Furthermore, the CBO assumes that scheduled SGR-dictated cuts to Medicare payments to physicians will not take effect, noting that SGR-based payments would otherwise be about 27% below current rates. Lastly, the Alternative Case assumes that the Budget Control Act sequester—a $1.2 trillion automatic spending cut scheduled for January 2013 after the Joint Select Committee on Deficit Reduction failed to reach an agreement—does not take effect.

This page serves as an appendix examining the "Clinton Recovery" from 1992 to 2000, which was characterized by 19% equity returns, 3.8% annualized real GDP growth, 265,000 monthly payroll gains, and an average budget deficit of less than 2% of GDP. The author questions how much presidential policies truly drive business cycles but analyzes the policy mix of the Clinton era to understand what might have contributed. The argument highlights that the recovery was fueled by a combination of progressive and non-progressive policies: raising top marginal income tax rates and cutting defense spending, alongside cutting capital gains taxes, supporting free trade, and pursuing significant industry deregulation.

Four charts support this analysis. The first chart, "Top tax rate on ordinary income and long term capital gains," displays rates from 1990 to 1999. It shows the ordinary income tax rate jumping from 28% to nearly 40% in 1993, while the long-term capital gains rate remained flat at 28% until being cut to 20% in 1997. The second chart, "US military spending, in between combatants," tracks defense spending as a percentage of GDP from 1975 to 2010. It illustrates a steady decline during the shaded Clinton Recovery period, falling from around 4.5% of GDP in the early 1990s to a low of nearly 3.0% in 2000, before rising again to around 4.5% by 2010. The third chart, "US trade and trade policy," measures exports and imports as a percent of GDP from 1990 to 1999. Trade activity rose from approximately 20.5% of GDP in 1990 to over 24% by 1999, with a visible upward inflection point following the enactment of the North American Free Trade Agreement around 1993–1994. The fourth chart, "Deregulation and business capital spending," spans 1987 to 2001 and compares a product market regulation index against nonresidential business investment as a percentage of capital stock. The chart displays a sharp drop in regulation for both electricity (noting FERC 888 on Wholesale Competition) and telecom (noting the Telecommunications Act of 1996). Simultaneously, nonresidential business investment rose from around 9.5% of capital stock in the early 1990s to nearly 12.0% by 2000, demonstrating how regulatory relief spurred capital spending. 

The accompanying text discusses broader historical context, noting that the drop in military spending was a temporary window of peace between the collapse of the Soviet Union and post-2001 conflicts, the roots of which the author partially traces to Operation Cyclone under Carter and Reagan. Additionally, the text highlights that while NAFTA signaled free-trade support, external global events like Deng's reforms in China and Rao's reforms in India also played a vital role in boosting global trade.

This page analyzes the policy drivers of the Clinton Recovery, focusing on centrist approaches to welfare, healthcare, and housing that had long-term economic structural consequences. The author begins by examining welfare reform, specifically the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996, which introduced work requirements and shifted responsibility to the states. A line chart illustrating the average monthly recipients of Federal assistance from 1962 through the late 1990s shows that recipient numbers peaked near 14 million in the early 1990s before sharply dropping to around 7 million following the 1996 reform. 

In healthcare, the author notes that while universal healthcare failed to pass, private-sector competition via Health Maintenance Organizations (HMOs) successfully curbed expenditure growth during the 1990s. A chart tracking the five-year moving average of year-over-year real growth in national healthcare expenditures shows a decline from around 7% in the late 1980s to below 4% by the late 1990s, though the author warns that 3% to 4% growth remains problematic given the nation's declining structural growth rate.

The remainder of the page argues that while the 1990s housing market benefited from conservative underwriting, federal policies planted the seeds of the eventual subprime housing crisis. The author points to the Federal Housing Enterprises Financial Safety and Soundness Act of 1992 (FHEFSSA) passed under President Bush, which allowed the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to set affordable lending targets. The Clinton Administration subsequently raised these GSE affordable lending targets from 30% to 50%. 

This shift is illustrated in two housing charts. The first shows the national average downpayment on home mortgages declining precipitously from approximately 26% in 1990 to below 20% by 1995. The second housing chart, depicting the origins of the housing crisis from 1980 to 2007, plots HUD affordable lending targets against the percentage of FHA and Fannie Mae home purchase volumes with a loan-to-value (LTV) or combined loan-to-value (CLTV) ratio of 97% or greater. This second metric rose from near 0% in the early 1990s to over 15% by 2007, while HUD targets rose from 30% to 55% over the same period. Detailed footnotes criticize these relaxed lending standards, quoting a 2000 HUD report encouraging GSEs to underprice competitors in subprime lending, as well as a highly optimistic 2002 risk assessment by economists Joseph Stiglitz and Peter Orszag.

This page explores the historical relationship between equity market rallies and weak economic growth indicators. The author argues that while equity rallies typically align with a global manufacturing PMI above 50 or at least rising, 2012 defied this trend as equities surged while the PMI remained weak and in decline. Historical analysis since 1960 shows that when equity markets and leading economic indicators disagree—meaning equities rise while the PMI falls below 50—the equity markets are usually eventually proven correct, with the sole exception being July 1980. 

A dual-axis chart titled "Equity rallies usually coincide with high or rising leading indicators, but not in 2012" tracks the index level of the MSCI World Equity Index against the global manufacturing PMI from 2010 to 2012. It visually highlights this divergence, showing the equity index rising to around 1,350 in 2012 while the manufacturing PMI dipped below the expansionary 50 threshold to around 48. 

An accompanying table, "When equity markets and leading economic indicators disagreed, the markets were usually right," provides historical data from 1961 to 2012 for instances where markets and indicators diverged. It tracks the four-month rise in S&P 500 or MSCI World equities, the global/US PMI index level, the four-month change in the PMI, and the subsequent two-year equity returns and PMI changes. For the September 2012 entry, the table notes a 13.9% rise in equities alongside a PMI of 48.4 (representing a four-month drop of 2.2), while leaving the subsequent two-year equity and PMI changes as open questions marked by question marks.

A second chart, "Reduction of 'tail risk' contributes to multiple expansion," plots forward price-to-earnings multiples from January to September 2012. It shows the S&P 500 P/E multiple expanding from roughly 12 to over 14, and the MSCI Europe multiple rising from around 9.5 to 12, demonstrating how easing tail risks drove multiple expansions over the summer. 

The author identifies aggressive monetary policy from global central banks as the primary catalyst for the rally, noting that banks are expanding base money until economies respond. This is illustrated in the chart "To infinity....and beyond!!," which projects central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP from 2008 to 2013. The data lines show the European Central Bank balance sheet climbing toward 35% of GDP, driven by an additional €1 trillion for Spain and Italy; the Bank of Japan's balance sheet rising above 30% following its announced program; the Federal Reserve's balance sheet projected to rise toward 23% under quantitative easing linked to Fed Governor Narayana Kocherlakota's advocated 5.5% unemployment threshold; and the Bank of England's balance sheet leveling off near 26% with no announced changes to its current program. The author highlights that the Federal Reserve now owns more than 25% of all duration in the US Treasury market.

The page concludes with the author reflecting on how this environment impacts money management. Having anticipated only a high single-digit return, the author notes that the 15% rally in global equities was unexpected, which led to a focus on public and private credit and hedge funds.

This page discusses private equity investing opportunities in Asia, focusing on two distinct themes: the growth of the luxury retail market and the rise of beer consumption in the region. 

In the luxury sector, the text details a retailer's geographical expansion into Tier 3 and Tier 4 Chinese cities, as well as emerging Indian urban centers like Chennai, Hyderabad, and Pune. This strategy is bolstered by exclusive brand distribution rights from high-end names such as Rolex, Jaeger-LeCoultre, A. Lange & Söhne, and De Beers, helping drive a 30 percent annual revenue increase. A line chart depicting the size of the worldwide personal luxury market from 1995 to 2011 shows a steady climb from around 75 billion Euros to nearly 190 billion Euros, despite a brief dip in 2009. Accompanying tables from Bain & Company illustrate that the Asia-Pacific region recorded the strongest regional growth, expanding by 28 percent in 2010 and 27 percent in 2011, while watches and jewelry led the sectoral growth with increases of 23 percent and 19 percent over the same periods.

The second half of the page shifts to beverage dynamics, highlighting that global consumers increasingly prefer beer over other spirits. The author describes a notable transaction involving a leading South Korean brewery established in 1933 that controls a 54 percent market share with local brands Cass, OB Golden Lager, and Cafri, alongside licensed brands Budweiser and Hoegaarden. This brewery operates with strong 30 percent operating cash flow margins, driven by South Korea's high beer consumption, which accounts for 50 percent of the domestic liquor industry. 

To illustrate this global shift, a line chart tracking global alcohol consumption from 1961 to 2003 shows beer volumes climbing from approximately 35 billion liters to over 150 billion liters, leaving wine and other beverages flat at under 30 billion liters. A final line chart displays the volume convergence of beer consumption from 1961 to 2009 across Asia, the Americas, and Europe. While European and American consumption steadily rose to plateaus of roughly 55 million tonnes, Asian consumption surged from near zero in 1961 to converge with Western volumes by 2009. The author suggests that while per capita consumption in Asia remains low compared to the West, total volume has caught up, highlighting massive expansion potential in markets like China.

In this publication, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that while central bank actions have boosted global equities, actual economic growth and employment must improve to justify these stock market rallies. On the positive side, corporations, households, and sovereign wealth funds possess massive idle cash balances; for instance, if S&P non-financial firms returned cash and leverage to their historic averages, they would have one point four trillion dollars available for mergers, acquisitions, and shareholder distributions. 

However, the author cautions that the economic situation in France is deteriorating markedly despite a twelve percent year-to-date rise in its equity markets. Cembalest frames France as a critical litmus test for redistributionist tax policies, noting that President François Hollande’s budget proposes a retroactive sixty-two percent long-term capital gains tax rate on gains above one hundred fifty thousand Euros. He questions whether such policies will simply lead to lower growth and fail to improve France’s budget deficit, suggesting Spain's recent economic history serves as a cautionary warning.

To illustrate the structural decline in France, the author presents three charts. The first shows French real exports as a percentage of German exports from 1970 to 2010, which reveals a steady decline from a peak of over sixty percent in the late 1990s down to nearly forty percent by 2010. The second chart tracks the seasonally adjusted France Manufacturing PMI from 2007 to 2012, showing a sharp drop after 2011 back down toward the forty-five level. The third chart compares unemployment rates in France and Germany from 2000 to 2012, highlighting a divergence where Germany's rate steadily fell to around seven percent while France's rate climbed back toward ten percent.

An appendix on Spain outlines the severe consequences of economic contraction through three additional charts. The first displays Spanish unemployment from 1983 to 2011, which skyrocketed from under ten percent in 2007 to twenty-five percent by 2011. The second chart shows Spanish retail sales index values from 2003 to 2011, illustrating a steep, continuous drop from a peak of one hundred ten down to eighty-five. The final dual-axis chart depicts non-performing loans and bankruptcies in Spain from 1990 to 2010. Following the 2007 financial crisis, bankruptcies spiked toward two thousand, while non-performing loans as a percentage of lending surged from under two percent to over eight percent. The page concludes with citations of academic research on historical Spanish financial crises.

This page analyzes how central banks globally are boosting equity markets ahead of actual economic improvements, focusing on the United States, China, and Japan. The main thesis is that central banks have successfully rebuilt market confidence despite weak on-the-ground economic data, presenting a test of whether these equity rallies can accurately predict subsequent economic recoveries or if they are simply a temporary triumph of central bank stimulus.

In the United States, the Federal Reserve’s aggressive intervention, including transitioning from "Operation Twist" to a continuous quantitative easing policy, has propelled the S&P 500 up 17% and the NASDAQ up 21% year-to-date, even though domestic growth remains weak. The mixed nature of this economic backdrop is represented in two top charts. The first, titled "Mixed messages on durable goods," plots the period from January 2010 to July 2012 and compares new orders for capital equipment (excluding aircraft, measured in billions of USD) against the ISM Manufacturing New Orders index. While capital equipment orders remained somewhat steady between 60 and 65 billion USD, the ISM index showed a sharp contraction, falling below the critical 50 level by mid-2012. The second chart, "US personal consumption growth hovering around 2%," shows year-over-year percent change from 2005 to 2012. Personal consumption, which plummeted below negative 3% during the 2009 recession, recovered to over 3% but has since drifted down, hovering just above 2% by mid-2012.

To evaluate whether stock markets can successfully act as a leading indicator during such weak economic phases, a table titled "Subsequent 2-year equity return and PMI change following periods of rising equities and low/falling PMIs" lists historical precedents. The table details eleven historical periods between 1961 and 1998 where equities rallied despite weak PMIs. For instance, following the January 1975 period, the subsequent two-year equity return was 39.6% with a 25.9-point increase in PMI. Similarly, May 1995 saw a 50.2% subsequent return and a 7.0-point PMI increase. Only one period, July 1980, yielded a negative equity return of negative 9.9%. The table leaves the subsequent two-year return and PMI change for September 2012 as an open question, symbolizing the ultimate test of current Fed policy.

The page notes a similar pattern in Asia, where Chinese and Japanese equity markets have risen despite deteriorating industrial data. In China, optimism is driven by infrastructure stimulus plans estimated at 3.5% to 4% of GDP, which represents about 30% to 40% of the massive 2009–2010 stimulus package. In Japan, weak growth has prompted the Bank of Japan to consider an explicit 2% inflation target, alongside past attempts to spur consumption using short-term shopping vouchers. 

These regional weaknesses are illustrated in the bottom-right chart, "Manufacturing in China and Japan: weak," covering January 2011 to July 2012. This dual-axis chart shows Chinese industrial profits on the left axis as a year-over-year percentage change, which plummeted from over 30% in early 2011 to below 0% by mid-2012. On the right axis, Japanese industrial production is plotted as an index level, showing a massive plunge to nearly 80 following the Fukushima disaster in early 2011, a recovery to around 95 later that year, and a subsequent decline back toward 90 by mid-2012.

This page analyzes Germany's ambitious post-Fukushima transition away from nuclear and coal toward renewable energy, examining whether this represents an impetuous and costly strategy. The author notes that while Germany is exceptionally energy-efficient with a low electricity-to-GDP ratio, it faces major challenges because wind and solar are highly intermittent. 

The first chart, "Snapshot of current German capacity and generation," illustrates this intermittency. It compares generating capacity to actual electricity generation as a percentage of the total. While coal represents about 27% of capacity, it produces nearly 40% of generation. In contrast, wind makes up about 17% of capacity but generates only 8% of output, and solar makes up 15% of capacity while producing just 3% of output. 

The second chart, "Levelized cost of electricity production in Germany," shows that the all-in costs (including construction, financing, operations, maintenance, fuel, and a carbon footprint estimate) for newer technologies are exceptionally high. Traditional sources like nuclear, natural gas, and coal are the cheapest, all clustered between roughly 60 and 90 USD/MWh. Onshore wind rises to about 110 USD/MWh, while offshore wind jumps to around 180 USD/MWh. Solar is by far the most expensive, spanning from 300 to over 400 USD/MWh. The text highlights that offshore wind connection costs alone, estimated at 1.1 million Euros per MW by transmission operator TenneT, exceed the total upfront capital cost of building a new natural gas plant.

The page then presents two charts comparing 2011 average retail electricity prices across European nations, broken down by basic price and taxes. In the residential segment, Germany has the highest rates in Europe at approximately 250 EUR/MWh, driven largely by high taxes. It is followed by Belgium, Italy, and Spain. In the commercial/industrial segment, Germany has the second-highest rates at roughly 160 EUR/MWh, just behind Italy, and ahead of Belgium and the Czech Republic. The author warns that the shift to renewables will likely drive these already-high prices even higher for both residential and business consumers.

In terms of forecasts and policy targets, Germany plans to raise renewable energy’s contribution to 35% of total consumption by 2020, and to 80% by 2050. According to DIW Berlin, financing this transition will cost an estimated 800 billion Euros in total, with the first stage through 2020 alone costing 200 billion Euros. The author raises concerns over this massive spending, especially at a time when Germany also faces financial commitments to support Spain and the rest of the European Periphery.

This analysis from J.P. Morgan evaluates the state of US equity valuations, focusing on several structural shifts that distinguish the contemporary market environment from historical patterns. The primary arguments address the strong cash position of corporations, the suppressed relative value of cyclical stocks due to low interest rates, and the historic decoupling of corporate profits from domestic GDP growth.

The first set of charts compares the profit recovery starting in 2008 against the average of the five prior recoveries in 1958, 1974, 1982, 1990, and 2001. Over fourteen quarters since the profit trough, the current recovery shows sales and corporate profits rebounding strongly to between five hundred billion and six hundred billion dollars, while labor compensation has remained highly depressed, barely rising above zero. By comparison, in past recoveries, labor compensation grew steadily alongside sales, while corporate profit growth was much more subdued. This divergence is partly explained by the rise of foreign-sourced corporate profits, which a third chart reveals have climbed steadily from under 0.5% of GDP in the mid-twentieth century to roughly 2.5% to 3.0% by 2012.

The next pair of charts highlights corporate cash generation and shareholder returns. The chart plotting the three-year moving averages of the dividend payout ratio and free cash flow yield from 1955 to 2012 shows that while the S&P 500 dividend payout ratio has dropped near its historic lows of approximately 30%, the free cash flow yield for large-cap stocks has risen to a very high level of about 6%. This dynamic leaves significant room for corporations to return capital to investors. Indeed, a companion chart tracking dividends and buybacks as a percentage of S&P 500 market cap (excluding financials) shows this return of capital rising from a post-crisis low of under 4.0% in 2009 to roughly 5.5% by early 2012, though still below the pre-crisis peak of over 7.0%.

The final segment addresses equity valuations and their relation to the broader economy. Low interest rates have driven a rush into defensive, dividend-paying stocks, pushing the relative valuation of cyclical stocks extremely low. This trend is demonstrated in a chart of the trailing P/E ratio of cyclicals versus defensives from 1974 to 2012, which shows the ratio sitting near 0.6, close to a forty-year low. Lastly, a chart measuring the ratio of two-year earnings growth to two-year nominal GDP growth from 1952 onwards reveals that corporate earnings have dramatically outpaced the underlying economy. This ratio reached unprecedented heights in the current cycle, spiking to 16.6x and 4.0x, compared to historical average peaks of 2.1x and 4.2x. The author notes that this delinking suggests investors are ignoring weak domestic growth because profits continue to rise, though this trend poses clear political and social risks. The data throughout these analyses is sourced from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, J.P. Morgan, Robert J. Shiller, Standard & Poor's, Empirical Research, and UBS.

In this entry of Eye on the Market, Michael Cembalest assesses US equity valuations in the wake of recent market rallies and evaluates the looming threat of the 2013 US fiscal cliff. He argues that the equity rally has been largely driven by anticipated central bank monetary stimulus and a fear of missing out rather than a strong economic recovery. With US equity valuations averaging 13x to 14x price-to-earnings ratios, equities have become compelling by default—or "at the point of a bayonet"—as the Federal Reserve’s low-rate policy has suppressed expected returns on alternatives like cash, Treasuries, credit, and real estate investment trusts. Cembalest projects slow US payroll growth, below-trend GDP expansion of around 2 percent, and the continuation of near-zero interest rates.

To support his view that central bank policies are inflating equity markets, Cembalest includes two charts. The first, titled "To infinity....and beyond!!," tracks central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP from 2008 projected into 2013. It illustrates a dramatic expansion across the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, the Bank of England, and the Bank of Japan, with several central banks reaching or approaching 30 to 45 percent of GDP by 2013. The second chart, "Equity rallies usually coincide with high or rising leading indicators, but not in 2012," reveals a stark divergence between economic realities and market performance. While the MSCI World Equity Index rose from around 1,100 to nearly 1,350 in 2012, the Global Manufacturing PMI Survey plummeted from about 54 down to 49, indicating that global equities rallied despite contractionary manufacturing data.

Cembalest then focuses on the potential economic drag of the upcoming US fiscal cliff, stating that any fiscal austerity measures totaling more than 2 percent of GDP would shock the market. An accompanying scorecard table outlines anticipated 2013 fiscal adjustments under three scenarios: the fully Legislated outcome, Scenario 1, and Scenario 2. The fully Legislated path represents a massive 4.3 percent of GDP drag, totaling 667 billion USD. This includes 535 billion USD in increased revenues—such as 115 billion USD from the expiring payroll tax holiday, 171 billion USD from expiring 2001 and 2003 tax reliefs, and 83 billion USD from expiring upper-income tax relief—and 132 billion USD in reduced expenditures, which is largely driven by 85 billion USD in sequester spending cuts. Cembalest presents Scenario 1 and Scenario 2 as compromise pathways that markets assume will ultimately be struck. In Scenario 1, the fiscal drag is reduced to 1.6 percent of GDP (255 billion USD) by preserving many of the tax reliefs and avoiding the sequester. In Scenario 2, the drag is further mitigated to 1.1 percent of GDP (172 billion USD) by additionally extending upper-income tax relief. 

The page concludes with a lighthearted "wildlife advisory alert" from South Carolina, where the author details a fishing trip with his son. He notes they caught a near-record 145-pound blacktip shark close to where people swim, heard of alligators in the local lagoons, and encountered a seven-foot diamondback rattlesnake under a porch, leading him to humorously advise readers to stay in their cars if traveling through the region.

In this commentary, the author critiques the decision to award the Nobel Peace Prize to the European Union, arguing that conditions for a lasting peace on the continent were already firmly established by 1954. Rather than cementing peace, the author suggests that the Euro currency project has instead heightened regional tensions by distorting current accounts, encouraging unsustainable debt-fueled consumption in Southern Europe, and blocking the currency adjustments that traditionally mitigated past recessions. To substantiate this claim of growing regional discord, the page presents three distinct visual datasets illustrating rising social and political stress across Europe.

The first chart tracks the share of parliamentary election votes won by extremist right-wing parties in nine European countries across seven periods from 1980 to 2012, based on Friedrich Ebert Foundation definitions. This data reveals a stark upward trend in right-wing populism, particularly in the 2010–2012 period. During this final window, right-wing populist parties captured nearly 30% of the vote in Austria and Switzerland, while support in France hovered around 15%, and Greece saw a dramatic climb from near-zero historical support to approximately 15%. 

The second chart indexes Google search volume from 2004 to 2012 to monitor the fracturing of the European social fabric, with maximum search volumes indexed to 100. This metric reveals dramatic spikes in public anxiety during the eurozone crisis, with searches for "Greece Depression" surging to an index level of nearly 80 in late 2011, searches for "Catalonia Independence" spiking to approximately 60 in late 2012, and searches for "Spain Riots" climbing toward 30 in the same period.

The final chart presents Eurobarometer poll data regarding public confidence in the European Union from 2004 to 2011, answering the question "Do you have trust in the European Union?" The line graph shows that public trust peaked at around 57% in 2007 but subsequently suffered a precipitous and steady decline as the financial crisis unfolded, ultimately hitting a low of nearly 32% by the end of 2011. Together, these visuals support the author's narrative that the European single-currency project is facing unprecedented social and political backlash.

On this page, the author outlines his first major investment demand for 2013 and beyond, calling for greater disclosure by US firms on their non-US operations as global economic growth cools. The author argues that while the US economy is growing at a modest two percent rate—propped up by very easy fiscal and monetary policies—and regions like China, Korea, and Taiwan are showing tentative signs of improvement, Europe remains weak. France, in particular, is experiencing significant economic strain under its new administration. This challenging global economic backdrop has reversed the previous trend of corporate profits outperforming nominal GDP, resulting in highly negative corporate guidance for the fourth quarter of 2012. The author asserts that generic regional revenue breakdowns, which group highly divergent economies together under broad labels like "Americas" or "Europe," are insufficient for analysts to forecast earnings accurately.

The page features four charts that illustrate these economic and corporate dynamics. The first chart, titled "Manufacturing: stable in US; improving in China; sluggish in Euro area," plots Flash Markit Manufacturing PMI data from January 2010 to September 2012. It shows the US ISM index remaining relatively stable above the critical 50 threshold, China's PMI beginning to recover toward expansionary territory, and the Euro area's PMI languishing deep in contraction territory around 46. The second chart, titled "France: Après Sarkozy, le Déluge?", highlights economic deterioration in France following François Hollande taking a fourteen percent lead over Nicolas Sarkozy in a second-round presidential poll. From January 2011 to July 2012, French business confidence plunged 22 points, the PMI survey fell from 57 to 42, export growth dropped from thirteen percent to four percent, and the number of job seekers rose thirteen percent.

The lower half of the page presents two historical charts tracking corporate profits. The third chart, "Unusual period of earnings outperformance ending," displays the ratio of two-year earnings growth to two-year nominal GDP growth from 1952 through 2008. It indicates that after historical average peaks of 2.1x and later 4.2x, the ratio spiked to an unprecedented peak of 16.6x before collapsing, signaling that the era of earnings vastly outperforming GDP is ending. The fourth chart, "US foreign-sourced corporate profits," tracks these profits as a percentage of US GDP from 1947 to 2012. It reveals a dramatic, volatile climb from under 0.5 percent in the mid-twentieth century to nearly 3.0 percent by 2012, underscoring the vital importance of international markets to US corporate health.

Looking forward, the author predicts that a decisive upturn in non-US leading indicators is necessary to revive US profit momentum. However, a silver-lining exists as companies have preemptively reduced inventories, potentially setting the stage for a rebound in the spring of 2013. The author concludes that with the S&P 500 at 1,400 trading at thirteen times 2013 earnings, stock prices are valued about as high as can be expected until a robust economic recovery takes hold.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues that the Congressional Budget Office should cease publishing its "Baseline Case" for US Federal debt, characterizing it as increasingly preposterous because it relies on legislative assumptions that Congress routinely defers, such as Medicare reimbursement cuts and the expiration of middle-class tax cuts. To highlight the unlikelihood of the baseline scenario, the author facetiously places a graphic of a unicorn on the chart. 

The page features two charts and one detailed table. The first chart, tracking capital spending from 2005 to 2012, compares planned capital expenditure from a composite index of Federal Reserve surveys against real core capital goods orders in billions of 2005 dollars. Both data series show a sharp contraction during the 2008 recession, a subsequent recovery, and a renewed decline in 2012, which the author suggests may be driven by anxieties surrounding the impending fiscal cliff. 

An accompanying table outlines three fiscal cliff scenarios: the fully "Legislated" path and two compromise iterations, labeled "#1" and "#2." The legislated scenario represents a total fiscal adjustment of $667 billion, or 4.3% of GDP, driven by $535 billion in revenue increases—including the expiration of the payroll tax holiday ($115 billion) and broad 2001/2003 tax relief ($171 billion)—alongside $132 billion in spending cuts. Under compromise scenario #1, the adjustment drops to $255 billion (1.6% of GDP), and under scenario #2, it falls further to $172 billion (1.1% of GDP), primarily by keeping various tax provisions intact.

The second chart maps long-term US net-debt-to-GDP projections from 2004 through 2022 across multiple policy paths. While the unrealistic CBO Baseline Case projects debt falling to just over 50% of GDP by 2022, the CBO Alternative Case, which assumes all tax cuts are extended and the sequester is avoided, shows debt rising toward 90% of GDP. Cembalest analyzes alternative paths, including President Obama’s proposed budget, which would stabilize debt at roughly 73% of GDP through tax increases on households with adjusted gross incomes over $250,000. These proposals include treating dividends as ordinary income, taxing long-term capital gains at 20%, capping itemized deductions at 28%, and taxing municipal bond income and 401k contributions. The author questions the political feasibility of this plan, noting that if the administration only passes top-bracket rate increases, the long-term debt trajectory would remain much higher, around 80% of GDP. 

Finally, a footnote dismisses as "ludicrous" an alternative idea, supported by Ron Paul and Dean Baker, that the Federal Reserve could simply write off the US Treasury debt it owns.

This page evaluates the fiscal challenges of the United States and the data inconsistencies of China's slowing economy. The discussion begins with an analysis of US presidential candidate Mitt Romney's fiscal proposals, noting that his tax-cut plans lack specifics and may not be politically feasible. The author argues that a pro-growth strategy can successfully reduce federal debt relative to the size of the economy, pointing to the 1950s under President Dwight Eisenhower as a key historical precedent. During this decade, the US debt-to-GDP ratio fell from 80% to 40% because of a 4.3% real compound annual growth rate, rather than austerity, sharp tax increases, or high inflation. 

This historical perspective is supported by a detailed table covering 1950 to 1960, which shows that while nominal net debt grew marginally from $219 billion to $237 billion (a 0.8% compound annual growth rate), real GDP expanded significantly from $273 billion to $415 billion. Over this same period, government outlays as a percentage of GDP remained relatively stable between 14% and 21%, while receipts hovered between 14% and 19%.

The page contrasts this historical fiscal flexibility with a line chart showing the percentage of US government revenue committed to mandatory programs and interest expense from 1962 to 2012. The chart illustrates a dramatic upward trend, starting at approximately 30% in 1962 and climbing to nearly 100% around 2010, before settling around 90% by 2012. This trend underscores how entitlement expansions, such as the signature healthcare bill under Barack Obama, have severely constrained the federal budget.

The second half of the page demands that China resolve contradictions in its reported economic data, especially as its economic growth moderates. The author details various internal inconsistencies in data published by China’s National Bureau of Statistics, such as conflicting month-on-month and year-on-year extrapolations for retail sales, GDP, and industrial profits, as well as an unchanged official unemployment rate of 4.1% for nine consecutive quarters. A final line chart tracks Chinese equity valuations from 2001 to 2012, measuring price-to-trailing-earnings (P/E) ratios for the Shanghai Composite Index and the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index. The chart shows that Shanghai Composite P/E valuations peaked near 60 in 2001 and near 50 in 2007, but have since experienced a structural decline, falling to around 10 to 15 by 2012. Similarly, the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index valuation fell from a 2007 peak of over 30 down to single digits by 2012. A brief footnote comments on US data reliability, referencing former GE CEO Jack Welch's public skepticism of a Bureau of Labor Statistics jobs report.

This page of J.P. Morgan's publication provides immediate post-election commentary following the 2012 US presidential election, focusing on the looming fiscal cliff, its potential resolutions, and the long-term outlook for US federal debt under a divided government. The author argues that while defusing the fiscal cliff is necessary to prevent a growth slowdown and a stall in capital spending, doing so will accelerate federal debt unless a long-term grand bargain is struck. 

To illustrate the options at hand, a table titled Fiscal cliff options, in billions and percentage of GDP, compares the legislated path to two alternative options. The fully legislated fiscal adjustment totals 667 billion dollars, or 4.3 percent of GDP, including 535 billion dollars in increased revenues—such as expiring payroll tax holidays, personal and business tax provisions, and Bush-era tax reliefs—and 132 billion dollars in reduced expenditures, which include Medicare physician reimbursement cuts and the Budget Control Act sequester. Option one represents a milder adjustment of 255 billion dollars, or 1.6 percent of GDP, while option two is a 172 billion dollar adjustment, or 1.1 percent of GDP; both alternative options limit revenue increases and dramatically scale back expenditure cuts. 

Directly adjacent, a dual-axis line chart titled Capital spending slows; fiscal cliff responsible? tracks real core capital goods orders in billions of 2005 dollars on the left axis alongside planned capital expenditures from a composite index of Federal Reserve surveys on the right axis from 2005 to 2012. Both series show a clear stalling and downward turn in late 2012, suggesting that policy uncertainty surrounding the fiscal cliff is indeed stalling business investment.

The central visual is a chart titled US long-term debt scenarios, which plots net debt to GDP from 2004 projected out to 2022. The chart contrasts the unrealistic CBO Baseline, where net debt falls back toward 40 percent of GDP by 2022 because it assumes current laws like doctor Medicare cuts and sunsetting tax rates actually take effect, with the CBO Alternative Case, where debt climbs toward 90 percent of GDP as tax cuts are extended and sequestration is avoided. The author notes that the CBO Baseline is preposterous and should feature a unicorn to indicate its low probability. Several alternative policy pathways are plotted: the President's budget as written plus the Budget Control Act sequester (represented by an orange triangle, bringing 2022 debt to around 64 percent), the President's budget as written without the sequester (represented by a purple square, ending around 73 percent), and a scenario where 2001 tax rates return only for those earning over 250,000 dollars in adjusted gross income (represented by a green diamond, ending around 78 percent). 

In his concluding forecast, the author notes that while the President's budget proposal stabilizes debt on paper, it is politically unfeasible with a Republican-controlled House. He warns that if the sequester is unplugged without a grand bargain, rating agencies may react negatively. Ultimately, because the public and politicians are reluctant to tackle the elephant in the room—mandatory spending on entitlements and interest, which eat up almost 100 percent of revenues—the US will continue to defer these choices, sliding into a high-debt economic model similar to Europe and Japan.

This page opens with reflections on the immediate aftermath of the 2012 U.S. presidential election, arguing that economic growth—not taxation, austerity, or inflation—is the true solution to high federal debt. The author questions whether the newly re-elected Obama administration will adopt a pro-growth agenda, citing a 1992 editorial by George McGovern that warned of public policies choking business expansion. Highlighting declining capital spending and massive corporate cash reserves, the author suggests businesses are waiting to see which direction the Democratic party will take, expressing doubt that centrist, pro-growth Democrats like those of the former Democratic Leadership Council will influence the administration.

Two charts at the top support this discussion of U.S. fiscal policy. The first chart shows that non-defense discretionary spending as a percentage of GDP, which hovered between 3.5% and 5.0% for much of the late 20th century, is projected to fall to approximately 2.5% by 2017 under Budget Control Act spending caps, excluding the sequester. The second chart, titled "The elephant in the room," reveals that mandatory programs and interest payments are crowding out discretionary spending. This line chart shows the percentage of federal revenues committed to mandatory programs and interest rising steadily from about 35% in 1962 to roughly 90% in 2012, even peaking above 100% around 2009.

The commentary then shifts to European competitiveness, focusing on France's position as a "worker’s utopia." While acknowledging that Europe’s work-life balance is beneficial, the author questions whether France can generate enough national income to service its debts as it loses competitiveness to Germany. He warns that France may become a major obstacle to a broader European economic recovery in 2013.

To analyze this issue, the page presents a "Worker’s Utopia Index" bar chart, which measures how favorable different countries are to workers based on average dispersion above or below the mean across nine factors. France ranks as the most favorable to workers with an index score of approximately 1.2, followed closely by Italy, Spain, and Portugal. Conversely, the United States ranks near the bottom at around -0.8, and Singapore is the least favorable to workers at roughly -1.4. An adjacent table details the nine indicators used to construct this index, which evaluate labor rules, government spending, and social protections. These factors include government expenditures to GDP, labor force participation, ease of hiring and firing, retirement age relative to life expectancy, annual working hours, vacation days, pay-to-productivity linkage, unemployment benefits, and employer social security contributions, compiled from major global organizations like the IMF, World Bank, and OECD.

This page introduces J.P. Morgan’s assessment of the global financial markets at the close of 2012, focusing on the highly unusual nature of the year’s equity market rally given the prevailing low global economic growth. 

To illustrate this performance, a table shows 2012 year-to-date returns and valuation changes from January to November. The data highlights strong returns across multiple asset classes: S&P 500 returned 14.4% as its P/E multiple expanded from 12.1x to 13.6x; MSCI Europe returned 15.1% with P/E expanding from 9.8x to 12.1x; MSCI Emerging Markets returned 11.2% with P/E rising from 9.4x to 11.4x; and US REITs returned 15.0%. In credit markets, US High Yield rose 12.5% as spreads compressed from 712 basis points to 592 basis points, while emerging market dollar debt returned 17.1% as spreads fell from 400 to 291 basis points. Meanwhile, the Barclays 7-10 Year US Treasury bond yielded a 4.9% return as yields declined from 1.95% to 1.64%.

A series of scatter plots analyze the historical relationship between annual global equity returns (on the y-axis, from negative 45% to positive 45%) and annual global GDP growth (on the x-axis, from negative 2% to 6%) from 1970 to 2012. The first chart, titled "Global equity returns vs. GDP growth, 1970-2012," features a highlighted box identifying anomalous "low-growth equity rallies." A red dot representing 2012 sits within this box, showing a double-digit equity return of approximately 15% despite low global GDP growth of around 2%. 

To determine just how unique 2012 was, the author filters out traditional drivers of low-growth rallies in two steps. In "Step 1," recession recovery years—specifically 1975, 1980, 1982, 1991, and 2009—are removed from the chart, which significantly thins the dots in the low-growth box. In "Step 2," the author removes years characterized by large declines in 10-year interest rates—namely 1986, 1993, and 1995. This leaves only two years in the low-growth, high-return box: 2012 and 1998.

The author concludes that 2012 was a exceptionally rare period where double-digit global equity returns occurred without the support of a recession rebound or a bond market rally, noting that the European rescue was a major factor in driving these returns. Looking ahead to 2013, the author cautions that without these unusual catalysts, a stronger recovery in global growth will be required to match 2012’s equity returns. While modest improvements in economic growth are expected for the United States, China, and Emerging Market Asia, the outlook is weaker for Europe and Japan.

In this J.P. Morgan commentary, Michael Cembalest reflects on the aftermath of Hurricane Sandy, criticizing the allocation of federal funding and highlighting New York City’s lack of preparedness for severe storm surges. Despite Mayor Bloomberg’s endorsement of the President citing climate change, and New York’s high-risk profile, Cembalest notes that virtually none of the eight billion dollars in American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA) funds spent in New York City was allocated to protecting energy, commercial, or residential infrastructure from flooding. He highlights the avoidable flooding of a Con-Ed substation in lower Manhattan and points out that funds were spent on federal building renovations rather than burying power lines or routing grids.

To illustrate the severity of this oversight, the page presents two tables. The first details global flood protection standards based on the worst storm expected per a given number of years. Rotterdam and Amsterdam design for 1-in-10,000-year events, and Shanghai, London, and Tokyo plan for 1-in-1,000-year events, whereas New York ranks last with a protective standard of only 1-in-100 years. The second table ranks global cities by assets exposed to coastal flooding in billions of 2007 dollars, showing Miami at the top with four hundred sixteen billion dollars, followed by New York in second place with three hundred twenty billion dollars, well ahead of New Orleans at two hundred thirty-four billion dollars and Tokyo at one hundred seventy-four billion dollars.

Cembalest argues that severe surges in the Northeast are predictable, historically occurring roughly once a decade. A bar chart tracking hurricanes impacting New York's coast since 1850 shows that three hit between 1850 and 1879, two hit in each block from 1880 to 1939, four hit between 1940 and 1969, three hit from 1970 to 1999, and two hit between 2000 and 2012. 

To demonstrate how close the city has previously come to disaster, a line chart plots the water level during Hurricane Gloria in 1985. It shows that while the actual storm surge peaked at roughly seven feet, it would have reached nearly ten feet had it coincided with high tide. 

A final bar chart displays 1995 estimates from the US Army Corps of Engineers, FEMA, and the National Weather Service regarding the critical storm surge elevations in feet above sea level at which major infrastructure systems become inoperable. This chart reveals that crucial transit networks fail at relatively low surge levels: the FDR Drive and Metro North Hudson lines flood at six feet, LaGuardia Airport and the A, C, M, N, and R subway lines fail at seven to seven and a half feet, the Holland Tunnel is compromised at eight feet, the Long Island Rail Road East River tunnels at nine feet, West Street at ten feet, Penn Station at just under eleven feet, and JFK Airport at thirteen feet.

Cembalest concludes by noting that while other global coastal cities have spent decades planning and building storm surge barriers, such projects are immensely expensive. He cites a six and a half billion dollar estimate for a barrier north of the Verrazano Bridge and leaves open the question of where this funding would come from, given already high state and local tax rates.

This page focuses on two major systemic risks for investors: the squeezing of discretionary US government spending due to rising entitlement obligations, and the accelerating threat of nuclear enrichment in Iran alongside the logistical challenges of a military response. 

The first section addresses the fiscal dilemma facing the US Congress over the next decade. The author argues that rising expenditures on Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid are gradually crowding out discretionary spending crucial for long-term economic growth, such as education, infrastructure, and energy. A multi-colored area chart titled "The Boiling Frog" tracks various spending components as a percentage of GDP from 1972 through projections for 2020. It illustrates how defense and discretionary spending are being squeezed under a growing block of entitlement spending and interest, while a dashed line representing government receipts remains well below total expenditures. To quantify the scale of the discretionary squeeze, an accompanying table shows estimated 2017 spending levels compared to their historical peaks in nominal terms. It lists dramatic declines, including a 33% drop for energy, a 69% drop for education, an 86% drop for teacher and worker retraining, a 4% drop for ground transportation, and a 9% drop for air transportation. The author notes that reducing the deficit to 3% of GDP by 2022 without touching these expenditures would require a plan that generates four times the revenue of the President’s 2011 proposal, warning that entitlement spending will only accelerate further after 2022.

The second section shifts to the geopolitical threat of Iran's nuclear enrichment program, which has continued to accelerate despite crippling economic sanctions. A chart tracking Iran's 19.75% enriched uranium stockpile in kilograms from February 2010 to February 2013 shows a steady climb driven by additional capacity from Fordow on top of Natanz. Despite a brief drawdown to replenish reactor fuel in mid-2012, the projected stockpile line is shown steeply climbing to cross the red horizontal threshold marking the minimum required for nuclear weapon production—approximately 150 kilograms—by late 2012 or early 2013. 

The final chart evaluates the viability of a US military option using conventional weapons, specifically the 30,000-pound Massive Ordnance Penetration (MOP) device, to destroy the underground Fordow facility.
