The primary argument of the first section is that standard metrics often understate active managers' success because they do not account for benchmark adjustments, size filters, or pricing structures. A detailed table presents seven years of trailing data through June 2013 on the percentage of active equity vehicles that outperform benchmarks across fifteen different investment styles. The baseline column, which shows equal-weighted outperformance against stated benchmarks, reveals relatively low success rates, such as 27 percent for Large Cap Core, 15 percent for Large Cap Growth, and 28 percent for Multi Cap Core, though Small Cap Value is a high outlier at 75 percent. When compared instead to investible ETFs and adjusted using vehicle size filters that incorporate 95 percent of assets under management, success rates rise significantly. For example, Large Cap Core outperformance rises by 11 percentage points to 38 percent, and International Large Cap Growth increases by 20 percentage points to 74 percent. Restricting the analysis to institutional share classes only similarly boosts outperformance figures, pushing Mid Cap Value up by 15 percentage points to 53 percent and Large Cap Growth up by 15 percentage points to 30 percent. The author notes that these consistent increases explain why institutional and individual investors retain substantial exposure to active management. Looking forward, the author suggests that if stock-to-stock correlations continue to decline, industry alpha measures may improve from where they stood at the end of 2012.

The second section of the page provides a follow-up to a previous note on private equity, focusing on database quality issues. The author explains that earlier academic studies by prominent researchers, including Phalippou of Oxford, Kaplan of Chicago, Schoar of MIT, and Rhodes-Kropf of Harvard, used the Venture Economics database because it was the best available at the time. These early papers frequently concluded that private equity underperformed the S&P 500. However, more recent research with access to superior datasets has concluded that private equity actually outperformed the S&P 500. The author clarifies that previous critiques of this literature were intended to highlight the newly discovered flaws of the Venture Economics database itself, rather than to criticize the scholarship of any specific academic.

This page explores whether Detroit’s historic financial collapse is a unique outlier or a warning paradigm for other municipal issuers, examining both the city's long-term credit deterioration and its underlying economic fundamentals. The commentary begins with the proposed Chapter 9 bankruptcy exit plan by Detroit's emergency manager, which involves substantial 80% to 90% writedowns on general obligation bonds and major reductions in retired city employee pension and healthcare obligations. The author questions if other cities face similar risks, pointing to two key dimensions: economic strength and finances. 

The first set of visual data connects Detroit's credit decline to the long-term retreat of its primary industry. A table tracking ratings on Detroit’s uninsured general obligation bonds from June 1998 to July 2013 shows a steady downward march from investment-grade tiers (such as Baa1 from Moody’s and A- from S&P in 1998) down to near-default ratings of Ca and C by July 2013. Beside this table, a line chart plots the three-month moving average of Big 3 domestic auto companies (GM, Ford, and Chrysler) as a percentage of total US auto sales from 1980 to 2012. This share contracted dramatically over three decades, falling from close to 80% in the early 1980s to roughly 45% by 2012, showing a clear structural parallel with the city's rating downgrades.

To evaluate Detroit’s economic foundation relative to the rest of the nation, the analysis compares Detroit against the other 381 US Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs) using two percentile-distribution charts. The first chart, tracking growth in Gross Metropolitan Product from 2001 to 2011 with an index baseline of 100, shows that while top-tier MSAs in the 95th percentile grew to an index value of nearly 190, Detroit’s economic output languished. Detroit’s line trends flatly below the 5th percentile, dropping below the index base of 100 after 2007. The second chart illustrates labor force growth from 2000 to 2012, with Jan 2000 indexed to 100. While the 95th percentile of US MSAs reached an index value of 130, Detroit’s labor force contracted steadily to an index value of approximately 90 by 2012, placing the city in the lowest 1st or 2nd percentiles nationally. 

The author concludes with critical questions regarding the bankruptcy process, noting that the plan to wipe the slate clean by fall 2014 is highly ambitious and faces complex legal challenges under the Michigan state constitution. Footnotes detail that the largest losses are likely to fall on unsecured general obligation bondholders, whereas essential service agency debt for water and sewer, which serves outside townships, is expected to see far milder impacts, although proposals to subordinate some of this debt remain highly contested.

This page, titled "How Different is Detroit: A story in pictures," argues that Detroit's labor force and demographic shifts have created highly unsustainable financial and economic dynamics. To illustrate this distress, the author compares the Detroit Police & Fire Pension structure (3,200 active workers supporting 9,300 beneficiaries) with Chicago's healthier ratio (12,000 active workers to 13,000 beneficiaries). Over the long term, weak local output has directly suppressed personal income and population growth, placing Detroit near the bottom fifth percentile of major metropolitan areas. 

To support this claim, the page presents six charts. The first, "Growth in personal income per capita" indexed to 1990, shows Detroit tracking at the very bottom along the 5th percentile line, reaching an index level of only about 175 by 2008 compared to the 95th percentile which exceeded 240. The second chart, "MSA-level population growth" indexed to 1970, displays Detroit flatlining near its 1970 baseline of 100, far below the 80th and 95th percentiles, the latter of which neared index level 380 by 2010. 

The author explains that even these metropolitan statistical area (MSA) metrics obscure the true depth of the crisis, as they include more stable suburbs like Warren and Livonia. Looking strictly at "city-proper" data reveals even more stark contrasts. The "Median household income" chart for 30 cities shows Detroit as the poorest city surveyed, with median household income falling below $30,000, while top-tier cities like San Francisco and Washington D.C. exceed $60,000 and $70,000 respectively. This economic strain is compounded by severe depopulation: the "Change in city-proper population from 1960 to 2010" chart shows Detroit's population plummeted by over 50% (ranking alongside St. Louis as the worst-performing cities), in sharp contrast to high-growth sunbelt cities like Phoenix, which grew by over 200%. This is further exacerbated by the fact that, according to Brookings, only 30% of jobs in Detroit are held by actual city residents.

The final two charts cement Detroit's position as the nation's most troubled major city across education and poverty. In "Percent of population over 25 years old with bachelor's degree or higher," Detroit has the lowest rate among the 30 benchmarked cities at roughly 12%, whereas Seattle, San Francisco, and Washington D.C. boast rates between 50% and 60%. Finally, the chart tracking the "Percent of individuals below poverty line" ranks Detroit at the extreme high end, with its poverty rate climbing above 35%—nearly four times higher than Seattle, which sits at the low end with under 10% of its population living in poverty.

This page explores the constitutional and legal frameworks governing municipal bankruptcy, focusing on the unresolved tension between federal bankruptcy law and states' rights regarding pension obligations. It begins by explaining that municipal bankruptcy under Chapter 9 is only available to cities if authorized by their state, noting that while Chapter 9 was historically used by small municipalities, recent filings by larger entities like Vallejo, Jefferson County, Central Falls, Stockton, and San Bernardino have changed this dynamic. The author details Michigan's specific distress statute, which allows an emergency manager to displace local governing bodies and potentially request bankruptcy authorization from the governor. 

A central side-by-side comparison highlights the legal conflict between federal and state authority. The "Federalist" argument relies on Article I, Section 8, Clause 4 of the U.S. Constitution, which grants Congress the power to establish uniform bankruptcy laws, and Chapter 9 rules requiring that bankruptcy plans do not discriminate unfairly and remain fair and equitable to all creditor classes. In contrast, the "State Rights" argument relies on the Tenth Amendment and specific state constitutional provisions, such as Michigan’s Article IX, Section 24, which defines pension benefits as contractual obligations that cannot be diminished. 

To demonstrate how this conflict plays out in practice, the author examines four ongoing municipal bankruptcies. In Central Falls, Rhode Island, retiree pensions were restructured, but because this was done by mutual agreement, it left the legal question of forced pension impairment unresolved. In Stockton, California, the city prioritized retirees over bondholders, leading to an ongoing dispute with capital markets creditors over whether such unequal treatment is legally "fair" under federal law. Meanwhile, a federal court ruling in Vallejo, California, suggested that federal law trumps state law, forcing both bondholders and retirees to make sacrifices by upholding the city's rejection of collective bargaining agreements. Finally, in San Bernardino, California, the court appointed a mediator to facilitate negotiations, leaving the final legal ruling on the city's petition pending. The page concludes that the core legal question of whether federal bankruptcy law can override state-level retiree pension protections remains open and highly contested.

This page presents a comparative analysis arguing that Detroit’s severe economic and demographic distress is an outlier when compared to the Metropolitan Statistical Areas of the 70 largest city General Obligation bond issuers held by J.P. Morgan’s municipal managers as of June 2013. These holdings, which represent about 70 percent of their city GO exposures, are mapped in blue across several charts to show that they possess far stronger economic fundamentals than Detroit in terms of crime, economic output, labor force, income, and population trends.

The first chart, displaying violent crime by MSA per 100,000 inhabitants in 2011, highlights Detroit as the highest-crime metro area in the cohort, with nearly 1,200 violent crimes per 100,000 people. It is followed by Chicago, Miami, Tallahassee, and Baltimore, with rates tapering down across dozens of other cities, ending with Provo, Utah, which has the lowest rate at under 200 violent crimes per 100,000.

The second chart, which tracks growth in Gross Metropolitan Product indexed to 2001, depicts Detroit's trend line lagging near the very bottom of the cohort at the 5th percentile, dropping below its 2001 baseline to an index value of approximately 95 by 2009. In contrast, the blue lines representing the rest of the municipal bond managers' holdings mostly show strong upward trajectories, with the 95th percentile index approaching 200 and the 80th percentile near 160 by 2011.

The third chart illustrates labor force growth, including both employed and unemployed individuals, indexed to January 2000. Detroit’s labor force contracted steadily over the decade, falling to an index value of roughly 85 by 2012, tracking the 5th percentile. Conversely, the vast majority of peer MSAs grew, with the 20th percentile resting just above 100, the 80th percentile near 120, and the 95th percentile peaking around 135.

The fourth chart examines growth in personal income per capita indexed to 1990. Detroit’s per capita income growth tracked the lowest tier of the peer group, rising to an index of only about 175 by 2008, placing it right at the 5th percentile. The broader group of MSAs experienced much more robust growth, with the 80th percentile index reaching 210 and the 95th percentile index exceeding 230. 

The final chart shows MSA-level population growth indexed to 1970. Detroit’s population flatlined, remaining right at the index baseline of 100 for four decades, placing it well below the 5th percentile. The peer MSAs experienced dramatic population gains over the same period, with the 20th percentile index at approximately 120, the 80th percentile index at 240, and the 95th percentile index surging to nearly 375 by 2010. A footnote notes that some large upward revisions in the population data occurred in 2010, coinciding with the Decennial Census.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication presents a commentary on the global economic and profit cycle, written in a pseudo-biblical narrative style. The main argument is that although corporate profit margins are high, they have been driven by low labor compensation as a share of GDP, leading to weak top-line revenue growth compared to past cycles. However, the author asserts that improving global economic "pillars" could bolster revenue and profits heading into 2014. 

The analysis is supported by five charts. The first, illustrating the S&P 500 trailing price-to-earnings ratio from 1926 to 2013, shows that while valuation multiples have recently risen back toward 17x or 18x, they remain roughly average on a long-term historical basis. The second chart, analyzing US growth across four key pillars, plots three-month annualized rates of change from January 2012 to July 2013. It depicts strong, albeit moderating, double-digit growth in housing alongside positive, stable contributions from production, consumption, and employment, demonstrating that the US economy is resiliently firing on all cylinders despite tax increases and budget cuts.

Global stabilization is also highlighted through manufacturing surveys. A chart of European Purchasing Managers' Index levels from 2010 to 2013 reveals a notable summer rebound in mid-2013, with the UK PMI surging above 55, Germany and the European Periphery climbing back toward or above the 50 expansion threshold, and France showing a modest uptick. Similarly, a chart of manufacturing PMIs in China and Japan shows stabilizing conditions in mid-2013, with Japan’s index climbing above 50 and China’s index recovering from its recent downward trend. Finally, a chart showing the ratio of global manufacturing orders to inventory displays a sharp rebound from a late-2012 low of around 1.01 to approximately 1.15 by mid-2013. 

In conclusion, the author raises the expectation that if these positive manufacturing and regional growth trends continue into 2014, they will likely catalyze a rise in corporate revenue and profits from their current stagnation, validating optimistic market expectations.

This page analyzes the potential consequences of the Federal Reserve’s plan to taper its monthly asset purchases despite an economic environment that remains fundamentally weak compared to previous cycles of monetary tightening. Written in a satirical biblical style, the commentary warns that while the Fed may keep short-term policy rates below one percent for several years, its tapering of quantitative easing could disrupt interest-rate-sensitive sectors and highly leveraged risk parity investors. 

A table compares economic indicators from the current cycle to the average of the five prior cycles when the Fed tightened policy. It highlights that the current environment is significantly weaker across all measures: core inflation is at 1.7% compared to a historical average of 3.1%, unemployment is elevated at 7.4% versus 6.2%, and the output gap stands at negative 5.8% of potential GDP versus the prior average of negative 0.9%. Furthermore, private sector credit growth is sluggish at 3.1% compared to a historical average of 9.2%, and capacity utilization relative to history is at negative 3.0% versus negative 0.3%.

The heavy reliance of the economic recovery on low interest rates is illustrated in a chart indexing GDP contributions from the second quarter of 2009 to 2013. The index shows that interest-rate-sensitive sectors, defined as durable goods consumption plus structures, surged to nearly 114 by mid-2013, whereas the rest of the economy—labeled "everything else"—lagged far behind, reaching only around 105. 

Another chart explores the vulnerability of risk parity strategies by showing a stylized risk parity portfolio's asset allocation from 1978 to 2013. While the equity weight remains stable and low, generally between 30% and 50%, the bond weight is highly leveraged and volatile, frequently fluctuating between 100% and nearly 300%. The author notes that because these portfolios use leveraged fixed income to mimic the risk profile of a traditional 60/40 stock/bond portfolio, they are highly sensitive to sudden changes in the yield curve as Fed policy normalizes.

The analysis also addresses whether the housing market can withstand rising interest rates. A chart of the US housing affordability index from 1970 to 2013 shows that housing affordability reached record-high levels in 2012, and although it declined slightly in 2013, it remains historically high. A complementary chart tracking new and existing home sales from 1990 to 2013 shows existing home sales recovering to around 5 million annualized units by 2013, though still below their 2005 peak of over 6.5 million. New home sales have shown a much weaker recovery, hovering around 400,000 units. The author projects that housing momentum will slow in 2014 compared to the 2012–2013 period, though the downturn may be cushioned because roughly 60% of recent home sales were all-cash transactions—often by institutional buy-to-rent funds—which are inherently less sensitive to mortgage rate hikes.

This page discusses the historical precedent of bipartisan support for major, nationally impactful U.S. legislation over the past century, arguing that the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010, or Obamacare, represents a historic departure due to its total lack of bipartisan consensus. To support this observation, the author includes a detailed table titled "Major nationally impactful legislation of the last 100 years, Obamacare and the 'disagreement gap' in gray."

The table lists twenty major pieces of legislation spanning from 1913 to 2010, detailing the percentage of Democratic and Republican "Yea" votes, as well as the percent difference, in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. Historically, massive and controversial changes—such as the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, the Social Security Act of 1935, the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and the Tax Reform Act of 1986—passed with significant support from both parties in both chambers. For example, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 was passed in the House with 61% Democratic and 80% Republican "Yea" votes, and in the Senate with 69% Democratic and 82% Republican "Yea" votes. Even highly polarized legislation, such as the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001, maintained a small level of cross-party support, passing with 15% Democratic support in the House and 28% in the Senate. 

In stark contrast, the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010, highlighted in yellow at the bottom of the table, passed with 87% Democratic and 0% Republican support in the House (an 87% voting difference) and 100% Democratic and 0% Republican support in the Senate (a 100% voting difference). 

The author poses an open question regarding whether the United States will successfully adapt to major societal changes when the country's elected representatives are so deeply divided on the issue. Highlighting this tension, the text notes that support for the healthcare law in a contemporaneous CNN poll stood at only 39%. The commentary closes with a quote from Benjamin Franklin: "We must hang together, or most assuredly, we will all hang separately."

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" addresses the short-term cyclical recovery in Europe and the profound, long-term structural challenges facing Italy. The main argument is that while European economies are emerging from a cyclical recession—supported by improving Purchasing Managers' Indices (PMIs) and a temporary growth boost from the Italian government repaying 40 billion Euros in arrears—Italy’s medium-term prospects remain highly troubled due to unrealistic official targets and structural decline within the Eurozone.

To illustrate the short-term cyclical rebound, the top-left chart, titled "A summer rebound in European manufacturing surveys," plots the Purchasing Managers' Index level from 2010 to 2013 for Germany, the UK, Spain, and Italy. It shows a clear upward trend across all four nations in mid-2013, with Germany and the UK breaking back above the expansionary threshold of 50, and Spain and Italy trailing closely behind. The top-right chart, "Italy: earnings growth vs. manufacturing/services survey" from 1999 to 2013, correlates the PMI business activity survey (index levels from 35 to 65 on the left axis) with year-over-year percentage changes in corporate earnings growth on a five-month lag (ranging from -50% to 50% on the right axis). The two series track each other closely, suggesting that the recent uptick in the PMI will likely lead to positive corporate earnings revisions in the coming months.

Despite these positive short-term signs, the author expresses deep skepticism regarding Italy’s medium-term outlook, specifically pointing out the unrealistic assumptions in Italy’s Stability Program. A middle-left chart, "Italy's primary surplus and SP target," tracks the primary fiscal balance as a percentage of GDP from 1962 to 2012. It shows that the 2017 target of a 5% to 6% surplus is an extreme historical outlier, achieved only briefly during the 1990s following currency devaluation, tax hikes, and asset sales. An adjacent chart, "Italian nominal GDP growth," tracks year-over-year changes from 2002 to 2012, highlighting that the Stability Program’s 3% growth target for 2014 to 2017 is far higher than the negative and near-zero rates recorded in the post-crisis years. 

The author argues that without realistic growth, Italy will remain burdened by a debt-to-GDP ratio nearly double that of the United States, as well as an unhealthy interdependency between domestic banks, the Italian government, and the European Central Bank. This structural malaise is illustrated in the middle-right chart, dramatically titled "Death in Venice." It plots industrial production indexed to 1999 for Germany and Italy. Following the fixing of the Euro exchange rate, Germany’s industrial production index rose steadily to nearly 130 by 2010, whereas Italy's index collapsed to roughly 80, suggesting that Euro membership has precipitated Italy's de-industrialization. 

Finally, a wide chart across the bottom of the page displays the "Change in 7-year real Italian GDP, percent, since 1861 (Unification)." This historical series shows that by 2012, Italy's seven-year real GDP growth rate fell to near-zero and slightly negative territory. This degree of economic stagnation has no modern precedent, matching the depths seen only during the disruptions of World War I and World War II. The author poses the open, critical question of whether Italy can tolerate languishing in the stagnation of the European Monetary Union indefinitely, warning that while the near-term EU news flow might be positive, Italy's structural decline is a major medium-term risk that will inevitably resurface.

This page addresses the emerging market balance of payments crisis focusing on the "Big 4" emerging market debtor nations of 2013: Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey. The author analyzes whether the present situation reflects past crises, such as the 1980s Latin American debt crisis and the 1997 Asian financial crisis, and evaluates the vulnerabilities these nations face.

To illustrate the macro environment of these four nations, the page features two line charts. The first, "Slowing growth in the Big 4," plots the Purchasing Managers' Index from 2010 to 2013. It shows declining trends for India, Turkey, Brazil, and Indonesia, with index levels falling from peaks near 55 to 60 down toward or below 50 by late 2013, indicating contracting economic activity. The second chart, "Rising vulnerability to capital outflows in the Big 4," plots net capital inflows and the current account balance as a percentage of GDP from 2002 to 2012. It highlights a widening vulnerability, where current accounts plummeted to nearly negative 4% of GDP while net capital inflows, despite a recent sharp drop, remained positive, pointing to a high dependence on foreign capital.

A central comparative table, titled "EM external account measures, past and present," compares the Big 4 of 2013 against past crisis cohorts: Latin America in the 1980s (represented by Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, and Venezuela) and Asia in 1996 (Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia, and Thailand). This comparison shows that while today’s external debt as a percentage of exports (152%) is higher than in 1996 (130%), it is far below the 1980s peak of 401%. Crucially, today’s interest on external debt is a manageable 4.7% of exports, and foreign exchange reserves cover a much larger 63.3% of external debt (circled in red for emphasis), compared to only 28.8% in 1996 and 7.7% in the 1980s. Furthermore, the Big 4 now use floating exchange rates rather than the managed rates of previous eras, and their year-to-date currency depreciation versus the US dollar is a relatively mild negative 13.3%.

To the right of the table, a line chart titled "Equity markets in the Big 4 vs. other EM countries" indexes stock performance from January to September 2013, using January 1, 2012, as a baseline of 100. It shows a sharp divergence: the Big 4 equity index fell from a peak of roughly 125 down to around 105 by September 2013, significantly underperforming a basket of other emerging market countries—including Colombia, Hong Kong, Malaysia, Mexico, the Philippines, Poland, Russia, South Korea, Taiwan, and Thailand—which hovered around 120.

The author concludes that although the Big 4's accumulation of reserves and floating exchange rates make this crisis less disruptive than those of the 1980s or 1990s—which is good news for highly exposed European banks—challenges remain. To defend their currencies, these countries must deplete reserves, which does not solve their underlying reliance on foreign capital. The author forecasts that further adjustments are likely, including higher interest rates and lower GDP growth, which could prevent recent equity market gains from lasting. Finally, the text touches on China, noting that while its growth has slowed due to tighter monetary policies targeting non-bank lending, stable indicators suggest a steady 7% to 8% growth rate. The author suggests that investors look for buying opportunities when emerging market surplus countries like China, South Korea, Taiwan, or Mexico become oversold, as they rely far less on volatile hot money inflows than the Big 4.

This commentary addresses the political debates in Washington, D.C., surrounding the continuing resolution and the debt ceiling, positioning Obamacare at the center of the impasse. The author highlights that Congress must pass a continuing resolution by October first to avoid a government shutdown, which is necessary since a formal budget has not been passed since 2009. A more difficult challenge is the debt ceiling deadline in mid-October. To avoid default, the author predicts that the House Speaker will likely have to split his caucus to pass an agreement, similar to the passage of the American Tax Relief Act in January 2013, where eighty-five moderate Republicans voted for it while one hundred fifty-one voted against.

To illustrate political division, a horizontal bar chart measures the partisanship gap of major domestic legislation from 1913 to 2010. The chart plots the "Yea" vote percentage differentials between Republicans and Democrats in both the Senate and the House. It highlights Obamacare in 2010 at the top, showing a near one hundred percent partisanship gap in both chambers, making it one of the most partisan pieces of legislation in a century. This stands in stark contrast to historically bipartisan laws, such as the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 or the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which had much narrower voting gaps between the parties.

The dynamics of a split caucus are further illustrated in a scatter diagram mapping the ideological orientation of House Republicans and their votes on the 2013 American Tax Relief Act. Using the Poole-Rosenthal methodology, representatives are plotted along an axis ranging from zero (less conservative) to one (more conservative). The diagram shows that the "Yes" votes were largely concentrated among moderate members, including key figures like Dave Camp, Speaker John Boehner, Paul Ryan, and Eric Cantor, while the "No" votes were overwhelmingly cast by the most conservative members of the caucus.

The commentary then shifts to the long-term outlook for federal debt, noting that the Congressional Budget Office projects debt held by the public to rise to one hundred percent of GDP between 2023 and 2038 due to demographics and entitlements. However, the projected gap in 2023 between the Baseline and Alternative scenarios has narrowed from thirty percent of GDP in the previous year's estimate to just ten percent of GDP, reflecting the impact of the American Tax Relief Act, the Budget Control Act, and the Sequester. 

A line chart shows federal debt held by the public as a percentage of GDP from 1940 to 2023. Historical debt peaked near one hundred ten percent after World War II, declined to a low of around twenty-five percent in the mid-1970s, and climbed back up to over seventy percent by 2013. For the future outlook, the chart plots two paths: the Baseline (current law) scenario, which stabilizes at around seventy-five percent of GDP by 2023, and the Alternative Fiscal Scenario, which climbs toward eighty-five percent. This alternative scenario assumes that business tax relief is extended, the Sequester is repealed, and the Medicare "Doc fix" physician payment limits are deferred.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s commentary, written by Michael Cembalest, focuses on the risks and outlook for investing in Japanese equities. Cembalest argues that while underweighting Japanese equities was a reliable strategy for decades, investors should now hold a normal allocation, provided they hedge their Yen exposure. He outlines key risks to Japanese economic recovery, particularly the potential for a Yen collapse combined with high oil and natural gas prices, which would drive up energy import costs. Consequently, he predicts that Japan will face growing pressure to re-commission its nuclear power plants, despite the deteriorating situation at Fukushima. He cautions that engineering a rise in Japanese equities is much easier than generating durable, consistent growth and inflation. 

The page also features a list of key acronyms used throughout the report, including CBO (Congressional Budget Office), CDC (Center for Disease Control), DSH (Disproportionate Share Hospital), ESRD (End-Stage Renal Disease), FAA (Federal Aviation Administration), NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration), NIH (National Institutes of Health), and PMI (Purchasing Managers Index). Additionally, a US Navy photograph titled "Giant oarfish captured off the California Coast" is displayed, showing a large line of military personnel holding up a massive, long, ribbon-like sea creature on a beach.

This page focuses on the return of underlying financial market trends, specifically examining how manufacturing surveys serve as leading indicators for corporate profits, alongside a brief historical look at healthcare cost underestimations. 

The page begins with a table comparing the initial estimated costs of various healthcare programs at the time of their enactment against their actual costs. It highlights substantial discrepancies, noting that the entire Medicare program was initially estimated to cost $12 billion but actually cost $110 billion, representing a 9.17 to 1 ratio. Similarly, the Medicaid DSH program had an initial estimate of $1 billion compared to an actual cost of $17 billion, a 17 to 1 ratio, while the Massachusetts Health Reform had a much closer ratio of 1.20 to 1, with an actual cost of $0.869 billion against a $0.725 billion estimate.

The main discussion shifts to purchasing managers' index (PMI) surveys in the United States and Europe, showing how they historically foreshadow corporate profit trends. Two side-by-side charts illustrate this relationship. The left chart, tracking the US from 1989 to 2013, plots the PMI business activity survey index (on a scale of 30 to 65) against year-over-year corporate earnings growth with a four-month lag (ranging from -50% to 50%). The right chart tracks the Euro-zone from 1998 to 2013, comparing the PMI index against earnings growth with a two-month lag. Both charts reveal a very tight historical correlation, suggesting that recent upturns in manufacturing surveys bode well for future earnings. 

The author explains that these rising PMI trends are crucial because US earnings growth has recently stagnated, and European earnings growth has only recently crawled back to zero. With equity price-to-earnings multiples back to their long-term average of approximately 15x, 2014 stock market returns are expected to be highly sensitive to whether actual earnings growth rebounds. Because benefits from declining interest, credit, and labor costs have already been largely realized, future profit growth must rely on rising GDP and top-line revenue growth. 

Despite these positive PMI indicators, the author notes several signs of market exuberance, including net margin debt reaching a cycle high, the outperformance of highly leveraged, lower-rated stocks, and the fact that more than 100% of equity market gains since January 2009 have occurred during weeks of Federal Reserve asset purchases, with non-purchase weeks yielding net negative returns. On the policy front, a major positive catalyst for 2014 is the expected decline in US fiscal austerity from around $300 billion to $50 billion. Since 2010, government austerity measures like discretionary spending caps and tax increases have shaved about 1% off real GDP growth annually, meaning their reduction should allow overall US GDP growth to align more closely with stronger private-sector levels in the coming year.

This page analyzes two major macroeconomic topics: the ongoing weakness in emerging market debtor nations and Japan's unprecedented monetary stimulus. 

The first section discusses the divergence within emerging markets. The author notes that while emerging market nations excluding debtor nations are experiencing a growth pick-up due to demand from the US, Europe, and Japan, five specific debtor nations—India, Indonesia, Brazil, Turkey, and South Africa—remain weak due to rate hikes implemented to defend their currencies. This is illustrated in two top charts. The first chart, "Industrial production," shows the six-month annualized percent change from 2007 to 2013, highlighting how emerging market debtor nations' production growth lagged behind other emerging markets in late 2013, dropping to near zero while non-debtor emerging markets hovered around five percent. The second chart, "Emerging market 5 year government bond yields," shows yields rising steeply through 2013, with Brazil exceeding eleven percent, Turkey and India approaching nine percent, and South Africa and Indonesia hovering between seven and eight percent. 

To contextualize this, a middle table compares external account metrics across three eras: the 1980s debt crises in Latin America, the 1996 Asian financial crisis, and today's situation in 2013. This comparison argues that the current episode is less severe than historical crises due to structural improvements circled in red. Specifically, current reserves cover 63.3 percent of external debt, compared to just 7.7 percent in the 1980s and 28.8 percent in 1996, and these countries now employ floating exchange rate regimes instead of managed ones. Although fundamentals are healthier, the author notes that growth adjustments are still needed and emerging market debtor equity valuations are not yet cheap enough relative to emerging market surplus countries.

The second half of the page covers Japan's dramatic monetary expansion. A bottom-right chart titled "Japan's massive money experiment" plots central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP from 2000 projected out to 2020 for the Bank of Japan, the European Central Bank, and the Federal Reserve. It shows the Bank of Japan's balance sheet exploding from roughly 35 percent of GDP in 2012 to a committed level of about 70 percent by 2016, with a "contingent" path that could see it exceed 100 percent of GDP by 2020 if inflation expectations fail to reach the government's two percent target. In contrast, the Federal Reserve and European Central Bank balance sheets remain steady below 30 percent of GDP. The author compares this massive planned increase in central bank holdings to a giant 20-foot oarfish. The goal of this expansion is to liquefy the Japanese economy, push investors out of government bonds and into riskier assets or foreign currencies to weaken the Yen, and drive an export-led recovery. To support this, Japan is considering tax-free equity-only investment accounts for its citizens.

This page outlines the potential consequences of a US Federal debt ceiling breach and default on federal debt. The core argument is that severe financial market disruptions, represented in blue charts, historically trigger adverse economic consequences, depicted in red charts, with a typical lag of two to six months. The visual layout uses downward-pointing arrows to connect specific market indicators to their corresponding real-world economic impacts.

The first connection pairs market liquidity with labor market health. A blue chart tracking a measure of market liquidity from Citigroup shows a massive spike in illiquidity during the 2008 financial crisis, scaling from a baseline of liquid conditions to a highly illiquid state above 1.0. This links directly down to a red chart of non-farm payrolls from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and J.P. Morgan Asset Management, which reveals that this liquidity freeze preceded a devastating drop in monthly employment, bottoming out at nearly negative 800,000 jobs during 2008 and 2009.

The second connection links equity volatility and broad financial stress to consumer spending and business sentiment. The blue chart for equity market volatility and financial stress, sourcing data from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City and the Wall Street Journal, displays a major surge in both the VIX index, which spiked near 60, and the financial stress index, which climbed above 5. This connects to a red chart of retail sales and business confidence from the Census Bureau. Following the market stress, year-over-year retail sales growth plunged to roughly negative 10 percent, while the business confidence index plummeted to nearly 20.

The third pair connects auto credit spreads with capital expenditures. The blue chart detailing credit spreads on automobile finance trusts, from Barclays, shows spreads spiking from a normal range of 2 to 4 percent up to nearly 11 percent in 2008. Below this, the red chart tracking businesses planning capital expenditures, from the National Federation of Independent Business, demonstrates that the share of firms planning capex plummeted from over 30 percent down to around 18 percent.

The fourth set focuses on capital markets and overall economic growth. A blue chart tracking initial public offerings and bond trading volumes, sourced from FINRA and Renaissance Capital, shows that IPO volumes ground to a virtual halt in 2008, coinciding with a severe drop in bond trading volumes. This connects directly to a red chart of real economic growth from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, which shows that year-over-year US gross domestic product contracted by nearly 4 percent.

The fifth pairing examines commercial paper and small business credit availability. A blue chart from the Investment Company Institute showing the rate of commercial paper issuance shows net issuance plunging below negative 400 during the 2008 crisis. This disruption corresponds directly with a red chart showing small and medium-sized firms reporting credit harder to get, from the National Federation of Independent Business, where the percentage of firms reporting difficulties rose from a typical 3 percent up to nearly 15 percent.

The final pair links wholesale funding strains to labor compensation. The blue chart for the Libor minus T-bill spread and haircuts on Agency repo lending, with data from Bloomberg and J.P. Morgan Securities, shows the Libor-Tbill spread spiking above 400 basis points and repo haircuts climbing to nearly 12 percent. This funding stress preceded a collapse in worker compensation, as shown in the red chart from the National Federation of Independent Business tracking firms raising worker compensation over the past three to six months, which fell from over 25 percent down to nearly 0 percent.

In this introductory page of J.P. Morgan's annual energy update, Michael Cembalest presents a realistic overview of global energy trends in collaboration with energy scholar Vaclav Smil of the University of Manitoba. The central thesis is that despite gains in energy efficiency, global growth remains heavily energy-intensive and deeply reliant on fossil fuels. Cembalest points out the contrast between Western environmental initiatives, like fossil fuel divestment petitions at three hundred US universities, and the reality of the developing world spending four hundred fifty billion dollars annually on fuel and electricity subsidies. 

The accompanying line chart, titled "A more efficient but still energy-intensive world," indexes world real GDP and primary energy consumption from 1965 to 2013, with 1965 set to one hundred. It shows that while real GDP has risen to over four hundred, global energy consumption has followed a similar, albeit slightly lower, upward trajectory, reaching approximately three hundred fifty by 2013. An inset pie chart showing the 2012 energy consumption breakdown highlights that fossil fuels still comprise the overwhelming majority of the energy mix, far exceeding hydro, nuclear, and non-hydro renewables.

The publication introduces five core topics for the 2013 update: an analysis of why US energy independence is unlikely to bring lower oil prices; the hidden system-wide costs of expanding renewable energy; potential over-optimism regarding US liquefied natural gas exports; the rising global share of coal, which has reached its highest level since 1970; and Japan's reconsideration of nuclear energy due to high gas prices, despite the Fukushima disaster. Cembalest concludes that the US is poised to maintain a significant manufacturing advantage due to electricity prices that are only half of European levels and fifty-five percent of China's, helping to drive foreign direct investment and job repatriation.

This page presents an update on progress toward US energy independence and explains why this milestone is unlikely to result in significantly lower global oil prices. The author argues that although domestic crude production is climbing rapidly and imports are falling, the rising capital costs and natural decline rates of legacy fields will keep the marginal cost of oil elevated. 

The first chart, titled "US net imports and domestic production of crude oil," plots monthly data from 1991 to 2013 in millions of barrels per day. It shows that net imports peaked near 10.5 million barrels per day around 2005 before falling to roughly 7.5 million by mid-2013. Meanwhile, domestic production reversed its long-term decline around 2008, surging from 5.0 million to over 7.0 million barrels per day by 2013. 

The second chart, "What US energy independence might look like," projects the components of US net crude oil imports through 2020–2025. It shows 2012 imports at approximately 8.1 million barrels per day, breaking down 2013 year-to-date imports by region, with the Americas representing the largest share, followed by the Middle East and Africa. By 2020–2025, projected net imports are expected to fall below 3.0 million barrels per day. This projected decline is driven primarily by a net increase in domestic production, alongside reduced consumption from CAFE standards and auto replacement cycles (estimated conservatively by J.P. Morgan to save 1.5 million barrels per day), oil imported for refined product exports, and minor displacement from natural gas vehicles. At these lower levels, imports from Canada and Mexico alone would be sufficient to satisfy total US import needs. 

The third chart, "Capital spending on legacy oil fields on the rise," tracks exploration and production maintenance capital expenditures (excluding new projects) from 2005 to 2011 in USD per barrel. It reveals a steep upward trajectory in costs across all analyzed sectors: Latin American oil capex rose from approximately $5 to $24 per barrel; Asian oils rose from $8 to $14; global oils rose from $4 to $13; and US integrated oils rose from $4 to $12. This rising capital intensity indicates that aging legacy fields—which suffer annualized decline rates of 3 percent to 6 percent across the US, Europe, and Latin America—require significantly more investment over time. 

The text notes that while the US oil boom could create 3 million jobs by 2020 according to IHS/CERA estimates and bolster the US dollar, high maintenance costs mean most global oil companies need oil prices between $100 and $125 per barrel to remain cash-flow neutral after accounting for capex and dividends. The author also cites external forecasts, including Leonardo Magueri’s projection of 10.4 million barrels per day of US production by 2017, driven by tight and shale oil expansion.

This page focuses on the complexities of calculating the levelized cost of energy for renewable sources, describing a "Rashomon effect" where different analysts produce widely varying estimates. To illustrate this, a central table compares cost projections and operational metrics—excluding subsidies—from the Energy Information Administration, Lazard, and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. For onshore wind, the Energy Information Administration estimates a levelized cost of eighty-seven dollars per megawatt-hour, whereas Lazard projects a range of forty-five to ninety-five dollars, and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory suggests sixty-two to seventy-two dollars. For solar photovoltaic, the Energy Information Administration estimates a levelized cost of one hundred forty-four dollars, while Lazard calculates a significantly lower eighty-nine to ninety-nine dollars. The author notes that on a stand-alone basis in optimal locations, renewable energy costs are declining rapidly—underlined by a forty-five percent drop in solar photovoltaic panel prices since mid-2011—making them cheaper than national-average government estimates.

However, the author argues that these standard levelized cost figures fail to capture the full system-wide costs of integrating intermittent renewables into the electricity grid. When renewable penetration grows, four distinct hidden costs emerge: stand-by power costs to maintain dispatchable conventional backup plants, over-production costs that strain grids during peak supply and require expensive high-voltage direct current transmission lines, balancing costs from constantly ramping peaking generators up and down, and grid transmission costs to connect remote solar and wind sites to population centers. As an example of these systemic challenges, the author cites research from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research showing that if wind energy reached a twenty percent share of Germany's electricity mix, its system-wide costs could be fifty percent higher than traditional levelized cost estimates. The text concludes by noting that these rising, subsidized costs are being passed on to struggling households in Europe, leading to political pushback and a recent reduction in renewable subsidies in Germany, Greece, and Spain.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s annual energy update presents an analysis of rising global oil production costs, geopolitical budget pressures on OPEC nations, and the economics of renewable energy. 

The author begins by highlighting the rising costs of US shale oil production outside of the Eagle Ford basin. While Eagle Ford boasts competitive breakeven costs of approximately $60 per barrel, other shale regions face higher costs. For instance, costs in the Bakken formation have risen due to a 15 percent decline in average well productivity from its peak, alongside rail infrastructure bottlenecks. Other basins like Anadarko, Utica, and Mississippi Lime are estimated to have breakeven costs ranging from $70 to $90 per barrel. 

Expanding to global marginal oil supplies, the author references Goldman Sachs data tracking E&P projects with over 300 million barrels of lifetime production. While some sites in Iraq, Brazil, the US Gulf, Norway, and specific Canadian heavy oil fields like Christina Lake and Foster Creek have low breakeven costs, no new projects added in the prior two years break even below $70. Most fall into the $80 to $100 range, which includes the majority of Canadian heavy oil sites. Because global consumption reaches approximately 90 million barrels per day, higher-cost marginal sources must be utilized. Furthermore, high domestic taxation contributes to steep Russian breakeven costs. Geopolitical dynamics, such as factionalism from the Arab Spring, also disrupt supply, leaving two-thirds of Libyan production offline. Consequently, OPEC nations have increased domestic spending to maintain stability, raising the average oil price needed to balance their budgets in 2015 to $100 per barrel—up from $20 a decade prior—particularly for Iran, Iraq, Russia, and Algeria.

These dynamics are visualized in an accompanying scatter plot titled "Cost curve for new projects (recently producing, under development or pre-sanction)." The chart plots USD per barrel on the vertical axis, from $20 to $110, against estimated cumulative lifetime production in thousands of barrels on the horizontal axis, ranging from 0 to 30,000. The curve starts at the low end around $20 to $30 with Northern Iraq and Brazil Deepwater, followed closely by Canada's Christina Lake and Foster Creek under $40, and US Eagle Ford shale oil near $50. The curve rises steadily through Norway, US Gulf Deepwater, and Bakken shale between $60 and $70. It continues upward past the Permian Basin, Utica, Mississippi Lime, and Angola Deepwater in the $70 to $80 range, before terminating at the highest-cost projects, including Russia, Nigeria Deepwater, and various Canadian heavy oil projects, which span $80 to $110.

The final section of the page shifts to the growth and costs of renewable energy. Global solar photovoltaic and wind capacity have grown annually by 60 percent and 25 percent respectively since 2007, with wind representing the largest share of US capacity additions in 2012. The US Energy Information Administration projects that by 2018, the all-in levelized cost of electricity for new wind capacity will be cheaper than coal and only 20 to 30 percent more expensive than natural gas, excluding subsidies. However, a footnote cautions that global renewable investment fell in 2012 and 2013, driven by a reduction in European subsidies.

This page analyzes global liquefied natural gas (LNG) markets, focusing on the viability of US LNG exports to Western Europe and Asia amid changing supply and demand dynamics. The author argues that while Western Europe imports significant volumes of LNG, high shipping costs compared to pipeline alternatives diminish the US cost advantage there. Consequently, US exporters are targeting major Asian markets where prices are significantly higher, though they face potential competition from Russian pipelines and rising global production.

An illustrative chart in the upper right, titled "Asia importing a lot of LNG at high prices, billion cubic meters," details gas imports and prices for four major Asian nations as of June 2013. Japan is the largest importer, receiving nearly 120 billion cubic meters (BCM) entirely as LNG at a premium price of $17 per mmbtu. South Korea imports about 50 BCM, also entirely as LNG, at $15 per mmbtu. China’s imports total approximately 45 BCM, split almost evenly between pipeline gas and LNG, with a lower price of $9 per mmbtu. India imports roughly 20 BCM of LNG at $13 per mmbtu.

To show the cost competitiveness of US gas in these high-priced Asian markets, a table at the bottom right, "Based on Sabine Pass, US LNG exports are cheaper than Asian imports," outlines the total delivered cost of US LNG at different US domestic price levels. At a Henry Hub spot price of $3.00 per mmbtu, adding liquefaction costs of $0.45, capacity charges of $3.00, and shipping fees of $2.51 results in a total indicated cost of $8.96 per mmbtu. If the Henry Hub price increases to $4.00, the liquefaction cost rises to $0.60, bringing the total cost to $10.11 per mmbtu. At a $5.00 Henry Hub price, liquefaction is $0.75, resulting in a total indicated cost of $11.26 per mmbtu. These figures indicate that US LNG remains cheaper than prevailing Asian spot prices, which have been elevated partly due to the Fukushima nuclear disaster.

However, the author cautions that a looming supply glut poses a major challenge for exporters. An area chart on the bottom left, titled "Some estimates of future LNG capacity exceed demand," plots projected demand against various layers of capacity from 2012 to 2025. While global LNG demand is projected to grow steadily from approximately 250 million tonnes per year to about 400 million tonnes per year by 2025, total potential capacity could scale past 700 million tonnes per year if all existing, under-construction, possible, and speculative projects are completed. 

This threat of oversupply is driven by extensive project pipelines globally, including Australian operations targeting 25% of global demand. The author notes that US "brownfield" projects enjoy a 30% to 40% cost advantage over new greenfield sites in Australia, where projects sponsored by Chevron and Inpex have faced 20% to 30% cost overruns due to rising labor and materials costs. Western Canada is also noted as an interesting competitor to watch, as its new sites benefit from lower shipping and raw material costs. Ultimately, the author suggests that the current high Asian price premium may be temporary, potentially deflating as Japan resumes nuclear power generation and Russia expands its pipeline capacity to China.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" focuses on Japan’s post-Fukushima energy dilemma and offers broader concluding thoughts on the slow pace of global energy transitions. The primary argument is that despite ambitious renewable energy targets, Japan is facing the harsh economic reality of soaring import costs, forcing the government to plan the reactivation of a significant portion of its idle nuclear fleet. 

The first chart, titled "Japan's rising cost of mineral fuel imports," tracks these import costs as a percentage of Japan's GDP from 1980 through 2012. The line shows that after peaking near 6.0% in the early 1980s, the import burden steadily fell to a low of approximately 1.0% around the year 2000. However, following the nuclear shutdowns, import costs spiked dramatically, returning to nearly 6.0% by 2012. This visual underlines the financial pressure on the nation’s trade balance.

Adjacent to this chart is a map of Japan titled "One-third of nuclear capacity applying for reactivation," which displays the plant capacities and locations of nine facilities seeking to restart 17 reactors. These restarts represent 36% of Japan’s total nuclear capacity. The map distinguishes between Pressurized Water Reactors, shown in blue, and Boiling Water Reactors, shown in red. The listed plants applying for reactivation include Kashiwazaki-Kariwa (2,630 MW, 6.0% of total capacity), Genkai (2,254 MW, 5.1%), Ohi (2,254 MW, 5.1%), Tomari (1,966 MW, 4.4%), Sendai (1,692 MW, 3.8%), Takahama (1,660 MW, 3.7%), Tsuruga (1,451 MW, 3.3%), Tokai (1,060 MW, 2.4%), and Ikata (846 MW, 1.9%). The text notes that almost all of these candidate plants use safer, more modern pressurized water reactors rather than the boiling water reactors associated with the Fukushima disaster. According to the Japanese Institute of Energy Economics, a full restart of these reactors would cut Japan's energy import bill by 30% and reduce its trade deficit by up to 3%.

A dedicated update box addresses the ongoing cleanup challenges at the crippled Fukushima site. It details how radioactive cooling water stored in leaking tanks has created hazardous localized radiation levels up to 40 times the allowed occupational exposure. Furthermore, at least 300 tons of contaminated groundwater, laden with cesium-137 and strontium-90, leak into the sea daily. In response, the Japanese government allocated half a billion dollars to build a giant underground wall of frozen earth to contain the flow. The International Atomic Energy Agency estimates that a complete cleanup will take at least 30 to 40 years, keeping nearby ocean fishing suspended indefinitely.

The page concludes with broader reflections on the global energy landscape, noting that 150 years after the start of the oil age, the global economy remains overwhelmingly dependent on fossil fuels. While energy efficiency has improved, actual reliance on coal has increased. The author references discussions with energy expert Vaclav Smil regarding the "fourth great energy transition" toward renewables, following the mastery of fire, the agricultural revolution, and the shift to fossil fuels. Smil cautions that the transition's complexities, costs, and limitations are frequently underestimated and will require many decades to unfold.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, titled "Our annual energy update: a reality check," addresses the question of why global coal consumption remains so high. The author argues that for countries lacking sufficient domestic natural gas reserves, coal is significantly cheaper than imported liquefied natural gas. Although operating and maintenance costs can be higher for coal plants, fuel costs dominate the overall economics. According to International Energy Agency estimates, fuel costs are five times operating and maintenance costs for coal and twelve times for natural gas, meaning coal's cheaper raw material costs easily offset any operational disadvantages.

To support this argument, the page features three charts. The first chart, "Global LNG and coal prices" in USD per mmbtu, compares LNG import prices across several countries with regional coal prices. LNG prices are shown to be substantially higher, ranging from around $9 per mmbtu in China to over $15 per mmbtu in Japan and Korea. Conversely, coal prices remain remarkably low and stable, hovering between $2 and $4 per mmbtu across all featured nations, including Indonesia, Russia, Germany, South Africa, Japan, and China.

The second chart displays the "Typical cost breakdown for 5,000 km transport" in USD per gigajoule, highlighting the disparity in logistics expenses between gas and coal. The total transport cost for gas is roughly $2.80 per gigajoule, with port and terminal costs accounting for nearly $1.90 and seaborne transport making up the remaining $0.90. In contrast, coal transport costs only about $0.50 per gigajoule, split between $0.20 for terminal costs and $0.30 for seaborne shipping. This visual demonstrates that shipping and terminal costs for liquefied natural gas are four to six times higher than those for coal.

The text notes that because coal’s negative environmental externalities are rarely priced into its market value, it remains the most economical option even in regions with carbon pricing policies. For example, a 2010 International Energy Agency analysis of Germany showed that combined operating and fuel costs for natural gas were 2.5 times higher than coal; even with a carbon tax of $30 per ton, gas remained 1.5 times more expensive. Consequently, unless coal prices rise to incorporate these externalities, significant reductions in global consumption are unlikely. This persistent global demand is reflected in the final chart, "US total coal exports," which tracks trailing 12-month exports in million short tons from 2005 to 2013. The chart depicts a strong upward trend, showing US coal exports rising from around 50 million short tons in 2005 to nearly 125 million short tons by mid-2013, despite a brief dip in 2009.

This page of the J.P. Morgan energy update focuses on two primary topics: the practical limits of US liquefied natural gas (LNG) export ambitions and the severe environmental consequences of rising coal usage. 

Regarding US LNG, the author questions whether there is a deep enough pool of actual buyers to support the 30 billion cubic feet per day that US companies are looking to export. Although the Department of Energy has approved projects representing about 6.4 billion cubic feet per day—including Sabine Pass, Freeport, Dominion Cove, and Lake Charles—and another 3.1 billion cubic feet per day is in the near-term pipeline via Cameron and Freeport Expansion, the author argues these volumes are likely overstated. Contracts have only been signed for 25% to 30% of proposed projects, largely because global demand may favor richer gas over US "lean" gas, and many contract signers are intermediaries who may ultimately cancel. Consequently, energy research firm Wood Mackenzie predicts that only 20% to 25% of proposed US LNG projects will actually succeed through the governmental, environmental, and financing stages to export LNG. Furthermore, a constriction of cheap capital could severely impact US shale gas production due to steep decline rates.

The second half of the page addresses the rise of US coal usage despite its severe health and environmental toll. The author lists several major impacts, including mercury emissions that prompt fish consumption advisories in over 40 states, mountaintop removal that has destroyed 500 Appalachian summits across 1.4 million acres, and the threat of radioactive toxins from 1,300 fly ash waste ponds receiving 130 million tons of waste annually. 

A line chart from the US Environmental Protection Agency illustrates the decline in US coal-fired sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions from 1990 to 2014, measured in millions of tons. The SO2 emission line drops sharply from approximately 15 million tons in 1990 to under 3 million tons projected for 2014. The chart identifies "fuel switching" as the primary driver of this decline prior to 2005, and "emission controls" as the primary driver after 2005. The NOx emission line shows a more gradual decrease from about 6 million tons in 1990 to under 2 million tons projected for 2014, a reduction attributed to emission controls. Despite these reductions, the author points out that the projected combined 4 million tons of SO2 and NOx emissions in 2014 still cause widespread damage, while newer regulatory efforts like the EPA's 2010 Mercury Air Toxics Standards face active court challenges from the coal industry.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s annual energy update presents a reality check on global coal usage, challenging the common perception that coal is in decline. Instead, the author points out that 2012 marked the highest global coal consumption on record, capturing its largest share of global primary energy since 1970. According to BP and IEA data, coal is the fastest-growing fossil fuel, with the IEA forecasting a 50% increase in global coal use by 2035.

To support this, the top-left chart, titled "World consumption of coal on the rise" (measured in million tonnes of oil equivalent from 1965 to 2012), shows a steep acceleration in consumption starting around the year 2000, rising to nearly 4,000 million tonnes. The top-right stacked area chart, "World consumption of primary energy still dominated by fossil fuels, percent," tracks energy shares from 1965 to 2010. It shows that fossil fuels—coal, oil, and natural gas—continue to dominate global energy consumption, with coal's share climbing to its highest level since 1970, while nuclear, hydro, and other renewables remain small fractions.

The commentary then zeroes in on the ten countries that account for 85% of worldwide coal use, splitting them into diversified and concentrated consumers. The bottom-left chart, "World's biggest coal consumers: diversified" (charting coal as a percentage of primary energy from 1995 to 2011), tracks nations where coal makes up less than a third of total energy. It reveals that while the US share has declined toward 20%—with an expected 20% capacity shutdown from 2011 to 2018 driven by cheap natural gas—other nations like Korea and Indonesia have seen substantial increases. Crucially, even Germany—despite its "die Energiewende" renewable initiative—and Japan have seen rising coal consumption, with Germany's coal use increasing by 10% from 2009 to 2012. Conversely, the US's shift from coal to natural gas dropped its carbon emissions to their lowest level since 1994, allowing it to meet Kyoto Protocol goals without ratification.

The bottom-right chart, "World's biggest coal consumers: concentrated," tracks countries where coal accounts for 45% to 80% of total energy consumption. South Africa and China lead this group, with coal representing over 70% of their energy mix, while Poland has seen a substantial decline from around 75% to under 60%, and India remains steady at just over 50%. The author notes that in absolute volume terms, coal consumption from 2000 to 2012 doubled in India and rose 2.7 times in China. Although China is rapidly expanding renewables—such that wind power growth surpassed coal power growth in 2012—electricity generation is projected to reduce coal's share of China's primary energy use by only 5% by 2017.

This page argues that Japan is likely to re-embrace nuclear energy despite the fallout from the March 2011 Fukushima Dai-ichi disaster, which prompted the country to idle 52 of its 54 nuclear reactors and saw operating capacity plummet from nearly 70% to under 5%. The core motivation for this reversal is economic survival: Japan imports 84% of its energy, leaving it vulnerable to soaring global fuel costs and volatile geopolitical situations, such as tensions in the Middle East. High energy import costs have resulted in domestic price hikes, with Japanese household electricity prices rising 8% to 12% and commercial rates jumping 12% to 18% in 2013. 

The economic and structural dynamics of this situation are illustrated across four charts. The first chart, depicting Japan's power plant capacity utilization by fuel type from 2007 through 2013, shows nuclear utilization collapsing to nearly zero percent after 2011. In contrast, coal and LNG capacity utilization have remained high and relatively steady, with coal hovering between 80% and 90% and LNG staying around 60% to 70%, while oil utilization has been highly volatile, fluctuating between 20% and 55%. 

The second chart presents the historical breakdown of Japanese power generation from 2006 to 2012 alongside three potential targets for 2031. This chart highlights that nuclear historically accounted for roughly 25% to 30% of total generation before nearly vanishing in 2012, forced out by increased LNG and coal generation. The 2031 planning iterations show varying strategies to reduce reliance on LNG and coal: Target 1 envisions zero nuclear energy, relying instead on a massive expansion of renewables, co-generation, and hydro; Target 2 includes a moderate nuclear contribution of around 15%; and Target 3 projects a nuclear return to over 20% of total generation. The author notes that plans relying heavily on renewables and waste-heat co-generation are highly ambitious given that their current contributions are negligible.

The third chart illustrates the dramatic "Fukushima premium" on natural gas prices from 1985 to early 2013. While global prices historically moved somewhat in tandem, Japanese natural gas prices spiked enormously after 2010, reaching roughly 16 USD per mmbtu. This stands in sharp contrast to prices in the European Union at 12 USD, the United Kingdom at 10 USD, and especially the United States, which enjoyed cheap domestic shale gas at around 3 to 4 USD. 

The final chart details regional electricity prices for households and industrial users in Q2 2012 across the United States, China, France, the United Kingdom, Germany, and Japan. This comparison highlights Japan's severe competitive disadvantage, with industrial electricity prices topping the chart at around 200 USD per MWh—higher than any other nation shown—and household electricity prices at nearly 300 USD per MWh, second only to Germany's. These unsustainable energy costs, combined with warnings from the former Japanese director general of the International Energy Agency regarding Middle Eastern supply shocks, form the backbone of the author's prediction that Japan will inevitably return to nuclear power.

This page is a reference document serving as an appendix for the J.P. Morgan publication "Our annual energy update: a reality check." It provides a comprehensive list of abbreviations and sources used throughout the annual update. The abbreviations section clarifies terminology related to energy metrics and regulatory bodies, including units like barrels per day, British thermal units, megawatt-hours, and terawatt-hours, as well as organizations like the Energy Information Agency, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. The sources listed represent a diverse collection of industry and academic literature, organized into four key areas: general energy databases, specialized research on wind, solar, and the levelized costs of energy, studies on energy independence and the marginal costs of oil production, and research focusing on liquefied natural gas markets.

This page of the J.P. Morgan energy update analyzes the total system-wide costs and diminishing capacity credits associated with integrating wind and solar power into electric grids. The author argues that while reducing coal reliance is environmentally necessary, transitioning to wind and solar introduces substantial, often-ignored grid-level costs that are not captured by standard Levelized Cost of Energy metrics.

The first chart, titled "Total system costs of wind in Germany," displays system costs in EUR per MWh on the y-axis against wind penetration as a percentage of annual energy demand on the x-axis, ranging from 5% to 40%. The chart demonstrates that while standard levelized costs remain flat at approximately 60 EUR per MWh, the total system cost rises progressively from around 78 EUR per MWh at 5% penetration to over 100 EUR per MWh at 40% penetration. This total cost increase is driven by expanding grid costs, balancing costs, overproduction costs, and stand-by power costs. This data is sourced from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.

Below this, two side-by-side charts from the Berkeley National Laboratory depict how "capacity credits"—the percentage of conventional, dispatchable power capacity that can be retired as renewables are added—decline as renewable penetration rises. The left chart, showing solar capacity credit on a y-axis of 0% to 80% against solar PV penetration on an x-axis of 0% to 35%, reveals a sharp downward trend across several regional studies, including NV Power, PGE, and California case studies. While the first additions of solar PV yield capacity credits of 40% to 70%, these credits shrink to 20% to 40% once solar penetration reaches just 10%. The right chart shows a similar trend for wind power capacity credits across various regions, including Germany, Ireland, the United Kingdom, and several US states. Wind capacity credits start lower than solar, generally between 20% and 40%, and drop to 10% to 20% as penetration approaches 20% to 30%, because wind generation is less likely to coincide with peak demand. 

The author notes that while these capacity credit analyses omit the benefits of lower greenhouse gas emissions, they highlight a pressing need for solutions to mitigate incremental system costs. Three primary strategies are proposed: the adoption of utility-scale electricity storage, consumer load shifting to off-peak hours, and greater regional integration of transmission grids. A detailed footnote addresses the current state of US storage, noting that the nation has 22 GW of permitted pumped hydro storage with an additional 50 GW in the permitting pipeline. Although pumped hydro is a net consumer of electricity, it creates economic value because daytime demand can be 1.6 times higher than at night. Additionally, the footnote highlights that pumped hydro has a highly favorable lifecycle energy ratio, storing more than 200 times the energy required to construct it, whereas newer utility-scale battery technologies like lithium-ion and sodium-sulfur only store 2 to 10 times their production energy.

This page serves as a reference list of source materials utilized in J.P. Morgan's annual energy update, categorized into two main subject areas: coal research and Japan’s nuclear energy policy. The coal research bibliography cites studies on the environmental impacts and life-cycle costs of coal power from organizations such as the Union of Concerned Scientists, the Harvard School of Public Health, and the New York Academy of Sciences, alongside media and advocacy reports regarding wind energy growth in China and the global geopolitical impact of fracking. The section on Japan's nuclear energy policy references publications detailing Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s stance on retaining nuclear energy, safety updates at the Fukushima Daiichi plant, utility applications for reactor restarts, solar energy subsidies, and economic analyses of the country's nuclear power options from publishers including Reuters, Bloomberg, the World Nuclear Association, and the Institute of Energy Economics, Japan.

This page defines the scope and data universe analyzed in a research paper on active equity management, focusing on the specific investment styles included and excluded. The text explains that the analysis evaluates over $7 trillion in total assets under management across various equity styles tracked by eVestment as of June 2013.

Exhibit 3 presents a detailed table listing twenty equity investment styles, along with their respective assets under management in millions of dollars and the total number of manager fund vehicles. Major categories featured in this analysis include Global equities, with nearly $1.2 trillion across 490 fund vehicles; Large Cap Value, representing over $1 trillion across 337 vehicles; Large Cap Growth, holding over $744 billion across 290 vehicles; EAFE, with over $675 billion across 260 vehicles; and Emerging Markets, with over $656 billion across 199 vehicles. Smaller categories, such as Mid Cap Core, are also tracked, representing roughly $51 billion across 52 vehicles. 

The author notes that several categories were excluded from the analysis due to overlapping definitions, sample sizes too small for statistical analysis, or negligible asset bases. Specifically, the paper excludes $189 billion in 204 U.S. smid-cap funds that overlap with small- and mid-cap classifications, $38 billion in 29 international large-cap growth funds, $12 billion in 61 U.S. micro-cap funds, and country-specific categories for the United Kingdom and Canada.

This publication from J.P. Morgan focuses on the critical divergence between rising equity valuations and stagnant corporate profits, as well as the distributional impacts of the Federal Reserve’s monetary policies. The author argues that while equity markets have surged, driven by S&P 500 price-to-earnings multiples rising from 14x in December 2012 to 16.5x today, corporate profits have stagnated for nearly a year. This valuation expansion matches pre-crisis levels seen in mid-2007, with other financial metrics also rallying back to pre-crisis levels. 

To assess whether profits can catch up to these elevated multiples, the author points to a chart titled "Rising business surveys point to a rebound in earnings." This chart plots the Purchasing Managers' Manufacturing Index business activity survey on the left axis, scaled from 30 to 65, against year-over-year earnings growth with a four-month lag on the right axis, scaled from negative 50 percent to positive 50 percent, from 1989 through 2013. The close historical correlation between these lines shows that the recent uptick in the PMI survey offers hope for a rebound in corporate profits, supporting a positive 2014 outlook. A second chart, "Investor optimism: P/Es and equity allocations rebound," illustrates a parallel recovery in investor sentiment from 2007 to 2013. It tracks the S&P 500 trailing P/E ratio on the left axis, from 11x to 23x, alongside individual investors’ portfolio allocations to equities on the right axis, from 40 percent to 70 percent, revealing that both metrics have rebounded aggressively since their 2009 lows, with equity allocations climbing back toward 65 percent.

The commentary then shifts to Federal Reserve policy, discussing two internal staff papers suggesting the Fed keep interest rates at zero until 2017 or later, lowering the unemployment threshold for rate hikes from 6.5 percent to 5.5 percent. The author notes that while cheap money supports asset prices, it has created a widening gap between household wealth and actual spending. This disparity is illustrated in a third chart titled "A stock market reflection of the distributional effects of Quantitative Easing." This chart plots equal-weighted performance indices, with a base value of 100 in January 2003, from 2003 to 2013. Following the inception of Quantitative Easing in late 2008, a massive gap emerged between luxury retail stocks, represented by Tiffany, Coach, and LVMH, which soared above 500 by 2013, and middle-market retail stocks, represented by Macy's, Kohl's, and J.C. Penney, which remained stagnant near 200. This divergence underscores the uneven wealth effects generated by the Fed's accommodative policies.

This page of the publication analyzes two main developments: the accelerating unwinding of the European credit bubble through bank deleveraging and the policy outcomes of the recent Chinese plenary session.
