The second chart, "S&P 500 vs. S&P 500 Buyback index," tracks the 100 companies with the highest share buyback ratios. This buyback index similarly outperformed the market, reaching a cumulative return of roughly 110% by late 2013, while the standard S&P 500 remained near 60%.

The second half of the page discusses how activist pressure has altered corporate defense mechanisms, noting a sharp drop in both the use of poison pills and the prevalence of classified boards, which prevent annual director re-elections. However, the author cautions that many companies mitigate these changes through standby poison pill arrangements and lower activation thresholds of 10% rather than the traditional 20%, aiming to deter activist investors. 

These governance shifts are detailed in two charts tracking corporate data from 1998 to 2012. The chart "Companies with a poison pill" illustrates a steep decline in poison pill usage for both large-cap S&P 500 and mid-cap S&P 600 companies, falling from peaks of around 55% in the early 2000s to approximately 10% and 15% respectively by 2012. The final chart, "Companies with classified board of directors," highlights a divergence between large and mid-cap firms. While the percentage of S&P 500 companies with classified boards plummeted from nearly 60% in 2002 to around 15% in 2012, S&P 600 mid-cap companies retained these structures at a much higher rate, declining only moderately from roughly 60% to 50% over the same period.

This page provides commentary on the Russian occupation of Crimea, analyzing the region's demographic ties to Russia and the geopolitical and economic consequences of the conflict. The discussion begins with the historical context of Crimea, noting its high concentration of ethnic Russians and its role as the home of the Russian Black Sea fleet in Sevastopol. 

To illustrate these demographics, the author presents two maps of Ukraine using data from the 2001 census. The first map highlights the distribution of ethnic Ukrainians and Russians, visually showing that Crimea is the only region with an outright ethnic Russian majority, while western and central Ukraine are dominated by Ukrainian speakers. The second map displays the percentage of ethnic Russians by province, showing that Crimea is 58.3% ethnically Russian and the city of Sevastopol is 71.6% ethnically Russian, whereas western regions drop to as low as 1.2% and the city of Kiev sits at 13.1%. 

A supporting table compares the percentage of ethnic Russians against the percentage of active Russian language users across fourteen former Soviet republics. The data reveals that Russian language usage often vastly exceeds ethnic Russian populations; for example, Ukraine has a 17% Russian ethnic population but 61% active language usage, Belarus has an 11% ethnic population with 78% language usage, and Kazakhstan has a 26% ethnic population with 67% language usage. This distinct gap suggests that Crimea's high proportion of actual ethnic Russians makes it a unique case among former Soviet states.

Looking forward, the author notes that while the press has drawn comparisons to Germany’s 1938 annexation of the Sudetenland, Western military intervention in Ukraine is highly unlikely. Instead, the United States is preparing economic sanctions and asset freezes. For global investors, the primary risks include increased pressure on emerging market assets, a rising risk of recession in Russia—where growth was already sluggish at just over 1%—and elevated geopolitical uncertainty for neighboring countries like Turkey. Lastly, the author addresses Europe's energy dependence on Russian natural gas pipelines crossing Ukraine, which limits Western leverage. This vulnerability could ultimately accelerate the sluggish approval process for US liquefied natural gas export projects as a strategic move to reduce Russia’s energy influence over Europe.

In this analysis, the author addresses whether US equity markets are currently too expensive to own, concluding that while they are not yet prohibitively expensive, they are no longer cheap, with large-cap valuations edging toward the higher end of historical mid-cycle ranges and small-caps becoming increasingly expensive. Consequently, future investor returns are expected to depend more heavily on organic earnings growth and the success of active management rather than multiple expansion. Consensus earnings growth expectations for 2014 have already fallen from 11% to around 9%. While recent economic weakness has been attributed to severe winter weather, the author notes that some housing weakness pre-dated the winter storms, meaning it will take several quarters of data to validate how much of the soft data was truly weather-related.

To illustrate these trends, the page features two line charts. The first chart plots the S&P 500 forward price-to-earnings ratio multiple from 1985 through late 2013 on a scale from 6x to 30x. This chart shows that while the multiple peaked near 25x in the late 1990s and fell to nearly 9x during the 2008 financial crisis, it has recently risen back to approximately 15x. A footnote explains that these P/E ratios actually look higher if the technology sector is excluded, as large tech companies are trading at a discount to their historical averages due to structural disruptions like cloud and mobile computing.

The second chart displays small-cap valuations by tracking the forward P/E multiple of the Russell 2000 index from 1986 to late 2013 on a scale from 9x to 24x. It highlights historical valuation spikes in early 2000 and late 2001, which are explained in a footnote as episodes where stock prices ran ahead of fundamentals or staged a post-9/11 relief rally while earnings estimates fell. At the far right of the timeline, the chart plots two scenarios for late 2013: one red dot indicating a multiple of roughly 17x assuming a consensus 20% earnings growth rate, and a higher red dot near 19x assuming a more conservative 10% earnings growth rate. The author argues that because top-line revenue growth is weak and earnings have been artificially supported by low labor, interest, and energy costs, the 10% assumption is more realistic, revealing that small-cap valuations are highly elevated. 

A stylized cartoon in the top right depicts financial markets as race cars taking a pit stop, representing the author's view that after a strong run, markets need a pause to verify the positive economic assumptions currently priced into equities.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market evaluates the structural challenges facing Bitcoin and explores the negative macroeconomic consequences if virtual currencies successfully gain broad adoption. The author outlines three primary challenges: transaction friction, regulatory hurdles, and safety. Under transaction friction, the author questions the long-term sustainability and capitalization of merchant services like Bitpay and Coinbase, which charge a fee to instantly convert Bitcoin to cash. On regulation, the text notes China’s decision to ban financial and payment institutions from utilizing Bitcoin or exchanging it for RMB, warning that other countries may implement similar anti-money laundering and know-your-client procedures. Safety concerns are underscored by the collapse of the Mt. Gox exchange and the theft of 6% of outstanding Bitcoins, which the author attributes to vulnerable digital wallets and clearance delays that expose transactions to fraudulent interference.

The author's primary long-term concern is that Bitcoin or a virtual competitor might actually succeed, shifting economic activity into an untraceable underground shadow economy. This shift would shrink the tax base and disproportionately burden the remaining regulated economy. To support this warning, the page includes a scatter plot titled "Large shadow economies coincide with less wealth," which visualizes the inverse relationship between the size of a nation's underground economy and its overall wealth. The y-axis measures the shadow economy as a percentage of GDP (from 0% to 70%), while the x-axis displays real per capita GDP in thousands of constant dollars (from $0 to $40). Each blue diamond represents a different country, and a red trendline curves downward to illustrate that wealthier nations keep their shadow economies small (generally below 20% of GDP), whereas countries with shadow economies exceeding 40% of GDP suffer from very low per capita wealth. This data is sourced from the October 2009 study "Shadow Economies and Corruption" by Buehn and Schneider for the Conference Board.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest addresses whether emerging market equities have become cheap enough to buy, concluding that they are not yet at capitulation levels and advising investors to slowly average into positions rather than trying to pick the bottom. Although emerging market debtor equities fell approximately 15 percent in US dollar terms since December 2012, their forward price-to-earnings multiples have only declined modestly because corporate earnings expectations have fallen at a similar pace. 

An accompanying chart, titled "EM debtor nations trade at higher multiples than surplus nations," tracks 12-month forward P/E multiples from January 2011 to January 2014. It compares debtor nations—specifically Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey—with the rest of the emerging markets, showing that these debtor nations consistently trade at a premium, ending early 2014 around 11.5x compared to roughly 10.5x for the rest of the emerging market universe. 

To assess potential technical capitulation, a second chart displays "Sectors trading below their 2-year moving averages" as a percentage of 62 MSCI EM sectors from 1997 through early 2014. Currently, only about 55 percent of sectors trade below their average, whereas past periods of true market distress and capitulation bottoms, such as in 1998, 2001, and 2008, historically saw this metric reach 80 to 90 percent. 

A third chart details the "Return on Equity (ROE)" from 2002 to 2014, comparing the S&P 500 against the MSCI Emerging Markets index. While S&P 500 ROE has steadily recovered to around 15 percent by 2014, emerging market ROE has deteriorated, dropping from a peak of nearly 16 percent in 2011 to around 12 percent in 2014. Cembalest highlights that this weaker emerging market trend may not be purely cyclical, pointing to research by Chief Economist Michael Vaknin suggesting the US outsourcing cycle may have reached its limit. 

A final chart illustrates that "EM debtors experience rising rates," plotting the average 1-year and 5-year interest rates for Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey from 2011 to early 2014. Both rates spiked sharply starting in mid-2013, with the average 5-year rate surging from around 7.0 percent to nearly 9.5 percent and the 1-year rate climbing from roughly 6.5 percent to approximately 9.0 percent. This rate surge continues to pressure domestic retail sales, employment, and capital spending. 

While India's current account has improved due to a collapse in gold imports, other debtor nations still have further to adjust. Turkey and Brazil lead in emerging market private sector debt growth since 2008, trailing only China. Cembalest highlights Brazilian oil major Petrobras as particularly vulnerable, noting it requires an estimated 20 billion dollars in annual borrowing to fund its capital expenditure plans. He concludes that economic stabilization for these nations remains at least several months away.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s executive summary, titled "A Quick Snapshot of Infrastructure Investing," provides an overview of infrastructure as an investment asset class, covering its sectors, global transaction values, and regional distributions. The introductory text highlights that institutional interest in infrastructure is driven by diversification, inflation protection, and stable, long-term yields derived from tolling, regulated utility models, and long-term power contracts. While Europe has led in public-private partnerships—with countries like the UK and Portugal financing 20% to 30% of infrastructure this way—the United States has historically relied on municipal bonds, though public-private partnerships are growing from low levels. Global private infrastructure funds invested $30 billion to $40 billion of equity annually from 2010 to 2013, with aggregate deal values recovering to pre-recession levels of $200 billion to $300 billion. Although current pension fund allocations sit at just 1% to 2%, industry surveys and projections by Bain & Co. suggest institutional allocations are poised to rise to 5% or more in the coming years.

The page includes a table titled "Infrastructure Overview" that categorizes the asset class into six major sectors and their corresponding subsectors. Regulated assets include water, wastewater, electricity transmission, and gas/power distribution. Transportation covers toll roads, airports, seaports, rail, and parking. Power generation spans conventional and renewable sources, while midstream covers pipelines, storage, and processing. Communications includes cell towers, cable networks, and satellite systems, and social infrastructure comprises hospitals, schools, and courts or prisons.

Two charts illustrate global investment trends using data from the Preqin Infrastructure Group. The first, "Estimated Aggregate Value of Infrastructure Deals Completed Globally by Private Funds," shows annual deal values in USD billions from 2007 through 2013. Deal activity peaked pre-recession in 2007 at approximately $260 billion, fell to a low of $150 billion in 2009, and steadily recovered to peak at roughly $300 billion in both 2012 and 2013. 

The second chart, "Breakdown of Infrastructure Deals by Region," tracks the percentage share of deals from 2008 to 2013 across Europe, North America, Asia, Australasia, Latin America, and other regions. Europe consistently represents the largest market share, ranging from about 40% to 55% of deals, with its highest share occurring in 2009. North America remains the second-largest region, holding a stable share of approximately 25% to 30% of global transactions. The remaining portion of deal activity is distributed among Asia, Australasia, Latin America, and other minor regions, which collectively make up the rest of the market.

This page analyzes the financial pitfalls of infrastructure investing, specifically focusing on over-optimistic transportation forecasts and the difficulties of estimating what drivers will pay for convenience. The main argument is that forecasting toll road economics has proven highly inaccurate, with actual traffic volumes and revenues consistently falling short of projections. 

The first chart, Exhibit 3, titled "Actual Traffic Volumes as a % of Initial Forecast," illustrates this systematic optimism bias using two probability distribution curves. For countries without prior experience building toll roads, actual traffic volumes peak at just 58% of the initial forecast. While countries with prior toll road experience perform better, their distribution still peaks well below the target, at 81% of the initial forecast. The data is sourced from Robert Bain's 2009 study on error and optimism bias in toll road traffic forecasts.

The second chart, Exhibit 4, shows the performance of U.S. toll roads opened between 1986 and 2004, plotting actual revenue as a percentage of projected operational results over their first five years of operation. Each dot on this scatter plot represents a different project. The majority of projects across all five years cluster far below the 100% dashed threshold, with a significant portion of roads capturing less than 60% of their projected revenue. This chart utilizes 2006 data from the National Cooperative Highway Research Program. Additionally, the text highlights a 2010 study by researchers at the University of Sydney, which found that traffic volumes for 14 Australian toll roads averaged just 55% of the forecasted level during their first year of operation.

At the bottom of the page, a detailed sidebar titled "Estimating the Value of Time (VoT)" explains why these forecasts fail. Traditional macro-level models, which are popular due to their low cost, predict regional-level traffic using demographics and income brackets, but they poorly anticipate the exact price points drivers are willing to pay to save time. Conversely, newer micro-level models analyze the Value of Time (VoT) dynamically, recognizing that VoT varies within income brackets and even on an individual level based on the trip's purpose and time of day. These micro-level frameworks utilize household-level surveys, GPS data, and smartphone activity to generate more accurate, activity-based demand distributions.

This page from the publication focuses on a key risk in infrastructure investing: projects whose success is overly dependent on subsequent, uncompleted development projects. The author warns that when infrastructure relies on the completion of other related public or private assets, any delays or cancellations place the entire investment at risk. 

To illustrate this, the author first presents a case study of the Northwest Parkway in Denver, Colorado. In 2007, local authorities signed a $603 million, 99-year concession agreement for this nine-mile highway. Investors paid a massive valuation multiple of 90 times 2006 revenues, driven by expectations that the remaining part of the beltway would be completed. Under the deal, investors agreed to pay an additional $40 million upon the beltway's completion, plus another $60 million if it was finished by 2020. However, despite political assurances, city council reports indicate the beltway is delayed by financing and design issues, leaving its completion in doubt and current parkway traffic at only 17% of capacity. An accompanying map, Exhibit 6, illustrates the Denver area highway system, highlighting the Northwest Parkway, the E-470 tollway, and the crucial unbuilt portion of the beltway represented by a red dotted line. The takeaway is to discount political assurances regarding factors they cannot control.

The second case study examines the South Bay Expressway in San Diego, California, a 10-mile express toll road built via a public-private partnership to link San Diego to the Mexican border. Completed in 2007 after a 13-month delay, the road failed to meet its projected 2009 traffic volume of 60,000 vehicles per day, instead averaging only 23,000 to 29,000. This underperformance was caused by overly optimistic suburban development projections and competition from existing free-to-use roads. Coupled with a $40 million litigation dispute with contractors, the expressway filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. It was eventually sold, resulting in a 30% loss for lenders and a complete equity write-down. Exhibit 7 displays a regional map of Southern California showing the path of the South Bay Expressway connecting down to the Mexican border. The author summarizes that investors must distinguish between linking already established commercial and residential areas versus relying on speculative future developments on either end of the asset.

This page begins with a final commentary on Puerto Rico's debt, advising investors that if an upcoming March debt offering goes well, it may be a strategic window to reduce exposure to uninsured general obligation and weaker revenue bonds. Two charts illustrate Puerto Rico's underlying economic challenges. The first chart, titled "CPR: labor force decline," indexes nonfarm payroll employees to March 2006 and shows a stark divergence starting around 2006: while the United States eventually recovered back toward its baseline, Puerto Rico's labor force steadily declined to about 85 index points by 2014. The second chart, titled "CPR: debt term structure," displays outstanding debt in billions of USD, revealing a heavily back-loaded maturity profile where the largest chunks of debt mature in 10 to 20 years (around $20 billion) and 20 to 30 years (approximately $23 billion).

The page then transitions to an analysis of Bitcoin, posing the question of whether it serves as a lifeline for the financially oppressed or is hampered by operational challenges. The author references research from J.P. Morgan's Investment Bank suggesting Bitcoin does not currently act as a true store of value because it is illiquid, highly volatile (with historical one-day drops exceeding 30%), and offers no interim yield. However, the author argues that Bitcoin may find a unique constituency among those living under severe capital controls, dual exchange rates, and negative real deposit rates—such as in Venezuela, where real interest rates have been negative for 25 years. 

To quantify this potential market, a table lists "Countries with capital account restrictions" categorized by Menzie and Ito. The "Most restrictive" tier, which includes Venezuela, Ukraine, Angola, and Myanmar, represents 260 million people and over $1.2 trillion in GDP. The "Next 10" tier, containing massive economies like China, India, Thailand, and South Africa, represents over 3.2 billion people and $22 trillion in GDP. Collectively, these restricted countries account for roughly half the world's population and 28% of global GDP. Finally, a dual-axis line chart plots Bitcoin's daily transaction volume against its USD price from June 2012 to December 2013. The chart notes low growth in daily transactions (which fluctuated between 30,000 and 60,000) even as the price of Bitcoin experienced a dramatic, speculative spike from under $100 to over $1,000 by late 2013.

In this analysis of infrastructure investment pitfalls, the author focuses on the case of Panda Energy in Texas to argue that constructing new power plants can be far more expensive than purchasing existing capacity, particularly when investments rely on speculative regulatory changes. In 2010, Panda Energy secured financing to build three natural gas-fired combined-cycle power plants at an estimated cost of $1,000 per kilowatt (kW). This high cost was likely justified internally by forecasts of rising electricity prices or by the assumption that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) would shift from "production pricing" to "capacity pricing," which would have helped reimburse construction costs. However, ERCOT maintained its production pricing system, leaving Panda Energy with a high-cost asset base competing in volatile merchant markets without stabilizing capacity payments, a risk that Standard & Poor's flagged in September 2012.

To illustrate this cost disparity, Exhibit 10 presents a table of select combined-cycle natural gas plant transactions in Texas from 2010 to 2013. The table compares Panda Energy's $1,800 million construction project—which yielded 1,800 megawatts of capacity at $1,000 per kW—with various acquisitions of existing assets. Nearly all contemporary acquisitions of existing capacity were significantly cheaper on a per-kilowatt basis. For example, the April 2010 transaction for the Colorado Bend Energy Center and Quail Run cost only $325 per kW ($365 million for 1,124 megawatts), while the October 2010 Oyster Creek Unit VIII transaction cost just $233 per kW ($100 million for 430 megawatts). Even the costliest acquisitions of existing capacity listed, such as the Freestone Energy Center in late 2010 at $836 per kW and Gregory Power in April 2013 at $565 per kW, remained below Panda Energy's new-build cost. 

Ultimately, the author warns that assuming Texas regulatory frameworks will shift to match the rest of the United States is a dangerous gamble. A footnote adds that because ERCOT has signaled a comfortable margin of power supply for the coming years, the likelihood of Texas transitioning to a capacity pricing model in the near term has decreased further.

This page, from a report analyzing infrastructure investing pitfalls, focuses on how excessive financial engineering and high leverage can undermine projects that otherwise perform well operationally. It presents two case studies to illustrate this point. 

The first case study examines the Indiana Toll Road, which was awarded as a 75-year concession in 2006. While the project’s revenues and operating cash flows grew steadily and met expectations, its financing structure proved disastrous. The project utilized a nine-year interest-only bullet loan paired with a 20-year accreting interest rate swap. As interest rates declined, the swap generated significant mark-to-market losses, nearly doubling the total project debt from $3.4 billion at acquisition to $6.0 billion by 2011 and preventing a planned early refinancing. 

This operational success versus financial struggle is shown in two charts. Exhibit 13, a bar and line chart titled "Indiana Toll Road Annual Revenue," shows that total revenues rose from approximately $145 million in 2007 to around $195 million in 2012, while EBITDA grew in tandem. The EBITDA margin, plotted as an orange line, steadily improved from roughly 73% in 2007 to over 81% by 2012. In contrast, Exhibit 14, titled "Indiana Toll Road Annual Debt Metrics," highlights the negative impact of the accreting swap. It shows that while long-term debt remained relatively flat at around $3.5 to $3.8 billion from 2006 to 2011, the swap liability surged to over $2 billion by 2011, bringing total debt close to $6 billion. Consequently, the debt-to-cash-flow multiple remained highly elevated, ending at 40x in 2011 instead of dropping to a projected, more manageable 20x.

The second case study looks at a diversified global marine and rail terminal operating company where a manager acquired a 49% stake in 210 terminal facilities worldwide. Bought at a high valuation of 20x cash flow with debt at 13x cash flow, the deal relied on the premise of global revenue diversification. However, a 7% annual revenue decline from 2006 to 2012 triggered financing covenants that increased interest coupons as debt-to-cash-flow multiples rose, raising borrowing costs at the worst possible time. The project was eventually refinanced under new ownership with less leverage and more equity. 

This shift toward more conservative financing is detailed in Exhibit 15, a table comparing financing approaches in 2007 versus 2014. It shows that loan-to-value ratios decreased from 65%–75% in 2007 to 55%–60% in 2014, while required equity increased from 25%–35% to 40%–45%. The cost of financing shifted from Libor plus 130 basis points with step-ups based on EBITDA multiples to a flat Libor plus 220–250 basis points. Finally, the minimum debt coverage ratio before default was tightened significantly from 1.0x–1.1x in 2007 to 1.4x in 2014. The author concludes that while geographic diversification is valuable, globalization has increased the correlation of growth patterns across countries, meaning that highly leveraged global infrastructure portfolios must be managed with caution.

This page presents an appendix on infrastructure performance based on a study from the Center for Private Equity Research, which analyzed returns and risks of specific private equity infrastructure transactions between 1971 and 2009. The study reveals that infrastructure investment returns significantly exceeded those of venture capital and private equity in similar vintage years, though dispersion across these investments was exceptionally high. The text notes that the study is heavily weighted toward U.S. and European telecommunication privatizations of the late 1990s, suggesting that past success may not predict future privatization outcomes. Sector-wise, telecommunications accounted for 59% of deals, followed by natural resources and energy at 25%, transportation at 13%, and alternative energy at 3%. Geographically, the transactions were concentrated in North America and Europe, each representing 43% of the sample, with Asia at 8% and the rest of the world at 6%.

A bar chart, Exhibit A2.1, illustrates the distribution of these infrastructure deals by year from 1971 to 2007. The chart shows that deal activity was minimal prior to the late 1980s, after which it began rising steadily, peaking around 1998 and 2001, where annual deal percentages reached approximately 12% to 13% before tapering off.

Exhibit A2.2 is a performance comparison table covering 1971 to 2007, categorizing investments into infrastructure, non-infrastructure, greenfield infrastructure, venture capital, brownfield infrastructure, and late-stage private equity. The table compares internal rates of return (IRR) and investment multiples. For overall infrastructure, the average IRR was 67% with a 19% median and a standard deviation of 300%, compared to non-infrastructure's average IRR of 20%, median IRR of 6%, and standard deviation of 197%. On a multiple basis, infrastructure achieved an average of 2.7x and a median of 1.7x, compared to 2.5x and 1.1x for non-infrastructure. When comparing early-stage greenfield infrastructure to venture capital, greenfield infrastructure registered an average IRR of 46% and a median IRR of 5%, whereas venture capital posted an average IRR of 6% and a median IRR of negative 22%. For brownfield infrastructure versus late-stage private equity, brownfield infrastructure saw an average IRR of 91% and a median IRR of 36%, outperforming late-stage private equity's average IRR of 40% and median IRR of 25%.

The key findings highlight that infrastructure investments consistently outperformed their private market counterparts. Despite high performance, the large gap between the median and average multiples indicates a significant skew from a few highly successful outlier projects. Furthermore, the risk of complete capital loss was lower for infrastructure, with brownfield infrastructure experiencing a 5.26% write-off rate compared to 9% for late-stage private equity. Lastly, European infrastructure investments outperformed other regions, which the study’s authors attribute to governments not prioritizing maximum sales prices and the subsequent ability of private owners to extract value by reducing operational inefficiencies.

This page focuses on the role, operational dynamics, and investment implications of natural gas peaker plants compared to baseload energy sources, utilizing a regional dispatch curve framework. The author argues that natural gas peaking facilities are unique investment assets because they only operate when baseload power sources cannot meet cresting demand. While peaker plants command high compensation rates during these critical windows, their overall revenue relies on highly variable capacity utilization, introducing substantial operating risk and requiring disciplined asset pricing.

Two charts illustrate these operational dynamics. The first, Exhibit A3.1, displays the monthly capacity factors by energy source as a percentage from January 2011 to July 2013. Nuclear power consistently occupies the highest tier, maintaining a capacity factor of approximately 80% to 90%. Geothermal follows at around 70%, while coal and combined-cycle natural gas fluctuate seasonally between roughly 40% and 70%. Wind and hydro hover lower in the 20% to 50% range. In stark contrast, natural gas peakers reside at the bottom of the chart, barely exceeding 0% capacity factor in the winter and spring, and spiking to only about 10% to 15% during peak summer demand.

The second chart, Exhibit A3.2, displays a hypothetical dispatch curve for the United States, showcasing variable operating costs on the vertical axis, from $0 to over $300 per megawatt-hour, plotted against capacity available to meet electricity demand, from 0 to 120 gigawatts. This curve depicts how energy assets are brought online sequentially based on their marginal operating costs. Extremely cheap baseload sources—such as renewables, nuclear, hydro, and coal—are utilized first to meet typical early-morning demand of around 65 gigawatts. As demand surges toward a peak of 115 gigawatts, grid operators must call on increasingly expensive single-cycle natural gas, petroleum, and finally natural gas peakers. At this peak point, variable operating costs skyrocket from under $50 per megawatt-hour for combined-cycle gas to between $150 and over $250 per megawatt-hour for peaking units.

The accompanying text explains how grid operators balance supply and demand to prevent localized brownouts or equipment damage from oversupply, citing an example where Czech grid operators had to take defensive actions to block wind-powered electricity surges originating in Germany. The author outlines how electricity providers are compensated at a single marginal market rate determined by the last and most expensive megawatt-hour of capacity brought online. Additionally, the text clarifies the technical distinctions among natural gas generation technologies, categorizing them into highly efficient baseload combined-cycle plants, less efficient single-cycle plants, and low-efficiency but rapid-starting combustion turbines used specifically as peakers. It concludes with a discussion of wind and solar as price-taking resources that can sometimes create oversupply, occasionally forcing grid operators to curtail renewable energy output to keep the grid stable.

This page, titled Infrastructure Pitfalls, Past and Present, focuses on Pitfall Number Five: Overly optimistic renewable energy projections, using wind power as a primary example. The author, Michael Cembalest, outlines how wind farm economics are shaped by a complex web of variables, including government subsidies, local mandate requirements, raw material costs like neodymium, technological degradation, curtailment, and wind speed variability. He warns that while wind power has significant positive momentum—making up 40 percent of all United States capacity additions in 2012—and is increasingly cost-competitive with natural gas, localized projects frequently underperform the highly optimistic projections originally laid out by consultants to investors and utilities.

To illustrate this gap, Exhibit 16 details projected versus actual capacity factors, measured as actual generation as a percentage of potential nameplate capacity, across two specific regional locations using data as of year-end 2013 from the EIA, American Municipal Power, and the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority. At the Blue Creek Wind project in Ohio, the projected capacity factor was 34.7 percent, but the actual capacity factors fell to 29.8 percent in 2013 and 26.7 percent in 2012. Similarly, for New York Wind Class 3 to 4, the projected capacity factor was modeled between 29 percent and 31 percent, whereas actual performance was lower, ranging between 25 percent and 27 percent.

On a broader scale, Exhibit 17 displays the distribution of wind capacity factors by year of installation using data from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the U.S. Department of Energy. The chart plots individual wind projects against their power generation-weighted average across ten vintage periods from 1998 through 2011. While the total capacity grew from 776 megawatts across 23 projects in the 1998 to 1999 period to a peak of 9,561 megawatts across 95 projects in 2009, the weighted average capacity factor remained fairly stable, hovering between roughly 28 percent and 34 percent. However, individual project performance varies wildly, with some installations achieving capacity factors near 50 percent while others in the same vintage years fell below 10 percent to 15 percent, emphasizing that national averages mask significant asset-level risks.

The page concludes with additional context on wind performance dynamics. While General Electric is developing new turbine technology designed to deliver capacity factors up to 50 percent, and Danish offshore wind farms frequently post capacity factors in the mid-40s, many newer wind farms are being built in less optimal wind locations, offsetting these technological improvements. Furthermore, because wind power is a function of wind velocity cubed, a minor 10 percent reduction in wind speed results in a roughly 30 percent reduction in power generation, a physical reality that contributed to low 2.5 percent annualized returns across 1,150 German wind farm investments examined in a study cited by Der Spiegel.

This page analyzes the risks associated with accreting swaps in infrastructure projects, specifically focusing on how they can negatively impact a project's refinancing prospects if interest rates fall. The author explains that infrastructure projects are typically funded with floating-rate bank loans, but owners often use accreting interest rate swaps—which start with low fixed rates and rise over time to match growing cash flows—to secure fixed payments. However, because a swap's mark-to-market loss adds to the project's total debt, a drop in interest rates can jeopardize refinancing even if the project's actual cash flows remain stable or improve.

To illustrate this, the page features a model simulation displayed in Exhibit A4.1, which calculates the time-weighted net present value gain or loss on a two billion dollar investment across various combinations of changing interest rates and cash flow growth. The horizontal axis represents changes in the long-term interest rate swap curve ranging from negative two point five percent to positive two point five percent, while the vertical axis represents annual cash flow growth versus original underwriting ranging from negative five percent to positive five percent. 

Three specific scenarios are highlighted within this matrix. Scenario one shows that with no change in cash flow growth and a negative one percent shift in interest rates, the project suffers a loss of three hundred twenty-eight million dollars due to swap mark-to-market losses. Scenario two displays a situation where cash flow growth actually improves by one percent, but a negative one point five percent shift in interest rates still results in a net loss of fifty-five million dollars. Scenario three depicts the worst-case outcome, where a negative three percent underperformance in cash flow combined with a negative one percent interest rate shift leads to a major loss of one billion five hundred seven million dollars. 

Below the matrix, the page lists the model's simulation assumptions. The hypothetical deal size is ten thousand with eighty percent leverage, resulting in eight thousand in debt and two thousand in equity. The model assumes a purchase multiple of free cash flow of twenty, a required internal rate of return of twelve percent, and an implied annual cash flow growth of four point zero nine percent. The bank loan features a credit spread of one percent with a nine-year term, with refinancing and valuation occurring in year eight. An accompanying table tracks the swap coupon percentage over a twenty-year horizon, showing how it rises from three point thirteen percent in years one through four, to four point nine zero percent in year ten, and eventually reaches eleven point twenty-nine percent in years eighteen through twenty.

This page analyzes historical bank and financial crises to argue that waiting for bank failures to subside before reinvesting in equities is a mistake, as stock markets consistently bottom out long before the banking industry's failures peak. To demonstrate this pattern, the author examines data from the Great Depression, the Savings and Loan Crisis, and the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, showing that cumulative bank failures are a lagging indicator.

The first chart, comparing equity markets to bank failures during the Great Depression from January 1929 to December 1933, plots the Dow Jones Industrial Average against cumulative bank failures. While the index fell from nearly 400 to its bottom in mid-1932, cumulative bank failures had only reached 48 percent of their eventual peak of roughly 9,000 institutions, showing that equities recovered well before the bank failure cycle ended. 

The second chart focuses on the Savings and Loan Crisis from March 1988 to October 1994, plotting the S&P 500 Bank Index against cumulative bank failures. When bank stocks bottomed in late 1990, cumulative bank failures had reached only 63 percent of their ultimate total of approximately 1,600 institutions. 

The third chart illustrates the 2008 financial crisis from January 2008 to January 2014, showing the S&P 500 Bank Index and cumulative bank failures. During this period, the disconnect was even more extreme: when bank stocks and equities bottomed in March 2009, only 8 percent of the banks that would eventually fail had actually done so out of an eventual total of around 500 institutions. 

The author concludes that rather than watching bank defaults, investors should focus on policy actions that restore confidence. During the 2008 crisis, the Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests, required by the US Treasury and announced in May 2009, as well as the Federal Reserve's expansion of its discount window operations, served as far better indicators for the market's recovery.

This page discusses the recovery of European equity markets following the Eurozone crisis, arguing that the durable portion of the recovery was tightly linked to the European Central Bank’s implicit guarantee and a turn in leading indicators rather than absolute levels of economic strength. The author notes that contrarian investors often find opportunities when markets begin to get "less bad," even if indicators like the Manufacturing PMI remain in contractionary territory below 50.

The first chart, titled "Equity recovery more closely aligned with ECB...", compares the STOXX European Broad equity index (ranging from 225 to 350 on the left axis) to the Spanish and Italian 5-year Credit Default Swap (CDS) spreads in basis points (ranging from 0 to 600 on the right axis) from 2010 to 2014. The chart highlights how Mario Draghi's "whatever it takes" speech in the summer of 2012 marked a major turning point, where soaring sovereign CDS spreads peaked above 500 basis points and subsequently collapsed, coinciding with a sustained rally in the STOXX equity index.

The second chart, "...and the turn in leading indicators," covers 2010 to 2013 and tracks the STOXX European Broad equity index against the Manufacturing PMI index level (ranging from 44 to 60 on the right axis). It shows that the bottoming of the equity index in late 2011 closely mirrored the bottoming of the PMI at around 44, demonstrating that the turn in PMI momentum was a more critical signal for equity investors than the index rising back above the expansionary threshold of 50.

To illustrate valuation opportunities at the market bottom, the page includes a table titled "Trailing price-to-earnings ratios across countries and sectors in September 2011." This table highlights extreme value dispersions that were masked by the overall European market average P/E of approximately 11 times trailing earnings. The data shows single-digit valuations across several key sectors and countries: German Consumer Discretionary at 5.9x, French Financials at 5.2x, Italian Industrials at 9.6x, and Spanish Industrials at 5.6x. In contrast, defensive sectors like Consumer Staples traded at higher multiples, such as 21.5x in France and 38.3x in Spain. 

The author concludes that when substantial subsets of the market trade at single-digit P/Es, markets have already priced in a vast amount of bad news. This historical pattern shows that equity recoveries often take place well in advance of what the financial press or consensus research views as necessary prerequisites before reinvesting.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, titled "The PMI survey in Europe," argues that the Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is highly effective at marking equity market bottoms in Europe, mirroring its utility in the United States. The author asserts that while the signal is not perfect, it consistently provides a reliable cue for investors to take on risk before actual economic conditions visibly improve. 

To support this observation, the page displays four charts comparing the STOXX European Broad equity index against the Manufacturing PMI across different historical crisis periods. The first chart, covering the Asia, Russia, and LTCM Crisis from December 1997 to June 2000, shows the Manufacturing PMI bottoming near a level of 48 in late 1998, which closely coincided with the trough in the STOXX European Broad equity index around 245, after which both indices experienced a robust recovery. 

The second chart focuses on the Tech Collapse from 2000 to 2006. It demonstrates that the Manufacturing PMI bottomed near 46 in late 2001, providing an early signal before the STOXX European Broad equity index finally established its ultimate bottom near 170 in early 2003. 

The third chart depicts the Global Financial Crisis from 2006 to 2009. During this severe downturn, both metrics collapsed in tandem, with the Manufacturing PMI bottoming at a low of approximately 35 in early 2009, aligning almost perfectly with the equity index's low point near 170, after which a sharp rebound commenced. 

The fourth chart illustrates the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis from 2010 to 2013. It shows that both indices reached a low point around mid-2012, with the Manufacturing PMI bottoming near 44 and the STOXX European Broad equity index bottoming near 230, marking the beginning of a sustained upward trajectory. 

Collectively, these charts, utilizing data from STOXX and PB Economics, demonstrate that the European Manufacturing PMI serves as an invaluable leading indicator for identifying key market turning points in European equities during major macroeconomic shocks.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes historical patterns in credit markets to show that bottom-feeding credit investors can successfully time the market using manufacturing activity and by ignoring trailing default headlines. The central argument is twofold: first, the bottom in credit (meaning the peak in credit spreads) aligns almost exactly with turning points in the Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI); second, high-yield credit spreads peak and begin to recover well before corporate defaults reach their cycle peak. 

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, titled "Peak credit spreads coincide with bottom in PMI," plots high-yield credit spreads (spread-to-worst) alongside the Manufacturing PMI index level against the number of months from the cyclical trough in PMI, using data from the 1991, 2001, and 2008 cycles. It demonstrates that the peak in high-yield credit spreads occurs almost precisely at month zero, matching the exact bottom of the PMI cycle. 

The remaining three charts illustrate the relationship between high-yield credit spreads and cumulative defaults (measured by the number of defaulting issuers) across three major economic crises. The "Savings and Loan Crisis" chart (covering 1987 to 1993) shows that high-yield spreads peaked when cumulative defaults were at only 55% of their eventual total. The "Tech collapse" chart (covering 1999 to 2004) shows that spreads peaked when cumulative defaults had reached 76% of their total. Finally, the "Financial crisis" chart (covering 2006 to 2013) highlights that only 30% of eventual defaults had occurred by the time high-yield spreads peaked in late 2008. Consequently, a diversified high-yield portfolio initiated in 2009 would have generated strong returns from tightening spreads, even as default news continued to dominate the headlines.

This page demonstrates how an upturn in the Institute for Supply Management Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index serves as a highly reliable buy signal for investors trying to time the bottom of major US equity market downturns since the end of the Gold Standard. 

To support this argument, the page features four historical charts plotting the S&P 500 index level on the left axis against the Manufacturing PMI index level on the right axis. The first chart, covering the 1970s stagflation crisis from 1973 to 1978, shows the S&P 500 bottoming near an index level of 70 and recovering to over 100, closely matching the trajectory of the Manufacturing PMI, which hit a low near 35 in early 1975 before rising back to 65. The second chart, analyzing the 1980s inflation and housing crisis from 1981 to 1984, illustrates the S&P 500 bottoming around 110 and climbing past 160, corresponding with a rebound in the PMI from its low of 35 to over 70. The third chart shows the tech collapse era from 1999 to 2006, where the S&P 500 fell from 1,500 to a low around 800; here, the PMI turned upward from a bottom of 40 in late 2001, providing an early signal before the equity market fully stabilized. The fourth chart displays the Global Financial Crisis from 2007 to 2013, showing that the S&P 500 bottomed near 700 in early 2009, aligning precisely with the PMI's recovery from its low of roughly 33 back up to 55, while the stock market subsequently rallied past 1,600. 

An explanatory text box at the bottom summarizes the structure of the PMI. It explains that the Purchasing Managers' Index provides a monthly snapshot of business activity compiled by Markit Group and the ISM, with the ISM being favored for US historical analysis due to its data stretching back to 1948. The ISM index is a diffusion index based on surveys sent to roughly 400 companies across 20 industries, weighted by each industry's share of US GDP. A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 represents contraction. The final headline PMI is a weighted average of five primary components: employment, new orders, inventories, production, and business activity.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market is an appendix focusing on the lagging nature of unemployment as a stock market indicator. The primary thesis is that by the time a convincing and durable decline in the unemployment rate is underway, equity markets have typically bottomed out about a year earlier. 

To support this claim, the page presents four dual-axis charts comparing the S&P 500 index level, represented as a 30-day moving average on the left axis, with the U.S. unemployment rate on the right axis across major economic downturns. In each chart, a brown circular marker identifies the market bottom on the S&P 500 curve to visually demonstrate how far it precedes the peak in unemployment.

The first chart illustrates the 1970s stagflation crisis from 1973 to 1978. It shows the S&P 500 bottoming in late 1974 at around 70, while the unemployment rate did not peak until mid-1975 at 9.0%. 

The second chart covers the 1980s inflation and housing crisis from 1981 to 1984. During this period, the S&P 500 bottomed in mid-1982 near 105, whereas the unemployment rate continued to rise, peaking at nearly 11.0% in late 1982 and early 1983 before starting its downward trend. 

The third chart displays the tech collapse from 1999 to 2006. Here, the S&P 500 hit its low point in late 2002 near 800, while the unemployment rate lagged, peaking at 6.3% in mid-2003. 

The final chart examines the Global Financial Crisis from 2007 to 2013. The S&P 500 bottomed in early 2009 near 700, yet the unemployment rate did not peak until late 2009 when it reached 10.0%. 

Across all four historical crises, the data consistently demonstrates that waiting for a recovery in the labor market before investing in equities would have caused an investor to miss the market bottom by several months to a year.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" uses the historical economic case study of Brazil from 1997 through 2000 to argue that a currency devaluation can act as an immediate, leading catalyst for an equity market recovery. The author notes that waiting for fundamental economic indicators like industrial production or exports to improve, or waiting for inflation to peak and decline post-devaluation, would have caused investors to miss the vast majority of the equity market rally. To illustrate this, the page features four charts that compare the Bovespa equity index level, shown on the left axis ranging from 6,000 to 18,000, against various macroeconomic variables on the right axis over the four-year period. 

The first chart, titled "Bovespa rise coincided with the Real devaluation...", plots the equity index against the exchange rate in Brazilian Real per USD, ranging from 1.00 to 2.00. It shows that the sharp devaluation of the Real in early 1999, where the exchange rate surged from roughly 1.20 to nearly 2.00 BRL per USD, directly coincided with the bottoming of the Bovespa index around the 6,000 to 8,000 level and its immediate, rapid rise. 

The second chart, "...preceded the rise in IP", overlays the Bovespa index with an index of Brazilian industrial production, where 2002 equals 100, on a scale of 84 to 104. This visual demonstrates that while the equity market rallied immediately in early 1999, industrial production continued to languish, only beginning a sustained recovery from its low of approximately 88 in late 1999 and into 2000. 

The third chart, "...and the export recovery by a year", compares the Bovespa index to nominal exports measured in billions of USD on a three-month moving average, scaled from $3.7 billion to $4.9 billion. This chart shows that nominal exports bottomed near $3.8 billion in early 1999 and did not embark on a sustained recovery until late 1999, meaning the equity market's rebound preceded the export recovery by nearly a full year. 

The fourth chart, "...and the downturn in inflation by 1.5 years", displays the equity index alongside year-over-year inflation, scaled from 0% to 10%. Following the devaluation, inflation rose steadily from under 2% in late 1998 to a peak near 9% in late 1999. Inflation did not begin to head downward until mid-2000, meaning that waiting for inflation to subside would have caused an investor to miss about a year and a half of the equity market's powerful upward trajectory. Data sources for these charts include the Financial Times, Banco Central do Brasil, IBGE, and the IMF.

This page analyzes United States public finance by evaluating state-level debt service ratios adjusted for Annual Required Contributions (ARC) for pensions and Other Post-Employment Benefits (OPEB). The analysis shows how accounting for actuarial assumptions rather than just actual current payments significantly alters the fiscal picture for several states, most notably New Jersey, which historically has made actual contributions far below its actuarial requirements. 

The first stacked bar chart, titled "Using the state's own assumptions for accruals," displays the percentage of state revenue collections required to pay interest on bonded debt alongside the state share of defined benefit plan contributions, retiree health care costs, and defined contribution plan expenses. It contrasts current payments in blue with the additional burden required under state actuarial assumptions for accruals in tan. While most states remain well below the green 15% warning threshold, a handful of states on the left side of the chart experience large increases. New Jersey's total burden rises from an active payment level of roughly 11% to over 30% under actuarial assumptions, crossing the red 25% threshold. Other states with total obligations exceeding the 15% mark include Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, West Virginia, Kentucky, and Delaware. 

The second stacked bar chart uses the same axis and 2012 data to break down these ARC-based debt service ratios into four specific cost components: interest on bonds in orange, pension contributions in blue, OPEB contributions in pink, and defined contribution plan expenses in black. This chart illustrates that the composition of the debt burden varies widely by state. For example, Hawaii and Delaware have a much larger share of their burden coming from OPEB than from pensions, whereas Illinois's burden is overwhelmingly dominated by pension contributions. In Connecticut, New Jersey, and West Virginia, the burden is split roughly equally between pensions and OPEB. The author notes that these distinctions are critical for future cost-mitigation strategies, as states have historically been more successful at restructuring OPEB liabilities than defined benefit pensions.

This page analyzes the economic ties between Europe and Russia compared to those between the United States and Russia, particularly in the context of geopolitical sanctions and natural gas dependence. The author argues that European-Russian economic relationships are roughly ten times larger than US-Russian ties, which complicates the debate over imposing severe sanctions. 

To support this claim, a bar chart titled "Russia-EU ties are 10x Russia-US ties" measures exports and imports with trading partners as a percentage of GDP. The chart shows that the importance of Russia as a trading partner to the European Union stands at 2.2 percent of GDP, compared to a negligible 0.2 percent for the United States. Looking from the Russian perspective, the European Union is a vital trading partner representing 18.7 percent of Russian GDP, whereas the United States represents just 1.6 percent of Russian GDP. The text highlights that Europe accounts for 80 percent of cumulative foreign investment in Russia, and energy-related products make up 65 percent of European imports from Russia. This deep integration is underscored by corporate exposure, such as BP warning British officials about the threat sanctions pose to its 20 percent stake in Rosneft. In contrast, US-Russia trade is minor, with Russia ranking as only the 22nd largest trading partner to the United States.

The analysis also addresses European reliance on Russian natural gas and whether US liquefied natural gas exports could offset this dependency. A table titled "Russia's share of natural gas imports across Europe" shows the percentage of total natural gas imports sourced from Russia by country. Exposure is highly concentrated in Eastern and Central Europe: Finland depends on Russia for 100 percent of its gas imports, followed by Slovakia at 93 percent, Poland at 82 percent, Hungary at 81 percent, Greece at 78 percent, the Czech Republic at 66 percent, Austria at 62 percent, and Turkey at 57 percent. Major Western European economies have lower but still significant dependencies, including Germany at 35 percent, Belgium at 24 percent, Italy at 20 percent, France at 16 percent, and the Netherlands at 14 percent. This exposure could be further compounded by Gazprom co-investing in Algerian gas projects, given that Algeria is Europe's third-largest gas supplier.

The author cautions that relying on US LNG to solve this dependency is unrealistic. Although the United States produces 723 billion cubic meters of natural gas per year—far exceeding the 130 billion cubic meters Europe imports from Russia—the infrastructure to export it is lagging. The first US export facilities are not scheduled for completion until 2015 and 2018, and Europe lacks the necessary import capacity. Furthermore, the private sector will ultimately direct US LNG to the highest bidders, meaning buyers in Japan, South Korea, and India could easily outbid Europe. Finally, the author notes that Russia’s geographic proximity and massive natural gas reserves allow it to consistently undercut US pricing, raising open questions about how much premium Europe would be willing to pay for more reliable American energy.

This page addresses the cheapness of Russian and Emerging Markets (EM) equities in early 2014. The author highlights that Russia is the least expensive of the major EM equity markets. Without normalizing for Russia's heavy oil-sector concentration, its forward price-to-earnings ratio is an exceptionally low 4.5x. Even on a sector-neutral basis, Russia trades at a significant discount. The author notes that while this extreme cheapness kept Russian equities on pace with broader EM markets throughout 2013, the worsening Ukraine crisis in early 2014 drove a sharp underperformance. Broadly speaking, EM equities as a whole continue to see their discount to developed markets widen because they lack an earnings catalyst, in contrast to the United States where forward earnings expectations continue to trend upward. 

Six charts support these observations. The first chart, "Russia trading at a discount to other EM countries," plots 12-month forward, sector-neutral P/E multiples from 2006 to 2014. It features curves for Taiwan, South Africa, Brazil, Korea, China, and Russia, demonstrating that Russia has consistently sat at the bottom of the valuation range, with its forward P/E hovering near 5x in 2014 compared to Taiwan and South Africa, which trade above 13x. The second chart, "Russian equities underperforming EM since February," indexes total returns starting in January 2013 at 100. The chart tracks MSCI Emerging Markets and MSCI Russia, illustrating that the two moved in tandem until early 2014, when the Russian index plummeted to nearly 75 by April, while the broader EM index remained around 90. 

The next two charts compare EM valuations to the US, Europe, and World indexes from 2008 to 2014. The "EM equities vs. the rest: price-to-book" chart shows EM trading at the lowest price-to-book multiple of approximately 1.4x in 2014, while Europe is at 1.7x, the World is at 2.0x, and the US is at nearly 2.6x. The "EM equities vs. the rest: price-to-earnings" chart shows a similar dynamic for sector-neutral forward P/Es, with EM cheapest at roughly 10x, followed by Europe at 12.5x, the World at 14x, and the US at 15x. 

The relationship between these valuations is further detailed in the chart "EM discount to the developed world," which measures the ratio of EM price-to-book to Developed World price-to-book from 2004 to 2014. This chart shows EM moving from a valuation premium of nearly 18% in late 2009 to a historical discount exceeding -30% by early 2014. Finally, the chart "No sign of an earnings catalyst for EM" tracks forward 12-month earnings per share from 2003 to 2014 for the S&P 500 and the MSCI Emerging Markets index. It shows that while S&P 500 forward EPS recovered sharply after the Great Recession to surpass $110, MSCI EM forward EPS has plateaued and stagnated since 2011, explaining why lower share prices have been required to attract investment back to EM equities.

This page of the publication explores the correlation between a state's debt service ratio and its level of responsibility for public pension contributions, particularly those of local schoolteachers. The author argues that states with lower debt ratios typically delegate pension funding responsibility to local entities, whereas states with high debt ratios shoulder a disproportionate share of local pension costs themselves.

To illustrate this, the first table categorizes states by their share of the aggregate state-run pension plan Annual Required Contributions (ARCs) in 2012. States are grouped into four categories representing their share of the contribution burden. States like Florida, Ohio, and Oregon fall into the 0% to 25% category, meaning local entities handle most of the pension funding burden. Conversely, states like Connecticut, Illinois, and Maryland fall into the 75% to 100% category, meaning the state government bears almost all of the pension obligation.

The second table zooms in on the ten states with the highest debt service ratios to analyze their specific teacher pension plan dynamics. For these states, the table lists the percentage of the state's total pension ARC devoted to the state-run teacher plan and the state's share of responsibility for those contributions. It shows that for almost all of these highly indebted states, the state bears 100% of the responsibility for employer contributions to the teacher plan. This includes New Jersey, where 60% of the pension ARC is devoted to the teacher plan; Illinois, at 52%; West Virginia, at 74%; Maryland, at 63%; and Massachusetts, at 60%. Hawaii and Delaware are noted as having no distinct teacher pension plans. Louisiana is a notable exception among this highly indebted group, with only 6% of its pension ARC devoted to the teacher plan and just 4% state responsibility. The author notes that even when cities make offsetting payments to the state, conversations with Moody's suggest these payments do not significantly reduce the state's ultimate net obligations.

This page examines the cumulative impact on US state budgets if they were to adopt level pension payments over a 30-year term paired with a more conservative 6% pension investment return assumption. The author argues that while the incremental change from adjusting the return assumption to 6% is modest, the overall impact compared to what states currently pay is massive and would be acutely felt by highly indebted states. 

The top chart illustrates the share of state revenue collections required to service interest on bonded debt, defined benefit plan contributions, retiree health care costs, and defined contribution plan expenses. The horizontal axis lists individual US states from the highest burden to the lowest, starting on the left with Illinois, Connecticut, Hawaii, New Jersey, and Kentucky, while the vertical axis spans 0% to 50% of state revenue. Two horizontal benchmark lines are highlighted: a green line at 15% and a red line at 25%. This chart breaks down the total projected burden into two components: the blue bars represent the baseline level payment of unfunded liabilities over 30 years, and the gold bars show the incremental addition of transitioning to a 6% pension investment return. For the most stressed states, such as Illinois and Connecticut, the total combined projection approaches 40% of state revenues.

The bottom chart utilizes the same axes and state ordering but compares actual current payments, represented by the blue bars, against the total required funding under the 30-year level payment and 6% return model, with the gold bars representing the gap. This visualization highlights a massive deficit in current funding levels. For the five most stressed states on the far left of the chart, the current actual payments sit well below the projected requirements, demonstrating that fully funding these obligations would result in an acute fiscal shock, pushing several states well past the 25% red benchmark line and into the 30% to 40% range. 

The accompanying text clarifies that other post-employment benefits, or OPEB, discount rate assumptions have not been revised in these charts. Because most states do not substantially prefund OPEB liabilities, they already utilize much lower discount rates to value them, with a national median rate of 4.5% and only five states using OPEB discount rates exceeding 6%. Consequently, OPEB liabilities and their annual required contribution payments remain unchanged in the displayed models. Data for both charts is sourced from J.P. Morgan Asset Management, state and pension plan Comprehensive Annual Financial Reports, BEA, Pew Research, Moody's, the Census, Merritt, and Loop Capital Markets, with all data reflecting the year 2012.

This appendix page details J.P. Morgan's methodology for calculating the "net tax-supported debt" of U.S. states at the end of 2012, which is used in the numerator of the Debt Service Ratio (DSR) formula. The DSR formula is depicted in a diagram as the sum of interest, principal, other, and debt terms, divided by revenue. Because the ratio's denominator accounts for state tax and general revenue collections, the numerator only includes bonds whose repayment originates from those same sources. 

A table sourced from Moody's outlines the specific types of included and excluded debt. Included categories feature general obligation debt paid from statewide taxes and fees, appropriation-backed bonds, lease revenue bonds, special tax bonds, highway bonds secured by gas taxes and DMV fees, GARVEE highway bonds, lottery bonds, moral obligation debt paid from statewide taxes and fees, capital leases, public-private partnerships with state concession obligations, and pension obligation bonds. Excluded categories consist of self-supporting general obligation debt and moral obligation debt with a history of being paid from non-tax or non-general revenues, tobacco securitization bonds without state backup, unemployment insurance obligation bonds, debt guaranteed but not paid by the state, special assessment bonds, and state enterprise revenue bonds such as those for toll roads. 

The author also notes that if large negative general fund balances were counted as additional bonded debt, the debt service ratios for states with substantial deficits, specifically California, West Virginia, and Illinois, would rise by one percent.

This page presents a scenario analysis regarding the amortization terms of public pension plans and the potential financial impact of a bear market correction on US states. The analysis centers on a recommendation by the Society of Actuaries to shorten amortization periods for public plans from longer terms to 15-to-20-year terms. The author explains that while shortening these terms is designed to address underfunding, it significantly increases near-term debt service ratios, especially for the most severely underfunded states, where the required revenue contribution can rise by an additional 7% to 10%.

The first chart, titled "Comparison of amortization terms," illustrates the percentage of state revenue collections required to pay interest on bonded debt, the state share of defined benefit plan contributions, retiree health care costs, and defined contribution plan expenses. It compares a 30-year amortization term against a 15-year term across all fifty states. The data reveals that under a 15-year amortization schedule, the worst-off states face massive budgetary pressures. Hawaii and Illinois, for example, see their required revenue share jump from approximately 32% under a 30-year term to over 40% under a 15-year term. Connecticut, New Jersey, and Kentucky also experience significant increases, pushing their required revenues well above the 35% mark, far exceeding the highlighted 25% red threshold line. 

The second section of the page details how pension systems relying on risky asset returns face severe risks during bear market corrections, as assets decline while liabilities continue to grow. The second chart, titled "Impact of a bear market correction," models this scenario by showing the incremental impact of a correction where assets remain flat for three years while liabilities grow at 5% per year, amortized over 30 years. This incremental impact is stacked on top of the level payment of unfunded liabilities under a standard 30-year term. The chart demonstrates that the immediate impact of such a correction is relatively modest because the resulting asset-liability gap is spread over thirty years. For instance, the required revenue share for the most heavily burdened state, Illinois, increases by only a few percentage points, rising from about 32% to approximately 35%, while the increases for other states are minor.

The author argues that market-capitalization-weighted equity indices can lead to severe concentrations of risk and overvaluation. To illustrate this point, the text highlights notable historical examples from the S&P 500, such as the US tech sector weight rising from 6% in 1990 to 29% by 1999, and the US financials sector weight rising from 7.5% in 1990 to 22% by 2006. 

To demonstrate the consequences of this concentration, the page features two scatter plots analyzing global equities divided into 40 region-sector buckets using MSCI World TR Index data from 1995 through 2011. The first scatter plot, on the left, shows that region-sector buckets tend to underperform the market after their index weights rise sharply. The horizontal axis measures the percent increase in region-sector weight over a 24-month period, from 50% to 250%, while the vertical axis plots the subsequent relative return over the next 18 months, ranging from -60% to 120%. The visual pattern shows that when a region-sector's weight balloons, the subsequent returns overwhelmingly cluster below the 0% line, showing underperformance. The second scatter plot, on the right, charts how region-sectors also underperform after their relative volatility rises sharply. It plots the 18-month relative return on the vertical axis against the region-sector volatility as a percentage of market volatility over a 36-month period on the horizontal axis, ranging from 125% to 250%. This plot similarly reveals a heavy concentration of negative relative returns at higher volatility levels. A cluster of outliers showing positive relative returns is circled; the text identifies these as late 1990s Asia ex-Japan tech stocks, noting that they too went on to underperform shortly after the measured time horizon. 

To address these risks, the author suggests an investment process that limits exposure to overvalued or highly volatile regions and sectors, combining this discipline with traditional stock-picking factors. This strategy is supported by the bar chart at the bottom of the page, titled "Excess returns generated by quintile and factor," which plots excess returns against the MSCI World Index using monthly data from December 1995 to December 2012. The chart breaks four factors—Value, Size, Momentum, and Low Volatility—into quintiles from Q1 to Q5. The first quintile, Q1, shows positive excess returns across all four factors, led by Momentum at nearly 5% excess return. In contrast, the fifth quintile, Q5, shows negative excess returns across all four factors, with Momentum showing the largest drag at around -5%. The author suggests that over the long run, avoiding Q5 characteristics and focusing on low valuations, smaller market caps, higher momentum, and lower volatility generates consistent excess returns.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest explores "The Resilience Project," a scientific endeavor led by Stephen Friend of the non-profit Sage Bionetworks and formerly of Merck that aims to prevent genetically predisposed childhood diseases. Rather than focusing on palliative care, the project seeks to discover why some individuals who carry genetic mutations for severe, single-gene childhood diseases never actually get sick. The project's premise is to find healthy adults over the age of 40 who carry these mutations—referred to as "EX-Men"—to isolate the genetic or environmental factors that blocked the disease. By analyzing these protective mechanisms, researchers hope to develop preventative therapies for 127 single-gene diseases, such as cystic fibrosis, Tay-Sachs, and ataxia, which typically manifest by age 18.

The page contains a schematic diagram on the left titled "DNA Mutations: some can be beneficial," which visually contrasts a normal DNA copying process with a mutated copying process, illustrating how base-pair mutations can occur. To the right, a table titled "The Resilience Project: snapshot of potential EX-Men so far" highlights nine early-stage candidates identified by Sage Bionetworks who possess disease-associated mutations but remain healthy. This table lists the number of potential EX-Men, their normal and mutated DNA sequences, and the associated disease they avoided. Specifically, the table displays two individuals with a mutated c.1558T sequence who avoided Cystic Fibrosis; two with a mutated c.964-1C sequence who avoided Smith-Lemli-Opitz Syndrome; and one individual each who carries mutated sequences protecting them from Familial Dysautonomia (mutated c.2204+6C), Sanfilippo Syndrome (mutated c.220T), Epidermolysis Bullosa (mutated c.373T), Pfeiffer Syndrome (mutated c.755G), and APECED (mutated c.769T).

To achieve its goals, Sage Bionetworks aims to analyze more than one million DNA swab samples, leveraging recent advances that have reduced analysis costs to under $100 per sample. The project proposes to partner with large corporations and institutions to integrate this screening into employee wellness programs. To accelerate the discovery process, Sage plans to employ an open-source, collaborative approach and keep findings in the public domain. Ultimately, the author highlights this initiative as a profound exercise in genetic pattern recognition that could shift medical focus from treatment to prevention.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the shifting dynamics of global equities as central bank zero interest rate policies fade, arguing that stock-picking will play a greater role in future portfolio returns. Specifically, it analyzes the European Central Bank's continued aggressive liquidity provisions, exploring why Germany has acquiesced to these easy money policies. The author suggests that despite sharp increases in German home prices, overall German wage and price inflation remain low. Additionally, the author argues that Germany is supporting these policies because France is in dire need of economic assistance, as French corporate profits and industrial production remain sluggish despite expanding valuation multiples.

Four charts support these arguments. The first, titled Germany: house prices, plots year-over-year percent change from 1999 to 2013. It demonstrates that while German home prices experienced negative or flat growth from 2000 to 2008, hovering between negative one percent and one percent, they surged dramatically after 2009, peaking near five percent by 2012 and 2013. Despite this housing heat, the second chart, Germany: wage inflation, shows that wage growth remains contained. This chart measures the year-over-year percent change of a three-month moving average for industry including construction from 1999 to 2013. It highlights that while wage inflation dipped to nearly negative two percent in 2009, it only recovered to around two to three percent by 2013, remaining far below its pre-crisis peak of over six percent in late 2008.

The third chart, Euro area core inflation, tracks the GDP-weighted average percentage of services and non-energy goods from 2008 to 2013 against the official two percent ECB inflation target. It visualizes three regions: Germany, Core Europe excluding Germany, and the Periphery. By late 2013, all three lines were well below the target, with Germany at approximately one point two percent, Core Europe excluding Germany at one point one percent, and the Periphery near zero point five percent, underscoring the broad-based absence of inflationary pressure.

The final chart, France: Vive la Difference, contrasts valuation expansions with stagnant real economy indicators from 2004 to 2014. It plots three series: French forward price-to-earnings multiples, year-over-year earnings growth on the left axis, and an industrial production index on the right axis. The chart shows that while France's forward P/E expanded significantly from around ten in late 2012 to nearly fourteen by mid-2014, year-over-year earnings growth hovered stagnantly near or below zero percent, and industrial production remained flat around an index value of one hundred, well below its 2008 peak of one hundred fifteen.

In terms of forecasts and open questions, the author poses whether French President François Hollande’s recent pension reforms and corporate tax cuts will repeat the successful market rebound seen after François Mitterrand’s similar policy volte-face in 1982.
