The author also notes that the Bundesbank expects German wage inflation to rise in 2015 due to a new minimum wage, though immigration may limit this trend. Ultimately, the author predicts that European valuation expansion has run its course, meaning that corporate earnings growth must now do the heavy lifting to carry equity markets higher.

This J.P. Morgan publication page examines the historically limited impact of geopolitical conflicts on global equity markets, arguing that the business cycle is far more critical for investors than war. The author notes that war-zone countries represent a very small share of the global economy outside of oil production. An accompanying table, titled War zone countries as a percent of total world, lists their minimal shares across several metrics, including population at 11.7%, oil production at 9.0%, GDP at 3.0%, corporate profits at 0.8%, and equity market capitalization at 0.7%. 

Two line charts illustrate the performance of the S&P 500 Index twelve months before and twenty-four months after major historical military events, with the index set to 100 at the month of invasion. The first chart covers conflicts from 1950 to 1968, including the Korean War, the Soviet invasion of Hungary, the Six-Day War, and the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia. It shows that these events generally did not trigger severe market declines. The text explains that the Vietnam War was omitted due to its unclear start date, though related deficit spending eventually drove up inflation and interest rates. The second chart covers conflicts from 1973 to 1983, tracing the S&P 500 during the Arab-Israeli War, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, martial law in Poland, the Falklands War, and the US invasion of Grenada. This chart highlights a major market decline following the 1973 Arab-Israeli War, which triggered a Saudi oil embargo and recession. In contrast, other conflicts in this period did not severely damage markets, with the 1981 downturn instead attributed to the Volcker Fed's anti-inflation policies.

This page presents an appendix titled "a petro-sectarian map of the Middle East," illustrating the tight geographical correlation between major oil and gas reserves and sectarian divisions, particularly Shi'ite majority populations. The commentary explains that oil markets are highly sensitive to sectarian violence because key reserves—such as those in Kurdistan and Basra in Iraq, Eastern Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait—frequently lie near sectarian fault lines. In Iraq, southern oil deposits near Basra are well-defended and comprise 75% of the country's production, whereas northern exports near Kirkuk have been severely disrupted by pipeline attacks and are currently under the control of Kurdish Peshmerga forces awaiting pipeline repairs in non-Kurdish territory. 

The primary visual is a detailed, color-coded map of the Middle East, Caucasus, and Central Asia, titled "Primary Oil and Gas Deposits in the Middle East and its Shia Majority Areas," reprinted from Columbia University's Gulf2000 Project. The map's legend categorizes religious demographics, highlighting Shi'ite-populated regions in light blue, Sunni regions in green, and Wahhabi or Salafi regions in light yellow-green, alongside other minority religions. Major oil fields, super-giant oil fields, and major gas fields are marked in black and red, demonstrating a striking geographical alignment with Shia-majority regions. This overlap is particularly pronounced in Iran, Azerbaijan, southern Iraq, and the eastern provinces of Saudi Arabia along the Persian Gulf, including Hasa, Qatif, and Hofuf. 

In the bottom-left corner, an inset bar chart displays proven developed combined oil and gas reserves in billions of barrels of oil equivalent at the end of 2004, using data from PFC Energy and The Economist. The chart compares five major resource holders: Russia leads with nearly 300 billion barrels of oil equivalent, followed closely by Iran and Saudi Arabia, both holding roughly 260 to 270 billion barrels. Qatar holds approximately 175 billion barrels, and Iraq possesses around 120 billion barrels of oil equivalent.

In this commentary, the author argues that the Federal Reserve is facing increasing pressure to abandon its emergency zero-interest-rate policy as the US economy transitions into a mid-cycle phase. With labor market slack and excess industrial capacity shrinking, the author suggests that Fed governors may need to raise rates sooner and faster than markets are pricing in. This situation is illustrated by a cartoon of a boiling pot labeled "United States Federal Reserve" heated by bright flames, containing five frogs representing the FOMC's more dovish members: Evans, Rosengren, Yellen, Kocherlakota, and Dudley. 

To the right of the pot, a color-coded list details twenty economic indicators acting as "heat" on the Fed to raise policy rates. "Hot" indicators highlighted in red include high JOLTS job openings, rapidly declining unemployment, inflation rising toward two percent, normalized capacity utilization, elevated credit market risk-taking, high M&A deal volumes, and expansionary ISM prices paid signals at sixty. "Warm" indicators in yellow include healthy corporate loan growth and a small uptick in the employment cost index to two percent. Meanwhile, "cool" indicators in blue, which do not yet signal a need for rate hikes, include weak residential mortgage demand, low average hourly earnings growth of two percent, and below-target inflation expectations in TIPS markets. 

The author concludes that while the Fed may not explicitly policy-target credit market liquidity, a broader recovery makes emergency rates hard to justify, predicting that upcoming monthly wage and consumer price inflation reports will be highly watched and will introduce volatility into US equity markets. Mentioned individuals include the FOMC members and former Fed governor Jeremy Stein.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication, published on September 2, 2014, discusses historical and current market behavior during Federal Reserve tightening cycles, alongside a positive economic outlook for the United States in 2014. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that initial Federal Reserve rate hikes typically trigger volatility and modest corrections in equity markets rather than outright bear markets, with equities rebounding once steady economic growth is established under controlled inflation. However, he cautions that the unprecedented scale of the post-crisis monetary experiment means future outcomes may differ from historical norms.

The first table, titled "2-year Treasury and S&P 500 reactions to Fed moves during tightening cycles," documents market performance during five cycles: 1987, 1988–1989, 1994–1995, 1999–2000, and 2004–2006. It shows that initial market reactions to the first rate hike consistently caused negative S&P 500 returns, ranging from negative five percent to negative nine percent, while two-year Treasury yields rose by 27 to 137 basis points. In contrast, the subsequent market reaction to the remaining hikes was positive in all periods, ranging from a seven percent return to a 32 percent return. Consequently, total S&P 500 price returns across the entire hike cycles were positive in four of the five periods, ranging from 10 percent to 26 percent, with only the 1994–1995 cycle ending in a minor decline of negative two percent. Meanwhile, total two-year Treasury yield increases ranged from 179 to 361 basis points across the tightening cycles.

The second section of the page focuses on how economic trends in 2014 are playing out as expected in the United States, pointing to a meaningful pick-up in growth. The author forecasts corporate profit growth expectations of eight to ten percent for 2015, stating that rising revenue growth and increased capital spending will be partially offset by rising labor and interest costs. 

To support this domestic outlook, the page displays three charts. The first chart, titled "Light vehicle sales and pending home sales," plots data from 2004 to mid-2014. Light vehicle sales, measured in millions of seasonally adjusted annual rate (saar) units on the left axis, shows a recovery from a low of nearly nine million units in 2009 back to approximately 17 million units by mid-2014. Pending home sales, plotted as a seasonally adjusted index on the right axis, shows a decline from its 2005 peak of over 125 down to a low near 80 in 2010, followed by a recovery to over 100 by mid-2014. 

The second chart, titled "Consumer confidence rising along with consumer credit," covers 2006 through mid-2014. Consumer confidence, plotted on a seasonally adjusted index on the left axis, dropped from a pre-crisis high of 110 to under 30 in 2009, before climbing back toward 90 by 2014. Consumer credit, represented on the right axis in thousands of 2014 USD per household, displays a steady upward trajectory from roughly $24,000 in 2006 to nearly $28,000 by mid-2014. 

The final chart shows "S&P 500 earnings and revenue growth (ex-financials)" measured in year-over-year percentage changes from first quarter 2010 to estimated second quarter 2014. Earnings growth, tracked on the left axis, peaked near 40 percent in early 2010, bottomed near zero percent in late 2012, and hovered around ten percent by mid-2014. Revenue growth, tracked on the right axis, followed a similar downward path from a peak of 12 percent in 2010 to a low of zero percent in late 2012, before showing a modest rebound toward five percent by mid-2014.

This page from the publication addresses "prophet warnings" from central banks, specifically the Federal Reserve and the Bank for International Settlements, which have expressed growing concern over stretched market valuations. The author highlights the irony of these central banks worrying about aggressive risk-taking when their post-2008 monetary policies were specifically designed to encourage it. To evaluate these warnings, the author reviews several key charts detailing historical market reactions to crises and current valuation multiples across different sectors and regions.

A chart titled "S&P 500 Index around military invasions and conflicts (1991 - today)" illustrates that equity markets are historically resilient to geopolitical shocks. Tracking the index from twelve months before to twenty-four months after a conflict begins (with the month of invasion indexed to 100), the data shows mild reactions to the US invasion of Kuwait in 1991, the Serbian invasion of Kosovo in 1998, and the US invasion of Iraq in 2003. Although the September 11 attacks and subsequent Afghan invasion in 2001 triggered a sharp decline, the market reversed within weeks. Similarly, the chart notes that South Korean equities typically recover within weeks of North Korean military provocations, such as the sinking of a South Korean Navy vessel in 2010.

Global equity valuation trends are analyzed in a chart titled "Equity valuations across regions," which tracks sector-neutral forward price-to-earnings ratios from 2008 to mid-2014. Since their lows in late 2011 and 2012, P/E multiples have expanded globally. By mid-2014, US valuations are the highest, approaching 16x forward earnings, followed by Europe at approximately 14x, the aggregate World index close behind, and Emerging Markets trailing at around 11.5x.

The author validates the Federal Reserve’s warnings about specific high-growth sectors in a chart titled "Internet and Biotech stocks: the 'secular growth' stories," which measures price-to-sales ratios from January 2011 to July 2014. While the broader Russell 1000 Index remained flat and inexpensive at around 1.5x to 2x sales, high-growth sectors experienced massive multiple expansion. The S&P 500 Biotechnology Index rose from 4x sales in 2011 to nearly 9x in early 2014, while a custom basket of "75 Secular growth stocks" peaked above 10x sales. The S&P 500 Internet Software & Services Index also expanded from 4x to approximately 6x sales, demonstrating the stretched valuations the Fed referenced in its Congressional testimony.

To round out the valuation analysis, the final chart, "S&P 500 P/Es: Forward and median trailing," compares market-cap-weighted forward P/E ratios to median trailing P/E ratios from 1985 to mid-2014. In mid-2014, the forward P/E stood at roughly 15x, which is elevated compared to its 2011 bottom of 10x but well below the tech-bubble peak of 24x. However, the median trailing P/E ratio, which avoids market-cap distortion, was higher at nearly 18x, suggesting that the average stock in the index is relatively more expensive than the cap-weighted forward metric implies.

In this executive summary titled "The Agony and the Ecstasy: The Risks and Rewards of a Concentrated Stock Position," Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management outlines the historically steep odds against holding concentrated stock positions. To illustrate the unpredictable and catastrophic nature of single-stock risk, the page features a cartoon graphic of a man holding an umbrella as a grand piano falls on him from above. 

Cembalest leverages data from the Russell 3000 Index since 1980 to show that approximately 40 percent of all stocks have suffered a permanent decline of 70 percent or more from their peak value, with even worse outcomes observed in the Technology, Biotech, and Metals and Mining sectors. Additionally, the median stock underperformed the Russell 3000 Index by 54 percent from its inception, two-thirds of all individual stocks underperformed the index, and 40 percent of all stocks posted negative absolute returns. When factoring in single-stock volatility, the author finds that 75 percent of concentrated stockholders would have benefited from diversifying. 

This trend of creative destruction is further supported by the fact that over 320 companies have been removed from the S&P 500 due to business distress since 1980. Cembalest points to globalization, specifically China's entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001, as a force that expanded opportunities but also escalated competitive, regulatory, and operational risks. The introduction sets up a forthcoming series of empirical analyses and sector case studies, reminding readers that while corporate failures look obvious in hindsight, they were unforeseen by management, boards, analysts, rating agencies, and employees alike.

This page addresses the risk of permanent, substantial price declines in individual stocks by analyzing approximately 13,000 companies that were members of the Russell 3000 Index at any point between 1980 and 2014. The author defines a "catastrophic loss" as a decline of 70% or more from a stock's peak price with little subsequent recovery, leaving an eventual loss of 60% or more. 

A table titled "Total % of companies experiencing 'catastrophic loss', 1980 - 2014" reveals that 40% of all analyzed stocks suffered this type of permanent decline. This rate varies significantly by sector. Information Technology experienced the highest rate of catastrophic loss at 57%, followed by Telecommunication Services at 51% and Energy at 47%. Consumer Discretionary and Health Care also showed high rates of permanent decline at 43% and 42% respectively. Conversely, Utilities was the most stable sector, with only a 13% loss rate, while Financials and Consumer Staples recorded relatively lower rates of 25% and 26%.

A line chart titled "Catastrophic loss rates on Russell 3000 companies" tracks the percentage of companies undergoing this distress at any given time from 1980 through roughly 2011. The y-axis ranges from 0% to 20%, and the x-axis spans from 1980 to past 2010. The chart demonstrates that while distress rates steadily persist during economic expansions, they spike during recessions and market corrections. Major peaks occurred in the early 1990s at around 15%, during the tech bust of 2001-2002 when it approached 20%, and during the 2008 financial crisis when it rose to about 13%. 

The chart shows a sharp drop in loss rates below 5% after 2010. The author warns against over-interpreting this post-crisis decline, attributing it to an unprecedented Federal Reserve monetary experiment that maintained negative real interest rates for over five years, alongside the fact that newer companies have simply had less time to fail. The high historical rate of permanent decline across sectors leads the author to conclude that diversification must be a foundational element of wealth management for concentrated stockholders.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" analyzes catastrophic loss rates by sector from 1980 through roughly 2012, defining these rates as the share of companies in the process of suffering sharp, unrecovered price declines. A key takeaway highlighted on the page is that a meaningful number of companies are always suffering these steep, unrecovered declines at any given time, even during economic expansions. While sectors like Consumer Discretionary, Materials, Health Care, and Industrials closely track the broad market benchmark—the Russell 3000—other sectors exhibit distinct patterns of higher or lower vulnerability, often tied to specific regulatory changes or macroeconomic shocks.

Five individual line charts, utilizing data from FactSet and J.P. Morgan Asset Management, illustrate these trends by plotting sector loss rates against the Russell 3000 benchmark on a timeline from 1980 to 2010. The first chart shows that Information Technology consistently experiences catastrophic loss rates higher than the broader market, with its y-axis ranging up to 50%. IT loss rates peaked near 30% in the mid-1980s and spiked dramatically to over 45% during the dot-com bust around 2000. 

Conversely, the second chart shows that Consumer Staples and Utilities consistently experience loss rates lower than the Russell 3000, measured on a 0% to 30% y-axis. Consumer Staples loss rates generally fluctuated between 5% and 15%, while Utilities remained exceptionally stable and low, rarely rising above 5% except for a small spike to around 8% in the early 2000s. 

The remaining three charts illustrate sectors where distress is highly concentrated around specific historical catalysts, plotted on 0% to 50% scales for Energy and Telecom, and 0% to 30% for Financials. The Energy chart reveals a massive spike in catastrophic loss rates to over 40% during the early 1980s oil price collapse, followed by a period of low distress during the mid-2000s energy price rally, and a subsequent spike to around 25% during the 2008–2011 natural gas price collapse. The Telecommunications chart highlights how deregulation altered the sector; telecom loss rates were very low in the 1980s and early 1990s but surged to nearly 50% in the early 2000s following the passage of the 1996 Telecommunications Act. Finally, the Financials chart shows that distress in the financial sector is generally lower than the broad market, with the notable exceptions of a 12% peak during the 1991 recession and a dramatic surge to nearly 25% starting during the 2008 global financial crisis.

This page argues that individual stock returns are characterized by a negative success/failure distribution across nearly all sectors, reinforcing the critical role of diversification in wealth planning over holding concentrated stock positions. 

To support this, a table analyzes the lifetime returns of stocks by sector from 1980 to 2014 compared against the Russell 3000 index. Across all sectors, the median excess return against the index was -54%, with 64% of stocks generating negative excess returns, 40% generating negative absolute returns, and only 7% qualifying as extreme winners. This underperformance pattern holds across every sector: median excess returns were negative across the board, ranging from -3% for Consumer Staples to -141% for Utilities. The proportion of stocks with negative excess returns exceeded 50% in every sector, peaking at 85% for Utilities and 72% for Energy. Except for Consumer Staples at 15%, every sector saw extreme winners limited to single digits, with Utilities at 0%. A footnote explains that while Utilities have a very low absolute negative return rate of 14% due to their low-risk nature, their high rate of negative excess returns reflects the sector's lower overall return rates.

The page contextualizes these findings with a life-cycle analysis designed to locate stocks that still delivered positive long-term returns despite catastrophic interim drops. This dynamic is illustrated in a chart of Cisco Systems’ stock price from 1990 to 2014. After peaking around $80 in 2000, Cisco suffered a maximum loss from its peak of -86% and ended the period with an eventual loss from its peak of -67%. Even with this dramatic collapse, Cisco's annual price return since inception was 27% compared to 8% for the broader market, illustrating how a concentrated holder could still benefit in the long run. However, the author notes that while Cisco survived, the negative skew of the distribution across the market indicates that most stocks suffering similar collapses do not recover. Ultimately, the page concludes that the high frequency of catastrophic declines and negative skew in individual stock returns compound the risk of concentrated stock holdings, making diversification essential for most entrepreneurs.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses why volatility, specifically defined as the volatility of negative stock price movements (semi-deviation), is a crucial signal of risk and how it impacts the optimal strategy for holding concentrated stock positions. The author argues that over the long run, higher volatility is closely linked to lower stock price returns, which has significant implications for how much of a single stock investors should hold relative to a diversified index. 

The first chart on the page is a scatter plot titled "Higher volatility usually associated with lower stock price returns," using data from Russell 3000 stocks with at least three years of returns between 1980 and 2014. The horizontal axis measures downside volatility (semi-deviation) from 0% to 140%, while the vertical axis shows annualized stock price returns from -100% to 200%. The dense cluster of data points exhibits a clear downward-sloping trend, visually demonstrating that as downside volatility rises, stock returns tend to fall. 

The second chart is a bar chart titled "Optimal mix of a concentrated stock position with the Russell 3000, 1980-2014, number of observations." It analyzes what combination of an individual stock and the Russell 3000 index would have delivered the best risk-adjusted return historically. The vertical axis represents the number of observations, ranging from 0 to 3,500, while the horizontal axis displays the optimal concentrated stock weight from 0% to 100%. The distribution is highly skewed to the left: the tallest bar shows that in over 3,000 instances, the optimal weight of the concentrated stock was 0%. The frequency declines sharply as the weight increases, though there is a small uptick at 100% weight, occurring in about 6% of the cases (roughly 500 observations) where owning only the concentrated stock was the optimal risk-adjusted path. The author concludes that because the vast majority of individual stocks underperformed the Russell 3000 index, a risk-adjusted framework typically dictates owning 30% or less of a concentrated stock, and often none of it, in favor of the diversified index. Both charts cite FactSet and J.P. Morgan Asset Management as their data sources.

This page of the report examines the history of the Information Technology sector, highlighting that while it has generated massive, historic winners like Google, Apple, Qualcomm, and Salesforce, the vast majority of tech companies fail to sustain success. In fact, only 6% of tech companies become extreme winners, while 70% underperform the Russell 3000 Index, and nearly 60% fall 70% from their peak price and never recover. The author argues that tech is defined by disruptive technologies that are eventually disrupted themselves. Even highly competent, smart industry leaders in the 1980s and 1990s, such as Wang Labs, Silicon Graphics, Digital Equipment Corporation, and Commodore, collapsed because they failed to adapt to the rise of personal computer platforms and Microsoft's operating system. 

To illustrate these corporate failures, the page displays four stock price charts. The first chart shows Wang Labs, Inc., a giant in dedicated word processing equipment, whose stock price peaked around $40 in 1983 before steadily declining to near $0 by 1993. The second chart focuses on Silicon Graphics Inc., which built dedicated 3D graphics servers; its stock spiked to over $15 in 1995 but crashed to almost zero by 2005 as PC platforms took over. 

The author notes that the late 1990s dot-com boom saw massive enthusiasm as global internet users grew ten-fold from 32 million in 1995 to 320 million in 2000. Despite this rapid growth, many companies could not survive the mild 2001 recession because their business models required unrealistic, exponential broadband adoption. This era is represented by the remaining two charts. The third chart details Exodus Communications Inc., a data center provider that saw its stock rocket to nearly $80 in 2000 before falling to zero by 2002 because its tech customer base collapsed and demand migrated from co-location to managed hosting. The fourth chart displays JDS Uniphase, whose stock experienced a dramatic, vertical climb to over $1,000 in early 2000 but collapsed just as quickly, flatlining near zero through 2014. This crash occurred because JDS's core customer base for optical equipment—including telecom giants like Alcatel, Cisco, Corning, Lucent, Motorola, and Nortel—suffered a simultaneous collapse in demand. Finally, a footnote highlights how difficult technological prediction can be, citing Digital Equipment Corporation CEO Ken Olsen's infamously wrong 1986 prediction that "the personal computer will fall flat on its face in business."

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market explores the distinct and substantial business risks across different subsectors of health care, including pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, medical devices, and service providers. The introductory text highlights that from 2003 to 2012, generic drug consumption saved the US health care system $1.2 trillion, which directly translated to lost revenue for branded, large-cap pharmaceutical companies. It emphasizes that biotechnology carries the highest event risk, citing Harvard professor Gary Pisano’s finding that Phase 3 clinical trials still face a failure rate of up to 50 percent, and noting that larger pharmaceutical firms often perform better in drug discovery than smaller biotech firms. Although the promise of mapping the human genome is now beginning to pay dividends, the 2000–2001 peak in biotech distress led to over 100 catastrophic failures of Russell 3000 biotech and life sciences companies since 2002.

To illustrate these diverse risks, the page presents six historical stock price charts. The first chart, tracking Boston Scientific Corporation from 1993 to 2013 on a scale of $0 to $50, demonstrates that device companies heavily reliant on a single product—such as drug-coated stents—operate like highly concentrated stock portfolios. The stock peaked near $45 in 2004 before dropping below $10 by 2010. 

The second chart displays HealthSouth Corporation from 1987 to 2014 on a scale of $0 to $160, cautioning CEOs on the importance of due diligence during stock-for-stock roll-ups. It shows how accounting fraud decimated the largest outpatient rehab roll-up, causing the stock to crash from nearly $160 in 1998 to near zero by 2003.

The third chart focuses on Dendreon Corporation from June 2000 to June 2014 on a scale of $0 to $60. It shows that FDA approval is not always a guarantee of commercial success if customer demand fails to materialize. The stock spiked to nearly $50 around 2010 following successful test results and FDA approval, but plummeted back to under $10 after the company withdrew its financial guidance.

The fourth chart plots Genesis Health Ventures Inc. from 1992 to 2001 on a scale of $0 to $40, showing how unanticipated declines in Medicare reimbursements can make a nursing home's capital structure completely inoperable. The stock fell precipitously from nearly $40 in late 1997 to near zero by 2000, spreading contagion to other providers.

The fifth chart tracks Neurocrine Biosciences, Inc. from 1997 to 2013 on a scale of $0 to $70. It shows how the FDA’s approval tolerance can shift over time, particularly when approved competitor drugs like Lunesta or Ambien show negative side effects. The stock crashed from roughly $65 to under $10 in 2006 when the FDA denied approval for a larger dose of its Indiplon insomnia drug.

The final chart tracks Human Genome Sciences Inc. from 1996 to 2012 on a scale of $0 to $120, arguing that advanced breakthroughs like gene mapping do not instantly translate into profitable business models. The stock peaked dramatically above $110 in 2000 before crashing. The chart also lists several other major biotech companies that suffered catastrophic price declines between 2000 and 2002, including Millennium, Celera, Abgenix, Protein Design Labs, Medarex, Maxygen, Curagen, Enzon, and Cell Therapeutics.

This page serves as a reference table listing the "Historical Winners," categorized into eight distinct sectors based on FactSet designations. Under the Consumer Discretionary sector, notable listed companies include Amazon, AutoZone, Bed Bath & Beyond, Best Buy, Comcast, Gap, Home Depot, Lowe's, McDonald's, Netflix, Nike, Starbucks, Target, TJX Companies, and the Walt Disney Company. The Consumer Staples sector lists firms such as Clorox, Colgate-Palmolive, Hershey, Monster Beverage, Sysco, Tyson Foods, Walgreen, Wal-Mart, and Whole Foods Market. The Energy sector features a shorter list, including Cheniere Energy, EOG Resources, and Patterson-UTI Energy. The Financials sector highlights major institutions such as Berkshire Hathaway, BlackRock, Charles Schwab, Franklin Resources, Progressive Corporation, and T. Rowe Price. The Health Care sector is highly populated, featuring Amgen, Biogen IDEC, Celgene, Express Scripts, Gilead Sciences, Medtronic, St. Jude Medical, and Stryker. The Industrials sector highlights companies like Danaher, Equifax, Illinois Tool Works, Southwest Airlines, and Stericycle. The Information Technology sector is particularly dense, naming tech giants and payment networks such as Adobe, Apple, Cisco Systems, eBay, Electronic Arts, Intel, Intuit, MasterCard, Microsoft, Oracle, Qualcomm, salesforce.com, and Yahoo. Finally, the Materials sector lists entities like Ecolab, Sherwin-Williams, Sigma-Aldrich, and Valspar. A critical footnote warning states that this list of historical winners is based purely on historical analyses and does not serve as investment recommendations or guarantee future results.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market summarizes an empirical analysis of concentration risk by combining three previously examined risk factors: the risk of catastrophic loss, the risk of underperforming the Russell 3000 index, and the risk of heightened volatility. The author argues that in about three-quarters of all cases between 1980 and 2014, some level of diversification would have been beneficial in sustaining family wealth. 

To support this, the page features a table titled "Percent of stocks whose concentrated holders would have benefited from diversification, 1980-2014," with data sourced from FactSet and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. Across all sectors, 74% of stocks met the criteria where diversification would have made sense. This vulnerability is highest in the Utilities sector at 87%, followed by Information Technology at 82% and Energy at 81%. Other sectors also show high percentages of stocks benefiting from diversification, including Materials at 75%, Industrials at 75%, Consumer Discretionary at 74%, Telecommunication Services at 74%, and Health Care at 72%. Even in the sectors with the lowest percentages, Financials at 63% and Consumer Staples at 58%, a clear majority of stocks would have benefited from diversification.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the vulnerability of industrial companies to systemic external shocks, noting that while airline bankruptcies are the most famous—with the US Government Accountability Office recording 162 airline bankruptcies between 1978 and 2005—many other long-standing industrial businesses have collapsed due to unexpected changes. The author points to factors such as rapid Asian growth, asbestos litigation, China's entry into the World Trade Organization, shifting demand in the digital age, unfavorable regulatory rulings, and the termination of government alternative energy subsidies. 

To illustrate these patterns of sudden failure, the page features six stock price charts tracing historical collapses of prominent companies. The first chart tracks Delta Air Lines from 1981 to 2005, showing its stock price peaking near $70 in the late 1990s before crashing to zero by 2005. This decline is attributed to high employee salaries, slow responses to low-fare competition, and spiked jet fuel costs, alongside a list of other catastrophic airline declines including Northwest, PanAm, TWA, and United. 

The second chart focuses on Harnischfeger Industries from 1981 to 2001, demonstrating how its stock collapsed from a peak near $45 in 1997 to nearly zero by 2000. The crash illustrates the risk of debt-fueled expansion and a heavy reliance on overseas consumption, which became exposed when orders from Indonesia dried up during its 17% GDP contraction in 1998. 

The third chart tracks Owens-Corning Fiberglass Corporation from 1981 to 2005, showing how the stock repeatedly crested near $40 to $50 before crashing to zero around 2000. This collapse was driven by massive asbestos litigation liabilities, part of a wave of nearly 100 asbestos producers filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. 

The fourth chart follows civil engineering and heavy construction firm Morrison Knudsen from 1981 to 1997. The stock plunged from nearly $60 in the early 1990s to near-zero by 1996, highlighting the financial danger of overextending and aggressively expanding into non-core business areas like mass transit. 

The fifth chart illustrates Cincinnati Milacron from 1980 to 2010. Once one of the world's largest machine tool manufacturers, its stock struggled under the weight of cheaper foreign competition and a general US manufacturing slowdown. After peaking at nearly $400 in the early 1980s and experiencing a secondary peak near $250 in the late 1990s, the stock plummeted to near zero following China’s entry into the WTO in 2001. 

The final chart shows the stock performance of lithium-ion battery manufacturer A123 Systems from September 2009 to September 2012. The stock plummeted from over $20 to near zero in just three years, demonstrating that while governments can subsidize the idea of electric cars, they cannot force consumers to buy them or their underlying battery technologies.

This page focuses on alternative energy stocks, analyzing their historical returns and highlighting the volatility and persistent underperformance of the sector relative to broader benchmarks and traditional energy stocks. The author contextualizes the eventual global shift toward renewable energy as the fourth major transition of the modern era, following coal in the early 1800s, oil in the early 1900s, and natural gas in the mid-1900s. He cautions, however, that this transition is a prolonged process characterized by fits and starts that pose substantial risks for concentrated stock holdings.

To visualize these risks, a line chart shows the rolling one-year excess return of clean energy stocks versus the S&P Small Cap Index from 2002 through mid-2014. This chart displays two primary data series: the Wilderhill Clean Energy Index minus the S&P Small Cap Index and the NYSE Bloomberg AME Clean Index minus the S&P Small Cap Index. The chart demonstrates massive cyclicality, with excess returns fluctuating widely between positive 50 percent and negative 50 percent. Crucially, the visual emphasizes that these cycles contain far more sustained valleys than peaks, illustrating how new clean energy ideas generate early excitement but frequently fail to deliver long-term returns.

An accompanying table displays the annualized total returns of clean energy indices compared with traditional benchmark indices over three multi-year periods: since 2002, since 2005, and since 2008. The performance metrics reveal that clean energy indices have severely lagged behind standard benchmarks. For example, the Wilderhill Clean Energy Index recorded negative annualized returns of negative 3.04 percent since 2002, negative 10.08 percent since 2005, and negative 4.11 percent since 2008. While other clean energy benchmarks fared somewhat better, such as the NYSE Bloomberg Americas Clean Energy Index returning 4.61 percent since 2005 and 11.82 percent since 2008, and the FTSE Environmental Opportunities Renewable & Alternative Energy Index returning 1.90 percent since 2008, they still fell far short of traditional equity indices. 

By comparison, the benchmark indices shown in the table posted strong, positive annualized returns across all periods. The S&P Small Cap Index returned 12.01 percent since 2002, 8.60 percent since 2005, and 18.39 percent since 2008. Traditional energy stocks, which make up the majority of S&P's sub-indices, also significantly outperformed clean energy; for instance, the S&P Small Cap Energy Index delivered returns of 20.01 percent since 2002, 12.49 percent since 2005, and 25.04 percent since 2008. Similarly, mid-cap and large-cap energy indices, alongside the S&P 500, consistently outperformed alternative energy options across every analyzed timeframe. The author concludes that regardless of the start date or the specific clean energy index chosen, alternative energy equities have struggled to compete with both the broader market and traditional fossil-fuel energy companies.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication analyzes structural and cyclical challenges within the Materials sector, focusing on how global policy shifts, overcapacity, environmental liabilities, and technological transitions have historically led to the collapse of major industrial firms. The main text argues that massive government subsidies following the Deng reforms in China and the Rao reforms in India created enormous overcapacity in capital-intensive industries like iron and steel. This capacity far exceeded domestic demand, flooding global markets and placing intense competitive pressure on US companies. Secular shifts, such as US newspaper readership falling from 62 million daily in 1990 to 52 million in 2006, structurally impaired materials providers. Cyclically, the 20% decline in global trade during the 2009 recession deeply wounded metals and mining firms, many of which never fully recovered.

To illustrate these points, the page features six stock price charts. The first chart shows Bethlehem Steel Corp. from 1981 to 2003, tracking its decline from peaks of around $30 in the 1980s and early 1990s to near-zero by 2003. An annotation notes that annual Chinese iron and steel exports jumped from $1.6 billion to $5.2 billion during this period, while management failed to reduce labor costs or improve plant productivity in time. 

The second chart illustrates Smurfit-Stone Container Corp. from 1995 to 2009, tracking a high-debt, low-margin packaging company whose stock peaked near $25 in 2000 before plummeting to zero during the 2009 trade collapse. 

The third chart depicts Solutia from 1998 to 2008, showcasing how legacy environmental liabilities can threaten solvency decades after the fact, dragging the stock from nearly $30 down to near-zero by 2004. 

The fourth chart follows Molycorp, Inc. from 2011 to 2014, demonstrating how the "insatiable" demand for rare earth elements in electronics and renewable energy collapsed once industries found technical workarounds, driving the stock from a peak of approximately $75 in 2011 to less than $10 by 2014. 

The fifth chart plots Abitibi-Consolidated Inc. from 1990 to 2006, showcasing the internet's role in the demise of newsprint. The stock fell from around $18 in 1997 to nearly zero by 2006. 

The final chart shows the Aluminum Company of America (Alcoa) from 1980 to 2013, illustrating how global capacity over-expansion and leveraged exposure to global growth dragged profits down. Alcoa’s stock peaked above $40 in 2000 and 2007 before crashing below $10 in 2009. An accompanying note explains that companies like US Steel, AK Steel, Walter Energy, Intrepid Potash, Century Aluminum, and Thompson Creek experienced similar devastating profiles due to the collapse in global trade.

This page presents an argument against shifting investment allocations away from a US-Emerging Markets (EM) "barbell" strategy toward Europe or Japan. The author contends that despite elevated US valuations, a regional rotation is unwarranted because European and Japanese valuations have risen without the support of underlying earnings growth or economic expansion. 

To support this, the first chart, "Regional price-to-earnings multiples," displays market-cap-weighted forward P/E ratios from 2008 to 2014. It shows that since 2012, valuations in the US, Europe, and Japan have all expanded, with the US reaching post-crisis highs of approximately 15x to 16x, while Europe and Japan have both climbed to around 14x. Emerging Markets remain the most inexpensive, trading near 10.5x. 

The disconnect between valuation and fundamentals is further analyzed in the second chart, "France: P/E multiples rise as profits/production stagnate." This graph tracks French financial metrics from 2004 to 2014, revealing that while the MSCI France P/E multiple surged to around 16x by mid-2014, industrial production remained stagnant near a level of 95, and corporate earnings growth remained flat.

The commentary notes that political headwinds—such as the rise of the Euroskeptic party Podemos in Spain and strong polling by the National Front in France—point to continued dissatisfaction with Europe's slow recovery. In assessing monetary policy, the author doubts the effectiveness of the European Central Bank's attempts to channel liquidity to the private sector. The chart "ECB capital markets interventions have less to work with" illustrates this structural hurdle, showing that capital market lending constitutes 68% of total private non-financial credit in the United States but only 12% in Europe as of the first quarter of 2014. Because European banks are not liquidity-constrained and rely far less on capital markets, cheap ECB funding is unlikely to spur growth if private credit demand remains weak.

Turning to Japan, the author characterizes the "Abenomics" program as an exercise in money printing rather than meaningful economic reform. Although Japanese corporations maintain strong balance sheets with lower debt-to-asset ratios than their US peers, domestic opportunities remain limited. This trend is captured in the chart "Signs of limited domestic opportunity in Japan," which tracks business capital spending as a percent of GDP from 2000 to 2014. While overall Japanese business capital spending recovered to roughly 7.0% of GDP by 2014, capital spending *within* Japan remained flat at around 4.7%, indicating that companies are increasingly choosing to invest their capital overseas.

In conclusion, the author predicts that despite potential headwinds in China, the US-EM barbell strategy is poised to deliver superior returns in 2015 compared to European and Japanese alternatives, especially in US dollar terms as both Europe and Japan aggressively ease their monetary policies.

This J.P. Morgan publication page discusses the tax implications of diversifying a concentrated stock position, arguing that investors should not let tax concerns solely dictate investment decisions. The author addresses older owners who worry about capital gains taxes versus receiving a step-up in basis upon death. Assuming a stock basis of twenty percent, a total Federal long-term capital gains tax rate of twenty-three point eight percent (including the Affordable Care Act Medicare surtax), and borrowing at four percent interest to cover taxes, the analysis compares keeping the stock versus selling to reinvest in the Russell 3000 Index.

A key table, titled Annualized gain or loss from disposition of concentrated stock and purchase of Russell 3000 Index, presents a matrix of scenarios based on an assumed eight percent annualized return for the Russell 3000. The horizontal axis measures the holding period until a step-up in basis from three to twenty-four years, while the vertical axis represents the excess annual return of the Russell 3000 Index over the concentrated stock position, ranging from negative fifteen percent to positive fifteen percent.

The table shows that if the concentrated stock outperforms the market (negative excess returns), selling results in losses, such as a negative twenty-one point five percent annualized loss at a negative fifteen percent excess return over a three-year horizon. However, if the stock underperforms the market (positive excess returns), selling is almost always beneficial. Only three specific short-term scenarios, highlighted in red, show taxation negating the benefits of selling when the stock underperforms: a negative four point zero percent loss at a two point five percent excess return over three years, a negative zero point four percent loss at a two point five percent excess return over six years, and a negative one point five percent loss at a five point zero percent excess return over three years. For all other underperformance scenarios, annualized gains are positive, reaching up to fourteen point six percent at a fifteen percent excess return over twenty-four years. The author concludes that tax issues should not discourage diversification, noting that alternative strategies like derivatives or charitable giving can also mitigate taxable gains.

This page focuses on the devastating long-term impacts of the 2001–2002 technology bust, showing how many dominant tech giants failed to recover because they did not adapt to changing industry trends. The author points out that of 212 internet and software service companies with peak stock prices in February 2000, only 17 ever reached higher prices between March 2000 and February 2014. The page highlights several of the largest decliners, the first three of which had peak market caps exceeding $100 billion. 

Six charts plot the historical stock prices of these failed or struggling technology leaders. In the telecom equipment sector, Lucent Technologies Inc.—which was the world’s largest telecom equipment company in 1999 with $38 billion in sales—suffered from relying too heavily on its incumbent status. Its stock price chart from 1997 to 2006 shows a peak of nearly $60 in late 1999 and early 2000 before plummeting to near-zero by 2002. Similarly, Lucent's Canadian competitor, Nortel Networks Corporation, drowned under overpriced, poorly integrated acquisitions and a corporate culture of arrogance. Nortel’s stock chart from 1981 to 2014 shows its stock skyrocketing to nearly $800 in 2000, only to completely crash to zero shortly thereafter.

In hardware and software licensing, Sun Microsystems fell victim to a market shift toward x86 processor machines and open-source software. Its stock chart from 1987 to 2008 shows a sharp spike peaking near $250 in 2000, followed by a permanent drop to single digits. A footnote includes a quote from former Sun CEO Scott McNealy in 2011, who lamented that wrapping their Solaris operating system in proprietary hardware was a critical mistake that paved the way for Linux. In the business software space, supply chain management leader I2 Technologies Inc. was crippled when Germany's SAP decided to compete directly and abandoned their joint venture. The stock chart for I2 Technologies from 1997 to 2009 shows a massive peak near $2,000 in 2000 before crashing to near-zero, demonstrating that a subsequent 2008 intellectual property judgment against SAP was too little, too late.

Finally, the page details how cheaper component parts and the migration to smartphones and tablets dragged down computer hardware manufacturers. Gateway 2000 was too slow to transition to portable laptops and shift its focus from retail to enterprise customers; its stock chart from 1994 to 2006 shows a peak of over $70 in 1999 before falling into a permanent flatline near zero. Dell Computer Corporation, once the world's top computer provider, struggled with a bruising price war, declining demand for customized hardware, and a difficult transition to mobile. Dell's stock chart from 1989 to 2013 shows a peak above $50 in 2000, a partial recovery to around $40 in the mid-2000s, and a long, grinding decline down to approximately $10 by 2013.

This page focuses on the stagnation of global equity markets outside of the United States, arguing that while US valuations are supported by rising corporate profits, European, Chinese, and Japanese markets suffer from weak fundamentals despite optimistic pricing. Because over thirty percent of US corporate profits are sourced internationally, these global developments significantly impact US equities. 

In Europe, equity valuations have risen without matching earnings or economic growth. The first chart, titled "France: P/E multiples rise as profits/production stagnate," tracks French performance from 2004 through 2014. It highlights a major divergence starting in 2012: while the MSCI France P/E multiple soared from around ten to nearly sixteen, French industrial production remained flat to down at index levels under one hundred, and earnings growth hovered in negative territory. The second chart, "European equity discount to the US," compares the Europe-to-US P/E ratio from 1995 to 2014. It demonstrates that although European equities historically trade at a discount to the US—reaching down to nearly forty percent in 2009 and 2012—the discount has recently narrowed to roughly fifteen percent, which is close to its tightest levels in fifteen years. This narrow discount exists despite Europe's return on equity being four percent lower than that of the US. The author questions how this situation will improve in 2015 given stagnant European profits and the European Central Bank's intention to debase the Euro.

The author points to other mediocrity clouds globally, including China and Japan. China's GDP growth is slowing due to a major pullback in private sector capital spending and high corporate debt, which has had a domino effect on commodity-exporting nations like Australia, Chile, Canada, and South Africa. This trend is visualized in the third chart, "One example of declining private sector activity," which plots China's year-over-year fixed asset investment from 2011 to 2014. The data shows investment by non-state private sector firms plunging from over thirty percent to around fifteen percent, dragging down the total Chinese investment rate from twenty-five percent to around seventeen percent, even as state-controlled investment stayed relatively flat. 

Meanwhile, Japan is struggling to rebound from its April VAT hike. This is illustrated in the final chart, "Japan struggling to recover after VAT hike," which spans January 2013 to July 2014. It tracks a seasonally adjusted Manufacturing PMI on the left axis and producers' shipments of capital goods on the right. Both metrics peaked sharply immediately before the April hike—with the PMI index near fifty-six and capital goods shipments index around one hundred thirteen—before collapsing, with PMI dropping below the expansion threshold of fifty and capital goods shipments falling to around one hundred two. Ultimately, the author notes that while these global economies are not necessarily imploding into recessions, markets are increasingly pricing in the risk that current economic stagnation is permanent.

This page discusses the historical timeline of global energy transitions to contextualize the current shift toward renewable energy. The author observes that while global energy efficiency (energy used per dollar of GDP) has doubled over the last 50 years, total global primary energy consumption is three times higher than it was in 1965. Drawing on the work of Vaclav Smil, a Distinguished Professor Emeritus at the University of Manitoba, the author argues that future transitions will likely be gradual due to sunk capital, behavioral issues, and complex systems, despite the modern urgency of climate change.

The page features a four-panel line chart titled "The Arc of Energy History, 1840 - 2012." Each panel shows the market penetration of an energy source after it reached a 5% share of global demand. The x-axes measure the number of years after this 5% threshold was met, ranging from 0 to 60 years, while the y-axes represent the percentage share of world energy, from 0% to 50%. The first panel shows coal, beginning in 1840, which rose steadily to reach nearly a 50% market share by year 60. The second panel shows oil, beginning in 1915, which reached a 30% share after roughly 35 years and ended near 40% by year 60. The third panel shows natural gas, beginning in 1930, which grew more slowly, reaching about a 25% share by year 60. The final panel shows modern renewables, excluding hydropower, starting in 2012 with a 3% share of global demand. The comparison emphasizes that prior transitions to coal, oil, and natural gas each took several decades to reach a 30% penetration rate.

In the footnotes, the author provides nuance regarding renewable energy adoption, pointing out that while Europe reported that 14% of its primary energy came from renewables in 2012, two-thirds of this was actually from hydropower and wood burning, and 13% came from biofuels. Ultimately, only 3% of Europe's total primary energy came from solar and wind. The page concludes with a biography of Vaclav Smil, highlighting his interdisciplinary research on energy systems and environmental change, his authoring of 35 books, and his recognition as one of Foreign Policy magazine’s top 100 global thinkers, as well as being named by Bill Gates as his favorite author.

This page discusses how the rise of US shale oil production has dramatically lowered and flattened the global marginal cost of oil, positioning US shale as the marginal supplier in the global market. 

The first chart, titled "Shale oil era has reduced estimated future marginal costs," plots the breakeven cost for new projects in USD per barrel (ranging from $20 to $120) against estimated peak cumulative production in millions of barrels per day (ranging from 0 to 35). The chart shows a sequential downward shift in the breakeven cost curves from 2009 through 2014. By 2014, the estimated marginal cost for probable levels of future demand had flattened to approximately $80 per barrel. A dotted line representing the "2014 with cost deflation impact" shows that technological improvements, fewer bottlenecks, and increased competition in oil services could push marginal costs down by an additional $5 to $10 per barrel.

The author notes that while lower marginal costs benefit oil-consuming nations, they pose severe challenges for countries with high fiscal break-even requirements, specifically naming Libya, Iran, Venezuela, and Russia. It also pressures highly indebted quasi-sovereign and private sector oil companies. The top 100 of these companies saw their collective debt rise from $300 billion in 2005 to $1.1 trillion in 2013, leaving many free cash flow negative and ill-equipped to maintain production and capital spending if oil remains at $80 per barrel.

The second chart, "The marginal barrel is now US shale," details the global cost curve for new projects in dollars per barrel (from $20 to $110) against estimated peak cumulative production (up to 45 million barrels per day). It illustrates that low-cost assets like Brazil's Lula field and Northern Iraq sit at the lower end of the curve ($20 to $40), followed by conventional shallower US Gulf reservoirs, Brazil deepwater, and the Utica shale in the $40 to $70 range. US shale plays—including the Bakken, Niobrara, Permian Basin, and Eagle Ford—cluster as the marginal unit of supply at the $75 to $80 range (marked by green diamonds). These US shale projects have effectively displaced more expensive options on the cost curve, such as Russian projects, Nigerian and Angolan deepwater, Norway, Canadian surface-mined heavy oil, and complex US Gulf deepwater reservoirs, which sit above $80 to $100 per barrel.

Looking forward, the author poses a question about how falling oil prices will affect energy independence. If oil prices fell below $70 to $75 on a sustained basis, some US shale operators would have to cut production, slowing the trend toward US energy independence. This potential adjustment period could last one to three years, during which inefficient shale operators would be squeezed out while survivors forced cost reductions through the supply chain. However, the author forecasts that even under this scenario, US energy independence remains achievable on a 2025 time horizon.

This page explores the challenges of investing in clean energy, highlighting that the transition to a renewable energy world is a volatile process characterized by temporary speculative excitement followed by long periods of underperformance. The author observes that while new alternative energy ideas frequently generate immense enthusiasm, very few survive or succeed in the long run, leading to investment returns with far deeper valleys than peaks.

To illustrate this volatility, a line chart shows the rolling one-year excess returns of two key clean energy indices compared against the S&P Small Cap Index from 2003 through 2013. Both the Wilderhill Clean Energy Index and the NYSE Bloomberg Americas Clean Energy Index exhibit sharp cyclical swings relative to the small-cap benchmark. The Wilderhill index, for example, saw its relative excess return spike near 50% in late 2007, only to fall below negative 50% by 2012, highlighting how rapidly these stocks fall in and out of favor.

A detailed performance table further maps this historical underperformance by comparing annualized total returns over three distinct periods starting in 2002, 2005, and 2008. Across almost every timeframe, clean energy benchmarks lagged behind traditional equity and energy indices. Since 2002, the Wilderhill Clean Energy Index lost an annualized 3.0%, while the S&P Small Cap Index gained 11.7% and S&P Small Cap Energy rose 18.6%. Since 2008, the FTSE Environmental Opportunities Renewable & Alternative Energy Index returned a mere 1.0% annualized, vastly trailing the S&P 500's 17.0% return and the S&P Small Cap Energy’s 21.9% return. 

The analysis covers various sectors involved in the clean energy value chain, defining the underlying indices as containing companies focused on solar, wind, bioenergy, energy efficiency, fuel cells, LED screen manufacturing, DC-AC energy conversion, and pollution control. Ultimately, the data indicates that alternative energy equities have significantly trailed the broader market and traditional oil and gas stocks, regardless of which alternative index or starting year is chosen for the comparison.

This J.P. Morgan publication features a market recap of 2013 and 2014, an outlook for 2015, and an introduction to the firm's annual energy paper. Author Michael Cembalest notes that as 2013 drew to a close, market valuations, investor sentiment, and risk-taking were exceptionally elevated, leaving little room for error. This observation is detailed in a table titled Dec 2013 valuation, positioning and sentiment, which tracks historical percentiles for ten metrics. It shows that the S&P 500 median trailing price-to-earnings ratio was in the 83rd percentile since 1979, and the S&P 600 US small-cap trailing P/E was in the 90th percentile since 1995. Sentiment indicators like the NAAIM active managers sentiment and hedge fund net long/short exposure both reached the 99th percentile. Meanwhile, protective and defensive metrics were historically low: implied equity market volatility was in the 22nd percentile since 1990, while hedge fund cash holdings and investment-grade corporate bond spreads were both at the 2nd percentile.

Because of these expensive entry points, 2014 experienced lower market returns than the previous two years. This is illustrated in a line chart titled Subpar growth outside US drags down 2014 portfolio returns, which maps the year-to-date total return of a stylized multi-asset portfolio from 2010 through late October 2014. The stylized portfolio consists of the S&P 500 (21%), S&P 600 Small Cap (9%), MSCI Europe (16%), MSCI Japan (5%), MSCI Emerging Markets (8%), Barclays US Aggregate (20%), JP Morgan Domestic High Yield (5%), Barclays US Treasury Bills (5%), S&P GSCI Commodities (5%), and HFRX Global Hedge Funds (5%). While 2012 and 2013 registered strong double-digit YTD returns, the 2014 trend sits in the low single digits, hovering just above 0% for much of the year and tracking below 2010 levels, though remaining ahead of the negative performance of 2011. Cembalest points out that while US growth and equity markets have held up well, subpar returns on non-US equities and currencies are dragging down the broader portfolio.

For the months ahead, the author forecasts minor improvements, highlighting expected economic resilience in Emerging Asia (excluding China), Poland, and Mexico, a rebound in German automotive manufacturing, and a boost to global retail sales driven by declining oil prices. Although Europe, Japan, and China are considering further fiscal and monetary stimulus, a footnote cautions that these tools are showing diminishing returns; for instance, the declining Japanese Yen has not boosted real exports, European Central Bank interventions have not revived weak private-sector bank lending, and outstanding Chinese bank loans as a percentage of GDP are falling. Given this constrained environment, the author projects another single-digit return year for portfolios in 2015. 

Finally, the page introduces the annual energy paper, outlining its core topics: the long-term history of energy and the transition to renewable sources, investment prospects in renewable energy equities, the impact of US shale oil on domestic energy independence, and technological trends in nuclear, wind, solar, and electricity storage.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication analyzes the progress and hurdles in achieving a 20 percent US wind energy penetration by 2030, noting that wind currently provides about 4 percent of US electricity. Drawing on data from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the author highlights several positive trends, including declining upfront capital costs, dropping rates of involuntary wind curtailment, and expanding transmission infrastructure. A key example of grid success is the completion of 3,600 miles of transmission lines for the Texas Competitive Renewable Energy Zone in 2013, which ERCOT reports has largely solved wind-related congestion between West Texas and other areas. Despite technological advancements like taller hubs and larger rotors, overall capacity factors have remained steady rather than rising because newer projects are increasingly being built in less optimal, less windy locations, offsetting efficiency gains.

To support these arguments, the page features five charts. The first chart, showing capacity-weighted project costs in 2013 dollars per kilowatt from 1983 to 2013, illustrates a long-term downward trend, falling from over $5,000 in 1983 to below $2,000 in recent years, despite a brief uptick around 2009. The second chart tracks involuntary curtailment as a percentage of annual potential wind generation from 2007 to 2013, showing that curtailment peaked at approximately 9 percent in 2009 before declining sharply to roughly 2 percent by 2013. The third chart details transmission lines added in miles from 2009 to 2013, categorized by voltage levels of 500 kilovolts, 345 kilovolts, and 230 kilovolts or less. It highlights a dramatic ramp-up in grid deployment, peaking at nearly 3,500 miles added in 2013, dominated heavily by 345 kilovolt lines. The fourth chart displays the average 2013 capacity factor of US wind fleets by their year of construction from 2000 to 2012, showing stable performance consistently hovering between 30 percent and 35 percent. The final chart explains this flat capacity trend by mapping the windiness of project locations using an index of wind quality at 80 meters, with 1998 to 1999 as the baseline of 100. This index reveals a steady decline from near 100 down to about 83 in 2012, signaling that developers have increasingly built in less windy locations, with only a modest rebound to around 87 in 2013 as new transmission lines began enabling projects in windier, more remote areas.

This page from Eye on the Market analyzes the future viability and challenges of wind energy in the United States, specifically exploring the potential fallout if federal tax subsidies lapse permanently. The author posits that without these subsidies, power purchase agreement prices would likely rise to between 5.5 and 6.0 cents per kilowatt-hour, potentially ending the need for tax equity partners. Although utilities might still find these prices attractive compared to volatile natural gas alternatives, they may delay signing new contracts in hopes that subsidies are eventually reintroduced. The author also notes ongoing arguments that wind generation should qualify for tax-advantaged Master Limited Partnership status, a benefit currently enjoyed by the natural gas industry to lower distribution costs but remains unavailable to power generation companies.

Ultimately, the analysis argues that the next decade is highly uncertain for wind compared to the prior one due to several compounding factors. Key headwinds include the prolonged expiration of the Production Tax Credit—marking its longest lapse since 1992—and persistently low natural gas prices, which fell below 6 dollars in 2009 and have averaged 4 dollars since, lowering the benchmark break-even cost for wind. Additionally, US electricity demand is growing at a slow rate of just 1 percent due to sub-trend GDP growth and increased efficiencies. Federal policy also lacks a carbon tax, a federally binding Renewable Portfolio Standard, or a national plan to integrate the electricity grid. While transmission investment is rising, local and regional grid capacity in wind-rich states like Wyoming and Montana remains insufficient to incentivize further development. 

To illustrate the regulatory landscape, the page features a map of the United States detailing Binding and Non-Binding Renewable Energy Portfolio Standards by state, using August 2014 data from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The map distinguishes between states with mandatory standards, shaded in blue, and those with non-binding goals, shaded in yellow. Highly ambitious mandatory targets include California's 33 percent by 2020, Maine's 40 percent by 2017, Colorado's 30 percent by 2020 for investor-owned utilities, and Hawaii's 40 percent by 2030. Examples of non-binding goals include Alaska's 50 percent by 2025 and North and South Dakota's 10 percent by 2015. The author emphasizes that many states are already well on their way to meeting their standards, and very few have adopted targets as high as California's. 

A detailed footnote highlights the 1.2 billion dollar TresAmigas project in Clovis, New Mexico, which aims to link the western, Texas, and eastern US grids for the first time. However, its initial phase is limited to an exchange capacity of 750 megawatts—roughly equivalent to the output of a single large coal plant—and is hindered by aging transmission systems subject to congestion, illustrating that broader grid integration still lacks national planning and government financial guarantees.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the dual trends of rising capacity factors and rapidly falling capital costs in solar energy, as well as the methodological difficulties of calculating consistent levelized costs. The author notes that while solar photovoltaic projects in low-irradiance areas with fixed-tilt panels generate capacity factors in the high teens, newer projects in the Southwest utilize single-axis tracking and DC panel over-building to achieve net capacity factors that are 10% to 12% higher. 

To illustrate these capacity trends, a table details a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory sample set of 64 projects totaling 1.5 gigawatts of capacity from the 2007 to 2012 vintage. Under low solar energy conditions of under 5 kilowatt-hours per square meter per day, a fixed-tilt system with low DC over-building yields a 17% net capacity factor, which increases to 19% with high DC over-building and 23% with single-axis tracking. In medium-irradiance conditions of 5 to 7 kilowatt-hours per square meter per day, the capacity factor ranges from 23% for low DC over-building with fixed-tilt up to 28% for single-axis tracking with high DC over-building. In high-irradiance areas of 7 or more kilowatt-hours per square meter per day, capacity factors reach 29% for fixed-tilt systems and up to 31% for single-axis tracking systems with high over-building. An accompanying text box adds perspective by comparing this 1.5 gigawatt solar sample set to the 6.3 gigawatts of total installed solar power in the US at the end of 2013, noting that solar capacity data remains much scarcer than wind capacity data.

The author stresses that levelized cost remains a moving target because capital cost estimates vary widely depending on the provider and methodology. A second table displays PV solar capital cost estimates converted to dollars per kilowatt-AC using a standard 1.25 DC-to-AC ratio. Completed projects from 2013 show higher, more consistent historical figures, with the Energy Information Administration reporting $3,873, the National Renewable Energy Laboratory reporting $3,750, and LBNL reporting $3,700. In contrast, estimates for future projects vary widely: the EIA models a $3,046 cost for 2019 delivery, while 2014-start estimates for crystalline silicon systems range from Bloomberg New Energy Finance at $2,463 and NREL at $2,250 down to Lazard’s outlier estimate of $1,750. 

Additionally, the author notes that operation and maintenance expenses are difficult to track accurately. A footnote cites a paper from the Syracuse Biophysical Economics Conference estimating that unexpected operating and maintenance expenses for solar plants in Spain could reduce the energy return on investment from an expected 8 times down to just 3 times.

This page, titled "The sun also rises: an early look at solar power in the US," examines the current state, future potential, and cost dynamics of solar power in the United States, placing it in a global context. The author notes that despite sunlight's immense theoretical potential, real-world adoption has been slower than wind, though falling component costs and subsidies have recently accelerated utility-scale photovoltaic and concentrated solar power. 

Currently, the United States gets only 0.2% of its electricity from utility-scale and large commercial solar installations over 1 megawatt, which represents 6.3 gigawatts of capacity. A table illustrating US electricity generation scenarios shows that even under optimistic forecasts, solar's contribution will remain modest. Under EIA projected additions of 9 gigawatts, solar's share is forecast to reach 0.6% by 2016, while SEIA projected additions of 16 gigawatts would bring it to 0.9%. Even if the entire 40-gigawatt queue of planned projects from late 2013 were completed, the share would rise to just 2.0%, leaving solar behind biomass. 

An international comparison table shows that the United States lags far behind major European nations in solar penetration. Italy leads with solar producing 7.8% of its total electricity, followed by Germany at 4.7%, Spain at 4.6%, Bulgaria and Greece at 3.2% each, the Czech Republic at 2.4%, and Belgium at 2.3%. Other notable shares include Slovakia at 2.1%, Denmark and Australia at 1.5% each, and Japan at 1.0%. The text points out that the rapid solar growth in the leading European countries—which averaged 65% annually from 2005 to 2012—has slowed dramatically to just 9% in 2013 as generous feed-in tariffs and subsidies are phased out due to budget constraints.

US solar installation growth is driven by subsidies, Renewable Portfolio Standards, and a historical decline in photovoltaic upfront capital costs. A bar chart from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory tracks these upfront capital costs for a modeled 185-megawatt project from 2009 to 2013. Total capital costs plummeted from over $4,000 per kilowatt-DC in 2009 to under $2,000 in 2013. This decline was heavily concentrated in module costs, which fell from roughly $2,000 to around $400. Inverter costs remained low and relatively flat, while "balance of system" costs—comprising labor, supply chain, permitting, and taxes—declined more modestly from about $1,900 to roughly $1,200, remaining the largest cost component. 

A line chart from Bloomberg confirms that silicon and thin-film module prices are leveling out. Between 2010 and 2014, the average silicon module price fell from nearly $2,000 per kilowatt-DC to around $700, while the average thin-film module fell from approximately $1,400 to the same $700 level. Both lines show a clear plateau starting in 2013, leading the author to state that substantial component cost declines are not expected in the near future. Footnotes clarify that solar project capacity is typically calculated in DC terms, which are higher than AC terms due to inverter conversion losses, and note that smaller residential and commercial systems under 1 megawatt have total capacity roughly equal to larger utility-scale projects but operate with lower capacity factors.

This page examines the outlook for solar energy, specifically discussing subsidy structures, pricing trends, and geographic limitations in the United States and Europe. The author argues that US solar module prices are unlikely to fall significantly further due to consolidation in China and the imposition of US tariffs on Chinese and Taiwanese panels in June 2014. Additionally, US subsidies face a major hurdle as the Investment Tax Credit for solar is scheduled to drop from 30% to 10% in January 2017, which the Energy Information Administration forecasts will trigger a dramatic decline in installations from 2.6 gigawatts in 2016 to just 0.1 gigawatts in 2017. The author suggests that even with potential multi-year extensions of these subsidies, it will take considerable time and grid investment for solar to account for 5% of US electricity generation, constrained further by the need for cost-effective electricity storage to handle solar's intermittency.

Centered on the page is a color-coded map of the United States detailing a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory sample set of utility-scale solar projects over 5 megawatts built between 2010 and 2013. The map correlates these project locations—categorized by technology type such as fixed-tilt crystalline silicon, fixed-tilt thin-film, tracking systems, concentrated photovoltaic, and concentrated solar power—against the country's solar resource quality. The direct normal irradiance ranges from under 4.0 kilowatt-hours per square meter per day in yellow-shaded northern regions to over 7.5 in deep red-shaded southwestern regions. The map illustrates a high concentration of tracking and concentrated solar systems in the high-irradiance desert Southwest, particularly in California and Arizona.

Transitioning to Europe, the text describes how feed-in tariffs initially fueled a 65% annual solar capacity growth rate from 2005 to 2012, highlighting major spending in Spain, Italy, and Germany. However, budget cuts stemming from the European debt crisis drastically altered the landscape. Spain ended its feed-in tariffs, leading to a collapse in solar sector employment from 60,000 to 5,000, while Italy reduced its program and levied a 10.5% tax on large producers. In Germany, high renewable energy surcharges now comprise about 18% of household electric bills, prompting utility companies like Eon and RWE to close power stations. The section concludes that European solar capacity growth slowed to 9% in 2013, with the European Photovoltaic Industry Association forecasting a low-end growth rate of 8% through 2018.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication discusses the critical challenge of matching electricity supply with demand as renewable energy capacity expands, focusing on the urgent need for cost-effective energy storage. The author argues that because wind and solar generation do not naturally align with demand patterns, an grid without storage forces inefficient compromises, such as curtailing natural gas or coal, wasting renewable energy through curtailment, maintaining expensive back-up peaker plants, or funding costly grid expansions. 

To illustrate these supply-demand mismatches, the page presents two charts. The first, using data from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, compares Texas electricity demand to actual wind output over a week in August 2011. The blue demand line peaks during midday heat at around 60 to 65 gigawatts, while dropping to 40 to 45 gigawatts at night. In contrast, the brown wind output line, measured on a secondary scale of 0 to 6 gigawatts, peaks primarily overnight when demand is lowest, highlighting the regional mismatch. 

The second chart, from the California Independent System Operator, illustrates how California's growing solar capacity creates the famous "duck curve," showing the hourly baseload power required on March 31 across different years. In 2012, the mid-day baseload requirement was relatively flat at around 20 gigawatts. However, as solar capacity grew through 2013, 2014, 2015, and into a projected 2020, midday net demand plummeted to under 14 gigawatts as solar flooded the grid, only to require a massive and rapid ramp-up to 24 gigawatts in the early evening as the sun set. 

The text transitions to explain that currently, global electricity storage capacity is equivalent to just 2% of total installed generation. Pumped storage, which involves pumping water uphill to a reservoir during low-demand periods and releasing it through turbines during peak times, represents 99% of all global stored electricity, operating at 70% to 85% efficiency according to the Electric Power Research Institute. 

An aerial photograph depicts the Seneca pumped storage and hydroelectric facility in Warren County, Pennsylvania. A footnote explains that a typical reservoir one kilometer in diameter and 25 meters deep holds roughly 10,000 megawatt-hours of electricity, noting for scale that Ann Arbor, Michigan, uses 5,000 megawatt-hours per day, while Dallas, Texas, uses 50,000.
