The text highlights that activist campaign returns are characterized by massive dispersion, with a standard deviation of 218 percent between 1994 and 2013, far exceeding the typical 22 percent to 62 percent range seen for individual S&P 500 stocks. 

The first chart on the page, "Distribution of absolute returns from activist events" using 13D Monitor data from 1994 to 2014, visualizes this dispersion. The frequency distribution of individual campaign returns is heavily right-skewed. The 15th percentile of returns lies near negative 50 percent, and the median return is positive but modest. Due to a small number of extremely high-performing campaigns—visualized by a spike in the 500 percent plus bucket—the average return is pulled to a level three times higher than the median return. The author concludes that while activism is an interesting, less-correlated source of return, it is highly volatile, and direct investment yields significantly better results than attempting to piggyback on campaigns after public disclosure.

The second section of the page explores the academic debate surrounding the long-term value of activism, presenting evidence of improved operating metrics and valuation multiples. The accompanying line chart, "Activism and improved operating and share price performance," plots activist-targeted company statistics relative to industry averages from the event year through five subsequent years (T+1 to T+5), based on a 2013 study by Lucian Bebchuk of Harvard and colleagues. The chart tracks two metrics: the relative return on assets on the left axis and Relative Tobin’s Q (representing the market-to-book ratio) on the right axis. In the event year, targeted companies underperform their industry peers significantly, with relative return on assets at nearly negative 2.8 percent and relative Tobin's Q near negative 1.5 percent. Following activist intervention, these gaps close substantially. The relative return on assets improves sharply to around negative 1.0 percent by year T+1 and remains stable, while the relative Tobin’s Q experiences a delayed rise, climbing to about negative 1.0 percent by year T+4 before stabilizing. The author adds that academic research supports a causal link, showing that these improvements do not systematically follow large passive stock purchases, but do occur after passive blockholders transition to active roles.

In this section, titled "Getting started," the publication highlights the extreme and characteristic volatility of oil as a commodity, noting that while price fluctuations of plus or minus 20% are frequent, sharper declines of 35% to 40% are less common, having occurred only seven times since 1974. Because current inventory levels are exceptionally high, the author forecasts that a rapid, V-shaped recovery is unlikely. Consequently, the analysis focuses on the broader market implications of oil prices remaining below $70 per barrel for a sustained period of three to four years.

These points are supported by three charts and one table. The first line chart tracks WTI Crude prices in USD per barrel from 2005 to early 2015, showing its rise from $60 to $140, its drop back to $40 during the financial crisis, and its subsequent recovery and sharp decline at the end of 2014. An accompanying table outlines annualized volatility from 2007 to 2009 to show that oil is more volatile than other energy, metal, and agricultural commodities. In this table, oil leads with 54% volatility, followed by natural gas at 51%, gasoline at 50%, lumber at 46%, copper at 43%, corn at 38%, soybeans at 33%, platinum at 32%, zinc at 30%, gold at 25%, and aluminum at 18%.

A second line chart compares WTI Crude and retail gasoline prices from January 2013 to January 2015, plotting oil on the left axis from $40 to $110 per barrel and gasoline on the right axis from $2.00 to $4.00 per gallon. This chart illustrates how gasoline tracked the dramatic plunge of crude oil starting in mid-2014, with both reaching multi-year lows by January 2015. Finally, a bar chart displays annual US crude inventories, excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, from 1990 to 2014. It reveals that US inventories steadily climbed after 2011, peaking at their highest level since 1990 at nearly 390 million barrels by December 2014, illustrating the supply glut that underpins the author's expectation of a prolonged period of low oil prices.

This page analyzes the potential systemic impacts of the sharp decline in oil prices in late 2014, arguing that the downturn's severity was worsened because the global energy sector was unprepared and heavily indebted. Believing in a "Peak Oil" scenario, the world’s largest energy companies increased their debt by one trillion dollars starting in 2003 when oil was at thirty dollars a barrel. Even before prices crashed, high extraction costs had already depressed the free cash flows of these companies. 

To illustrate this vulnerability, a dual-axis line chart displays the fundamentals of the top one hundred global energy companies from 2002 to 2014. It shows total industry debt rising from around two hundred and fifty billion dollars in 2002 to over one trillion dollars in 2014, while the percentage of companies with positive free cash flow plummeted from a peak of about seventy-five percent in 2005 to nearly fifty percent by 2013. A corresponding table identifies the top twenty energy companies by outstanding debt as of the third quarter of 2014, led by Petrobras, PetroChina, Rosneft, Total, China Petroleum, Gazprom, BP, Royal Dutch Shell, Kinder Morgan, and Eni, alongside other majors such as Statoil, Enbridge, JX Holdings, Chevron, TransCanada, Exxon Mobil, ConocoPhillips, Williams Cos, Repsol, and BG Group.

The commentary draws a historical parallel to the 1980s oil crash, which triggered a wave of regional bank failures and worsened the U.S. Savings and Loan crisis. A second chart tracks bank failures in Texas versus the rest of the United States from 1975 to 1995 alongside crude oil prices. As crude oil fell from a peak near forty dollars per barrel to under fifteen dollars by 1986, bank failures surged, with Texas institutions bearing the brunt of the damage, peaking at hundreds of failures in the late 1980s. While the author notes that modern banks have less direct oil exposure than in the 1980s—shifting the primary risk to high-yield bond investors—the historical example illustrates the dangers of sudden price declines following a debt-fueled capital spending boom.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the substantial improvements in global oil intensity—defined as the barrels of oil required to generate a unit of GDP—independent of broader economic growth levels. The author argues that rising fuel economy standards and structural shifts, rather than just weak growth, are driving down global oil demand.

The first chart, "Decline in oil intensity across economies" (indexed to 2005=100), shows a substantial downward trajectory for multiple nations from 2005 to 2014. Notably, China's oil intensity declined by approximately 35%, dropping at an annual rate of 4.3% to index around 65 by 2014. Other developed economies also saw marked improvements over this decade, with Taiwan reaching index levels near 66, Southern European nations like Italy, Portugal, and Spain reaching around 75, the United Kingdom near 78, and Japan, the United States, and France clustering around 81. 

A major driver for this trend is explored in the second chart, "Actual and projected fuel economy for new passenger vehicles by country," which plots historical and projected miles per gallon from 2000 to 2025 across key regions including the European Union, South Korea, China, the United States, and Japan. All featured regions show steep upward projections in fuel economy standards. For example, the European Union is projected to approach nearly 60 miles per gallon by 2021, South Korea and China are set for dramatic climbs to around 55 and 50 miles per gallon respectively by 2020, and the United States is projected to steadily rise to over 50 miles per gallon by 2025. 

The commentary notes that while the Energy Information Administration also projects energy intensity improvements across residential, commercial, and industrial sectors, the benefits from the transportation sector are significantly larger than those expected from electricity intensity. Furthermore, the author points out that outside of the United States, declining subsidies and price controls, conservation efforts, improvements in internal combustion engines, and fuel-switching away from petroleum in electricity generation are all contributing to the persistent decline in global oil intensity.

This page analyzes the primary supply-side dynamics driving the collapse in oil prices, focusing on a production rebound in unstable OPEC nations and Saudi Arabia's refusal to act as a swing producer. Despite severe military, economic, and social challenges, OPEC's most turbulent nations—specifically Libya, Iraq, Iran, and Nigeria—managed an unexpected production recovery of one million barrels per day in late 2014, reversing a sharp year-over-year decline seen during 2013. This trend is detailed in a chart titled "Production rebound in turbulent OPEC countries," which maps year-over-year production changes in thousands of barrels per day from early 2013 to late 2014. The chart reveals that total production change troughed at nearly negative 1.5 million barrels per day in late 2013 before recovering to positive growth in late 2014. 

At the same time, overall OPEC production has consistently run above its stated targets. A chart titled "OPEC producing more than its quota" plots OPEC output in millions of barrels per day against the group's quota from 2010 through 2014. It demonstrates that production has consistently exceeded the quota line of roughly 30 million barrels per day for the vast majority of the period since late 2011, peaking near 32 million barrels per day in late 2012. 

Historically, Saudi Arabia would counteract such oversupply to stabilize prices, but the author highlights that they are no longer willing to play this swing producer role. A supporting table titled "Saudi Arabia refusing swing producer role this time around" compares the percentage decline in oil prices and output across five major market downturns. In previous crises, Saudi Arabia cut its output aggressively to support prices, slashing production by 14.1% during the 1996-1999 crash, 19.2% in 2000-2002, 8.8% in 2006-2007, and 18.1% in 2008-2009. However, during the 2014-2015 cycle, despite a severe 59.5% plunge in the price of oil, Saudi Arabia cut its output by only 3.3%, while total OPEC output declined by just 2.4%. Consequently, the author notes that without Saudi cooperation, unilateral efforts by countries like Iran and Venezuela will do little to alter the current downward pressure on oil prices.

This analysis focuses on the demand-side factors driving the decline in global oil prices. The author argues that weak global GDP growth and negative economic growth surprises outside the United States have been major culprits, particularly a structural slowdown in China and historically weak growth in Europe. The text notes that Europe is experiencing its slowest trend growth—outside of wartime—in approximately 100 years. Furthermore, the prominent 2010 spike in Chinese oil demand is characterized as an artificial, unsustainable byproduct of a massive fiscal stimulus and strategic reserve accumulation rather than organic economic demand. 

Five charts support these observations. The first chart, titled "Lower GDP growth only explains part of the demand decline," plots year-over-year percentage changes from 2001 to 2015. It compares global GDP growth to oil demand alongside an EIA forecast. The data shows that while global GDP growth stabilized around 3% to 4% after 2010, oil demand growth plummeted from a peak of nearly 4% down to 0% by 2014, illustrating that slower GDP growth is only a partial explanation for the demand drop. 

The second chart, titled "Global growth expectations falling with oil prices," tracks Brent crude oil in USD per barrel against the global growth ex-US surprise index from 2006 to late 2014. It highlights a tight correlation between the two, with Brent crude collapsing toward $50 per barrel as the ex-US surprise index fell sharply from over 117 to around 108 by the end of 2014. 

The third chart, "Slowing growth of the 'old' China," depicts year-over-year real growth percentages from 2004 to 2014 for both industrial production and GDP. Following a post-recession rebound in 2010 where industrial production neared 18% and GDP reached 12%, both metrics steadily declined, with GDP dropping to about 7% and industrial production to 8% by the end of 2014. 

The fourth chart, "Annual growth in Chinese crude oil demand," measures growth in thousands of barrels per day from 2003 to 2014. It visualizes the massive 2010 spike, which approached 1,000 thousand barrels per day due to strategic reserve accumulation and the aftermath of the 2009 stimulus, before falling back to a more modest level of roughly 400 thousand barrels per day in 2014. 

The final chart, titled "Remembrance of things past: a return to 19th century stagnation in Europe," displays the six-year percentage change in real GDP for Italy, France, and Spain from 1825 through the mid-2000s, excluding wartime and subsequent rebuilding periods. The chart shows that by the end of the data series, six-year real GDP growth for these European nations had plummeted to near 0% or negative territory, representing a return to stagnation levels last seen in the nineteenth century.

This page analyzes the economic benefits of lower oil prices on the United States economy, balancing the positive impacts of increased household and corporate disposable income against the negative impacts of reduced oil-related capital spending. The author notes that US exploration and production stocks have already announced 2015 capital spending reductions of 10% to 15%, citing data from Empirical Research Partners. Despite this drag, J.P. Morgan's analysis forecasts a modest net positive economic impact on US GDP. When oil prices were at $65, the estimated net GDP boost was 0.1% to 0.4%. However, if West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil prices fall to the $40 to $45 range, the net positive effect on 2015 and 2016 GDP could expand by an additional 0.10% to 0.15%.

The page includes a visual breakdown titled "Estimated effects of $65 oil on US GDP." This diagram illustrates that a consumption benefit of 0.5% to 0.6% of GDP is counteracted by a capital spending drag of -0.5% to -0.2%, yielding a net positive effect of 0.1% to 0.4%. To provide context for the capital spending drag, a companion pie chart titled "Capital spending detail" shows that out of $1.5 trillion in total annual US business spending on equipment and structures, the oil, gas, and mining sectors account for 11.1%, or $171 billion.

The author concludes with a timeline prediction for when these net benefits will materialize in US economic data. Based on historical trends from prior oil price declines, the lag times are estimated at 6 to 7 months for stronger personal consumption, 7 to 9 months for higher non-energy-related capital spending, and 10 to 12 months for stronger employment growth. Given that oil prices began falling in autumn 2014, J.P. Morgan expects these positive impacts to start appearing in US economic indicators by mid-2015.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, published in January 2015, discusses the performance and valuation of the energy sector following a steep decline in oil prices. The author examines whether energy stocks have become cheap enough to buy, arguing that current cheapness is deceptive because it is based on trailing twelve-month cash flows from when oil was still around $90 per barrel. Ultimately, the author concludes that energy stocks are only attractive if oil prices recover to approximately $75 per barrel over the next two to three years.

A bar chart titled "Energy down across the board" illustrates the percentage change in performance for various energy sub-industries since the 2014 oil peak. While the broader Russell 1000 index gained 5%, all energy sub-industries declined. Pipelines fell by 6%, refiners by 9%, and integrated oil companies by 14%. The broader Russell 1000 Energy index dropped by 22%, followed by steeper declines in crude producers at negative 31%, equipment and services at negative 34%, coal at negative 40%, and offshore drillers as the worst performers at negative 47%. 

To assess potential rebounds, a table titled "Oil price behavior after prior 35%+ declines" compares seven historical oil drawdowns since 1984, indexing the trough of each decline to 100. The table lists the peak price, trough, and subsequent performance in years one, two, and three, along with the recovery type. For example, during the 1984–1986 decline, the peak index was 222, and the recovery was U-shaped, reaching 121 by year three. The 1987–1988 and 1997–1998 declines saw V-shaped recoveries, with the latter surging to an index level of 275 in the first year and 288 in the second year. The 2008–2009 decline featured a peak index of 375 and followed a U-shaped recovery to 319 by year three. The ongoing 2014–Today cycle shows a peak index of 214 and a trough of 100, with subsequent years marked as not applicable. The author notes that while V-shaped recoveries do occur, they rarely manifest during the first year after a collapse. 

In terms of valuation, the text points out that last December, large-cap oil and oil service companies were trading near historic lows, at the 15th and 9th percentiles of their historical range. Drawing a parallel to the severe energy selloff of the mid-1980s, the author compares current valuations to July 1986. Currently, price-to-book ratios have fallen to 0.5x relative to the overall market, matching the level seen in July 1986. Similarly, relative price-to-sales ratios are at 0.6x today, which is very close to the 0.5x ratio recorded in July 1986.

This page analyzes the viability of US shale oil production in the face of declining oil prices, drawing a key distinction between existing and future production. The author argues that existing production is relatively insulated from price drops because it only needs to cover operating costs, which exclude upfront capital costs and typically fall below $40 per barrel. Consequently, operating wells will likely continue pumping until depleted, while future production—which must cover both operating and capital costs—is more vulnerable. Evaluating marginal viability requires looking at the forward curve rather than the spot market, leading the author to forecast that oil prices will rise over the next two years as higher-cost locations are depleted and not replaced.

Three key charts support this analysis. The first chart, titled "WTI crude oil futures curve," plots USD per barrel against months until delivery up to 60 months out. It shows three curves: six months ago, one month ago, and the current curve. The current curve has dropped dramatically from six months prior, starting near $47 per barrel and rising gradually to around $65 at 60 months, whereas the older curve remained high, between $85 and $100. 

The second chart, titled "Cash costs of current production," tracks cumulative global oil production in millions of barrels per day against operating costs in USD per barrel, both with and without royalties. It shows that massive low-cost producers like Saudi Arabia, Iraq, and Iran have operating costs below $10 per barrel, while regions like Mexico, China, the US, Russia, and the UK scale up to around $20 to $30 per barrel. The most expensive production, Canada oil sands and Venezuela, tops out around $40 to $50 per barrel, reinforcing the point that most global production remains profitable on an operating basis even at lower prices.

The final chart, titled "Breakeven prices by region and formation," presents full lifecycle breakeven costs in dollars per barrel for dozens of shale formations, comparing them against a vertical dashed line indicating a two-year forward WTI price of $60. Low-cost formations like Bakken - Sanish ($34), Bakken - Mountrail ($41), and Permian - Bone Spring ($45) sit comfortably below the line. Conversely, a large segment of formations, including Eagle Ford ($61), Three Forks - Sanish ($62), and Three Forks - McKenzie ($91), require prices above $60 to justify future drilling. Although the chart suggests that the lower third of these shale locations could stop future production at $60 oil, the author notes that anticipated cost reductions may eventually bring breakeven costs down across many of these locations.

This page analyzes the broader sector consequences of falling oil prices, observing that while lower oil prices typically boost consumer sectors, this expected upward revision has not yet materialized in 2015 consensus earnings forecasts despite a massive decline in projected energy sector earnings. 

The analysis begins with a table tracking sector outperformance relative to the market following five historical occasions since 1970 where oil prices declined by 40%. The data shows that Consumer Discretionary stocks outperformed the market more consistently than any other sector, doing so in all 5 instances over both the subsequent six-month and one-year periods. Other relatively strong performers include Basic Materials (outperforming 4 times in the subsequent six months and 3 times in the subsequent year) and Consumer Staples (outperforming 3 times in both periods), while Industrials fared the worst over the longer term, outperforming zero times in the subsequent year.

This historical relationship is further illustrated in a horizontal bar chart modeling sector earnings growth sensitivity to oil price changes between 2000 and 2014. The chart estimates the percentage response in US earnings growth to a 1% decline in oil prices, controlling for the business cycle and other factors. It shows that Consumer Discretionary and Consumer Staples earnings benefit the most, growing by approximately 0.25% and 0.20% respectively for every 1% drop in oil. Utilities and Telecom also show positive sensitivities. Conversely, Energy earnings growth experiences a severe negative impact of roughly -0.85%, while IT, Materials, and Industrials also see minor negative impacts.

Despite these historical patterns, the page highlights a disconnect in current market expectations using a line chart tracking 2015 calendar year EPS forecasts indexed to December 31, 2013. While the overall S&P 500 forecast remains stable near 100, the Energy sector EPS forecast plummeted from about 100 in mid-2014 to roughly 55 by December 2014. However, the EPS forecasts for Consumer Discretionary and Consumer Staples have not yet picked up, remaining flat or slightly declining over the same period. The author notes that mass-market retailers, who are typically the primary beneficiaries of increased disposable consumer income, are already trading at P/E multiples that are well above the market, approaching their highest relative premiums of the last 15 years.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market argues that an impending hiring slowdown in the energy sector will not significantly derail the broader US job market because energy-related jobs have comprised only a tiny fraction of post-recession employment gains. Specifically, of the roughly 10 million jobs created since the labor market trough in February 2010, energy-related positions represent only 3%. 

This is illustrated in the first chart, "Energy jobs are a very small share of recent US job gains," which breaks down the 9,800,000 total jobs added since February 2010. Core oil and gas extraction accounts for 198,000 jobs (2%), closely-related energy industries account for 82,000 jobs (1%), and other non-energy industries make up the vast majority at 9,520,000 jobs (97%). 

The author acknowledges that while energy jobs have had a strong multiplier effect on overall employment growth in North Dakota and Texas, this dynamic is inconsistent across other energy-producing states. A scatter plot titled "Inconsistent multiplier effect from oil & gas job growth" compares the annualized growth rate of total jobs since 2009 against the energy intensity of each state's job market. North Dakota exhibits high overall job growth of over 4.0% with moderate energy intensity, and Texas sits above 2.0% job growth. However, other highly energy-intensive states like Oklahoma, Wyoming, West Virginia, and Louisiana show overall job growth closer to or even below the national average growth line of approximately 1.5%.

A slowdown in the energy sector is indeed on the horizon, as detailed in the chart "Energy companies are likely to begin reducing payrolls." This dual-axis line chart tracks the year-over-year percentage change in oil industry payrolls alongside the year-over-year percentage change in WTI Crude Prices advanced by nine months from 1990 to 2014. The historical tracking shows a very tight relationship, signaling that the recent steep drop in oil prices will soon drag oil industry payroll growth deep into negative territory.

Nevertheless, the final chart, "Fastest pace of employment gains since 2000," demonstrates that the rest of the US economy is strong enough to absorb this shock. This dual-axis chart plots the six-month moving average of non-farm payroll changes alongside the job openings rate from 2000 to late 2014. With non-farm payroll monthly gains rising well above 200,000 and the job openings rate climbing toward 3.5%, the broader US labor market is growing at its fastest pace in fourteen years, making it highly resilient to a localized slowdown in energy hiring.

This page analyzes the potential long-term impact of lower oil prices on the United States natural gas industry, arguing that the threat of users switching from natural gas to petroleum products is overstated. The author asserts that high switching costs, a lack of infrastructure (such as pipeline availability and the cost of converting vehicles to compressed natural gas), and favorable pricing protect current natural gas demand. 

To support this, the page includes three charts. The first line chart compares the price of West Texas Intermediate Crude, measured on the left axis from $40 to $110 per barrel, with natural gas prices based on Henry Hub, measured on the right axis from $2.50 to $6.50 per MMBtu, spanning January 2013 to January 2015. It illustrates that natural gas prices remained firm even as WTI crude fell from $108 to $75, though gas prices eventually declined once oil broke below $70. The second line chart tracks the price ratio of natural gas to propane at their respective hubs from 2002 to late 2014 on a scale from 0.0x to 1.2x. It shows that even after a forty-percent drop in propane and oil, natural gas remains significantly cheaper per MMBtu, with the price ratio ending around 0.6x.

The final visual is a stacked bar chart showing US electricity generating capacity additions in gigawatts from 1985 through 2030, categorized by fuel type such as coal, nuclear, natural gas, wind, solar, and other renewables. The chart identifies historic phases: the nuclear era ending in the late 1980s; a massive debt-fueled natural gas boom-bust that peaked above 50 gigawatts of annual additions around 2002; and a subsidy-fueled wind power expansion in the late 2000s and early 2010s that subsided as wind subsidies lapsed. 

Looking forward, the page highlights the Energy Information Administration forecast, which shows that future capacity additions through 2030 will be overwhelmingly dominated by natural gas. The EIA projects 185 gigawatts of new electricity generation capacity from 2014 to 2030, with seventy-five percent expected to come from natural gas as it takes market share from coal, which faces strict emissions rules, and nuclear, which faces rising costs. The author concludes that while gas production volumes may decline due to lower spending on wet shale plays, electricity generation will remain the primary driver for the industry, making federal and localized fracking rules a larger potential obstacle than lower oil prices.

This page analyzes the impact of the mid-2010s oil price decline on the high-yield bond market and US banking sector. The author presents a mixed outlook: the good news is that US banks are less exposed to oil price declines than in previous eras like the 1980s, because modern US oil and gas producers rely primarily on the high-yield bond market rather than bank loans for debt. The bad news is that energy companies have grown to represent an increasingly massive portion of the high-yield bond market, climbing from just 4% of the market in 2000 to nearly 20% by 2014, leaving the broader credit market vulnerable to energy sector distress.

This transition of debt sourcing is illustrated in a chart titled Energy Debt Mostly Sourced from High Yield Market, which plots various debt types as a percentage of shareholders' equity and total debt from 2000 to 2014. The data shows bank loans steadily declining from over 20% in 2000 to around 10% in 2014, while other debt—including bonds and commercial paper—remained dominant, fluctuating between 30% and 45% and driving total debt to around 50% by the end of the period. A companion chart, Growing Impact of High Yield Energy Companies, tracks issuance from 1996 to 2014. It shows that high-yield issuance by energy companies surged to nearly 60 billion USD by 2014, representing roughly 18% of total annual high-yield issuance, up from low single digits in the early 2000s.

The consequence of this heavy concentration is explored in two subsequent charts detailing the pressure on credit spreads. The chart High Yield Under Pressure plots basis point spreads to worst from January 2012 to January 2015. While the overall JPM Domestic High Yield index remained relatively stable between 400 and 500 basis points, both the JPM Domestic High Yield Energy index and the Bloomberg USD High Yield Energy index spiked dramatically starting in mid-2014, with the JPM energy index climbing past 800 basis points and the Bloomberg energy index exceeding 1,000 basis points by January 2015. 

To contextualize this spike, the final chart, Energy High Yield Pressure Points, subtracts overall high-yield spreads from energy high-yield spreads from 1995 to 2015. This spread difference peaked near 300 basis points in early 2015, representing the widest gap in the twenty-year history shown. The only comparable historical period occurred in 1997 to 1998, when a drop in oil prices from 22 dollars to 11 dollars prompted a spread difference of around 200 basis points and led to The Economist publishing its infamously mistimed "Drowning in Oil" cover. The author notes that between 1999 and mid-2014, high-yield energy bonds consistently traded at tighter spreads than the broader market, particularly during the collapses of the technology and financial sectors, making the sudden 2014–2015 divergence highly unusual and severe.

This page analyzes the geopolitical and macroeconomic impacts of falling oil prices on major oil-exporting nations across the Middle East, Latin America, and Central Asia. The author argues that while declining oil prices have dropped below both the fiscal and external breakeven levels for almost all exporters, standard breakeven metrics overlook the critical stabilizing role of massive sovereign wealth funds, which aggregate over $2 trillion for Gulf nations like the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Qatar. 

This argument is supported by a scatter plot comparing fiscal and external breakeven oil prices in USD per barrel, with the size of each nation's sovereign wealth fund labeled in billions of dollars. The x-axis tracks external breakeven prices from $20 to $140, while the y-axis tracks fiscal breakeven prices from $40 to $180. A red dot represents the current Brent price near $50 per barrel, sitting well below the 2014 peak Brent crude price of approximately $115. Plotted countries with massive stabilizing reserves include the United Arab Emirates ($1,079 billion fund), Saudi Arabia ($757 billion), Kuwait ($548 billion), and Qatar ($256 billion). Conversely, highly vulnerable nations like Venezuela have exceptionally high breakevens (around $130 fiscal and $105 external) but possess only a $1 billion sovereign wealth fund. Libya is plotted as an extreme outlier near the top right, with an external breakeven of $189 and a fiscal breakeven of $317, alongside a $66 billion fund. 

An accompanying table outlines the estimated impact of a drop in oil prices from $80 to $40 on the fiscal balances and current accounts of selected countries as a percentage of GDP. The nations most severely impacted are Azerbaijan, facing a negative 9.6 percent fiscal balance hit and a negative 14.5 percent current account hit, followed by Venezuela at negative 6.0 percent fiscal and negative 11.2 percent current account. Other listed countries suffer moderate impacts, such as Russia (negative 4.4 percent fiscal, negative 7.6 percent current account) and Iraq (negative 3.6 percent fiscal, negative 7.9 percent current account). At the bottom of the list, Mexico suffers a much smaller direct impact of negative 0.8 percent to its fiscal balance and negative 0.4 percent to its current account. 

In the commentary, the author provides specific context for several nations. Brazil is noted for having low overall economic sensitivity to oil price declines despite its domestic struggles with Petrobras and the broader commodity collapse. Mexico's primary risk is identified not as direct fiscal sensitivity, but rather the potential postponement of its oil and natural gas block privatizations due to dampened investor interest. Finally, the author highlights Venezuela as a prime example of the natural resource curse. Despite holding 18 percent of global oil reserves, the nation faces severe economic mismanagement, 80 percent inflation, acute goods shortages, and high crime rates. With its external debt trading at distressed levels of 35 to 45 cents on the dollar, the author suggests that Venezuela will ultimately require a massive political adjustment and assistance from the IMF and World Bank.

This page examines potential investment alternatives to traditional fixed income in a prolonged low-interest-rate environment, which the author describes as a "financial euthanasia" for savers, pension plans, and insurers—recalling John Maynard Keynes’s 1936 concept of the euthanasia of the rentier. With yields on US Treasuries and the Barclays Aggregate Index hovering around 2% in early 2015, the author proposes using a diversified portfolio of relative value and market-neutral hedge funds to complement fixed income allocations. The goal is to identify investments capable of delivering a return of 4% or more with an annualized volatility of less than 5%.

A line chart in the upper right, titled "Barclays Agg & Treasury yields back to January 2012 levels," illustrates the yield trends for the 10-year Treasury and the Barclays US Aggregate Index from 2011 to early 2015. Both series show yields fluctuating between roughly 1.5% and 3.5%, ultimately declining from their late 2013 peaks back down to approximately 2.0% by early 2015.

To evaluate whether hedge funds could meet the desired risk-adjusted return target, the author constructed equal-weighted, four-fund portfolios randomly selected from a filtered universe of low-volatility hedge funds using data available at the end of 2011. The performance of these portfolios from 2012 to 2014 is shown in two scatter plots at the bottom of the page, mapping annualized return against annualized volatility. 

The bottom-left chart, focusing on "Relative value hedge funds," reveals that 84% of the randomly constructed portfolios successfully landed within the target zone of more than 4% return with under 5% volatility. Furthermore, 97% of these portfolios outperformed the Barclays Aggregate Index, which returned an annualized 2.7% over the same period. The bottom-right chart, depicting "Market-neutral and other low vol long-short equity HFs," shows similar success, with 79% of the portfolios meeting the primary target return and volatility criteria, and 95% outperforming the Barclays Aggregate benchmark.

This page begins with an analysis of portfolio construction and hedge fund returns, highlighting that selected funds showed tight, risk-adjusted returns due to a low pairwise correlation of 0.25 or less and low return sensitivity against the S&P 500 ranging from 0.17 to 0.25. Two line charts illustrate this distribution for market-neutral and low-volatility equity hedge funds compared to relative value hedge funds. The first chart, showing the correlation distribution of these portfolios, reveals that both fund types cluster tightly in low positive correlation space, with market-neutral funds peaking around 0.20 to 0.25 and relative value funds peaking around 0.30 to 0.40. The second chart, displaying the beta distribution relative to the S&P 500, shows relative value portfolios peaking sharply around a beta of 0.15 to 0.20, while market-neutral and low-volatility equity portfolios peak broadly around 0.30.

The commentary then addresses the unexpected collapse of oil prices in 2014 to highlight the dangers of concentrated stock risk. It notes that energy, metals, and mining companies represent a massive portion of the steep decliners in both the Russell 1000 and Russell 2000 indices. Specifically, for value buyers, the price-to-book value of large-cap energy stocks relative to the overall market reached 0.5, marking its lowest level since 1928. The author mentions several smaller-cap Russell 2000 companies that fell more than 70% over the preceding year, including Energy XXI, Hercules, Alpha Natural Resources, Rex Energy, Goodrich Petroleum, and Solazyme.

A concluding table highlights the largest trailing one-year total return declines in the Russell 1000 index. Leading the declines is Ocwen Financial Corp in the financials sector with an 82% loss on a starting market cap of 7.53 billion USD. This is followed closely by several energy and materials names, including Sandridge Energy (-68%), McDermott International (-67%), Cliffs Natural Resources (-67%), and Seadrill Ltd (-58%, which began with a massive 19.28 billion USD market cap). Other notable decliners listed include Pandora Media (-57%), 3D Systems (-57%), Oasis Petroleum (-57%), Theravance (-54%), MRC Global (-54%), Zulily (-52%), Chicago Bridge & Iron (-52%), and Peabody Energy (-52%).

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication analyzes Russia's economic crisis, arguing that a triple threat of falling oil prices, international sanctions, and capital flight is severely harming the country's economy. The author draws a historical parallel to the collapse of the Spanish Empire in the 1500s and the Soviet Union in the 1980s, suggesting that while commodity declines often act as a catalyst for collapse, they ultimately expose deep-seated, systemic inefficiencies.

To support this historical comparison, the top-left chart, titled "Commodity declines and the end of empires," plots Spanish gold inflows in millions of pesos from 1525 to 1645 alongside Russian oil exports to capitalist countries in billions of USD from 1971 to 1989. The chart illustrates how sharp drops in resource revenues—such as Spain's falling gold inflows in the early 17th century and Soviet oil exports cutting in half during the 1980s—coincided with geopolitical disintegration, leading to Spain losing control of Portugal, Aragon, and Catalonia, and Russia losing Eastern Europe. 

The top-right chart, "Economic collapse of the Soviet Union," shows that this downfall was already in motion. Plotting the rate of return on invested capital from 1950 to 1982, the chart reveals a steady, decades-long decline. The return on capital for the total economy plummeted from approximately 0.50 in 1950 to under 0.10 by 1982, while the rate of return for industry sank close to 0.00, demonstrating structural failures long before the 1980s oil price shock.

Turning to modern Russia, the author notes that crude oil and petroleum products constitute 54% of Russia's exports, with natural gas making up another 14%. The bottom-left chart, "Another episode of a falling Ruble and rising inflation," tracks the relationship between the year-over-year percentage change of the trade-weighted Ruble index (inverted, where an upward trend denotes a weaker currency) and inflation from 2006 to 2014. It shows that by late 2014, a sharp depreciation in the Ruble (well over 30% weaker year-over-year) was accompanied by a spike in inflation to 11% in December 2014, despite the government spending $100 billion of its reserves to defend the currency.

The bottom-right chart, "Impact of sanctions on Russian corporate debt issuance," tracks trailing six-month corporate loan and bond issuance in billions of USD from 2002 to 2014. It highlights a dramatic drop-off in both loan and bond issuance to near-zero levels by late 2014, illustrating how international sanctions have effectively cut Russian corporations off from foreign credit markets. 

Ultimately, these compounding pressures have forced Russia's central bank to raise policy rates to 17%, the highest level since the country’s 1998 default. This economic strain will make it increasingly difficult for President Vladimir Putin to deliver promised increases in public sector salaries and pensions. The author concludes by dismissing claims from Russian policymakers that this crisis will force beneficial economic restructuring and productivity gains, noting that true reform would require weakening the power of oligarchs and fostering an independent class of small- and medium-sized businesses, which is highly unlikely to happen.

The page opens with a brief geopolitical observation on the conflict in Ukraine, noting that its immediate prognosis is dim and validating President George H.W. Bush’s cautious 1990s stance, which was once mocked by William Safire. 

The primary market commentary focuses on the high hurdle US equity markets face in 2015 due to highly elevated market sentiment and positioning at the start of the year. To support this, a detailed table titled "Market sentiment and positioning elevated heading into 2015" compares various historical percentiles from December 2013 and December 2014. By December 2014, the median trailing price-to-earnings ratio for the S&P 500 was at the 85th percentile, and the S&P 600 small-cap trailing P/E was at the 80th percentile. Extreme bullishness is further evidenced by the Investors Intelligence Newsletter Advisory Sentiment at the 94th percentile, the NAAIM Active Managers Sentiment at the 98th percentile, and Bank of America hedge fund net long/short exposure at the 99th percentile. Concurrently, cash levels were exceptionally low, with Bank of America hedge fund cash holdings dropping to the 1st percentile, where 1 represents the most bullish, least-cash state. 

The author points to slowing economic indicators, such as weak Q4 GDP components, slowing manufacturing orders, and flat S&P 500 sales growth of only 2%. S&P Q4 earnings reflected deep sector divergence, with energy down 21%, flat results in materials, financials, and staples, and gains of 8% to 17% in other sectors. Consequently, 2015 S&P estimates are projected to be flat compared to 2014, factoring in an expected 50% decline in energy earnings. To drive US equities higher, the market will require confirmation of a consumer spending rebound. 

Some fundamental support is visible in labor markets, as shown in a dual-axis line chart tracking "Improving labor market conditions" from 2004 to early 2015. The chart displays a steady recovery in the employment-to-population ratio for 25-to-54-year-olds, climbing back toward 77%, alongside a sharp rebound in the percentage of businesses planning to raise worker compensation, which reached nearly 18% in early 2015. 

The final bar chart compares year-to-date total returns across major equity regions in both USD and local currency terms as of February 9, 2015. It reveals flat to slightly negative returns for the US market. Meanwhile, Europe leads with exceptional local currency returns of roughly 8% (though closer to 1.5% in USD terms), followed by positive returns of about 2% for Japan, China, and emerging market manufacturers, while emerging market commodity exporters remain in negative territory.

This page critiquing central bank policies features an editorial cartoon titled "Central Bankenstein's Monster: turning out the lights on savers to revive the patient," illustrated by Anni Betts. The elaborate, gothic-style artwork depicts a mad-scientist central banker inside the "Castle of Central Banks" using a high-voltage generator to shock a patient labeled "Economy." To power this resuscitation, the machine drains energy away from a dark, freezing village on the left where retirees, savers, insurers, pension plans, and endowments huddle around a small fire. The diverted energy is instead channeled to illuminate a shining city on a hill labeled "Riskier Assets." 

In the accompanying text, the author discusses the historical scale of modern central banking experiments that drive bond yields below inflation. The policy aims to reduce the cost of capital and spark a wealth effect by forcing savers into riskier assets and pushing banks toward riskier loans. While US policies appear successful in the short term, the author questions their long-term viability. To illustrate the danger of upfront policy benefits hiding eventual systemic crises, the text cites several historical examples: Lyndon B. Johnson's "guns and butter" policies in the 1960s, Richard Nixon's wage and price controls coupled with easy Federal Reserve policy in the 1970s, HUD's 1990s lending targets for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, negative real Federal Reserve rates in the early 2000s, and the SEC's 2004 decision to eliminate the Net Capital Rule, which allowed broker-dealers to increase their leverage from a 12-to-1 cap up to 30-to-1 or 35-to-1 by 2006.

This page analyzes how central bank policies have impacted financial markets, driving investor sentiment, positioning, and asset valuations to highly elevated levels. The author argues that markets are nearing the end of a "forced march" into riskier assets, meaning future equity gains must rely on earnings growth rather than further valuation expansion. 

To illustrate extreme investor optimism, a table on market sentiment shows that by December 2014, multiple positioning metrics were near historic highs. The Bank of America hedge fund net exposure was in the 99th percentile of its history since 2005, while both NAAIM active manager sentiment and net long futures positions of market participants were in the 98th percentile. Individual investor and newsletter advisory sentiment also sat in the low 90s. 

Despite this enthusiasm, a line chart of trailing 12-month price-to-earnings ratios for the United States, United Kingdom, and European Monetary Union demonstrates that while valuations have risen significantly since 2011, they remain well below the late-1990s tech bubble peaks of over 30x, hovering instead between 15x and 20x. 

In real estate, a chart tracking average US cap rates adjusted for five-year core inflation shows values returning to tight 2007 credit-bubble levels. Apartment cap rates are the lowest at around 4.0%, with office and retail rates sitting near 5.0% and 5.2% respectively. 

Credit markets show a distinct divergence, illustrated in a chart tracking high-yield spreads-to-worst from 2004 to 2015. While US high-yield energy spreads spiked dramatically to nearly 900 basis points in late 2014, the high-yield ex-energy market experienced only a modest selloff, remaining tight at around 450 basis points. 

Lastly, a commentary box highlights a mixed signal in Europe. Following European Central Bank interventions, 70% of European companies now yield more in dividends than their corporate bonds yield, compared to just 5% to 15% pre-crisis. The author cautions that rather than being a straightforward buy signal, this divergence reflects severe deflationary pressures and emergency monetary policy rather than healthy underlying corporate cash flows.

In this concluding section of the publication, the author analyzes the state of the post-2009 economic recovery, noting that while fundamental improvements in US corporate profits, employment, and housing demand are genuine, a significant portion of the global equity market rally has been forced by aggressive central bank interventions. This phenomenon is illustrated by the Bank of Japan directly purchasing equities and a massive global central bank balance sheet expansion of nearly eight trillion dollars since 2007 across regions including the United States, Europe, the United Kingdom, Japan, Canada, Australia, Sweden, and Norway. The author poses an open question about how much demand was artificially pulled forward by these ultra-low rates, warning that the "Central Bankenstein" strategy of using ultra-low real policy rates has created an exceptionally volatile environment for investors.

To substantiate this historical perspective on volatility, a table compares Dow Jones Index volatility across different Federal Reserve eras. The data shows that the combined Greenspan and Bernanke era was more volatile than the inflationary era of the 1970s under Arthur Burns and G. William Miller, the tight-money eras under William McChesney Martin and Paul Volcker, and the Great Depression and World War II era under Marriner Eccles. Specifically, volatility reached 20.3 percent during Ben Bernanke's tenure from 2006 to 2014 and 17.4 percent during Alan Greenspan's tenure from 1987 to 2006. This combined average of roughly 18 percent is comparable to the 18.1 percent volatility seen between 1896 and 1914, prior to the creation of the Federal Reserve when the US was frequently beset by recessions and depressions. By comparison, volatility under William McChesney Martin from 1951 to 1970 was only 10.3 percent.

An accompanying bar chart illustrates the potential casualties of prolonged negative real long-term interest rates by showing private pension fund and insurance company assets as a percent of GDP across OECD countries using data from 2012 and 2013. The chart highlights that nations relying heavily on funded private pensions and insurance assets are highly vulnerable to prolonged low-rate environments. The Netherlands represents the highest exposure, with private pension assets nearing 160 percent of GDP. Other highly exposed nations include Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Denmark, Australia, and the United States, where private pensions account for roughly 80 percent of GDP and insurance companies make up about 40 percent. In contrast, countries like France, Germany, and Italy are less affected by these specific dynamics because over 95 percent of their pensions are public and not pre-funded with assets.

This page explores the connection between environmental degradation in the emerging world, specifically China, and the growing demand for US agricultural exports, which directly benefits US farmland investors. Although the United States faces its own water pollution issues, the situation is far worse in parts of the emerging world. Adjusted for its stage of economic development, China's environmental conditions are worse than any other country measured. 

This relationship is first illustrated in a scatter plot titled "China: farthest away from wealth-environment curve," which plots composite environmental scores from 1 to 100 against log-scale per capita GDP. While wealthier nations generally enjoy cleaner environments—with the United States scoring near the top—China’s large bubble, representing its massive population, sits well below the upward-sloping trendline, far lower than countries with similar GDP per capita like India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. 

This environmental strain, particularly the degradation of over 40% of China’s arable land and the heavy-metal contamination of 20% of its surveyed farmland, has forced the country to increasingly rely on food imports. A bar chart titled "US agricultural trade with China" shows a dramatic surge in US agricultural exports to China, rising from negligible levels in the 1990s to roughly $25 billion by 2014, while US agricultural imports from China stayed flat below $5 billion. 

Two line charts illustrate this rising import demand from 2000 to 2014 in net millions of metric tons. The first, "China's imports of grains and soybeans," shows net soybean imports skyrocketing from around 10 million metric tons in 2000 to nearly 80 million metric tons by 2014, while cereal and dried grains transitioned from a net export position to nearly 30 million metric tons in net imports. The second, "China's imports of meats and dairy," details a parallel rise in livestock products, with meat imports climbing to over 2 million metric tons and dairy imports steadily rising from near zero to about 1.8 million metric tons by 2014. 

As China overtakes Japan, Mexico, and Canada as the largest US agricultural trading partner, these import trends are expected to continue. For investors, despite low single-digit crop and livestock product returns since 1980 and falling farmland rental yields, US farmland remains an attractive asset. Incorporating rental growth and lease participation payments, the author projects annual return targets of 7% to 9% for farmland owners.
This page is a cover and title page for a J.P. Morgan Asset Management "Investment Insights" publication titled "What if we live in a low-return world? Implications for pension funds."

This page of the publication examines healthcare investing and the "free-rider" phenomenon in the developed world. Michael Cembalest argues that healthcare stocks have historically delivered some of the strongest nominal and risk-adjusted returns because of a structural 40-year shift away from out-of-pocket spending toward government and private insurance. For example, in 1982, US out-of-pocket spending on prescription drugs accounted for 70% of total drug spending, but by 2012, that share had dropped to 18%. This shift lowers direct consumer costs and drives up consumption.

The first table displays annual total returns and volatility by sector across three regions: the United States since September 1989, Europe since January 1995, and Japan since January 1995. Across these geographies, the healthcare sector consistently showcases outstanding risk-adjusted performance. In the US, healthcare delivered an annual return of 12.4% with 15.6% volatility, yielding a return-to-volatility ratio of 0.80. In Europe, healthcare returned 11.0% with 13.3% volatility, resulting in a ratio of 0.83. In Japan, healthcare returned 7.4% with 16.7% volatility, leading to a ratio of 0.44. In all three cases, healthcare outperformed most other major sectors, including financials, energy, and industrials, on a risk-adjusted basis.

To illustrate the demand-driving effect of subsidized healthcare, a second table compares the initial estimated costs of major US government programs to their actual costs, based on a 2009 Joint Economic Committee report. Because planners consistently underestimated consumer demand, actual expenditures dramatically exceeded projections. For example, the entire Medicare program was initially projected to cost $12 billion but actually cost $110 billion—a ratio of 9.2 to 1. Medicare hospital insurance cost $67 billion against a $9 billion estimate (7.4 to 1), while the Medicaid DSH program ballooned from an estimated $1 billion to an actual cost of $17 billion (17 to 1). Even more recent programs, like the Massachusetts Health Reform, experienced cost overruns, costing $869 million against an estimated $725 million. 

The final chart tracks the inexorable rise of US healthcare spending from 1960 to 2020, incorporating CMS projections for the outer years. The chart shows three rising trends: government and private insurance as a percentage of healthcare spending climbed from around 50% in 1960 to nearly 90% by 2014; healthcare spending as a percentage of GDP rose from about 5% to over 17%; and inflation-adjusted per capita healthcare spending surged from under $1,000 to over $10,000, with projections targeting nearly $14,000 by 2020. 

Looking forward, the author highlights important intra-sector shifts for investors to follow, such as rising unit prices for branded drugs, declining hospital profit margins on Medicare and Medicaid, and growth in biotech prescription sales. Ultimately, the author expects diversified healthcare exposures to remain highly attractive, pointing to CMS projections of continued spending increases and a Brookings Institute paper forecasting healthcare spending to grow at GDP plus 1.2% annually over the next two decades.

This page contains biographical profiles and headshot photographs for two key contributors to J.P. Morgan Asset Management: Michael Cembalest and Anthony Gould. 

The first profile is of Michael Cembalest, the Chairman of Market and Investment Strategy for J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The text highlights his responsibility for leading strategic market and investment insights across the firm's Institutional, Funds, and Private Banking businesses, noting that J.P. Morgan Asset Management oversees $1.8 trillion of client assets worldwide as of March 31, 2015. It details his roles on the J.P. Morgan Asset Management Investment Committee and the retirement plan investment committee. His career history at the firm is noted, including his eight-year tenure as Chief Investment Officer for the Global Private Bank, his leadership of a fixed income division, and his start at J.P. Morgan in 1987 in the Corporate Finance division. His educational background includes an M.A. from the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs in 1986 and a B.A. from Tufts University in 1984.

The second profile is of Anthony Gould, the Head of Global Pension Solutions & Advisory for J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The text describes his 28 years of financial industry experience, including more than 15 years as a global fixed income manager. It notes his career beginnings at J.P. Morgan Securities, his return to the firm in 2011 to lead the Long Duration Client Portfolio Management team, and his work as a senior portfolio manager for liability-aware multi-asset portfolios. Prior to 2011, he led the Pension Solutions Group at another major investment bank. Additionally, his professional accomplishments include publishing a book on fixed income portfolio management and articles in the Journal of Alternative Investments and the Journal of Fixed Income. He holds a B.Sc. in Economics from the London School of Economics and is a member of the CFA Institute and the CAIA Association.

This page focuses on Mexico’s ambitious "Big Bang" structural reforms, framing them as a necessary response to a decade of stagnant economic growth, flatlining corporate profits, and falling oil production. To highlight the country's historical underperformance, the author features two line charts comparing Mexico to its emerging market peers. The first chart, tracking per capita GDP growth in thousands of 1990 GK dollars from 1990 to 2011, shows Mexico's per capita GDP stagnating around eight thousand dollars, far behind Chile, which climbed past fourteen thousand dollars, as well as Poland, Malaysia, and Thailand. The second chart, indexing trailing twelve-month earnings per share in local currency from 2007 through early 2015, illustrates that Mexican corporate profits flatlined near the base level of one hundred, trailing nearly all other listed nations—including Indonesia, China, India, and Korea—with only Brazil showing worse performance. 

The author explains that the newly proposed reforms are highly ambitious and designed to boost Mexico's potential growth by two percent per year to five percent, while restoring oil production to three and a half million barrels per day. The broad scope of these reforms is detailed across five main sectors. In energy, the reform seeks to lower costs and end the state monopolies of Pemex and CFE by allowing private and foreign firms to participate in deepwater and shale drilling. Financial reforms aim to lower borrowing costs and foster banking competition. Fiscal reforms are designed to raise public spending and non-oil tax revenues, which includes introducing a general sixteen percent value-added tax and closing tax loopholes. Labor reforms focus on increasing workforce flexibility by lowering hiring and firing costs and utilizing temporary contracts. Finally, telecom reforms will permit up to one hundred percent foreign ownership and cap market share at fifty percent to prevent monopolies.

To show the potential impact of these actions, a table lists the economic performance of several countries before and during historical liberalizations, including Argentina, Colombia, Chile, Indonesia, Sweden, Peru, Brazil, and Mexico. Across these historical precedents, average annual GDP growth rose from two point three percent in the five years prior to four point two percent during liberalization. Meanwhile, average productivity growth experienced a substantial turnaround, shifting from negative zero point two percent prior to the reforms to three point six percent during liberalization. 

In terms of future outlook, the author expresses optimism, noting that Mexico’s current account vulnerability is lower than that of other emerging markets and that its export share in sectors like vehicles and machinery is already rising. However, the author cautions that the recent decline in global oil prices adds significant urgency to these reforms, as the government's upcoming oil and gas auctions will likely yield much lower prices than they would have a year prior.

This analysis examines the severe structural and political challenges facing the Eurozone, arguing that despite a cyclical rebound, the monetary union is in a race against time. The core issue is the dramatic economic divergence between Germany and other major members like France and Italy. Germany is currently overheating, characterized by record-low unemployment, a fifteen-year high in job vacancies, and rising wages. In contrast, France and Italy face high unemployment and stagnant productivity. The author warns that if this gap does not close over the next few years, a potential Greek exit or a populist victory in the 2017 French election—where Marine Le Pen of the National Front campaigned on reclaiming monetary sovereignty—could break the union. Italy’s labor market is highlighted as particularly inflexible, ranking 136th out of 144 countries in the World Economic Forum’s Labor Market Efficiency index, making a rapid productivity catch-up unlikely.

The publication supports these arguments with several charts. The first, illustrating unemployment rates from 2000 to 2014, shows that while rates are beginning to decline, they remain extremely high in Southern Europe, with Greece and Spain peaking near twenty-five to twenty-eight percent post-financial crisis, while France and Italy hover around ten to twelve percent. This high unemployment has fueled a surge in populist politics, as shown in a chart detailing support for anti-establishment parties from 2009 to 2014. By late 2014, Italy’s Five Star Movement and Lega Nord, along with Greece’s Syriza, polled near thirty to thirty-five percent of intended votes, while Spain’s Podemos and France’s Le Pen both commanded around twenty-five percent.

The structural divergence is further illustrated by a chart showing industrial production indexed to December 31, 1999. Prior to fixing the Euro exchange rate, Germany, France, and Italy tracked each other closely. After 1999, Germany’s industrial production climbed to over 120 by 2014, whereas France fell to around 85 and Italy crashed to approximately 75, underscoring the divergence that has occurred since the single currency was adopted. 

Finally, two tables analyze economic and structural dispersion among country groups based on World Economic Forum data, measuring divergence on a scale where the Eurozone scores a high 31.9. The Eurozone has far greater internal dispersion than any other feasible but non-existent monetary union, such as Anglo-Saxon countries at 17.7, Northern Europe at 22.9, or Gulf countries at 27.1. Remarkably, the Eurozone is also more diverse and less economically aligned than historical empires like the Austro-Hungarian Empire at 30.2 and a reconstituted Soviet Union at 31.4, and is only surpassed in divergence by highly arbitrary groupings such as the Ottoman Empire at 33.5 or an imaginary union of all countries beginning with the letter "M" at 39.3.

This page presents an appendix of six charts and tables covering global energy economics, geopolitical risks, demographics, and cultural integration. 

The first chart, A1, illustrates the price ratio of natural gas to propane at their respective hubs from 2002 to 2014. Despite a greater than 40 percent decline in propane and oil prices, the chart demonstrates that natural gas remains substantially cheaper per million British thermal units (mmBTU), with the price ratio hovering around 0.4x in late 2014, well below its peak of 1.2x in 2005.

The second chart, A2, projects the impact of spending and Brent Crude oil prices on Saudi Arabian government reserves in billions of Saudi Riyals through 2019. It contrasts four scenarios: at ninety-dollar oil with a 3 percent fiscal adjustment, reserves remain stable near 1,500 billion Riyals; without adjustment, they drop to around 1,000 billion. At sixty-five-dollar oil, reserves drop sharply, reaching approximately 300 billion Riyals with a fiscal adjustment, and falling into a deficit of roughly negative 250 billion Riyals by 2019 if no adjustment is made.

Table A3 details the global footprint of war zone countries as of November 2014. It highlights a sharp divergence between demographic weight and financial integration: while these conflict areas account for 11.7 percent of the global population and 9.0 percent of oil production, they represent a negligible fraction of global financial activity, including only 0.7 percent of equity market capitalization and 0.4 percent of portfolio investment inflows.

Chart A4 tracks the rising demographic imbalance of elderly populations aged 65 and older as a percentage of the total population from 1980 through projections to 2050. Japan leads the aging trend, projected to reach nearly 40 percent by 2050. The European Union and China show similar steep trajectories, with both projected to reach 25 to 30 percent, while the United States is projected to experience a more gradual increase, reaching roughly 22 percent.

The final two charts focus on Muslim populations in Western nations. Chart A5 displays the estimated percentage of Muslim populations in major European cities, showing high concentrations in Marseille (ranging between 20 and 30 percent), Blackburn, Brussels, and Rotterdam, while cities like Milan, Vienna, and Berlin sit below 10 percent. Chart A6 uses an International Assimilation Index from a Manhattan Institute study to show that Muslim immigrants are far more integrated in North America than in Europe. Canada and the United States score highest on the index (at roughly 72 and 62, respectively), while European nations such as Switzerland and Italy score the lowest, both registering under 20.

This page features three distinct sections covering global corporate tax rates, Arctic environmental data, and a personal hobby visual related to sport fishing. 

The first section focuses on marginal effective corporate tax rates (METR) on capital, arguing that the United States is at a competitive disadvantage due to its high tax rates and its worldwide tax system, which contrasts with the territorial tax systems used by most OECD nations. A set of tables details these rates from 2005 through 2013. The United States’ METR remained virtually flat, hovering between 35.3 percent and 35.9 percent over this period. Meanwhile, other countries and regions substantially reduced their rates. For example, Canada’s rate fell from 38.8 percent in 2005 to 18.6 percent in 2013, the G-7 average dropped from 34.2 percent to 27.6 percent, and the average for the 34 OECD nations fell from 22.4 percent to 19.6 percent. Consequently, the United States ranked first for the highest tax rate within both the G-7 and the OECD every year from 2007 to 2013, and ranked second within the G-20 from 2010 to 2013. The text references recommendations from the President’s Bipartisan Fiscal Commission on Fiscal Reform in 2010, as well as several other presidential advisory councils, all advocating for a transition to a territorial tax system.

The second section presents a line chart tracking the average monthly Arctic sea ice extent from 1978 to 2013, sourced from the National Snow and Ice Data Center. Utilizing a dual-axis format to show extent in millions of square kilometers, the chart displays two distinct seasonal series. The January sea ice series, plotted on the left axis, shows a steady, gradual decline from around 15.5 million square kilometers in the late 1970s down to approximately 14.0 million square kilometers by 2013. The September sea ice series, plotted on the right axis, shows a much more dramatic downward trend, plummeting from nearly 7.5 million square kilometers in the early years of the data set to a record low of roughly 3.5 million square kilometers in 2012, before recovering slightly in 2013.

The final section is a creative infographic titled A Periodic Table of Fishing, which organizes various sport fish species like elements on a periodic table, ordered by average adult weight. The table serves as a personal checklist for the author, color-coding species into those already caught, which are shaded in blue, and those the author is still searching for, shown in white. Shaded species include Sea Trout, Striped Bass, Amberjack, Yellowfin Tuna, Atlantic Cod, Mahi Mahi, and Rainbow Trout, while unshaded "undiscovered elements" include False Albacore, Wahoo, Goliath Grouper, and Southern Stingray. Three photographs in the center of the graphic illustrate successful catches, depicting fishers holding a redfish, a massive tuna, and a giant grouper.

This page, titled The Case for Lower Growth: A Focus on Productivity Trends, argues that long-term interest rates are highly likely to remain low because nominal GDP growth remains sluggish, contrary to more optimistic consensus forecasts. The author examines the relationship between nominal growth, interest rates, and productivity to make a case for a sustained low-return world.

To establish the link between interest rates and economic growth, the author provides two charts spanning from 1965 to 2015. Exhibit 1A plots the ten-year U.S. Treasury yield against nominal GDP expectations four quarters ahead, sourced from the Survey of Professional Forecasters and the Federal Reserve Board. This chart shows that while expectations and yields have structurally declined from peaks above fourteen percent in the early 1980s to low single digits, forecasters lately project a rise in future nominal GDP growth expectations. However, Exhibit 1B, which plots the ten-year Treasury yield against actual trailing two-year nominal GDP growth, reveals a different reality. Actual nominal growth has remained steady below four percent, suggesting that ten-year Treasury yields are likely to stay well below four percent if current growth rates persist.

The discussion then shifts to what drives real economic growth, specifically focusing on productivity. Exhibit 2A plots five-year trailing real GDP growth alongside five-year trailing U.S. labor productivity from 1965 to 2015. While labor productivity generally drives real GDP growth, the two series occasionally disconnect. For instance, during the mid-1980s, real U.S. GDP growth surged toward four percent, while labor productivity remained low near one and a half percent, a divergence the author attributes to the end of a decade of stagflation rather than productivity gains. 

To find a more reliable leading indicator for growth and interest rates, Exhibit 2B compares five-year trailing real GDP growth with five-year trailing total factor productivity, which accounts for both labor and capital efficiency. This chart shows a much stronger, tightly correlated relationship where total factor productivity closely mirrors the cyclical peaks and valleys of real GDP growth, including a drop below zero percent around 1980 and a decline near zero percent after the 2008 financial crisis. The author concludes that analyzing total factor productivity is the key to understanding future economic growth and interest rate trajectories. All productivity data is sourced from the Bureau of Economic Analysis and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, current as of late 2014 and early 2015.

This page discusses the demographic and global structural factors that point toward lower economic growth and lower interest rates in the future. The author argues that declining labor force growth and an aging population place a speed limit on nominal growth, which in turn implies lower nominal and real interest rates. To support this, several charts examine demographic shifts in the United States relative to other major global economies, alongside historical trends in labor force growth and sovereign bond yields.

The first visual analysis compares demographic trends across the United States, Japan, Germany, the United Kingdom, and China. Exhibit 4A tracks working-age population growth for ages 15 to 64 from 1950 to 2040, utilizing United Nations actual data through 2014 and forecasts beyond. The chart shows that while five-year annualized growth in the U.S. working-age population is projected to remain slightly positive through 2040 at around 0.25% to 0.50%, it is far below its late 20th-century peaks of over 1.5%. Meanwhile, working-age population growth in Germany, Japan, and China is projected to decline deeply into negative territory by 2040, with Germany and Japan dipping below negative 0.5% annually. 

Compounding this issue, Exhibit 4B illustrates the rising dependency ratio, which measures minors and retirees as a percentage of the working-age population. In the U.S., this ratio is forecasted to rise from around 50% in 2010 to nearly 65% by 2040. Similar upward trajectories are visible for all other featured countries, with Japan's ratio expected to approach 80% and Germany's forecasted to surpass 75% by 2040, demonstrating that active workers worldwide will have to support a much larger inactive population.

Turning to domestic labor dynamics, Exhibit 5 displays annual U.S. labor force growth from 1985 through 2014 using Bureau of Labor Statistics data. This chart highlights a clear downshift in labor supply: the average annual growth rate was 1.5% from 1985 to 2000, but plummeted to an average of just 0.75% from 2001 to 2014. This structural decline in labor force participation directly restrains the country's long-term GDP growth prospects.

Finally, the author explains that U.S. growth and interest rates cannot be analyzed in a vacuum, as developments abroad are transmitted domestically through trade, capital markets, and international corporate revenues. Exhibit 6 underscores this global integration by plotting 10-year sovereign bond yields from 1980 to 2015 for both the United States and a GDP-weighted average of developed markets excluding the U.S. The chart shows a highly correlated downward trajectory over three decades, with yields collapsing from peaks of over 13% in the early 1980s to historic lows near 1.5% by early 2015. This close relationship suggests that global capital market forces and structural adjustments in Europe, Japan, and China exert a powerful downward pull on U.S. yields.

This page focuses on the structural headwinds to global growth, specifically highlighting how U.S. corporate profits are increasingly linked to international markets and how structural imbalances within the Eurozone continue to hinder European growth. The author argues that because U.S. companies have steadily increased their foreign exposure, future U.S. growth assessments must closely incorporate developments in Europe and China. A regional breakdown of U.S. profits reveals that while the U.S. accounts for 60%, Europe makes up 17%, emerging markets comprise 15%, and other developed markets represent 8%. 

Two charts illustrate the rising foreign exposure of U.S. firms. Exhibit 7A shows the percent of total corporate profits from foreign sources over trailing four quarters from 1947 to 2012. The share of foreign profits rose from below 5% in 1947 to a peak of over 30% by 2012. Exhibit 7B displays S&P 500 foreign pretax income as a percentage of the total from 1984 to 2012, tracking both the overall S&P 500 and the S&P 500 excluding Financials. Both series show a steady upward march, with the overall S&P 500 foreign profit share peaking near 50% in 2008 before settling around 40% in 2012, while the series excluding financials peaked near 70% in 2008 and ended close to 45% in 2012.

The discussion then shifts to Europe, arguing that the adoption of the euro in the late 1990s drove a wedge between Northern and Southern Europe by exaggerating macroeconomic and microeconomic differences. A footnote contrasts this with the United States' monetary union in the 19th century, which led to economic convergence rather than divergence. 

This European divergence is illustrated in two additional charts. Exhibit 8A displays the Industrial Production Index from 1982 to 2014, indexed to December 31, 1999, which equals 100. A vertical line marks the late-1998 period when the Euro exchange rate was fixed. Before this fixing, Germany, France, and Italy moved in relative alignment. Afterward, Germany's industrial production surged to nearly 130 by 2008 and remained above 120 in 2014, whereas France stagnated near 90 to 100, and Italy fell significantly, dropping below 90 by 2014. 

Exhibit 8B tracks real unit labor costs relative to Germany from 2000 to 2014, indexed to the first quarter of 2000. Higher values on this index represent a less competitive labor market. The chart shows that while Spain, Italy, and France all saw their relative labor costs rise significantly to peak near 125 to 130 between 2008 and 2012, Spain subsequently achieved dramatic competitiveness improvements, with its index falling back toward 110 by 2014. In contrast, labor cost issues have not yet been successfully addressed in France and Italy, where relative unit labor costs remained elevated near 115 and 125, respectively, by late 2014.

This page explores the global implications of massive central bank interventions, focusing on Japan's unprecedented monetary experiments, and discusses how unresolved global debt burdens continue to constrain economic growth. The author argues that central bank asset purchases drive down global yields and create structural instability in equity markets, while the lack of genuine deleveraging post-2008 has forced fiscal austerity that dampens economic performance.
