In this commentary, the author evaluates whether consensus financial projections for 2016 are realistic, ultimately forecasting another year of single-digit returns for US equities that will be only slightly better than 2015. 

The author begins by agreeing with the market's confidence in corporate profit margins. While S&P 500 margins have declined to a degree that has historically signaled recessions, a line chart titled "US net profit margin decline mostly an energy story" shows that this downturn is driven entirely by the collapse in the energy sector, reminiscent of the mid-1980s. This chart, which tracks margins from 1973 to 2015, illustrates that while the total market margin has dipped, the margin excluding the energy sector remains robust and nearly unchanged near its historical peak of approximately 9%. Additionally, the author supports expectations of a Consumer Discretionary earnings bounce in 2016, buoyed by lower energy prices, an improving labor market, rising home prices, and low inflation.

However, the author strongly questions the market's optimism for a technology sector earnings recovery. A second chart, "Tech revenues declining, after excluding AAPL & GOOG," plots year-over-year sales growth from 2006 to 2015. It demonstrates that when tech giants Apple and Google are removed from the data, the remaining tech sector's sales growth has fallen to around negative 4%, matching the weakness of the Industrials ex-Defense sector. This stagnation is due to Tech having the highest foreign sales exposure of any S&P sector, making it highly vulnerable to global headwinds. 

Two subsequent charts analyze the currency environment. "The rise of the dollar" displays the real effective exchange rate index from 1980 to 2015, comparing the US dollar against a foreign exchange basket both including and excluding the Chinese RMB, showing a dramatic surge after 2011. A companion chart, "After a rapid climb, the Dollar has stabilized despite Chinese devaluation," zeroes in on the trade-weighted USD index from 2010 to 2015, showing the index soaring from roughly 70 in late 2011 before plateauing between 90 and 95 in 2015. While the author believes the dollar's sharp rise is mostly over, they do not anticipate a significant decline. Coupled with stagnant international growth outlooks for Brazil, China, Europe, Japan, and the Far East, the foreign exchange drag on Tech earnings is expected to persist into 2016.

Finally, the author warns of headwinds for smaller enterprises using a chart titled "Proxy for small business operating margin trends." This chart measures the net percentage of businesses planning to raise prices minus those planning to raise wages from 1987 to 2015. The metric has plummeted from nearly 10% down to approximately 0% by late 2015, signaling mounting margin pressures as rising labor costs outpace pricing power. Without a major acceleration in top-line sales growth, the small business earnings outlook for 2016 remains only modestly better than 2015.

This page features a commentary by Michael Cembalest on the rise of ideological polarization in the United States Senate, contrasting historical bipartisan voting habits with the modern era of political "zealots." Cembalest reflects on his father’s belief in a bipartisan America, citing historical Democratic senators like Pat Moynihan, John Glenn, Sam Ervin, Hubert Humphrey, Henry Jackson, Claude Pepper, and Harry Truman, who frequently voted across party lines. To illustrate this shift, he presents two charts based on DW-Nominate voting record data compiled by Keith T. Poole of the University of Georgia. 

The first chart, titled "Ideological uniformity of Senate Democrats, 1937-2014," measures ideological purity on a scale where 1.0 represents the most liberal voting pattern. Modern senators sit at the extreme left of this distribution, led by Bernie Sanders of Vermont at approximately 0.85 and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts at approximately 0.75. In contrast, the historical figures praised by Cembalest’s father occupy much more moderate positions, such as John Glenn at roughly 0.3 and Pat Moynihan at 0.25, while older Southern Democrats like Sam Ervin of North Carolina and Allen Ellender of Louisiana fall below 0.0, indicating they regularly voted with the opposing party. 

The second chart, titled "Ideological uniformity in the US Senate, 1937-2014," displays the distribution curves for both Democrats and Republicans, where 1.0 represents the most polarized voting pattern. The chart shows that both parties have steep polarization curves, though the Republican curve is slightly higher overall than the Democratic one. Cembalest notes that contemporary Republican senators like Mike Lee, Jim DeMint, and Tom Coburn occupy the same highly polarized territory on their side of the aisle as Senator Warren does on hers. He concludes with advice to economists and academics to keep a low profile in this deeply polarized climate, warning that modern political zealots are closed off to opposing viewpoints.

This page explores the potential connection between stagnant US productivity, rising government regulation, and a decline in business dynamism. The author introduces the topic by noting that despite steadily rising private research and development (R&D) spending, US productivity remains stagnant. While acknowledging that certain regulations—like fracking oversight or Sarbanes-Oxley—are necessary, the author highlights that the massive expansion of the Code of Federal Regulations may explain why the United States ranks a dismal 49th out of 189 countries in the World Bank’s category for starting a new business. 

Four visuals support this argument. The first chart, titled "Why isn't R&D growth helping productivity?", compares the two-year annualized change in non-farm productivity with private R&D spending as a percentage of GDP from 1980 to 2015. It shows that while private R&D steadily increased from approximately 1.25% of GDP in 1980 to over 1.75% by 2015, non-farm productivity dropped from peaks around 4% in the late 1990s and early 2000s to nearly 0% by 2015. An adjacent table displays select World Bank "Starting a Business" rankings for 2015, highlighting that the United States (ranked 49th) falls behind nations like Canada (3rd), Hong Kong (4th), Singapore (10th), and Korea (23rd). 

Below these, a third chart, titled "The ever expanding Code of Federal Regulations," tracks the total number of pages in the Code alongside the actual number of regulatory restrictions from 1975 to 2011. During this period, the total pages rose from roughly 70,000 to over 170,000, while the actual number of restrictions—such as "shall," "must," or "prohibited"—nearly tripled, climbing from 350,000 to over 1 million. The final chart, "A decline in business dynamism," links this regulatory growth to weakening business activity from 1977 to 2013. It depicts a steady decline in the job reallocation rate, which fell from around 36% of total jobs down to 26%, and a sharp drop in the net firm entry rate, which fell from around 4% of US firms to below 0% in the post-financial crisis years.

The page concludes with a discussion of researcher Bob Litan’s sudden resignation from the Brookings Institution, a think tank where he spent 40 years. Litan resigned after testifying in Congress about the potential adverse impacts of proposed changes to financial advisor disclosures, presenting an opinion that differed from the White House and Senator Elizabeth Warren. Although Litan testified as an independent consultant funded by a mutual fund company—and fully disclosed this sponsorship—the political fallout ultimately led to his resignation, raising concerns about the state of independent academic research and policy debate.

This page analyzes the economic disparities resulting from the decline of US manufacturing, arguing that the consequences have been particularly negative for African American workers. The author asserts that both job loss and earned income consequences were worse for African American workers than for white workers, driven by a faster and deeper decline in manufacturing employment over the entire period analyzed. These employment trends are proposed as a key explanatory factor behind the renewed widening of the racial wealth gap in the United States.

To support this observation, the page features two charts. The first chart displays US manufacturing employment by race from 2000 to 2015, measured as an employment-to-population index set to 100 in January 2000 on a three-month average. It tracks three demographic groups: White, African American, and Hispanic workers. While all groups show a severe downward trend, African American manufacturing employment suffered the steepest and deepest decline, dropping below an index level of 50 around 2010 before recovering slightly to finish near 55 by 2015. In contrast, manufacturing employment for White workers experienced a less severe decline, ending the period around 60. Hispanic manufacturing employment closely tracked the decline of African American workers, also ending near 55.

The second chart illustrates the racial wealth gap by plotting the median net worth of households in 2013 US dollars on a log scale from 1983 to 2013, comparing White and African American households. Over this thirty-year span, the median net worth of White households consistently hovered between $80,000 and $160,000, while the net worth of African American households remained much lower, fluctuating between approximately $5,000 and $20,000. The chart details the ratio of White to African American wealth over time, showing that the gap narrowed to its lowest levels of 6x in 1998 and 2001, but expanded dramatically in the following decade, reaching 10x in 2007, dropping to 8x in 2010, and then rising to 13x by 2013. Data sources cited include the Bureau of Labor Statistics, J.P. Morgan Asset Management, and the Pew Research Center.

This page from the publication discusses the historical disconnect between political policymaking and the practical realities of running a business, focusing on the late Senator George McGovern's post-political career. 

The page features a chart illustrating the degree of liberalism among prominent U.S. Senators based on Senate voting records from 1937 to 2014, where a score of 1.0 represents the most liberal. According to the DW-Nominate algorithm data compiled by Keith T. Poole of the University of Georgia, George McGovern of South Dakota ranks near the very top of the spectrum with a score of approximately 0.75. He is positioned just below Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who scores around 0.85, and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who scores around 0.80. The chart plots dozens of other senators in descending order of liberalism, including Ted Kennedy, Hillary Clinton, Al Gore, Harry Reid, Dianne Feinstein, Harry Truman, and Lyndon B. Johnson, ending with southern Democrats like John Stennis and Sam Ervin scoring near or below zero. 

The accompanying text explains that in 1992, after retiring from the Senate, McGovern used his lecture earnings to purchase a leasehold interest in a New England hotel. After the business went bankrupt during a recession, McGovern penned a reflective op-ed titled "A Politician's Dream Is a Businessman's Nightmare." The page presents excerpts from this piece, in which McGovern laments that he did not possess firsthand knowledge of business hardships while serving in public office, stating that such experience would have made him a better senator and a more understanding presidential contender. 

In the excerpts, McGovern argues that government must actively encourage business growth and praises figures like Bill Clinton, Paul Tsongas, and Bob Kerrey for shifting the Democratic Party's debate toward supporting capital-risking entrepreneurs. He criticizes rigid, "one-size-fits-all" regulatory thresholds—such as rules targeting businesses with 50 or more employees or over $500,000 in sales—for failing to account for profit margins, labor versus capital intensity, and local market economics. McGovern poses an open question to lawmakers regarding where to set regulatory standards so they do not choke off opportunities, concluding that leaders must start asking these practical questions more often. A footnote references a prior publication from November 4, 2015, which discussed Elizabeth Warren and a high-profile resignation at the Brookings Institution.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" argues that the impact of tort reform—specifically punitive damage caps and medical malpractice reform—is far smaller than proponents typically claim. 

To support this observation, the page features three scatter plots analyzing punitive awards relative to compensatory awards, plotted in millions of USD on a log scale ranging from $0.0 to $100.0 million. Sourced from Theodore Eisenberg of Cornell University, these charts display regression best-fit lines of individual court cases. The first chart illustrates the impact of the landmark 1996 Supreme Court decision BMW v. Gore, which theoretically should have limited punitive damages. However, the best-fit regression lines showing the relationship between punitive and compensatory awards before and after the decision are nearly identical. The second and third charts examine the 2005 Supreme Court case State Farm Mutual Auto v. Campbell, looking at bench trials and jury trials respectively. In both instances, the regression lines tracking awards before and after the ruling are almost entirely overlapping, demonstrating that these landmark judicial limits had very little real-world impact on relative punitive damage amounts.

The text also addresses medical malpractice tort reform, citing a 2014 study conducted by the University of Illinois and Northwestern University Schools of Medicine and Law. Examining nine states that adopted damage caps between 2002 and 2005, the researchers found that tort reform did not lead to a reduction in "defensive medicine" or lower healthcare costs. Instead, the reforms had no significant impact on Medicare Part A and Part B spending and were actually associated with a small ex-post rise in spending on physician services. The page explains that while physicians routinely practice defensive medicine to mitigate malpractice risk, liability is only one of many reasons they do so, meaning liability caps alone cannot solve the issue. The author concludes by quoting David Hyman, a professor of law and medicine at the University of Illinois, who describes tort reform as "a very small idea" that fails to deliver the system-wide cost savings promised by its proponents.

This page argues against the idea of abolishing the Environmental Protection Agency, countering common complaints of regulatory overreach with historical data showing that state-level environmental regulation prior to 1970 was highly ineffective. The author points out that as late as 1968, 70% of industrial waste discharges in the United States were entirely untreated, and by 1972, 15 million gallons of raw sewage were being dumped into the Potomac River daily. A historical footnote adds political context, noting that the EPA was originally proposed by Senator Ed Muskie and established by President Richard Nixon in 1970, and that Congress later overrode Nixon’s veto to pass the landmark Clean Water Act of 1972. 

To support the defense of federal regulation, the page features two line charts and a data table. The first chart, tracking air pollutants from 1970 to 2010 against an index where 1970 emissions equal 100, shows dramatic declines following key federal policies. After the passage of the Clean Air Act, the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, the Clean Air Act Amendments, and the Clean Air Interstate Rule, emissions of sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide plummeted to roughly 20% of their 1970 levels, while nitrogen oxide emissions were cut nearly in half. 

The second chart tracks national ambient lead levels from 1980 to 2012, illustrating a steep decline in lead concentration from over 1.6 micrograms per cubic meter in 1980 to nearly zero by 2012. This reduction is attributed to the federal phase-out of leaded gasoline, stricter point-source emission limits on smelters and battery plants, and the elimination of lead from paints and coatings. 

Finally, a table titled "Plenty of work still to do" underscores that water pollution remains a significant challenge, detailing that 54% of assessed US rivers (out of 3.5 million miles), 68% of lakes (out of 41.7 million acres), and 78% of estuaries (out of 87,000 square miles) are currently classified as polluted, while 42% of wadeable streams are in poor condition. Ultimately, the author concludes that the historical success of federal clean air and water initiatives makes returning environmental oversight entirely to the states a dangerous proposition.

This page analyzes the impact of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) of 2002, arguing that its implementation has coincided with a material improvement in the quality of corporate financial statements. Although SOX has faced criticism over compliance costs, the author notes that these expenses appear manageable. He cites a 2015 survey from Protiviti showing that 95% of small companies spend less than $500,000 annually on compliance, while most large companies with revenues over $10 billion spend between $1 million and $2 million. This burden was further reduced by regulatory changes in 2007 and the 2012 Jumpstart Our Business Startups (JOBS) Act, which exempted smaller firms. Additionally, while international cross-listings in the US declined after the act's passage, the author suggests this is a reasonable trade-off for increased investor confidence.

To support these assertions, the page features nine charts displaying steady improvements in corporate reporting and internal controls. The first chart, showing SEC Accounting and Audit Enforcement Releases from 2002 to 2014, details a drop in investigations and injunctive actions from a peak of nearly 250 in 2003 to around 125 by 2014. The second and third charts track Section 4.02 restatements, where prior statements are deemed unreliable, from 2005 to 2014; overall restatements plummeted from over 1,000 to under 400, while restatements for accelerated filers fell from approximately 400 to below 100. 

The next three charts focus on the diminishing impact of these restatements. The average net income adjustment per restatement shrank from a negative adjustment of over $20 million in 2005 to just a few million dollars in 2014, despite a brief spike to negative $11 million in 2011. Meanwhile, the share of restatements with an impact on the income statement fell from about 75% in 2005 to roughly 45% in 2014, and the size of the single largest restatement dropped from a peak of over negative $6 billion in 2005 to negligible levels by 2014. 

The final three charts demonstrate improved internal accounting health. The number of 4.02 filing companies declaring material internal controls weaknesses plummeted from nearly 140 in 2005 to under 20 by 2012. Similarly, the proportion of restatements involving multiple issues fell from a peak of 60% in 2005 to 30% in 2012, and the percentage of restatements affecting core earnings decreased from 65% in 2003 to around 42% in 2012. Together, these metrics indicate that corporate financial reporting has become significantly cleaner and more reliable in the post-SOX era.

This page serves as the Executive Summary for the 2016 Outlook, titled "Planet of the Aches." The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that while diversified portfolios are positioned for mid-single-digit returns in 2016—representing a slight improvement over 2015's returns of 0% to 3.5%—global growth remains slow and sluggish. While consumer spending sustains real retail sales growth at 3% to 4% annually, key pillars like manufacturing, trade, and capital spending are stagnating. This stagnation persists despite unprecedented monetary stimulus from major central banks. The flattening of global profits since mid-2014 is blamed in part on severe declines in the energy and mining sectors that have not been offset elsewhere, resulting in diminishing equity returns.

The first chart, "Global manufacturing, exports and capex: stagnating," tracks year-over-year percentage changes from 2010 through late 2015 for manufacturing output, export volume, and equipment capex, excluding China. All three metrics show a steady decline from their post-recession peaks of 10% to 15% in 2010 down to near-zero growth by the end of 2015, highlighting the broader economic stagnation.

The second chart, "Developed world central bank assets and policy rates," illustrates the massive scale of global monetary easing from 2005 to 2015 across a broad group of developed nations, including the United States, Eurozone, Japan, United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, Denmark, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, and Switzerland. The GDP-weighted policy rate plummeted from a peak of over 4.0% in 2007 to roughly 0.5% in 2015, while central bank assets surged from around $3.5 trillion to over $12 trillion. The author projects that, with ongoing ECB asset purchases of 60 billion Euros per month, Bank of Japan programs, and Federal Reserve reinvestments, these assets could swell by another $2 to $3 trillion over the next two years.

The third chart, "Slowdown in global earnings, with or without EM," tracks trailing 12-month earnings per share from 2010 to late 2015. It contrasts MSCI World Equity Index earnings excluding emerging markets on the left axis against earnings including emerging markets on the right axis. Both lines reveal a distinct flattening and downturn starting in mid-2014. The index including emerging markets fell from a peak near 26 down to approximately 24, indicating that the profit slowdown is global and not solely concentrated in emerging markets.

The final chart, "Despite central bank policy, diminishing returns on global equities," displays the rolling 1-year total return in local currency for the MSCI World Equity Index, both with and without emerging markets, from 2010 to late 2015. Despite supportive central bank policies, rolling returns fell from highs of 25% to 30% in late 2013 and early 2014 down to around 0% or slightly negative territory by late 2015. 

Footnote details provide additional performance context for 2015, noting that a 60/40 portfolio returned 0% for US dollar investors and 3.5% for Euro investors under specific currency-hedged assumptions. In both cases, emerging markets exposure dragged down returns by approximately 1%, and a 10% allocation to US high yield bonds subtracted another 0.5%.

This page of the publication analyzes the emerging markets component of the global slowdown, focusing on how the growth premium of emerging markets over developed economies has been steadily shrinking since 2010. While emerging markets face economic challenges, economic conditions in developed economies remain stable, as stronger services sector activity offsets weak manufacturing. The author addresses a key question for 2016: whether economic distress in emerging markets will trigger contagion in developed markets, presenting the assessment that contagion will remain largely limited. A primary driver of this economic divergence is a five hundred and fifty billion dollar annual wealth transfer from oil-producing countries to oil-consuming countries. This transfer disproportionately benefits regions with low gasoline taxes like the United States, where consumer-facing gasoline prices fell thirty to thirty-five percent from June 2014 to September 2015, compared to twenty-five percent in China, fifteen percent in the rest of the developed world, and only five to ten percent in emerging markets excluding China.

Four charts visually support this argument of divergence between emerging and developed markets. The first chart, titled Falling emerging markets growth premium, displays year-over-year real GDP growth from 1997 to 2015. It highlights that while emerging market growth historically peaked near eight percent in 2010, it has consistently declined to around four percent by 2015, whereas developed market growth has stabilized around two percent. The adjacent chart, titled Advanced economies stable despite EM weakness, shows a three-month average of manufacturing and services PMIs from 2010 to 2015. It demonstrates that while PMIs for China and emerging markets have slid down toward the contraction threshold of fifty, the combined PMI for the United States, Eurozone, and Japan has remained comfortably in expanding territory at around fifty-four.

The bottom half of the page illustrates this divergence in credit and consumer metrics. The third chart, titled A divergence in bank credit growth, uses dual axes to track year-over-year percentage change from 2009 to 2015. It shows developed market credit growth recovering from negative three percent in 2010 to nearly four percent in 2015, while emerging market credit growth fell from nearly twenty percent to roughly eleven percent over the same period. The final chart, titled and in real retail sales, shows year-over-year percentage changes from 2013 to 2015. Mirroring the credit trend, developed market real retail sales growth climbed from about one percent to over three percent, while emerging market real retail sales growth fell from over eight percent to around four percent, indicating that consumer spending momentum is shifting toward developed economies.

This page from the publication argue that while emerging market vulnerabilities played a role, the August correction in US equities was primarily driven by domestic factors, specifically slow core revenue and earnings growth. The author points out that even after stripping out the hard-hit energy sector, core sector revenues grew only in the single digits, with healthcare being the lone standout in Q2 with growth over five percent. This outperformance led to overcrowding and a subsequent healthcare-specific correction in late summer. 

To support these points, the page features four key visual charts. The first chart tracks the impact of the Chinese Renminbi devaluation on the S&P 500 and the MSCI Emerging Markets index throughout 2015. Both indices dipped sharply around the initial August devaluation, with the S&P 500 falling from over 2,100 to about 1,860, and the MSCI EM dropping from approximately 950 to under 800. The second visual is a trio of small line charts showing year-over-year percentage changes from early 2014 through late 2015. It highlights that S&P 500 core revenues dropped from a five-percent growth rate to below two percent, while S&P 500 core earnings fell from twelve percent to six percent, mirroring a broader slowdown in nominal global GDP growth from five percent to three percent.

The bottom half of the page addresses the toll that a strong dollar and weak earnings growth have taken on future expectations. The third chart displays consensus earnings per share estimates for the S&P 500 for the years 2015 and 2016. It shows that expectations for 2015 fell twelve percent from their peak to below one hundred twenty dollars, while expectations for 2016 dropped fifteen percent from a peak of nearly one hundred forty-five dollars down to around one hundred twenty-seven dollars. The final chart presents a long-term proxy for small business operating margin trends from 1987 to 2015, calculated by subtracting the percentage of businesses planning to raise wages from those planning to raise prices. This margin proxy fell sharply toward zero percent in late 2015, suggesting significant downward pressure on margins for 2016.

In conclusion, the author asserts that lower earnings growth justifies price-to-earnings multiples closer to historical averages rather than peak valuations. He expresses skepticism toward market participants who argue that low interest rates and low inflation should justify higher multiples in the face of a sub-par earnings outlook. Furthermore, a footnote highlights that during the late 2015 healthcare selloff, stock correlations spiked to sixty percent—roughly double the average historical level since the mid-1970s—pushing healthcare forward price-to-earnings multiples below parity with the overall market for the first time in two decades.

This page from the publication discusses how the slowdown in equity and credit returns in 2015 was predictable given the highly elevated expectations that preceded it. It contrasts the over-optimism of both private investors and policymakers with reality, focusing on market valuation metrics, Federal Reserve GDP growth projections, and rising global debt levels.

At the top left, a table displays the Market and Investor Optimism Barometer, comparing historical percentiles from December 2013 to December 2015, where the 99th percentile represents peak bullishness. The data shows a severe decline in investor sentiment and credit metrics over this two-year period. For instance, the individual investor bull/bear ratio plunged from the 93rd percentile to the 8th percentile, and independent advisor optimism fell from the 96th to the 52nd percentile. High grade bond spreads shifted from the 99th percentile to the 24th percentile, while high yield bond spreads fell from the 98th to the 29th. Valuation metrics also cooled, with small cap P/E ratios dropping from the 89th to the 54th percentile, though large cap forward P/E ratios remained elevated, moving from the 75th to the 78th percentile. 

To the right of the table, a line chart plots the cumulative total return in US dollars since January 1, 2005, of a simplified portfolio of risky assets, rebalanced quarterly. This portfolio is weighted with 30 percent S&P 500, 30 percent MSCI Europe, 20 percent US high yield, and 20 percent Europe high yield. The chart demonstrates that after the publication of the barometer in October 2014, when cumulative returns peaked near 110 percent, the portfolio's return trended sideways through late 2015.

The bottom-left line chart, titled Federal Reserve growth expectations too high, illustrates real year-over-year US GDP growth percentage changes from 2010 to 2014. It compares actual GDP growth, shown as a solid blue line that fluctuated between 1.5 percent and 2.5 percent, against various ex-ante FOMC projections made twelve months prior. The chart highlights a persistent gap where the Fed's forecasts were consistently too optimistic; for example, the projection made in 2010 estimated 2011 growth would approach 4 percent, whereas the actual growth rate was below 2 percent.

The bottom-right line chart, titled Despite a painful recession, overall economy-wide debt levels did not decline, tracks total non-financial debt as a percentage of GDP from 2000 to 2015. It features three series: developed markets, global, and emerging markets. Developed market debt steadily climbed from about 210 percent of GDP in 2000 to approximately 260 percent by 2015. Global debt mirrored this trend, rising from roughly 190 percent to 230 percent. Emerging market debt remained relatively flat at around 100 percent of GDP until 2009, after which it climbed sharply to about 165 percent by 2015. 

In the concluding text, the author explains that during the global recession, debt in much of the developed world shifted from households to governments. This accumulation of sovereign debt is expected to limit the fiscal ammunition available to governments for boosting growth, unless they choose to monetize fiscal deficits through central banks. The author projects that while fiscal austerity in the developed world has finally eased, the overall fiscal impact in 2016 will be neutral rather than stimulative.

This page analyzes whether the consensus financial projections for S&P 500 earnings and sales growth in 2016 are realistic. The discussion centers on a comprehensive table detailing year-over-year earnings and sales growth from the second and third quarters of 2015, estimates for the full year of 2015, and consensus projections for the full year of 2016. Overall, consensus forecasts project S&P 500 earnings growth to jump from a negative 2% in 2015 to an 8% increase in 2016, with sales growth rising from negative 4% to positive 5%. The table highlights optimistic projections for a Consumer Discretionary earnings bounce from 8% in 2015 to 14% in 2016, and an Information Technology earnings bounce from 4% in 2015 to 9% in 2016. Meanwhile, Energy sector earnings are projected to improve from a steep 59% contraction in 2015 to a milder 10% decline in 2016.

The author evaluates these forecasts, agreeing that lower energy prices, low inflation, and a stronger labor market support the Consumer Discretionary rebound, though noting that elevated valuations and crowded institutional positioning pose risks. However, the author remains highly skeptical of the projected technology earnings rebound. After stripping out Apple and Google, tech revenues are as weak as industrials, largely because of high foreign sales exposure and economic flatness in regions like Brazil, China, Europe, and Japan. Energy is also unlikely to rebound until 2017 due to expiring corporate hedges. Ultimately, the author expects consensus estimates are 1% to 2% too high, proposing a base case of mid-single-digit growth for both earnings and sales in 2016. 

A footnote extends the valuation discussion to key growth stocks. Amazon is cited as a prime example of soaring valuations, as its 2015 market capitalization equaled Walmart, Costco, and Target combined, despite having only 15% to 25% of their revenues and cash flows. The author compares Amazon's current trajectory to Walmart's historic rise from 1971 to 1988, noting that Amazon's stock price reflects high assumptions of 10% to 20% revenue growth over the next decade. Additionally, a basket of five major growth stocks—Google, Facebook, Amazon, Netflix, and Salesforce.com—displays late-cycle behavior. Their relative price-to-earnings ratios are 3.3 times that of the broader market, and their daily excess return correlations peaked at 45% in December 2015, mimicking the patterns of late-1990s market leaders Microsoft, Intel, Cisco, and Dell.

This page analyzes the state of credit markets, arguing that spreads are widening and that higher volatility is ahead for 2016. The primary driver of this trend is rising yields on energy bonds, reflecting increased expectations of default. A J.P. Morgan Securities report estimated that 30% of the high yield energy market could default by 2017 under a scenario of $45 oil and $2.75 natural gas. Crucially, the author notes that rising spreads have begun to broaden beyond energy and mining, historically a precursor to broader equity market downturns, as seen in the late 1990s and 2007. This stress follows a period of heavy inflows driven by low interest rates, which fostered easy credit conditions; for instance, covenant-lite loans comprised 70% of US loan issuance in 2015 compared to only 10% in 2009. The author also warns of severely reduced credit market liquidity, referencing the December 2015 gating of a $3.5 billion distressed credit mutual fund managed by Third Avenue.

Four charts support these points. The first, "US high yield corporate bond spreads," tracks the spread to worst over 10-year treasuries from 1995 to 2015. It compares energy bonds with ex-energy bonds, showing that energy spreads spiked dramatically in 2015 to around 10% or more, diverging significantly from the ex-energy spread which hovered near 6%. 

The second chart, "Impact of high yield energy companies," plots two metrics from 1996 to 2015. The blue line, representing high yield issuance by energy companies in billions of US dollars, shows a massive spike to over $60 billion around 2013 and 2014. The brown line tracks energy companies' share of total annual high yield issuance, peaking near 18% in the same period before falling sharply towards 10% in 2015.

The third chart, "The frantic search for yield," shows total mutual fund and ETF holdings of debt from 2005 to 2015 in trillions of US dollars. The stacked area chart details how total holdings ballooned from about $0.5 trillion to roughly $1.6 trillion by late 2015. This massive growth is broken down into four categories: High Yield, Municipal, Emerging market, and Inflation-linked debt.

The final chart, "Less liquidity in high-grade corporate bonds," measures the days required to trade the entire high-grade corporate bond market using a five-quarter average from 2006 to 2015. The line rises steadily over the decade, climbing from around 200 days in 2006 to over 300 days in 2015, signaling a substantial decline in market liquidity.

This page focuses on the economic and equity market outlook for the United States in 2016, arguing that improving labor markets and falling gas prices will boost consumption and housing, leading to projected GDP growth of 2.5% to 3.0%. The publication notes that consumer credit is accelerating beyond student loans into auto loans and credit cards, and that fiscal headwinds from federal and local governments have largely subsided. 

Several charts support this domestic macroeconomic view. A chart on steady employment growth shows year-over-year job growth stabilizing around 2% in 2015, following its deep drop to negative 5% in 2010. Another chart displays consumer credit growth rebounding to nearly 7% year-over-year by late 2015. Private wages as a percentage of GDP, shown on a six-month average, are normalizing upward to around 36.5% after bottoming near 34.5% in 2011. Additionally, a chart tracking home and auto sales shows both indicators trending higher; by late 2015, three-month average light vehicle sales reached roughly 5.5% of the population, while new and existing home sales climbed back to over 4% of households. A final chart in this macroeconomic section tracks bank loans to consumers alongside nominal consumer spending, showing that six-month annualized growth in bank loans reached over 6% in 2015, while consumer spending steadily expanded at a 3% to 4% rate.

Addressing the equity markets, the author forecasts a single-digit US equity market return as the central scenario for 2016. He addresses concerns over declining corporate profit margins, which historically can precede recessions. A historical chart of US profit margins from 1973 to 2015 shows that the 2015 margin decline was primarily an energy sector phenomenon, much like the margin decline in 1985 which also did not lead to a recession. The chart demonstrates that while the total market profit margin dropped, the ex-energy profit margin remained robust and stable near its peak of 9%, while the energy sector's margin plummeted toward 3%. This suggests that outside of energy, profit margins across the other nine S&P sectors remain stable, and the overall margin dip is not signaling an imminent economic recession.

This page analyzes how the rising US dollar has hindered corporate revenue, profit growth, and exports, while asserting that the domestic consumer rebound should nevertheless sustain economic momentum. The author posits that the majority of the dollar’s appreciation is now complete, particularly against the Euro and the Yen. A whimsical cartoon map of the United States illustrates key economic concerns across the country, labeling the Pacific Northwest with "Dollar Altitude Sickness," the South with "Shale Gas Acid Reflux," the Midwest with "Earnings Anemia," and the Northeast with "Toxic Political Sclerosis." 

To support the analysis of the currency's trajectory, the first chart, "Fast and furious: the rise of the dollar," displays the real effective exchange rate index from 1980 through late 2015. It plots two series: one comparing the dollar against a foreign exchange basket excluding the Chinese RMB, and another including the RMB. Both lines show a sharp appreciation beginning around 2011, rising from an index level of roughly 85 to over 110 by 2015, representing one of the swiftest climbs in historical record.

The adjacent chart, "Domestic demand strong, exports weak," details the contribution to GDP growth from 2012 to 2015. It contrasts a robust domestic final demand, which consistently contributed between 1.5% and 3.5% to GDP growth, with net exports, which acted as a drag for nearly the entire period, dipping to a negative 1.5% contribution in early 2015. 

The commentary explains that the dollar's strength has created a severe divergence between domestic services and globally exposed manufacturing. While capital spending is growing at 10% to 15% for domestic firms, it is falling at the same rate for global and energy companies. The commercial real estate sector remains strong, bolstered by significant Chinese capital outflows seeking safe-haven assets in rule-of-law nations like the US, UK, Canada, and Australia. 

This sectoral gap is illustrated in the third chart, "Unusually large gap between services & manufacturing," which plots three-month average PMI survey levels from 1998 to 2015. By late 2015, services remained in solid expansion territory near 58, whereas manufacturing had fallen close to the stagnation line of 50. 

Finally, the chart "Domestically oriented labor markets holding up" shows the six-month average change in payrolls from 2010 to 2015. It reveals that while services and construction added over 200,000 jobs monthly by late 2015, the manufacturing and mining sectors experienced a contraction, falling from a peak gain of 40,000 jobs in late 2014 to a loss of roughly 10,000 jobs per month by the end of 2015.

This page discusses the trajectory of Federal Reserve interest rate hikes and the underlying labor market dynamics in the United States. The author argues that while market expectations point to the weakest tightening cycle on record, these projections are likely too low due to a tight labor supply that could eventually trigger wage inflation. This potential spike in wage growth is highlighted as the single biggest risk for global markets in 2016.

The first chart, titled "Current expectations vs. historical Fed tightening cycles," plots the change in the policy rate from month zero to 24 months, comparing previous tightening cycles since 1964 in grey to current market expectations in blue. The blue line shows that markets anticipate a rate of only 1.35% two years out—representing a minimal increase that would be the lowest trajectory of Fed tightening on record.

The second chart, titled "Labor market dropouts by category since 2008," displays the U.S. labor force participation rate from 2008 to 2015. The rate declined from approximately 66.0% down to roughly 62.5%. This chart breaks down the dropouts into three stacked categories: retired, disabled, and other. The accompanying text explains that 3% of the labor force dropped out between 2008 and 2014, with Federal Reserve analysts concluding that nearly half of these leavers retired, a large portion self-diagnosed as disabled, and the remainder left for other reasons. 

The third chart, "Three measures of wage growth," tracks the year-over-year percent change from 1997 to 2015 for median wages, average hourly earnings, and wages and salaries from the Employment Cost Index. Although these metrics have only recovered to normal historical levels, they indicate a steady upward trend.

The final chart, "Net percentage of small businesses planning to raise worker compensation," spans 1987 to 2015. It shows that the net percentage of small businesses planning raises recovered sharply in late 2015 to around 15%, which is the highest reading since 2007. This sharp upward trend suggests that despite low overall goods price inflation, rising wages could compel the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates more quickly than markets currently anticipate.

This page from the Outlook 2016 report analyzes the macroeconomic landscape of Japan, focusing on the disconnect between corporate profits and consumer welfare under government intervention policies. The core argument is that while government-induced yen devaluation has successfully boosted large, multinational corporate profits, it has harmed Japanese households and smaller businesses by inducing imported inflation without triggering a corresponding recovery in household incomes.

The top portion of the page features two side-by-side charts comparing the United States and Japan from 2007 through 2015. The first chart, showing trailing twelve-month earnings per share, highlights that both nations experienced robust corporate profit rebounds following the global financial crisis. The S&P 500 index recovered from a low of around sixty dollars to nearly one hundred twenty dollars, while the MSCI Japan index rose from zero to roughly sixty yen. In contrast, the second chart reveals a stark divergence in real household earnings. While US real household earnings steadily rose to an index value near one hundred sixteen by 2015, Japan's real household earnings index steadily deteriorated, dropping from a base of one hundred in 2007 to approximately ninety-two by late 2015. Accompanying these charts is a cartoon illustration of the Japanese archipelago labeled "Japan Consumercurry Poisoning," emphasizing the plight of domestic consumers.

The bottom-left chart tracks Japan's real GDP and its components from 2008 to 2015, indexed to the first quarter of 2008. It shows that while real GDP and consumer spending recovered and stabilized near their 2008 levels, they remain flat. Real GDP dipped during the global financial crisis but clawed back to an index level of one hundred, while consumer spending fell following the introduction of a Value Added Tax in 2014 and has failed to rebound. Exports suffered a massive collapse to an index level of sixty-three in the first quarter of 2009 before recovering fitfully to around ninety-five. 

A adjacent table, titled "The incredible, shrinking benefits of massive Japanese money printing," underscores the diminishing returns of Japan's monetary easing since 2012. It shows that despite a massive one hundred forty-four percent expansion of the Bank of Japan's balance sheet and a twenty-seven percent real devaluation of the yen, annualized real GDP growth stood at a meager zero point eight percent as of September 2015. Annualized nominal GDP growth was only one point nine percent, annualized core inflation was one point three percent, and annualized bank loan growth reached just two point four percent. 

The text forecasts that Japanese GDP growth will remain volatile and expects 2016 growth to mirror the one point five percent average seen in 2015. In a footnote, the author highlights another systemic barrier for domestic consumers: Japan's highly elevated OECD producer protection ratio of one point nine, which keeps domestic agricultural prices artificially high compared to international standards. This ratio is significantly higher than that of the United States at one point zero two and the European Union at one point zero five. The author expresses skepticism that the Trans-Pacific Partnership will successfully dismantle these protectionist agricultural barriers.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2016 Outlook analyzes Japan’s macroeconomic landscape, corporate governance reforms, and the unprecedented monetary policy actions of the Bank of Japan, colloquially termed the "Japanese experiment." In October 2015, the Bank of Japan surprised market participants by opting not to increase its asset purchases, which included annual targets of three trillion yen in equity ETFs, ninety billion yen in REITs, and eighty trillion yen in government bonds. This pause, likely influenced by concerns over the domestic impact of a weakening Yen, is expected to persist until November 2016. However, several tailwinds exist for Japanese equities, such as nominal GDP growth accelerating to three percent compared to a flat zero percent average from 1991 to 2013, aggressive equity buying by the Bank of Japan and the Government Pension Investment Fund, and the privatization of massive financial institutions like Japan Post Bank and Japan Post Insurance. These newly privatized entities control three hundred trillion yen in assets, currently heavily concentrated in Japanese government bonds, which could eventually migrate toward equity risk.

Corporate governance reforms are also attempting to address the massive cash piles built up by Japanese corporations. A series of charts comparing US and Japanese companies reveals that Japanese firms hold cash equal to nearly forty-eight percent of their market capitalization and around thirty-seven percent of GDP, whereas US firms hold less than ten percent on both counts. Despite these massive reserves, Japanese corporations do less with their cash; their dividend payout ratio stands at about thirty-two percent compared to over fifty percent in the US, and their share buybacks account for a mere 0.6 percent of GDP compared to 3.0 percent in the US.

The final section of the page highlights the extreme and untested nature of the Bank of Japan's monetary policy. A line chart, humorously subtitled "A professor I once had told me this was impossible," plots the velocity of money against central bank assets as a percentage of GDP from 1970 to 2015. The velocity of money has collapsed in a near-continuous downward trend from a value of 1.0 in 1980 to about 0.4 by 2015. Meanwhile, Bank of Japan assets have surged from historical levels of around ten percent of GDP to nearly eighty percent of GDP by late 2015. The author warns that at this current pace of purchasing, private sector banks could run out of government bonds to sell by the end of 2016, forcing the central bank to buy bonds directly from the non-bank private sector. This creates an unprecedented situation of debt monetization with unknown consequences. A footnote highlights an additional unique policy: a Bank of Japan initiative to buy equity ETFs targeting firms that raise wages and capital expenditures, financed by selling its other stock holdings.

This page analyzes the global ramifications of China's economic slowdown, focusing on its impact on commodity markets, regional economic growth, and emerging market debt vulnerabilities. The author notes that while most commodity prices have fallen sharply since 2011, many remain higher than their year-2000 baseline levels. 

To illustrate these commodity trends, two charts are presented. The first, indexing oil, coal, copper, aluminum, natural gas, and agricultural prices to January 2000, shows that despite major post-2011 declines, copper, coal, and oil remain above their 2000 levels. The author adds that Barclays projects the copper market will face excess supply until 2020. The second chart tracks iron ore prices delivered to Qingdao, China, showing a dramatic drop from peak levels of nearly one hundred ninety dollars per metric tonne in 2011 down to around forty dollars per metric tonne by late 2015.

The analysis then shifts to how a one percent growth decline in China would impact global GDP by region. A bar chart based on data from 2000 to 2015 reveals that the developed world is largely insulated, with the United States, Euro Area, and Japan experiencing less than a zero point four percent cumulative growth impact. In contrast, emerging markets face substantial exposure; EM ex-China, EM Asia ex-China, Latin America, and EM EMEA all face cumulative growth declines of approximately zero point eight percent to over one percent. 

The major "wild card" identified by the author is the massive expansion of emerging market non-financial corporate debt, which the IMF reports doubled from nine trillion dollars in 2008 to eighteen trillion dollars in 2014. This surge is heavily linked to commodities, construction, and real estate in China. To assess which countries are most at risk, a final chart compares external debt as a percentage of exports, broken down by government, banks, intercompany loans, and other sectors as of the second quarter of 2015. Brazil and Turkey emerge as the most vulnerable, with external debt ratios exceeding two hundred percent of exports, followed by Chile, Indonesia, and Poland. Meanwhile, China appears highly resilient on this metric, with its external debt-to-exports ratio staying well below one hundred percent, alongside other lower-risk countries like Thailand, Taiwan, and South Korea.

This page from the publication focuses on cyclical economic improvements across Europe, arguing that while 2016 is showing signs of widespread recovery, the true test of this growth will arrive in 2017. The author notes that positive signals, including rising employment, improved business surveys, stronger bank lending, and healthier consumer confidence, are evident not just in core nations like Germany but also in recovering peripheral economies like Spain and Italy.

The top-left chart, which tracks eurozone employment and hours worked as a year-over-year percentage change from 2001 through 2015, illustrates this labor market recovery. Both metrics dipped sharply during the financial crisis of 2008 to 2009, with hours worked falling to negative four percent, and declined again in 2012. By late 2015, both series show positive momentum, rising back toward one percent growth. To the right, the Eurozone business surveys chart displays composite manufacturing and services PMI indices from 2010 to 2015. It highlights that while Germany leads with a PMI near 55, and the average for Italy and Spain has rebounded strongly from a 2012 low of 43 up to approximately 53, France is trailing the recovery, barely holding above the expansion threshold of 50.

In the middle row, the chart on Eurozone bank lending and consumer confidence reveals a parallel recovery in financial conditions and sentiment from 2005 to 2015. Eurozone bank lending, measured as a three-month average in billions of euros, has climbed from a contraction of negative 15 billion euros in 2013 to positive territory around 15 billion euros by late 2015. Consumer confidence, measured as a net balance of responses, has similarly improved from around negative 30 percent in 2013 to nearly negative five percent. This is mirrored in the adjacent chart tracking Eurozone retail sales and car registrations. Both series, plotted as three-month averages of year-over-year percentage changes, show a sharp recovery in late 2015, with retail sales rising toward three percent and new car registrations climbing to around ten percent.

The bottom of the page analyzes credit demand in Spain and Italy, plotting the net percentage of banks reporting higher demand on a two-quarter average from 2003 to 2015. In Spain, where credit demand fell to near negative 100 percent for mortgages and negative 75 percent for corporate debt around 2012, demand has rebounded significantly. By late 2015, corporate and consumer credit demand have both entered positive territory at roughly 30 percent and 50 percent respectively, while mortgage demand is hovering just below neutral. In Italy, the rebound is even more pronounced: consumer credit demand is near 50 percent, mortgage demand has surged to approximately 60 percent, and corporate credit demand has turned positive for the first time in years.

Despite these positive developments, the author notes that Italy’s turnaround remains fragile. While households and businesses are expanding, exports are rising, and unemployment is falling, Italy will require long-term easy money support from the European Central Bank and permission from the European Commission to delay fiscal tightening and debt reduction. Furthermore, a rising stock of non-performing loans in Italian banks continues to limit their lending capacity, posing a persistent structural challenge.

This page analyzed the rising importance and global footprint of emerging markets (EM), arguing that these economies have transitioned from exotic niches to mainstream financial powerhouses that command far more attention than they did during the 1998 Asian and Russian financial crises. The central driver of this shift is China, whose rapid expansion has exerted an immense economic gravitational pull on other emerging nations through commodity demand and trade linkages. 

A detailed table tracks the footprint of emerging markets from 1980 to 2015, revealing that EM inflows as a percentage of global GDP surged from 1.0% to 17.5%, while the developed world's asset allocation to EM rose from under 0.5% to 5.75%. Over the same period, the EM share of global output expanded from 27% to 47%. The rise of debt markets is particularly stark: EM annual corporate bond issuance exploded from just $2 billion in 1990 to $931 billion by 2015. China's dominance within this space is clear, with its share of annual EM corporate bond issuance rising from 0% in 1990 to 72% in 2015, while its share of global fixed investment leaped from 3% in 1980 to 27% in 2015. 

To demonstrate China's specific impact, a horizontal bar chart compares China's share of various global economic categories between 2000 and 2014. Over this span, China's share of global growth rose from roughly 8% to 30%, and its share of global fixed investment shot up from about 4% to 26%. The shift is most extreme in industrial materials, with China's share of global commodity consumption rising from approximately 12% to 43%, and steel consumption climbing from 15% to 46%.

This commodity demand is further explored in an area chart tracking global copper consumption from 1900 to 2010. While copper demand in the rest of the world flattened at around 10 million metric tons after the year 2000, China’s consumption exploded, driving total global consumption toward 18 million metric tons and making up nearly half of the entire global copper market by 2010. 

As a result of this scale, other emerging economies have become deeply tied to China’s business cycle. A line chart tracking the 10-year rolling correlation between China’s GDP growth and that of all other EM countries shows this relationship rising from nearly zero in the mid-1990s to a peak of around 0.45 in 2010, remaining highly elevated at approximately 0.43 in 2014. A medical-themed cartoon map illustrates this vulnerability, depicting South Asia as an "Asian Tigers" region suffering from "Sinoverexposure" and "Balance Sheet Inflammation," alongside Chile afflicted with "Copperiodontitis," visualising the overexposure of commodity exporters and manufacturing partners to any potential slowdown in China.

This page, from the Emerging Markets section of the Outlook 2016 report, asks whether emerging market (EM) equities have corrected enough, concluding that a bottom in EM asset prices will likely occur over the next 12 to 18 months. The author notes that EM price-to-book ratios and trade-weighted EM currencies (excluding China) are approaching 1998 levels, while investor positioning is extremely underweight. The commentary highlights that market bottoms typically occur before macroeconomic distress indicators—like unemployment, defaults, and export declines—peak, and that rising manufacturing surveys are useful timing signals.

To support this view, a table and three charts examine EM valuations, positioning, and balance of payments metrics. The first table, "Balance of payments pressures in the emerging world," documents current accounts and peak-to-current declines since 2010 for Malaysia, Brazil, Colombia, Turkey, Indonesia, and South Africa. It shows significant current account adjustments, such as Turkey improving from its worst level of -10.2% of GDP to -4.3% today. It also highlights steep currency depreciation, with Brazil and South Africa falling 47% and 44% respectively, and significant declines in unit labor costs, such as Colombia dropping 31%.

The second visual, a chart titled "On a P/B basis, EM getting closer to 1998 levels," tracks the relative price-to-book value of emerging markets against both EAFE and the US from 1990 to late 2015. It illustrates that EM's relative price-to-book value has fallen sharply since 2010, dropping to approximately 0.6x versus EAFE and roughly 0.4x versus the US, which approaches the historical lows of late 1998 and the early 2000s.

The third chart, "Global fund managers underweight EM vs. DM," depicts fund manager relative positioning from 2001 to late 2015. It demonstrates that investor sentiment is highly pessimistic, with positioning dropping below negative 40% towards deep underweight territory for EM, a level of extreme underweighting not seen since the early 2000s.

The final chart, "Emerging markets: real effective exchange rates," displays the GDP-weighted broad real effective exchange rate from 1995 to late 2015 for both China and EM excluding China. The data shows a stark divergence: while China's exchange rate has steadily risen to nearly 130, the EM ex-China index has depreciated back down to around 90, matching the low valuation levels observed during the Asian Financial Crisis around 1998 to 2002.

This page analyzes emerging market vulnerabilities, focusing on Brazil and Turkey as the countries experiencing the greatest economic distress heading into 2016, with additional context on Russia, Chile, and South Africa. 

Brazil's economic downturn is characterized by rising domestic debt, fiscal deficits, double-digit inflation, falling growth, and a sharp unemployment surge from 4.6% in the second quarter of 2014 to 8% in the third quarter of 2015. While the author notes that Brazil's $350 billion in foreign exchange reserves and lower reliance on external debt make a sovereign default unlikely, domestic assets remain under heavy pressure. This economic reality is paired with a cartoon map of South America depicting satirical ailments like "Dilma-cular Degeneration," "Iron Ore Deficiency," and "Petrobranchitis." To illustrate these troubles, a line chart titled "Brazil: if you forgot what stagflation looks like, this is it" tracks year-over-year real GDP growth and inflation from 1990 to 2015. The chart highlights historical inflation peaks of 4,922% in June 1994 and 17% in May 2003, and shows a stark divergence in late 2015 as inflation spikes toward 10% while GDP growth plummets to nearly negative 4%.

The discussion of Turkey emphasizes its status as one of the most capital-reliant nations globally, with a negative net international investment position second only to Greece among major emerging markets. Turkey's balance of payments crisis is exacerbated by political instability, capital flight, a falling Lira, shrinking central bank reserves, and currency mismatches within its banking sector. A cartoon map of the region features illustrative afflictions such as "Erdogangrene," "Greece Conjunkdebtivitis," and "International Capital Addiction." An accompanying line chart plots Turkey’s net international investment position in billions of US dollars from 1997 to 2015. This metric, which measures household, corporate, and sovereign liabilities to foreigners minus domestic holdings of foreign assets, shows a persistent decline from near-zero in 1997 to approximately negative $400 billion by late 2015.

Lastly, the page addresses Russia, noting that while the nation faces flat growth in 2016 following a 4% GDP contraction in 2015, much of this pain has already been priced into financial markets. The Russian equity market is noted as trading at the lowest price-to-earnings ratio in the emerging market space, and its currency has depreciated by 60% from its 2011 peak. Russia's situation is accompanied by a cartoon depicting diagnoses like "Pu-tinnitus" and "Petronucleosis." The author concludes by mentioning that, aside from Brazil, other commodity exporters like Chile and South Africa exhibited the weakest economic momentum at the close of 2015.

This page details the broadening economic slowdown in China, arguing that the nation's competitive edge has diminished since the financial crisis. Consequently, in 2016, China is projected to experience its lowest economic growth rate since 1990. The author notes that a fifty percent appreciation in the Renminbi has created currency headwinds, while stagnating industrial profits, excess capacity, and slowing investment continue to put downward pressure on wages. Additionally, a massive rise in corporate debt and severe environmental degradation—referenced by a cover cartoon snippet depicting environmental and public health hazards as "Cirrhosis of the River"—threaten to drag down long-term growth.

Six charts illustrate these domestic economic pressures. The first chart, comparing gross fixed capital formation as a percentage of GDP, demonstrates that Chinese capital investment peaked at nearly forty-five percent of GDP between 1981 and 2012. This level of investment significantly eclipsed the peak investment levels seen during the historical industrializations of Japan, Korea, and Germany, which topped out between thirty percent and thirty-eight percent. 

The second chart tracks China's Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) from 2010 to 2015, illustrating that the services sector has remained relatively stable and expansionary, fluctuating between fifty-four and fifty-eight. Conversely, the manufacturing sector weakened steadily, dipping below the expansionary fifty-threshold to around forty-eight by late 2015. 

The third chart displays the year-over-year percentage change in fixed asset investment by sector from 2008 to 2015. It shows a dramatic collapse in real estate and construction investment growth, which plunged from over thirty-five percent to nearly zero percent. Industrial investment also fell to single digits, while infrastructure and other service sectors remained somewhat more resilient. 

A fourth chart details the decline in electricity consumption and railway traffic growth from 2010 to 2015. Year-over-year electricity consumption growth fell from nearly twenty percent to near zero, while railway traffic growth plunged deep into negative territory, bottoming out near negative fifteen percent in 2015. 

The fifth chart shows the rapid accumulation of non-financial corporate debt as a percentage of GDP, which surged from roughly one hundred percent in 2008 to over one hundred fifty percent by 2015. 

The final chart shows that year-over-year growth in China's industrial profits collapsed from nearly thirty percent in 2011 to negative five percent by late 2015.

This page of the publication analyzes China's slowing economic growth and its impact on consumer activity, housing, labor, and financial markets, arguing that the country is on its way to a lower annual GDP growth rate of four percent by 2020. The author notes that while home prices have bounced, an overhang of inventory remains a major barrier to residential construction, and a sharp boom-and-bust cycle in onshore equity markets has caused medium-term damage to the inner workings of Chinese financial systems. 

This domestic slowdown is illustrated across six charts. The first chart, tracking the China real consumer activity index year-over-year percentage change from 2004 to 2016, shows that activity peaked near forty percent in 2010 but steadily declined to just under five percent by late 2015. This is mirrored by the second chart on China retail sales from 2012 to 2015, which shows nominal growth declining from sixteen percent to eleven percent and real growth dipping from twelve percent to around nine percent.

The third chart highlights the inventory issues in the property sector by comparing housing inventory levels relative to 2010. While Tier 1 cities have inventory levels around one hundred fifty percent of 2010 levels, Tier 2 cities are at roughly two hundred ten percent, and Tier 3 cities face a massive overhang of nearly three hundred thirty percent. Weakness is also evident in the fourth chart, which tracks deteriorating labor market conditions. This index, combining wage growth, employment growth, and PMI surveys, fell from a positive reading in 2011 down to around negative one point one by late 2015.

The final two charts address Chinese equities. The fifth chart displays the close correlation between margin debt as a percentage of GDP and onshore equity prices represented by the CSI 300 index. Both skyrocketed in tandem in early 2015, with the CSI 300 peaking above five thousand and margin debt surpassing three percent of GDP, before collapsing together later that year. The sixth chart compares forward price-to-earnings multiples for offshore H-shares and onshore A-shares from 2004 to 2015. Onshore A-shares have historically been highly volatile, spiking to over twenty-two times forward earnings in 2015, whereas offshore H-shares remained much more conservative, trading between ten and twelve times forward earnings by the end of 2015 as international investors began pricing in the reality of slower growth.

In this publication, the author argues that the positive impact of stock buybacks and share count reductions on the equity markets is likely peaking. Although buybacks have historically added approximately two percent annually to earnings per share (EPS) growth during periods of scarce organic earnings growth, rising credit spreads and elevated corporate debt suggest that the EPS contributions from buybacks and mergers and acquisitions (M&A) could be cut in half by 2017. 

To support this outlook, the page features four charts tracking corporate spending, leverage, and tech IPO profitability. The first chart, titled "Another strong year for buybacks," tracks annual buyback announcements by S&P 500 companies in billions of US dollars from 1997 through 2015. The data shows buyback announcements surging back toward their 2007 peak of around 700 billion dollars, with 2015 annualized at nearly 600 billion dollars. The second chart, "S&P 500 M&A transactions and buybacks," shows this combined spending as a percentage of earnings before interest, taxes, and intangibles using a four-quarter average from 1999 to 2015. This ratio has risen to over 20 percent, surpassing its 2007 peak and indicating that corporate expenditures on M&A and buybacks relative to cash flow are at historic highs.

The third chart addresses corporate leverage, titled "Rising S&P 500 leverage, particularly ex-tech," plotting net debt to EBITDA from 2000 to 2015. By comparing a series for "Ex-financials" with "Ex-financials & technology," the chart reveals that the cash-rich technology sector masks a dramatic increase in leverage across the rest of the non-financial corporate landscape. While the ex-financials line stands at a moderate net debt to EBITDA ratio of around 1.3 in 2015, the ex-financials and technology line has risen sharply since 2012 to exceed 2.0, approaching levels last seen during the early 2000s recession.

Finally, the fourth chart, "Remembrance of things past: low percentage of technology company IPOs with profits," acts as a late-stage market signal. It displays the annual percentage of technology companies with positive net income at their IPO date from 1980 to 2015. In 2014 and 2015, this profitable share fell below 20 percent, a level almost as low as the dot-com bubble era of 1999 and 2000. A footnote contextualizes this by noting that while the tech IPO market has structurally improved since 1999 with longer pre-IPO lifespans and lower price-to-sales ratios, the current low profitability at IPO still signals a high market appetite for risk. Ultimately, the author highlights shifting dynamics, noting that acquiring companies experienced positive relative stock market returns from 2010 to the third quarter of 2015, but these relative returns turned negative in the fourth quarter of 2015, signaling a potential turning point.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Outlook 2016 focus publication argues that global banking systems are far more resilient than they were before the 2008 financial crisis. Due to higher capital ratios and a reduced reliance on volatile wholesale inter-bank funding, banks are in a much better position to handle write-downs. Furthermore, the risk from energy-sector debt and emerging market exposure has largely shifted away from highly leveraged banking systems and toward less leveraged corporate, institutional, and individual investors, which typically results in less pronounced market corrections.

The page supports this thesis with four distinct charts. The first chart, titled "Developed world banks have increased capital," tracks Tier 1 capital ratios from 2000 through 2015 for the United Kingdom, Eurozone, United States, and Japan. Across all these regions, Tier 1 ratios rose significantly after the financial crisis, climbing from pre-crisis lows of roughly 7.5% to 10.0% up to a range of 12.5% to nearly 15.0% by the third quarter of 2015. 

The second chart, titled "and reduced reliance on wholesale funding," illustrates loan-to-deposit ratios for the same four regions over the same fifteen-year period. Since peaking around 2008, loan-to-deposit ratios have dropped substantially, signifying a greater reliance on stable customer deposits over wholesale funding markets. The loan-to-deposit ratio in the Eurozone and the United Kingdom fell from over 130% down to around 110% by 2015, while the United States dropped from approximately 100% to under 80%, and Japan remained low and stable near 65%.

The third chart demonstrates the changing structure of emerging market credit, showing "Foreign funding to emerging markets by creditor type" from 1985 to 2015. In 1985, banks provided the vast majority of emerging market funding, accounting for over 80% of the total. By 2015, the share of bank credit had shrunk to roughly 30%, with the remainder distributed among investors, corporates, and other non-bank entities. This shift means that emerging market stress is less likely to trigger a systemic banking crisis in developed markets.

The final chart, "US energy debt mostly from high yield market, not banks," displays US energy debt as a percentage of shareholders' equity from 2001 to 2015, covering mining and oil and gas extraction industries. While total energy debt surged in 2014 and 2015 to nearly 80% of equity, the vast majority of this increase was driven by non-bank debt such as bonds and commercial paper, which spiked to over 60% of equity. In contrast, direct energy bank loans remained low and flat, accounting for only about 10% to 15% of equity. This indicates that the high-yield bond market, rather than the banking system, bears the primary exposure to the energy sector's downturn.

This page outlines J.P. Morgan's outlook for the oil market in 2016, presenting a narrative roadmap that suggests prices will remain rangebound near-term—potentially falling temporarily to around $30 per barrel—before modest recovery drivers take effect in 2017–2018. The current market is characterized by severe oversupply and brimming storage capacity. 

A chart tracking the world oil supply balance from 1970 to 2015 shows trailing twelve-month production exceeding consumption as a percentage of production, with a stark upward spike in oversupply toward the end of 2015. This oversupply is corroborated by a chart of global floating crude oil storage from 2010 to late 2015, which shows the four-week average of floating storage rising dramatically throughout 2015, surging from under 85 million barrels to over 160 million barrels.

The primary structural drivers behind this oversupply are declining Chinese demand growth and broader global improvements in energy efficiency. A bar chart tracking the annual growth of Chinese crude oil demand from 2003 to 2015 shows that growth spiked at nearly 1,000 thousand barrels per day in 2010—driven by strategic reserve accumulation and the aftermath of the 2009 stimulus program—but subsequently declined, ending 2015 at approximately 200 thousand barrels per day. This decelerating demand is paired with a steady decline in energy intensity among major global economies. An energy intensity index chart, tracking barrels of crude oil demand per unit of real GDP from 2005 to 2015, shows consistent downward trajectories for Europe, Russia, Japan, India, the United States, and China. China is leading this efficiency trend, with its energy intensity index falling to nearly 60 by 2015.

The supply glut is further compounded by geopolitical shifts and changes in producer behavior. An oil production chart for Iran from 2010 to 2016 illustrates historical production falling from 3.75 million barrels per day in 2010 to a low of nearly 2.50 million barrels per day in 2013 due to sanctions. J.P. Morgan Securities forecasts that, assuming the nuclear deal is successfully implemented, Iranian production will rise back toward 3.25 million barrels per day in 2016. 

Compounding the surplus, Saudi Arabia has refused to act as a swing producer to stabilize prices. A supporting table compares historical oil market downturns from 1996 to 2015, showing that in previous market declines, Saudi Arabia and OPEC slashed output to defend prices. For instance, during the 2008–2009 downturn, when oil prices collapsed by 74.9%, Saudi output fell by 18.1% and OPEC output fell by 15.6%. In contrast, during the 2014–2015 downturn, when prices fell 62.9%, Saudi output actually rose by 5.4% and OPEC output rose by 5.9%. The commentary notes that many US producers are unlikely to shut in production until prices drop below $40.

This page analyzes the deep deflationary effects of an oil price bust on the energy sector’s supply chain, earnings, valuations, and default rates. The author highlights that price busts drive down the marginal cost of oil, noting that well development costs in some locations have plummeted from 4.0 million dollars to 2.2 million dollars per well. An index chart of nominal and real well costs from 1975 to 1985 illustrates that the dramatic cost increases of the late 1970s and early 1980s completely reversed in real terms by 1984, returning to baseline 1975 levels. 

Looking forward, a line chart of Brent and WTI oil futures projects a modest price rebound over 36 months, with Brent rising from approximately 37 dollars to 53 dollars per barrel, and WTI rising from about 35 dollars to 51 dollars per barrel. This price pressure has deeply impacted corporate performance. A bar chart comparing S&P 500 sector earnings shows energy sector earnings plunging by 59 percent in 2015 and an estimated 10 percent in 2016, whereas non-energy S&P 500 sectors remain stable with projected growth of 5 percent in 2015 and 8 percent in 2016. 

Despite the earnings crash, the publication asserts that credit conditions alone will have a modest impact on the sector's operational capacity because investment-grade producers represent 75 percent of US oil output, and only 8 percent are rated B or lower. However, high-yield credit spreads show a stark divergence. A chart tracking US high-yield corporate bond spreads from 1995 to 2015 shows that while non-energy spreads remained low, energy spreads spiked near 12 percent in late 2015. 

At the same time, large-cap energy stocks have fallen to their lowest relative valuations in decades. A chart of the price-to-book ratio of energy relative to the large-cap universe from 1925 to 2015 shows the ratio dropping to approximately 0.6x, which is comparable to historic lows from the early 1930s and late 1990s. 

To assess the potential for distress if low prices persist, a bottom-up energy default analysis table outlines cumulative default rates from 2015 through 2017 under three scenarios, all assuming gas prices of 2.75 dollars.
