In a modest recovery scenario with 55-dollar oil, the total default rate is projected to reach 20.0 percent, peaking at 11.6 percent in 2017. In a spot market scenario of 45-dollar oil, the total default rate rises to 29.6 percent, with an 18.6 percent rate in 2017. Under an unsustainably low scenario of 35-dollar oil, the cumulative default rate is projected at 35.3 percent, with default rates spiking rapidly to 20.0 percent in 2016 before settling at 10.7 percent in 2017. Data for these visualizations are sourced from the Energy Information Administration, Bloomberg, Morgan Stanley, Barclays Research, Empirical Research Partners, and J.P. Morgan Securities.

This page provides a financial market update focused on credit and equity markets, addressing whether a US profits recession will trigger a full GDP recession. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that while manufacturing surveys are weak, other domestic indicators like services and payrolls remain supportive. He forecasts low but non-recessionary US GDP growth of 1.5% to 2.0% in 2016. In terms of earnings, he expects S&P 500 earnings for Q4 2015 to be down 3% year-over-year (but up 2% excluding energy) and forecasts 2016 ex-energy earnings growth of 4% to 6%. Consequently, he suggests equity markets may remain range-bound since valuations are not cheap and the benefits of central bank interventions are fading. He expects US and European consumer spending to rise due to payroll growth and lower oil prices, though he warns of diminishing returns from cheap oil due to low bank loan-loss reserves and high-yield energy market disruptions. Additionally, he expects China to devalue its currency further due to weak growth, capital outflows, and labor unrest.

The analysis is supported by four key charts. The first chart, in the top left, is titled "Manufacturing surveys are in territory that has coincided with combined profit/GDP recessions in the past." It plots the ISM Manufacturing index from 1960 to 2015 against historical economic recessions, shaded in gray, and profit recessions, shaded in orange. The index line is shown dipping below the key expansion threshold of 50 in late 2015, reaching levels that historically have aligned with combined profit and GDP downturns.

To the right, the second chart, "When services hold up better than manufacturing, GDP recessions can be avoided," shows the three-month average PMI survey levels for services and manufacturing from 1998 to 2015. This visual highlights a divergence in late 2015, where the manufacturing PMI is dipping below 50, but the services PMI remains resilient at around 55, supporting the author's view that a GDP recession can be averted.

The bottom-left chart, titled "China real effective exchange rate," displays the CPI-based real effective exchange rate (REER) from 1995 to 2015. The index shows a steady, massive appreciation from a base of around 70 in 1995 to a peak of nearly 130 in late 2015, illustrating why the author believes China's currency peg has created significant structural problems that may force a market devaluation.

The final chart, in the bottom right, is titled "After correction, stocks cheaper but not that cheap" and displays the combined price-to-sales ratio on MSCI US, Europe, and Japan equities, excluding financials and energy, from 2004 to early 2016. It compares the forward 12 months ratio to the trailing 12 months ratio. Although the ratio declined from a peak near 1.5x down to approximately 1.3x following the late 2015 correction, it remains significantly higher than its historical bottom of around 0.6x in 2009, reinforcing the author's point that valuations are not yet extraordinarily cheap.

This page, titled Act III: Changes to the regulatory landscape, explores how regulatory reforms since the 2008 financial crisis have made a repeat scenario less likely. The text explains that risk-based capital ratios are now higher, banks rely less on wholesale funding, stress-testing of portfolios has increased, and potential bank failures would see bondholders take on the majority of the risk rather than taxpayers or depositors. 

To support this observation, the top of the page features two line charts tracing bank metrics from 2000 to 2015 across the United Kingdom, Eurozone, United States, and Japan. The first chart, depicting Tier 1 capital ratios, shows a marked upward trend for all regions starting after 2008, with ratios rising from historic lows near 7.5 percent to between 12.5 percent and 15.0 percent by late 2015. The second chart, tracking loan-to-deposit ratios, shows a significant reduction in wholesale funding reliance. Loan-to-deposit ratios in the United Kingdom and Eurozone, which peaked at nearly 140 percent around 2006 to 2008, fell to roughly 110 percent by 2015, while the United States fell from above 100 percent to near 80 percent, and Japan maintained a lower, stable ratio around 70 to 80 percent.

The middle and bottom sections of the page contextualize the necessity of these post-crisis protections by illustrating the extreme severity of the Great Recession. The commentary notes that deposits in failed and assisted US banks as a percentage of GDP in 2009 actually surpassed the peak of the Great Depression in 1933, prompting former Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke to call the 2008 crisis the worst in global history. A bar chart below shows deposits in failed and assisted US banks as a percentage of GDP during three eras. During the Great Depression, the peak reached just over 6 percent of GDP in 1933. During the Savings and Loan Crisis of 1982 through 1992, bank failure deposits consistently remained below 2 percent of GDP. In contrast, during the Great Recession, the figure rose past 3 percent in 2008 and spiked to over 8 percent of GDP in 2009.

Finally, an accompanying table lists the emergency facilities created by the Federal Reserve during the crisis to prevent widespread defaults, along with their peak outstanding balances in billions of dollars. The Term Auction Facility saw the largest peak at 493 billion dollars, followed by the Commercial Paper Funding Facility at 348 billion dollars, and the Term Securities Lending Facility at 236 billion dollars. Other facilities included the Asset-Backed Commercial Paper Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility at 152 billion dollars, the Primary Dealer Credit Facility at 147 billion dollars, Term Repurchase Transactions at 80 billion dollars, the AIG Revolving Credit Facility at 72 billion dollars, and the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility at 48 billion dollars.

This page, titled "Act IV: A chorus of concern emerges," argues that despite assurances from Paul Volcker and Federal Reserve officials that increased regulations have not significantly harmed credit market liquidity, a broad consensus of academic and industry experts has warned of negative consequences since at least 2012. The author expresses skepticism toward official claims, drawing a parallel to the Federal Reserve and the Department of Housing and Urban Development's historically unacknowledged roles in the housing crisis. 

To support this critique, the page presents a compilation of quotes from prominent financial figures and academics. Anjan Thakor of Washington University in St. Louis warns that the Volcker Rule retrenches banks from market making in riskier, smaller securities where liquidity is most valuable. Darrell Duffie of Stanford University notes that the rule increases borrowing and hedging costs for investors and may push market-making activities to less regulated non-bank entities, threatening financial stability. Charles Calomiris of Columbia University warns that separating proprietary trading from market making is nearly impossible and amounts to a "Volcker lobotomy" that strips banks of essential human capital, referencing similar liquidity concerns raised by Central Bank of Mexico Governor Agustin Carstens. Paul Asquith of MIT provides empirical data showing that mandated market transparency led to a 41.3% reduction in trading activity and a 24.7% decrease in daily price standard deviation for high-yield bonds, suggesting transparency can harm market participation. Finally, Howard Marks of Oaktree Capital Management cautions that curbing banks' ability to buy assets during market crises will likely result in severe liquidity shortages precisely when support is most critical.

This page examines the factors that could eventually drive oil prices higher, focusing on supply adjustments in both the United States and global markets, alongside the fiscal pressures facing Saudi Arabia. The author predicts that while oil prices may remain below $40 per barrel for a few months in 2016, a gradual supply-demand rebalancing—including the absorption of idle storage—will be well underway by early 2017, leading to rising prices.

The top-left chart analyzes key US shale oil plays, specifically the Bakken, Eagle Ford, and Permian basins, from 2007 to 2015. It tracks the oil rig count on the left axis and oil production in millions of barrels per day on the right axis. The data shows that while the oil rig count plummeted dramatically from a peak of around 1,000 in late 2014 to roughly 400 in late 2015, oil production only recently began to turn downward after peaking at over 4.5 million barrels per day, illustrating how production laggingly follows drilling activity. The top-right chart shows that a wider global supply adjustment is underway among 97 major oil companies. Annualized capital expenditure peaked near $525 billion in 2014 and fell to around $425 billion in 2015, with the 2016 capex estimate dropping further to approximately $375 billion. This reduction in spending comes as annualized cash from operations fell below capital expenditures in late 2015, a pressure expected to intensify as prior oil hedges roll off in 2016 and 2017.

The page then transitions to Saudi Arabia's fiscal runway and the potential pressure on the kingdom to tighten oil supply. The middle-left chart displays the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency (SAMA) balance sheet in billions of Saudi Riyals from 2000 to 2015. Total assets peaked near 2,800 billion Riyals in 2014 before declining in 2015, driven entirely by a drop in government deposits. This is a critical vulnerability given that oil accounts for 90% of government revenues. The middle-right chart projects the impact of government spending and Brent crude prices on SAMA government deposits from 2013 to 2019. In a favorable scenario of $90 oil with a 3% fiscal adjustment, deposits remain stable around 1,500 billion Riyals. However, in a scenario of $65 oil with no fiscal adjustment, government deposits are projected to deplete entirely and enter negative territory by late 2018. 

The bottom-left chart contextualizes Saudi Arabia's capacity to handle low oil prices by comparing Saudi government debt as a percentage of GDP against the Brent crude oil price from 1991 to 2015. When Brent crude prices were low in the late 1990s, Saudi government debt peaked at 100% of GDP, which subsequently fell to nearly 0% as Brent prices rose above $100 per barrel in the 2010s. This history suggests that while current low oil prices are depleting reserves and raising debt, the Saudis have a high tolerance for debt and may take a long time to experience enough financial distress to unilaterally tighten global oil supply.

This page focuses on Brazil’s economic vulnerabilities, analyzing its sovereign debt structure, inflation indexing, and corporate debt risks, specifically regarding the state oil giant Petrobras. The author argues that high indexation of wages and debt to inflation exacerbates a downward economic spiral of recession, currency depreciation, and capital flight. Brazil reversed its 1990s de-indexing progress between 2003 and 2011, leaving collective bargaining to cover 60% of labor contracts, which is far higher than levels in Argentina, India, and Mexico. 

However, the author notes that sovereign default risk on external debt is significantly lower than in 2002 because financing has shifted from external to domestic markets; public external debt to GDP fell from 18% in 2002 to just 5% in 2015. Thus, unlike Greece in 2009 or Argentina in 2001, sovereign external debt is not Brazil's primary issue. Nonetheless, public finances remain pressured by short-term and inflation-indexed debt, even if credit spreads might currently overestimate default risk after Brazil was downgraded to junk status by S&P and Fitch.

This shift in vulnerability is supported by a table comparing indicators of external vulnerability from 2002 to 2015. Across all metrics—percentage of GDP, percentage of exports, and percentage of international reserves—vulnerabilities have decreased. For example, gross external debt as a share of international reserves fell from 598% in 2002 to 151% in 2015, while the non-bank public sector’s gross external debt dropped from 18% to 5% of GDP and from 246% to 24% of international reserves over the same period. Two-year amortization requirements for the non-bank public sector also fell from 7% of GDP to less than 1%.

An accompanying line chart plots Brazil's credit spread on external sovereign debt using 5-year credit default swap (CDS) spreads in basis points from 2001 to 2015. It shows a dramatic peak in October 2002 at 3,950 basis points, followed by a long period of lower spreads that stayed well below 400 basis points for most of the decade, before rising again toward 500 basis points by 2015.

A second line chart illustrates foreign financial exposure to Brazil as a percentage of world GDP (excluding Brazil) on a four-quarter average from 1980 to 2015. Exposure grew from around 0.5% in the 1980s and 1990s to a peak of over 2.0% around 2011 before dipping slightly toward 1.8% in 2015, indicating that global markets are much more exposed to Brazil than in past crisis periods.

Finally, the text addresses "Petrobranchitis," noting that Petrobras debt quintupled between 2009 and 2014, and the firm has failed to generate free cash flow since 2008. Facing 24 billion US dollars in debt maturities over the next two years, the company risks running out of cash by the end of 2016 without asset sales, a government bailout, local bank support, or highly dilutive equity offerings. Rating agencies S&P and Moody's suggest a high probability of state support, but the exact mechanism is uncertain, prompting the author to warn investors to exercise caution despite enticing bond yields of 12% to 14%.

This page explores the argument that post-financial crisis regulatory efforts to reduce systemic risk may have come at the cost of increased market risk. Specifically, many of these regulations make it harder for banks to expand their balance sheets during crises, reducing their capacity to take on risk or facilitate trading for others. 

To support this claim, the author provides a detailed overview of several key credit-market regulatory scopes, their real-world impacts, and the applicable rules governing them. For bank capital, rules like Basel III, the Basel Fundamental Review of the Trading Book, the Supplementary Leverage Ratio, and the Global Systemically Important Bank Surcharge require higher capital against corporate bond trading inventories, phase out lower-quality capital, and apply leverage ratios to total assets rather than risk-weighted assets. This limits asset transfers and reduces the appetite of banks to hold volatile positions. In bank liquidity, the Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio require banks to hold high-quality liquid assets, which reduces the money multiplier in the banking system. Meanwhile, stress testing via the Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review creates a more robust capital framework but diminishes banks' incentives to participate in certain business lines.

Under structural reforms, the Volcker Rule and EU Bank Structural Reform prohibit proprietary trading, restrict speculative investing, and require ex-ante assessments of client demand, making banks less willing to hold inventory that could become illiquid. Money market reforms, specifically the SEC Money Market Reform, introduce floating net asset values and could lead to reduced investor participation in prime money market funds during periods of stress. J.P. Morgan Securities research estimates that the combined impact of fund conversions and investor outflows could shift $600 billion to $650 billion in assets away from prime money market funds.

For credit market transparency, the European Securities and Markets Authority's Markets in Financial Instruments Directive introduces pre- and post-trade transparency and mandatory buy-ins, while US TRACE rules increase transparency requirements for 144a securities, affecting the bulk of the high-yield market. Finally, new Securitization Capital Rules impose capital charges on retained positions, altering the balance sheet economics of securitization. 

A critical footnote elaborates on these credit market transparency initiatives, drawing parallels to equity market mandates from the 1990s and 2000s. A J.P. Morgan Securities report from November 2015 highlights that when similar transparency was mandated in equity markets, principal traders disappeared and large trades became significantly harder to execute, forcing institutional investors to use multiple venues and tickets. The author warns that the resulting agency-driven, high-frequency trading model is not a panacea for bond markets, as these traders show low commitment and quickly withdraw liquidity during times of heightened volatility and uncertainty, raising the risk of "flash crashes."

This page explores whether high-yield bond spreads currently offer a fair-value margin of safety for investors. The author notes that while implied default rates are quite high—standing at 18 percent for energy bonds and 6 percent for non-energy bonds—investors must weigh several historical precedents. Specifically, credit spreads historically lead default rates, suggesting that defaults are likely to rise further from current levels. 

The top chart, titled Relationship between high yield default rates and credit spreads, plots rolling 12-month default rates on the left axis and spreads on the right axis from 1985 through 2015. This visual highlights how spikes in credit spreads consistently precede peaks in default rates, particularly around recessionary periods marked in grey. 

To determine the optimal timing for purchasing credit, three historical case studies are presented under the heading Time capsule: in the past, it made sense to buy credit before defaults peaked, but not before they began. In each panel, high-yield credit spreads are mapped against the cumulative number of defaulting issuers. During the Savings and Loan Crisis from 1987 to 1993, credit spreads peaked when 55 percent of cumulative defaults had occurred. In the Tech collapse from 1999 to 2004, spreads peaked when cumulative defaults reached 76 percent. During the Global Financial Crisis from 2006 to 2013, spreads peaked when only 30 percent of defaults had been realized. These examples demonstrate that spreads rally well before defaults peak, though buying before defaults even begin remains an aggressive strategy. 

The author concludes by discussing valuation methodology, suggesting that investors estimate default and recovery rates to determine a minimum spread. However, the text warns that because liquidity conditions are substantially changing, investors require an additional spread cushion, similar to the illiquidity premium demanded by private equity investors compared to public equity markets.

This page examines the risks and potential opportunities in the credit market, focusing on the substantial redemptions and rising leverage that signal a breaking levee in high-yield credit. Michael Cembalest argues that while high-yield spreads peaked in tight territory back in April 2014, the current risk environment for weak credits is healthier than it was in 2000, yet heavily resembles the conditions of 2007. 

An accompanying chart showing cumulative flows into global high-yield bond funds in USD billions from 2005 to 2015 illustrates this shift, showing a steep drop from a peak of nearly 140 billion dollars down to around 80 billion dollars by late 2015 as redemptions accelerated. 

A second chart tracking US high-yield corporate bond spreads over 10-year Treasuries from 1995 to 2015 highlights the widening gap between the energy sector and ex-energy sectors. Spreads for energy bonds surged past 15 percent by late 2015, while ex-energy spreads remained lower but climbed to between 6 percent and 8 percent. This widening reflects the immense pressure on energy and mining, alongside potential forced selling risks from crossover buyers and collateralized loan obligations facing downgrade limits, as most CLOs have a 7.5 percent cap on CCC-rated exposure. 

A quarterly bar chart displays the median gross debt-to-EBITDA leverage multiple for US high-yield issuers between 2000 and 2015. The multiple has risen steadily from its post-crisis lows of around 3.0x to approach 4.0x by late 2015, driven by weak sales growth of just 2 percent to 3 percent annually since 2013. 

To assess systemic risk, a horizontal bar chart compares the percentage of the high-yield index comprised of weak credits across five metrics: leverage greater than six times cash flow, cash-to-debt below 5 percent, interest coverage below 2x, negative free cash flow to debt, and enterprise value to sales above 4x. These metrics are compared across three periods: 2000, 2007, and the current period in early 2016. This comparison shows that while current credit metrics are significantly stronger than they were in 2000, they are nearly identical to the warning signs seen in 2007, particularly with leverage over six times cash flow sitting above 50 percent. 

Cembalest notes that refinancing risk is relatively contained since the bulk of high-yield maturities fall after 2020, although the concentration of bonds due within four years remains similar to 2008 levels. Additionally, he addresses the high-profile gating of a Third Avenue high-yield mutual fund, clarifying that it is not representative of the broader market because it held more than 85 percent of its assets in CCC-rated and non-rated securities.

In this report, J.P. Morgan’s Michael Cembalest addresses the question of why US equity markets are declining if services, rather than manufacturing, dominate the domestic economy. He argues that while services drive US GDP, manufacturing, business capital spending, energy, and the strength of the US dollar have a disproportionately large impact on S&P 500 corporate profits. 

To illustrate this divergence, a central table compares GDP metrics directly with S&P 500 metrics. While international exposure via US exports represents only 12% of GDP, foreign-sourced profits account for 40% of S&P 500 profits. Conversely, personal consumption expenditures make up 69% of GDP, but consumer-related services generate only 35% of S&P 500 profits. The disparity is most evident in manufacturing, which employs just 14% of the workforce but accounts for 65% of S&P profits. Business capital spending constitutes 13% of GDP, yet business spending is equivalent to 20% of S&P earnings. Similarly, oil and natural gas represent only 1% of total US employment but accounted for 11% of S&P profits in 2014. Historically, a surging US dollar has caused only a modest decline in overall economic growth, but it has led to stock market crashes or corrections. This equity-market sensitivity is underscored by a 59% correlation between manufacturing surveys and S&P returns from 2005 to 2015, compared to just a 39% correlation for service sector surveys. A footnote adds that a rising US dollar has reversed two-thirds of the US unit labor cost competitiveness gains against emerging markets achieved between 2000 and 2010.

Two supporting charts further detail these trends. The first chart, titled "Manufacturing weakness may be affecting services," plots PMI survey levels on a three-month average from 1998 to early 2016. It shows that manufacturing PMI has fallen toward the 50-level contraction threshold, and the services PMI is beginning to follow it downward. The second chart, "Global and US earnings revisions remain weak," measures the net proportion of earnings upgrades minus downgrades relative to total revisions from 2008 to early 2016. It tracks both the S&P 500 and the MSCI All Country World Equity Index ex-US, showing that both indexes remain deeply negative, with net revisions hovering between negative 20% and negative 40% in early 2016. Cembalest concludes that regardless of whether a recession occurs, markets in 2016 are repricing for very low revenue and earnings growth, with S&P 500 sales growth consensus standing at just 2% due to weak corporate guidance.

This page analyzes how credit hedge fund managers positioned themselves ahead of 2016. The author divides these managers into three distinct categories: directional managers who are primarily long-only, dynamic low net managers with balanced long and short exposures, and distressed managers targeting heavily discounted securities. The overarching finding is that as 2015 concluded, managers across all three groups significantly reduced their exposure in response to worsening market conditions, prioritizing cash conservation to capitalize on expected volatility in 2016.

The first chart, titled Directional credit hedge funds, tracks fund exposure throughout 2015. It shows that net exposure peaked near 80 percent and long exposure reached approximately 72 percent around April 2015, before both steadily declined to around 60 percent and 58 percent, respectively, by the end of the year. Similarly, gross exposure for these funds, measured on the right axis, peaked at about 112 percent in April before falling to roughly 92 percent by December.

The second chart, titled Dynamic low net credit hedge funds, presents the net and gross exposure for these relative-value players over the same period. Net exposure, on the left axis, rose from around 11 percent in January to nearly 18 percent by mid-year, only to plummet back to around 5 percent by December. On the right axis, gross exposure peaked at over 280 percent in July 2015 before dropping to approximately 255 percent at year-end, signaling a significant reduction in overall leverage.

The third chart, Distressed credit hedge funds, illustrates the asset exposure of distressed debt managers in 2015. Net exposure, measured on the left axis, peaked at about 70 percent in the spring of 2015 but fell sharply to around 52 percent by December. Meanwhile, their long exposure, on the right axis, started the year near 88 percent, ticked up to 92 percent in April, and ultimately wound down to roughly 82 percent by the year's close.

The final chart, Cash balances, measures the three-month average cash holdings as a percentage of total assets for both directional and distressed funds from 2012 through late 2015. This metric serves as a proxy for risk appetite. It shows that cash balances for directional funds spiked dramatically toward the end of 2015, reaching nearly 18 percent. Distressed funds' cash levels also rose to around 12 percent by late 2015. These elevated cash reserves confirm that credit managers actively pulled back risk in late 2015 to prepare for more volatile, yet potentially lucrative, buying opportunities in 2016.

This page addresses the ongoing debate over whether the US was in an earnings recession in 2015, explaining that the answer depends entirely on the earnings definition used. The author highlights the stark difference between GAAP/reported earnings, S&P operating earnings, and "Pro-Forma" operating earnings. A visual breakdown of S&P 500 earnings per share for Q4 2015 shows GAAP/reported earnings at $91 per share, championed by Robert Shiller. Standard & Poor's adds back $13 in restructuring and acquisition charges to reach $104 for S&P operating earnings, supported by S&P, Goldman Sachs, and Barclays. Finally, major brokerage firms like J.P. Morgan, Morgan Stanley, and others add back an additional $14 of non-recurring items—such as asset write-downs and non-cash compensation—to calculate Pro-Forma operating earnings of $118 per share. An accompanying line chart of year-over-year trailing 4-quarter EPS growth from 2011 to 2015 demonstrates how these definitions diverge: the Pro-Forma metric stayed flat to positive near 0% in late 2015, while the S&P operating metric dropped to nearly -5% and Shiller’s reported metric plummeted toward -10%, indicating a clear earnings recession under the stricter guidelines.

Looking forward to Q1 2016, the page warns that earnings expectations are rapidly declining. A table detailing these shifts shows that between December 31 and February 5, expected growth for almost all sectors was revised downward. Only three out of ten sectors remained in positive territory: Consumer Discretionary (falling from 16.0% to 13.2%), Telecom (falling from 13.7% to 12.8%), and Healthcare (falling from 5.3% to 4.8%). The rest fell into negative territory, with Technology dropping to -7.4%, Materials to -15.8%, and Energy collapsing to -84.0%. The table also notes foreign sales percentages, highlighting that highly exposed sectors like Tech (59% foreign sales) are seeing significant revisions.

Finally, the author analyzes market valuations using a chart of S&P 500 enterprise value to operating cash flow before capital spending from 2002 to early 2016. Tracking Staples, Healthcare, Consumer Discretionary, and Technology, the chart shows that while multiples have fallen from their peak in 2015, they remain elevated compared to the "oversold" troughs of 2009-2012, indicating that the market is not yet deeply discounted.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, explores two separate financial topics: the disconnect between economic growth and equity returns in emerging markets, and the valuation correction in the high-growth cloud computing sector. 

Cembalest first discusses emerging markets, explaining how economic expansion does not always translate to investment success. In 2012, when the International Monetary Fund reported that emerging markets surpassed a 50 percent share of global GDP, McKinsey published a highly bullish report forecasting that annual consumption in these regions would reach 30 trillion dollars by 2025. However, 2012 ultimately marked the peak of emerging market equity outperformance. Stress points included a heavy sensitivity to Chinese demand for commodities and intermediate goods, combined with a high reliance on dollar-denominated debt, which grew increasingly expensive as local currencies depreciated. 

Two charts illustrate this emerging market narrative. The first, titled "Emerging market equities hit the wall in 2012...", displays a total return index from 1995 to 2015, set to a base of 100 in December 2012. It shows developed market equities rising steadily to nearly 140 by late 2015, while emerging market equities fell and fluctuated between 80 and 100. The second chart, titled "...just when the EM share of global GDP hit 50%", utilizes IMF data from 1980 to 2012 to show world GDP share at purchasing power parity. This chart depicts the steady convergence of the two segments, with developed markets falling from around 70 percent to just under 50 percent, and emerging markets rising from 30 percent to meet them at the 50 percent threshold in 2012.

The second half of the page addresses the sharp decline in fast-growing, high-margin cloud computing stocks, which fell by a third in early 2016. Cembalest explains that while these companies boasted high gross margins of approximately 70 percent and strong revenue growth of around 25 percent, valuations remained elevated at 7x to 8x sales. Furthermore, roughly two-thirds of these firms still had negative operating cash flow. He highlights key downside risks for 2016, including potential cuts in corporate IT spending and intensifying price competition from industry giants Google and Amazon. Cembalest notes that the sell-off reduced the valuation premium of cloud stocks relative to legacy tech giants Microsoft and Oracle, raising the broader question for 2016 of how to price growth appropriately, irrespective of a potential recession.

Two additional charts support the technology analysis. The first, titled "Remembrance of things past: low percentage of technology company IPOs with profits", uses data from Jay Ritter to show the percentage of tech companies with positive net income at their IPO date from 1980 to 2015. This figure has declined significantly from levels above 80 percent in the early 1980s, bottoming out below 20 percent during the dot-com bubble, and remaining low at around 40 to 50 percent in the mid-2010s. The final chart, "Valuations and profitability of cloud computing sector", tracks a 45-company Bessemer cloud universe from 2011 to 2016. It plots two metrics: the average enterprise value to sales ratio, which peaked near 11x in early 2014 before dropping to around 6x by 2016, and the percentage of companies with negative operating cash flow, which climbed from roughly 30 percent in 2011 to more than 60 percent by 2016.

This page analyzes the potential tax rates under a hypothetical Bernie Sanders administration, noting that such reforms would require substantial Democratic legislative gains of at least 30 House seats and 4 Senate seats to be enacted. The proposed changes include a 6.2 percent Social Security tax on earned income over 250,000 dollars, a 2.2 percent premium tax on ordinary income across all brackets, capping itemized deductions as a 28 percent tax credit for high earners, taxing long-term capital gains and qualified dividends as ordinary income for incomes above 250,000 dollars, and introducing new marginal tax brackets of 43 percent, 48 percent, and 52 percent for incomes starting at 500,000 dollars, 2 million dollars, and 10 million dollars respectively. The author distinguishes effective tax rates from marginal rates, emphasizing that while marginal rates grab headlines, effective rates, which measure total taxes paid as a percentage of total taxable income, are what ultimately matter to taxpayers.

To illustrate the impact, four charts compare current effective tax rates with proposed Sanders tax rates across different taxpayer profiles as income scales from 25,000 dollars to 10 million dollars. For a salaried worker, whose income is 90 percent wages, the effective tax rate under the Sanders plan begins to diverge significantly from current levels around the 300,000-dollar mark, eventually rising above 50 percent at the 10 million-dollar income level, compared to the current rate of around 42 percent. For a retiree with no wage income and 30 percent of income from 401k distributions, the impact is more muted but still leads to higher effective rates, rising to around 37 percent at the highest income levels versus current rates under 30 percent. 

The most dramatic change occurs for a control investor or private equity principal who relies on long-term capital gains and qualified dividends for 80 percent of income. Because capital gains would be taxed as ordinary income under the proposal, their effective tax rate under Sanders climbs sharply from a current rate of roughly 20 percent to over 50 percent for incomes above 1 million dollars. Similarly, a hedge fund manager or active investor relying on ordinary unearned income for 50 percent of their earnings would see effective rates climb from a current rate of approximately 32 percent to nearly 50 percent at high income levels. These effective tax rate models assume specific baseline conditions, including a 1 percent property tax rate, 1 percent charitable contributions, 7 percent state and local taxes, and a 5 percent mortgage rate.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management examines the public market performance of "unicorn" companies—private startups valued at over $1 billion—arguing that very few manage to sustain material gains once they transition to public stock exchanges. 

The primary visual is a line chart titled "Many unicorns finding it hard to survive in the wilderness," which plots the stock price performance of 17 public unicorns for up to 900 days post-IPO, indexed to 100 on their first day of trading. The chart reveals that stock price weakness typically intensifies around the expiration of the standard 180-day lock-up period, leaving the vast majority of these stocks well below their initial index of 100. Specific companies tracked on the chart include Facebook, LinkedIn, Alibaba, Mobileye, GoPro, Twitter, Zynga, Groupon, LendingClub, Atlassian, Pure Storage, Sunrun, Shopify, Fitbit, Etsy, Box, and Square. In the long-term "Current" column on the right side of the chart, only Facebook and LinkedIn show positive index gains, while Zynga and Groupon sit near the bottom of the scale. 

The author shares several key observations regarding these listings. Although there are about 150 unicorns globally with an aggregate valuation exceeding $500 billion—where nearly half of that value is concentrated in ten major firms like Uber, Xiaomi, Airbnb, Palantir, China Internet Plus Holding, Snapchat, Flipkart, Didi Kuaidi, SpaceX, and Pinterest—their transition to public markets has been challenging. Even though these 17 IPOs had an average first-day jump of 45%, only Facebook, LinkedIn, and Shopify have managed to keep gains above 15% relative to their IPO price, and ten of them are deeply in negative territory. 

Despite these public market struggles, the text explains that early-stage unicorn investors can still reap substantial profits. This is because IPO valuations averaged 55% higher than final private-round valuations, which were already 75% to 100% higher than previous private funding rounds. However, late-round investors face considerable risk of loss, particularly when IPO valuations fall below final private-round valuations, as occurred with Zynga, Square, and Box. Looking forward, the author predicts that the ongoing struggles of post-IPO investors will eventually depress private unicorn valuations, limit their access to public markets, and lead to much more restrictive investment terms.

In this commentary, the author analyzes the complex investment terms and protections surrounding late-stage "unicorn" valuations. High-valuation fundraising rounds can box companies in through restrictive clauses like blocking rights, ratchets, and senior liquidation preferences. These provisions, which may have been granted too easily during the optimistic market of 2014 and early 2015, protect later-stage investors but can severely hamper future fundraising and impede realistic mergers and acquisitions. 

The author warns that these market stresses, along with IPO delays and internal corporate turnover, could trigger a substantial shake-out over the next year or two. Consequently, strategic and non-venture-capital investors might soon be able to acquire stakes in surviving unicorns at deep discounts. The author highlights the polarization in the market by noting that among ten privately acquired unicorns, outcomes were highly mixed: WhatsApp and zulily generated substantial gains, while Good Technology, Better Place, Gilt Groupe, and Fab resulted in substantial losses.

To illustrate the trade-offs investors demand when buying in at high premiums, the page features a detailed table titled "Select Unicorn terms and conditions," utilizing data from Fenwick & West covering the second quarter of 2014 through the fourth quarter of 2015. The table displays metrics across five categories: Financing Overview, Price Change, Acquisition Protection Terms, IPO Protection Terms, and Participation. Key trends reveal a decline in the number of unicorn financings from 37 in the earliest period down to 12 by the fourth quarter of 2015. Over the same period, investor protections intensified sharply. For example, the share of deals containing a senior liquidation preference jumped from 15% in the third quarter of 2015 to 42% in the fourth quarter. Similarly, deals featuring either a blocking right or a ratchet reached 50% in the fourth quarter of 2015, up from 30% in the initial 2014 to early 2015 period. Other metrics, such as cumulative dividends and liquidation preferences at a multiple greater than 1.0, also spiked to 17% in late 2015, underscoring how late-stage unicorn investors increasingly insulated themselves from downside risk as the market cooled.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, published on March 16, 2016, presents six key observations and associated charts monitoring current macroeconomic and market indicators. The overall discussion covers stock performance drivers, earnings growth revisions, labor incomes, credit downgrade cycles, and energy default sensitivities.

In the first observation, the author argues that short covering played a large role in the performance of the best and worst S&P 500 stocks since late January. This is illustrated by a bar chart showing the total return by short interest deciles, where the most shorted decile achieved an average total return of over eight percent, while the least shorted decile returned nearly nine percent, creating a U-shaped return distribution across S&P 500 members.

The second and third observations address slowing corporate earnings and the potential for a consumer-led recovery. A line chart tracking consensus earnings per share growth estimates for 2016 reveals that expectations for the S&P 500 have tumbled from twelve percent in mid-2015 to just two percent, with European earnings following a similar downward trajectory. Meanwhile, expectations for Japan have held relatively steady near ten percent, and emerging markets have ticked up with rebounding oil prices. The author points out that while declining earnings often signal the end of a cycle, past cycles show corporate profits can rebound, particularly when supported by rising labor incomes. This support is reflected in another line chart showing year-over-year growth in developed world disposable personal income from 2005 to 2016, with recent figures trending upward at roughly three percent in the United States, two percent in Germany, and over two percent in France.

The final sections analyze high-yield credit markets and energy defaults. A bar chart compares investment-grade downgrades as a percentage of the high-yield market during the 2000 to 2003 tech cycle against the current cycle's forecast. The downgrade wave is projected to be much milder today, reaching under twenty percent of the high-yield market compared to nearly sixty percent in the earlier cycle, which the author notes is marginally positive for high-yield credit. Lastly, a chart tracking West Texas Intermediate oil prices from January 2014 through early 2016 highlights the non-linear relationship between crude prices and energy defaults. The chart estimates that the two-year high-yield energy bond default rate drops dramatically from sixty percent if oil remains at twenty-five dollars per barrel, down to thirty-six percent at thirty-five dollars, twenty-seven percent at forty-five dollars, and just eleven percent if oil climbs to fifty-five dollars, demonstrating how quickly default risks subside with stabilizing energy prices.

This commentary by Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management explores what the election of a political novice, specifically Donald Trump, might mean for investors and the broader market by examining historical precedents of extreme political uncertainty. The author notes potential impacts of Trump's proposed policies, such as Medicare drug negotiation pressures on the healthcare sector and a projected ten trillion dollar rise in the budget deficit over ten years, which is contrasted with an eight hundred billion dollar projected deficit under Ted Cruz. 

To understand how markets react to severe political volatility, the analysis turns to the historical example of Huey Long's dominant and highly controversial reign in Louisiana during the late 1920s and 1930s. The page features a vintage black-and-white campaign flier from around 1928 with a portrait of Huey Long, bearing the slogan Huey P. Long for Governor, A Sure Winner. 

The text outlines Long's dictatorial grip on Louisiana, citing biographer accounts of voter fraud, physical assaults, bribery, kidnapping, and his open ambition to bypass democratic norms. Despite his authoritarian methods and being considered by Franklin D. Roosevelt to be one of the most dangerous men in America, Long oversaw massive public works, including increasing paved roads from three hundred and thirty miles to thirteen thousand miles, providing free school textbooks, and funding hospitals. 

Strikingly, economic research from American University and the University of Iowa reveals that Huey Long's volatile political career, spanning from 1924 through his 1929 impeachment proceedings to his 1935 assassination, had very little impact on Louisiana-domiciled stocks or bonds. When compared to national averages, even targeted sectors like oil companies showed no substantial performance divergence. Cembalest concludes that this historical case study illustrates how financial markets can remain surprisingly resilient and stable even during periods of extreme political uncertainty and transition into the unknown.

This page focuses on three main macroeconomic and market observations: the continued economic slowdown in China, the sudden end of the momentum investment era in equity markets, and the resilience of the non-energy US economy despite a severe downturn in the oil and mining sectors. 

In China, the author observes that nearly all tracked economic indicators are slowing, with the exception of property-related data, prompting the government to curtail capital outflows and leading to a spike in labor unrest. This trend is visualized in the chart titled "China: The Year Of The Draggin'," which displays various indicators from 2011 to 2016. These series—comprising employment surveys, exports, business conditions, GDP, corporate earnings, industrial production, and retail sales—all show a clear and persistent downward trajectory over the five-year period, converging near their lowest levels by early 2016.

The second section explains how the multi-year outperformance of momentum stocks ended abruptly in early 2016. The author notes that investors had overpaid for scarce growth, driving relative valuations of momentum stocks to extreme levels compared to value stocks. This is depicted in the chart "Expensive momentum stocks hit a wall in 2016." The blue line, representing the total return index of a long-short basket of "Best" minus "Worst" momentum stocks, peaked above 32 in late 2015 before falling sharply in early 2016. Meanwhile, the brown line shows that the forward P/E valuation gap between the best momentum stocks and the best value stocks peaked near 9x in late 2015 before retreating.

The final section argues against an impending US recession, pointing to the resilience of the non-oil economy. While energy sector default rates have spiked to 12%, non-energy high-yield default rates remain stable at 2%. This divergence is illustrated by two charts. The chart "US business capital spending" displays the year-over-year percentage change in non-residential fixed investment. It shows that while oil and mining capital expenditures collapsed to nearly -50% by early 2016, all other capital expenditures remained stable, fluctuating in a positive range between 5% and 10% during 2015. Similarly, the chart "US jobs: a tale of 2 economies" plots the six-month average of annualized monthly employment changes. It shows that job growth in all other sectors remained steady, averaging between 1.5% and 2.0% from 2014 through early 2016, while employment in the oil and mining sectors plummeted from over 15% growth in 2014 to around -15% by 2016.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the economic and social drivers behind the political appeal of outsider candidates in the 2016 primary elections. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that the best explanation for the primary election results is the devastating impact of China’s 2001 entry into the World Trade Organization on US workers. This event triggered rising foreign exchange intervention by China, a collapse in US manufacturing jobs, and a sharp decline in the share of corporate profits going to US labor. Academic papers from the Federal Reserve, Yale, MIT, CEMFI, and UC San Diego support this connection, arguing that the granting of Permanent Normal Trade Relations to China in 2000 directly drove the decline of US manufacturing, rather than general declines in US competitiveness. 

Two charts at the top of the page illustrate these economic changes from 1960 to 2015. The first chart, on the top left, tracks the ten-year percentage change in US manufacturing jobs alongside Chinese FX intervention as a percentage of GDP on an inverted scale. Following China's entry into the WTO in 2001, US manufacturing job losses rapidly accelerated, dropping past negative thirty percent, while Chinese FX intervention surged, peaking near forty percent. The second chart, on the top right, shows that this period coincided with a sharp decline in US labor’s share of non-financial gross profits, which plunged from around sixty-four percent before 2001 to historical lows of around fifty-seven percent by 2010.

On the bottom left, the page addresses the issue of unauthorized immigration, noting that data does not support the idea of a recent spike. The chart tracks the total foreign-born US population in millions from 2000 to 2014, showing a steady rise from thirty-one million to over forty million, while the unauthorized immigrant population remained relatively flat. The unauthorized immigrant population peaked at thirty-two percent of the total foreign-born population in 2007 and has since declined to twenty-seven percent.

Finally, the chart on the bottom right connects these anxieties to primary voter turnout as a percentage of eligible voters from 1980 to 2016. It shows that Republican primary turnout has surged to nearly thirteen percent through the March 15, 2016 primaries, a modern-era high for the party. Meanwhile, Democratic turnout, though rebounded from 2012 levels, remains lower than its 2008 peak of nearly eighteen percent.

This page analyzes the impact of recent Chinese economic stimulus and evaluates the resilience of global credit markets in the face of significant fund outflows. 

The author begins by addressing China's aggressive monetary and fiscal stimulus, noting that while it has triggered a temporary economic response—such as a minor pickup in industrial production and a slowing of capital outflows—it remains unconventional, unusual, and unsustainable over the long term, with underlying private sector data still pointing to sub-6% growth. This situation is illustrated by two charts covering the period from 2011 to early 2016. The first chart, titled "Pump Up the Volume," shows the year-over-year percentage change of stimulus measures. It highlights a massive surge in mortgage lending, which approached 25% by early 2016, and a sharp increase in capital expenditure by state-owned enterprises to over 20%, while government spending and total social financing hovered between 10% and 20%. In contrast, the second chart, "China: The Year Of The Draggin'," tracks a broad range of indicators including employment surveys, exports, business conditions, GDP, corporate earnings, industrial production, retail sales, and non-state-owned fixed asset investment. These metrics show a synchronized, multi-year decline, demonstrating that broad economic activity has continued to drag downward despite targeted state stimulus.

The second half of the page focuses on credit markets, arguing that they have successfully navigated a major liquidity test characterized by massive withdrawals from high-yield and emerging market debt funds. Two cumulative flow charts from 2005 to early 2016 quantify these historic redemptions. Global high-yield bond funds saw cumulative flows drop by $86 billion from their May 2014 peak, while global emerging market debt funds experienced a substantial decline of $110 billion from their May 2013 peak. Despite these severe headwinds, credit spreads have held up remarkably well. The final two charts show the subsequent market recovery from January 2014 to early 2016. A chart tracking emerging market dollar-denominated debt and US high-yield ex-energy spreads shows that after spreads peaked in early 2016—with EM corporate and sovereign spreads climbing toward 5.0% and US high-yield ex-energy spreads reaching nearly 7.5%—they began a sharp rally and compression. Finally, a total return index chart for emerging market local currency government debt shows that after falling from a peak of over 310 in 2014 to a low of around 230, the index staged a notable recovery, rising back toward 260 by April 2016.

This page discusses opportunities in structured credit and provides an update on the economic conditions in the Eurozone. Michael Cembalest argues that post-crisis structured credit underwriting has become significantly more conservative and investor-friendly compared to the pre-crisis era. He points out several improvements, such as credit enhancement for BBB- rated commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) rising from 3.5%–4.5% to 8%–13%, lower loan-to-value ratios, and a decrease in interest-only loans from 75% of pools down to 25%. Additionally, upcoming regulatory changes in late 2016 requiring sponsors to retain 5% of structured credit transactions are seen as positive. He suggests that the recent price sell-offs in these markets present a compelling investment opportunity relative to expected default rates.

This commentary is supported by two price index charts spanning January 2013 to January 2016. The first chart, tracking structured credit backed by commercial real estate, shows CMBS price indices for BBB- rated 2012, 2013, and 2014 vintages. It illustrates a sharp drop across all vintages in early 2016, with the 2014 vintage dropping toward 70. The second chart shows post-crisis collateralized loan obligation (CLO) price indices for corporate loans across A, BBB, BB, and B tranches. This chart displays a similar sell-off in early 2016, with the lower-rated B tranche suffering the most significant decline, dropping to around 60 before starting a slight recovery.

The latter half of the page evaluates the European economic climate, noting that European equity markets are flat for the year and forecasting a pronounced V-shaped corporate earnings trajectory. Although Eurozone GDP growth remains tepid at 1.5% to 2.0%, several recovery indicators are highlighted through three final charts. The first Eurozone macro chart tracks the three-month average year-over-year percentage change for retail sales and new car registrations from 2006 to 2016, showing a clear upward trend leading into 2016, where car registrations grew by roughly 10% and retail sales grew by about 2%. The other two charts display bank credit demand in Spain and Italy, reporting the net percentage of banks experiencing higher demand for corporate, consumer, and mortgage loans from 2004 to 2016. Both nations reflect a deep, post-recession trough followed by a robust turnaround, with most credit categories returning to positive net demand by 2016, signaling renewed economic activity and consumer confidence in these regions.

This page analyzes the strength of the German domestic economy—specifically in housing, retail sales, and household income—and explores why aggressive European Central Bank monetary policies are meeting fierce resistance in Germany. The author suggests that while low core inflation of one percent and moderate wage growth of two to three percent give the ECB breathing room for now, the booming domestic sectors could pressure the central bank by 2017. 

Three charts support this analysis. The first chart, titled German housing market: booming, tracks mortgage lending, house prices, and residential investment from 2002 to 2016. It shows that after years of stagnation, German house prices and residential investment indexes have risen steadily since 2009, with residential investment climbing from an index level of under 100 in 2009 to over 135 by 2016, alongside rebounding mortgage lending growth. The second chart, German retail sales and household income: surging, illustrates real retail sales and real household income from 1996 to 2016. It demonstrates a sharp upward surge in real household income after 2010, rising to an index level of over 106 by 2016, which has pushed real retail sales up as well. 

The discussion then turns to the ECB’s extraordinary monetary intervention plans, which include acting as an anchor investor in corporate bonds. Under this framework, the ECB will purchase up to 70 percent of individual corporate bond issues rated BBB- or better, include small companies by setting no minimum issuance size, and allow eligibility for Eurozone-incorporated firms even if their parent companies are located outside the region. The author notes that these interventions, combined with the fact that approximately 40 percent of European government bonds trade with negative yields, are stoking intense debates in Germany over the "expropriation" of savers. German Finance Minister Schäuble is noted as having partially blamed these ECB policies for the rise of the right-wing, Eurosceptic party Alternative for Deutschland (AfD). 

The final chart, German households have a strong preference for cash relative to their disposable income, explains why Germans are uniquely sensitive to these low and negative interest rates. Plotting cash as a percentage of financial assets against real household disposable income per capita, the chart shows that German households, despite having a high per-capita disposable income of nearly 27,000 euros, hold approximately 38 percent of their financial assets in cash and deposits. This is a much higher preference for cash than seen in other high-income nations such as France, where cash represents around 31 percent of assets, the Netherlands at roughly 24 percent, or Sweden at roughly 15 percent. This high cash exposure explains the deep-seated German opposition to current ECB monetary policies. A concluding footnote highlights that this economic tension is playing into a broader, existential European election cycle, citing the rise of the AfD in Germany and the electoral success of Austria's right-wing Freedom Party.

This publication page addresses the sustainability of state pension systems by analyzing pension discount rates against historical and projected market returns, as well as the impact of tightening pension valuation assumptions on state budgets. The author argues that average state assumptions of a 7.6% return—which equates to a 5.6% real return assuming 2% inflation—are overly optimistic and rely on historical periods of extraordinary returns that are unlikely to recur. Instead, J.P. Morgan proposes a more conservative real return assumption of 4.0%, representing a 6% nominal return minus 2% inflation.

The first chart, titled "Historical real returns for hypothetical 65% stock, 35% bond portfolio, 30-year rolling real return," plots the trailing 30-year rolling real returns from 1956 to 2016 against these two return assumptions. The y-axis shows real return percentages ranging from 3% to 8%. A volatile blue line representing actual rolling returns dips to a low of just above 4% in the early 1980s before climbing to over 7% by the mid-2010s. The average state pension return assumption of 5.6% is marked with a red dotted line, while J.P. Morgan's conservative assumption of 4.0% is marked with a black dotted line near the historical bottom of the cycle. The text notes that a 2014 US Society of Actuaries panel similarly recommended basing return assumptions on forward-looking risk-free rates plus risk premia rather than past performance alone.

The second chart evaluates how tightening these assumptions impacts state budgets by displaying the Interest, Pension, OPEB, and Defined Contribution (IPOD) ratio, which measures the percentage of state revenue collections required to cover these combined fixed costs. Titled "IPOD ratio: the impact of a lower discount rate and shorter amortization term," this chart compares a baseline scenario of a 6% discount rate and 30-year amortization (represented by blue bars) against a stricter scenario of a 5% discount rate and 20-year amortization (represented by brown circles) across fifty US states. The y-axis scales from 0% to 50%, with reference lines at 15% (green line) and 25% (red line). Under the stricter assumptions, highly indebted states see severe increases in their IPOD ratios. Illinois remains the most affected state, with its ratio jumping from approximately 39% to nearly 47%. Hawaii, Massachusetts, Texas, and Maryland all cross the critical 25% red line threshold under the stricter assumptions, while states at the far right of the chart, such as North Dakota, Nebraska, and Wyoming, remain comfortably below 5% under both scenarios.

This page analyzes the severe fiscal challenges facing several US states—specifically Illinois, New Jersey, Connecticut, Kentucky, Hawaii, and Massachusetts—that carry high ratios of debt service and retirement obligations relative to state revenues. The author uses the term IPOD to represent this ratio, which sums interest on bonds, pension payments, other post-employment benefits (OPEB), and defined contribution payments, divided by state revenues. To meet all future accrued obligations, these states must transition from their current IPOD levels to much higher full accrual IPOD ratios. This transition requires raising taxes, cutting direct non-retirement spending, or increasing public sector worker contributions over a 30-year period.

A table titled "Mutually exclusive means of raising incremental revenues required to meet full accrual payments to retirees" outlines the scale of these adjustments. For Illinois, moving from a 22 percent current IPOD to a 39 percent full accrual ratio would require either a 17 percent increase in tax revenues, a 16 percent cut in direct spending, or a 400 percent increase in worker contributions. New Jersey must bridge a gap from 12 percent to 38 percent, requiring either a 26 percent tax increase, a 24 percent spending cut, or a 471 percent increase in worker contributions. Connecticut needs to move from 21 percent to 35 percent, which translates to either a 14 percent tax increase, a 14 percent spending cut, or a 699 percent increase in worker contributions. Kentucky, transitioning from 11 percent to 32 percent, would require a 20 percent tax increase, a 13 percent spending cut, or a 435 percent worker contribution hike. Hawaii and Massachusetts face smaller but still daunting gaps, needing 8 percent and 7 percent tax hikes, 6 percent spending cuts for both, or 327 percent and 164 percent worker contribution increases, respectively.

The author points out that tax increases are politically difficult because several of these states already impose some of the nation's highest tax burdens. A second table shows the effective state tax rates on middle-quintile earners and their national ranks. Hawaii ranks 3rd highest in the nation with an 11.4 percent effective tax rate, Illinois ranks 4th at 10.8 percent, Kentucky ranks 6th at 10.8 percent, and Connecticut ranks 7th at 10.7 percent, while Massachusetts and New Jersey rank 26th and 30th respectively. 

If these states try to avoid tax hikes, spending cuts, or worker contribution increases by relying entirely on asset investment returns over the next 30 years, the required annual returns are historically unrealistic. Kentucky would require a 16.8 percent annual return, Illinois would need 13.8 percent, Connecticut 13.6 percent, Hawaii 13.2 percent, and Massachusetts 10.6 percent. For New Jersey, the deficit is so large that solving the funding gap through investment returns alone is not mathematically solvable. Footnotes add that defined contribution plans comprise a negligible 0.31 percent of state revenues, and pension obligation bonds are not a viable solution, as even a large-scale issuance would only cover about 5 percent of the states' incremental funding needs.

This page discusses how US states can manage and reduce their Other Post-Employment Benefit (OPEB) liabilities—specifically retiree healthcare—either through leveraging the Affordable Care Act (ACA) or by implementing state-level plan reforms. 

In SM Exhibit 7, a bar-and-dot chart illustrates the potential impact of an ACA transition on state IPOD ratios, which measure the percentage of state revenue collections required to cover bond interest, unfunded pensions, retiree healthcare, and defined contribution payments. The y-axis ranges from 0% to 40%, and the x-axis lists states by abbreviation. The chart compares an "Original scenario," represented by blue bars, to an alternative scenario where OPEB obligations are capped at the 25th percentile of the distribution with COLA adjustments, represented by brown dots. A red line marks the 25% threshold, and a green line marks the 15% threshold. The visualization demonstrates that Hawaii and Delaware would experience the largest fiscal benefits under this reform, as seen in the sharp drops from their original blue bars to the brown dots. Meanwhile, states like Illinois, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Kentucky see some declines but still remain at or above the 25% red line, indicating that pensions, rather than OPEB, remain the dominant driver of their fiscal pressure. 

Complementing this analysis, SM Exhibit 8 details specific OPEB plan reforms enacted by various states, referencing a survey showing that two-thirds of state respondents modified retiree healthcare in recent years. The listed actions include Delaware extending vesting terms and raising contributions; Georgia raising premiums and linking subsidies to years worked; and Idaho ending coverage for Medicare-eligible retirees and dependents. Indiana, Maryland, and Nevada increased copays, deductibles, or premiums, with Nevada also eliminating eligibility for employees hired after 2011. New Jersey shifted costs to the federal government by transitioning to an official Medicare Part D plan, while Ohio increased service requirements and is phasing out spousal coverage and Medicare Part B reimbursements. Finally, Pennsylvania increased service requirements, Utah closed its plan to post-2005 hires, and West Virginia restricted and capped subsidies for its employees.

This page serves as an introduction and table of contents for J.P. Morgan's annual energy paper by Michael Cembalest. It outlines five main sections focusing on the realities of the renewable energy transition alongside commodity and oil dynamics. The first section explores the commodity super-cycle and predicts a global oil supply deficit by mid-2017. The second section discusses why the adoption of hybrid vehicles is progressing more impactfully than over-projected electric vehicles. The third section critically analyzes New York State's ambitious 2030 plan to reach 50% renewable electricity and cut building energy use by 23%, noting that parts of the plan are highly aspirational given New York's limited solar and wind resources. Section four covers changes to utility customer billing that could decelerate distributed residential and commercial solar growth in the United States. Finally, section five looks at the modest future of US hydropower, drawing comparisons to countries like Norway, Switzerland, Canada, Austria, and Brazil, where hydropower accounts for more than half of electricity generation. 

The page highlights that the paper is overseen by Vaclav Smil, a distinguished energy systems expert and professor emeritus at the University of Manitoba, whom Bill Gates describes as his favorite author. A featured photograph at the bottom of the page, credited to katoh123, shows long-exposure light trails on Jinshui Road in Taiwan. This image serves as the report's cover, symbolizing the mixture of reality and imagination inherent in modern energy planning.

This page focuses on assessing the fiscal health of U.S. states by comparing their financial obligations against market yields, while also defining the assumptions used in the underlying analysis. 

The first section features a dual-axis chart comparing full accrual Interest, Pension, and OPEB Debt (IPOD) ratios to the current yields on 30-year general obligation (GO) bonds and their associated Moody’s credit ratings across all fifty states. The IPOD ratio, shown as blue vertical bars on the left axis ranging from 0% to 40%, measures the percentage of state revenue collections required to pay the sum of interest on bonds, the state's share of unfunded pension and retiree healthcare liabilities, and defined contribution plan payments. The right axis shows the yield on 30-year GO bonds from 2.00% to 4.50%, represented by dots color-coded by Moody's credit ratings, including AAA, AA+ to AA-, A+ to A-, BBB+ to BBB-, and unrated bonds. States are ordered from highest to lowest IPOD ratio, starting with Illinois at nearly 37% and New Jersey at roughly 35%, and ending with Wyoming and Nebraska at under 5%. The chart demonstrates that markets apply a modest yield premium of 0.5% to 1.5% for states with the highest IPOD ratios. For example, Illinois’s yield falls in the BBB+ to BBB- category and approaches 4.5%, whereas states with much lower IPOD ratios generally enjoy lower yields.

The second half of the page provides detailed definitions and methodology assumptions for the analysis. Revenues include state tax collections, sales taxes, select General Fund items, and profits from state liquor monopolies. Bonds are restricted to those supported by state taxes and general revenues, explicitly excluding revenue bonds. Pension and OPEB liabilities are measured via the entry-age normal method and amortized over 30 years using a harmonized level dollar amortization. The analysis assumes a 6% discount rate for plans using higher investment return expectations. State spending definitions cover key public service areas like education, public welfare, corrections, and highways. 

In terms of legal and structural flexibility, the author references findings from the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College, noting that out of 17 states that altered pension Cost of Living Adjustments (COLAs) between 2010 and 2013, 12 faced court challenges. In 8 of the 9 cases decided by courts, the adjustments were upheld under the legal view that COLAs are not a contractual right and can be modified by the state. Finally, the duration of pension plans is modeled at an average of 11.5 years based on GASB disclosures, while OPEB liabilities are modeled with a 14.3-year duration based on California's 2015 CAFR.

In this publication, the author argues that the global transition to a renewable energy future is taking significantly longer than most analysts and government agencies historically predicted. Despite rapid declines in the capital costs of wind and solar technology, past and current forecasts for both the renewable share of primary energy and the adoption rate of electric vehicles have consistently proved over-optimistic.

To illustrate this point, the top-left chart tracks the actual share of US primary energy derived from renewable sources from 1960 to 2015 against several notable historical forecasts. While the actual renewable share slowly grew from roughly 6% to around 10% by 2015, past projections predicted far faster transitions. For instance, physicist Bent Sorensen projected that renewables would comprise nearly 45% of US primary energy by 2000, while Amory Lovins of the Rocky Mountain Institute projected over 30% by the same year. The Carter Administration similarly projected that solar energy alone would reach 20% by 2000. Looking forward, the chart also shows ambitious, steeply upward-sloping trajectories from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory and the Google 2030 Clean Energy Plan, both aiming for 30% to 35% by 2030. 

Similarly, the top-right chart illustrates how forecasts for electric vehicle (EV) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV) sales have consistently run ahead of reality. Plotting EV and PHEV sales as a percentage of total car sales from 2009 to 2020, the chart shows actual US and global sales flatlining near 0.6% by 2015. In contrast, forecasts made by major financial and consulting institutions for 2020 predicted aggressive growth. Deutsche Bank, PwC, Frost & Sullivan, and Bloomberg New Energy Finance projected sales to reach 8% to 11% of the market by 2020, while the International Energy Agency, Roland Berger, BCG, and Deloitte projected market shares ranging from 3% to 7%.

Despite these lagging milestones, the author notes that renewable energy is finally making a measurable impact on the global power grid due to capital cost reductions. According to the bottom-left chart, annual global investment in renewable energy reached an all-time high of $286 billion in 2015, despite falling fossil fuel prices. This chart, spanning 2004 to 2015, reveals a shifting regional landscape. While investment in Europe peaked around 2011 and subsequently declined, spending in China and the broader Asian region surged. By 2015, China represented the largest single share of global renewable investments, followed by the United States, Europe, and Asia excluding China. 

Even with these record investments, the global power generation mix remains heavily reliant on traditional sources. The bottom-right chart displays global renewable electricity generation as a percentage of total generation from 1985 to 2015. Total renewable generation hovered between 20% and 24% over this thirty-year period, but the chart underscores that this remains predominantly a hydroelectric story. Hydroelectricity made up the vast majority of renewable generation, though its share of the total global power mix slipped slightly from 20% in 1985 to around 17% in 2015. Meanwhile, non-hydro renewables have slowly expanded. Wind generation has shown steady growth, and solar, despite its rapid growth rate, still accounted for only 1% of total global electricity generation in 2015. 

Footnotes on the page provide additional context, noting that electricity and transportation account for 39% and 28% of US primary energy use, respectively. The author also references an extreme 2009 proposal by Jacobson and Delucchi that envisioned a 100% renewable global energy system by 2030, dryly noting the colossal physical infrastructure requirements—including 3.8 million wind turbines and 1.7 billion rooftop solar installations—by adding, "Assembly required." Lastly, the author highlights the underlying solar technology learning curve, which saw solar module costs fall from $100 per watt in 1976 to $1 per watt by 2015, while wind turbine cost declines stalled after 2004 due to rising labor and component costs.

This page discusses the over-optimism surrounding electric vehicle (EV) adoption compared to the quieter, more practical progress of hybrid vehicles. While much excitement centers on upcoming EVs like the Tesla Model 3 and Chevy Bolt, actual sales tell a different story. The author details four levels of hybrid technology—micro, mild, full, and plug-in (PHEV)—arguing that hybrid vehicles (the "tortoise") currently have a more significant real-world impact than pure EVs (the "hare"). 

To demonstrate the gap between expectations and reality, the top-right line chart, titled "Another generation of electric car projections out of sync with reality," compares actual US EV and PHEV sales as a percentage of total car sales against various analyst projections for 2020. From 2009 to 2015, actual sales remained flat, hovering below 1%, whereas firms like Deutsche Bank, PwC, Frost & Sullivan, Bloomberg NEF, IEA, Roland Berger, BCG, and Deloitte projected 2020 market shares ranging from roughly 4.5% to over 11%. A note mentions that actual global EV and PHEV sales in 2015 were similarly low at around 0.6%.

The bottom-left chart, titled "US full hybrid, plug-in hybrid & electric vehicle sales," shows sales volume in thousands of units from 1999 to 2015. Full hybrids—such as the Toyota Prius, Camry, Ford Fusion, Hyundai Sonata, and Lexus CT 200h—have consistently dominated the market, driving the overall sales curve to a peak of nearly 500,000 units in 2013 before dipping slightly by 2015. In comparison, plug-in hybrids (like the Chevy Volt, Ford Fusion Energi, and BMW i8) and pure electric vehicles (like the Tesla Model S, Nissan LEAF, and BMW i3) only began showing minor sales volume starting in 2011, remaining a tiny fraction of total light vehicle sales at around 0.7% combined, compared to 3% for full hybrids.

The bottom-right dual-axis bar chart, titled "Full hybrids: fuel savings and cost vs. non-hybrid," plots fuel consumption reduction against the initial price premium for various manufacturers based on data from ICCT and Vincentric in July 2015. Across all hybrids, the average fuel consumption reduction is about 22% for an average price premium of approximately $3,500. Toyota leads with the highest fuel savings at over 30% for a modest price premium of around $3,000, while luxury and specialty brands like BMW, Mercedes, and Subaru show lower fuel savings of about 15% with a higher premium of nearly $4,000. The author notes that because only about 60% of analyzed full hybrids recoup their extra costs over their lifespan through lower fuel expenses, hybrid costs must fall further to become more widely competitive.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest addresses the sustainability of the 2016 oil price recovery, arguing that the bounce is indeed real. While the market remains well supplied, a massive 35% to 40% reduction in global oil capital spending and a drop of over 75% in the US rig count are paving the way for a supply deficit by 2017 or 2018. This decline in capital expenditure is concentrated outside of OPEC. According to research from Wood Mackenzie, non-OPEC field decline rates are expected to climb back to 5% by 2017 after dropping to 3% to 4% during the high-price years of 2013 and 2014. Additionally, extremely bearish investor positioning in early 2016 made the market ripe for a sharp rebound on any rumors of OPEC production freezes. 

The dynamics of this price recovery are shown across four charts. The first chart, titled "The wild ride in oil prices in 2016," tracks the WTI crude oil futures curve in USD per barrel across months until delivery up to 60 months. It compares curves from three dates: January 4, March 31, and June 14, highlighting how the short end of the curve rose from under $38 per barrel in March to nearly $48 per barrel by mid-June. The second chart, "World oil supply-demand balance," plots million barrels per day of excess supply or demand from 1995 to 2015, depicting a historically large supply glut that peaked close to 2 million barrels per day in late 2015. The third chart, "World oil capex," shows upstream capital spending as a share of global GDP from 1985 through 2016 estimates using Barclays and IMF data.
