Estimates for the US remain steady around 11% for both years, while Europe is expected to see a slight moderation from roughly 12% in FY 2017 to 10% in FY 2018. Japan exhibits strong projected growth, rising from 16% in 2017 to around 18% in 2018, while Emerging Markets are expected to experience a sharp deceleration, dropping from over 22% expected growth in 2017 down to around 12% in 2018. Overall, the author argues that Europe’s high operating leverage positions it well to translate global growth into continued earnings strength, even if profit margins stall.

This page addresses the persistent valuation differences between European and United States equity markets, arguing that Europe's lower valuations are a direct reflection of its lower return on equity (ROE) across most sectors. The author also analyzes the long-term effectiveness of a "barbell" investment strategy that overweights the US and Emerging Markets while underweighting Europe and Japan. Although this strategy has consistently outperformed since 1988, the author takes a neutral stance for 2018, recommending a balanced global portfolio instead.

To support the ROE argument, the first chart displays the difference in return on equity between European and US sectors as of November 2017. Only three European sectors show superior ROE compared to their US counterparts: Communication Services at roughly positive seventeen percent, Insurance at around eleven percent, and Energy at about six percent. The remaining twenty-one sectors show negative differentials, indicating poorer ROE in Europe. This underperformance is most severe in Tech Hardware and Consumer Services, which lag by nearly twenty percent. 

The next chart illustrates that while Europe trades at a large price-to-earnings discount compared to the US, it is not currently in deep value territory. Looking at the Stoxx 600 P/E discount versus the US S&P 500 based on forward earnings from 2006 to late 2017, the discount has fluctuated, reaching its widest point of over negative thirty percent during the Eurozone crisis in 2011 and 2012, recovering to near negative five percent in 2015, and settling near negative twenty percent by late 2017. A footnote explains that this analysis begins in 2006 because pre-2006 International Financial Reporting Standards required substantial goodwill amortization that distorts P/E comparisons. Furthermore, the author notes that adjusting for sector weight differences between the S&P 500 and the Stoxx 600 does not materially change this persistent discount.

The historical performance of the overweight US/EM and underweight Europe/Japan barbell strategy is shown in a three-year rolling performance chart from 1991 through 2017. The strategy has consistently generated positive excess returns, peaking near ten percent in the early 1990s and suffering only two brief periods of minor underperformance around 2001 and 2006. 

A regional equity market performance table highlights how the barbell performed through late 2017. The table compares the standard MSCI weights to the barbell weights, showing the US overweight at sixty-seven percent versus fifty-seven percent, the EM overweight at seventeen percent versus twelve percent, the Europe underweight at twelve percent versus twenty-two percent, and the Japan underweight at four percent versus nine percent. In 2017, US dollar returns were twenty-two percent for the US, thirty-four percent for Emerging Markets, twenty-five percent for Europe, and twenty-four percent for Japan. However, local currency returns paint a different picture: the US returned twenty-two percent, EM returned twenty-eight percent, Japan returned twenty percent, and Europe returned just fourteen percent. This demonstrates that Europe's competitive USD returns were entirely a byproduct of a strong Euro. Ultimately, the barbell strategy achieved a modest year-to-date excess return of zero point three percent in 2017.

This page outlines a broad recovery across emerging markets, highlighting that bank lending conditions are picking up, foreign direct investment is returning, exports are rebounding, and emerging market growth is accelerating in tandem with a recovery in US oil and gas investment. 

To illustrate these trends, the author presents four charts. The first chart displays improving emerging market bank lending conditions from 2009 to 2017 using a diffusion index. It tracks three series—trade finance, demand for loans, and performing loan health—all of which bottomed out around 2015 or 2016 before turning upward. By late 2017, trade finance and demand for loans both climbed above 50, while performing loan health improved toward 48.

The second chart tracks capital inflows, encompassing both foreign direct investment and portfolio investment, into emerging markets in billions of US dollars from 2000 with estimates through 2018. Inflows peaked near 1.5 trillion dollars in 2013 before plunging to a low of approximately 400 billion dollars in 2015. Since then, inflows are estimated to have rebounded sharply, projected to reach about 1 trillion dollars by 2018.

The third chart demonstrates a rebound in Emerging Asian exports from 2011 to 2017, measured as the three-month moving average of year-over-year percentage change in export value. After falling from nearly 25% growth in 2011 to roughly negative 10% in late 2015, export growth recovered to approximately 10% in 2017, reclaiming levels last seen in 2013 and 2014.

The final dual-axis chart suggests that the commodity supercycle downturn is coming to an end by comparing emerging economy real GDP growth against US oil and gas real investment from 2012 to 2017. Emerging economy real GDP growth declined from over 5.0% in 2012 to a trough of 4.0% in 2016, while US oil and gas investment crashed from positive growth territory down to nearly negative 40% over the same period. In 2017, both series experienced a dramatic turnaround, with US oil and gas investment surging to nearly 90% year-over-year growth and emerging market GDP growth rising back to about 4.6%.

In this J.P. Morgan publication, Michael Cembalest argues that despite current optimism surrounding the Eurozone’s recovery, several deep-seated, unresolved structural issues remain. He predicts these issues will become highly problematic for markets when the next recession arrives, potentially in 2020 or later. Key concerns include a decline in the euro's appeal as a global reserve currency, Germany's economic divergence from France, stagnation in Italy's industrial sector, and a sharp pullback in lending by German banks to periphery nations like Spain and Italy. While Cembalest acknowledges positive domestic labor reforms in France under President Emmanuel Macron, he expresses skepticism that Macron's calls for broader Eurozone-level reforms, such as fiscal, military, asylum, and tax harmonization, will materialize anytime soon.

To support his argument regarding the euro's declining status, a chart titled Global currency reserves displays the percentage of global currency reserves allocated to the euro and the US dollar from 1999 to 2017. The euro's share peaked near 28 percent in 2009, then steadily fell to around 19 percent by 2015, showing only minor stabilization around 20 percent by 2017. Over the same period, the US dollar’s share fluctuated between approximately 62 percent and 71 percent, ending near 64 percent in 2017.

The growing economic imbalance within Europe's core is visualized in a chart titled Franco-German wealth gap, which plots Germany's real per capita GDP divided by France's from 1850 to 2015. Historically volatile with massive peaks during world wars, the ratio fell to near parity around 1.00 in the early 2000s but has since trended upward. By 2015, the ratio reached nearly 1.15, highlighted by a red circle, indicating that Germany is pulling significantly ahead of France in per capita wealth.

Another chart, titled Death in Venice, shows the Industrial Production Index for Germany, France, and Italy from 1980 to 2017, with December 31, 1999, indexed to 100. A vertical dashed line marks the fixing of the Euro exchange rate in 1999. Prior to this, the three nations exhibited highly synchronous economic cycles. Afterward, their paths diverged dramatically: Germany's industrial production surged to nearly 130 by 2017, while France's stagnated below 100, and Italy's steadily deteriorated to around 85.

The final chart, titled German banks less willing to lend to periphery banks, tracks German outbound lending to Italy and Spain in US dollars from 2005 to 2017. Both series peaked around 2008, with lending to Italy reaching over 300 billion dollars and lending to Spain surpassing 250 billion dollars. By 2017, German bank lending to both nations had plummeted to under 100 billion dollars each, a contraction that has forced the European Central Bank to step in and handle a significant amount of the lending burden.

This page focuses on the unique structure of China's economy, analyzing why its massive debt load may not trigger a Western-style financial crisis, and tracking its gradual transition from an investment-led to a consumption-led growth model. The author argues that because China is not a free-market country, the government controls the key levers that usually catalyze banking crises. Specifically, about eighty-five percent of China's debt is held internally, external debt is only fifteen percent of GDP, and domestic banks hold foreign assets five hundred billion dollars greater than their external liabilities. Furthermore, fifty-five to sixty percent of corporate debt is issued by state-owned enterprises with government backing, the bad debt is concentrated in the central government-controlled top five banks and the Postal Savings Bank, and stable retail deposits account for eighty percent of state bank liabilities. 

To illustrate these debt dynamics, the page features two charts. The first, titled Total China economy-wide debt as a percentage of GDP, shows a stacked bar chart of debt rising steadily from 2007 to the third quarter of 2017. Over this decade, government debt increased from forty-two percent to fifty-six percent, household debt grew from eighteen percent to forty-eight percent, and corporate debt climbed from eighty-nine percent to one hundred sixty-six percent of GDP. The second chart, Pre-crisis household and corporate debt, compares China's private sector debt trajectory to historical pre-crisis periods in other nations, including Japan, Thailand, Sweden, Ireland, Spain, and the United States. While China's trajectory rises steeply past two hundred percent of GDP by 2016, exceeding Sweden, the United States, and Thailand, the author suggests China's state-controlled buffers mitigate these systemic risks.

The lower half of the page details the good news regarding China's long-run economic rebalancing. As production wages in developing Asia rise, China is transitioning toward greater efficiency and a growing contribution from new economy sectors like consumer staples, consumer discretionary, healthcare, and technology. A scatterplot titled Slowly switching from investment to consumption plots gross fixed capital formation against private consumption as a percentage of GDP. A cluster of industrial and emerging economies from 2008 to 2014 sits in the region of twenty to thirty percent investment and fifty to seventy percent consumption. In 2011, China was a massive outlier, with capital formation near forty-seven percent and consumption around thirty-six percent. By 2016, China had made slow progress toward the global average, with capital formation falling to roughly forty-three percent and private consumption rising to about thirty-nine percent. 

Finally, a bar chart titled China A-share reported profits in trillions of RMB from 2008 to 2016 displays the shifting composition of corporate earnings. Total profits generally rose over this period, peaking in 2016. Within this total, profits from the energy sector, which includes major entities like Sinopec and PetroChina, shrank significantly, while the old economy segment remained large but volatile. Meanwhile, new economy profits expanded consistently year-over-year, demonstrating a rising share of overall corporate profitability and supporting the narrative of a gradual structural shift in the Chinese economy.

This page analyzes how Brazil's improving economic fundamentals are overriding its persistent political scandals and negative press. The author argues that despite unending corruption revelations, such as those from Operation Car Wash, Brazil is undergoing a classic balance of payments adjustment and recovery. This recovery sequence begins with currency depreciation that narrows the current account deficit, followed by a slowdown in inflation that allows the central bank to ease interest rates. Over time, credit, employment, and foreign direct investment begin to rise, bolstered by rising industrial metals prices and government privatizations involving major companies like Vale, Petrobras, and Eletrobras. Ultimately, recovering business and consumer confidence drives a rebound in equity markets regardless of political turmoil.

Six charts from late 2017 illustrate this macroeconomic turnaround. The first chart displays the current account deficit and the USD to BRL exchange rate from 2013 to 2017, showing how the currency's depreciation toward 4.0 Reals per Dollar in late 2015 helped shrink the current account deficit from over four percent of GDP in 2014 to nearly zero by late 2017. The second chart traces consumer price inflation and the central bank's policy rate, showing that inflation peaked above ten percent in late 2015 before plummeting to around three percent in late 2017, which allowed the policy rate to be slashed from over fourteen percent down toward eight percent. 

The third chart plots business and consumer confidence indexed to January 2013, showing that both measures bottomed out in early 2016 near sixty before staging a recovery, with business confidence reaching above ninety by late 2017. The fourth chart displays employment growth, which fell from over one percent in 2013 to a low of nearly negative three percent in 2016, followed by a sharp rebound back to positive territory in late 2017. The fifth chart tracks industrial metals prices, showing a price index that bottomed out around sixty-two in early 2016 and recovered to nearly one hundred by late 2017. The final chart shows the MSCI Brazil Index, which bottomed out near thirty-five in early 2016 and recovered to around seventy-five by late 2017, with markers indicating that major developments in the Operation Car Wash investigation did not halt the equity market's upward trajectory.

This analysis examines Japan's cyclical economic recovery and explains why it has not yet altered the country's challenged long-term outlook. The author highlights that while Japan is participating in the global recovery—evidenced by seven straight quarters of real GDP growth, strong export growth, and rising labor demand—the recovery is fundamentally unbalanced. Although corporate profits have boomed to the point of becoming a political issue, household incomes have failed to recover. This "one-legged recovery" contrasts sharply with the United States, where household incomes rose alongside corporate profits, and leaves global investors hesitant to take overweight positions in Japanese equities.

The first chart on the page tracks Japanese business conditions using the Bank of Japan's Tankan survey diffusion index of favorable less unfavorable responses from 1990 to late 2017. After plunging to nearly -50% during the 2008 financial crisis, the index has steadily climbed to nearly 20%, marking its highest level since the early 1990s. 

The second chart compares the USD/Yen exchange rate (left axis, ¥75 to ¥130) with MSCI Japan equities (right axis, index level 400 to 1,100) from 2010 through late 2017. While the two series historically moved in tandem, they decoupled in 2017, with MSCI Japan equities climbing toward 1,100 even as the Yen exchange rate remained relatively stable around ¥110 to ¥115 per dollar.

Two lower charts compare corporate profits and household incomes in the United States and Japan from 2007 to 2017. The first of these shows trailing 12-month earnings per share for the S&P 500 (left axis, $50 to $130) and MSCI Japan (right axis, ¥0 to ¥70). Both indices suffered major profit drops during the financial crisis but have since rebounded strongly, with the S&P 500 rising to about $130 and MSCI Japan climbing to nearly ¥70 by late 2017. 

In contrast, the final chart plots the real household earnings index for the US (left axis, 98 to 122) and Japan (right axis, 91 to 101). While the US index rose from a post-recession low of 100 in 2010 to over 120 in 2017, Japan's index steadily declined from 100 in 2007 to roughly 94 in 2017. 

The author questions whether Japan's tight labor market—where the ratio of vacancies to applicants is at its highest since 1974—will finally force wages higher and resolve this stagnation. For now, a JP Morgan footnote indicates that foreign institutional and retail investors maintain a neutral position on Japanese equities, sitting midway between the pre-Abenomics lows of 2012 and the post-Abenomics peak of 2015.

This page discusses the fiscal health of the United States municipal market, focusing on the debt burdens of various US cities, counties, and states. The author explains that J.P. Morgan, which manages over $70 billion in municipal bonds, closely monitors these issuers' unfunded pension and retiree healthcare obligations. A deep-dive analysis reveals a highly varied fiscal landscape; while some municipal issuers enjoy manageable debt levels, others face severe financial challenges. To protect portfolios from asymmetric downside risk, J.P. Morgan keeps its exposure to the general obligation bonds of the highest-risk cities and counties at around 1% of total assets. Furthermore, the author warns that the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act could compound these fiscal strains by motivating high-income residents to migrate away from high-tax states.

The analysis is visualized in a line chart titled "The IPOD ratio: State, City and County debt burdens." This ratio represents the percentage of a municipality's revenues required to pay the sum of interest on net direct debt, its share of unfunded pension and retiree healthcare liabilities, and defined contribution plan payments. This metric assumes a 6% plan return and a 30-year level dollar amortization, using fiscal year 2015 data. 

The chart's vertical axis measures this revenue percentage from 0% to 70%, plotting three distinct series representing cities (in purple), counties (in green), and states (in brown), ordered from highest burden to lowest. 

Cities generally carry the heaviest burdens. Chicago is the most extreme outlier, with an IPOD ratio exceeding 60%. Following Chicago, a long line of highly burdened cities is labeled in descending order, including Lubbock, Atlanta, Pittsburgh, Baton Rouge, Austin, Honolulu, Oakland, Phoenix, Los Angeles, Houston, San Jose, Dallas, Fort Worth, Omaha, Sacramento, El Paso, and Jersey City, with the overall city trend line gradually sloping down to around 15%. 

Counties occupy the middle tier of debt burdens. The highest-burden county shown is Prince George’s County in Maryland at approximately 45%, followed by Shelby County in Tennessee, King County in Washington, Santa Clara County in California, Bexar County in Texas, Clark County in Nevada, Montgomery County in Maryland, and Bergen County in New Jersey, with the remaining county line declining to just under 20%. 

States generally have the lowest IPOD ratios, though there are significant exceptions. Illinois is a major outlier among states with an IPOD ratio of approximately 50%, followed by New Jersey at about 37%. Other notable states with elevated burdens include Connecticut, Kentucky, Hawaii, and Maine. The state trend line eventually falls and levels off below 10% for the least burdened issuers.

This page discusses the dynamics affecting stock-pickers and hedge fund managers, focusing on the relationship between declining stock correlations and historically compressed valuation dispersions. The author explains that stock-pickers benefited from a decline in the correlation among stocks, meaning equities stopped moving in lockstep, as well as from a hedge fund preference for growth-oriented sectors like technology and healthcare. 

This drop in stock-to-stock relation is illustrated in the first chart, titled S&P 500 and its average stock correlations, which tracks average pair correlations using 100-day daily rate of change data from 1997 through late 2017. The chart shows that average pair correlations spiked near 0.7 during the post-crisis period around 2011 but fell dramatically to below 0.2 by 2017, marking a favorable environment for active stock selection.

However, the author highlights a persistent headwind for hedge funds: the compression of valuations. While stock correlations have fallen, the valuation dispersion across stocks remains extremely low. This narrow gap limits the potential returns that managers can generate by identifying undervalued versus overvalued stocks. The author attributes this compression to massive central bank stimulus programs that have distorted equity, corporate, municipal, and real estate markets. The publication forecasts that it may take until 2020 or even later for the lingering distortions of central bank interventions to clear from the financial markets. 

This phenomenon is supported by the second chart, titled Valuation dispersions across stocks: lowest on record. This chart measures the difference between the 90th percentile of cheapness and the 10th percentile of cheapness across five key valuation metrics: earnings yield, free cash flow yield, dividend yield, book to price, and sales yield. Indexed to 100 in January 1978, the data series run from 1978 to mid-2017. The chart reveals that while previous eras—such as the late 1990s tech bubble and the 2008 financial crisis—saw massive spikes in valuation dispersion where index levels surged to between 140 and over 200, dispersions across all five factors have converged to historic lows near or below 40. An accompanying footnote emphasizes that this valuation gap between cheap and expensive stocks has narrowed by 50% to 75% since the 1980s, bringing it close to the narrowest level ever recorded.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" analyzes the concentration of U.S. equity market returns in 2017. It explores how a small group of stocks, specifically the FAAMG cohort (Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google), accounted for a disproportionate share of the S&P 500's overall performance. In 2017, the top five stocks contributed 5.0% of the total index return of 21.9%. While this is higher than the historical 1991–2016 average return contribution of 3.4% and median of 2.6%, the author points out that their contribution share of total positive market returns (around 25%) is roughly average.

The page features two bar charts tracking historical return concentration from 1991 through 2017. The first chart, "Impact of removing top 5 S&P 500 stocks each year," displays the total return foregone. It shows that 2017's 5.0% foregone return was elevated but not unprecedented, as the late 1990s saw even higher peaks, with 1999 reaching nearly 9%. The second chart, "Share of market returns from top 5 stocks" (with values capped at 50%), shows that 2017's concentration share of roughly 25% is moderate compared to several years, such as 1999, 2007, 2010, and 2015, where the top five stocks accounted for 50% or more of the index's returns.

A table at the bottom of the page details the top S&P 500 contributors in 2017. Apple Inc. ranks first with a 1.62% return contribution, marking its ninth appearance in the top five since 2005. Microsoft Corp. ranks second with a 1.04% contribution, which represents its 13th year in the top five since 1991 and its fifth consecutive year. Amazon.com Inc. (1.02% contribution), Facebook Inc-A (0.76% contribution), and Alphabet Inc-C (0.50% contribution) round out the top five, with all three having appeared in the top five at least once before. The commentary emphasizes that repeat appearances are normal: between 1991 and 2017, twenty-six companies made multiple appearances in the top five, while only twenty companies appeared just once.

This report addresses the shrinking number of publicly listed companies in the United States, a phenomenon described as the "listing gap" because the number of US public companies is falling while listings in the rest of the world are rising. 

To illustrate this trend, the first line chart compare the growing listing gap between the US and the rest of the world from 1975 to 2015. On the left axis, domestic US-listed companies peaked in the mid-1990s at around 8,000 before steadily declining to approximately 4,000-5,000 by 2015. Meanwhile, measured on the right axis, non-US listings grew from under 15,000 in the late 1970s to over 40,000 by 2015. The second chart shows the additions and subtractions to listed companies from 1976 to 2016. The total number of listed firms, represented by a black line, peaked in the late 1990s at over 8,000 and dropped to under 4,000 by 2016. This chart uses blue bars for new listings and red bars for delistings, showing that the overall contraction is driven by both rising delistings and fewer new listings.

The report attributes delistings primarily to mergers and acquisitions and business consolidation, noting that the average US company has a market capitalization of $7 billion, which is ten times higher in real terms than in 1976. This consolidation is reflected in the Herfindahl index, which measures industry concentration and increased by 45% from 1995 to 2015. Despite these trends, the annual rate of delistings has remained relatively steady at 8% to 10% of listed firms since 2002. 

The decline in new listings is explained by two primary factors. First, increased regulatory costs, complexity, and litigation risks have discouraged companies from going public. In a PwC survey, 45% of firms stated that the cost of being public exceeded their expectations, and US companies spend 166% more on legal services per dollar of revenue than their global counterparts. Second, the deregulation of private capital has made it easier for companies to remain private. For example, the financial thresholds defining "accredited investors" established under Regulation D Rule 501 in 1982—such as an individual income of over $200,000 or a net worth over $1 million—have not been adjusted for inflation. In 2016, Congress expanded the accredited investor definition, and the 2012 JOBS Act further eased private fundraising by repealing bans on general solicitations, creating crowdfunding exemptions, raising the private shareholder limit from 500 to 2,000, and introducing the "Regulation A+" exemption for small companies.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, Eye on the Market, analyzes the ramifications of private capital deregulation in the United States, specifically focusing on the rise of venture capital and the corresponding decline in public market participation. The author begins by highlighting that deregulation has led to a sharp increase in US venture capital investment and a longer runway before tech companies go public. To support this, the text cites that venture capital investors funded 2,888 private US companies in 2006, which grew to 4,244 companies in 2015. Additionally, as of late 2017, there remained one trillion dollars in unspent private equity and venture capital dry powder available for private investments.

The top-left bar chart, titled Global venture capital investment by quarter, displays quarterly funding in billions of US dollars from Q1 2010 to Q1 2017. The stacked bars partition funding between the United States and the rest of the world. The chart illustrates a dramatic escalation in quarterly global venture capital, climbing from under ten billion dollars in 2010 to a peak near forty-five billion dollars in late 2015, with the US consistently accounting for the largest share. 

To the right, a line chart titled Waiting longer to go public tracks the median age of technology companies at their initial public offering from 1980 to 2016. This age, measured in years, dipped to a low of four years during the dot-com boom of 1999 and spiked to an all-time high of approximately thirteen years around 2008. By 2016, the median age remained elevated at roughly eleven years, visualising how tech companies are remaining private for significantly longer periods.

The commentary addresses why this shift away from public markets is problematic, focusing on two main issues. The first issue is fairness to the average investor. Since high-growth, pre-IPO investments are kept private, ordinary investors are locked out of wealth-creation opportunities. This concern is illustrated by the bottom-right line chart, Number of participants in pension plans, which plots the number of participants in millions from 1975 to 2011. While traditional defined benefit plans flatlined and eventually decreased to under forty million participants, defined contribution plans surged from under twenty million to over ninety million participants. Because individual retirement savers rely heavily on defined contribution plans, which cannot easily or safely access illiquid private assets, they are deprived of early-stage investment gains.

The second issue is the reduction of public market knowledge and the potential for private companies to free-ride on public disclosures. The author argues that fewer public companies mean less overall information available for investors. This information is highly valuable, as demonstrated by the fact that expert networks like GLG can cost up to one thousand dollars per hour. Duke Law Professor Elisabeth de Fontenay is cited from her 2017 paper, arguing that the current equilibrium is unsustainable because public companies face increasing disclosure burdens while their private competitors benefit from this shared knowledge without incurring any of the same regulatory costs.

This page analyzes the potential financial and political implications of a Democratic victory in the 2018 midterm elections. The author argues that if Democrats retake the House or Senate, market sentiment could reverse, noting that historically, the lowest S&P 500 returns from 1945 to 2017 occurred under a Republican President with a split or unified Democratic Congress. The piece also raises concerns that markets could react negatively to an increased risk of a constitutional crisis or political gridlock that would stall infrastructure legislation, despite the post-election surge in CEO confidence and capital spending plans seen after the GOP victory in 2016.

Four key graphics support this analysis. The first chart, "Number of House challengers that have raised over five thousand dollars," tracks Democratic and Republican challengers from 2003 to 2017. It shows an unprecedented spike in Democratic challengers in 2017, reaching 391 compared to just 71 for Republicans, signaling a strong progressive mobilization. The second chart, "A century of wave elections," displays the number of House seats gained by either party during wave elections from 1912 to 2010, illustrating that substantial shifts are common and noting the threshold of seats Democrats need to regain control of the House of Representatives. At the bottom left, a line chart titled "Capex plans and CEO confidence: the post-election spike" plots CEO confidence on a one-to-ten scale against capital expenditure plans as a percentage of respondents from 2010 to 2017. It clearly illustrates a sharp upward trajectory for both indicators immediately following the November 2016 presidential election.

Finally, a table on "S&P 500 returns during periods of US political unity and gridlock, 1945 to 2018" compiles historical performance data over 74 years, which has an overall average return of 11.4 percent. Under unified government, the S&P 500 averaged a 13.9 percent return over 30 years, with a Republican president averaging 16.0 percent and a Democratic president averaging 13.1 percent. Under a unified Congress, the overall return drops to 9.8 percent over 32 years, with a dramatic split: a Democratic president saw returns of 16.4 percent, while a Republican president saw just 6.9 percent. Under a split Congress, the return averaged 9.6 percent over 12 years, yielding 16.7 percent under a Democratic president and only 6.2 percent under a Republican president. The author concludes by noting that polling and political futures markets place a two-thirds probability on Democrats taking the House, which would represent the tenth wave election in his lifetime.

This page discusses how the Trump Administration's decision to end the Temporary Protected Status program for migrants from El Salvador, Honduras, and Haiti could inadvertently trigger higher wage inflation and prompt a more aggressive monetary policy response from the Federal Reserve. The author argues that deporting these workers will worsen labor shortages in states currently trying to rebuild after devastating natural disasters. According to the National Association of Homebuilders, over 30% of construction workers in Florida and Texas are foreign-born. Removing these workers risks exacerbating construction backlogs, driving up labor costs, and slowing the broader economic recovery.

An illustrative map of the United States visualizes the concentration of temporary protected status holders from these three nations. California, Texas, Florida, and New York are highlighted as having the highest concentrations, with more than 50,000 holders each. Map callouts emphasize the scale of local rebuilding needs, noting that 15,000 homes were damaged or destroyed by wildfires in California, 200,000 homes were damaged or destroyed by Hurricane Harvey in Texas, and insurance claims were filed on 800,000 residential and commercial buildings following Hurricane Irma in Florida. 

Two supporting line charts illustrate the broader macroeconomic context of a tightening labor market. The first chart displays the seasonally adjusted US unemployment rate from 1970 through late 2017. It shows the unemployment rate falling sharply from its post-financial crisis peak of 10.0% down to approximately 4.1%, nearing historical lows. The second chart compares various measures of US wage inflation against goods inflation from 1997 through late 2017, using a three-month average of year-over-year percentage changes. This chart shows that the employment cost index, average hourly earnings, and median wages are all rising faster than core CPI and core PCE. While core goods inflation measures hover near 1.5%, median wages are rising at a pace of nearly 4.0%, highlighting that wage pressures are already accelerating across the economy.

This page analyzes the rising trade disputes between the United States and China, arguing that while pending administration decisions under the 1962/1974 Trade Acts—including recent tariffs on washing machines and solar panels, and potential ones on steel and aluminum—cause concern, investors should not overreact. These targeted goods represent a mere 0.25% of Chinese exports and US imports. 

The primary components of the US-China trade imbalance are instead detailed in a bar chart titled "Largest contributors to US-China net goods deficit." This chart displays trailing 12-month figures in billions of US dollars, showing that the top ten categories combine for a total deficit of $384 billion. The single largest contributor is "Phones, TVs, Radios" at nearly $95 billion, followed by "Toy, Jewel, Bldg Fixture Etc" at around $60 billion, and "Computers" at approximately $45 billion. The fundamental imbalance is further illustrated in a scatter plot titled "A general lack of tariff reciprocity," which compares the average tariffs applied by the US against those applied to the US. China sits significantly below the diagonal y=x reciprocity line, facing an average US tariff of roughly 2.5% while charging an average tariff of approximately 8.5% on US imports. Other nations like Brazil, India, and Egypt also demonstrate heavily non-reciprocal tariff rates on US goods.

Beyond trade, the page discusses potential US investment restrictions under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act. This reciprocal investment regime would restrict Chinese foreign direct investment in the US to match China's domestic restrictions, specifically targeting sectors within China's "Made in China 2025" plan, such as aerospace, robotics, electric vehicles, and medical devices. This initiative is framed alongside a bar chart titled "Regulatory restrictions on inbound Foreign Direct Investment," which indexes restriction levels on a 0 to 1 scale. China ranks as one of the ten worst nations for inbound investment restrictions with a score of about 0.33, trailing only the Philippines and Saudi Arabia. For comparison, the United States scores below 0.10, and European nations like Germany, France, the UK, and Spain show much lower regulatory barriers. 

The author concludes with the bottom line that the administration faces a difficult task in renegotiating these inherited, one-sided trade arrangements. The primary risk is doing so without driving up US inflation or triggering a wave of retaliatory protectionist measures. Footnotes highlight that China's tech sector has grown from 1% to 10% of the global tech sector over the past decade, and that bilateral pressure has led to a major $250 billion purchase agreement for US goods, including liquefied natural gas, semiconductors, and aircraft.

In a Q&A structured as a letter to "Addie" from a reader in Canberra, Michael Cembalest addresses concerns regarding the stability of the global financial system in the event of faster interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve. The author argues that systemic risk is much lower today than before the 2008 financial crisis, pointing to substantial increases in bank and insurance capitalization alongside marked declines in wholesale funding risks, securities lending, asset-backed securities issuance, and money market fund risks. 

To support this view, six charts illustrate structural improvements across the financial sector. The first chart, showing bank risk-weighted capital ratios, compares 2007 to 2017, demonstrating that capital ratios have risen significantly in both the United States, from approximately 9% to nearly 14%, and Europe, from under 9% to around 16%. Similarly, bank liquid assets as a percentage of short-term liabilities increased over the same decade, rising from roughly 42% to 48% in the US and from about 35% to 41% in Europe. Looking at leverage and funding, a chart of bank loan-to-deposit ratios from 1995 to 2017 shows a dramatic decline for both US and Eurozone banks; Eurozone ratios fell from a peak of nearly 140% in 2008 down to around 110%, while US ratios dropped from a peak of 100% to approximately 75%. 

The insurance sector displays comparable strengthening. A dual-axis chart tracking insurance company capitalization from 2004 to 2016 shows that the life insurance risk-based capital ratio climbed from under 400% to nearly 480%, while property and casualty operating leverage steadily declined from around 1.1x in 2004 to roughly 0.8x by 2016. 

Capital markets also show reduced risk profiles. The volume of outstanding debt supported by securities lending as a percentage of GDP peaked near 15% in 2007 before sharply declining to just over 4% by 2016. Additionally, a stacked area chart of US asset-backed securities shows total outstanding issuance peaking near $5.0 trillion in 2007, largely driven by non-agency residential mortgage-backed securities, before shrinking to below $3.0 trillion in 2016 with a much smaller share of non-agency mortgages. Finally, the author highlights a significant risk reduction in cash management vehicles, tracing US money market fund assets from 2002 to 2018. Following the Lehman Brothers crash in 2008 and institutional money market reforms in 2016, assets shifted heavily out of riskier prime funds, which fell from over $1.5 trillion to under $500 billion, and into safer government money market funds, which grew to exceed $2.0 trillion.

Michael Cembalest addresses the question of whether blockchain technology will take over the consumer payments landscape anytime soon, concluding that such a transition is unlikely in the near future. 

To illustrate the current landscape, the page features two tables. The first table outlines the key participants in consumer payments and their functions, listing retailers, merchant acquirers such as Vantiv, card networks like Mastercard and Visa, and issuing banks. The second table breaks down US consumer payments in 2016 by volume and percentage share of the total. It shows that credit cards held the largest share at $3.153 trillion (32%), followed by debit cards at $2.561 trillion (26%), cash at $1.572 trillion (16%), preauthorized electronic payments at $790 billion (8%), checks at $830 billion (8%), remote electronic payments at $638 billion (6%), other cards at $322 billion (3%), and other paper at $69 billion (1%). 

Cembalest argues that while blockchain is theoretically proposed to eliminate centralized card networks to lower fees, the economic benefits are overstated. Visa and Mastercard only receive about 0.15% of the total retailer discount fee of 2.0% to 3.0%, with the rest going to merchant acquirers and issuing banks; thus, eliminating card networks would not radically alter overall payment economics. Additionally, displacing these networks introduces immense governance challenges, and incumbent networks like Visa can process over 50,000 transactions per second, compared to just hundreds of transactions per second on private blockchain networks. 

The author poses the open question of whether a more radical blockchain solution—one directly connecting retailers to customers—could succeed. However, he notes that such a system would have to replicate complex services currently managed by issuing banks, including dealing with fraud, providing consumer protections, and extending $3 trillion in annual float and credit. A footnote clarifies that approximately 30% to 35% of credit card users rely on float by paying their bills in full monthly, while 40% to 45% carry a balance. Cembalest suggests that while giant retail entities like Walmart or Amazon have the scale to attempt such a ledger, its massive operational complexity and funding requirements mean it is highly unclear if it would be cheaper or more efficient than the existing financial infrastructure.

In this publication, Michael Cembalest evaluates the practical applications of blockchain technology, questioning the industry's hype. He notes that while some point to the wholesale global payments market as a prime target for blockchain, this market already functions well. Instead, blockchain might find utility in resolving payments that are bounced due to input errors or compliance issues. He cites the Australian Securities Exchange, which represents 1.7 percent of global exchange capitalization, as a real-world example of using blockchain to cut settlement and clearing costs. Blockchain could also facilitate peer-to-peer business lending, lower underwriting costs, and serve as a record-keeping ledger. Ultimately, Cembalest remains underwhelmed by blockchain's disruptive capacity in finance, suggesting blockchain companies may simply be temporary cost-cutting service providers whose programming skills will soon be commoditized, casting doubt on their high valuations.

The page shifts to a lighter topic regarding online dating trends. A line chart titled Increase in percentage of couples meeting online tracks various meeting methods from 1940 to 2010. It shows that meeting online has risen sharply since the mid-1990s to reach roughly 23 percent by 2010, nearly surpassing meeting through friends, which dropped from a peak of nearly 40 percent in the 1990s to about 27 percent. Other categories, such as bars or restaurants, coworkers, college, family, neighbors, primary or secondary school, and church, all represent much smaller shares, with meeting in church sitting near the bottom at under 5 percent. 

An accompanying table titled Change in inbound messages based on food mentions in dating profile analyzes the response rate associated with mentioning specific foods. It shows that mentioning guacamole increases inbound messages by 144 percent, chocolate by 100 percent, sushi by 93 percent, hamburger by 68 percent, ice cream by 62 percent, pizza by 48 percent, hot dogs by 41 percent, and ribs by 20 percent. Conversely, mentioning yams leads to a 70 percent decrease in inbound messages. The page concludes with references to other J.P. Morgan publications from early 2018.

This page from the publication argue that US trade deficits are largely driven by structural macroeconomic forces rather than just past trade deals. The author, Michael Cembalest, asserts that factors such as structural US budget deficits, rising oil prices where the US still imports about six million barrels per day, the stimulative impact of US tax cuts, and an overvalued dollar are the primary drivers of the trade deficit. Consequently, the administration's tariff policies are described as tilting at windmills because they do little to alter these underlying forces, especially as the government runs budget deficits that naturally expand the trade deficit. 

The analysis is supported by four charts. The first chart, titled Large US non-oil goods deficit, plots the deficit as a percentage of GDP from 1990 to 2016. It shows the non-oil goods deficit worsening from roughly negative half a percent of GDP in 1990 to its lowest point of nearly negative four percent in 2005 and 2006, followed by a temporary recovery to negative two percent in 2009, before sliding back down to around negative three point five percent by 2016. 

The second chart, titled Federal budget balance and current account balance, compares these two measures as percentages of GDP on dual axes from 1960 to 2020, with projections extending through 2019. This chart highlights the twin-deficit phenomenon, showing that the budget deficit and current account balance historically move in tandem. The budget deficit is projected to widen significantly toward negative five percent of GDP by 2019, while the current account deficit is projected to hover around negative two point five percent of GDP.

The third chart, titled Trade weighted dollar, indexes the dollar from 1988 to 2016, with March 1973 set as the baseline of one hundred. The index peaked above one hundred five in the early 2000s, dropped to its lowest point near seventy during the 2008 financial crisis and again around 2011, and steadily rose back to nearly one hundred by 2016, illustrating the overvaluation cited by the author.

The fourth chart, titled A general lack of tariff reciprocity, is a scatter plot comparing the simple average of tariffs applied by the US on the vertical axis against tariffs applied to the US by other countries on the horizontal axis. A diagonal reciprocity line marks where tariffs would be equal. Because almost all plotted countries fall below this line, they impose higher average tariffs on the US than the US imposes on them. China is prominently highlighted in red, showing that the US applies about a two point five percent tariff on Chinese goods, while China applies a nearly ten percent tariff on US goods. Nations like Bangladesh, Pakistan, Brazil, India, and Nigeria apply tariffs ranging from ten percent to fourteen percent on US goods, whereas the US tariff on their goods remains below six percent. Conversely, closer trade partners like Canada, Mexico, Chile, and Israel cluster near the origin, showing low, nearly reciprocal tariffs of under two percent. 

The page ends with a brief note directing readers to the February twenty-first, twenty-eighteen edition of Eye on the Market, which covered inflation, US equities, hedge funds, and blockchain.

This page, titled "Pressure on the Fed," argues that the Federal Reserve is behind the curve in raising interest rates, given tightening labor markets, rising budget deficits, and rising unit labor costs. Michael Cembalest points out that negative real policy rates have historically been reserved for wartime and the immediate aftermath of the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. Despite US economic conditions returning to normal years prior, the real Fed Funds rate has remained negative. 

To support this argument, the first chart, "Lowest real yields on cash since 1830, other than during wartime," shows the five-year average of the T-bill/Funds rate less inflation from 1830 to 2017. The data reveals that negative real yields have only occurred during the Civil War, World War I, World War II, and the five-year period ending in 2017. A companion chart, "Why is the real Fed Funds Rate still negative?", plots the unemployment rate, economy-wide inflation, and the real Fed Funds rate from 1995 to early 2018. This chart shows that while unemployment surged toward 10% in 2009 and inflation collapsed, unemployment has since fallen back to around 4% and inflation has stabilized near 2%, yet the real Fed Funds rate has remained negative.

Cembalest notes that markets are beginning to recognize the need for rate adjustments, as evidenced by rising yields. J.P. Morgan projects six rate hikes over the next 18 months, with the Fed Funds rate peaking at approximately 3.5% in 2019. He forecasts that while corporate earnings typically rise during tightening cycles due to an improving economy, price-to-earnings multiples will likely decline this time, aligning with J.P. Morgan's 2018 Outlook of 8% to 10% equity returns. A footnote adds that rising unit labor costs, driven by flat productivity, may serve as the primary catalyst for Fed policy.

The bottom-left chart, "US bond yields and cash rates," tracks the US 10-year bond yield and the US current cash rate from 2014 to early 2018. It shows the cash rate rising from near 0% in late 2015 to roughly 1.4% by early 2018, while the 10-year bond yield rose from a 2016 trough of around 1.5% to nearly 3.0% by early 2018. 

Finally, a table titled "US equity performance during periods of rising rates" provides historical context by analyzing fifteen periods of rising 10-year bond yields from 1991 through early 2018. The table details the trough and peak yields, the basis point change, and the subsequent S&P 500 12-month forward P/E and forward EPS percentage changes. Across these periods, the average trough yield was 3.8% and the peak was 5.3% (a 149 basis point increase), resulting in an average 4% increase in forward P/E and an 8% increase in forward EPS. The most recent period listed, from July 2016 to March 2018, saw yields rise from 1.4% to 2.9% (a 152 basis point increase), with forward P/E increasing by 3% and forward EPS rising by 26%.

This page outlines the primary arguments advanced by proponents of Net Neutrality, categorizing them into four major themes alongside illustrative examples, data, and supplementary notes. 

The first thematic section argues that Net Neutrality is essential to prevent content discrimination and monopolistic practices by Internet Service Providers. Advocates assert that without these protections, ISPs could engage in anti-competitive behaviors such as paid prioritization, zero-rating, throttling, or blocking rival content. This concern is highlighted by media consolidations, such as Comcast’s acquisition of NBC Universal and AT&T’s proposed acquisition of Time Warner. A historical example is cited from 2005, when DSL provider Madison River blocked Vonage to protect its own landline business. Proponents also note that past Republican FCC chairs historically favored an open internet, including attaching lifetime net neutrality conditions to 4G spectrum auctions in 2008, and argue that these rules are needed to prevent ideological or political blocking of content. A footnote clarifies that while paid prioritization at the ISP level is contested, technical prioritization via Content Delivery Networks and transit providers already exists to optimize web traffic.

The second section details the FCC’s role in promoting communications network growth. Under the authority of the 1996 Telecom Act, the FCC is meant to encourage product development and investment rather than rent-seeking. Advocates warn that allowing ISPs to maximize profits through deregulation harms entrepreneurs developing broadband-reliant technologies like mobile streaming, gaming, and smart devices. They also argue that ISPs overreacted to Title II classification, pointing out that post-2015 ISP capital spending trends are inconclusive.

The third argument frames the internet as a public good requiring utility-like regulations to ensure universal, affordable access. A footnote highlights a significant barrier to this goal, noting that over twenty US states restrict or prohibit local governments from building municipal broadband networks. Advocates argue that customer dissatisfaction is too entrenched for market forces to correct ISP behavior, citing a 2017 survey where cable operators and ISPs tied for last place across 43 industries with a 64% satisfaction rating. They also warn that platforms like YouTube, which function as public goods for news and education, might be forced to pass down new ISP access fees to individual content creators.

Finally, the text argues that most consumers lack competitive options and are forced to use single, expensive ISPs. This is backed by data showing that as of June 2015, 78% of developed census blocks had one or fewer fixed broadband providers offering downstream speeds of at least 25 Mbps. Similarly, a 2014 Department of Commerce report found that 67% of the US population had only one option at that speed. These limitations leave the US with low broadband penetration rates relative to other OECD countries. Advocates point out that cable and satellite TV inflation over the past 20 years averaged 3.4%, outstripping overall core inflation of 2.0%, and warn that losing price transparency rules will exacerbate this trend. Furthermore, they note that mobile devices are unlikely to replace home broadband due to the high costs and infrastructure challenges of 5G deployment.

This page presents a comprehensive overview of the common arguments made by opponents of Net Neutrality, structured across several key themes. 

First, opponents argue that the 2015 Net Neutrality rule was a regulation in search of a problem, noting that instances of content throttling, blocking, or favoring for pay were historically rare. They assert that market discipline and the mutual economic incentives of internet service providers and content creators naturally discourage restricted access. Furthermore, the page highlights that consumers have ample choices; as of December 2016, 56 percent of the US population had more than one fixed broadband provider offering speeds greater than 25 megabits per second, a figure that excludes mobile and satellite options. 

The text outlines how utility-like regulations under the 2015 FCC Order deter business investment, create market uncertainty, and discourage consumer-friendly innovations like "Zero Rating" plans, which do not count streaming protocols against monthly data caps. Opponents also argue that Net Neutrality functions as a form of regulatory capture by powerful content creators and tech giants. By prohibiting prioritized pricing, the rules force ISPs and end-user consumers to subsidize the heavy traffic of streaming services like YouTube and Netflix, which comprise about 50 percent of downstream traffic during peak demand. 

Instead of FCC Title II classification, opponents suggest relying on the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice to police anti-competitive behaviors, as was done prior to 2015. They also contend that the US internet market is already highly competitive and affordable, citing that entry-level US broadband prices as a percentage of gross national income are among the lowest in the OECD, the US has the second lowest cost per gigabit in the OECD as of February 2018, and quality-adjusted broadband services have experienced negative one percent inflation since 1997.

To support the argument that wireless options are becoming viable alternatives to wired access, the bottom of the page features a horizontal bar chart displaying the peak download rate per second of mobile generations on a logarithmic scale ranging from 1 bit to 10 gigabits. The chart illustrates exponential speed increases from 1G, 2G, 3G, and 4G, up to 5G, with a callout pointing out that 5G is 20 times faster than 4G, pushing peak download rates toward the 10 gigabit mark.

This page analyzes the historical context of the upcoming 2018 midterm elections, questioning if the Republican Party is headed for an unprecedented rejection despite a strong economy characterized by a rising stock market and falling unemployment. The author observes that while the President's party almost always loses House seats during midterms, large losses are historically tied to falling stock markets, rising unemployment, or both. 

To illustrate this relationship, the page features a scatter plot mapping midterm elections since 1910. The vertical axis shows the trailing two-year change in the unemployment rate, ranging from a negative eight percent change at the top to a positive eight percent change at the bottom. The horizontal axis represents the trailing two-year real equity market return, ranging from negative fifty percent to fifty percent. The chart is divided into four quadrants based on these indicators: falling unemployment and falling stock market; falling unemployment and rising stock market; rising unemployment and falling stock market; and rising unemployment and rising stock market. Midterm election years are plotted as bubbles, where blue denotes a Democratic President and red denotes a Republican President, with the bubble size representing the number of House seats lost. 

The data shows that the top-right quadrant, which represents the favorable economic conditions of falling unemployment and a rising stock market, has historically seen very minimal seat losses for the President's party. Examples include a loss of nine seats in 1926, five seats in 1986, and thirteen seats in 2014. In contrast, massive losses are concentrated in the quadrants with weaker economic conditions, such as seventy-two seats lost in 1938 and fifty-two seats lost in 1930. The chart inserts a projected red bubble for the 2018 midterm election in the top-right quadrant, using an estimated GOP loss of twenty-five to forty seats based on a forecast by Seth Masket. A loss of this magnitude during a strong economic period would represent a historic anomaly. 

The author discusses several competing factors shaping the 2018 election. Factors supporting the GOP include the lowest unemployment rate in decades and a high number of non-competitive, gerrymandered districts. Conversely, factors pointing to a Democratic wave include strong Democratic performances in recent special elections, historically low presidential popularity, robust Democratic fundraising, and satirical cultural indicators like John Oliver's parody book about Mike Pence's rabbit outselling Pence's own book. Ultimately, the author posits that the 2018 midterms may serve as a referendum on presidential unorthodoxy rather than standard economic or market data.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Annual Energy Paper argues that there are clear structural limits to decarbonizing the global economy through electrification alone. The author emphasizes that electricity accounts for only 17% of global final energy consumption, with the vast majority of energy used directly for applications like combustion engines, industrial smelting, heating, and raw materials. Furthermore, electricity represents less than one-third of global fossil fuel use, as direct consumption in sectors like transportation and industry dominates. 

A bar chart illustrating global energy consumed by end-user in quadrillion BTUs breaks down primary energy used for electricity (around 210 quadrillion BTUs) and shows how energy is consumed across the industrial, transport, and residential/commercial sectors. The industrial sector is the largest consumer, relying heavily on direct fossil fuels alongside electricity. The transport sector is almost entirely dependent on petroleum, with only a negligible fraction of electricity used for electrified rail. An accompanying pie chart shows that 341 quadrillion BTUs of fossil fuels are used directly for non-electricity purposes, compared to 141 quadrillion BTUs used indirectly to generate electricity. 

A historical line graph tracks the share of global primary energy consumption derived from fossil fuels (coal, oil, and natural gas) from 1965 to 2015. This share sat above 94% in the late 1960s, declined to around 86% during the nuclear adoption era of the 1970s and 1980s, and hovered around 85% by 2016 as the solar and wind era began. 

The final chart projects global urbanization trends from 1950 to 2050, showing the percentage of the population living in cities across various countries and regions. Japan leads with urbanization rates projected to exceed 90% by 2050, followed closely by the United States, Europe, South America, and China, which are all forecasted to rise past 80%. Urbanization in Africa and India is also projected to rise significantly, reaching roughly 55% and 50% respectively by 2050. The author argues that because society is becoming increasingly urbanized, decentralized or off-the-grid energy solutions are becoming less relevant, meaning energy solutions must be designed for dense, grid-dependent urban populations.

This J.P. Morgan analysis explores the slow pace of decarbonization in the industrial sector, highlighting that only fifteen percent of OECD industrial energy use comes from electricity, while the rest relies on direct fossil fuel consumption. The author explains that industrial decarbonization is uniquely challenging because key sectors require fossil fuels both as raw material feedstock and as fuel to generate sustained high-temperature process heat.

The page contains several graphics illustrating these dynamics. A pie chart depicting OECD industrial sector energy consumption by source shows that liquid fuels dominate at thirty-seven percent, followed by natural gas at twenty-nine percent, electricity at fifteen percent, coal at eleven percent, and renewables at just eight percent. Next to this, a horizontal bar chart breaks down OECD industrial sector energy consumption by product as a percentage of the total. The chemical industry represents the largest share at nearly twenty percent, followed by iron and steel at around thirteen percent, oil refining at approximately eleven percent, and paper manufacturing at about eight percent. Nonmetallic minerals and food products each account for roughly five percent, while nonferrous metals make up about three percent of the total.

Two tables further detail these uses. The first table covers the industrial use of fossil fuels as raw materials, listing four major applications: metallurgical coke is used as a carbon source for smelting pig iron to make steel; methane serves as a hydrogen source to synthesize ammonia for crop fertilizers; methane, naphtha, and ethane are used to synthesize monomers for plastics; and heavy petroleum products are used to produce carbon black for rubber fillers in tires. The second table highlights the industrial use of fossil fuels for generating process heat, specifically for producing construction materials such as cement, bricks, tiles, glass, and kiln-dried timber; manufacturing petrochemicals and plastics; and smelting iron ore in blast furnaces. The author notes that while electricity could in theory supply some process heat, progress in this area has been modest.

This page examines the speed of electric vehicle (EV) adoption and questions whether it represents a rapid transition or a gradual evolution, framed by the title "Electric vehicles: a 2% or a 20% solution?" The author points out that despite tenfold growth in renewable power generation since 2004, fossil fuels still supply 85% of primary energy. Because road transportation accounts for half of all global oil consumption, decarbonizing this sector is critical to achieving climate goals. However, the author argues that the shift to EVs will likely be slow and gradual, potentially defying the geometric projections of some futurists.

To contextualize the scale of energy use, the page presents two visual breakdowns of global oil and transportation energy consumption. A table of global consumption of oil products shows that road transportation dominates at 50% of the total (1,823 million tons of oil equivalents), followed by feedstocks at 16% (588 mtoe), other transportation like air and marine at 15% (539 mtoe), heating at 8% (313 mtoe), industry at 8% (303 mtoe), and agriculture at 3% (116 mtoe). Alongside this, a stacked bar chart breaks down world transportation energy consumption by mode in quadrillion Btu. Passenger transport is heavily dominated by light-duty vehicles, which consume around 45 quadrillion Btu, vastly exceeding air, bus, and other passenger modes combined. Freight transport energy is more evenly divided, led by heavy trucks, followed by marine transport, medium-sized trucks, and rail.

The page then compares public policy mandates against manufacturer commitments to illustrate the landscape of the EV transition. A table detailing government policy goals maps out vehicle sales and electrification targets for various nations. China, the largest vehicle market with 28.3 million light vehicle sales in 2017, has a pending internal combustion engine (ICE) ban alongside a cap-and-trade policy targeting 5% EV sales by 2020. The United States, the second-largest market with 17.2 million sales, has no stated federal goal. Among other nations, Japan, Brazil, Italy, Canada, South Korea, and Mexico target 30% EV sales by 2030. Meanwhile, European nations and India have set outright ICE bans, with Germany and India targeting 2030, the United Kingdom and France aiming for 2040, and the Netherlands and Norway planning to phase out ICE sales by 2025.

A corresponding table details company policy goals, matching corporate EV ambitions against 2016 production volumes. Chinese OEMs, which produced 11.9 million vehicles in 2016, target 4.5 million annual EV sales by 2020. Toyota aims for 5.5 million annual EV sales by 2030, and Volkswagen targets 2 to 3 million by 2025. Other manufacturers have unique metrics: Renault-Nissan targets 1.5 million cumulative EV sales by 2020; GM targets 1 million annual EV sales by 2026; and Honda wants two-thirds of its 2030 sales to be EVs. Hyundai and Ford plan to expand product lineups with 38 and 40 new electric models by 2035 and 2022, respectively. Volvo, with a smaller 2016 production footprint of 0.5 million vehicles, aims for 100% EV sales by around 2024, while Tesla targets 0.5 million EV sales by 2018 and 1 million by 2020.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Annual Energy Paper analyzes the highly varied and historically overoptimistic forecasts for global electric vehicle (EV) adoption by the year 2030. Cembalest argues that current projections, which range from 2% to 20% of a projected 1.4 billion-car global fleet, likely suffer from the same wishful thinking that plagued forecasts from a decade prior. He advises that the median forecast of approximately 125 million EVs by 2030 is likely too high, stating that he is taking the “under” on these projections.

The first chart on the page, titled "Electric vehicle projections for the year 2030: from 2% to 20% of the global fleet," plots global EV fleet sizes in millions from 2016 through 2030, alongside a companion dot plot showing projected 2030 EV penetration as a percentage of the global fleet. The most aggressive projection comes from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) using a "horse-to-car" transition method, which forecasts nearly 250 million EVs, or an 18% market penetration. Cembalest strongly critiques this model, pointing out that switching from internal combustion engines to EVs does not offer the massive utility leap that switching from horses to cars did, and notes that the IMF got the historical timeline of horse displacement wrong by ignoring the early role of electric streetcars and subways. Other plotted forecasts include the International Energy Agency (IEA) high-end at around 15% and low-end at 12%, followed by Bloomberg New Energy Finance, the UN Paris Agreement, Morgan Stanley, Wood Mackenzie, BP, and Smil regression clustered between 6% and 9%. The lowest projections come from Goldman Sachs, IHS Automotive, and Exxon, which forecasts penetration of only around 2% to 4%.

To ground these numbers, the second chart, "Prior generation of electric car projections out of sync with reality," displays EV and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) sales as a percentage of total car sales from 2009 to 2020. It compares actual U.S. sales, which remained flat and below 2% through 2017, with highly optimistic forecasts made around 2009 by various institutions. These historical projections estimated that by 2020, EV and PHEV market share would rise dramatically, led by Deutsche Bank at nearly 11%, followed by PwC, Frost & Sullivan, Bloomberg NEF, IEA, Roland Berger, BCG, and finally Deloitte, which had the lowest forecast at roughly 4%. 

Ultimately, Cembalest cautions investors that while battery prices have declined and subsidies have been introduced, cars are not smartphones; they face higher upfront costs, complex supply chains, refueling needs, and strict safety standards that naturally slow down product displacement.

This page analyzes the potential bottlenecks that could slow the pace of the electric vehicle revolution, focusing on massive infrastructure funding requirements and the technological challenges of reducing battery costs. 

The author argues that transitioning to electric vehicles requires substantial upgrades to power generation and distribution networks rather than just building charging stations and factories. For example, India, China, and Europe face a combined estimated capital investment of $1.7 trillion to meet their respective EV targets. A cumulative bar chart sourced from Bridgewater Associates illustrates the total investment required through 2030 to meet specific EV targets: 100% EV sales for India, 25% for China, 50% for Europe, and 12% for the United States. Across all four regions, the overwhelming majority of the required funds must go to power generation and distribution rather than production facilities or charging stations. Under these assumptions, India requires approximately $600 billion, China around $500 billion, Europe roughly $450 billion, and the United States slightly over $100 billion.

The second key hurdle is the trajectory of battery costs. A line chart detailing the capital cost of lithium-ion battery packs per kilowatt-hour shows a dramatic decline from over $1,200 in 2006 to approximately $200 by late 2017, highlighting specific progress markers for Tesla and GM. However, while the US Department of Energy aims for a target of $100 per kilowatt-hour on a cell basis to achieve cost parity with internal combustion engine vehicles, researchers from the Advanced Research Projects Agency suggest this threshold may be difficult to achieve using current battery designs.

A concluding table from the US Department of Energy compares current and future vehicle energy storage technologies. Current lithium-ion graphite/NMC technology has a current cost of $235 per kilowatt-hour, a potential future cost of $100 to $160, and a long cycle life of 1,000 to 5,000 cycles, but it requires research into high-voltage cathodes and extreme fast charging. Next-generation lithium-ion batteries using silicon composites or high-voltage NMC have a current cost of $256 per kilowatt-hour and can potentially reach $90 to $125, though their current cycle life is lower at 500 to 700 cycles. Finally, longer-term lithium metal technology offers the lowest potential cost of $70 to $120 per kilowatt-hour, but currently costs $320 and suffers from a very low cycle life of only 50 to 100 cycles, necessitating extensive R&D in lithium protection and solid electrolytes.

This page addresses the global supply and demand of rare earth metals and critical materials required for clean energy technologies, focusing specifically on the impact of electric vehicles. While overall reserves are ample—amounting to 478 megatons of global rare earth oxides that could sustain current production for over a century—the page highlights potential supply chain vulnerabilities for specific critical minerals. Citing a 2011 U.S. Department of Energy report and a 2017 study from the University of Science and Technology in Beijing, the author notes that electric vehicles are projected to consume 68% of all rare earth demand by 2030, up from 50% in 2018. 

Three main charts support this discussion. The first, a "Medium Term Criticality Matrix" from the U.S. Department of Energy, maps clean energy importance against supply risk on a four-point scale. It places dysprosium and neodymium in the highest-risk, highest-importance categories, while other elements like terbium, europium, yttrium, lithium, and tellurium sit at medium-to-high risk levels. The second chart shows "Global rare earth production and demand" in metric tons from 1950 to 2015, illustrating how production and demand have historically tracked each other closely, climbing from near zero in 1950 to around 120,000 metric tons by 2015. The third chart indexes "EV battery metals prices" to January 2014 baselines. It demonstrates that while prices for copper, terbium, dysprosium, and neodymium remained relatively flat or fell through early 2018, cobalt and lithium experienced massive price spikes, nearly tripling in value by the start of 2018.

Finally, a callout box titled "A brief comment on autonomous car energy use" introduces research from the University of Michigan Center for Sustainable Systems. It highlights that while autonomous driving can offer efficiency benefits that offset the energy drag of onboard computing and hardware weight, testing on larger vehicle platforms, such as Waymo autonomous systems installed in minivans, resulted in higher net energy consumption.

This page focuses on the technology, grid efficiency benefits, and cost dynamics of high voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission lines, arguing that they are highly economic for long-distance power transport compared to standard high voltage alternating current (HVAC) lines. This distinction is critical for large nations like China, the United States, Brazil, India, and Australia, where renewable energy resources—such as wind, solar, and hydro—are often located far from major population centers. Without efficient long-distance transmission, grids suffer from high transmission losses and substantial involuntary curtailment of renewable power.

The analysis is supported by four key data visuals. First, a scatter plot of transmission and distribution losses as a percentage of total generation against population density reveals that lower-density countries suffer higher grid losses. For instance, Canada and the United States experience losses of roughly 8% and 6% respectively, whereas high-density South Korea experiences around 4.5% losses. Second, a table detailing involuntary wind and solar curtailment ratios reveals that while European nations and regional US grids like ERCOT have successfully limited curtailment to under 2% (and even 0% in Denmark and Portugal), China has struggled with severe curtailment, which reached 17.0% in 2016. 

To explain how HVDC addresses these issues, the bottom of the page presents two comparative line charts. The first shows active power losses in megawatts across distances from 200 to 400 kilometers. While HVAC losses rise steeply from approximately 83 megawatts to over 110 megawatts, HVDC losses increase much more gradually, reaching only about 88 megawatts at 400 kilometers. The second line chart compares lifetime system costs, demonstrating that while HVDC carries higher initial capital costs due to conversion terminal requirements, its lower per-kilometer costs make it the cheaper option once transmission distances exceed 600 to 700 kilometers. For underground or underwater transmission, this breakeven threshold drops to just 50 to 80 kilometers due to the high electrical capacitance and reactive power losses inherent to insulated AC cables near the ground. 

Finally, the text notes that major industrial firms Siemens and ABB report similar breakeven distances, with both companies currently working on the world’s first 1,100 kilovolt HVDC transformers for use in Guquan, China.

This page analyzes China's leadership in installing high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission lines to connect remote wind, solar, and hydro facilities with its major urban demand centers. Although China holds 30% of global wind and solar capacity, these sources generate only 5% of its electricity due to transmission challenges and severe renewable curtailment. To support its mandatory goal of reducing coal's share of primary energy from 62% in 2016 to 58% by 2020, China is building numerous HVDC projects, with 20 currently operating or under construction.

An included map of China depicts these HVDC transmission lines, separating operational lines (solid) from those projected for completion by 2020 (dotted), with color-coding to show pathways for hydropower (blue) and PV and wind energy (red).

To put China's efforts into a global perspective, a table lists announced domestic HVDC projects above 400 kV for eight countries, ranking them by the ratio of project distance (in kilometers) to total electricity generation capacity (in gigawatts). Mexico leads with a ratio of 40.6 (2,740 km of projects and 67 GW of capacity), followed by Brazil at 29.8 (4,640 km and 156 GW), China at 18.4 (27,953 km and 1,519 GW), Indonesia at 15.3 (876 km and 57 GW), the UK at 12.5 (1,187 km and 95 GW), Germany at 12.2 (2,495 km and 204 GW), the USA at 7.5 (8,075 km and 1,074 GW), and India at 6.2 (2,021 km and 325 GW). The author highlights that China's HVDC ratio is more than double that of the US, a comparison made more worrisome by the likelihood that some announced US transmission projects may never actually be built.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Annual Energy Paper argues that while modeling sea level rise is complex, constructing flood mitigation infrastructure is straightforward. The author highlights that sea-based systems, such as hydraulic locks, dams, and gates, have proven highly effective during severe storms.
