The chart reveals that despite a notable margin shortfall of about negative 0.4x, a massive multiple expansion of nearly 0.9x successfully offset the operational underperformance to keep overall returns positive. 

Additionally, the author notes that buyout Public Market Equivalents (PMEs) show very little dispersion based on fund size, and that venture capital managers show greater performance persistence over time than buyout managers. Cembalest argues that private equity's illiquid nature demands an outperformance premium, especially given the steep discounts to net asset value (NAV) often seen in secondary markets. 

To illustrate these discounts, a second chart from Coller Capital tracks average secondary market pricing for private equity LP positions as a percentage of NAV from 2007 through 2016. The chart compares buyout and venture positions. Buyouts fell from over 100% of NAV in 2007 to roughly 63% in 2009, eventually recovering to around 95% by 2016. Venture capital followed a similar path, dropping to roughly 65% in 2009 but recovering more modestly, hovering between 75% and 80% of NAV through 2016. 

The page concludes by addressing the overstatement of risk-adjusted returns caused by the stale pricing of LP NAVs. When de-smoothing techniques are applied to private equity returns to estimate true volatility, the optimal portfolio allocation for private equity in a traditional mean-variance model (assuming a 10% projected absolute return) falls significantly from 20% to just 14%.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication focuses on the measurement of private equity dry powder, noting that estimates range widely between $500 billion and $1.5 trillion depending on whether the count includes all private equity categories or just buyouts. The author observes that dry powder now exceeds the peaks of 2008 and 2009, driven by the largest managers and the most recent vintage years. However, the text highlights that dry powder may be overstated by $350 billion to $400 billion due to the rise of subscription loans used by managers to temporarily fund investments and boost internal rates of return. Conversely, dry powder can be understated because separate accounts are typically excluded from these industry estimates.

A bar chart titled "Global dry powder by category" displays the growth of dry powder from 2003 to 2017 in trillions of US dollars, utilizing data from Bain Global Private Equity. The total volume has climbed from under $0.4 trillion in 2003 to approximately $1.7 trillion in 2017. The columns are stacked by strategy, showing that buyouts consistently represent the largest share of dry powder, followed by real estate, other categories like infrastructure and distressed debt, private credit, and venture capital. 

An accompanying text box details subscription loans, noting that while Cambridge Associates estimates these loans can theoretically boost internal rates of return by up to 3% annually, data from the Institutional Limited Partners Association indicates a median annual impact of no more than 0.45%. Additionally, industry polling shows that 87% of private equity CFOs and COOs use or plan to use subscription loans, and about 95% report that limited partners view them positively or neutrally.

At the bottom of the page, two charts from Pitchbook illustrate where this capital is concentrated. The first chart, "Dry powder concentrated in largest funds," tracks PE dry powder in billions of US dollars by vintage year from 2010 to 2017. It shows a dramatic upward trend, peaking in 2017 at over $300 billion, with the vast majority of that capital concentrated in mega-funds sized at over $5 billion or between $1 billion and $4.99 billion. The final chart, "Current dry powder by vintage year," stacks current undeployed capital to show a total of nearly $900 billion. The largest portion of this total is held in the 2017 vintage, followed sequentially by 2016, 2015, and 2014, highlighting that the bulk of the dry powder is highly concentrated in the most recent vintages.

In this section, Michael Cembalest examines why private equity dry powder has been rising, pointing out that capital commitments from investors have outpaced the actual deployment of capital by fund managers. This dynamic is supported by a rising number of buyout funds, strong fundraising over the previous five years, distributions outpacing capital calls, and commitments relative to stock market capitalization reaching their highest levels since 2007. Furthermore, surveys show that institutional limited partners remain highly committed to the asset class, with only a small fraction planning to decrease their allocations.

To illustrate these trends, the page presents five visual graphics. The first chart shows the number of active buyout firms from 1990 to 2017, revealing a steady increase from roughly 200 active firms in 1990 to over 1,200 by 2017. North American and European firms make up the vast majority of this count, though the Asia-Pacific region and the rest of the world have also shown growth. The second chart details global private equity capital raised by year from 2003 to 2017 in billions of US dollars. Capital raised climbed from under $200 billion in 2003 to a pre-crisis peak of over $600 billion in 2007, before dropping sharply and then steadily recovering to nearly $700 billion by 2017. Buyout funds represent the largest segment of this fundraising, followed by venture capital, real estate, infrastructure, and other strategies like growth and distressed debt.

A third area chart tracks private equity fundraising by fund size and vintage year from 2010 to 2017. It demonstrates that mega-funds, specifically those over $5 billion, have captured an increasingly large share of total commitments over time, while smaller funds under $500 million have seen their relative share shrink. Two final bar charts display 2017 Preqin survey data regarding investor private equity intentions. For both the short term (next 12 months) and the long term, fewer than 10% of surveyed investors expected to decrease their commitments, while the remaining 90% or more were roughly split between maintaining or increasing their allocations. 

In a detailed footnote, the author highlights the $100 billion SoftBank Vision Fund raised in 2017 as a prominent example of aggressive investing by limited partners, especially given the managers' limited history in deploying such vast sums of capital. Cembalest observes that while SoftBank achieved early successes with Flipkart and Guardant Health, it would need to generate gains of $23 billion per year to meet its 20% internal rate of return target. He also questions the prudence of some of their high-profile venture deals, citing a $300 million investment in the dog-walking startup Wag.

This page analyzes the dynamics of private equity fundraising, investment pacing, and capital commitments. Drawing on data from the Bain Global Private Equity Report, the author highlights strong fundraising in 2017, noting that over two-thirds of private equity funds met or exceeded their target amounts, with approximately 40 percent taking less than a year to close. Buyout funds performed even better, with an 85 percent success rate in meeting targets and 68 percent closing in under a year. 

Two middle charts examine capital activity and market commitments. The first, illustrating global private equity capital calls and distributions as a percentage of fund size from 2000 to 2017, reveals a slower pace of capital calls in recent years compared to distributions. While distributions peaked sharply near 5.5 percent before the 2008 financial crisis and recovered to solid levels of 3 percent to 4 percent, capital calls have remained relatively low, suggesting a strong seller's market for private companies. The second chart details commitments to US private equity partnerships as a percentage of public stock market capitalization from 1980 to 2016. It shows a massive divergence between sectors; commitments to buyout, growth, and distressed assets spiked near 1.2 percent in 2007-2008 and remained elevated around 0.9 percent by 2016, while venture capital commitments peaked around 0.4 percent in 2000 and have since plateaued at very low levels under 0.2 percent.

The author also addresses the ongoing debate over whether private equity capital is being called more slowly than usual, pointing out conflicting signals in the data. Although the first chart suggests a slowdown relative to overall fund size, a chart analyzing the median buyout percentage called by fund age paints a different picture. Tracking various vintage groupings from 1998 through 2018 over a three-year fund life, this chart demonstrates that the median percentage called is relatively consistent across cycles. Crucially, the 2015-2018 vintage shows a call pace right in the middle of historical ranges, reaching approximately 60 percent by year three, indicating that recent investing speeds are not slower than usual. Specific sources and authors referenced on this page include Steve Kaplan, eFront Insight, Hamilton Lane, and Bain.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest argues that regardless of whether the pace of private equity investment is slow, the acquisition prices paid for buyouts are climbing rapidly. This trend is fueled by a growing pool of dry powder, cheap and covenant-light debt, high levels of equity capital, and intensifying competition from corporate strategic buyers whose average deal sizes have doubled. Additionally, the shrinking pool of US public companies limits options, driving up acquisition multiples to new cyclical highs. A cited study by Verdad Capital notes that private equity firms typically double a target company's leverage from 2.5x to 5.0x. Cembalest attributes these elevated asset prices to a historic decade of interest rates trailing inflation—an anomaly seen only three times prior in US history, specifically during the Civil War, World War I, and World War II.

To illustrate these market dynamics, the page features four charts based on data from the Bain Global Private Equity Report. The first chart, tracking global buyout deal value in billions of US dollars from 1996 to 2017, shows that total buyout activity peaked near $800 billion in 2006 and 2007 before plummeting during the financial crisis. By 2017, global deal values recovered significantly to around $450 billion, with North America consistently representing the largest regional share, followed by Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the rest of the world. 

The second chart details average EBITDA purchase price multiples for US LBO transactions from 2008 through the third quarter of 2017. Total multiples escalated from around 9x EBITDA in 2008 to over 11x by late 2017. This valuation expansion has been driven primarily by expansions in the senior debt-to-EBITDA portion and the equity-to-EBITDA component, while subordinated debt has played a minimal role.

The third chart tracks LBO leverage, showing average debt-to-EBITDA multiples for large US LBO deals from 2001 to 2017. After peaking near 6x in 2007 and dropping below 4x in 2009, total leverage returned close to 6x by 2017, with first-lien debt making up the vast majority of the debt structure. 

The final chart highlights increasing competition from strategic buyers by measuring global corporate venture capital deal value in billions of US dollars from 2008 to 2017. Corporate VC deal value exploded over this decade, surging from less than $10 billion in 2008 to nearly $45 billion by 2017, led heavily by North American and Asia-Pacific corporate investors.

This page analyzes how the declining number of public US companies is driving up private equity acquisition multiples, while highlighting that a growing pool of private companies, particularly in the technology sector, is absorbing significant amounts of private equity "dry powder." The author argues that because tech companies are waiting longer to go public, they require more private capital, meaning that measuring dry powder solely against the market capitalization of public companies is no longer a sufficient metric. Technology now represents 15% to 20% of US private equity activity, driven by a dramatic improvement in tech company fundamentals that has reduced their cash-flow volatility.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, "The growing listing gap between the US and the world," compares domestic US listings with non-US listings in thousands from 1980 to 2016. It shows a stark divergence: while non-US listings steadily climbed from under 15,000 in 1980 to over 40,000 by 2016, domestic US listings peaked at around 8,000 in 1996 before falling back down to around 4,000 by 2016. The second chart, "Additions and subtractions to listed companies," details this trend by plotting the total number of listed US firms alongside new listings and delists from 1976 to 2016. The total number of listed firms peaked near 8,000 in the late 1990s and has since steadily declined toward 4,000 as delists outpaced new listings.

The third chart, "Tech companies waiting longer to go public," tracks the median age in years of technology companies at the time of their IPO from 1980 to 2016. After dropping to a low of 4 years during the dot-com boom in 1999, the median age at IPO rose sharply to nearly 14 years in 2008 and remained high, hovering between 10 and 11 years by 2016. The final chart, "Tech sales growth more stable," measures the five-year volatility of quarterly sales growth for the median S&P 500 tech company from 1991 to 2015. This volatility peaked near 30% in the early 2000s but steadily declined to around 15% by 2015. Notably, this level of volatility is now lower than that of the broader S&P 500 index, demonstrating why technology companies are no longer considered too volatile for conservative private equity investment strategies.

This page addresses the question of whether the current volume of private equity dry powder is problematic for investors, with the author arguing that these levels are stable and not as alarming as absolute dollar figures suggest when measured against either the market capitalization of target small- and mid-cap companies or the pace of investment. 

To support this view, the first chart compares buyout dry powder to the market capitalization of the Russell 2000 index from 2000 to 2017. While the Russell 2000 market cap expanded to over $2.0 trillion by 2017, buyout dry powder grew at a much slower rate, reaching approximately $0.5 trillion. Consequently, the ratio of buyout dry powder to the Russell 2000 market cap, which peaked near 50% ahead of the 2008 financial crisis, has stabilized at a more moderate level of around 20% to 25% by 2017. This suggests the relative scale of dry powder is not historically overextended.

The second chart evaluates dry powder using an inventory approach, calculating the years of private equity inventory on hand from 2006 to 2017 based on annual investment pace. The "In year" measure peaked at over 2.0 turns in 2009 but subsequently fell and stabilized at around 1.0 turn by 2017. The "3-year trailing" measure displays a similar trajectory, peaking around 1.3 turns in 2010 and settling at roughly 1.0 turn by 2017, indicating a healthy and stable relationship between dry powder and actual deployment.

The third chart illustrates the time required to deploy capital overhang, measured in years at a trailing 12-month pace for both buyout and venture capital from 2001 to 2017. The deployment time for buyout funds peaked at over 5 years in 2003 and nearly 5 years in 2010, but declined to under 3 years by 2017. Venture capital followed a comparable path, peaking above 4 years in 2002 and 2010 before declining to approximately 2.5 years by 2017. Together, these metrics suggest that the dry powder overhang remains well within historical norms and does not present an immediate crisis for private equity managers.

This page argues that due to substantial growth in private equity assets and high buyout multiples, absolute and relative private equity returns over the next decade are likely to be lower than they were in the 1990s, unless a major market correction occurs. The author, Michael Cembalest, points out that high starting valuations historically lead to lower subsequent returns, and while the investible universe for private equity is expanding—driven by technology companies and mega-funds—fundraising is growing even faster, which pushes acquisition multiples higher. 

To illustrate the historical relationship between valuation and returns, the first chart, a scatter plot titled "Higher S&P multiples generally followed by lower returns," plots the subsequent 10-year price-only returns from 1930 to 2017 against S&P P/E multiples based on trailing three-year earnings. The chart reveals a clear downward-sloping trend, showing that higher starting P/E multiples, which range from under 10 to nearly 40, are strongly correlated with lower subsequent 10-year returns, which span from positive 15% down to negative 10%. 

To demonstrate how rapid asset growth impacts alternative investment performance, the second chart, "Hedge funds: assets under management and returns," displays data from 1995 to 2016. This dual-axis line chart tracks hedge fund assets under management (AUM) in trillions of US dollars on the left axis against their rolling 5-year annualized returns on the right axis. As AUM steadily climbed from near zero in 1995 to approximately 3.0 trillion dollars by 2016, the rolling 5-year annualized returns experienced a major long-term decline, falling from peaks above 20% in the late 1990s down to around 5% by the mid-2010s. 

The author draws a parallel from this hedge fund trend, where rising competition for investment ideas eventually eroded investor returns, to the current state of private equity. Ultimately, the author forecasts that future diversified private equity portfolio returns will be lower than in the 1990s, with outperformance versus public equities remaining positive but at the lower end of its historical range.

This page addresses the question of whether investors should attempt to time their commitments to private equity. Michael Cembalest presents findings from a November 2018 study by finance professors Brown, Harris, Jenkinson, Kaplan, and Robinson analyzing buyout funds from vintage years 1987 to 2013. The study evaluated two approaches: a counter-cyclical strategy, which allocates more when fundraising conditions are difficult, and a pro-cyclical strategy, which commits more during overheated fundraising periods. The author explains that the benefits of market timing are historically modest because fund managers use their discretion to call and deploy capital at similar rates regardless of LP timing, effectively neutralizing LP-level decisions. The lowest relative returns typically occurred in vintages raised three years before a market peak because capital was fully deployed before the correction, whereas vintages raised just one year before the peak performed better by investing post-correction.

These findings are supported by a detailed table of private equity commitment strategies comparing the Multiple on Invested Capital, the Internal Rate of Return, and the Public Market Equivalent. In the baseline case, buyout funds achieved a Multiple on Invested Capital of 1.80, an Internal Rate of Return of 16.5 percent, and a Public Market Equivalent of 1.15. Under an investment strategy based purely on fundraising dollars, the pro-cyclical strategy underperformed the baseline with a 1.74 Multiple on Invested Capital, a 14.3 percent Internal Rate of Return, and a 1.10 Public Market Equivalent. Conversely, the counter-cyclical strategy outperformed with a 1.89 Multiple on Invested Capital, an 18.9 percent Internal Rate of Return, and a 1.20 Public Market Equivalent. When evaluated using fundraising dollars relative to market capitalization, the pro-cyclical strategy produced a 1.68 Multiple on Invested Capital, a 14.9 percent Internal Rate of Return, and a 1.12 Public Market Equivalent, while the counter-cyclical strategy achieved a 1.91 Multiple on Invested Capital, an 18.1 percent Internal Rate of Return, and a 1.16 Public Market Equivalent.

This page discusses how record levels of private equity "dry powder" are pressuring general partners to deploy capital, leading to a rise in secondary buyouts—transactions where one private equity firm sells a portfolio company to another. The author notes that these secondary buyouts typically involve higher purchase multiples and higher leverage, while academic literature indicates their investment performance is often lower than traditional private equity investments. 

Academic research cited on the page reveals several key vulnerabilities of secondary buyouts. First, funds facing pressure to invest near the end of their investment period, or to sell near the end of their fund lives, are more likely to engage in secondary buyouts, which then tend to underperform. Second, companies undergoing multiple rounds of ownership across different private equity firms rarely experience subsequent rounds of operational improvement, as the first round is typically the most impactful. Consequently, public market equivalent ratios for secondary buyouts are often below 1.00, with particularly weak performance for deals executed during the latter half of a firm's investment period.

Three charts support these observations using data through 2017. The first chart, tracking sales from one private equity firm to another, shows that both the number of exits and total exit values in billions of US dollars recovered sharply after the financial crisis. By 2014 through 2017, the annual number of exits stabilized at a high level of around 500, while total exit values peaked near 80 billion dollars in 2015. 

The second chart displays the purchase price as a multiple of EBITDA, comparing sponsor-to-sponsor deals against all buyouts from 2007 through the first half of 2017. Sponsor-to-sponsor transactions consistently command higher valuation multiples than the broader buyout market, rising from roughly 9.5x in 2007 to nearly 11.0x by the first half of 2017. 

The third chart illustrates the average debt-to-EBITDA ratio over the same period, showing that sponsor-to-sponsor deals are consistently more leveraged than general buyouts. This leverage ratio bottomed out near 4.0x in 2009 but climbed back to nearly 6.0x by the first half of 2017, approaching the pre-crisis leverage peak seen in 2007.

This page analyzes the factors driving increased demand for private equity, focusing on the role of underfunded public pensions and the growing pool of eligible individual investors. A pie chart titled "Top 100 Private Equity LPs by type," using February 2017 data from Preqin, shows that public pension funds represent the largest share of capital by a wide margin. Other represented limited partners include asset managers, insurance companies, sovereign wealth funds, endowment plans, private sector pension funds, banks, and foundations. 

To explain why public pensions are heavily allocating to private equity, the page highlights their severe underfunding issues, which drive them to chase high-return assets to try to "earn their way out" of deficit. A supporting table from fiscal year 2017 details the financial strain on several distressed state plans. For instance, Illinois has a reported pension funding ratio of only thirty-eight percent, requiring fifty-one percent of government revenues to meet future obligations and necessitating a twenty-five percent increase in state tax collections. New Jersey is in a similar position with a thirty-six percent funding ratio, requiring thirty-eight percent of revenues and a twenty-two percent tax hike. Other listed states facing similar pressures to varying degrees include Hawaii, Connecticut, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Delaware, West Virginia, and California. The author notes that this is a global phenomenon, referencing a study from Harvard and the National Bureau of Economic Research that identified a one point eight trillion dollar shift into alternative investments by major global pensions between 2008 and 2017.

Finally, the text addresses a second driver of demand: the expanding pool of individual buyers. Since 1982, SEC Regulation D Rule 501 has defined "accredited investors" eligible to buy unregistered securities, such as private equity and hedge funds, as individuals with an annual income over two hundred thousand dollars or a net worth over one million dollars. Because these thresholds have never been adjusted for inflation, a larger number of individual investors qualify each year, naturally growing the pool of retail capital flowing into the asset class.

This page serves as the final reference section of the publication, compiling acknowledgements, acronym definitions, and sources. Author Michael Cembalest expresses gratitude for draft reviews to Steve Kaplan of the University of Chicago and Berk Sensoy of Vanderbilt University. The acronym guide defines standard finance and private equity terms, such as assets under management (AUM), earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT), earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), general partner (GP), internal rate of return (IRR), leveraged buyout (LBO), limited partner (LP), multiple of invested capital (MOIC), net asset value (NAV), private equity (PE), public market equivalent (PME), secondary buyout (SBO), and venture capital (VC). A bibliography of seventeen academic and industry sources details research on private equity performance, cash flow liquidity, compensation structures, sovereign wealth fund investing (focusing on the Norwegian pension fund), secondary buyouts, valuation pricing issues, portfolio company fees, and market outlooks from organizations like Bain & Company, McKinsey, and Pitchbook. Key referenced authors include Gregory Brown, Robert Harris, Tim Jenkinson, Steven Kaplan, David Robinson, Berk Sensoy, Per Strömberg, Victoria Ivashina, Josh Lerner, and Ludovic Phalippou.

This page examines private equity fees, dividing them into three distinct categories and estimating the fees earned since 2008 by major publicly listed firms Carlyle, KKR, Blackstone, and Apollo. 

The first category, carried interest, accounts for twenty billion dollars in fees. While academic research generally supports the alignment of interests between managers and limited partners, it highlights a potential agency conflict: managers tend to accelerate asset realizations in the "waterfall quarter" immediately after the limited partners' preferred return is satisfied to secure their own catch-up returns. This phenomenon is depicted in a bar chart showing excess realizations in the waterfall quarter compared to average quarters as a percentage of original committed capital. According to the chart, excess realizations reach approximately 38% for buyout managers and nearly 58% for venture capital managers.

The second category is management fees, representing thirteen billion dollars. These fees are typically earned based on committed rather than invested capital. A stacked bar chart breaks down this approach across various manager types, illustrating that over 90% of buyout managers charge fees on committed capital. While other categories show a slightly higher use of invested capital models—such as direct lending at roughly 40% and natural resources at nearly 37%—committed capital remains the dominant fee base across all categories, including growth, venture capital, and real estate.

The third category, net monitoring and transaction fees, also known as "company fees," accounts for three billion dollars. These fees generate controversy because they are paid by portfolio companies whose boards are controlled by the general partner, sometimes leading to SEC fines for inadequate disclosure. The text notes that between 2011 and 2014, about 80% to 85% of these fees were rebated to limited partners. Furthermore, a 2016 study found that less skilled limited partners were typically the ones backing general partners that charged higher levels of these company fees, though these allocations declined once information about the fees became more transparent.

This page serves as an introduction to Michael Cembalest’s holiday-themed commentary, which departs from typical financial analysis to address the 2020 US Presidential election. Cembalest sets the stage by observing that while US GDP and corporate profits are expected to continue rising in 2019, asset prices historically peak about a year before profits and the broader economy do during a business cycle. Consequently, rising corporate profits late in the cycle may not translate to higher asset prices, a challenge compounded by the current US President's policy alignment with historical figures like Andrew Jackson and Herbert Hoover rather than Ronald Reagan. Cembalest forecasts a low single-digit return for 2019 at best, following returns of negative three percent to one percent for diversified stock-bond portfolios in 2018. He identifies the long-term US-China trade and political conflict as the primary binary variable capable of driving either a substantial market recovery or decline. Additionally, the page lists several key research topics covered in 2018, including monetary interventions, de-carbonization, private equity dry powder, state pension obligations, midterm election losses, and Trumpism.

Supporting this market outlook is a dense, color-coded bar chart titled "2018: US growth stocks up, almost everything else flat/down as the global stimulus cycle comes to an end," which shows year-to-date returns in US dollars. The y-axis ranges from negative twenty-five percent to twenty percent, displaying performance across various asset categories, including US growth sectors, US equities, US fixed income, European and developed world equities, emerging market equities, EM bonds, and commodities. The visual demonstrates that positive performance was heavily concentrated in US growth sectors and safe-haven assets, such as S&P healthcare, FANG stocks, consumer discretionary, the trade-weighted US dollar, technology, US REITs, and T-bills. Conversely, the vast majority of global assets—including international equities, emerging markets, and commodities like oil—ended the year in negative territory. The chart highlights extreme outliers in its footnotes, noting off-chart positive returns for Natural Gas at fifty-five percent and US Steel at thirty-three percent, contrasted against deep losses such as South African equities down twenty-seven percent, Turkish local bonds down thirty-one percent, Shenzhen Chinese equities down thirty-three percent, Turkish equities down forty-one percent, and Argentine local bonds down fifty-three percent.

This page from Michael Cembalest's newsletter discusses the consequences of growing political polarization and the erosion of the political center in the US Congress. Cembalest argues that the decline of moderate politicians has hindered the government's ability to address complex policy problems, leading to one-sided policymaking and contributing to a slowdown in long-term economic growth.

The first chart, titled "Moderates in Congress and GDP growth that followed," displays two historical trends from 1950 to 2010. The first trend line tracks moderates as a percentage of the House of Representatives, based on a Voteview score between negative 0.25 and positive 0.25. This metric peaked near 45% in the late 1960s and early 1970s before steadily collapsing to under 10% by 2010. The second trend line tracks the subsequent 10-year cumulative real GDP growth, which similarly declined from peaks of around 60% in the late 1950s and early 1960s to roughly 20% by the 2010s. The author uses this correlation to argue that US prosperity has historically aligned with a higher concentration of moderate politicians who can foster stable, long-term policymaking.

This argument is supported by an adjacent table titled "The Decline in Congressional problem-solving," which uses academic data to highlight a steep drop in legislative engagement and solution-oriented hearings across three distinct eras. During the 92nd Congress (1971–1973), congressional hearings averaged 15 witnesses, and 65% of those hearings were devoted to proposed solutions. By the 100th Congress (1987–1989), those figures fell to 11 witnesses and 48% of hearings devoted to solutions. By the 111th Congress (2009–2011), the average number of witnesses dropped to just 6, and only 20% of hearings focused on finding solutions, signaling that the capacity of government to assess complex problems has severely declined.

Looking ahead to the 2020 election and beyond, Cembalest outlines major structural headwinds facing the US, which he terms "negative productivity agents." Commissioned by J.P. Morgan Chairman Jamie Dimon, this assessment identifies critical systemic issues including crumbling transportation and electricity infrastructure, high healthcare and litigation costs, sub-par reading and math education, and land-use regulations that hinder labor mobility. Additionally, Cembalest warns of an impending fiscal crisis, citing Congressional Budget Office projections that by 2030, 100% of Federal tax revenues will be consumed by mandatory entitlements and interest payments, leaving zero room for discretionary spending. He concludes that resolving these complex problems will require a level of pragmatic, moderate problem-solving that current polarized dynamics make difficult to achieve.

Michael Cembalest argues that hoping for a moderate consensus in the 2020 U.S. presidential election is unrealistic, as the political pendulum is swinging toward ideological extremes rather than the middle. To support this, he notes that forty-four percent of Democratic House primary candidates in 2018 identified as Progressive, up from twenty-nine percent in 2016, and that Gallup polling showed more young Democrats aged eighteen to twenty-nine holding a positive view of socialism than of capitalism for the first time. 

This ideological polarization is illustrated in a chart tracking the political ideology of presidential administrations from 1916 to the 2020 outlook. The chart plots administrations on an axis ranging from most liberal at negative zero-point-seven to most conservative at zero-point-seven, using Nokken-Poole Voteview congressional roll-call data to score key administration officials and supportive members of Congress. Historically, the data reveals a zig-zag pattern between parties, with the ideological divide widening over time. On the conservative side, the Coolidge and Hoover administrations score near zero-point-six-five, Eisenhower at zero-point-two-five, Nixon and Ford at zero-point-three, Reagan and Bush at zero-point-five, George W. Bush at zero-point-six, and the Trump administration at a highly conservative score of nearly zero-point-six-five. On the liberal side, the FDR and Truman administrations score near negative zero-point-four-five, JFK and LBJ at negative zero-point-four-two, Carter at negative zero-point-four-five, Clinton at a more moderate negative zero-point-two-five, and Obama at negative zero-point-four-five. 

Looking ahead to 2020, potential Democratic candidates are categorized into three distinct ideological groups. The ultra-progressives, including Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, Kamala Harris, and Cory Booker, represent an extreme left shift with an average score of negative zero-point-six. The progressive tier, including Sherrod Brown, Kirsten Gillibrand, and Jeff Merkley, scores around negative zero-point-four-five, aligned with the historic average of the Obama and Carter administrations. The moderate tier, including Joe Biden, Michael Bennet, Bob Casey, Amy Klobuchar, and Beto O'Rourke, sits at roughly negative zero-point-three, which is closer to the Clinton administration's positioning. The author suggests that voters in 2020 may face a choice between the historic ideological extremes of Donald Trump on the far right and an ultra-progressive nominee on the far left.

This appendix page details the methodology and rationale behind the Political Pendulum chart, focusing on how political polarization in the United States is tracked and analyzed. The author explains that the chart utilizes Voteview data, a spatial model of parliamentary voting that assigns liberal or conservative scores to American politicians since the first Congress in 1789. Originally developed by Keith Poole and Howard Rosenthal, and currently maintained by UCLA, this data is used by the author to compute overall ideological scores for various presidential administrations by averaging the scores of closely aligned executive branch officials and prominent congressional supporters. The author admits that selecting which administration officials and supporters to include is subjective but argues it reasonably captures each administration's actual political orientation. For further reading on polarization, references are suggested to scholars at Princeton, Yale, Duke, the University of Texas, and the American Enterprise Institute.

The commentary goes on to detail specific historical observations arising from this analytical framework. It notes a distinct rightward shift in Republican administrations since the 1950s, while highlighting the Clinton administration as a notable moderate outlier due to the influence of the Democratic Leadership Council's efforts to steer the party away from progressive defeats in the 1970s and 1980s. To illustrate the subjectivity of mapping administration supporters, the author explains why Eugene McCarthy is categorized as an ally to John F. Kennedy and Lyndon B. Johnson based on his legislative support for the Great Society, despite his subsequent anti-Vietnam War campaign against Johnson. Defining supporters for Jimmy Carter proved particularly challenging because of deep-seated conflicts with congressional Democrats, most notably House Speaker Tip O'Neill and primary challenger Ted Kennedy. Finally, the page discusses Richard Nixon's relatively moderate placement, quoting Nixon's private criticisms of the Republican Party's far-right wing represented by Barry Goldwater, despite the irony that Goldwater ultimately was the one to tell Nixon he faced certain impeachment and conviction in 1974.

In this market commentary, Michael Cembalest outlines a "Bear market barometer" analyzing the catalysts behind the late-2018 market selloff. He attributes the downturn to three main factors: first, prolonged low interest rates from the Fed and aggressive bond-buying by the European Central Bank, which previously drove cash allocations to record lows and pushed equity valuations to the 90th percentile; second, economic slowdowns in China and Europe, where earnings revisions are falling and France and Italy are reverting to one percent growth despite 2.6 trillion Euros of ECB intervention; and third, market-unfriendly political moves, highlighted by President Trump's reported inquiries into firing the Fed Chairman, comparing this potential instability to conditions in Turkey under Erdogan and Argentina under Kirchner where lack of investor trust keeps P/E multiples in the single digits. Cembalest supports this political critique by quoting FedEx CEO Fred Smith regarding bad political choices hurting corporate forecasts.

Turning to market outlooks, Cembalest suggests that market pessimism is finally priced in, with stock and corporate bond valuations falling below median levels. While acknowledging downside risks from high-volume algorithmic trading—which accounts for 70 percent of equity trading and 40 to 50 percent of options and futures volume—and reduced liquidity from the Volcker rule, he identifies key guardrails against a major 1970s- or 2000s-style collapse. These include strong US banking capitalization, improved global current account balances, and a slowing global economy that is not yet in recession. Furthermore, he points out a historical pattern where in 15 out of 20 historical episodes since the 1920s where P/E multiples contracted by 20 percent or more, US equities rebounded with positive returns averaging 12 percent over the following year. 

Finally, he observes that FAANG stocks, banks, metals, and emerging market equities have collapsed to depressed valuations, currently pricing in a high probability of a 2019 recession and a poor resolution to trade tensions. He frames the ultimate direction of the 2019 market as highly dependent on binary geopolitical outcomes, namely whether the US can strike a trade deal with China and whether the administration decides to impose Section 232 tariffs on 270 billion dollars of European and Japanese automotive imports.

This infrastructure-focused page illustrates how the United States lags significantly behind many developed and developing nations in high-speed rail development. The central visual is a table compiled using 2018 data from the Environmental and Energy Study Institute and the International Union of Railways, comparing the length of operational high-speed rail lines alongside those currently under construction across 22 countries. 

China overwhelmingly leads the global rankings, boasting an unparalleled 26,869 kilometers of high-speed rail lines in operation and another 10,738 kilometers under construction. European and Asian leaders also show significant networks, with France operating 3,220 kilometers, Spain operating 3,100 kilometers (with 1,800 kilometers under construction), Japan operating 3,041 kilometers, and Germany operating 3,038 kilometers. Even much smaller economies and developing nations far outpace the U.S.; for instance, Turkey has 802 kilometers of operational lines and is constructing 1,208 kilometers more, while Uzbekistan has 600 kilometers in operation. 

Highlighting the stark contrast, the United States is positioned at the very bottom of the list in a bright red row, with a mere 54 kilometers of high-speed rail currently in operation and 192 kilometers under construction. This position ranks the U.S. below countries like Luxembourg, Switzerland, and Norway in active high-speed rail mileage.

This page, titled "The early 2000’s: large cost overruns on defense projects" under the broader heading "WAR," illustrates the history of budget excesses in United States military procurement. The central visualization is a scatter plot showing defense project cumulative cost overruns versus their baseline budgets in percentage terms, spanning projects initiated from 1997 through 2015. The chart distinguishes between active projects, represented by solid blue circles, and completed projects, represented by open grey circles. 

The data reveals that the late 1990s and early 2000s were characterized by extraordinary cost overruns. Extreme outliers are highlighted at the top of the chart with upward-pointing arrows, led by the MH-605 with an 849% overrun, the GMLRS at 750%, and the RQ-4A/B Global Hawk at more than 250%. Other notable defense projects with massive budget overruns during this period include the completed Joint MRAP at approximately 175%, the UH-60M Black Hawk at roughly 160%, and the JTRS HMS at around 150%. 

A wide range of other high-profile programs also saw substantial cost increases, including the Chem Demil-ACWA, WGS, JTN, EELV, and LHA 6, all of which exceeded 100% cost overruns. Well-known platforms like the Stryker, MQ-8 Fire Scout, AEHF, MQ-9 Reaper, and the F-35 are plotted with overruns ranging from 50% to nearly 100%. Visually, the concentration of severe overruns is densest for projects started between 1997 and 2007, whereas programs initiated after 2009 cluster much closer to the 0% baseline, indicating a potential moderation in defense acquisition overruns in later years. The data is sourced from the Department of Defense's 2016 report, "Performance of the Defense Acquisition System."

This page from a J.P. Morgan infrastructure presentation highlights the challenge of aging power generation capacity across the United States, pointing out that the issue is particularly acute in the Northeast. The primary visual is a geographic map of the United States plotting power plants, with the data sourced from Joshua Rhodes of the University of Texas Energy Institute in 2017. On the map, each power plant is represented by a circle. The size of the circle indicates the capacity of the facility, distinguishing between large and small plants. The color of the circles is mapped to a gradient scale representing depreciation as a proxy for age, transitioning from red for more depreciated, older plants to blue for less depreciated, newer plants. The map reveals a high concentration of large, deeply red circles clustered throughout the Northeast corridor, the Mid-Atlantic, and parts of the Midwest, demonstrating that these heavily populated areas rely on highly depreciated and aging infrastructure. In contrast, newer, less depreciated blue circles are more prominent in parts of the Great Plains, Texas, and the West Coast.

This page argues that increased land use regulation is a primary driver of lower housing affordability across major United States metropolitan areas. It features a scatter plot titled Zoning rules and housing affordability, which maps the Wharton Residential Land Use Regulatory Index on the horizontal axis against the 2013 National Association of Realtors Housing Affordability Index on the vertical axis. A higher value on the regulatory index indicates more zoning restrictions, while a higher value on the affordability index represents greater housing affordability. A distinct downward-sloping trend line indicates that more regulated markets suffer from lower affordability. Highly regulated cities like Boston, San Francisco, New York, and Los Angeles cluster on the right side of the chart, showing high regulatory scores up to 1.5 and low affordability levels, with many index values dropping near 50. In contrast, less regulated Midwestern cities such as Indianapolis, Cincinnati, Dayton, and Cleveland cluster on the left, displaying regulatory index scores below zero and high affordability index values well above 250. The data for this chart is sourced from a 2015 Council of Economic Advisors report titled Barriers to shared growth: the case of land use regulation and economic rents.

This page compiles multiple financial indicators to analyze the late 2018 market correction, focusing on global growth momentum, corporate earnings revisions, equity valuations, inflation pressures, and investor sentiment. 

The top section notes that while the world economy is still expanding, fewer countries are growing above their historical trends. The first chart shows that although nearly 80 percent of developed and emerging market business surveys indicate expansion (above 50), the share of surveys indicating performance above their two-year trend has plunged from near 100 percent in 2017 to under 25 percent by late 2018. Concurrently, corporate earnings revisions have deteriorated sharply. A chart on revisions shows the net percentage of positive less negative revisions, as a three-month moving average, falling into negative territory across the S&P 500, Europe, and offshore China, with offshore China dipping past negative 20 percent.

To contextualize the market selloff, a chart tracks S&P 500 drawdowns since 1969, framing the late 2018 drop. An accompanying table details the resulting valuation compression. Between the 2018 peak and late December 2018, forward price-to-earnings ratios dropped significantly: US equities fell from 18.5 (the 86th percentile) to 13.6 (the 32nd percentile); European equities fell from 15.1 (the 91st percentile) to 12.0 (the 34th percentile); and Emerging Market equities declined from 13.2 to 10.2 (the 16th percentile). Meanwhile, high-yield spreads rose from 305 to 533 basis points, and high-grade spreads increased from 108 to 182 basis points. To assess the potential for recovery, another chart shows subsequent twelve-month S&P 500 returns after historical forward P/E ratio declines of 20 percent or more. While a few major crisis periods like 1929 and 1973 saw further declines over the subsequent year, the majority of historical episodes resulted in positive returns, with the average post-1950 subsequent twelve-month return exceeding 15 percent.

On the macroeconomic and sentiment front, a chart of US wage and core price inflation shows wage growth rising steadily toward 3.0 percent by late 2018, while core CPI remains relatively stable around 2.2 percent. In terms of market positioning, short interest in the S&P 500 spiked to levels near 3.5 percent, matching the elevated levels seen just prior to the 2016 market correction. Finally, a long-term chart from 1980 to 2016 highlights that cash allocations among key investor groups—including households, pension funds, and non-US investors—had fallen to record or near-record lows by 2016, indicating that market participants held very low defensive cash buffers leading into the late-cycle period.

This page features a collection of charts and data tables analyzing equity valuations, structural economic shifts, historical tariff trends, and financial system health as of late 2018. 

The top portion of the page examines market valuations across different cycles and sectors. A line chart tracking the FAANG premium to the S&P 500 shows the average forward price-to-earnings ratio relative to the market for Facebook, Amazon, Apple, Netflix, and Google. This premium peaked near 3.4x in late 2012 and June 2015 but fell to roughly 2.2x by mid-2018. To place this in historical context, a neighboring bar chart compares tech P/E ratios relative to the market at cycle peaks dating back to 1953. This comparison reveals that the mid-December 2018 peak of approximately 1.3x was far more conservative than previous cycle peaks, particularly the tech bubble peak of March 2000, which reached nearly 2.5x. Valuation contraction is also visible in financial equities, with bank P/E ratios relative to the market at cycle peaks dropping steadily from over 1.1x in 1960 to around 0.5x in mid-December 2018. Additionally, a chart of the metals and mining sector shows its price-to-sales ratio relative to the market oscillating cyclically from 1952 through 2016, ending the period at around 0.6x.

The middle section shifts focus to global trade and macroeconomic trends. One chart depicts a substantial decline in global imbalances, measured as the absolute value of all country current account surpluses and deficits as a percentage of world GDP. This metric peaked at nearly 6% in 2006—driven by Asian manufacturing, oil exporters, and Northern European financing of housing booms in the Anglo-Saxon world and Iberia—before retreating to below 4% by 2016. Alongside this, a chart mapping US import tariffs from 1900 to 2018 shows a dramatic drop in the US tariff rate on total imports from nearly 20% in the early 20th century to below 2% in the 2010s. However, the chart flags a potential reversal of this trend due to recent and proposed protectionist policies, including imposed tariffs on washing machines, solar, steel, aluminum, and Chinese imports under Section 301, alongside proposed 25% tariffs on autos and parts.

The bottom portion of the page highlights structural improvements in bank balance sheets since the global financial crisis. A table detailing bank risk metrics reveals that between 2007 and 2017, risk-weighted capital ratios rose significantly in both the US (from 8.5% to 13.9%) and Europe (from 8.0% to 16.0%). Concurrently, bank liquid assets as a percentage of short-term liabilities rose in both regions, while loan-to-deposit ratios declined sharply, dropping from 97% to 76% in the US and from 139% to 105% in Europe. 

Despite these healthier bank balance sheets, a final chart tracking changes in debt stock and liquidity from 2006 to 2017 points to a growing mismatch in fixed-income markets. While the total market size of outstanding debt expanded aggressively—particularly for investment-grade corporate bonds and US Treasuries, which grew by roughly 175% and 230% respectively—trading turnover, measured as trading volume divided by debt stock, contracted across nearly all major asset classes, including mortgages, high-yield debt, investment-grade debt, and US Treasuries.

This page, categorized under the topic of behaviors, explores how policy proposals addressing gun ownership and regulation in the United States are stymied by a deep partisan divide. It features a table titled "Partisan gaps on gun control issues" using 2017 data from the Pew Research Center, showing the percentage of Republicans and Democrats who strongly or somewhat favor various policies, along with the percentage-point difference between the two groups. 

Under gun control policies, there is strong bipartisan consensus on preventing the mentally ill from purchasing guns, favored by eighty-nine percent of both Republicans and Democrats, and barring gun purchases by people on no-fly or watch lists, favored by eighty-two percent of Republicans and eighty-five percent of Democrats. However, political divides widen on other measures. Requiring background checks for private sales and at gun shows is favored by seventy-seven percent of Republicans and ninety percent of Democrats. Banning assault-style weapons has a twenty-six-point gap, favored by fifty-four percent of Republicans and eighty percent of Democrats. Creating a federal database to track gun sales is supported by fifty-six percent of Republicans and eighty-four percent of Democrats. The largest divide in this category is over banning high-capacity magazines, supported by forty-seven percent of Republicans compared to seventy-nine percent of Democrats, a thirty-two-point gap.

For gun-friendly policies, the gaps remain wide, with Republicans being significantly more supportive. Allowing concealed carry in more places has the largest overall gap at forty-six percentage points, favored by seventy-two percent of Republicans and only twenty-six percent of Democrats. Allowing teachers and officials to carry guns in K-12 schools is favored by sixty-nine percent of Republicans versus twenty-six percent of Democrats. Shortening waiting periods for buying guns legally is supported by fifty-one percent of Republicans and twenty-five percent of Democrats. Finally, allowing concealed carry without a permit is supported by thirty percent of Republicans and ten percent of Democrats.

This page addresses the relationship between gun ownership and gun deaths, presenting the argument that higher gun ownership correlates with higher rates of gun deaths both internationally and across different states within the United States. A key note at the top of the page highlights that while the United States accounts for only 4 percent of the world’s population, it possesses 22 percent of civilian-owned guns and suffers the highest rate of gun deaths in the developed world.

The first chart, titled Gun ownership vs gun deaths by country, plots gun-related deaths per 100,000 people on the vertical axis against the number of guns per 100 people on the horizontal axis. A clear positive trend line indicates that countries with more guns per capita generally experience higher gun death rates. The United States is positioned as a stark outlier at the top right of the chart, with nearly 90 guns per 100 people and approximately 9 gun deaths per 100,000 people. In contrast, most other countries cluster near the bottom left, including Japan, Singapore, the United Kingdom, Spain, and Germany, all of which have fewer than 20 guns per 100 people and fewer than 2 gun deaths per 100,000 people. Canada and Switzerland represent mid-range examples, with Canada having roughly 30 guns per 100 people and 5 deaths per 100,000, and Switzerland showing higher gun ownership at about 45 guns per 100 people but a lower death rate of around 3.5 per 100,000. Argentina is a notable outlier on the higher end of deaths relative to its lower ownership rate.

The second chart, titled Gun ownership vs gun deaths by state, illustrates the same positive correlation at the domestic level, plotting gun deaths per 100,000 residents against the percentage of adult gun ownership by state. States like Alaska, Wyoming, Montana, and Arkansas cluster on the far right with adult gun ownership rates between 50 percent and 60 percent, corresponding to high gun death rates ranging from 15 to over 20 per 100,000 residents. Louisiana also displays one of the highest gun death rates at over 20 per 100,000 residents with an ownership rate near 48 percent. Conversely, northeastern states like New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Massachusetts sit in the bottom left, with adult gun ownership rates below 15 percent and gun death rates under 5 per 100,000 residents. Hawaii serves as a distinct outlier in this dataset, maintaining an adult gun ownership rate of roughly 45 percent but experiencing a very low gun death rate of around 3 per 100,000 residents. 

The analysis is based on 2018 data compiled from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the Small Arms Survey, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and Vox.

This page, titled "Opioid use and labor market participation by state: a clear pattern" under the category of "Behaviors," presents a compelling analysis of how the opioid crisis correlates with economic engagement. The central argument is that labor market participation is negatively correlated with opioid use across the United States. 

To support this claim, the page features a scatter plot charting all fifty U.S. states and the District of Columbia using 2016 data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The vertical axis tracks opioid prescriptions per 100 persons, ranging from 20 to 130, while the horizontal axis represents the labor market participation rate as a percentage, ranging from 50% to 75%. A clear, downward-sloping regression line visually emphasizes the negative relationship: states with higher prescription rates consistently display lower labor force participation. 

Several notable outliers and data points help illustrate this trend. On the far left, West Virginia exhibits one of the lowest labor participation rates at approximately 53% alongside roughly 95 opioid prescriptions per 100 persons. Alabama sits near the top of the chart with an exceptionally high prescription rate of nearly 120 per 100 persons and a low participation rate of around 57%. Arkansas, Mississippi, and Tennessee also occupy the upper-left quadrant, representing high prescription rates and low economic participation. In contrast, states toward the right side of the chart, such as North Dakota, display high participation rates of nearly 74% paired with lower prescription rates of approximately 55 per 100 persons. The District of Columbia appears as a distinct outlier near the bottom right, featuring a very low prescription rate of about 35 per 100 persons alongside a high participation rate of roughly 70%. Overall, the visualization demonstrates a stark geographic and economic pattern linking public health challenges with regional labor force dynamics.

This page, titled "Behaviors," highlights the severe economic impact of the opioid epidemic, illustrating that the annual cost of opioid use in the United States has reached approximately $78.5 billion. To put this massive figure into perspective, the publication notes that this national-level cost is greater than the entire annual GDP of 13 different US states: Hawaii, West Virginia, New Hampshire, Delaware, Idaho, Alaska, Maine, Rhode Island, North Dakota, South Dakota, Montana, Wyoming, and Vermont. 

A detailed table breaks down these annual opioid costs into nonfatal and fatal categories, referencing a 2013 CDC study by Florence et al. titled "The Economic Burden of Prescription Opioid Overdose, Abuse and Dependence in the United States." Nonfatal costs comprise the majority of the economic burden, accounting for $57.0 billion, or 72.6% of the total. Within nonfatal costs, health care is the largest driver at $26.1 billion (33.2% of the overall total), with private insurance bearing the largest portion of this subcategory at $14.0 billion (17.9%), followed by Medicaid at $5.5 billion (7.0%), uninsured or other payers at $4.0 billion (5.0%), and Medicare at $2.6 billion (3.3%). Nonfatal lost productivity represents another massive component at $20.4 billion (26.0%), which is primarily driven by reduced productive time and increased disability at $16.3 billion (20.7%), alongside $4.2 billion (5.3%) in production lost for incarcerated individuals. Criminal justice costs total $7.7 billion (9.7%), which includes spending on correctional facilities ($3.2 billion), police protection ($2.8 billion), legal and adjudication services ($1.3 billion), and property lost due to crime ($0.3 billion). Substance abuse treatment is the smallest nonfatal component at $2.8 billion (3.6%), primarily funded by state and local governments ($1.8 billion), followed by federal ($0.7 billion) and private ($0.3 billion) funding. 

Fatal costs represent the remaining 27.4% of the total economic burden, summing to $21.5 billion. This category is almost entirely composed of lost productivity due to premature death, which accounts for $21.4 billion (27.3%), while fatal healthcare costs account for just $0.1 billion (0.1%). Together, these nonfatal and fatal costs combine for the final total of $78.5 billion.

This page, under the litigation section of the publication, argues that a higher degree of corporate innovation corresponds to a greater likelihood of a company facing a meritless class action lawsuit in the following year. The main visual is a scatter plot with an upward-sloping linear regression line titled "Probability of a meritless class action lawsuit filing in the following year vs innovation success." The vertical y-axis measures the probability of a meritless filing, scaled from 0.0% to 2.5%. The horizontal x-axis measures "innovation success," ranging from negative 0.1 to positive 0.3. The plot reveals a strong positive correlation: at low levels of innovation success near negative 0.08, the probability of a lawsuit is around 0.5%, whereas at higher levels of innovation success near 0.25, the probability rises to over 2.2%. 

A footnote clarifies that meritless class action lawsuits are defined as those that are eventually dismissed, while innovation success is evaluated based on the economic value of patents granted. The data is sourced from a 2018 paper titled "Litigating Innovation: Evidence from Securities Class Action Lawsuits" from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication, categorized under the theme of behaviors, highlights that the United States has the highest incarceration rate in the world, which is a significant anomaly for a highly developed, high-income nation. 

The primary visual is a scatter plot titled "Incarceration rates and national income," which plots the adult incarceration rate per 100,000 people against per capita GDP using 2017 data from the World Prison Brief and the IMF. The vertical y-axis measures the incarceration rate from 0 to 700, while the horizontal x-axis tracks per capita GDP from $0 to $80,000. 

The chart demonstrates a clear trend where wealthier nations generally maintain lower rates of incarceration. Most developed countries with a per capita GDP over $40,000—such as Japan, Germany, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Ireland, and Norway—cluster near the bottom of the chart with incarceration rates well under 100 per 100,000 people. Other wealthy peers like Canada, Australia, Singapore, and the United Kingdom also maintain relatively low rates, mostly remaining under 150. 

In stark contrast, the United States is positioned as a massive outlier in the upper-right quadrant of the chart, combining a high per capita GDP of approximately $60,000 with an exceptionally high adult incarceration rate of nearly 650 per 100,000 people. This rate is higher than those of developing or lower-income nations with notorious incarceration challenges, including El Salvador, Turkmenistan, Thailand, Cuba, Rwanda, Russia, Belarus, and Brazil, all of which have much lower per capita GDPs. Additional countries plotted for comparison include Taiwan, Saudi Arabia, the Czech Republic, Spain, Slovakia, Portugal, Greece, Italy, Belgium, and France, further emphasizing that the United States' incarceration rate is uniquely elevated compared to both developing and developed economies.

This page, under the education topic, explores academic performance gaps among 15-year-olds using two scatter plots based on 2018 World Bank data. The central observation is that girls demonstrate substantially better reading skills than boys across almost all countries, whereas no clear gender gap exists for mathematics. Each chart plots average female scores on the vertical axis against average male scores on the horizontal axis, with axes spanning from 290 to 570. A diagonal 45-degree line indicates equal performance; points above the line show girls outperforming boys, while points below the line favor boys. The size of each dot represents the country's population.

The first chart, titled "Average reading score by gender," shows that virtually every country lies above the diagonal line, indicating a global trend where girls' reading scores exceed those of boys. Even in top-performing nations like Singapore, Finland, and South Korea, which achieve average scores above 500, girls hold a clear advantage. This gap persists in lower-scoring nations such as Macedonia, Algeria, and Lebanon, where average scores fall below 400 but remain visibly skewed in favor of female students. 

The second chart, titled "Average math score by gender," presents a contrasting picture. Here, the country dots cluster tightly along the diagonal line, indicating that math scores between boys and girls are nearly identical in most nations. Singapore, China, and Japan lead the math rankings with scores above 520, sitting almost perfectly on the diagonal line. Other nations like the United States, Germany, and Italy cluster near the middle of the distribution around 470 to 500, similarly showing no significant gender disparity. The Dominican Republic represents one of the lowest-performing outliers on this chart, with scores for both genders averaging around 320 to 350.

This page serves as the executive summary of J.P. Morgan's 2019 Outlook, titled "The Decline of Western Centralization, Part II." The main thesis is that the longest and largest era of central bank intervention in history is coming to an end. For the first time in almost twenty years, demand for financial assets will have to be sustained by institutional and individual investors without central bank assistance. Author Michael Cembalest argues that the late 2018 market selloff was not a mere mid-cycle correction, as global growth and earnings revisions are rolling over, and unresolved trade issues alongside a shift away from market-friendly policies by the Trump administration will likely limit any post-correction rebound. For 2019, Cembalest forecasts a volatile but positive single-digit return year for diversified portfolios, recovering from a weak 2018 where typical 65/35 stock-bond mixes fell between -4% and -7%. He identifies a potential U.S.-China trade deal as a key source of substantial upside, particularly for emerging market assets.

To support the thesis of fading liquidity, the page features a line chart plotting the rolling 12-month net purchases of G4 financial assets by developed and emerging economy central banks as a percentage of world GDP from 1975 through late 2018. The G4 cohort represents the United States, the Eurozone, the United Kingdom, Japan, and Switzerland. The visual trend reveals that central bank purchases hovered generally below 2% of global GDP for decades before embarking on a massive twenty-year expansion starting in the late 1990s. This intervention peaked at over 5% of global GDP during the Great Recession around 2008 and remained highly elevated through 2017, before suffering a sharp, near-vertical collapse toward 0% in late 2018. This dramatic drop visually underscores the end of the historical central bank intervention era.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, explains why emerging market central banks are slowing their purchases of G4 assets. Historically, these central banks purchased G4 assets to build up rainy-day reserves and prevent their own higher-yielding currencies from appreciating too much. This trend is now reversing due to several key factors. First, as US interest rates rise, the pressure for EM currencies to appreciate has diminished; in fact, EM currencies fell by approximately 10% in 2018, led by sharp declines in the Turkish Lira, Russian Ruble, South African Rand, Brazilian Real, and Chilean Peso. Second, investor credit concerns have prompted capital outflows, forcing EM central banks to liquidate reserves. Finally, declining oil and commodity prices have squeezed budgets, forcing nations like Saudi Arabia to draw down their foreign exchange reserves. A footnote highlights that while developed world central banks drove 60% of G4 asset transactions since 2000, EM nations—principally China, Russia, Saudi Arabia, India, Brazil, and Korea—drove the remaining 40%.

Four charts illustrate these dynamics over the period from 2000 to late 2018. The first chart, depicting an EM currency index, shows that concerns over currency appreciation peaked around 2011 when the index reached nearly 115, before steadily declining to around 65 by late 2018. This trend is mirrored in the second chart, which tracks EM foreign-exchange reserves (excluding gold) in US dollars; reserves grew from about $1 trillion in 2000 to a peak near $9.5 trillion in 2014, followed by a decline and leveling off around $9 trillion. The third chart shows the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency balance sheet in billions of Saudi Riyals, revealing that assets peaked at approximately 2.8 trillion Riyals in 2014 before falling to roughly 1.9 trillion Riyals by 2018 as the country funded entitlement spending. The final chart plots Brent crude oil prices in US dollars per barrel against an industrial metals index level, showing that both peaked dramatically around 2008 and again in the 2011 to 2014 period, and were declining once more by the end of 2018, illustrating the persistent pressure on commodity-dependent emerging market reserves.

This page, titled "Regulations make critical contributions to public welfare" under the "Other Regulation" section, presents six charts illustrating how post-financial crisis regulations have strengthened the banking and financial systems in the United States and Europe. The overall theme is that post-crisis reforms have successfully bolstered bank capital, enhanced liquidity, reduced reliance on riskier wholesale funding, and diminished the size of the shadow banking sector.

The first chart, "Rising capital ratios since crisis," displays risk-weighted capital ratios for the United States and Europe, comparing 2007 with 2017. Capital ratios rose substantially in both regions, with the US ratio increasing from approximately 9% to 14%, and the European ratio rising from around 8% to about 15.5%.

The second chart, "Improving liquidity ratios since crisis," measures liquid assets as a percentage of short-term liabilities for the same two regions. Between 2007 and 2017, the ratio for US banks climbed from roughly 41% to 47%, while the ratio for European banks grew from 35% to 40%.

The third chart, "US commercial banks: deposits and interbank loans," spans from 1990 to late 2018, showing a structural shift in bank funding. Interbank loans, plotted on the left axis, declined from a peak of nearly 6% of assets in the mid-1990s to under 1% by 2015. Meanwhile, deposits, plotted on the right axis, steadily increased from about 60% of assets in the early 2000s to over 75% by 2015, demonstrating a transition toward more stable deposit-based funding.

The fourth chart, "Bank loan-to-deposit ratios," compares US and Eurozone banks from 1995 to 2017. Eurozone banks saw their loan-to-deposit ratio peak near 140% around the 2008 crisis before falling to about 110% by 2017. US banks historically maintained lower ratios, which fell from a peak near 100% in 2008 to a safer range of 75% to 80% by 2017.

The fifth chart, "A shift to lower risk money market funds," tracks assets under management in trillions of US dollars from 2002 to 2018, highlighting the impact of major financial events. Following the Lehman Brothers crash in 2008 and the implementation of Money Market Reform in late 2016, assets shifted dramatically. Prime money market fund assets plummeted from approximately $1.2 trillion down to $0.4 trillion, while safer Government money market fund assets surged from about $1.2 trillion to over $2.0 trillion.

The final chart, "US: shadow banking and traditional banking," maps liabilities as a percentage of GDP from 1960 to 2015 across three sectors: commercial banking, shadow banking, and bank holding companies (BHC) or broker-dealers. Shadow banking liabilities grew rapidly before the crisis, peaking at over 110% of GDP in 2008 before shrinking to roughly 80% by 2015. In contrast, traditional commercial banking liabilities grew post-crisis to reach approximately 100% of GDP, reclaiming dominance over shadow banking, while BHC and broker-dealer liabilities declined from a peak of 40% of GDP in 2008 to around 20% by 2015.

This page examines the trajectory and market implications of declining G4 central bank balance sheets, diverging interest rate policies, and fading fiscal stimulus in the United States and Europe. The author argues that while the decline of central bank balance sheets will be gradual, markets are highly sensitive to the sudden drop in asset purchase flows, which resembles going "cold turkey." 

To support this point, a chart titled "G4 central bank balance sheets" displays total assets in US dollars from 2008 to 2022. It shows assets peaking near fifteen trillion dollars in early 2018, followed by a projected steady decline down to approximately twelve trillion dollars by 2022. A companion chart, "G4 central bank asset flows by central bank," tracks the twelve-month change in asset purchases across the Federal Reserve, the Bank of Japan, the European Central Bank, and the Bank of England. This flow chart demonstrates a dramatic plunge from peak annual injections of nearly three trillion dollars down into negative territory for the 2019 and 2020 projections, indicating that only Japan remains a minor net buyer.

The discussion then turns to interest rate projections. The text notes that the Federal Reserve intends to raise rates twice in 2019, even though modest hikes have already begun to damp US housing growth. A chart titled "Number of Fed hike expectations" compares expectations of twenty-five-basis-point hikes through year-end 2019. It shows that the Median FOMC Projection, HSBC, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, and Goldman Sachs all forecast two hikes, while Macroeconomic Advisers, Deutsche Bank, and J.P. Morgan expect three. In stark contrast, a note on the chart highlights that the futures market expects zero hikes. 

For Europe, the author highlights a massive gap between market expectations and potential inflation realities. The chart "Markets expecting another decade of low rates in Europe" plots the Eurozone policy rate from 2000 through a forward curve extending to 2028. Although the Eurozone rate previously peaked near five percent before falling below zero percent after 2012, the forward curve shows market pricing rising at an incredibly slow pace, barely reaching one and a half percent by 2028, which is far below the current US rate. The author warns that this expectation of another decade of low rates leaves markets highly vulnerable to disappointment if rising German inflation forces the European Central Bank to raise rates earlier than expected. 

Finally, the page briefly addresses fiscal stimulus, stating that US fiscal support is peaking and set to decline, while stimulus in the rest of the developed world already peaked several years prior and has settled around a neutral level.

In this executive summary page of the J.P. Morgan 2019 Outlook, Michael Cembalest addresses the question of why central bank stimulus is winding down, arguing that central banks are focused on long-term wage and price stability rather than equity markets. He explains that G4 central bank asset purchases are slowing because the severe economic slack of a decade ago has been replaced by the tightest labor market conditions in decades, returning inflation to normal levels. 

To support this, five charts illustrate the macroeconomic environment. The first chart, showing developed world unemployment and labor shortages from 1983 to 2018, highlights how closely the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate matches an inverted measure of labor shortages. By late 2018, unemployment is down to approximately five percent, while labor shortages have risen to extreme, tight levels. The second chart traces developed world consumer price inflation and wages from 2000 to 2018, demonstrating that Core CPI is rising toward one point six percent year-over-year and wages are recovering toward two point six percent year-over-year, indicating a return to normal ranges that do not require emergency monetary policy. Regional differences are highlighted in the third chart, which tracks developed world wage growth by region from 2007 to 2018; it shows US average hourly earnings rebounding strongly to nearly three percent, while Eurozone wage growth is slower but recovering toward two percent. The fourth chart depicts the US output gap from 1970 to 2018, showing how capacity constraints have shifted from a deep abundance of negative five percent during the post-2008 recession into shortage territory above two percent, signaling that economic slack has been entirely absorbed. Finally, the fifth chart plots the real US federal funds rate—the fed funds rate minus trailing annual consumer price inflation—from 1958 to 2018. It illustrates that for most of post-war history, the real rate was positive, making the extended post-2008 period of deeply negative real rates an anomaly that Cembalest notes will be debated for a long time. Ultimately, he concludes that US central bankers have every historical and economic reason to continue raising rates above the inflation rate, regardless of market disappointment.

In this section of the J.P. Morgan 2019 Outlook, Michael Cembalest discusses why the softening of global growth makes the withdrawal of monetary stimulus more difficult for financial markets to absorb. Global growth is estimated to have declined from approximately 3.75 percent to 3.00 percent over the prior year. Although manufacturing surveys do not yet indicate a recession, this marginal slowdown significantly impacts corporate revenue and earnings growth, leading to a visible rolling over of corporate earnings revisions.
