While the majority of developed and developing economies are still expanding, a rapidly shrinking number of countries are experiencing growth that is above their recent trend.

Three charts illustrate these economic dynamics. The first chart, titled Global Business Surveys, tracks monthly purchasing managers' index levels for manufacturing and services from 2014 through late 2018, with levels above 50 indicating expansion. The services survey peaked at around 55.5 in 2014 and has fluctuated between 52 and 55 since, ending 2018 near 53. The manufacturing survey peaked near 54.5 in late 2017 but steadily declined through 2018 to just above 51.5. This shows that while both sectors are still expanding, momentum is slowing.

The second chart, Global Earnings Revisions, shows the net percentage of positive minus negative corporate earnings revisions as a share of total companies using three-month moving averages from 2010 to late 2018. Two series are depicted: developed world equities and global equities including emerging markets. Both series peaked around early 2018 with net-positive revisions at nearly 20 percent. However, throughout 2018, these revisions rolled over sharply. By late 2018, net revisions for global equities fell to roughly negative 15 percent, while developed world equities dropped to around negative 5 percent.

The final chart, World Still Expanding, But Fewer Countries Above Trend, plots data from 2000 to late 2018 representing nineteen developed and emerging economy business surveys. One line tracks the percentage of surveys that are in expansionary territory above 50, which remains historically high at approximately 80 percent in late 2018. In contrast, the second line tracks the percentage of surveys performing above their two-year trend. This trend line peaked near 90 percent in late 2017 but collapsed to below 25 percent by the end of 2018, illustrating that the global economic slowdown is highly synchronized despite continued nominal expansion.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, focuses on the consequences of central bank stimulus withdrawal and slowing growth, which have prompted a repricing of overpriced assets. Cembalest argues that aggressive intervention by the European Central Bank (ECB) created historic market distortions, forcing yields below zero percent for a large portion of Eurozone government bonds and pushing investors into extreme risk-taking. 

To demonstrate this financial repression, the first visual compares ECB purchases against net issuance since the inception of the CSPP in 2016 and PSPP in 2015. For corporate bonds, the ECB’s purchases of approximately €175 billion significantly exceeded the estimated Eurozone term debt issuance of roughly €130 billion. For sovereign bonds, the trend is even more pronounced: ECB purchases reached about €1.8 trillion, vastly eclipsing the net Eurozone issuance of around €1.1 trillion.

The second chart, which details the pricing of BB-rated Italian high-yield bonds from 2005 to 2018, highlights the scale of this distortion. By mid-2017, nearly the entire outstanding face value of Italian high-yield debt—representing about €35 billion—traded at a tighter spread, or lower yield, than risk-free US Treasury bonds. Cembalest characterizes this as perhaps the single largest fixed-income distortion he has seen in his 31 years at J.P. Morgan.

A third chart, using data from Bridgewater Associates spanning 1980 to 2018, shows how these interventions forced investor cash allocations to record lows by 2016. Over this period, household cash allocations fell from over 50% to roughly 20%, pension fund cash allocations hit a low near 8%, and non-US investor cash levels bottomed out below 5%. This trend began to reverse in late 2018 as US policy rates rose and investors took profits, highlighted by a record-setting $32 billion weekly outflow from active US equity mutual funds in mid-December 2018.

The final chart shows how this reversal has compressed asset valuations in the Eurozone. Tracking 12-month forward earnings per share (EPS) and P/E multiples from December 2016 to December 2018, the chart shows that while forward EPS steadily grew from around 235 EUR to nearly 270 EUR before plateauing, the forward P/E multiple collapsed sharply from a peak of nearly 14.5x in mid-2017 to under 11.5x by late December 2018. Cembalest notes that this phenomenon of falling multiples despite relatively stable corporate earnings is characteristic of what is occurring globally in the US, China, and Japan.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, outlines several structural guardrails that argue against a major, systemic equity collapse similar to those experienced in the 1970s and 2000s, despite developed world equities falling 15% to 20% in late 2018. Cembalest attributes this resilience to three main factors: a decline in global current account imbalances, improved banking sector health, and technical support from low growth in global equity supply.

The first visual is a historical line chart tracking S&P 500 drawdowns from 1969 through late 2018. It illustrates major historic market drops, showing deep troughs reaching down toward negative 50% to 60%, providing long-term context for the late 2018 market correction. 

The second chart details the decline in global imbalances from 1980 to 2016, measuring the absolute value of all country current account surpluses and deficits as a percentage of world GDP. Imbalances peaked near 6% in the mid-2000s, fueled by capital flows from Asian manufacturers, oil exporters, and Northern Europe that financed housing booms in Anglo-Saxon nations like the United States, Australia, Ireland, and the United Kingdom, as well as Spain and Portugal. By 2016, this figure had fallen to under 4%, significantly reducing the risk of destabilizing capital flights.

The banking system's increased safety is illustrated through three tables comparing 2007 and 2017 metrics in the United States and Europe. US bank risk-weighted capital ratios rose from 8.5% to 13.9%, while European ratios doubled from 8.0% to 16.0%. Bank liquid assets as a percentage of short-term liabilities rose from 41% to 48% in the US and from 35% to 40% in Europe. Furthermore, bank loan-to-deposit ratios decreased from 97% to 76% in the US and fell from 139% to 105% in Europe. Cembalest also notes that shadow banking has retreated to 2000 levels, and the gross market value of over-the-counter derivatives plummeted from $35 trillion in 2008 to $10 trillion in 2018.

The final dual-axis chart tracks global equity supply from 1997 to 2018. The S&P divisor, which serves as a proxy for US equity supply, declined from its peak of over 9.0 in the early 2000s back to its 2001 level of around 8.3 in 2018. Over the same period, the annual expansion of the MSCI All Country World Index fluctuated, peaking near 900 billion US dollars in 2007 before collapsing and remaining low through 2018. Looking ahead, Cembalest notes that while the US S&P divisor is poised to decline further due to stock buybacks in 2019, investors should be cautious, as Flow of Funds data suggests the peak of corporate stock buybacks may already be behind us.

This page from Michael Cembalest's "Eye on the Market" series discusses the Trump administration's impact on financial markets by comparing its policy choices to those of prior US Presidents. Cembalest argues that while Trump's market-positive impacts occurred mostly in 2017, market-negative policies began in 2018 and are expected to continue, driven by what FedEx CEO Fred Smith called "bad political choices." The author also highlights unprecedented senior-level staff turnover in the Trump administration that exceeds the prior four Presidents combined.

An illustrative grid titled "Elements of Trumpism for investors" pairs six historical Presidents with two defining policy traits that parallel Trump’s approach. Under Andrew Jackson, the parallels are anti-globalization and loyalty-based political patronage. For Herbert Hoover, they are tariffs and trade wars alongside the deportation of undocumented workers. John F. Kennedy represents re-engineering the economy (and triggering a bear market) alongside attacks on individual companies. Richard Nixon aligns with bullying the Federal Reserve Chairman and political scandals or constitutional risks. Ronald Reagan is matched with deregulation/tax cuts and government shutdowns. Finally, George W. Bush is associated with large fiscal deficits outside of a recession and conservative court appointments.

The page goes into greater detail on several of these elements. Regarding anti-globalization, the text compares Trump’s "America first" stance to Jacksonian foreign policy, where the US has little interest in spreading democracy but reacts with full force when attacked. Under tariffs, Cembalest warns that if all mentioned tariffs are implemented, US tariff rates could surge from 1.5% to 10%, representing the largest increase in 50 years, affecting Chinese imports and auto imports from Europe and Japan. He draws a historical parallel between JFK’s 1962 public battle with US Steel—which led to a 20% bear market—and Trump's public attacks on companies like Amazon, Comcast, Boeing, Delta, ESPN, GM, Lockheed Martin, Merck, Nordstrom, Toyota, and the Washington Post. Finally, the text compares Trump's pressuring of the Federal Reserve to Richard Nixon's bullying of Arthur Burns, warning that questioning Fed independence mirrors actions by Turkish and Argentine autocrats, which historically damages investor confidence and depresses price-to-earnings multiples.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the dramatic selloff in the fourth quarter of 2018, which pushed global equity and credit valuations well below their historical medians. While cheaper valuations lower the bar for investors entering 2019, Cembalest cautions that the upside remains limited due to risks like central bank stimulus withdrawal and the unorthodox policies of the Trump administration. He forecasts volatile, single-digit returns for diversified portfolios in 2019 unless a substantial trade deal is reached with China.

To illustrate the severity of the selloff, an opening table compares peak 2018 levels against valuations at the end of December across major asset classes. The forward price-to-earnings ratio of the S&P 500 fell from a peak of 18.5, which was in the 86th historical percentile, to 14.3, representing the 42nd percentile. European equities on the Stoxx 600 dropped from a forward P/E of 15.1 (91st percentile) to 12.0 (34th percentile), and emerging market equities on the MSCI EM index fell from 13.2 (59th percentile) to 10.3 (18th percentile). In the corporate bond market, US high yield spreads widened from a peak of 305 basis points to 534 basis points (dropping from the 89th to the 35th percentile), while investment grade spreads expanded from 108 to 182 basis points (moving from the 89th to the 35th percentile). 

A bar chart titled "S&P 500 returns after P/E ratio declines of 20%+" shows the subsequent 12-month returns following twenty historical episodes of significant multiple contractions since the 1920s. In fifteen of these twenty episodes, US equity returns were positive over the next year, averaging 12%, though severe economic environments like November 1929, October 1931, April 1937, and November 2000 led to further double-digit declines. 

Finally, a dual-axis line chart titled "Short interest in S&P similar to levels before 2016 correction" plots short interest percentages on the left axis and the S&P 500 index level on the right axis. Comparing the period from late 2015 to late 2016 with the period from mid-2018 to late 2018, the chart shows that a late December surge in short interest on the S&P ETF reached levels similar to those seen prior to the 2016 market correction. This suggests that a near-term market rebound could be sparked by short-covering, particularly during thin year-end trading.

This page serves as the Executive Summary for the 2019 Outlook edition of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest. The primary argument is that despite the recent fall selloff, US growth and profits often continue to expand even after asset prices have peaked. To support this, a table titled "Asset prices tend to peak before growth/profits" examines historical business cycle peaks. In five cycles prior to 2000—specifically January 1966, November 1968, December 1972, November 1980, and August 1987—the peak of the equity market preceded the peak of economic data by 9 to 19 months. In these periods, earnings growth over the subsequent 12 months remained positive, ranging from 2% to as high as 41%, despite initial equity market declines between 7% and 19%. The September 2018 peak is noted as having a subsequent 12-month return of negative 15%, with the months to economic peak and earnings growth yet to be determined, though the author suggests 2018 will likely fit into this pattern of continued growth. Conversely, the recessions starting after August 2000 and October 2007 represent exceptions where economic peaks followed market peaks very quickly, by just 1 and 4 months respectively, accompanied by sharp contractions in 12-month earnings growth of negative 16% and negative 23%. 

In the commentary, Cembalest reflects on the exceptional decade-long bull run from March 2009 to December 2018, noting that its 13% annualized price return was matched only three other times in the postwar era: briefly in 1959, 1992, and the late 1990s. Looking ahead to 2019, the author expects modestly positive returns following the market correction. He recommends holding significant liquidity, as US cash is poised to yield a positive real return, and suggests that Emerging Markets present highly attractive valuations, especially if the ongoing international trade war sees a cease-fire. 

Finally, the page outlines the contents of the report, directing readers to sections on the United States, Europe, China, and Japan, as well as a retrospective analysis of the financial crisis ten years prior. This retrospective promises to examine critical crisis points beyond the banking sector, including the balance sheets of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, broker-dealer deregulation, the collapse of bond reinsurers, and systemic risk contributions from individual firms.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2019 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, serves as an executive summary outlining several key policy trends, economic indicators, and historical parallels under the Trump administration. 

Under the theme of deregulation, the author notes that the Federal Register expanded in 2017 by its lowest number of new pages since 1992, falling 25% below the 2009–2016 average. Consequently, "Regulation and Red Tape" dropped to the third-largest concern for small businesses in the NFIB survey, down from the top spot in 2014. Regarding fiscal policy, the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act is highlighted as the fourth-largest tax cut as a percentage of GDP since 1950, which successfully brought US corporate marginal effective tax rates from the highest in the OECD to below the median. However, Cembalest notes that the personal tax cuts lacked bipartisan consensus and were partially funded by taxing non-repatriated offshore earnings, which Trump had previously promised to direct toward infrastructure projects with higher growth multipliers.

The summary highlights a growing concern over fiscal health, noting that the US is running its largest fiscal deficit during a period of full employment in over 50 years. The 2018 deficit stood at 3.8% of GDP, and the Congressional Budget Office projects it to rise to 4.6% in 2019. A brief mention of loyalty-based political patronage cites Trump's proposal to install his personal pilot as head of the Federal Aviation Administration. 

On immigration, the author points out that ICE arrests of non-criminal undocumented immigrants rose by 171% in 2017 compared to 2016. This shift occurred during full employment and construction labor shortages. Cembalest compares these actions to Herbert Hoover's deportations in the 1930s but notes a critical difference: Hoover acted when unemployment was between 10% and 20%, whereas restricting immigration during today's labor shortages drives wage inflation. This makes the administration's criticism of the Federal Reserve's rate hikes seem inconsistent.

Turning to political and constitutional crises, the text references the October 1973 "Saturday Night Massacre" under Richard Nixon, which caused a sudden 15% decline in US equity markets within a broader 40% stagflation-driven selloff, prompting parallels to modern executive conflicts. Additionally, the author notes that Reagan popularized government shutdowns for policy leverage, experiencing three during his first term. He also highlights judicial trends, stating that 80% of Trump's federal judiciary nominees have ties to the conservative Federalist Society, mirroring the judicial appointment strategy of George W. Bush. The page concludes by directing readers to a holiday piece analyzing the potential for extreme voter polarization in the 2020 presidential election.

This page outlines the late-2018 economic outlook for the United States, balancing highly positive current indicators against emerging headwinds. The author notes several strengths, including expansionary business surveys, multi-decade highs in retail sales, strong consumer and small business confidence, and rising wages driven by intense hiring demand. However, rising interest rates and the fading benefits of tax cuts are expected to drag down U.S. gross domestic product growth. The author forecasts that GDP growth will slow from 3.40% in the third quarter of 2018 to an estimated 2.60% in the fourth quarter, eventually landing at 2.25% by the end of 2019, with early signs of cooling visible in housing, capital spending, and new orders.

Four charts support this analysis. The first, titled "Small business and consumer confidence surging," plots a three-month moving average of personal finances and small business optimism from 1975 to late 2018. Both series show a dramatic upward trend, with small business optimism on the left axis and personal finances on the right axis reaching heights not seen in decades, near levels of 105 and 110 respectively. The second chart, "Wages picking up," runs from 2000 to the third quarter of 2018 and compares annual private sector wage growth on the left axis to the share of companies reporting higher wages on a four-quarter moving average on the right axis. This chart highlights that private sector wage growth has climbed to over 3.0%, while the proportion of companies raising wages has surged toward 50%, reflecting the tightest labor market and highest wage-growth intentions since 2000.

The bottom two charts illustrate the emerging soft spots in the economy. The chart "US core capital goods" measures the rolling three-month percentage change in orders and shipments from 2014 through late 2018. After recovering from negative growth in 2015 and 2016, both orders and shipments peaked in late 2017 and early 2018 at around 3% to 4% growth before moderating back toward 1% to 2% by the end of 2018. Finally, the chart "US business surveys rolling over from high levels" tracks capital spending and new orders from 2000 through December 2018. Capital spending expectations for the next 12 months, plotted on the left axis, and the ISM new orders Purchasing Managers' Index, plotted on the right axis, are both beginning to decline. Although they remain expansionary, with capital spending expectations around 5% and the new orders PMI index remaining well above the neutral 50 threshold at approximately 60, their downward trajectory points to a gradual loss of momentum.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2019 Outlook focuses on the resilient financial health of United States households while highlighting a growing labor shortage in the construction sector that could pressure the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. The author argues that US households are in much better shape than they were a decade ago, supported by five distinct charts showing strong consumer fundamentals alongside a tight labor market.

The first line chart, titled "Homeowners' equity above pre-crisis levels," plots US household equity in trillions of dollars from 2000 to late 2018. The data shows that equity peaked near thirteen trillion dollars in 2006, plummeted to a trough of six trillion dollars in 2011, and has since steadily climbed to surpass fifteen trillion dollars. 

To the right, the "Household debt" line chart tracks debt and debt service as a percent of disposable income from 1980 through late 2018. The blue line representing household debt peaked near one hundred and thirty percent in 2008 before falling to approximately one hundred percent. Similarly, the grey debt service line peaked near thirteen point five percent and has declined to around ten percent, indicating a much lower debt burden on average citizens.

A dual-axis chart titled "Signs of a healthy US labor market" displays the three-month average percentage of the labor force from 2001 to late 2017. The blue line tracks the firing rate on the left axis, which sits near historic lows of around one point three percent. Meanwhile, the grey line tracks the voluntary quit rate on the right axis, which has risen to a healthy one point eight percent, indicating high worker confidence.

The chart titled "Sharp upward revision in US savings rate" shows the personal savings rate as a three-month moving average from 1990 to 2018. It compares the pre-revision data, which showed a worrying decline toward three percent, with the post-revision data, which reveals a much stronger savings rate of around seven percent in 2018. This revision removes what had previously been labeled as the economic recovery's Achilles' heel.

The final chart, "Job openings rate: construction," tracks vacancies in the construction sector from 2001 to late 2017. The rate has climbed to its highest level in twenty years, approaching four percent. The accompanying text notes that this shortage could worsen if the Trump administration succeeds in terminating the Temporary Protected Status program, which currently allows three hundred thousand Central American individuals to work in the US. This policy decision could significantly impact recovery efforts in Florida, Texas, and California, where rebuilding is underway following major natural disasters.

On this page of the 2019 Outlook, Michael Cembalest analyzes United States corporate debt as a key longer-dated risk. He argues that while household debt is low, US corporate debt relative to equity and cash flow is near record highs. A primary concern is that the current median net debt-to-cash-flow ratio of approximately 2.0x masks a wide distribution of highly leveraged and negative-cash-flow companies. Furthermore, research from J.P. Morgan Global Markets Strategy shows that half of US and European BBB-rated issuers now exhibit higher leverage than the average BB-rated issuer. Cembalest predicts that as corporate debt reprices to higher yields, rising debt service costs will gradually impact highly leveraged sectors such as consumer staples, telecommunications, and utilities.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, tracking corporate debt for the largest 1,500 stocks from 1974 through 2018, compares median net debt-to-equity with median net debt-to-EBITDA. Both metrics have risen steeply since 2010, with net debt-to-EBITDA approaching 2.0x, close to previous cyclical peaks. The second chart illustrates the wide distribution of this leverage across the Russell 2000 and S&P 500 equity indexes as of the third quarter of 2018. It shows that while many companies hold net cash, a significant share of small-cap and large-cap firms have net debt-to-EBITDA ratios exceeding 12x or operate with negative EBITDA entirely. 

The third chart depicts the S&P 500 debt service ratio, measured as the median company's interest expense relative to operating income. This ratio fell from around 25% in 1990 to an all-time low of roughly 13% after the financial crisis, but it has recently ticked back up to around 15%, reflecting the onset of rising debt service burdens. The final chart plots the high yield default rate against non-financial corporate debt as a percentage of GDP from 1987 through 2018. While non-financial debt-to-GDP has climbed back to its historical peak of nearly 46%, the high-yield default rate remains exceptionally low at around 2%. Cembalest attributes this low default rate to easy monetary policies from central banks that fueled demand for high-yield credit, but he warns that this disconnect is unlikely to persist indefinitely.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, discusses two major economic headwinds facing the United States: rising interest rates and trade tariffs. 

The first section outlines how interest rates are dampening the housing and automotive sectors. The author points out that housing is already showing signs of a slowdown after only a 0.5% increase in mortgage rates. For the first time in ten years, the average US homeowner lacks an financial incentive to move because prevailing mortgage rates have risen above their existing outstanding mortgage rates. While housing and autos underperformed the S&P 500 by 20% in 2018, the author expects only a modest downturn rather than a crash due to strong underlying demand from household formation and young adults. 

This argument is supported by the first chart, "Housing measures declining as rates rise," which plots the year-over-year percentage change across eight indicators, comparing 2017, the first half of 2018, and the period from September to November 2018. The indicators include housing affordability, building permits, housing starts, home sales, and the MBA purchase index. Across almost all measures, the robust growth seen in 2017 has turned negative in late 2018, with single-unit building permits flatlining at 0.0% and the MBA purchase index slipping to -0.1%.

The second section addresses the threat of tariffs. The author warns that if proposed tariffs are fully implemented, consumer price inflation could spike, leading to the largest rollback of globalization in 50 years. This historical context is visualized in the chart "A century of globalization: US import tariffs, 1900-2018," which tracks the US tariff rate on total imports. The chart highlights a long-term decline from around 20% in the early 1900s to near-zero levels in the 2010s, but notes five recent policy steps: implemented tariffs on washing machines, solar, and steel/aluminum; two rounds of implemented Section 301 tariffs on China (25% on $50 billion and 10% on $200 billion); and two potential actions—a 25% tariff on $460 billion of Chinese goods and a 25% Section 232 tariff on $290 billion of autos and parts.

The composition of these trade actions is examined in the chart "Consumer products would be hit by next round of tariffs." It breaks down US imports from China by economic category (capital, intermediate, and consumer goods) across three rounds. While Round 1 ($50 billion) and Round 2 ($200 billion) focused heavily on capital and intermediate goods, the proposed Round 3 ($267 billion) would heavily penalize consumer goods, which make up over $100 billion of the total, alongside roughly $110 billion in capital goods.

The final chart, "US tariffs on China as a share of selected measures," argues that looking at tariffs relative to broad aggregates like GDP or overall consumer spending understates their true damage. While total tariffs represent less than 1% of US GDP and consumer spending, and only about 2% of overall S&P 500 earnings, the "relevant tariffs as a share of affected companies' earnings" tell a different story. In specific sectors, the burden is highly concentrated, representing roughly 10% of earnings for industrial capital goods and about 13% of earnings for technology hardware. The page also references White House National Trade Council head Peter Navarro and his book "Death by China" in a footnote.

This page of the publication focuses on United States market valuations and earnings expectations heading into 2019. The author argues that while earnings growth should continue, it will do so at a much slower rate than in 2018, which was boosted by tax cuts and a stronger global economy. Higher interest rates are also projected to weigh on earnings for value sectors like financials, consumer staples, and healthcare. Although a market correction in late 2018 reduced some extreme valuations, the author notes that high valuations remain a general headwind, even if very low valuations historically only occur during recessions or high-inflation periods.

To illustrate the expected slowdown, a line chart of consensus S&P 500 earnings growth shows year-over-year earnings-per-share growth expectations. The line representing 2018 peaked above twenty percent in mid-2018, whereas the line for 2019 growth steadily declined over the year, stabilizing between seven and eight percent. 

An adjacent chart explores how rising interest rates pressure value sector earnings. It compares the percentage of S&P value stocks with positive earnings revisions to the change in the ten-year US Treasury yield, which is advanced eighteen months and inverted. The visual correlation demonstrates that when Treasury yields rise, positive earnings revisions for value stocks tend to decline significantly.

A detailed valuation table ranks various S&P 500 metrics against their historical percentiles dating back to 1976, revealing a median metric in the seventieth percentile. Highly elevated measures include US market cap to GDP at one hundred sixty-four percent (the eighty-eighth percentile), enterprise value to sales at two times (the eighty-seventh percentile), and cyclically adjusted P/E at twenty-four times (the eighty-first percentile). In contrast, more moderate metrics include a forward P/E of fourteen point three times (the fifty-sixth percentile) and a free cash flow yield of five point one percent (the twentieth percentile). Footnotes clarify that the low free cash flow percentile is influenced by a post-2002 reduction in capital spending intensity among large-cap companies. Additionally, the author notes that percentile rankings are highly sensitive to historical start dates; for instance, using a 1985 start date instead of 1976 would drop the current forward P/E to the forty-second percentile.

Finally, a chart plotting US valuation measures as deviations from their long-term averages from 1950 through late 2018 shows the trajectory of the S&P 500 forward P/E ratio, home prices, and commercial real estate prices. While the equity forward P/E ratio pulled back toward its historical average during the late 2018 correction, home prices and especially commercial real estate prices remained highly elevated, with commercial real estate prices hovering nearly two standard deviations above their historical average.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication analyzes why technology, banks, and mining sectors appear oversold in late 2018, while the outlook for healthcare remains highly uncertain due to proposed regulatory reforms. 

The first chart, a line graph tracking the average forward price-to-earnings ratio of FAANG stocks (Facebook, Amazon, Apple, Netflix, and Google) relative to the S&P 500 from June 2012 to June 2018, demonstrates a severe collapse in their market premium. After hovering near 3.4x in 2012 and seeing multiple peaks, the FAANG premium steadily declined to around 2.0x by late 2018, representing one of its lowest points in years. 

To provide historical context on technology valuations, a bar chart displays tech sector price-to-earnings ratios relative to the market at cycle peaks dating from July 1953 to mid-December 2018. This chart shows that the mid-December 2018 premium of approximately 1.4x is remarkably subdued, standing far below historical cycle peaks such as December 1969 at 2.5x and the March 2000 dot-com peak at roughly 2.4x. 

Similarly, a bar chart of bank price-to-earnings ratios relative to the market at cycle peaks indicates that late 2018 bank valuations are depressed. In mid-December 2018, banks traded at approximately 0.5x, a level comparable to the pre-financial crisis lows of December 2007 at roughly 0.55x. The author notes that despite these low multiples, systemic risks in the financial sector are currently much lower than they were in 2007.

The fourth chart is a historical line graph showing the price-to-sales ratio of metals and mining stocks relative to the market from 1952 through late 2018. This ratio has plunged back toward multi-decade lows of roughly 0.4x. According to the author, these depressed valuations are tied to secular and cyclical slowdowns in China, but are also pricing in a high probability of a global recession in 2019 and a damaging outcome to the US-China trade war. 

Finally, the author addresses the healthcare sector, presenting a list of Democratic proposals aimed at controlling drug pricing. Although congressional and presidential support remains uncertain, the author predicts that some reform may pass in 2019, clouding the investment outlook. These proposals include introducing drug price controls to prevent gouging, allowing "dual eligible" drugs to be purchased at lower Medicaid pricing, empowering the government to negotiate drug pricing, establishing an independent price-tracking board, limiting tax deductions for advertising, requiring disclosure of development costs, increasing Medicaid rebates, reducing biologic patent terms from 12 years to 7 years, capping out-of-pocket patient costs at $250 per month, reducing Medicare Part B drug prices, requiring FDA pre-approval for advertisements, and allowing drug re-importation.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, titled Non-US markets overview, argues that while global growth was synchronized and rising a year prior, indicators have since softened, with conditions outside the United States looking particularly weak. Author Michael Cembalest points to disappointing economic data in Europe, noting that the European Central Bank has very limited options to counter a negative growth surprise because its short-term interest rates are already negative, it already owns 20% to 30% of many Eurozone government bonds, and German wages and home prices are starting to heat up. A footnote adds that the private sector only owns 20% to 25% of German and Dutch government bonds, compounded by large holdings from non-EU central banks and the ECB. Because of these constraints, the publication expresses a preference for Emerging Markets over Europe as a deep-value investment for 2019.

Four charts support this analysis. The first chart, tracking manufacturing PMI surveys from 2013 to late 2018, shows that US growth is holding up better than the rest of the world. While both indices softened in 2018, the US PMI remained elevated at around 57, whereas the Global PMI slid toward 52. The second chart, covering earnings revisions from 2010 to 2018, displays the number of positive revisions less negative revisions as a percentage of total companies. It highlights that S&P 500 earnings revisions, despite dropping from a peak near 40% in early 2018, remained positive at about 10%, while earnings revisions for Europe and Offshore China fell deep into negative territory, ending near negative 10% and negative 20% respectively.

The third chart illustrates global business confidence excluding the US and China from 2013 to 2018, measured as a deviation from the long-term average. This metric peaked in late 2017 at over 1.0 standard deviation above average and fell sharply throughout 2018 to around 0.3. The fourth and final chart traces German home prices and wages from 2010 to Q3 2018, showing year-over-year percentage changes. It demonstrates that German house prices surged to around 5.5% and hourly wages climbed to approximately 3.0%, while unit labor costs rose to about 1.5%, signaling a heating economy even as the GDP deflator and Core CPI remained lower, between 1.0% and 2.0%.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication details the rising structural risks in the United States credit markets, highlighting how massive central bank security purchases since 2009 drove down interest rates, sparking immense growth in corporate debt. Concurrently, the implementation of the Volcker Rule dampened market-making and proprietary trading, creating a dangerous combination of expanding fixed-income supply and collapsing market liquidity. The author argues that this conundrum, which could trigger severe market disruptions if investors attempt a sudden exit, should have been anticipated by policy architects.

The author supports this thesis with four charts illustrating credit quality deterioration and liquidity contraction. The first chart, titled "Debt stock expanding while liquidity shrinks," shows the percentage change in market size and turnover from 2006 to 2017 across different debt classes. It demonstrates that while the debt stock for high yield, investment-grade corporate bonds, and US Treasuries ballooned by up to 200% or more, their corresponding turnover ratios plummeted, with investment-grade and US Treasury turnover dropping by roughly 25% to 50%. 

The second chart, "BBB rated bonds take over post-crisis," tracks the percentage of the US investment-grade corporate bond index by rating, comparing December 2007 to December 2018. It illustrates a clear migration toward lower-tier investment-grade debt: the share of BBB3, BBB2, and BBB1 bonds rose significantly—with BBB1 increasing to over 15%—while top-rated AAA bonds shrank from around 5% to under 2%. 

This credit migration is further examined in the third chart, "Highest rated corporate bonds squeezed out by BBBs," which plots Single A or better bonds as a percentage of investment-grade supply in Europe and the United States. In the US, the historical 2008–2017 range of top-tier bonds sat between 47% and 75%, but fell to 51% in 2016 and hit a low of roughly 45% in 2017. Europe saw an even steeper squeezing out of high-rated debt, with top-tier supply dropping from its historical range down to approximately 32% in 2017. 

Finally, the fourth chart, "Rise in US corporate borrowing costs," plots the ratio of US BBB yields to their trailing 5-year average from 1925 through 2018, with NBER-defined recessions marked by grey vertical bars. The chart shows a sharp upward spike in the ratio toward the end of the timeline, indicating that BBB yields have widened by their largest amount versus trend since the 1980s, excluding the 2008 financial crisis. This rise in corporate borrowing costs historically signals increased credit market stress, often preceding or coinciding with recessions.

In this section of J.P. Morgan's 2019 Outlook, Michael Cembalest discusses the persistent underperformance of European equities relative to US equities. Despite trillions of Euros of ECB intervention helping European stocks rise 62% since December 2011, the S&P 500 surged by 116% in the same timeframe. Cembalest notes that 2018 was another year of US outperformance and predicts that this trend will continue into 2019, driven by rapidly weakening European earnings revisions and slowing economic growth in France and Italy, both of which are heading back toward 1% growth. 

The first chart, titled "US outperformed for most of the last 30 years," displays the 3-year rolling outperformance or underperformance of a simulated portfolio against the MSCI All World Index from 1991 to 2018. The portfolio is defined as an all-equity, quarterly rebalanced allocation with no currency hedging, featuring a 15% overweight to the US, a 10% underweight to Europe, and a 5% underweight to Japan. The vertical axis ranges from -10% to 15%. This chart visualizes that the US-overweight strategy generated positive relative returns for almost the entire three-decade span, with the sole exception of the mid-2000s growth boom in Southern Europe when underperformance dipped to around -7% before returning to positive territory around 2010.

The second chart, titled "Europe: P/E discount vs the US is par for the course," tracks the Stoxx 600 forward price-to-earnings discount relative to the S&P 500 from 2006 through late 2018. The vertical axis, representing the discount percentage, ranges from 0% to -30%. The line fluctuates entirely in negative territory, hitting its lowest points of nearly -28% during the 2009 financial crisis and the 2011–2012 Eurozone crisis, and ending 2018 at around a -15% to -20% discount. This visual supports the author's point that a valuation discount in Europe is historically normal rather than a signal for a near-term rebound.

Footnotes clarify that the Stoxx 600 includes both Eurozone and non-Eurozone countries, noting that pre-2006 P/E multiples are not comparable due to past European goodwill amortization rules. Furthermore, the author addresses potential counterarguments by explaining that US outperformance is not merely a consequence of the higher technology sector weighting in the S&P 500. When adjusting to look at sector-neutral P/E ratios, the valuation discount remains very similar, and US outperformance has been broad-based across financial, consumer discretionary, and energy sectors.

This page focuses on Europe's economic history, the creation and viability of the Euro, and its future prospects. It centers on a discussion between Michael Cembalest and Henry Kissinger regarding Europe's post-World War II recovery, contrasted against a perceived loss of vitality among its current leaders. Cembalest poses the open question of whether the political and economic efforts required to maintain the Euro are currently bolstering or draining European energy. 

To support this analysis, the page features two key charts. The first, titled "Post-war recovery in per capita GDP, 1946-1960," shows the ratio of 1960 per capita GDP compared to the 1946 level. This chart highlights Germany's dramatic economic recovery, known as the Wirtschaftswunder, where GDP per capita more than tripled, achieving a ratio of nearly 3.3. Other recovering nations shown in descending order of growth include Austria, Taiwan, Japan, Italy, the Philippines, Greece, Hungary, the USSR, and France, which had the lowest recovery ratio on the chart at just under 2.0. 

The second chart, titled "Economic efficiency based on goods markets, labor markets, innovation, corruption, legal framework and investor protections," rates countries on a 100-point scale where 100 represents the best possible score. This metric exposes a severe divergence within the Eurozone, showing Germany with a strong score of approximately 90, while Italy scores roughly 45. The author compares this to the Americas, where the United States scores around 93 and Mexico scores around 35. This comparison demonstrates that the economic efficiency gap between Germany and Italy is almost as wide as that between the US and Mexico, raising concerns that these nations do not possess the aligned economic structures necessary for a typical monetary union. 

The page also includes two historical text boxes illustrating the extreme devastation of post-war Europe from which these economies rebuilt. The first, written by Oxford history professor Margaret MacMillan in 2009, details ruined infrastructure, destroyed housing—including 70% of Germany's housing and thousands of towns in the Soviet Union—and widespread starvation, where many survived on fewer than 1,000 calories a day. The second is an excerpt from a letter written in August 1945 by the author’s uncle, describing Vienna as a starving ghost town of bombed-out landmarks, destroyed bridges, and black-market looting by the occupying Russian Army.

In this section of the J.P. Morgan 2019 Outlook, Michael Cembalest provides a brief commentary on Brexit, summarizing the key forecasts of J.P. Morgan economist Malcolm Barr. Notably, Barr does not view a second referendum as the most likely outcome. Instead, he predicts that while the initial withdrawal agreement will fail to pass the House of Commons on its first attempt in early January due to political divisions, and Prime Minister Theresa May will likely face and survive another no-confidence vote, the current agreement will ultimately pass once MPs realize no better options exist. 

Following the deal's eventual passage, the analysis projects that Prime Minister May will step down in 2019, yielding power to a more staunchly pro-Brexit Conservative leader. However, the signed withdrawal agreement, including the contentious Irish backstop, will constrain the new leader's negotiating power. Cembalest emphasizes that the agreement is merely a roadmap for complex future discussions on trade, the Irish border, citizen movement, and legal jurisdictions. Consequently, he expects the status quo transition period will be extended to 2022, with an outside chance of a long-term Norway-type arrangement. Cembalest concludes by reflecting on the historical legacy of British parliamentary democracy, dating back to Simon de Montfort in 1258, questioning whether Brexit will ultimately be remembered as a high or low water mark in English history.

This page focuses on the economic challenges and structural underperformance facing Europe, noting that the region-wide economic revival anticipated in early 2018 peaked and rolled over, with third-quarter 2018 earnings ranking as some of the weakest since 2014. The author forecasts that 2019 will bring another year of sub-2% growth for Europe. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) may consider further low-cost financing to encourage private-sector lending, particularly in Italy, the author highlights that previous massive ECB interventions have done little for investors. Specifically, Eurozone equities ended 2018 near where they started in 2014, despite 2.6 trillion Euros in cumulative asset purchases. Structural reasons for this underperformance include a lower return on equity across most European industries compared to the United States and a significantly smaller, less profitable, and more expensive technology sector.

The economic and financial data on this page is illustrated through three charts and one comparative table. The first line chart, "Tracking Eurozone GDP growth," plots actual quarter-over-quarter percentage growth against business survey predictions from 2010 to 2018, showing a clear downward trajectory after a peak in late 2017. The second line chart, "Eurozone bank lending to non-financial corporations," measures year-over-year percentage changes from 2005 to 2018 for Germany, France, Spain, and Italy. This chart demonstrates that while corporate lending has recovered from the abysmal contraction of the 2013–2015 period, it remains far below pre-crisis levels. The third chart, "Eurozone equities and ECB asset purchases," uses dual axes to contrast the volatile MSCI Eurozone index level against the steadily rising curve of cumulative ECB asset purchases from 2014 through late 2018, underscoring that massive quantitative easing failed to translate into sustained equity market gains. 

The structural deficit in European technology is detailed in the table titled "Tech sector: US vs Europe," which compares composition metrics across the S&P 500, MSCI US, MSCI Europe, and MSCI Eurozone as of late December 2018. The data reveals that tech represents a 20% index weight in the US compared to just 5% in MSCI Europe and 9% in MSCI Eurozone. Additionally, US tech firms boast far superior profitability, with operating margins of 22% to 24% and returns on equity of 26% to 27%, compared to European tech operating margins of 12% to 15% and returns on equity of 11% to 14%. Despite these weaker metrics, European tech companies trade at higher valuations, with 12-month forward P/E ratios of roughly 16.0 compared to 14.0 in the United States.

Finally, the page details the vulnerabilities of the Italian banking sector. Italian bank reliance on ECB funding is noted to range from 6% of assets for Unicredit to 12% for Monte dei Paschi and Banco BPM. Italian banks also hold a substantial portion of domestic sovereign risk, owning 20% of all Italian government bonds, which equates to 15% of their total assets. This concentration poses risks regarding deposit flight and rising borrowing spreads. However, the author notes that the two largest Italian banks, Unicredit and Intesa, are expected to maintain Tier 1 Capital ratios above 10% even under conservative liquidation values of 20 to 40 cents on the Euro for their non-performing loans.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the economic underpinnings of recent strikes in France. The author argues that while many observers attribute the unrest to typical French worker activism, the root causes run much deeper. Key issues include a stagnant economy, a historically wide wealth gap with Germany, and an extremely high tax burden. Specifically, President Emmanuel Macron’s shelved fuel tax hike, though billed as an environmental measure, was perceived as a regressive tool to meet Eurozone fiscal targets, which triggered intense public backlash because France already boasts exceptionally low carbon emissions and some of the highest gasoline prices and tax rates in the developed world.

Six charts support these observations. The first chart, titled "Franco-German wealth gap," plots the ratio of Germany's real per capita GDP to France's from 1850 to 2015. It highlights a sharp upward trend since 2000, circled in red, where the ratio approaches 1.15, representing the widest wealth disparity between the two nations in 50 years. 

The second chart, "Remembrance of things past: low French growth," illustrates the six-year percentage change in real GDP from 1825 to recent years, excluding world wars. It marks historical economic low points, such as the Franco-Prussian War, the phylloxera agricultural epidemic, the Paris Bourse crash of 1882, the rise of factory strikes in the early 20th century, the Great Depression, and the Euro crisis, demonstrating that France's recent economic stagnation is comparable to historic non-wartime crises.

The third chart, "France CO2 emissions versus OECD," shows tons of CO2 per $1,000 of GDP across 46 countries. France ranks near the bottom (sixth lowest) at roughly 0.1 tons, indicating that its carbon footprint is already incredibly low compared to international peers. 

The fourth chart, "France: taxed to the gauls," illustrates total personal tax revenue as a percentage of GDP. France ranks first among all listed countries, with personal taxes consuming nearly 45% of GDP. 

The fifth chart, "Gasoline prices per gallon," ranks global gasoline prices as of late 2018, showing that France ranks near the top (11th out of 46 countries) with prices hovering close to $6 per gallon, as indicated by a red arrow. 

The final chart, "Average days not worked due to strikes," compares European nations across two time frames: 2000–2009 and 2010–2017. France leads by a wide margin in both periods, averaging over 100 days lost to strikes annually, far outpacing runner-up nations like Belgium and Spain.

This page of the publication, focused on Europe, argues that contrary to historical precedents like the US monetary union, the inception of the Euro has widened economic disparities rather than narrowing them, leading to reverse integration. 

To support this observation, the top-left chart, titled "Death in Venice," plots the Industrial Production Index for Germany, France, and Italy from 1980 to late 2018, setting December 31, 1999, as the baseline of 100. The chart demonstrates that economic cycles were highly synchronous among the three nations before the Euro exchange rate was fixed in 1999. Following the Euro's introduction, Germany's industrial production diverged upward, climbing toward 130, while France stagnated near 100, and Italy suffered a severe decline to approximately 80 by 2018. Nearby, the top-right chart, titled "German banks less willing to lend to periphery banks," tracks German outbound lending to Spain and Italy in billions of US dollars from 2005 to 2018. Lending to both countries peaked between 2007 and 2008—with Spain reaching over $300 billion and Italy exceeding $250 billion—before steadily collapsing to under $100 billion by 2018, showing a dramatic retreat in cross-border financial integration.

The narrative then focuses on Italy, explaining that while a budget agreement with Brussels has lowered near-term default risk, the resulting cuts to infrastructure investment and corporate tax hikes have heightened Italy's recession risk. The author notes that Italy's infrastructure quality already ranks near the bottom of the OECD, exceeding only Mexico and Poland, making infrastructure cuts highly counterproductive. 

Two bottom charts detail Italy’s financial strains. The bottom-left chart, "Italy: the cost of protecting against default," shows the Italian 5-year CDS contract price in basis points from 2010 to 2018. It contrasts the ISDA 2003 contract with the ISDA 2014 contract, which includes protection against redenomination risks. Spreads peaked during the 2011–2012 crisis at over 550 basis points and rose again in late 2018, with the ISDA 2014 contract climbing to around 250 basis points, reflecting renewed investor anxiety. The bottom-right chart, "Foreign investors lose confidence in Italy, again," shows annualized quarterly debt flows by non-Italian investors in billions of euros from 1996 to 2018. Capital flows plunged into deep negative territory during the 2011–2012 crisis and saw another severe contraction in 2018, falling below negative 200 billion euros as foreign capital fled the country.

In conclusion, the author offers a cautious outlook for the region. Angela Merkel's decision not to run for German Chancellor again in 2021, combined with disruptive labor strikes in France, are predicted to stall any meaningful progress toward fiscal integration or risk-pooling in the Eurozone. Without these necessary precedents, the author believes the valuation gap between European and US markets is unlikely to narrow.

This page of the J.P. Morgan 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the investment and economic risks associated with a "hard" Brexit for the United Kingdom. Cembalest argues that while Brexit has exerted a modest drag on the UK economy so far—with growth lagging the developed world by one percent—the primary source of weakness has been slower business investment. He suggests that if the UK can transition into a multi-year negotiation process rather than experiencing a sudden, disruptive divorce, UK equities could become strong relative performers in 2019 because substantial no-deal risks are already priced into the market.

To demonstrate the UK's vulnerability, a table titled Tracking UK exposure to the European Union outlines the economic contributions and EU exposures of three vital UK sectors: production, distribution/transport, and finance/insurance. These sectors account for significant shares of corporate tax (14 percent for production, 20 percent for distribution, and 18 percent for finance) and employment (9 percent, 26 percent, and 3 percent respectively). Their exposure to the EU is notably high: the foreign workforce comprises 11 to 14 percent of their totals, and the EU share of total exports ranges from 37 percent for finance to 51 percent for production. Additionally, the imports to inputs ratio reaches 51 percent in the production sector, highlighting a heavy reliance on EU supply chains.

Alongside these economic figures, a sidebar highlights the medical risks of a hard Brexit, referencing British Medical Association concerns. Leaving the Euratom atomic energy agency could severely disrupt imports of radioactive cancer-treatment isotopes—80 percent of which are currently imported from the Netherlands, France, and Belgium—which cannot be stockpiled due to rapid radioactive decay.

Two charts support the economic assessment. The first, Real business fixed investment, plots the percentage change in investment relative to the Brexit vote level from 2014 through late 2018 for the US, EU, and UK. Following the mid-2016 Brexit referendum, UK business investment flatlined, hovering around 3 percent to 4 percent above pre-referendum levels by late 2018, while investment in the EU rose to nearly 8 percent and the US surged past 12 percent, illustrating the drag of Brexit uncertainty on UK corporate spending. 

The second chart, UK: P/E discount vs Europe, tracks the MSCI UK price-to-earnings discount or premium based on forward earnings from 2006 to late 2018. It compares the UK valuation to both the broader European market and the Eurozone. By late 2018, the UK traded at a steep discount of roughly 5 percent to 10 percent versus Europe. Meanwhile, its valuation premium against the Eurozone, which peaked at over 20 percent around 2015, had evaporated down to near parity. 

Finally, a footnote addresses media sensationalism, noting that the Financial Times corrected an erroneous report claiming one trillion dollars in UK equity outflows post-Brexit, revising the figure down to twenty billion dollars after J.P. Morgan pointed out the error.

This page analyzes China’s dominant position within the emerging markets and the implications of its slowing economic growth. The author emphasizes that China’s weight in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index has climbed to 30%, a figure expected to rise even further as more companies qualify for eligibility. Beyond equity market weight, other emerging market nations have become increasingly dependent on China's economic cycle. While the author is not concerned about an imminent balance of payments crisis due to China's exceptionally low external debt-to-GDP ratio, there is a prominent risk of lower trend growth. The author notes that fiscal and monetary stimulus, alongside rising corporate debt, have artificially boosted recent performance; the International Monetary Fund estimated that without this debt accumulation, Chinese growth would have averaged 5.5% rather than 7.25% between 2012 and 2016. Consequently, the author supports a 2014 Conference Board forecast predicting that Chinese growth will decelerate and converge to 4% by 2020–2025. This slowdown is already visible in recent indicators, with November car sales dropping 15% year-over-year and retail sales and industrial production hitting ten-year lows.

Four charts illustrate these arguments. The first, "Emerging Market equities: China then and now," plots the percentage weight in the MSCI EM Index from 1998 to 2018. It showcases China's remarkable trajectory, surging from near 0% to 30% over the period, while Latin America's weight fell from around 34% to 11%. Over the same timeframe, South Korea, Taiwan, India, and other Asian countries saw their weights stabilize or decline, leaving South Korea at roughly 13%, Taiwan at 12%, and India at approximately 8%. The second chart, "EM countries becoming more tied to China," tracks the GDP-weighted, ten-year rolling correlation of GDP growth across 19 emerging market countries to China from 1989 to 2016. This correlation climbed from below 20% in the early 1990s to nearly 60% by 2016, visually representing how tightly other emerging markets are linked to China's economic fortunes.

The bottom left chart, "China economy monitor," tracks eight domestic economic variables from 2011 to 2018, including employment surveys, exports, business conditions, GDP, corporate earnings, industrial production, retail sales, and non-state owned enterprise fixed asset investment. The overlapping lines demonstrate a clear downward trend across almost all variables, illustrating a broad economic rollover after a brief recovery in 2017. Lastly, the chart titled "Chinese credit growth slowing, but from high debt level" displays data from 2003 to 2017. It shows credit growth as a year-over-year percentage change on the left axis and total credit as a percentage of GDP on the right axis. While annual credit growth has slowed from its massive post-financial crisis peak of over 30% in 2009 down toward 10% in 2017, the overall debt burden has continued to rise, with total credit as a percentage of GDP climbing steadily from 120% in 2008 to over 200% by late 2017.

This page, titled "Where to from here on tariffs?", analyzes the outlook for global trade negotiations, focusing on lessons from the newly minted USMCA agreement and the high-stakes trade friction between the United States and China. The author begins by summarizing takeaways from the USMCA with Mexico and Canada, noting that tariffs are increasingly being used as leverage to extract concessions rather than as final policy goals, and that the net economic impacts of the new agreement versus NAFTA are modest. Looking to China, the US is demanding greater market access, enforcement against cyber intrusions targeting intellectual property, and the elimination of subsidies tied to the "Made in China 2025" initiative. Although China has made concessions—such as lowering auto tariffs, banning fentanyl exports, and purchasing more US goods—tensions remain high, with a February deadline looming before "Round 2" tariffs of 25% could be reinstated. 

To illustrate how trade uncertainty is weighing on the global economy, the page includes a line chart titled "Expectations declining faster than current conditions, which could reverse with a comprehensive deal." The chart tracks two data series from 2012 through November 2018: the Current Global Output Survey (plotted on the left axis from 46 to 56) and the Future Global Output Survey (plotted on the right axis from 58 to 68). The visualization reveals that while actual current output has remained relatively resilient, the forward-looking expectations index has plummeted sharply in 2018, falling from a peak of nearly 66 down toward 60. This divergence underscores that business sentiment is preemptively pricing in trade war damage, presenting a potential upside if a comprehensive deal is struck.

The author concludes with strategic forecasts, recalling a discussion with Henry Kissinger, who warned that trade disputes carry a risk of unintended consequences similar to those that precipitated World War I. The author predicts a potential "mixed result" by March: a deal with China that averts further tariff hikes, paired with the onset of a new tariff conflict with Europe and Japan regarding $300 billion of US automotive imports. If negotiations fail and more tariffs are implemented, the author warns that costs will be split among Chinese and European producers absorbing lower margins and US consumers paying higher prices, likely triggering a negative market reaction where investors "shoot first and ask questions later."

This page from J.P. Morgan’s emerging markets analysis focuses on the dynamics of tariff risks and semiconductor warfare between the US and China. The author argues that while China has reduced its overall economic reliance on exports, its technological dependence on the US for advanced semiconductors remains absolute. This vulnerability is demonstrated by how the US export ban on ZTE effectively disabled the company due to its reliance on US networking chips from Broadcom, optical chips from Inphi, and microprocessors from Intel. Similarly, Huawei remains heavily dependent on US semiconductor suppliers like Intel, Qualcomm, and Micron, as well as software from Microsoft and Oracle. 

To illustrate the dominant position of US technology, a table outlines estimated market shares held by US semiconductor firms. It shows that Intel and AMD command a 99% market share in microprocessor chips for PCs and servers. NVIDIA and AMD capture 95% of graphics processors for artificial intelligence and deep learning. Broadcom dominates 95% of networking chips for cloud datacenters. In mobile technology, Qualcomm and Intel hold 70% of smartphone cellular processing chips for 4G/5G. Meanwhile, Texas Instruments, Analog, and Maxim hold 90% of electric vehicle power management chips, and Intel and NVIDIA capture 90% of next-generation fully autonomous car processors.

Four charts visually support this discussion. The first chart, showing exports as a percentage of GDP, highlights China’s decreasing reliance on exports, which declined from a peak of approximately 36% in 2006 to less than 20% in 2018. The second chart details China's semiconductor imports in US billions by partner country in 2017, distinguishing between equipment and chips. Japan and the United States are the top suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment, each providing around $1.7 to $2.0 billion in total goods, whereas imports from South Korea, Singapore, and Taiwan consist primarily of completed semiconductor chips rather than fabrication equipment. 

The third chart illustrates that China has been the primary equity market loser in the trade war. It indexes the 2018 performance of equities based on their geographic exposure; while US, European, and Japanese stocks with international exposures hovered between indices of 90 and 100, Chinese stocks with US exposure plunged, ending the year down near 75 relative to a starting index of 100. The final chart presents Chinese equity market valuations using 12-month forward P/E multiples from 2005 to 2018. Multiples for both onshore and offshore Chinese equities collapsed to around 10x, representing their lowest levels in a decade. Looking ahead to 2019, the author cautions that tariff issues are beginning to negatively affect corporate behavior, noting that front-loaded investments in 2018 will likely set the stage for weaker demand in 2019 as companies increasingly move production out of China.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, focuses on the growing risk of a significant decline in the Chinese Renminbi (RMB) amid escalating trade tensions with the United States. Cembalest argues that if the trade war intensifies, China may allow the RMB to depreciate to restore its export competitiveness. While China has historically used its foreign exchange reserves to prop up the currency, several conditions make a large currency decline more viable now. Specifically, capital outflows have stabilized, FX reserves have dipped slightly below the International Monetary Fund’s estimate of adequacy, and China's current account surplus has effectively evaporated. The author notes that a 10% to 15% depreciation could offset the impact of US tariffs, but warns that such a move would be highly destabilizing for other emerging market nations whose corporate sectors hold substantial debt in hard foreign currencies.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, titled "The RMB sold off as the trade war progressed," displays the inverted USDCNY exchange rate from 2016 to late 2018. The vertical axis ranges from an inverted 6.2 to 7.0, meaning lower positions on the chart indicate a weaker Chinese Yuan. The data series shows the currency strengthening to roughly 6.3 in early 2018 before sharply weakening toward 6.9. A vertical dashed line marks the moment President Donald Trump announced $50 billion in tariffs on China, which immediately preceded this steep currency depreciation.

The second chart, "China capital flows," illustrates the change in foreign exchange reserves minus the current account balance in billions of US dollars from 1998 to 2018. The vertical axis spans from negative $300 billion to positive $200 billion. The chart highlights that while China suffered extreme net capital outflows approaching nearly negative $250 billion around 2015 and 2016, these capital flows stabilized close to the zero line by late 2018.

The third chart, "China current account balance," tracks the nation's balance as a percentage of GDP from 1998 to 2018, with the vertical axis ranging from negative 2% to positive 12%. This graphic reveals that China's historical current account surplus, which peaked at approximately 10% of GDP around 2007, has steadily declined and entered near-deficit territory, hovering around 0% by mid-2018.

The final chart, "Shrinking net interest carry between China and US," shows the spread between the 12-month SHIBOR and LIBOR from 2015 to late 2018, with a vertical axis running from 0% to 5%. This spread has contracted dramatically from about 4.5% in 2015 down to approximately 0.5% by the end of 2018, illustrating that a weaker RMB is a natural consequence of a narrowing interest rate differential. 

In addition to these charts, the footnotes clarify that China's balanced trade account is a result of a massive services deficit with the rest of the world and substantial overall deficits with trading partners such as Taiwan, South Korea, Australia, and Brazil, despite its highly publicized goods surplus with the United States.

This page focuses on the outlook for emerging markets, specifically examining how trade tensions and domestic margin pressures have impacted Chinese corporate profits and equities. It argues that while Chinese profits were recovering in early 2018, the introduction of tariffs caused profits to roll over and triggered a selloff in Chinese equities. This market decline was further worsened by Chinese CEOs who borrowed heavily against their own stock to secure corporate liquidity or personal investments, which ultimately triggered a wave of margin calls as equity prices fell. Despite these headwinds, the publication highlights that a comprehensive trade deal could offer significant upside for both Chinese and global markets.

The analysis is supported by four charts. The first, "China onshore profits growth," tracks year-over-year EBIT growth on a three-quarter moving average from 3Q 2008 through 3Q 2018, broken down by state-owned, private, and total enterprises. The chart shows that while private enterprise profits peaked near 50% growth in late 2017, they plummeted alongside state-owned profits in 2018, dragging total onshore profit growth close to 0% by the third quarter of 2018. 

The second chart, "Margin calls on Chinese CEOs exacerbate market decline," illustrates the relationship between market performance and executive leverage from January 2017 to October 2018. It plots the year-over-year change of the Shenzhen Composite Index against the rising number of firms where the CEO has pledged at least 80% of their stock and the stock price has fallen by 40% or more. As the Shenzhen Composite Index steadily fell towards a 40% year-over-year decline, the number of highly vulnerable, leveraged firms surged from under 100 to over 300, demonstrating how margin calls on CEOs exacerbated the broader equity selloff.

The third chart, "Earnings revisions," plots the net percentage of positive minus negative earnings revisions for China Offshore and Asia ex-Japan equities from 2010 through 2018. Throughout 2018, both series fell sharply into negative territory, with China Offshore revisions dropping from positive levels to nearly negative 40%, reflecting widespread analyst downgrades.

Finally, the waterfall chart titled "China 2019 earnings outlook" details how J.P. Morgan Economic Research adjusted its growth expectations for 2019. Starting from an initial consensus estimate of roughly 15% year-over-year profit growth, the chart incorporates a positive contribution from tax cuts, which is then offset by negative drag from CNY depreciation, trade issues, and slower GDP growth. This results in an adjusted, more conservative 2019 earnings growth forecast of 10%.

This page of the report examines the economic landscape in Japan, highlighting a critical disconnect where booming corporate profits and rising capital investments have failed to benefit workers and consumers. The author argues that while Japanese corporate profits have kept pace with those in the United States and corporate spending has steadily risen, Japanese real household incomes have stagnated or fallen for many years. 

To illustrate this disparity, the top two charts compare corporate and household indicators between the US and Japan from 2007 through late 2018. The first chart shows that both nations experienced a dramatic corporate profits rebound. The MSCI Japan index saw trailing twelve-month earnings per share recover from a low of around 20 yen in 2009 to nearly 80 yen in late 2018, mirroring the S&P 500's rise from under 65 dollars to over 140 dollars. Despite this lockstep corporate growth, the second chart demonstrates that real household incomes only rose in the US. While the US real household earnings index climbed steadily from 100 in 2010 to around 126 in 2018, Japan’s index plummeted from 101 in 2007 to 92 in 2015, showing only a meager recovery to around 95 by late 2018. 

The bottom half of the page tracks year-over-year changes in Japan's capital and software investments, with a vertical line marking the start of the Abenomics policy era in late 2012. The chart on capital investments reveals that year-over-year fixed asset spending rebounded from deep contractions of nearly negative 25 percent in 2009 to steady, positive growth mostly between 0 and 10 percent post-Abenomics. Meanwhile, Japanese software investments also stabilized after the implementation of Abenomics, maintaining steady positive year-over-year growth that reached nearly 11 percent by late 2018. Ultimately, the data shows that while Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s economic policies successfully revived corporate health and capital spending, the benefits have not trickled down to the broader Japanese population.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, argues that Emerging Markets present a more compelling contrarian deep-value investment opportunity for 2019 than Europe. The author bases this on several key observations. First, although corporate earnings in both regions have tracked a similar path since 2014, Europe currently trades at a significant premium to Emerging Markets. Additionally, valuation spreads show a higher concentration of deep-value opportunities within Emerging Markets, while global investor positioning in these markets is hovering near a ten-year low, signaling that the asset class is highly unloved.

To support these assertions, the page displays four distinct charts. The first chart, titled Europe vs Emerging Markets: 12-month forward earnings, plots indexed earnings from January 2015 to July 2018, with January 1, 2015, established as the baseline of 100. This chart tracks the Stoxx 600 alongside the MSCI Emerging Markets index, demonstrating that both indices followed nearly identical trajectories, peaking near 110 in late 2017 and early 2018 before sliding downward together. 

The second chart, titled Europe: P/E premium vs the Emerging Markets, shows the Stoxx 600 P/E premium or discount relative to MSCI Emerging Markets based on forward earnings from 2006 through late 2018. This visual highlights that Europe currently trades at a 15% to 20% premium over Emerging Markets. While this is down from a peak premium of nearly 40% around 2014, it stands in stark contrast to the period between 2008 and 2011 when Europe traded at a discount.

The third chart, Europe and Emerging Markets valuation spreads, shows the deviations of the top valuation quintile from its long-term average from 2000 through 2018. In this chart, higher values indicate wider valuation disparities, meaning more deep-value stocks are available. The data reveals that valuation spreads in Emerging Markets are elevated, holding above the long-term average at around 1.0 standard deviation. In contrast, Europe’s spreads are negative, sitting at roughly -0.5 standard deviations, indicating narrow disparities and fewer exceptionally cheap stocks.

The final chart, EM countries no longer worried about too much FX appreciation, tracks an EM currency index from 2000 to 2018, with December 31, 2009, set to 100. The chart illustrates a dramatic, roughly 40% depreciation of the EM currency index from its peak of over 110 in 2011 to a low of approximately 65 in 2018. The author notes that while stabilization in this currency index is critical for an EM recovery, any such progress ultimately depends heavily on economic developments in China.

This J.P. Morgan analysis of Japan highlights the nation's ongoing struggle with low consumer demand and investor skepticism, arguing that a persistent deflationary mindset remains difficult to break while foreign investors continue to withdraw capital despite low equity valuations. Author Michael Cembalest points out that Japanese inflation remains below the central bank's target and spending intentions have only crawled back to neutral from deep lows two years prior. Additionally, Japan faces economic headwinds from trade conflicts, particularly if they lead to a devaluation of the Chinese RMB. 

To support the consumer spending argument, the page features two top charts. The first chart plots Japan's consumer price index excluding food, alcoholic beverages, and energy from 2005 to 2018. This year-over-year percentage change spent most of the decade before 2013 in negative territory, spiked briefly to nearly 2% following the April 2014 VAT hike, and subsequently drifted back down toward zero by late 2018. The second chart illustrates Japanese consumers' spending plans from 1991 through late 2018, tracking the net percentage of respondents planning to spend more on services such as entertainment tickets, housekeeping, eating out, amusement parks, and self-enlightenment. Throughout this multi-decade period, all categories remained deeply in negative territory, mostly fluctuating between negative 10% and negative 40%, demonstrating an entrenched reluctance to spend.

Turning to equity markets, the text explains that international investors ignored positive corporate earnings news in 2018, pulling money out of Japan at a pace that rivaled the major sell-offs of 2008 and 2016. Cembalest observes that while Japanese equities look cheap and could attract value investors, a sustainable rally would likely require a broader global economic recovery in 2019, in which case emerging markets would probably outperform Japan anyway. 

This market behavior is depicted in two bottom charts. The bottom-left chart shows non-resident net purchases of Japanese equities on a rolling six-month basis in trillions of Yen from 2005 to 2018. It highlights that the massive capital flight in late 2018 reached net outflows of nearly five trillion Yen, matching the capitulations seen in 2008 and 2016, and contrasting sharply with the massive ten-trillion-Yen buying wave that occurred when Abenomics began in late 2012. Finally, the bottom-right chart tracks Japan's forward 12-month P/E ratio from 2005 to late 2018. Since the start of Abenomics, the P/E ratio has repeatedly flirted with the 15x level only to fall back down, ending 2018 near the bottom of its historical post-crisis range at around 11x to 12x.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the role of policymakers in the housing crisis, focusing on how changes to Government-Sponsored Enterprise balance sheets laid the groundwork for the subprime mortgage collapse.
