The author argues that a 1993 law allowing Housing and Urban Development to set low and moderate-income lending targets forced Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to lower their underwriting standards. Consequently, these GSEs flooded their balance sheets with low-quality loans well before the private sector began its own subprime and Alt-A expansion. Cembalest highlights that many experts at the time, including Nobel Laureate Joseph Stiglitz and future OMB Director Peter Orszag, drastically underestimated the risks, predicting in 2002 that the probability of a GSE balance sheet shock was less than one in 500,000.

The accompanying chart visually demonstrates this timeline, tracking annual underwriting percentages from 1990 to 2009. It shows the HUD low and moderate-income lending target rising from 30% in 1993 to 50% by 2001, driving the overall Fannie/Freddie share of the mortgage market from roughly 35% in 1990 to a peak near 55% in 2003. Concurrently, five indicators of Fannie and Freddie underwriting that exceeded traditional standards—including non-traditional loans, high combined loan-to-value ratios, and high debt-to-income ratios—escalated steadily throughout the late 1990s and early 2000s. In contrast, the private sector subprime and Alt-A share of total origination remained under 10% until 2003, after which it ballooned to nearly 40% by 2006. This lag support's the author's thesis that the private sector merely followed the high-risk path forged by public policy and the GSEs.

This page introduces a retrospective on the tenth anniversary of the Global Financial Crisis, with Michael Cembalest arguing that the crisis resulted from a complex web of interactions involving banks, broker-dealers, investors, insurance companies, rating agencies, the Federal Reserve, and policymakers, rather than being a simple tale of bank failures. To illustrate the scale of the crisis, the page features a bar chart comparing deposits in failed and assisted US banks as a percentage of GDP across three historical eras: the Great Depression, the Savings and Loan Crisis, and the Great Recession. The chart demonstrates that failed and assisted bank deposits in 2009 spiked to approximately 8% of GDP, exceeding the Great Depression peak of around 6% in 1933, while the Savings and Loan Crisis peaked at less than 2% of GDP in the late 1980s.

To show the massive scale of emergency liquidity needed to prevent further damage, an accompanying table lists emergency facilities created by the Federal Reserve and their peak outstanding balances in billions of dollars. Key facilities highlighted include the Term Auction Facility at $493 billion, the Commercial Paper Funding Facility at $348 billion, the Term Securities Lending Facility at $236 billion, the Asset-Backed Commercial Paper Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility at $152 billion, the Primary Dealer Credit Facility at $147 billion, Term Repurchase Transactions at $80 billion, the AIG Revolving Credit Facility at $72 billion, and the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility at $48 billion.

Lastly, the text outlines the topics covered in the subsequent pages of this section, which aim to provide a more nuanced view of the crisis. These include the role of policymakers in hijacking Government-Sponsored Enterprise balance sheets during the housing crisis, the impact of deregulation on broker-dealers, underwriting decisions by rating agencies, bond reinsurers, and institutional investors, and individual financial entities' contributions to systemic risk. Cembalest concludes by noting that the final pages will review the substantial and welcome post-crisis regulatory changes in capital requirements, liquidity, leverage, and shadow banking.

This page, part of a retrospective on the tenth anniversary of the Global Financial Crisis, discusses the critical role of broker-dealer deregulation in driving the scale of the 2008 financial crisis. The author argues that changes to broker-dealer regulations, specifically the relaxation of the SEC Uniform Net Capital Rule in 2004, played a more prominent role in the crisis than changes in commercial banking regulations. Following this regulatory shift, the five largest US broker-dealers saw immense balance sheet growth. Lehman Brothers serves as a key example: by 2007, its balance sheet grew to 690 billion dollars—larger in real terms than all failed banks during the Great Depression combined—while supported by only 22 billion dollars in equity and funded heavily by short-term repurchase agreements with maturities as short as 24 hours.

Two charts illustrate these trends. The first chart, "Growth in assets and major financial sector legislation," tracks asset growth indexed to December 1992. It shows that after the SEC Uniform Net Capital Rule change in 2004, the assets of the five largest broker-dealers skyrocketed to an index level near 900, reaching 4.2 trillion dollars by late 2007. In contrast, the assets of 513 commercial banks with over one billion dollars in assets grew at a much steadier pace, ending at 10 trillion dollars with an index level near 400. The second chart, "Lehman's evolution into a leveraged, risky portfolio accelerated after SEC rule repeal," plots Lehman's stock price alongside a simulated portfolio of stocks, high-yield bonds, and high-grade bonds leveraged at 85 percent from 1994 to late 2007. Prior to the rule change, Lehman's stock did not track this portfolio, but after the 2004 SEC policy change, the stock price closely mirrored the highly leveraged, high-risk index, highlighting how leveraged Lehman's balance sheet had become.

The page concludes with observations from Eric Rosengren, President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, regarding broker-dealer stability. Rosengren points out that the most dramatic runs of the financial crisis targeted broker-dealers, noting that Lehman's collapse was part of a systemic vulnerability that also caused the failure of Bear Stearns, the acquisition of Merrill Lynch, and the conversion of Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley into bank holding companies. Because broker-dealers fund their holdings in uninsured, short-term credit markets, they remain inherently vulnerable to sudden liquidity runs when confidence falters. While capital ratios and liquidity have improved since the crisis, the author notes that broker-dealers' reliance on wholesale funding remains high, even though broker-dealer repo usage has declined from 70 percent of liabilities in 2008 to 50 percent.

This page, from J.P. Morgan’s "GFC: Ten Years Later" retrospective, examines how individual bank and broker-dealer actions contributed to systemic risk leading up to the Global Financial Crisis. The analysis centers on a multidimensional bubble chart titled "Changing leverage, pre-crisis compensation and post-crisis writedowns." This chart plots the change in balance-sheet leverage (assets to equity) from 2003 to 2007 on the horizontal axis, ranging from -40% to 120%, against writedowns from 2007 to the second quarter of 2011 as a percentage of pre-crisis tangible common equity on the vertical axis, ranging from 0% to over 350%. The size of each bank's bubble represents how much management paid itself and its employees as a percentage of operating income from 2004 to 2007. 

The primary takeaway is that institutions positioned in the lower-left quadrant with smaller bubbles behaved more prudently. These firms, such as J.P. Morgan, Wells Fargo, and US Bancorp, reduced their leverage heading into the crisis, suffered far lower writedown rates, and shared a larger portion of their net income with shareholders instead of management. In contrast, institutions like Wachovia, Washington Mutual, and National City experienced devastating writedowns that exceeded 300% of their tangible common equity. Meanwhile, Merrill Lynch is depicted as an exceptionally large bubble on the far right, signaling high pre-crisis compensation alongside a leverage increase of roughly 100% and writedowns near 200%. 

The author includes several critical notes to provide context for these metrics. First, the relatively low writedowns shown for Goldman Sachs are subject to lingering debate because the firm was bailed out of its American International Group exposure at 100 cents on the dollar by the Federal Reserve, ultimately receiving the largest share of AIG bailout funds directly attributable to specific counterparties. Second, the losses for Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers are understated on the chart because the data only reflects realized losses through 2008, when both entities were either acquired or liquidated. Lastly, the losses shown for European banks, such as Deutsche Bank, Barclays, Royal Bank of Scotland, and HSBC, are also understated because they only capture the first wave of European bank losses from 2007 to 2010, omitting the second wave that transpired between 2011 and 2015.

This page, titled "Underwriting decisions by rating agencies, bond reinsurers and institutional investors," is part of a series reflecting on the Global Financial Crisis ten years later. Michael Cembalest argues that the pre-crisis market euphoria was fueled by banks originating poorly underwritten loans, rating agencies approving their designs, reinsurers insuring them, and institutional investors purchasing them. He highlights that in 2007, the cushion below AAA investors in securitized commercial real estate transactions fell to a critical level of 5%, meaning a minor 5% property writedown would inflict losses on AAA investors. Furthermore, monoline insurers worsened the risk by diversifying away from stable municipal bonds to untested structured credit, while a low Federal Reserve interest rate of 1% starting in 2004 further accelerated credit growth.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, "Property decline cushion for AAA CMBS Investors," traces AAA CMBS subordination adjusted for rating agency loan-to-value ratios from 2001 to 2018. It shows the protective cushion collapsing from approximately 35% in 2001 down to 5% in 2007, spiking back to around 35% by 2010, and then drifting down to just under 20% by 2018.

The second chart, "US asset-backed securities," shows the total amount outstanding in billions of US dollars from 1990 to 2016. The structured credit market peaked in late 2007 at around $5.5 trillion, dominated by non-agency residential mortgage-backed securities, collateralized debt obligations, and non-agency commercial mortgage-backed securities, before steadily declining to under $3 trillion by 2016.

The third chart, "Monolines become multi-lines," illustrates municipals as a percentage of annual industry net par insured risk from 1991 to 2005. Looking at a universe of insurers including AMBAC, MBIA, American General, CIFG, FGIC, FSA, SCA, ACA, and Radian, the share of municipal risk plummeted from roughly 90% in the early 1990s to a low of nearly 35% in 1999, before hovering around 40% to 50% by 2005. This demonstrates how monolines rapidly shifted their portfolios toward structured credit.

The final chart, "Structured credit market accelerated in 2004, in the wake of a 1% Fed Funds rate," plots the Federal Funds rate against structured credit as a percentage of GDP from 1990 to 2008. It highlights that the Fed's decision to lower rates to 1% in the early 2000s catalyzed a dramatic rise in structured credit, which rose from roughly 10% of GDP in 2000 to nearly 40% of GDP by 2008.

This page, titled "Aftermath: substantial improvements in capital, liquidity and shadow banking," argues that post-financial crisis regulatory changes have significantly reduced systemic risk in the banking sector. To support this observation, the page features four charts comparing metrics from the pre-crisis era to the decade following the Great Financial Crisis.

The first chart, "Rising capital ratios since crisis," shows risk-weighted capital ratios in the US and Europe, comparing 2007 to 2017. Risk-weighted capital ratios rose significantly in both regions, with the US ratio increasing from approximately 9 percent to 14 percent, and the European ratio doubling from about 8 percent to nearly 16 percent. 

The second chart, "Improving liquidity ratios since crisis," measures liquid assets as a percentage of short-term liabilities. Between 2007 and 2017, this ratio grew in the US from roughly 41 percent to 48 percent. In Europe, it experienced a similar upward trajectory, rising from about 35 percent to 43 percent, reflecting a stronger buffer of liquid assets.

The third chart illustrates "Bank loan-to-deposit ratios" from 1995 to 2017. US banks steadily lowered their loan-to-deposit ratios from a peak of nearly 100 percent in 2001 and 2008 to around 75 percent in 2017. Eurozone banks experienced a more dramatic shift, with their ratio climbing to nearly 140 percent around 2008 before falling sharply to just above 100 percent by 2017. This downward trend indicates a healthier, deposit-backed funding structure across both regions.

The fourth chart, "A shift to lower risk money market funds," tracks assets under management in US trillions from 2002 to 2018, comparing Prime funds with Government funds. Key events are marked on the timeline, including the Lehman Crash in late 2008 and the implementation of Money Market Reform in late 2016. Following the Lehman Crash, government funds experienced a noticeable influx, but the 2016 reform triggered a massive structural shift: assets in higher-risk Prime funds plummeted to under 0.5 trillion dollars, while assets in safer Government funds surged past 2.0 trillion dollars.

Overall, the page illustrates how regulatory measures, such as the 2016 Money Market Reform, and institutional adjustments have successfully funneled capital into safer, more liquid instruments while bolstering the capital buffers of major US and European banks.

This page examines the economic foundations of Senator Elizabeth Warren’s proposed wealth tax, which would impose a two percent annual levy on household assets exceeding fifty million dollars. The author argues that the underlying research supporting the proposal—specifically the wealth and income inequality estimates by economists Emmanuel Saez, Thomas Piketty, and Gabriel Zucman—relies on sensitive assumptions and may overestimate the growth of inequality in the United States. 

The critique is supported by two line charts. The first chart, titled Top 1% Wealth Share in the US, plots the share of total national wealth held by the top one percent from 1960 to 2010. It compares three different estimation techniques: the estate tax multiplier method, the Survey of Consumer Finances method, and the capitalization method developed by Saez. While the Saez capitalization method shows a steep upward trend starting in the late 1970s, climbing from under thirty percent to nearly forty percent, the alternative approaches depict a much flatter trajectory. The Survey of Consumer Finances method peaks around thirty-four percent, and the estate tax multiplier method actually declines to around twenty percent, suggesting that top wealth shares may not have risen significantly since the 1960s. 

The second chart, Top 1% Income Shares in the US, displays the top one percent’s share of total national income from 1960 to 2015, comparing the Saez/Piketty method to a revised Treasury and Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) method. The Saez/Piketty data depicts a sharp rise in the income share of the top one percent, surging from approximately nine percent in the late 1970s to over twenty percent by 2015. In contrast, the Treasury/JCT method, which adjusts for changes in tax law distortions and uses a broader definition of income, shows the top one percent's share rising only modestly from around nine percent in 1960 to roughly ten percent in 2015. The JCT and Treasury authors conclude that the actual increase in income inequality over this multi-decade period is just one-tenth of what Saez and Piketty report, pointing out that unadjusted tax returns present a highly distorted view of inequality trends.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market report, themed around the tenth anniversary of the Global Financial Crisis, analyzes individual financial institutions' contributions to systemic risk during the crisis. Michael Cembalest focuses on the collateral pledged to the Federal Reserve's emergency Primary Dealer Credit Facility (PDCF), which extended $9 trillion in collateralized loans to banks and broker-dealers in 2008 and 2009. The author argues that examining these cumulative balances and the riskiness of the collateral pledged—such as junk bonds, unrated securities, and equities—helps quantify each firm's systemic risk footprint at the time, even though the facility was successfully closed in 2010 with all loans repaid in full.

A horizontal bar chart illustrates the cumulative collateral postings to the PDCF in trillions of dollars, broken down by collateral quality: investment grade, non-investment grade, unrated/loans, and equities. Merrill Lynch led all firms, posting over $2.2 trillion in total collateral, characterized by substantial portions of non-investment grade assets, unrated loans, and equities. Citigroup followed closely with nearly $2.2 trillion in cumulative postings of a similarly diverse and risky collateral mix. Morgan Stanley occupied the third spot at over $2.1 trillion, standing out for its exceptionally large share of high-risk equity collateral. In contrast, Bear Stearns, which ranked fourth at roughly $1.1 trillion, pledged almost entirely lower-risk investment-grade collateral. Other major institutions like Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, and Barclays posted much smaller cumulative amounts, each below $0.7 trillion. 

To provide a comprehensive view of government support, an accompanying table displays total facility usage by firm across twelve emergency facilities, including the PDCF, various Maiden Lane vehicles, AIG facilities, and the Term Auction Facility. Citigroup was the largest total user of these facilities at $2.830 trillion, representing 14.0% of the total program usage. Merrill Lynch was second at $2.449 trillion (12.1%), followed by Morgan Stanley at $2.305 trillion (11.4%). Other significant users of these facilities included Bank of America at $1.129 trillion (5.6%), AIG at $1.047 trillion (5.2%), Goldman Sachs at $1.033 trillion (5.1%), Barclays at $1.030 trillion (5.1%), BNP Paribas at $1.002 trillion (5.0%), and Bear Stearns at $976 billion (4.8%). All other participants collectively accounted for $3.323 trillion, or 16.5% of total facility usage.

This page contains legal and regulatory disclosures for the publication. It outlines the compliance requirements and restrictions across different jurisdictions, specifically detailing regulations under the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission and the Australian Securities and Investment Commission. The text clarifies that the material is intended solely for wholesale clients in Australia and explains licensing exemptions under the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) for J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, which is regulated by the US SEC, FINRA, and CFTC. It concludes with standard disclaimers regarding currency references, non-Australian financial standards, tax issues, and restrictions on distribution.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market," authored by Michael Cembalest, examines how United States banks have restructured their funding ten years after the Global Financial Crisis. The central argument is that the banking system has become safer by shifting away from fragile wholesale funding sources, like interbank loans and repos, in favor of stable customer deposits, which has subsequently shrunk the footprint of the shadow banking sector. 

This structural shift is illustrated first through a chart showing US commercial bank assets from 1990 to 2018. It shows that customer deposits as a percentage of assets climbed dramatically from a low of around 60% before the crisis to over 75% by 2018, while interbank loans simultaneously cratered from around 5% of assets to less than 1%. 

Another chart details repo usage by financial intermediaries from 1970 to 2018. The overall repo market declined from $4.2 trillion to $2.2 trillion after 2008, driven by broker-dealers shrinking their balance sheets. Consequently, repos as a share of broker-dealer liabilities fell from a pre-crisis peak of over 70% to approximately 50%, while foreign banks in the US stayed around 15% and domestic US banks remained near zero. Cembalest notes that while 50% remains high, the risk is mitigated by higher-quality collateral and longer-term repo structures.

The middle of the page addresses the contraction of the shadow banking sector, noting that its share of liabilities has fallen back to levels last seen in the year 2000. This is partly due to a reduction in securities lending by institutional investors, as shown in a stacked area chart from 2007 to 2015. Securities lending against cash collateral—primarily driven by retirement and pension plans, mutual funds, and insurance companies—plummeted from an pre-crisis peak of nearly $1.2 trillion to around $0.4 trillion by 2015. The remaining activity is structured with higher-quality investments than in 2008.

The bottom portion of the page, featuring data from economists Stephen Cecchetti of Brandeis and Kermit Schoenholtz of NYU, visually contrasts shadow banking and traditional banking liabilities as a percentage of GDP from 1960 to 2015. Traditional commercial banking liabilities have remained relatively stable, whereas shadow banking liabilities surged from near-zero in the 1960s to a peak of over 110% of GDP just before the crisis, subsequently retreating to around 80% by 2015. Bank holding companies and broker-dealers also saw their liabilities decline to around 20% of GDP. This contraction is reflected in the final chart, which shows the commercial bank share of intermediation. This share had steadily plummeted from 95% in 1960 to a trough of about 35% during the financial crisis, but has since rebounded to nearly 50% as traditional commercial banks reclaim market share from broker-dealers and other non-banks.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the political economics of wealth and income redistribution, challenging arguments that advocate for a 70% top marginal tax rate or Elizabeth Warren's proposed wealth tax on households with assets over $50 million by appealing to historical precedent. He argues that progressive advocates and journalists should not justify these taxes by claiming that the rich used to pay much higher tax rates in the past, as the top 1% paid roughly the same effective tax rate decades ago as they do today. He also cautions that the academic research on wealth taxes by Emmanuel Saez, Thomas Piketty, and Gabriel Zucman has faced significant criticism regarding its assumptions and methodology from the US Treasury, the Federal Reserve, the Joint Committee on Taxation, and professors at Columbia University.

To support his argument, Cembalest points out that statutory tax rates are misleading without context regarding deductions and tax brackets. For example, in 1955, the top tax bracket applied only to incomes equivalent to $3.5 million in today's dollars, compared to just $466,000 in 2019. 

The page contains two line charts illustrating effective tax rates over time. The first chart, titled "What the top 1% pay in Federal taxes hasn't changed much despite the decline in the top statutory rate," covers the years 1979 to 2015, with the vertical axis representing percentages from 0% to 70%. It compares two series using data from the Congressional Budget Office and the Internal Revenue Service. The first series shows the top statutory Federal income tax rate, which starts at 70% in 1979, falls sharply to around 28% in the late 1980s, and then hovers between 35% and 40% through 2015. The second series represents the effective Federal tax rate for the top 1%, including income, payroll, and excise taxes. Despite the massive drop in the statutory rate, this effective rate remains extremely stable, fluctuating within a narrow band between roughly 20% and 25% over the entire thirty-six-year period.

The second chart, titled "Average effective tax rate on the top 1% including all Federal, state and local taxes," covers 1955 to 2015, with a vertical axis spanning 0% to 50%. Based on data from Piketty, Saez, and Zucman, the chart shows that even when including all layers of taxation—such as payroll, property, and excise taxes—the total effective tax rate on the top 1% has historically stayed within a steady range. The line starts at nearly 40% in 1955, experiences modest declines to a low of about 30% around 1985, rises back toward 40% in the late 1990s, and ends at approximately 35% in 2015. 

Cembalest concludes by noting a fundamental shift in the composition of government spending since the 1960s. He highlights that in the 1960s, the Federal government spent $0.60 on entitlements for every dollar spent on growth-fueling discretionary programs like infrastructure, job retraining, and R&D. Currently, the government spends $3.30 on entitlements for every dollar of discretionary spending, and Congressional Budget Office projections estimate this will rise to $4.50 per dollar by 2025.

Michael Cembalest begins the commentary by addressing the erosion of truthfulness in political discourse, highlighting that neither political party possesses an unblemished record. He warns that the United States may be heading toward its most ideologically charged presidential election in a century. Supporting this argument are two charts. 

The first chart plots the cumulative false or misleading claims by President Trump according to the Washington Post Factchecker Database. The curve climbs dramatically from zero in January 2017 to nearly 8,000 by January 2019. 

The second chart, titled "Presidential administration ideology and a look at 2020," utilizes roll-call vote data to map the ideological stance of US administrations since 1916 on a scale from most liberal (-0.7) to most conservative (0.7). It shows Donald Trump situated near 0.6, while mapping potential 2020 Democratic candidates. These challengers are grouped into moderates around -0.25 (such as Joe Biden, Michael Bennet, Amy Klobuchar, and Beto O'Rourke), progressives around -0.45 (Sherrod Brown, Kirsten Gillibrand, and Carol Moseley Braun), and ultra-progressives clustered near -0.55 (Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, Kamala Harris, and Cory Booker). This layout underscores a widening ideological divide.

The page also features an appendix examining the constitutionality of wealth taxes and potential de facto alternatives known as Wealth Integration Methods. Cembalest explains that while direct wealth taxes face constitutional hurdles under the 16th Amendment, Wealth Integration Methods would instead use wealth as an input for income tax calculations to achieve a similar outcome. Citing a January 2019 paper by law professor Ari Glogower, the text suggests that courts are likely to accept these integration methods, which might ultimately pave the way for Congress to tax wealth directly. Expected tools of this policy include deduction phase-outs, increased marginal tax rates based on wealth levels, mark-to-market valuation for liquid assets, and unified tax rates for income and capital gains. Footnotes on the page provide additional context, referencing President Obama’s 2013 "Lie of the Year" regarding the Affordable Care Act to illustrate bipartisan exaggerations, and highlighting existing tax code precedents that already function as de facto wealth taxes.

This page consists entirely of standard legal disclaimers and regulatory disclosures for J.P. Morgan, specifically outlining licensing exemptions and compliance notifications under Australian financial services regulations for wholesale clients, as well as general copyright information.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest analyzes the dramatic equity market rebound from late December lows, attributing the initial rally to intensive short-covering rather than long-term institutional inflows, while exploring how a shift in Federal Reserve policy has provided further support.

The first chart, titled "Mirror images: as the shorts cover, equity market rallies," illustrates a tight inverse relationship between the S&P 500 index level on the right axis and short interest percentage on the left axis from June 2018 to February 2019. When the S&P 500 bottomed near 2,350 in late December 2018, short interest peaked at nearly 7%. As the index rebounded back toward 2,750 by February 2019, short interest collapsed to approximately 2%, confirming that short covering catalyzed the rebound. 

The second chart, "S&P 500 rebound not accompanied by real money flows," plots the S&P 500 index level against cumulative U.S. equity flows in billions of dollars from January 2018 to January 2019. It highlights a stark divergence: while the S&P 500 recovered significantly from its December trough, cumulative equity flows continued their steep decline, falling to a deficit of nearly negative $80 billion by January 2019, proving a lack of "real money" participation in the early stage of the rally.

The third chart, "Valuations for stocks and corporate bonds," shows historical valuation percentiles across five asset classes: U.S. equities, European equities, Emerging Market equities, high-yield debt, and high-grade debt. The chart compares three periods: the peak of 2018, the trough on December 26, and current February 2019 levels. Valuations across all asset classes plummeted on December 26—with Emerging Markets dropping to about the 10th percentile and US equities and high yield dropping below the 30th percentile—before recovering to near-median levels between the 40th and 60th percentiles by February.

The final chart, "Fed models suggest that equilibrium policy rates might only need to be 50-100 bps over inflation," displays two versions of the modeled equilibrium real rate of interest from 1980 to 2018 based on research by Holston, Laubach, and Williams at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Both versions illustrate a structural decline in the equilibrium real rate from a range of 3.0% to 4.0% in the 1980s and 1990s down to approximately 0.5% to 1.0% by the end of the period.

Cembalest attributes the Federal Reserve’s pause in rate hikes to this research alongside a fear of market volatility and political pressure from the President. He observes that real Fed policy rates remain slightly below these modeled equilibrium levels. Looking ahead, Cembalest warns that if the labor market continues to tighten—noting that U.S. job openings reached an all-time high in December—the Fed will face difficult policy decisions, concluding with the prediction that one more interest rate hike is coming later in 2019.

This page addresses two separate topics: the escalating US-China technology rivalry and a critique of Senator Marco Rubio's proposal to tax corporate stock buybacks. 

First, a commentary box highlights the next steps in the China-US rivalry, detailing more aggressive US export controls aimed at denying Chinese firms access to US technology. This includes restricting cross-border sales containing US components and enforcing deemed export restrictions that might require US tech companies to segregate Chinese nationals from projects involving critical emerging and foundational technologies. Highlighted technology sectors subject to these controls include biotechnology, neurotechnology, advanced computing, machine learning, robotics, hypersonics, advanced materials, and surveillance. 

The primary article critiques a December 2018 proposal by Senator Marco Rubio to change US tax laws so that corporate stock buybacks trigger an imputed dividend tax for all shareholders. The author questions the senator's underlying assumption that buybacks divert resources away from hiring and capital spending, pointing to robust economic data instead. This counterargument is supported by two charts. 

The first chart, titled Job openings rate, tracks US job openings from 2000 through late 2018 using Bureau of Labor Statistics data. It shows the job openings rate climbing from a post-recession low of under two percent in 2009 to a historic high near four and a half percent in late 2018, representing the largest number of US job openings on record. 

The second chart, titled US fixed investment, indexes various categories of non-residential investment from December 2011 to late 2018, with December 2011 set as one hundred. Drawing from Bureau of Economic Analysis data, the chart tracks five key areas: Research and Development, Software, Structures, Information processing equipment, and Industrial equipment. All five series exhibit upward trajectories, particularly after 2016, with Research and Development and Software leading the growth by reaching index values near one hundred and forty-five to one hundred and fifty by late 2017. The author concludes that US companies are actively investing and hiring despite ongoing trade tensions. A footnote adds context on US dividend tax rates, noting they are typically taxed at twenty percent plus a three point eight percent Affordable Care Act tax.

This page from the publication discusses the key drivers behind the early 2019 market rebound and outlines the investment outlook for the remainder of the year. Michael Cembalest points to a shrinking universe of publicly traded equities as a favorable technical backdrop that aids market recovery during institutional rebalancing. This trend is illustrated in the first chart, "A proxy for US equity supply," which plots the S&P 500 Index Divisor from 1997 through 2018. Reflecting buybacks, mergers and acquisitions, and de-listings, the divisor peaked near 9.3 around 2004 before steadily declining to approximately 8.6 by 2018. 

The author also highlights expected positive momentum from Chinese fiscal stimulus and potential trade resolutions that could postpone or cancel 25% tariffs on $200 billion to $460 billion of Chinese imports. This stimulus is detailed in the bar chart "More China fiscal stimulus on the way," which breaks down tax and spending measures as a percentage of GDP from 2015 to a 2019 estimate. Total stimulus is projected to reach approximately 2.9% of GDP in 2019—consisting of roughly 1.9% in tax cuts and 1.0% in spending—reversing the lower levels seen in 2017 when spending stimulus fell below -0.1%.

However, Cembalest cautions that the stock rally may stall due to corporate profit deceleration and risks surrounding auto tariff threats on Europe and Japan. He notes that leading indicators for US earnings and earnings breadth are softening, raising the possibility of slightly negative year-over-year growth in S&P 500 earnings for 2019, with a low point expected in the second quarter. This is demonstrated in the line chart comparing S&P 500 year-over-year earnings-per-share growth with an earnings leading indicator from 1989 to 2019. The leading indicator has turned sharply downward, converging toward 0% growth. This negative sentiment is further supported by the chart "S&P 500 earnings revisions," which measures the three-month moving average of positive minus negative earnings revisions as a percentage of total companies. This line shows a dramatic collapse from a peak of nearly 35% in 2018 down past -20% by February 2019. 

In conclusion, Cembalest maintains a steady investment strategy for 2019, recommending normal risk allocations. Although US GDP growth is forecasted to slow to 2% by year-end, J.P. Morgan does not foresee a significant risk of a US recession in 2019. A dovish Federal Reserve and ongoing Chinese stimulus are expected to support equity valuations, potentially lifting them toward 2018 highs. From a regional allocation standpoint, the publication expresses a preference for Emerging Markets over Europe for deep value, noting that their overweight position in US and Emerging Markets equities relative to Europe and Japan is outperforming once again, on track to achieve this outperformance for the 10th time in the last 13 years.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the historic performance slump of New York professional sports teams during the 2017–2018 period. He highlights that, for a fan of all New York major sports teams, the recent stretch has been one of the worst in history. Since 1950, the combined winning percentage of these teams has only been lower once, which was during the 1966–1967 season. Furthermore, the number of playoff appearances has plummeted to levels not seen since the 1950s and 1960s, a time before several franchise expansions even occurred. Cembalest connects this poor performance to the cost of ticket prices, analyzing whether New Yorkers are overpaying for their sports entertainment.

To support his observations, Cembalest presents three charts. The first line chart, titled Average winning percentage of NY sports teams, tracks the combined winning percentage of nine teams: the Mets, Yankees, Knicks, Nets, Jets, Giants, Bills, Rangers, and Islanders from 1950 to 2018. The line fluctuated generally between 44% and 58% over the decades, but the 2017–2018 period shows a steep drop to near 41%, nearly matching the historical low of the mid-1960s. 

The adjacent line chart, titled Number of playoff appearances, NY sports teams, tracks playoff appearances for the same nine teams on a scale of 0 to 7. While playoff appearances peaked at 7 in the early 1980s and 2000s, they crashed to just 1 in 2018, which is the worst mark since the pre-expansion era of the 1950s and 1960s.

A stacked bar chart at the bottom, titled Daily ticket price package for 4-sport cities, displays the cost of general seating ticket packages for cities with teams across four major sports leagues: the NFL, NBA, MLB, and NHL. The chart distinguishes two separate New York team combinations. The NYC 1 package, which includes the Giants, Knicks, Yankees, and Rangers, is the most expensive in the country at over $350. Meanwhile, the NYC 2 package, featuring the Jets, Nets, Mets, and Islanders, is much more moderate at roughly $230, making it cheaper than Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Washington D.C., and Philadelphia.

A historical footnote details the disastrous 1966 season, noting that the Giants finished 1-12, the Yankees finished last for the first time since 1912, and Yankee Stadium saw a record-low paid attendance of 413 people on September 22. Announcer Red Barber lost his contract shortly after drawing attention to the nearly empty stadium.

This analysis focuses on the immense challenges of decarbonizing the global industrial sector, which is currently the largest global user of energy. While transport and electricity generation have seen progress in decarbonization, the industrial sector remains heavily reliant on fossil fuels. Achieving deep decarbonization in this sector would require two major, difficult steps: substituting electricity for direct thermal heat and pressure, and significantly increasing the share of renewable energy on the power grid.

The dominance of fossil fuels is illustrated by a pie chart showing global industrial energy consumption by source. Only 15 percent of industrial energy is currently derived from electricity, and a mere 7 percent comes from renewables. In contrast, liquid fuels lead at 29 percent, followed by coal at 26 percent and natural gas at 23 percent. This fossil fuel consumption is concentrated in a few key product sectors, as shown in a horizontal bar chart of global industrial energy consumption by product. Basic chemicals and iron and steel are the largest consumers, each accounting for roughly 15 to 16 percent of the total, followed by refining at around 9 percent, nonmetallic minerals at 7 to 8 percent, and smaller shares for food, paper, and nonferrous metals.

A major economic barrier to electrifying these industrial processes is cost. A bar chart comparing the ratio of industrial electricity prices to natural gas prices per megajoule reveals that electricity is consistently three to five times more expensive. For instance, in coal-heavy Germany and the United Kingdom, electricity is approximately five times more expensive than natural gas, while in major US industrial states like Texas, Indiana, and Ohio, the ratio is still three to four times higher. In California, the ratio exceeds five times. Compounding this price disparity is the fact that switching to electricity would require massive capital investments in new power generation. Additionally, in nations like China and Germany where coal remains a substantial share of grid electricity, substituting electricity for natural gas could actually increase carbon emissions in the near term. This economic reality is contrasted with a theoretical 2018 study by the Wuppertal Institute in Germany, which estimated that in the absence of cost considerations, 100 percent of German industrial steam and 25 percent of industrial fuel use could successfully be displaced by electricity. 

To illustrate why fossil fuels are so deeply embedded in industry, two tables detail their specific applications. The first table outlines the use of fossil fuels as raw materials, where metallurgical coke acts as a carbon source for smelting pig iron into steel, methane serves as a hydrogen source for ammonia synthesis to make fertilizers, methane, naphtha, and ethane are used to synthesize plastics, and heavy petroleum products are converted into carbon black for rubber tires. The second table highlights the use of fossil fuels for generating high-temperature process heat, which is essential for manufacturing construction materials like cement, bricks, tiles, glass, and kiln-dried timber, as well as for producing petrochemicals, food and beverage processing, and smelting iron ores in blast furnaces.

This page argues that decarbonizing the electricity grid has clear limits because electricity represents only seventeen percent of total global final energy consumption, while the remaining eighty-three percent consists of direct energy use such as combustion engines, industrial heating, smelting, and raw materials. To illustrate these constraints, the page presents several charts detailing global energy flows, fossil fuel reliance, and demographic trends.

The first visual, a stacked bar chart of global energy consumed by end-user in 2017, demonstrates how primary energy for electricity—consisting of renewables, nuclear, natural gas, coal, and petroleum—flows to end-users. When distributed across the industrial, transport, and residential or commercial sectors, electricity makes up only a small fraction of the total energy consumed. The industrial sector is shown to be the largest overall energy consumer, relying heavily on direct fossil fuels. Meanwhile, the transport sector is almost entirely dependent on petroleum, with electricity representing a negligible sliver. 

An adjacent pie chart reinforces this point by illustrating that electricity accounts for less than one-third of global fossil fuel consumption. Out of the global total, three hundred forty-one quadrillion BTUs of fossil fuels are used directly for non-electrical purposes, compared to one hundred forty-one quadrillion BTUs used indirectly to generate electricity. 

A third chart tracks the historical and projected percentage of global primary energy consumption derived from fossil fuels from 1965 to 2040. It shows that fossil fuels accounted for approximately eighty-five percent of global energy in 2017, down from over ninety-four percent in the mid-1960s. This decline is marked by two distinct periods: the nuclear adoption era of the 1970s and 1980s, and the solar and wind era starting around 2010, during which fossil fuel market share began declining by about a quarter of a percent per year. International Energy Agency estimates project this share to drop further, reaching roughly seventy-eight percent by 2040. 

A final line chart displays global urbanization trends from 1950 to 2050 using United Nations data, showing rising urban population percentages for Japan, the United States, Europe, South America, China, Africa, and India. The author uses these upward trajectories—which project most regions to be majority-urban by 2050—to argue that energy solutions must be tailored for highly urbanized societies, making decentralized, off-the-grid approaches largely irrelevant. 

The commentary notes that because electricity and fossil fuel shares in the United States, China, and Europe are similar to these global averages, Germany faces immense challenges in meeting its target of a forty percent emissions decline by 2030. It likewise notes the steep hurdles the United States faces with any plan aiming for net-zero emissions by the same year. A footnote highlights regional differences, pointing out that the United States uses more energy for transport than industry and relies more heavily on natural gas than coal, whereas China exhibits the opposite pattern. Nonetheless, in both countries, electricity makes up less than twenty percent of energy use, and fossil fuels account for more than eighty percent of primary energy.

This page presents a historical overview and future consumption projections for the four industrial pillars of modern society: cement, steel, ammonia, and plastics. The author notes that although production growth for these materials has recently slowed due to a cooling Chinese economy, the International Energy Agency expects global consumption for all four to rise significantly by 2050. Specifically, consumption is projected to rise by 12% for cement, 30% for steel, 60% for ammonia, and 150% for plastics. The text highlights the critical role of ammonia in the global food supply, noting that half of the world's population relies on it as a fertilizer input, while also pointing out that 40% to 70% of applied ammonia is lost to leaching, erosion, or de-nitrification, making usage efficiency key to decarbonization goals.

The page features several charts tracing the production history of these materials from 1950 through approximately 2017. The top two charts display production indices set to 1 in 1950 to illustrate relative growth and carbon-based inputs. The first shows that by 2010, the production of ammonia (relying on methane as an input) and cement (using coal and petroleum coke) grew roughly 30-fold, while steel (using metallurgical coke and natural gas) grew about 7-fold. The second top chart depicts a dramatic, near-exponential surge in plastics production (relying on methane, naphtha, and ethane), which expanded to around 170 times its 1950 level by 2010.

Four subsequent charts display absolute production volumes in millions of tonnes. The cement chart illustrates a rise from less than 500 million tonnes in 1950 to over 4,000 million tonnes, noting that China produced 2,500 million tonnes of cement in 2017—nearly ten times the volume of the next largest producer, India—and consumed almost all of it domestically. The steel chart shows global production rising from approximately 200 million tonnes in 1950 to more than 1,600 million tonnes, highlighting that China's share of global production grew from 36% in 2007 to 50% in 2017. The ammonia chart documents an increase from under 20 million tonnes to about 150 million tonnes, pointing out that China produces 33% of the world's ammonia (followed by India, Russia, and the US) and that 85% of it goes toward fertilizer. Finally, the plastics chart tracks production growing from near zero to roughly 400 million tonnes, categorized by sector. Packaging is shown as the largest single demand driver, followed in descending order by building and construction, textiles, consumer and institutional products, transportation, and electrical or electronic applications.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market examines the immense physical and economic scale challenges facing carbon capture and storage as a primary de-carbonization strategy. While a 2018 US Congressional bill introduced tax credits of thirty-five to fifty dollars per tonne of sequestered carbon dioxide to encourage development, actual global progress remains minimal, with operating facilities capturing just one-tenth of one percent of global emissions by the end of 2018. The author details numerous head-winds, including a thirty-percent energy penalty on coal plants, legal liabilities, and massive project failures like the Kemper Clean Coal plant in Mississippi, which Mississippi Power and Southern Company abandoned after going four billion dollars over budget. 

The primary argument focuses on the sheer physical scale required to make a difference. To sequester just fifteen percent of global emissions, or five billion metric tons of carbon dioxide, the transport and storage infrastructure would need to handle six billion cubic meters of gas annually. An accompanying bar chart illustrates this point by comparing the mass and volume of sequestered carbon dioxide against global oil extraction. The chart show that five billion metric tons of sequestered carbon dioxide translates to more than six billion cubic meters of volume under supercritical storage conditions. In contrast, total global oil extraction stands at roughly four point four billion metric tons, which equates to five point one billion cubic meters of volume. The author highlights that building a carbon-handling infrastructure larger than the global oil ecosystem, which took over a century to construct, is a daunting task. Consequently, the author remains highly skeptical of its feasibility, predicting that global carbon capture is unlikely to exceed five percent of total carbon dioxide emissions by 2030 and awarding the technology a low overall grade.

This page analyzes the potential and limitations of forest management, specifically reforestation and afforestation, as a low-tech means of sequestering carbon dioxide in the United States. US forestland currently covers roughly 750 million acres and captures 10% of annual US greenhouse gas emissions. However, returning to historical levels of forestation—such as the 900 million acres that existed in 1850—is deemed highly unlikely due to infrastructure conversion and a sixfold increase in the US population since then. 

To illustrate the historical context, a line chart titled "US forests offset 10% of annual GHG emissions" displays data from 1990 to 2014 in million metric tons of CO2 equivalents per year. The chart plots total GHG emissions and GHG emissions from energy, which both hover between 5,000 and 7,000 million metric tons, alongside a negative line representing the carbon sink from forests and land use changes, which remains stable near the -750 to -1,000 million metric ton level. A neighboring pie chart, titled "Cleared US forestland by disturbance source, 2014," breaks down why US forests are cleared. Fire is the dominant driver at 62%, followed by other natural causes at 12%, grazing at 11%, insects at 5%, timber harvesting at 4%, drought at 3%, and disease at 3%. 

The text details the operational hurdles of scaling up these natural solutions. Reforestation—replanting cleared areas without changing land use—could sequester 50 million metric tons of GHGs annually if 20 million acres of disturbed land were replanted, offsetting nearly 1% of US emissions. However, this is a massive undertaking; in 2017, the US Forest Service reforested just 122,000 acres. Reforestation is increasingly needed to offset aging, less-absorbent forests, emissions from wildfires (which have averaged 60 to 80 million metric tons per year since 2013), and severe weather events, such as Hurricane Michael, which destroyed 3 million acres of trees in Florida in 2018. 

Afforestation—planting trees on previously unforested land like cropland or pastures—presents a separate opportunity. A 2018 study estimated that a carbon price of $15 per tonne could incentivize farmers to sequester 150 million metric tons of CO2 annually. However, this would require converting 7 to 10 million acres of agricultural land, a transition complicated by farmer decision-making, competing land demands for food or biofuels, and carbon verification risks. Ultimately, the author concludes that while reforestation and afforestation are viable, achieving an additional 3% sequestration of US emissions would require unprecedented private-sector participation and substantial economic costs.

This page analyzes and tempers the hype surrounding a May 2018 headline celebrating a joint venture financed by Apple, Alcoa, and Rio Tinto to develop a "carbon-free" aluminum smelting method. While the venture successfully created an advanced conductive material that releases oxygen instead of carbon dioxide during aluminum electrolysis, the author argues the technology's real-world impact is marginal. 

To support this, a bar chart sourced from the International Aluminum Institute illustrates greenhouse gas emissions by stage of the aluminum production process, measured in tonnes of CO2 equivalent per tonne of aluminum produced. The chart breaks down emissions across five stages: bauxite mining, alumina production, anode production, electrolysis (smelting), and ingot casting. While stages like alumina production generate around two tonnes of CO2 equivalent (primarily from thermal energy), electrolysis is by far the most carbon-intensive phase, totaling nearly 13 tonnes. Crucially, the chart shows that approximately 84% of these smelting emissions are derived from electricity generation, whereas the carbon anode itself accounts for only 16% (and a mere 10% of total emissions across the entire aluminum production lifecycle).

Because of this, even if the carbon anode were universally eliminated from global production, the maximum annual global CO2 reduction is capped at 138 million tons (assuming 63 million tons of global aluminum production). This represents a mere 0.4% reduction in annual global CO2 emissions. Consequently, the author concludes that the technology does not live up to claims of being "carbon-free smelting" or "changing global manufacturing," awarding it the lowest grade on a five-tier visual scale at the bottom of the page.

This page focuses on the viability of cellulosic ethanol as a renewable fuel source, expressing deep skepticism about its future prospects despite recent media hype, such as a segment on the television show 60 Minutes highlighting a company using electron beam accelerators to break down plant material. The author, Michael Cembalest, warns that the industry has a history of failed expectations, citing a 2006 prediction by venture capitalist Vinod Khosla that cellulosic ethanol production would reach 24.8 billion gallons by 2017, whereas actual production reached only about 10 million gallons. Many of the major companies that built plants to scale this technology, including DuPont, Abengoa, INEOS Bio, Range Fuels, and Cello Energy, are no longer in operation. 

The primary physical barriers to cellulosic ethanol are its low energy and volumetric density. Corn stover, the primary feedstock, has a volumetric density of just 6% compared to gasoline. Consequently, storing and transporting cellulosic ethanol at a scale that could rival gasoline would require an ecosystem 110 times larger than the existing gasoline infrastructure. Even under highly optimistic assumptions where all available US corn stover is harvested, the fuel would displace a negligible amount of oil. 

A detailed model in the accompanying table demonstrates this calculation. Beginning with 385 million metric tons of US corn production and a 1:1 stover-to-grain ratio, the model assumes a 40% midpoint stover removal percentage to protect soil health, yielding 154 billion kilograms of raw stover. After applying a 15% haircut for harvesting, evaporation, and transportation losses, 130.9 billion kilograms remain for conversion. Utilizing a conversion ratio of 0.32 liters per kilogram, this biomass produces 41.89 billion liters of ethanol. Because the energy density of cellulosic ethanol is only 66% of gasoline, this volume translates to 7.34 billion gasoline-equivalent gallons. Against the 142.98 billion gallons of total US gasoline consumption in 2017, this best-case scenario displace a mere 5% of total demand.

The page concludes with a horizontal bar chart depicting the US Energy Return on Investment (EROI) for various fuel sources. The data shows that while traditional energy sources and established renewables have high ratios—hydropower exceeds 100x, wind turbines return nearly 20x, oil and gas returns 15x, and photovoltaic solar returns roughly 6x—corn-based and cellulosic fuels perform exceptionally poorly. Corn-based ethanol, cellulosic n-butanol, cellulosic ethanol, cellulosic iso-butanol, and biodiesel are all grouped at the bottom of the chart, barely registering an energy return of 1.0x. A grade scale at the bottom left points toward a very low rating for the technology's overall viability.

This page examines the potential of supercapacitors as an alternative or complement to lithium-ion batteries for utility-scale energy storage. The author explains that supercapacitors store energy as a static charge rather than through electrochemical reactions, which gives them superior durability, faster charging, and negligible performance degradation over time. However, they currently trail lithium-ion batteries significantly in energy density and cost, though Tesla's acquisition of Maxwell Technologies could catalyze commercial scaling. 

The core of the page is a comparison table detailing the technical and economic trade-offs between the two technologies. Supercapacitors boast a massive lifecycle advantage of 1,000,000 cycles compared to just 2,000 to 10,000 for lithium-ion. They also function across a much wider temperature range (-30°C to 85°C, versus 0°C to 40°C for lithium-ion) and maintain a constant 99% round-trip DC efficiency with no risk of thermal runaway. On the other hand, lithium-ion batteries hold the edge in upfront capital costs, at $350 per kWh compared to $500 per kWh for supercapacitors before mass-production scaling. Lithium-ion also possesses a far superior system-level energy density of 150 to 260 Wh/kg (with potential for 400 to 500), whereas supercapacitors range from only 5 to 30 Wh/kg. Regarding environmental impact, supercapacitors defer disposal issues due to their long life, and while their carbon-based graphene construction is less toxic than lithium-ion, studies still show potential environmental impacts from graphene exposure.

The author concludes that utility-scale battery storage is still in its infancy, with unresolved engineering challenges around degradation, maintenance, and durability. This real-world degradation is highlighted by footnotes detailing how the French utility EDF de-rated its Illinois-based storage project by 30%, and how US utility AES experienced similar capacity losses, aligning with simulations by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL). Another real-world application cited is South Dakota-based Northwestern Energy’s partnership with Kilowatt Labs to use supercapacitor storage in low-density regions. 

Ultimately, both technologies receive low-to-moderate marks on the author's proprietary graphical grading scale, with lithium-ion rated slightly ahead of supercapacitors. However, the author notes that these grades could improve by 2025 if production scaling drives capital costs for either technology below $200 per kWh. Additional sources cited for this analysis include the Brattle Group, the Electric Power Research Institute, the National Graphene Institute, and Argonne National Laboratory.

This page examines the progress and impacts of Germany's "Energiewende" energy transition, arguing that its primary achievement has been successfully substituting solar and wind power for thermal and nuclear energy without sacrificing grid reliability. The author notes that renewable generation reached 38% of Germany's total electricity mix in 2017, and highlights Germany's target to reach 65% renewable generation by 2030. 

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, showing the share of total electricity generation in Germany from 1991 to 2017, illustrates the decline of thermal coal and gas from over 60% to around 45%, and nuclear from nearly 30% to roughly 12%. Simultaneously, all renewables rose to 38%, with solar and wind specifically climbing from near zero to about 20%. The second chart tracks Germany's capacity in gigawatts from 1991 to 2015, depicting how the dramatic build-out of solar and wind capacity rose from zero to approximately 85 gigawatts, successfully matching the country's thermal capacity. 

The third chart demonstrates that Germany possesses the largest wind and solar footprint in the developed world, plotting installed capacity in kilowatts per square kilometer against kilowatts per capita. Germany stands out in the upper right quadrant of the scatter plot with approximately 250 kilowatts per square kilometer and over 1.00 kilowatt per capita, surpassing other nations like Denmark, Belgium, and the Netherlands. Lastly, the fourth chart addresses grid reliability by comparing average annual power supply interruptions in minutes for 2016. It shows that Germany's average outage times actually improved from around 22 minutes in 2006 to just 15 minutes in 2017, representing one of the lowest outage rates in Europe, second only to Switzerland. By comparison, nations like Ireland and Norway experienced over 80 minutes of interruptions, and the comparable United States figure according to the Energy Information Administration was 128 minutes.

This page addresses the financial and structural challenges of Germany’s Energiewende energy transition policy, focusing on the high current costs of household electricity and the looming regional grid imbalances. The author argues that German household electricity costs are already among the highest in Europe, even before accounting for upcoming expenses related to transmission expansion, nuclear power substitution, and deeper renewable integration. While German household incomes align with those in France, Ireland, and the United Kingdom, making Germany's high electricity rates comparatively heavier, lower incomes in Italy and Spain mean those nations face real financial burdens closer to Germany's than nominal prices suggest.

A stacked bar chart titled "Electricity prices for household consumers," displaying data in EUR per kWh from the second quarter of 2018, highlights these disparities across dozens of European nations. Denmark and Germany lead the list with the highest overall consumer prices, with Germany positioned second at approximately 0.30 EUR per kWh, as highlighted by a red arrow. The chart breaks down electricity prices into three components: VAT, renewable energy levies and other taxes, and the cost without taxes. In Germany, renewable energy levies and other taxes make up a substantial portion of the consumer price, nearly matching the base electricity cost of roughly 0.13 EUR per kWh. The Euro Area and European Union averages sit much lower, at about 0.22 and 0.20 EUR per kWh, respectively, while France is significantly cheaper at around 0.17 EUR per kWh. 

Below the price chart, a geographical visualization titled "German regional power deficits expected to rise by 2030" illustrates the physical supply-demand challenge of the transition using data from Amprion GmbH. Comparing two maps of Germany—one representing the power balance in 2015 and the other projecting the balance for 2030—the graphic uses a color scale ranging from blue for power surplus to purple for power deficit. The 2015 map shows a largely balanced country with mild surpluses in the north and only faint, isolated deficits in the south. In contrast, the 2030 forecast predicts a stark divide: while the north remains in surplus due to concentrated wind generation, a massive, deep purple deficit area covers almost the entire southern and western halves of the country, where major population and industrial centers reside. This visual underscores the critical, unmet need for massive transmission infrastructure to connect northern wind supply to southern demand centers.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication evaluates the challenges facing Germany's Energiewende energy transition program, arguing that its targets are far broader than just the electricity grid and are highly unlikely to be met. Specifically, the author focuses on the goal of achieving a 30% reduction in primary energy use from 2015 levels by 2030, a target that faces severe headwinds because Germany's overall energy consumption has remained virtually unchanged since 2000. 

An accompanying line chart titled "Germany primary energy consumption, Mtoe" plots energy consumption from 2000 to 2030. It shows historical consumption hovering consistently between 300 and 340 million tonnes of oil equivalent (Mtoe) up to 2018. To hit the 2030 Energiewende target of a 30% decline from 2015 levels, which would bring consumption down to around 220 Mtoe, the energy trajectory must follow a steep, dotted-line downward path that diverges sharply from historical trends. 

A second line chart, "Energy intensity," measures Mtoe of primary energy per unit of nominal GDP from 2000 to 2016 across several major developed nations: the United States, Germany, France, Japan, and the United Kingdom. While the chart demonstrates that all of these nations have successfully improved efficiency—with Germany's energy intensity falling from roughly 0.15 in 2000 to about 0.09 in 2016—these efficiency gains have been offset by economic growth, keeping total energy consumption flat.

The author highlights that the German Federal Government's Expert Commission has itself given failing grades to several key transition areas, listing transportation energy use, changes in the fuel mix, overall primary energy use, and transmission grid expansion as unlikely to meet 2020 targets. Looking forward, the author assesses the feasibility of several long-term goals. While Germany might reach 65% renewable power generation by 2030, doing so will require politically challenging transmission infrastructure projects—80% of which are still on the drawing board—and likely further electricity rate hikes. A footnote explains that household resistance to prices above 35 cents per kilowatt-hour may force regulators to burden industrial users, whose rates of 12.5 to 15.5 cents per kilowatt-hour are already among the highest in the industrialized world. Ultimately, the author concludes that cutting greenhouse gas emissions in half by 2040 is highly unlikely due to the slow pace of de-carbonization outside the power sector, and the newly announced goal of phasing out all coal and lignite by 2038 is completely unrealistic.

This page analyzes the rising financial and environmental risks facing utility companies in fire-prone US regions, driven by anthropogenic climate change. The author uses the catastrophic collapse of PG&E stock following severe wildfire seasons in 2017 and 2018 to illustrate that such events are not anomalies but persistent risks that utility investors must confront. 

The first chart on the page tracks PG&E's market capitalization in billions of US dollars from January 2017 to January 2019. The line graph shows the utility's valuation starting above thirty-five billion dollars in early 2017 before experiencing successive, sharp drops. By January 2019, following consecutive devastating fire seasons, PG&E’s market capitalization collapsed to under five billion dollars.

The text connects these financial consequences to scientific research on climate change. It references a 2016 study by Abatzoglou and Williams from Columbia’s Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory and the University of Idaho to show how man-made climate change amplifies wildfire activity. This is illustrated in the second chart, which plots the cumulative millions of hectares of US forest fires from 1984 to 2016. 

The second chart compares a blue line representing the "non-anthropogenic burn area baseline"—the forest area burned due to natural causes, which would have accumulated to roughly four to five million hectares by 2016—against the actual forest area burned, shown as gray dots, and the total estimated burn area, represented by a red line. The actual and estimated total burn area reaches nearly ten million cumulative hectares by 2016, with the gap between the two lines representing the forest area burned due to anthropogenic climate change. Both lines include shaded areas representing ninety-five percent confidence intervals. The visual data demonstrates that man-made climate change is responsible for roughly doubling the cumulative forest area burned in the United States over this thirty-two-year period, highlighting a permanent, escalating risk for utilities operating in these regions.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Annual Energy Paper examines how human activities contribute to wildfire frequency and severity in the United States, focusing on both the indirect impacts of climate change and the direct impact of human-caused ignitions. 

The author begins by illustrating the link between human-induced climate change and wildfires using two charts sourced from Abatzoglou and Williams. The first line chart, titled "Estimated temperature change in Western forest region due to human activities," tracks estimated temperature change in degrees Celsius from 1900 to 2010. It shows that temperatures remained relatively flat or slightly negative until approximately 1970, after which they rose sharply to over 1.0 degree Celsius by 2010. 

The second chart, a scatter plot titled "US forest fire area versus fuel aridity by year," plots forest fire area in thousands of hectares on a logarithmic y-axis, ranging from 20 to 1,280, against fuel aridity relative to a non-anthropogenic baseline on the x-axis, ranging from negative 1.5 to 2.0. The data is split into two eras: 1984 to 1999, represented by blue dots, and 2000 to 2015, represented by orange dots. The earlier period exhibits lower fuel aridity and lower burned forest area, whereas the later period shows markedly higher fuel aridity and an exponential increase in burned forest area, demonstrating a strong correlation between rising fuel aridity—driven by human climate impacts—and wildfire severity. A footnote defines fuel aridity as a composite measure of forest fire risk based on factors such as vapor pressure deficit, the Palmer drought severity index, and the Fire Weather Index.

Beyond climate change, the author discusses how humans directly initiate wildfires. Accompanying text notes that while natural events like lightning play a role, humans account for 84 percent of all fires and nearly half of the total forest area burned in the US. A detailed table, based on a January 2017 study by Balch et al. at the University of Boulder covering the years 1992 to 2012, breaks down fire numbers and burned areas across different US ecological regions. For the Total Continental US, the table shows that humans started 1,272,076 fires, which is 84 percent of the total, compared to 245,446 started by lightning. In terms of area, human-started fires burned 16,027,412 hectares, representing 44 percent of the total, while lightning-started fires burned 20,126,852 hectares. 

Regionally, human influence varies significantly. In Mediterranean California, humans started 97 percent of fires representing 89 percent of the area burned. Conversely, in the Northwest Forested Mountains, humans started 45 percent of fires accounting for 25 percent of the area burned. Despite these statistics, the author notes that overall fire frequency peaked around 1980 and has since declined due to fewer arsons, fewer uncontrolled agricultural burns, and fewer cigarette ignitions.

In this commentary, the author discusses the dramatic global market rebound in early 2019, which was fueled by the Federal Reserve’s sudden pivot away from monetary tightening—a phenomenon visually symbolized by an illustration of a rising blimp labeled "Fed Zeppelin." This recovery from the December 2018 equity bear market stands as the fastest post-war recovery in history. The rally was heavily supported by the Fed’s decision to halt balance sheet reductions and interest rate hikes. While some market observers compare this shift to the Fed's mistake in 1966, when easing too early ignited inflation, the author argues that current wage and price inflation metrics are stable enough to justify the pause. The author forecasts that the next policy move will likely be a rate hike in early 2020, despite political pressure to ease coming from Trump's Fed nominees. Aside from the Fed, China acted as a major market driver due to economic stimulus, rising leading indicators, and the high probability of a US-China trade deal. Although global growth and earnings are currently in a soft patch—most visible in European manufacturing—the author does not believe the economic cycle is ending, though he expects only modest market gains for the remainder of 2019, favoring US and Emerging Market equities.

The core visual on the page is a dense bar chart titled "2019 YTD returns," which plots year-to-date total returns in US dollars across dozens of global asset classes as of April 5, 2019. The chart's data series are color-coded into US growth equities, US equities, US fixed income, European and developed world equities, developed world fixed income excluding the US, emerging market equities, emerging market bonds, and commodities. The vertical axis spans from negative 15% to positive 20%. The visual highlights a massive, broad-based surge in risk assets, with several top performers rising so high they exceed the chart's vertical boundary. These outstanding performers include Shenzhen equities at positive 44%, oil at positive 36%, Shanghai equities at positive 33%, and S&P Tech, FANG stocks, and MSCI China equities all returning between 21% and 22%. Other major equity indices, such as the Nasdaq, S&P 500, and various European sector equities, occupy the upper half of the chart with positive returns generally ranging from 10% to 15%. In contrast, the far right of the chart displays assets with negative returns, which are dominated by safe havens and select commodities. These lagging assets include gold, Italian and Japanese local bonds, the Yen, the Euro, silver, natural gas, corn, and local bonds from Turkey and Argentina, with the lowest performers dipping toward negative 15%.

This page analyzes the rapid rebound of global equity markets in early 2019 despite slowing economic growth, attributing the bounce largely to the Federal Reserve's pivot to a more patient monetary policy. The author observes that while valuations have quickly risen back above their historical medians, global GDP and earnings growth are declining. For the US, the author forecasts zero or negative year-over-year earnings growth in the first and second quarters of 2019, and modest full-year growth of just 3% to 5%, warning of rising labor costs squeezing corporate profits. Regionally, the author highlights a severe contraction in Europe's manufacturing sector.

The page features six charts illustrating these trends. The first, titled "Fed Zeppelin: the Fed fuels the bounce," compares the 2018/2019 S&P 500 recovery over the 70 days following its market bottom against the historical median recovery. The 2018/2019 recovery curve rises steeply, approaching a 100% recovery by day 70, markedly outperforming the median historical recovery which typically reaches only about 30% in the same timeframe. This rise is annotated as being driven by the Federal Reserve's pivot to patience. An adjacent chart compares this rebound against twelve historical post-war bear market recoveries since 1957, demonstrating that the 2018/2019 recovery is tied for the fastest on record.

A bar chart titled "Valuation percentiles back above median" details the valuation percentiles of US, European, and emerging market equities, alongside high-yield and high-grade bonds. Across all categories, valuations at the December low had dropped to the 20% to 35% range but have since rebounded to current levels between 50% and 75%, placing them back above their historical medians. 

To contextualize the macroeconomic environment, the line chart "Global GDP and profits: soft patch not recession" plots global nominal GDP growth against trailing corporate profits from 1998 through 2019 estimates. While both metrics are declining in 2019, nominal GDP remains above 5% and corporate profit growth is slowing but positive, suggesting a soft patch rather than a formal global recession.

Geographic disparities in manufacturing are shown in the chart "Black hole in European manufacturing," which tracks manufacturing new orders indices from 2013 to 2019 for the US, Eurozone, China, and Japan. The Eurozone index has plummeted sharply below the 50 expansion line down to approximately 45, highlighting severe contraction. Japan and China also hover slightly below the expansion threshold, while the US manufacturing index remains in expansionary territory but is trending downward. 

Finally, the chart "US capital spending surveys rolling over" tracks US corporate investment sentiment from 2000 to 2019. It plots the Duke CFO survey on plans to increase capital expenditures alongside the National Federation of Independent Business survey on expected growth over the next 12 months. Both series show a clear rollover from their post-2016 peaks, indicating that US business investment momentum is softening.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication analyzes China’s role as a major market catalyst, focusing on its rebounding economic indicators, fiscal stimulus, and the strong incentives for a US-China trade deal driven by deep historical economic linkages. The author, Michael Cembalest, notes that despite anticipated criticisms that a potential trade deal might only deliver modest concessions on intellectual property and joint venture rules, any concessions would still exceed those achieved by the Bush or Obama administrations. He references the negative historical impact of China's 2001 WTO entry, which estimated annual US economic losses of $250 billion to $600 billion from counterfeit goods and trade secret theft. Additionally, he notes that Europe is also exploring tighter regulations on Chinese foreign direct investment in high-tech and infrastructure sectors.

The page features three charts supporting these observations. The first chart, titled "More China fiscal stimulus on the way," presents fiscal stimulus as a percentage of GDP from 2015 through an estimated 2019, categorized by tax cuts and spending. It shows that stimulus is projected to rebound to nearly 3.0% of GDP in 2019, with tax cuts comprising a significantly larger portion of the total package compared to the spending-dominated stimulus of 2016, which peaked around 2.3% of GDP.

The second chart, titled "China business surveys rebounding," tracks the monthly Caixin and Markit Manufacturing PMI and Services PMI from 2010 to 2019, where a level above 50 indicates expansion. Both lines show a clear upward turn in early 2019.
