Second, in 2017, PetSmart's sponsor, BC Partners, transferred its stake in Chewy.com, which had been purchased for three point four billion dollars, to a subsidiary shielded from bondholders, and later went public without using any proceeds to pay down PetSmart's eight billion dollars in debt. Third, in September 2018, Neiman Marcus transferred its online store, MyTheresa, to a holding company owned by Ares and the Canadian Pension Board to protect the asset from creditors.

The author points out that this behavior has attracted regulatory attention, notably in a Federal Reserve speech, though the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is sending mixed signals by softening its EBITDA leverage guidance. Another concerning practice highlighted is sponsor-designated counsel, where sponsors mandate which law firm syndicated loan-arranging banks must use. Looking ahead, the author forecasts that while these trends will not drive higher default rates—which instead depend on the depth of the next recession—they will lead to significantly lower loan recoveries. Historically, loan recoveries averaged seventy percent, but the author predicts they could drop to a midpoint of fifty-five percent in the next cycle, concluding that issuers are clearly winning the covenant battle against lenders.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest analyzes the slowing global business cycle, arguing that despite imminent Federal Reserve monetary easing, leading indicators suggest weaker sales, negative second-quarter S&P earnings per share growth, and slower global growth. He maintains that a US or global recession is unlikely, pointing to a resilient services sector and planned rate cuts by twenty global central banks. However, he warns that US stock markets, despite reaching record highs, require a clear upward turn in economic leading indicators to sustain their rally, predicting flat markets after the July Fed meeting as the benefits of monetary easing are largely exhausted.

To support his assessment, Cembalest presents six economic charts. The first, charting global business surveys and S&P sales surprises from 2010 to 2019, shows a strong historical correlation where global manufacturing surveys—advanced by two quarters on a scale of 48 to 56—have fallen to near 49, dragging down the percentage of S&P companies with positive sales surprises from a 2018 peak of 75% to below 45% in 2019. This cyclical weakness is further illustrated in a long-term chart comparing S&P earnings per share to Japanese machine tool orders from 1995 to 2020. This visual demonstrates that Japanese machine tool orders—historically a reliable leading indicator advanced six months—have plunged to nearly negative 40% year-over-year, signaling a contraction in S&P EPS growth into negative territory.

A third chart examines global business surveys and GDP growth from 2011 to 2019, showing how the combined manufacturing and services PMI indicator has slid to around 51, closely tracking a deceleration in quarter-on-quarter global GDP growth toward 2.5%. This slowdown is driven primarily by manufacturing, as detailed in a fourth chart tracking global output surveys from 2013 to 2019. Here, a clear divergence shows the services sector remaining resilient above the expansionary threshold of 50, while manufacturing has fallen into contraction territory below 50.

The final two charts confirm this industrial slowdown. A chart tracking global manufacturing new orders from 2013 to 2018 shows a steady decline from a peak near 56 down to contraction levels. Lastly, a chart tracking real-time world trade indicators from 2012 to 2019 shows both a world trade volume proxy and J.P. Morgan's world trade indicator falling from peaks of over 6% year-over-year in 2017 to near 0% by the June 2019 estimate, highlighting a stark deceleration in global trade.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the rising risks in the leveraged loan market, arguing that healthy-looking interest coverage metrics mask rising leverage due to the widespread practice of EBITDA add-backs. These add-backs, which allow companies to artificially inflate EBITDA by adding back non-recurring expenses and projected merger synergies, are analyzed using data from S&P, Moody's, and Fitch. S&P data shows that add-back usage has tripled, growing from 10% of all deals to approximately 30%, with add-backs typically representing 10% to 15% of unadjusted EBITDA. Fitch Covenant Review reports that 35% of middle-market loan issuers utilize these adjustments, while Moody's points out that some deals permit uncapped add-backs or caps up to 20% to 30%. Furthermore, Moody's research on European corporate acquisitions reveals that issuers achieve only 45% of their projected cost savings on average, and nearly 20% fail to realize any add-back targets at all.

These leverage dynamics are visualized in two charts from S&P Global Market Intelligence. The first line chart, titled "Rising interest coverage, but rising leverage as well," plots historical data from 2002 to 2019. It shows interest coverage on outstanding loans on the left axis and debt-to-EBITDA on new loans on the right axis. While interest coverage has climbed back to over 4.0x, debt-to-EBITDA on new loans has simultaneously risen to elevated levels, exceeding 5.0x by 2018. The second stacked bar chart, "M&A loan leverage trends using unadjusted EBITDA (excluding the benefit of assumed merger synergies)," tracks the annual distribution of leverage tiers from 2006 to 2018. This chart reveals a clear shift toward higher leverage: by 2018, roughly half of all M&A loans had leverage ratios above 6.0x, including a significant cohort exceeding 7.0x, once adjusted to exclude projected synergies.

The author also addresses the growth of covenant-lite (cov-lite) loans, refuting the argument that cov-lite structures are safe because they are dominated by larger, well-known issuers. While smaller loans under $300 million have shrunk from 50% of the market in 2000 to just 10% today, these larger issuers remain mostly non-investment grade junk credits. To demonstrate this growing risk, the author notes that the portion of the loan market rated below split BB has risen from 50% to 60% since 2016. Lastly, the page warns about low recovery expectations for cov-lite loans. Though defaults have been sparse during the low-default environment since 2010, the 13 cov-lite loans that did default experienced an average recovery rate of only 56%, compared to the much stronger 80% to 85% historical recovery rates seen for standard bank loans and senior secured bonds.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest challenges the assumption that private equity sponsors will step in to support portfolio companies' loans during times of economic stress. He argues that while sponsor-backed loan default rates historically appeared lower than non-sponsor rates during the financial crisis ten years prior, this advantage disappears once corporate debt exchanges—which often result in heavy losses for lenders—are factored in. As examples of significant debt exchanges from the 2009 and 2010 period, he cites TXU, Harrah's, Freescale, Realogy, Intelsat, and Hexion. 

This argument is supported by the first chart on the page, titled "Sponsored vs non-sponsored default rates" from 2000 to 2012. The y-axis measures the default percentage from 0% to 25%. While sponsor-backed loans excluding debt exchanges peaked at a modest 8% in 2009-2010, the gold line representing sponsor-backed loans including debt exchanges peaked near 22%, which actually exceeded the blue line for non-sponsored loans that peaked near 18%. 

Cembalest then transitions to the disconnect between market pricing and ultimate realized losses, noting that peak loan defaults of 20% to 22% in 2010 should have only translated to 6% to 8% in peak realized losses under normal 65% to 70% recovery rates. However, investor panic and low dealer liquidity caused the broader market to sell off far more aggressively. This dynamic is mapped in the second chart, "Leveraged loans: market pricing versus realized losses," which indexes the period from January 2006 to January 2010 with a baseline of September 15, 2008, equal to 100. The S&P/LSTA Leveraged Loan Index plummeted to a low near 70 in late 2008, whereas J.P. Morgan's estimates of actual peak realized losses only drop the index value to around 90. Cembalest projects that in a future, milder recession with lower recovery rates, the loan total return index could decline by 7% to 10%. He advises loan investors that they must be prepared to ride out paper declines that far exceed ultimate losses. 

Finally, a third chart, "Leveraged loan default rates" from 2012 to 2019, shows that default rates have remained benign over the prior few years, averaging 1% to 2%. The chart, plotted on a scale of 0% to 5%, reveals that the only major disruption during this multi-year stretch was a temporary wave of energy defaults in late 2014 and 2015 that pushed the default rate up toward 4% before it subsided.

This page analyzes the structural headwinds driving down inflation in the United States and globally. The author argues that several factors—including a decline in labor bargaining power, online price transparency, globalization, corporate margin absorption, and automation—have suppressed inflation, making low-inflation regimes a dominant global characteristic.

The first chart, titled "Decline in labor bargaining power," displays two trends from 1947 to 2017. The first is the labor share of output in the non-farm business sector, which has fallen from around 65% in the late 1940s to approximately 57% by 2017. The second is private sector union membership, which shows a continuous, steep decline over the same period, dropping to under 10%. 

The second chart, "Online retailing increases price transparency, reduces pricing power," tracks the average duration of price changes in months from 2008 to 2017. Across three categories—recreation and electronics, furnishings and household, and food and non-alcoholic beverages—the time between price changes has collapsed. For recreation and electronics, the duration dropped from a peak of nearly 16 months in 2011 to around 6 months in 2017, illustrating that online transparency forces faster, more frequent pricing adjustments.

The third chart demonstrates "Globalization: less US price sensitivity to domestic conditions, more to global conditions." From 1960 to 2015, world trade as a percentage of GDP rose from under 30% to nearly 60%. Over a similar period, world cross-border capital stock as a percentage of GDP surged from near-zero to more than 110%, signaling that global economic conditions now hold greater sway over inflation than domestic indicators alone.

The fourth chart shows "Companies now responding to labor cost changes through margins rather than prices." It compares the change in core PCE inflation resulting from a 1% increase in unit labor costs against the corresponding change in profit margins (inverted). Since the late 1980s, the pass-through of labor costs into inflation has dropped from around 0.8% to virtually 0%, while the negative impact on corporate profit margins has widened significantly, dipping past -0.6%. This indicates that companies are absorbing labor cost increases internally rather than raising prices for consumers.

The fifth chart shows the rise of automation via the density of US industrial robots per thousand workers from 1993 to 2018. Data compiled by Acemoglu at MIT, the Institute for Employment Research, and the Bruegel Institute in Belgium all align to show a consistent rise from fewer than 0.5 robots per thousand workers in 1993 to roughly 2.0 per thousand by 2018.

The final chart presents the "Percentage of world GDP with low, positive headline inflation (0-4%)" from 1960 to 2015. It shows that while low, positive inflation represented nearly 0% of world GDP during the inflationary spikes of the late 1970s and early 1980s, it has steadily climbed to encompass nearly 90% of global GDP in recent years, indicating that these disinflationary forces are a widespread, global phenomenon.

This page of the publication analyzes the impact of the US-China trade war on corporate profits while presenting counterarguments for why a US recession is unlikely in 2019 or 2020. 

The author begins by detailing how the trade-war induced slowdown is suppressing corporate profits, noting that S&P 500 earnings growth decelerated to 2% to 3% compared to 7% to 9% in the fourth quarter of 2018, excluding tax-cut benefits. Absent stock buybacks, organic S&P earnings growth for the first half of the year was near zero. Furthermore, economy-wide profit restatements suggest the "Trump profits boom" was overstated, and the divergence between S&P profits and economy-wide profits historically signals aggressive accounting and an impending end to the business cycle. While most research puts the trade war's impact on US profits at 3% to 5%, this is enough to offset corporate tax cuts, with uneven impacts hitting tech hardware by up to 22% and capital goods by 10%. If passed through to consumers, J.P. Morgan Equity Research estimates a cost of $600 to $1,000 per household, wiping out household tax cut benefits. 

On the positive side, the author argues that a US recession is not imminent for 2019 or 2020, driven primarily by a strong US consumer supported by a 50-year low in unemployment and wage growth exceeding 3%. This consumer strength is visible in picking-up mortgage refinancing, home purchases, retail sales, and credit statistics. While commercial loan demand grows, the author warns of deteriorating leveraged loan underwriting standards. The inverted US yield curve is dismissed as an unreliable recession indicator due to negative yields in Europe and Japan forcing capital into long-duration US assets. Multinationals are adapting by shifting final assembly to countries like Vietnam, though labor shortages there present limitations. Other stabilizing factors include a tentative agricultural and auto trade deal with Japan, anticipated central bank easing across major global economies, and falling net equity supply driven by weak issuance combined with strong merger-and-acquisition and buyback activity. 

Footnotes expand on free-trade stances from Heritage and the American Enterprise Institute (AEI), the pricing of European Central Bank interest rate hikes, and the specific exposure of several US multinationals to China revenues, citing high exposures for tech firms like Qualcomm at 80%, Micron at 57%, Broadcom at 49%, Texas Instruments at 44%, AMD at 39%, Intel at 27%, Apple at 20%, Nike at 16%, and Boeing at 14%. No charts or tables are visualised on this text-based page, though several are referenced as external callouts.

This page features an executive summary and analysis by Michael Cembalest regarding the shifting impacts of Donald Trump's economic and trade policies on the financial markets. Cembalest argues that the initial phase of "Trumpism"—characterized by deregulation, corporate tax cuts, and pro-business judicial appointments favored by conservative organizations like the Heritage Foundation and the American Enterprise Institute—spurred a substantial equity rally and temporarily boosted manufacturing jobs. However, once protectionist trade policies and tariffs took center stage, US manufacturing stalled and the stock market entered a volatile, sideways pattern. The author predicts this range-bound behavior will persist through the next presidential election, suggesting that investors should range-trade equities around the highs and lows established since early 2018. To back up his cautious outlook, Cembalest notes several negative global trends: US tariffs are at a forty-year high, global trade volumes are at their weakest since 2010, manufacturing surveys indicate contractions (particularly in Germany and Europe), US manufacturing hours worked are declining, and consumer spending is beginning to suffer from tariff impacts.

The primary visual on the page is a line chart mapping the S&P 500 Index level from January 2015 through September 2019, with the vertical axis scaling from 1,800 to 3,200. The chart tracks a relatively flat market fluctuating around 2,000 to 2,100 until the 2016 election. Following the election, a highlighted yellow line—dubbed the "yellow brick road"—depicts a steep, steady climb up to nearly 2,800, which is annotated as the period when market participants celebrated deregulation, tax cuts, and pro-business court appointments. This upward march halts abruptly on January 22, 2018, when the trade war officially commenced with the imposition of tariffs on washing machines and solar panels. From that point forward, the index behaves erratically, exhibiting sharp sell-offs and recoveries within a wide, sideways band labeled the "Trumpism trading range," which spans roughly between 2,400 and 3,100. Footnotes at the bottom cite various policy research papers from 2017 and point out that recent stock market volatility of 14% aligns with long-term historical averages dating back to 1958, casting the lower volatility periods of 2016 to 2018 as anomalies.

In this commentary page, Michael Cembalest argues that central banks cannot fully offset the market volatility stemming from the US-China trade war because of deeply integrated global economic ties. Although the broader US economy is heavily driven by domestic consumption (at 70%), the US equity market is disproportionately reliant on production and global trade, leaving corporate profit margins vulnerable to de-globalization. Cembalest predicts that a substantial unwinding of the trade war is unlikely under Donald Trump or potential Democratic successors, meaning the range-bound equity market observed since January 2018 will likely persist.

To support these assertions, the page presents four charts. Chart 1, "Ease of starting a new business," tracks the US percentile rank relative to the world and the OECD from 2005 to 2017. It shows a steady decline in both metrics, with the US rank against the world slipping from around 95% to 75%, and its rank against the OECD dropping from about 80% to under 50%, signaling a regulatory environment that has grown relatively harder for new business creation.

Chart 2 displays "US manufacturing sector labor dynamism" from 2000 to 2018 in thousands of workers. It plots new hires, voluntary quits, and layoffs, highlighting a recovery since the Great Recession where hires and quits gradually rose to approximately 350,000 and 200,000 respectively by 2018, while layoffs stabilized at around 100,000.

Chart 3 illustrates "US tariff history and projections assuming no change in US import demand from targeted foreign exporters" from 1910 to beyond 2010. The historical timeline highlights the Smoot-Hawley tariff peak near 20% in the 1930s, followed by a long-term decline to near-zero levels. A series of numbered points trace the impact of recent and proposed tariffs under the Trump administration, starting with steel and aluminum duties and moving through successive Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods. These actions, culminating in proposed tariffs on remaining goods by December 2019, threaten to push the effective US tariff rate back up to around 6% to 7%, a level not seen since the mid-20th century.

Finally, Chart 4 shows "Global industrial production and world trade" as a six-month over six-month percentage change from 2004 to 2019. This visual highlights a sharp deceleration starting in 2018, with global trade volume contraction dipping below 0% and global industrial production slowing to near-flat levels by mid-2019, underscoring the real-world economic drag of recent trade barriers.

This page consists entirely of legal disclaimers and regulatory disclosures for J.P. Morgan Private Bank. It outlines licensing requirements and exemptions for J.P. Morgan Securities LLC under Australian law, specifically referencing the Corporations Act 2001, the SEC, FINRA, CFTC, and limitations for wholesale clients. It also details distribution restrictions and private placement regulations for Latin American jurisdictions, specifically highlighting compliance requirements under the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission and platforms in Mexico.

This page analyzes the ongoing global manufacturing slowdown, the contraction of hours worked, and the domestic impacts of the trade war, specifically showing how tariffs have failed to boost the US sectors they were designed to protect. 

Chart 5 illustrates that the ratio of orders to inventories, lagged by three months, points to a deeper slowdown in German manufacturing production. The year-over-year manufacturing production growth rate, which hovered near five percent in early 2018, has dropped into negative territory toward negative five percent in 2019, closely tracking the decline in the orders-to-inventory survey.

Chart 6 tracks global manufacturing and employment business surveys, where index levels above 50 signal expansion. Both global manufacturing and employment measures have experienced a continuous downturn since their early 2018 peaks. By mid-2019, the global manufacturing survey has fallen below the critical 50-expansion threshold, while global employment has dipped to right on the line.

Chart 7 highlights regional differences in manufacturing business surveys from 2016 to 2019 across the US, China, Eurozone, and Japan. The Eurozone shows the steepest contraction, with its purchasing managers' index plummeting to around 47. The US, China, and Japan have also trended downward over this period, with all four regions converging around or below the 50 expansion threshold by mid-2019.

The US manufacturing slowdown is also showing clear signs in labor utilization. Chart 8 displays the year-over-year growth in US manufacturing aggregate weekly hours of all employees. This growth rate peaked near two and a half percent in early 2018 but steadily deteriorated throughout 2018 and 2019, entering negative territory at approximately negative zero point three percent.

Chart 9 addresses the consumer impact of the trade dispute by indexing US real consumer spending from 2015 to 2019, with February 2018 set to 100. Following the implementation of the first round of tariffs in early 2018, spending on tariff-impacted categories—such as housekeeping supplies, furniture, major appliances, floor coverings, and auto parts—flattened and declined slightly below the 100 mark. Meanwhile, spending on all other core goods continued its steady upward trajectory, reaching approximately 107 by mid-2019.

Finally, Chart 10 analyzes US employment indexed to February 2018, revealing that employment has actually been weaker in tariff-protected industries like steel, aluminum, household appliances, and furniture. Following the implementation of the first round of tariffs, employment in these protected sectors stagnated and ultimately rolled over, dropping to around 99 by mid-2019. In contrast, employment in all other industries continued to climb steadily, reaching an index level of nearly 103.

This page analyzes the potential tax and regulatory consequences of a hypothetical Democratic sweep in the 2020 elections. The author begins by highlighting that funding ambitious progressive programs—such as Medicare-for-All, free college, student debt forgiveness, infrastructure, affordable housing, universal pre-K, and the Green New Deal—would require substantial new sources of revenue. Since a Democratic president would only need three additional seats to regain effective control of the Senate, the author emphasizes the importance of understanding the specific policy proposals of various Democratic presidential candidates, drawing from research by Cornerstone Macro and The American Banker.

The page details several key policy proposals across five major categories. Under higher taxes on income and capital gains, Joe Biden suggests doubling the capital gains tax rate for those earning over one million dollars and eliminating the step-up in basis for heirs. Ron Wyden proposes taxing unrealized capital gains, while Bernie Sanders wants to tax capital gains and dividends at standard income rates, apply a top estate tax rate of 77 percent, and establish a new 12.4 percent payroll tax on incomes over $250,000. Elizabeth Warren supports a wealth surtax, including an annual 2 percent tax on assets exceeding $50 million. 

Regarding corporate taxes, the progressive wing of the party has shifted away from previous bipartisan efforts to lower corporate rates, with conservative Blue Dog Democrats now accounting for only 27 of 227 House seats. Most candidates favor raising corporate rates, with Warren proposing an additional tax on corporate profits over $100 million to raise $900 billion over a decade, which is roughly equivalent to a 9 percent corporate tax rate increase. 

On the topic of stock buybacks, Sanders and Chuck Schumer propose blocking share repurchases unless companies meet certain requirements, such as establishing a $15 minimum wage, sick leave, and improved benefits. Warren, Sanders, and Kirsten Gillibrand co-sponsored the Reward Work Act to prohibit open-market buybacks and require public companies to have employees elect one-third of their board of directors. Additionally, Sherrod Brown has introduced legislation requiring companies to pay workers one dollar for every one million dollars in increased shareholder returns from buybacks.

For financial industry reforms, Sanders has proposed the Inclusive Prosperity Act, which would impose transaction taxes of 0.5 percent on stocks, 0.1 percent on bonds, and 0.005 percent on derivatives, potentially raising $400 billion to $800 billion over ten years. Kamala Harris proposes a new bank tax modeled on Barack Obama's proposed 0.07 percent fee on bank liabilities, while Amy Klobuchar would tax banks to fund infrastructure. Both Warren and Sanders support retroactively breaking up large bank and big tech mergers. Finally, Warren’s plan to rein in Wall Street would force private equity firms to guarantee the debt and pensions of companies they acquire, while restricting their ability to pay themselves dividends and monitoring fees.

Morgan Securities LLC in Australia, explaining that it operates under an exemption from holding an Australian Financial Services Licence and is intended solely for wholesale clients. Additionally, it details restrictions on the distribution of materials and financial offerings in Latin American jurisdictions, specifically highlighting compliance requirements and limitations related to Brazilian and Mexican platforms, as well as the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission. Finally, the page contains standard brand references and copyright information for JPMorgan Chase & Co.

This page presents a collection of six charts analyzing corporate profits, the financial impact of trade tariffs on specific sectors and household tax benefits, and trends in the US housing market as of late 2019. 

Chart 11 tracks S&P 500 12-month forward earnings per share as a percentage year-over-year from 2014 to 2019. It shows a steep deceleration in earnings growth from a late-2018 peak of over 20% down to approximately 2% by mid-2019. Chart 12 provides crucial context to this slowdown by illustrating US economy-wide after-tax non-financial corporate profits in trillions of US dollars. It reveals a massive downward post-revision correction by the Bureau of Economic Analysis; what originally appeared as a pre-revision climb toward $1.25 trillion in late 2018 was revised to a flat-to-declining trend hovering around $1.0 trillion. Chart 13 compares S&P 500 reported earnings per share against broader economy-wide profits from National Income and Product Accounts, indexed to December 2001. This ratio, which historically plunges during recessions, climbed steadily to around 140 in 2019, indicating that public market S&P profits are significantly outperforming the broader economy's profit trend.

The next two charts address the impact of trade policy. Chart 14 shows tariffs on Chinese imports as a percentage share of various financial measures. While the tariffs are relatively minor as a share of US GDP (around 1%) and broader S&P 500 earnings (around 3.5%), they severely squeeze specific sectors, representing over 11% of Industrial Capital Goods earnings and approximately 22% of Technology Hardware earnings. Chart 15 details how these tariffs are eroding the benefits of the 2017 tax reform, comparing the estimated tariff cost per household against a tax cut benefit baseline of roughly $1,300. Across three progressive tariff stages—Phase I & II; Phase I, II, and partial implementation of Phase III; and full implementation of Phases I, II, & III—the chart displays estimates from both the Federal Reserve and a consensus of external groups, which includes the Peterson Institute, Oxford Economics, UC Davis, and the "Tariffs Hurt the Heartland" coalition. Under the final, full-phase scenario, both Federal Reserve and consensus estimates project tariff costs of approximately $1,400 to $1,600 per household, completely wiping out and exceeding the initial tax cut benefit.

Finally, Chart 16 tracks the US housing market using seasonally adjusted 12-week average home refinancing and purchase indices from 2014 to 2019, indexed to March 1990. The purchase index shows a steady multi-year upward climb, reaching around 260 by late 2019. Meanwhile, the highly rate-sensitive refinancing index, which had plummeted to a low near 800 at the end of 2018, experienced a dramatic surge throughout 2019, climbing back above 2,000 as mortgage rates declined.

This page of the publication focuses on global economic integration, trade dynamics, equity supply, and banking performance. 

Chart 23 illustrates unprecedented low levels of net equity supply globally from 1999 to 2019, measured in billions of US dollars based on the MSCI All Country World Equity Index. The data shows a significant contraction in net equity supply over the decade, with the total turning negative in 2018 and 2019, driven primarily by negative net equity supply in the United States. 

Chart 24 compares the total return performance of US and European banks from 2009 to 2019, indexing both to 100 in January 2009. The chart reveals a dramatic divergence: while the S&P 500 banks index steadily climbed to over 300, the Euro STOXX banks index underperformed significantly, languishing near or below its 100 base value.

Chart 25 argues that the economic integration between China and the US is far deeper than that of any major historical or potential adversaries of the last 100 years. Expressed as a percentage of combined GDP, the bilateral linkages between the US and China in 2014 approached 8%, driven by a combination of annual trade, central bank holdings of government debt, and foreign direct investment. This is compared to much lower levels of integration in historical conflicts, such as the US and Japan in 1940 or the UK and Germany in 1930. An accompanying footnote adds that US-China linkages also include $450 billion in sales of US affiliates in China, massive enrollment of Chinese college students in the US, and the world's largest bilateral scientific research relationship.

Chart 26 maps the relationship between global profit margins and global trade to GDP from 1995 to 2017. The visual demonstrates a close correlation between the two metrics over the two decades, showing that as global trade to GDP expanded to nearly 30% by 2017, global profit margins rose in tandem, peaking at over 9%. 

Chart 27 compares KOF globalization index scores to actual trade volumes (imports plus exports as a percentage of GDP) across major economies like Sweden, Germany, the US, China, and Brazil. The chart highlights that while the United States has a low trade-to-GDP ratio compared to European nations, its overall globalization score is among the highest in the world, exceeding 80%. An accompanying text box explains that the KOF globalization index captures a broader set of de jure and de facto measures, including capital account openness, foreign direct investment, portfolio investment, embassies, and international patents, rather than just raw trade flows.

This page of the publication provides a critical commentary on US presidential candidate proposals for a nationwide ban on hydraulic fracturing. Michael Cembalest argues that such a ban would have severe consequences, as fracking has fueled a massive domestic energy boom that erased the long-standing US net energy deficit. 

The transition from a net energy importer to energy independence is illustrated in two initial charts. The first chart, depicting the US net energy deficit in dollar terms as a percentage of GDP from 1978 to 2018, shows the deficit peaking above 3.0% around 2008 before plunging to nearly 0.0% by 2018. The second chart measures the deficit in physical energy terms, showing net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal peaking near 700 million tonnes of oil equivalent in the mid-2000s before falling precipitously toward zero by 2016. 

A third chart shows the percentage of US oil and gas production derived from hydraulic fracturing from 1995 to 2019. By 2019, hydraulic fracturing accounted for approximately 80% of natural gas production, over 60% of crude oil production, and over 60% of natural gas liquids (such as ethane, propane, and butane). A fourth stacked bar chart demonstrates that unconventional oil, gas, and NGLs requiring hydraulic fracturing make up 40% of all US primary energy consumption, dwarfing conventional oil and gas sources at roughly 20%, coal at 15%, nuclear at 8%, and renewables like biomass, hydro, wind, and solar. 

Despite the economic benefits, the author acknowledges the substantial environmental risks associated with fracking. He notes that the US is unique in its widespread adoption of the practice, with only minor activity in Canada, China, and Argentina. Specific risks discussed include aquifer contamination from shallower wells (1,000 to 2,000 feet deep), exponential growth in water usage in the Permian Basin, well integrity issues, and toxic flowback water containing hazardous substances like lead, arsenic, barium, chromium, uranium, radium, radon, and benzene. He also points out that the EPA's own Advisory Board questioned a 2016 EPA report that found little evidence of systemic impacts on drinking water. A final footnote contrasts these concerns with alarms over the Trump administration's rollback of federal oversight of US waterways.

This page compiles six diverse macroeconomic and financial charts monitoring US domestic health, global capital flows, shifting trade dynamics, monetary policy, and corporate actions. 

The first two charts assess the health of the US consumer. Chart 17 displays US same-store retail sales growth as an eight-week average of year-over-year percentage changes from 2005 through 2019. After plunging to a low of nearly negative six percent during the 2008–2009 financial crisis, retail sales growth staged a strong recovery, peaking at over six percent in 2019. This consumer strength is supported by Chart 18, which monitors US ninety-day-plus loan delinquency transition rates for credit cards, second mortgages, autos, and first mortgages. Delinquency rates for first and second mortgages have plummeted from their respective crisis peaks of roughly six percent and four percent down to near-historic lows under one percent. Auto loan delinquencies remain stable at around one to two percent, while credit card delinquencies have leveled off near four percent, showing only a mild upward trend.

The next two charts highlight global capital and trade shifts. Chart 19 tracks cumulative net purchases of foreign bonds by Japanese and Euro area residents in trillions of dollars since March 2015. Driven by aggressive domestic monetary easing, Euro area residents dramatically increased their foreign bond holdings to nearly one point five trillion dollars by 2019, far outpacing Japanese residents, who accumulated approximately zero point six trillion dollars over the same period. Chart 20 shows the six-month average share of total US imports by country from 2010 to 2019. It highlights a notable shift in US trade relations: China’s share of US imports, which peaked at over twenty-two percent around 2017 to 2018, fell sharply to approximately eighteen percent by mid-2019. Meanwhile, the import shares for Mexico and Canada remained steady at around thirteen to fifteen percent, with Japan, Korea, and Vietnam capturing smaller, stable shares.

The final two charts focus on policy and corporate deployment of capital. Chart 21 illustrates how central bank rate cuts lead global manufacturing activity by demonstrating the relationship between the global manufacturing survey and a net count of central banks cutting rates or holding negative rates, adjusted for an eight-month lead. Although global manufacturing recently dipped below the fifty-point expansion threshold, a dramatic surge in net central bank rate cuts suggests that global manufacturing could soon find support and rebound. Lastly, Chart 22 displays quarterly S&P 500 corporate buybacks in billions of dollars from 1998 to 2019. Following a post-crisis recovery, buybacks reached an all-time high of well over two hundred billion dollars in late 2018 and 2019, significantly exceeding the previous pre-crisis peak of roughly one hundred seventy-five billion dollars in 2007.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues against an outright ban on hydraulic fracturing, suggesting that associated environmental and regulatory issues are manageable and far less complex than processes like crude oil refining or nuclear energy. He asserts that a sudden ban on fracking would jeopardize 40 percent of the United States energy supply, posing major risks to economic growth, employment, energy prices, geopolitical stability, and the strength of the dollar. Because domestic renewable energy is not growing fast enough to replace decommissioning coal and nuclear plants, natural gas remains an indispensable bridge fuel that complements intermittent renewables, especially given the lack of cheap energy storage and a unified national grid.

To illustrate the scale of domestic fossil fuel dependency, a line chart displays US sources of primary energy consumption from 1965 to approximately 2018. The data shows that oil has consistently remained the largest source of primary energy, hovering around 40 percent in recent years, down from a peak of nearly 48 percent in the late 1970s. Natural gas represents the second-largest share, rising back to about 31 percent after dipping in the 1980s. Coal consumption has steadily declined from over 20 percent in the early 2000s to around 13 percent, while nuclear energy has remained flat at roughly 8 percent since 1990. Hydroelectric power and modern renewables constitute the smallest shares, with modern renewables only recently ticking up to around 4 to 5 percent of primary energy consumption by the end of the period, demonstrating why fossil fuels cannot be easily or quickly abandoned.

Cembalest highlights the practical hurdles of expanding clean energy infrastructure by pointing to the failed Northern Pass transmission line project. Supported by Massachusetts regulators to deliver 1 gigawatt of clean hydropower from Hydro-Quebec to Southern New England, the 192-mile project was ultimately blocked by a New Hampshire siting committee due to concerns over local disruption and tourism impact. Despite concessions to bury parts of the line, the New Hampshire Supreme Court permanently killed the proposal in July 2019, leading to warnings from the grid regulator ISO New England about potential future rolling blackouts. Furthermore, he emphasizes the severe physical limitations of utility-scale storage, noting that while the nation generates over 4 billion megawatt-hours of electricity annually, it possesses only about 1,500 megawatt-hours of utility-scale energy storage, with pumped-storage hydropower in geological reservoirs accounting for 95 percent of that capacity.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest examines how active institutional equity managers are performing in a market landscape heavily influenced by central bank quantitative easing programs. By evaluating 6,700 institutional equity managers across 23 different style categories with historical performance data dating back to 1996, the publication addresses the viability of active management. The primary finding is that while manager outperformance between 2014 and 2019 was almost universally weaker than during the 2010 to 2014 period, a substantial number of equity categories still boast more than half of their managers outperforming net of fees. Notably, outperformance remains consistently stronger in non-US categories than in domestic ones.

The central chart, titled Active equity manager outperformance trends, displays the percentage of managers outperforming their respective exchange-traded fund on a one-year basis using monthly data. The vertical axis ranges from 30% to 70%, with a dashed line marking the 50% threshold where the majority of managers beat the benchmark. The horizontal axis categorizes the 23 styles, showing three distinct timeframes: January 1996 to December 2009 in grey, January 2010 to June 2019 in gold, and January 2014 to June 2019 in red. The chart visually demonstrates a general downward trend in outperformance, as the red bars representing the most recent period are typically shorter than the gold and grey bars. However, international and small-cap segments show resilient active success, whereas US large-cap categories show much lower rates of outperformance. 

The text provides a grading system to summarize these trends since 2014. Grade A categories, which maintained average outperformance above 50%, include small-cap growth, small-cap value, global, ACWI ex-US, Europe, Asia ex-Japan, Japan, EAFE, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Emerging Markets. Grade B categories, averaging between 45% and 50% outperformance, comprise large-cap value, mid-cap core, mid-cap growth, mid-cap value, small-cap core, all-cap growth, and Australia. Grade C categories, which fell below the 45% outperformance threshold, include large-cap core, large-cap growth, all-cap core, all-cap value, and US defensive.

In terms of methodology, managers were evaluated directly against their stated benchmarks rather than a single category index, and their returns were compared to actual or derived pro forma ETFs. Calculations assumed a separate account size of 50 million dollars to compute net-of-fee returns, with the author noting that minor differences in fees for smaller account sizes did not materially alter the overall findings.

This page analyzes the challenges facing active equity managers, attributing their declining outperformance to unorthodox central bank policies, such as quantitative easing and negative real interest rates. The author argues that the rise of negative-yielding government bonds—totaling 14 trillion dollars in Europe and Japan—has created severe market distortions that coincide with a deterioration in manager outperformance across both US and non-US style categories. This trend is compounded by the historic length of the current US economic expansion, as active managers historically achieve better relative performance during down markets rather than prolonged bull markets.

Three charts illustrate these dynamics. The first chart, depicting negative-yielding debt as a percentage of global investment grade debt from 2014 to 2019, shows the ratio spiking from near zero in 2014 to roughly 25% in 2016, before retreating slightly and then surging to nearly 30% by mid-2019. The second chart traces the three-year rolling average of one-year manager outperformance against exchange-traded funds from 2000 to 2019. It reveals that during the quantitative easing era starting around 2014, outperformance rates fell precipitously. US style categories, which peaked near 75% in the early 2000s, dropped below the 50% mark to lows near 42%, while non-US style categories fell from around 70% down to approximately 47% by 2019. The third chart shows the percentage of managers outperforming their respective benchmarks in up versus down markets since 1996 across various styles and global regions, including the US, Europe, Japan, Asia, Australia, Canada, the UK, and Emerging Markets. In almost every category, active managers perform significantly better during down markets, with outperformance rates frequently exceeding 60% to 70%, compared to up markets where outperformance rates often languish below 50%.

The author notes several specific market distortions that hinder active managers, such as high market concentration, where a small number of stocks drive the majority of returns, and rising pairwise stock correlations that limit the benefits of individual stock-picking. Additionally, the market has seen a long period of growth stock outperformance since 2010 and substantial gains in bond proxy stocks, which are interest-rate-sensitive, high-yielding, low-beta equities. Most notably, the author highlights a prolonged and anomalous period of value underperformance, which runs contrary to 70 years of historical data that typically underpins active investment models.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s September 2019 "Eye on the Market" by Michael Cembalest argues that despite significant market distortions, the fact that over 50% of active managers in many categories have outperformed since 2014 bodes well for the long-term viability of active equity management. The author highlights the potential for a value stock recovery, pointing to early signs of a turnaround detailed in the report's appendix. 

Six charts support this analysis of market distortions, valuation spreads, and performance trends. The first chart, tracking the rolling 12-month contribution of top firms to the overall US market return from 1963 to 2018 (during periods with a 10% or higher annual return), shows the percentage of returns driven by the top five and top twenty firms. The second chart depicts average trailing one-year pairwise correlations in the S&P 500 index from 1992 to late 2018. It shows correlations peaking near 0.5 to 0.55 during the Federal Reserve's QE1, QE2, and QE3 quantitative easing phases, before falling below 0.2 and subsequently rising slightly toward 2019.

Two charts illustrate the global divergence between growth and value investing. The first shows the US growth versus value cumulative net total return ratio (using Russell 1000 indices indexed to January 2005), which steadily climbed from around 0.9 in 2007 to roughly 1.45 by 2019, reflecting massive growth outperformance. The second displays growth versus value cumulative net total return ratios indexed to January 2010 for international regions, including Europe, Emerging Markets, Asia excluding Japan, and Japan. Europe saw the most dramatic rise in its growth-to-value ratio, climbing to over 1.4, while Japan remained the lowest but still experienced an upward trend, illustrating that growth outperformance is a global phenomenon.

The final two charts look at stock valuations. A chart comparing bond proxy stock valuations to the broader Russell 1000 valuations (from 1989 to 2019) plots the ratio of P/E multiples, illustrating how bond proxies have become historically expensive, climbing well above their long-term average to around 1.1 by 2019. Lastly, a historical chart on a log scale from 1926 to 2016 plots the cumulative excess return of the cheapest value stocks over the most expensive value stocks. This chart highlights a significant and unusual flatlining and eventual downturn in the post-2007 period, breaking sharply below its long-term pre-2007 upward trend line.

This page examines the relationship between the frequency of active managers outperforming their benchmarks and the magnitude of that outperformance. The author, Michael Cembalest, defines the magnitude of outperformance as the average alpha of successful managers minus the average underperformance of lagging managers. A key observation is that a direct positive correlation exists between these two metrics: when active managers outperform more frequently, the net manager alpha is also higher. For instance, in categories where the frequency of outperformance is above fifty percent, the reward of picking a successful manager is larger than the penalty of picking an unsuccessful one. Conversely, when outperformance is scarce (under fifty percent frequency), the penalty of a bad selection is magnified because underperforming managers lose more alpha than successful ones gain, which is typified by US large- and mid-cap categories. The author concludes that the magnitude of outperformance tends to amplify frequency results, making active management experiences exceptionally positive when it works, but severely worse when it does not.

These concepts are supported by two visual elements based on post-2010 rolling monthly data from eVestment and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. On the bottom-left is a scatter plot titled "Outperformance frequency vs outperformance magnitude, 2010 - 2019." The horizontal axis shows the frequency of manager outperformance ranging from forty percent to seventy percent, and the vertical axis plots the average annual successful manager alpha less average annual unsuccessful manager alpha, ranging from negative one percent to three percent. The plot shows a clear upward-sloping trend from the bottom left to the top right. Lower-frequency, underperforming styles—such as Large Cap Core, Large Cap Growth, Large Cap Value, and Mid Cap Value—cluster in the bottom-left quadrant with frequencies under forty-five percent and negative net alphas. Highly successful regions—such as Australia, Japan, Emerging Markets, and Europe—cluster in the top-right quadrant, showing both high frequencies of outperformance and positive net alphas.

To the right, a detailed table titled "Magnitude of out/underperformance" provides specific percentage breakdowns for twenty-three distinct style categories. The table columns outline the style category, the average positive alpha of successful managers, the average negative alpha of unsuccessful managers, and the resulting net difference. According to this data, Australia boasts the highest net alpha at two point eight percent, derived from an average positive alpha of six point one percent and an average negative alpha of negative three point three percent. Japan follows closely with a net alpha of two point four percent (five point five percent positive versus negative three point one percent negative), and Emerging Markets achieves a net alpha of one point nine percent. On the underperforming end, Mid Cap Value and US Defensive both show the lowest net alphas at negative zero point five percent, with Mid Cap Value showing a three point seven percent positive alpha overshadowed by a negative four point two percent negative alpha.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market publication presents historical data analyzing active investment manager performance across six distinct style categories. Grouped under the designation "Grade A," these categories represent style areas where the post-2014 average percentage of managers outperforming their respective benchmark exchange-traded funds (ETFs) is at or above 50%. 

Each of the six charts plots rolling one-year monthly data from 1997 through June 2019 on a vertical axis from 0% to 100%. The blue line tracks the percentage of outperforming managers over time, measured against a dotted 50% horizontal line. Every chart also displays horizontal bars indicating historical average outperformance over three key periods: January 1996 through December 2009 in grey, January 2010 through June 2019 in gold, and January 2014 through June 2019 in red.

The first chart, Small Cap Growth, shows a highly volatile track record of outperformance that frequently swings between 30% and 80%, though its post-2014 average remains just above the 50% threshold. The Small Cap Value chart shows a similar pattern, with a post-2014 average at roughly 55%, despite experiencing a sharp dip toward 20% around 2018 before recovering. 

The Global chart demonstrates that active global managers have averaged right around the 50% mark since 2014, recovering substantially from a historical low point near 20% in the late 1990s. The ACWI ex-US chart displays stronger relative manager performance, with the post-2014 average hovering around 58% and the blue trendline spending the majority of the post-2011 period comfortably above the 50% line. 

In the European equity category, active managers have maintained a post-2014 average of roughly 57%, despite a severe dip below 40% near the end of 2018. Finally, the Asia ex-Japan category demonstrates some of the strongest active manager results, with the post-2014 average sitting near 60%, showing persistent strength throughout the late 2010s. Collectively, these charts suggest that active management has maintained a strong, viable track record in these specific asset classes and geographical regions. All chart data is sourced from eVestment and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page evaluates active investment managers by asset class, assigning them a "Grade B" because their post-2014 average outperformance against their respective exchange-traded funds falls within the 45% to 50% range. The analysis features seven line charts tracking the percentage of active managers outperforming their benchmark ETF on a rolling one-year basis from 1997 through 2019, utilizing data from eVestment and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. Each chart includes a dotted horizontal line indicating the long-term historical average and a solid red/brown horizontal line representing the lower post-2014 average. 

The first chart, focusing on Large Cap Value, displays highly volatile rolling outperformance that spiked near 80% around 2001 and 2009 but features a post-2014 average that sits slightly below 50%. The Mid Cap Core chart illustrates a similar cyclical pattern, peaking near 80% in the early and late 2000s before declining to a post-2014 average just under 50%. For Mid Cap Growth, rolling outperformance frequently surpassed 60% historically but has been dragged down to a post-2014 average of roughly 47%. Mid Cap Value managers also show a historical tendency to exceed 60% outperformance, yet their post-2014 average has settled between 45% and 50%. 

The Small Cap Core chart shows active managers historically maintaining a solid track record, with outperformance often hovering above 50%, though their post-2014 average has slipped just below the 50% threshold. The All Cap Growth chart reveals significant cyclicality, with sharp drops and subsequent recoveries, ending with a post-2014 average in the mid-40s. Finally, the Australia chart tracks Australian active managers, showing exceptionally high outperformance in the late 1990s and early 2000s, followed by a steady downward trend that leaves their post-2014 average within the same 45% to 50% Grade B bracket.

This page, titled "Grade A (continued)," provides a visual assessment of active fund manager performance relative to passive index alternatives across five major global equity markets from 1997 through 2019. Each of the five line charts tracks the percentage of active managers outperforming their respective exchange-traded fund (ETF) on a rolling one-year basis. A dotted horizontal line at fifty percent represents the threshold where half of the active managers beat the benchmark, while solid horizontal lines represent historical averages over different horizons, showing a general long-term average around sixty percent that has recently stepped down in the final five years of the period. 

The first chart examines Japan, where active manager outperformance has historically fluctuated between thirty percent and eighty percent. While Japanese managers frequently exceeded the fifty percent mark—averaging over sixty percent historically—there is a distinct decline at the end of the series, with outperformance plunging toward twenty-five percent in 2019. 

The second chart focuses on the EAFE region, representing Europe, Australasia, and the Far East. After starting near ninety percent in 1997, EAFE active manager outperformance fell sharply to twenty-five percent in 1999 before recovering to spend most of the 2000s and 2010s fluctuating between fifty percent and eighty percent. However, a sharp downward turn is visible leading into 2019, where outperformance drops to approximately thirty percent. 

The third chart displays Canada, which exhibits a highly volatile cyclical pattern. Canadian active managers experienced deep lows near twenty percent in 2000 and mid-2016, interspersed with peaks near eighty percent. By 2019, the percentage of outperforming Canadian managers sat well below the fifty percent mark at around thirty-five percent. 

The fourth chart covers the United Kingdom, where data begins around late 1999. UK active managers saw high points near eighty percent in the early 2000s and mid-2010s but suffered a major drop to around twenty percent around 2016. By 2019, the outperformance rate remained depressed at approximately thirty percent, continuing a trend below its historical sixty-five percent average. 

The final chart tracks Emerging Markets, which also experienced a sharp early drop to twenty percent in late 1999. For the next two decades, emerging market managers fared relatively well, often keeping outperformance rates between fifty percent and eighty percent, though the trend steadily drifted down toward forty percent by 2018 before hovering near fifty percent in 2019. Together, these charts suggest a widespread global challenge for active managers in consistently outperforming passive benchmarks in the years leading up to 2019.

This page focuses on active investment manager performance, specifically grouping together asset classes that receive a "Grade C" due to their post-2014 average outperformance rate falling below 45%. The page features five individual line charts illustrating the rolling one-year percentage of active managers outperforming their respective benchmark ETFs from 1997 to 2019, with data sourced from eVestment and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. 

The first chart analyzes Large Cap Core managers. Historically, the percentage of outperforming managers fluctuated widely, occasionally peaking above 80% in the early and late 2000s, but the post-2014 average, depicted by a solid red horizontal line, has settled below the 45% threshold. The second chart, focused on Large Cap Growth managers, shows a similar dynamic where active managers frequently bested their passive peers in the late 1990s and mid-2000s, but have languished post-2014, with their average outperformance level also depicted below 45%. 

The third and fourth charts display All Cap Core and All Cap Value managers, respectively. Both charts demonstrate strong historical eras—especially around 2001 to 2005, when outperformance reached near or above 80%—contrasted against a significant post-2014 decline. For both groups, the post-2014 average outperformance is marked by a red horizontal line well below 45%. Lastly, the fifth chart tracks US Dividend Focused managers, showing highly cyclical historical outperformance that peaked around the 2001, 2008, and 2011 market downturns. However, this group has also suffered a substantial decline in active success since 2014, with the recent rolling average outperformance dropping below 45%. Together, these charts emphasize that across large cap, all cap, and dividend-focused strategies, active managers have found it increasingly difficult to beat passive benchmarks in the post-financial crisis era.

This page serves as a section outline and transition page for Appendix II: Methodology, listing the four primary topics covered in the upcoming section. These methodology topics include the most frequently used manager benchmarks by style category; assets under management, the number of managers, and benchmark/ETF availability; manager fee assumptions and sensitivity; and ETF tracking error by style category.

This page focuses on the potential normalization of US monetary policy and its implications for value stocks, particularly in the underperforming energy sector. The author begins by discussing the high demand for "bond proxies" driven by low and negative real interest rates. Despite low inflation in Europe and Japan, the author argues that the US is seeing the "beginning of the end" of super-loose monetary policy. This argument is supported by two charts. The first, illustrating the US "output gap" as actual GDP relative to potential GDP from 1990 to 2018, shows that the post-crisis excess capacity has been fully exhausted, with the gap rising from below negative five percent in 2009 to above zero percent by 2018. The second chart shows US core CPI year-over-year from 2008 to 2019, highlighting that core inflation has remained at or above two percent for over a year, hovering near two and a half percent in 2019. The author expects that as rates normalize, value stocks will recover at the expense of over-bought bond proxies.

The discussion then pivots to the energy sector, one of the market's primary value laggards, which has suffered from a well-acknowledged lack of capital discipline. A chart indexing US oil and gas production and exploration and production sector performance from 2008 to 2018 demonstrates this dynamic. While actual production soared from an index level of 100 to approximately 260, the E&P sector's financial performance peaked around 2012 and subsequently collapsed back to its starting level of 100 by 2018, completely erasing prior gains. The chart also indicates that without external capital, production would have risen much more modestly, to around 140, which analysts suggest would have kept prices and profitability higher.

Finally, the author highlights signs of returning capital discipline. A chart tracking energy sector capital raises from 2008 to 2019 (annualized through July) illustrates a significant decline in funding. Total capital raises—comprising US E&P equity issuance and US energy high-yield bond issuance—peaked near seventy billion dollars annually in 2012 and 2013, but have steadily declined in recent years, falling to around thirty billion dollars in 2019. The author concludes that this ongoing rationalization and decline in capital issuance signals a major industry shake-out that should ultimately pave the way for improved returns in the future.

This page, titled "Appendix I: Possible catalysts of a value recovery, and signs that it may already be underway," outlines the potential reversal of value investing's historic underperformance. The author suggests that a recovery could be driven by "exhaustion"—where the extreme discount of value stocks relative to momentum and low-volatility stocks forces underweight investors to rebalance—or accelerated by upcoming policy and regulatory headwinds facing high-performing growth stocks.

The top-left chart, "Premiums paid for momentum and low vol at historic highs," illustrates the Forward P/E premium over value from 1986 to 2018. The line representing momentum minus value shows the premium spiking back toward historic highs near 15, which is close to the peak seen during the dot-com bubble. Meanwhile, the low-volatility minus value premium has reached an all-time high of roughly 10. To the right, the "Broad market premium over value" chart shows the S&P 500 P/E premium over value rising sharply after 2014, climbing past 7 by late 2018 to approach its peak tech-bubble level. 

The commentary identifies antitrust action as a primary threat to dominant growth stocks. A stacked bar chart on the bottom left, titled "Number of Department of Justice antitrust investigations initiated," details the sharp, multi-decade drop in regulatory actions across mergers, monopoly, and competition categories. Annual investigations peaked at over 500 during the 1970s and late 1990s but collapsed to roughly 100 by 2018. 

The bottom-right chart, "Technology companies' share of industry sales," demonstrates why these platforms are increasingly targeted by regulators. Looking at the years 2011 to 2019, Google maintained a dominant though slightly declining share of interactive media and services, sliding from over 90% to around 70%, while Facebook’s share in the same sector grew from near 0% to over 20%. During this same timeframe, Amazon’s share of internet retailing climbed from roughly 45% to nearly 70%, and Apple’s share of tech hardware rose from around 10% to over 40%. 

The author concludes that while major federal antitrust legislation is unlikely before the 2020 election, active Department of Justice investigations, state-level investigations by dozens of Attorneys General, and proposed privacy rules could restrict data-sharing with advertisers and slow the pace of tech-sector acquisitions, thereby dampening the earnings growth of key momentum and growth stocks.

This page analyzes the outlook for the US banking sector, arguing that while certain catalysts like yield curve steepening and institutional investor reweighting could trigger a modest recovery, bank valuations are unlikely to return to their pre-financial crisis peaks. The author points out that structural changes, such as post-crisis re-equitization, have permanently lowered the sector's return on equity. Furthermore, political forces in Washington are unlikely to permit banks to reduce their capital buffers, and the wave of major interstate bank consolidation has already passed, leaving mostly small- to mid-cap mergers that have historically underperformed the broader sector.

To illustrate these trends, the page features several historical charts and a detailed data table. A line chart showing the S&P 500 banks' return on common equity from 1990 to 2018 demonstrates that profitability peaked near 20% in the late 1990s and early 2000s, plunged to a low of approximately -15% during the 2008 financial crisis, and recovered to only about 10% to 12% by 2018. A companion line chart tracking the S&P 500 banks' price-to-book value over the same period reveals that valuations exceeded 3.0x in the early 2000s but have largely hovered between 1.0x and 1.5x since the crisis, supporting the author's claim that price-to-book ratios are unlikely to exceed 2.0x again soon.

Additionally, a line chart tracking the total number of US commercial banks from 1934 to 2014 shows a steady decline from a peak of over 14,000 banks in the mid-1980s to under 6,000 by the end of the period. An accompanying FDIC table from the second quarter of 2019 breaks down the industry's consolidation and financial performance by asset size. The data highlights a highly concentrated landscape where just 9 massive banks with assets exceeding $250 billion control over 53% of all bank assets, achieving a 1.37% return on assets and a 12.66% return on equity. In contrast, the smallest tier of 1,090 banks with assets under $100 million controls a mere 0.38% of industry assets and struggles with a lower return on equity of 6.75%. The intermediate tiers include 2,884 banks with assets between $100 million and $1 billion (controlling 5.50% of assets with an 11.42% return on equity), 531 banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion (8.17% of assets and a 10.64% return on equity), and 116 banks with assets between $10 billion and $250 billion (holding 32.73% of assets with an 11.88% return on equity).

This page focuses on the methodology used to assess investment manager performance, arguing that comparing returns directly to each manager's self-stated preferred benchmark or ETF provides a more accurate picture than over-simplifying with a single standard benchmark per equity style. 

To support this approach, a comprehensive reference table presents the top three most frequently used benchmarks across twenty-three distinct style categories. Each entry details the benchmark name, the total assets under management in millions, and the exact number of managers utilizing that benchmark. 

In the domestic style categories, Russell and S&P indices dominate. For Large Cap Core, the S&P 500 is the leading benchmark with 249 managers representing 555,350 million dollars in assets, followed by the Russell 1000 with 89 managers. Large Cap Growth is heavily dominated by the Russell 1000 Growth index with 226 managers representing 722,351 million dollars, while Large Cap Value is led by the Russell 1000 Value index with 274 managers representing 996,494 million dollars. Similar trends of Russell index dominance appear in Mid Cap, Small Cap, and All Cap sub-styles, with the Russell MidCap, Russell 2000, and Russell 3000 families acting as the primary benchmarks for their respective categories. 

For global and regional styles, MSCI indices are the clear favorites. In the Global category, the MSCI World-ND index leads with 303 managers and 849,671 million dollars in assets, ahead of the MSCI ACWI-ND. For ACWI ex US, the MSCI ACWI ex-US-ND is the top choice with 142 managers. Regional categories such as Europe, Asia excluding Japan, EAFE, and Emerging Markets are similarly led by their respective MSCI Net Daily Total Return (ND) indices. For instance, the MSCI EAFE-ND index is used by 210 managers managing 628,423 million dollars, and the MSCI EM-ND index is used by 246 managers managing 651,039 million dollars. In single-country categories, local benchmarks prevail: TOPIX dominates in Japan with 186 managers, the S&P/ASX 300 leads in Australia with 68 managers, the S&P/TSX Composite leads in Canada with 140 managers, and the FTSE All Share is the clear favorite in the United Kingdom with 94 managers. All data on this page is sourced from eVestment and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page, titled "Early signs of a value recovery?", examines whether the historical performance gap between growth and value stocks is beginning to close. Michael Cembalest observes that in mid-September 2019, value stocks outperformed growth stocks by their largest magnitude since 2009 across both the S&P 500 and Russell 1000 indices. He notes that Bloomberg's factor analysis showed the second-largest weekly return of value versus growth since 2009. While acknowledging that this trend could eventually reverse, he poses the open question of whether this nascent recovery will continue and boost active manager outperformance in the coming months.

The analysis is supported by four charts. The first chart, located on the upper left, displays the cumulative growth return minus the cumulative value return for the S&P 500 and Russell 1000 from January 2019 to September 2019. It shows growth steadily outperforming value throughout the year, peaking in late August at approximately 10% for the Russell 1000 and 5% for the S&P 500, before both lines drop sharply in September, showing a sudden narrowing of the performance gap to roughly 7% and 2.5%, respectively. 

The upper right bar chart shows the largest weekly S&P 500 value versus growth returns since 2009, measured as the weekly value index return minus the growth index return. The week of September 9–13, 2019, highlighted in red, ranks as the fourth-largest weekly outperformance since 2009 at approximately 2.8%, trailing only three periods in 2009: March 9–13 (about 5.2%), May 4–8 (about 5.1%), and August 3–7 (about 3.3%), while coming in just ahead of November 7–11, 2016 (about 2.7%).

The bottom left chart depicts the largest weekly Russell 1000 value versus growth returns since 2009. Here, the week of September 9–13, 2019, is again the fourth-largest at roughly 3.1%, following May 4–8, 2009 (about 5.4%), March 9–13, 2009 (about 4.4%), and August 3–7, 2009 (about 3.1%), and exceeding October 1–5, 2018 (about 2.6%).

The final chart on the bottom right measures the largest weekly value versus growth factor returns since 2009, showing the weekly value factor return minus the growth factor return. For this factor-based metric, the week of September 9–13, 2019, represents the second-highest weekly return since 2009 at 2.0%. This is surpassed only by the week of November 7–11, 2016 (about 2.15%), and is significantly higher than the next three periods—May 4–8, 2009, November 28–December 2, 2016, and March 31–April 4, 2014—which all registered factor return spreads of around 1.1%.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market report analyzes active investment managers by assets under management, manager count, and the availability of exchange-traded funds that correspond to their benchmarks. The author argues that matching managers to representative ETFs rather than abstract market indices offers a more realistic comparison for investors because ETFs incorporate actual fees and tracking error. 

The analysis is based on the eVestment database, covering managers reporting since 1996 with assets under management compiled as of December 2018. To keep the comparison fair, the dataset excludes managers who do not report gross-of-fee performance, those who do not report in U.S. dollars, and those using benchmark-agnostic or custom-blended benchmarks, which accounted for 4% of total assets and 9% of all managers. 

A comprehensive table details these metrics across twenty-three different investment style categories, showing total assets under management in millions of U.S. dollars, the total number of managers, and the percentage breakdown of ETF availability, lack of ETF availability, or lack of benchmark availability. This breakdown is presented in two separate sections: one calculated by total assets under management, and the other by the raw count of active managers. 

At the aggregate level across all categories, the dataset represents over $11.9 trillion in assets under management across 6,707 managers. Overall, 76% of aggregate assets have a corresponding ETF available, 20% have no ETF available, and 4% have no benchmark available. By count of managers, 68% have an ETF available, 23% have no ETF, and 9% have no benchmark. 

The largest single category is Global equities, containing nearly $2.49 trillion in assets across 1,290 managers, with 66% of these assets having an ETF available. Other massive categories include Large Cap Value, with over $1.25 trillion in assets across 389 managers, and EAFE, with over $1.05 trillion in assets across 428 managers, showing 97% and 68% ETF asset availability respectively. Large Cap Growth also represents a major segment with over $1.04 trillion across 294 managers, boasting 100% ETF availability by assets. Emerging Markets represent another significant asset pool at $969,505 million across 527 managers with 71% ETF availability by assets. Conversely, All Cap Growth and All Cap Value show some of the lowest ETF availability rates by assets, at just 18% and 30% respectively.

This page serves as a reference guide defining the acronyms used throughout the J.P. Morgan publication. It outlines general financial concepts, including assets under management, exchange traded funds, price to earnings ratios, and quantitative easing. It also lists standardized abbreviations for capitalization and style investment categories, covering large cap, mid cap, small cap, and all cap segments across core, growth, and value investment styles. Finally, the page defines abbreviations for broader index and geographic classifications, specifically highlighting U.S. dividend focused strategies, the All Country World Index, Europe, Australasia, and the Far East, the United Kingdom, and emerging markets.

This page focuses on exchange-traded fund tracking error by style category. The commentary defines tracking error as the annualized standard deviation of monthly return differences between an ETF and its underlying index. It explains that liquidity constraints often prevent ETF managers from holding all of a benchmark’s constituent stocks, which can result in significant deviations. In some cases, these tracking errors are comparable to the tracking error budgets of active managers seeking outperformance. 

An extensive table lists the assets under management weighted average annualized tracking errors and the corresponding top benchmarks analyzed for twenty-three different investment styles. Domestic US equity styles generally exhibit lower tracking errors. Large Cap Core, Large Cap Growth, and Large Cap Value show tracking errors of 0.58%, 0.65%, and 0.57% against benchmarks such as the S&P 500 and Russell 1000. Mid-cap styles fall between 0.47% and 0.68%, while small-cap styles have higher tracking errors, with Small Cap Value reaching 1.01% against benchmarks like the Russell 2000. 

International, global, and regional categories show much higher levels of tracking error. The Global category has a tracking error of 2.02%, and ACWI ex US has a tracking error of 3.01%. Regional and country-specific categories display some of the highest tracking errors in the table, with Europe and Emerging Markets both at 5.09%, Asia ex Japan at 4.93%, EAFE at 2.98%, Japan at 2.39%, Australia at 1.80%, Canada at 1.75%, and the United Kingdom at 1.39%. The underlying indices for these calculations include regional MSCI benchmarks, the TOPIX, the FTSE All Share, and local Canadian and Australian indices. According to the footnote, the tracking errors were calculated using historical monthly return data from June 2004, or the inception of the ETF, through June 2019.

This page serves as a professional biography for Michael Cembalest, the Chairman of Market and Investment Strategy for J.P. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management. Accompanied by a color headshot of Mr. Cembalest, the text details his extensive career at the firm, which he joined in 1987 in the Corporate Finance division. In his current role, he leads strategic market and investment insights across J.P. Morgan's Institutional, Funds, and Private Banking businesses, representing an asset management division with two trillion dollars in client assets under management as of mid-2019. The biography highlights his previous positions within the firm, including an eight-year tenure as Chief Investment Officer for the Global Private Bank, head of a fixed income division of Investment Management overseeing high grade, high yield, emerging markets, and municipal bonds, and head strategist for Emerging Markets Fixed Income. It also mentions his service on key internal bodies, such as the Asset & Wealth Management Investment Committee and the Investment Committee for the J.P. Morgan Retirement Plan. Finally, the page outlines his academic background, noting that he earned a Master of Arts from the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs in 1986 and a Bachelor of Arts from Tufts University in 1984.

This page, titled "Manager fee assumptions and sensitivity," evaluates how different separate account fee assumptions impact the calculated net-of-fee outperformance statistics for various asset managers. Using gross return and fee schedule data from the eVestment database, the analysis uses a baseline of $50 million separate account fees to compute net-of-fee manager returns. The author's primary finding is that utilizing the higher fees associated with smaller $10 million separate accounts yields only a negligible difference in overall outperformance statistics.
