Citing a Brookings Institution paper by Adam Looney and Constantine Yannelis, the author notes that net college costs are actually thirty to forty-five percent lower than gross costs once institutional aid and federal grants are factored in. 

The first line chart demonstrates this cost dynamic, tracking gross and net tuition, room, and board in real 2018 thousands of dollars from 1999 to 2019. While gross costs for four-year private nonprofits climbed from approximately thirty-three thousand dollars to forty-eight thousand dollars, net costs rose much more modestly, ending near twenty-three thousand dollars. Similarly, gross costs for four-year public institutions grew from eleven thousand dollars to over twenty thousand dollars, while net costs remained relatively flat, hovering between ten thousand and twelve thousand dollars.

The core of the issue is highlighted in the second visual, a comparative column chart detailing the top ten institutions where students hold the most debt in the years 2000 and 2014. In 2000, the list was dominated by selective and somewhat selective traditional schools like New York University, the University of Minnesota, the University of Southern California, and Pennsylvania State University, with only the University of Phoenix representing a for-profit entity. By 2014, the list had inverted completely to consist almost entirely of for-profit institutions, including Ashford University, Argosy University, Kaplan University, Strayer University, Capella University, DeVry University, Walden University, and the University of Phoenix, leaving NYU as the only traditional university in the top ten.

The third visual, a stacked bar chart from 2011 and 2012, displays cumulative debt ranges for bachelor's degree recipients. It reveals that graduates of for-profit universities carry dramatically higher debt loads than those from public or private nonprofit institutions, with a very high percentage of for-profit graduates carrying over forty thousand dollars in debt and almost none graduating debt-free. 

Finally, a line chart tracking the percentage of undergraduates receiving federal student loans from 1993 to 2015 shows that students at private, for-profit institutions have consistently relied on federal loans at a higher rate than any other group. This reliance peaked near eighty percent around 2009 and finished near seventy-five percent in 2015, far exceeding the borrowing rates of students at private nonprofits, public universities, and the overall undergraduate average.

This page examines the structural failures of for-profit colleges and proposes policy reforms to improve the broader student loan system. The author argues that for-profit colleges exhibit low graduation rates, higher student unemployment, lower median earnings, and consequently, higher loan default rates. 

To support this argument, the author presents four charts. The first chart illustrates graduation rates within six years for students seeking bachelor's degrees who started between 1996 and 2011. It shows that nonprofit institutions maintain the highest graduation rates, rising from 55 percent to over 60 percent, while public institutions hover slightly below them. For-profit colleges perform poorly by comparison, with graduation rates consistently lingering between 25 percent and 30 percent. The second chart tracks the tight historical correlation between the for-profit share of Federal student loans and the student loan default rate after two years from 1970 through 2012. Both metrics experienced a massive spike in the late 1980s, peaking near 35 percent, and began rising in tandem once again starting in the mid-2000s.

The third chart plots the relationship between graduate median earnings and unemployment rates in their second year of repayment, categorized by institution type. For-profit graduates experience the worst outcomes, with median earnings around 20,000 dollars and unemployment rates exceeding 20 percent. As institutional selectivity increases up to graduate-level education, median earnings rise steadily to over 50,000 dollars, and the unemployment rate drops below 10 percent. The fourth chart displays the total number of outstanding borrowers as of 2014 alongside the five-year average default rate through 2011. The data reveals that for-profit and two-year programs represent both the highest volume of outstanding borrowers, peaking above 10 million, and the highest cohort default rates, which approach 30 percent. In contrast, selective four-year and graduate programs show significantly lower default rates, dropping under 10 percent.

Rather than implementing proposals to write off all student loans—which the author notes could cost 955 billion dollars, excluding the cost of making public university tuition free—the text outlines several targeted reforms. These include preserving the successful elements of the current student loan system, linking loan repayments to post-graduation income via automatic paycheck withholding, reintroducing risk-based underwriting based on the risk profile of the institution or field of study, and targeting grants and subsidies to underserved populations. The author cautions that preserving government resources is vital, particularly because projections indicate that by the year 2027, entitlements, mandatory payments, and interest will consume 100 percent of Federal tax revenues.

This page argues that economic and market reactions to pandemics are driven more by mortality rates than by contagion itself. Analyzing early COVID-19 data from China’s Center for Disease Control, the author notes that while overall mortality rates drifted from 2.2% to 3.5%, the virus primarily affects older demographics and those with pre-existing conditions. 

Two bar charts illustrate these vulnerabilities. The first chart, depicting the coronavirus mortality rate by age, shows a steep age gradient: mortality peaks near 15% for those aged 80 and older, drops to roughly 8% for ages 70 to 79, falls to about 4% for ages 60 to 69, and declines to near 0% for individuals under 40. The second chart, analyzing mortality by pre-existing conditions, highlights that cardiovascular disease presents the highest risk with a mortality rate exceeding 10%, followed by diabetes at roughly 7.5%, chronic respiratory disease at 6.5%, hypertension at 6%, and cancer at 5.5%, compared to under 1% for individuals with no pre-existing conditions.

Because palliative care has had a limited impact on outcomes, the author suggests that behavioral and environmental factors that compromise lung capacity—specifically smoking and air quality—may play a dominant role in cross-country mortality differences. A bottom scatter plot, mapping countries by their Air Quality Index (where 100 is best) against smoking prevalence, highlights a high-risk zone of poor air quality and high smoking rates. China, Laos, Bangladesh, and Nepal fall into this high-risk category, with China showing an air quality index below 20 and a smoking prevalence of around 25%. Countries like India and Pakistan have poor air quality but lower smoking rates, while Russia, Greece, and Indonesia have high smoking rates but better air quality. The United States enjoys both high air quality, near 95, and lower smoking rates, near 15%. The author posits that if these environmental and behavioral factors are indeed major drivers of the virus's lethality, COVID-19 mortality rates outside of China may turn out to be lower.

This page discusses the economic impacts of the coronavirus pandemic on global and US economies, specifically evaluating the extent of US supply chain reliance on China. The author argues that while US reliance on Chinese intermediate goods is notable, it should not be overstated because no single sector's reliance exceeds 20%. Additionally, healthy levels of manufacturing and wholesaling inventories are expected to help buffer potential supply chain disruptions. 

The first chart, "US reliance on China by industry," displays the percentage of intermediate goods inputs sourced from China by sector in 2018. The electronics sector shows the highest reliance at roughly 17%, followed closely by machinery and miscellaneous manufacturing at 16% and non-metallic mineral products at 15%. Other sectors like furniture, apparel and leather, and plastics and rubber fall between 8% and 12%, while printing, paper and wood, metals, and textiles all remain under 6%.

The second chart, "Coronavirus estimated impact on first quarter growth," illustrates the projected annualized quarter-over-quarter percentage change across various global economies as of February 2020. The estimated impact on the US and UK is negligible (around 0%), while Europe and Japan show modest estimated impacts of roughly -0.5% and -1.0%, respectively. Conversely, Asian economies face much more severe impacts, with projected GDP drops of about -4.0% for Thailand, -4.5% for Taiwan, -5.8% for Singapore, and -7.1% for both Hong Kong and China. 

The remaining two charts present historical US inventory-to-sales ratios from 1997 to 2019, highlighting where inventory cushions exist. The first of these charts compares computer and electronic products against general manufacturing, showing that while computer and electronic product ratios have risen to around 2.2, manufacturing ratios remain steady around 1.4. The second ratio chart contrasts retail and wholesale, showing that wholesale inventory ratios are relatively high at around 1.35, whereas retail ratios are tighter at approximately 1.43 compared to historic highs near 1.55. These trends underscore the author's point that while wholesaling and manufacturing inventories are high, tighter conditions exist within retail and electronics.

This publication page from JP Morgan's Eye on the Market examines the severity and global economic impacts of the emerging COVID-19 pandemic. Author Michael Cembalest outlines several key observations: while infection rates inside China are slowing, they are rising internationally; mortality is heavily skewed toward older people with pre-existing conditions; and China's high smoking rates and poor air quality may make its mortality rate higher than what will be seen elsewhere. Additionally, although Chinese factories are starting to reopen, activity indicators remain near post-Lunar New Year lows, which disrupts global supply chains, though the impact on the United States is expected to be manageable. Cembalest notes that markets are pricing in major earnings declines, suggesting the impact on Chinese corporate earnings may be worse than expected, whereas the hit to US earnings might be milder, raising questions about the appropriate risk premium for Chinese financial assets.

Four charts support these points. The first, titled "New confirmed coronavirus cases per day in China," tracks daily cases in thousands from January 21 to February 25, showing separate lines for Hubei using an old definition, Hubei using a newer, broader definition, and the rest of China. It highlights a sharp decline in cases after a peak in early February, noting the exclusion of about 14,000 cases recognized on February 12 due to a shift in Hubei's testing procedures. The second chart, "Actual vs forecast total reported coronavirus cases in Wuhan, Thousands," plots cumulative cases in thousands from January 10 to March 10. It compares actual cases against two January models by York University epidemiologists: a high-growth projection of up to 600,000 cases before quarantine policies and a severe quarantine and lockdown scenario from January 23. The actual case data closely aligns with the low-growth quarantine scenario, demonstrating that containment policies have been effective.

The bottom half of the page shifts focus to the growing international spread. The third chart, "Coronavirus confirmed cases outside of China," displays cumulative cases from January 21 to February 25, reaching over 2,400 cases. An embedded pie chart details the distribution of these cases as of late February, led by South Korea with 977 cases, the Diamond Princess cruise ship with 691 cases, Italy with 229 cases, Japan with 157 cases, Singapore with 90, Hong Kong with 81, Iran with 61, the United States with 51, and 244 cases across other locations. Finally, the fourth chart, "Coronavirus confirmed cases per day outside of China," tracks the daily count of new cases over the same period, illustrating a dramatic spike to nearly 400 daily cases by February 25, reflecting the rapid global acceleration of the virus that is beginning to alarm financial markets.

This page contains only regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for various jurisdictions, including Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America, detailing the distributing J.P. Morgan entities and their respective regulatory overseers.

Michael Cembalest discusses the presence of weak economic signals in the United States, even amid expectations of an eventual post-coronavirus bounce in global economic activity. He highlights three specific negative pressures: falling US job openings, declining domestic freight activity, and the inventory and production fallout from the Boeing 737 Max grounding. While the Boeing issue is a direct blow to first-quarter growth due to unsold aircraft, the jobs and freight declines are interpreted as lingering aftershocks of the Trump administration's trade wars. 

The first chart, titled "Composite help wanted index and job openings rate," plots historical US job openings and help-wanted data from 1951 through late 2019 on a scale of 1.5% to 5.5%. Shaded vertical grey bars represent recessions. The blue line illustrates that while the job openings rate had risen to historic highs near 5.0% by 2018, it experienced a sharp, sudden downturn heading into late 2019, signalling a softening labor market. 

The second chart, "North American freight volumes and expenditures," tracks year-over-year percentage changes from 1991 through early 2020. It displays two series: freight volumes in blue and freight expenditures in gold, with the y-axis ranging from -30% to 30%. Both lines show a clear downward trend at the far right of the chart, with freight volumes contracting into negative territory to nearly negative 10% by early 2020, representing a distinct slowdown in shipping and logistics. 

The third chart, "Aircraft output and change in inventories," examines the impact of the Boeing 737 Max grounding. It uses dual axes spanning from 2010 to 2020: a left axis index where the 2012 average equals 100, and a right axis in billions of US dollars. The blue line represents aircraft and parts output, showing a sharp drop from its peak near 110 down to around 95 by the start of 2020. Concurrently, the gold line representing the change in transportation equipment inventory, excluding motor vehicles, climbed dramatically to over $20 billion as unsold planes accumulated. J.P. Morgan's first-quarter 2020 average projection, marked by a blue dot, forecasts a severe correction in inventory accumulation down to approximately negative $12 billion, which is expected to drag down near-term GDP growth.

This page examines the severe disruption to global supply chains and the Chinese domestic economy following the early 2020 lockdown, arguing that China’s Asian trading partners will experience more severe economic damage than the United States. It highlights that domestic economic activity in China has recovered only marginally from the post-Lunar New Year low point. 

To illustrate the scale of global supply chain disruptions, the first chart displays the month-over-month change in suppliers' delivery times from 2002 to early 2020, averaging data from Japan, the Euro Area, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The inverted index reveals that supplier delivery times in early 2020 spiked dramatically toward much longer delays, surpassing the disruptions seen during the 2011 Fukushima disaster and approaching the levels of the 2008 financial crisis. 

A second chart tracks high-frequency Chinese economic indicators as a percentage of their historical average, comparing levels 20 days after the Chinese New Year on February 14 against more recent mid-February readings. These indicators—including traffic jams, railway coal deliveries, coal consumption, road and rail travel, transport hub passenger flows, home sales, and box office revenues—remain severely depressed. For instance, box office revenues were virtually at zero percent of historical averages, while transport hub passenger flows and home sales remained below 20 percent, underscoring the slow rate of economic recovery.

The author projects a massive hit to China’s corporate sector in the first quarter of 2020. Prior to the virus outbreak, assuming a 7 percent nominal GDP growth rate, China’s corporate sector was projected to generate RMB 5.7 trillion in net operating cash flow. Instead, Q1 net cash flow is forecast to plunge to as low as RMB 750 billion. 

The commentary notes that emergency government funding and bond market investor preferences will likely favor state-owned enterprises due to implicit state guarantees, dealing another major blow to China’s private sector. This division is depicted in a chart showing net debt issuance in RMB billions from 2014 through late 2019. While state-owned enterprises maintained solid positive net issuance, private companies saw their net issuance plummet into negative territory by the end of 2019, reflecting a loss of debt market access. Consequently, the final chart shows the yield spread of Chinese private debt over state-owned enterprise debt from 2017 to early 2020. This yield spread rose from a low of around 0.5 percent in early 2018 to over 2.0 percent by early 2020, demonstrating the escalating borrowing costs faced by private Chinese firms relative to their state-backed competitors.

This page from JP Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the emerging market and economic implications of the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on asset risk premiums, historical market recoveries, and unique US political risks. Michael Cembalest points out that while MSCI and Barclays are increasing China's weight in global indices, the Chinese government's initial repression of whistleblowing scientists raises critical questions about the risk premium required to hold Chinese assets. He notes that if the virus spreads widely in the United States and triggers disruptions, any market selloff should likely be viewed as a buying opportunity. This perspective is shaped by historical trends where pandemics cause temporary market drops followed by sharp economic rebounds, though Cembalest cautions that a US political front-runner proposing radical economic restructuring—combined with discussions around ending the Senate filibuster—could introduce unpredictable asset repricing risks. 

The first chart, titled "Average S&P 500 performance during and after start of pandemic outbreak," displays the average total return percentage across past pandemics, including SARS, H1N1, H7N9, Ebola, and MERS. The data shows that while the average maximum drawdown within a six-month window is roughly negative seven percent, the market historically rebounds quickly, averaging a positive return of approximately one percent at one month, four percent at three months, and exceeding ten percent by six months. 

The second chart, titled "Impact of coronavirus on global real GDP forecast," displays global real GDP growth on a quarter-over-quarter, seasonally adjusted annualized rate from 2012 with projections through 2021. It compares the forecast made on January 24, before the coronavirus impact was integrated, with the updated current forecast. While the initial forecast expected steady global growth at around two and a half percent, the revised outlook projects a sharp V-shaped shock, with growth plunging to nearly one and a half percent in early 2020 before surging to a peak of nearly three and a half percent later in the year as economic activity normalizes.

In this analysis, J.P. Morgan’s Michael Cembalest assesses the late February 2020 market selloff triggered by the emerging COVID-19 pandemic. He notes that the S&P 500’s 8.1% decline was the second-largest four-day drop from an all-time high on record. While the market priced in an earnings decline of 20% to 25% in China and 10% to 15% in the US and Europe, Cembalest suggests that actual US earnings may prove better than expected, whereas Chinese earnings could be worse. Since he does not anticipate a US recession due to a resilient consumer, he predicts a historical pattern where the market rebounds within six months. He also argues that fears of collapsing interest rates are overstated, pointing to a steepening yield curve.

A chart tracking the spread between the 30-year and 10-year US Treasury from 2014 to early 2020 illustrates this steepening trend. The yield spread declined from approximately 1.0% in 2014 to a low near 0.1% in late 2018, before steadily recovering to around 0.45% by February 2020.

Cembalest emphasizes that financial markets were highly vulnerable to a global shock because equity valuations were extremely elevated in December 2019. A table detailing S&P 500 valuation metrics highlights that the median historical percentile across these metrics was in the 89th percentile. Most notably, US market cap to GDP reached 199% and the Enterprise Value to Sales ratio reached 2.5x, both in the 99th percentile of historical expensiveness. Other highly valued metrics included Enterprise Value to EBITDA at 12.7x (93rd percentile) and the Cyclically Adjusted P/E ratio at 27.8x (89th percentile). In contrast, the S&P earnings yield minus the 10-year US Treasury rate was in the 28th percentile at 362 basis points, reflecting a more moderate relative valuation compared to bonds. 

Two index charts at the bottom of the page display performance from March 2017 to March 2020. The S&P 500 index chart shows a strong upward trend from 2,300 to above 3,300, marked by several sharp historical selloffs, including the early 2020 decline. Conversely, the MSCI Emerging Markets index chart demonstrates more volatility over the same period, peaking near 1,250 in early 2018, dropping below 950 in late 2018, and experiencing a renewed downturn in early 2020 down to the 1,050 range.

This page analyzes the projected impact of Senator Bernie Sanders' Medicare for All proposal on the United States federal debt. Michael Cembalest argues that the healthcare plan alone would dramatically increase government debt, even after factoring in massive tax increases. These offsets include four trillion dollars in new employer healthcare contributions and taxes, another four trillion dollars in new individual healthcare contributions and taxes, one point seven trillion dollars in new individual income and wealth taxes, and five hundred billion dollars in new business taxes. The analysis warns that younger generations, specifically Millennials, will ultimately bear the burden of this debt, and notes that even under the standard baseline, mounting debt servicing costs risk consuming all federal tax receipts.

A line chart details the federal debt as a percentage of GDP from 1940 to 2030, annotating historical levels alongside presidential inauguration dates. Historically, federal debt peaked around one hundred and ten percent of GDP under Harry Truman post-World War II, declined to a low near twenty-five percent in the mid-to-late 1970s, and then trended upward through the administrations of Ronald Reagan, George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Donald Trump to reach approximately eighty percent of GDP by 2020. Looking forward to 2030, the chart compares two trajectories: the Congressional Budget Office baseline, which shows debt steadily rising to about one hundred percent of GDP, and the Sanders healthcare plan projection, which shows debt sharply accelerating to surpass one hundred and forty percent of GDP by 2030.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the surprising outcome of the 2020 Democratic Primary following Super Tuesday, where Senator Joe Biden unexpectedly gained a delegate lead over Senator Bernie Sanders. The author, Michael Cembalest, posits that voters may have been searching for moderation and traditional Democratic Party alignment. To illustrate this, the page features a chart titled "Partisanship and ideology score for candidates seeking the Democratic Presidential nomination in the modern era," which relies on Congressional voting records from the UCLA VoteView project. 

The vertical axis ranges from 0.0 to 0.8, where a score of 1 indicates the highest degree of political partisanship and ideological liberalism. The chart plots dozens of candidates from the modern primary era starting in 1960. On the far left, representing the most moderate positions, are figures like Lloyd Bentsen, Jim Webb, and Joe Lieberman with scores between 0.1 and 0.2. On the far right, representing the most progressive and partisan figures, are Bernie Sanders (the highest at roughly 0.75), Elizabeth Warren, and Kamala Harris. Joe Biden sits near the middle of this historical spectrum with a score of approximately 0.4. Detailed footnotes discuss Super Tuesday delegate projections from 538.com, NPR, and the New York Times, alongside historical details of pre-1960 conventions and the methodology behind the Voteview spatial voting scores.

This page examines the economic assumptions of Senator Bernie Sanders’s previous presidential bid by reproducing a critical open letter written during his 2016 campaign. Michael Cembalest introduces the document as a response from mainstream Democratic economists to what he characterizes as the campaign's unrealistic economic assumptions. 

The reprinted letter, dated February 17, 2016, is addressed to Senator Sanders and his economic advisor, Professor Gerald Friedman. It is signed by four former Chairs of the Council of Economic Advisers under Presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama: Alan Krueger, Austan Goolsbee, Christina Romer, and Laura D’Andrea Tyson. In the letter, these economists argue that the Sanders campaign is citing extreme, unsupported claims regarding the positive impacts of Sanders’s economic plan on growth rates, income, and employment. They assert that no credible economic research supports these projections, which they describe as exceeding even the most grandiose claims made by Republicans about tax cuts. The authors warn that making such unrealistic promises undermines the Democratic Party's reputation for evidence-based policy and "responsible arithmetic," ultimately making it more difficult to challenge the fiscal claims of political opponents and damaging the credibility of the progressive economic agenda.

This J.P. Morgan report page, titled "Appendix charts: COVID-19 in context," provides historical and statistical perspective on the emerging COVID-19 pandemic as of late February 2020. In the introductory text, the author notes that the first chart compares the infection and mortality rates of COVID-19 against SARS and the Swine Flu, while the second chart compares a broader array of communicable diseases. To put these figures into perspective, the author shares the US CDC's preliminary estimates for the concurrent US seasonal flu, which stood at 29 to 41 million illnesses, 280,000 to 500,000 hospitalizations, and 16,000 to 41,000 deaths.

The first chart, titled "Contagion from coronavirus vs SARS and swine flu," plots days since the outbreak on the horizontal axis (from 0 to 200 days) against the number of global cases in thousands on the left vertical axis (from 0 to 100) and total deaths on the right vertical axis (from 0 to 2,600). The data, sourced from Johns Hopkins University as of February 24, 2020, illustrates a stark contrast in transmission speed. The coronavirus case trajectory rises almost vertically, reaching approximately 80,000 cases in just over 50 days, whereas the Swine Flu took roughly 100 days to reach 100,000 cases, and SARS cases plateaued under 10,000. In terms of total deaths, the coronavirus also shows a steep upward trajectory, exceeding 2,400 deaths by day 50, compared to SARS which plateaued near 800 deaths around day 120.

The second chart, titled "Diseases by contagiousness (reproductive number) and mortality," maps dozens of infectious diseases on a grid. The horizontal axis measures contagiousness using the average basic reproductive number, or R0, ranging from 0 (not contagious) to 18 (extremely contagious). The vertical axis shows the mortality rate, utilizing a non-linear scale at the bottom (ranging from 0.0% to 1.0%, then progressing to 10.0% and up to 100.0%) to distinguish diseases with lower mortality rates. Early coronavirus estimates are represented by red dots, positioning the virus with an R0 of roughly 2 to 3 and an estimated mortality rate of 1.0% to 3.0%. This places the virus near the historical Spanish Flu in terms of both severity and spread. In comparison, seasonal flu is shown to be less contagious (R0 of roughly 1.3) and far less deadly (mortality below 0.1%). Meanwhile, other diseases on the chart occupy extreme positions, such as untreated rabies with a 100% mortality rate and an R0 near 10, measles with an R0 between 12 and 14 and a mortality rate around 1%, and malaria with an exceptionally high R0 of 17.

This page evaluates the general election electability of Democratic presidential candidates Bernie Sanders and Joe Biden against incumbent Donald Trump, focusing on swing state polling and potential electoral college paths to victory. The author notes that while both Sanders and Biden have polled well against Trump in key swing states, polling may fail to capture the full picture due to some voters' reluctance to admit their support for Trump. 

The analysis is supported by two scatter plots tracking polling margins in key swing states as of February 2020. The first plot displays Trump-versus-Sanders polling, where negative values indicate a Sanders lead and positive values indicate a Trump lead. The second plot displays Trump-versus-Biden polling on the same scale. Both Democrats show strong leads (negative spreads reaching down to -8% or lower) in several critical swing states, including Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Colorado, while Trump shows leads in states like Iowa and Florida. 

Additionally, a stacked bar chart illustrates four possible electoral paths for a Sanders victory, based on the assumption that Ohio leans Republican. All scenarios require a baseline of safe and likely Democratic electoral votes combined with leaning Democratic states like Nevada, Minnesota, and Michigan. Scenario one reaches 278 electoral votes by winning Florida. Scenario two achieves 279 votes by securing Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Scenario three reaches 275 votes by winning North Carolina and Arizona. Scenario four secures exactly the required 270 votes by winning Arizona and Wisconsin. The author cautions that these combinations rely on polling estimates that had already shown discrepancies in primary contests just prior to publication.

This page of the report addresses whether the onset of spring and summer could slow COVID-19 transmission rates. The author outlines three main theories behind why influenza peaks in the winter, focusing on increased indoor clustering in cold weather, colder and drier air facilitating airborne travel and longevity of viruses, and reduced winter sunlight limiting natural UV sterilization. The discussion highlights scientific consensus that influenza peaks during cold, dry conditions, with animal studies demonstrating that high temperatures and humidity sharply slow or halt transmission. It notes that while the 2003 SARS epidemic declined from March to May as temperatures rose, concurrent public health interventions made isolating weather's impact inconclusive. The author explains the biological mechanisms, noting that low winter humidity impairs protective mucus function and that influenza virions are less stable in high humidity, which causes respiratory droplets to settle more quickly. The role of sunlight is emphasized, citing a study from Brazil correlating smoke-blocked UV radiation with rising influenza admissions, and a US military study where UV sterilization prevented flu spread in a veterans hospital. Ultimately, the author cautions that COVID-19's relationship with temperature, humidity, and sunlight remains unclear and distinct from influenza and SARS, adding in a footnote that MERS showed no weather seasonality due to its animal-to-human transmission. The open question is posed that if weather indeed influences COVID-19, infection rates may fall in the Northern Hemisphere as temperatures rise but rise in the Southern Hemisphere during its winter months of June, July, and August.

This page of the report, authored by Michael Cembalest, addresses the potential economic and market impacts of a hypothetical Bernie Sanders presidency. Cembalest argues that a progressive, unified government would likely lead to a repricing of financial assets, noting that a fundamental restructuring of the economic sectors that have driven equity market gains over the past decade cannot occur without market disruption. 

To illustrate the scope of these proposed changes, the page presents a comprehensive, two-column table listing thirty major progressive policy proposals synthesized from the Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren campaigns. Key financial and tax proposals include taxing unrealized capital gains annually, unifying capital gains with ordinary income tax rates, repealing individual and corporate tax cuts, imposing a wealth tax of two percent on wealth over fifty million dollars, and placing a surtax on corporate profits over one hundred million dollars. Additional financial market proposals include breaking up big banks, implementing new financial transaction taxes, reversing anti-competitive mergers, and banning or curbing stock buybacks. Environmental and labor proposals feature a ban on hydraulic fracturing on public and private land, banning fossil fuel exports, banning state "right to work" laws, and requiring worker election of at least forty percent of corporate board members. Major social and welfare policies listed include implementing Medicare for All with a ban on private health insurance, wiping out student debt for seventy-five percent of students, establishing a national rent control standard at one-and-a-half times the consumer price index, and providing a three trillion dollar subsidy for a clean energy transition.

Cembalest then analyzes the feasibility of implementing such sweeping reforms, noting that success under a Democratic president would depend heavily on three key political dynamics. First, the margin of control in the Senate is critical. Democrats would need to gain at least three seats to win a majority with the Vice President's tie-breaking vote, but projections suggest any majority would be very slim. Cembalest contrasts this tight margin with historical progressive legislative expansions, noting that the Affordable Care Act in 2010 barely reached the necessary sixty-vote threshold even with fifty-eight Democratic seats, whereas the Great Society and New Deal programs were passed during eras of dominant Democratic Senate majorities of sixty-five percent to eighty percent. Second, the fate of these policies depends on whether a Democratic Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer would scrap the legislative filibuster to allow passage via a simple majority, a move recommended by his predecessor Harry Reid. Cembalest poses that Schumer's decisions may be influenced by political pressures from the left of his party, citing a story in The Atlantic about potential primary challenges in 2022. Finally, the author questions whether a Democratic president would bypass a gridlocked Congress entirely by using executive orders to implement changes in areas like energy, immigration, and trade, following precedents set by Donald Trump.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures, legal disclaimers, and distribution warnings for various jurisdictions, including Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America, with no financial charts, tables, or market commentary.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" uses six charts to demonstrate how proposed policy changes, if enacted, could challenge US equity markets by disrupting the key drivers of their recent performance. The overall argument highlights the reliance of equity markets on stock buybacks, hydraulic fracturing for energy independence, tech sector profit margins, competitive international tax rates, and deregulation.

The first chart, "Sources of 2018 net US equity demand," shows that corporations are the primary driver of equity demand, contributing over $600 billion in net demand through share buybacks. This far outpaces foreign investors, while net sellers are led by pension funds, mutual funds, households, and life insurance. 

The second chart, "Total banks' shareholder yield based on approved capital plans," details how this corporate buyback reliance manifests in the banking sector. Across major US financial institutions—including Wells Fargo, Citigroup, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, and J.P. Morgan—the vast majority of the total shareholder yield comes from approved share buybacks rather than dividend yields. The average bank shareholder yield sits at approximately 10%, with Wells Fargo leading at around 14% and U.S. Bancorp at the lower end near 6%.

The third chart, "Percentage of US oil and gas production derived from hydraulic fracturing," illustrates the critical role of fracking in US energy independence from 1995 to 2019. By 2019, hydraulic fracturing accounted for nearly 80% of US natural gas production and roughly 60% of both crude oil and natural gas liquids, such as ethane, propane, and butane. 

The fourth chart, "Tech: the primary driver for US margin expansion," plots the trailing 12-month average operating margin for S&P 500 companies from 1991 to 2018. The data shows that the overall expansion in S&P 500 profit margins has been almost entirely driven by information technology, which rose to around 24% by 2018, and communication services, which reached roughly 17%. Conversely, other sectors—including consumer discretionary, consumer staples, healthcare, and industrials—have remained flat, hovering between 8% and 10% for nearly thirty years.

The fifth chart, "Marginal effective tax rate," compares the effective corporate tax rate on new investment in manufacturing and services across different regions. Prior to tax reform, the US marginal effective tax rate was around 35%, significantly higher than competitors in Asia-Oceania, Europe, Canada, and Mexico, which ranged from 18% to 26%. The 2017 tax bill reduced the current US marginal effective rate to approximately 18%, aligning the US with global averages and leveling the playing field.

The final chart, "Small business concerns about regulation," tracks the percentage of respondents citing regulation as their largest problem from 1986 to 2018. This metric peaked at over 23% in the early 1990s and again between 2012 and 2014, but steadily declined to around 13% by 2018, indicating that regulatory relief has been a significant support for small businesses in recent years.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s publication explores two distinct epidemiological topics regarding COVID-19: the significance of virus reproductive numbers across Chinese provinces and the survival persistence of coronaviruses on hard surfaces. 

In the first section, Cembalest discusses the basic reproductive number, or R0, explaining that it is an empirical measurement reflecting not only the inherent transmission risk of a disease but also human behavior and healthcare infrastructure. Consequently, early January measurements of R0 differed widely across Chinese provinces depending on living density, mass gatherings, and local isolation protocols. Although aggressive interventions like quarantines and contact tracing sharply reduced reproductive numbers by mid-February, the author notes that controlling the outbreak requires the reproductive number to fall below one. Because most Chinese provinces remained above this threshold in mid-February, researchers cautioned that lifting quarantine restrictions prematurely could risk reaccelerating the infection rate. 

These dynamics are illustrated in a scatter plot titled "COVID-19 reproductive numbers in Chinese provinces," which lists 30 provinces along the horizontal axis, ordered from highest to lowest initial basic reproductive number. The vertical axis measures reproductive numbers from zero to six, with a horizontal dashed line marking the critical threshold of one. The blue squares display the initial basic reproductive number, which ranges from a high of around 5.5 in Jilin and 5.0 in Heilongjiang down to about 1.5 in Fujian. In comparison, the gold squares represent the reproductive numbers as of February 12, showing dramatic declines across the board. On this date, almost all provinces clustered between one and two, with only a few, such as Yunnan, Qinghai, and Fujian, dropping below the critical threshold of one. 

In the second section, the author addresses how long viruses can survive on hard surfaces, known as fomites, pointing out that even five seconds of exposure can transfer 31 percent of influenza’s viral load to hands. Drawing from a March 2020 report in the Journal of Hospital Infection, he highlights that SARS and other human coronaviruses persist at room temperature for four to five days on surfaces like glass, plastic, steel, ceramic, and Teflon. Notable exceptions include aluminum, where survival is limited to two to eight hours, and environments where temperatures exceed 86 degrees Fahrenheit, which significantly shortens virus persistence. To provide further context, Cembalest references a 2007 study from the American Society of Microbiology showing that influenza and coronaviruses lose 90 percent of their infectivity within a few hours. Additionally, he notes that contaminated surfaces can be disinfected in just one minute using standard concentrations of household bleach or ethyl alcohol.

This page explores the crucial distinction between being infected and being clinically sick during a pandemic, urging caution when interpreting early coronavirus mortality rate estimates. The author begins by noting that while reported infections outside of China are accelerating at a rate similar to China's early outbreak, early mortality statistics are highly unreliable because the actual number of asymptomatic infections is unknown. 

An included line chart, titled "Coronavirus T days after respective region's outbreak," compares the cumulative number of cases over a 36-day period for Mainland China (starting January 21, 2020) and the world excluding China (starting February 4, 2020). The curves show that the rest of the world is tracing China's early exponential path, even though Mainland China's cumulative cases eventually plateaued around 81,000. Beside the chart, a list of global control measures highlights major disruptions, including Italy's quarantine of 16 million people, school closures in France, food rationing in the United Kingdom, and high-profile event cancellations by entities like Adobe, Facebook, Google, IBM, Microsoft, the IMF, and the Geneva Motor Show.

The core of the page’s argument outlines four variables that define pandemic data: total population, total infected (including asymptomatic individuals), self-reported sick individuals, and the deceased. Early pandemic estimates divide deaths by self-reported cases, which inflates the mortality rate. To illustrate this, the author points to the 2009 H1N1 Swine Flu, where early World Health Organization estimates of 1.0% to 1.3% were eventually revised down to just 0.02% four years later in a study with the Imperial College of London once asymptomatic cases were factored into the denominator. 

Finally, the text addresses a forecast by Harvard epidemiologist Marc Lipsitch that 40% to 70% of the world's population could become infected. The author strongly warns readers not to multiply this projected infection rate by early, inflated mortality rate estimates. He emphasizes that the vast majority of infected individuals will never become clinically ill, and approximately 80% of those who do show symptoms will only develop mild infections.

This page from Michael Cembalest's J.P. Morgan publication examines the environmental factors that influence viral transmission and details the aggressive measures required to control a pandemic like COVID-19. The top portion of the page features two charts assessing weather-related trends in disease spread. The first chart, titled SARS daily incidence and air temperature, shows the daily incidence of SARS patients in 2003 as a function of mean daily air temperatures in Celsius from March to May. As temperatures rose from 15.5 degrees to 29.5 degrees Celsius, daily incidence fell sharply from peak levels near 75 cases to near zero. The second chart, titled Global influenza peaks, plots precipitation in millimeters on the y-axis against specific humidity in grams of water vapor per kilogram of air on the x-axis. This visual shows that primary influenza peaks, marked as black dots, cluster heavily in winter-like conditions of low humidity (under 5 grams per kilogram) and low precipitation, with another distinct cluster in tropical summer conditions of high humidity and precipitation.

The bottom half of the page shifts to outbreak mitigation, emphasizing that controlling COVID-19 requires aggressive isolation of infected individuals and contact tracing within three to four days. The author expresses doubt regarding whether Western democracies can execute contact tracing as aggressively as China. A final chart, titled Aggressive isolation of infected individuals' traced contacts is required to control COVID-19 outbreaks, models the percentage of simulated outbreaks controlled against the percentage of contacts traced and isolated. The chart plots three curves representing different reproductive numbers. For a reproductive number of 1.5, control is relatively easy to achieve. However, at a reproductive number of 2.5, a circled dot on the chart emphasizes that an 80 percent contact isolation rate is necessary to achieve a 90 percent chance of controlling the outbreak. If the reproductive number is 3.5, the curve shows that almost 100 percent of contacts must be traced and isolated to control the outbreak. These simulations assume that 100 percent of identified cases and contacts are isolated after a three-to-four-day delay, and that 15 percent of individuals transmit the infection before showing symptoms.

This page consists entirely of legal and regulatory disclosures concluding the publication. It details distribution restrictions, regulatory compliance, and licensing exemptions for J.P. Morgan entities operating in various jurisdictions, specifically covering Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America. The text highlights that the materials are intended for wholesale clients in Australia and private placements in Latin America, while noting that the content has not been reviewed by local regulatory authorities in certain areas. No charts, financial tables, or market analyses are present on this page.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market argues that the 1918 Spanish Flu is a poor historical proxy for the COVID-19 pandemic due to massive advancements in modern medicine and healthcare infrastructure. The author presents several key differences: first, while no vaccine was ever developed for the Spanish Flu, modern researchers benefit from an 86% genetic similarity between COVID-19 and SARS, allowing them to build on previous vaccine and antibody research led by institutions like Harvard and the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. Second, most deaths during the 1918 pandemic were caused by secondary bacterial pneumonia infections rather than the virus itself, which could be treated with modern antibiotics that did not enter mass production until the 1940s. Additionally, the US CDC reports that the 1918 virus is sensitive to modern FDA-approved anti-influenza drugs like rimantadine and oseltamivir. Finally, modern innovations like ICU-level care, ventilators, and antivirals are now widely available, whereas pre-1918 US life expectancy hovered at just 50 to 55 years.

To support these points, the page features two charts. The first is a line chart showing US life expectancy at birth in years from 1900 to 2015, split by gender. It illustrates a dramatic, sharp spike downward in 1918, where male life expectancy plunged to around 37 years and female life expectancy dropped to roughly 42 years. Following this shock, both lines steadily climb, showing how twentieth-century medical innovations helped raise life expectancies to approximately 76 for men and 81 for women by 2015. 

The second chart is a stacked bar chart showing the percentage of cultures containing bacteria that caused secondary respiratory infections and pneumonia during the Spanish Flu in 1918. Breaking the data down by military samples, civilian samples, and the overall total, the chart reveals that more than 80% of all cultures in each category contained bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae/hemolyticus or Staphylococcus aureus. Only a small sliver, representing roughly 10% to 15% of samples, showed no bacteria found. This data supports the scientific consensus that secondary bacterial infections were the true driver of high case fatality rates during the 1918 pandemic, highlighting why the modern availability of antibiotics makes COVID-19 a very different medical challenge.

This page focuses on the trajectory and potential spread of COVID-19, comparing real-world data from China with hypothetical UK government estimates. The author argues that outside of the outbreak's epicenter in Wuhan and Hubei, Chinese infection and mortality rates are remarkably low—comparable in some cases to seasonal flu mortality for elderly populations in developed nations. 

To support this observation, the page features a detailed table of COVID-19 statistics across select Chinese provinces as of March 8, 2020. The data shows that while Wuhan and Hubei experienced high death rates among the sick of 4.75% (2,370 deaths) and 4.41% (2,986 deaths) respectively, other provinces recorded vastly milder outcomes. For example, populous Guangdong, with over 113 million people, reported only 1,352 sick cases and 7 deaths, translating to a 0.52% death rate among the sick. Other major regions, such as Zhejiang, Henan, Hunan, and Beijing, also show death rates among the sick mostly below 2%, with total infection-to-population rates rounding to 0.00%. 

The author contrasts these actual figures with two modeling scenarios for the United Kingdom to analyze what a projected 100,000 UK deaths would imply. The first estimate assumes that 38% of the 66.44 million UK population becomes infected, with 40% of those infected getting sick and experiencing a 1% mortality rate. The second estimate assumes a 33% infection rate where only 10% of those infected get sick, but they experience a 4.43% mortality rate, which mirrors the epicenter in Wuhan. 

The author notes that both UK models present scenarios magnitudes worse than the reality observed in China and South Korea, leaving a puzzling pandemic gap. He poses the question of why Hubei's mortality rates were so much higher than other regions, concluding that a collapse in Hubei's healthcare infrastructure due to a sudden flood of infections prevented doctors from providing the round-the-clock care that kept patients alive in other cities.

This page focuses on the unprecedented scale of China's quarantine measures during the early phase of the COVID-19 outbreak, comparing the transmission dynamics of this new disease against the 2003 SARS outbreak, while also illustrating the severe economic fallout on Chinese activity and global tourism. The author argues that containing COVID-19 is fundamentally more difficult than SARS because evidence suggests its serial interval may be shorter than its incubation period. This means asymptomatic individuals could be highly contagious before they even show symptoms, rendering patient isolation protocols at healthcare facilities far less effective than they were during the SARS outbreak. 

To demonstrate the domestic economic shock of these strict quarantine measures, a line chart shows Chinese manufacturing and services business surveys from 2006 through early 2020. Both indices plummeted in February 2020 to all-time lows, far deeper than the declines seen during the 2008 financial crisis. A companion bar chart tracks high-frequency Chinese economic indicators as a percentage of their historical averages, comparing levels 20 days after the Chinese New Year against the most recent levels in late February and early March. While some indicators show a slight rebound—such as electricity usage and factory capacity climbing to roughly 60 percent by late February, and coal consumption and railway deliveries also recovering—the author cautions that electricity figures may overstate actual productivity. Meanwhile, travel and leisure indicators remain severely depressed, with road and rail travel, transport hub flows, and home sales sitting at a fraction of their historical averages, and box office revenues lingering near zero.

The final portion of the page shifts to the vulnerability of global markets to a disruption in tourism, utilizing data from OECD countries in 2018. The first bar chart details domestic and inbound tourism spending as a percentage of gross domestic product, showing that nations like Mexico, Portugal, and New Zealand are particularly vulnerable, with tourism revenues making up more than 11 percent of their GDP, compared to the United States at around 5 percent. A final bar chart maps tourism employment as a percentage of total employment, illustrating the potential impact on labor markets. Iceland is the most exposed with over 15 percent of its workforce dependent on tourism, followed closely by Spain, Ireland, Greece, and Portugal, while US tourism employment represents about 4 percent of the country's total workforce.

This page analyzes the challenges of comparing COVID-19 mortality rates during the early stages of the pandemic, arguing that mortality figures are highly sensitive to local factors such as testing volume, regional healthcare quality, and the disproportionate impact of initial epicenters. The author emphasizes that the heavy concentration of deaths in Wuhan and Hubei province skews both Chinese and global mortality measures, while nations like South Korea, which implemented widespread testing, show much lower mortality rates that may closer reflect the true ratio of deaths to total infections. Iran is highlighted as a region of concern due to a fragile healthcare system exacerbated by sanctions and the emigration of medical professionals.

A large bubble chart on the page plots mortality rates from zero to five percent, comparing COVID-19 across different regions against other notable infectious diseases. For COVID-19, represented by blue bubbles scaled by relative fatalities, high mortality rates are concentrated in Wuhan at 4.7 percent and Hubei at 4.4 percent, which pulls China's overall rate to 3.8 percent. Outside of Hubei, however, China's mortality rate drops to 0.9 percent, with local rates ranging from 1.9 percent in Beijing to 0.1 percent in Jiangxi. In the rest of the world, Italy shows a high mortality rate of 4.0 percent, while Iran is at 2.5 percent, and the global average excluding China sits at 2.0 percent. In contrast, the Diamond Princess cruise ship reports a 1.0 percent rate, and South Korea stands at 0.7 percent. These are compared against historical and seasonal diseases, shown as orange dots, which include yellow fever at 4.9 percent, West Nile virus at 4.2 percent, the Spanish flu at 3.5 percent, cholera at 3.2 percent, initial swine flu estimates at 1.3 percent, measles at 0.7 percent, and seasonal US flu at 0.1 percent overall, rising to 0.8 percent for individuals aged 65 and older. 

Supporting the discussion on healthcare system vulnerability, two bar charts compare international medical infrastructure. The first chart, illustrating the Healthcare Access and Quality Index, shows top-performing nations like Switzerland, Japan, and Germany scoring well above 90, while Iran is highlighted in red with a lower score of approximately 72. The second chart measures physicians per 1,000 people, where leading European nations boast more than 4.0 physicians per 1,000 people, whereas Iran, also highlighted in red, possesses just over 1.0 physician per 1,000 people, placing it near the bottom of the tracked nations alongside Chile and Thailand.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" focuses on the concept of economic resilience and recovery following severe crises. The author introduces a quote from John Stuart Mill’s 1848 work, *Principles of Political Economy*, which observes how rapidly nations recover from devastating events like earthquakes, floods, and wars. Cembalest applies this historical optimism to the COVID-19 pandemic, arguing that modern medical advances will facilitate a similar road to recovery. He references updates to J.P. Morgan’s online materials, which track infection rates, the efficacy of treatments like Remdesivir and Chloroquine, and geopolitical factors like Chinese information repression. 

To support the narrative of progress, the page presents two historical charts focused on demographic data from France since 1740. The first chart, "Male life expectancy in France since 1740," tracks life expectancy in years from 1740 to 2010. It shows a dramatic upward trajectory, rising from under 30 years in the 18th century to nearly 80 years by 2010. The chart demonstrates that major drops in life expectancy were primarily driven by human conflict rather than natural disasters, highlighting sharp declines during the Napoleonic wars, the War of 1870, World War I, and World War II, alongside a gap in data during the French Revolution. 

The second chart, "Infant mortality in France since 1740," measures the risk of a newborn dying before their first birthday per 1,000 live births. Infant mortality plummeted from nearly 300 deaths per 1,000 births in the mid-1700s to almost zero by 2020. The chart highlights historical spikes caused by cholera outbreaks in 1834, 1859, and 1871, an exceptionally hot summer in 1911, the Spanish influenza pandemic in 1918, and a smaller disruption in 1945. Together, these charts serve as a proxy for the extraordinary medical achievements of the 20th century, suggesting that modern scientific tools leave society far better equipped to handle the COVID-19 pandemic than previous generations were during historical plagues.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication presents a historical argument for economic resilience, suggesting that economies often rebound from major crises faster than they decline. To illustrate this, the author highlights the aftermath of the US Civil War, which was the deadliest conflict in US history, causing six times the number of war deaths as a percentage of the population compared to World War II. Despite the complete destruction of the southern United States and minimal federal assistance, agricultural income rebounded remarkably quickly. 

A line chart titled "Post Civil War recovery in Confederate farm income" illustrates this trend using an index where 100 represents the level in 1859. The chart shows that farm income plunged to a low of approximately 84 in 1865 at the end of the war, but then recovered rapidly, experiencing some volatility before ultimately climbing above 104 by 1880. 

Applying this historical resilience to the COVID-19 pandemic, Michael Cembalest posits that while the economic situation is likely to worsen in the near term, the world is poised to feel seventy to eighty percent back to normal within a year. He attributes this anticipated recovery to twenty-first-century medical advancements, the application of artificial intelligence and big data in drug development, and the inherent adaptability of modern economies. For investors, he notes that financial markets historically bottom out before crisis indicators like bank failures and defaults actually begin to improve. Additionally, a footnote references research by Hideki Toya and Mark Skidmore on natural disasters, noting that countries with higher incomes, better education, open financial systems, and developed supply chains tend to suffer fewer long-run losses from severe systemic shocks.

In this section of the publication, Michael Cembalest examines historical economic contractions that required many years for GDP to recover to put the potential long-term impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic into perspective. He argues that deep, prolonged economic declines are typically the result of colossal wartime destruction of capital stock or massive economic mismanagement, suggesting that the economic aftershocks of COVID-19 will likely be much shorter than these extreme historical episodes. 

The first case study focuses on the decade required for Germany and Japan to recover pre-war levels of per capita GDP following World War II. An accompanying line chart plots real per capita GDP in thousands of 1990 dollars from 1930 to 1960. Both nations saw their per capita GDP peak during the war before experiencing catastrophic collapses in 1945, with Germany dropping from nearly 450,000 to 150,000 dollars and Japan dropping to nearly 100,000 dollars. Neither nation fully recovered to pre-war peaks until approximately 1955. To illustrate the scale of wartime destruction, the author notes that by 1945, Germany had lost 20% of its housing stock, saw food production halved compared to 1938 levels, and experienced a drop in daily caloric intake to 1,250 calories. Japan lost 40% of its capital stock, 25% of its housing, and sustained destruction across 67 cities. Furthermore, Germany lost over 8% of its population, while Japan lost 4%. 

The second case study details China’s Great Leap Forward, which the author describes as a catastrophic instance of economic mismanagement. A dual-axis line chart from 1955 to 1964 illustrates the relationship between daily caloric intake and the national mortality rate during this period. As daily caloric intake plunged from roughly 2,100 calories in 1958 to a low of 1,500 calories in 1960, the national mortality rate spiked dramatically from approximately 12% to over 25%. This crisis resulted from forced collectivization, the rejection of agricultural science, and unrealistic industrial quotas that led to the melting down of household tools. This mismanagement resulted in an estimated 30 to 60 million unnatural deaths between 1958 and 1961. The text cites historian Frank Dikötter, who argues that a portion of the death toll was intentional, involving victims who were executed or tortured rather than simply starving. 

Finally, a footnote highlights other notable long-recovery periods, including the 15 years required for Iran to regain its 1978 per capita GDP level after the Iranian Revolution, and the 13 years required for Peru to regain its prior economic peak during the rise and fall of the Shining Path movement.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication, containing no financial commentary, charts, or market analysis. It details compliance guidelines and distribution restrictions across multiple global jurisdictions, specifically addressing regulatory requirements in Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America, with mentions of Brazil and Mexico. The text defines the specific J.P. Morgan entities distributing the material and identifies their governing regulatory bodies, such as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Securities and Futures Commission of Hong Kong, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, and the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission. Additionally, it highlights restrictions limiting the distribution of the material to wholesale clients in Australia and private placements in Latin American jurisdictions.

This page discusses the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on US GDP and corporate earnings, comparing current market-priced expectations against historical cycles of decline and recovery. J.P. Morgan economists, including Michael Feroli in his paper titled "The lamps are going out all across the economy," estimate a sharp 14% annualized quarter-over-quarter decline in US GDP for Q2 2020. This contraction would represent the largest since 1947, surpassing the 10% decline in Q1 1958. This baseline scenario assumes that lockdown restrictions gradually lift in May, with mobility and transport returning to normal by June, followed by a slow recovery with lingering weakness through the end of the year. 

To evaluate what is currently priced into equity markets, the author presents a chart of the US earnings per share level implied by dividend futures as a percentage of the pre-virus level, using data from Bridgewater. The chart compares market expectations from January 20, which anticipated steady growth to nearly 20% above pre-virus levels by 2030, to expectations in mid-March 2020. The updated pricing shows a severe bottoming out at a 45% earnings decline by late 2022, followed by an incredibly slow recovery that fails to reach the prior peak even by 2030, remaining roughly 10% below pre-virus levels at the end of the decade.

The author notes that such a prolonged recovery would be highly anomalous compared to historical corporate earnings drawdowns. This point is supported by two historical charts. The first, utilizing data from Robert J. Shiller and S&P Dow Jones Indices, plots S&P 500 earnings drawdowns from 1870 to 2010, measuring the maximum drawdown of reported and operating earnings per share. It highlights historic collapses, including the Great Depression and the 2008 financial crisis, where reported earnings fell by over 80% and 90% respectively. 

The final chart provides a peak-to-trough-to-peak analysis of large US earnings declines exceeding 15% across twelve historical periods, sourced from Bloomberg and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The stacked bar chart shows the years spent from peak to trough in blue and the years required to regain the prior peak in gold. While extreme cases like the November 1894 and November 1932 troughs required roughly 21 and 18 years respectively to fully recover, the post-war era shows a much swifter recovery pattern. For troughs in 1952, 1958, 1983, 1991, 2001, and 2009, the entire process of falling and regaining the prior peak generally took less than four years, and occasionally under three years, suggesting that the decade-long recovery currently priced into dividend futures is historically pessimistic.

This page presents a historical analysis of financial crises, arguing that asset prices and credit spreads consistently bottom out or peak well before the associated defaults, bank failures, and delinquency rates reach their worst points and begin to improve. 

The first row of charts focuses on high-yield credit spreads versus cumulative defaults across three distinct periods of stress. In the Savings and Loan Crisis from 1987 to 1993, high-yield spreads peaked when cumulative defaults were at only 55% of their eventual cycle total. During the Tech Collapse from 1999 to 2004, spreads peaked when cumulative defaults stood at 76%. During the Global Financial Crisis from 2006 to 2013, high-yield credit spreads spiked to their highest level in late 2008, a point at which cumulative defaults were only at 30% of their final cycle total.

The second row of charts examines equity prices and bank stock performance against cumulative bank failures. In the Great Depression chart spanning 1929 to 1933, the Dow Jones Industrial Average bottomed in mid-1932, when cumulative bank failures had reached only 48% of their ultimate total. For the Savings and Loan Crisis from 1988 to 1994, the S&P 500 Bank Index hit its low in late 1990, when cumulative bank failures were at 63%. Most notably, during the Global Financial Crisis from 2008 to 2014, the S&P 500 Bank Index bottomed in March 2009—coinciding with the Supervisory Capital Assessment Program—when cumulative bank failures were at a mere 8% of their eventual count. 

The third row highlights the relationship between pricing indicators and ongoing delinquency or default performance. The first chart displays the Leveraged Loan Price Index against the trailing 12-month default rate from 2006 to 2011. The price index hit its bottom in late 2008 and began a sharp recovery, while the default rate continued to rise, peaking about a year later in late 2009. The final chart details AAA Commercial Mortgage-Backed Securities spreads against 60-day-plus delinquency rates from 2006 to 2014. Spreads spiked to nearly 1,600 basis points in late 2008 and normalized rapidly thereafter, whereas the associated delinquency rate steadily climbed for several more years, finally peaking near 9% in late 2011 and early 2012.

This page features a comprehensive reference table outlining the global pipeline of vaccine and antiviral developments for COVID-19, compiled from sources such as Cortellis, Bioworld, Johns Hopkins, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management as of March 5, 2020. The author notes that while it is impossible to know which of these treatments will ultimately prove successful, the table serves to illustrate the massive scale of research currently underway. The medical countermeasures are classified into three overarching categories: vaccines, immunomodulators, and direct viral inhibitors, the latter of which includes antivirals, anti-retrovirals, prophylactic polypeptides, nanoviricides, cell therapies, and antibody-based therapies.

The table organizes dozens of therapeutic candidates by their developmental status, ranging from launched treatments to those in Phase II/III trials, preclinical testing, and early discovery. 

Four therapies are listed in the "Launched" category, meaning they are approved for other indications but are being deployed or tested for COVID-19. This includes Fujifilm, Medivector, and Zhejiang Hisun Pharmaceutical's antiviral Favipiravir (Avigan), which entered Chinese clinical trials in February 2020. It also includes Bayer's immunomodulator Chloroquine (Resochin), which showed efficacy against COVID-19 pneumonia in China, and Genentech and Roche's Actemra, which Chinese authorities approved for use in patients with severe lung damage. Finally, Aim Immunotech's immunomodulator Rintatolimod, approved elsewhere for chronic fatigue syndrome, entered COVID-19 discovery in February 2020.

Advanced clinical trials highlight several key treatments. In Phase III, Ascletis Pharma initiated trials in China for its anti-retroviral ASC-09 and ritonavir combination, while Gilead’s antiviral Remdesivir is being evaluated for COVID-19. Regeneron and Sanofi's immunomodulator Kevzara is in Phase III/II clinical trials in the United States, targeting 400 patients with severe cases. In Phase II, Beijing Defengrei received approval in China for clinical trials of its antibody BDB-1, and Innovation Pharmaceuticals is exploring the antibody Brilacidin for MERS, SARS, and COVID-19.

The preclinical category contains various vaccines, polypeptides, and cell therapies. These include INO-4800, a DNA vaccine developed by Beijing Advaccine Biotech, GeneOne Life Science, and Inovio, which planned Phase I trials in the US and China. Sorrento Therapeutics and Celularity are evaluating CYNK-001, a cell therapy, while Novavax, Chongqing Zhifei Biological, and the Jenner Institute (developing ChAdOx1 nCoV-19) are preparing or conducting early-stage vaccine studies. Sichuan Kelun Pharmaceutical's prophylactic polypeptide S-protein/ACE2 showed promising safety in primate studies, and Wuhan Hamilton Biotechnology planned clinical trials in China for its mesenchymal stem cells.

The discovery phase includes numerous early-stage projects. Key vaccine developments include Moderna’s mRNA-1273, which planned Phase I trials with the National Institutes of Health, and Curevac's mRNA vaccine. Sanofi Pasteur, Vaxart, Clover Biopharmaceuticals (utilizing GlaxoSmithKline adjuvant technology), and the University of Queensland are also pursuing protein subunit and recombinant vaccine candidates. In terms of antibodies, Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Vir Biotechnology (partnering with Wuxi Biologics), and Immunoprecise are actively developing human antibody therapies, while Nanoviricides has initiated preparations to test nanoviricide candidates in cell cultures against coronaviruses.

This page outlines the limits of government intervention during a pandemic, arguing that while public policy can address credit availability, credit costs, and income loss, it cannot easily control economic activity during lockdowns or speed up medical advancements. The author focuses on early indicators from high-frequency US manufacturing and consumer data to assess the economic impact of the pandemic and the potential effectiveness of unprecedented Federal Reserve and Congressional intervention. 

A prominent historical chart tracks US jobless claims as a percentage of the active working population from 1970 to 2020, highlighting an unprecedented vertical spike in March 2020 that reaches over 2.0 percent, dramatically eclipsing previous historic recessions where claims never exceeded 0.8 percent. An accompanying commentary argues that this virus-led spike differs from traditional demand-led recessions. Because of the speed with which lockdowns might be lifted and provisions in the two-trillion-dollar fiscal stimulus bill that turn corporate loans into grants if workers are retained, many unemployed people may return to work much faster than in typical downturns.

Two high-frequency tracking charts for the first quarter of 2020 illustrate the real-time economic fallout of rising COVID-19 infections. The first chart tracks manufacturing and daily infections, showing that a rolling four-week year-over-year measure of industrial activity—spanning lumber, steel, and coal production, electricity output, and railroad traffic—dropped from approximately negative 4.3 percent in early February to negative 7.5 percent by late March. This decline directly correlates with the vertical rise in daily infections, which skyrocketed to nearly twenty thousand cases by late March. The second chart focuses on the consumer sector, illustrating divergent shopping behaviors. As daily infections surged, weekly year-over-year discount store sales jumped from roughly 7 percent to nearly 18 percent due to panic buying, while department store sales collapsed from flat levels down to negative 10 percent.

In this report, Michael Cembalest analyzes the historical relationship between stock market bottoms and unemployment rates to understand whether the S&P 500 low of 2,237 reached on March 23, 2020, will mark the bottom of the COVID-19 market cycle. He posits that in most historical US and European downturns, equities have bottomed well before unemployment rates peaked and began to decline, with the tech collapse of the early 2000s serving as a rare exception. 

To support this observation, the page features six charts mapping equity indices alongside unemployment rates across different historical crises. The first chart, covering the 1970s stagflation crisis from 1973 to 1978, shows the S&P 500 bottoming in late 1974, just as the US unemployment rate was starting a steep rise toward its peak of 9.0% in 1975. The second chart details the 1980s inflation and housing crisis from 1981 to 1984, revealing that the S&P 500 reached its low point in mid-1982, whereas unemployment did not peak until late 1982 and early 1983 at nearly 11.0%. The third chart highlights the early 2000s tech collapse from 1999 to 2006, demonstrating the exception where the S&P 500 bottom in early 2003 closely coincided with the peak of the US unemployment rate at roughly 6.3%. 

The fourth chart traces the Global Financial Crisis from 2007 to 2013, showing the S&P 500 bottoming in March 2009, months before US unemployment peaked at 10.0% in late 2009. The fifth chart examines the UK equity market and unemployment rate in the 1970s, illustrating that UK equities bottomed around late 1974, while the UK unemployment rate continued to rise from under 1.5% to a peak of around 4.0% in late 1977. The final chart presents European equities and the Eurozone unemployment rate during the European debt crisis from 2010 to 2014, demonstrating that the STOXX European Broad equity index bottomed in late 2011, long before the Eurozone unemployment rate peaked at over 12.0% in 2013.

This page analyzes the Federal Reserve's capacity to alleviate a credit and liquidity crunch through upcoming credit facilities, which include loans, asset purchases, and relaxed accounting standards for banks. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that the current spread increases are far smaller than those experienced during the 2008 financial crisis, indicating a healthier, better-capitalized banking sector with improved underlying structure. He predicts that the benefits of these Fed facilities will materialize within weeks, particularly at the short end of the yield curve. Consequently, he highlights investment value in investment-grade credit, select municipal issuers, and upper-tier non-energy high-yield bonds.

The analysis is supported by six charts tracing historical financial market spreads from the early to mid-2000s through late March 2020, with red dots indicating the current levels. The first chart, measuring the 3-month LIBOR minus the 3-month forward Fed Funds rate in basis points, shows a recent spike to approximately 140 basis points, which is elevated but remains well below the peak of over 350 basis points in 2008. Similarly, the second chart presents the TED spread—the US 3-month Libor minus the 3-month Treasury rate—showing a recent rise to about 140 basis points, far below its 2008 peak of over 450 basis points.

The third chart illustrates US commercial paper spreads relative to the 3-month Treasury, showing that Financial Commercial Paper (CP) recently rose to about 230 basis points and Asset-Backed CP rose to roughly 180 basis points, both remaining far below their respective 2008 highs. The fourth chart displays AAA asset-backed securities spreads versus Treasuries, tracking Prime auto, Credit card, and Commercial Real Estate (CRE) since 1998. It shows current spreads spiking to roughly 100 basis points for Prime auto, 125 basis points for Credit cards, and 150 basis points for CRE, representing a minor fraction of their 2008 heights when spreads neared 600 basis points. 

The fifth chart shows US investment-grade corporate bond spreads using the JULI index versus Treasuries, detailing a sharp spike to around 320 basis points, which is substantial but still below the nearly 600 basis points recorded in 2008. Finally, the sixth chart presents the spread difference between financial and non-financial investment-grade bonds using the JULI index.
