It emphasizes that this spread difference has barely budged and sits slightly below zero, indicating that bank debt has not faced disproportionate selling pressure relative to non-bank corporate issuers, in stark contrast to 2008 when the spread difference skyrocketed to over 300 basis points.

This page, titled "The Chloroquine controversy," argues that the development of anti-viral medications and vaccines is a highly complex, lengthy process requiring rigorous randomized trials, control groups, and large populations. The author cautions against drawing concrete conclusions from premature, non-randomized trials of only twenty or thirty people, which are often conducted under " wartime" conditions in China and elsewhere, posing risks to healthcare providers. To highlight the steep challenges of drug development, the author notes that out of thousands of anti-viral inhibitors proposed in scientific literature from 1963 to 2016, only 90 were eventually approved for final use. Furthermore, several therapies once tested against Ebola—such as chloroquine, favipiravir, brincidofovir, monoclonal antibodies, antisense RNA, and convalescent plasma—ultimately failed to prove safe or effective in randomized clinical trials.

To visualize this historical difficulty, the page features a line chart tracking the cumulative number of approved drugs from 1960 to 2015 across nine different viral infections, based on a study by De Clercq and Li in Clinical Microbiology Reviews. The chart's vertical axis ranges from 0 to 40 approved drugs. The data shows that the vast majority of successful anti-viral drug development has been concentrated in just two areas. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) treatments show a dramatic exponential surge beginning in the late 1980s, rising to reach 40 approved drugs by 2015. Hepatitis C (HCV) treatments represent the second-largest category, growing slowly from the late 1980s before climbing sharply after 2010 to reach nearly 20 approved drugs by 2015. Approved drugs for all other tracked infections remain extremely low by comparison. Herpes simplex (HSV) treatments plateaued at around 10 approved drugs in the early 2000s, while treatments for Influenza, Hepatitis B (HBV), Chickenpox (VZV), Human herpesvirus 5 (HCMV), Human orthopneumovirus (RSV), and Human papillomavirus infection (HPV) all remained below 10 approved drugs, with most under 5 by the end of the period.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the scientific uncertainty and lack of rigorous clinical data supporting various proposed COVID-19 treatments, arguing that small, uncontrolled studies are insufficient. It highlights a paper by Alfred Kim of the Washington University School of Medicine and Jeffrey Sparks of Harvard Medical School, published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, which warns against the off-label use of hydroxychloroquine due to a lack of prophylactic evidence and the risk of creating shortages for patients with rheumatic diseases who rely on the drug. The author also notes inconclusive results from a 199-person randomized trial of Lopinavir-Ritonavir in Wuhan, which showed statistically similar 28-day mortality rates between the treatment group at 19.2% and the placebo group at 25.0%. Additionally, Genentech is expanding studies on the immunomodulator tocilizumab under the brand name Actemra after a small 20-patient trial in China. Ultimately, the page argues that the scientific community must transition away from small, single-group front-line studies of 20 to 50 patients and instead rely on randomized clinical trials, as echoed by Andre Kalil of the University of Nebraska Medical Center in his praise of the National Institutes of Health's rapidly deployed adaptive clinical trials. The section concludes with a list of bibliographical sources on early COVID-19 drug efficacy trials from February and March 2020.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication. It details regional distribution regulations, licensing, and compliance requirements for various jurisdictions, specifically addressing Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin American countries such as Brazil and Mexico. The text outlines the regulatory bodies overseeing JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and its affiliates in these regions—including the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission—and provides guidelines regarding the restricted distribution of materials to wholesale clients. It concludes with standard copyright information and brand-name definitions for J.P. Morgan Private Bank.

This page analyzes the severe dislocations across global credit, mortgage, and bond markets during the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic, alongside a list of Federal Reserve facilities established to stabilize these financial systems. 

The first chart tracks the spread between a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage and the 10-year Treasury in basis points from 2005 through late March 2020. It shows that this spread spiked dramatically to approximately 320 basis points, approaching the historical peaks of nearly 330 basis points seen during the 2008 financial crisis. 

The second chart shows US high-yield corporate bond spreads, utilizing the JPDFHYI index versus Treasuries from 1995 to 2020. In March 2020, high-yield corporate spreads spiked violently to roughly 1,000 basis points. High-yield energy sector spreads, highlighted by a separate data point, spiked even higher to approximately 2,150 basis points, which is near the historic high-yield peak of late 2008. 

The third chart illustrates the option-adjusted spread for fixed-rate preferred securities using the P0P1 index from 2000 to 2020. By late March 2020, this spread shot up to around 400 basis points, representing a notable dislocation, though still well below the 2008 crisis peak of over 1,500 basis points. 

The fourth chart documents the spread of emerging market dollar-denominated bonds versus US Treasuries from 2002 to 2020. This spread surged to about 600 basis points in early 2020, representing a rapid rise from its typical post-2010 range of 300 to 450 basis points. 

The fifth chart plots the S&P 500 leveraged loan price index from 2000 to 2020. The index experienced a sharp downward plunge in late March 2020, dropping to approximately 82, showing a severe contraction but not quite reaching the depths of the 2008 crash when the index fell below 65. 

To address these severe market pressures, a dedicated panel lists the specific Federal Reserve emergency lending facilities deployed at the time. These policy interventions include the money market lending facility, Fed purchases of US Treasuries, the commercial paper funding facility for municipals, Fed purchases of mortgage-backed securities, the term asset-backed securities loan facility, the commercial paper funding facility for corporates, the primary investment-grade credit funding facility for direct lending, the secondary corporate credit funding facility for asset purchases, and Fed lending to the Exchange Stabilization Fund to support the Main Street lending fund.

This page discusses why J.P. Morgan does not find value in predicting infection curves for COVID-19, arguing that by the time epidemic models can be accurately calibrated, the actual outcomes are already known. The author explains that popular Kermack/McKendrick "SIR" (susceptible, infected, and removed) models rely heavily on manual curve-fitting and are highly sensitive to parameters like infectiousness (beta), removal rates (gamma), and the exposed population percentage (Nper). These models struggle with unreported or asymptomatic cases and fail to transfer successfully across different countries due to differing national policies and public behaviors.

To demonstrate this limitation, the page features two comparative charts showing active infections in thousands over a 100-day period. The first chart, titled "A good fit for Korea in mid-February," shows actual versus estimated active cases in South Korea. Using parameters of Beta at 3.5, Gamma at 1.74, and Nper at 0.10%, the estimated curve aligns almost perfectly with the actual data, peaking at around 7,500 active infections. 

The second chart, titled "Korea parameters: a really, really bad fit for Italy," applies those exact same South Korean parameters to Italian data. While the model estimates a mild peak of approximately 9,000 active infections around day 50, the actual data line for Italy skyrockets exponentially, reaching over 60,000 active infections by day 60. This discrepancy underscores a massive estimation failure caused by different behavioral and containment dynamics in Italy compared to South Korea.

Additionally, a humorous footnote features a dialogue between the author and his son, Max, who assisted with the mathematical section and prefers Python over the author's favored Excel VBA programming.

This page evaluates the weaknesses of COVID-19 infection prediction models, focusing on how easily they can be manipulated to fit historical data while remaining unreliable for future forecasting. The author highlights the tail-chasing exercise of recalibrating model parameters after the fact using the case of Italy, noting that even a model that fits historical data well can require arbitrary, extreme adjustments—such as increasing a parameter by ten times—and can still be completely wrong. 

The analysis is supported by two charts showing active COVID-19 infections in Italy in thousands over a 200-day period, utilizing data from Johns Hopkins and J.P. Morgan Asset Management up to March 26, 2020. The first chart, titled "The model, recalibrated for Italy: 10x higher infected population," plots actual infections against a recalibrated estimated curve using a Beta of 3.6, Gamma of 1.74, and Nper of 1.0%. While the actual data points match the rising slope of the curve up to day 60, the model predicts active infections peaking at over 100,000 around day 70. 

The second chart, "Which set of assumptions best predicts Italy? Still totally unclear," demonstrates that multiple distinct sets of assumptions can fit the same actual data up to day 60 but project dramatically different future trajectories. This chart compares three curves: a brown curve (3.6 Beta, 1.74 Gamma, 1% Nper peaking near 100,000 cases), a grey curve (3.8 Beta, 1.74 Gamma, 0.7% Nper peaking around 90,000 cases), and a red curve (2.7 Beta, 1.74 Gamma, 3% Nper peaking much higher at approximately 160,000 cases). 

The author concludes that predictive models have almost no cross-country utility and are highly sensitive to shifts in testing and public policy. Ultimately, these models are deemed highly inaccurate for forecasting future peaks and only become reliable once the infection curve has already peaked, rendering them redundant. A footnote further critiques the necessity of complex Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered (SIR) models, noting that J.P. Morgan successfully replicated South Korea's infection curve with similar precision using a simple modified Gaussian function.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication examines the early-pandemic controversy surrounding potential anti-viral treatments for COVID-19, specifically focusing on Gilead’s Remdesivir and Bayer AG’s Chloroquine. While both drugs initially showed promise by reducing viral loads in cell cultures with low toxicity, the author emphasizes the crucial caveat that in vitro success often fails to translate to successful live clinical trials. 

To support this point, a line chart on the top left from the Wuhan Institute of Virology displays the test results of Remdesivir (solid blue line) and Chloroquine (dotted blue line) in cell cultures. The y-axis measures the percentage of virus inhibited and cytotoxicity from negative twenty percent to one hundred percent, while the x-axis shows the dosage in micromoles on a logarithmic scale from zero point one to one hundred. Both drugs reach near one hundred percent viral inhibition at higher dosages, while cytotoxicity (damage to cell cultures, shown as a flat gold line) remains close to zero percent. 

The author then addresses a highly publicized, though ultimately discredited, French study by Gautret et al. that combined hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin. The line chart on the top right shows the percentage of patients testing positive for infection over a six-day period. In this chart, the control group’s positive rate (grey line) drops only slightly from one hundred percent to about ninety percent by day six, while the hydroxychloroquine-only group (blue line) falls to about sixty percent. The combination therapy group (gold line) drops precipitously to zero percent positive by day five. Cembalest highlights that this study was quickly discredited due to severe methodological flaws: it was a non-randomized trial of only thirty-six patients, excluded six patients who deteriorated or died, started with higher initial viral loads in the control group, imputed over a third of the control group’s test results, and sourced treatment patients from a single medical center.

To counter the flawed French study, the page presents a bar chart at the bottom displaying findings from a small thirty-patient study by Chen Jun et al. at the Shanghai Public Health Clinical Center, which compared a treatment group receiving hydroxychloroquine (blue bars) against a control group (gold bars). This study found no benefit from the drug. Specifically, on day seven, eighty-five percent of the treatment group tested negative for COVID-19 nucleic acid, which was actually lower than the ninety percent negative rate observed in the control group. Additionally, abnormal liver function was more prevalent in the treatment group at twenty-eight percent compared to twenty percent in the control group. Finally, radiological progression occurred in thirty-three percent of the treatment group versus forty percent of the control group, leading the researchers to conclude that the drug offered no clinical benefits.

This page analyzes COVID-19 infection trends, advising investors and analysts not to over-extrapolate temporary fluctuations or rely on overly simplistic binary categorizations of countries as accelerating or decelerating. Michael Cembalest argues that flattening the curve often means stretching out an outbreak, resulting in sustained high infection rates that keep healthcare systems under severe pressure even after a peak is passed. To illustrate these differences, the page presents three charts depicting new daily infections per one million people on a linear scale, using a three-day trailing average, plotted against the number of days since total reported cases reached one hundred. 

The first chart focuses on regions with relatively minimal virus exposure, where the vertical axis peaks at just sixteen cases per million. This group includes Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, and Taiwan. While daily infection levels stayed very low overall—mostly under four per million—Singapore shows a distinct uptick to about fifteen cases per million near day thirty-eight, and Japan displays a mild upward drift toward two cases per million by day forty-five. 

The second chart, which uses a much higher vertical scale maximizing at one hundred cases per million, showcases nations where infection rates have more clearly rolled over. Austria peaked dramatically near ninety cases per million around day twenty before falling to approximately forty by day twenty-eight. Meanwhile, Australia and South Korea managed to contain their peaks below twenty cases per million, with both subsequently trending lower. 

The third chart uses the largest vertical scale, peaking at two hundred cases per million, to display countries like Spain, Switzerland, and Italy. Here, the worst of the initial surge may be over, but ongoing daily infection rates remain extremely high. Spain peaked near one hundred eighty cases per million around day twenty-five and remains above one hundred forty on day thirty-five, while Switzerland peaked around one hundred thirty and has dropped toward ninety. Italy presents a stark example of plateauing, with its curve flattening but remaining stubbornly high between eighty and one hundred cases per million for over fifteen days. The author emphasizes that these high plateaus pose a continuous threat of reacceleration and illustrate the severe, ongoing stress on local healthcare systems.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication argues that while global COVID-19 infections remain on the rise, there is positive news in that most large US states, which represent seventy percent of US GDP, are on a lower infection trajectory compared to the severe outbreaks seen in New York and New Jersey. 

The first chart on the page tracks US new daily infections per one million people on a linear scale using a three-day trailing average, plotted against the number of days after total reported cases in each state reached one hundred. The data, sourced from Johns Hopkins University, the IMF, and JPMAM, shows New York and New Jersey with exceptionally steep curves, with New York rising past five hundred daily infections per million and New Jersey peaking near four hundred and fifty. In comparison, other major states—including Massachusetts, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, Washington, Florida, Virginia, California, Ohio, Texas, and North Carolina—display much flatter trajectories, with most remaining well below two hundred infections per million. 

In the accompanying commentary, the author notes that real-world infection curves are highly idiosyncratic rather than following neat theoretical exponential decay models. For example, Italy flattened its curve but has still struggled with a high rate of new infections for over a month. Globally, the pace of new infections is either rising or stable at a high level. Looking ahead, the author forecasts a sharp decline in new infections in the Developed World during April, though this prediction remains subject to incoming data. 

The second chart illustrates this broader global trend by comparing new daily infections per one million people between China and the rest of the world over seventy days after reaching one hundred cases. While China’s rate peaked early at around five daily infections per million before dropping back to near zero, the "World ex China" series shows a relentless upward climb, reaching nearly fourteen daily infections per million by day sixty-five, indicating that the global pandemic was still accelerating outside of China at the time of publication.

This page details research on convalescent plasma as a potential treatment option for COVID-19. It explains that Houston Methodist Hospital received the first FDA approval to use this treatment, which involves infusing virus-neutralizing antibodies collected from recovered patients into active COVID-19 patients. The author notes that while this historical technique dates back to the Victorian era and is currently used to treat immunodeficient individuals against pathogens like measles and mumps, its application to COVID-19 requires clinical trials to prove efficacy. 

Furthermore, because antibody half-lives are only 30 days, convalescent plasma would only offer temporary, short-term protection, though this might be sufficient during a pandemic wave. Other key challenges discussed include difficulty in scaling and the risk of transmitting undiscovered viruses or triggering adverse immunological reactions like serum sickness. To provide historical context, the text references a paper by Arturo Casadevall of the Johns Hopkins School of Public Health, citing a past SARS study of 80 patients in Hong Kong where early treatment improved patient prognosis, as well as positive outcomes during the 2009–2010 H1N1 influenza pandemic where treated individuals showed reduced viral burden and lower mortality. Ultimately, the author frames convalescent plasma as a potentially vital tool for high-risk cases, provided that risks are mitigated through rigorous pathogen screening and blood type matching.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the volatility of early COVID-19 infection curves, analyzing why simple trend-following models fail during temporary downward trends, and exploring potential environmental factors behind lower infection rates in emerging markets. The author warns that initial declines in infection rates can be "head-fakes," as seen in the top-left chart tracking new daily infections per one million people on a linear scale with a three-day trailing average. This chart shows that in France, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Germany, initial drops in daily infections were subsequently reversed; for example, France’s daily infections dipped near day 30 before spiking sharply to nearly 180 per million by day 35. The top-right chart plots the same metric for the United States, Ireland, Great Britain, and Canada, showing that their infections are either still accelerating or experiencing brief, unreliable downturns, with the United States and Great Britain climbing past 80 and 70 daily cases per million, respectively, by day 30.

The commentary then addresses the surprisingly low reported infection rates in the emerging world. The author notes that day-20 infection rates per million people in these nations ranged from below 1 to 5, which is drastically lower than the day-20 rates in developed nations, such as 73 in Spain, 40 in Italy, 36 in Germany, 25 in France, 22 in the United States, and 17 in the United Kingdom. The bottom-left chart tracks these low rates for Brazil, the Philippines, Thailand, Pakistan, Indonesia, and India, where Brazil shows the highest rate in the group, peaking at just under 6 daily infections per million. 

To explore whether environmental or weather factors could explain these differences, the bottom-right chart plots the percentage of infections and the percentage of the world population as a function of latitude. The data reveals that 95% of reported infections have occurred between 22.5°N and 57.5°N, a latitudinal band containing 59% of the world’s population. The blue line representing the percentage of infections peaks dramatically at nearly 16% around 47.5°N. Additionally, the author notes that between January and March, 90% of infections occurred in regions with temperatures ranging from -5°C to 15°C and humidity between 0 and 8 grams per kilogram, leaving the impact of climate as an open question still under intense study.

This page contains regulatory disclosures, distribution restrictions, and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication. It details specific compliance and regulatory information for various jurisdictions, including Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America.

This page analyzes the severity and economic impact of the COVID-19 lockdown in the United States compared to China. To contrast the immediate public health outcomes, the author presents a chart tracking total infections per one million people after initial outbreaks began. The chart reveals a stark divergence starting around day 15 after total cases reached 100: the US infection curve climbs sharply to over 1,000 cases per million people by day 35, while the line for China remains virtually flat and near-zero, pointing to a massive gap even after allowing for potential under-reporting by Chinese authorities.

To measure how much economic activity each lockdown suppressed, the author compares high-frequency energy data as a percentage of 2019 levels. The corresponding chart plots weekly US electricity production against daily Chinese coal consumption. While China's coal consumption plummeted to around 60% of its 2019 level during its peak February lockdown before initiating a volatile recovery, US electricity production remained highly resilient, hovering between 90% and 100% of its 2019 baseline through late March. 

Further examining US energy trends, a regional bar chart details the percentage change in US electricity demand for the week ending March 25. It shows that although power demand dropped by nearly 7% in New York, declines were far more modest in other regions like New England, California, the Southeast, and the Northwest, which fell by only 1% to 4%. Meanwhile, some power markets, including MISO, Florida, and Ercot, actually experienced positive demand growth of 1% to 4%. 

The author contextualizes these energy comparisons by noting that the US is undergoing a secular shift from coal to natural gas and renewables. In contrast, China increased its coal-fired generation capacity by 43 gigawatts from January 2018 to June 2019, with another 121 gigawatts under construction, while the rest of the world reduced its capacity by 8 gigawatts. Finally, a footnote highlights car sales as another proxy for lockdown severity, noting that US car sales were down 35% compared to 2019 by late March, whereas Chinese car sales collapsed by over 90% in February, illustrating that China implemented a far more extreme version of a lockdown.

This page of the publication argues that the shape of an economic recovery, such as whether it is a "U vs. V" shape, is less relevant to investors than understanding the historical lead time of equities over the broader economy. The author, Michael Cembalest, asserts that the S&P 500 historically leads the trough in economic data (specifically GDP) by four to eight months. Therefore, when second-derivative changes in economic data begin to improve, signaling that a bottom is forming, it has historically been an optimal time to start searching for value in equities.

To support this claim, the page presents four charts comparing the index level of the S&P 500 on the left axis against US GDP (indexed to 2012 = 100) on the right axis across different historical recessions. 

The first chart illustrates the Eisenhower recession from May 1957 to December 1958. It shows the S&P 500 bottoming around December 1957 at an index level just above 40, while US GDP hit its trough several months later in early-to-mid 1958 at an index value of approximately 18.2. 

The second chart focuses on the stagflation era from June 1973 to December 1976. During this period, the S&P 500 reached its low point around December 1974 near an index level of 70, whereas US GDP did not find its bottom until roughly mid-1975 at a level of about 34.5. 

The third chart depicts the double-dip recession of the 1980s, spanning October 1980 to October 1983. The equity market found its trough in mid-1982 around an index level of 110, well ahead of US GDP, which bottomed in late 1982 at an index level of 42.4. 

The final chart examines the Global Financial Crisis from May 2007 to May 2013. The S&P 500 hit its bottom in March 2009 near the 700 to 800 index level range, leading the GDP trough which occurred in mid-2009 at an index value of approximately 94. 

The author concludes by noting that a full collection of historical market bottom charts is available on their web portal, which further explores the lead times between bank stocks and bank failures, high-yield spreads and defaults, and equities and unemployment. All charts cite the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) and Shiller as data sources.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market publication. It details distribution terms, licensing, and regulatory compliance across various jurisdictions, including Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America.

This page details the significant uncertainties and clinical caveats surrounding COVID-19 serology testing and its application in epidemiological modeling and back-to-work strategies. The author notes that models are highly sensitive to input parameters, such as the timing of outbreaks and testing results, and warns of false positives, unrepresentative sample populations, and patients with insufficient antibodies. A referenced study from Fudan University showed that one-third of a 175-person cohort of recovered patients lacked high antibody levels, suggesting their immune response relied instead on T-cells or cytokines, which leaves their long-term susceptibility to reinfection an open question. 

Despite these limitations, serology tests are positioned as critical tools for summer or fall back-to-work plans. Globally, countries are scrambling to utilize them: the United Kingdom has ordered 3.5 million tests, Germany is exploring immunity certificates, and China and Singapore are leveraging them to measure exact infection rates. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration allows doctor-led testing to find antibody donors for emergency treatments, and over fifty companies intend to distribute self-validated testing kits. The author emphasizes that these kits come with strict FDA-mandated disclosures stating they are not formally FDA-reviewed, negative results do not rule out active infection, antibody tests cannot be the sole basis for diagnosis, and positive results may occur due to past exposure to other non-SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus strains. Nonetheless, many nations appear ready to accept these risks to jumpstart economic activity.

This J.P. Morgan publication page examines how countries can safely transition back to normal life after the first wave of COVID-19 infections subsides. Author Michael Cembalest highlights that Asian nations, along with European countries like Austria and Norway, are already grappling with this challenge, with some—like Singapore—facing worrisome spikes. To illustrate the initial trajectory of the pandemic across different regions, the page features two side-by-side charts showing the number of new daily infections per one million people using a linear scale and a three-day trailing average, plotted against the number of days since total reported cases reached one hundred. 

The left chart showcases regions with relatively lower per-capita infection rates, including Japan, Australia, Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, and China, where daily infections peak below eighteen per million. China and South Korea saw early, sharp peaks around fourteen infections per million before declining, whereas Japan exhibits a slower, steady climb to about four per million by day fifty. The right chart highlights countries with much higher infection densities, utilizing a scale up to one hundred twenty. In this comparison, Austria peaks near ninety infections per million around day twenty, Norway peaks near sixty around day twenty-five, and Singapore shows a distinct late-stage upward trend to nearly forty infections per million around day forty. 

The text details three potential strategic approaches for exiting lockdowns, assuming travel restrictions remain in place to prevent importing cases. The first strategy is to continue flattening the curve and slowly return people to work as infections decline. Cembalest notes a major flaw in this approach is that a tiny cluster of active cases can quickly trigger a second wave without robust tracing systems, especially given the uncertainty surrounding whether seasonal elements like summer heat will dampen virus transmission before a potential autumn resurgence. The second approach involves relaxing lockdowns while using an aggressive contact-tracing strategy to isolate and quarantine new outbreaks immediately. Cembalest considers this the most likely path for many nations, though it demands a highly organized healthcare system, strict public compliance, and invasive government surveillance tools like GPS and credit card tracking. The third strategy relies on serological testing to identify individuals who possess antibodies and can safely return to work, though this relies heavily on herd immunity, which presents its own set of challenges. Footnotes reference educational animator Grant Sanderson of 3 Blue 1 Brown for epidemic visualizations and compare aggressive tracing to the "Code 2319" protocol from the movie Monsters Inc.

This page analyzes early random serological test results in Europe to estimate how quickly COVID-19 herd immunity might be achieved. The author highlights findings from Denmark, where 2.7% of 1,500 people tested positive for antibodies 34 days after the outbreak; Gangelt, Germany, where 14.0% of 509 people tested positive 73 days after; and Scotland, where 1.2% of 500 people tested positive 21 days after. These figures indicate that actual exposure levels are at least one order of magnitude higher than official numbers suggest, revealing a high volume of undetected, mild, or asymptomatic cases. 

A bar chart titled "How widespread is COVID-19? Serology test results vs reported cases as a % of population" compares serology results against reported case-to-population ratios. With the vertical axis displaying percentages up to 16%, the chart shows Denmark at 2.7% serology versus 0.1% reported, Gangelt at 14.0% serology versus 3.4% reported, and Scotland at 1.2% serology versus 0.1% reported. 

The second chart, "When might herd immunity occur, after which serology tests could have a greater 'return to work' impact?", maps these real-world data points onto an epidemiological Susceptible-Infected-Removed (SIR) model. The horizontal axis measures days after the outbreak from 0 to 180, while the vertical axis tracks the percentage of the population from 0% to 100%. The model shows a red curve for the susceptible population falling rapidly, a green curve for the removed (recovered or deceased) population rising to nearly 80%, and a brown curve for active infections peaking at around 12% near day 110. A horizontal dotted black line highlights the 40% susceptibility threshold, which represents the 60% exposure level needed to reach herd immunity, assuming an initial reproductive number of 2.5. 

By tracking Denmark and Gangelt’s serology findings along the susceptible curve, the author projects that herd immunity is closer than linear projections suggest. The model forecasts that much greater levels of immunity could be just one month away in Gangelt, Germany, and two months away in Denmark.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest analyzes the sudden and sharp equity market rally that began on March 23, 2020. He argues that prior to this date, markets had overreacted by pricing in an entire decade for corporate earnings to recover to their prior peak, compared to the historical average recovery period of less than three years. This extreme pessimism, combined with high short interest, slowing COVID-19 infection acceleration, and unprecedented Federal Reserve liquidity injections, created the perfect conditions for a rapid rebound. However, looking ahead, Cembalest warns that markets are now pricing in a large amount of optimistic news. With price-to-earnings multiples having quickly risen from a low of 13 times back to 16 times 2021 consensus earnings, and with corporate earnings estimates likely to be revised downward, he predicts that future market advances will be slower and much less one-directional.

To support his argument, Cembalest presents four charts. The first chart, titled S&P 500 index, plots the index level on a vertical axis from 1,800 to 3,400 against a timeline from January 1 to April 10, 2020. It illustrates a steep drop from a high near 3,400 down to a trough of around 2,200 on March 23rd, followed by a recovery to approximately 2,800. Key annotations highlight that this March 23rd market bottom coincided with peak short interest on the SPY exchange-traded fund, a shift in the acceleration of regional coronavirus infections, and aggressive Federal Reserve intervention. 

The second chart, NYC and Italy: change in new daily infections, displays the five-day percent change in new daily infections from March 10 to April 9, 2020, using two different vertical axes. The left axis, tracking New York City, scales from 0% to 2,000% and shows a growth rate peaking near 1,800% in mid-March before plunging toward 0% by early April. The right axis, tracking Italy, scales from negative 50% to 300% and depicts infection growth peaking near 200% in mid-March before dropping to negative territory by early April, illustrating how the momentum of the virus was breaking around the March 23rd turning point.

The third chart, Quantity-On-Loan of the SPY US ETF, shows the short-sale indicator of on-loan quantity as a percentage of shares outstanding from January 2016 through early 2020. This indicator spiked to nearly 6% on March 23rd, reaching its highest level since late 2018, demonstrating that the market was highly vulnerable to a short squeeze once positive news arrived.

The fourth chart, Fed balance sheet, tracks total assets in trillions of US dollars from 2008 to 2020. It depicts a historic, vertical spike in early 2020 that brought the Federal Reserve's balance sheet to nearly 6 trillion dollars through massive purchases of US Treasuries, agency debt, and mortgage-backed securities. 

This balance sheet expansion was driven by a series of aggressive emergency policies announced on March 23rd, which are detailed at the bottom of the page. These policies include the Primary Market Corporate Credit Facility for new bond and loan issuance, the Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facility to support liquidity for outstanding corporate bonds, and the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility to purchase consumer and small business loans. Additionally, the Fed expanded the Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility to include municipal variable rate demand notes and bank certificates of deposit, and expanded the Commercial Paper Funding Facility to include high-quality, tax-exempt commercial paper.

This page focuses on the general guidelines announced by the White House regarding what constitutes a reduced COVID-19 infection rate. The author notes that because individual states have the latitude to define these parameters, he has constructed a state-by-state assessment of potential litmus tests that governors might use to judge whether pandemic declines are truly meaningful. 

The primary visual component is a comprehensive table detailing the status of each U.S. state and Washington D.C. across four core metrics evaluated over a two-week period ending around the publication date. The first metric measures the positivity rate of all tests, checking for at least a three percent decline over the last two weeks. The second metric tracks the three-day average of new cases, looking for a decline of ten percent or more over the last two weeks. The third metric evaluates the three-day average of current hospitalizations, also seeking a ten percent decline. The fourth metric evaluates the three-day average of current intensive care unit admissions, requiring a ten percent decline as well. For each metric, the table lists the values from two weeks prior, the values today, and whether the state passes or fails the threshold, or if there is no data available.

The overall takeaway from the table is that very few states meet the criteria for a meaningful decline in infections, hospitalizations, or ICU usage, with the word "FAIL" dominating the status columns. For example, in New York, the positivity rate fell only slightly from forty point four percent to thirty-nine point three percent, resulting in a fail status, while its three-day average of new cases fell from nine thousand eight hundred eighty-three to six thousand eight hundred thirty-four, marking a pass. However, New York failed on hospitalizations, which rose from fifteen thousand seven hundred thirty-one to sixteen thousand seven hundred seventy-nine, and on ICU cases, which grew from four thousand seventy-eight to five thousand thirty. California failed across all assessed metrics: its positivity rate dropped marginally from eleven point five percent to ten point eight percent, its average new cases remained nearly flat, dropping only from one thousand four hundred sixteen to one thousand three hundred eighty-four, and its hospitalizations and ICU cases both more than doubled. Texas similarly failed on all fronts, with positivity rising from nine point six percent to ten point four percent, new cases rising from seven hundred fourteen to eight hundred twenty-three, and hospitalizations surging from four hundred six to one thousand four hundred thirty-eight. The data source is cited as covidtracking.com and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, "Eye on the Market," explores the relationship between cultural traits and the management of COVID-19, specifically contrasting societal collectivism against individualism and its apparent impact on infection rates. 

The author shares a firsthand account from a colleague returning to Hong Kong who detailed the region's strict containment measures, including GPS tracking verification, electronic wristbands, immediate saliva testing at the airport, and random compliance phone calls during a mandatory two-week quarantine. These rigorous protocols, along with credit card receipt tracking, closed-circuit television monitoring, and mandatory smartphone "virus passports," represent policy choices typical of Developed Asian countries and China. 

To analyze the efficacy of these intrusive containment strategies against cultural backdrops, Cembalest presents a scatter plot comparing total COVID-19 infection rates per million people against Geert Hofstede's index of societal collectivism versus individualism, using data up to April 17, 2020. The horizontal axis scales from collectivism on the left to individualism on the right, while the vertical axis tracks infections per million up to 4,500. 

On the left side of the chart, representing highly collectivist cultures, a cluster of red dots shows very low infection rates—mostly well under 500 cases per million—for places like Taiwan, China, South Korea, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Japan. On the right side, representing highly individualistic Western nations plotted as blue circles, infection rates are substantially higher. Spain sits near the top of the plot with roughly 4,000 infections per million, while Switzerland, Belgium, Ireland, and Italy group closely together between 2,500 and 3,200 cases per million. The United States and France are positioned near 2,000 cases per million, and the United Kingdom and Germany are charted between 1,500 and 1,700 cases per million. 

A standard cluster analysis of this data, marked by diamond-shaped centroids, yields a cluster significance coefficient of 82%. This high statistical correlation supports the author's argument that a society's position on the collectivism-individualism spectrum is an indispensable factor in explaining regional differences in early infection rates, as collectivist societies more readily accept the aggressive tracking and quarantine protocols necessary to suppress the virus.

This page consists entirely of standard regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication. It outlines the specific legal entities and regulatory authorities governing the distribution of the material across various global jurisdictions, including Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America (specifically highlighting Brazil and Mexico). The text clarifies the registration status of J.P. Morgan entities under relevant regional laws, restrictions regarding wholesale clients in Australia, and limitations on public offerings in Latin American jurisdictions. There are no charts, tables, financial data, or investment analyses on this page.

This page analyzes when and how the United States might begin to reopen its economy during the COVID-19 pandemic. The author, Michael Cembalest, suggests that if the US has indeed entered a decline phase of the virus, its recovery trajectory can be modeled by overlaying the decline paths of other nations. He argues that because the US did not implement broad quarantine or contact tracing efforts like China or South Korea, those countries' rapid recoveries are less relevant benchmarks. Instead, Austria and Germany are presented as more realistic paths, while Italy serves as a very slow-decline outlier. 

The analysis features a line chart plotting US new daily infections on a five-day average, which peaked near 35,000 in early April. From a hypothetical terminal peak on April 20, the chart projects various potential recovery paths based on actual declines observed in other countries. An accompanying table details these decline dynamics from peak infection levels. China experienced the fastest drop with a 98 percent decline from peak at a 35.1 percent daily pace. South Korea and Australia also saw swift drops of 97 percent and 90 percent respectively, declining at daily paces of 8.4 percent and 7.2 percent. Thailand and Austria followed with daily decline paces of 5.4 percent and 4.1 percent. Germany’s daily pace was 2.9 percent (a 55 percent decline from peak), and Italy experienced the slowest progress, showing only a 43 percent overall decline from peak at a 2.0 percent daily pace. 

Regarding the mechanics of reopening, the author posits that individual states will dictate the process more than the federal government. He highlights common elements in "Phase I" proposals, such as restricted non-essential travel, reopening schools and businesses with strict social distancing, demanding a 14-day downward trajectory in documented cases, ensuring hospital capacity is not breached, and keeping high-risk populations isolated. The author warns that any significant rise in infections would trigger immediate re-lockdowns, citing Singapore as an active example of this risk. Ultimately, he concludes that balancing public safety with economic needs in the absence of a vaccine or herd immunity points to an elongated, rather than rapid, economic recovery.

This page examines the progress of the COVID-19 drug Remdesivir and analyzes Sweden’s alternative pandemic lockdown strategy compared to other Scandinavian countries. 

Regarding Remdesivir, the author critiques a highly publicized trial of 125 patients by Gilead, noting that the study lacked a control group and screened out the most severe patients, making the positive results less scientifically rigorous. In contrast, a controlled study on twelve rhesus macaque monkeys yielded more promising findings, with treated primates showing lower viral loads, less lung damage, and milder breathing difficulties, though the author notes that an approved anti-viral treatment remains far off.

The discussion then shifts to Sweden, which opted for voluntary recommendations rather than strict lockdowns to achieve herd immunity faster. Sweden kept schools for children under sixteen, cinemas, gyms, and borders open while restricting only large gatherings and advising older citizens to self-isolate. 

To evaluate the success of this strategy, the page presents two charts comparing Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Norway, and a European composite, plotted by the number of days after total reported cases reached one hundred. The first chart, showing new daily infections per million people on a three-day trailing average, demonstrates that Sweden’s infection rate peaked between 60 and 70 per million around day 35, far higher than Denmark, Finland, and Norway, which mostly remained below 30. The second chart depicts case fatality rates on a one-day trailing average. It reveals that Sweden’s mortality rate climbed steeply to over 10% by day 40, exceeding the broader European average of around 9% and dwarfing Denmark, Finland, and Norway, all of which stayed below 4%.

The author concludes that while serology testing may eventually lower these reported fatality rates across all nations, Sweden currently shows worse outcomes than its neighbors. Sweden is betting that other countries will experience a resurgence in infections and greater economic damage once they lift their lockdowns, a premise the author leaves as an open question.

This page addresses the question of whether US equities reached their ultimate bottom on March 23, 2020, during the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic. The author argues that a market bottom during a period of escalating crisis is historically consistent, pointing out that if US equities did indeed bottom in March, they did so when COVID-19 infections were at only six percent of their late-April levels. To support this observation, the page features a detailed table titled "Market appreciation during times of ample economy-wide distress," which lists seventeen historical precedents dating back to the Great Depression where markets rallied substantially from their lowest levels or widest spreads before key economic pain points actually peaked.

The historical data shows that equity markets frequently start to recover before GDP officially bottoms, as seen in US equity rallies of four percent in 1957, twenty-five percent in 1974, twenty-six percent in 1982, and twenty-four percent in 2009. Similarly, equities often rally long before unemployment peaks; the table highlights US equity rallies of thirty-five percent in 1974, twenty-seven percent in 1983, seventeen percent in 2003, and thirty-three percent in 2009, alongside a thirty-three percent rally in European equities in 2012. 

The pattern extends to credit and banking sectors during major financial crises. For example, the Dow Jones rallied sixty-seven percent in 1932 before bank failures reached seventy-five percent of their eventual total, while the S&P Bank Index rallied ninety percent in 1990 and one hundred and eighty percent in 2009 before bank failures peaked. High-yield and securitized debt markets also rebounded well ahead of peak defaults and delinquencies. US High Yield spreads began to recover before high-yield defaults reached seventy-five percent of their eventual totals in 1990 by three hundred and fifty basis points, in 2002 by zero basis points from the widest spread, and in 2008 by one thousand one hundred and seventy-seven basis points. In 2009, AAA CMBS spreads tightened by nine hundred and seventy-five basis points before delinquency rates reached seventy-five percent of their maximum, and leveraged loans rallied six percent before defaults hit seventy-five percent of their peak. Ultimately, the table reinforces the premise that forward-looking financial markets regularly discount the worst of an economic crisis and begin their recovery well before fundamental indicators show actual signs of improvement.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the most ambitious COVID-19 vaccine timetables announced during the early stages of the pandemic. The author, Michael Cembalest, contrasts disappointing news regarding anti-viral treatments, specifically pointing to setbacks with Gilead's Remdesivir trial, with more optimistic timelines for vaccine development. 

Two primary initiatives are highlighted. First, Oxford University's Jenner Institute is working on a vaccine based on an altered chimpanzee virus coding for SARS-CoV-2 spike proteins, aiming for one million doses by the fall of 2020 if current clinical trials involving 1,100 volunteers succeed. Notably, the Serum Institute of India announced plans to proactively manufacture 40 million doses of Oxford’s vaccine before clinical trials are even finished. Second, Johnson & Johnson is leveraging the technology platform from its Ebola, Zika, RSV, and HIV programs to target Phase I trials in September 2020, with production potential by spring 2021. 

Additional long-term initiatives mentioned include those from Sanofi/GlaxoSmithKline, CanSino, BioNTech/Pfizer, Sinovac/Dynavax, Moderna, and Inovio. Cembalest cautions that many of these candidates utilize novel RNA, DNA, or viral vector technologies that have never before received approval for communicable diseases.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers, detailing J.P. Morgan's compliance, licensing, and distribution guidelines across various international jurisdictions including Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America, with no financial analysis or market data presented.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market analyzes whether different global regions are ready for lockdown relaxation and economic reopening. The author argues that while Europe and Asia are showing clear signs of readiness, other regions such as the United States, South America, and the Middle East are not yet prepared. 

To support this argument, the page presents five regional area charts that track COVID-19 infection trends from February to late April 2020, categorized by the share of each region's gross domestic product (GDP) affected. Each chart's vertical axis represents 0% to 100% of regional GDP, and the horizontal axis tracks time. The visual data is color-coded using a legend: dark red indicates infections rising faster than tests; orange represents infections rising slower than tests; yellow, purple, blue, and green indicate varying degrees of falling infections from peak levels; and white represents areas with no infections or fewer than five cases per million people.

The Europe COVID infection monitor shows that in late March, countries comprising almost 100% of European GDP were experiencing rising infections, colored entirely in dark red. By late April, this red zone fell below 10%, with the majority of European GDP shifting to purple, blue, and green, indicating sharp declines from peak levels. Conversely, the Asia COVID infection monitor shows that outbreaks were never sustained at high levels, with the vast majority of Asia's GDP remaining in the white zone throughout the entire spring. 

The US COVID infection monitor by state GDP reveals that after a rapid rise in dark red in mid-March, the country transitioned largely to orange, indicating infections rising slower than tests. By late April, a significant portion of state GDP remained in the orange and dark red zones, with only a moderate share showing falling infection rates in purple and blue. 

Lastly, the Middle East and South America monitors both illustrate picking up infection trends toward late April. In the Middle East, dark red and orange segments continue to dominate the majority of GDP. In South America, after a sharp drop in infections in early April, dark red and orange segments surged back to capture nearly the entirety of the continent's GDP by April 26. All charts cite Johns Hopkins University, the IMF, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management as data sources.

This page analyzes early COVID-19 serology antibody test results, arguing that while they must be interpreted with caution, they offer a better picture of infection and mortality rates than standard reported data. The author outlines several key caveats regarding antibody testing, including findings from a 175-person cohort in China where one-third of recovered patients lacked high antibody levels, leaving their long-term immunity an open question. Additionally, the specificity and sensitivity of manufacturer kits vary, though a UCSF and UC Berkeley study of 12 tests showed promising sensitivity after three weeks of disease progression and specificity exceeding 95% for most kits. Other challenges include a lack of FDA quality control, small study sizes relative to broader populations, and demographic adjustments that complicate interpretation. A footnote emphasizes that any counterarguments regarding high rates of false positives must be backed by rigorous disease prevalence estimates and PCR kit accuracy comparisons.

To illustrate these points, the author provides a table titled "Serology test results to date" compiled from JPMAM and Johns Hopkins University sources. The table lists eight regions, showing that case fatality rates based on serology estimates are consistently and significantly lower than official reported case fatality rates. For instance, in New York State, 52 days after the outbreak, the estimated population with antibodies was 13.9%, which translates to a serology-based case fatality rate of 0.7%, compared to the officially reported 7.4% fatality rate based on a study size of 3,000. In Gangelt, Germany, with a study size of 500 at day 73, the estimated antibody prevalence was 14.0%, bringing the estimated case fatality rate down to 0.4% from a reported 2.3%. Similar trends are visible in smaller study areas: Geneva, Switzerland shows an 8.8% reported fatality rate compared to an estimated 0.8% serology-based rate, while Los Angeles shows a 2.9% reported fatality rate compared to an estimated 0.1% serology-based rate. Even in regions with very low estimated antibody prevalence, such as Scotland at 1.2% and Santa Clara at 3.3%, the estimated fatality rates based on serology are low, at 0.04% and 0.1% respectively, showing that the virus was likely far more widespread than official testing numbers captured.

This page of the publication challenges the hypothesis that the Bacille Calmette-Guerin tuberculosis vaccine, commonly administered to children, explains regional differences in COVID-19 severity. Michael Cembalest outlines several reasons for widespread skepticism regarding this theory among the epidemiological, mathematical biology, and medical communities. First, the World Health Organization has noted a lack of medical evidence supporting the BCG thesis. Furthermore, because BCG vaccination is more prevalent in less-developed nations with younger population demographics, age distribution likely explains cross-country variations far better than the vaccine itself, as research from the Imperial College of London indicates that hospitalization and mortality rates closely track age. Cembalest also points out that COVID-19 cases are actively rising in developing regions where the BCG vaccine is widely used. 

The critique also highlights fundamental medical and logical disconnects, noting that tuberculosis is a bacterial infection while SARS-CoV-2 is a virus. Additionally, Chinese healthcare professionals, as reported by epidemiologist Salim Karim, observed no variation in COVID-19 outcomes based on patient BCG vaccination histories. Other academic reviews, including research from the University of Goettingen, highlight that supportive BCG studies failed to account for population heterogeneity, actual vaccination rates, or individual response differences. Cembalest emphasizes that the primary methodological flaw in these studies is their reliance on quick cross-country comparisons that commit an ecological fallacy by comparing broad groups rather than individuals, which confuses average exposure with individual risk. He warns against making policy decisions based on such weak evidence, comparing the situation to the controversial promotion of hydroxychloroquine, and directs readers to a chart on the following page.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest critiques the hypothesis that Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) tuberculosis vaccination policies provide protection against COVID-19, calling the theory sloppy science. Although there is a cluster of low death rates in countries with long-standing BCG vaccine policies, Cembalest argues the thesis falls apart for three main reasons. First, the group of countries with no widespread BCG policy is extremely small, consisting of only six nations, and shows highly dispersed death rates. Second, many countries that terminated their BCG programs after 1970, such as France and Spain, still recorded high COVID-19 death rates despite their older populations over age fifty having received the vaccine. Third, countries that only started BCG policies after 1970 also show low COVID-19 death rates, raising the question of how their older, unvaccinated populations are protected.

To support this critique, the page features a scatter plot titled COVID-19 deaths per million people as a function of BCG vaccine policy, mapping 157 countries across six categories. The vertical axis ranges from zero to 600 deaths per million. Group one, representing twenty-six countries with BCG policies established before 1970, shows a tight cluster of very low death rates. Group two, with eighty-nine countries where start dates are unavailable, also clusters near zero. Group three, which includes fifteen countries that terminated their policies after 1970, shows several high-mortality outliers reaching up to 450 deaths per million, highlighted by a red question-mark arrow. Group four has no countries listed. Group five, comprising twenty-one countries that began BCG vaccination after 1970, displays consistently low death rates, flagged by another red question-mark arrow pointing out the logical inconsistency regarding older citizens. Group six, which has no widespread BCG policy, shows extreme dispersion among its six countries, with death rates ranging from nearly zero to over 500 per million. The author concludes that while clinical trials will be interesting to monitor, the current observational data fails to support the BCG vaccine thesis.

This page from the publication argues that US states should be granted emergency access to Chapter 9 bankruptcy provisions to ensure fair treatment of creditors and allow flexible budget allocations during fiscal distress. The primary visual element is a side-by-side comparison table presenting the legal arguments for both sides. On the left, highlighted in yellow, the Federalist argument relies on Article I, Section 8, Clause 4 of the US Constitution, which empowers Congress to establish uniform bankruptcy laws, alongside Chapter 9 provisions requiring fair, non-discriminatory treatment of creditor classes. This viewpoint is supported by Supreme Court rulings from the 1930s that validated municipal bankruptcy laws without violating state sovereignty. On the right, highlighted in blue, the State’s Rights argument is presented using the Tenth Amendment and Michigan State Constitution Article IX, Section 24 as examples, arguing that federal bankruptcy laws would result in tortious interference with public sector contracts and state pension protections. 

The author aligns with the Federalist perspective, referencing former FDIC Chairman William Isaac's 2016 remarks urging Chicago and the state of Illinois to restructure their liabilities using Chapter 9 tools similar to those provided to Puerto Rico. The text also notes decades of scholarly support for state Chapter 9 access, specifically citing bankruptcy expert David Skeel of the University of Pennsylvania Law School. A footnote references Skeel’s April 2020 work warning of a massive wave of corporate bankruptcies due to the coronavirus pandemic, advocating for policies to flatten the bankruptcy curve through prepackaged bankruptcies, government-provided debtor-in-possession financing, and an increase in temporary bankruptcy judges.

This introductory commentary summarizes key updates regarding the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, tracking indicators, medical treatments, fiscal policy, mortality demographics, and major corporate events. Michael Cembalest highlights that while most of the United States' GDP is experiencing declining or testing-driven infection rates, the nation still has the highest infection rate per million people globally outside of Singapore. J.P. Morgan's unofficial reopen criteria are met by states representing just fifteen percent of US GDP, even though states representing twenty-five percent of GDP have already initiated partial reopenings. Concurrently, US tracking models are showing initial signs of recovery in areas such as petroleum demand, intermodal rail traffic, new business applications, GPS driving usage, hotel occupancy, and mortgage applications.

In medical developments, Remdesivir trials have shown positive but incremental benefits in reducing recovery time without yet demonstrating a mortality benefit, making it a marginal improvement rather than a game-changer. The author emphasizes that vaccines from Johnson & Johnson and Oxford, along with Regeneron's monoclonal antibody therapy, are the key treatments to watch. Regarding fiscal stimulus, the note references Goldman Sachs research indicating that government transfers could offset an eleven percent hit to worker incomes by eight percent, resulting in only a three percent decline in overall incomes for 2020. Furthermore, because sixty-five to seventy-five percent of laid-off workers may receive unemployment benefits exceeding their lost wages through July, personal disposable income could remarkably increase by half a percent compared to 2019.

Demographic data reveals that the risk of COVID-19 mortality for individuals under sixty-five is only two to three percent of the risk for those over sixty-five in most regions, though it reached seven percent in New York City. This is notable because roughly seventy-five percent of the US workforce is under the age of fifty-four, which is the point where mortality risk begins to rise sharply. Finally, the page highlights a historic corporate event where Boeing executed the largest non-mergers-and-acquisitions bond deal in history, selling over twenty-two billion dollars in bonds at five to six percent yields. This successful sale occurred despite a fifty-seven percent year-to-date decline in Boeing's stock price, a BBB- credit rating, and a first-quarter cash burn of nearly six billion dollars that left the company with fifteen point five billion dollars in cash and marketable securities along with nine point six billion dollars in undrawn revolvers.

This page consists entirely of legal disclosures and regulatory disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication, detailing distribution compliance, licensing, and regional regulatory oversight for Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin American jurisdictions including Brazil and Mexico.

This page discusses the estimated impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on unfunded state pension and retiree healthcare obligations in the United States, utilizing J.P. Morgan's "ARC & The Covenants" framework and Interest, Pension, and Other Debt (IPOD) ratios. To estimate this impact, the author models an upfront financial shock to state financial results based on three key assumptions. First, on revenue declines, the model assumes that two-thirds of the Moody's projected 13% to 15% fiscal year 2021 revenue declines are recovered by 2022. Second, it assumes an upfront 10% valuation shock to pension plan asset portfolios. Third, it maintains a conservative 6% long-term investment return assumption instead of the 7.0% to 7.25% rate typically used by many US states. 

A stacked bar chart titled "The cost of unfunded pensions and retiree healthcare as a % of state revenues" displays the results for all 50 US states, sorted from highest total obligation to lowest. The vertical axis ranges from 0% to 60% of state revenues. Each state's bar is composed of three colored segments: what states are currently paying (gray base), what they would have to pay under a revised scenario assuming a 6% plan return and 30-year level dollar amortization (blue middle), and the additional simulated COVID-19 impact (red top). 

The data highlights a stark disparity between states. Highly indebted states see their total required payments rise to levels that appear unsustainable from a long-term public policy perspective, which was largely the case even prior to the pandemic. For instance, Illinois's total obligation climbs to over 55% of state revenues, and New Jersey's approaches 45% once the revised return and COVID-19 shocks are factored in. Other highly burdened states include Hawaii, Connecticut, Kentucky, and Massachusetts, which all exceed 30%. Meanwhile, the estimated COVID-19 impacts are small for less indebted states on the right side of the chart, such as Nebraska and North Dakota, where total obligations remain well under 10% of revenues. The author notes that this analysis focuses on long-term state resource adequacy to meet pension commitments and is separate from short-term questions regarding whether rainy day funds or the Federal Reserve’s Municipal Liquidity Facility can fund immediate 2020 state operating deficits.

This page explores the critical vulnerabilities and geographical dependencies of the United States food and energy supplies, especially in light of COVID-19 disruptions. The author points out that the US is highly urbanized, with eighty-five percent of the population living in cities that rely heavily on non-urban areas to sustain their large consumption footprints. Despite these vulnerabilities, the US goods sectors of food and energy are uniquely self-sufficient and represent the largest segments of the domestic goods economy.

To illustrate this, the first horizontal bar chart compares domestic and foreign content across various goods sectors in 2018. It shows that the largest sector, "Oil, gas, coal and electricity," represents nearly two trillion dollars in economic activity, with foreign content making up just thirteen percent of the total. Similarly, the second-largest sector, "Agriculture and food production," valued at over 1.6 trillion dollars, has a foreign content share of only ten percent. These figures demonstrate a high level of domestic reliance compared to other sectors, such as apparel, which has eighty-eight percent foreign content, or computers and electronics, which is fifty-three percent foreign-sourced.

The second chart, a stacked vertical bar chart, tracks the top twenty-five states in food and energy production for 2018, which collectively represent eighty-seven percent of total US output. Texas leads by a wide margin, generating nearly 160 billion dollars of total production, which is heavily dominated by energy. California ranks second at approximately eighty billion dollars, driven primarily by food production. Other significant contributing states include Pennsylvania, Ohio, Oklahoma, Louisiana, and Illinois, demonstrating how the nation's vital resources are concentrated in a diverse mix of Western, Southern, and Midwestern states.

This page discusses a hypothetical adjustment to the United States Electoral College that factors in a state's economic burden of producing food and energy. The author argues that because cities rely heavily on food- and energy-producing states to survive, representation could logically reflect this vital contribution. In this academic exercise, electoral votes are allocated using a formula where population represents a sixty-seven percent weight, and the remaining thirty-three percent is split between food and energy production. 

Two horizontal bar charts illustrate the potential shifts in electoral votes under this modified approach across various US regions, including Texas, the Northeast, California, the Southwest, Oklahoma to North Dakota, the Pacific Northwest, the Rockies, the Upper Midwest, the Southeast, and the Ohio Valley. 

The first chart weights food and energy production equally at seventeen percent each. Under this model, Texas is the largest beneficiary, gaining over thirty electoral votes, while California gains around ten. These gains come almost entirely at the expense of the Northeast, which loses nearly twenty-five electoral votes. All other regions experience negligible changes of just a few votes. 

The second chart addresses uncertainty in future domestic energy production by reducing the energy weight to eleven percent and raising the food weight to twenty-two percent. Even with this adjustment, the regional impact remains highly concentrated: Texas gains over twenty electoral votes, California gains around twelve, and the Northeast loses roughly twenty votes, while all other regional changes remain minor. 

The author concludes by noting that this is a purely academic exercise, as the high constitutional hurdle of a two-thirds vote in Congress and ratification by thirty-eight state legislatures makes changing the Electoral College highly unlikely. However, the analysis suggests that, despite its criticized flaws and the prominent Texas-Northeast divide, the current system already doing a reasonable job of balancing political power between major population centers and the regions that feed and power the country.

This page discusses the severe fiscal impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on US state budgets, arguing against framing the issue as a crude partisan divide following comments by Senator McConnell. Instead, the author characterizes the crisis as a significant state's rights and structural issue, involving the long-term servicing of revenues over the next 30 years and the potential sharing of fiscal burdens by more solvent states in the event of federal bailouts. For FY 2021, state revenue shortfalls are estimated to reach a substantial $200 billion to $250 billion. Although federal stimulus measures and the concentration of job losses among lower-income workers may help income tax revenues hold up better than during the 2008 recession, natural resource extraction and motor vehicle taxes are projected to experience steeper declines. To balance their budgets, states face difficult choices after already depleting $75 billion in cash reserves, enacting $30 billion in spending freezes, and utilizing $50 billion from the CARES Act. Some states, including Arkansas, Illinois, Kansas, Kentucky, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania, are particularly vulnerable, with cash reserves amounting to less than 3 percent of state expenditures.

The page features two charts illustrating these fiscal dynamics. The first chart displays FY 2021 revenue forecasts for the twenty states with the highest interest, pension, and other debt (IPOD) ratios. It compares base-case and bear-case percentage revenue decline estimates from Moody's Analytics and Morgan Stanley across twenty states, including Illinois, New Jersey, Hawaii, Connecticut, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Maryland, West Virginia, Delaware, Pennsylvania, California, Texas, Georgia, South Carolina, Maine, Montana, Rhode Island, Missouri, Vermont, and New York. The projected revenue declines vary significantly; for instance, Illinois shows revenue decline estimates ranging from roughly -10 percent to a bear case of nearly -37 percent, while New York and West Virginia show bear-case declines approaching -35 percent to -40 percent. This chart excludes Alaska, which faces even steeper declines due to its reliance on natural resource extraction taxes.

The second visual is a bubble chart plotting projected job layoff rates on the y-axis against average weekly earnings on the x-axis by industry, where the bubble size represents each industry's share of the employed population. This chart demonstrates that job losses are heavily concentrated among lower-income workers. The leisure sector has the lowest average weekly earnings of approximately $550 to $600 but the highest projected layoff rate of nearly 50 percent. Similarly, retail and other low-wage sectors face high projected layoff rates between 40 percent and 50 percent. Conversely, higher-paying industries—such as finance, professional business services, information, manufacturing, and wholesale trade—boast average weekly earnings exceeding $1,100 and maintain much lower projected layoff rates, generally under 15 percent. This stark skew explains why state income tax receipts might be relatively shielded compared to the severe impacts on employment and sales tax revenues.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" analysis discusses three medical developments in the fight against COVID-19: vaccine progress by Moderna, the potential of monoclonal antibody therapies, and a newly released clinical trial for an antiviral drug combination. 

The author first notes that Moderna is advancing its messenger RNA vaccine into Phase II clinical trials with 600 participants, following a 45-person Phase I trial in Seattle that began in March. He reminds readers that Phase I only tests safety, not efficacy, so it remains to be seen if the vaccine is effective. 

Next, the text outlines the mechanics, advantages, and limitations of monoclonal antibody therapies, which involve infusing engineered antibodies to neutralize SARS-CoV-2 by binding to its spike protein. While Regeneron is expected to start clinical trials in the summer of 2020, these therapies present distinct trade-offs. They can be deployed quickly as acute therapy or as a prophylactic for healthcare workers, but they are expensive, difficult to scale, and only offer temporary protection lasting a few weeks. 

The final section details a randomized Phase II clinical trial conducted by Hong Kong physicians evaluating a multi-drug regimen of lopinavir, ritonavir, ribavirin, and interferon-1 beta on hospitalized COVID-19 patients. The full regimen reduced the average time to symptom resolution from 12 days to 7 days and accelerated the decline in viral load compared to a control group. However, the author cautions that the trial has significant limitations, including a small sample size of 127 patients, a complex hospital-only setup, and a lack of efficacy for patients who initiated treatment more than seven days after symptom onset. As a result, this combination is mostly relevant to a narrow demographic of patients hospitalized with mild to moderate symptoms. 

The page concludes with a brief reference to other recent publication topics, which span the impact of COVID-19 on state pensions, US fiscal stimulus, vaccine timetables, and market bottom history.

This page discusses the onset of COVID-19 reopening policies in the United States, pointing out that states representing 45% of US GDP have initiated reopening plans despite the nation having one of the highest infection rates in the world, surpassed only by Russia among large countries. Author Michael Cembalest characterizes this decision as a "Logan’s Run" moment, implying a heightened risk of generational sacrifice for the elderly. He notes that J.P. Morgan will be tracking the healthcare consequences of these reopenings, which typically take three to four weeks to appear in the data, as well as real-time consumer spending patterns.

To support this discussion, the page includes three charts. The first chart displays new daily infections per million people on a linear scale using a three-day trailing average, plotted against the number of days after total reported cases reached 100. It shows the United States plateauing at a very high level of roughly 75 to 85 daily infections per million people at day 80, far exceeding the declining infection rates of Western Europe, which peaked near 70 and fell below 30, as well as the lower rates in Eastern Europe, South America, and the Middle East.

The second chart traces Georgia's mobility trends, specifically looking at the percentage change in residential location activity relative to a baseline. This data shows that stay-at-home residential activity spiked to more than 20% above baseline during the state's shelter-in-place order in early April. However, as the state moved into its "preparing to reopen" phase on April 24 and its "partial reopening" phase on April 27, residential activity sharply declined back toward 10% to 15% above baseline, illustrating a rapid decrease in stay-at-home behavior.

The third chart presents a high-frequency US data tracker from late February to mid-May, indexing ten separate economic and mobility indicators where 0 represents the lowest observed value and 100 represents the highest.
