The series tracked include IRS new business applications, Apple maps driving usage, mortgage applications, rail traffic for consumer goods, GPS workplace mobility, hotel occupancy rates, petroleum products demand, TSA checkpoint travelers, department store sales, and heavy industrial production. Virtually all of these indicators bottomed out between late March and mid-April. By early May, the tracker reveals the initial signs of a revived economic pulse, with clear upward turns visible in driving usage, mortgage applications, and petroleum demand.

This page contains regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan clients in various global jurisdictions, including Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America, with no investment charts, tables, or analytical content.

Michael Cembalest analyzes the stark and unprecedented divergence between a rapidly rebounding financial market and severely deteriorating real-world economic conditions during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. He points out that while massive Federal Reserve interventions, totaling eight trillion dollars in asset purchases and commitments, alongside historic fiscal deficits are supporting asset prices, the market's swift recovery relies on three highly optimistic assumptions. These assumptions are that second waves of infections will not lead to renewed state lockdowns, that further federal and state aid will offset income loss if lockdowns persist, and that the economic recovery will show high elasticity upon reopening. He supports this latter point by noting that over ninety-five percent of April Bureau of Labor Statistics survey respondents classified their layoffs as temporary. Cembalest cautions that the high certainty with which these assumptions are priced into markets seems premature given the outstanding epidemiological, behavioral, policy, and growth risks, identifying upcoming second-quarter earnings as a key indicator for investors.

The left side of the page features two charts illustrating the recovering financial markets. The top-left chart plots the Bloomberg Financial Conditions Index on an inverted scale from negative fourteen to two, comparing the 2008/2009 Financial Crisis with the 2020 Covid Crisis. It demonstrates that while the financial crisis saw a severe spike to around negative thirteen followed by a slow, multi-month recovery, the 2020 Covid crisis experienced a much milder shock to negative six before recovering almost instantly. Below this, a second chart from Morgan Stanley tracks the US equity risk premium in basis points from three hundred to seven hundred and fifty, comparing the same two periods. While the risk premium peaked over seven hundred basis points in late 2008 and remained elevated, the 2020 premium spiked to five hundred and fifty basis points and plunged rapidly back to around four hundred basis points, showing an even speedier recovery in equity valuations relative to bonds.

The right side of the page illustrates the collapsing economy with two more charts. The top-right chart traces the US unemployment rate from 1869 to 2020 using data from Christina Romer, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and the Economic Policy Institute, demonstrating how the current crisis rivals the Great Depression. The historical peak during the Great Depression approached twenty-five percent, and the 2020 spike reaches similar heights when adjusted for specific segments. One red data point at approximately twenty percent includes workers erroneously classified as employed, while another near twenty-five percent incorporates an additional six point three million unemployed individuals who are not looking for work. Finally, the bottom-right chart displays J.P. Morgan's forecast for quarterly global GDP growth. The chart highlights a historically unprecedented dotted-line forecast, showing global GDP plunging by nearly twenty-five percent quarter-over-quarter in early 2020 before a projected sharp rebound of almost thirty percent.

This page analyzes the stark divergence in corporate profits across different sectors during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. Michael Cembalest argues that the partial recovery of the equity market reflects a concentration of earnings strength: 72% of the S&P 500 market capitalization is projected to suffer relatively minor earnings hits, while the worst damage is heavily concentrated in cyclicals and financials. 

To illustrate this market composition, a pie chart of S&P 500 sector weights shows that Tech, Internet Retail, and Media make up 40% of the index, while Non-Cyclicals account for 32%. This leaves Cyclicals at 18% and Financials at just 10% of the index. 

A bar chart of consensus earnings-per-share (EPS) growth comparing Q2 2020 to Q2 2019 highlights this divergence. While the total S&P 500 EPS is projected to decline by roughly 40%, Tech, Internet Retail, and Media are expected to experience a minimal drop of only about 2%. Non-cyclicals are projected to decline by about 20%, whereas Financials face a decline of around 45%, and Cyclicals face a dramatic contraction of over 120%, pushing them into net losses. 

For the subsequent recovery, a second bar chart projects consensus EPS growth for 2021 versus 2020. The total S&P 500 is expected to rebound by about 30%, driven heavily by a projected surge in Cyclicals of over 130%. Financials are projected to grow by roughly 35%, Tech, Internet Retail, and Media by 20%, and Non-Cyclicals by 15%. 

Finally, a line chart plots actual S&P 500 EPS on a rolling four-quarter basis from January 2016 through January 2020 against 2021 consensus EPS projections. Actual earnings rose steadily from roughly $100 in early 2016 to peak around $163. The consensus projections for 2021 EPS, which started near $190, have been revised downward to approximately $165 to $170. Cembalest expresses skepticism about these 2021 projections, noting that expectations for earnings to remain flat compared to actual 2019 levels seem overly optimistic. He cautions that because many US companies have high operating leverage, earnings can fall far more sharply in a weak economy than forecasters expect.

This page analyzes the structural outperformance of US and Emerging Market equities over European and Japanese equities, a persistent market trend that has continued despite differing COVID-19 trajectories. The author argues that while Europe has seen a faster decline in infections and Japan has maintained very low infection rates, their equity markets continue to underperform. This is attributed to structural advantages in the US market: higher exposure to high-growth technology sectors rather than low-growth, volatile cyclical sectors, and superior profitability within individual sectors.

A series of charts and tables supports this thesis. The first chart, tracking new daily COVID-19 infections per million people, shows that despite the US maintaining high infection levels of around 80 cases per million, Europe’s rate has fallen sharply to around 30, and Japan’s rate remains near zero. The second chart illustrates a three-year rolling outperformance of an active portfolio overweighting the US and Emerging Markets while underweighting Europe and Japan. This barbell strategy has consistently beaten the MSCI All World Index since 1991, except for a brief period in the mid-2000s.

A Year-to-Date performance table as of mid-May 2020 confirms that both the US dollar and local currency barbell strategies achieved 0.9% outperformance. The table details regional weights and returns, showing US dollar returns of -8.7% for the US (62% weight) and -17.7% for Emerging Markets (12% weight), compared to -20.1% for Europe (18% weight) and -12.2% for Japan (8% weight). 

The structural sector composition is visualized in a column chart showing that technology represents roughly 30% of the US index market cap, while materials, energy, and industrials make up only about 13%. Conversely, Europe and Japan have tech exposures of only 10% and 12%, respectively, with cyclical sectors dominating both at around 28% of their index market caps. 

Finally, two tables compare corporate profitability across sectors. The first shows that the US leads in Return on Assets (ROA) across all key sectors; for instance, US technology shows a 10.1% ROA compared to 6.0% in Europe and 4.1% in Japan. The second table displays a similar trend in Return on Equity (ROE), where the US dominates with a technology ROE of 27.5% compared to Europe's 12.3% and Japan's 9.4%. This profitability advantage for US companies holds true across consumer staples, consumer discretionary, healthcare, communication services, and financials.

This page discusses the risks present in the leveraged loan market amid rising corporate bankruptcies, arguing that the lack of covenant protections will make the recovery road much longer and more difficult than in prior recessions. The author points out that covenant protections have been surrendered at a record pace. This is illustrated by the first chart, which displays Moody's loan covenant quality score from 2012 to 2019, where a score of 5.0 represents the weakest quality. The score climbed from around 3.2 in 2012 to nearly 4.4 by the end of 2019, indicating the weakest covenant quality on record. Consequently, the author projects defaulted loan recovery rates could fall to 60–65 cents on the dollar, significantly lower than the historical average of 75–80 cents. 

The second chart tracks par-weighted, 12-month trailing leveraged loan default rates from 1998 through April 2020. Historically, default rates peaked near 8% in 2001 and reached nearly 14% in 2009, whereas the rate in early 2020 shows only a minor uptick to around 2% or 3%. The author attributes this slow rise to rapid loan growth since 2010 expanding the denominator, payment waivers, loose covenants preventing technical defaults, and the lag time of the recession. 

Two total return index charts compare the market pricing behavior of the 2008–2009 crisis with the early 2020 downturn. During the Great Financial Crisis, the S&P/LSTA Leveraged Loan Index plummeted from an index level of 100 in Jan-07 to a bottom near 70 in late 2008 before embarking on a sharp V-shaped recovery back past 105 by 2010. This index drop vastly overshot actual peak realized losses, which J.P. Morgan estimates were only around 8%. In the second total return index chart, covering January to May 2020, the index dropped from approximately 180 in January to a low of 145 in March—a 25% selloff—before recovering partially to around 163 by May. 

Unlike the clean V-shaped recovery of 2009, the author warns of a high risk of relapse or stagnant loan prices due to eroded creditor protections. While zero interest rates make leveraged loans tempting, the author advises maintaining a balance of distressed debt and loans, expecting a substantial surge in distressed debt toward the end of 2020. Data sources throughout the page include Moody's, J.P. Morgan, S&P LCD, S&P/LSTA, and Bloomberg.

This page introduces a J.P. Morgan analysis on the post-lockdown recovery of the United States consumer, utilizing real-time, aggregated, and anonymized Chase credit and debit card transaction data through May 11, 2020. The author, Michael Cembalest, notes that while he has been discussing macroeconomic and political developments with clients—such as swing state polls shifting toward Joe Biden, the potential for a Democratic sweep, debt burdens, and inflation risks—he is focusing this analysis on the consumer. He argues that aggregate national data, which combines fully locked-down states with those that have partially or fully reopened, is insufficient for understanding the recovery. To address this, J.P. Morgan has created tools to differentiate consumer transactions by state-level policy and virus severity, with the goal of identifying lasting secular shifts in retailing, commercial real estate, and e-commerce. 

The transaction data is presented in two line charts tracking spending changes from March 7 to May 16, 2020, compared to the same period in 2019, utilizing a seven-day smoothing average. The first chart, which covers all spending categories and all transaction types, shows that overall national spending began March up nearly 10% year-over-year, plummeted to a low of nearly negative 40% in mid-April, and recovered to a decline of 15% by mid-May. The second chart isolates "card present" transactions to exclude e-commerce and emphasize physical, in-person retail. This metric fell from slightly positive territory in early March to a deep trough of negative 50% in mid-April, recovering only to a decline of approximately 35% to 40% by mid-May. Comparing these two charts highlights how significantly e-commerce buffered the broader retail downturn. Cembalest also notes in the footnotes that the United States has proceeded with reopening its economy despite having one of the highest COVID-19 infection rates per million people in the world.

This page analyzes how consumer spending on social distancing services and oil or gasoline is recovering across US states grouped by their COVID-19 infection rates. The author argues that states in the lowest quartile of infections per capita are experiencing faster spending recoveries, a pattern that also holds true when analyzing spending relative to deaths per capita and recent infection trends. 

The first line chart presents credit and debit card spending trends in social distancing categories, which include card-present transactions for retail, lodging, restaurants, amusement parks, theaters, and other recreational services. It compares spending in 2020 against 2019 using a seven-day smoothing average from March 7 to May 16, 2020. The data is divided into four lines representing quartiles of total COVID infections per million people. All groups saw a sharp contraction in March, bottoming out between late March and early April with spending down between 60% and 70%. By mid-May, the lowest quartile of infections showed the strongest rebound, rising to approximately negative 40% year-over-year, while the highest infection quartile lagged significantly, remaining near negative 60%.

The second line chart tracks spending trends specifically for oil and gasoline transactions over the same period, categorized by the same infection quartiles. The overall pace of recovery for fuel spending is more muted. After dropping to lows of negative 55% to negative 60% in early April, the lowest-infection quartile recovered to around negative 40% by mid-May, while the remaining quartiles showed weaker recovery, clustered between negative 50% and negative 55%. Both charts utilize internal Chase debit and credit card data to demonstrate that lower regional infection rates correlate with a faster return of consumer economic activity.

This page focuses on analyzing discretionary "social distancing spending" (SDS), which is defined as card-present transactions for activities requiring physical presence, such as retail, lodging, restaurants, theaters, and amusement parks. The author notes that SDS represented about one-third of all consumer spending in 2019, and its decline during the pandemic was much sharper than the decline in overall spending, which includes non-discretionary items like groceries and recurring bills.

To illustrate this, a bar chart displays 2019 spending categories broken down by card-present and card-not-present transactions. Major card-present SDS categories include retail, restaurants, lodging, and other travel and entertainment, with retail representing the largest overall category at approximately 27% of transactions. 

A companion line chart tracks the national credit and debit card spending trend for social distancing categories in the spring of 2020 compared to 2019. It shows a precipitous drop starting in early March, bottoming out at nearly a 70% year-over-year decline in mid-April, before recovering slightly to around negative 50% by mid-May. 

The core analytical focus of the page is how quickly these spending patterns will recover as lockdowns end. To explore this, the bottom line chart breaks down credit and debit card spending trends based on each state's current reopening status. The data reveals that states with "no lockdown ever" suffered the least severe contraction, bottoming out at negative 60% before recovering strongly to roughly negative 35% by mid-May. States in the "reopening" category also showed a relatively strong rebound, recovering to about negative 45% of 2019 levels. In contrast, states under "shelter in place" mandates, "regional reopening" plans, or scheduled to reopen the following week experienced the deepest spending drops (reaching negative 75% to negative 80%) and faced a much slower recovery, remaining stuck around negative 60% by mid-May. The author emphasizes that for investors, the crucial metric is the pace of the recovery rather than the absolute year-over-year spending levels. All card spending charts are based on smoothed, seven-day average Chase transaction data.

This page consists entirely of legal and regulatory disclosures for the publication, containing no charts, economic analyses, or investment commentary. It outlines distribution details and governing regulatory bodies across various international jurisdictions. For Switzerland, it lists distribution by J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA, regulated by the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority. For Hong Kong and Singapore, it details distribution by the local branches of JPMorgan Chase Bank, regulated by their respective monetary and securities authorities. The disclosure also covers Australian regulatory requirements under the Corporations Act 2001, defining restrictions for wholesale clients and noting that the material has not been prepared specifically for Australian investors. Additionally, the page details distribution restrictions across Latin American jurisdictions, highlighting regulatory rules for offering unregistered securities or funds in countries such as Brazil under the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission and Mexican platforms. It concludes with standard copyright information and personal-use limitations.

This page of Michael Cembalest's report provides an update on three COVID-19 vaccine candidates—Moderna, Oxford, and Sinovac—as well as clinical findings on the use of anticoagulants for hospitalized COVID-19 patients. 

For Moderna, the author reports encouraging interim Phase I trial results showing dose-dependent immunogenicity in all 45 recipients and neutralizing antibodies in the 8 patients with detailed results available. Although no serious adverse reactions were found and mouse studies look promising, the author notes that Phase II and III trials are required to confirm if these antibodies are generated in sufficient quantities to overcome the virus. 

Oxford’s vaccine trials in rhesus monkeys showed antibody generation within 28 days and protection against lung damage, but sparked controversy because the virus continued to replicate in the monkeys' noses. While biotech pioneer William Haseltine criticized the Oxford trial for a lack of difference in viral load compared to the placebo group and low overall antibody levels, others point out that vaccinated monkeys avoided viral pneumonia, which affected two-thirds of the placebo group. 

Sinovac’s monkey trial results appeared more favorable, achieving sterilizing immunity in the highest-dosed group, though the author cautions that different study designs and viral load levels make direct comparisons between Sinovac and Oxford difficult, leaving human trials as the next critical indicator for both. 

Finally, the page highlights a medical study of 2,773 COVID-19 patients in New York City hospitals published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology. The study reveals that intubated patients treated with anticoagulants experienced a 71% survival rate compared to only 37% for those who did not receive them, illustrating how blood thinners can serve as an effective non-antiviral intervention to reduce mortality.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, investigates whether any countries or US states are experiencing a second wave of COVID-19 infections as of mid-May 2020. The analysis defines a second wave as a scenario where infection rates dropped sharply from prior peaks, appeared to be contained, and then rose again. 

On the international stage, only Greece, Lebanon, and South Korea came close to meeting this definition. The top-left chart, which plots new daily infections per million people on a linear scale using a three-day trailing average against the number of days after total cases reached 100, shows Greece peaking around 9 cases per million before dropping and rising slightly to about 6 cases around day 40. Lebanon and South Korea show even smaller secondary bumps, peaking below 5 and 12 cases per million respectively before flattening out. The top-right chart provides broader context by adding a data series for Europe as a whole, which peaked near 75 daily infections per million people. This comparison reveals that the potential second waves in Greece, Lebanon, and South Korea are negligible compared to overall European infection levels, indicating that despite reopenings across Europe and Asia, there is no material evidence of a second wave.

The same litmus test is applied to US states. Montana is the only state to show a potential second wave after its stay-at-home order expired on April 26 and restaurants reopened on May 4. The bottom-left chart tracks Montana's daily infections per million people, showing a peak of over 20 cases early on, a drop to near zero, and a minuscule uptick to 2 cases per million people around day 50. The bottom-right chart compares Montana to Washington, demonstrating that Washington's infection rate peaked near 65 cases per million around day 30 and has stubbornly fluctuated between 30 and 40 cases per million through day 60. The author concludes that the primary issue for the US is not second waves, but rather the persistence of the first wave in early outbreak zones like Washington, where infection rates have shown little improvement.

This page introduces key topics from J.P. Morgan's recent client Zoom calls, focusing primarily on an analysis of inflation risks. While clients are concerned about inflation due to aggressive Federal Reserve and Treasury actions, the author highlights that the US experienced a full decade of negative short-term interest rates and high fiscal deficits leading up to 2020 without an inflation overshoot. Historically, structural factors like declining labor bargaining power, online retailing, globalization, China's entry into the World Trade Organization, and industrial automation have kept inflation low. Although the current growth of the money supply is much faster than during the Global Financial Crisis, and US-China tensions or wealth redistribution could eventually drive up prices, the author expects deflation to be the primary concern over the next one to two years due to corporate restructuring and the eventual expiration of federal and state unemployment benefits.

Two charts illustrate these monetary dynamics. The first chart displays the five-year average of the T-bill or Funds rate less inflation from 1830 to 2010 to show the lowest real yields on cash since 1830. The data shows that real yields on cash have historically dipped below zero almost exclusively during major conflicts, specifically the Civil War, World War I, and World War II. However, the five-year period ending in 2019 stands out as a rare peacetime anomaly, with real yields falling into negative territory at around negative one percent. 

The second chart compares the expansion of the money supply, measured by M2 plus institutional money market fund balances, indexed to the start of the Global Financial Crisis in August 2008 and the Global Coronavirus crisis in 2020. During the Global Financial Crisis, represented by a gold line, the money supply grew gradually, peaking near an index level of 110 about a year into the crisis. In contrast, the blue line representing the Global Coronavirus crisis climbs almost vertically, soaring to an index level of nearly 120 in just a few months, illustrating the unprecedented speed of recent money supply growth.

This page of the publication, titled "COVID lockdowns: do they do any good?", discusses the challenge of analyzing how COVID-19 lockdowns affected mortality rates and stresses the importance of waiting for rigorous, peer-reviewed counterfactual studies. The author cautions readers against flawed logic and non-peer-reviewed papers. Specifically, he dismantles a common argument comparing Germany and Italy: even though Germany experienced lower infection and mortality rates with less stringent lockdowns than Italy, one cannot logically conclude that lockdowns provided no benefit to Italy. The analysis must account for each country's unique demographic and healthcare dynamics.

The author critiques a widely circulated paper claiming lockdowns had no impact in Europe, noting its author is an oceanographer at the Woods Hole research center rather than an epidemiologist. Detailed methodological flaws in this paper are explored, including a lack of pre-lockdown data, the erroneous assumption that everyone follows a median disease course, mischaracterizing the United Kingdom as having a full lockdown when the Oxford Stringency Index showed otherwise, overestimating initial reproductive numbers by double the consensus, lacking statistical support, and failing to account for daily reporting anomalies.

Conversely, the author highlights research by Jeff Shaman at Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health. Shaman's team utilized county-level infection, death, and mobility data to conclude that implementing lockdown and control measures in the United States just one to two weeks earlier could have avoided fifty-five percent of the deaths that occurred between March 15 and May 3. 

Ultimately, the author remains open to the idea that lockdown costs might have exceeded their benefits, but emphasizes that such conclusions must be proven through peer-reviewed research rather than internet missives, opinion pieces from unrelated disciplines, or unreliable news sources like the London Daily Mail, which has been flagged by NewsGuard for irresponsible reporting.

This J.P. Morgan newsletter highlights COVID-19 updates, focusing on real-time spending, healthcare capacity, infection trajectories, vaccine progress, and European fiscal proposals. US real-time spending indicators, such as business and mortgage applications and petroleum demand, are rising quickly compared to March lows, with credit and debit card tracking showing sharp improvements in social distancing spending in reopened states with low infection rates.

Regarding healthcare capacity, ICU bed utilization in New York and New Jersey has finally fallen below seventy-five percent, while the median ICU utilization rate across other states is just seven percent. This, paired with a fifty percent median hospital bed utilization rate, suggests the US has sufficient excess capacity to handle a potential second wave of infections. To analyze these waves, the page presents two charts tracking new daily infections per million people on a linear scale with a three-day trailing average, plotted against the number of days after total reported cases reached one hundred. 

The first chart, focused on US states experiencing second waves, shows Arkansas peaking at around eighty infections per million near day sixty, while West Virginia exhibits a more modest secondary rise peaking near thirty-five infections per million around day twenty-five. The second chart compares the broad trajectories of the United States and the United Kingdom. While the United Kingdom's infections peaked near seventy per million around day forty and declined to around thirty by day eighty, the United States remains flat, hovering between sixty and ninety infections per million from day forty onward, indicating that the nation is still struggling to end its first wave of infections.

In vaccine development, the US Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority has agreed to provide one point two billion dollars to AstraZeneca and Oxford to fund trials and secure three hundred million doses for the US, with delivery potentially starting in October. However, recent monkey trials showed mixed results due to low antibody responses and active virus replication, and declining UK infection rates mean that upcoming large-scale US trials this summer will be critical to proving the vaccine's efficacy. Finally, in Europe, France and Germany have proposed that the European Commission borrow five hundred billion euros, representing about two to three percent of EU GDP, to distribute as grants to struggling member states. This proposed step toward fiscal burden-sharing could relieve pressure on the European Central Bank, making historically undervalued Italian and Spanish equities potentially attractive investments if the proposal secures unanimous EU approval.

This commentary discusses how the United States successfully managed its post-World War II debt ratio, arguing that the nation did not actually reduce its absolute debt levels but instead rapidly expanded its real gross domestic product. Under President Eisenhower’s administration from 1952 to 1960, the U.S. implemented several pro-business policies that spurred a three percent real and five percent nominal economic growth rate, while private-sector employment reached a historic peak of eighty-six percent. 

The author details specific Eisenhower-era measures that supported this growth, including the elimination of double-taxation for small businesses under Subchapter S, accelerated depreciation for plant and equipment investments, research and development tax write-offs, and lower excise and foreign profit taxes. Additionally, the administration dismantled wage and price controls, decreased agricultural subsidies, lowered import tariffs, vigorously applied antitrust laws under the Sherman Act to limit monopolies, and scaled back easy government-underwritten mortgages as well as military and foreign aid spending. The author addresses personal tax rates, noting that economists Emmanuel Saez, Thomas Piketty, and Gabriel Zucman conceded that effective tax rates on the top one percent in 2015 were only five to seven percent lower than they were in 1955. Ultimately, the author concludes that while some of these policies may clash with today's aging demographics and alternative Keynesian approaches could be considered, Eisenhower’s approach represents the sole historical precedent for rapidly lowering the federal debt ratio. 

The page concludes with a summary of recent publication topics from April and May of 2020, which cover diverse economic and medical issues related to the coronavirus pandemic, including tracking the rebirth of the consumer, regional equity performance in Europe and Japan, vaccine timelines and monoclonal antibody applications, corporate profit and pension impacts, and the effectiveness of fiscal stimulus.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclaimers and jurisdictional disclosures for J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market publication. It details the specific legal entities responsible for distributing the material and their respective regulatory oversight bodies across several global regions. Mentioned jurisdictions and regulatory bodies include Switzerland, regulated by the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority; Hong Kong, regulated by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the Securities and Futures Commission; and Singapore, regulated by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. The page also outlines compliance disclosures for wholesale clients in Australia under the Corporations Act 2001, detailing regulatory exemptions for J.P. Morgan Securities LLC under U.S. laws overseen by the SEC, FINRA, and CFTC. Finally, it addresses private placement and distribution restrictions across Latin American jurisdictions, specifically referencing compliance with the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission as well as Mexican financial platforms.

This page focuses on the rapid acceleration of e-commerce retail spending during the COVID-19 pandemic, with Michael Cembalest arguing that shifting consumer preferences toward online shopping could become one of the pandemic's most enduring structural legacies, impacting a wide array of industries. 

To support this observation, the page features three charts based on internal Chase credit and debit card transaction data, tracking the year-over-year percentage change in spending from March 7 to May 16, 2020, using a seven-day smoothing average. 

The top chart illustrates retail-only e-commerce spending trends categorized by US state reopening statuses: "No lockdown ever," "Reopening," "Reopening next week," "Regional reopening," and "Shelter in place." The data reveals a massive surge in online retail shopping across all state categories. E-commerce growth rose from roughly 10% to 20% in early March to peak levels by late April and May. States under "Shelter in place" mandates saw the most dramatic spike, peaking near 70% growth. Conversely, states with "No lockdown ever" experienced the lowest growth, yet still rose significantly to around 40%. States categorized as "Reopening" or "Regional reopening" also maintained robust e-commerce growth of 50% to 60%, showing that the online shopping boom persisted even as physical economies began to unlock.

The bottom-left chart directly compares national retail-only "E-commerce" transactions against "Card Present" (in-person) transactions. While retail e-commerce growth climbed steadily from around 20% in early March to over 40% by mid-May, Card Present retail spending collapsed from 0% down to nearly -60% in mid-April, recovering only slightly to around -40% by the end of the observed period. 

The bottom-right chart expands this comparison to include all spending categories in the dataset rather than just retail. In this broader view, Card Present transactions plummeted from 0% in early March to a trough of -50% in mid-April, lingering near -45% by mid-May. E-commerce across all categories exhibited more volatility than in the retail-only sector, starting near 15% growth, dipping briefly below 0% in late March and mid-April—likely due to the suspension of travel and event bookings—before recovering to 10% to 15% growth by mid-May.

In this publication, Michael Cembalest investigates a historical economic anomaly in an article titled "The explosion in the US Federal debt and the Eisenhower blueprint." The author poses a central question: how did the United States successfully reduce its gross federal debt-to-GDP ratio by almost half during the 1950s? This historical mystery is highly relevant to contemporary policy, especially given the rapid surge in US federal debt shown in the accompanying charts, which project debt levels for 2020 and 2021 to reach nearly 100% of GDP. The author notes that this dramatic post-World War II debt reduction did not rely on standard playbook options such as drastic cuts in government spending, massive tax hikes, negative interest rates engineered by the Federal Reserve, or runaway inflation.

The first chart, titled "Gross federal debt held by the public as a percentage of US GDP," tracks debt levels from 1940 to 2020 using Congressional Budget Office data. It highlights a massive spike peaking above 100% of GDP in the mid-1940s, followed by a dramatic decline to under 50% by 1960. An arrow points to this precipitous drop, asking, "How did this happen in just a decade?" After bottoming out at around 25% in the mid-1970s, the ratio rises again, culminating in projected estimates for 2020 and 2021 that approach the post-World War II high.

The second chart, titled "Interest burdens don't always track debt levels," presents interest payments on federal debt as a percentage of US GDP from 1940 to 2020, sourcing data from the Office of Management and Budget. It demonstrates that despite the massive debt-to-GDP ratios of the 1940s and 1950s, the national interest burden remained relatively low, hovering between 1.0% and 2.0%. The interest burden actually peaked much later, around 1990, at over 3.0%, before falling back to between 1.5% and 2.0% in the 2000s and 2010s.

To explain how the post-World War II debt ratio fell so quickly, a detailed table presents annual economic data from 1950 to 1960, sourced from the OMB, BEA, the Robert Shiller dataset, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The table reveals that the gross federal debt held by the public in absolute terms actually rose slightly over the decade, from $219 billion in 1950 to $237 billion in 1960, representing a compound annual growth rate of just 0.8%. However, nominal GDP expanded rapidly, rising from $273 billion to $519 billion, reflecting a stellar compound annual growth rate of 6.6%. Real GDP also grew at a robust compound annual growth rate of 4.3%, rising from $273 billion to $415 billion. Throughout this decade, government outlays remained relatively steady, ranging from 14% to 21% of GDP, while receipts fluctuated between 14% and 19% of GDP. Meanwhile, the average real 10-year interest rate remained mostly positive but modest, starting at 1.3% in 1950, dipping to a low of negative 5.3% in 1951, and rising to 2.7% by 1960. This dataset demonstrates that the debt-to-GDP ratio fell from 80% to 46% primarily because nominal economic growth far outstripped the minimal growth of the nominal debt.

This analysis focuses on Joe Biden’s 2020 taxation and spending agenda, presenting it as a highly progressive platform that may surprise younger voters who dismiss him as a centrist establishment candidate. To frame the political landscape, two charts examine polling and market predictions leading up to late May 2020. The first chart, showing Trump vs. Biden polling in swing states since March 1, displays the polling spread between the candidates across twelve swing states, such as Colorado, Florida, Iowa, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Wisconsin. The majority of these polling data points cluster below the zero line, indicating a Biden lead in critical states like Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, while Trump leads primarily in Iowa and Ohio. The second chart traces the betting odds of a Democratic sweep from late February to late May 2020. It shows the probability of a Democrat winning the presidency rising from roughly 55 percent to nearly 60 percent, while the odds of Democrats controlling both the House and the Senate surged from around 23 percent to approximately 45 percent over the same period.

The core of the page is a detailed table comparing Biden’s proposed tax increases against his planned spending initiatives, drawing data from Cornerstone Macro Research and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. On the taxation side, the agenda proposes a total of 3.994 trillion dollars in tax increases. The largest revenue generators are raising the corporate tax rate to 28 percent, which is estimated to raise 1.3 trillion dollars, and applying a 12.4 percent payroll tax on incomes above 400,000 dollars, split evenly between employers and employees, which is estimated to raise 962 billion dollars. Other significant tax measures include raising the top rate and limiting itemized deductions to raise 520 billion dollars, taxing capital gains as ordinary income for those earning over 1 million dollars to raise 448 billion dollars, and establishing industry-specific taxes to raise 343 billion dollars, primarily targeting commercial and multifamily real estate depreciation schedules. 

On the spending side, the agenda outlines 6.030 trillion dollars in total spending increases. The largest outlays are for healthcare expansion, including a public option and ACA expansion, costing 2.250 trillion dollars, followed by 1.3 trillion dollars for infrastructure, 850 billion dollars for Pre-K and K-12 education, and 750 billion dollars for higher education. Clean energy research is budgeted at 400 billion dollars, while expanding social security and paid family leave are estimated at 450 billion dollars and 430 billion dollars, respectively. Drug price reforms are expected to offset spending by saving 400 billion dollars. Ultimately, Cembalest argues that Biden’s agenda represents a very progressive platform characterized by base-broadening corporate tax hikes, increased antitrust enforcement, and significant public investments in progressive causes.

This page evaluates the potential impact on investors of upcoming policy changes, focusing particularly on the reversal of corporate tax cuts and a potential antitrust revival targeting the technology sector. The author projects that a corporate tax reversal could reduce the S&P 500 by 200 to 300 points, given today's elevated price-to-earnings multiples. An antitrust crackdown poses a significant headwind to megacap tech companies, which are characterized by high market concentration, massive outperformance compared to the broader market since 2010, and aggressive acquisition strategies.

To demonstrate how dominant megacaps have become, a chart on year-over-year financial growth in the first quarter of 2020 shows that tech and large-cap companies survived the pandemic best. While the Nasdaq 100 saw positive sales growth of 8% and earnings growth of 4%, the broader S&P 500 saw sales growth of only 1% and an earnings decline of 14%. Small-cap companies in the S&P 600 were hit hardest, seeing a 2% drop in sales and a severe 72% collapse in earnings.

Another chart shows that industry consolidation, measured by the revenues of the largest 15 companies as a percentage of US GDP, is approaching its historic 1969 peak. In 1969, the top 15 industrial companies accounted for approximately 9% of US GDP. This ratio fell to around 4% for tech and telecom companies in 2000, but rose to nearly 8.5% by 2019 for tech, telecom, and e-commerce companies combined. 

The historical context of antitrust enforcement is presented in two additional charts. A stacked bar chart displaying the number of Department of Justice antitrust investigations initiated from 1970 to 2018 shows a pronounced downward trend. Total cases, which include merger, monopoly, and competition investigations, peaked at over 500 per year in the early 1970s but have steadily dwindled, remaining well below 200 annually throughout the 2010s. 

A final chart illustrates that the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice have historically enforced antitrust laws at much lower rates in the tech sector than in other industries. Specifically, the FTC's rate of agency challenges is over 12% across all sectors, but sits at 0% for the tech sector, which is defined here to include data processing, hosting, and related services that primarily identify Google, Amazon, and Facebook. For the DOJ, the challenge rate is roughly 17% across all sectors, compared to only about 6% for the tech sector.

This page analyzes the early stages of the US economic recovery following the initial COVID-19 lockdowns, comparing positive consumer spending rebounds with emerging indicators of second-wave virus infections in select states. Michael Cembalest highlights several encouraging economic metrics, including a payroll increase of 2.5 million jobs, a 40 percent monthly rise in auto sales, weekly unemployment claims dropping below 2 million, and a 60 percent surge in mortgage applications from their April lows. Short-term vacation rental bookings have also rebounded above pre-pandemic levels. Although these indicators remain significantly below 2019 levels, the author argues they represent a clear inflection point in the recovery, supporting his earlier prediction that the economy would be 70 to 80 percent back to normal within a year of the lockdowns. 

The first chart on the left, which tracks national credit and debit card spending trends from March 7 to May 26, visualizes this consumer rebound. It compares overall spending to social-distancing-sensitive card-present transactions in states with low COVID infection rates. Overall spending bottomed out at nearly negative 30 percent in April before recovering to roughly negative 15 percent by late May. Meanwhile, social-distancing transactions—which include retail, lodging, restaurants, amusement parks, and theaters—fell much further to a trough of nearly negative 60 percent in mid-April, recovering to approximately negative 30 percent by late May. 

The author cautions that a severe second wave of infections could prompt a return to lockdowns and reverse these spending trends. He notes that median state ICU utilization is currently at a low 7 percent and median hospital bed utilization is at 52 percent, indicating ample healthcare capacity. However, based on epidemiological research, he warns it may take four to six weeks rather than two to three weeks to observe the viral impact of economic reopening. 

The second chart, on the right, plots new daily infections per million people on a 10-day trailing average over the number of days after total reported cases reached 100. This chart tracks Arkansas, Washington, and Montana to identify potential second waves. Montana’s case rate remains flat and near zero. Washington shows an initial peak of around 60 daily infections per million near day 35, followed by a decline and a modest climb back to around 40 by day 90. Arkansas displays a distinct second wave, with daily infections rising sharply from around 20 near day 40 to over 90 infections per million by day 80. 

The page mentions entities such as J.P. Morgan, Johns Hopkins University, the International Monetary Fund, and Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart, whose famous quote on obscenity is used to describe the subjective identification of a second infection wave. Additionally, a footnote highlights supply shortages in the construction sector, noting that Riverhead Building Supply ran out of specific timber screws due to a backlog of renovation projects.

This page of Michael Cembalest’s report explores the hypothesis that COVID-19 acts as a vascular disease rather than strictly a pulmonary one, exploring how this perspective could lead to more effective treatment strategies. The author highlights observations from medical directors at Harvard's Brigham and Women's Hospital, who suggest that SARS-CoV-2 behaves as a vasculotropic disease by infecting the endothelial cells that line blood vessels. This infection damages endothelial cells and causes inflammation, which can trigger plaque rupture and subsequent heart attacks. It also explains why individuals with pre-existing conditions like high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, and heart disease face a much higher risk of severe complications. Furthermore, this vascular damage explains why mechanical ventilation often fails to rescue patients, as proper oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange requires healthy blood vessels in and around the lungs. 

To mitigate this damage, the author discusses the potential benefits of existing drugs like statins, ACE inhibitors, and anticoagulants. The text cites a New England Journal of Medicine study of nine thousand COVID-19 patients that linked statins and ACE inhibitors to higher rates of survival. Similarly, a study of over two thousand seven hundred COVID-19 patients in New York City hospitals published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology revealed that the survival rate for intubated patients treated with anticoagulants was seventy-one percent, compared to only thirty-seven percent for those who were not treated.

This page consists entirely of standard regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's financial services and materials distributed across various jurisdictions, including Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America.

This page analyzes the profound impact of the Federal Reserve’s massive monetary expansion on the post-COVID-19 market rally, arguing that recent equity and credit gains are heavily driven by this unprecedented liquidity. To illustrate this, the first chart compares the growth of the money supply—measured as M2 plus institutional money market fund balances—during the current crisis against the Global Financial Crisis of 2008. The index, starting at 100, shows that during the COVID-19 crisis, the money supply surged vertically to over 120 in just a few months, whereas during the Global Financial Crisis, the index grew much more slowly, peaking around 107 over two years later.

An accompanying table displays the recovery of various credit spreads from their peaks over the preceding six months, demonstrating how Fed interventions repaired credit market distress. Notable recoveries include US asset-backed commercial paper versus the 3-month Treasury at 99%, AAA asset-backed credit cards at 96%, AAA asset-backed prime auto at 93%, and the TED spread at 92%. In contrast, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage versus the 10-year Treasury recovered the least, at 39%. This influx of capital also led to a historic $35 billion inflow into US high-yield bonds, representing 18% of all high-yield assets under management.

The bottom half of the page details the performance and valuation divergence between resilient sectors and COVID "victim" sectors. A line chart of year-to-date S&P 500 sector returns shows that resilient sectors—comprising Tech, Communication Services, Utilities, Health Care, Staples, and Amazon—grew by 5.7% year-to-date, while victim sectors—consisting of Discretionary excluding Amazon, Energy, Financials, Industrials, Materials, and REITs—fell by 11.2%. 

Despite this underperformance, an adjacent bar chart shows a substantial expansion in valuation multiples for these victim sectors based on consensus 2021 forward price-to-earnings ratios. While resilient sectors saw their median P/E rise modestly from approximately 18x on January 1 to 19x, the victim sectors saw their median P/E jump from about 14x to 18x over the same period. The author notes that while the performance of the resilient sectors makes sense, the rapid valuation recovery in the harder-hit victim sectors suggests that investors, faced with decimated cash and bond yields, are aggressively pricing in an overly rapid economic recovery to chase any available return.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication counsels realism regarding the timelines for a COVID-19 vaccine, particularly hopes for an early 2021 rollout. Cembalest emphasizes that many widely reported vaccine candidates rely on novel methodologies that have never been approved for use in developed markets like the United States or Europe, which raises the bar for successful Phase III trials and regulatory approvals. 

To illustrate these challenges, the author provides a table classifying five distinct vaccine development methods along with select candidate developers. Type one involves a live but weakened virus. Type two uses a killed virus, with Sinovac and Dynavax listed as representative candidates. Type three involves using an engineered different virus, such as an adenovirus, to deliver genetic components for spike proteins; candidates in this category include CanSino, Oxford, J&J, and Merck with Themis. A footnote details that no adenoviral vector vaccine has yet demonstrated disease prevention in humans, noting that while China approved one for Ebola, Phase II trials did not prove infection prevention. Type four uses DNA or RNA to prompt cells to make proteins, represented by Moderna, Inovio, and BioNTech with Pfizer; the table notes that no DNA or RNA vaccines have ever been approved or previously tested in large-scale clinical trials. Type five uses industrially produced coronavirus proteins, a method pursued by GlaxoSmithKline, Sanofi, and Novavax. 

Furthermore, Cembalest points out that vaccine approval standards are high because the infection mortality rate for COVID-19 is relatively low, estimated at 0.6% to 1.0%. He references a controversial, lower CDC estimate of 0.4% that was heavily criticized as scientifically inaccurate and potentially politicized by researchers at Harvard, Berkeley, and the University of Washington.

Michael Cembalest argues that globalization is highly resilient and difficult to dismantle, primarily because the financial benefits of offshoring are often misunderstood. While S&P 500 manufacturer profit margins have climbed significantly since the early 2000s, only a small portion is driven by offshoring labor cost savings. A line chart tracking market cap-weighted net profit margins for S&P 500 manufacturers reveals that margins crashed from over 12% in 2000 to a low of nearly 3% in 2002, before embarking on a long-term upward trend to peak near 18% by late 2019. An accompanying pie chart illustrates the drivers of this growth between 2000 and 2019. It reveals that only 20% of the margin expansion was driven by wage savings from offshoring. The remaining drivers consist of wage savings from more efficient domestic plants, the use of tax havens, declines in developed world effective tax rates, and declining interest rates. This suggests that a partial reversal of globalization would have a smaller impact on corporate profit margins than commonly assumed.

Furthermore, much of the offshore production by US multinationals is designed to meet local demand rather than to be imported back to the United States. A stacked bar chart of US multinationals' foreign affiliates' sales across manufacturers, capital goods, computer and electronics, and pharmaceuticals shows that host-country sales make up the largest share of revenue, with US-bound sales remaining minimal. 

This dynamic is particularly critical in the context of US-China trade relations. A line chart plotting the US trade exposure to China from 2003 to 2017 compares the officially reported US-China trade balance against a broader measure that includes the in-country sales of US subsidiaries operating within China. While the officially reported US-China trade deficit worsened from negative 120 billion dollars in 2003 to roughly negative 330 billion dollars in 2017, the adjusted balance factoring in US subsidiary sales stayed close to flat, ending near zero in 2017. This indicates that US multinational sales inside China are nearly as large as the trade deficit itself, granting China massive retaliatory leverage against US business interests. Consequently, proposed Trump administration measures—such as banning Chinese ADRs, restricting Huawei's access to semiconductor designs, or restricting student visas—may have more bark than bite, ensuring the globalization of profit margins persists.

This page analyzes Sweden's controversial and unorthodox COVID-19 strategy during the early months of the pandemic, arguing that its policy choices were driven more by constitutional constraints and public policy history than by epidemiological evidence. The author highlights that Sweden performed significantly fewer COVID-19 tests per million people (27,000) compared to its Nordic neighbors—Finland (35,000), Norway (47,000), and Denmark (97,000)—which makes its comparatively poor public health metrics even more striking. 

Two charts illustrate this disparity over a 100-day period following each nation's 100th reported case. The first chart, depicting new daily infections per million people on a linear scale with a three-day trailing average, shows Sweden's infection rate spiking wildly up to approximately 140 infections per million near day 90, whereas Denmark, Finland, and Norway all remained consistently low, generally below 20 infections per million after day 40. The second chart, tracking the case fatality rate on a one-day trailing average, reveals Sweden's cumulative death rate peaking near 12% around day 70 and remaining above 10% by day 100, while Denmark and Finland plateaued around 4% to 5%, and Norway remained below 3%. 

The text explains that despite domestic academic criticism and rising infection rates, Sweden maintained a lax policy stance, illustrated by its maximum Oxford Stringency Index score of 58 compared to scores of 76 to 85 among its neighbors. The author attributes this rigid policy adherence to Sweden's "epistocracy," a system where appointed experts dictate policy independently of political interference, coupled with a constitutional lack of peacetime emergency powers to restrict personal mobility. Consequently, the author concludes that Sweden's policy trajectory was path-dependent, locked in by its historical and legal frameworks rather than responsive to ongoing public health data.

This page analyzes the steep cost and physical challenges of electrifying the industrial sector, which is the largest consumer of fossil fuels. The central argument is that industrial electrification is heavily constrained because electricity is three to six times more expensive than direct natural gas combustion on a per-megajoule basis for industrial users. This price gap is detailed in a bar chart comparing electricity-to-gas price ratios across major industrial states and nations. In California and Germany, for example, electricity is over five times more expensive than natural gas, while in Texas it is over five times, and in China, it is more than three times more expensive. This economic hurdle could be partially mitigated by carbon taxes or efficiency gains, but full electrification remains highly expensive.

Beyond costs, physical limitations present major obstacles. Many processes utilize combustion waste heat through combined heat and power systems, meaning electrification would force producers to buy energy they previously captured for free. Furthermore, non-metallic, non-conductive solids like glass, brick, and cement require temperatures exceeding 1400 degrees Celsius, which are difficult to achieve with electric heating. A table outlining sectors with high electrification potential illustrates these steep thermal demands; primary metals require temperatures of 1200 degrees Celsius (with 75 percent of fuel consumed as process heat), and secondary steel requires temperatures between 1425 and 1540 degrees Celsius (with 87 percent consumed as process heat). 

The author also highlights the "four pillars of modern society"—steel, cement, ammonia, and plastics—which rely on fossil fuels not only for high-temperature process heat but also as essential raw material feedstocks. For instance, metallurgical coke is needed to smelt iron into steel, methane is used to synthesize ammonia for fertilizers, and methane, naphtha, and ethane serve as monomer sources for plastics. 

Finally, a production table provides historical data and forecasts showing that global demand for these four pillars is projected to continue growing through 2050, albeit at a slower rate than during China's rapid industrialization era. Between 2018 and 2050, global steel production is projected to rise from 1,817 to 2,170 million tonnes; cement is expected to grow from 4,100 to 4,682 million tonnes; ammonia is forecast to increase from 171 to 281 million tonnes; and plastics are projected to more than double from 359 million tonnes to 818 million tonnes, driven by a 2.6 percent compound annual growth rate.

This section of the J.P. Morgan Annual Energy Paper addresses the challenges of grid de-carbonization proposals that rely on over-building wind and solar combined with energy storage to retire natural gas peaker plants. The author argues that utility-scale electrochemical battery storage is still in its infancy and faces significant deployment hurdles. 

To illustrate the current state of energy storage, a bar chart titled "Only 1% of US electricity generation is stored, and most storage is via decades-old pumped hydro storage" shows that in 2019, 99% of US electricity generation was immediately consumed, with only 1% stored. Of the existing US storage capacity, a staggering 94% consists of pumped hydro, while other methods—including batteries, thermal, compressed air, and flywheels—make up just 6%. Below the text, an aerial photograph of the Seneca pumped storage and hydroelectric facility in Warren County, Pennsylvania, visualizes the scale of this dominant, decades-old pumped hydro technology.

A second chart, "Much larger storage buildout needed to reduce peaker plant usage," measures electricity in terawatt-hours (TWh) to compare current storage dispatch against peaker plant output. The chart shows that electricity generated, stored, and then consumed later is a tiny fraction (around 25 TWh) compared to the massive generation from peaker plants, which stands at over 250 TWh. Because peaker plant generation is roughly ten times larger than currently stored-and-dispatched electricity, a massive storage buildout would be required to displace these gas plants. 

Finally, the author critiques "hockey stick" growth forecasts for electrochemical battery deployment, drawing a parallel to overly optimistic electric vehicle forecasts from a decade prior. He warns that battery storage forecasts are likely too high due to complex utility reimbursement and cost recovery regulations.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, argues that while reforestation and afforestation are helpful, their potential to offset US greenhouse gas emissions is often overestimated. US forests currently cover roughly 750 million acres—about one-third of the country's land area—and have remained relatively stable for the past century, offsetting about 10 percent of annual US emissions. The author explains that to offset an additional 5 percent of emissions, the US would need to plant 130 million acres of forest, returning forested land area to its 1850 level. Doing so would be an enormous undertaking because current USDA reforestation efforts are three orders of magnitude smaller, and substantial reforestation is already required just to counter the effects of aging forests, wildfire emissions, and hurricanes.

Four charts support this analysis. The first chart, illustrating US forest carbon sinks against annual greenhouse gas emissions from 1990 to 2014, shows that the carbon sink from forests and land use changes remains a flat, minor offset of around negative 700 to 800 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent per year, compared to total emissions that hover between 6,000 and 7,000 million metric tons. 

The second chart tracks US forest area and population trends from 1850 to 2010. It shows that while the US population rose from near zero to over 300 million, forest area declined sharply from over 900 million acres in 1850 to a low of nearly 730 million acres around 1920, before stabilizing near 750 million acres. 

The third chart depicts the annual millions of acres burned by wildfires in the US from 1989 to 2019. The data shows a volatile but rising trend, with several years in the 2000s and 2010s seeing between 8 million and 10 million acres burned, which releases significant amounts of CO2 back into the atmosphere.

The final chart shows total USDA reforestation per year in thousands of acres from 2004 to 2019. Reforestation peaked in 2006 at over 200,000 acres but has since experienced a downward trend, falling to approximately 100,000 acres by 2019. This visual highlights the immense gap between current federal reforestation rates and the scale of planting required to achieve meaningful additional carbon sequestration.

This page addresses why primary steel production is extremely carbon-intensive and evaluates the practical challenges of decarbonizing the sector. The author highlights that the two main drivers of carbon emissions in integrated steel-making are the conversion of coking coal into coke and the subsequent blast furnace iron-making process. 

To support this, a table titled "CO2 emissions, integrated steel-making" lists the kilograms of CO2 emissions per tonne of steel produced across different stages: coal and coking accounts for 990 kilograms, blast furnaces for 610 kilograms, basic oxygen furnaces for 85 kilograms, and iron ore sintering for 15 kilograms, resulting in a substantial total of 1,700 kilograms of CO2 per tonne of steel. 

An accompanying chart, "Iron/steel production: energy usage and intensity," tracks global data from 2000 to 2015. The chart's left axis shows energy intensity in gigajoules per tonne, which hovered between 18 and 21, indicating little change over the years despite Sweden producing steel more efficiently at 16 gigajoules per tonne compared to China's 20 gigajoules per tonne. The right axis shows overall energy usage rising from under 20 exajoules in 2000 to nearly 35 exajoules by 2015, heavily dominated by coal, with gas, electricity, and other sources playing much smaller roles.

The page then examines the prospects of hydrogen-based direct reduction for steelmaking, focusing on an initiative by ArcelorMittal. The author expresses skepticism regarding near-term solutions, pointing out that ArcelorMittal's demonstration plant has an initial planned output of 100,000 tonnes, which is a mere 0.01 percent of the 1.8 billion tonnes produced globally in 2018. Furthermore, the company initially plans to use hydrogen sourced from fossil-fuel steam methane reformation for economical operation, rather than green hydrogen. 

Finally, the author critiques a forecast by Bloomberg New Energy Finance suggesting that half of global steel could be produced via green hydrogen by 2050. Citing a Swedish steel industry expert, the author describes this target as highly implausible due to the 50-plus-year lifespan of existing blast furnaces and the decades required to build new hydrogen reduction infrastructure from scratch. Illustrating this slow transition timeline, Sweden is currently working on a demonstration plant to master the chemistry of iron ore reduction and is only targeting full operation by 2045.

This page addresses the environmental impact of ride-hailing services, arguing that they lead to a substantial net increase in vehicle miles traveled and greenhouse gas emissions, potentially by 60% to 80% compared to a world without ride-sharing. A primary driver of this increase is dead-heading, which refers to the miles drivers travel while waiting for passengers or commuting. 

Four charts illustrate these trends. The first chart, depicting US ride-hailing and taxi ridership, shows annual ridership in billions from 1990 to 2018. While taxi ridership remained stable at around 1 billion rides annually from 1990 to 2012, the introduction of ride-hailing pushed total annual ridership to nearly 4 billion by 2018, with ride-hailing services accounting for more than 3 billion of those rides. The second chart details the volume of rides in New York City in millions of trips from 2010 to 2018. It illustrates the dramatic displacement of yellow cabs, whose annual trips fell from around 175 million in 2010 to under 100 million in 2018, while total trips expanded to nearly 350 million, driven predominantly by the rise of Uber and Lyft.

The third chart focuses on ride-hailing emissions, measured in grams of CO2 equivalent per trip-mile. A typical ride-hailing trip produces nearly 600 grams of CO2 equivalent, which is 69% more emissions than the displaced trip it replaces. An electric ride-hailing trip with 50% pooling can achieve 52% lower emissions than a displaced trip, reducing emissions to approximately 150 grams per trip-mile. However, footnotes highlight the difficulty of reaching this ideal, noting that in California in 2018, only 1% of ride-hailing vehicles were electric, and only 15% of trips were pooled. 

The fourth chart compares total vehicle miles traveled by ride-hailing services against the displaced choices of transportation. It demonstrates that ride-hailing often replaces environmentally friendly choices. For instance, ride-hailing generated approximately 800 million miles of travel that replaced public transportation, and nearly 500 million miles of travel from people who otherwise would not have traveled at all. Even when replacing private travel, such as driving alone, ride-hailing generates more vehicle miles traveled (approximately 900 million miles) than the displaced drive alone option (around 700 million miles) due to dead-heading. 

Ultimately, the author notes that while entities like California and the City of Chicago have begun implementing penalties and incentives to encourage electrification, rider pooling, and mass transit, the convenience of personalized ride-hailing remains difficult to dislodge.

This page discusses whether the "stranded asset" theory is the primary driver of underperforming oil and gas stock prices, or if poor industry cash flows and a supply glut are more plausible explanations. The author notes that if BP's "evolving transition" base case holds—wherein global oil consumption remains flat through 2040 due to growth in emerging economies offset by energy efficiency and a fifteen percent global electric vehicle penetration rate—it is too early for stranded asset concerns to dictate stock prices. Highlighting investor confidence in persistent demand, a footnote mentions Berkshire Hathaway's ten billion dollar investment in Occidental Petroleum to support its acquisition of Anadarko. 

A line chart illustrating global oil use with BP projections to 2040 in million barrels per day shows historical demand steadily climbing toward one hundred million barrels per day by 2019. From 2020 onward, the chart plots three possible paths: "Greater emerging country energy demand," which rises past one hundred twenty million barrels per day; the flat "Evolving transition" base case near one hundred million barrels per day; and a "Rapid transition" scenario where demand declines to around seventy million barrels per day by 2040.

To evaluate what could substantiate the stranded asset theory, the author compares two International Energy Agency scenarios in a set of tables measuring quantities in million tons of oil equivalent. Under the Stated Policies Scenario, which assumes currently announced policy intentions, cumulative extraction between 2019 and 2070 exceeds 2018 proven reserves for both oil and natural gas. Consequently, zero percent of oil and natural gas reserves are stranded, while sixty-seven percent of coal reserves—amounting to three hundred ninety-eight thousand six hundred fifty million tons—become stranded. 

Conversely, the Sustainable Development Scenario, designed to limit global warming to one point eight degrees Celsius, projects substantial stranded asset risks. In this scenario, cumulative extraction is sharply curtailed, resulting in forty-two percent of oil reserves being stranded (ninety-eight thousand four hundred fifty-four million tons out of two hundred thirty-five thousand nine hundred thirty-one million tons of proven reserves), twenty-six percent of natural gas reserves being stranded (forty-four thousand seventy-five million tons out of one hundred sixty-nine thousand three hundred thirty-four million tons of proven reserves), and eighty-seven percent of coal reserves being stranded (five hundred eighteen thousand nine hundred eighty million tons out of five hundred ninety-six thousand five hundred forty million tons of proven reserves). A footnote adds that J.P. Morgan European Equity Research estimates actual proven reserves could be roughly half of BP's estimates when applying stricter commercial return thresholds and carbon density distinctions.

This page focuses on the environmental pressures of hydraulic fracturing, specifically examining the industry's rising water requirements. The author notes that fractured wells require eight to ten times more water than conventionally drilled wells. While overall water demand peaked in 2014 and declined only modestly through 2016, this demand is driven by both the number of wells and a 20% to 30% increase in the lateral length of wells from 2011 to 2016. 

To illustrate these trends, the page features two stacked bar charts comparing the years 2012 through 2016 across major US shale oil and gas basins, including the Permian, Marcellus, Haynesville, Eagle Ford, Niobrara, and Bakken. The first chart, tracking water use in millions of cubic meters, shows that total water consumption peaked in 2014 at around 225 million cubic meters and remained high in 2016 at roughly 210 million cubic meters. In contrast, the second chart, showing the number of new wells drilled in thousands, reveals that well starts peaked in 2014 at over 12,000 but fell sharply to around 7,000 by 2016. This divergence highlights that water demand remained elevated despite a drop in drilling activity.

To control for the changing number and physical dimensions of wells, the author introduces "liters of water per gigajoule of energy" as the preferred measure of water intensity. Two line charts track this metric from 2011 to 2016 during the first 12 months of well production. The first line chart, focusing on shale oil, shows rising water intensity across all basins; the Permian Basin experienced the sharpest increase, rising from approximately 20 to nearly 50 Liters/GJ, while Eagle Ford and Niobrara climbed to nearly 40 Liters/GJ, and Bakken rose more modestly to just over 20 Liters/GJ. The second line chart, focusing on shale gas, shows a dramatic surge in the Permian Basin after 2014, spikes to over 50 Liters/GJ by 2016. Eagle Ford gas wells rose to around 25 Liters/GJ, while the Marcellus and Haynesville basins remained relatively stable and low, fluctuating between 10 and 15 Liters/GJ.

The page concludes with a discussion of the broader environmental context of natural gas extraction. Although switching from coal to natural gas for electricity generation from 2013 to 2016 reduced water consumption by 1 cubic meter and water withdrawal by 40 cubic meters per megawatt-hour, roughly 50% of natural gas extraction still occurs in water-stressed areas. Additionally, the toxicity of produced water from fracking is described as comparable to the toxic acidic drainage from abandoned coal mines and the heavy metal and radioactive contamination risk posed by coal ash ponds leaching into groundwater.

This page, titled "Maiming the Swamp: Trump and the Environment," presents a detailed status report of forty-two distinct environmental regulatory rollbacks under the Trump administration. The visual presentation consists of a grid of forty-two policy changes, color-coded to distinguish between those implemented as of January 2020, shown in white boxes, and those pending implementation, shown in shaded gray boxes.

The implemented policies, represented by the white boxes, span multiple sectors including energy, chemical safety, and wildlife preservation. Key implemented actions include the elimination of methane reporting requirements for oil and gas companies, the revocation of California's authority to establish its own vehicle emissions limits, and the lifting of the oil and gas drilling ban in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. Other significant implemented rollbacks consist of rescinding water pollution rules for fracking on federal lands, rejecting a ban on pesticides linked to childhood developmental problems, and reversing a rule requiring braking system upgrades for trains hauling flammable liquids.

The shaded gray boxes detail pending regulatory rollbacks that further target environmental and consumer standards. These pending actions include weakening fuel economy standards for passenger vehicles, eliminating carbon capture requirements for new coal plants, weakening the Endangered Species Act, and doubling the time allowed to remove lead pipes from high-lead water systems. Additionally, pending items include relaxing mercury emission standards for coal plants, limiting EPA research that relies on confidential patient data, and scaling back energy-efficiency requirements for residential furnaces, water heaters, and light bulbs.

Sources for this comprehensive tracker include environmental law centers at Harvard and Columbia, the Brookings Institution, the Federal Register, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Department of the Interior, the US Chamber of Commerce, the New York Times, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page addresses the paradox of the ongoing economic recovery in the United States despite the country experiencing a massive surge in COVID-19 infections. Among the 50 largest nations by GDP, the US ranks third in infection rates, and it ranks second behind Brazil when sorted by population. The author poses the critical question of whether this infection surge will derail the economic recovery, noting that state-level countermeasures—such as closing gyms, bars, and limiting indoor dining—have been mild compared to previous lockdown measures.

Two charts provide data on infection rates to contextualize this situation. The first chart displays infection levels for the 50 largest GDP countries, comparing their peak infection rates per million people against their latest rates using a trailing 7-day average. The US and Brazil stand out at the top of the list, both operating at 0% reduction from their peak rates of approximately 175 infections per million people. In contrast, other hard-hit nations have seen significant declines, such as Chile, which is down 67% from a peak of over 200 infections per million. European nations like France, Germany, Italy, and Spain, along with Asian nations like China and South Korea, show infection rates down 90% to 100% from their peaks.

The second chart tracks the progression of new daily infections per million people over time, starting from the day each region reached 100 total cases. It compares highly infected areas—Brazil, the United States, South Africa, Sweden, and Mexico—with Europe and Hubei, China. The trajectories reveal a stark divergence. Brazil and South Africa show steep, late-stage rises, with Brazil nearing 180 cases per million by day 120 and South Africa climbing past 140. The United States exhibits a double-wave pattern: an initial peak of around 100 cases per million near day 40, followed by a decline and a subsequent, sharper surge past 140 cases per million by day 120. Sweden's curve peaked near 130 cases per million before turning downward, and Mexico shows a gradual upward slope reaching about 50 cases. Meanwhile, the lines for Europe and Hubei remain completely flat and near zero, illustrating successful virus suppression compared to the resurgent or unchecked outbreaks in the other featured nations.

This appendix page presents three detailed tables compiling key energy and electricity statistics by country and region, sourcing data from JPMAM and the US Energy Information Agency's 2019 International Energy Outlook. The tables cover global and regional metrics for the World, US, OECD, OECD Europe, Japan, Canada, Non-OECD, China, India, Brazil, the Middle East, and Russia. 

The first table, focused on electricity, details primary energy used for electricity and actual electricity consumed, which accounts for thermal conversion, plant energy consumption, and transmission losses. It also measures electricity's share of primary and consumed energy, alongside the renewable share of primary energy used for electricity.
