Globally, 248.4 quad BTUs of primary energy are used to generate 80.3 quad BTUs of consumed electricity, representing a 13% share of primary energy and 18% of consumed energy, with renewables accounting for 31% of the primary energy used for electricity. On a regional level, Canada and Brazil stand out for their high renewable shares of primary energy used for electricity at 75% and 88%, respectively, while the Middle East is the lowest at 9%. 

The second table breaks down primary and delivered energy across total primary energy, total consumed energy, industrial sector consumption, transport sector consumption, and the renewable share of consumed energy. Globally, total primary energy stands at 627.0 quad BTUs, with 453.5 quad BTUs consumed, where 238.7 quad BTUs go to the industrial sector and 122.4 quad BTUs go to the transport sector, resulting in renewables making up an 11% share of consumed energy. Regionally, China leads total primary energy consumption at 152.7 quad BTUs, with a heavily industrial footprint of 70.6 quad BTUs compared to only 15.5 quad BTUs in transportation. Brazil showcases the highest renewable share of consumed energy at 36%, while the Middle East records the lowest at just 1%. 

The third table examines the role of fossil fuels, specifying their share in electricity generation and primary energy, as well as the portion of fossil fuels used directly for electricity. Globally, fossil fuels make up 57% of electricity generation, 80% of primary energy, and 29% of fossil fuels are used for electricity. The Middle East relies most heavily on fossil fuels, which represent 90% of electricity generation and 97% of primary energy. In contrast, Brazil and Canada demonstrate remarkably low fossil fuel reliance for electricity generation, at 9% and 11% respectively, reflecting their high adoption of alternative power sources.

In this report, Michael Cembalest argues that the global economic recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic is progressing rapidly, clawing back approximately half of the initial 17 percent contraction in global GDP observed between January and April 2020. This positive momentum is evidenced by rising global manufacturing and service sector business surveys and a stronger-than-expected US employment report, which saw the addition of nearly five million private-sector jobs and a drop in the unemployment rate to 11 percent from its peak of 16 percent. Cembalest also highlights that corporate profits can grow during post-recession periods through aggressive expense management—a concept known as operating leverage—even before top-line revenue recovers.

The first line chart, titled "Estimated virus impact on global GDP," traces the estimated percentage impact to global GDP from February 7 to June 26, 2020. It illustrates a sharp downward plunge starting in early March, bottoming out at around negative 17 percent in mid-April, followed by a steady recovery that climbs back to about negative 8 percent by late June. 

The second chart, "Regional manufacturing & services business surveys," plots monthly purchasing managers' index (PMI) data from September to June for China, the Eurozone, the United States, and Asia excluding China, using a threshold of 50 to denote economic expansion. The visual shows China plunging first to nearly 25 in February before bouncing back above 50. The other regions experienced their troughs in April, with the Eurozone dropping most severely to below 20, followed by sharp V-shaped recoveries for all regions heading back toward or above the expansion line by June.

The third chart, "Leisure and hospitality: changes in spending and employment," compares J.P. Morgan's internal Chase card spending data with Bureau of Labor Statistics employment data from March 1 to June 29, 2020. Both data series bottomed out in mid-to-late April, with restaurant, hotel, and travel spending plummeting nearly 80 percent compared to 2019 levels, and total employment dropping about 50 percent compared to February 2020. By June 29, spending had recovered to negative 45 percent and employment improved to negative 25 percent, demonstrating that job recovery in these sectors has closely mirrored credit and debit card spending.

The final bar chart, "Contribution to S&P 500 profits from operating leverage after recessions and other market declines," breaks down the year-over-year percentage change in operating EPS growth into contributions from operating leverage and sales. Examining quarterly data across five historic recovery periods—the post-Savings and Loan crisis (1993), the post-Long-Term Capital Management crisis (1999), the post-tech bubble (2002), the post-Global Financial Crisis (2010), and the post-emerging markets and oil collapse (2016–2017)—the chart demonstrates that cost-cutting and operating leverage consistently act as the primary engines of earnings-per-share growth during early recovery phases, often while top-line sales contributions remain flat or negative.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market analysis discusses the shifting dynamics of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States during the summer of 2020, focusing on the trend of rising infections and hospitalizations even as death rates remained low. The author, Michael Cembalest, notes that while hospitalizations are starting to catch up to the rising infection numbers, daily deaths have continued to fall. He attributes this divergence to improved medical interventions, such as anti-coagulants and corticosteroids, though he cautions that time lags could still play a role. He also explores the theory that younger, less vulnerable cohorts are driving the new wave of infections. Despite lower mortality rates among the youth, the author warns of serious, lingering health consequences for survivors of all ages, including lung scarring, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, neurocognitive issues, and abnormal blood clotting.

The analysis is supported by three charts. The first chart, showing seven-day averages for US infections, hospitalizations, and deaths from mid-March to mid-July 2020, utilizes two axes. The left-hand scale measures current hospitalizations and new daily infections up to 70,000, showing a dramatic rise in new daily infections starting in June, with current hospitalizations beginning to curve upward shortly after. The right-hand scale tracks daily deaths up to 2,500, showing a steady decline from the April peak, save for a temporary statistical spike in late June caused by a one-time addition of probable deaths in New York and New Jersey. 

The second chart focuses on the same metrics within specific hotspot states, including North Carolina, Arkansas, Utah, California, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Nevada, and Louisiana. From late March to early July, daily infections on the left-hand scale surged to over 35,000, with current hospitalizations following a very similar sharp upward trajectory starting in June. Conversely, daily deaths, measured on the right-hand scale up to 350, remained relatively flat. 

The third chart investigates the demographics of the virus spread using data from the Vanderbilt School of Medicine for Tennessee from March to June 2020. It plots the trend of new cases against an age-adjusted Case Mix Index, which acts as a proxy for COVID risk. The chart shows that while new cases began climbing steadily in May, the Case Mix Index declined, indicating that the virus was increasingly infecting a younger and less clinically vulnerable demographic in that state. The author notes that while this supports the "younger infection age" theory, the lack of regular age distribution disclosures from most other states makes it difficult to confirm this trend nationwide.

This page consists entirely of standard legal disclaimers and regional regulatory disclosures concluding the publication. It outlines the compliance terms and supervising authorities for J.P. Morgan entities across various global jurisdictions, including Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America, specifically noting restrictions for private clients and distribution rules under local securities laws.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, titled "Blinded by Science: the American scientific trust gap," explores the cultural and behavioral factors driving the uniquely severe surge of COVID-19 in the United States. The author argues that despite the United States leading the world in medical patents and hosting twenty-two of the top forty clinical research universities, its citizens demonstrate an exceptionally low level of interest and trust in science compared to the rest of the world. This distrust is further compounded by a highly individualistic culture—with the US ranking highest globally on the Geert-Hofstede individualism dimension—and was exacerbated by the Trump administration's marginalization of science, as highlighted by a bipartisan group of fifty-seven former government scientists. Additionally, the author references pandemic simulations by educator Grant Sanderson of 3Blue1Brown, which show that even a small minority of non-compliant individuals can disproportionately accelerate viral transmission, explaining why American skepticism has had such a devastating impact.

A column chart titled "How Americans rank globally on trust in science, medicine and vaccines" illustrates this gap using 2018 data from the Wellcome Trust/Gallup Global Science and Health Monitor across 144 countries. The vertical axis measures the US percentile rank from zero to one hundred percent, showing that the US consistently ranks in the bottom half of all nations surveyed. Specifically, for the desire to know more about science, the US ranks at roughly the 38th percentile. Trust in the national government and government health advice are particularly low, landing at approximately the 24th and 25th percentiles, respectively. Trust in corporate scientists to benefit the public ranks around the 33rd percentile. Regarding vaccines, US agreement that they are important for children ranks at about the 33rd percentile, agreement that they are safe ranks at about the 34th percentile, and the self-reported vaccination rate for children stands at roughly the 33rd percentile. Collectively, these statistics underscore the profound scientific trust deficit that hindered the US response to the pandemic relative to other developed nations.

This page is an energy paper client Q&A titled "What about..." in which Michael Cembalest addresses three follow-up questions from readers of J.P. Morgan's tenth annual energy paper. 

In the first section, Cembalest discusses low energy nuclear reactors (LENR) that theoretically convert hydrogen to helium to produce heat without radiation. He explains that LENR does not yet meet the J.P. Morgan standard of having reached early-stage commercialization, unlike deep geothermal in Iceland or utility-scale lithium-ion battery storage. While the author notes that commercial applications for space heating at temperatures up to 200 degrees Celsius might emerge in the next 5 to 10 years, he highlights deep skepticism, citing a May 2019 study by Google, MIT, the University of British Columbia, the University of Maryland, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory that failed to find evidence of fusion or heat.

Next, the author addresses renewable natural gas (RNG) made from landfills and agricultural waste. Current US volumes are 200 to 300 million gallons per year, with Platts and NREL estimating maximum potential limits between 2.9 and 4.8 billion gasoline gallon equivalents (GGE) per year. This potential maximum represents only about 2.5 percent of the 142 billion gallons of US motor gasoline consumed in 2019, meaning RNG is not a transformative energy solution, though it could still support new industry entrants. Cembalest also mentions Germany's use of waste-to-energy biogas, which produces electricity at a relatively high cost of nearly 20 cents per kilowatt-hour, compared to just 9 cents for onshore wind, due in part to the energy-intensive process of gathering waste over large areas.

Finally, the page explores the feasibility of electrifying global container ships. Cembalest compares a small, first-generation electric container ship with Maersk's massive Triple-E class vessels, which carry 150 times more cargo, travel 400 times further, and sail three to four times faster. Using current state-of-the-art batteries with energy densities of 300 Wh/kg, an electric Maersk-sized vessel would have to dedicate 40 percent of its cargo capacity to batteries. To keep battery and motor weight equivalent to today's diesel engines and fuel, battery energy densities would need to improve tenfold, which is highly unlikely given that commercial battery densities have not even quadrupled over the past 70 years.

This page from Michael Cembalest's "Eye on the Market" explores the drivers behind the mid-2020 surge in US COVID-19 infections, challenging the assumptions that the spike was simply due to increased testing or changes in public mobility. 

To debunk the argument that the surge in infections is a mere artifact of more testing, the author presents two side-by-side line charts tracking data relative to the number of days after a state's total reported cases reached one hundred. The first chart, "US new daily infections per mm people," shows that a designated group of hotspot states—including North Carolina, Arkansas, Utah, California, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Nevada, and Louisiana—saw daily infections soar toward 250 per million people by day 100, while "Other States" remained flat and under 50. Meanwhile, the second chart, "US daily tests per mm people," shows that testing rates in these hotspots were not substantially different from "Other States," rising to roughly 2,200 and 1,700 daily tests per million people respectively. This minor difference in testing volume cannot account for the massive divergence in infection rates. For comparison, the early-outbreak states of New York and New Jersey saw infections spike and then plummet as their daily testing rates climbed past 3,000 per million.

The author also argues that mobility levels and reopening dates do not consistently predict infections, either globally or domestically. A line chart titled "Country mobility changes do not predict infections" tracks mobility across retail, restaurant, transit, and workplace categories from February to late June 2020. Despite experiencing similar deep mobility declines, the United States ended up with a massive infection rate of 146.5 new daily infections per million people (IPM), whereas Japan, Germany, Thailand, and Italy maintained extremely low rates ranging from 0.1 to 4.8 IPM. 

Domestically, a scatter plot titled "US mobility changes only partially explain infection rise" maps the change in recent infections per million people against peak declines in mobility. The data reveals that even among states with similar peak mobility declines of -50% to -60%, hotspot states like Georgia, Florida, Arizona, and South Carolina saw infection increases of 300 to over 500 per million, while non-hotspot states at the same mobility levels saw virtually no change. 

In terms of economic outlook, the author suggests that if falling death rates remain the primary barometer for state governments to stay open with only mild restrictions, the US economy and equity markets may continue to rise gradually through the summer. Cembalest identifies the upcoming US presidential election and the potential market consequences of a Democratic Sweep in the fall as the next major litmus test, noting that J.P. Morgan's future virus research will focus on analyzing deaths relative to rising infections and hospitalizations.

This page analyzes coronavirus tracking dynamics in mid-2020, focusing on how ramping up testing capacity helps suppress positivity rates and questioning the consistency of reported infection data across Sub-Saharan Africa. 

The first chart, titled "Italy virus tracking," plots the positive testing rate on the left axis against total daily tests in thousands on the right axis from late February through late June 2020. The data shows Italy’s positive testing rate, represented by a gold line, peaking at approximately 25% in late March. As daily testing (the blue line) surged from near zero to around 50,000 by late April, the positivity rate steadily fell, eventually stabilizing below 2% by late June when daily tests hovered around 30,000. 

Mirroring this trend, the second chart, "New York virus tracking," illustrates a similar containment strategy from early April to mid-July 2020. New York's positive testing rate plummeted from a peak of nearly 45% down to under 2% as the state successfully scaled up its daily testing volume from 20,000 to over 60,000 tests. The author highlights that New York adopted the same approach as Italy and states an expectation that other U.S. states will follow this trajectory.

The final chart, "New daily infections per mm people [Africa]," tracks the seven-day trailing average of new infections against the number of days since total cases in each country reached 100. It compares South Africa, Ghana, Kenya, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Mozambique, Angola, and Tanzania. The chart reveals a dramatic divergence: South Africa’s curve rises exponentially, exceeding 200 new daily cases per million people by day 100, while the curves for all other compared African nations remain flat near the bottom axis. The author expresses skepticism regarding this data, doubting that the true rates of infection in South Africa differ so significantly from other sub-Saharan African countries, which points to a likely underreporting or testing deficit in the rest of the region.

This J.P. Morgan publication presents a set of COVID-19 charts and commentary detailing trends in US hotspot states, the infection gap between the United States and other developed nations, and state-level epidemiological trajectories. The author, Michael Cembalest, begins by noting that infections in US hotspot states have rolled over and that doctor visits for COVID-like symptoms have declined, signaling further infection decreases ahead. He also shares a political anecdote involving Republican Representative Liz Cheney and NIAID Director Dr. Anthony Fauci, suggesting that political divisions in the US may be a primary driver behind the country's infection gap with the rest of the developed world. 

These trends are illustrated in two side-by-side charts. The left chart, titled "Hotspots: rollover in infections and COVID symptoms," covers hotspot states such as South Carolina, Arkansas, Florida, North Carolina, Nevada, Utah, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia, and Idaho from April 1 to July 30. It plots the daily number of doctor visits with COVID-like symptoms on the left axis against the percentage of new daily infections on the right axis. Doctor visits peaked near 40,000 in early July before falling sharply to under 30,000, while new daily infections peaked at just over 10% in mid-July before beginning to roll over. The right chart, titled "The US infection gap," compares the 7-day average of new daily infections per million people in the US against peer nations, including Australia, France, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, and South Korea, indexed by the number of days after total cases reached 100. While peer nations successfully suppressed daily infections to near zero by day 150, the US line surges late in the timeline, peaking above 200 new daily infections per million people.

Lastly, the page examines state-level virus trajectories using a three-factor test from J.P. Morgan's Technical Strategy group. To achieve a positive trajectory, a state must demonstrate cumulative case growth under 3%, a testing positivity rate under 10%, and an infection rate under 60% of its peak. The bottom line chart, "US population share with positive epidemiological trajectory," tracks the percentage of the US population meeting this test from March 6 to July 24. After dropping to 0% in March, the share of the population meeting these criteria rose to peak at nearly 50% in mid-June before declining to approximately 25% by late July.

This page focuses on two main topics: a comparison of COVID-19 second-wave transmission rates and mitigation policies between Hong Kong and Western nations, and an analysis of promising Phase I trial results for the Oxford/AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. 

The author begins by analyzing Hong Kong’s second wave of infections, highlighting that despite experiencing lower levels of infection than the West, the Hong Kong government implemented strict mobility restrictions. These policies included delaying school reopenings, limiting dining to take-out only, restricting gatherings to four people, mandating face masks with hefty fines, and enforcing quarantines for foreign arrivals. The author contrasts these aggressive measures with the much more modest restrictions in the United States, a country with an infection rate ten times higher than Hong Kong’s. 

This policy comparison is supported by two line charts plotting new daily infections per million people (7-day average) against the number of days after total reported cases reached 100. The first chart, which focuses on Hong Kong’s second wave alongside regional peers, shows both Hong Kong and Australia rising sharply to peak around 16 daily infections per million near day 150, while Japan rises to about 6, and South Korea and Taiwan remain flat near zero. The second chart places Hong Kong’s wave in a global context on a much larger scale. It reveals that the United States and Israel experienced massive surges peaking near 200 daily infections per million people, with Costa Rica rising past 100 and Romania near 50, illustrating how flat Hong Kong's infection curve remains by comparison.

The second half of the page highlights positive vaccine developments, specifically looking at immunogenicity results from the Oxford/AstraZeneca Phase I trials. The author notes that after a second booster shot administered on Day 28, the vaccine generated antibody response levels similar to those seen in convalescent plasma samples from recovered patients. While this antibody response is a key milestone for progressing to Phase II and III trials, the author cautions that it does not prove durable, long-term immunity, noting that the wide variation in antibody levels reflects the complex nature of human immune responses. 

This analysis is accompanied by a scatter plot showing neutralizing antibody responses measured by IC50 on a log scale ranging from 16 to 16,384. The chart tracks patients at 0, 28, 35, and 42 days since receiving either the Oxford COVID vaccine or a meningitis vaccine placebo, alongside a comparison group of convalescent plasma samples. Prior to the Day 28 booster, Oxford vaccine recipients show modest antibody levels, but by days 35 and 42 post-vaccination, their antibody response levels (marked by red dots) rise significantly, clustering between 128 and 1,024. This range closely mirrors the distribution of the green convalescent plasma samples, while the placebo group shows no neutralizing antibody response.

This page discusses severe emerging market COVID-19 outbreaks, government patent rights, and the nuances of herd immunity research. The author begins by highlighting that Latin America has the most severe reported outbreak among emerging market regions, driven by high infection rates in Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, and Peru. An accompanying line chart plots new daily infections per million people (on a 7-day average) against the number of days after total reported cases reached 100. The data reveals that South America has experienced a massive spike, climbing sharply to over 160 infections per million around day 150. This stands in stark contrast to other emerging market regions like the Middle East, which hovers below 40, Eastern Europe and Africa, which remain below 30, and EM Asia, which tracks lowest of all at under 10 daily cases per million.

The page then addresses legal mechanisms the US Federal Government can use to control pharmaceutical patents. Under "march-in" rights, the government can directly produce or license medications developed with federal funds, which could apply to Gilead's drug Remdesivir. Additionally, under 28 U.S.C. Section 1498, Health and Human Services can seize control of private patents, manufacturing, and distribution with "just compensation." The author notes this section was used as leverage during a 2001 anthrax scare to reduce the price of generic Cipro to under $1 a tablet, and was proposed in 2018 for hepatitis C drugs.

Finally, the author explores herd immunity research. While original estimates for COVID-19 herd immunity were between 60% and 70%, newer models accounting for "heterogeneity in susceptibility"—meaning differences in social interaction intensity across ages and demographics—suggest a lower aggregate national threshold of 43%. However, the author cautions that achieving this aggregate level still requires immunity rates of 70% or higher among younger, more active populations. The author predicts that this lower 43% figure will likely go viral in media and independent research reports without this crucial qualifying context.

This page consists entirely of legal disclosures, regulatory compliance statements, and terms of use for J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market publication. It outlines the data security and confidentiality protocols applied to aggregated Chase credit and debit card transaction data used in the report. Additionally, it details regulatory notices and licensing information for various global jurisdictions, including the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Europe, the Asia Pacific region, Singapore, Taiwan, Japan, and Australia, while emphasizing that the material is intended exclusively for institutional, wholesale, professional, and qualified investors.

This page of the report analyzes the direct relationship between US COVID-19 severity—specifically hospitalizations—and the nation's economic recovery, as measured by consumer spending. Michael Cembalest argues that the economic recovery is tightly bound to public health metrics, noting that as soon as hospitalizations stopped falling, consumer spending stopped rising. 

The top chart illustrates this relationship by plotting the seven-day average of current US hospitalizations against year-over-year changes in in-person credit and debit card spending from March to July 2020. In early April, hospitalizations peaked near 60,000 while card spending hit a trough of nearly negative fifty percent. As hospitalizations steadily declined through mid-June, card spending recovered to around negative fifteen percent. However, once hospitalizations bottomed out around June 17 and began rising back toward 55,000, consumer spending plateaued. The author suggests that if hospitalizations begin to decline again, in-person spending should resume its recovery. 

Two charts at the bottom of the page focus on specific hotspot states, which include South Carolina, Arkansas, Florida, North Carolina, Nevada, Utah, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia, and Idaho. The bottom-left chart tracks new daily infections, current hospitalizations, and daily deaths in these hotspots from April to July 2020. As daily infections surged to nearly 40,000 and hospitalizations climbed past 35,000 by mid-July, daily deaths lagged but eventually rose to approximately 400. Cembalest notes that a recent rollover in infections indicates that hospitalizations and deaths in these regions may soon follow a downward trajectory. 

The bottom-right chart puts this mortality data into perspective by plotting US daily deaths per million people against the number of days after total cases reached one hundred. It compares these hotspot states against other US states and the hard-hit region of New York and New Jersey. While New York and New Jersey experienced an early, massive spike of roughly sixteen daily deaths per million people, other states peaked much lower at around five deaths per million. The hotspot states show a delayed and more gradual increase, reaching approximately four daily deaths per million people around day 135. The author highlights that while mortality in these hotspots is rising, it remains far below the peak levels seen in New York and New Jersey during the initial April surge.

In this issue of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, Michael Cembalest evaluates the public debate between President Donald Trump and Dr. Anthony Fauci regarding COVID-19 testing. While President Trump argued that the high number of virus cases in the United States was merely a reflection of its high testing rate, Cembalest uses data to demonstrate that the high case numbers are actually driven by elevated infection levels. 

The first chart on the page, titled "Total tests to date per million people for the largest 50 countries by GDP," shows that the United States does indeed rank near the top globally for per capita testing. The US ranks fifth, conducting roughly 160,000 to 170,000 tests per million people, trailing only the United Arab Emirates—which leads with more than 250,000 tests per million—Denmark, Russia, and Israel. While the US tests more than peer countries like the United Kingdom, Canada, Germany, and Japan, this high volume does not tell the full story.

To explain why, the second chart, titled "Positive share of tests," plots the positive testing rate as a percentage against the number of days after total reported cases reached 100. The chart reveals that the United States maintains an exceptionally high positive test rate compared to other developed nations. By day 160, the positive testing rate in the US sits near eight percent, whereas a cluster of peer countries including France, Canada, Italy, Germany, South Korea, and the United Kingdom remains flat near or below one percent. Other notable trends on this chart include Sweden, whose positive rate declined sharply from around eight percent down to two percent, and Japan, which shows a late surge approaching five percent by day 160. The author argues that this high positive rate indicates that the US is testing heavily precisely because it has much higher infection levels, rather than its case count being an artificial product of broad testing.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest argues that the higher COVID-19 infection rate in the United States cannot be attributed solely or even primarily to higher testing rates. By modeling what other nations' infection rates would look like if they matched US testing levels—assuming their positive testing shares remained constant—the publication demonstrates that other countries would still maintain much lower infection rates than the United States. Cembalest attributes this disparity to larger initial mobility declines in Europe and greater compliance with social distancing measures, echoing observations made by Dr. Anthony Fauci and other public health officials.

This argument is first illustrated with a bar chart comparing actual and testing-adjusted seven-day average infection rates per million people across various countries in August 2020. The United States exhibits an actual infection rate of approximately 170 per million. In comparison, actual rates in other countries like France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom, South Korea, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Sweden are extremely low, mostly remaining under 20 per million. Even when adjusting these nations' infection rates upward to simulate US-equivalent testing levels, their rates remain significantly lower than the US actual rate. Germany and Italy adjust to only around 15 and 20 per million, respectively, while France rises to about 40 per million. Even Sweden and Japan, which show the highest adjusted rates at roughly 80 and 115 per million, remain well below the actual US infection level.

A second scatter plot reinforces this point by showing that mobility declines in the United States never reached European levels during the initial wave of the pandemic, despite the US experiencing similar or higher peak infection rates. The chart plots the peak percentage decline in mobility—averaging retail, transit, and workplace data—against the peak seven-day average of new daily infections per million people before May 1, 2020. The United States is a clear outlier, experiencing a peak mobility decline of only about 52% despite reaching a peak infection rate of approximately 100 per million. 

In comparison, European nations with similar peak infection rates implemented much deeper mobility cutbacks. Italy and Austria, which experienced peak infection rates of roughly 100 and 95 per million, saw mobility declines of about 90% and 85%, respectively. Nations with lower infection peaks than the US also experienced much larger mobility drops, such as the United Kingdom and Germany, which saw mobility declines of approximately 80% and 82% with infections peaking under 80 per million. Even Switzerland and Belgium, which had higher peak infection rates than the US at roughly 135 and 130 per million, saw mobility drop significantly further, by 74% and 85%. Spain, which had the highest peak infection rate in the group at 175 per million, recorded a peak mobility decline of approximately 91%. Other nations included in this analysis, such as France and the Netherlands, also achieved mobility declines well over 70%.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the emergence of mini-second waves of COVID-19 in Australia and Europe during mid-2020, comparing their infection trajectories and policy responses to those of the United States. He highlights how regions with far lower infection rates than the US, such as Australia and Hong Kong, have instituted much tighter mobility restrictions. For example, Melbourne implemented strict Stage 4 emergency restrictions, including nighttime curfews, mandatory masks, and severe travel limits, despite experiencing a second wave that is relatively small. Conversely, parts of Europe, such as Spain and Belgium, are seeing mild mini-second waves in cases, but these have not yet translated into rising mortality rates, and mobility restrictions there remain mild.

Two line charts support this analysis, plotting data against the number of days after total reported cases reached one hundred. The first chart displays new daily infections per million people on a seven-day average. It shows the United States experiencing a massive second surge, climbing to nearly 200 daily cases per million by day 150. Meanwhile, Spain and Belgium, which saw sharp initial peaks of roughly 160 and 140 daily cases per million respectively, show much smaller secondary upticks of around 50 cases per million by day 150. The combined curve for Australia and Hong Kong remains extremely low, barely rising above zero throughout the 150-day period.

The second chart tracks daily deaths per million people on a seven-day average. It reveals that although Europe suffered a higher initial mortality peak, reaching nearly 9 deaths per million around day 50 compared to the US peak of approximately 6 per million, European deaths subsequently flattened to near zero. In contrast, the US death rate shows a clear secondary increase, rising back up to around 3.5 deaths per million by day 150, illustrating the divergent paths of the two regions.

This page focuses on the contrast between depressed economic realities and positive expectation surprises, alongside tracking the progression of the COVID-19 pandemic's summer wave in the United States. Michael Cembalest notes that while second-quarter S&P 500 earnings are projected to suffer a disastrous decline of 35% to 40% compared to 2019 levels—with only healthcare equipment, utilities, and semiconductors posting positive year-over-year growth—actual results are significantly outperforming pessimistic forecasts. An accompanying chart titled "US earnings and economic surprises" tracks the S&P 500 earnings surprise percentage alongside the Citi Economic Surprise Index level from 2008 to mid-2020. The chart reveals a dramatic, near-vertical spike in both metrics in mid-2020, with the earnings surprise leaping above 15% and the Citi Economic Surprise Index surging to an unprecedented level near 250. Cembalest cautions that these positive surprises are highly dependent on continued congressional stimulus, which J.P. Morgan expects will be extended in August. Additionally, he previews an upcoming analysis concerning the difficult measures required to eventually bring US debt levels back down to 80% of GDP.

The bottom half of the page addresses a sharp decline in COVID-19 infection rates across several Southern US states, which is beginning to slow national transmission rates. This trend is illustrated in two charts. The first, "Sharp decline in Southern US infections," displays the seven-day average of new daily infections per million people against the number of days after total reported cases reached 100. It tracks Florida, Arizona, South Carolina, and Texas, showing that all four states peaked between 100 and 120 days—with Florida peaking near 500 cases per million and Arizona near 450—before starting to decline. The second chart, "United States virus tracking," plots national daily infections and current hospitalizations on the left axis against daily deaths on the right axis from April to late July 2020. It shows new daily infections peaking around 65,000 and hospitalizations rising near 60,000 in late July. Daily deaths, which had bottomed near 500 in early July, climbed back to approximately 1,000 by the end of the month. Based on the downward shifts in infections and hospitalizations, Cembalest forecasts that the rise in US mortality should reverse and begin to decline within two weeks.

This page of Michael Cembalest’s commentary addresses recent COVID-19 news and developments surrounding the 2020 US Presidential election, focusing on the security and public perception of voting by mail. Cembalest begins by criticizing a note from Fundstrat Research that used a question mark to suggest herd immunity might be achieved at 15% to 20% infection levels without presenting scientific evidence. He draws a parallel to President Trump using a similar questioning tactic to suggest postponing the election. Addressing the logistical security of voting by mail, Cembalest references a study by Charles Stewart of MIT showing that while about 4% of mail-in ballots were lost or miscounted in the 2016 election, this share is comparable to the 4% to 6% of in-person ballots lost due to administrative issues in the 2000 election. Consequently, Stewart argues that the net risk of a surge in mail-in voting is negligible to the 2020 election outcome. 

The page features a scatter plot titled Public support for Vote by Mail expansion, which tracks polling data from 1996 to May 2020, separated by political party. Sourced from Vanderbilt University and the University of Pennsylvania, the chart's vertical axis represents the percentage of support from 0% to 100%, while the horizontal axis tracks various polls over time, splitting the data into pre-2020 and 2020 periods. The data shows that prior to 2020, support for mail-in voting expansion was virtually identical between Democrats and Republicans, closely aligned and hovering between 30% and 45% in polls conducted by Pew, NBC/WSJ, and AP. In April and May of 2020, however, a massive partisan divide emerged. While Republican support remained flat or declined slightly to a range of 30% to 40%, Democratic support skyrocketed, rising from about 75% in mid-April to nearly 90% by late May, as recorded in Fox News and ABC/Washington Post polls. Cembalest notes that this sharp divergence in partisan support occurred for reasons unique to the respondents.

This page analyzes COVID-19 transmission trends in Arizona and Western Europe, evaluating potential leading indicators and tracking the emergence of secondary infection waves as economies reopen. 

First, the author examines whether "doctor visits with COVID-like symptoms," collated by Carnegie Mellon, serves as a reliable leading indicator of infection. A dual-axis chart titled "Arizona virus tracking" plots daily new infections per million on the left axis against the percentage of symptom-related doctor visits on the right axis from late March to early August 2020. While both metrics historically tracked closely—peaking in early July with infections near 500 per million and visits around 12%—they have recently diverged. In late July, infections plummeted toward 200 per million, but doctor visits spiked sharply back up toward 15%. The author poses an open question, noting that the coming weeks will reveal whether this symptom-based metric is a valid leading indicator.

Next, the page shifts focus to rising infections in Western Europe as schools, restaurants, and other public spaces reopen. The author highlights that mobility is returning, showing only 15% to 25% declines from January baselines compared to the 50% to 80% drops seen in April and May. An accompanying chart, "Western Europe infections," plots the 7-day average of new daily infections per million people against the number of days after total reported cases reached 100. It tracks eight countries: Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands, France, Switzerland, Austria, Germany, and Italy. After initial spring spikes that peaked between 60 and 160 cases per million, most countries flattened by day 100. However, by day 150, a second wave is emerging, particularly in Spain, where daily infections have climbed back to around 80 per million. France and others show smaller upticks, while Italy has notably maintained the flattest trajectory with the smallest second wave among the group.

In this publication of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, Michael Cembalest analyzes the trajectory of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, focusing on infections, hospitalizations, and mortality trends. The author observes that while US infections and hospitalizations have recently rolled over, which should lead to a decline in mortality within the next few weeks if past trends repeat, the overall level of the virus remains high globally. In fact, only a handful of Latin American countries show higher infection rates than the United States. Cembalest questions why US infections are not declining more rapidly despite significant drops in former hotspots like California, Texas, Florida, and the Carolinas. He argues that the lack of internal border controls allows citizens to easily cross state lines, shifting the virus from former hotspot states to new, often less-dense states.

This analysis is supported by two key visuals. The first is a line chart titled "United States virus tracking," which maps current hospitalizations and daily infections on the left axis (from zero to 70,000) and daily deaths on the right axis (from zero to 2,500) using a seven-day average from April through late July. The data series reveal that new daily infections peaked near 30,000 in April, fell to approximately 20,000 in June, and then spiked to nearly 70,000 in July before starting to roll over. Current hospitalizations followed a similar path, peaking near 60,000 in April, bottoming out under 30,000 in June, and rising past 50,000 in late July. Daily deaths peaked at over 2,000 in April, fell to a low of about 500 in July, and then rose back to around 1,000 by the end of the month. 

The second visual is a map of the United States titled "Without border controls, Hotspots keep shifting." The map highlights current hotspot states in red—including California, Texas, Florida, and Georgia, alongside several states in the South and Midwest—with large black arrows indicating the outward movement of infections from former hotspot states into neighboring and more distant states. Together, these visuals and commentary demonstrate how interstate mobility distributes the virus to new areas, preventing a swift nationwide decline in cases.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures, legal disclaimers, and confidentiality notices for J.P. Morgan's institutional, wholesale, and professional clients. It includes a brief statement explaining the rigorous security and anonymization protocols used to protect Chase credit and debit card transaction data referenced elsewhere in the publication, ensuring all unique identifiable personal information is removed prior to analysis.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market by Michael Cembalest analyzes US healthcare capacity and the shifting trends of e-commerce spending during the COVID-19 pandemic. 

The first section examines hospital and ICU bed utilization rates across various US states using data from the US Department of Health and Human Services. The author notes that hospital systems are typically built for a 60 percent to 70 percent utilization rate during normal periods, utilizing 2018 data as a proxy baseline. A dual-series bar and scatter chart titled Hotspot state hospital bed and ICU bed utilization rates presents current utilization rates alongside 2018 baselines for states including Alabama, Georgia, Nevada, Oregon, Arkansas, Mississippi, North Dakota, Hawaii, Montana, Indiana, Missouri, Oklahoma, Illinois, and Virginia. The visual demonstrates that states like Alabama, Arkansas, and Mississippi are experiencing utilization rates well above normal. For instance, Alabama's ICU bed utilization rate is shown near 90 percent, noticeably higher than its historical 2018 benchmark of roughly 74 percent.

The second section addresses the evolution of e-commerce, questioning the narrative from futurists of a permanent mega-shift in retail spending. While e-commerce shares spiked in April 2020 during the first wave of infections, they have since declined rapidly, even while overall US infection levels remained only 20 percent below peak levels. The author forecasts that when infection levels eventually decline, e-commerce shares of spending will likely return much closer to 2019 levels than to their April 2020 peaks. A table tracking the evolution of e-commerce shares during the COVID pandemic using internal Chase data supports this observation. It breaks down online spending shares across five sectors, comparing 2019 averages, April 2020 averages, and July/August 2020 averages. Retail rose from 43 percent to 70 percent before falling to 56 percent. Healthcare and Pharmacy went from 27 percent to 45 percent, then dropped to 32 percent. Supermarkets rose from 4 percent to 11 percent and remained flat. Wholesale and Discount clubs went from 10 percent to 28 percent, then settled at 21 percent. Restaurants spiked from 8 percent to 39 percent, then dropped back to 25 percent in the July/August period.

This page features a critique by Michael Cembalest of a bullish COVID-19 vaccine forecast report published by Goldman Sachs. Goldman Sachs had predicted that the FDA would approve at least one vaccine in 2020, leading to large-scale vaccinations in the US and Europe by the second and third quarters of 2021, respectively. Cembalest challenges the methodology behind this optimistic forecast, questioning Goldman’s reliance on "superforecasters" from the Good Judgment project. He also critiques the assumption that vaccine success scales linearly with the number of attempts—which led to the implication that 43 of 115 COVID-19 vaccine attempts could succeed. Pointing out that vaccine development is highly non-linear, Cembalest notes that some diseases like HIV and Hepatitis C have zero successful vaccines despite numerous attempts, while others like Hepatitis B have high success rates. Additionally, he cautions that because most COVID-19 vaccine candidates target the same coronavirus spike protein, there is a heightened risk of collective success or collective failure.

To offer a more rigorous historical perspective, the page includes a stacked bar chart titled "Clinical trial outcomes for drug treatments entering Phase II," using 2018 data from the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab. The chart illustrates the percentage of trials that failed Phase 2, failed Phase 3, or were approved across nine distinct medical categories. Oncology exhibits the lowest success rate, with roughly 85% of candidates entering Phase II failing. Conversely, the category "Infectious Disease (vaccines only)" shows the highest historical success, with an approval rate of approximately 50%, while roughly 40% failed in Phase 2 and around 10% failed in Phase 3. Other categories charted for comparison include the Central Nervous System, Autoimmune, Endocrinology, Genitourinary, Cardiovascular, Infectious Disease (all), and Ophthalmology. While Cembalest acknowledges that infectious disease vaccines historically have higher approval rates once they pass Phase I safety trials, he warns against over-interpreting this data, as it bundles together diseases with vastly different vaccine susceptibilities.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the surprising year-to-date outperformance of US and Emerging Markets equities over Europe and Japan in 2020. Despite the US and Emerging Markets being significant epicenters for the coronavirus, overweighting these regions continued to add value to portfolios, primarily driven by the earnings resilience and massive scale of US megacap technology and internet stocks.

A table titled "YTD United States/Emerging Markets vs Europe/Japan regional equity market barbell performance" illustrates this dynamic. It shows a US dollar barbell outperformance of 1.5% and a local currency barbell outperformance of 2.2%. The US accounts for 62% of the weight (revised to 72%) and delivered a 5.1% return in both US dollar and local currency terms. Emerging Markets, with a 12% weight, returned negative 0.5% in US dollars but achieved a positive 3.8% return in local currency. Conversely, Europe, at an 18% weight, saw a US dollar return of negative 7.7% and a local currency return of negative 10.7%, while Japan, at an 8% weight, suffered a US dollar return of negative 5.5% and a local currency return of negative 8.0%. 

An accompanying chart, "US equity market earnings," tracks the percentage change in forward 12-month earnings compared to January 2020. It highlights that the top five firms—Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Facebook—maintained highly resilient forward earnings expectations, remaining nearly flat and hovering around 0% through late June. In contrast, the S&P 500 excluding these top five firms saw forward earnings decline to roughly negative 25%, while the small-cap Russell 2000 suffered an earnings collapse, bottoming out near negative 80% before a slight recovery to around negative 70% by the end of June.

Another chart, "High growth tech drives US markets, growth laggards drive Europe and Japan," compares index composition by percentage of total market cap. In the US, high-growth technology represents roughly 34% of the market cap, while old-economy sectors like materials, energy, and industrials combine for only about 13%. In Europe, this relationship is inverted, with materials, energy, and industrials commanding 26% of the market cap compared to just 7% for technology. Japan shows a similar pattern, with technology representing about 13% and the older industrial sectors representing 25%. 

Cembalest argues that Europe's implementation of digital service taxes on US tech companies, justified by the concept of user-created value, amounts to de facto tariffs on US service sector exports. He suggests these taxes are a subconscious admission that Europe will struggle to produce megacap tech companies of its own, punctuating this point with a brief reference to the collapse of Germany's Wirecard AG.

This page from Michael Cembalest's Eye on the Market addresses the unprecedented levels of international cooperation and funding for COVID-19 vaccine development, while tempering optimism with scientific reality. The author highlights that many leading vaccine candidates rely on either RNA/DNA platforms or Trojan Horse vector approaches, technologies that had never been approved for use in developed countries at the time of writing in August 2020. He expresses hope for an approved vaccine by late 2020 and distribution by early 2021, but stresses that this expectation is a hopeful feeling based on early Phase I trial immunogenicity results rather than an empirical forecast.

The page features a table outlining five distinct methods of provoking an antibody response to SARS-CoV-2 along with select developers. The first type involves live, weakened coronaviruses to infect cells and produce viral proteins, which lists no major candidates. The second type uses industrially produced coronavirus proteins recognized as foreign matter in the blood, associated with candidates from GlaxoSmithKline/Sanofi and Novavax. The third type utilizes a killed coronavirus, with Sinovac and Dynavax listed as candidates. The fourth type employs a different engineered virus, such as a human or ape adenovirus, to deliver genetic components coding for spike proteins; candidates include CanSino, Oxford, Johnson and Johnson, and Merck/Themis. A footnote warns that no adenoviral vector vaccines had yet demonstrated disease prevention in humans, noting that China's approved Ebola vector vaccine did not prove prevention in Phase II studies, and Johnson and Johnson's Ebola vaccine was still under European review. Lastly, the fifth type uses DNA or RNA to cause cells to produce coronavirus proteins, represented by Moderna, Innovio, and BioNTech/Pfizer. A corresponding footnote cautions that there were no approved DNA or RNA vaccines at the time and none had ever been tested in a large-scale clinical trial prior to the pandemic.

This page examines why United States COVID-19 infections are not declining more rapidly and presents global serology data to show that populations remain far from herd immunity. The author argues that because the US lacks internal border controls, focusing too closely on state-level data ignores how easily citizens cross borders, causing infections to constantly shift from former hotspots to new, often less-dense states. A map of the United States illustrates this phenomenon, marking active hotspot states in red and showing arrows that track how infections migrated from prior hotspots—predominantly located in California, the South, and Florida—into adjacent and interior states. 

The second part of the page addresses how far global populations are from herd immunity, highlighting serology tests from the United Kingdom conducted between late June and mid-July. These tests revealed antibody prevalence rates of only 6% for England overall and 13% for London, which were lower than many had hoped. An accompanying bubble chart plots estimated antibody prevalence across various global regions from March through September 2020, with the vertical axis representing antibody detection from 0% to 25%. Notable data points include New York City with the highest prevalence at approximately 22%, followed by New York State and Gangelt, Germany at around 14%, and London at 13%. Aside from these outliers, the vast majority of analyzed regions exhibit antibody levels well under 10%. This includes Wuhan at 10%, Miami-Dade at roughly 6%, Spain at 5%, and Tokyo, Belgium, Los Angeles, and Santa Clara all sitting below 5%. The author uses this data to demonstrate that, except for extreme hotspots like New York City, the presence of COVID-19 antibodies is globally too low to suggest any substantial progress toward herd immunity.

This page serves as a reference list titled "Sources (that were not hard to find)" concluding a discussion on COVID-19 misinformation and treatments. It contains five hyperlinked sources addressing the controversies surrounding hydroxychloroquine and the group known as America's Frontline Doctors. The listed web resources include investigative and reporting articles from Snopes, MedPage Today, Rolling Stone, and ABC News, which track the spread of unproven COVID-19 treatments and related political endorsements, alongside a scientific commentary thread on Twitter by Professor Shane Crotty.

This page provides an update on the status of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States as of mid-August 2020. The main observation is that while US coronavirus infections have fallen from their peak summer levels, the rate of decline has flattened, and daily mortality remains high at approximately 1,000 deaths per day. Additionally, the vast majority of US states continue to experience infection levels far higher than those in Europe.

To illustrate these trends, the page features three visual data tracking displays. The first chart, titled "United States virus tracking," plots current hospitalizations and new daily infections on the left-hand scale (ranging from 0 to 70,000) and daily deaths on the right-hand scale (ranging from 0 to 2,500) from early April through mid-August. The visualization reveals two distinct waves. The first wave peaked in April with daily deaths exceeding 2,000 and hospitalizations near 60,000. The second wave peaked in July, with daily infections spiking near 70,000 and hospitalizations rising back up to 60,000. By August 15, hospitalizations had descended to around 40,000, and daily infections fell to approximately 50,000, though both lines show signs of leveling off as daily deaths plateau near 1,000.

The second chart, also titled "United States virus tracking," compares new daily infections per million people (left scale, 0 to 250) against the percentage of doctor visits for patients with COVID-like symptoms (right scale, 0.0% to 9.0%). The two data series mirror each other closely. After peaking in July with doctor visits surpassing 7% and infections topping 200 per million, both metrics declined gradually by mid-August, with doctor visits hovering around 5% and infections around 150 per million. The author notes that the gradual downward trend in doctor visits is a key indicator that the overall virus decline will be slow rather than abrupt.

The final chart compares peak versus current infection levels across all 50 US states, sorted from left to right by their trailing seven-day average infection rate per million people. For each state, the chart displays the peak infection rate with a red marker and the latest rate with a blue marker, alongside the percentage change from their respective peaks. A dotted horizontal reference line marks the European average of 30 infections per million. This visual makes the point that 46 out of 50 US states still have higher infection levels than Europe. Southern and Sunbelt states like Georgia, Florida, and Texas show the highest current infection levels, remaining well above 200 per million despite notable drops from their peaks, such as Florida's 53% decline. Only a handful of northeastern states, including New York, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Maine, and Vermont, have managed to reduce their infection rates to or below the European baseline.

This page of Michael Cembalest’s commentary, titled "Lost in translation: T-cells and financial industry co-conspirators in the war on science," addresses the widespread misinterpretation of T-cell research during the COVID-19 pandemic. Cembalest explains the critical distinction between "cross-reactive immune memory," which merely reduces disease severity, and full "immunity," which prevents infection and transmission entirely. He cites immunologist Shane Crotty from the La Jolla Institute of Immunology, who emphasized that T-cells do not eliminate the need for masks. Cembalest criticizes an unnamed financial research firm for spreading dangerous claims by citing a former ophthalmologist associated with America's Frontline Doctors. This doctor falsely claimed that herd immunity could be achieved at 10% to 20% COVID-19 penetration and that pharmaceutical companies were aggressively pushing lockdowns. Cembalest highlights that this doctor has an expired medical license, has launched a blockchain fund, and has no experience treating COVID-19, warning that the mindless regurgitation of unvetted sources hinders the United States' efforts to flatten the virus curve. He concludes with the observation that while the exact role of T-cells in disease severity and reinfection remains an open question, spreading scientific misinformation harms public health.

This commentary by Michael Cembalest focuses on the unprecedented scale of monetary and fiscal policy responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, arguing that it represents the largest debt monetization exercise in recorded history. Although the International Monetary Fund projects that advanced economy fiscal deficits will decline in 2021 from their 2020 peaks, they are still expected to remain more than double 2019 levels, pushing advanced economy debt from 105 percent to 132 percent of gross domestic product. Cembalest contrasts the potential impact of these actions on emerging markets—where such actions would typically trigger capital flight, soaring interest rates, and balance of payments crises—with developed countries, where substantial excess capacity allows governments to support private consumption, investment, and economic growth without immediate threats of inflation or crowding out private investment. While he acknowledges the risk of an eventual stagflationary failure similar to the economic issues of the 1970s, he agrees with the equity market's current bullish stance, noting that these policies successfully support private sector demand and provide meaningful near-term benefits to public and private sector companies.

The visual evidence is presented in a scatter plot titled "Debt monetization response to global virus crisis eclipses everything else." The chart compares the change in fiscal deficits on the y-axis, ranging from negative five percent to twenty percent of GDP, against the change in central bank balance sheets on the x-axis, ranging from four percent to eighteen percent of GDP, with both metrics measured relative to pre-crisis levels. The scatter plot maps data points for the 2020 Global Virus Crisis, the 2008 to 2009 Global Financial Crisis, the 1930s Great Depression, World War II, and the 2012 Eurozone Balance of Payments Crisis across the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, and the Eurozone. 

The data points illustrate how the 2020 Global Virus Crisis response dwarfs previous historical interventions. For the United States, the 2020 crisis triggered a fiscal deficit change of roughly fifteen percent of GDP and a central bank balance sheet expansion of more than fourteen percent of GDP, compared to a seven-and-a-half percent deficit increase and a ten percent balance sheet expansion during the Global Financial Crisis. The United Kingdom's 2020 response shows a twelve percent balance sheet expansion and a thirteen-and-a-half percent deficit increase. Japan recorded the largest central bank balance sheet expansion during the 2020 crisis at nearly eighteen percent of GDP, alongside an eleven percent deficit change. The Eurozone's 2020 metrics sit at a fourteen-and-a-half percent balance sheet expansion and a seven-and-a-half percent deficit increase. In comparison, US spending during World War II shows a slightly higher fiscal deficit change of eighteen percent but a much smaller balance sheet expansion of five-and-a-half percent, while the 2012 Eurozone Balance of Payments Crisis is situated at a negative one-and-a-half percent deficit change and an eleven percent balance sheet expansion. This comparison underscores that the synchronized fiscal and monetary actions taken during the pandemic represent a uniquely aggressive economic intervention.

Michael Cembalest discusses whether the rise of work-from-home policies has driven homebuyers to less dense locations with cheaper land, concluding that this shift is occurring in some major US cities but not all of them. The page features a chart titled "Post-COVID shift to lower land price locations," which plots the change in the share of mortgage rate locks compared to 2019 against the land price of a median lot as a share of the total median home price. 

The chart's Y-axis measures the change in mortgage rate lock share from negative 4.0 percent to positive 5.0 percent, while the X-axis details the land price share from 10 percent to 80 percent. Five population density quintiles, numbered 1 for the lowest density to 5 for the highest density, are plotted for five metropolitan areas. 

In Los Angeles-Long Beach, California, represented by a red line, the lowest density quintile shows a significant positive change in rate locks of about 3.5 percent at a 40 percent land price share, while its highest-density quintile shows a decline of nearly 3.0 percent at a 70 percent land price share. A similar shift toward lower-density, lower-land-price quintiles is observed in New York-Newark, represented by a black line, which falls to negative 4.0 percent in its densest quintile, as well as in Phoenix-Mesa, Arizona, and Miami-Port St. Lucie-Fort Lauderdale, Florida. Conversely, Houston-The Woodlands, Texas, serves as an exception where the densest quintile actually shows a slightly positive change in rate lock share. 

Based on data from the American Enterprise Institute, Census, USDA, FHFA, and Optimal Blue, the author notes that while economic incentives to relocate have always existed, work-from-home policies are actively enabling these shifts. He characterizes this as an early read on post-COVID residential demand trends that J.P. Morgan will continue to monitor.

This page contains only standard legal disclaimers, data privacy disclosures, and regulatory boilerplate information for J.P. Morgan Asset Management. It details the security protocols used to aggregate and anonymize Chase credit and debit card transaction data and outlines the distribution restrictions and regulatory entities governing the report across various global jurisdictions.

This page of the commentary analyzes the controversy surrounding the Trump administration's decision to issue an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for convalescent plasma to treat COVID-19. The author contrasts this decision with the EUA for Remdesivir, which was supported by rigorous randomized controlled trials. While a Mayo Clinic observational study showed lower mortality rates for patients treated early—with a 7-day mortality rate of 8.7% for those treated within three days of diagnosis versus 11.9% for those treated after three days, and a 30-day mortality rate of 21.6% versus 26.7%—the author emphasizes that observational studies cannot conclusively prove efficacy or determine optimal dosing. The commentary expresses disappointment that over 70,000 US patients received the treatment without generating any scientifically rigorous control data. 

The text also details political friction, noting that despite opposition from Dr. Anthony Fauci and the National Institutes of Health director, the Food and Drug Administration proceeded with the authorization. This resulted in public controversy when the FDA Commissioner later admitted to misrepresenting study results, particularly a 35% mortality improvement statistic cited by the White House that the study's own authors could not verify. A quote from Derek Lowe at Translational Medicine warns that these actions undermine public trust in eventual vaccine approvals ahead of the November election and refutes the President's claims of a "deep state" block at the FDA. Finally, the author discusses the scaling challenges of convalescent plasma due to donor variability and notes that scientists are far more optimistic about manufactured monoclonal antibodies than donor-sourced plasma.

This page analyzes the state of COVID-19 infections, mobility trends, and mortality rates across the United States and Europe. The central observation is that while US infections are falling rapidly—resembling Europe's decline from three months prior—the ongoing reopening of schools and businesses makes a continuous, linear decline unlikely. At the same time, Europe's reopening has led to a modest uptick in new cases. However, a crucial trend is that second-wave infections in both regions exhibit much lower mortality rates. The author attributes this positive shift to a younger average age of newly infected individuals and improved medical treatments for hospitalized patients, including the use of steroids like Dexamethasone and anti-coagulants.

Four charts support these insights. The first, titled "US vs Europe infections," plots the seven-day average of new daily infections per million people against the number of days after total reported cases reached one hundred. The data shows that the US experienced a massive second wave peaking at over 200 daily infections per million around day 130 before falling sharply, while Europe's initial wave peaked near 75 daily infections per million and remained low before a slight rise at the end of the timeline. 

The second chart, "Regional mobility data," tracks the percentage change from baseline for retail, restaurants, transit, and workplace activity from February 12 to mid-July. Both regions saw mobility collapse in March, with Europe dropping to nearly negative 75 percent and the US falling to around negative 50 percent. By July, both regions recovered to similar levels, hovering between negative 20 percent and negative 30 percent.

The final two charts compare new daily infections against mortality per million people from March through late July. The chart for Europe shows that during the first wave in April, infections peaked around 70 per million and deaths peaked near 8 per million. During the second wave of infections in July, which climbed back to around 40 per million, deaths remained extremely low, near zero. Similarly, the US chart shows that while first-wave infections peaked near 100 per million with daily deaths reaching 7.5 per million, the massive July wave of over 200 infections per million only led to a modest rise in daily deaths to around 3 per million, illustrating the significantly lower lethality of recent infections.

This page presents a critical commentary on reports that the Trump Administration might fast-track the Oxford/AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine before the 2020 U.S. presidential election. According to the Financial Times, the administration is considering granting an Emergency Use Authorization based on partial Phase III data, a shortcut that AstraZeneca itself has rejected and not applied for. The text describes the vaccine's novel adenovirus vector technology, which uses a chimpanzee virus to trigger an antibody response and has never been approved for use in the developed world. 

While AstraZeneca is running global trials with fifty thousand participants across the United Kingdom, United States, South Africa, and Brazil, the administration reportedly contemplated approval based on the UK trial of just ten thousand participants, far below the standard Food and Drug Administration minimum requirement of thirty thousand Phase III results. The author warns that because vaccines are given to healthy populations for a disease with an infection mortality rate under one percent, safety standards must be extraordinarily high. Premature approval risks severely damaging public trust in a nation where vaccine confidence is already well below the global median. The commentary concludes by citing several media and medical sources, highlighting a New York Times piece by Thomas and Fink on recent FDA actions as a troubling reflection of the federal government's scientific competency.

This page addresses the puzzle of why Latin America has experienced far higher COVID-19 infection rates than other parts of the developing world, while also evaluating the fitful recovery of consumer spending and air travel in the United States. 

The author begins by noting that no obvious health system, mobility, or behavioral dynamics explain why Latin America's infection levels are so much higher than those of other emerging markets. For comparison, the current US infection level at the time of writing was 125 per million people, and Europe's was 40 per million. 

This regional disparity is illustrated in a chart of emerging market world infections, which tracks the seven-day average of new daily infections per million people against the number of days since total reported cases reached 100. South America dramatically outpaces all other regions, surging past 160 daily infections per million people around day 160. In contrast, Eastern Europe, the Middle East, Emerging Asia, and Africa all remain flat and well below 40 cases per million throughout the 200-day period. 

A companion chart provides a country-by-country breakdown of Latin American infections using a 14-day average of daily infections per million people. It shows that Chile experienced an early, sharp spike that peaked near 250 cases per million around day 75 before declining. Meanwhile, Colombia, Argentina, and Peru show steep upward trajectories later in their outbreaks, with Colombia and Argentina rising past 200 cases per million near day 150, and Peru spiking back up toward 250. Brazil peaked at around 220 infections per million around day 130 before beginning a slight decline, whereas Mexico and Ecuador experienced flatter curves peaking under 100, and Venezuela remained extremely low.

The discussion then shifts to the United States, where a July spike in infections caused a temporary plateau in the year-over-year recovery of "social distancing spending," which represents card-present transactions at retail stores, hotels, restaurants, and amusement parks. This spending has since resumed its rise, as depicted in a chart tracking national credit and debit card spending from March 7 to August 4, 2020. The data shows that after crashing to nearly negative 70 percent year-over-year in mid-April, social distancing spending recovered to roughly negative 25 percent by early August. 

In contrast, airline spending has shown almost no improvement since its March collapse. A final chart compares airline credit and debit card spending against TSA checkpoint travelers, showing year-over-year percentage changes. While both metrics plummeted to near negative 100 percent in April, TSA checkpoint travelers have recovered more quickly, rising to about negative 70 percent by August. Meanwhile, airline spending has lagged, recovering only to roughly negative 85 percent. The author notes that this divergence suggests travelers are taking shorter trips, buying more heavily discounted fares, and participating in far less business travel.

This page opens a broader analysis of the financial and economic cost of the US recovery during the COVID-19 pandemic. The author, Michael Cembalest, contrasts the current economic landscape with the historically strong tailwinds President Donald Trump possessed in January 2020. While China is lagging behind its trade agreement purchase commitments, the primary focus has shifted to the pandemic's toll on Trump's reelection tailwinds, which have fallen far below late-2019 levels and the historical averages enjoyed by Dwight D. Eisenhower and Bill Clinton during their second terms. Despite this setback, the US economic recovery is moving much faster than the post-2009 rebound. The author projects that third-quarter annualized GDP growth could hit 35 percent, while unemployment is forecast to fall to 7 percent by the end of 2020 and 5.5 percent by the end of 2021. Meanwhile, the prospect of an additional congressional fiscal stimulus package is described as a toss-up.

To illustrate the recovery's trajectory, the page features four economic charts. The first, detailing US manufacturing industrial production indexed to 2012, displays historical data from 2006 through mid-2020, highlighting a steep plunge in early 2020 to an index level below 85, followed by a partial rebound to around 97. The second chart tracks real retail sales in billions of 1982-1984 dollars, depicting a dramatic pandemic-induced plunge in early 2020 to approximately 160 billion, followed by a rapid, near-vertical surge that brought sales back above 205 billion. 

The third visual is a dual-axis chart analyzing unemployment and job openings between 2006 and 2020. This chart tracks the ratio of unemployed persons per job opening on the left axis alongside the overall unemployment rate on the right axis; both metrics experienced historic, nearly vertical spikes in early 2020, with the unemployment rate peaking near 15 percent and the ratio of unemployed per opening jumping past 5 before both began to moderate. Finally, a high-frequency tracker for US manufacturing in 2020 measures the year-over-year weekly percentage change in industrial inputs, including lumber, steel, coal, electricity output, and railroad traffic. This series bottomed out near negative 23 percent in April before steadily clawing back to around negative 9 percent by late August.

This page discusses the potential trajectory of US Federal debt under the proposed policies of the Biden campaign, contrasting them with the fiscal policies of the Trump administration. The author argues that while Biden’s extensive tax and spending proposals would likely increase the federal debt by an additional $3 trillion under a Democratic Sweep, they should not be viewed as an automatic negative for economic growth. This is because a significant portion of Biden’s spending is directed toward areas with historically high growth multipliers. However, the author warns that these policies could negatively impact short-term corporate profits and equity valuations due to a substantial increase in corporate taxes.

The page features three primary charts to support this analysis. The first chart, titled "The Biden Agenda," illustrates the projected taxation and spending initiatives over a ten-year period in trillions of dollars. Under taxation, which totals around $5 trillion, the largest contributors are taxes on the wealthy, industry-specific taxes, and corporate tax hikes/base broadening, along with a payroll tax on incomes over $400,000, slightly offset by small tax cuts for homebuyers and caregivers. Under spending, which totals approximately $8 trillion, the major categories include entitlement expansion, housing, education, infrastructure and jobs, and healthcare, partially offset by savings from drug price reforms. 

The second chart, titled "CBO estimates of growth multipliers by policy," shows the range of change in economic output per dollar of fiscal policy based on February 2015 Congressional Budget Office data. It contrasts tax cuts with spending measures, demonstrating that spending policies generally yield higher growth multipliers. For instance, federal government purchases of goods and services have a multiplier range of roughly 0.5x to 2.5x, and federal transfers to states for infrastructure range from 0.4x to 2.2x. In contrast, tax cuts show lower multipliers, with corporate tax cuts generating only 0.2x to 0.8x in output, and one-year tax cuts for higher-income individuals generating 0.1x to 0.6x. 

The third chart, "Biden proposed corporate tax increase vs Trump corporate tax cuts," displays the net impact on corporate and pass-through taxes over ten years.
