The second chart, S&P 500 megacap outperformance, tracks the percentage difference between the market-cap weighted and equal-weighted S&P 500 index. It overlays the 1997–2002 tech bubble period with the 2017–2020 period. This comparison illustrates that while megacap outperformance in the late 1990s peaked above 50%, the current cycle's outperformance has peaked much lower, at around 20%, indicating that recent market excess is not quite at 1999 levels. 

The third chart illustrates the Median free cash flow margin for 10 largest stocks within S&P 500 by market cap, showing a volatile but clear upward trajectory from under 10% in the early 1990s to over 20% by 2020, underlining the immense profitability of today's largest firms. 

The fourth chart, Top 10 companies in S&P 500 by market cap compared to bottom 100 companies by P/E, plots the ratio of median forward P/E ratios from 1995 to 2020. This valuation metric peaked at roughly 5.5x in 2000, fell to near 1.0x after the 2008 financial crisis, and has climbed back up to around 3.0x in 2020.

Finally, a table presents selected secular growth stocks with lower antitrust risks, categorizing them by GICS sector. These companies met specific fundamental criteria: S&P 500 membership, historical and projected sales growth exceeding 10%, a free cash flow margin over 15%, and a subindustry market revenue share below 33%. 

The highlighted companies include TransDigm Group in Aerospace & Defense; Arista Networks in Communications Equipment; Align Technology in Health Care Supplies; Xilinx in Semiconductors; Adobe, Autodesk, ANSYS, Intuit, and Paycom Software in Application Software; Mastercard, PayPal, and Visa in Data Processing & Outsourced Services; Take-Two Interactive Software in Interactive Home Entertainment; Monster Beverage in Soft Drinks; Vertex Pharmaceuticals in Biotechnology; ABIOMED and Intuitive Surgical in Health Care Equipment; Etsy in Internet & Direct Marketing; and Fortinet and ServiceNow in Systems Software.

This page from the report discusses how the high yield and leveraged loan markets have become beneficiaries of financial repression, supported by substantial monetary and fiscal stimulus backstops. The author observes that while the 2020 recession was twice as deep as the 2009 recession, high yield and leveraged loan default rates, as well as bankruptcy filings, peaked at only half of the 2009 level. However, a flood of investor liquidity has led to weakened underwriting standards and covenant protections. Consequently, credit spreads have rallied, but investors are paying a price in the form of declining recovery rates on defaulted high yield bonds and loans. For investment grade corporate bonds, the author passes on making any recommendations, noting that the inflation-adjusted yield on the Barclays Investment Grade Corporate Bond Index is slightly negative.

The page features four key charts supporting this analysis. The first chart, showing US high yield bond and leveraged loan default rates from 1999 to 2020, compares the last twelve-month par-weighted default rates of high yield bonds and leveraged loans. It highlights that both rates peaked at around 14% and 10% respectively in 2009, but reached peaks of only about 6% to 7% in 2020. 

The second chart displays US high yield corporate bond spreads from 1995 to late 2020, measuring the JPDFHYI index spread versus Treasuries in basis points. Spreads peaked near 1,400 basis points in 2009 and spiked to over 1,000 basis points in early 2020 before rapidly contracting back to around 400 basis points. A specific point indicates that high yield energy spreads remained slightly elevated, near 600 basis points, toward the end of 2020.

The third chart illustrates quarterly US high yield and leveraged loan fund flows in billions of dollars from 2017 to 2020. This visual highlights a massive surge of inflows into high yield funds during 2020, reaching upwards of $20 billion, while leveraged loan funds experienced persistent net outflows over the same period, often losing between $5 billion and $15 billion per quarter. 

The fourth chart presents US high yield bond and institutional loan recovery rates in cents on the dollar from 1990 to 2020. It demonstrates a clear downward trend in recovery values. First lien loans, which historically yielded recoveries of 70 to 80 cents on the dollar, dropped to approximately 50 cents in 2020. Similarly, high yield bond recovery rates fell to their lowest recorded levels near 20 cents on the dollar in 2020, down from historical averages of 30 to 50 cents.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2021 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, presents an executive summary focusing on vaccine rollouts, consumer spending potential, Federal Reserve policy, and global output gaps. The author argues that while it will take three to four months for COVID-19 vaccinations to meaningfully lower hospitalization and mortality rates in the developed world—partly due to logistics and a high rate of vaccine resistance in the United States, where fifteen to thirty percent of Americans do not plan to get vaccinated—vaccine rollouts will eventually unleash significant pent-up consumer demand. Despite this potential surge in spending, the author predicts the Federal Reserve will do little to constrain it, likely waiting for a major surge in inflation before raising interest rates due to a decade of repeatedly overestimating recovery strength and inflation risks.

To support these points, the page features four charts. The first chart, titled "Due to COVID, potential spending exceeds actual consumption," plots year-over-year percentage changes from 1972 to 2020. It illustrates a historic divergence in 2020: while actual consumption growth plunged, spending potential, bolstered by massive government transfer payments, spiked sharply to around thirteen percent. The spending potential metric is defined as sixty-five percent of taxable income, one hundred percent of transfer payments, ten percent of housing wealth, and one point five percent of financial wealth.

The second chart, titled "Fed projections vs actual Fed funds rate," compares the effective Fed funds rate from 2012 through late 2020 against median FOMC projections extending to 2022. The chart visualizes the Federal Reserve's consistent forecasting errors, showing a series of grey projection curves that repeatedly anticipated steep rate hikes that never materialized. Instead, the actual rate, represented by a solid black line, remained near zero percent for years, peaked at only about two point two percent in late 2018, and fell back to zero percent in 2020. 

The final two charts show global output gaps, which measure actual GDP relative to potential GDP as a gauge of spare capacity. One chart displays the long-term trend from 2006 to 2020, while the other focuses closely on the period from January 2019 to July 2020. Both charts track China, Emerging Asia, the Developed World, Emerging Asia excluding China, and Latin America. The data reveals that the COVID-19 pandemic caused severe negative output gaps across all regions in 2020. By mid-2020, China’s output gap recovered dramatically back toward zero percent, whereas other regions faced persistent, massive gaps, with Latin America and Emerging Asia excluding China dropping below negative fifteen percent, and the Developed World lingering near negative five to ten percent.

This page serves as an executive summary of the J.P. Morgan 2021 Market Outlook by Michael Cembalest. The author projects a year of approximately 10% gains in the US equity market, though with expected volatility from profit-taking and legislative policy decisions surrounding the filibuster and taxes. 

The summary outlines several key tactical recommendations. The report favors overweighting US and Emerging Market equities while underweighting Europe and Japan. While bullish on renewable energy as a long-term secular theme, the author advises investors to wait for better entry levels following a sharp run-up. Cembalest anticipates that the Biden administration will implement policy adjustments—such as tighter fracking rules on public lands, climate risk disclosures, and higher mileage standards—without passing a full Green New Deal. For value, the report recommends traditional energy, noting that even after a late 2020 rally, the S&P 500 oil and gas sector traded at only half the book value of the broader market, marking its lowest relative valuation since 1928. Additionally, the author notes that infrastructure stocks could benefit from bipartisan legislative support, while expressing caution on large-cap pharma due to the potential for bipartisan drug pricing bills.

The text also challenges the conventional wisdom that congressional gridlock is universally positive for equities, warning that intense partisan polarization is at a century-long peak. This phenomenon is visualized in a line chart titled "Moderates in Congress and GDP growth that followed," which plots the percentage of moderates in the House and Senate against the subsequent 10-year cumulative real GDP growth from 1950 to 2020. The chart demonstrates a striking parallel decline: congressional moderates dropped from roughly 40% of the legislature in the mid-20th century to under 10% by 2020, coinciding with a drop in subsequent 10-year real GDP growth from peak levels above 50% in the 1960s to around 20% by the end of the historical series.

A second chart, titled "Global alternative vs traditional energy performance," uses an index starting in January 2016 at 100 to compare the MSCI Global Alternative Energy Index against the MSCI All-Country World Energy Index. Through late 2020, alternative energy skyrocketed to an index level of over 250, while traditional energy plummeted below its 2016 starting value, ending 2020 under 100. This stark divergence underpins the author's call to wait for a better entry point in renewables while seeking deep value in traditional energy.

This page analyzes the ongoing US-China economic conflict, arguing that while trade war intensity may decrease under the Biden administration, fundamental tensions are here to stay. The author suggests that political pressures will prevent a quick reversal of policies, noting that Chinese import competition historically boosted Republican vote shares in key swing states like Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania. Furthermore, bipartisan concern remains elevated over human rights abuses, highlighted by the near-unanimous passage of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, as well as China's low compliance (ranging from 30% to 70%) with the Phase I trade deal. A potential future compromise could involve scrapping tariffs in exchange for China easing market access for US services firms.

Four charts support this analysis. The first chart tracks the relative stock performance of companies with high exposure to the US-China trade war against the S&P 500 from January 2018 to December 2020. This index of exposed companies bottomed out at roughly 77% of its initial value in mid-2020 before rebounding to about 95% by late 2020 as investors anticipated a less volatile bilateral relationship. 

The second chart details the lagging progress of the US-China Phase 1 purchase agreement. Across all designated sectors, China fell significantly short of its 2020 targets: agriculture imports reached $22 billion against a $33 billion target (67% complete), manufacturing reached $48 billion against an $83 billion target (57% complete), and energy imports reached only $8 billion against a $26 billion target (31% complete). 

The third chart labels China as the world's most mercantile country, comparing its policy scores on a scale where 100 is best and 0 is worst. China sits on the far-left, low-scoring side of the spectrum across several metrics, including the overall Mercantilism Index—which accounts for forced local production, intellectual property theft, and currency manipulation—as well as barriers to market access, weak trade secret protections, and public ownership of the private sector. 

The final chart measures "The Rights of the Individual versus the State" on a 100-point scale evaluating judicial independence, freedom of expression, and rule of law. Along a descending curve of global nations, the United States and Hong Kong rank near the top with scores around 75 to 85, whereas mainland China ranks near the absolute bottom with a score of approximately 45, illustrating its high degree of state control.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Trade War analysis examines the ongoing consequences of the US-China economic conflict, focusing on bilateral investment, semiconductor exports, and the supply chain decisions of US multinationals. The author argues that the drop in bilateral foreign direct investment may be permanent as definitions of national security expand. Additionally, while US semiconductor exports to China grew through mid-2020, they dropped sharply following strict export regulations in August. The author notes that US semiconductor companies command a dominant 90% to 95% global market share in advanced chips and equipment essential for artificial intelligence, 5G, autonomous vehicles, and other advanced technologies, meaning China's reliance on US equipment is likely to continue despite its self-sufficiency goals. Finally, the text highlights that most US multinationals do not plan to relocate out of China because they primarily operate there to serve local and regional demand rather than to export goods back to the US.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, a bar graph showing bilateral foreign direct investment in billions of dollars from 2004 to mid-2020, illustrates a dramatic collapse in Chinese FDI into the US. This category peaked at over $45 billion in 2016 before plummeting to nearly zero by 2020, whereas US FDI into China remained remarkably steady over the same sixteen-year span, generally fluctuating between $5 billion and $15 billion annually.

The second chart is a line graph tracking US semiconductor exports to China from 2015 to late 2020. It demonstrates a steady rise from about $0.5 billion in 2015 to a peak of nearly $1.1 billion in mid-2020. Annotations highlight key policy shifts: a May 16, 2019 restriction placing US-produced technology out of reach for Huawei, and a stricter August 17, 2020 restriction banning any technology based on US technology from reaching Huawei, which triggered a sharp downturn in export values toward the end of 2020.

The third chart, a stacked bar graph based on AmCham China survey data from 2017 to 2019, shows the percentage of US multinationals planning to relocate manufacturing out of China. In all three years, the overwhelming majority—upwards of 80% to 85% of respondents—had no plans to move, while only a small single-digit percentage had actually relocated and roughly 10% to 15% were considering it.

The final stacked bar graph explains this reluctance by breaking down the destination of sales for US multinational foreign affiliates across four sectors: Manufacturers, Capital Goods, Computer and electronics, and Pharmaceuticals. In each sector, only a small fraction of sales, around 10% to 15%, goes back to the United States. Instead, the largest portion, ranging from roughly 45% to over 50%, goes directly to the host country, with the remainder going to other foreign countries. This pattern underscores that these foreign operations are strategically placed to serve their local markets rather than act as export hubs for the US.

This appendix page, titled "Executive Summary Appendix: The US, at war with itself," examines the intense social and political polarization in the United States around late 2020 and early 2021. The author argues that the partisan balance across federal and state levels of government has reached an almost exact 50/50 split, and that the Democratic majority in the House of Representatives is at one of its narrowest points since 1901. This political division is accompanied by deep mutual animosity and a notable surge in domestic firearm purchases.

Six charts illustrate these dynamics in detail. The first chart, "Federal/State Partisan Balance Index, 1937-2021," plots percentage control of the House, Senate, Governorships, State Senates, and State Houses. Shaded in blue for Democratic control and red for Republican control, it shows that the balance has converged to an almost exact 50/50 split in 2021 after decades of shifting majorities. The second chart, "Partisan House leadership by majority party since 1901," lists the majority party's percentage advantage in descending order. It highlights historic eras of high dominance, such as the FDR era in 1937 (approaching a 60% advantage), the LBJ era in 1965 (around 48%), and the JFK era in 1961 (around 31%). By comparison, the Republican "red wave" of 2015 saw about a 12% advantage, and the 2021 balance is sitting near 0%, representing one of the smallest House advantages in over a century.

The next sequence of charts shifts focus to public sentiment. A bar chart of "GOP voter surveys" from mid-December 2020 displays the percentage of Republican respondents holding specific views: roughly 67% believed the election was unfair, 67% believed mail-in voting led to fraud, 53% believed the courts were biased against Trump, and 42% believed Trump should not concede under any circumstances. 

Another bar chart displays the "Percentage of respondents who believe members of opposing party are immoral," comparing survey results from 2016 and 2019 on a scale of 0% to 60%. The data shows a rising sense of moral condemnation on both sides. In 2016, 35% of Democrats viewed Republicans as immoral, and 46% of Republicans viewed Democrats similarly. By 2019, those proportions increased to 45% for Democrats viewing Republicans and 53% for Republicans viewing Democrats.

This growing division is further analyzed in the chart "Survey respondents' feeling toward own vs opposing party," which tracks sentiment from 1976 to 2020 on a scale of warmth to antipathy from -40 degrees to 40 degrees. While warmth toward one's own party has remained stable between 20 degrees and 30 degrees, antipathy toward the opposing party has steadily worsened, dropping from nearly neutral (just under 0 degrees) in the late 1970s to nearly -30 degrees in 2020. This indicates that for the first time, negative feelings for the opposing party outweigh positive feelings for one's own.

Finally, the chart "Monthly firearm sales, proxied by background checks" demonstrates a tangible real-world outcome of these tensions. Measuring the deviation from the expected number of background checks in millions from 2010 to 2020 on a scale of -1.0 to 2.0 million, the line chart highlights significant demand spikes during major national events. Notable historic peaks occurred after the Sandy Hook shooting in late 2012 (around 1.1 million deviation), the San Bernardino shooting in late 2015 (around 1.4 million deviation), and the Parkland shooting in early 2018 (around 0.8 million deviation). These are eclipsed by a massive double-peak in 2020 associated with the onset of COVID-19 and the general election, which drove background checks more than 1.0 million above expected levels.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the evolving geopolitical and military dynamics between the United States and China, specifically examining Taiwan as a potential flashpoint. Author Michael Cembalest argues that while rhetoric has deteriorated, the unprecedented depth of economic integration between the US and China challenges the "Thucydides Trap" theory of inevitable military conflict. However, the military balance of power in the region has shifted dramatically, potentially reducing the likelihood of US intervention if China were to challenge Taiwan's independence.

The first chart, titled "China and the US: much deeper economic linkages than actual and potential adversaries of the last 100 years," plots economic integration as a percentage of combined GDP across fifteen historical adversary dyads. The data series consists of bilateral annual trade, bilateral central bank holdings of each other's government debt, and bilateral foreign direct investment stock. The US-China relationship in 2014 stands out dramatically at nearly 8% of combined GDP, whereas historical rivals like France and Germany in 1930, the US and Japan in 1940, or the US and Russia in 1983 barely reached 1% of combined GDP. This highlights that the modern economic interdependence between the US and China has no historical precedent among global rivals.

The second chart, "Global energy vs semiconductor market capitalizations" in trillions of US dollars from 2004 to 2020, compares the MSCI AC World Energy Index and the MSCI AC World Semiconductor Index. It illustrates a structural shift in global market reliance from traditional oil and gas to microchips. The energy index peaked above $4.0 trillion in 2008 before falling to under $2.0 trillion in 2020. Conversely, the semiconductor index rose from under $0.5 trillion in 2004 to over $2.0 trillion in 2020, overtaking the energy index. This shift underscores Taiwan's growing strategic value to global supply chains, given that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company has surpassed Intel in market capitalization.

A third chart tracks "US arms sales to Taiwan" in billions of US dollars from 1990 to 2018. It shows sporadic, multi-billion-dollar annual transactions, featuring a massive spike of over $8 billion in 1992 and a rising trend of substantial purchases throughout the late 2000s and 2010s. Cembalest points out that in 2019, US arms sales to Taiwan hit their highest dollar figure on record, reflecting deteriorating US-China relations and Taiwan’s efforts to bolster its defense. 

The final chart, "China and US military spending" in billions of US dollars, visualizes defense budgets broken down into hardware, structures, and personnel. While China's officially reported defense budget is shown to be relatively modest at around $175 billion, the second bar shows that normalizing China's budget for wage levels and purchasing power parity (PPP) skyrockets its effective military spending to roughly $450 billion. This adjusted figure represents about 90% of the reported US defense budget of approximately $550 billion. This adjusted budget reveals that Chinese spending on military hardware and structures is nearly on par with that of the United States, illustrating how the regional balance of power has shifted and eroded the US military's ability to reliably enforce its protective umbrella over Taiwan.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan Outlook, titled China Index Weight, examines the characteristics of Chinese fixed income and credit risk. The author argues that while China is typically treated as an emerging market for equity investors, its scale, low volatility, high yields, and favorable creditor status make it look more like a developed market for fixed-income investors. 

The first chart, titled Foreign investment in Chinese stocks and bonds, shows total foreign investment in trillions of RMB from 2014 to 2020. The chart illustrates a steady rise in foreign holdings, growing from under one trillion RMB in 2014 to over four trillion RMB by 2020, split roughly evenly between stocks and bonds. The author notes that the two trillion RMB added to bonds since 2014 represents just two percent of China's domestic fixed income market, and that China’s three percent weight in the Barclays Global Aggregate is set to rise to six percent upon full inclusion. 

The second chart, Yield to worst vs volatility of aggregate bond indices from 2013 to 2020, plots annualized volatility against yield to worst. It highlights China as an attractive outlier, boasting a yield of over three percent with relatively low volatility of around three percent. In contrast, the US offers a yield of roughly one percent, while European nations like Germany and Spain trade at negative yields with higher annualized volatility.

The second section addresses Chinese credit risk and how its debt structure differs from the United States. Although the line between public and corporate debt is blurred due to state-owned enterprises, the chart General government and non-financial corporate debt shows that both the US and China have overall combined debt levels reaching roughly 210 percent of GDP as of late 2020. However, China’s pure government debt remains low, hovering around 40 percent of GDP, meaning the bulk of its leverage resides in non-financial corporate debt. 

Importantly, the author emphasizes that Chinese debt is predominantly held internally rather than externally. This dynamic is illustrated in the final chart, Net international investment position as a percentage of trailing four-quarter GDP in the second quarter of 2020. This chart contrasts net creditor nations against net debtor nations. China stands as a net creditor nation at around 15 percent of GDP, alongside countries like Switzerland, the Netherlands, Germany, and Japan. Conversely, the United States is a major net debtor at nearly negative 70 percent of GDP, joined by other nations such as Brazil, France, and the United Kingdom. The author concludes by noting that China's net external debt to GDP is only 15 percent, compared to a substantial 95 percent in the United States, cementing China's favorable risk profile for global bond investors.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication addresses why the United States equity market consistently outperforms Europe and Japan. Cembalest argues against contrarian calls to overweight Europe and Japan, noting that since January 2010, US equities generated total returns of 319 percent, compared to 124 percent for Japan, 87 percent for Europe, and 73 percent for Emerging Markets. He attributes this outperformance primarily to microeconomic factors: a heavier index concentration in high-growth technology and structurally higher profitability within individual sectors. Demographically, a footnote adds that the prime income population aged 30 to 49 is projected to expand by 5 percent in the US from 2020 to 2025, while declining by 3 percent in Europe.

Several visuals support this analysis. The first chart, titled Overweight US, underweight Europe and Japan, displays the three-year rolling outperformance and underperformance versus the MSCI All World Index from 1991 through 2018. It shows a prolonged period of positive rolling performance for the overweight US strategy starting around 2012, which contrast with a deep period of underperformance leading up to the 2008 financial crisis. 

The adjacent line chart, titled US outperforming Europe and Japan, tracks cumulative total returns in US dollars from January 2010 to early 2021, starting at a base value of 100. By late 2020, the S&P 500 line rises to nearly 400, while the MSCI Japan and MSCI Europe lines both lag significantly, ending near 200.

A bar chart titled High growth tech drives US markets, growth laggards drive Europe and Japan shows the percentage of total index market cap as of late December 2020. The US has over 30 percent of its market cap in technology and less than 15 percent in materials, energy, and industrials combined. In Europe, tech represents less than 10 percent while cyclicals represent nearly 30 percent. Japan similarly has only about 13 percent in tech and over 25 percent in cyclicals.

Finally, two tables demonstrate superior US corporate profitability across major sectors, including consumer staples, consumer discretionary, technology, healthcare, communication services, and financials. In the Return on Assets table, the US leads all regions in every sector; for example, US technology return on assets is 9.9 percent compared to 5.4 percent in Europe and 3.9 percent in Japan, while US consumer discretionary is 4.1 percent compared to Europe's 0.6 percent and Japan's 1.7 percent. In the Return on Equity table, the US shows similar dominance, with US technology return on equity at 27.6 percent compared to Europe’s 14.6 percent and Japan’s 9.3 percent, and US consumer discretionary return on equity at 25.1 percent compared to 5.5 percent for Europe and 5.0 percent for Japan.

This page outlines a bullish case for emerging markets, asserting they offer investors a "trifecta of value" consisting of improved current account balances, undervalued currencies, and lower equity valuations compared to Europe. Although emerging market equity investors have faced headwinds in recent years—such as a growth slowdown in China, commodity price collapses, US trade tensions, and COVID-19—several supportive factors are now in play. These include subsiding pandemic risks, underway economic recoveries, low US real interest rates, a rapid Chinese recovery, and stimulative policies across many emerging market nations. Notably, despite record inflows in November, emerging market equities were still on track for their largest yearly outflows on record in 2020.

Four charts support this value thesis. The first chart, depicting emerging market current account balances as a percentage of GDP in Q2/Q3 2020, compares current levels against their worst levels from 2014 to 2016. Across the vast majority of analyzed countries—including Taiwan, Malaysia, Mexico, South Africa, South Korea, India, and China—current account balances have significantly improved compared to their mid-decade lows. Taiwan shows the strongest current account balance at roughly 13% of GDP, while Saudi Arabia displays the deepest deficit near negative 15% of GDP.

The second chart traces the real trade-weighted emerging market currency basket from 2004 through November 2020 to illustrate valuation. The currency basket entered deeply undervalued territory in late 2020, hovering around negative 4%, a stark contrast to the overvalued peaks of nearly 6% observed around 2010 and 2013.

The third chart illustrates the price-to-earnings discount of emerging markets versus Europe from 2006 to early 2021, measured as the MSCI EM forward P/E discount or premium relative to the Stoxx 600. After reaching premium levels of up to 15% prior to 2010, emerging market valuations have traded at a persistent discount, sitting at roughly a 10% to 15% discount heading into 2021.

The final chart shows regional equity returns since December 2014, indexing total returns in US dollars to a baseline of 100. By the end of 2020, the MSCI US and MSCI China indexes led performance, both nearing a total return index value of 200. The broader MSCI Emerging Markets index trailed these leaders at approximately 140, but still outperformed MSCI Europe, which remained the lowest-performing region with a total return index value of around 120.

This page, titled "Antitrust enforcement: coming to a tech company near you," outlines the rising tide of regulatory scrutiny facing major US technology giants. Michael Cembalest argues that after reaching a postwar low in late 2017, antitrust enforcement is seeing a rebirth. He highlights key regulatory actions, including the Department of Justice's and various State Attorneys General's lawsuits against Google, consumer class-actions over data privacy, ongoing debates around amending or revoking Section 230 indemnity, and the FTC's antitrust lawsuit targeting Facebook to unwind its acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp. He also points to the aggressive, though politically uncertain, antitrust agenda laid out in the October 2020 House Judiciary Report under a narrow Democratic congressional majority.

To illustrate the historical context of enforcement, a bar chart displays the number of Department of Justice antitrust investigations initiated from 1970 to 2018, broken down by mergers, monopolies, and competition cases. The data shows a precipitous decline from peak levels of over 500 annual investigations in the late 1970s and early 1980s to significantly lower levels by the late 2010s. An adjacent column chart demonstrates that industry consolidation has returned to its historic 1969 peak, measuring the revenues of the largest 15 companies as a percentage of US GDP. While the 1969 peak of roughly 9% was driven by industrial conglomerates, the matching 2020 peak of about 9% is dominated by tech, telecom, and e-commerce giants, contrasting with a lower intermediate peak of around 4% in 2000.

Finally, a comprehensive market share table for US digital markets underscores the dominance of Big Tech firms, specifically Google, Apple, Facebook, Amazon, and Microsoft. Notable statistics include Google and Apple capturing 99% of phone operating systems (52% and 47%, respectively); Google commanding 91% of search services (including images, maps, and YouTube) and 80% of navigation apps; Amazon holding 73% of video game streaming, 70% of eBooks, 84% of e-readers, and 54% of e-commerce; and Facebook controlling 51% of social media and 50% of social media digital photos. Together, these five tech giants, along with Microsoft, frequently secure dominant combined subtotals across crucial digital categories, reinforcing why regulators are intensifying their focus.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market series argues that negative policy rates have had a highly detrimental impact on European banks. The author, Michael Cembalest, asserts that European bank equity returns and valuations have severely lagged behind their US peers since the European Central Bank introduced negative rates in 2014. Highlighting a concept from Princeton economist Markus Brunnermeier, the page discusses the "reversal rate," a tipping point where further rate reductions do more harm to bank profitability and credit supply than they do to stimulate the economy. The author strongly cautions against bringing negative interest rate policies to the United States.

To support this argument, the page features three charts and one table. The first chart, showing total return performance in US dollars from 2009 to 2021 (normalized to 100 in January 2009), shows a stark divergence following the start of the ECB's negative interest rate era in 2014. While the S&P 500 banks index climbed steadily to peak near 300, the Euro STOXX banks index stagnated and eventually fell to around 50 by late 2020. A second, adjacent chart tracking price-to-book ratios from 2009 to 2021 shows a similar gap. After 2014, the price-to-book ratio for S&P 500 banks recovered to trade between 1.2 and 1.4, whereas the Euro STOXX banks index languished at a heavily discounted valuation of 0.4 to 0.6.

A third chart examines the components of European bank profitability in billions of euros from 2007 to 2019. It demonstrates that recent profit gains are not organic. Operating income remained flat at roughly 500 billion euros and operating expenses remained stable at roughly negative 300 to 350 billion euros. Instead, the slight recovery in bottom-line profits—reaching close to 100 billion euros by 2019—was driven almost entirely by a sharp reduction in loan loss provisions, which shrank from nearly negative 200 billion euros during the eurozone crisis to near zero.

Finally, a table details the percentage of the J.P. Morgan GBI Broad Index trading with negative yields as of November 30, 2020. It reveals that 64% of the total index trades at negative yields, including 100% of all debt maturing in 1 to 5 years. In Denmark, Finland, Germany, and the Netherlands, 100% of all outstanding government debt across all maturities trades with negative yields. Even in the 10-plus year maturity bucket, 54% of Austrian debt, 45% of French and Belgian debt, and 39% of Irish debt offer negative yields, illustrating how deeply negative interest rates have permeated European financial markets.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2021 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, explores whether investors can generate marginal returns without taking on excessive portfolio risk by utilizing "hybrid" investments. These hybrids include high-yield bonds and loans, collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS), convertible bonds, equity and mortgage REITs, preferred stock, and utility stocks. The author synthesizes J.P. Morgan's Global Long Term Strategy Team's analysis, which compares traditional 60-40 stock-bond portfolios with a hybrid-inclusive portfolio composed of 40% hybrids, 40% stocks, and 20% bonds.

The first visual, a scatter plot titled "Traditional 60/40 portfolio vs portfolio with hybrids," plots forward-looking annualized return over 10 years against 10-year annualized volatility of compound returns from 1987 to 2019. It evaluates four regions: the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and Japan. The traditional portfolios, shown as blue dots, are compared against the hybrid-inclusive portfolios, shown as gold dots. In every region, the shift to a hybrid-inclusive allocation projects a modest increase in return alongside a modest increase in volatility. For instance, the US traditional portfolio points to roughly a 2.8% return with about 6.0% volatility, while the hybrid portfolio shifts up to around a 3.3% return with similar volatility. Japan’s traditional portfolio sits at approximately a 2.5% return with 9.0% volatility, while its hybrid equivalent increases the projected return to about 3.2% with roughly 9.2% volatility.

The second visual is a performance table assessing nine hybrid asset classes during calmer periods and major crises. It outlines their annualized returns from 2011 to 2019 alongside their daily, monthly, and quarterly maximum drawdowns during the 2008–2009 Great Financial Crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 recession. On average, the hybrid classes delivered a 7.0% annualized return from 2011 to 2019, but they suffered significant daily maximum drawdowns: averaging a loss of 51% during the Great Financial Crisis and 31% during the 2020 recession. Highly volatile sub-sectors like mortgage REITs saw maximum daily drawdowns of 72% in the 2008–2009 recession and 71% in the 2020 recession, despite an annualized return of just 4.5% during the stable period. In contrast, utility stocks achieved a high annualized return of 12.3% with relatively lower daily drawdowns of 50% in 2008–2009 and 37% in 2020. Across all categories, drawdowns appear less severe when viewed through a monthly or quarterly lens rather than a daily one. 

Ultimately, the author cautions that while long-term risk measures calculated over decades can smooth over periods of extreme volatility, hybrid investments often experience equity-like drawdowns during market crises. Investors must firmly commit to a truly long-term horizon to successfully capture the benefits of these diversified hybrid portfolios.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2021 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, discusses the characteristics and historical patterns of gold rallies, highlighting that while gold can rally significantly, these periods of outperformance are highly infrequent and separated by long stretches of underperformance. The author notes that gold's rise of approximately 80 percent from its post-financial crisis low is modest compared to three prior historical spikes: the 1930s Great Depression, the 1970s stagflation era, and the 2000s post-tech collapse and financial crisis. 

The first chart on the page, titled "When gold prices rise, they usually rise by a lot," plots gold prices in US dollars per Troy ounce on a log scale from 1900 to 2020. It illustrates four distinct historical periods of rapid price increases: a 68 percent rise during the Great Depression when major nations abandoned the gold standard, a massive 2,333 percent surge during 1970s stagflation as the fiat money era began, a 644 percent increase in the 2000s when the Federal Reserve embraced negative real interest rates, and a more modest 79 percent rise associated with perpetual deficits and the COVID-19 response. 

The second chart, titled "The infrequent outperformance of gold," shows the five-year rolling outperformance or underperformance of gold compared to a balanced portfolio of 65 percent stocks, 25 percent bonds, and 10 percent T-Bills from 1932 to 2020. This visual emphasizes that gold underperformed for several decades prior to World War II and went through a 22-year period of negative relative returns following the 1970s peak before showing net portfolio benefits again in the 2000s. 

Looking forward, Cembalest notes that massive COVID-19 stimulus, a surge in the money supply relative to gold production, political indifference to US deficit reduction, and the popularity of Modern Monetary Theory all support the case for gold. He observes that central banks had recently turned into net buyers of gold, and despite a brief pause in the third quarter of 2020 when financially stretched countries like Turkey sold gold to fund pandemic responses, he forecasts that central banks will resume buying gold in 2021. Ultimately, he cautions investors that while a gold rally has significant potential, poor timing on a gold investment can take a generation or more to reverse.

This page consists entirely of legal and regulatory disclosures and distribution disclaimers for J.P. Morgan entities operating across multiple global jurisdictions, including Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s financial outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, focuses on the role of gold in macroeconomic history and modern monetary policy through four distinct charts. 

The first chart, titled "The earlier a country abandoned its gold standard, the faster its economy recovered," visualizes historical research by Barry Eichengreen. It plots an economic activity index starting in 1929 at 100 against years ranging from 1929 to 1937 on the horizontal axis, and index values from 50 to 175 on the vertical axis. The chart tracks Japan, the United Kingdom, Germany, the United States, and France, marking the specific year each nation exited the gold standard. Japan, which abandoned the gold standard early, recovered fastest, with its index climbing near 175 by 1937. Conversely, France, which remained on the standard longest, stayed depressed, remaining below an index value of 100.

The second chart displays the "Lowest real yields on cash since 1830, other than during wartime," showing the five-year average of T-bill and Fed Funds rates minus inflation. The horizontal axis covers nearly two centuries, from 1830 to 2020, while the vertical axis represents real yields from negative 10 percent to positive 15 percent. Blue and red bars track historical yields, showing that negative real interest rates are historically unprecedented outside of wartime periods like the American Civil War, World War I, and World War II. However, following the tech collapse and the 2008 financial crisis, the Federal Reserve implemented policies that pushed real yields into negative territory once again during peacetime.

The third chart analyzes the "Growth in US money supply vs global gold production," plotting the ratio of the increase in M2 relative to the increase in gold production from 1966 through a 2020 estimate. The vertical axis measures this ratio from 0x to 45x. Significant spikes in M2 growth relative to gold production are evident, particularly a spike of over 40x in the early 1970s and a 2020 estimate rising toward 25x. Shaded pink regions indicate historic gold rallies, demonstrating that periods when the U.S. money supply surged relative to gold production have historically preceded major gold market expansions.

The final chart, titled "Global central bank gold purchases and holdings," utilizes a dual-axis layout to display quarterly data from 2010 to 2020. Net purchases in tonnes are plotted on the left-hand vertical axis, ranging from negative 50 to 300 tonnes, while holdings as a percentage of total reserves are plotted on the right-hand axis, ranging from 9 percent to 14 percent. Blue vertical bars show net central bank purchases, which fluctuated but remained largely positive over the decade. An olive line tracks central bank gold holdings as a percentage of total reserves, showing a steady rise from around 10 percent in 2015 to nearly 14 percent by late 2020, representing the highest share of reserves held in gold since 2002.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market 2021 Outlook focuses on the long-term sustainability of US federal debt and the potential threat it poses to the US dollar's status as the world's primary reserve currency. Author Michael Cembalest argues that standard debt-to-GDP metrics, while concerning, understate the true burden because they ignore demographic shifts. By analyzing federal debt per working-age person, he highlights the pressure on the tax base responsible for servicing this debt, noting that similar fiscal strain has historically marked the end of prior reserve currency nations.

The page features two line charts tracking gross federal debt from 1940 through 2020, with estimates for 2020 and 2021. The first chart plots debt as a percentage of US GDP, showing a steep climb from about 40% in the late 2000s to around 80% by 2020, with 2020 and 2021 estimates rising sharply toward the historic World War II peak of over 100%. The second chart displays gross federal debt per working-age person in real 2012 dollars. This demographic-adjusted metric reveals an unprecedented spike, with debt per working-age person soaring past 70,000 dollars and approaching 80,000 dollars in the 2020 and 2021 estimates, far eclipsing the post-World War II peak of roughly 30,000 dollars.

To put this fiscal trajectory into historical perspective, the page lists a timeline of global reserve and dominant trade currencies, emphasizing their temporary nature. The timeline spans from Rome in the first century BC to the fourth century AD, the Byzantine Empire in the fifth century, the Arabian Dinar from the seventh to tenth centuries, Florence from the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries, Portugal from 1450 to 1530, the Iberian Union from 1530 to 1640, the Netherlands from 1640 to 1720, France from 1720 to 1815, the United Kingdom from 1815 to 1920, and finally the United States from 1920 to the present.

A final pie chart details the currency composition of global foreign exchange reserves as of the second quarter of 2020, showing that the US dollar still maintains a major share at 61.3%. The Euro follows at 20.3%, with other allocations including the Japanese Yen at 5.7%, Pounds Sterling at 4.5%, the Chinese Renminbi at 2.0%, the Canadian Dollar at 1.9%, the Australian Dollar at 1.7%, the Swiss Franc at 0.2%, and other currencies making up the remaining 2.5%. Together, these visuals present an open question regarding how much longer the US can maintain its monetary dominance under its current debt trajectory.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest analyzes the legal challenges surrounding the 2020 US presidential election, the mischaracterization of certain executive orders, and the shifting political landscape for both major parties. On the legal front, Cembalest references legal expert Charles Geyh to highlight how Trump's lawyers struggled to transition from political rhetoric to strict judicial standards. While the US Supreme Court could eventually rule on certain election administration cases—specifically whether state legislatures hold exclusive constitutional authority over election rules as opposed to state courts—such decisions would only affect future elections and not alter the 2020 results, including those in Pennsylvania. Cembalest points to a Wisconsin Supreme Court ruling and disputes over "indefinitely confined" voter status in Dane County to illustrate the near-impossible hurdle of reversing election results after they have occurred. 

Additionally, the author debunks viral social media theories regarding Executive Order 13848, clarifying that it deals solely with foreign election interference sanctions and holds no jurisdiction over domestic election results or internal challenges. Looking ahead to the political future of the GOP, Cembalest notes the looming threat of primary challenges for Republicans who refuse to object to the electoral votes during the January 6 Joint Session, referencing a famous Ben Franklin quote to underscore the party's internal tension. Finally, he outlines the fragile position of the Democratic Party, which holds one of its smallest House majorities since 1900 and faces historical headwinds in the 2022 midterms. He points to the J.P. Morgan Partisan Balance Index to demonstrate that the 2020 elections actually shifted state and national legislative balance further to the right rather than delivering a predicted "Blue Wave."

This J.P. Morgan report by Michael Cembalest discusses the rules of engagement and the legal, political, and statistical background surrounding the contentious upcoming Joint Session of Congress on January 6 to certify the 2020 US Presidential Election. The author highlights how COVID-19 prompted widespread changes to state election laws in 2020, leading to a wave of pre-election litigation. Courts in states like Minnesota, Wisconsin, Ohio, South Carolina, Georgia, and Arizona successfully struck down attempts to relax certain rules, such as signature requirements and absentee deadlines. After the election, the Trump campaign and associated groups launched numerous lawsuits that were overwhelmingly dismissed. The author notes that out of 40 post-election cases, the campaign suffered 36 defeats, had 4 pending, and achieved 0 wins. Bipartisan judges cited a lack of standing, unsubstantiated fraud claims, and the legal principle of "laches" as reasons for dismissal. Despite this, over 100 Republican House Representatives and at least 13 Republican Senators, led by Senator Josh Hawley, are poised to challenge the Electoral College results.

To illustrate the unprecedented nature of the election, the page features a bar chart titled "Absentee/mail-in ballot share, 2016 vs 2020," which displays mail-in votes as a percentage of total votes cast across key swing states: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Iowa. The chart demonstrates a dramatic surge in absentee voting; for example, Michigan’s share increased from approximately 25% in 2016 to over 60% in 2020, while both Pennsylvania and Wisconsin rose from under 10% to more than 40%. 

An accompanying table titled "Rejected absentee/mail-in ballot percentage" shows rejection rates across the same states for the years 2016, 2018, and 2020. The data reveals that despite the massive surge in absentee ballot volume, rejection rates fell significantly in 2020. Georgia’s rejection rate declined from 6.42% in 2016 to 0.60% in 2020; Pennsylvania’s dropped from 0.95% to 0.28%; and Iowa's fell from 0.65% to 0.15%. Data points for Arizona and Wisconsin in 2020 are marked as unavailable. 

The author raises an open question regarding how Senator Josh Hawley, who once clerked for Chief Justice Roberts, will respond to criticisms of Roberts' character and judicial rulings that have been promoted by Donald Trump.

This commentary by Michael Cembalest analyzes the upcoming January 6 Joint Session of Congress, explaining why the Electoral Count Act of 1887 will govern the proceedings rather than a twelfth amendment contingent election. The author provides historical context, noting that the Act was passed in the decade following the bitter 1876 election crisis to resolve disputes over competing electors. He outlines how the law requires both chambers to vote separately on competing slates of electors under ordinary voting rules where each member casts a single vote. Given that Democrats hold a slim ten-seat margin in the House, and the Senate stands at 51 Republicans to 48 Democrats, the author points out that it would take only two Republican Senators voting with Democrats to accept the certified Joe Biden electors, dooming any competing Donald Trump slates in the Senate.

Cembalest further explains that if the House and Senate disagree on competing slates, the tie-breaker by law goes to the slate certified by the state's governor. Because the governors of Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, Arizona, and Georgia have already approved the Biden slates, the only way for Donald Trump to win would be if both chambers accepted three or more uncertified Trump slates that lack governor, legislative, or court approval. Although Vice President Mike Pence holds procedural roles, the author asserts that none of these decisions allow the Vice President to unilaterally determine the election outcome. Additionally, objections to single certified slates are expected to fail because discarding a slate requires approval from both chambers, which the Democratic-controlled House would not grant.

Finally, the page addresses media coverage concerning twelfth amendment contingent elections, clarifying that they are highly unlikely and only occur under specific circumstances, such as an Electoral College tie, faithless elector scenarios, or candidate incapacitation. In a detailed footnote, the author notes that while some scholars argue the Electoral Count Act is unconstitutional, ignoring it would plunge the country into a constitutional crisis where, if unresolved by January 20, the Speaker of the House—presumably Nancy Pelosi—would have the opportunity to resign and be sworn in as Acting President.

This page introduces the "Fear of Flying" commentary, which explores soaring equity markets, the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, and corporate political shifts in the aftermath of the January 6th Capitol Building riot. Author Michael Cembalest observes that equity markets have been on an extraordinary tear since April 2020, with multiple indices rising at annualized rates of 90% to 130%. While J.P. Morgan forecasts a global rebound in growth, corporate profits, and employment for the year, the author advises investors to keep some "dry powder" on hand. He warns against assuming one-directional market growth given lingering uncertainties over COVID-19 mutations and vaccine efficacy, predicting a rising market in 2021 punctuated by bouts of intense profit-taking. The upcoming sections of the report are outlined to cover topics such as megacap stock headwinds, recovering oil consumption, lagging European equities, and vaccine progress, highlighting an upcoming webcast with Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel.

A prominent line chart titled "All Systems Go" illustrates total returns in U.S. dollars from January 2019 to January 2021, with all series indexed to 100 at the start date. The chart visualizes a dramatic recovery and divergence across asset classes following the March 2020 pandemic market bottom. Bitcoin is the top performer by a massive margin, surging completely off the chart's vertical axis to reach an index level of 987 by mid-January 2021. Among traditional equity indices, the MSCI Global Alternative Energy index experienced a dramatic year-end spike to near 300, closely followed by S&P 500 Semiconductors and FAANG stocks, which ended in the 225 to 250 range. The NASDAQ index rose to around 200, outperforming the S&P 500 Consumer Discretionary index at approximately 175, the broader S&P 500 at roughly 150, and the MSCI Emerging Markets index, which finished the period just under 150.

This page addresses the factors driving the soaring equity markets, concluding that widespread investor participation and high optimism are primary drivers. The author highlights rapidly rising gross and net hedge fund exposures, which toward the end of 2020 rose faster than the market itself. This trend is illustrated in two top-level charts. The first, measuring North American hedge fund exposures versus the S&P 500 from January 2020 to January 2021, shows both gross and net notional exposures sharply climbing by over 40% and 50% respectively, far outstripping the S&P 500 total return of nearly 20%. The second chart shows the six-month percentage change in hedge fund net exposure and S&P 500 returns from 2015 to 2020, depicting a dramatic parallel surge in both series during the latter half of 2020. 

In addition to rising exposures, the market experienced a painful short squeeze and a sharp decline in risk aversion. A middle-left chart tracking the index level of the 50 highest short interest names in the Russell 3000 from 2008 to late 2020 shows a massive spike, skyrocketing past an index level of 250 toward 300 as forced short covering took hold. This speculative behavior is mirrored on the middle-right by a chart of the equity put-call ratio from 2000 to 2020. The ratio, representing the number of put options purchased relative to call options, collapsed to around 0.4 in late 2020, a level last seen during the dot-com era of 2000, indicating a complete drop-off in demand for portfolio insurance. Furthermore, the author notes that 59 stocks trading at over ten times sales have doubled in the prior three months.

Despite the soaring stock market, demand remains resilient for long-duration fixed income. A chart at the bottom-left tracks investor demand at 30-year US Treasury auctions as a percentage of total demand from 2006 to 2020, including direct bidders like pension funds and individuals, and indirect bidders like monetary authorities bidding through the Federal Reserve. This demand reached nearly 90% in late 2020, marking its highest level since 2006. The author explains that a mere 20 basis point backup in long-end yields was enough to attract this massive wave of interest. Looking ahead, the publication forecasts that treasury yields will rise further as the United States tracks toward a 10% deficit in 2021. This deficit projection is expected even before factoring in any potential future stimulus, such as President Joe Biden’s proposed $1.9 trillion spending package, which still faces a challenging path through Congress.

This page discusses the mounting challenges facing megacap technology stocks, characterizing their recent regulatory and public scrutiny as an "Icarus Moment." The author argues that megacaps are hitting severe headwinds due to antitrust actions, rising corporate tax rates, and proposed digital service taxes, suggesting that the peak era of megacap outperformance has passed. Historically, extreme concentrations of corporate power have triggered heavy government and citizen backlashes, a point illustrated by a reference to Senator John Sherman and the passage of the 1890 Sherman Antitrust Act. The text also touches on the difficult content moderation choices faced by web platforms, referencing the legal battle between Amazon Web Services and Parler, which may seek hosting via a firm in Russia.

To support this thesis, a table presents total returns across three periods: since June 2020, September 2020, and January 2021. It compares a group of equal-weighted antitrust targets—comprising Apple, Amazon, Facebook, and Google—against the S&P 500 on both a market-cap-weighted and equal-weighted basis. While the antitrust targets performed strongly from June 2020 with a 30.1% return, they subsequently struggled, returning negative 4.7% since September 2020 and negative 4.6% since January 2021. In contrast, the equal-weighted S&P 500 significantly outperformed these megacaps over those same intervals, gaining 18.7% and 2.8% respectively.

An accompanying line chart tracks S&P 500 megacap outperformance, plotted as the percentage performance of the market-cap-weighted S&P 500 minus the equal-weighted version. The chart compares the modern cycle of 2017 through 2021 against the historical dot-com boom and bust era from 1997 to 2002. The historical line shows outperformance peaking at nearly 50% in 2000 before plummeting to negative 20% by 2002. The modern line shows a similar, albeit less extreme, pattern, rising to a peak of around 20% in late 2020 before starting to decline, signaling a potential repeating cycle of mean reversion.

This page consists entirely of legal and regulatory disclosures for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication across multiple international jurisdictions. It outlines the specific distributing entities and governing regulatory bodies responsible for oversight in countries including Spain, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and various Latin American nations. The text details local licensing requirements, restrictions on public offerings of securities, limits of liability, and definitions of eligible client types, such as the restriction of materials to wholesale clients in Australia. No financial charts, market analysis, or investment forecasts are present on this page.

This page analyzes the critical race between surging COVID-19 mutations and the global vaccination rollout, while debunking online misinformation regarding the pandemic's true mortality rate. The author emphasizes that even if new virus mutations are not inherently more lethal, their high transmissibility inevitably drives up total deaths by vastly increasing the overall number of infections. 

This trend is visualized in three side-by-side charts tracking daily infections versus mortality from March 2020 to January 2021 for the United Kingdom, South Africa, and Ireland. In the United Kingdom, daily infections per million spiked to nearly 1,000 by early January 2021, with deaths per million climbing sharply toward 16. In South Africa, infections peaked near 350 per million, driving deaths to around 12 per million. Ireland's chart illustrates an even sharper vertical spike in early January 2021, where infections surged past 1,200 per million, causing hospitalizations and deaths to rise precipitously. 

Addressing vaccine efficacy, the author notes that while early laboratory research on Pfizer's vaccine shows its antibodies successfully neutralize some mutations found in the UK and South African variants, the E484 mutation from South Africa remains an open question that may demand new rounds of vaccine development. Furthermore, the rollout faces logistical bottlenecks and human hurdles. The text highlights significant vaccine resistance among US healthcare workers, citing resistance rates of 15 percent at Miami’s Jackson Healthcare System, 22 percent at Michigan’s Henry Ford Health System, 30 percent in New York City, and up to 60 percent among Ohio nursing home staff. The author expresses confidence in current vector and mRNA vaccines but states a personal preference for upcoming recombinant protein vaccines.

Two bottom charts emphasize the scale of the vaccination effort and actual mortality. The first, tracking total vaccinations as a percentage of the population from mid-December 2020 to mid-January 2021, shows the United Kingdom leading the transition at over 5.5 percent, followed by the United States at around 3.5 percent, while Italy, Canada, Germany, and France lag behind below 2 percent. The final chart tracks weekly excess deaths in the United States from 2017 to early 2021 to debunk the online fallacy that COVID-19 deaths merely offset other causes of death. By comparing actual weekly deaths from all causes against the standard threshold for excess deaths, the chart reveals massive, unprecedented surges far above normal baseline levels, peaking near 90,000 deaths per week in early 2021 and proving COVID-19's severe net impact on mortality.

This page focuses on the fallout from the January 6, 2021, DC insurrection, specifically analyzing corporate PAC funding for Congressional objectors. In the wake of the event, several US companies announced plans to halt political donations to members of Congress who objected to the Electoral College results. To contextualize this shift, the author examines political funding sources across the US House and Senate, utilizing data compiled by the Center for Responsive Politics and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. 

The first visual, a stacked bar chart titled "Political funding sources," displays average funding sources for the 2014, 2016, and 2018 election cycles divided by political party and Congressional chamber. The chart shows that political action committees (PACs) are a much larger funding source for the House of Representatives than for the Senate. In the House, PACs make up roughly 40% of the funding for both Democrats and Republicans. In the Senate, PACs represent a smaller share, accounting for roughly 18% of funding for Democrats and 23% for Republicans. Large individual contributions over $200 make up the largest portion of funding for Senate candidates—over 50% for both parties—while small individual contributions under $200 and self-financing or other funding sources make up the remaining fractions.

The second visual is a pie chart titled "Congressional candidate funding by type of PAC, % of total," focusing on the top 50 recipients in the 2020 election. This chart illustrates that corporate PACs dominate overall PAC funding at 66%, followed by ideological PACs at 25%, and labor PACs at 9%. 

In addressing who receives corporate PAC donations, the author evaluates the common belief that corporate funding is primarily directed toward moderate politicians. The analysis reveals this is only partially true. While corporate PAC donations to Republican Senators align proportionally with their ideological spectrum—indicating no specific preference for moderates—funding to Democratic Senators is notably skewed toward centrist members, with the most progressive Democratic Senators receiving virtually no corporate PAC funding.

Footnotes on the page provide additional legal and financial context. Constitutional law advisor Michael Morley explains that establishing an election audit commission after Congress begins counting electoral votes is procedurally impossible under the Electoral Count Act. Additionally, the author notes that these datasets exclude SuperPACs, which are prohibited from contributing directly to candidates. SuperPAC spending exploded to $2 billion in 2020, with 55% of that spending leaning conservative and 45% liberal, and with just twenty-five mega-donors accounting for half of all individual contributions to SuperPACs.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication explores the complex debate surrounding corporate PAC funding for Congressional politicians, specifically addressing the aftermath of the January 6, 2021 objections to the US presidential election certification. 

To contextualize corporate donation patterns, the page features two charts illustrating how political ideology, scored on an x-axis from -1.0 (more liberal) to 1.0 (more conservative), relates to 2020 corporate PAC funding in millions of dollars. The left chart displays US Senate data, comparing the number of senators in each political ideological band to total corporate PAC donations. The bar graph shows that the majority of senators cluster in moderate-left and moderate-right camps, and the line graph indicates that PAC funding closely follows this pattern. Moderate conservatives around the 0.5 ideology score received a peak of nearly $18 million in 2020 corporate PAC donations, while moderate liberals around the -0.3 score received a peak of about $8 million. Extreme liberals and extreme conservatives received almost zero funding. The right chart shows similar dynamics for the House of Representatives, where moderate-liberal donations peaked around $12 million and moderate-conservative donations peaked near $14 million, with political extremes again receiving negligible funding. This data illustrates that corporate PAC contributions already heavily favor centrist politicians.

The text presents the competing arguments regarding whether corporations should halt PAC donations to the members of Congress who objected to the election results. Arguments to cease funding center on the premise that the objections were groundless, as no states officially submitted competing elector slates and court cases uniformly rejected claims of fraud; thus, the objections represented attempts to disenfranchise voters, violating the core values of many corporate PACs. Conversely, arguments against ceasing funding emphasize that the objecting politicians, such as Josh Hawley and Ted Cruz, were exercising legal rights established by the Electoral Count Act of 1887 to resolve disputes peacefully. This perspective warns that corporate punishment for using legal avenues could incentivize politicians to seek extralegal means in the future. It also points out that House Democrats raised similar objections in 2000, 2004, and 2016 without facing corporate sanctions. 

Cembalest concludes that he would not cut off corporate PAC funding solely based on the January 6 objections. Instead, he suggests that corporations should evaluate politicians across a broader range of issues to ensure alignment with corporate values, including supporting voting rights. A footnote details his perspective on voting rights, noting that updating federal voting legislation to survive Supreme Court challenges is the most practical way to address voter suppression.

This page examines the structural and cyclical reasons behind the long-term underperformance of European equities compared to US equities, metaphorically comparing Europe's stock market to the extinct, flightless moa bird. Between 2010 and late 2020, US equities generated cumulative returns of 335% while European equities yielded only 88%. The author attributes this gap to multiple factors, with the largest driver being stock-specific outperformance within sectors rather than broad sector weightings or currency fluctuations. While the currency tailwind of a strong US dollar may eventually fade, other fundamental advantages for US companies, such as superior return on equity and return on assets, are expected to endure over the long term. Despite these headwinds, a cyclical recovery is anticipated for Europe in 2021 as its trade-dependent economy begins to reopen.

The first line chart, titled "US vs Europe performance," traces total returns from January 2010 to January 2021, starting at a base value of 100. It shows a step-by-step build-up from the lower line, representing the MSCI Europe in USD index, to the top line, representing the MSCI US in USD index. The stacked performance drivers added to the MSCI Europe baseline include the outperformance of the US dollar over the Euro, sector weight differences like the US overweight in tech and Europe's overweight in financials, industrials, and staples, and stock-specific outperformance within the financial, consumer discretionary, and technology sectors. The chart illustrates how within-sector stock selection was the primary force widening the performance gap.

The second line chart, titled "Lockdown stringency index: US vs Europe," measures strictness on a scale from 0 to 100, where 100 represents the highest level of strictness, from February to December 2020. This index highlights how Europe maintained more severe restrictions than the US during the COVID-19 pandemic. After both regions experienced sharp spikes in lockdown severity in March and April 2020, Europe's stringency index dropped to around 50 in the late summer before climbing back up to over 70 by December 2020. Conversely, the US stringency index remained more stable, hovering around the 50 mark in the latter half of the year. The page also features a vintage scientific illustration of the flightless extinct moa bird to visually anchor the core metaphor.

This page introduces a commentary on the surge in capital raising by Special Purpose Acquisition Companies (SPACs), which the author terms "Hydraulic Spacking." Michael Cembalest argues that while the SPAC boom has revived a quiet US new issue market, it raises critical issues regarding wealth transfers among participants, increased market entry for highly risky and early-stage companies, and underwhelming relative returns for long-term buy-and-hold investors compared to other rising market alternatives. 

To explain how these vehicles function, the page features a horizontal timeline diagram depicting the key stages of a SPAC. The process begins with sponsors launching a SPAC IPO and placing the proceeds into a trust. The sponsor then has approximately two years to search for a target merger candidate. Upon finding a candidate, the merger is announced, and the sponsor enters a letter of intent while arranging Private Investment in Public Equity (PIPE) financing to bolster the IPO proceeds. Before the merger closes, SPAC arbitrage investors can exit the stock via the secondary market or a redemption option, or trade their warrants. Finally, the merger closes, PIPE investors fund the deal at the IPO price, and the new company begins trading publicly, subject to a typical 180-day lock-up period for target sellers and sponsors.

The commentary provides several key metrics on the market's scale. Since January 2019, SPACs have accounted for roughly half of all new US IPOs by both volume and company count. Among the 85 completed SPAC IPOs in this period, the dominant sectors were technology, electric vehicles, healthcare, and industrials, with 69 of these companies reporting negative free cash flow or negative net income. The momentum remains strong, as mid-January figures showed 52 announced but uncompleted mergers and another 264 SPACs actively searching for target companies. The author notes that this lack of profitability is not isolated to SPACs; in 2020, 80% of traditional IPOs also had negative earnings, driving the market share of unprofitable companies relative to total US equity market capitalization to its highest level since the dot-com bubble in 2000. Additionally, the page touches on the role of PIPE investors who conduct "over the wall" due diligence on company projections before public announcements to help finance these large transactions.

Michael Cembalest argues that despite a persistent "fear of flying" depressing airline spending, global oil demand and energy stocks have rebounded sharply. He contends that the poor performance of the energy sector from 2017 to 2020 was primarily caused by a lack of capital discipline among investors and oil and gas firms, rather than renewable energy penetration or stranded asset risks. Cembalest asserts that renewable energy adoption is simply too slow to have driven that decline, and notes that capital discipline has now returned to the sector. Looking forward, he forecasts that the Biden administration is unlikely to revive the Iran nuclear deal in 2021 or 2022, which prevents the release of another 1 million barrels per day of supply into the global oil market.

To support these observations, the page presents four charts. The first two utilize Chase card transaction data to compare 7-day smoothed national credit and debit card spending trends against 2019 baselines from March 2020 to January 2021. The airline spending chart shows a severe collapse to nearly negative 100% in spring 2020, recovering only slightly to between negative 70% and negative 80% by January 2021. In contrast, the oil spending chart reveals a shallower initial drop to about negative 50% in mid-2020, followed by a robust recovery back to roughly negative 10% by January 2021.

The third chart tracks global gasoline and diesel demand as a percentage change from 2019 levels, showing a historical dip in mid-2020 followed by a projected recovery. Diesel and gasoil demand, which fell to nearly negative 20% in mid-2020, is forecasted to exceed 2019 levels by mid-2021, while gasoline demand is projected to recover from its low of negative 30% to near-pre-pandemic levels over the same period. 

Lastly, a chart illustrating total returns for the S&P 500 energy industry from 2016 to early 2021, indexed to January 2016, tracks "Oil, Gas & Consumable Fuels" and "Energy Equipment & Services." Both sub-sectors experienced multi-year declines from their 2018 peaks, bottoming out in 2020 before showing a clear upward rebound heading into 2021, with the fuels index rising back toward 90 and the equipment index recovering to approximately 50.

This page provides an in-depth return analysis of eighty-five completed SPAC IPOs and five SPAC liquidations occurring between January 1, 2019, and January 22, 2021. The author, Michael Cembalest, analyzes returns across multiple SPAC participant scenarios on both an absolute basis and relative to benchmarks like traditional IPOs and the Russell 2000 Growth Index. 

Several key observations emerge from the analysis. First, SPAC sponsor returns are exceptionally high due to large share allocations relative to upfront costs, with sponsors only losing money if post-merger share values fall below upfront expenses or in the event of a liquidation. Second, SPAC Arbitrage investors, who cash out stock and warrant positions right before a merger, experience highly attractive and low-risk returns. Third, while buy-and-hold investors achieve high absolute returns, their median relative returns are negative across all benchmarks. This gap between high average returns and negative median returns is driven by a small number of massive successes, such as DraftKings, Virgin Galactic, and Immunovant. Furthermore, buy-and-hold returns degrade significantly for seasoned SPACs where more than 180 days have elapsed since the merger, a drop likely caused by the expiration of private equity lock-up periods. PIPE investors can enhance their returns through sponsor concessions, though these concessions have been declining. Ultimately, the high standard deviation across all investor groups points to an enormous dispersion of returns, suggesting that active management is essential for navigating this asset class.

These points are supported by a detailed table of cumulative returns broken down by investor scenarios. SPAC Arbitrage investors earned an average return of 40 percent and a median of 14 percent, with standard deviation at 78 percent. SPAC investor buy-and-hold gross returns averaged 90 percent, with a median of 45 percent, but dropped to a median of just 8 percent for seasoned holdings. Relative to the IPO Index, these buy-and-hold returns averaged negative 24 percent with a median of negative 73 percent, worsening to negative 115 percent for seasoned investments. Compared to the Russell 2000 Growth Index, buy-and-hold returns showed an average of 27 percent but a median of negative 21 percent. 

For PIPE investors, gross returns averaged 63 percent, with a median of 26 percent, which falls to negative 24 percent average relative to the IPO Index. When sponsor concessions are included, PIPE gross returns rise to an average of 96 percent and a median of 41 percent. Post-merger buy-and-hold investors saw gross returns average 44 percent, with a 10 percent median, but underperformed the IPO Index by an average of negative 34 percent and a median of negative 53 percent. Finally, SPAC sponsor returns were exceptionally high, averaging 958 percent with a 682 percent median, and remaining robust at a 648 percent average and 418 percent median even after accounting for concessions, forfeiture, and vesting. The table's 15th and 85th percentiles underscore the extreme performance dispersion; for example, gross buy-and-hold returns range from negative 17 percent at the 15th percentile to 218 percent at the 85th percentile.
