In this concluding section on special purpose acquisition companies, Michael Cembalest analyzes the viability of SPACs, warning that while they offer compelling low-risk arbitrage opportunities and major gains for sponsors, long-term buy-and-hold investors face poor median relative returns. He predicts that sponsor and arbitrage returns will eventually decline through reduced subsidies, tighter vesting rules, and higher transaction failure risks. He also highlights conflicting perceptions among market participants, such as PIPE investors and SPAC structurers, regarding concession trends and forward purchase commitments. 

The analysis is accompanied by four exhibits. The first chart, "US IPOs by type," tracks the annual number of IPOs from 1990 to 2020. This visual compares traditional IPOs with SPAC IPOs, demonstrating that while traditional listings peaked during the late 1990s tech bubble, SPAC IPOs exploded to unprecedented levels in 2020, making up a massive share of total listings. A companion stacked bar chart, "Traditional vs SPAC IPO deals," measures deal proceeds in billions of dollars from 2010 to 2021. It underscores a massive surge in total proceeds to over $160 billion in 2020, where the combination of SPAC deal sizes and PIPE deal sizes collectively eclipsed traditional IPO proceeds for the first time. 

A third bar chart, "Average percentage of SPAC holders who voted to redeem their shares in completed mergers," shows a dramatic decline in shareholder redemptions at the time of merger. Based on a sample of 85 companies, redemptions fell from approximately 60% in 2019 to roughly 33% in 2020, and further down to around 20% in 2021. Finally, a pie chart provides a sector breakdown for these same 85 companies brought public via SPACs since 2019. Tech, Media & Telecom represents the largest share at 34%, followed by Industrials at 16%, Healthcare at 13%, Electric Vehicles at 12%, Consumer at 11%, Finance at 8%, Energy at 4%, and Real Estate at 2%.

This page consists entirely of legal and regulatory disclaimers for various international jurisdictions, including Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Latin America, and Australia, containing no market commentary, charts, or analytical content.

This page analyzes the economic dynamics of Special Purpose Acquisition Companies (SPACs), specifically examining why risk-return opportunities are highly attractive for SPAC sponsors and arbitrage (Arb) investors, even as they facilitate massive wealth transfers away from buy-and-hold investors and selling companies. 

The author outlines several factors driving the SPAC boom. First, speed to market is a primary driver for private companies attempting to capitalize on a massive, potentially fleeting surge in investor demand for risky assets. Second, SPACs offer a lenient avenue for younger, riskier companies with negative free cash flow to go public, allowing management to market themselves using their own optimistic financial projections. Third, SPACs may minimize the money issuers "leave on the table" compared to traditional IPOs. Citing academic Jay Ritter from the University of Florida, traditional IPOs averaged a first-day pop of 20% to 40% between 2018 and 2021. Fourth, performance data suggests SPACs are a cheaper capital-raising vehicle for issuers because they underperform traditional benchmarks. Comparing deals since January 2019 against the Russell 2000 Growth Index, SPAC median and average excess returns were -21% and 27%, respectively, compared to much higher IPO median and average excess returns of 17% and 58%. A footnote adds that SPAC Arb investors welcome stock volatility because they can cash in their shares while retaining warrants to delta-hedge against the stock.

The page features two key visuals. The first chart, titled "Release the Krakens: investors load up on equity risk," plots global equity fund flows in billions of dollars as a 12-week rolling sum from 2006 through early 2021. Based on EPFR data, it highlights that while historical equity flows typically fluctuated between positive $150 billion and negative $100 billion, they skyrocketed in late 2020 and early 2021 to an unprecedented peak of nearly $250 billion. The second visual, a stylized diagram titled "SPAC Wealth Transfers," illustrates the directional flow of capital among the Sponsor, SPAC IPO investor, SPAC Arb investor, Selling company, PIPE investor, and Buy-and-hold post-merger investor. The diagram's arrows demonstrate that wealth is systematically transferred away from buy-and-hold post-merger investors and the selling companies, concentrating instead in the hands of the SPAC Arb investors and the transaction Sponsors.

This page of J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" assesses the real-world impact of President Biden's early energy agenda, including the Keystone XL pipeline termination, federal fleet electrification, and particularly the ban on new oil and gas leases on Federal lands. The author argues these policies are more likely to increase US energy imports than reduce emissions in the short and medium term, as they restrict supply faster than they reduce demand. 

Two historical charts trace the dramatic rise in US energy production over the last decade. The first, charting the US net energy deficit in energy terms from 1972 to 2020, illustrates how net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal peaked in the mid-2000s at around 700 million tonnes of oil equivalent before falling to cross the zero line into net-positive territory, achieving energy independence in October 2020. The second chart details US crude oil and natural gas production from 2010 to 2021, showing crude oil production rising from approximately 5.5 million to nearly 13 million barrels per day, and natural gas production growing from 75 billion to roughly 115 billion cubic feet per day over the same timeframe. 

The text then shifts to the ban on new federal leases. The author notes that because the moratorium only restricts new permits rather than existing leases, the immediate nationwide impact will be small, especially since onshore federal lands only account for 9% of US production. However, certain states like Colorado, Utah, and New Mexico will see larger local economic hits. If all federal lands—both onshore and offshore—were eventually fully decommissioned as older wells age out, US oil production would drop by 24% and gas by 12%. 

This context is supported by two bottom charts detailing production trends from 2003 to 2019. The chart on US crude oil production shows that private land accounted for almost all of the dramatic production increase, rising to over 8 million barrels per day by 2019, while federal offshore and onshore production remained flat. The final chart on US natural gas production displays a near-identical trend, with private land production driving total output to over 40,000 billion cubic feet by 2019 while federal contributions lagged far behind.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues that reducing domestic oil and gas supply, such as through the cancellation of the Keystone XL pipeline or Federal leasing restrictions, will not curb US carbon emissions unless policies also reduce overall energy demand. Without demand-side reductions, the US will simply import oil to fill the gap. 

To illustrate this point, he analyzes the cancellation of the Keystone XL pipeline, which was designed to deliver 500,000 barrels of oil per day from Canada to the US. This volume translates to 3.5 billion gallons of gasoline per year, enough to power 5.7 million internal combustion engine passenger cars. By comparison, only 328,000 electric vehicles (EVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) were sold in 2020. At this current pace of adoption, it would take 17 years of EV sales growth to offset the lost pipeline supply, meaning the US must import oil to fuel remaining internal combustion vehicles in the interim. Cembalest highlights further supply losses from the cancellation, including 2.3 billion gallons of distillate fuels and 800 million gallons of jet fuel. He suggests that President Biden's policy may ultimately penalize Canada, a close ally, while benefiting Middle East oil exporters.

The page features two charts to support these points. The first, "US electric vehicle sales," shows annual sales in thousands of vehicles from 2011 to 2020. It illustrates that combined sales of EVs and PHEVs grew from near zero in 2011 to a peak of around 360,000 in 2018, before settling at approximately 328,000 in 2020. The second chart, "US oil production by type," tracks production from 2000 to 2018 in millions of barrels per day. It shows that total production hovered around 5 to 6 million barrels per day until 2010, when fracking-dependent "tight oil" began to dominate, driving total production past 10 million barrels per day by 2018. Other sources, such as conventional onshore, Alaska, and the Gulf of Mexico, remained relatively flat. 

In a concluding footnote, Cembalest notes that despite overall energy independence, the US still imports about 2.5 million barrels of crude oil per day. He suggests the US may eventually need the Keystone supply because fracking-dependent tight oil, which comprises more than half of US production, faces slower growth as investors demand positive cash flow and environmental regulations tighten.

Michael Cembalest discusses the limitations of federal vehicle electrification and highlights the necessity of demand-side policies to match supply-side energy cuts proposed by the Biden administration. He argues that immediately electrifying the federal government's 645,000 vehicles would only reduce gasoline demand by 390 million gallons annually. This demand-side reduction is vastly overshadowed by supply-side policy impacts, such as canceling the Keystone XL pipeline and slashing onshore federal oil production by 30 percent, which together would cut gasoline supply by 5.5 billion gallons per year. Furthermore, he points out that retiring federal vehicles are typically sold into the used car market rather than being destroyed, meaning they will continue to consume fuel. 

To bridge this policy gap, Cembalest outlines several interventions needed to lower oil and gas demand. These include accelerating wind and solar transitions with subsidies, and investing hundreds of billions or even trillions of dollars into the US electricity grid to manage reliability and avoid wasted energy. He suggests the federal government may need to utilize eminent domain to bypass local opposition that has previously stalled projects like Arkansas's Clean Line Plains and Eastern transmission line and New Hampshire's 1 gigawatt Northern Pass hydroelectric project. Other options include reinstating strict auto mileage standards to curb the heavy gasoline consumption of popular US pickup trucks, such as the Ford F series, Chevy Silverado, and Dodge Ram, and introducing a carbon tax. 

To demonstrate the public's reluctance toward consumer energy taxes, a stacked bar chart titled "Low support for gas and electricity taxes" is included, displaying data from an August 2019 Washington Post-Kaiser Family Foundation poll of 2,293 respondents. The chart measures support for two proposals: increasing the federal gasoline tax by 25 cents per gallon and adding a 10 dollar monthly tax on US residential electric bills. For both proposals, about 50 percent of respondents strongly oppose the measure, while an additional 18 to 22 percent somewhat oppose it. Only about 26 to 32 percent of respondents express any level of support, highlighting the deep political challenges facing these demand-side taxation policies.

This page from Michael Cembalest's J.P. Morgan market analysis evaluates the heightened speculation and lack of profitability in the US initial public offering (IPO) and special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) markets. Drawing on database research from Jay Ritter at the University of Florida, the author highlights a concerning trend of unprofitable listings driven by a decade of interest rates lagging behind inflation. 

The first chart, titled "US IPOs with negative earnings," plots the percentage of companies listing with negative trailing twelve-month earnings from 1980 through 2020, excluding SPACs. It shows that unprofitable listings peaked near eighty percent in 2000, receded, and have climbed back up to nearly eighty percent in 2020. The adjacent chart, "Average first-day return of US IPOs," measures the equal-weighted average first-day percentage return over the same forty-year period. While the historic bubble of 1999 and 2000 saw average first-day returns spike to over seventy percent, the metric has recently surged back up to roughly forty percent in 2020 after hovering between ten and twenty percent for most of the intervening two decades.

The publication also details the financial weakness of companies going public via SPACs. A bar chart titled "Poor profitability of companies brought public via SPACs since 2019" shows that out of eighty-five studied companies, only a tiny fraction of about fifteen have positive net income or positive free cash flow. Conversely, the vast majority—roughly sixty-five companies—exhibit negative net income and negative free cash flow. 

To quantify this broader market trend, Cembalest highlights J.P. Morgan's "YUC" model. A line chart titled "Market cap of young unprofitable companies" measures YUCs—defined as firms less than five years from their IPO with annual revenue growth exceeding fifteen percent and negative net income in two of the last three years—as a percentage of total market capitalization. This metric peaked near six percent during the dot-com bubble in 2000, languished around one percent for a decade, and has recently climbed back to roughly two and a half percent as of late 2020.

Reflecting on these trends, the author notes that while current conditions are frothy, they still do not match the historic height of 1999. In an anecdotal footnote, he recalls that the two CEOs of TheGlobe.Com were invited to speak at a J.P. Morgan managing director meeting in 1999 despite having no publicly announced business model, preceding the rapid disintegration of their stock. Cembalest also shares a personal motivation story from 1997, noting how his status as a vice president barred him from attending a professional dinner hosted at his own home by his spouse, Rachel, who was already a managing director. This exclusion served as his primary incentive to seek a promotion and ensure he would never be left out again.

This page explores the localized obstacles to implementing regional renewable energy transitions, focusing on the canceled Northern Pass transmission line. Author Michael Cembalest discusses how local and state-level interests can stymie broader climate goals, even when the overall regional environmental benefits are substantial. For example, while HydroQuebec seeks to export hydropower to the United States, and New York is successfully forging its own path with a planned 1.3 GW transmission line buried under Lake Champlain and the Hudson River, progress elsewhere is often delayed when individual states control transmission networks. 

The Northern Pass, a planned 1.1 GW transmission line designed to bring Canadian hydropower to New England through New Hampshire, was blocked primarily due to local concerns about tourism and property values. Canadian hydropower has lifetime CO2 emissions that are only 5% of natural gas plants. After factoring in 5% transmission losses and an estimated 83% utilization rate, the Northern Pass could have delivered 7.5 GWh of clean power to New England each year. This would have reduced regional emissions by 3.0 million metric tons of CO2 annually, more than offsetting the 2019 shutdown of the Pilgrim nuclear plant. 

An accompanying bar chart, titled "CO2 emissions: New Hampshire vs Northern Pass," contrasts local emissions with the potential savings of the blocked project. The left bar shows that the entire New Hampshire electricity grid emits 2.1 million metric tons of CO2 annually. The right bar shows that the emissions from New England natural gas plants that could have been eliminated by the Northern Pass project total 3.0 million metric tons annually. The chart illustrates how New Hampshire, whose own electricity generation is dominated by nuclear power, impeded a neighboring regional emission-free generation project that would have offset more carbon than New Hampshire’s entire grid emits.

In the epilogue, the author notes that Massachusetts is currently trying to import Canadian hydropower through Maine via the New England Clean Energy Connect, but that project has already run into injunctions from environmental groups. The author outlines alternative pathways for clean baseload power, such as adding 7 GW of utility-scale, commercial, and residential solar combined with expensive battery storage. Ultimately, research from the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research indicates that the most cost-effective solution for a zero-emission power system would be to build 4 GW of new two-way transmission lines between New England and Quebec. However, given the intense political and environmental opposition to such infrastructure, the author concludes with extreme skepticism regarding the feasibility of completing four projects of this scale.

This page of the publication introduces a collection of short commentaries focusing on the global economic recovery from COVID-19, rising inflation risks, and energy infrastructure challenges. Michael Cembalest argues that the global economic rebound is in full swing, particularly in the United States and China, driven by sharp rises in shipping demand, petroleum consumption, manufacturing, and capital spending. Notably, Q4 2020 S&P 500 earnings surpassed Q4 2019 levels, despite steep declines in specific sectors like energy at negative 102 percent, airlines at negative 367 percent, and restaurants and hotels at negative 117 percent. While slow vaccination rollouts in Europe—reaching only about 5 percent of the population outside the United Kingdom—present a headwind, the primary risks identified as potential disrupters to this recovery are a bond market revolt and vaccine-unresponsive COVID-19 variants.

To illustrate the strength of the recovery, the page features three charts. The first, charting Chinese shipping rates and US petroleum demand from 2011 to early 2021, displays a sharp, simultaneous upward spike in the China Container Freight Index toward the 2,100 mark and US petroleum product demand recovering toward 20 million barrels per day. The second chart, tracking the Global Manufacturing Survey from 2012 to 2021, displays a sharp V-shaped recovery for both current manufacturing and expected future output, with both measures well above the 50-expansion threshold. The third chart shows a global capital expenditure forecast using annualized three-month-on-three-month percentage changes. It illustrates a historic collapse to nearly negative 30 percent in 2020, followed by a near-vertical rebound to almost positive 30 percent by early 2021.

The text outlines five upcoming "very short stories" covering a range of topics. These include the conflict between state rights and renewable energy imperatives in New Hampshire; the rapid decline of reported COVID-19 infections in the US and Europe; Larry Summers's warnings that a mega-stimulus bill could reignite inflation and drive up bond yields; the misalignment of incentives between SPAC sponsors and long-term investors; and the internal political battles of the Republican Party, drawing comparisons to the historical dissolution of the Whigs.

Finally, a dedicated analysis addresses the February 2021 Texas power outage, arguing that frozen wind turbines were not the primary culprit. Cembalest explains that wind was only expected to provide 6 gigawatts of power during the winter, whereas peak energy demand during the storm hit 67 gigawatts. The primary issue was that 30 gigawatts of thermal power went offline due to natural gas plant outages. Texas's reliance on just-in-time production from the Permian Basin and its limited gas storage capacity led to natural gas production cutting in half when gathering lines and electric pumps froze. Pointing to the successful winterization of natural gas facilities in sub-zero Canadian climates, such as the Muskeg River plant in Alberta, the author notes that the Texas ERCOT system has failed to make these necessary infrastructure investments, which will likely dominate future policy discussions.

This page consists entirely of legal disclaimers and regulatory disclosures regarding the distribution of the publication across various global jurisdictions, including Spain, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Latin America, and Australia. It outlines the specific regulatory bodies overseeing J.P. Morgan's entities in these regions and provides legal warnings, terms of service, and client classification details, particularly for wholesale clients in Australia. There are no charts, tables, or financial analyses on this page.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, investigates the rapid and sudden decline in reported COVID-19 infections across the United States, the United Kingdom, Denmark, and other European nations in early 2021. Cembalest poses the central question of why this dramatic fall is occurring, especially since the highly contagious B117 variant has become highly prevalent, accounting for 90% of infections in the United Kingdom, 21% in Denmark, and projected by the Scripps Institute to dominate the United States by March. 

To evaluate potential drivers, the author presents four charts. The first chart, titled "US, UK and Denmark infections," displays daily infections per million people with a seven-day smoothing from early 2020 through early 2021. It shows a massive late-year surge that peaked in January, with the United Kingdom exceeding 800 infections per million, the United States topping 700, and Denmark peaking near 600, before all three regions experienced a sharp, synchronized drop. 

Cembalest first assesses vaccinations, noting that US vaccination rates were under 5% when infections began to tumble in mid-January. A chart titled "Unique people vaccinated as percentage of population" tracks the percentage of vaccinated individuals from December 13, 2020, to February 21, 2021. It reveals that the United Kingdom led with a rapid rise toward 23%, followed by the United States at roughly 12%, while Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, and Canada all remained clustered below 5%. The low coverage during the initial infection turnaround suggests vaccinations were not the primary driver.

The author then looks at holiday travel. The chart "US air travel and driving directions" plots the percentage decline from a pre-COVID baseline, tracking TSA checkpoint travelers and Apple driving directions. While driving directions recovered above baseline during the summer and saw a minor bump around late December, TSA travel remained severely depressed between 60% and 80% below baseline, indicating that travel changes were too small to fully explain the infection drop. 

Finally, Cembalest examines changes in testing volume. The chart "United States virus tracking" shows daily tests per million on a seven-day average, which rose steadily throughout 2020 to peak at over 6,000 in early January 2021 before falling back toward 5,000. While testing declined moderately, this shift does not match the rapid speed of the infection decline. A detailed footnote addresses client inquiries about changes to PCR test "Ct" cycle thresholds, stating there is no evidence that altering these positivity standards caused the decline in reported infections, particularly given the lack of standardization across testing platforms. Cembalest ultimately concludes that none of these three factors—vaccines, travel, or testing—appear sufficient to explain the sheer speed of the plummeting infection rates.

This page of the publication, titled "Money for nothing: an epilogue on SPAC sponsors and long term investors," focuses on the significant misalignment of financial outcomes between SPAC sponsors and buy-and-hold investors. Michael Cembalest observes that while sponsors typically receive 25% of SPAC IPO shares—leading to median and average sponsor returns of 418% and 648% since 2019—buy-and-hold investors often experience much weaker or even deeply negative returns. 

To illustrate this disparity, the page presents six historical charts showing share prices over time for completed SPAC mergers, tracking four critical timeline milestones: the IPO, the merger announcement, the merger closing, and 180 days after the merger close. 

In the case of Allied Esports Entertainment, the share price dropped sharply from the traditional $10 IPO level to under $3, resulting in a 74% loss for buy-and-hold investors compared to a 30% loss for the sponsor. For Glory Star New Media Group, the share price dropped to around $3, giving the sponsor a positive 35% return while buy-and-hold investors lost 61%. OneSpaWorld and Accel Entertainment both saw sponsors capture huge returns of 420% and 323%, respectively, while buy-and-hold investors remained essentially flat at losses of 4% and gains of 3%. For high-flying deals like Nikola Corporation and Immunovant, where share prices spiked dramatically before falling, sponsors secured staggering returns of 981% and 451% because one-time vesting tests allowed their shares to unlock before the subsequent price crashes, leaving buy-and-hold investors with much lower returns of 91% and 59%.

Cembalest highlights a nascent trend aimed at better aligning interests through multi-year vesting schedules that do not release sponsor shares unless long-term price targets are maintained. He points to Hamilton Lane’s Alliance I SPAC as an example, where sponsor shares vest gradually over four years only if price targets of $12.50 and $15.00 are met. While such structures are currently present in only a small minority of the hundreds of active SPACs, Cembalest suggests they may indicate where the SPAC market is headed as investors digest the poor performance of the latest wave.

This page analyzes the rapid decline in COVID-19 infections and the impact of stringent lockdowns versus vaccinations in the United States, United Kingdom, and Denmark in early 2021. The author notes that while the exact speed of the decline in infections is difficult to explain, US hospitalizations have dropped 50% from peak levels and mortality is down 15%. The author remains optimistic that vaccines provide strong efficacy against the B117 variant, though he notes concerns regarding the South Africa B1351 strain, which represented roughly 5% of European infections at the time.

This US data is supported by two tracking charts. The first, "United States virus tracking," plots new daily infections and current hospitalizations on the left axis alongside daily deaths on the right axis from March 2020 through January 2021. It shows a steep drop in new daily infections from a peak of nearly 300,000 down to around 100,000 by late January, with hospitalizations and deaths following a downward trajectory from their respective peaks of roughly 130,000 and 3,400. The second chart, "Tracking excess deaths from COVID," shows total weekly deaths from January 2017 to January 2021. It highlights a dramatic surge in actual weekly deaths from all causes starting in early 2020, peaking near 90,000 in early 2021, well above the baseline threshold for excess deaths.

Turning to Europe, the author argues that recent declines in infections and mortality in the UK and Denmark are primarily driven by highly stringent lockdowns rather than early vaccine success. He raises the open question of whether Europe can sustain these declines when lockdowns are lifted, especially given that continental European vaccination rates remain below 5% due to narrow vaccine contracts and logistical issues. 

To illustrate the severity of these European measures, the page includes two comparative charts for the US, UK, and Denmark. The "Lockdown stringency index" tracks lockdown strictness on a scale of 0 to 100 from February 2020 to February 2021. By early 2021, the UK's index surged past 80 and Denmark's rose above 70, while the US remained comparatively relaxed at around 50. The adjacent "Regional mobility data" chart measures the percentage change from baseline for retail, restaurants, transit, and workplace activities. Consistent with lockdown stringency, mobility in the UK plunged to nearly negative 70% and Denmark fell to around negative 60% in early 2021, whereas US mobility remained higher, hovering between negative 30% and negative 40%.

In accompanying footnotes, the author compares the risk of getting COVID-19 against vaccine side effects, citing a Koch Institut report showing a mere 0.02% probability of serious vaccine side effects compared to the much higher risk of long-term debilitating COVID-19 symptoms. Additionally, he highlights the strictness of international travel policies, contrasting the US's daily infection rate of 230 per million with Hong Kong's low rate of 2 per million, which was maintained through a mandatory three-week quarantine in government-run hotels.

This page serves as the introduction and table of contents for the J.P. Morgan publication, "The Agony & the Ecstasy 3.0: an update on our concentrated stock research for high net worth families." Written by Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management, the introduction notes that although a third version of their concentrated stock research was originally planned for 2024—following version 1.0 in 2004 and version 2.0 in 2014—current market and economic factors prompted an earlier release. The report is structured to review 40 years of business survival risk in the United States, discuss the market and economic forces that will affect business survival in the coming years, examine business failures across sectors from the last decade, and outline diversification and hedging strategies for families holding concentrated stock portfolios. Cembalest emphasizes that while many of the severe macroeconomic risks analyzed are not the firm's base-case forecasts, understanding them is critical for families with concentrated wealth because the consequences of being wrong are far higher than for diversified investors. 

The Table of Contents outlines four distinct sections of the report:
* "Business failure risk, 1980-2020: measures and catalysts," co-authored by Michael Cembalest and Kirk Haldeman.
* "Market, macroeconomic and microeconomic risks," authored by Michael Cembalest.
* "Business failure review, 2017-2020," co-authored by Chris Baggini and Jake Manoukian.
* "Concentrated portfolio diversification and hedging strategies," authored by Kirk Haldeman.

This page, titled “The Not So Civil War: the Whigs, and what happens next in the Republican Party,” discusses the internal conflicts within the modern Republican Party (GOP) following the Trump presidency. Author Michael Cembalest analyzes whether current divisions—such as the creation of a "Patriot Party" or a "center-right" party—will lead to a viable third-party movement. He argues that history shows third parties rarely succeed in the U.S. "winner-take-all" legislative system and predicts that the conflict will instead result in intense primary battles in 2022 and 2024. 

To support this analysis, the page features a line chart titled “Dissolution of the Whigs,” which plots the percentage of congressional members by political party from 1826 to 1866. The chart illustrates how the Jacksonians and Anti-Jacksonians of the late 1820s transitioned into a stable system dominated by the Democrats and the Whigs, with the Whigs holding roughly 30% to 50% of congressional seats through the 1840s. Following the 1852 election, intense disputes over slavery caused a rapid collapse of the Whig Party, which fell to 0% of congressional representation by 1855. This collapse coincided with the rise of the newly formed Republican Party, which quickly grew from its inception in 1854 to claim over 50% of congressional seats by the late 1850s. The chart also traces the brief emergence of smaller, transient groups during this transition, such as the Opposition, American, and Unionist parties, which never achieved long-term dominance. 

The author asserts that the dissolution of the Whigs does not serve as a template for today's GOP factions because the creation of the Republican Party required the immense, singular issue of slavery to drive massive defections. He warns that a modern center-right party would likely suffer the same fate as Teddy Roosevelt’s 1912 Progressive Party, which only succeeded in splitting the Republican vote and allowing Democrat Woodrow Wilson to win the presidency with 42% of the popular vote. 

Cembalest also addresses the feud between Donald Trump and Mitch McConnell by consulting historian Michael Beschloss for historical precedents of presidential conflicts with Senate majority leaders. Beschloss points to Senator Alben Barkley’s dispute with FDR over a World War II tax hike, and Senator Mike Mansfield’s opposition to LBJ regarding the Vietnam War. Both historical disputes were ultimately resolved without prompting third-party movements. The author also notes in a footnote that FDR attempted a failed "purge" of Southern Democrats in 1938, where almost all of the incumbents FDR opposed won their primaries. The page concludes that the Trump-McConnell dispute is similarly unlikely to result in a third-party movement, and that the party's future will instead be decided by primary challenges from the Trump wing in the 2022 and 2024 elections.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest evaluates whether economist Larry Summers is correct in predicting that a potential $1.5 trillion fiscal stimulus bill could spark significant wage and price inflation alongside rising bond yields. Summers' thesis relies on rapid labor market healing, the deployment of pent-up savings triggered by herd immunity, and a historic post-war deficit. Cembalest explores this argument using four key charts.

The first chart, "US output gap (spare capacity measure)," tracks actual and projected output gaps as a percentage of actual GDP relative to potential GDP from 1949 to 2029. It illustrates how a $1.5 trillion stimulus package could eliminate spare capacity entirely; under a 0.5x multiplier, the output gap is projected to enter positive territory, while a 0.75x multiplier would push it to roughly 4%, a level not seen since the inflationary era of the 1970s. Although some economists, such as Jan Hatzius and Sven Jari Struyven of Goldman Sachs, argue that potential GDP is understated and more slack exists, Cembalest notes that predicting these metrics is nearly impossible in an era of unprecedented monetary and fiscal experimentation.

The potential for a sudden release of consumer demand is highlighted in the chart "Pent-up spending will be unleashed sometime in 2021," which measures year-over-year percentage changes from 1972 to 2020. This visual shows a massive gap between the historically high estimated spending potential (climbing near 10%) and the sharply depressed actual consumption growth following the pandemic. This release of pent-up demand is expected to align with herd immunity, as analyzed in the chart "US vaccinated individuals and survivors." This chart plots the percentage of the unique US population vaccinated or carrying survivor antibodies from January to July 2021. Under various growth scenarios—ranging from a constant vaccination rate to a 30% increase—the combined contribution of vaccines and antibodies is projected to reach between 70% and 80% by June or July 2021.

Finally, the chart "US real GDP vs long-run growth expectations" indexes GDP to Q4 2019 levels and maps expectations through mid-2022. It compares the dramatic drop in actual real GDP in 2020 (which fell to an index level of 90) against a Morgan Stanley forecast showing real GDP recovering sharply to an index level of 108 by mid-2022. This non-consensus projection is notably higher than the Federal Reserve’s own projection of long-term GDP growth, which trends at a lower trajectory around index level 105. 

Ultimately, Cembalest agrees that Summers may be onto something, warning that Fed Chair Jerome Powell will face difficult policy exit decisions well before the 2022 midterm elections. Markets may currently price in a dormant Fed, but Cembalest poses that a rapid move toward 2.5% inflation and 3.5% yields on 10-year US Treasuries could lead to substantial equity and credit market corrections.

This page, authored by Michael Cembalest and Haldeman, explores the theme of business failure risk and the relentless force of creative destruction from 1980 to 2020. Despite the dramatic rise in global wealth and the United States' strong standing as an entrepreneurial, innovative nation, the authors emphasize that even dominant market leaders face significant risks of displacement and decline.

To illustrate this ongoing corporate displacement, a cumulative line chart shows that between 1980 and 2019, more than 400 companies were removed from the S&P 500 due to business distress. This steady upward climb highlights a constant rate of failure among major companies. Furthermore, an accompanying table details the percentage of companies within the Russell 3000 Index that experienced a catastrophic stock price loss, defined as a 70 percent unrecovered decline from peak price levels. Across all sectors, 44 percent of companies suffered such a catastrophic loss. Sector-by-sector data shows that Energy was the most volatile, with 65 percent of its companies experiencing catastrophic losses, followed closely by Information Technology at 59 percent, whereas Utilities experienced the lowest rate of catastrophic loss at just 14 percent.

The analysis further investigates concentration risk by evaluating how single-stock positions compare to cash or a diversified market position. A large performance table indicates that, across all sectors, 42 percent of stocks generated negative absolute returns, meaning holding them was worse than holding cash. Additionally, 66 percent of stocks suffered negative excess returns relative to the Russell 3000 Index, meaning investors would have been better off in a diversified index. Only 10 percent of stocks since 1980 were classified as megawinners, defined as having a cumulative price return at least 500 percent higher than the Russell 3000 Index. Sector breakdowns reveal that Energy and Utilities performed poorly, with 84 percent and 85 percent of their stocks underperforming the Russell 3000, respectively, and only 5 percent and 4 percent achieving megawinner status. Conversely, Consumer Staples proved to be the most resilient sector, boasting the highest proportion of megawinners at 17 percent and a relatively low 35 percent of stocks experiencing negative absolute returns. This data suggests that while concentrated stock positions can occasionally generate massive wealth, they carry a high probability of underperformance compared to diversified index strategies.

This page of the report examines the distribution of individual stock performance relative to the Russell 3000 Index from 1980 to 2020 and analyzes the external drivers of business failure. The central observation is that while a small group of winning stocks generates enormous excess returns, the typical median stock ultimately underperforms the broader index. The author poses the question of what drives business failure, concluding that most instances of corporate ruin are caused by factors outside the control of management, boards, or analysts.

The stock return dynamics are illustrated in a bar chart titled "Distribution of excess lifetime returns on individual stocks vs. Russell 3000, 1980-2020." The vertical axis measures the number of stocks, ranging from zero to 3,500, while the horizontal axis displays the annualized lifetime return of individual stocks relative to the index, divided into ten-percent brackets ranging from underperformance of more than negative 70 percent to outperformance of more than 70 percent. The chart displays a clear leftward skew, with the largest volume of stocks clustered in the negative excess return categories. A red dashed vertical line marks the median stock's performance, which falls under the negative ten percent bucket, visually proving that most individual equities fail to keep pace with the index.

The text outlines several primary reasons for business failure, arguing that external macroeconomic, regulatory, and competitive forces are the true culprits. Commodity price risks that cannot be hedged present a major threat to stability. Government intervention is another primary driver of failure, manifested through changing service reimbursement rates, slow FDA approval timelines, public domain privatizations, shifting subsidies for renewable energy, carbon taxes, fracking rules, and government-sponsored enterprises crowding out private capital. The author notes that deregulation can be just as disruptive as re-regulation, as seen in the boom-and-bust cycles of the telecommunications, utilities, and broker-dealer sectors. 

Global competition and trade policies also present existential risks, notably from foreign competitors backed by state subsidies and currency manipulation, with China's support of its automotive, steel, solar, paper, and glass sectors cited as key examples. Furthermore, intellectual property infringement and patent trolls cost US businesses over 20 billion dollars per year. Other critical factors include sudden tariff adjustments, employee fraud (which SEC investigations show accounts for about 30 percent of cases), technological innovations that disintermediate traditional distributors, customer consolidation that erodes seller pricing power, and aggressive competitor expansion that collapses industry prices.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication analyzed by Michael Cembalest discusses the heightened market, macroeconomic, and microeconomic risks facing concentrated stock families, focusing on historical valuation extremes and indicators of intense investor optimism. The author argues that valuations are exceptionally high across almost all historical measures, supported primarily by unsustainably low ten-year Treasury yields that sit below the rate of inflation.

A table detailing S&P 500 valuation percentiles compares December 2019 to current levels, where a percentile of one hundred percent represents the most expensive on record. Current percentiles have reached one hundred percent for US market cap to GDP, Enterprise Value to Sales, and Enterprise Value to EBITDA. The median across all tracked metrics sits at the ninety-fifth percentile, up from eighty-nine percent in late 2019. The only metric displaying below-median valuations is the S&P earnings yield minus the ten-year US Treasury yield, which is in the fortieth percentile.

An adjacent line chart illustrates real yields, calculated as the yield less core inflation, from 1980 to early 2021. It tracks BBB corporate bonds alongside ten-year US Treasuries. The chart shows both series hitting historic lows, with ten-year US Treasuries dropping deeply into negative territory below negative one percent by 2020.

The text highlights massive retail and institutional optimism, noting that since 2016, the American Association of Individual Investors sentiment is in the ninety-eighth percentile, Investors Intelligence Advisory Sentiment is in the ninety-fifth, the NAAIM Active Managers Sentiment is in the ninety-ninth, and cash holdings of the twenty largest US equity mutual funds are at the one-hundredth percentile for lowest cash levels.

To visualize the surge in retail participation, a chart shows online broker and retail trading volume from 2017 to early 2021. It tracks the daily average of online broker trades on the left axis, which spiked from around two million trades to over eight million trades following the late 2019 move where major brokers cut trading commissions to zero. The right axis tracks wholesaler trading volume as a percent of total US trading volume, which surged as a proxy for retail trading from under sixteen percent to over thirty-two percent by early 2021.

Finally, the author warns of deteriorating market depth, illustrated by a chart showing the S&P 500 futures contracts volume measuring the average number of bid-offer contracts from 2007 to late 2020. This metric has fallen sharply from peaks of over five hundred contracts in 2008 and 2013 to just over one hundred contracts recently. The author cautions that this low market depth suggests prices could evaporate rapidly if selling pressure suddenly intensifies.

In this analysis, the author explores the potential risks of the Federal Reserve's current policy path, questioning whether the Fed is underestimating the inflationary pressures of massive fiscal stimulus. The author notes that even a conservative 0.5x multiplier on a new $1.5 to $2.0 trillion spending bill could push the US output gap—the measure of spare capacity in the economy—into positive territory, meaning no spare capacity remains. While structural shifts like globalization, automation, and declining unionization make 1970s-style hyperinflation unlikely, the chief risk for concentrated stock families is whether the Fed will raise interest rates at all. The author warns that a yield of 3.0% to 3.5% on the 10-year Treasury could trigger severe equity market losses. 

This thesis is supported by four key charts detailing the coming economic surge. The first chart displays the US output gap as a percentage of actual GDP relative to potential GDP from 1949 projected out to 2029. It illustrates a sharp historical drop during the pandemic but points out that a new $1.9 trillion stimulus bill in 2021 could push the output gap positive, reaching nearly 2% under a 0.5x multiplier assumption and over 4% under a 0.75x multiplier. 

To explain the rapid economic acceleration that will fuel this shift, the second chart traces the trajectory of US vaccinated individuals and survivors as a percentage of the population from January to June. It projects that the combined vaccination contribution and non-vaccinated survivor antibodies will easily surpass the critical 70% threshold by June, depending on whether vaccination rates remain constant or increase by up to 30%. 

Concurrently, the third chart examines pent-up consumer demand by plotting the year-over-year percentage change in estimated spending potential against actual consumption growth from 1972 to 2021. This visual reveals a massive divergence in late 2020 where actual consumption plummeted, yet estimated spending potential surged, setting the stage for a dramatic unleashing of consumer spending in 2021. 

Lastly, the fourth chart plots US real GDP against long-run growth expectations, indexing values to Q4 2019. It shows actual real GDP making a sharp V-shaped recovery, with Morgan Stanley forecasting that real GDP will rise well above the Fed's projected long-term growth line by mid-2022, reaching an index level of roughly 108. This rapid recovery above pre-crisis trends marks a stark contrast to the sluggish recovery following the 2008-2009 financial crisis. Together, these charts raise open questions about whether Fed Chair Jerome Powell's tolerance for transitory post-COVID inflation might lead to policy errors as unprecedented monetary and fiscal experiments unfold over the next two to three years.

This page focuses on the macroeconomic risks of unprecedented post-COVID fiscal and monetary stimulus, arguing that the Federal Reserve may have made an unrecognized mistake by initiating the largest monetary policy experiment in central banking history. The author warns that massive fiscal deficits, combined with easy monetary policy, could compound eventual inflationary pressures, particularly if rising interest rates increase the government's debt service burden and impact equity markets. 

To support this argument, the page features six charts. The first chart, comparing the stimulus response to COVID against previous crises, plots fiscal stimulus against monetary stimulus as a percentage of GDP. It shows that the "Global Virus Crisis" responses from Japan, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Europe represent vastly larger combined interventions than those of the "Global Financial Crisis." While World War II saw higher fiscal stimulus for the US at around 18%, its monetary stimulus was much lower than the post-COVID response, where Japan's monetary stimulus exceeds 30% of GDP. 

The second chart compares M2 money supply and institutional money market fund growth, indexed to 100. During the Global Coronavirus Crisis, this index rocketed from 100 in January 2020 to nearly 125 by July 2020, continuing upward towards 130 into 2021. In contrast, during the Global Financial Crisis from August 2008 to September 2010, the index barely peaked above 107, demonstrating much faster money supply growth in the current era. 

The third chart illustrates the five-year average of real yields on cash (T-bill/Funds rate less inflation) from 1830 to 2020. It reveals that recent real yields have fallen below zero to around -2%, marking the lowest real cash yields in nearly two centuries outside of major conflicts like the Civil War, World War I, and World War II. 

The fourth chart displays the US fiscal deficit as a percentage of GDP from 1930 to 2020. The deficit spiked to nearly -30% during World War II, and has plunged again to a projected estimate of approximately -15% of GDP for 2021, excluding any pending stimulus legislation. 

The fifth chart tracks gross federal debt held by the public as a percentage of US GDP from 1940 to 2020. Public debt is shown rising rapidly from around 40% in the early 2000s to a 2021 estimate of nearly 100%, approaching the historic World War II peak of approximately 110%. 

The final chart details the interest burden on federal debt, measured as interest payments as a percentage of US GDP from 1940 with projections to 2030. Although the interest burden peaked above 3.0% in the late 1980s and has since hovered around 1.3%, Congressional Budget Office projections estimate a sharp rise back toward 2.5% by 2030, presenting a looming fiscal risk if rates rise.

This page focuses on the potential permanent transition to remote work in a post-COVID world, highlighting a significant disconnect between employee desires and employer expectations. Citing research from Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom, and Steven J. Davis of the Becker Friedman Institute at the University of Chicago, the author argues that how this gap is resolved will have major economic consequences across various sectors of the United States. 

The first chart illustrates the historical and projected percentage of paid days worked from home. Prior to the pandemic, work-from-home days accounted for less than ten percent of paid days, which then spiked to over sixty percent in May 2020 before settling into the low forty-percent range by late 2020. Looking forward to a post-COVID environment, employees prefer to work from home for roughly forty-five percent of paid days, whereas employers only plan for this to occur on about twenty percent of paid days. 

The second chart examines the preferences of workers who have the ability to work from home, indicating that the largest single cohort, at more than twenty-five percent, wants to work remotely five days per week. The next most popular preferences are two days and three days per week, at roughly fifteen percent and fourteen percent respectively, while only about ten percent of these workers wish to never work from home. 

The third chart plots the number of post-COVID paid work-from-home days against annual earnings from 2019 to reveal how income influences this expectations gap. Across all income brackets from twenty thousand dollars to over two hundred and fifty thousand dollars, employee desire for remote work remains consistently high, averaging between two and two and a half days per week. In contrast, employer plans for remote work start extremely low—under one day per week for those earning between twenty thousand and seventy thousand dollars—but rise steadily with income. The gap only closes at the highest income bracket of over two hundred and fifty thousand dollars, where employer plans align with employee desires at approximately two and a half days per week.

This page from J.P. Morgan's report highlights the substantial public health and economic challenges of a longer-lasting COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on its higher lethality compared to seasonal influenza, its impact on excess deaths, and the long-term aftershocks reported by survivors.

A chart comparing estimated infection fatality rates for seasonal influenza and COVID-19 demonstrates a stark difference in lethality. While seasonal flu estimates from the World Health Organization (WHO), Oxford, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) hover near or below 0.1%, COVID-19 fatality rate estimates are significantly higher, ranging from approximately 0.25% from the Stanford Meta-Research Innovation Center to 1.0% from Imperial College London, with various CDC and University of Wollongong estimates placed in between.

A second chart, tracking weekly excess deaths from January 2017 to January 2021, compares actual deaths from all causes to the threshold for excess deaths. Prior to 2020, weekly deaths fluctuated seasonally between roughly 50,000 and 65,000, staying near or below the excess threshold. Following the arrival of COVID-19, actual weekly deaths repeatedly spiked far above this baseline, peaking near 80,000 in the spring of 2020 and reaching nearly 90,000 in early 2021.

Finally, the text details the persistent, long-term effects of the virus on survivors. A University College London study of 3,700 individuals with prolonged symptoms found that 96% reported symptoms beyond 90 days, 65% beyond 180 days, and 45% required reduced work schedules, with fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and post-exertional malaise being the most common lingering issues after six months. These findings align with a Wuhan study of 1,700 hospitalized patients, which found that 76% experienced ongoing fatigue, muscle weakness, and sleep difficulties six months post-illness.

This page explores the concept of "Zoomshock," which represents the geographic shock to local labor markets caused by a transition to permanent work-from-home policies during the pandemic. Based on classifications developed by the University of Chicago and applied by researchers in the UK, the analysis estimates the shift in hours physically worked across various districts, assuming overall employment levels and employers remain unchanged while only the location of the work shifts. 

The first visualization is a bar chart titled "Estimated change in work activity based on ability to work from home in the UK, % change in number of workers." It illustrates a clear divergence: less densely populated residential areas see substantial positive growth in physical work activity, while highly dense urban centers experience steep declines. Outlying districts like Redbridge, Lewisham, Harrow, and Waltham Forest see increases in work activity ranging from roughly 40% to 60%. In contrast, major commercial and civic hubs experience severe contractions, with Westminster and the City of London suffering declines in physical work activity of approximately 60% to 80%.

This geographic redistribution is illustrated in greater detail through two maps of the Greater London area. The first map, depicting net employment change, reveals a stark core-periphery pattern. The central core of London is dominated by dark red shading, indicating net losses of more than 5,000 workers, while the outer ring of suburbs is filled with dark blue shading, indicating net gains of over 1,200 workers. The second map shows the employment flow per 100 workers, reinforcing this core-periphery split. Central London exhibits deep red and orange shading representing outward flows of greater than 25 workers per 100, while the outer residential boroughs are shaded in deep blue, showing inward flows of more than 40 workers per 100. Together, these maps demonstrate how the rise of remote work physically decentralizes economic activity away from city centers and into residential neighborhoods.

This page addresses the microeconomic risks associated with the possibility that COVID-19 does not fade away. While J.P. Morgan's base case assumes a gradual return to normal in 2021 driven by mass vaccination and improved clinical treatments, the author warns that this outcome is not guaranteed. Emerging UK and South African variants have already diminished vaccine efficacy. Continued viral evolution could compromise the spike-protein target of current vaccines, potentially forcing developers to design new vaccines from scratch and prompting permanent shifts in business consumption, mobility, investments, and residency patterns.

A detailed comparison table outlines the specifications and efficacy of five vaccines: Moderna, Pfizer, AstraZeneca, Johnson & Johnson, and Novavax. Moderna and Pfizer are mRNA vaccines, both approved, that demonstrated high initial efficacy against the 2020 prevailing D614G strain, at 94% and 95% respectively. However, both show reduced neutralizing activity against variants; Moderna has a twofold reduction in neutralization against the B.1.1.7 UK variant and a sixfold reduction against the B.1351 South African variant, while Pfizer experiences a modest decline against the UK variant and a two-thirds decline against the South African variant. Both see their effectiveness cut in half against the B.1.427/9 California variant. Regarding storage, Moderna is kept under normal refrigerated conditions, whereas Pfizer requires ultra-cold storage at minus 94 degrees Fahrenheit.

AstraZeneca and Johnson & Johnson are vector vaccines. Approved AstraZeneca shows 84% symptomatic efficacy against the prevailing strain and 75% against the UK strain, but clinical trials indicate minimal protection against mild-to-moderate illness caused by the South African variant. Johnson & Johnson's pending vaccine shows 72% efficacy against the prevailing strain and 64% against the South African strain, rising to 86% and 82% respectively against severe infection. Novavax, a pending recombinant vaccine, boasts 95.6% efficacy against the prevailing strain, 85% against the UK variant, and 60% against the South African variant. AstraZeneca, Johnson & Johnson, and Novavax all utilize normal refrigerated storage.

In trial and real-world roll-out observations, Pfizer demonstrated no COVID-related deaths across global trials, and real-world data from Israel showed infections in those aged 60 and older fell by two-thirds after the first dose, with only a 0.1% infection rate after the second. A UK study of Pfizer reported a 75% drop in hospitalizations after one dose. Real-world roll-out of AstraZeneca in Scotland reduced hospital admission risk by 94%, while clinical trials showed 100% prevention of severe illness and deaths across the UK, Brazil, and South Africa. Johnson & Johnson trials showed 85% prevention of severe disease and 100% prevention of deaths. Novavax trials reported no hospitalizations or deaths among vaccinated participants.

This page, authored by Baggini and Manoukian, reviews notable business failures and sector distress between 2017 and 2020, focusing on iconic blue chips and the collapse of the United States shale oil industry. The authors argue that even the most valuable companies can fail due to poor strategic decisions, heavy debt, lack of innovation, and market oversupply. 

The first section highlights the decline of blue-chip companies, specifically General Electric and Kraft-Heinz. A stock price chart for General Electric from 1996 to 2020 shows its fall from a peak near sixty dollars in 2000 to approximately ten dollars by 2020, detailing a history of succession and strategic issues, including a disastrous Sarasota conference that caused massive management turnover and subsequent dividend cuts. Beside it, a stock price chart for Kraft-Heinz from 2015 to 2021 shows its slide from nearly one hundred dollars down to approximately thirty dollars, indicating that the merger was doomed by high debt, severe cost-cutting at the expense of innovation, and rising competition from fresher, healthier food options.

The second section addresses the US shale bust, explaining how an aggressive drilling mentality created oil oversupply and depleted shareholder returns, leaving exploration and production companies down over seventy-five percent from 2014 levels despite a ninety percent post-vaccine rally in late 2020. This collapse is illustrated by a stock chart for Occidental Petroleum from 1991 to 2021, which shows the stock peaking over one hundred dollars before crashing below twenty dollars in 2020, a trend mirrored by peers like Antero, Apache, Concho, and Continental. Accompanying this is a stock chart for Schlumberger from 1999 to 2020, showing its price dropping from past highs of one hundred twenty dollars down to nearly twenty dollars as active US rig counts halved, dragging down other major oil service providers like Baker Hughes and Halliburton.

This page, titled "The Mall Rats," examines the prolonged decline of brick-and-mortar retail since the mid-2010s, illustrating how weakness has spread from individual stores to the broader ecosystem, including real estate and private label credit cards. The author notes that while online sales still only represented about twelve percent of total retail before the pandemic, the weakest retail links have suffered tremendously. To demonstrate this trend, the page features six stock price charts tracking major retail-associated companies from the mid-2000s or 2010s through late 2020.

The first chart tracks Men's Warehouse, illustrating how relaxed office dress codes, a shift toward working from home, and an ill-conceived hostile merger with Jos. A Bank led to a collapse in stock price. The stock peaked around sixty to seventy dollars in 2015 before falling to near zero in 2020; the chart features a quote from former CEO George Zimmer admitting the acquisition was a mistake. The second chart shows Signet Jewelers, which suffered from declining mall traffic and digital competitors that increased price transparency. Its stock plummeted from a peak of nearly one hundred fifty dollars in late 2015 to roughly twenty dollars in 2020. The third chart highlights Express, whose stock slid from a peak of twenty-five dollars in 2012 to near zero by 2020 due to inventory mismanagement, a consumer shift toward fast fashion, and a failed private equity takeover. The fourth chart focuses on COTY Brands, showing its descent from over thirty dollars in 2015 to below five dollars in 2020, driven by an overreliance on mergers and acquisitions, excessive debt, and high CEO turnover.

The final two charts show how this retail pain infected real estate and retail services. The fifth chart displays Tanger Outlets, a freeway-exit outlet mall landlord that failed to overcome secular retail declines, seeing its stock drop from a peak of around forty dollars in 2016 to under ten dollars in 2020. The sixth chart profiles Alliance Data Systems, which struggled to pivot away from private label card partnerships with struggling retailers like J. Crew, Pier 1, and Pottery Barn, and botched the forced sale of its marketing services business. Alliance Data Systems saw its stock price plunge from a peak of approximately three hundred dollars in 2015 down to around fifty dollars in 2020. All charts utilize data sourced from Bloomberg and Factset as of December 2020.

This page of the publication addresses the long-term, structural consequences of "Zoomshock"—the shift to remote work during the COVID-19 pandemic—on urban commercial real estate, municipal transportation, and surrounding businesses. The author, referencing Nicholas Bloom's research at Stanford University on the "doughnut effect," argues that the pandemic-induced migration away from dense urban centers has created severe, ongoing challenges for cities.

The page features four charts that illustrate how density, remote work viability, and public transit reliance correlate with real estate and office utilization declines. 

The first chart tracks commercial office prices by density across the twelve largest metro areas from January 2018 through mid-2020, indexing prices to January 2020. While low-density office prices rose from 100 to over 101 after March 1, 2020, high-density commercial properties saw their price index plummet to around 90. Mid-density office properties remained relatively flat near 98. 

The second chart displays residential rental prices by density over a similar period, extending to January 2021. It shows a severe divergence following the start of the pandemic: while low-density rental indexes climbed to nearly 104, high-density residential rents dropped to 91, and dense urban center rents cratered to approximately 86.

The third chart demonstrates a clear negative correlation between the share of jobs that can be done from home and local residential property price appreciation. Aggregating data from roughly 2,400 zip codes into 20 points, the chart plots the year-over-year percentage change in property values against the percentage of remote-friendly jobs. Zip codes with only a 34% share of remote-compatible jobs saw strong residential appreciation of nearly 9%, whereas zip codes with a high share of remote jobs (exceeding 52%) saw appreciation drop significantly to around 3% to 4%.

The final chart compares public transit reliance with office utilization rates across major U.S. metropolitan areas. It shows that cities with very low public transit usage, such as Dallas, Houston, and Austin (under 5% transit commute share), had the highest office utilization rates in early 2021, though these rates were still low at 35% to 40%. Conversely, cities with high public transit reliance, such as San Francisco and New York (where public transit commute shares exceed 15% and 30% respectively), suffered from much lower office utilization rates of 12% to 15%. San Jose is pictured as an outlier with low public transit usage but an office utilization rate of only about 17%. 

Ultimately, the author stresses that the full extent of these "Zoomshock" consequences remains an open question, representing a multi-billion-dollar challenge for urban commercial real estate and public infrastructure over the long run.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market examines the Reddit-fueled retail stock phenomenon of late January 2021. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that prior to this unprecedented short squeeze, these target companies were popular hedge fund shorts for sound fundamental reasons, having been severely disrupted by digital transformation, e-commerce, and the pandemic. To illustrate this, the page features three charts tracing the long-term stock market declines of GameStop, AMC Theaters, and Bed Bath & Beyond leading up to December 2020. 

The first chart displays GameStop’s stock price from 2001 to late 2020, on a axis of $0 to $70. The stock peaked above $60 in late 2007 and hovered around $50 between 2013 and 2015, before embarking on a steady downward trajectory that brought it down to single digits by late 2019 and 2020. This trend reflects the company’s struggle to remain relevant in an era dominated by digital video game downloads. 

The second chart tracks AMC Theaters from 2014 through late 2020, on a scale of $0 to $40. AMC shares saw highs near $35 in 2015 and 2017 but plummeted to under $5 by late 2020 due to the devastating impact of COVID-19 lockdowns. Cembalest notes that AMC was on the verge of bankruptcy until it managed to raise capital during the retail squeeze, posing an open question as to whether the company can ever fully recover. 

The third chart illustrates Bed Bath & Beyond's stock price from 1999 to late 2020, on a scale of $0 to $90. The retailer’s stock peaked near $80 during the 2013 to 2015 period, after which it collapsed to under $10 in 2020. The commentary attributes this decline to the competitive pressures of the Amazon effect, bad shareholder management, and a failure to modernize and improve the physical store experience. Ultimately, the author suggests that while the Reddit squeeze disrupted the market, these companies were fundamentally catastrophic losers by the close of 2020.

This page begins a discussion on concentrated portfolio diversification and hedging strategies, framing the analysis around the rapid market recovery and surge in wealth creation following the initial COVID-19 lockdowns. Although the pandemic paralyzed many businesses, financial markets quickly rebounded from a brief, one-month selloff to reach all-time highs within five months. This market recovery coincided with a major renaissance in equity issuance. The author notes that 2020 marked the most active year for Initial Public Offerings since 2007, and by early 2021, the market counted over five hundred "Unicorns"—private companies valued at more than $1 billion. 

To illustrate this trend, a bar chart titled "2020 saw most global IPO value since 2007, 2021 off to strong start" details the annual global IPO value in billions of US dollars from 1994 through 2021. The chart shows that IPO activity peaked in 2007 at nearly $500 billion before dropping significantly during the 2008 financial crisis. Activity surged again in 2020, reaching approximately $400 billion. The data for 2021, which only extends through March 3, already shows a gold-colored bar reaching nearly $150 billion, illustrating an extraordinarily rapid pace of equity issuance at the start of the year. 

The text explains that while the formation of these emerging companies has generated vast new wealth, it has also created "victims of success" by leaving investors with highly concentrated stock positions. Whether acquired through the sale of a business, option compensation, or long-term investment, these concentrated holdings introduce significant idiosyncratic risk to a portfolio, increasing the likelihood of dramatic financial losses. To help investors manage these risks, the author outlines a framework of wealth planning strategies categorized into five key actions: Sell, Monetize, Diversify, Give, and Hedge.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" discusses outright sale strategies for investors looking to mitigate the idiosyncratic risks of holding a concentrated stock position. It explains that selling strategies involve a trade-off between execution speed and price, and outlines five distinct approaches. 

The first approach is staged selling, which uses a pre-defined plan specifying share quantities, timeframes, and price levels to reduce downward market pressure and manage tax burdens. This section highlights 10b5-1 plans, which are rigid, pre-programmed selling strategies utilized by corporate executives and insiders of U.S. listed companies to avoid insider trading conflicts. The second strategy is block trades, which enable investors to quickly liquidate large positions, albeit often at a discount to the prevailing market price. Third, the author describes covered call options, where investors collect an upfront premium and set a future strike price to sell their shares if the stock rises. Fourth, target price selling strategies are discussed as a method to sell equal daily portions of shares at a target price, typically five to fifteen percent above the current market price, featuring a knock-out clause if the stock drops below a set price. Fifth, private company sales are presented as an option for venture-backed companies, noting that the private market has grown dramatically to nearly two trillion dollars from just twenty-five billion dollars fifteen years prior, offering a path to liquidity despite being less liquid than public markets. 

The page concludes by addressing tax considerations, noting that the threat of a one-time tax payment on unrealized gains creates a "tax drag" that discourages selling, though various planning and investment strategies can help mitigate this impact.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market outlines various financial strategies designed to help clients monetize or diversify concentrated stock positions without executing an immediate sale. To monetize a position, the text details four primary options. Principal Installment Stock Monetization strategies combine a hedge with a non-recourse cash advance to help de-risk a holding, though this approach may limit participation in stock appreciation above a set cap. Alternatively, Charitable Remainder Trusts let investors donate shares to a trust in exchange for an annual income stream, allowing the trust to diversify the holdings and eventually distribute any leftover assets to charity. Investors can also secure capital through security-based lines of credit by pledging their concentrated shares as collateral, though this increases portfolio risk if the stock value drops and triggers collateral requirements. To mitigate this risk, hedge and borrow strategies combine protective options, like puts and collars, with borrowing to stabilize the collateral's value, which often secures higher liquidity at lower costs. 

For diversification, the author highlights the utility of exchange funds. This mechanism allows investors to swap their concentrated stock directly for units in a diversified fund without triggering an immediate tax liability. After a holding period of seven years, the investor can redeem their fund units for a diversified basket of securities while retaining their original cost basis. Finally, the page mentions that some investors may opt for a "do-it-yourself" Personal Exchange Fund to maintain more direct control over their portfolio investments.

This page examines "healthcare disappointments" to counter the common belief that investing in healthcare innovation is an easy win, emphasizing that 90% of drugs entering clinical trials never reach the market due to innovation deficits, poor M&A execution, or political and regulatory challenges. This narrative is supported by five distinct historical stock price charts of pharmaceutical and biotech companies, each illustrating a specific type of failure.

The first chart tracks Bluebird Bio from 2014 to 2021, demonstrating the hazards of hype cycles. In 2018, the stock was covered by 23 analysts—compared to only 17 for industry giant Merck—helping drive the share price to a peak near $250. However, the excitement was short-lived, and the company had nothing to show for it by February 2021, when it suspended clinical trials for its sickle cell gene therapy, sending the stock price plunging below $50.

The second chart traces Clovis Oncology from 2012 to 2020, showing the consequences of failing to develop a differentiated star drug. After peaking near $100, the stock suffered a massive drop to around $20 in 2016 following a delayed FDA approval for a lung cancer drug. A subsequent wave of hype for Rubraca, an ovarian cancer treatment, briefly pushed the stock back up near $90 in 2017, but management's eventual guidance of flat sales for the drug left investors cold, dragging the stock down toward $10 by late 2020.

The third chart illustrates Mylan from 2005 to 2020, highlighting a flawed M&A strategy that spent $15 billion over four to five years merely to keep cash flows flat against rising biosimilar competition. The stock reached its peak of approximately $75 in 2015, around the time it bought Abbott Labs and subsequently acquired Meda & Renaissance. The aggressive acquisitions failed to sustain growth, leading to a long decline that ended in a low-value merger with Pfizer's Upjohn generics business, with the stock trading under $20.

The fourth chart follows Perrigo from 2005 to 2021 to illustrate political and generic-sector headwinds. The stock peaked near $200 in 2015, but a major downturn was triggered by a tweet from Hillary Clinton concerning drug prices. This political headwind, combined with generic drug industry pressures and the departure of the company's "Growth Czar," doomed the stock to a steady multi-year decline, bottoming out around $40 by 2021.

The final chart details Akorn Inc. from 2010 to 2020, tracking a chaotic period for the ophthalmic pharmaceutical manufacturer. The stock rose from near-zero to almost $55 in 2015 before restating its 2014 earnings and suffering a customer database hack. Although the stock temporarily rebounded when Fresenius offered to buy the company at a premium, the deal fell through and Fresenius sought damages. This legal and operational turmoil culminated in Akorn filing for bankruptcy in 2020, with the stock price collapsing to zero.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, titled "Give it away," details various strategies for transferring wealth using concentrated, appreciated stock positions to minimize tax liabilities. The author outlines four main options for investors looking to pass wealth to loved ones or charitable organizations. 

First, direct gifts to family and friends remove both the current value and future appreciation of the stock from the grantor's taxable estate, while potentially allowing recipients in lower tax brackets to liquidate the shares at a reduced income tax rate. 

Second, Grantor Retained Annuity Trusts (GRATs) allow grantors to transfer a concentrated position to an irrevocable trust that pays back the principal plus a minimum return set by the IRS, known as the 7520 rate, in annual annuities. Any remaining appreciation is transferred to beneficiaries free of transfer taxes. The author notes that the price fluctuations of concentrated positions can act as a tool in estate planning, as high-performing stocks that beat the 7520 rate result in significant wealth transfer, while underperformance only risks stock depreciation and trust setup costs. 

Third, direct charitable contributions of appreciated stock allow investors to maximize philanthropic impact, as tax-exempt charities can sell the shares without incurring capital gains taxes, wiping out the embedded gain. 

Finally, Charitable Remainder Trusts let investors defer capital gains taxes by transferring shares to a trust in exchange for an annual income stream, enabling the trust to sell the concentrated position and reinvest in a diversified portfolio, with the remaining assets eventually passing to charity.

This commentary page discusses various hedging strategies available to investors holding a concentrated stock position, allowing them to mitigate downside risk without triggering a taxable event, losing voting rights, or sacrificing dividend income. The text details four primary approaches: protective puts, protective put spreads, collars, and proxy hedges. Protective puts act like insurance, where the buyer pays an upfront premium to secure a minimum sale price, with longer options and higher strikes costing more.
