The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that despite the common perception of private equity returns being driven primarily by multiple expansion or financial leverage, operational cash flow improvements actually play the primary role in generating returns. To demonstrate this, the page analyzes company-specific data from three consecutive buyout funds managed by a major unnamed buyout manager, decomposing enterprise value changes into EBITDA growth, changes in valuation multiples, and changes in debt levels. In all three analyzed funds, operating cash flow improvements accounted for more than half of the total change in enterprise value and exceeded the impact of multiple expansion. 

The data is presented in three rows of charts, each featuring an individual investment breakdown on the left (sorted by cumulative enterprise value growth) and an enterprise-value-weighted aggregate chart on the right. The first row examines a Pre-GFC fund. The individual investment breakdown on the left shows the return components for about 17 investments, with the highest-performing asset achieving over 400% cumulative enterprise value growth, largely led by EBITDA growth. The right-hand chart shows the aggregate results for this fund, indicating a total change in enterprise value of approximately 80%, indicated by a black diamond. This total is driven by an EBITDA growth contribution of roughly 65% and a multiple expansion contribution of about 20%, offset slightly by a negative change in debt of about -5%.

The second row focuses on the Post-GFC Fund I. The individual investment breakdown on the left shows the top performer achieving over 700% cumulative enterprise value growth, driven by a combination of EBITDA growth and a positive change in debt. On the right, the aggregate results show a total enterprise value change of about 160%, where EBITDA growth is the dominant driver at roughly 95%, multiple expansion contributes about 50%, and change in debt contributes approximately 15%.

The third row presents data for the Post-GFC Fund II. The individual investment breakdown on the left reveals that the top-performing asset reached approximately 450% cumulative enterprise value growth, driven by both massive multiple expansion and EBITDA growth. The aggregate chart on the right depicts a total change in enterprise value of just over 50%, with EBITDA growth contributing around 26%, multiple expansion contributing approximately 16%, and the change in debt accounting for about 8%. 

The author notes that while this specific case study may not represent the entire private equity industry, it clearly demonstrates the crucial role that operational improvements can play in driving buyout performance. All charts are sourced from the JP Morgan Private Bank.

This page of the report examines the performance dispersion of private market managers, focusing on how the risks of choosing a below-average manager have evolved over time. Michael Cembalest observes that while average and median managers have consistently outperformed the public markets, the performance gap between top-quartile and bottom-quartile buyout managers has narrowed significantly since 2010. As a result, the degree of underperformance for bottom-quartile managers has become relatively modest.

The first chart, titled "US buyout PME quartiles by vintage year," plots the Public Market Equivalent ratio against the S&P 500 for vintage years 1991 through 2016. It displays three data series: top quartile, median, and bottom quartile managers, alongside a horizontal reference line at 1.0 indicating parity with the benchmark. While the median manager has consistently remained above the 1.0 threshold, the bottom quartile line demonstrates notable improvement. After bottoming out around 0.7 to 0.8 in the 1990s and mid-2000s, the bottom quartile's PME ratio climbed closer to 0.9 and above since 2010, narrowing the gap with top quartile performance, which has generally fluctuated between 1.2 and 1.6 in recent years. This data is sourced from Steve Kaplan of Chicago Booth and Burgiss.

The second chart, titled "US buyout direct alpha quartiles by vintage year," measures annualized direct alpha against the S&P 500 over the same 1991 to 2016 timeframe, using the same sources. This visual shows that top-quartile direct alpha peaked at over 25% in the early 1990s and around 22% in the early 2000s before stabilizing near 10% after 2010. Meanwhile, bottom-quartile direct alpha, which dipped to nearly -10% in the early 1990s and -5% in the late 1990s and mid-2000s, has narrowed to a modest range of roughly -1% to -3% since 2010.

The third chart, titled "Distribution of performance by strategy," illustrates absolute performance dispersion across different private asset classes using Hamilton Lane data from January 2021 for the 2010 to 2019 vintage years. The chart plots the percentage of funds on the y-axis against the trailing 10-year annualized return on the x-axis, ranging from 0% to 30%. Private credit shows the tightest distribution and lowest dispersion, with a sharp peak near 8% of funds earning roughly an 8% annualized return. Real estate displays a slightly wider but still relatively tight curve that peaks at a 10% return. Buyouts show a broader distribution spanning returns from approximately 5% to 20%, peaking around 12% to 13%. Venture capital displays the widest dispersion and flattest curve, with returns spanning from 5% to well over 25%, peaking more moderately around 17% to 20% annualized return.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes secondary private equity funds, which are pooled investment vehicles that buy existing private equity units or companies. The author explains the evolution of this market, starting with traditional LP-led transactions where limited partners sell their units for liquidity or portfolio rebalancing. Since 2010, average secondary market buyout prices for LP units have ranged from 85% to 100% of Net Asset Value (NAV), while venture capital secondary prices have ranged between 75% and 85% of NAV. A newer segment, GP-led transactions, emerged around 2014, allowing general partners to roll remaining seasoned investments into a new fund, giving assets a new lease on life and offering LPs the choice to cash out or reinvest. While early GP-led deals sometimes involved low-quality zombie managers looking to extend management fees, the quality of these transactions has generally improved since.

The first chart, using data from Credit Suisse, details secondary market volume by deal type in billions of US dollars from 2010 to 2020. Total volume grew from under 20 billion dollars in 2010 to a peak of approximately 80 billion dollars in 2019, before declining to around 65 billion dollars in 2020. The chart shows that GP-led secondaries and single-asset continuation funds have captured a substantial and growing portion of this total market volume since 2014.

The second chart tracks average secondary market pricing for private equity LP positions as a percentage of NAV from 2005 to 2021, sourced from Coller Capital. Buyout secondary positions hit a low near 60% of NAV during the 2008 financial crisis but have since rebounded to trade mostly in the 90% to 100% range, while venture capital secondary pricing consistently lags behind buyout pricing, generally hovering between 70% and 85% of NAV before rising sharply to nearly 90% in 2021.

The third chart showcases alternative investment performance by type using data from Cambridge Associates from Q3 2020, comparing median IRR to median total value to paid-in capital (TVPI) for the 1999 to 2018 vintage years. On this scatter plot, secondary funds demonstrate the highest median IRR at approximately 13% (with a TVPI around 1.35), outperforming buyouts (roughly 12.2% IRR, 1.55 TVPI), growth equity (11.2% IRR, 1.45 TVPI), fund of funds (10% IRR, 1.58 TVPI), private credit (8.9% IRR, 1.28 TVPI), real estate, venture capital, and infrastructure.

Despite this strong performance, the author highlights two key caveats. First, the performance data relies on self-reported performance from Cambridge Associates rather than J.P. Morgan's regular sources. Second, and more critically, some GP-led secondary funds utilize 30% to 50% leverage at the fund level, stacked on top of the leverage already present within the underlying portfolio companies. This creates a significant risk profile, presenting a large amount of leverage to carry into an economic downturn.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses venture capital performance benchmarking and manager dispersion, arguing that the S&P 500 might not be the most appropriate benchmark for venture capital given the historically small deal sizes associated with VC. He notes that because the S&P 500 has outperformed smaller-cap indices like the Russell 2000 and the Russell Microcap since 2010, using those smaller-cap benchmarks would actually make venture capital's outperformance look even larger. 

To support this argument, two charts illustrate US venture capital average and median public market equivalent (PME) ratios by vintage year from 2004 to 2016 across different benchmarks, using data from Steve Kaplan of Chicago Booth and Burgiss. Both the average and median PME charts show that benchmarking against the S&P 500 consistently yields lower PME ratios than benchmarking against the Russell 2000 or Russell Microcap. For the peak vintage year of 2012, the average PME versus the Russell Microcap exceeded 2.2, whereas the average PME versus the S&P 500 was around 1.8. Similarly, the median PME for 2012 vintages peaked near 1.5 against the Russell indices compared to approximately 1.25 against the S&P 500.

Cembalest also addresses manager dispersion, noting that the gap between top-performing and bottom-performing VC managers has narrowed since 2010, and that bottom-quartile managers have shown surprisingly modest underperformance against public equities. A chart displaying US venture capital PME quartiles by vintage year against the S&P 500 highlights this narrowing gap. The bottom-quartile PME ratio improved from roughly 0.5 for 2005 vintages to nearly 0.8 by 2016, while the top-quartile PME ratio generally fluctuated between 1.5 and 2.0. 

Finally, a stacked bar chart sourced from Pitchbook details US venture capital deals by size as a percentage of total deal value from 2006 through the first quarter of 2021. This chart reveals a massive shift toward larger deal sizes over the fifteen-year period. In 2006, deals valued at 50 million dollars or more represented only a small slice of total deal value, whereas by 2021, these large deals grew to dominate the market, capturing well over half of the total venture capital deal value. Meanwhile, categories representing smaller deals, particularly those under 10 million dollars, shrank significantly in terms of their share of total value.

This page analyzes absolute and relative venture capital performance, focusing on vintage years from 2004 onward to avoid the distortions of the late-1990s boom and bust. The author notes that the massive gains of the mid-1990s—such as the peak 1996 vintage which achieved a 7.0x multiple on invested capital (MOIC) and a 120% internal rate of return (IRR)—are no longer relevant to modern VC investing. A footnote also points out the rapid decline following that era, where the 1999 vintage fell to a 1.0x MOIC and a negative 1% IRR. The central argument is that while VC managers have generally outperformed public equity markets on average, a massive gap exists between average and median returns. This gap indicates that a small number of top-tier VC managers and larger funds generate outsized returns that pull up the averages, whereas the median manager often underperforms. Additionally, the author notes that after 2012, VC manager MOIC and IRR diverged; IRRs rose even as MOICs fell, driven by subscription lines and quicker distributions.

Four charts based on data from Steve Kaplan and Burgiss illustrate these dynamics across vintage years from 2004 to 2017. The first chart displays US venture capital MOICs, showing a persistent gap between average and median results. The average MOIC rose from under 2.0x in 2004 to a peak of nearly 3.7x in 2012, before declining to roughly 2.3x by 2017. In contrast, the median MOIC peaked earlier in 2009 at around 2.6x and steadily declined to approximately 1.7x by 2017. 

The second chart tracks US venture capital IRRs by vintage year. It depicts a steady upward trend for both metrics post-2008, despite the falling MOICs shown in the first chart. The average IRR climbed from about 7% in 2004 to nearly 35% in 2017, while the median IRR rose from approximately 3% in 2004 to just over 20% in 2017. 

The third chart presents US venture capital Public Market Equivalents (PMEs) relative to the S&P 500, where a PME ratio above 1.0 indicates outperformance. The average manager's PME remained almost entirely above the 1.0 threshold, peaking at roughly 1.75 for the 2012 vintage. Conversely, the median manager's PME fell well below 1.0 for vintage years 2004 to 2008, dropping to nearly 0.7 in 2006, meaning the typical manager substantially underperformed the S&P 500 during this period. The median PME only crossed above the 1.0 line for vintages after 2008, peaking at around 1.25 in 2012. 

The final chart shows US venture capital direct annualized alphas versus the S&P 500. This metric further highlights the median manager's struggle in earlier vintages, with median alpha dipping into negative territory from 2004 to 2008, reaching lows of around negative 8% in 2004 and 2005. While the average manager's alpha remained mostly positive and climbed to nearly 18% by 2017, the median manager's alpha only hovered around 5% for the later vintage years.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" addresses the debate over whether venture capital investors capture the majority of the benefits from tech IPOs, leaving public market investors holding the bag. Cembalest argues that, over the decade spanning 2010 to 2019, the reverse has been true: post-IPO investor gains have often been substantial, with public market equity investors capturing the vast majority of the total value created. 

The analysis covers 165 US tech, internet retailing, and interactive media IPOs. The visual centerpiece is a scatter-line chart titled "Value creation in pre-IPO and post-IPO markets," which plots these 165 IPOs along an ascending S-curve. The left y-axis displays the percentage of value created post-IPO (ranging from -50% to 150%), while the right y-axis displays the inverted percentage of value created pre-IPO (ranging from -50% to 150%). 

The chart is divided into three distinct shaded regions. The bottom-left red region comprises companies where pre-IPO investors earned virtually all the value, leaving public market investors with losses or no gains; notable examples highlighted here include Rocket Fuel, Quotient, Groupon, Green Sky, Blue Apron, SolarWinds, Sabre, Eventbrite, and The RealReal. The middle yellow region highlights where pre- and post-IPO investors shared the value creation, containing companies such as Dropbox, Switch, Surveymonkey, Yelp, Twitter, DataDog, Pinterest, and LinkedIn. The upper-right blue region shows the vast majority of the companies, where post-IPO investors earned the vast majority of total value creation. This region includes high-performing stocks such as Chewy, Cloudflare, Zoom, CrowdStrike, Snap, DocuSign, Facebook, Square, and First Data. 

Methodologically, the analysis defines pre-IPO performance to include the post-IPO lockup period, after which pre-IPO investors are treated the same as public investors. Value creation shares are capped at 150%, meaning values over 100% reflect instances where one group of investors experienced negative value creation. The data is sourced from PitchBook, Bloomberg, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page explores the performance and downside mitigation benefits of private equity co-investments, which typically arise when a target acquisition requires more capital than a sponsor can provide from their fund alone. The author explains that the premise behind co-investments is that lower fees increase limited partner returns, while security selection is expected to be at least as strong as in standard diversified private equity funds. Historically, buyout and growth co-investment funds have demonstrated clear outperformance versus the overall industry. For 2009 to 2016 vintages, 80 percent of co-investment funds outperformed primary private equity funds, delivering a net median internal rate of return of 18.9 percent compared to 14.6 percent for primary funds. Over the longer 1998 to 2016 period, 60 percent of co-investment funds outperformed. 

To illustrate these downside risk mitigation benefits, the page features two charts sourced from Capital Dynamics in 2020. The first chart, which plots net total value to paid-in capital, compares the lower quartile and lower decile performance of primary private equity funds versus co-investment funds. It reveals that primary private equity funds have a lower quartile net TVPI of 1.20x and a lower decile of 0.93x. In comparison, co-investment funds exhibit higher values, with a lower quartile net TVPI of 1.27x and a lower decile of 1.09x, showing that even the lower-performing co-investment funds generally avoided capital losses. 

The second chart displays the proportion of loss-generating funds, defined as those with a net TVPI of less than 1.0x, across two vintage periods. For the 1998 to 2016 vintage years, primary private equity funds had a loss-generating rate of approximately 12 percent, whereas co-investment funds stood lower at around 8 percent. For the 2009 to 2016 vintage years, this difference is even more pronounced, with about 11 percent of primary private equity funds generating losses compared to only about 3 percent for co-investment funds. This visual data reinforces the author's point that co-investments have historically offered both superior return profiles and superior downside protection.

This page analyzes the performance differences between private equity buyout funds and venture capital (VC) across four key metrics. Michael Cembalest argues that while VC has outperformed buyout since 2010, the gap is smaller than commonly assumed when evaluating the performance of the median manager. Although average manager performance metrics show a massive VC advantage, median results offer a more realistic reflection of the opportunity set available to an individual limited partner (LP).

Four charts plot performance by vintage year from 2004 to 2016, utilizing data from Steve Kaplan at Chicago Booth and Burgiss. The top-left chart compares median Multiple on Invested Capital (MOIC). It shows VC median MOICs starting low in 2004 near 1.1 but rising steadily to peak at over 2.5 in 2009 and 2012, while buyout median MOICs remained relatively stable between 1.5 and 2.0, ultimately converging with VC near 1.4 by 2017. The top-right chart illustrates median Internal Rates of Return (IRRs), showing VC starting at near 0% in 2004, climbing to match buyout’s mid-teen IRRs around 2009, and remaining closely matched or slightly ahead of buyout through 2017, where both end near 22%. The bottom-left chart details median Public Market Equivalent (PME) ratios versus the S&P 500, showing buyout consistently outperforming the public benchmark (PME above 1.0) for almost all vintage years, while VC underperformed in earlier vintages but consistently beat the index starting with 2010 vintages, peaking near a PME of 1.2 in 2012. The bottom-right chart tracks annualized median direct alphas against the S&P 500, displaying buyout direct alpha hovering in positive territory between 0% and 5% for most years, whereas VC direct alpha starts significantly negative near -7% in 2004 before rising into positive territory around 2010 and peaking near 4% in 2012.

Two tables at the bottom summarize these performance metrics for the 2004 to 2017 vintage years. The first table shows that for the median manager, buyout actually outperformed VC in three out of four metrics. While VC had a slightly higher MOIC of 1.8 compared to buyout's 1.7, buyout delivered a superior median IRR of 15.3% (versus VC's 14.3%), a higher PME of 1.1 (versus 1.0), and a much stronger direct alpha of 2.4% (versus 0.3%). In contrast, the second table highlights the average manager performance over the same period, where VC heavily outpaced buyout across the board, achieving a 2.6 MOIC (versus 1.7 for buyout), a 21.4% IRR (versus 16.1%), a 1.3 PME (versus 1.1), and a 6.7% direct alpha (versus 3.2%). This stark contrast underlines how outsized returns from top-tier VC funds skew average metrics upward, emphasizing the author's point that median figures represent a more grounded guide for individual investors.

This page analyses fundraising trends and the pace of investment in private equity, observing that global dry powder has surged from $2 trillion to approximately $3 trillion due to new investment trailing fundraising. The author clarifies that buyout and venture capital only account for about $1 trillion of this dry powder, and the widespread use of subscription lines—estimated at $500 billion outstanding—artificially inflates the apparent level of committed capital. 

Two stacked bar charts from the Bain Global Private Equity Report support these points. The first, titled Global Private Equity Capital Raised by Year (spanning 2003 to 2020 in trillions of US dollars), shows capital raised climbing to nearly $1.1 trillion by 2020. The second, titled Global Dry Powder by Category, depicts total dry powder climbing steadily to nearly $3.0 trillion in 2020. Both charts break down figures into Buyout, Venture Capital, Real Estate, Infrastructure, and "Other" categories, where "Other" includes segments like Direct Lending, Secondary, Growth, Distressed, SPACs, and Natural Resources.

The author also notes that during periods of elevated valuations, exits and distributions tend to exceed capital calls, particularly in the United States. Many 2020 exits were conducted through IPOs and SPACs; because much of this capital is public but not yet distributed, distributions are predicted to remain elevated throughout 2021. This dynamic is illustrated in two line charts sourced from Burgiss measuring capital calls and distributions as a percentage of fund size from 2000 to 2020. The US Private Equity Capital Calls and Distributions chart demonstrates that US distributions have surged to over 4% of fund size, comfortably outpacing US capital calls, which sit below 3%. A parallel chart, Global Private Equity Capital Calls and Distributions, shows a similar divergence globally, with distributions rising to approximately 3.5% of fund size, outperforming capital calls.

This page analyzes the structure and impact of private equity fees, dividing them into three distinct categories based on estimates of fees earned from 2008 to 2020 by major publicly listed private equity firms: Carlyle, KKR, Blackstone, and Apollo. 

The first category is carried interest, which totaled thirty billion dollars over this period and is paid only if returns exceed a specified threshold. The author notes that while academic research generally suggests an alignment of interest between general partners and limited partners, a notable agency conflict occurs during the waterfall quarter. During this time, general partners tend to accelerate realizations right after the limited partner's preferred return has been paid to secure a catch-up return, which sacrifices potential upside for the limited partner. This phenomenon is illustrated in a bar chart titled "Managers cluster realizations around waterfall quarter," which plots excess realizations in the waterfall quarter compared to an average quarter as a percentage of original committed capital. The chart reveals that excess realizations reach approximately thirty-eight percent for buyout funds and jump to roughly sixty-three percent for venture capital funds.

The second category discussed is management fees, which brought in twenty-six billion dollars and are typically earned based on committed rather than invested capital. An accompanying bar chart titled "Private equity management fee approach by manager type" displays the percentage of managers charging fees based on committed capital versus invested capital across ten different fund types. The data shows that ninety percent of buyout managers charge fees on committed capital, while other strategies utilize invested capital more frequently. For instance, while private equity funds of funds almost exclusively charge on committed capital, categories like direct lending, distressed debt, mezzanine, infrastructure, real estate, and natural resources show a significantly larger share of managers charging on invested capital.

The third category covers net monitoring and transaction fees, also known as company fees, which accounted for four point six billion dollars. The author notes that these fees generate controversy because they are paid by portfolio companies whose boards are controlled by the general partner, a practice that has previously drawn SEC fines for inadequate disclosure. While these fees are not specified in limited partnership agreements, they are outlined in management services agreements, and the text notes that eighty to eighty-five percent of such fees were rebated to limited partners between 2011 and 2014.

This page analyzes US private equity and venture capital fundraising relative to overall stock market capitalization, arguing that while absolute commitments to buyouts and venture capital have risen sharply, they appear less ominous when measured against the total size of the stock market. To support this point, J.P. Morgan presents four charts based on 2020 data from Steve Kaplan of Chicago Booth and Burgiss. 

The first chart shows absolute commitments to US private equity and leveraged buyout partnerships in billions of dollars, illustrating a steady long-term climb from nearly zero in 1980 to cyclical peaks of about $100 billion in 2000, $250 billion in 2007, and a record peak approaching $350 billion around 2018. However, the adjacent chart scales these same commitments as a percentage of all-cap stock market capitalization. This relative view reveals that buyout commitments actually peaked in 2007 at over 1.2% of total market capitalization, whereas the recent absolute record-high funding represents a lower relative percentage of roughly 1.0% or less. 

A similar dynamic is visible in the venture capital charts. The absolute dollar commitments to US venture capital partnerships show a massive spike during the dot-com bubble, peaking near $75 billion in 2000, followed by a long drop and a subsequent multi-decade recovery that brought absolute commitments back close to that $75 billion mark by 2020. When adjusted as a percentage of all-cap stock market capitalization in the final chart, the contrast is even more pronounced. The dot-com bubble peak exceeded 0.40% of market capitalization, while the 2020 fundraising level reached only about 0.20%, demonstrating that modern venture capital expansion is significantly smaller relative to the scale of the broader public equities market.

This page presents insights and findings from five academic papers regarding private equity performance, secondary markets, fund sizing, and post-IPO manager behavior. The author outlines key takeaways for institutional investors, highlighting issues like performance persistence, mature fund volatility, scaling difficulties, and inefficient post-IPO stock management. 

The first chart on the left, titled "Dispersion of remaining buyout fund performance over fund life, Remaining direct alpha," illustrates the performance dispersion of buyout funds as they mature. Drawing on data from Burgiss and a June 2020 study by Brown et al., the line graph displays remaining direct alpha on the y-axis, ranging from negative 80 percent to 100 percent, against fund age in years on the x-axis, spanning from year zero to 15. The chart shows five series: the 90th, 75th, 25th, and 10th percentiles, along with the median. While the median remains close to zero percent throughout the fund's life, the gap between the 90th percentile and 10th percentile widens dramatically starting around years 7 and 8. By year 15, the 90th percentile reaches nearly 60 percent, while the 10th percentile falls below negative 60 percent. This dramatic divergence highlights the rising volatility in mature funds, which has significant implications for secondary private equity funds purchasing older assets.

The second chart, on the right, is titled "Faster exits post-IPO improve fund performance" and is sourced from a February 2021 paper by Jenkinson et al. of Oxford. This bar chart depicts the net internal rate of return (IRR) of the median deal under four different post-IPO exit strategies. The y-axis shows net IRR from zero percent to 45 percent. The first bar reveals that the fastest exit (top quartile) produces the highest return at approximately 38 percent IRR. Spacing share sales equally over three years results in a lower return of about 32 percent IRR. The actual historical performance of these funds is even lower, delivering roughly 26 percent IRR. The slowest exit (bottom quartile) performs the worst, yielding only about 14 percent IRR. This data underscores the author's argument that private equity funds holding public companies for an average of three years post-IPO fails to add value and needlessly forces limited partners to pay ongoing management fees.

Beyond these charts, the text details several academic findings. Research on top performer persistence indicates that while top-quartile venture capital and buyout fund performance tends to persist, buyout interim performance is not an accurate predictor of future performance, whereas venture capital interim performance remains a useful signal. Additionally, private equity firms that raise larger subsequent funds after strong cycles often see performance declines, which is likely due to difficulties scaling investment operations or simple reversion to the mean. Finally, timing private equity commitments has historically yielded very modest benefits because general partners actively adjust their pacing to market cycles and valuations. These insights are drawn from researchers at institutions such as the University of Virginia, University of North Carolina, University of Arizona, and Oxford University.

This page contains only standard legal disclaimers, regulatory information, and jurisdictional disclosures for JPMorgan Chase Bank and its affiliates across various international regions, including Europe, Asia, Latin America, and Australia.

This appendix section, titled "Appendix III: Sources for private equity manager performance," addresses historical issues and modern solutions in measuring private equity portfolio returns against public markets. The author explains that data aggregators like Venture Economics were once the primary resource for performance tracking, but research from the University of Oxford in 2013 revealed severe database anomalies, such as survivorship bias and incomplete data. Specifically, over forty percent of active funds in the database stopped updating, and incomplete funds missed over sixty percent of their cash distributions, causing a significant downward bias in benchmark returns. Correcting these errors turned a previously estimated underperformance of three to six percent against the S&P 500 into an annual outperformance of four percent. Additionally, some analysts incorrectly treated constant residual values as worthless "living dead investments" when calculating returns.

To overcome these data quality issues, the author notes a shift toward the Burgiss database, which collects net-of-fee cash flow data directly from limited partners rather than relying on self-reported figures. The Burgiss investor universe comprises three hundred state and corporate pension funds, endowments, and foundation limited partners across fourteen hundred private equity funds. This dataset is estimated to represent at least seventy percent of all private equity funds ever raised, leading the author to rely exclusively on this source rather than self-reported performance data. The text references academic papers by Rudiger Stucke of Oxford and Steve Kaplan of Chicago Booth to support these points.

This page compiles multiple charts analyzing trends in private equity, venture capital, institutional portfolio allocations, and buyout performance during market crises. 

The author begins by noting that the number of private equity funds has now surpassed the number of hedge funds, warning that this proliferation could negatively impact private equity returns, similar to the historical trend seen with hedge funds. This is illustrated in the first chart, "Global active private capital firms by asset class," which tracks the number of firms from 1990 to 2020. It demonstrates that the number of firms in private markets overall has risen to nearly 11,000, driven heavily by private equity, which overtook hedge funds around 2020, while real estate, natural resources, private debt, and infrastructure remain much lower.

The next chart details the "Distribution of US LBOs by type" from 2002 to the first quarter of 2021. The author highlights that sponsor-to-sponsor buyouts have declined as a percentage of overall US deals since their 2014 peak, when they represented over 50% of transactions. Conversely, public-to-private buyouts and corporate division divestitures have taken up an increasing share of overall transaction volume by 2021.

The middle of the page features two charts analyzing "US venture capital exits by type" from 2006 to 2021, with one measuring the number of exits and the other measuring value in billions of US dollars. Together they show that while acquisitions consistently represent the highest number of exits—accounting for 65% of exits in 2021—public listings represent a massive 90% of the total exit value, which spiked near $300 billion in 2020.

Looking at institutional investor behavior from 2008 to 2019, the "Institutional investors' portfolio allocation" chart shows a steady rotation away from public equities toward bonds, private equity, and alternative assets. Public equity's share of portfolios declined from approximately 50% in 2008 to roughly 40% by 2019, while allocations to bonds, private equity, infrastructure, and other alternatives grew incrementally.

Finally, the bottom-right chart, titled "Impact of rapid central bank response," shows the loss rate for buyout deals by their year of exit from 2005 to 2020. The author observes that buyouts suffered far fewer poorly performing investments during the COVID-19 shock of 2020, with a loss rate of only about 11%, compared to the Global Financial Crisis, where the loss rate peaked near 30% in 2009. This resilience is attributed to the unprecedented speed of the central bank policy response. Data sources cited across these charts include McKinsey, S&P Global, Pitchbook, and Bain.

This page of Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market discusses the performance and return dispersion of individual buyout and venture capital transactions within commingled funds. Using a database of transactions from the mid-1990s to 2018 sourced from a academic study of Burgiss holdings data by Brown, Harris, Hu, Jenkinson, Kaplan, and Robinson, the analysis demonstrates that while venture capital offers strong average returns, these returns are heavily dependent on a very small fraction of highly successful transactions. Because of this high level of dispersion, the author advocates for investors to focus on diversified private equity funds rather than concentrated individual bets.

A performance table compares TVPI, which is equivalent to Multiple on Invested Capital, and Public Market Equivalent metrics for buyout and venture capital deals. For buyouts, the value-weighted mean TVPI is 1.9, the median is 1.6, and the standard deviation is 2.8, with only 27% of transactions losing money. For venture capital, the TVPI standard deviation is a much wider 6.9, with a value-weighted mean TVPI of 2.2 and a median of 1.0. Crucially, 61% of venture capital transactions lose money, and 54% of transactions yield a TVPI of less than 0.5x. 

The concentration of performance is further illustrated by a line chart tracking the cumulative percentage of value creation against the cumulative percentage of transactions. While the buyout curve shows a relatively steady accumulation of value across transactions, the venture capital curve remains nearly flat for the first 80% of deals. This stark curve illustrates that venture capital managers rely on just the top 20% of their transactions to drive virtually all of their overall fund returns, offsetting the fact that more than 60% of all venture capital transactions end up losing money.

This page, titled Appendix IV: On IRR, Direct Alpha, cash flow timing and subscription lines, presents a scenario analysis examining how the timing of capital commitments and distributions, along with the use of subscription lines, affects Internal Rate of Return and Direct Alpha. The analysis assumes a hypothetical 2010 vintage fund with a four-year investment period and a seven-year harvesting period that ultimately returns two times the committed capital, benchmarked against the S&P 500 Index. Under the subscription line scenario, an extreme case is modeled where every dollar called is funded by the line and not repaid until the end of the investment period in 2014.

An initial chart titled Illustrative net cash flows plots net cash flows as a percentage of committed capital from 2010 to 2020. It illustrates three scenarios: a Base Case, a Front Loaded case, and a Back Loaded case. The Front Loaded scenario shows capital being called and returned earlier, peaking around 45% in 2015, while the Back Loaded scenario delays cash flows, peaking around 45% in 2019.

Four tables detail the resulting IRR and Direct Alpha metrics under different combinations of commitment and distribution schedules, comparing performance with and without subscription lines. 

Without subscription lines, the IRR table shows that the highest return of 26% is achieved under a Front Loaded distribution and Back Loaded commitment schedule, while the lowest return of 9% occurs with a Back Loaded distribution and Front Loaded commitment. The corresponding Direct Alpha table without subscription lines shows a range from a high of 10% (Front Loaded distribution, Back Loaded commitment) to a low of -4% (Back Loaded distribution, Front Loaded commitment), with the Base Case combination yielding 2% Direct Alpha.

With subscription lines, performance metrics improve significantly across the board, particularly for front-loaded distributions. Under the IRR table with subscription lines, the Front Loaded distribution and Back Loaded commitment combination reaches 43%, and the Base Case combination rises to 22%. In the Direct Alpha table with subscription lines, the Front Loaded distribution and Back Loaded commitment combination jumps to 32%, whereas the Back Loaded distribution and Front Loaded commitment combination only improves to 0%. The comparisons demonstrate that subscription lines have a much larger distorting impact on performance metrics when fund distributions are front-loaded rather than back-loaded.

This page, titled "COVID and Thy Brother’s Keeper," examines the impact of the COVID-19 Delta variant on public health and financial markets, arguing that while the variant poses severe risks to unvaccinated individuals, developed world equities will withstand its spread because the economic reopening momentum is unlikely to be reversed. Author Michael Cembalest points out that while the Delta variant causes few breakthrough infections in vaccinated people, the unvaccinated face serious risks. In the United Kingdom, where ninety-six percent of people over fifty are vaccinated, a major spike in Delta infections has not triggered a corresponding rise in overall hospitalizations or deaths. However, for the unvaccinated over-fifty population in the UK, fourteen percent of Delta infections resulted in hospitalization and nearly four percent died—rates four times higher than their vaccinated peers. In contrast, the United States has a lower vaccination rate of approximately seventy-five percent among people over fifty, which is even lower in rural areas and hotspot states such as Arkansas, Florida, Louisiana, Missouri, Nevada, and Wyoming, causing hospitalizations to rise more rapidly than in the UK. 

Cembalest predicts that the US reopening remains on track because governments are highly unlikely to reimpose mobility restrictions to protect individuals who actively choose not to get vaccinated, reflecting a political shift away from intergenerational sacrifices. 

This decoupling of infections and severe illness is illustrated by two charts. The first chart, focused on the United Kingdom, plots daily infections and current hospitalizations on the left-hand axis (ranging from zero to seventy thousand) alongside daily deaths on the right-hand axis (ranging from zero to fourteen hundred) from February 2020 to June 2021. It shows that while daily infections surged dramatically in mid-2021, hospitalizations and deaths remained exceptionally low compared to the severe peaks seen in late 2020 and early 2021. The second chart, titled "Lockdown stringency index: US, UK and Europe," measures lockdown strictness on an index from zero to one hundred (with one hundred being the highest level of strictness) from February 2020 to August 2021. It tracks three series: the United States, the United Kingdom, and an aggregate of France, Germany, Italy, and Spain. By mid-2021, lockdown stringency had dropped significantly across all regions, with the US falling to around twenty and the UK and European countries also showing a steady downward trend in restrictions, reinforcing the idea that mobility limits are unlikely to return.

This page outlines several concerning market developments, described as "ashes" that can be attributed to Federal Reserve policies, focusing on loose credit, speculative equity activity, surging real estate, and collapsing underwriting standards. 

The first chart tracks the US corporate high-yield bond index spread over the 10-year Treasury from 2001 to 2021, revealing that spreads have compressed to historically low levels near 3% in mid-2021, which is reminiscent of the pre-crisis lows of 2007. To illustrate speculative equity trends, a second chart displays net secondary offerings as a percentage of the US stock market from 1982 to 2021, plotting the offerings of profitable firms minus those of unprofitable firms. This metric has plummeted below zero, indicating that unprofitable companies have flooded the market with secondary offerings. Furthering this point, a third chart highlights the market capitalization of young unprofitable companies as a share of the total market cap from 1990 to 2020. Defining these entities as having negative net income in two of the last three years, less than five years since IPO, and annual revenues growing over 15%, the chart shows their share spiking toward 4% by early 2021, nearing the peak levels seen during the dot-com bubble in 2000.

Real estate pressures are captured in a chart of US home price appreciation year-over-year from 2013 to 2021. It shows that appreciation for both low-to-medium and medium-to-high price tiers surged dramatically to between 15% and 25% in 2021. 

Finally, the author details a collapse in loan underwriting standards using Moody’s data. A line chart of the loan covenant quality score from 2012 to 2021 shows the score climbing steadily from 3.2 to nearly 4.5, where a score of 5 represents the weakest possible covenant quality. A companion bar chart directly compares individual quality scores from 2007 against the 2019–2020 period. Across every category examined—including overall score, financial covenants, subordination of liens and structural protections, restricted payments, debt incurrence, risky investments, asset sales with mandatory prepays, and voting and assignments—the credit discipline in 2019–2020 was significantly weaker than in the famously free-wheeling environment of 2007. The author concludes that these discarded protections will likely become a major problem when the business cycle hits a rough patch.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest characterizes the Federal Reserve as acting simultaneously as a firefighter and an arsonist. While the central bank resuscitates private sector demand, it is simultaneously eroding underwriting and investment discipline through the easiest monetary policy in US history outside of wartime. This monetary policy is reinforced by a symbiotic relationship with the US Treasury, in which the Fed has purchased nearly the entire stock of net Treasury issuance. Cembalest warns that while a powerful global economic recovery is underway—supported by pent-up demand and US household debt service ratios at their lowest levels in forty years—markets have already priced in much of this positive news, driving valuations near record highs. 

The publication includes four charts to support this assessment. The first chart displays the five-year average of real yields on cash, defined as the Treasury bill or Funds rate less inflation, spanning from 1830 to 2020. The chart demonstrates that real cash yields have historically only dipped below zero percent during major national crises, specifically annotated as the Civil War, World War I, and World War II. The far right of the chart highlights that current non-wartime real yields have once again entered negative territory.

The second chart, plotted from 2003 to 2021, displays Fed Treasury purchases covering net issuance in trillions of US dollars on a three-month average. It compares Treasury net issuance, shown as a solid gold line, against Fed purchases of Treasuries, shown as a dashed blue line. The visual shows that during the 2020–2021 pandemic intervention, both metrics spiked dramatically, with the Fed’s Treasury purchases almost entirely matching the massive net issuance peak near one trillion dollars.

The third chart tracks the S&P 500 price-to-earnings ratio based on forward two-year earnings per share from 1990 to 2021. The ratio peaked near 24x during the dot-com bubble, fell to approximately 10x during the Great Recession, and has climbed back up to approximately 20x as of July 8, 2021. 

The fourth chart presents the S&P 500 cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio from 1880 to 2021, which is based on trailing ten-year average inflation-adjusted earnings. This Shiller P/E ratio highlights a historic low of 6x on July 8, 1932, and contrasts it with a exceptionally high level of 37x recorded on July 8, 2021, a level surpassed only by the peak of the dot-com bubble in 2000. 

Looking forward to 2022, Cembalest envisions a transition back toward trend growth accompanied by modestly higher inflation. In this macroeconomic environment, he forecasts that equity returns will be driven by earnings growth rather than expanding valuation multiples, and he predicts that reflation sectors, including industrials, energy, and financials, will outperform.

This page examines the regulatory pressures weighing on Chinese technology companies, contrasting US policies against Beijing's own domestic crackdown. Michael Cembalest lists several US initiatives introduced under the Biden administration targeting China, such as Executive Orders restricting data access and investment, the Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act, the CHIPS Act, the Endless Frontier Act, the Strategic Competition Act, and the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act. However, he argues that the most severe risks for Chinese tech stocks and American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) originate from China's own regulators, who are cracking down on monopolies, data privacy, fintech, education, and foreign listings—noting a new rule requiring cybersecurity reviews for firms with over one million users listing abroad, which heavily impacted Didi's ride-hailing app. 

A bar chart on the left illustrates the year-to-date total return in US dollars for various China equity indices as of July 8, 2021. Performance is highly divergent: mainland and Hong Kong-focused indices like MSCI China B Shares, Shenzhen Composite, and Shanghai Composite posted positive returns, with MSCI China B Shares leading at around 13%. In contrast, tech-heavy and offshore indices suffered steep losses, with Hang Seng Tech, FTSE China Tech, and the China ADR index—which is composed of 70% technology and consumer services—down between 10% and 15%. 

A line chart on the right displays US and China technology valuations from 2017 through mid-2021, measured by price divided by forward two-year earnings per share. Historically volatile, China technology valuations peaked at roughly 36x forward earnings in early 2021 but sharply de-rated to around 24x by July 2021. This rapid decline brought Chinese tech valuations down to roughly the same level as US technology stocks, which traded steadily around 24x. The author concludes that because Chinese tech giants face substantial domestic policy hurdles, they now require lower valuations than their US counterparts.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market publication. It provides jurisdiction-specific legal notices regarding the distribution and supervision of the material by local financial authorities. Countries and regions covered include Spain, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Latin America, and Australia. The page does not contain any charts, market analysis, forecasts, or economic discussions, serving strictly as legal boilerplate.

Michael Cembalest discusses the concept of a US-China economic divorce, arguing that while the twenty-five percent decline in the stock price of Didi has renewed investor anxiety about this rift, a high level of normalcy still characterizes the broader US-China economic relationship. To support this thesis, he presents six charts analyzing trade shares, stock performance, semiconductor exports, asset holdings, and foreign direct investment.

The first chart, tracking the trade war’s impact on US import counterparties through six-month average shares from 2015 to 2021, demonstrates that China's share of US imports has only modestly declined. After peaking near twenty-two percent in 2017 and 2018, China's import share fell to about seventeen percent in 2020 before recovering slightly to roughly eighteen percent in 2021. Meanwhile, Europe remains the largest counterpart at around twenty-five percent, with Canada and Mexico steady at twelve to fourteen percent, and the combined share of Korea, Vietnam, and Taiwan holding between five and eight percent.

The second chart illustrates the relative performance of US companies with high exposure to the US-China trade war against the S&P 500, indexed to one hundred in January 2018. This relative index fell to a low of approximately seventy-three in early 2020 during the pandemic's onset but recovered sharply to about ninety-five by mid-2021, indicating that trade-war-exposed US companies are performing nearly on par with the broader market.

The third chart plots US semiconductor exports to China in billions of dollars from 2015 to 2021. It highlights two key regulatory events aimed at Huawei: the May 16, 2019 policy putting US-produced technology out of Huawei's reach, and the August 17, 2020 policy extending this ban to any technology based on US tech. Despite these barriers, semiconductor exports rose from a stable base of around five hundred to six hundred million dollars between 2015 and 2018 to a record high of nearly one point three billion dollars by early 2021.

The fourth chart displays US holdings of Chinese stocks and bonds from 2012 to 2020 in billions of dollars. It shows a steady accumulation of Chinese assets by US investors, growing from around one hundred billion dollars in 2012 to approximately three hundred billion dollars by late 2020, with stocks consistently making up the overwhelming majority of these holdings.

The fifth chart compares the ownership of US Treasuries in trillions of dollars by China and Russia from 1995 to 2020. Unlike Russia, which liquidated almost all of its US Treasury holdings from a peak of about two hundred billion dollars in 2010 to near zero by 2018, China has not weaponized its holdings. China's US Treasury holdings rose from near zero in 1995 to a peak of roughly one point three trillion dollars around 2011 to 2013, before stabilizing at just over one trillion dollars in 2020.

The final chart examines the decline in bilateral foreign direct investment, measured in billions of dollars from 2004 to 2020, which the author notes may be permanent due to changing national security policies. While US foreign direct investment into China has remained relatively stable, fluctuating between ten and fifteen billion dollars annually over the period, Chinese foreign direct investment into the US tells a different story. It spiked dramatically to over forty-five billion dollars in 2016 and thirty-five billion dollars in 2017, but subsequently plummeted to negligible levels below five billion dollars by 2020.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses why he is skeptical that wage inflation will subside quickly. While he agrees that broader consumer price inflation may soon fall back into the Federal Reserve's comfort zone once short-term supply chain bottlenecks resolve, he questions the common assumption that the scheduled expiration of federal COVID-19 unemployment benefits will easily resolve labor market tightness. Instead, he points to multiple underlying factors suggesting that wage pressures are structural and possess strong momentum independent of temporary government aid.

To support his argument, Cembalest presents six charts detailing various aspects of the labor market and business expectations. The first chart, depicting workers losing federal unemployment benefits, illustrates the massive cliff coming in September 2021, when roughly 14 to 15 million people are scheduled to lose benefits entirely or experience a three-hundred-dollar weekly reduction through programs like Pandemic Unemployment Assistance and PEUC.

The remaining charts demonstrate why labor markets may remain tight despite these benefit cuts. The second chart compares total private employment against total wages using an index set to 100 in February 2020. This data shows a sharp divergence: while private employment remains depressed at an index level below 95, total private wages have surged, recovering rapidly to an index value near 104 by mid-2021, proving that wages are growing much faster than hiring.

This dynamic is further explained by NFIB small business survey data. The third chart shows that the share of small businesses planning to raise worker compensation and prices has skyrocketed to historic highs in 2021, with price-raising intentions hovering around 45% and compensation-raising intentions close to 40%. Simultaneously, the fifth chart reveals that the percentage of small businesses with hard-to-fill job openings has reached an all-time high of nearly 50% in 2021, a level far surpassing previous business cycles.

Structural shifts in the labor supply are detailed in the fourth chart, which tracks those not in the labor force. The percentage of the population aged 16 and older who are not in the labor force and do not want a job has climbed steadily to approximately 36% in 2021, while the share of those who do want a job has dwindled to just around 2%. Finally, the sixth chart highlights the reservation wage, which measures the lowest wage respondents are willing to accept for a new job. For lower-income workers earning under sixty thousand dollars annually, this reservation wage index has surged dramatically to over 125 relative to late 2019, whereas the reservation wage for higher-income earners has actually declined, showing that businesses must pay a substantial premium to attract lower-wage workers back into employment.

On this page, author Michael Cembalest discusses the outlook for inflation, globalization, and the booming US economy. He argues that while President Biden's China agenda is unlikely to derail China's economy, a broader decline in globalization alongside rising US national security enforcement points toward higher long-term inflation. This transition is framed under the broader section title, "The Pig and the Snake: a unified theory of the US, China, wages, jobs, inflation, opioid use, the WTO and investment portfolios for 2022 and beyond." Despite some unusually high inflation readings, the author notes that professional economic forecasters view these as temporary anomalies, supported by strong capital spending and hiring tailwinds.

The page features six charts that support these observations. The first chart, depicting a globalization index from 1970 to 2020, measures global trade, portfolio flows, and foreign direct investment as a percentage of global GDP. The index peaked above 120 in the mid-2000s and has since steadily declined, falling back to around 80 by 2020, signaling a clear structural shift toward deglobalization. 

Adjacent to this, a stacked bar chart illustrates the activities of the US Committee on Foreign Investment (CFIUS) from 2010 to 2019. It shows a substantial increase in notices and investigations, rising from roughly 90 cases in 2010 to well over 200 cases per year by late decade. The growth is led by the manufacturing and finance, information, and services sectors, while a separate trend line for cases involving China shows investigations peaking near 75 in 2017 and 2018 before tapering off slightly.

Addressing capital expenditure, a chart on US leading indicators compares actual capital expenditure growth to demand-based estimates across seven sectors. While resource equipment experienced negative growth of about 5%, its demand-based estimate sits at nearly 50%, reflecting massive latent demand. Similarly, vehicles show a demand-based capex estimate of over 45%, while actual tech equipment capex growth leads other sectors at roughly 25%.

The next chart tracks US CEO hiring plans using an index where a value above 50 signifies increased hiring expectations. This index plunged to near zero in 2009 and hit a low of roughly 25 in 2020, but skyrocketed to over 100 in mid-2021, highlighting exceptionally strong hiring intentions.

The final two charts address the inflation debate. One graph tracks the year-over-year percentage change in the US Core Consumer Price Index from 2001 to 2021. For two decades, core inflation fluctuated predictably between 1% and 3%, but spiked sharply above 4% in 2021. A final chart on used car prices, indexed to 2012, illustrates the specific supply-chain anomalies driving these numbers. Historically range-bound between 80 and 100, the used car price index experienced a near-vertical climb to over 110 in 2021, providing a clear example of the temporary, extreme price pressures current forecasters are looking past.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication by Michael Cembalest discusses the interconnected relationship between China’s economic rise, US manufacturing decline, and the modern distribution of corporate profits. The author argues that rising wages are positive for the US economy, but they may eventually challenge the Federal Reserve's zero-rate policy. He frames the current rise in wages as a long-awaited correction: after China entered the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2001, a massive wave of currency intervention suppressed US import prices but accelerated domestic manufacturing job losses. This shift dramatically reduced the share of corporate profits going to US workers rather than capital, contributing to deep social crises like the opioid epidemic. Because rising wages are finally helping the labor share recover toward its post-war average, the author predicts the Federal Reserve will be very reluctant to interfere with rate hikes initially, which favors reflation investment strategies for portfolios in 2022 and beyond.

The page features four key charts to illustrate this structural narrative. The first chart, at the top left, displays the 10-year percentage change in US manufacturing job losses on the left axis alongside Chinese foreign exchange intervention as an inverted percentage of GDP on the right axis. It shows that following China's accession to the WTO in 2001, Chinese FX intervention spiked dramatically, peaking near 40% of GDP, while US manufacturing job losses plunged to a nearly 40% decline on a 10-year basis by 2010. 

The top right chart connects these same US manufacturing job losses to the US labor share of non-financial gross corporate profits. Historically fluctuating between 62% and 66%, the labor share plummeted sharply after 2001, dropping from roughly 64% down to a historic trough of approximately 57% in the early 2010s, showcasing how the benefits of economic growth shifted heavily toward capital during this period of globalization.

The bottom left chart correlates these economic shifts with social distress, comparing US manufacturing job losses with per-capita opioid prescriptions measured in morphine milligram equivalents on an inverted right-hand axis. As manufacturing job losses accelerated in the decade after 2001, opioid prescriptions surged dramatically, peaking at nearly 800 to 900 morphine milligram equivalents per capita around 2011, illustrating the societal scarring of deindustrialization.

Finally, the bottom right bar chart puts the scale of China's economic rise into a broader global perspective by comparing the largest 30-year increases in real per capita GDP across various countries. China’s economic transformation from 1981 to 2011 stands as the largest in modern history, boasting a real per capita GDP growth of roughly 1,400%. This extraordinary expansion dwarfs other major post-war economic miracles, such as South Korea's 1965–1995 boom of about 900%, and the mid-century expansions of Oman, Japan, Greece, and Taiwan, which all saw peak 30-year growth clustered between 600% and 800%.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, explores the strong correlation between political ideology and COVID-19 vaccine resistance in the United States during the rise of the highly contagious Delta variant. Cembalest argues that while vaccine hesitancy is not unique to one political party, distinct ideological factors are at play. He notes that despite 95% to 99% of recent COVID-19 hospitalizations occurring among unvaccinated individuals, vaccine skepticism remains deeply entrenched, citing an Associated Press poll showing that 80% of unvaccinated Americans definitely or probably will not get vaccinated. He also references political tensions within the GOP, mentioning a conservative talk show host who questioned whether Florida’s Governor was being bribed or threatened after he publicly encouraged vaccinations.

The analysis is supported by two scatter plots illustrating these political dynamics. The first chart, "Congressional Representatives: political ideology and district vaccination levels," plots the percentage of fully vaccinated residents in each of the 435 Congressional districts against the representative's ideological voting score, ranging from -1.00 (most liberal) to 1.00 (most conservative). The data splits into two distinct clusters: districts with liberal representatives (colored blue) generally see higher vaccination rates, mostly between 35% and 70%, while districts with conservative representatives (colored red) see lower vaccination rates, typically between 25% and 50%. Georgia’s 14th district is singled out at the lower-right margin of the conservative cluster, displaying a particularly low vaccination rate of roughly 27%.

The second chart, "Trump share of 2020 vote and vaccination by county," plots the percentage of fully vaccinated people in a county against the percentage of that county's population who voted for Donald Trump in the 2020 presidential election. The visual reveals a clear negative correlation: as the percentage of Trump voters increases, the vaccination rate steadily declines. In counties where Trump’s vote share was low (under 20%), vaccination rates often exceed 50% and reach up to 75%. Conversely, in counties with high Trump support (above 80%), vaccination rates are significantly lower, with many hovering between 10% and 30%.

This page analyzes the relationship between COVID-19 infection rates, vaccination progress, and subsequent hospitalizations and deaths, comparing the United Kingdom's success with emerging challenges in the United States. The author highlights an optimistic trend in the UK where high vaccination rates—exceeding 95% for those aged 65 and older—have resulted in a very low pass-through from infections to hospitalizations and mortality. In contrast, US senior vaccination rates lag by 10% to 15%, leading to severe surges in specific regions, particularly in Missouri and Florida where hospitalizations among the vulnerable, unvaccinated population are approaching or matching winter peaks.

To support this argument, a chart of the United Kingdom shows that while daily infections surged to nearly 900 per million in July 2021, current hospitalizations remained low at around 100 per million, and daily deaths stayed extremely low at under 2 per million, a stark contrast to the winter peak when hospitalizations topped 600 and daily deaths hit nearly 20 per million. A comparative vaccination chart tracks unique people vaccinated as a percentage of the population, showing Canada leading at nearly 75%, followed closely by the United Kingdom above 70%, Continental Western Europe at around 65%, the United States plateauing near 55% to 60%, and China flatlining near 45%.

The situation in the United States is illustrated by a chart comparing US hotspot states—specifically Arkansas, Florida, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, and Nevada—with the rest of the country. Daily infections in these hotspots are shown rising sharply to approximately 500 per million by late July 2021, whereas the rest of the US remains low at around 100. A detailed view of these same six hotspot states demonstrates that this spike in daily infections is closely trailed by rising hospitalizations, which are climbing back toward 300 per million, and a ticking upward of daily deaths.

Finally, state-level data for Florida and Missouri isolates hospitalization rates per million people, comparing the vulnerable population against the entire population. In Florida, hospitalizations for the vulnerable population have spiked dramatically to nearly 500 per million, surpassing the winter peak of about 400, while the entire population rate is near 300. In Missouri, a similar trend is visible, with the vulnerable population hospitalization rate surging to nearly 400 per million, close to its winter peak of 450, while the overall population rate lags behind at approximately 250.

Michael Cembalest argues against reimposing lockdowns to address the Delta variant of COVID-19, asserting that it is already too late for such measures given the high prevalence of the variant. Instead, he presents data indicating that the risk-reward ratio of mRNA and vector vaccines is overwhelmingly positive, and provides visual evidence that vaccinations are successfully suppressing community-level transmission. 

The first chart displays COVID variant reproductive number estimates, which represent the number of people infected by a single infectious individual. It shows a clear upward trend in transmissibility: the original variant had a reproductive number ranging from approximately 1.5 to 3; the Alpha (UK) variant rose to between 4 and 5; and the Delta (India) variant spans a much higher range of 5.5 to 8. This extreme transmissibility is reflected in the adjacent horizontal bar chart showing Delta variant prevalence as of late July 2021. The Delta variant accounted for nearly 100% of cases in the United Kingdom, Singapore, Denmark, and Australia, and surpassed 80% prevalence in the United States, Germany, Switzerland, and Ireland, reinforcing the author's point that the variant is already too pervasive to control via lockdowns.

To illustrate the highly favorable risk-reward profile of vaccination, two charts compare foregone COVID risks against expected adverse vaccine outcomes. For the Johnson & Johnson vaccine, analyzed per 6 million doses given to adults aged 30 to 65+, the vaccine prevents approximately 13,000 long-haul COVID cases and 3,000 deaths, whereas the expected severe adverse event is limited to 50 to 60 cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome. For mRNA vaccines, analyzed per 4 million doses given to individuals aged 12 to 30+, the vaccines prevent roughly 5,000 long-haul cases and over 1,000 deaths, while the associated risk is only 50 to 60 cases of generally treatable myocarditis. 

Lastly, a scatter plot comparing US county infections against vaccination rates demonstrates that vaccines are working on a community level. The chart plots daily infections per million on a seven-day average against the percentage of fully vaccinated people in each county. The data shows a dense concentration of low infection rates (well below 200 per million) in counties where more than 60% of the population is vaccinated. In contrast, counties with vaccination rates below 40% show a wide vertical spread of infection rates, with many experiencing severe outbreaks that exceed 1,000 daily cases per million.

This page consists entirely of standard regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan. The text outlines the relevant supervising authorities in each country, such as the Spanish Securities Market Commission, the European Central Bank, the French Autorité des Marchés Financiers, and the Australian Securities and Investment Commission, while defining local restrictions on product offerings and client classifications.

In this update on US economic recovery metrics, Michael Cembalest argues that further lockdowns in the United States are unlikely, regardless of the severity of the Delta variant, as it is politically difficult to justify broad shutdowns to protect those who refuse vaccination. While manufacturing, services, and CEO confidence remain strong, and retail inventories are at 25-year lows, rising prices for housing and consumer goods present a headwind that may slow consumer purchases and has already prompted a rollover in COVID recovery stocks. 

This analysis is supported by six charts. The first, detailing regional manufacturing and services business surveys from 2016 to mid-2021, shows the US purchasing managers' index (PMI) surging to nearly 70 by mid-2021, comfortably above the 50-level that indicates expansion. The Eurozone also shows strong expansion above 60, while Asia and Japan lag closer to 50. The second chart, illustrating US CEO hiring plans and economic expectations from 2005 to 2021, shows that CEO hiring plans have spiked near a reading of 100, while CEO confidence has rebounded sharply to around 75, both indicating highly optimistic outlooks. 

The third chart compares year-over-year pent-up spending potential against actual consumption growth from 1972 through early 2021. It highlights a massive divergence in 2021, where estimated spending potential—calculated from taxable income, transfer payments, housing wealth, and financial wealth—spiked to approximately 25%, while actual consumption growth hovered near 3%, suggesting significant untapped demand. The fourth chart tracks card-present social distancing spending (covering lodging, restaurants, parks, and theaters) as a change relative to 2019. It shows a recovery from a low of nearly -75% in March 2020 to positive territory of around 10% by June 2021. 

In contrast, the fifth chart shows a sharp decline in US buying conditions from 2000 to mid-2021. The net percentage of consumers who think it is a good time to buy houses has plunged to nearly -50%, vehicles have dropped to around -30%, and household durables have fallen toward 0%, indicating that high prices are severely damaging consumer purchase sentiment. Finally, the sixth chart indexes the performance of COVID recovery stocks relative to the S&P 500 from January to July 2021. It reveals that COVID Domestic recovery, COVID International recovery, and Consumer recovery indices all peaked around April or May 2021—with the domestic index reaching nearly 120—before rolling over in June and July, with the international and consumer recovery series falling back to near or below their starting index value of 100.

This commentary page of J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" covers several updates under the theme of investor odds and ends, spanning corporate earnings, commercial real estate, and shifting tax policy. Michael Cembalest begins with strong initial corporate performance, noting that with a quarter of S&P 500 companies reporting, 88 percent have beaten consensus earnings-per-share expectations and 86 percent have beaten revenue forecasts. 

In contrast, the recovery of commercial office space remains weak, with central business district office utilization reaching 50 percent in Texas but only 20 to 30 percent in other regions. In New York City, available office space has expanded by 40 million square feet to a total of 80 million square feet, a much larger increase than the 25 to 35 million square feet observed after previous recessions. Hotel real estate is also experiencing distress; the 725-room Lexington Hotel in New York recently sold for 255,000 dollars per key, nearly half of its 2011 price. According to the American Hotel and Lodging Association, New York City hotel revenues are down 67 percent compared to 2019, placing it alongside Seattle, Boston, Minneapolis, Washington D.C., Chicago, and San Francisco on the association's list of hotel markets in economic depression. 

The author then turns to US and international tax policy. While President Biden's original tax proposal outlined aggressive measures—such as a 28 percent domestic corporate tax rate, a 26.25 percent GILTI minimum tax, higher oil and gas taxes, a new SHIELD tax, unified capital gains and ordinary income tax rates for high-net-worth individuals, and forced capital gains realization at death—ongoing negotiations suggest a more moderate path. The current expectation is a 25 percent corporate tax rate, a GILTI tax of 15 to 19 percent, partial commingling of foreign tax credits, an increase in capital gains tax to 28 percent, and a potential doubling of the SALT deduction cap to 20,000 dollars. Finally, Cembalest expresses skepticism regarding a global minimum tax rate agreement. He argues that without a universally applied definition of taxable income—which would require nations to agree on complex treatments for R&D credits, opportunity zones, drilling expenses, inventory valuation, and write-offs—countries will still find ways to compete on effective rates, potentially delaying actual implementation for years. The page concludes with a list of recent archive topics covering SPACs, energy, China regulations, and private equity.

This page addresses the reliance of the big four technology and social media companies—Google, Apple, Amazon, and Facebook—on acquisitions to fuel their expansion. The author poses the critical question of whether an antitrust revival by the House Judiciary Committee or through executive orders will curtail these acquisitions, noting that the market currently anticipates little to no impact on the companies' earnings. 

The first chart, titled Big Tech Acquisitions: Core vs New Sectors, tracks the cumulative number of acquisitions from 1988 through 2021 across various business categories such as e-commerce, search, advertising, social, software, artificial intelligence and machine learning, media, cloud, data, mobile, and location services. It compares acquisitions within each firm's core business against those in new sectors. Google has the highest volume of acquisitions, with roughly 80 in its core business and over 180 in new sectors. Apple has around 20 core acquisitions compared to over 100 in new sectors. Amazon shows roughly 40 core e-commerce acquisitions and over 70 in new sectors, while Facebook features about 20 core social media acquisitions versus approximately 70 in new sectors, emphasizing how crucial expansion into new business segments has been for their growth strategies.

The second chart, Contribution of Top Firms to Overall US Market Cap, plots historical data from 1990 to 2020 showing the growing concentration of market capitalization in the largest companies. The top 20 firms accounted for around 30 percent of market capitalization in 2015 before rising dramatically to over 40 percent by 2020. More strikingly, the top five firms—specifically Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Facebook—saw their combined share jump from around 10 percent in 2015 to more than 20 percent by 2020, underlining their massive influence on the broader market.

The final chart, Forward Earnings per Share for Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, and Facebook, indexed with December 2019 as zero, illustrates the historical and projected trajectory of aggregate forward earnings per share from 2015 to 2023. The trend line rises from around negative 60 percent in 2015 to zero at the end of 2019, before surging to approximately 40 percent in 2021. The forecast, represented by a dotted estimation line, continues on a steady upward trajectory to reach nearly 80 percent by 2023. This projection highlights the market's expectation that the earnings growth of these tech titans will remain unaffected by prospective regulatory headwinds.

This page provides an update on SPAC (Special Purpose Acquisition Company) merger performance, arguing that while sponsors and arbitrageurs continue to reap massive profits, the vast majority of other investors experience poor or negative returns. The author humorously notes that if individuals had avoided SPACs instead of COVID-19 vaccines, the public would be wealthier. 

The central data table reviews 98 SPAC mergers brought public or liquidated between January 1, 2019, and March 5, 2021, tracking median cumulative returns across two dates: March 11 and August 17. The data reveals a significant decline in returns over this period for almost every investor class except arbitrageurs and sponsors. SPAC arbitrage investor returns held steady at 16% for both periods. Meanwhile, SPAC sponsor returns, though declining, remained extraordinarily high, falling from 712% in March to 507% as of August 17 (or from 468% to 284% when accounting for concessions, forfeiture, and vesting). 

In stark contrast, other investors suffered. SPAC buy-and-hold investor gross returns collapsed from 41% down to 4%, underperforming the IPO Index by 100% and the Russell 2000 Growth Index by 48% as of August 17.
