Fire losses historically account for less than one percent of all U.S. forestland per year. Although public lands face the highest fire density—such as in Oregon, where the U.S. Forest Service owns sixty percent of forestland but accounted for eighty-six percent of burned acreage over the last decade—extreme weather events like the high winds of 2020 can still impact private lands, where forty percent of the one million burned Oregonian acres were industrial or private. Post-fire rehabilitation and replanting mature forests can reach costs of fifteen hundred dollars per acre. Lastly, hurricanes and storms pose a relatively minor threat, impacting only zero-point-two to zero-point-five percent of U.S. timberland annually.

This page analyzes the changing dynamics of Emerging Market portfolio inflows, focusing particularly on China's growing dominance and the resilience of its long-term investment outlook despite recent regulatory actions. The author argues that Emerging Market equity indices have become less geographically diverse, with China, South Korea, and Taiwan now representing two-thirds of the entire MSCI EM equity index. Furthermore, China's index weight could potentially rise from 35 percent to 45 percent. Despite the regulatory purge of 2021, the author asserts that China's massive middle class and strong venture capital inflows indicate that private investors still believe in the country's long-term growth prospects.

This perspective is supported by four charts. The first chart, titled Emerging markets country weights, displays the percentage weight in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index from 2000 to 2020. It shows how Latin America and other nations have steadily lost share, while Taiwan, South Korea, and China have grown to dominate the index, with China's slice expanding dramatically since 2015. The second chart, China VC investments by US dollar denominated funds, shows venture capital investment in billions of US dollars from 2010 to 2021 year-to-date. Investments peaked around 120 billion dollars in 2018, dipped in 2019, and rose again to reach an all-time high of nearly 130 billion dollars in 2021, signaling sustained private investor confidence.

The third chart, Private equity performance versus public equity in Asia, looks at the ten-year annualized return through the second quarter of 2020. This visual compares public equities to private equity and venture capital, demonstrating that public equity in MSCI EM Asia and MSCI Pacific returned around 6 percent, whereas Asia Developed Markets private equity and venture capital returned nearly 11 percent, and Asia Emerging Markets private equity and venture capital led with a return of roughly 13 percent. The final chart, Middle class consumption in 2020, shows consumption in trillions of US dollars based on 2011 purchasing power parity. China leads the world with over 7 trillion dollars in middle-class consumption, followed by the United States at about 4.5 trillion dollars, India at 3 trillion dollars, Japan at 2 trillion dollars, and several other countries with lower levels. Additionally, a detailed footnote explains that from 2000 to 2020, MSCI EM Asia outperformed MSCI EM Latin America, though both vastly underperformed the S&P 500's ten-year cumulative performance of 267 percent.

This page, titled "Brexit and the high price of national sovereignty," provides an early assessment of the economic impacts of Brexit on the United Kingdom, focusing specifically on the banking, real estate, and trade sectors. Author Michael Cembalest notes that while many British economists offered highly pessimistic outlooks, many of these analysts worked in finance or owned London real estate—two sectors directly exposed to the fallout of leaving the European Union. 

To illustrate these regional impacts, the page features four charts. The first chart, "UK banks vs Eurozone banks," indexes bank performance to June 2016. It shows that UK banks have significantly lagged behind their Eurozone peers since the referendum, with the index for UK banks dropping from over 140 in 2014 to hovering around 90 to 100 by early 2022, while Eurozone banks recovered to a higher level of around 120. This trend is exacerbated by the European Central Bank’s ongoing pressure on EU banks to relocate staff and facilities from London back to the continent. The second chart, "London home prices," indexed to Q2 2016, shows that London home prices did experience a post-referendum decline, dropping to an index level near 95 in 2019 before rebounding alongside global real estate trends to reach nearly 110 by late 2021.

Cembalest cautions that a definitive assessment of Brexit remains difficult because the UK did not formally leave the EU single market until the end of the transition period in December 2020, and the COVID-19 pandemic has heavily distorted recent economic data. The trade effects are detailed in two subsequent charts, both indexed to June 2016 with a 12-month moving average. The chart "UK trade volumes with the European Union" shows that trade initially rose after the referendum, peaking in late 2018, before declining sharply; by late 2021, UK exports to the EU stabilized near an index level of 95, while EU exports to the UK dropped to around 90. 

The final chart, "UK trade volumes with non-EU countries," demonstrates that while non-EU exports to the UK rebounded sharply to an index level of 110 in 2021, UK exports to non-EU countries remained stagnant around 95. This reveals that, contrary to the hopes of Brexit proponents, increased trade with the rest of the world has not offset the loss of EU trade. Nonetheless, Cembalest points out that a 15% depreciation of the Pound since the referendum has helped stabilize the nation's balance of trade, keeping the UK current account deficit at 3.3% of GDP in the third quarter of 2021, which is in line with its 20-year average. Ultimately, he concludes that while the trade data is not encouraging, it is still too heavily influenced by the pandemic to draw definitive long-term conclusions.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest assesses Chinese portfolio inflows, arguing that although Chinese growth slowed in late 2021 due to new real estate standards, high energy prices, and power rationing, the positive factors will likely outweigh the negatives for onshore Chinese stocks in 2022. In contrast, the author remains cautious about offshore Chinese internet stocks due to increased antitrust enforcement and tighter regulatory oversight of overseas listings. Positives supporting onshore equities include modest stimulatory actions, such as a 50-basis-point reserve requirement ratio cut, and pro-growth statements. J.P. Morgan Equity Research projects 19% earnings growth and 4.7% real GDP growth for 2022, despite headwinds like the zero-COVID policy and property developer defaults.

The economic situation is analyzed across three index charts relative to a January 2018 baseline. The chart for positive signs shows exports soaring past an index level of 140 by late 2021, alongside stable corporate earnings for A-shares. The chart for stable signs shows that electricity consumption, industrial production, retail sales, and construction and real estate GDP recovered from their deep 2020 troughs to stabilize between 110 and 130. Conversely, the negative signs chart demonstrates sharp downturns in late 2021 for crude steel production, residential construction starts, and commercial construction starts, with the latter dropping below an index level of 70.

Underneath these economic indicators, two additional charts detail consensus expectations and monetary policy. The first shows declining MSCI China year-over-year earnings expectations over the course of 2021, with expected 2021 EPS expectations dropping from 18% to around 13%, and 2022 expectations falling from 19% to 15%. J.P. Morgan's own forecasts sit at approximately 12% for 2021 and 19% for 2022. The final chart details Chinese lending rates and reserve requirements from 2012 forecasted through 2023, highlighting a December 15 reserve requirement ratio cut that reduced the ratio toward 12%, while various policy lending rates on the left axis remained low or drifted slightly downward. An explanatory footnote clarifies that China’s domestic power constraints resulted from a combination of surging global energy demand, reduced hydropower output, coal production curbs tied to climate goals, and utility price controls.

This page examines the negative economic impacts of Brexit on the United Kingdom, focusing specifically on capital spending, construction output, and real disposable income. Michael Cembalest argues that business investment, a key indicator of overall economic health, has suffered significantly since the 2016 referendum, with the UK lagging behind other developed nations. 

The first chart, titled "UK business investment relative to developed markets," indexes the data to the second quarter of 2016. It shows that while UK investment was on a steady upward trajectory relative to developed markets between 2011 and 2016, it broke sharply away from this trend post-referendum, falling to roughly 15% below its peers by 2019 and plunging even further to nearly 25% below after the onset of COVID-19. 

A second chart, titled "Real business investment," compares indices from June 2016 for the US, Euro Area, Japan, and the UK. While the US and Euro Area steadily grew their real business investment to index levels of approximately 120 and 115 respectively by late 2019, the UK flatlined near 100, subsequently dropping to 80 during COVID-19 and recovering only to roughly 90 by late 2021, well below its peers.

The narrative notes that construction and consumer income follow similar downward trends. In the chart "Construction sector output," indexed to June 2016, the UK output gap widens relative to the US and Euro Area post-Brexit. Following a sharp contraction during the pandemic, the UK's construction index remained below 100 in 2021, while the Euro Area hovered around 105 and the US reached approximately 115.

In the final chart, "US vs UK real disposable household income," a stark divergence is shown after the 2016 referendum. While US household income climbed steadily and spiked to over 140 during pandemic-era stimulus programs, UK disposable income barely rose above its 100 baseline, ending 2021 at roughly 105. This stagnation is partly attributed to the 2016 depreciation of the Pound, which the London School of Economics estimated raised consumer prices by 2.9%, costing the average household an additional £870 per year. The author concludes by noting that while these relationships are complex, the timing suggests Brexit-related structural deficiencies may have permanently hindered the UK's pandemic recovery, a trend that warrants close observation.

This page focuses on the massive influx of venture capital into cryptocurrency and blockchain investments, culminating in a historic surge in 2021. While the author acknowledges that capital is mobilizing rapidly and drawing top-tier talent from Silicon Valley, he raises the open question of whether these investments will deliver viable long-run returns, rather than just impressive initial fundraising. He notes that the current breakdown of venture capital crypto investments allocates roughly 40 percent to trading, investing, and lending businesses; 20 percent to Web 3.0 applications and non-fungible tokens; 10 percent to custody; and the remainder to compliance, mining, and data security. 

To support this analysis, the page presents four charts compiled using data from Pitchbook and Galaxy Digital Research. The first chart, which displays venture capital investments by sector in billions of US dollars from 2017 to 2021, compares crypto to other fields like quantum computing, cloud technology, robotics, artificial intelligence, and fintech. While fintech remained the clear leader, topping 100 billion dollars in 2021, crypto investment experienced an unprecedented spike in 2021, rising to roughly 30 billion dollars and rivaling other major innovation categories. 

The second chart tracks quarterly venture capital investments in crypto and blockchain from 2016 to 2021, showing both total capital invested and overall deal counts. This visual highlights a dramatic spike in 2021, where quarterly deal counts surged toward 500 and total quarterly capital invested skyrocketed to peak levels of around 8 billion and 10 billion dollars, dwarfing the activity of all prior years. 

A third chart breaks down this venture capital funding by stage, including pre-seed, seed, Series A, and later stages. It reveals that while seed and pre-seed rounds historically accounted for most activity, the late-2021 investment surge was heavily driven by massive later-stage and Series A rounds, which pushed quarterly funding totals near the 10-billion-dollar mark. 

Finally, the fourth chart compares pre-money valuations for crypto and blockchain startups against the broader venture capital market in millions of US dollars. While average valuations for both categories tracked closely from 2016 through 2020 at under 15 million dollars, crypto and blockchain pre-money valuations decoupled dramatically in 2021, soaring to nearly 70 million dollars compared to the broader venture capital average of approximately 30 million dollars.

This page focuses on the rising adoption and changing attitudes toward cryptocurrency across various investor types and global regions. While institutional ownership has historically been low, the author notes that it is growing steadily, citing a Bridgewater estimate that institutional investors hold approximately 1 million Bitcoin, representing about 5% of the total issued supply, via custodial intermediaries. Corporate and retail adoption trends are also highlighted through anecdotes: Square and Tesla combined have invested nearly $2 billion in Bitcoin, and retail clients of Square and PayPal reportedly purchase a majority of the new daily Bitcoin supply entering the market.

The commentary is supported by four charts reflecting data from the September 2021 Fidelity Institutional Digital Assets Survey. The first chart, illustrating crypto adoption by region as a percentage of investors with digital asset allocations, shows consistent growth from 2019 to 2021. The United States saw allocations rise from roughly 22% to 33%, while European allocations grew from about 45% in 2020 to 56% in 2021. By 2021, Asia led the regions shown with an adoption rate of 71%. 

The second chart details crypto adoption by investor type, showing the percentage of investors owning digital assets across different categories. Financial advisors and high-net-worth individuals display the highest adoption rates, particularly in Asia (98% and 84%, respectively) and Europe (73% and 83%, respectively). In contrast, US financial advisors sit at 40% and US high-net-worth individuals at 17%. Conversely, US family offices lead their global peers with 50% adoption, compared to roughly 33% in Europe and 32% in Asia. Institutional segments like pensions show very low overall adoption—under 5% in the US and Europe, though reaching 16% in Asia—while US endowments and foundations show 15% adoption. 

The third chart breaks down ownership by specific digital assets, revealing that Bitcoin is the most widely held asset, owned by 46% of surveyed investors in Europe, 45% in Asia, and 22% in the US. Ethereum is the second most popular asset, held by 27% of European, 22% of Asian, and 12% of US investors. Alternative coins like Litecoin, XRP, Bitcoin cash, and Binance coin see moderate ownership in Europe and Asia but remain under 10% in the US. 

The final chart tracks future purchase intent, demonstrating a rising willingness to invest in digital assets. In the US, purchase intent increased from 50% in 2019 to 60% in 2021. European purchase intent rose from 60% in 2020 to 75% in 2021, while Asian purchase intent reached 82% in 2021. For all charts, missing bars represent data that was not published in the original Fidelity study rather than zero values.

This page examines the "store of value" thesis for digital currencies, using Bitcoin as a primary proxy due to its dominant market share. The author expresses understanding of why investors are drawn to cryptocurrencies with fixed supplies, arguing that massive expansions in debt and fiat money creation by modern central banks have created a profound confidence void. This currency debasement mirrors the economic degradations that historically accompanied the collapse of past global reserve currencies. 

To support this analysis, several charts depict the cryptocurrency landscape and the macroeconomic pressures driving interest in it. The first chart illustrates the market capitalization of the top twenty cryptocurrencies by segment as of January 2022. Bitcoin dominates the "Currency" segment with a market cap of nearly $700 billion, followed by Ethereum representing the "Platform" segment at approximately $300 billion, and Tether representing "Stablecoins." Other segments defined include decentralized finance (DeFi), remittances, and exchanges. 

Three subsequent charts illustrate the unprecedented expansion of global debt and money supply. One chart tracks developed world government debt and central bank balance sheets from 2009 to 2021, showing government debt rising from roughly 90% of GDP to nearly 140%, while central bank balance sheets skyrocketed from around $5 trillion to nearly $30 trillion. Another chart indexes U.S. money supply growth, comparing the 2008 Global Financial Crisis to the Global Coronavirus Crisis. While the index for M2 money supply plus institutional money market fund balances only rose to about 107 during the 2008 crisis, it surged rapidly to over 140 between January 2020 and January 2022. Additionally, a chart on total global debt shows it rising from approximately 110% of GDP in 1970 to nearly 250% in 2020, with public debt making up an increasingly large share alongside household and non-financial corporate debt.

Finally, a timeline chart illustrates the lifespan of major reserve currencies since 1250 AD, tracing the rise and fall of the Florentine Florin, Venetian Ducat, Portuguese Real, Spanish Real, Dutch Guilder, French Livre, British Sterling, US Dollar, and the Eurodollar. This historical perspective underscores the author's point that reserve currencies have historically experienced limited lifespans, often ending when issuing nations faced severe economic degradation.

This page discusses an approaching fiat currency reckoning and explores whether Bitcoin can serve as a viable digital store of value to complement gold. The author argues that by the year 2030, United States Federal tax revenues will be entirely consumed by mandatory outlays on entitlements and interest, leaving no money for the non-defense discretionary spending that drives long-term economic growth unless funded through deficit spending. 

This fiscal trajectory is illustrated in a line chart showing revenues and outlays as a percentage of GDP from 1970 through projections to 2030. In this chart, the line representing entitlements, other mandatory outlays, and interest is projected to trend upward and cross over the revenue line at approximately 19% of GDP by 2030. Concurrently, non-defense discretionary spending, which was suppressed by the Budget Control Act of 2011, is projected to slide toward 2% of GDP. To emphasize the global scope of sovereign debt issues, a companion table lists the short universe of countries that have never defaulted, imposed exchange controls, or confiscated assets, noting that many of these safe havens still carry immense debt burdens. This list is led by Singapore with a 150% national debt-to-GDP ratio, followed by the United States at 128%, Canada at 114%, and Belgium at 113%, down to Taiwan at 37%.

Against this backdrop of sovereign debt risk, the author addresses skeptics of digital currency. While critics argue that gold took thousands of years to establish its status as a store of value, the author contends that modern behavioral shifts occur rapidly. For Bitcoin to succeed as a store of value, it must see expanding adoption, its volatility must settle into an acceptable range, and it must hold its value during systemic crises. 

Two bottom charts examine Bitcoin's progress. A bar chart comparing the market capitalization of Bitcoin to gold (excluding jewelry) from 2010 to 2022 shows that while gold remains dominant—ranging between roughly $3.0 trillion and $6.5 trillion—Bitcoin has steadily captured a larger share of the store-of-value market, rising to nearly $1.0 trillion in market capitalization by 2021. However, a final line chart of the Bitcoin price from 2017 to early 2022 illustrates its persistent volatility, showing a massive price spike that peaked over $60,000 in 2021 before falling back toward $40,000 by early 2022.

This page of the publication analyzes and critiques the thesis of Bitcoin as a "store of value," focusing on its high volatility, extreme ownership concentration, and the challenges of establishing a reliable valuation model. The author argues that Bitcoin's volatility remains too high to support the store of value claim, pointing out that this volatility may be driven by extreme wealth concentration where just two percent of Bitcoin holders own seventy-two percent of its total value. By comparison, wealth in the United States is less concentrated, with the top ten percent of households holding seventy percent of national wealth. The author also expresses skepticism regarding cryptocurrency valuation models, noting that while Metcalfe's Law—which posits that a network's value scales with the square of its users—is helpful for relative comparisons, it is ineffective at determining absolute fair value.

Four charts illustrate these arguments. The first chart, titled "Bitcoin volatility vs S&P 500, gold and US dollar," plots rolling three-month daily annualized volatility from 2015 to 2022. It shows that Bitcoin's volatility fluctuates wildly, frequently peaking over one hundred percent and reaching as high as one hundred twenty-five percent, whereas the volatility of gold, the US dollar, and the S&P 500 Index consistently remains below twenty-five percent. 

The next two charts compare historical drawdowns. The "Gold vs Bitcoin drawdowns" chart measures percentage declines from prior peaks from 1960 to 2020. It demonstrates that gold's largest drawdown over six decades approached seventy percent, while Bitcoin has repeatedly experienced rapid declines of eighty to ninety percent in its much shorter history. Similarly, the "S&P 500 vs Bitcoin drawdowns" chart, covering 2011 to 2021, shows that S&P 500 drawdowns rarely exceed twenty percent, except for a brief drop of around thirty percent in 2020, while Bitcoin regularly suffers steep crashes of fifty to over eighty percent.

The final chart, titled "Metcalfe's Law: Valuation vs network size," utilizes Goldman Sachs research to show the relationship between active addresses and crypto market capitalization. Plotted on log scales, the chart shows various cryptocurrencies—including Zcash, Dash, Ethereum Classic, Cardano, Litecoin, Ripple, Bitcoin Cash, Ethereum, and Bitcoin—aligning closely along a positive diagonal trendline. This visualization supports the idea that larger network size correlates with higher market capitalization, indicating that Metcalfe's Law serves as a useful framework for relative valuation across different digital assets.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest examines the historical performance of gold to challenge the common assumption that it serves as a reliable inflation or currency hedge. He argues that while gold was an effective inflation hedge from 1790 to 1900 because its real price remained highly stable under the gold standard, its real value has gyrated wildly since 1900 and particularly after the end of the gold standard. Instead, Cembalest suggests that gold acts primarily as a hedge against the fear of inflation or financial instability, which is closely mirrored by expanding government deficits. He also references academic research by Claude Erb and Campbell Harvey indicating that changes in Emerging Market Central Bank gold reserves may be a more significant driver of gold prices.

To illustrate these points, the page includes three charts. The first, "Real price of gold since 1790," plots the ratio of the gold price to the US Consumer Price Index. The chart shows a stable, flat line hovering between 1x and 2.5x for over a century, which abruptly transitions into violent, volatile swings beginning in the 1970s, reaching multiple peaks near 8x. 

The second chart, "Real price of gold since the advent of US futures trading," provides a detailed look at this post-1970 volatility. It tracks the same ratio of gold price to the US Consumer Price Index from 1970 to 2020, revealing a sharp peak of approximately 8.5x in 1980, a multi-decade decline to a low of about 1.5x around the year 2000, and subsequent massive rallies that peaked near 8x in both 2011 and 2020.

The third chart, "Gold prices vs developed markets deficit," compares the gold spot price (in dollars per ounce on the left axis) to the fiscal deficit of G10 countries (as a trailing four-quarter average percentage of GDP on the right axis) from 1970 to 2020. This visual highlights a strong correlation between the two trends. Notably, during the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, G10 fiscal deficits spiked to nearly 10% of GDP around 2010 while gold spot prices climbed toward $1,800 per ounce in 2011. This pattern repeated during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, when G10 fiscal deficits surged to approximately 14% of GDP and gold spot prices peaked above $2,000 per ounce, reinforcing the author's point that gold correlates heavily with government deficit expansion.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" examines the potential for cryptocurrency, specifically stablecoins, to disrupt the traditional cross-border remittance market. The author explains that while global remittances have ranged between $500 billion and $600 billion per year over the last decade, the vast majority are sent via traditional wire or bank transfers, with crypto accounting for only about 1% according to MoneyGram's CEO. 

A line chart titled "World personal remittances received" tracks global remittance flows in billions of US dollars from 2008 to 2020, showing a steady climb from under $400 billion in 2008 to a peak of nearly $650 billion in 2019, followed by a slight dip in 2020. 

A bar chart titled "Personal remittances and bank account ownership" highlights major remittance recipient countries and reveals a key hurdle for crypto adoption: the necessity of having a bank account to cash out. The chart shows that while some major recipient countries like India, which receives around $80 billion, and China, which receives around $60 billion, enjoy high bank account ownership rates of 80%, other massive markets have much lower bank account penetration, such as Mexico at 37% of its roughly $40 billion in remittances and the Philippines at 35% of its roughly $30 billion in remittances. 

A third chart titled "Global remittance costs" illustrates that traditional remittance costs have been steadily falling. From 2009 to 2021, the global average cost dropped from nearly 10% to around 6.5%, while the global weighted average, which is weighted by the size of remittance flows, declined from 8% to approximately 5%.

To contrast these traditional costs with stablecoin alternatives, a table titled "Select stablecoin off-ramp costs to fiat" details the fees associated with converting stablecoins to local currency via local crypto exchanges. The table highlights that total off-ramp fees (combining transaction and withdrawal fees) are exceptionally low compared to traditional channels, sitting at 0.1% in Mexico via Bitso, 0.2% in India via CoinDCX, 0.2% in South Africa via Luno, 0.7% in Brazil via Mercado Bitcoin, and 2.1% in the Philippines via PDAX. 

The author concludes that although stablecoin use for remittances is currently negligible, it is poised to rise among banked individuals because off-ramp costs are significantly lower than traditional channel fees. This transition, supported by high crypto ownership rates among remittance senders, will likely exert deflationary pressure on legacy remittance companies like Western Union. However, because this trend relies on stablecoins, the author notes it is unlikely to drive up valuations for broader cryptocurrency assets.

This page explores the challenges and future outlook for the Ethereum network, focusing on its high transaction costs, low speeds, and the rising threat of competitive programmable public blockchains. Michael Cembalest highlights that Ethereum's poor interoperability and high network fees have opened the door for rivals to gain significant ground.

The author uses several charts and diagrams to illustrate these points. A line chart detailing Ethereum's average daily transaction costs in Gwei from February 2021 to February 2022 shows that transaction "gas" fees—paid to compensate miners for computational power—have been highly volatile, frequently spiking above 300 Gwei. A secondary bar chart tracks Ethereum's market capitalization against its competitors in billions of dollars from Q1 2020 to Q4 2021. This chart shows competitor market cap rising from negligible levels in early 2020 to over $250 billion by the end of 2021, closing the gap with Ethereum, which peaked near $450 billion in late 2021. 

A table on processing speeds compares the transaction capacity of various financial infrastructures. It reveals that Ethereum handles only 15 transactions per second, slightly faster than Bitcoin at 7, but vastly slower than alternative networks like Ripple at 1,500, EOS at 8,000, VISA at 45,000, and Paypal at 56,000. Competitors like Solana aim to surpass these rates with claimed speeds of 50,000 transactions per second. Other mentioned rivals seeking to address scalability and interoperability include Cardano, Polkadot, Avalanche, Hedera, and Algorand. The author notes that while many competitors are thriving, only a few are likely to survive the venture capital cycle.

To address these limitations, Ethereum is planned to undergo a major upgrade shifting from Proof-of-Work to Proof-of-Stake to improve speed, cost, energy efficiency, and scalability. This transition is mapped out in an upgrade timeline diagram showing key milestones from the initial October 2020 deposit contract deployment and December 2020 Beacon chain launch to the August 2021 London upgrade, "The Merge" in early 2022, and planned data sharding in 2022–2023. Additionally, the text notes that "zero knowledge proof" Layer-2 offerings are already showing 100x to 1000x improvements in latency and transaction costs.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues that blockchain adoption does not correlate with cryptocurrency valuations, pointing out that corporate blockchain use cases validate the technology itself, not crypto. He highlights J.P. Morgan's own permissioned, private blockchain repo system, which has cleared more than $200 billion in transactions. Because this system is closed, software-verified without mining rewards, and uses a stable-value JP Morgan Coin for intraday transactions, its adoption has no positive impact on public token values. Other non-financial companies like Walmart and Alibaba leverage blockchain to improve supply chains and track orders, while enterprise vendors like IBM, Oracle, and Microsoft design these systems. Cembalest emphasizes that any financial value generated by these private systems accrues to corporate shareholders and technology vendors rather than public token holders. 

To contextualize blockchain as merely the latest productivity and data-transmission tool, the page compares it to the historical evolution from carrier pigeons to telegraphs, telephones, faxes, and the internet. During these technological cycles, incumbent service providers usually vanish, but incumbent users—like today's J.P. Morgan, Walmart, and Alibaba—simply shift to the next technology. 

This historical perspective is illustrated by two visuals. A line chart titled "The life cycle of the Telegraph" shows the millions of messages handled per year in the United States from 1860 to 1980. The volume of messages starts near zero in 1860, rises steadily to a peak of roughly 225 million in the mid-1940s, and then drops sharply to below 100 million by the 1970s. Beside the chart is a historical photograph from August 1940 showing British soldiers in the south of England training a carrier pigeon to deliver messages during World War II, illustrating how older technologies often persist and overlap with newer ones like the telegraph.

This page explores the challenges and potential of using cryptocurrency for cross-border remittances, specifically focusing on the high execution costs for unbanked receivers and the emerging role of stablecoins. The author notes that Bitcoin-to-fiat conversions are costly and inaccessible for many, citing Coin ATM Radar data showing only two such ATMs in India, 11 in Mexico, and 13 in the Philippines, with conversion fees typically charging 5 percent to cash out and 10 percent to buy Bitcoin. The author highlights potential changes, such as Moneygram's project to offer 4 percent conversions and its partnership with the Stellar Development Foundation to facilitate stablecoin-to-cash transactions.

The discussion then shifts to stablecoins, which are pegged to external reserve assets to avoid crypto price volatility. While stablecoins could facilitate cheaper remittances, the author raises concerns about reserve transparency, comparing some private stablecoins to the structured investment vehicles that contributed to the 2008 financial crisis. A footnote details how Tether's convertibility was temporarily suspended in 2017 when Wells Fargo withdrew support, causing it to trade as low as 92 cents on the dollar, and reveals that Tether's first published reserve breakdown showed 49 percent backing by unspecified commercial paper. The text also notes a January 2022 US Federal Reserve report discussing the possibility of a Fed-backed US dollar stablecoin to eliminate private liquidity and reserve risks.

Two charts illustrate the rapid growth and price behavior of these digital assets. The first chart shows the market capitalization of select stablecoins from January 2020 to January 2022 in billions of US dollars. The total market cap surged from near zero to approximately 160 billion dollars, dominated by Tether and USD Coin, with smaller shares held by Dai, Binance USD, HUSD, and Paxos. The second chart tracks the historical prices of USD Coin and Tether from 2016 to early 2022 to demonstrate how increased market participation has lowered volatility. Although Tether experienced wide price fluctuations early on, dropping to 92 cents in 2017 and spiking above 1.06 dollars in 2018, both Tether and USD Coin converged tightly to their 1.00 dollar par value by 2021 and 2022.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management utilizes a cinematic analogy from the 1941 film The Maltese Falcon to describe his skeptical outlook on cryptocurrency. He recounts the plot of the movie, where characters desperately chase a legendary, jewel-encrusted golden statue that ultimately turns out to be a fake, and detective Humphrey Bogart's character refuses to play the sap for his deceptive love interest, turning her in to the police despite his feelings. 

Cembalest applies this narrative directly to his own personal financial view, explaining that he refuses to buy cryptocurrency even though part of him wants to, resisting the psychological FOMO that crypto holders rely on to entice new buyers. He asserts that current crypto valuations and their widely discussed use cases are merely the stuff that dreams are made of, quoting Bogart's final line about the worthless statue. Cembalest poses that he would only reconsider investing in the sector if valuations for cryptocurrencies and their linked companies plummeted to deeply distressed levels. Accompanying the text is a black-and-white archival movie still featuring Humphrey Bogart holding a cigarette while examining the falcon statue.

This appendix section, titled "Tracking creative destruction," examines the dynamics of business obsolescence. The author argues that the optimal time to sell legacy assets—such as Wang Labs, newspaper stocks, DSL providers, and electronics retailers—is when they are still on top, which typically coincides with the infancy of the disruptive technologies that will eventually replace them, such as personal computers, digital advertising, high data demand, and e-commerce.

A series of five charts supports this thesis. The first chart shows the cumulative number of companies removed from the S&P 500 due to distress from 1980 to 2019. The cumulative count rises steadily over these four decades, starting at zero and climbing to over 400 companies, illustrating the ongoing process of creative destruction. 

The second chart focuses on the demise of data processing equipment, specifically tracking Wang Labs from 1980 to 1994. It plots the percentage of households with at least one computer on the left axis against the Wang Labs stock price on the right axis. As household computer ownership rose from under 5% in 1980 to roughly 25% by 1994, Wang Labs' stock price plummeted from a peak of around $40 in the early 1980s to near-zero by 1994.

The third chart illustrates the decline of the newspaper industry from 1999 to 2020. It plots the newspaper share of advertising revenue on the left axis against stock performance on the right axis, indexed to December 1998. Newspaper ad revenue share fell from approximately 35% in 1999 to under 5% by 2020. Consequently, a newspaper stock index consisting of Tribune (TRB), New York Times (NYT), Knight Ridder (KRI), and McClatchy (MNI) collapsed to near-zero after peaking in the early 2000s, drastically underperforming the S&P 500, which rose to nearly 400.

The fourth chart covers electronics retailers from 1999 to 2020, charting the e-commerce share of electronics sales on the left axis against stock indices on the right axis. The online sales share climbed from under 5% to around 35%. While the S&P 500 rose to nearly 600, an index of traditional electronics retailers—including Circuit City (CC), CompUSA (CPU), Office Depot (ODP), and RadioShack (RSH)—briefly peaked in the mid-2000s before collapsing to zero.

The fifth chart explores wireline telecom and DSL stocks from 2010 to 2022, comparing monthly household data use in gigabytes on the left axis to stock performance on the right axis, indexed to December 2009. Although household data demand surged from under 50 GB to roughly 350 GB per month, the Telecom/DSL index—featuring Lumen (LUMN), Frontier (FTR), and Windstream (WIN)—steadily deteriorated to near-zero, while the S&P 500 index climbed above 500.

This appendix outlines the rapid technological advancements that support the viability and growth of the Metaverse, showcasing improvements across computing power, storage costs, artificial intelligence capabilities, and cellular connection speeds. 

The first chart tracks CPU improvement rates relative to a 1979 baseline on a logarithmic scale from 1980 to 2020. It highlights that while CPU speed growth began to flatten out around 2010 at roughly 100,000 times the baseline, transistor density and overall efficiency continued their steep upward trajectory, both approaching a one-million-fold improvement by 2020. In tandem with more powerful processing, the cost of information storage has collapsed exponentially. Measured in US dollars per gigabyte on a log scale, the average hard drive storage cost plummeted from nearly $1,000,000 in 1980 to approximately $0.02 by 2020. 

Developments in artificial intelligence have also advanced rapidly, both in speed and capability. The third chart shows that the time required to train an AI model to classify images fell drastically from 10 hours, 41 minutes, and 37 seconds in September 2017 to just 1 minute and 28 seconds by August 2019. Over a similar timeframe, computer image identification accuracy rose from under 55% in 2016 to roughly 77% by late 2019, closing in on the established human baseline of approximately 80%. 

Lastly, high-speed connectivity is analyzed through a comparison of average 5G and 4G download speeds in megabits per second across ten global telecommunication providers. Across all featured carriers—T-Mobile, AT&T, Sprint, Vodafone, EE, Telstra, KT, SK telecom, LG U+, and Verizon—5G dramatically outperforms 4G. Verizon leads with average 5G download speeds exceeding 500 Mbps, while South Korea's LG U+ and SK telecom represent the next fastest tiers, averaging over 200 Mbps. These rapid wireless speeds provide the necessary infrastructure to handle the massive data loads required by real-time virtual environments.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses several immediate headwinds forcing global markets to digest significant bad news, resulting in year-to-date declines of 3% to 10% in global equity indices and 3% to 4% in global fixed-income indices. Michael Cembalest highlights three major pressures: persistent global inflation that has dismantled the transitory narrative, Europe's precarious energy dependence on Russia in the shadow of potential conflict in Ukraine, and slower-than-hoped-for improvements in US supply chains. 

To illustrate the sudden shift in monetary policy expectations, a line chart titled "Market implied Fed hikes, derived from futures market" tracks the number of expected 25 basis point rate hikes over the next 12 months. The chart shows that expectations rose from virtually zero in August 2021 to over six anticipated hikes by February 2022, reflecting the market's aggressive repricing of central bank actions. 

A second line chart compares electricity prices in the US against Europe from 2015 to early 2022, measured in US dollars per megawatt-hour on a 30-day average. The chart reveals a stark divergence. While US electricity prices remained low and stable at $51, European prices across Germany, Spain, and France spiked dramatically starting in late 2021, reaching $218. This visual emphasizes Europe's unique vulnerability, supported by a footnote explaining that Europe imports roughly as much oil and gas from Russia as it produces for itself.

Lastly, the author references his recent J.P. Morgan publication, "Maltese Falcoin," which evaluates cryptocurrencies and blockchains. He discusses whether stablecoins and private, permissioned blockchains will fulfill popular blockchain use cases without impacting directional crypto valuations. To support this cautious view on decentralized finance, he notes that the SEC is reportedly negotiating a $100 million fine with DeFi lender BlockFi for selling unregistered securities, and highlights emerging options for NFT buyers to transact with fiat currency rather than Ethereum tokens.

This page focuses on the unfolding risk unwind in the credit and equity markets, analyzing how various market segments are adjusting as monetary policy shifts. The author attributes the large credit overweight accumulated by investors over the last decade to the Federal Reserve engineering the longest period of negative real rates since the 1860s. He notes that while the credit unwind has a long way to go, equity repricing is much further along. He suggests that a potential 50 basis point Fed hike in March, combined with additional equity market capitulation, could represent an attractive entry point for investors.

The first chart, titled "Implied investor credit overweight," tracks the percentage of investor credit overweight from 2005 to early 2022. It shows that credit overweight dropped significantly during the 2008 financial crisis, bottoming near 2% in 2009, before steadily climbing to a peak of nearly 18% in late 2021. By early 2022, it had begun a downward turn, landing around 14%.

The second chart, "Retail favorites performance," is an index baseline set at 100 in January 2020. It compares retail favorites against the S&P 500 through early 2022. Retail-favored stocks spiked dramatically to over 220 in early 2021 but have since steeply declined to around 160, converging back down toward the S&P 500, which rose steadily to around 140 over the same period.

The third chart, "S&P 500 valuation vs real rates," compares the S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings ratio on the left axis against the inverted 10-year US real yield on the right axis from 2016 to early 2022. S&P 500 forward valuations closely tracked the real yield, peaking at over 22x when real yields neared negative 1.0% in late 2020. As real yields climbed back toward 0.5% in early 2022, the forward P/E valuation fell back toward 19x, though the author notes valuations remain high in a historical context.

The fourth chart, "Drawdowns of individual NASDAQ stocks from their respective peaks," displays a bar graph of 2,915 NASDAQ stocks. It reveals a striking distribution of drawdowns, showing that while about 275 stocks experienced no drawdown, the vast majority suffered significant declines. Many hundreds of stocks are down over 50%, with a notable portion down more than 75% or 90%, contributing to an average NASDAQ stock drawdown of 42% from its peak.

The final chart, "Weak links crumbling," shows a total return index from August 2020 to February 2022, with a base of 100, tracking the IPO Index, SPAC Index, S&P Renewable & Clean Tech, and Solactive Fintech Index. These speculative growth sectors all peaked dramatically in early 2021, with the SPAC and Renewable indices reaching nearly 180 to 200. By early 2022, all four indices collapsed back toward or below their baseline of 100, marking what the author views as a predictable repricing of overpriced, adversely selected assets.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s commentary addresses the market and geopolitical implications of the escalating crisis in Ukraine. Cembalest begins by warning that full sanctions on Russia could severely disrupt markets, expressing skepticism about Europe’s ability to withstand a protracted trade war due to its heavy reliance on Russian energy. To analyze the roots of the conflict, he references political scientist John Mearsheimer’s realist perspective, which attributes the crisis to Western foreign policy mistakes, starting with the post-Cold War enlargement of NATO under the Clinton administration. This expansion added more European landmass than the combined territories of France, Germany, and Italy. Cembalest highlights historical warnings, such as George Kennan’s 1998 caution that NATO expansion was a tragic mistake, and the subsequent 2008 announcement that Georgia and Ukraine would eventually join NATO, which ignored explicit Russian red lines. 

The text is accompanied by a map of Europe illustrating the stages of NATO enlargement. Original 1949 members are shown in black, with subsequent expansions from 1950 to 1980 in brown, 1999 to 2004 in purple, and 2009 to 2020 in red. Ukraine is colored orange, indicating its status in the "Intensified NATO dialogue" phase, while non-NATO nations are depicted in gray. 

Ultimately, Cembalest contrasts Western foreign policy's liberal and realist factions, suggesting the realists may be proven right. He notes that the West has made clear it will not defend Ukraine militarily, explaining in a footnote that the 1994 Budapest Memorandum only offered security assurances rather than a binding defense treaty. The page concludes by suggesting that a neutral status, or some form of Finlandization for Ukraine, might be the best outcome to resolve the conflict.

In this commentary, JP Morgan Asset Management’s Michael Cembalest argues that COVID-19 mortality is severely underreported in many countries, particularly within emerging markets. He refutes the claim that developing nations suffered lower death rates despite having lower vaccination rates, pointing out that strained healthcare systems and inadequate statistical tracking mask the true scale of the pandemic. 

To illustrate this point, a scatter plot compares excess total mortality per million against reported COVID-19 mortality per million from February to December 2020. Countries plotted on the diagonal line, such as Belgium, accurately matched excess deaths with reported COVID-19 deaths. However, many nations lie far above this line, indicating significant underreporting; extreme outliers include Peru, Russia, Bulgaria, Ecuador, Bolivia, and Mexico. A cluster of countries in the bottom-left quadrant, including New Zealand, Japan, Australia, Taiwan, and South Korea, actually recorded negative excess mortality. 

The discrepancy is further highlighted in three line charts tracking deaths per million from 2020 to early 2022 across different income tiers. In high-income countries, estimated excess deaths slightly exceed official reports, reaching roughly 2,000 per million compared to 1,500 reported. In upper-middle-income countries, the gap is wider, with estimated excess deaths exceeding 2,000 per million while reported deaths remain under 1,000. The divergence is most extreme in lower-middle-income countries, where estimated excess deaths spike to nearly 3,000 per million by early 2022, even though officially reported deaths stay below 500. This massive gap persists despite these countries having younger average populations, proving that developing country deaths are heavily undercounted. Chart data is sourced from research published in JAMA Network Global Health Research Letter and Nature.

This page serves as an appendix illustrating that global supply chain conditions remain highly constrained, though there are early signs of minor improvements from peak crisis levels. 

The first chart examines the massive imbalance in the container freight rate between Los Angeles and Shanghai for a 40-foot box from 2012 to early 2022. While the outbound rate from Los Angeles to Shanghai remained flat and negligible under $2,000, the inbound rate from Shanghai to Los Angeles skyrocketed starting in late 2020, peaking at approximately $12,000 in late 2021 before a slight decline. 

This shipping cost pressure is further illustrated by a second chart comparing container freight rates to the backlog of anchored containerships off the port of Los Angeles and Long Beach from 2019 to early 2022. Both the Freightos China to West Coast index, which peaked near $20,000, and the WCI Shanghai to LA index, which peaked near $12,000, rose in tandem with the count of anchored vessels. This backlog spiked to over 100 containerships in late 2021, though all three metrics began showing modest declines by early 2022. 

A third chart tracks global manufacturing delivery times using an inverted index where higher values indicate longer lead times. This index reached near-historical extremes around late 2021, dropping to index levels near 35 before stabilizing slightly by early 2022. 

These severe supply chain disruptions have heavily hampered global auto production. A fourth chart displaying the trailing 12-month sum of auto production by region from 2000 to early 2022 shows deep declines across major manufacturers during the pandemic. By early 2022, production remained significantly depressed, with US output at roughly 9 million units, Japan at around 8 million, and Germany at roughly 3.5 million units.

Domestically, a fifth chart shows the truckstop market demand index, which measures the demand for trucks versus available supply. This index spiked dramatically from a low base under 50 in 2019 to multiple peaks exceeding 200 in early 2021 and early 2022, indicating severe inland logistics bottlenecks. 

Shippers seeking alternatives to ocean transport faced high costs in the air, as shown in a sixth chart of average air freight rates. Air shipping rates climbed from under $3 per kilogram in late 2019 to near-record highs of approximately $8 per kilogram by late 2021 and early 2022. 

A final chart compares shipping rates from 2018 to 2022, highlighting a divergence between dry bulk and container shipping. While the Baltic Dry Index peaked sharply at over 5,000 in late 2021 and plummeted back toward 2,000 by early 2022, container freight rates remained stubbornly high near the $10,000 mark.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the historical context of the geopolitical crisis in Ukraine, focusing on the long-running debate between Liberalism and Realism in Western foreign policy. Michael Cembalest reviews political scientist John Mearsheimer’s 2014 essay, which argued that the West's actions, particularly NATO's eastward expansion, provoked Russia. The narrative traces this expansion back to the Clinton administration in the 1990s, noting that it added more territory than the landmass of France, Germany, and Italy combined. The text quotes diplomat George Kennan's 1998 warning that NATO expansion was a tragic mistake that would eventually trigger an adverse Russian reaction. Despite Russian objections, NATO announced in 2008 that Georgia and Ukraine would become members, crossing what Russia viewed as a red line. 

An accompanying map of Europe visualizes the historical phases of NATO enlargement. Original 1949 members are shaded black, and expansions from 1950 to 1980 are shown in brown. The post-Cold War eastward push from 1999 to 2004 is colored purple, followed by Balkan additions from 2009 to 2020 in red. Countries with a NATO Membership Action Plan are shown in blue, while Ukraine is highlighted in orange to represent its "intensified NATO dialogue" status, bordering non-NATO nations shown in gray. 

The author suggests that because the West has made it clear it will not defend Ukraine militarily, the Realist school of thought may be proven right. A footnote explains that while the 1994 Budapest Memorandum provided Ukraine with security assurances from the US, UK, and Russia in exchange for giving up its nuclear weapons, the agreement only required signatories to raise issues with the UN Security Council and was not a legally binding defense treaty. Ultimately, the page highlights Mearsheimer's conclusion that a neutral "Finlandization" of Ukraine would have been a better outcome for all sides.

This page analyzes the escalating European energy crisis following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, emphasizing the structural limitations that prevent liquefied natural gas imports from easily replacing Russian pipeline gas. The author argues that because LNG exporters price their supplies close to European spot pipeline prices, it would take an unprecedented flood of imports to drive prices down. 

To illustrate these supply dynamics, the page features four visual data displays. The first chart, "European natural gas imports: Russia vs LNG" (in billion cubic meters per week from 2015 to early 2022), tracks the historical reliance on Russian pipeline gas, which has typically fluctuated between 2.5 and 3.5 Bcm per week but trended downward into 2022. Meanwhile, total LNG imports and US LNG imports have surged to record highs. The second chart, "Natural gas prices" (in dollars per MMBTU from 2019 to 2022), reveals how European natural gas and Asian LNG prices have spiked in tandem to over $60 per MMBTU, while US Henry Hub domestic gas prices have remained flat and cheap at under $10 per MMBTU. 

On the bottom left, the "Europe energy prices" chart (in US dollars per MWh from 2015 to 2022) highlights a massive, concurrent spike in regional utility costs, with electricity prices reaching $225 per MWh and natural gas prices hitting $140 per MWh. On the bottom right, a pie chart detailing the "Annual capacity of EU27 natural gas imports" (in TWh) highlights the scale of Europe’s dependency. Russia represents the largest pipeline import source at 2,800 TWh, followed by Norway at 1,100 TWh, North Africa at 800 TWh, and Azerbaijan at 130 TWh. Total LNG import capacity is fragmented across individual nations, led by Spain at 700 TWh and France at 440 TWh, followed by smaller capacities in Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Greece, Portugal, Poland, Lithuania, and Croatia.

The commentary notes that even if more LNG cargo were available, Europe suffers from severe infrastructure bottlenecks. For instance, Spain has the greatest excess LNG capacity but lacks adequate pipeline connections to transport this gas to Central Europe. Furthermore, global regasification facilities and exporter liquefaction facilities are already running at very high utilization rates. While the Netherlands possesses additional gas capacity at its Groningen fields, a drilling moratorium remains in place due to local earthquake risks. The author warns that if Russian gas imports were cut in half, LNG capacity could not cover the deficit, likely forcing EU governments to implement mandatory gas rationing. This industrial demand curtailment has already begun, as high prices have prompted production cuts among steel and aluminum makers, chemical and fertilizer companies, and silicon producers like Ferroglobe in Spain.

This page analyzes timber investing, focusing on its steady yields and potential upside for carbon sequestration compared to other real assets. The commentary details how US timber returns have lagged since the 2008 housing crisis due to a surplus of Southern Pine in the US Southeast. According to J.P. Morgan timber managers, while sawlog prices could rise in two to four years, it may take eight to ten years to fully restore the Southern Pine supply-demand balance. The author notes that timber has served as a steady, modest-yield portfolio addition over the past 20 years, though they caution against relying on risk-adjusted returns like Sharpe ratios for illiquid, appraisal-based assets. A footnote references an October 2018 Wall Street Journal article to illustrate how a large institutional investor suffered losses by acquiring timber at peak 2008 valuations with high leverage and poor diversification.

The analysis is supported by two tables and one chart tracking NCREIF unleveraged real asset returns. The author explains that these indexes track unleveraged property returns and are not directly investable, whereas most managed commercial property funds employ leverage, typically around 25%. 

The first table, covering 1991 to 2021, shows farmland leading with a 10.6% annualized return, a 5.8% standard deviation, and a 1.36 Sharpe ratio. Industrial properties follow at a 9.9% annualized return, while timberland posted an 8.9% annualized return, a 6.8% standard deviation, and a 0.91 Sharpe ratio. Other categories in this period include apartment properties at 8.7%, retail properties at 7.5%, and office properties at 6.9%. 

The second table, covering 2000 to 2021, demonstrates a shift as timberland returns drop to 5.6% with a 0.95 Sharpe ratio. Farmland and industrial properties lead this period with annualized returns of 11.6% and 10.9% respectively, followed by retail and apartment properties both at 8.5%, office properties at 7.6%, and hotel properties at the bottom with 4.6%. 

The bottom line chart plots the total return index from 2000 to 2021, starting with a base of 100 in late 1999. It visually emphasizes farmland’s outperformance, climbing to nearly 1,100 on the index with a 12% annualized return since 2000. Industrial properties achieved an 11% return, followed by retail and apartment properties at 9%, office properties at 8%, timberland at 6%, and hotel properties at 5%.

This page discusses Europe's energy and agricultural vulnerabilities amidst rising geopolitical tensions with Russia, while also offering a critical observation on Bitcoin’s market behavior. Addressing the debate over whether long-term US liquefied natural gas (LNG) contracts are cheaper for Europe than the LNG spot market, the author cautions that historical Asian data shows long-term contracts are not always the more economical choice. Specifically, in 2018 and 2019, long-term contracts traded at a premium to spot prices, though spot prices surged significantly higher after 2020. Securing long-term LNG contracts would require Europe to commit to 5-to-15-year deals at prices well above historical pipeline levels. This is critical given that 30% of Europe's energy imports flow through pipelines in Ukraine, putting them at immediate risk. Furthermore, Europe relies heavily on Russia for oil, which accounted for 27% of its oil imports in 2021. This dependency is exacerbated by OECD oil inventories sitting at 15-year lows relative to global demand, and a severe drop in global oil and gas capital expenditures.

The first chart, titled "Global fossil fuel use vs energy capital spending," illustrates this capital divergence. Measured in exajoules on the right axis and US dollars on the left, it shows that while global primary energy fossil fuel use rose steadily from 400 exajoules in 2005 to around 500 exajoules in 2019—experiencing only a brief dip during the 2020 COVID-19 decline—capital spending by S&P Global 1200 Energy companies collapsed from a peak near $400 billion in 2013 to roughly $150 billion by late 2021.

The second chart, "Cereal prices rising as supply remains tight," tracks the stocks-to-use ratio of major exporters alongside cereal prices from 2014 to 2023. The stocks-to-use ratio declined from about 17% in 2017 to under 10% in J.P. Morgan's 2022 and 2023 forecasts. Meanwhile, the cereal price index remained stable near 100 before surging dramatically toward 140 by late 2021. Forecasted dots show wheat and corn prices remaining historically elevated.

Transitioning to cryptocurrency, Cembalest argues that Bitcoin does not behave as an independent store of value, but rather as standard high-beta market exposure. The chart "Bitcoin vs relative performance of high Beta stocks" plots the ratio of the S&P 500 High Beta Index to the Low Volatility ETF on the left axis against the log-scale Bitcoin price on the right from July 2019 to January 2022. The two curves move in near-perfect lockstep, showing Bitcoin's price rising from around $10,000 to over $60,000 and falling in tandem with broader high-beta equity trends.

Finally, the chart "Asia long-term and spot vs US LNG contracts" tracks prices in US dollars per MMBTU from 2018 through 2021. It shows the US Henry Hub price remaining consistently low, under $5, while the Japan Customs Cleared (JCC) long-term oil-linked LNG contracts remained steady between $5 and $15. Conversely, the JKM LNG spot price remained low (under $10) until late 2020, when it experienced an extreme spike, peaking over $35 by the end of 2021.

This page of the report evaluates the International Energy Agency's highly ambitious "shock treatment" plans to rapidly wean Europe off of Russian energy, with Michael Cembalest arguing that these plans are unrealistic in the short term. He critiques four major pillars of the IEA's proposal. First, diversifying gas suppliers will likely narrow European supply and drive up prices rather than curb global demand, especially since 80% of US liquefied natural gas is already exported to Europe, new US liquefaction facilities will not arrive until 2025, and building new German import terminals and Spanish pipeline connections will take significant time. Second, accelerating wind and solar is hindered by transmission bottlenecks and the fact that electricity represents only 19% of final European energy consumption, meaning the region still heavily depends on thermal fossil fuels for industrial production, transport, and heating. Third, increasing residential heat pump usage is a slow-moving transition currently confined mostly to Scandinavia, while electrification of residential heating has remained flat at 25% since 2013. Finally, maximizing nuclear power is limited by European reactors already operating at their realistic capacity limit of 80% due to required maintenance downtimes.

Four charts support these observations by detailing the structural realities of European energy and the resulting price shocks. A pie chart depicting OECD Europe's total final energy consumption shows that industry consumes 35% and transport accounts for 27%, while electricity is only 19%, followed by residential heating at 13% and commercial heating at 6%. To the right, a line chart tracking European reliance on Russian energy in thousands of barrels of oil equivalent per day from 1980 to 2020 reveals that while domestic European oil and gas production peaked in the late 1990s and has since steadily fallen to around 5,500 thousand barrels per day, imports from Russia have steadily climbed to approximately 6,000 thousand barrels per day. This leaves Russian imports nearly neck-and-neck with domestic production and represents a significant portion of all other European oil and gas imports, which hovered around 10,000 thousand barrels per day in 2020. 

Two pricing charts at the bottom illustrate the extreme divergence between North American and European energy markets in early 2022. The chart for wholesale electricity prices, measured in US dollars per megawatt-hour on a 7-day average from 2015 to 2023, shows European prices spiking dramatically in early 2022 to $571 for Germany, Spain, and France, and $522 for the UK, compared to a flat $34 in the United States. Adjacent to this, the wholesale natural gas prices chart, measuring US dollars per million British thermal units from 2019 to 2022, shows the US Henry Hub benchmark remaining low at $5 while European and UK natural gas prices spiked to $87. 

Ultimately, Cembalest asserts that Europe’s energy reliance on Russia is too high to reduce quickly. He projects that any near-term decline in European energy costs is primarily dependent on three external factors: a resolution of the conflict in Ukraine, a large 2.5-times seasonal drop in gas demand during March and April, and an end to strategic reserve buying by the United States and the European Union.

This page analyzed the historical and economic context surrounding the Russian invasion of Ukraine, reflecting on missed geopolitical opportunities and drawing comparisons to historical military imbalances. The author discusses the brief window of Russian weakness in the 1990s, when a sovereign debt default, collapsing oil prices, and depleted reserves coincided with NATO’s eastward expansion. This expansion proceeded despite warnings from prominent U.S. foreign policy figures and a 1999 NATO report which correctly predicted that Russian society would lean back toward authoritarianism. 

To illustrate Russia's subsequent rebuilding of its economic defenses, two charts are presented. The first shows Russia’s foreign exchange reserves rising from near zero in 1998 to over $600 billion by 2022, despite temporary dips in 2008 and 2014. The second chart details Russia’s current account balance as a percentage of GDP, which spiked past 15% in 2000 and consistently maintained a surplus, fluctuating between 2% and 10% over the next two decades.

The author raises the question of whether different paths—such as "Finlandization" or immediate NATO membership with explicit military protections—could have prevented the war. Instead, a late 2021 U.S.-Ukraine strategic partnership offered aspirations of NATO membership without actual protection. The stark consequence is depicted in a table of the 2022 Russia-Ukraine military balance, revealing a massive asymmetry. Russia vastly outmatches Ukraine in ground forces (850,000 versus 200,000), tanks (12,420 versus 2,596), armored vehicles (30,122 versus 12,303), total aircraft (4,173 versus 318), and attack helicopters (544 versus 34). 

Reflecting on Ukraine's history, including the Holodomor terror-famine imposed by Stalin that killed 4 million Ukrainians, the author searches for hope. A final table compares this conflict to the American Revolutionary War, where the United States faced similarly daunting odds against Great Britain. In that conflict, Britain possessed 500 naval ships by 1782 compared to the U.S. force of 20, and commanded 194,000 soldiers against a peak American force of 30,000. This parallel suggests that, much like the early United States, Ukraine’s survival against an overwhelming adversary will depend heavily on the determination of its defenders and historical resilience.

This page analyzed the state of the Chinese economy, global equity market performance, and the mounting pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. The analysis suggested that China’s 5.5% GDP growth target would likely require additional fiscal stimulus to achieve, especially given the government’s firm stance against real estate speculation. While Chinese economic and corporate earnings data stabilized, its equity markets had sold off in tandem with other major global regions. The primary headwind for global equities was the expectation of substantial monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve, alongside geopolitical risks. The author warned that the markets had likely not yet seen the worst of the ongoing war or the bottom of the stock market downturn.

To dissect China's economic health, three charts plotted index values where January 2018 equals 100, tracking data through late 2021 or early 2022. The first chart, showing positive economic signs, illustrated robust activity in exports, electricity consumption, and a sharp late-2021 rebound in crude steel production. The second chart, tracking stable signs, showed that industrial production, construction and real estate GDP, retail sales, and corporate earnings for A-shares were holding steady, clustering between index levels of 100 and 120. In contrast, the third chart highlighted negative signs, showing a severe and ongoing contraction in both residential and commercial construction starts, with commercial starts dropping to an index level near 60 by the end of 2021. 

Global and regional equity performance was depicted in two charts showing year-to-date total returns in U.S. dollars through March 4, 2022. The major equity markets chart showed negative returns across all major regions; Canada and Australia fared the best with a modest decline of roughly three percent, US Large Caps and China onshore equities both fell about ten percent, and Europe and the Eurozone suffered the heaviest losses, down roughly seventeen and nineteen percent, respectively. A dedicated chart on China's YTD equity returns broke down performance across various indices and MSCI subcomponents. Every single tracker was in negative territory, with MSCI Red Chips declining the least at around two percent, while technology-heavy segments like China ADRs, the five largest China tech stocks, and the Hang Seng Tech index fell between sixteen and eighteen percent.

The final two charts focused on the Federal Reserve's policy path. The chart displaying market-implied Fed hikes derived from the futures market showed a massive shift in investor expectations, with the projected number of 25 basis point hikes over the next 12 months rising from zero in August 2021 to nearly seven by February 2022. This market pricing aligned with the final chart, which plotted the required Fed Funds rate according to various policy guidelines, including the Taylor rule, Balanced approach, Balanced approach for shortfalls, Adjusted Taylor, and First difference models. By late 2021, most of these policy rules, particularly the Taylor and Balanced approaches, indicated that the required policy rate should have spiked to between five and seven percent, illustrating the intense pressure on the central bank to aggressively tighten monetary policy.

This page from the publication surveys the severe geopolitical, humanitarian, and economic damage caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, putting the conflict into historical and energy-market contexts. The author begins by highlighting the massive humanitarian toll, projecting that the invasion could displace four to five million refugees—comparable to major crises in Syria, Venezuela, and Afghanistan—and push ninety percent of the Ukrainian population into extreme poverty by the end of 2022. To demonstrate that this brutal subjugation is not without precedent, the author references the Holodomor, a terror famine imposed by Soviet Russia on Ukraine in the 1930s. 

A line chart titled Ukraine Holodomor terror famine compared to other famines illustrates this point by tracking death rates per one thousand people over a five-year span. The data shows the Holodomor peaking dramatically in year three at nearly one hundred and thirty deaths per one thousand people, dwarfs other historical famines. In comparison, the Irish Potato Famine of 1845 to 1850 and the North Korean Arduous March of 1993 to 1998 both peak around thirty-five to forty deaths per thousand, while the Indian Bengal famine and China's Great Leap Forward famine show peak death rates below thirty per thousand.

The commentary then shifts to the energy crisis and the feasibility of Europe reducing its reliance on Russian energy. The author expresses skepticism regarding Europe's ability to quickly scale up liquefied natural gas imports, expand wind, solar, and heat pump installations, build out non-existent hydrogen infrastructure, and maximize nuclear power. However, if Europe successfully achieves this energy independence, the author predicts Russia's global economic standing will decline so sharply that it will essentially become an energy vassal state for China. The author notes that China is already Russia's largest trading partner, yet Russia represents a mere two percent of Chinese exports. 

Two charts at the bottom of the page support this economic and energy analysis. The first, titled Russia/USSR share of World GDP since 1820, maps the historic rise and fall of the Russian economy's global weight. It traces the additions of Georgia, Azerbaijan, Central Asian republics, and postwar Eastern European annexations, which drove the Soviet Union's share of world GDP to a peak of nearly sixteen percent in the mid-twentieth century. Following the dissolution of the USSR, the share plummeted, with the modern Russian Federation holding less than four percent of world GDP. 

The final chart, Energy dependence and independence, plots net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal in million tonnes of oil equivalent from 1980 to 2020. It contrasts the roles of major global powers, showing Europe as a persistent net importer of energy, hovering between six hundred and eight hundred million tonnes. China has rapidly transformed from energy self-sufficiency in the 1980s to a massive net importer of nearly six hundred million tonnes by 2020. Conversely, the United States successfully transitioned from a major net importer peaking near six hundred million tonnes in 2005 to a net exporter by 2020, while Russia has steadily grown its position as a dominant net exporter, reaching nearly eight hundred million tonnes of energy exports.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market discusses the resilience of global credit markets alongside a deep selloff in Chinese equities, particularly within the internet sector. The author highlights that while credit spreads are widening, they are nowhere near levels typically seen during recessions. Meanwhile, the intense selloff in Chinese markets is pricing in significant bad news, though China possesses a substantial reservoir of stimulus ammunition to help meet its government-mandated five point five percent growth target for the year. 

To support the credit spread argument, the page features two charts spanning 1987 to early 2022, with shaded areas indicating historical recessions. The first chart, showing US and emerging market high yield credit spreads, illustrates that both the US high yield spread and the emerging market high yield sovereign spread have risen slightly but remain far below historical recessionary spikes, which often exceeded fifteen to twenty percent. The second chart tracks US investment grade credit spreads, showing that although spreads have recently ticked up to around two percent, they remain well below the recessionary peaks of four to six percent observed during the Great Financial Crisis and the early COVID-19 pandemic.

The discussion then focuses on China, where the author notes that investors must grapple with tough COVID-19 lockdowns in Shenzhen and Shanghai, the potential elimination of all Chinese ADRs, and higher capital costs. This market anxiety is visualized in two additional charts. The first compares Chinese internet stocks from September 2019 to early 2022 against the historical NASDAQ bubble and bust from 1999 to 2004, with both series indexed to one hundred at their peak. The comparison shows that the Chinese internet index has closely tracked the dot-com crash, plummeting to a level near thirty. The second China chart tracks MSCI China equity index drawdowns from prior peaks between 2007 and early 2022. It shows that the latest drawdown has reached negative forty-five percent, marking a severe decline, though still less than the near eighty percent drawdown experienced during the 2008 financial crisis.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication evaluates whether the market decline around March 8, 2022, offers a bottom-fishing opportunity for investors. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that if a US recession is avoided, the March 8th low likely represents a market bottom, as its magnitude matches historical non-recessionary sell-offs. While he considers recession risk a close call due to rising energy prices, credit spreads, wages, geopolitical shortages, and aggressive Federal Reserve policy tightening, he predicts the United States will avoid a recession. 

To analyze the scale of the correction, the page includes two bar charts comparing different stock indices, including the S&P 500, Russell indices, and Nasdaq. The first chart, titled March 8 a likely bottom if no US recession occurs, displays the average stock decline from its prior peak. It shows that March 8th declines (depicted in red) closely track the historical averages of other large non-recessionary sell-offs (depicted in gold), which typically range between fifteen percent and thirty-five percent. In contrast, historical recessionary declines (depicted in blue) are much deeper, often exceeding forty percent to fifty percent. The second chart, titled The average stock fell a lot more than the index it is in, measures the decline from fifty-two-week highs as of March 8th. This visual compares the market-cap-weighted index declines (blue) to their median stocks (gold) and average stocks (red). It illustrates that while the Nasdaq Composite index itself fell about twenty percent, its average and median constituent stocks dropped over forty percent, indicating severe underlying damage to individual equities.

The bottom half of the page examines market valuations and investor positioning. A line chart titled P/E ratio of top 25 stocks vs the market plots forward price-to-earnings ratios from 1986 to early 2022. It reveals a wide valuation gap, with the twenty-five largest stocks, including Apple, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Tesla, trading at an elevated forward ratio of around twenty-seven times earnings. Meanwhile, the rest of the S&P 500 trades at a much lower multiple of around seventeen times earnings.
