The final chart, titled Hedge fund gross leverage, shows gross leverage percentages from January 2020 to January 2022. It indicates that while hedge fund leverage has declined from its late 2020 peak of over two hundred five percent down to approximately one hundred eighty-eight percent by early 2022, it has not undergone the drastic capitulation typical of past recessions. Additionally, the text notes that while CFTC futures positions in the S&P 500 and NASDAQ are approaching their 2018 and 2020 lows, small-cap futures positions have reached their lowest levels since the 2008 financial crisis.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest assesses the deteriorating economic outlook for Europe, arguing that while European nations are historically among the most energy-efficient on Earth, the sheer scale of recent energy and producer price increases is large enough to completely overwhelm these efficiency gains. Characterizing the situation as a massive commodity shock comparable to the OPEC oil embargoes of 1973 and 1979, Cembalest notes that European electricity and natural gas prices have quadrupled. He warns that a European recession appears inevitable as companies either absorb these producer price surges through lower margins, less hiring, and reduced capital spending, or pass them along to consumers, prompting central banks to tighten policy. Consequently, European equities, currently trading at thirteen times earnings, look overvalued, as European recessions historically cause earnings to drop by twenty-five percent and price-to-earnings ratios to fall below ten. This bleak outlook is unlikely to improve unless there is an unexpectedly swift resolution to the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Four charts support this argument. The first chart, which illustrates the energy intensity of growth, displays primary energy consumption in exajoules per trillion US dollars of real GDP for 2020. It shows that European nations like Switzerland, the UK, Italy, Germany, Spain, France, and Sweden are exceptionally efficient, consuming fewer than three exajoules per trillion dollars of GDP. In contrast, Canada and Russia consume between seven and eight exajoules, China consumes around five, and the United States consumes about four. 

The second chart tracks the percentage gap between producer price and consumer price inflation from 1970 to February 2022. While both the United States and Europe have historically seen this gap hover between negative five percent and positive five percent, Europe has recently experienced an unprecedented spike, with producer prices exceeding consumer price inflation by nearly thirty percent. The United States has experienced nothing close to this degree of producer price pressure.

The third and fourth charts detail wholesale energy prices. The third chart shows wholesale electricity prices in US dollars per megawatt-hour on a seven-day average from 2015 to early 2023. While US prices remained stable at thirty-three dollars, European wholesale electricity prices experienced a massive spike, ending at two hundred sixty-one dollars in the UK and two hundred fifty-eight dollars in Germany, Spain, and France. Similarly, the fourth chart shows wholesale natural gas prices in US dollars per million British thermal units from 2019 to early 2022. European and UK gas prices surged to thirty dollars, compared to the US Henry Hub benchmark, which remained at just five dollars.

This page analyzes the performance of growth stock allocations from January 2017 to February 2022, demonstrating that while growth stock exposure generated substantial excess returns over other equity alternatives, nearly half of this outperformance over value was concentrated in just four mega-cap stocks: Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Google. 

The first line chart, titled "Equity benchmark performance," tracks total return indices starting in January 2017, where all indices are set to a base of 100. By February 28, 2022, the Russell 1000 Growth and NASDAQ indices significantly outperformed the S&P 500, MSCI World Small Cap, Russell 1000 Value, Russell 2000 Small Cap, MSCI Emerging Markets, and MSCI Europe. Both growth leaders peaked above 325 in late 2021 before experiencing a selloff. 

To illustrate how concentrated these returns were, a second line chart, "Closer look at the Russell 1000," isolates the impact of the four mega-caps. This chart compares the full Russell 1000 Growth Index against the Russell 1000 Growth Index excluding its four largest stocks, alongside the Russell 1000 Index and the Russell 1000 Value Index. A substantial performance gap is visible between the full Growth index and the Growth index excluding Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Google, proving that these four giants drove a massive share of the overall growth index gains.

A supporting data table compares growth equity against other benchmarks from January 2017 through February 2022. The Russell 1000 Growth and NASDAQ delivered cumulative returns of 171% and 168% respectively, translating to an annualized return of 21% for both. In contrast, the S&P 500 achieved a cumulative return of 115% (16% annualized), while the Russell 1000 Value returned 64% (10% annualized). Growth stocks also achieved a superior return-to-risk ratio of 1.2x compared to 1.0x for the S&P 500 and 0.6x for the Russell 1000 Value, despite having similar annualized volatility levels, with the Russell 1000 Growth at 17% volatility versus 16% for both the S&P 500 and the Russell 1000 Value. At the end of the period, the growth indices stood at 88% of their peak values, while value stocks sat at 97% of their peak.

This page analyzes how rising metals prices threaten to impact the electric vehicle (EV) industry, focusing on whether sustained commodity price hikes will lead to vehicle sticker shock due to ballooning battery costs. The author, Michael Cembalest, compares the raw metal costs of a hypothetical 60 kWh battery across three major chemistry types: Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC), Lithium Nickel Cobalt Aluminum (NCA), and Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP).

A line chart titled "Metals cost per EV battery" tracks the cost in U.S. dollars per 60 kWh battery from January 2020 through January 2022. It reveals that the raw metals cost for both NMC and NCA batteries sat around $1,500 in early 2020 before surging to nearly $3,000 by early 2022. LFP battery metals costs remained much lower, rising from roughly $500 to about $1,000 over the same period. 

A companion stacked bar chart, "EV battery cost breakdown using current metals prices," highlights why these costs diverge. For NMC and NCA batteries, which total roughly $2,700 and $2,500 respectively under current pricing, nickel and cobalt make up the largest share of the expenses. LFP batteries, totaling just under $1,000, are dominated by lithium and copper, with the cost of iron and steel being negligible. 

An accompanying table outlines battery chemistries by manufacturer and vehicle type. Traditional auto brands including Audi, BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, Ford (for the F-150 EV), and Volkswagen (for high-end passenger EVs) rely on NMC batteries. LFP batteries, which are cheaper but less energy-dense, are favored by Chinese manufacturers like BYD and Hongguang, Rivian (for trucks, SUVs, and delivery vans), Volkswagen (for entry-level EVs), and Tesla (for short-range passenger EVs). Tesla uses NCA for its long-range passenger vehicles. 

A third line chart, "Metal prices," indexes metal costs starting in December 2019 through early 2022. By January 2022, lithium experienced the most dramatic surge, reaching a final index value of 597. It is followed by cobalt at 257, nickel at 228, manganese at 222, aluminum at 193, copper at 168, iron at 160, and steel at 146. 

Cembalest observes that while LFP-based EVs face manageable battery cost increases of around $500 since early 2020 (mostly driven by copper), NMC and NCA-based EVs face a steep $1,500 battery cost increase. Additionally, all EVs face an extra $500 cost increase for non-battery copper and aluminum. Consequently, he predicts sticker shock for nickel- and cobalt-reliant EVs, which could further hinder U.S. EV adoption rates that stood at just 2% of sales in the prior year. He suggests this pressure might require more generous Federal subsidies. A detailed footnote calculates that EV owners can still save about $1,250 annually on fuel—assuming 25 mpg for a gas car, 3 miles per kWh for an EV, $4 gasoline, and 14 cents per kWh electricity—which helps determine the payback period for the upfront premium of an EV.

This page analyzes the performance of growth equity mutual funds from January 2017 to February 2022, arguing that scarce active manager outperformance is largely driven by regulatory diversification rules that forced them to underweight the market's biggest winners. Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan highlights Section 5-b-1 of the 1940 Investment Company Act, which dictates that for a mutual fund to remain classified as diversified, holdings that exceed five percent of the portfolio cannot collectively total more than 25 percent of the fund. This rule creates a structural hurdle for growth managers because the benchmark indices have become highly concentrated in a few mega-cap technology stocks. For example, in March 2022, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Google combined for 36 percent of the Russell 1000 Growth Index and 41 percent of the S&P 500 Growth Index. Consequently, active managers seeking to comply with the 25 percent diversification threshold were legally forced to underweight these dominant stocks, which severely dragged down their relative returns. 

Three charts illustrate the quantitive impact of this constraint. The top-left chart displays a histogram of the relative cumulative performance of 138 Russell 1000 Growth benchmarked funds over the five-year period. It shows that a vast majority of these funds underperformed the benchmark, with the largest clusters of funds falling into the negative ten percent to negative twenty percent underperformance ranges, and only a tiny fraction achieving positive excess returns. 

The top-right chart traces the cumulative performance of the growth indices starting from a base value of 100 in January 2017. It shows that the S&P 500 Top Four stocks—Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet—skyrocketed to an index value approaching 600 by early 2022, vastly outstripping the S&P 500 Growth Index and the Russell 1000 Growth Index, which both finished the period around the 250 to 300 level. This stark divergence illustrates the massive opportunity cost of being underweight in these four names. 

The bottom-left chart quantifies this opportunity cost directly, plotting the cumulative outperformance of an unconstrained growth portfolio versus one that is restricted by the diversification rule. Assuming constrained managers maintained a combined weight of 23 percent across the four largest stocks, the unconstrained portfolio steadily pulled ahead, building a cumulative outperformance gap of nearly 14 percent to 15 percent by early 2022. Together, these visualizations make the case that growth fund underperformance is less about poor stock selection and more about the structural drag imposed by decades-old regulatory frameworks in a highly concentrated stock market.

This page evaluates the performance of long-short hedge funds using two distinct databases, HFR and eVestment, comparing them to a beta-adjusted benchmark of the Russell 1000 Growth Index with 45% net exposure over a period spanning January 2017 to February 2022. 

The first analysis focuses on the HFR database, examining 55 tech and healthcare long-short hedge funds. The accompanying line chart and table illustrate that the median (50th percentile) manager performed close to the beta-adjusted benchmark, with the 75th and 25th percentile managers distributed on either side. Specifically, the 75th percentile manager significantly outperformed, achieving a 126% cumulative return (17% annualized) with 24% volatility, resulting in a return-to-risk ratio of 0.7x. The median manager achieved a 65% cumulative return (10% annualized) with 17% volatility, closely matching the Russell 1000 Growth benchmark's 60% cumulative return (9% annualized). The 25th percentile manager lagged significantly with a 31% cumulative return (5% annualized) and a 0.4x return-to-risk ratio. The author notes that while top-quartile managers outperformed the median by a larger margin than bottom-quartile managers underperformed it, there remain concerns regarding the self-reporting bias inherent in the HFR dataset.

To address data gaps, the author presents a second analysis using the eVestment database, which tracks 231 high-beta hedge funds that exhibited a beta to the S&P 500 Growth Index of at least 0.45 over the prior two years. Despite eVestment having a lower rate of missing data, the performance distribution remains nearly identical to the HFR results. The eVestment line chart and table show the 75th percentile manager achieving a 103% cumulative return (15% annualized) with 18% volatility. The median manager recorded a 66% cumulative return (10% annualized) with 15% volatility, again tracking near the benchmark. The 25th percentile manager finished with a 38% cumulative return (6% annualized) and 13% volatility. 

A key takeaway across both datasets is that while top-quartile active managers generated high cumulative returns, their risk-adjusted returns—ranging from 0.5x to 0.8x—were substantially lower than the passive, beta-adjusted Russell 1000 Growth benchmark, which delivered a 1.2x return-to-risk ratio due to its much lower volatility of 8%.

This page analyzes hedge fund performance using PivotalPath data, focusing on Technology long-short funds and generalist growth-oriented Tiger Cub descendants of the original Tiger fund. Out of 104 Technology long-short funds, only 27 had consistent monthly data from January 2017 to February 2022, illustrating how data limitations present a constant challenge in hedge fund analysis. The performance of these 27 funds displayed a normal distribution, where the median manager generated returns close to the beta-adjusted Russell 1000 Growth benchmark at 45 percent net exposure, but with higher risk-adjusted returns.

A chart titled PivotalPath Tech hedge funds plots the index performance from January 2017 to early 2022, revealing that the 75th percentile outperformed significantly, while the 25th percentile underperformed. According to the accompanying table of Tech fund performance by quartile, the 75th percentile reached a 90 percent cumulative return (13 percent annualized) with 13 percent volatility, while the median manager achieved a 63 percent cumulative return (10 percent annualized) with a low volatility of 6 percent, resulting in a strong return-to-risk ratio of 1.6x. In comparison, the 25th percentile manager returned 37 percent cumulatively (6 percent annualized), and the Russell 1000 Growth benchmark at 45 percent net exposure returned 60 percent cumulatively with an 8 percent annualized volatility.

The second section of the page focuses on 12 out of 29 Tiger Cub funds that had consistent performance data over the same five-year period. The corresponding chart, PivotalPath Tiger Cub hedge funds, shows that the 75th percentile manager kept pace with the Russell benchmark, but the median manager suffered a deep correction in early 2022. The performance table shows the 75th percentile Tiger Cub matched the Russell 1000 Growth benchmark with a 60 percent cumulative return (10 percent annualized). However, the median Tiger Cub manager achieved only a 37 percent cumulative return with an elevated 11 percent volatility, and the 25th percentile manager underperformed dramatically with a 14 percent cumulative return (3 percent annualized) alongside 12 percent volatility, translating to a poor return-to-risk ratio of 0.2x. The author notes that one unnamed Tiger Cub fund exhibited extreme volatility, posting high returns initially but subsequently experiencing a severe drawdown of 37 percent by February 2022, with reports of further heavy drawdowns in March despite a rebound in the Russell benchmark.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s analysis examines how growth-oriented asset allocations and hedge fund managers performed relative to growth benchmarks from January 2017 through February 2022. The central argument is that while growth generated substantial portfolio benefits despite the early 2022 selloff, only top-quartile managers delivered excess returns over their growth benchmarks. The author notes that most growth mutual funds underperformed the Russell 1000 Growth Index because managers were reluctant or unable to hold market-weight positions in the market's four largest stocks, which outperformed the rest of the equity market by 300 percent during this period. 

To illustrate these trends across different tiers of hedge fund management, the page features three line charts indexing performance starting from a baseline of 100 in January 2017 through early 2022. The charts compare several manager datasets—including eVestment high beta, PivotalPath Tech, HFR Tech/Healthcare, and Tiger Cub managers—against a benchmark of the Russell 1000 Growth Index at 45 percent exposure. 

The first chart shows the 50th percentile, or median, manager performance. Most median managers closely tracked the beta-adjusted benchmark, which rose to around 160 by late 2021, though the Tiger Cub manager was an exception that trailed the benchmark. The second chart, tracking 25th percentile underperforming managers, shows all manager datasets lagging behind the benchmark; the benchmark ended near 150, while underperforming manager indices struggled, with the Tiger Cub index falling sharply toward 120 by early 2022. The third chart shows the 75th percentile outperforming managers, where three of the datasets—HFR Tech/Healthcare, eVestment high beta, and PivotalPath Tech—dramatically outperformed the benchmark, with indices peaking near 240 to 280 in late 2021. In this top tier, the Tiger Cub fund was the lone exception, merely tracking the benchmark instead of beating it. 

The accompanying text addresses broader issues of volatility, benchmarking, and data quality. The author points out that despite large drawdowns in early 2022, some hedge funds had accumulated such high prior returns that long-term investors remained ahead of the benchmarks, a nuance often missed by media coverage. Furthermore, the author cautions that standard beta-adjusted benchmarks do not capture specific manager styles, which typically requires customized benchmarks. Finally, the analysis notes that data issues such as selective reporting, survivorship bias, and missing manager data—particularly in the PivotalPath dataset where less than half of existing managers could be analyzed—complicate overall performance measurements.

In this executive summary of the JP Morgan Annual Energy Paper, Michael Cembalest argues that despite a rapid decline in the market price of wind and solar power, global reliance on fossil fuels remains stubbornly high—representing about 83% of primary energy use globally and 70% even in Europe. He asserts that popular "levelized costs" comparing renewables to fossil fuels are misleading because they omit the costly necessities of high grid penetration: transmission expansion, thermal backup power, and utility-scale battery storage. Furthermore, the benefits of grid decarbonization are severely limited by low electrification across industrial processes, heating, and transportation. 

Four distinct charts support these observations. The first line chart, titled "The world uses fossil fuels for ~83% of its energy," tracks the percentage of global primary energy consumption from coal, oil, and natural gas from 1965 to 2050. It details the transition from the nuclear adoption era to the beginning of the solar/wind era. Looking to 2050, it plots two International Energy Agency (IEA) projections: the Stated Policies Scenario, which leaves the world roughly 66% reliant on fossil fuels, and the Announced Pledges Scenario, which drops fossil fuel reliance to about 46%.

The second line chart, "Average power purchase agreement by year of operation," shows how renewable procurement costs in real 2020 dollars per megawatt-hour plummeted between 2010 and 2020. Global solar photovoltaic fell from nearly $200 to $40, while US solar PV dropped from $160 to approximately $30. US wind decreased from about $60 to under $30, and global wind followed a similar downward trajectory. However, the author cautions in the footnotes that power purchase agreement levels are starting to rise again due to inflation in industrial metals and interest rates, forcing wind turbine manufacturers like GE and Siemens to raise prices.

The third chart, "Low levels of electrification in global industry and transport," displays final energy consumption in quadrillion BTUs across sectors. It shows that the massive industrial sector (consuming about 225 quads) and the transport sector (consuming nearly 90 quads) remain overwhelmingly dependent on direct fossil fuels, with electrification representing only a small sliver of their energy mix. Conversely, residential and commercial buildings consume far less overall energy but exhibit much higher relative shares of electrification.

The final chart, "US electricity uses," breaks down electricity consumption by sector in quadrillion BTUs. It shows that electricity in residential and commercial sectors is predominantly consumed by space cooling, lighting, ventilation, refrigeration, and electronic equipment, while industrial electricity is largely used for space heating, water heating, motors, and process heat. Transport electricity use is noted as too small to plot, registering at just 0.04 quads.

This page explores the significant challenges Europe faces in rapidly pivoting its energy strategy away from Russian imports, while contextualizing these difficulties within global investment trends and supply chain realities. The author argues that while replacing Russian crude oil imports of 2.6 million barrels per day is theoretically achievable through increased imports from the United States, Canada, Norway, the United Kingdom, and Denmark, replacing natural gas imports is far more complex. Europe's 174 billion cubic meters of annual Russian gas imports cannot easily be substituted due to limited liquefied natural gas regasification capacity and inadequate pipeline connectivity across the continent. While the author notes that Europe will try to diversify in the short term, any lasting solution will require long-term structural adjustments, as alternative paths like rapid wind and solar adoption, residential heating electrification, and nuclear power face severe bottlenecks, high costs, or political resistance. 

This regional struggle is part of a broader global dilemma. A chart titled "Fossil fuel capex falling despite no change in consumption" illustrates a widening divergence between global primary fossil fuel use and capital spending by S&P Global 1200 Energy companies from 2005 to 2021. While fossil fuel consumption has steadily risen to nearly 500 exajoules, capital spending has collapsed from its peak of over 400 billion dollars in 2013 to less than 150 billion dollars by 2021. This capital starvation is further highlighted in a chart showing the collapse in global investment in energy-intensive industries for 2022 compared to their ten-year averages. While sectors like media and the internet saw positive investment growth, capital spending for oil and gas producers plummeted by nearly 50 percent, with steel, mining, marine shipping, and oil refining all experiencing declines of 20 to 30 percent.

These investment shortfalls leave countries with difficult choices: increase domestic fossil fuel production, accept reliance on politically sensitive exporters, or confront the immense hurdles of the renewable transition. A table of the largest proven oil and natural gas reserves based on 2020 data highlights the geopolitical risks of importing energy, showing that the largest natural gas reserves are concentrated in Russia with 1,320 trillion cubic feet and Iran with 1,134 trillion cubic feet, while the largest oil reserves reside in Venezuela at 304 billion barrels and Saudi Arabia at 298 billion barrels.

If countries choose to accelerate the renewable transition, the author emphasizes that simply increasing the cost of capital for fossil fuel companies or pursuing institutional divestment will not suffice. Policymakers must address local project delays, transmission constraints, and carbon pricing. Furthermore, a table on renewable production global market share reveals that any rapid shift to green energy heavily benefits China, which dominates the clean energy supply chain. As of recent years, China controls 63 percent of solar photovoltaic module shipments, 46 percent of the wind capacity order book, 79 percent of lithium-ion battery manufacturing capacity, 79 percent of electric vehicle mineral processing, and 85 percent of electric vehicle cathode and anode production, leaving the United States and Europe with single-digit market shares in most of these categories. A final footnote notes that while a revival of the United States Build Back Better bill could marginally assist the transition through building efficiency and electric vehicle tax credits, its proposed funding for critical long-term technologies like hydrogen, carbon capture, and transmission infrastructure remains relatively small.

This page examines the stark energy divide between the developed and developing worlds, focusing on how carbon-intensive manufacturing has shifted to emerging markets, driving up their energy consumption and maintaining a heavy reliance on coal. The author argues that because global economic growth outpaces efficiency gains, deep decarbonization will require a physical replacement of fossil fuels rather than just reducing per-capita consumption.

The first chart, titled "A shift in energy intensive manufacturing to the emerging world, % of global production," compares the share of production held by developed versus emerging economies across several key industrial sectors. Looking at manufacturing (1995 vs. 2020), ammonia (1998 vs. 2021), steel (1998 vs. 2020), cement (1998 vs. 2021), and plastics (2005 vs. 2020), a massive migration of industrial output is visible. For instance, the developed world's share of steel production shrank from roughly 60% in 1998 to just 20% in 2020, while its share of cement production plummeted from over 30% to less than 10% in 2021. Emerging economies now dominate all five of these energy-intensive sectors.

The second chart, titled "China is the only EM country projected to slow primary energy consumption growth over the next three decades," compares historical change in primary energy from 2010 to 2020 against projected changes from 2020 to 2050 in exajoules. Developed regions like the European Union, Japan, and the United States are projected to experience declines in primary energy consumption of around 5 to 10 exajoules. In contrast, emerging regions are projected to grow significantly, led by India with a projected increase of over 30 exajoules, followed by Africa, Southeast Asia (excluding China and India), and the Middle East, which are all projected to grow by 20 to 25 exajoules. China is the notable exception among emerging markets; after expanding by over 30 exajoules between 2010 and 2020, its projected growth slows to roughly 15 exajoules through 2050.

The third chart, "Wind, solar, hydro and other renewables share of primary energy," tracks these resources as a percentage of primary energy from 1965 to 2025, using solid lines for overall renewables and dotted lines for wind and solar specifically. It compares the OECD, China, and Non-OECD nations excluding China. While the OECD and China have both pushed their total renewable share to nearly 14% and their wind and solar shares to around 6%, Non-OECD nations excluding China lag far behind, with total renewables flatlining under 10% and wind and solar comprising only about 2% of primary energy.

The fourth chart, "Coal share of primary energy consumption," highlights the persistent reliance on coal from 1990 to 2020 across selected countries. Coal remains the dominant energy source in South Africa (at over 70%), China (at nearly 60%), and India (at around 55%). Coal’s share has risen dramatically in Vietnam to nearly 50% and in Indonesia to roughly 40%. While the United States and Germany have steadily reduced their coal share to around 10% and 15% respectively, Japan has maintained a flat coal share of roughly 25% over the past three decades.

The final chart, "Global CO2 intensity declining, CO2 emissions rising," illustrates why efficiency gains are insufficient on their own. Plotting data from 1965 to 2020, the chart shows a steady decline in global CO2 intensity (measured on the left axis in tonnes of CO2 per thousand dollars of 2020 GDP) from over 0.50 down to approximately 0.23. Despite this improved efficiency, absolute global CO2 emissions (measured on the right axis in billion tonnes) have more than tripled, rising from approximately 11 billion tonnes in 1965 to over 33 billion tonnes in 2020. This divergence underscores the author’s point that decarbonization must rely on fuel substitution.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market energy paper argues that Europe made a critical strategic error by rapidly winding down its domestic fossil fuel production while its consumption remained high, leaving the continent highly vulnerable to Russian energy leverage. The author lists several severe consequences of this dependence, including an impending recession, reduced competitiveness of energy-intensive exports, and potential mandatory industrial curtailments in sectors like steel, fertilizer, and cement. These energy shortages also drive up food prices and foster anti-establishment political tensions. To emphasize the historical context, the text notes that Mitt Romney warned of Russian geopolitical threats during the 2012 U.S. presidential election, though his warnings were dismissed at the time.

The first chart, titled Europe curtails oil and gas production while keeping imports unchanged, tracks European energy trends in thousand barrels per day of oil equivalent from 1980 to 2020. It demonstrates that while domestic European oil and gas production fell steadily after 2000, imports from Russia remained stubbornly flat and overall foreign imports stayed high. 

An adjacent chart, Energy dependence and independence, displays the net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal in million tonnes of oil equivalent from 1980 to 2020. It shows Europe as a major net importer, plateauing near 800 to 900 million tonnes. China has also become a massive net importer, rising toward 500 million tonnes. Conversely, Russia has grown its position as a dominant net exporter, reaching around negative 700 million tonnes, while the United States successfully transitioned from a net importer to a net exporter by 2020.

The middle section of the page highlights the widening economic divergence between the United States and Europe through two price charts. The US-Europe electricity gap plots wholesale electricity prices in US dollars per megawatt-hour on a seven-day average from 2015 to 2023. While U.S. prices remained stable near 50 dollars, prices in Germany, Spain, and France spiked to 235 dollars, and the United Kingdom climbed to 209 dollars. Similarly, the US-Europe natural gas gap chart shows wholesale natural gas prices in US dollars per MMBTU from 2019 to 2022. The U.S. Henry Hub price remained low at 8 dollars, whereas the United Kingdom rose to 21 dollars, and continental Europe spiked to 32 dollars.

The bottom of the page analyzes gas infrastructure and supply dynamics. A pie chart titled Russia dominates European gas import capacity details the annual gas import capacity for the EU 27 in terawatt-hours. Russian pipeline imports dominate at 2,800 TWh, far exceeding Norway at 1,100 TWh, North Africa at 800 TWh, and Azerbaijan at 130 TWh. Liquefied natural gas import capacity is highly fragmented across several countries, led by Spain at 700 TWh, France at 440 TWh, Italy at 200 TWh, and Belgium at 170 TWh, down to Croatia at 30 TWh. 

Lastly, a stacked area chart, Russian natural gas exports to Europe, tracks flows in million cubic meters per day from January 2019 to early 2022. This visualization shows a clear decline in total Russian exports over time, driven by reductions in flows via Yamal through Poland and pipelines transiting through Ukraine, while Nord Stream 1 and LNG volumes fluctuated but remained more resilient prior to mid-2022.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication presents introductory commentary on the "electrification of everything," questioning the feasibility of electrifying major parts of a modern economy given historical trends. The author highlights that over the last 20 years, electricity's share of primary energy use has risen by a mere 2% to 3% in most countries. While a few small, resource-rich nations have reached 25% to 30% electrification, larger nations still rely on electricity for less than 20% of their energy use, suggesting that many transition blueprints currently lack a proven proof of concept.

A bar chart titled "The slow advance of electrification, 2000 to 2020" illustrates this slow progress by plotting the electricity share of primary energy consumption for twenty nations. Each country’s bar shows the share in 2000 in blue, with a gold segment representing the increase by 2020. Iceland leads the list, rising to nearly 33% by 2020, followed closely by Norway at roughly 28% and Sweden at around 27%. In contrast, major economies exhibit limited progress: the United States and Germany both hover around 17% in 2020, showing almost no growth since 2000. China is a notable exception, experiencing more rapid growth as its electricity share rose from roughly 10% to nearly 20% over the same period.

The author shifts focus to the challenges of maintaining and expanding the U.S. electricity grid, which consists of 7,700 power plants, 3,300 utilities, and 2.7 million miles of power lines. To demonstrate existing grid vulnerabilities, a stacked bar chart tracks "US reported electric disturbances by season" from 2002 to 2021. The chart reveals a stark upward trend in grid disruptions. Annual disturbances, which routinely totaled under 100 in the early 2000s, surged to over 350 disturbances in both 2020 and 2021. These disruptions are distributed across all seasons, with significant occurrences in winter, spring, summer, and autumn in the most recent years. 

To further evaluate these grid issues, a scatter plot displays the System Average Interruption Duration Index, measuring 2020 annual average outage minutes per customer against electricity sales per utility in terawatt-hours. The data indicates that smaller utilities, specifically those with under 10 terawatt-hours in sales, experience the most severe disruptions, with several utilities reporting average customer outages between 4,000 and 8,000 minutes. Larger utilities generally cluster below 1,000 average outage minutes, though one prominent outlier with roughly 53 terawatt-hours of sales suffered over 5,000 average outage minutes per customer. Ultimately, the author poses an open warning to policymakers, noting that they must preserve the stability of this massive, increasingly strained grid machine while attempting to dramatically expand its load.

This page presents executive summary exhibits one through three, analyzing energy use by sector and fuel type across three key global areas: the United States, OECD Europe, and China, accompanied by a comprehensive list of energy acronyms. Each regional section features a column chart showing final energy consumption in quadrillion BTUs (Quads) across the industrial, transport, residential, and commercial sectors, broken down by oil, coal, natural gas, renewable energy, and nuclear power, with dotted segments indicating electricity consumed. Each chart is paired with a key statistics table highlighting critical energy metrics.

For the United States, final energy consumption is highest in the industrial and transport sectors, both approaching twenty-five Quads. Key stats reveal that primary energy consumption is 93.3 Quads, with final consumption at 70.1 Quads. Electricity makes up 18% of total energy consumed, dominated by the residential sector at 44%, while transport is 0%. Fossil fuels comprise 79% of primary energy, and passenger cars represent 60% of transport energy. Renewable energy accounts for 20% of electricity generation and 13% of primary energy, while low-carbon options constitute 43% of electricity generation and 21% of primary energy. Coal represents 10% of primary energy, with a low coal-to-natural gas ratio of 0.3, and hydropower makes up 37% of renewable electricity.

OECD Europe demonstrates a relatively lower primary energy consumption of 76.8 Quads and final consumption of 56.7 Quads. Industrial use is the largest sector at over twenty Quads, followed by transport at around fifteen Quads. Electricity constitutes 19% of energy consumed, with 30% in residential and 2% in transport. Fossil fuels are lower than in the US, representing 69% of primary energy. Renewables have a stronger footprint, accounting for 44% of electricity generation and 22% of primary energy, while low-carbon sources make up 69% of electricity generation and 31% of primary energy. Coal remains at 10% of primary energy with a coal-to-gas ratio of 0.4, and hydropower holds a 43% share of renewable electricity.

China shows vastly larger energy consumption dynamics, with primary energy consumption at 160.2 Quads and final consumption at 109.6 Quads. China's industrial sector is exceptionally dominant, consuming more than seventy Quads, heavily reliant on coal and electricity. Electricity makes up 20% of overall energy consumed, with 21% in industrial, 4% in transport, and 32% in residential. Fossil fuels comprise 84% of primary energy, with industrial fossil fuels representing 59% of primary energy. Passenger cars account for only 25% of transport energy. Renewable energy makes up 25% of electricity generation and 14% of primary energy, while low-carbon sources represent 30% of electricity generation and 16% of primary energy. Coal represents a massive 59% of primary energy, shown by a very high coal-to-natural gas ratio of 7.9. Hydropower accounts for 57% of China's renewable electricity.

At the bottom of the page, a reference list of energy acronyms defines key units and organizations, including billion cubic meters (Bcm), barrels per day (Bpd), British thermal unit (BTU), carbon capture and storage (CCS), US Energy Information Agency (EIA), exajoule (EJ), enhanced oil recovery (EOR), Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), greenhouse gases (GHG), gigawatt (GW), hydrogen (H2), International Energy Agency (IEA), independent system operator (ISO), kilowatt hour (kWh), liquefied natural gas (LNG), cubic meter (m3), megajoule (MJ), million metric tons (MMT), metric ton (MT), million tonnes of oil equivalent (Mtoe), megawatt hour (MWh), power purchase agreement (PPA), quadrillion BTUs (Quad), and terawatt hour (TWh).

This page of the J.P. Morgan annual energy paper, authored by Michael Cembalest, argues that the United States transmission grid is a slowly changing quagmire that is failing to expand quickly enough to support electrification and Net Zero goals. Historically, the US transmission infrastructure has grown at just two percent per year since the late 1970s, but more recently, that expansion has slowed even further to just one percent. This slow growth is contrasted against the massive grid expansion required under various decarbonization pathways, such as the Princeton Net Zero requirement.

The first chart, titled "US transmission grid growing at just 2% per year since 1978," displays grid capacity in thousands of gigawatt-miles from 1978 to 2048. Based on data from the Department of Energy and UT Austin, the chart shows that a standard two-percent annual growth trajectory will fall drastically short of the Princeton Net Zero requirement for 2050, which targets well over one thousand gigawatt-miles. 

The second chart, "Most recent growth has been just 1% per year," tracks the miles of transmission lines added annually by region from 2013 to 2020. The stacked bar chart includes regions such as CAISO, ERCOT, MISO, New England, New York, PJM, SPP, and Non-RTO/ISO areas. The visual highlights a clear downward trend in grid expansion, with total annual transmission line additions dropping from approximately 2,500 miles in 2013 to around 1,000 miles in 2020. 

The text attributes these difficulties to local opposition, NIMBYism, and state-level regulatory hurdles that block major transmission initiatives. Several specific projects and political actions are detailed. For example, the Northern Pass project and the New England Clean Energy Connect—both designed to bring Canadian hydropower to Massachusetts—were blocked by New Hampshire and Maine, respectively. In Maine, fifty-nine percent of voters approved a referendum blocking the lines, a campaign reportedly funded by NextEra and other local utilities, which halted a project where Avangrid, a subsidiary of Iberdrola, had already spent 350 million dollars. 

Similar roadblocks exist across the Midwest and West. Iowa passed a law preventing the use of state eminent domain for transmission lines, shelving projects intended to export its high wind capacity to Illinois and Wisconsin. Arkansas blocked a wind transmission project from Oklahoma to the Southeastern United States, Missouri blocked a Kansas-to-Indiana project, and Colorado blocked a line carrying Wyoming wind power to the Southwest. Furthermore, California's state environmental protection laws are often leveraged to delay solar farms and mass transit, whereas Florida took the opposite legislative stance by preventing local entities from blocking solar and renewable natural gas projects. Finally, a footnote notes that thirty-nine gigawatts of coal, gas, and nuclear capacity have retired since 2013, with another twenty-seven gigawatts scheduled for retirement by 2028.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Annual Energy Paper analyzes the severe bottlenecking and gridlock occurring in US electricity transmission interconnection queues, which presents a major obstacle to the deployment of clean energy. The author uses the Midcontinent Independent System Operator region as a primary case study, pointing out that while the volume of proposed generation projects entering the queue has surged, less than half are ultimately constructed, with the rest being withdrawn. Nationally, from 2010 to 2020, only 24 percent of projects in interconnection queues across major grid regions—including CAISO, ISO-NE, MISO, NYISO, and PJM combined—reached commercial operation. Completion rates were particularly low for wind at 19 percent and solar at 16 percent, while queue wait times nearly doubled from an average of 2.0 years in the 2000–2010 period to 3.7 years in the 2011–2021 period. 

Four charts illustrate these backlog trends. The first chart, titled "The clogged MISO interconnection queue," plots the requested gigawatts in the region's queue from 2000 to 2020, broken down by fuel type. It illustrates a transition from gas and wind dominance in the early 2000s to a massive surge in proposed capacity around 2019 and 2020, when solar and hybrid projects pushed the total queue volume to over 50 gigawatts. 

The second chart, "Less than 50% of MISO queue projects are completed," correlates this influx with falling completion rates. It tracks MISO queue requests in gigawatts using blue bars against the percentage of completed interconnection agreements shown in a red line. As the queue requests climbed in the late 2010s, completion rates plummeted from historical averages of 40 to 60 percent to nearly zero percent for the most recent project cohorts.

The third chart, "Renewable capacity in interconnection queues dwarfs existing capacity" as of December 2021, compares capacity currently waiting in US queues to existing operating capacity across solar, storage, wind, and natural gas. For solar, the queue capacity exceeds 600 gigawatts compared to less than 100 gigawatts of existing capacity. For energy storage, queue capacity is over 400 gigawatts while existing capacity is negligible. Wind has over 250 gigawatts in the queue versus roughly 150 gigawatts currently active. In contrast, natural gas has massive existing capacity of nearly 500 gigawatts but less than 100 gigawatts of new capacity in the queue. 

The final chart, titled "US interconnection queue by fuel type," details the national expansion of the queue from 2014 to 2021. Total requested capacity grew from roughly 400 gigawatts in 2014 to over 1,400 gigawatts in 2021. This rapid growth has been driven almost entirely by solar and battery storage proposals, while wind remains stable and natural gas is flat. The page references data from MISO, the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the Energy Information Administration, J.P. Morgan Asset Management, and a report by Scott Madden Management Consultants.

Michael Cembalest explores the real-world friction facing transition plans to renewable energy, emphasizing how local objections and interconnection delays lead to the underutilization of wind and solar resources across several US states. To demonstrate this underutilization, the author presents two scatter plots comparing resource potential, measured by capacity factors on projects built from 2015 to 2019, against actual generation per capita in 2020. 

The first scatter plot, mapping wind resource potential, shows wind capacity factor on the horizontal axis from 38 percent to 48 percent against wind generation in MWh per capita on the vertical axis from 0 to 18. North Dakota leads the nation with nearly 17 MWh per capita, but states like Illinois, Vermont, Colorado, Montana, Minnesota, and Wisconsin exhibit clear underperformance, generating close to zero to 3 MWh per capita despite having high wind capacity factors exceeding 38 percent. The second scatter plot maps solar resource potential, with capacity factors on the horizontal axis from 26 percent to 32 percent and solar generation in MWh per capita on the vertical axis from 0.0 to 1.0. While Nevada stands out with around 0.85 MWh per capita, states like Colorado, Texas, Idaho, and Washington generate nearly zero solar MWh per capita despite boasting capacity factors over 26 percent.

Cembalest then pivots to regional grid issues in New England and New York. Following decisions by Maine and New Hampshire to block low-cost Canadian hydropower, Massachusetts has grown increasingly reliant on electricity imports. The author warns of potential sticker shock for consumers as the state pivots to offshore wind, where procurement prices for projects expected by 2025 range from 70 dollars to 100 dollars per MWh, compared to average wholesale prices of 50 dollars per MWh in 2021. Offshore wind is planned to cover nearly 50 percent of Massachusetts' electricity consumption, with 10 GW in advanced permitting across the Eastern Seaboard. Meanwhile, in New York, the shutdown of the Indian Point Nuclear Plant forced the state to close its energy gap with fossil-fuel-powered imports. Although construction is starting on a 339-mile high-voltage transmission line to bring in Canadian hydropower, this project has taken 17 years to permit and is not expected to be completed until 2025. 

These trends are illustrated by two historical line charts showing electricity generation by source in terawatt hours from 1990 to 2020. The Massachusetts chart shows that imports surged from under 5 terawatt hours in 1990 to nearly 30 terawatt hours in 2021, becoming the state's primary source of power as coal and nuclear fell to zero, while natural gas peaked around 25 terawatt hours in 2012 before sliding to roughly 15 terawatt hours. In the New York chart, natural gas generation rose steadily to reach nearly 50 terawatt hours by 2021, hydro remained steady around 30 terawatt hours, and nuclear plummeted from over 40 terawatt hours to around 30 terawatt hours following the Indian Point shutdown, driving a corresponding rise in imports to over 20 terawatt hours. Cembalest concludes that the disconnect between transmission grid assumptions in Net Zero plans and ground-level reality is as wide as the gap between expectations and reality in carbon sequestration.

This page of J.P. Morgan's annual energy paper explores the slow rate of electric vehicle transition in the United States, raising critical questions about how to deal with gasoline super-users amid rising battery and metal costs. The author argues that while global EV sales experienced a meaningful jump to nearly 9% of total sales in 2021, EVs still make up a tiny 1.5% of the global vehicle fleet on the road. The primary barrier to rapid fleet conversion is the longevity of modern cars, which limits turnover unless governments offer aggressive incentives and subsidies. 

A pair of top charts illustrates these dynamics. The first, "Global electric vehicle market share," highlights the stark divergence between the rapidly growing EV share of annual global vehicle sales—climbing from near zero in 2010 to almost 9% in 2021—and the nearly flat line of EV share in the existing global fleet, which barely register at 1.5%. The second chart, "Cars last a lot longer than they used to," shows that the average age of US light vehicles in operation has steadily climbed from roughly six years in the early 1970s to nearly twelve years by 2020, confirming that old vehicles remain on the road longer than ever.

The bottom half of the page demonstrates the unique uphill battle the US faces compared to international peers. A chart tracking "Electric vehicle market shares in 2021" reveals that while Norway dominates with an EV share of annual vehicle sales exceeding 70%, and Sweden and the Netherlands sit at roughly 45% and 30% respectively, the US trails far behind at just 4.5%. This puts the US on par with Spain and only slightly ahead of developing economies like Indonesia and Brazil. 

This sluggish adoption is contextualized by a chart detailing the top twenty vehicles sold in the US in 2021, which is heavily dominated by large, low-mpg SUVs and light trucks. The top three best-selling vehicles are the Ford F-Series (selling over 700,000 units at 24 mpg), the Ram Pickup (at 21 mpg), and the Chevrolet Silverado (at 20 mpg). Only one pure electric vehicle, the Tesla Model Y, makes the top twenty, selling roughly 160,000 units. The author concludes that the US faces structural hurdles to EV transition, including high vehicle ownership per capita, long driving distances, low public transit usage, cheap gasoline, and a strong cultural preference for heavy trucks. A personal footnote from Cembalest underscores the economic challenge, noting that his own 2022 Jeep Wrangler hybrid has a thirteen-year payback period due to his low annual mileage of 2,000 miles.

This page from the publication focuses on the challenge of US gasoline "super-users" and the mismatch between where high gasoline consumption occurs and where electric vehicles are being adopted. The author highlights that the top 10% of gasoline consumers in the United States account for nearly one-third, or 32%, of total gasoline consumption, which is more than the bottom 60% of drivers combined. 

An accompanying bar chart titled "The US gasoline super-users" plots gasoline consumption in billions of gallons across deciles of the driver population, from the tenth decile representing the lowest consumption to the first decile representing the highest consumption. The chart shows a steep upward curve, where the bottom 60% of drivers in deciles five through ten collectively burn less gasoline than the top 10% of drivers in the first decile, who consume over 40 billion gallons of fuel. 

The text defines these super-users as individuals who drive three times more miles than the average driver, are more likely to drive pickups and SUVs, and predominantly live in rural areas. While their income and education levels are comparable to the general population, their high fuel usage means they spend between 8% and 13% of their income on gasoline, which is more than twice the proportion spent by the average driver. 

To illustrate the geographical mismatch of this consumption, the page presents two comparative maps of the United States sourced from Coltura in July 2021. The map on the left, "Superusers' share of state gasoline consumption," shows that super-users make up the largest share of gasoline consumption, ranging from 25% up to 35%, across the Great Plains, the South, and the Rocky Mountain states, highlighted in dark red. Conversely, the map on the right, "EV registrations by state," depicts EV registration shares from 0.2% to 1.4%, with the highest concentrations, shown in dark green, heavily clustered on the West Coast, particularly California, and parts of the Northeast. The author points out that the EV registration map is nearly the inverse of the super-user map, emphasizing the core decarbonization challenge: electric vehicles are being purchased least in the areas where the highest-volume gasoline consumers actually live.

This page examines the impact of soaring metals prices on electric vehicle (EV) battery costs, analyzing a hypothetical 60 kWh battery across three chemistry types: Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC), Lithium Nickel Cobalt Aluminum (NCA), and Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP). The author argues that rising prices for cobalt, nickel, and copper have drastically increased battery costs, risking "sticker shock" for EV buyers. LFP batteries, which are cheaper but less energy-dense, are mostly manufactured in China and utilized by Tesla, BYD, Hongguang, and Rivian. They saw a modest cost increase of about $500 since January 2020. Conversely, NMC and NCA batteries, largely produced by LG Chem and Samsung and favored by legacy automakers like Audi, BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, and Ford, saw a steep $1,500 cost increase due to nickel and cobalt price spikes. An additional $500 cost increase is estimated for non-battery copper and aluminum. While EV buyers can offset this via lower fuel costs—saving an estimated $1,250 per year based on $4 gasoline and 14 cents per kWh electricity—supply chain pressures remain severe. The author quotes Rivian’s CEO, who warns that 90% to 95% of the battery supply chain needed in ten years does not yet exist, casting doubt on aggressive EV market share forecasts.

The first chart, a line graph showing the estimated metals cost per EV battery type from January 2020 to May 2022 in US dollars per 60 kWh battery, illustrates the divergent trajectories of the chemistries. While NMC and NCA battery costs track closely together—rising from roughly $1,000 in early 2020 to peak near $3,000 in early 2022—the cost of LFP batteries rises much more gradually, starting below $1,000 and ending near $1,000. 

A stacked bar chart breaks down these battery costs using May 2022 metals prices. NMC and NCA batteries both total around $2,500, heavily dominated by the costs of nickel (the largest segment in blue), lithium carbonate (purple), and cobalt (red), with smaller shares for copper, aluminum, manganese, steel, and iron. LFP batteries, totaling just under $1,000, are primarily driven by lithium carbonate and copper, completely avoiding the expensive nickel and cobalt inputs. 

The third chart is a bar graph indexing EV metals prices as of May 2022 against a December 2019 baseline of 100. It shows that lithium carbonate prices have surged nearly sixfold to an index value around 600. Other essential metals have also risen by 20% to over 150% from the baseline, with cobalt near 250, nickel near 220, aluminum near 170, copper near 150, manganese near 130, and iron and steel both near 120.

Finally, a table details the specific battery chemistries deployed by different automotive manufacturers. Audi, BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, and Porsche all utilize NMC batteries for their passenger EVs. Ford uses NMC for its F-150 EV, Volkswagen plans NMC for its high-end passenger EVs, and Chinese OEMs use NMC for Class 8 trucks. Tesla relies on NCA for its long-range passenger EVs, while utilizing LFP for its short-range models. LFP batteries are also utilized by BYD (China), Hongguang, Volkswagen (for entry-level passenger EVs), and Rivian (for electric trucks, SUVs, and delivery vans).

This page from Michael Cembalest's Annual Energy Paper analyzes the viability and economic incentives of transitioning residential heating to electric heat pumps, focusing on the logistical challenges of grid peak loads and the relative costs of heating fuels. The author questions whether it is economically viable for the natural gas industry to maintain residential pipeline infrastructure purely for backup purposes on extreme cold days to prevent grid surges. If this is not viable, alternative solutions like residential fuel cells would likely introduce significantly higher structural and all-in costs.

An initial table compares non-electric backup power scenarios on cold days to show how they affect grid buildout needs. Under the current scenario, space heating shares are split among resistance heating at twenty percent, heat pumps at six percent, and fossil fuels at sixty-nine percent, resulting in five hundred eighty-nine million metric tons of CO2 emissions. If all residences transitioned to heat pumps without backup thermal power, sixty-three percent of census tracts would experience a peak load increase, with the average peak load in those affected tracts rising by one hundred nine percent. Conversely, if all residences transitioned to heat pumps but kept backup thermal power in place, only three percent of the space heating share would rely on fossil fuels, reducing total residential emissions to two hundred eighty-one million metric tons of CO2 while completely eliminating peak load increases across all census tracts.

A second table details the economic incentives for homeowners to switch to heat pumps depending on their current fuel source. Although seventy-nine percent of propane users and forty percent of fuel oil users have an economic incentive to switch, they represent only six percent and eight percent of the housing stock, respectively. Meanwhile, natural gas users make up the largest segment of the housing stock at fifty-six percent, yet only eight percent of these households have an economic incentive to switch. 

This low incentive is explained by an accompanying line chart displaying residential fuel prices in US dollars per million BTU from the year 2000 through 2020. Throughout this twenty-year period, natural gas prices remained consistently low and stable, generally hovering between ten and fifteen dollars per million BTU. In contrast, heating oil and propane prices fluctuated widely and were significantly more expensive, frequently climbing above twenty-five dollars and occasionally spiking near thirty-five to forty dollars per million BTU. Footnotes cite studies from Columbia University, the University of Texas at Austin, and the University of Michigan, noting that heat pump installation costs typically range from three thousand three hundred to four thousand eight hundred dollars, with additional expenses for capacity and ductwork.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" explores the transition to electric vehicles, highlighting the critical difference between the share of new vehicle sales that are electric and the share of the actual vehicle fleet on the road that is electric. Cembalest explains that standard EV analyses group battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids together because their primary propulsion is electric, while excluding conventional hybrids since they rely primarily on internal combustion engines. He notes that while he finds BloombergNEF forecasts to be generally overly optimistic, they are useful for demonstrating the long lag time between growth in new sales and growth in the overall fleet.

The first chart displays electric vehicle battery capacity in kilowatt hours, sorted in descending order across dozens of specific vehicle models, sourced from Car and Driver and manufacturers as of February 2021. It categorizes vehicles into four types: battery electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids, hybrids, and mild hybrids. Battery electric vehicles, marked with blue dots, lead the capacity rankings, with the Tesla Model X and Tesla Model S reaching up to 100 kilowatt hours, followed by models like the Audi e-tron, Porsche Taycan, Jaguar I-PACE, Polestar 2, Chevrolet Bolt, and Nissan LEAF, ending with the Mini Cooper Electric at roughly 33 kilowatt hours. Plug-in hybrids, marked in gold, cluster between 10 and 30 kilowatt hours, including models like the Chevy Volt, Chrysler Pacifica, BMW i8, and Toyota Prius Prime. Standard hybrids, in red, and mild hybrids, in dark blue, possess negligible battery capacities under 5 kilowatt hours, including models like the Toyota Camry Hybrid and the Dodge Ram 1500 eTorque.

The remaining four charts depict global BloombergNEF forecasts through 2040, illustrating how new vehicle EV sales translate into actual fleet penetration across four distinct vehicle categories: passenger, light-duty, medium-duty, and heavy-duty vehicles. For passenger vehicles, the forecast shows that while the EV share of new vehicle sales is projected to rise steadily to over 70% by 2040, the EV share of vehicles on the road will reach only about 45%. In light-duty vehicles (under 3.5 tons), new vehicle EV sales are projected to reach nearly 60% by 2040, while the share of light-duty EVs on the road lags behind at approximately 38%. For medium-duty vehicles (3.5 to 15 tons), the EV share of new sales is forecasted to rise to about 33% by 2040, compared to a fleet share of only 13%. Similarly, in heavy-duty vehicles (over 15 tons), the EV share of new sales is expected to climb to about 27% by 2040, while the actual heavy-duty EV fleet on the road rises to only about 14%. Together, these charts emphasize that because of slow fleet turnover, even rapid adoption of electric vehicles in new sales requires decades to replace the existing fossil-fuel-powered global fleet.

This J.P. Morgan research page discusses the reality versus the hype surrounding the emerging hydrogen economy. The author argues that while hydrogen is highly anticipated—and frequently cited as a key solution for Europe to reduce its dependency on Russian energy—its actual use cases are far narrower than advertised and its timeline is very long. Currently, the hydrogen economy is in its infancy and remains almost entirely reliant on fossil fuels. Almost no hydrogen is utilized for power, transport, home heating, shipping, rail, or aviation. 

To illustrate this reality, the page features four charts. The first chart, showing the performance of hydrogen-linked equities, tracks several ETFs and indices, including the Solactive Hydrogen Economy Index, Direxion, VanEck, Global X, and Defiance Next Gen H2 ETFs, from January 2019 to early 2022. It demonstrates that these equities quadrupled from 2019 to 2021 before experiencing a sharp 35 percent to 40 percent decline from their peak levels. 

The second chart, depicting hydrogen demand by sector, is a stacked bar chart showing annual demand in million metric tons from 2000 to 2020. Over this period, total demand rose from approximately 60 to 90 million metric tons, driven almost entirely by refining for desulfurization and chemical production for ammonia fertilizer, with only a negligible fraction used for iron and steel production. 

The third chart is a pie chart showing the energy sources used to create hydrogen. Out of the 90 million metric tons produced, it reveals that practically all hydrogen is produced from fossil fuels without carbon capture. Natural gas without carbon capture and storage accounts for 59 percent, followed by by-products from reforming naphtha into gasoline at 21 percent, coal at 19 percent, oil at 0.6 percent, and fossil fuels with carbon capture at a mere 0.7 percent. This indicates that less than 1 percent is green hydrogen created via electrolysis using renewable energy. 

Finally, the fourth chart shows the share of global primary energy used to create hydrogen from 1975 to 2020. It illustrates that hydrogen is an energy carrier rather than a native source, with the share of global primary energy converted into hydrogen rising from just over 1.0 percent in 1975 to about 2.0 percent in 2020, remaining relatively flat over the last decade. Footnotes reference major reports on hydrogen by the International Energy Agency, Goldman Sachs, Barclays, J.P. Morgan, and the International Renewable Energy Agency.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan Annual Energy Paper focuses on the viability and environmental impact of blue hydrogen and carbon capture and storage. Presented as a dialogue between Cembalest and an interlocutor, the text argues that blue hydrogen is not as environmentally friendly as often proposed. Citing research by Robert Howarth at Cornell University, Cembalest explains that the greenhouse gas impact of blue hydrogen is over twenty percent higher than simply burning natural gas or coal directly. This high footprint is attributed to the additional energy required for carbon capture and storage, capture rates that remain well below one hundred percent, and the high energy intensity of grey hydrogen production. 

Cembalest also addresses arguments regarding commercial demand for captured carbon dioxide, specifically for enhanced oil recovery. He highlights that carbon dioxide is used in only two point five percent of United States crude oil production, with global enhanced oil recovery consumption in 2019 representing just zero point two percent of global emissions at seventy-two million metric tons. He casts skepticism on optimistic McKinsey forecasts for synthetic and algae-based fuel demands by 2030, calling them unrealistic. Furthermore, Cembalest doubts the feasibility of repurposing large portions of the United States natural gas pipeline network for carbon transport in his lifetime.

The first chart on the page, titled Global carbon capture and storage capacity as a percentage of global CO2 emissions, spans from 2010 to 2021 using data from the Global CCS Institute. It reveals that global carbon capture capacity represents a minuscule fraction of global emissions, staying consistently below zero point five percent over the entire decade. The chart breaks capacity down into operational, construction, advanced development, and early development stages. Actual operational capacity remains flat and accounts for roughly zero point one percent of global emissions, while the vast majority of capacity exists only in early or advanced development stages. 

The second chart, titled Blue hydrogen GHG higher than direct natural gas combustion, measures emissions in grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule of energy, based on Howarth's 2021 study. The stacked bar chart separates emissions into methane and carbon dioxide for grey hydrogen, blue hydrogen, natural gas, coal, and diesel oil. It shows that blue hydrogen generates roughly one hundred thirty-five grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule, which is significantly higher than burning natural gas directly at about one hundred ten grams or coal at about one hundred ten grams. This is largely due to high methane emissions associated with blue hydrogen production, which offset the reduction in carbon dioxide emissions achieved through carbon capture. Grey hydrogen is shown to have the highest total footprint on the chart at over one hundred fifty grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule.

This page from J.P. Morgan's energy paper evaluates the viability of hydrogen fuel cells in ground transportation, specifically focusing on long-haul trucking versus electric battery vehicles. While hydrogen is deemed uncompelling for passenger vehicles due to tank space constraints and high conversion losses, the author notes that it could be viable for long-haul heavy-duty trucking. This is because compressed hydrogen allows for longer range, faster refueling, and faces fewer space constraints than passenger vehicles. The text compares the pending Freightliner eCascadia class 8 electric truck, which weighs 82,000 pounds with a 250-mile range, against Hyzon’s pending class 8 hydrogen fuel cell truck, which has the same weight but achieves a longer range of 375 to 500 miles on 50 to 70 kilograms of hydrogen. Despite this potential, the author advises caution, noting that hydrogen truck companies are in their infancy and have unproven track records, citing the regulatory and staging scandal involving Nikola Motors as a warning. Furthermore, a medium-term forecast from Cummins Engine projects just a 2.5 percent market share for hydrogen in long-haul heavy-duty trucking by 2030. 

A horizontal stacked bar chart illustrates the breakdown of global carbon dioxide emissions from transport based on 2020 data from Our World in Data. Road passenger transport (cars, motorcycles, buses, and taxis) represents the largest share at 45 percent, followed by road freight (including trucks and lorries) at 29 percent, aviation at 12 percent, shipping at 11 percent, other sources at 2 percent, and rail at 1 percent.

A process flow chart details the round-trip efficiency of hydrogen in vehicles, starting with 1 kilowatt-hour of renewable AC electricity, sourced from the Center for Sustainable Road Freight in the United Kingdom. The chart outlines five sequential stages of energy conversion and delivery. The AC/DC conversion operates at 95 percent efficiency (leaving 95 percent of the original energy), followed by electrolysis at 75 percent efficiency (bringing remaining energy to 71 percent). Next, hydrogen compression operates at 90 percent efficiency (leaving 64 percent energy), followed by hydrogen transport and transfer at 80 percent efficiency (leaving 51 percent energy). Finally, the fuel cell itself operates at 50 percent efficiency, resulting in a final remaining round-trip energy of just 26 percent. In contrast, the chart notes that a standard electric vehicle battery achieves a final round-trip efficiency of 69 percent.

This page examines the viability and potential market size of hydrogen-powered passenger and freight rail as an alternative to diesel. While hydrogen trains have proven their concept in China, Germany, and the United Kingdom, and the manufacturer Alstom has orders for more fleets in Europe, the overall market for hydrogen rail faces significant headwinds. Rail only accounts for a tiny fraction of global transport emissions, and passenger rail is already highly electrified, with seventy percent of global passenger-kilometers electrified by 2016. While the United States presents a massive opportunity for replacing diesel-powered freight, there is minimal traction for hydrogen there, with battery-electric powertrains emerging as a highly competitive and cost-effective alternative for diesel-electric locomotives. The author concludes that the timeline for hydrogen adoption in rail is very long-term. 

The analysis is supported by three charts. The first, illustrating global passenger rail transport activity by fuel type from 1995 to 2016, shows overall passenger activity growing from just over two trillion passenger-kilometers to over four trillion. This growth was driven almost entirely by electrified rail, including high-speed, urban, and conventional electric transport, while conventional diesel activity remained flat and stagnant. 

The second chart compares rail energy consumption across major economies to show that North America is the largest non-electrified rail opportunity. North America consumes nearly fifteen million tonnes of oil equivalent in rail energy, of which ninety-six percent is diesel, almost entirely comprised of heavy freight diesel. In contrast, China’s rail energy consumption is nearly as high but only thirty-one percent diesel, with the remainder electrified. Other regions also show much lower diesel shares, with Europe at twenty-seven percent, Russia at thirty-three percent, Japan at four percent, and India at fifty-three percent. 

The third chart contextualizes these figures by displaying the global share of carbon dioxide emissions from transport. Road passenger transport, such as cars and buses, accounts for forty-five percent of emissions, followed by road freight trucks at twenty-nine percent, aviation at twelve percent, and shipping at eleven percent. Rail emissions account for a mere one percent of the global transport total. Footnotes on the page detail the high cost of extending overhead catenary electricity infrastructure, citing a SINTEF study indicating that catenary expansion costs fifty-five million Euros per year, which is two and a half times more expensive than hydrogen fuel cell or electric battery-powered alternatives.

This page presents J.P. Morgan's sobering outlook on the hydrogen economy, arguing that its widespread adoption will be a long, challenging journey filled with potential dead ends. Michael Cembalest emphasizes that success depends not only on reducing the production cost of green hydrogen but also on the monumental task of building out electrolyzers, storage facilities, and distribution systems, as well as redesigning end-use machines and engines. Over the next decade, rather than experiencing the explosive, hockey-stick growth often predicted by renewable energy advocates, hydrogen demand is expected to remain limited to modest niche applications. These pockets of demand may include natural gas pipeline blends, shipping, trucking, steel production, commercial back-up power, and non-electrified rail. 

To contextualize this skepticism, the author highlights that hydrogen has a long history of being hyped as "right around the corner." The page lists several historical publication headlines from 1972 to 2003, including articles from Science, The New York Times, Grist, and the International Journal of Hydrogen, alongside books and commentary by figures such as Amory Lovins and Jeremy Rifkin, all of which previously heralded the imminent arrival of the hydrogen age.

A table of summary statistics outlines the severe efficiency losses and scale challenges facing the sector. Key data points reveal that global carbon capture and storage (CCS) accounted for only 0.1% of global emissions in 2021, and the emissions potential of developing US and European CCS projects is just 1% to 2% of regional emissions. Nordic countries, often watched for green steel, represented only 0.5% of steel production in 2020. The table also details significant energy penalties: conversion losses from natural gas to hydrogen using Steam Methane Reformation (SMR) stand at 30%, while energy conversion losses from Alkaline and PEM electrolysis range from 25% to 35%. While fuel cell efficiency in converting hydrogen back to electricity is 50% to 60%, the round-trip efficiency of fuel cells in transportation is only 25%. This drops further to 15% to 30% when liquefaction, shipping, and regasification are required, and plunges to 11% to 19% for liquid ammonia produced from green hydrogen for shipping. Additionally, liquefying gaseous hydrogen into liquid hydrogen consumes 30% to 40% of the energy.

Finally, the page defines the hydrogen color spectrum to clarify the different production methods. Green hydrogen is produced via electrolysis using renewable sources with zero carbon emissions. Yellow uses grid electricity, and pink, purple, or red uses nuclear power. Turquoise hydrogen is produced by the thermal splitting of methane, yielding solid carbon instead of gaseous carbon dioxide. Black or gray hydrogen is extracted from natural gas using steam-methane reforming, while blue hydrogen applies carbon capture and storage to gray or brown processes. White hydrogen is generated as a byproduct of industrial processes like fracking, and brown hydrogen is extracted from fossil fuels, typically coal, via gasification.

This page examines the challenges facing China’s decarbonization efforts, arguing that deep decarbonization projections rely on highly aggressive assumptions given the country’s massive energy footprint and heavy reliance on coal. The author emphasizes that China’s industrial sector is a major global energy consumer, using four times more energy than its own transportation sector and more than the combined industrial sectors of the United States, Europe, and Japan. 

To illustrate this scale, a bar chart titled "The elephant in the room: China's industrial sector" shows final energy consumption in quadrillion BTUs. China’s industrial sector consumes nearly 75 quads of energy, dwarfing its transportation sector at roughly 15 quads and exceeding the combined industrial energy consumption of the United States (around 22 quads), Europe (around 20 quads), and Japan (around 8 quads).

A second line chart, "China & coal: declining shares versus declining consumption," tracks data from 1990 to 2020. It reveals a critical distinction: while coal's share of China’s primary energy has steadily declined from about 75% to just under 60%, its absolute coal consumption has surged, rising from approximately 20 Exajoules in 1990 to around 80 Exajoules by 2020. The accompanying text points out that during 2020 and 2021, China built 67 gigawatts of new coal plants—nearly double the 35 gigawatts built by the rest of the world combined. This led to a net growth of 52 gigawatts in China's coal fleet, compared to a net decline of 23 gigawatts in the rest of the world. Furthermore, China initiated another 106 gigawatts of new coal plants during those two years.

The text also addresses China’s nuclear power strategy, noting plans to expand nuclear capacity from 50 gigawatts to 130 gigawatts by 2030. However, the author notes that this expansion will only represent about 6% of China’s electricity generation and 3% of its primary energy by 2030, meaning nuclear power is not a solo game-changer. Currently, coal accounts for roughly 60% of China's primary energy, compared to just 10% in Europe and the United States.

At the bottom of the page, two additional charts reinforce China's dominant role in global coal markets. The chart "The impact of China on global coal capacity" tracks annual additions and retirements in gigawatts from 2000 to 2020. It illustrates that China's net capacity additions have consistently dominated global activity, offsetting net retirements in the United States and Europe. Finally, the chart "China coal production" shows monthly domestic output in million tonnes from 2005 to 2021, detailing a clear upward trend from around 150 million tonnes in 2005 to over 350 million tonnes by the end of 2021.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, Eye on the Market, analyzes the International Energy Agency’s September 2021 report, An Energy Sector Roadmap to Carbon Neutrality in China.
