This page analyzes the relationship between equity market bottoms and macroeconomic indicators—such as GDP, corporate earnings, and payrolls—across historical recessions to contextualize the bear market of 2022. Author Michael Cembalest argues that the Dot-com collapse was a historical outlier because corporate earnings declined before equities did. In contrast, most economic cycles see the equity market bottom out while headline economic data like profits, GDP, and payrolls are still worsening. He anticipates that the 2022 bear market will follow this typical pattern. To help time the market bottom, Cembalest advises closely watching the ISM manufacturing survey, which historically coincides with stock market troughs. He projects that an S&P 500 index level between 3,200 and 3,300 would represent attractive value for long-term investors if reached during the fall or winter of 2022.

The analysis is supported by four line charts indexing the S&P 500, GDP, Payrolls, and Earnings to a value of 100 at the start of each observed cycle. The first chart, covering the Global Financial Crisis from March 2007 to March 2013, shows the S&P 500 bottoming in early 2009, well before earnings and payrolls recovered. The second chart, tracking the Global COVID Pandemic from December 2019 to December 2021, displays a sharp decline and rapid recovery in the S&P 500 in early 2020 that preceded the recovery of employment payrolls. The third chart shows the Dot-com Bubble Recession from December 1999 to January 2004, where earnings led the downward trend and the S&P 500 did not bottom until late 2002. The final chart, titled "Negative real rate experiment implodes as inflation returns," covers June 2021 to October 2022, showing a steep decline in the S&P 500 even as payrolls and GDP remained relatively resilient.

A final table compares historical equity market bottoms to ISM Manufacturing survey bottoms to demonstrate their strong correlation. Across seven periods, the months between the equity market bottom and the ISM manufacturing bottom are minimal: the Eisenhower recession (equity bottom 12/31/1957, ISM bottom 1/31/1958, +1 month), the Stagflation era of the 1970s (equity bottom 9/30/1974, ISM bottom 1/31/1975, +4 months), the 1980s double-dip recession (equity bottom 7/31/1982, ISM bottom 5/31/1982, -2 months), the S&L crisis of the 1990s (equity bottom 10/31/1990, ISM bottom 1/31/1991, +3 months), the Dot-com bubble (equity bottom 9/30/2002, ISM bottom 10/31/2001, -11 months), the Global Financial Crisis (equity bottom 2/28/2009, ISM bottom 12/31/2008, -2 months), and the Global COVID pandemic (equity bottom 3/31/2020, ISM bottom 4/30/2020, +1 month).

This page of the publication critiques the tendency of media outlets to hold up small countries with high shares of renewable energy, such as Uruguay, Iceland, Norway, and Costa Rica, as models for larger, more industrialized nations. The author coins the term "The Pitcairn Problem" to describe this issue, arguing that these tiny nations possess unique characteristics that make their energy transition pathways highly context-specific and mostly irrelevant to major global economies. 

Specifically, these countries benefit from small shares of global GDP, low populations, and low population densities, which reduce the challenges of siting wind and solar power and lower the required transmission infrastructure investments. Furthermore, they typically have lower economic complexity, meaning they require less complex industrial energy systems to support. They also possess disproportionately abundant hydroelectric assets, which are mostly tapped out in larger developed nations, and unique geothermal or highly efficient sugarcane-based biomass resources. For instance, Denmark and Uruguay rely heavily on wind and biomass for backup power and stabilize their grids thanks to their close physical proximity to major neighboring systems like Germany and Brazil.

To support this argument, the page features a comprehensive Energy Profiles data table comparing three cohorts: high renewable share countries, large developed countries, and large developing countries. The table presents metrics including primary energy per capita, carbon emissions, electricity generation sources, and socio-economic indicators. Under the high-renewable cohort, nations like Iceland, Costa Rica, and Nepal boast a 100% total renewable electricity share, largely driven by hydro (92% in Norway, 100% in Nepal) and geothermal (31% in Iceland). In contrast, large developed economies show far lower renewable shares, such as 20% in both the United States and Japan, which rely heavily on natural gas, coal, and nuclear. Among developing nations, Brazil stands out with an 84% renewable share due to its massive 64% hydroelectric generation, whereas South Korea has just a 6% renewable share. The table also highlights stark demographic and economic contrasts; for example, Iceland has a population density of just 9 people per square mile, while South Korea has a density of 1,340 people per square mile and an economic complexity score of 98.

Ultimately, the author concludes that larger, urbanized nations pursuing a renewable transition must tackle complex issues involving raw material supply chains, massive project siting, transmission investments, and thermal backup power, noting that these challenges will be explored further in the firm's upcoming annual energy paper.

This page examines the landmark CHIPS and Science Act of 2022, analyzing its unique bipartisan passage, its funding limitations, and the massive geopolitical and technical challenges of global semiconductor manufacturing. Michael Cembalest argues that the CHIPS Act represents a rare moment of modern political cooperation. An accompanying chart, "Partisanship gap for major US legislation," measures the average difference in "yea" votes between parties in the House and Senate on a scale from 0% to 100%. While highly partisan bills like the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, the 2021 American Rescue Plan, and the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act saw partisanship gaps close to 100%, the CHIPS Act recorded a much lower gap of around 35%, receiving critical cross-party support. 

Despite this political success, a second chart titled "Semiconductor bill spending and estimated amounts required for US self-sufficiency" reveals a massive funding shortfall. While the CHIPS bill allocates roughly $50 billion for domestic semiconductor manufacturing, the estimated amount needed for complete US semiconductor self-sufficiency ranges between $400 billion and $500 billion. 

The text transitions to the highly delicate geopolitical dynamics surrounding China and Taiwan. China commands 60% of global semiconductor demand but produces only 10% of that demand domestically. The remaining 90% relies on foreign imports, with Taiwan accounting for a massive 70% share of total Chinese chip consumption. This extreme reliance dwarfs Europe's pre-war reliance on Russian energy, which was around 25% in 2021. 

Furthermore, a significant technological divide exists between Chinese foundries, which are mostly limited to producing older 14-28 nanometer chips, and advanced global leaders like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). A chart detailing "TSMC semiconductor capabilities" plots the exponential shrinkage of chip node sizes over time, falling from 1,500 nanometers in 1987 down to 5 nanometers by 2022. Cembalest notes that fabricating the most advanced chips (10, 7, 5, and 3 nanometers) requires highly specialized extreme ultraviolet photolithography (EUV) machines produced exclusively by the Dutch company ASML, which builds only 45 to 55 of these complex systems per year. The commentary concludes by outlining the immense physical and logical hurdles in the advanced semiconductor supply chain, which demands clean rooms 10,000 times cleaner than surgical suites, weeks-long multi-step manufacturing processes, and highly specialized inputs sourced from thousands of companies globally.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s report presents an appendix of six charts illustrating that various market indicators are generally downbeat and signaling economic strain. 

The first chart tracks the year-over-year percent change in the US dollar from 1990 to late 2022, highlighting that the recent dollar surge of approximately 20% mirrors levels that historically preceded major financial crises. These historical episodes include the Mexican debt crisis, the Russian default, the tech bubble recession, the housing bubble peak, the Global Financial Crisis, sovereign debt crises, and the Chinese devaluation. A question mark is placed above the current peak, raising the question of what crisis this current surge might trigger. Alongside this currency pressure, a chart of US consumer price inflation measures shows the Cleveland Fed median CPI, the Cleveland Fed trimmed mean CPI, and the Atlanta Fed sticky CPI. All three measures have spiked in 2022 to between 6% and 7%, representing the highest underlying inflation rates seen since the early 1990s. 

Looking forward, corporate profitability appears vulnerable. A chart on leading earnings indicators plots actual trailing year-over-year earnings growth against two predictive models from 2001 through 2022. Although actual earnings growth hovered near 40% recently, both model 1 and model 2 point sharply downward toward negative territory, between negative 10% and negative 20%, suggesting a notable contraction ahead. In response to these inflation and economic conditions, the Federal Reserve has raised interest rates rapidly. A chart tracking Fed tightening cycles from 1958 to 2022 shows that the 2022 cycle is one of the steepest on record, climbing over 300 basis points within its first twelve months. Dotted lines representing expectations from Overnight Interest Swaps project this tightening cycle peaking near 400 basis points before beginning to level off.

The final two charts illustrate severe imbalances in the housing and labor markets. The US housing affordability index, tracking data from 1970 to 2022, shows that affordability has plummeted from an index level of nearly 180 down to approximately 100, indicating that homes are less affordable than at any point since the mid-2000s housing bubble. Simultaneously, the US is experiencing its largest worker shortage of the post-war era. A chart of job openings plus employment as a percentage of the labor force from 1951 to 2022 shows a spike to nearly 3%, indicating a historic mismatch where there are significantly more jobs than available workers, surpassing previous tight labor markets in the late 1960s and the late 1990s.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest provides a preliminary assessment of the 2022 midterm election results, noting that the projected net loss of 11 Democratic House seats represents a better-than-expected outcome for the President’s party given the prevailing below-average economic and market conditions. He contextualizes this by discussing historical exceptions where the President's party suffered major midterm losses despite robust economic conditions due to specific non-economic factors, pointing to Warren G. Harding in 1922 (prohibition), Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1942 (early World War II frustrations and wage controls), and Lyndon B. Johnson in 1966 (the Vietnam War and backlash to New Deal policies). He observes that the projected narrow majority for the Republicans would result in one of the smallest governing margins in nearly a century. Cembalest asserts that the market consequences of this midterm outcome are likely negligible compared to broader business cycle issues, and notes that control of the Senate remains a toss-up.

The primary visual is a bubble chart titled "Midterm White House party losses since 1910 adjusted for economic & market conditions." The vertical axis tracks an economic index composed of employment, wages, and inflation, where 100 represents the best conditions and 0 the worst. The horizontal axis measures market conditions based on the trailing two-year real return on equities, home prices, and government bonds, ranging from -30% to 30%. Each bubble represents a midterm election year, with its color indicating the President's party (blue for Democrats, red for Republicans) and its size reflecting the number of House seats lost. 

The 2022 midterm (labeled D-11) is plotted in the lower-left quadrant, marking a period of weak market returns (around -23%) and poor economic conditions (scored at 33). Despite these headwinds, the relatively small size of the 2022 bubble illustrates that the 11-seat loss was exceptionally mild compared to other historical periods with similar economic distress, such as 1974 (R-48), or eras of severe market downturns, such as 1930 (R-52). Conversely, the chart highlights anomalies like 1922 (R-77), where the President's party lost 77 seats despite strong market returns of roughly 20%. The chart excludes the midterms of 1934, 1998, and 2002, when the President's party actively gained House seats.

In this entry, Michael Cembalest discusses the fallout of the FTX collapse and critiques the crypto industry's complaints regarding a "lack of regulatory clarity." He argues that criticizing SEC Commissioner Gary Gensler and the SEC for the failure of FTX is highly hypocritical unless critics meet specific, stringent criteria. This "Gensler Rule" specifies that critics must acknowledge that most cryptocurrencies are securities under the decades-old Howey test, support the SEC's over one hundred enforcement actions against entities like Grayscale, Coinbase, and BlockFi, and not have accepted political campaign contributions from major crypto and venture capital firms like Coinbase, Ripple, and Andreessen Horowitz. He specifically points out that eight House members wrote to Gensler in March 2022 complaining that the SEC's inquiries into FTX were burdensome and stifling innovation. 

Cembalest highlights that US investors trade on offshore platforms like Binance, Bitfinex, Huobi, and FTX.com—where an estimated 60% of US crypto derivative trades occurred—not due to regulatory ambiguity but to evade stringent US rules and access high-margin lending and unrestricted token selections. He asserts that securities laws are intentionally flexible and principles-based rather than prescriptive, pointing out that the crypto industry actively lobbied against anti-fraud reporting requirements in the 2021 Infrastructure Act. 

The page includes an image of the cover of J.P. Morgan's February 3, 2022 report, titled "The Maltese Falcoin: On cryptocurrencies and blockchains." The black-and-white illustration features a film-noir-style caricature of a detective in a fedora standing behind a bald man at a desk, who is closely examining a Bitcoin token with a magnifying glass. Cembalest concludes by suggesting readers compare J.P. Morgan's skeptical "Maltese Falcoin" analysis with the highly complimentary, now-archived profile of FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried formerly hosted on Sequoia Capital's website.

This page analyzes the effectiveness of mRNA vaccines in mitigating COVID-19 mortality and highlights the consequences of vaccine hesitancy in the United States. Author Michael Cembalest emphasizes that while current mRNA vaccines are not highly effective at preventing transmission or infection, they are remarkably successful in reducing hospitalization and death. He notes that bivalent booster uptake in the US is low at 12% to 15%, ranking the country 73rd globally, while newer variants like BQ.1.1 and XBB show increased resistance to treatments such as Bebtelovimab and Evusheld. He advocates for the development of nasal vaccine deliveries and pan-coronavirus vaccines to better target infection and transmission. To accurately compare mortality globally, the author cites studies showing that high-income country excess death rates are 1.3 times higher than reported COVID-19 death rates, rising to three times higher in middle-income countries and six times higher in lower-income countries, making all-cause mortality statistics a critical tool for global analysis.

The analysis is supported by four charts. The first chart, showing US COVID-19 deaths per 100,000 people among those aged six months and older from April 2021 to July 2022, contrasts the high peak death rate of the unvaccinated (reaching nearly 27 deaths per 100,000 in January 2022) with the consistently low death rate of the vaccinated, which remained below 4 deaths per 100,000. The second chart focuses on US COVID-19 deaths per 100,000 people for adults aged 50 and older from April 2022 to August 2022. It reveals that unvaccinated individuals in this bracket experienced significantly higher death rates, peaking at over 10 deaths per 100,000, whereas those with a primary series, one booster, or two or more boosters maintained much lower mortality rates, with the lowest deaths seen in those with multiple booster doses.

The third chart illustrates preventable US COVID-19 deaths from January 2021 to April 2022. It tracks actual cumulative deaths among adults, which reached 641,305, against an estimated path of 322,324 deaths if 100% of adults had been fully vaccinated, indicating that nearly half of these deaths were preventable. The final chart presents age-adjusted all-cause excess death rates by registered political party in the US from January 2018 to January 2022. The data shows that while Republicans and Democrats tracked closely prior to late 2020, a substantial gap opened after vaccine availability in early 2021. Excess death rates for registered Republicans spiked significantly higher, peaking at nearly 40% in late 2021, compared to a lower peak of around 10% to 15% for registered Democrats during the same period.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication "Eye on the Market" by Michael Cembalest focuses on the massive market repricing of unprofitable and speculative companies during the 2019 to 2022 market cycle, drawing strong parallels to the dot-com crash of 2000 to 2002. Cembalest opens with a satirical visual of a custom-commissioned "APE Innovation ETF" cartoon—featuring a bored ape holding a burning hundred-dollar bill—skewering the speculative bubble in NFTs and the Metaverse. A footnote highlights that virtual real estate trading volumes and prices collapsed 98% and 88% from their peak levels, respectively, even as McKinsey estimates that $120 billion has been invested in the Metaverse.

The commentary argues that while 2022 brought a painful repricing of unprofitable companies, this recent cycle was arguably dumber than the dot-com era because investors ignored clear historical precedents. To illustrate this, a line chart titled "Dumb and Dumber" indexes performance to 100 to compare a basket of "profitless innovation" sectors (such as Metaverse, Hydrogen, Fintech, SPACs, crypto, software, e-commerce, and biotech) from 2019 to 2022 against the NASDAQ 100 from 1998 to 2003. The profitless innovation index peaked near 480 in early 2021 before crashing down toward 150 by late 2022, closely tracking the trajectory of the NASDAQ 100's historic peak near 400 and subsequent decline to around 120.

Two additional charts monitor how the price for equity risk is being corrected. The first, "The YUCs: Young Unprofitable Companies," measures companies with less than five years since their IPO, annual revenue growth exceeding 15%, and negative net income in two of the last three years as a percentage of equity market capitalization. YUCs peaked at nearly 5% during the dot-com boom, remained under 1% for most of the 2000s and 2010s, surged past 3% in 2021, and corrected back down to roughly 1.8% by late 2022. The second chart, "The MUCs: Megavalued (P/E >50x) or Unprofitable Companies," tracks these entities as a percentage of total US market capitalization from 1990 to 2022. This share peaked at approximately 43% in 2000, fell to around 12% in 2010, spiked to nearly 37% in 2021, and has since fallen sharply to about 18% in late 2022. Cembalest observes that approximately 60% to 70% of the recent YUC and MUC surge has now been reversed.

This page, titled "The End of the Affair," serves as an introduction to Michael Cembalest’s 2023 market outlook, arguing that the era of massive fiscal and monetary stimulus, negative real rates, and speculative market catalysts like unregulated crypto and profitless innovation is coming to an end. While anticipating a major growth slowdown in the United States and Europe, Cembalest advises investors against becoming overly bearish as markets decline. He highlights that in the history of US recessions—with the exception of the 2001 dot-com collapse—equity markets have historically bottomed well before key lagging economic indicators like GDP, payrolls, corporate earnings, housing starts, and real estate delinquencies. Consequently, he predicts that the equity market will bottom during the first half of 2023, with the October 2022 lows holding, closely coinciding with a pause in Federal Reserve interest rate hikes at around five percent in the spring. 

The accompanying chart, titled "When recessions occur, the ISM survey has been the best coincident indicator of a bottom in equities," plots the S&P 500 index (indexed to 100 at the start of each period) across seven historical US recessions: the Eisenhower recession, Stagflation, the Double-dip recession, the S&L recession, the DotCom collapse, the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), and the COVID-19 pandemic. The chart features color-coded markers pinpointing when various indicators reached their cyclical bottoms relative to the stock market's path. These indicators include the ISM survey, GDP, payrolls, S&P 500 earnings, housing starts, and real estate delinquencies. Across almost all displayed recessionary periods, the ISM bottom marker, represented by a blue circle, aligns almost perfectly with the absolute trough of the S&P 500 line. In contrast, other indicators such as GDP, S&P Earnings, and real estate delinquencies lag significantly, bottoming well after the stock market has already begun its rebound. The text also previews upcoming sections of the report, which address topics such as the retreat of globalization, value stock opportunities, a coming regulatory wave for fintech and crypto, and opportunities in global fixed income.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the normalization of monetary and fiscal policies following years of negative real interest rates and massive fiscal deficits. Michael Cembalest argues that this macroeconomic shift is correcting unrealistic valuation premiums, driving capital out of speculative digital and "innovation" assets and back into physical "old economy" assets and traditional energy sectors. 

To support this transition thesis, the author presents the chart "The Tortoise and the Hare," which indexes performance starting in December 2016. It tracks the ARK Innovation ETF against an "old economy basket" of farm equipment, industrial REITs, and office cleaning supplies and uniforms. The speculative ARK ETF soared from an index level of 100 in late 2016 to a peak of over 800 in early 2021 before precipitously crashing below 200 by late 2022. Conversely, the old economy basket maintained a steady, slower upward trajectory, ultimately overtaking the ARK ETF in late 2022 at an index level near 400. 

A second chart, titled "Reports of my death were greatly exaggerated," displays the annual returns for 2021 and 2022. It compares the MSCI World Energy Index, which covers traditional oil, gas, and pipeline companies, to a Renewables Composite that includes indices such as NASDAQ Clean Edge, Wilderhill Clean Energy, FTSE Renew/Alt Energy, S&P Global Clean Energy, and MAC Global Solar. In 2021, traditional energy returned nearly 40% while renewables lost over 10%. In 2022, traditional energy gained around 50% while renewables lost roughly 8%, reinforcing that real-world thermal energy demands continue to outperform green alternatives during this transition period.

The commentary then shifts to Russia's critical geopolitical influence on energy and fertilizers, noting that many market participants mistakenly dismissed the country because its share of global GDP has fallen to a 200-year low. This historical context is visualized in the chart "Russia/USSR share of World GDP since 1820." The chart tracks the economic weight of the region through various expansionary eras, including the creation of the USSR and its postwar annexation of Eastern Europe, which saw its global GDP share peak near 15% in the mid-20th century. Following the dissolution of the USSR, the Russian Federation's share fell to approximately 3%. 

Despite this diminished economic footprint, Russia's capacity to disrupt global markets remains massive. In response to energy vulnerabilities, European nations are adjusting their strategies, with Germany building floating LNG regasification units and France planning a nuclear energy expansion. Meanwhile, China has strengthened its ties with Russia. This geopolitical realignment is illustrated in the final chart, "Cross-border syndicated loans to Russia" in billions of US dollars from 2010 to 2022. A vertical marker denotes the 2014 invasion of Crimea, after which loans from Western nations—including France, Germany, Italy, Great Britain, the United States, and Japan—steadily declined toward zero. In contrast, cross-border syndicated loans from China surged from around $16 billion in 2014 to over $44 billion by 2022.

Looking ahead, Cembalest suggests that despite Russia's ongoing attacks on Ukraine's infrastructure, investors should not be surprised by an eventual ceasefire. He posits that such an outcome may be partially driven by Europe's pragmatic, urgent need to restore access to Russian land-based oil and natural gas pipelines, especially given the physical destruction of the Nord Stream pipelines.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" analyzes declining leading indicators in the United States and Europe, forecasting a major growth slowdown that will drag down corporate profits in 2023. The author predicts that while a recession may occur, it will likely be milder than the downturns of 2008 and 2020, with manufacturing surveys expected to bottom out in the first half of 2023. 

The analysis is supported by four key charts. The first two charts compare manufacturing new orders less inventories against composite PMI indices to predict downturns. The first chart, tracking the US from 1983 to 2022, plots the ISM manufacturing PMI composite index on the left axis (scale of 30 to 70) against the ISM new orders less inventories with a three-month lead on the right axis (scale of -20 to 30). The second chart shows the same relationship for the European Union from 1997 to 2022, using the EU manufacturing PMI composite index and EU new orders less inventories (scale of -30 to 30 on the right axis). Both charts show their respective leading indicator lines plunging sharply in late 2022, signaling an imminent composite PMI downturn.

The third chart illustrates leading earnings indicators pointing to a decline in S&P 500 earnings, measured as a percentage change from -30% to 60% between 2001 and 2022. It tracks trailing year-over-year S&P 500 earnings—which stood at 14% late in the series—against two proprietary leading indicator models. Model one includes manufacturing PMI, business surveys, credit spreads, and housing starts, while model two incorporates business surveys, supplier deliveries, wage trackers, inflation, and a cyclical GDP indicator. Both models show a steep drop below zero percent by late 2022, supporting the author's prediction of a 10% to 15% year-over-year decline in S&P earnings for 2023.

The final chart examines Europe’s energy crisis, titled "Europe's energy bill goes off the rails." It plots the net exports of energy products as a percentage of GDP from 1978 to 2022, with a scale ranging from net imports at -5% to net exports at 1%. The chart contrasts the United States, which has transitioned from a net importer to a net exporter (rising above 0%), with the European Union, whose net imports plunged precipitously to nearly -5% of GDP in 2022. This visualization underscores the author's point that rising energy costs are crowding out other forms of European consumption. Despite government interventions to shield consumers, high energy bills are expected to drag down employment, housing, and production, while the European Central Bank is forced to tighten policy due to 5% core inflation.

Michael Cembalest argues that Chinese assets hit "deep value" pricing in late 2022, suggesting that the massive pricing-in of bad news has set the stage for a sharp recovery upon marginal policy improvements. He notes that the Chinese government has introduced property market support measures, such as central bank relending programs and loosened fundraising restrictions, while domestic households are flush with cash, boasting deposits 60% higher than pre-pandemic levels alongside mortgage rates matching 2017 lows. This setup could lead to the outperformance of a US-EM equity barbell in the coming year once the country's intense COVID-19 wave subsides. 

To support this outlook, the page presents four charts. The first, "Equity index drawdowns: China vs World," tracks the percentage decline from prior peaks from 2005 to late 2022. It reveals that the MSCI China index suffered a steep drawdown of 49% by late December 2022, far deeper than the MSCI World drawdown of 18%. The second chart, "China earnings yields," displays 12-month forward earnings yields for the Hang Seng Index and MSCI China from 2006 through late 2022. Yields spiked to 11% to 12% in late 2022, near Global Financial Crisis levels, before settling at 9% for the Hang Seng and 8% for MSCI China by late December. 

The third chart, "Chinese bank valuations," details the average price-to-book ratio from 2010 to 2022 for major institutions, specifically the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, China Construction Bank, Agricultural Bank of China, and Bank of China. This average ratio steadily deteriorated from nearly 1.8x in 2010 to less than 0.5x by late 2022. Finally, the fourth chart, "China property high-yield bond price distribution," presents Goldman Sachs data from November 2022 detailing the cumulative percent of notional outstanding across defaulted, exchanged, and undefaulted/unexchanged bonds. It demonstrates unprecedented distress in the Chinese real estate sector, showing that only 5% to 10% of the high-yield property bond universe is priced above 60% of par value, while 85% is trading at or was exchanged at less than 20% of par. Cembalest compares this to emerging market crises since 1987, stating he cannot recall any sector-wide restructuring episode this severe.

This page from the report analyzes the current state of the US banking system amid slowing economic growth. The author argues that while banks are structurally in a much stronger position than they were ahead of the 2008 financial crisis, rising interest rates have created a significant new headwind in the form of massive unrealized bond losses. To support the positive view, the author notes that riskier lending has migrated away from banks, wholesale funding has dropped from 17.5 percent of liabilities in 2000 to 7.5 percent, and liquidity has improved dramatically. This liquidity improvement is illustrated in a historical line chart of the US loan-to-deposit ratio for all commercial banks from 1973 to late 2022, which shows the ratio falling from its 1.00x peak in 2008 to approximately 0.65x in 2022. Capital strength is further demonstrated by a line chart of US bank tier 1 capital ratios, which tracks tier 1 capital as a percentage of risk-weighted assets climbing from under 10 percent in the mid-2000s to over 14 percent by 2022.

The primary vulnerability highlighted on the page is that rising rates have left US banks holding high-quality bonds that trade below par, resulting in roughly 700 billion dollars in unrealized losses on securities designated as Available-for-Sale or Hold-to-Maturity. This trend is shown in a bar chart of FDIC third-quarter unrealized bank losses on investment securities from 2008 to 2022, where the net losses plunge precipitously to nearly negative 700 billion dollars in 2022, split between Available-for-Sale and Held-to-Maturity securities.

To analyze individual bank risk, a scatter plot compares US bank loan-to-deposit ratios, plotting retail deposits as a share of total deposits on the y-axis against loans plus securities as a percentage of deposits on the x-axis for third-quarter 2022. This chart categorizes banks with high retail deposit shares and low loan-to-deposit ratios as having a lower-risk deposit base, such as J.P. Morgan, which sits at roughly 52 percent retail deposits and 72 percent loans plus securities. Conversely, banks with lower retail deposit shares and higher loan-and-security concentrations, like Citigroup and Comerica, are positioned closer to the higher-risk deposit base. Other analyzed banks, including US Bank, PNC, Truist, KeyBank, and Capital One, cluster between 90 percent and 115 percent for loans plus securities.

Lastly, a line chart tracking Fed assets and liabilities from January 2022 through late 2023 displays quantitative tightening trends. It plots Fed assets, which are projected to decline from 9.0 trillion dollars to roughly 7.8 trillion dollars, alongside bank reserves, which fall from around 3.8 trillion dollars to 2.0 trillion dollars, and overnight reverse repo agreements, which hover between 1.5 trillion and 2.5 trillion dollars. This highlights the contraction of liquidity in the broader financial system.

This page from the report focuses on the repricing of financial assets as the extraordinary gap between asset yields and policy rates finally begins to close. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that this narrowing gap has catalyzed a severe repricing of profitless innovation that is now spreading to the broader equity market. He predicts a modest valuation correction early in 2023 to bring public equities closer to their long-term averages as an economic slowdown approaches, while noting that private equity and private credit markets have yet to fully reprice. Additionally, he anticipates that physical assets will continue to outpace digital assets, traditional energy will outpace renewable energy, and fintech returns will continue giving back their post-2019 outperformance compared to traditional banks.

To support these arguments, the page presents six charts. The first chart, titled Gap between asset yields and short rates is finally closing, plots percent values from 1960 to late 2022. It contrasts developed world asset yields against developed world short rates adjusted for quantitative easing, showing that the unprecedented gap between the two since 2008 is rapidly closing as QE-adjusted short rates spike upward.

The second chart, Dumb and Dumber, overlays two historical speculative bubbles indexed to 100. It shows an uncanny similarity between the 1998 to 2003 dot-com crash of the NASDAQ 100 and the 2019 to 2022 rise and fall of a basket of profitless innovations including the metaverse, hydrogen, fintech, SPACs, crypto, software, e-commerce, and biotech. Both indices peaked near 450 before crashing down toward 150 to 200.

The third chart, Forward PE ratios: Russell 1000, growth and value, tracks price-to-consensus 12-month forward earnings per share from 2006 to 2022. It compares the Megacap 8, which includes Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Netflix, Nvidia, and Tesla, against the Russell 1000 Growth, Russell 1000, and Russell 1000 Value indices. It highlights how the Megacap 8 forward PE ratio skyrocketed toward 45 during the pandemic but has since collapsed back to the mid-20s, converging closer to the broader Russell 1000 indices.

The fourth chart displays the S&P 500 price to earnings ratio based on 12-month forward earnings from 1990 to late 2022. After peaking near 24x during the pandemic, the forward PE has corrected back down to 16.7x, resting just slightly above its historical average.

The fifth chart, titled The Tortoise and the Hare, indexes performance to 100 starting in December 2016. It shows the ARK Innovation ETF, representing the high-flying hare, peaking above 800 in early 2021 before crashing to around 150 by late 2022. In contrast, the old economy basket, representing the steady tortoise and consisting of farm equipment, industrial REITs, and office cleaning supplies and uniforms, steadily climbed to over 300, ultimately outperforming the speculative tech ETF.

The final chart, titled Reports of my death were greatly exaggerated, indexes performance to 100 starting in December 2018. It compares an equal-weighted renewables composite, consisting of NASDAQ Clean Edge, Wilderhill Clean Energy, FTSE Renew/Alt Energy, S&P Global Clean Energy, and MAC Global Solar, with the MSCI World Energy Index for traditional oil, gas, and pipelines. While the clean energy composite peaked near 450 in early 2021 and has since slid down to around 250, traditional energy has staged a massive comeback, rising from a low of around 50 in 2020 to approximately 150 by late 2022.

This page analyzes the deep headwinds facing Chinese equities, focusing on pandemic mismanagement, a demographic crisis, and detrimental political shifts under President Xi Jinping. The author notes that due to a combination of strict pandemic restrictions, low consumer spending, and a failing property market, China is expected to grow slower than most other Asian economies for the first time in thirty years. A key failure highlighted is China's refusal to approve highly effective mRNA vaccines from Moderna or Pfizer because Moderna refused to hand over its intellectual property. Consequently, by late 2022, a third of China's elderly population over 60 lacked booster shots, yet the nation began a rapid and risky reopening. 

The author suggests that a demographic emergency may have forced China’s sudden reopening. The chart titled China Total Births shows annual births plummeting from peaks of roughly 30 million in the late 1960s and late 1980s to a historic low of approximately 10 million by the 2022 estimate. This birth rate collapse dramatically worsens long-term forecasts, as illustrated in the China Working Age Population Projections chart, which tracks population aged 15 to 64 from 1950 out to 2090. While 2019 UN projections estimated the working-age population would peak near 1 billion in 2015 and decline to roughly 600 million by 2090, the updated 2022 estimates project a far steeper collapse to just 400 million by 2090.

Turning to equity markets, the author outlines how years of market-friendly policies had successfully increased China’s representation in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index to a peak of 40% by 2020. However, as shown in the chart tracking China’s index weight, performance, and policy changes, the commencement of Xi Jinping's progressive authoritarianism campaign sparked a historic sell-off. This political pivot resulted in the largest underperformance of Chinese equities compared to world equities on record, reaching roughly negative 50% on a rolling three-year basis by late 2022. 

Despite this drag from China, the final chart, Overweight US & EM, Underweight Europe & Japan, demonstrates the long-term success of J.P. Morgan's core equity allocation thesis. Tracking the three-year rolling performance of a portfolio with a 10% overweight to the US, a 10% underweight to Europe, a 5% overweight to Emerging Markets, and a 5% underweight to Japan against the MSCI All World Index from 1991 to 2021, the strategy has consistently generated positive outperformance. Except for a minor dip in the mid-2000s, this barbell strategy has steadily outperformed the benchmark, peaking above 8% in the 1990s and remaining firmly in positive territory through the recent market volatility.

This page addresses a major concern heading into a potential recession: the minimal repricing of leveraged loans despite a decade of declining investor protections and rising leverage. The author points out that loan investors have surrendered protections at a record pace, partially driven by the Federal Reserve's financial repression, which forced investors to lose their bearings. Similar issues plague the private credit market, which has grown to 1.2 trillion dollars, equivalent to the US high yield market. The decline in investor protections, often exacerbated by the practice of sponsor-designated counsel, has resulted in relaxed leverage criteria, weakened interest coverage maintenance tests, and a rise in EBITDA add-backs. According to S&P data cited on the page, the share of deals using EBITDA add-backs tripled from 10 percent to roughly 30 percent by 2019, with add-backs often making up 10 percent to 30 percent of unadjusted EBITDA. 

Four charts illustrate these deteriorating dynamics. The first chart, showing Moody's loan covenant quality score from 2012 to 2021 on a scale where 5 represents the weakest quality, illustrates a clear upward trend of weakening covenants. The score deteriorated from approximately 3.3 in 2012 to nearly 4.6 by 2021. The second chart compares specific loan covenant quality categories between 2007 and the 2019–2020 period. Across every single metric—including financial covenants, restricted payments, risky investments, and voting assignments—the scores in 2019–2020 were significantly closer to the weakest rating of 5 compared to 2007, with financial covenants spiking from over 3.0 to nearly 5.0. 

The third chart displays the distribution of leveraged loan issuance by debt-to-EBITDA ratio from 2008 to 2022. It shows that higher-quality, lower-leverage loans of under 4x represented a substantial portion of the market in 2008 but have since shrunk to a tiny sliver of the market. Conversely, highly leveraged loans, particularly those with leverage ratios of 6x to 6.9x and above 7x, have steadily expanded to dominate issuance. The final chart plots the US high yield spread alongside the leveraged loan price index from 1988 through late 2022 to argue that risky credit is not pricing in a recession. Historically, during recessions in 2000 and 2008, high yield spreads spiked past 10 percent and 15 percent respectively, while the loan price index crashed below 70. In contrast, the current market shows only a mild rise in spreads and loan prices remaining relatively high near the index level of 90, presenting a disconnect given the underlying structural weaknesses.

This page focuses on Federal Reserve policy and the path of inflation, with Michael Cembalest arguing that inflation pressures will likely subside, allowing the Fed to pause its tightening cycle at 5% while the 10-year US Treasury yield remains below 4%. He notes that market-derived inflation expectations have fallen from a 3% peak back to 2.25%, giving the Fed room to claim victory after its fastest tightening cycle on record. However, he warns that the projected rapid decline in inflation is historically unusual and that the Fed's primary challenge lies in wages and an exceptionally tight labor market, where job shortages are at post-war highs and layoffs remain concentrated mostly in the technology and homebuilding sectors.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, titled "Fed tightening cycles, 1958-2022," plots the basis point change from the start of various tightening cycles over a timeline of thirty-six months before and after the first Fed action. The 2022 cycle stands out as a steep, dark blue line that surges roughly 400 basis points in less than a year, visually demonstrating that this tightening cycle is one of the fastest and most aggressive on record compared to dozens of historical cycles shown in light gray.

The second chart, "Developed market inflation episodes since 1970," tracks year-over-year percent inflation change against the number of months since inflation first rose above 8%. It plots the current US and Eurozone inflation cycles along with Bloomberg consensus forecasts, shown as dotted lines, against historical medians and quartiles. While consensus expectations project a remarkably swift decline in inflation back to around 2% to 3% within twenty months of crossing the 8% threshold, the historical median and third quartile lines demonstrate that inflation typically takes much longer to recede, remaining well above 6% at the twenty-month mark.

The third chart, "Largest worker shortage in the post-war era," shows job openings plus employment as a percentage of the labor force from 1951 through late 2022. The line plots the balance of jobs versus workers, showing that the post-pandemic period has seen an unprecedented spike to nearly 5%, indicating a massive labor shortage that far exceeds any prior peak in the post-war era.

The fourth chart, "Wage growth measures," tracks alternative wage metrics from 2008 to late 2022, avoiding the distortion seen in average hourly earnings due to pandemic-related labor composition shifts. It displays the Atlanta Fed Tracker as a three-month average year-over-year percent change and the Employment Cost Index as an annualized quarter-over-quarter percent change on the left axis, alongside a monthly wage survey average index on the right axis. All three measures peaked dramatically in late 2021 and early 2022, with the Atlanta Fed Tracker nearing 7%, but they show clear signs of beginning to roll over by late 2022.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s market outlook focuses on the housing market as a primary driver of cooling inflation in 2023, arguing that a sharp decline in housing activity will allow the Federal Reserve to pause its rate hikes at 5.0%. The author explains that although official core consumer price index data for housing is heavily lagged, leading indicators like apartment asking rents are already slowing significantly. This shift is driven by a combination of surging mortgage rates and a massive volume of new multifamily construction. Furthermore, the Federal Reserve’s quantitative tightening is further tightening credit conditions, as shown by a record gap between the actual Federal funds rate and the San Francisco Fed’s proxy funds rate.

The argument is supported by six detailed charts. The first chart, depicting US new rents, shows a divergence between lagging CPI rent of primary residences and real-time measures. While the CPI rent measure on the left scale continues its upward trend toward 8% annualized in late 2022, Apartment List asking rents and RealPage asking rents on the right scale have both plummeted from peak levels near 35% in late 2021 down toward zero or negative rates by November 2022. The second chart shows multifamily units under construction relative to rental stock as a percentage from 1970 to 2022, highlighting that the level in late 2022 has spiked to over 2.0%, the highest supply injection since the mid-1970s. 

The third chart illustrates annual mortgage cost as a percentage of household income from 1948 to 2022. It reveals a dramatic vertical spike in late 2022 to 45%, a level of unaffordability matching the peak of the 2006 housing bubble and the high-interest-rate environment of the early 1980s. The fourth chart indexes the decline in existing home sales over 16 months across several historical economic episodes, showing that the current housing market collapse is exceptionally rapid, tracking the steep paths of the Great Financial Crisis and the double-dip recession of the 1980s by falling to roughly 65% of its starting value. 

The fifth chart compares the federal funds rate to the San Francisco Fed’s proxy funds rate, which accounts for balance sheet shrinkage. In late 2022, the proxy rate surged to nearly 6.0%, creating the widest recorded gap above the actual federal funds rate. Finally, the sixth chart tracks three major US consumer price inflation measures—the Cleveland Fed median CPI, the Atlanta Fed sticky CPI, and the Cleveland Fed trimmed mean CPI—showing that after decades of low stability, all three measures surged in 2022 to peak annualized rates between 6% and 8% before showing tentative signs of stabilization.

This page analyzes the contrasting energy inflation dynamics in Europe and California, emphasizing how market design, infrastructure issues, and policy choices drive extreme price disparities. 

The analysis begins with the Euro Area energy inflation chart, a line graph showing year-over-year percentage changes from 1997 through late 2022. Historically fluctuating between negative ten percent and fifteen percent, Euro Area energy inflation skyrocketed in late 2021 and 2022, peaking near fifty percent. This surge is attributed to Europe’s pre-war reliance on Russian energy and a marginal pricing mechanism where clean energy producers (wind, solar, hydro, and nuclear) are paid the same high rates as natural gas generators when fossil fuels set the marginal price. 

An accompanying table, showing the percentage of all hours that different sources set marginal electricity prices across Europe, illustrates this vulnerability. In Germany, fossil fuels set the marginal price ninety-one percent of the time, followed by Spain at eighty-nine percent, Portugal at eighty-seven percent, Italy at eighty-six percent, the United Kingdom at eighty-four percent, Greece at seventy-seven percent, and Ireland at sixty-one percent. The primary exceptions are France, where non-fossil sources set prices ninety-three percent of the time, and Denmark, where imports dominate at sixty-two percent. To mitigate this shock, European nations have implemented household subsidies and caps on non-gas producers to offset roughly sixty percent of the impact. The author notes that uncapped December 2022 electricity prices ranged from one hundred to three hundred fifty Euros per megawatt-hour, whereas new price caps are set at two hundred forty-five Euros in the United Kingdom, one hundred fifty Euros in Germany, one hundred Euros in France, and sixty-seven Euros in Italy and Spain. 

Looking forward, the author highlights fiscal and operational challenges, such as Germany’s first of five liquefied natural gas import regasification facilities tripling its original budget to approximately ten billion dollars. Additionally, France’s nuclear power industry has been running at only fifty percent capacity, threatening further price strains across Europe if nuclear exports remain constrained through the winter.

The bottom portion of the page contrasts these dynamics with the United States, displaying two line charts tracking prices from January 2021 to January 2023. The first chart, showing wholesale natural gas prices in dollars per million British thermal units, reveals a dramatic gap. The US Henry Hub benchmark remained flat and low, ending around five dollars, while Europe's Title Transfer Facility index peaked over eighty dollars in mid-2022 before dropping to twenty-six dollars. Notably, California gas prices surged to thirty-eight dollars near the end of 2022. The second chart illustrates the resulting wholesale electricity price gap in dollars per megawatt-hour. The average price for Germany, Spain, and France shows immense volatility, spiking repeatedly to peaks near four hundred fifty dollars before settling around two hundred fifty dollars. In contrast, the US PJM region remained extremely low and stable under one hundred dollars, while California electricity prices spiked sharply to nearly three hundred dollars in late 2022. 

The author concludes by blaming California’s electricity and gas spikes on a series of structural vulnerabilities, questioning what else could be expected from a state that closed PG&E natural gas storage facilities, shut down nuclear power plants, faced urban outmigration to high-energy-demand rural and suburban areas, suffered pipeline maintenance delays, and now faces heightened natural gas competition from Canadian and Mexican exports.

This page analyzes the gradual decline of globalization, arguing that while globalization is not in a complete collapse, it has clearly receded from its historical peaks. To support this, the author first presents three line charts showing global macroeconomic trends as a percentage of world GDP from 1970 to 2020 or 2022. The first chart, tracking global exports, shows that while services have climbed steadily to around 6% of GDP, goods exports peaked near 22% around 2008 and have since declined to just under 20% in 2021. The second chart shows that global foreign direct investment flows have historically been volatile, peaking near 5% of GDP in 2000 and 2007, before sliding to roughly 1.5% in early 2022. The third chart illustrates global portfolio equity flows, which also show high volatility, peaking above 1.5% of GDP in the late 1990s and mid-2000s, and resting near 1.25% in 2021. The text notes that only a portion of the decline in goods trade is due to reshoring, with much of it driven by declining commodity prices. 

The core of the page’s argument focus shifts to the collapse of the Western strategy of constructive engagement through trade with Russia and China. Specifically, Germany's "Ostpolitik" approach to Russia has failed, resulting in Europe's energy and financial embargo, while US-China relations have rapidly deteriorated. The author highlights aggressive US policies, such as placing restrictions on AI chips, expanding the restricted entity list to 500 Chinese companies, and enforcing the Foreign Direct Product Rule. These rising tensions are cited by US companies in the 2022 AmCham China survey as their single largest challenge. Furthermore, the author notes that the US is poised to implement new restrictions on outbound FDI into critical Chinese technology sectors. 

Two final charts illustrate this geopolitical fracturing. The first, measuring the trade war's impact on US import counterparties from 2015 to 2022, reveals that China’s share of US imports peaked near 22% in 2018 but fell sharply to around 17% by late 2022. Meanwhile, imports from Europe, Mexico, Canada, and a combined group of Korea, Vietnam, and Taiwan have gained ground or remained resilient. The final chart indexes OECD greenfield capital spending from 2012 to 2022, demonstrating a severe retreat from China. While OECD investments into the European Union and the United States rose to index levels of approximately 210 and 170 respectively by 2022, OECD greenfield investments into China collapsed from a peak index value of 150 in 2018 to below 30 in 2022.

This page from the report focuses on the performance of active investment managers, arguing that a decade of financial repression by central banks after the 2009 recession severely hindered active equity and hedge fund managers. Michael Cembalest explains that central bank interventions, particularly the European Central Bank purchasing split-rated bonds near junk status, artificially compressed credit spreads and kept insolvent companies solvent. Citing data from the Bank for International Settlements, he notes that "zombie" companies in the developed world rose from just 1% of total market capitalization in 1990 to 12% by 2018, a figure that likely increased further by early 2021. 

Four charts illustrate these trends, showing that active managers historically struggle when real interest rates and inflation are low. The two top charts focus on active equity managers, plotting an index of average US large-cap core managers against the S&P 500 starting from a base value of 100 in January 1990. The top-left chart compares this index against the five-year average of the Fed funds rate less core CPI, revealing that active managers steadily underperformed, with the index falling from near 100 in 2010 to around 86 by late 2022, closely mirroring the decline of real policy rates into negative territory. The top-right chart compares the same active manager index against the five-year average of consumer price inflation, demonstrating a similar long-term downward trend as inflation remained subdued before spiking after 2020. 

The bottom two charts shift the focus to hedge funds, plotting the HFRI Equity Hedge Funds versus the S&P 500 index from a base of 100 in December 1989. In the bottom-left chart, which compares hedge fund performance against the real Fed funds rate, the HFRI index peaks near 250 around 2010 before suffering a steep decline down to near 100 by 2022 as real rates plummeted. The bottom-right chart tracks this same hedge fund index against the five-year average of consumer price inflation. Together, these charts suggest a strong correlation between low-yield, low-inflation environments and active management underperformance. Looking forward, the author suggests that if the financial system is returning to a period of positive real interest rates, value-oriented portfolio managers may finally experience more favorable stock-picking and bond-picking conditions than they have seen in many years.

This page analyzes the deepening geopolitical divide between the Western sphere of influence, led by the United States, and the emerging alignment between China and Russia. The author argues that this structural divergence explains the speed with which Chinese financial institutions and energy markets stepped in to replace Western partners following Russian aggressions in 2014 and 2022, reflecting the "no-limits" partnership between Beijing and Moscow.

The primary visual, titled "The structure of global public allegiances," maps nationally representative public opinion surveys across 137 countries. The horizontal axis measures the positive view of the United States from 0% to 100%, while the vertical axis shows the average positive view of China and Russia from 0% to 100%. The chart reveals an increasingly inverse relationship, where countries are migrating away from a moderate middle position into two distinct clusters. One branch, extending toward the top-left, shows countries with highly favorable views of China and Russia (above 80%) and low favorability toward the US (below 30%), including Laos, Iran, and Serbia. The opposite branch, extending toward the bottom-right, highlights the US sphere of influence, featuring nations like Japan, South Korea, Great Britain, Poland, and Germany, which hold highly positive views of the US (above 70%) and very low favorability toward China and Russia (below 20%). 

The second chart, "Cross-border syndicated loans to Russia," tracks bank lending from 2010 to 2022 in billions of US dollars, highlighting the 2014 invasion of Crimea as a pivotal turning point. Before the invasion, European nations like France, Germany, and Italy, along with the US and Japan, were significant lenders to Russia. Following the 2014 invasion, lending from these Western countries and Japan plummeted, with most falling toward zero by 2022. In contrast, syndicated lending from China rose dramatically, climbing from approximately $20 billion in 2014 to over $40 billion by late 2021, demonstrating how Chinese banks successfully substituted for Western capital.

The final chart, "Chinese vs European purchases of Russian energy," covers the period from 2019 to late 2022 to show how energy trade shifted following the invasion of Ukraine. It plots European purchases of Russian energy in million tonnes of oil equivalent per day on the right axis and Chinese purchases of Russian energy in billions of US dollars on the left axis. While European purchases remained steady between 0.7 and 0.8 million tonnes per day through 2021, they fell sharply to around 0.3 million tonnes per day by late 2022 due to embargoes. Concurrently, Chinese spending on Russian energy, which fluctuated between $2 billion and $4 billion from 2019 through mid-2021, surged to over $8 billion in 2022, highlighting how China absorbed Russian energy exports displaced by Western sanctions.

This page focuses on the extreme geopolitical and industrial complexity of global semiconductor supply chains, specifically analyzing the heavy reliance of China on Taiwan and the sheer difficulty of manufacturing advanced chips. The author argues that China's reliance on Taiwan for high-value semiconductor imports is historically unprecedented, with only ten percent of Chinese semiconductor demand being met by its domestic production. As of 2021, Taiwan accounted for a seventy percent share of China's chip consumption, with TSMC producing ten percent in its Nanjing and Shanghai factories and exporting the remaining sixty percent directly from Taiwan.

A column chart titled "Regional reliance for critical goods" visualizes this dynamic by comparing China’s seventy percent chip reliance on Taiwan to Europe’s pre-war reliance on Russian energy, which stands at only about twenty percent. The comparison highlights that no other country is so disproportionately dependent on another for a critical high-value import. To counter this vulnerability, China’s National Integrated Circuit Investment Fund has backed national champions with mixed success. While companies like SMIC (achieving seven-nanometer chips), YMTC, San'an Optoelectronics, AMEC, and JCET have made progress, others like Tsinghua, Wuhan Hongxin, and Quanxin Circuits have gone bankrupt, leaving China short of its domestic semiconductor production goals.

Another visual, a line chart titled "TSMC semiconductor capabilities," shows the dramatic historical decline in transistor node sizes, measured in nanometers, from 1987 to 2022. The curve starts at fifteen hundred nanometers in 1987, steadily shrinking past one hundred and eighty nanometers in 2001, twenty-eight nanometers in 2011, and reaching five nanometers by 2022. This demonstrates how global leaders like TSMC have maintained a massive technological lead, while most Chinese foundries are still working on older fourteen to twenty-eight nanometer chips.

In concluding, the page characterizes advanced semiconductors as the "Faberge eggs of industrial complexity." The author describes the near-impossible barriers to entry for manufacturing ten, seven, five, and three-nanometer chips. These advanced nodes depend entirely on extreme ultraviolet photolithography machines designed and built by ASML in the Netherlands, which produces only forty-five to fifty-five of these machines per year. The manufacturing process itself requires clean rooms ten thousand times cleaner than hospital surgical suites, chip etching processes consisting of seven hundred distinct steps over several weeks, and a supply chain involving components flown thousands of miles between specialized global sites using exotic chemicals, gases, and rare metals from thousands of international suppliers.

This page analyzes the long-term fiscal challenge of rising entitlement spending crowding out non-defense discretionary spending, which is vital for productivity and future growth. To ground the discussion, the page first defines non-defense discretionary spending, listing key areas such as transportation infrastructure, education and training, science and energy, healthcare initiatives like vaccine development, and law enforcement. 

A central line chart displays federal spending as a percentage of GDP from 1970 through CBO projections reaching 2032. The chart contrasts the relatively stable, low path of non-defense discretionary spending, which hovers around 3% to 4% of GDP, with the climbing trajectory of entitlement spending, which rose from around 5% of GDP in 1970 to over 10% in recent years. This shift is highlighted by the rising ratio of entitlement spending to discretionary spending, which stood at 1.0x in 1970, grew to 2.0x in 1990, reached 2.8x in 2021, and is projected to hit 4.0x by 2032. By this point, entitlement payments plus interest are expected to permanently consume all federal revenue.

To address this widening gap, the author highlights several partial and politically challenging solutions. These include Senator Sanders’ proposal to raise income and capital gains taxes on earnings over $250,000 to raise 1% of GDP annually, Senator Warren’s proposed wealth tax of 1% on fortunes over $20 million to raise 0.5% to 0.7% of GDP, and removing the cap on income subject to Social Security taxes without raising benefits. Other options include means-testing Medicare benefits, raising the retirement eligibility age, and cutting defense spending, which currently stands at 3.5% of GDP. 

Footnotes provide historical and structural context. The author notes that programs like Social Security and Medicare were historically decried as socialism or communist plots by political opponents when first introduced in the mid-20th century. Additionally, the author addresses whether a single-payer healthcare system could curb entitlement costs, concluding that while it would grant the government more leverage to lower Medicare and Medicaid costs, it is unlikely to reduce overall spending unless healthcare access and availability are restricted, especially given that entitlement program costs have historically vastly exceeded initial projections.

This page, titled "Topic #7: Just the Vax and nothing but the Vax," concludes the J.P. Morgan report with Michael Cembalest's analysis of COVID-19 mRNA vaccine efficacy and booster uptake. While Cembalest avoids evaluating the societal costs and benefits of broader policy measures like lockdowns or mask mandates, he strongly supports the efficacy of mRNA vaccines, particularly for older populations. He highlights CDC data from September to November 2022 showing that bivalent booster vaccines boast a 73% to 84% efficacy rate against hospitalization for immunocompetent individuals over the age of 65. This efficacy spanned major variants of the time, including BA.5, BQ.1, and BQ.11. Furthermore, CDC data from April to September 2022 indicated that COVID-19 mortality was roughly 14 times higher for unvaccinated individuals than for those who were fully vaccinated. Despite these figures, Cembalest notes a concerning gap in vaccine uptake: while 94% of Americans over 65 completed the primary vaccination series, only 36% received the updated bivalent booster, which likely accounts for why seniors represent the largest share of hospitalizations. 

The author criticizes Florida Governor Ron DeSantis's call to investigate vaccine manufacturers for fraud, pointing out the contradiction of taking such a stance in a state with the nation's second-oldest population. He compares modern vaccine skepticism with the belief held by 10% of Americans that the 1969 moon landing was a hoax, accompanying this observation with a historical photograph of Buzz Aldrin on the moon in July 1969, taken by Neil Armstrong. 

An accompanying line chart displays the reproductive rate of various COVID-19 variants over a 90-day period, using data from Trevor Bedford and JP Weiland as of December 2022. The chart reveals that while older variants like BA.5, BA.4, BQ.1, BA.2, BA.2.12.1, and standard XBB see their reproductive rates drop sharply from initial levels of 1.4 to 1.8 down to near or below 1.2 by day 90, the newer XBB.1.5 variant exhibits a persistently high reproductive rate. XBB.1.5 starts at approximately 1.8 and only marginally declines to about 1.7 by day 90, illustrating its high potential to outcompete other variants due to increased resistance to vaccines and acquired immunity.

On this page, J.P. Morgan’s Michael Cembalest argues that several fixed income categories are currently unattractive because their spreads or yields are too tight relative to the broader economic outlook, failing to provide enough compensation for the underlying risks. While he does not foresee a major crisis for investors in high-grade corporate bonds, he contends that a spread of 150 basis points does not represent good value. 

To illustrate these tight spreads, the page displays five historical charts, each showing data up to late December 2022. The first chart plots US investment grade corporate spreads using the JULI index versus US Treasuries from 2000 to 2022. Spreads peaked near 550 basis points during the 2008 financial crisis and have now compressed to a red dot at around 150 basis points. The second chart shows Emerging Markets dollar bond spreads against US Treasuries from 2002 to 2022, highlighting a historical peak near 950 basis points during the financial crisis and a current spread of approximately 420 basis points. The third chart tracks US high yield bond spreads using the JPDFHYI index against US Treasuries from 1995 to 2022. Spreads crested above 1,200 basis points in both 2002 and 2008, with high-yield energy highlighted near the low point in 2020, and currently sit at about 450 basis points. The fourth chart tracks US leveraged loan prices from 2000 to 2022 using the SPBDALB index, showing a crash below 65 in 2008 and a current price of roughly 92 to 93. The fifth chart depicts Pan European high yield percent yields from 2000 to 2022, which spiked to nearly 18% in late 2008 and are currently at roughly 5.5%.

The second half of the page shifts focus to Brazil, noting that "the jury is out." The J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Debt portfolio management team is adopting a cautious, highly tactical stance on Brazil local bonds rather than adding to long-term positions. They are waiting for clarity on the newly elected Lula administration's fiscal framework, potential tax reforms, and plans for large state-owned enterprises, despite Brazil offering one of the highest risk premiums among emerging market local bonds. This situation is illustrated by a chart of Brazil's sovereign 10-year local currency bond yields from 2006 to late 2022. The yield, which peaked near 16.5% in 2016 and bottomed near 7% in 2020, has risen back to roughly 13%. An annotation on the chart emphasizes that the team remains cautious until Lula's spending plans are revealed, though a possible upgrade could follow.

This page analyzed by Michael Cembalest at J.P. Morgan outlines attractive opportunities in global fixed income markets for yield-oriented investors at the beginning of 2023. While spreads have widened, Cembalest argues that solvency and systemic risks in the financial sector are not comparable to the 2009 financial crisis. However, due to historically low market depth and liquidity, he warns that investors could see "flash crash" fixed income volatility in 2023. This risk is compounded by the Federal Reserve's balance sheet reduction and a potential replay of the disruptive 1995 and 2011 "GOP House / Democratic President" debt limit negotiations, with Congress likely needing to raise the debt limit by autumn. 

The analysis is supported by eight charts. The first chart, tracking US Municipal yields from 2000 to late 2022, shows both long duration munis and Municipals 1-17 spiking significantly in 2022, with long-duration munis rising to over 4% and Municipals 1-17 climbing above 3%, reversing a decade of low yields. A second chart of 10-year sovereign bond yields for Europe and China shows European yields reversing from negative territory in 2020 to reach roughly 2.5% by late 2022, while Chinese yields stabilized near 3.0%. A third chart highlights the spread between 30-year mortgages and 10-year Treasuries from 2005 to late 2022, showing that this spread surged in late 2022 to approximately 275 basis points, approaching the peaks seen during the 2008 financial crisis. 

Further charts focus on specific credit segments. A chart of AAA asset-backed securities spreads versus Treasuries across commercial real estate, auto, and credit cards from 1998 to 2022 reveals that while spreads widened slightly in 2022 to around 100 to 150 basis points, they remain far below the massive spikes of 2008, where commercial real estate spreads exceeded 600 basis points. Looking at emerging markets, a chart of 10-year sovereign bond yields for South Africa and Mexico from 2006 to late 2022 shows local currency yields rising in late 2022, with South Africa exceeding 11% and Mexico approaching 9%. A chart tracking floating-rate instruments in USD from 2000 to late 2022 illustrates a dramatic yield surge, with US Investment Grade Corporate Floating Rate Notes yielding over 5% and AA Bank Commercial Paper over 4.5%. 

The final two charts examine preferred securities. One chart plots the preferred option adjusted spread (the POP1 index of basis points versus US Treasuries) for US investment-grade preferred stock from 2000 to late 2022. The spread rose to roughly 150 to 200 basis points by the end of 2022, which is only a fraction of the 1,600 basis point peak seen in 2008. The final chart covers yields to worst for preferred yields from 2010 to late 2022, showing Europe Contingent Capital yielding nearly 9%, US High Yield Preferred near 8%, and US High Grade Preferred around 6.5%. An accompanying note explains that European Contingent Capital (CoCos) trade at higher yields than US preferred stocks due to the lower overall credit rating of the CoCo market, explicit write-down and payment triggers linked to capital ratios in their prospectuses, and the inclusion of 10% to 15% emerging market bank securities.

On this page, Michael Cembalest warns that failure to sustainably resolve US debt and spending issues will eventually invite disruptive economic and political forces, metaphorically described as the "Visigoths." While he suspects the immediate crisis will be resolved, he cautions that the structural problem will inevitably return for a true day of reckoning. 

To illustrate this warning, the page features a reproduction of Joseph-Noël Sylvestre’s 1890 painting, *The Sack of Rome in 410 AD*, depicting the chaos of Alaric I and the Visigoths looting the Roman capital. The accompanying narrative details how Rome was attacked for the first time in 800 years and was spared further destruction only after paying a steep tribute of gold, silver, luxury goods, and captives. This historical collapse is punctuated by a quote from Saint Jerome lamenting the fall of the city that had once conquered the world.

Below this historical parallel, Cembalest provides a detailed glossary outlining various mechanisms and options surrounding the contemporary US debt ceiling impasse. First, it defines "Debt Prioritization," a proposal by some House Republicans to selectively pay certain obligations, which Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen has dismissed as a default, though the FOMC has historically discussed similar contingency plans. Second, it notes "Spending Cuts with a Debt Limit Vote," where House Speaker Kevin McCarthy and his caucus have demanded tying the debt limit to capping discretionary spending at FY22 levels and balancing the budget within ten years. Third, the glossary covers Senator Joe Manchin’s proposal for a "Bipartisan Commission" to negotiate fiscal reforms, echoing the 2011 Congressional deficit reduction committee. Fourth, it addresses the hypothetical issuance of a "Trillion Dollar Coin" by the Treasury, which Yellen has dismissed as a gimmick. Finally, it explains the "Discharge Petition," a procedural maneuver that would allow House Democrats to bypass the Speaker and force a vote on a clean debt ceiling increase if they can secure the support of at least five Republican members.

This page discusses the unexpected economic resilience in the United States and Europe, which has been bolstered by an unusually warm Northern Hemisphere winter and a sequence of positive economic surprises. The author highlights several positive US indicators, including retail sales, strong manufacturing output, low jobless claims, and resilient residential construction employment. Concurrently, Europe has successfully navigated the winter with high natural gas inventories, and China's economic reopening has further brightened the global growth outlook.

To illustrate these trends, the top-left chart shows population-weighted historical heating degree days in the Northern Hemisphere during January and February from 1973 to 2023. The data reveals that the winter of 2023 was exceptionally mild, with heating degree days dropping near the 4,200 mark, representing one of the lowest points in the fifty-year dataset. Beside this, a line chart displays the OECD Economic Surprise Index from January 2021 to January 2023 for the Eurozone, Japan, and the United States. This chart shows a coordinated upward spike across all three regions in early 2023, indicating that economic data consistently outperformed analyst expectations, particularly in the Eurozone, which rebounded sharply from deep negative territory.

Despite this near-term economic resilience, the author cautions that monetary policy rates have not yet fully normalized. Real US three-month and ten-year yields remain negative when measured against trailing inflation. Although consumer and producer price increases are falling, the author anticipates that it is too soon for the Federal Reserve to halt its rate-hiking cycle, predicting two to three more Fed hikes ahead and a mild US recession, though the likelihood and potential severity of that recession may be shrinking. 

This inflationary picture is represented in the bottom-left chart, which tracks US core consumer and producer prices from 2015 to 2023. The chart depicts both Core CPI and Core PPI peaking in late 2021 to early 2022 before beginning a steady descent, with Core CPI dropping to around 5.5% and Core PPI falling even faster. Finally, the bottom-right chart plots the ISM manufacturing PMI composite index alongside the three-month leading indicator of ISM new orders less inventories from 1983 to 2023. This chart demonstrates that the new orders minus inventories metric has plunged well below zero, suggesting an impending downturn in the broader ISM manufacturing PMI despite current pockets of economic strength.

This page presents a collection of appendix charts illustrating the long-term fiscal health and structural budget challenges of the United States, focusing on interest payments, historical tax changes, under-budgeted healthcare costs, defense spending, and projected deficits. 

The first chart tracks US government net interest payments as a percentage of GDP from 1960 through Congressional Budget Office projections to 2035. Net interest payments peaked near 3.0% of GDP in the late 1980s and early 1990s before falling, but they are projected to climb sharply in the coming decade, approaching 3.5% of GDP by 2035. 

To put potential solutions in context, a second chart maps historical US tax increases by legislative year, plotting the additional taxes raised annually against federal receipts as a percentage of GDP prior to the legislation. This scatter plot demonstrates that while the US has successfully passed tax increases exceeding 2.0% of GDP in the past, such as in 1950 and 1951, these occurred when overall federal receipts were much lower. The chart contrasts these historical points with Senator Sanders' high-net-worth tax proposal, Senator Warren's wealth tax proposal, and a benchmark required increase of roughly 2.5% of GDP represented by a red square, which would be necessary to restore the ratio of entitlements to non-defense discretionary spending back to its historical 2.2x level.

A table on healthcare entitlement programs illustrates the historical tendency to underestimate public spending. For example, the 1965 Medicare hospital insurance program was estimated to cost $9 billion annually but actually cost $67 billion, representing a 7.4 to 1 actual-to-estimated cost ratio.
