Similarly, the 1967 Medicare entire program had a 9.2 to 1 overrun ratio, and the 1987 Medicaid DSH program actualized at $17 billion versus an estimated $1 billion, a 17 to 1 ratio.

Defense spending trends are explored in two visuals. A historical line chart of US defense spending as a percentage of GDP shows a massive peak of 37% in 1944, followed by a steady downward trend to around 3% to 4% in the 2010s and 2020s, with a projected slight decline continuing out to 2030. An adjacent table ranks the top 15 nations by defense spending per capita in 2021, with Qatar leading at $3,955, followed by Israel at $2,769, and the United States in third at $2,405.

Finally, a crossover point chart projects when US federal revenues will be surpassed by mandatory spending and interest payments. Looking at the years 2019 to 2032, the chart highlights the temporary spike in outlays caused by pandemic-era Covid spending, which briefly pushed spending above 22% of GDP. More critically, the long-term projection shows that by 2032, the combined cost of entitlements, mandatory outlays, and rising interest payments is expected to permanently cross and exceed federal revenues, which are projected to remain flat near 17% to 18% of GDP.

In this J.P. Morgan publication, Michael Cembalest advises investors against chasing the early 2023 US equity market rally, arguing that it is built on shaky foundations. He attributes the market's gains to the appreciation of low-quality and highly shorted stocks, a massive six-trillion-dollar rebound in China's money supply, and overly optimistic expectations that Federal Reserve rate hikes will not severely impact corporate earnings or the broader economy. To support this cautious view, the page displays six charts and highlights a significant downgrade in corporate earnings estimates.

The first chart, titled "What kind of rally is this?", plots performance indices indexed to January 2022 for low-quality and high short-interest stocks. Both indices show a sharp, speculative spike in early 2023 after hitting multi-month lows around October 2022 and January 2023. The second chart, "Market implied Fed funds rate," plots expectations for the policy rate from March 2023 through January 2024. The curve peaks at approximately 5.3% around July and September 2023 before descending toward 4.9% by early 2024, showing that the market anticipates rate cuts later in the year. 

To evaluate the broader economic impact of these interest rate hikes, two charts examine consumer debt. "Household debt service share of disposable income" breaks down total debt service into mortgage and consumer components from 1980 through mid-2022. It shows that overall debt service relative to disposable income remains near historic lows at around 9% to 10%, well below the peaks of over 13% seen in 2007. However, the next chart, "Annual mortgage cost for new homebuyers," reveals a more alarming trend. It shows that mortgage costs for new buyers have spiked dramatically to 40% of household income by late 2022, a level not seen since the housing bubble and previous periods of extreme interest rates in the early 1980s.

The final two charts focus on deteriorating corporate health. "Costs rising faster than sales" measures year-over-year percentage changes from 2000 through late 2022, illustrating that cost growth has recently overtaken sales growth, a pattern that historically pressures profit margins. Adjacent to this, "Leading margin indicator predicts downside ahead" compares S&P 500 net margins against an NFIB small business composite indicator measuring demand versus wage costs with an 18-month lead. The NFIB indicator has collapsed deep into negative territory, signaling a sharp imminent decline in S&P 500 profit margins. The author cements this warning by noting in a footnote that Q4 earnings-per-share estimates have fallen by 1.7% since the close of the earnings season, compared to a historical average increase of 2.8%. This represents the largest non-recessionary downgrade in 24 years, trailing only the 2001 recession, the 2008 financial crisis, and the initial wave of the pandemic.

This page of the publication examines the future profitability of the internet search business, analyzing the economic and computational challenges that arise from integrating large language models into search engines. With Microsoft's CEO asserting that search gross margins are set to drop forever and OpenAI's Sam Altman highlighting the vulnerability of existing search monopolies, Google faces potential headwinds. Since 2018, Google's operating margins, which include YouTube, have averaged roughly 24 percent. While standard Google search queries cost a mere 0.2 to 0.3 cents in infrastructure expenses, ChatGPT queries are estimated to cost between 0.4 and 4.5 cents, with a midpoint of 2 cents. According to research from Morgan Stanley, every 10 percent increase in Google queries powered by AI could degrade Google’s operating margin by 1.5 percent to 1.7 percent. This economic pressure raises the open question of whether Google and Microsoft will offer premium, LLM-enhanced search products only to users with high expected ad revenue potential.

The author notes that these cost concerns might be overstated. Google's Bard AI relies on a lightweight, less computationally demanding version of its LaMDA model. Additionally, sparse models like Google's GLaM can narrow the necessary field of knowledge to answer questions; GLaM is seven times larger than GPT-3, yet it requires two-thirds less energy to train and half the computing effort. 

These arguments are contextualized by two charts. The first, a line chart tracking the month-over-month percentage change in search and chat website traffic from January 2022 to January 2023, shows a sudden divergence starting around November 2022. While both series fluctuated near a 0.0 percent change for most of the year, the combined ChatGPT and Bing traffic grew by roughly 0.5 percent month-over-month by January 2023, whereas Google's traffic growth dipped to about negative 0.3 percent. Despite this shift, an adjacent pie chart displaying search engine market share from January 2022 to January 2023 highlights Google's near-monopoly. Google commands 92.0 percent of the market, while Bing holds just 3.2 percent, Yahoo! stands at 1.3 percent, Yandex at 1.1 percent, Baidu at 0.9 percent, DuckDuckGo at 0.6 percent, and other engines make up the remaining 0.2 percent. This overwhelming volume suggests that Google's LLM could learn and improve much faster than ChatGPT due to the sheer scale of its daily user interactions.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, discusses the future of Large Language Model capabilities by examining the Big Bench project, a collaborative benchmarking effort involving Google, OpenAI, and over one hundred other artificial intelligence firms. This project evaluates LLMs against human performance across more than two hundred diverse, complex tasks designed to push the limits of language models. The author argues that while increasing parameter sizes and providing more context examples improve performance, AI models still have a long way to go before catching up to humans on highly difficult tasks. Additionally, OpenAI and Google models perform similarly when calibrated at the same scale, indicating the competitive landscape is just beginning. Cembalest forecasts that the next frontiers for LLMs will include integration into productivity suites like Microsoft Office 365 and Google Docs, longer context windows, the ability to digest visual charts and data matrices, and shorter latency periods for bulk users.

The page features two line charts displaying data from the June 2022 Big Bench project. The first chart, which evaluates performance with one-shot prompting against human raters, plots normalized performance on a scale where one hundred represents very good performance against an effective parameter count ranging from ten to the sixth power to ten to the eleventh power. It reveals a stark gap between AI and human capabilities: while the average human rater scores around forty-five and the best human rater scores around seventy-five, the Google BIG-G and OpenAI GPT models both score below fifteen even at their largest parameter sizes of ten to the eleventh power. The second chart illustrates performance on JSON multiple choice tasks using the same parameter scale. This chart compares one-shot and three-shot prompting for both BIG-G and GPT, demonstrating that performance climbs steadily with scale, reaching scores of fourteen to sixteen at ten to the eleventh parameters. It also highlights that three-shot prompting consistently yields slightly better results than one-shot prompting for both developers' models.

At the bottom of the page, the author outlines several indicative Big Bench challenges to illustrate the complexity of the tasks being tested. These include asking models to identify dark humor or sarcasm, translate English descriptions into Python code, solve logic grid puzzles, and find winning chess moves. Other tasks test the models' ability to guess movies from emoji plot descriptions, answer cryobiology questions in Spanish, pass GRE reading comprehension tests, determine shape intersections from verbal descriptions, solve crime stories, match equivalent English and Russian proverbs, align choices with human ethical judgments, and even have one instance of a model teach and evaluate another.

This page analyzes the sudden regulatory shutdown of Silicon Valley Bank (SIVB) due to inadequate liquidity and insolvency. Author Michael Cembalest highlights the scale of the collapse, noting SIVB’s $209 billion in assets represent roughly two-thirds of Washington Mutual’s 2008 failure, and evaluates the bank's extreme structural liability issues stemming from a heavy reliance on venture capital and institutional funding rather than stable, traditional retail deposits. 

To illustrate SIVB's precarious positioning, the page features a scatter plot of US bank loan-to-deposit ratios based on Q3 2022 data. The chart compares the estimated retail deposit share of total deposits on the y-axis (ranging from 0% to 100%) against loans plus securities as a percentage of deposits on the x-axis (ranging from 70% to 120%). While peer banks like J.P. Morgan, Citigroup, and Bank of America cluster in safer zones with higher retail deposit shares and lower asset-to-deposit ratios, SIVB is a severe outlier in the "Higher Risk Deposit Base" region. SIVB's retail deposit share sits near 10% while its loans plus securities exceed 110% of deposits, exposing it to massive capital shortfalls during rate hikes and deposit outflows.

The bank's deposit profile is further dissected in two pie charts representing Q3 2022 funding. SIVB's $177 billion in deposit funding was heavily concentrated in the tech sector, with early-stage technology accounting for 29%, general technology for 20%, international clients for 18%, and US global fund banking for 14%. A mere 7% was classified as private banking, which resembles traditional retail deposits. SIVB's off-balance-sheet funding, also totaling $177 billion, shows similar concentrations: 31% in technology, 23% in early-stage technology, 22% in early-stage life science and healthcare, and 13% in general life science and healthcare. This extreme concentration meant that by the end of 2022, $152 billion of SIVB’s $173 billion in customer deposits were uninsured, with only $4.8 billion fully insured under the FDIC limit. Cembalest questions the underwriting discipline of VC firms that concentrated liquidity in a single bank with such a risk profile, especially given SIVB offered only a minor deposit premium of 0.60% over peers. A footnote mentions that deposit exclusivity arrangements required by SIVB on its borrowers, as reported by Mark Suster of Upfront Ventures, likely contributed to this concentration.

Finally, a historical sidebar outlines the percentage of bank resolutions where losses were imposed on uninsured depositors. Historical precedents show that uninsured depositors faced losses in 24% of bank resolutions from 1980–1987, 14% from 1988–1991, 65% from 1992–2007, 28% during the 2008 crisis, and 6% from 2009–2013, providing historical context for the potential losses facing SIVB's uninsured clients.

This page analyzes a critical systemic issue facing US banks in early 2023: the accumulation of massive unrealized losses on investment portfolios purchased during a period of generational lows in bond yields. The author explains that a massive $5.4 trillion surge in deposits occurred between Q4 2019 and Q1 2022. Because of weak loan demand, only about 15% of these deposits were lent out, forcing banks to invest the rest in cash or securities designated as either available-for-sale (AFS) or hold-to-maturity (HTM). Silicon Valley Bank (SIVB) is highlighted as a primary example of this behavior, as its HTM portfolio grew from $14 billion to $99 billion since 2019. The author notes that selling HTM securities is exceptionally complicated because doing so forces a mark-to-market accounting treatment on the rest of the portfolio, potentially triggering an urgent need for a capital raise. To evaluate the systemic risk, the author poses the question of how much duration risk banks took on and models the impact on capital ratios if all unrealized losses were immediately realized.

The first chart on the page, titled "Impact of unrealized securities losses on capital ratios," plots both the official Common Equity Tier 1 Capital Ratio and an adjusted capital ratio that accounts for these unrealized losses across various major US banks at the end of 2022. Most banks, such as JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Capital One, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo, show moderate declines in their adjusted capital ratios, generally remaining above 5%. SIVB, however, is a severe outlier, with its adjusted ratio collapsing from a healthy official level of around 12% to near or below 0%, underscoring its unique vulnerability given its high level of uninsured deposits. Other regional banks analyzed include Signature Bank, First Republic Bank, PacWest, and Zions Bancorporation. 

To the right, a chart titled "FDIC Q4 unrealized bank losses on investment securities" tracks total industry losses from 2008 through late 2022. It shows that while unrealized gains and losses fluctuated within a modest range of roughly positive $75 billion to negative $75 billion for over a decade, they plunged to an unprecedented deficit of nearly negative $675 billion by the end of 2022. This total is split between massive unrealized losses on both held-to-maturity and available-for-sale securities.

At the bottom of the page, two charts provide historical context on bank health. The first, "US bank tier 1 capital ratios," shows the industry-wide Tier 1 capital ratio as a percentage of risk-weighted assets from 1991 to 2022. While these capital ratios steadily climbed from roughly 8% in 1991 to nearly 14% by 2021, the author cautions that these official figures are exaggerated because they do not account for the steep unrealized losses in HTM portfolios. The final chart, "US loan-to-deposit ratio, all commercial banks," plots the loan-to-deposit ratio from 1973 through early 2023. This ratio peaked near 1.00x in the late 1990s and mid-2000s before embarking on a long-term decline that accelerated during the pandemic, bottoming at a historic low of under 0.65x in late 2021 and early 2022 due to the deposit surge, before ticking up slightly to around 0.70x by early 2023.

This page features J.P. Morgan's analysis of Charles Schwab alongside an appendix of charts detailing bank deposit trends and the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank. 

Michael Cembalest argues that Charles Schwab should not be grouped with vulnerable regional banks. Although Schwab holds a massive portfolio of underwater available-for-sale and held-to-maturity securities that would push its Common Equity Tier 1 ratio below zero if marked to market, the firm's fundamental liquidity metrics remain incredibly robust. Specifically, Schwab boasts a conservative loan-to-deposit ratio of just 10 percent and has only 20 percent of its deposits uninsured, which is the lowest uninsured ratio among its peers. Furthermore, the firm manages 7.5 trillion dollars in client assets that drive significant earnings, helping it post a 1.39 percent return on assets as of December 2022, the third-highest among thirty-two major US and European banks monitored by J.P. Morgan.

The appendix contains five charts explaining the broader banking crisis. The first chart, tracking Silicon Valley Bank's asset growth alongside the IPO cycle from 2016 to 2022, demonstrates a near-perfect correlation between quarterly asset growth and the volume of tech public offerings, both of which peaked dramatically in 2020 and 2021. The second chart illustrates that this massive surge in Silicon Valley Bank's asset growth unfortunately coincided with historically low yields, as the influx of deposits arrived precisely when the 10-year US Treasury yield dipped below 1 percent and the 30-year mortgage rate hovered near 3 percent, locking the bank into low-yielding assets just before rates spiked.

The next two charts examine system-wide deposit flight. One chart tracks the historical drawdown of US commercial bank deposits from peak levels between 1973 and 2023, revealing an unprecedented, steep deposit drawdown of roughly 5 percent in early 2023, a contraction far worse than any previous cycle in fifty years. The adjacent chart explains this flight by comparing money market fund yields to bank deposit rates from 2010 to 2023. It displays a widening, historically large gap as money market rates surged past 4 percent while bank deposit rates remained anchored near zero, creating a powerful incentive for depositors to move cash out of commercial banks. 

Finally, a stacked bar chart breaks down deposit types for select large institutions, including Bank of America, Citigroup, J.P. Morgan, PNC, Truist, U.S. Bancorp, and Wells Fargo. The visual categorizes deposits into stable retail, operational wholesale, other retail (comprising foreign deposits, accounts exceeding FDIC insurance limits, and non-relationship CDs), and non-operational wholesale. This breakdown illustrates that these major banks retain a high percentage of highly sticky, stable retail and operational wholesale deposits, differentiating them from more vulnerable regional institutions.

In this page from J.P. Morgan’s annual energy paper, titled "Growing Pains: The Renewable Transition in Adolescence," author Michael Cembalest assesses the progress and hurdles of the global clean energy transition. The opening text highlights several major milestones: clean technology investment is outperforming fossil fuel capital spending; combined wind and solar generation surpassed nuclear energy for the first time in 2021; and the International Energy Agency (IEA) projects peak fossil fuel demand this decade. Additionally, the next five years are expected to see 2,500 gigawatts of new renewable capacity, which equals the total added over the previous two decades. Rapid electric vehicle sales, heat pump adoption, and domestic US battery manufacturing plants are accelerating, with China alone matching the rest of the world combined in 2022 renewable additions. 

Despite these positive developments, Cembalest cautions that global decarbonization will be a slow, gradual process. Over $9.6 trillion has been spent on renewable energy and electricity grids since 2005, yet fossil fuels still account for roughly 80% of global primary energy consumption, falling only 5% since 2005. The transition remains challenging because heavy industrial, transport, commercial, and residential sectors are difficult to electrify, and the core pillars of modern infrastructure—such as steel, cement, ammonia, and plastics—remain fundamentally dependent on fossil fuels. 

To support these points, the author includes four charts. The top-left chart, "Clean tech spending outpacing fossil fuels," tracks the annual ratio of clean technology capital spending to fossil fuel spending from 2015 to 2023. Using data from S&P Global and the IEA, it shows that the investment ratio has steadily risen. S&P Global’s measure, which includes renewable power, grids, and storage, rose from under 0.8x in 2015 to around 1.3x by 2023. The broader IEA metric, which adds electric vehicles, biofuels, nuclear, and carbon capture, rose even higher, approaching 1.5x in 2023.

The top-right chart, "Fossil fuel share of primary energy since 1965," shows the long-term trend in the percentage of global primary energy consumption derived from coal, oil, and natural gas. It traces the gradual decline of fossil fuels through different historical periods, including the pre-existing hydropower era, the nuclear adoption era, and the beginning of the solar and wind era. Regionally, the European Union has made the most progress, with its fossil fuel share falling to roughly 70% by 2020. In contrast, the United States and China remain slightly above 80%, while emerging markets excluding China stand at roughly 86%.

The bottom-left chart, "Future global fossil fuel demand: depends who you ask," presents highly divergent projections for global fossil fuel demand in exajoules from 1990 to 2040. Under the EIA's slower transition scenario from late 2021, fossil fuel demand continues to rise, reaching nearly 650 exajoules by 2040. Under the EIA's faster transition scenario, demand peaks and holds steady around 520 exajoules. Meanwhile, the IEA's Stated Policies scenario from January 2023 shows a peak and gradual decline to roughly 470 exajoules by 2040, while its Announced Pledges scenario anticipates a steep drop to approximately 350 exajoules.

The bottom-right chart, "IEA consistently underestimated solar capacity growth," compares actual global annual solar additions from 2000 to 2022 against the IEA's consecutive ten-year forecasts. The actual solar additions line, plotted in red, spikes sharply to nearly 250 gigawatts by 2022, consistently and dramatically outperforming every annual IEA forecast curve published between 2009 and 2022. However, a concluding note on this chart puts this rapid growth into context, reminding readers that solar energy still represented only 2% of global primary energy use in 2022.

Michael Cembalest argues that while physical evidence clearly demonstrates the urgent need for a rapid energy transition, the process faces severe structural obstacles. These hurdles include permitting delays, a lack of eminent domain in the West, critical mineral shortages, rising resource nationalism, the high costs of decarbonizing industrial heat, grid integration issues, and the massive backup thermal power and storage costs required to support intermittent wind and solar energy. Because of these constraints, Cembalest contends that starving the oil and gas industry of capital will not accelerate the transition; instead, it risks causing severe energy shortages, similar to what Europe experienced due to mismanaged energy supplies. He advises fossil fuel-rich nations that their resources will be needed for many years to come. In support of this view, he highlights Warren Buffett's 60 billion dollar stake in Chevron and Occidental, alongside other natural gas and pipeline assets. Looking ahead, Cembalest predicts that future Energy Information Administration projections will show lower trajectories of fossil fuel use as a result of recent US energy legislation and European policy responses to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. 

To support his observations on the physical drivers of the transition, Cembalest presents four charts. The first is a dual-axis chart tracking ocean heat content and sea levels from 1955 to 2025. Ocean heat content, measured in zettajoules against a 1957 baseline, has steadily climbed to roughly 330 zettajoules, absorbing 10 zettajoules per year over the last decade—an amount equal to about 20 times annual global primary energy consumption. Concurrently, sea levels measured against a 1993 baseline have risen to approximately 100 millimeters. 

The second chart displays the variation in ice sheet mass for Antarctica and Greenland from 2002 to 2022. Both regions show a continuous loss of mass in gigatonnes, with Antarctica losing over 2,000 gigatonnes and Greenland experiencing a much steeper decline of approximately 5,000 gigatonnes by late 2022. 

The third visual is a stacked area chart measuring the greenhouse effect via radiative forcing in watts per square meter from 1979 to 2021. Total radiative forcing has nearly doubled, rising from 1.5 to over 3.0 watts per square meter, with carbon dioxide representing the vast majority of the impact, followed by methane, nitrous oxide, chlorofluorocarbons, hydrochlorofluorocarbons, and hydrofluorocarbons. 

The final chart compares absolute carbon dioxide emissions in billions of tonnes against emissions intensity per GDP in developed and emerging markets from 1965 to 2020. It shows that while emissions intensity has successfully declined in both developed markets (falling from roughly 0.35 to 0.15) and emerging markets (falling from 0.55 to 0.25), absolute emissions have diverged. Developed market emissions peaked around 2005 at 15 billion tonnes and have since fallen to around 11 billion tonnes, while emerging market emissions have risen dramatically from under 5 billion tonnes in the mid-1960s to over 22 billion tonnes.

This page of the J.P. Morgan annual energy paper presents an executive summary examining the feasibility of the energy transition, arguing that Western nations have set wind and solar targets that are historically unprecedented and highly ambitious, while China’s goals are comparatively realistic but paired with continued coal expansion. The primary analytical tool is a set of four charts showing gross electricity capacity additions in watts per year per capita, contrasting historical additions from all generation sources (solid lines) against the wind and solar capacity additions required by 2030 to meet official targets (dotted lines). 

The chart for the United States reveals that under the 2022 Energy Bill, the required annual capacity additions for wind and solar will need to rise to between 180 and 300 watts per capita, which surpasses the historical peak of all generation sources combined, which was just over 200 watts per capita set in the early 2000s. Similarly, the European Union's chart indicates that its REPowerEU target requires wind and solar additions of roughly 125 watts per capita, far exceeding the historical peak of about 70 watts per capita seen around 2010. Germany exhibits the most aggressive target; its 2023 Renewable Energy Sources Act mandates annual capacity additions approaching 350 watts per capita, which is nearly double its historical peak of around 200 watts per capita achieved in 2012. 

Conversely, China’s chart shows that its targets are within reach. The stated gigawatt target requires only about 40 watts per capita, and its 25% non-fossil target sits at around 90 watts per capita, both well below China's recent peak historical capacity addition of nearly 140 watts per capita in 2022. However, the commentary highlights that China is also building substantial fossil generation, approving 106 gigawatts of new coal capacity in 2022, an amount equal to the last five years of decommissioned coal capacity in the United States and Europe combined.

The text heavily focuses on the economic and operational risks of Germany's transition. Germany plans to decommission its final three nuclear plants, accelerate its exit from coal to 2030, and double the size of its electricity grid to support a 33% projected increase in electricity demand from electric vehicles, heat pumps, and electrolyzers. The author cites Bloomberg NEF's estimate that the German plan will cost $1 trillion by 2030, raising concerns about escalating electricity prices that could drive manufacturing out of the country. This risk is highlighted by the Verband der Chemischen Industrie warning that Germany could transition from an industrial country into an industrial museum. Additionally, the author references a McKinsey estimate that Germany faces a potential 30 gigawatt power shortfall by 2030, with peak load capacity falling to 90 gigawatts while peak load demand rises to 120 gigawatts.

This page examines the relationship between rising electric vehicle (EV) sales and future global oil demand, analyzing how long it takes for EV adoption to meaningfully displace fossil fuel consumption. The author begins by highlighting the rapid growth of EV sales, which reached 10% of global passenger car sales in 2022 after a 68% year-over-year increase, with an additional 40% gain projected for 2023. This growth is led globally by manufacturers such as Tesla, BYD, SAIC, and VW Group. Additionally, EV performance metrics continue to improve, with Argonne National Laboratory noting longer average ranges of up to 300 miles, faster acceleration, and better fuel efficiency. 

To illustrate these trends, the first column features a bar chart titled "Global sales of battery electric vehicles," measuring the number of vehicles in millions from 2021 to an estimated 2023. It reveals that global sales are projected to climb from approximately 6.5 million in 2021 to about 11 million in 2023, with China consistently representing the largest market share, followed by Europe, the United States, and other regions. Directly adjacent, a line chart titled "It takes time for EV sales to impact entire fleet" plots percentages from 2010 to 2022 to show why rapid sales growth lags in overall impact. Although the three-month average EV share of light-duty vehicle sales rose sharply to around 7% by the end of 2022, the actual EV share of the total vehicle fleet, the EV share of vehicle miles traveled, and the share of gasoline consumption displaced by EVs all remained flat and well below 1%. This delay is driven by the 12-to-13-year average lifespan of modern combustion engine vehicles.

The page poses the critical question of what global oil demand will look like in 10 to 15 years, noting the complexity of such projections given that nearly half of global oil consumption comes from non-transport sectors. This breakdown is shown in a donut chart titled "Global oil demand by sector," which divides consumption into transport (53%) and non-transport (47%). Within transport, passenger vehicles account for 27%, road freight accounts for 16%, and aviation and shipping make up 11%. Within non-transport, chemicals represent 17%, followed by other uses at 12%, buildings at 8%, oil refineries at 6%, and power generation at 4%. 

The final chart, titled "Oil demand, supply from existing fields and demand projections," plots oil in million barrels per day against a timeline from 1970 to 2050. It depicts historical demand rising steadily toward 100 million barrels per day by 2020. It forecasts a steep decline in oil supply from existing fields, assuming no new development, down to roughly 45 million barrels per day by 2050. In contrast, various demand projections for 2030, 2040, and 2050 remain highly resilient. Under the OPEC Reference and Advanced Technology cases, demand is expected to stay flat or even increase to around 105 million barrels per day through 2050. Middle-ground scenarios from Wood Mackenzie, Bloomberg New Energy Finance (BNEF), and BP New Momentum suggest demand will plateau but take at least 20 years to meaningfully decline. The most aggressive decarbonization scenario, the IEA Announced Pledges, still projects global demand of around 60 million barrels per day by 2050. 

A concluding footnote details the policy landscape, specifically referencing the US Treasury's guidance on EV subsidies. Influenced by Senator Manchin, this policy restricts the $7,500 tax credit to vehicles whose battery assembly and critical minerals are predominantly sourced from the United States or its allies, excluding components from "foreign entities of concern" under rules that will become increasingly stringent over time.

This page from J.P. Morgan's energy paper argues that despite significant attention and policy support, biofuel contributions to fuel supplies remain small outside of Brazil and Indonesia, and face steep hurdles in costs and feedstock availability. A bar chart showing the biofuel share of transport demand in 2021 compared to projections for 2027 demonstrates this disparity. Brazil leads with a biofuel share of around 17% in 2021, projected to exceed 20% by 2027, followed by Indonesia rising from approximately 12% to 16%. In contrast, the United States hovers around 6% to 8%, and the global average remains well under 5%. Even with ten billion dollars in US tax credits, biofuels are expected to add only two to three percent to transport fuel share on top of existing ethanol. Similarly, renewable aviation fuels are projected to reach just one percent of global consumption in five years.

A second bar chart details renewable jet fuel cost estimates in Euros per liter, comparing various production pathways against fossil jet fuel, which sits below one Euro per liter. The data shows that renewable pathways are two to eight times more expensive than fossil fuels. Hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids, utilizing feedstocks like soy oil, palm oil, and used cooking oil, are the least expensive options but still range from one point one to nearly two Euros per liter. More complex pathways, such as power to liquids using renewable electricity, soar to three point five Euros per liter, while synthesized isoparaffins using agricultural residues or energy crops range up to nearly four Euros per liter.

Feedstock availability presents another major constraint, as illustrated by a line chart tracking biofuel demand share of global production and supply from 2010 with forecasts to 2026. While vegetable oils, sugar cane, and maize have steady demand shares of ten to twenty percent, the demand for used cooking oil, animal fats, and other waste oils is projected to surge dramatically. After rising from ten percent in 2010 to around forty percent in 2022, this category is forecast to consume sixty to ninety percent of total global supply by 2026, signaling severe imminent feedstock constraints.

Finally, a text box highlights the ongoing scientific dispute over corn ethanol's environmental benefits. A 2022 study by researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences concluded that corn ethanol's carbon intensity is twenty-four percent higher than gasoline due to emissions from land-use changes like tilling. This directly contradicts a 2019 US Department of Agriculture study that found ethanol's carbon intensity to be thirty-nine percent lower than gasoline, a discrepancy that has drawn strong criticism from the Renewable Fuels Association.

This page focuses on the decarbonization of commercial and residential building heat, arguing that transition gains in this area are outpacing those in the industrial sector. The primary drivers of this shift are electrification via heat pumps, cleaner electricity grids, renewable district heating, and direct geothermal or solar thermal applications. 

A bar chart tracking annual European heat pump sales from 2010 to 2022 illustrates rapid adoption, with total sales rising from under one million units in 2010 to approximately three million units by 2022. This expansion is heavily dominated by air-to-water and air-to-air systems, while brine-to-water and sanitary hot water installations remain small, stable segments. This trend is mirrored in the United States, where a line chart from 2009 to 2022 demonstrates that heat pump sales have overtaken gas furnaces. While US gas furnace sales plateaued and recently dipped below three and a half million units, heat pump sales climbed steadily to surpass them, approaching four million annual units by the end of the period. 

The financial incentive to switch is clarified by a line chart showing US residential pricing for heating oil, propane, and natural gas in dollars per million BTU from 2000 to early 2023. Heating oil and propane are consistently much more expensive, frequently spiking between twenty-five and forty dollars, while natural gas remains comparatively cheap, typically staying below fifteen dollars. This pricing gap explains why heating oil and propane users have the strongest financial incentive to transition to heat pumps. 

Technological advancements have also dramatically reduced the carbon footprint of these systems. A bar chart comparing the heat pump carbon dioxide emissions ratio to a highly efficient natural gas boiler baseline of one point zero shows that in 2010, heat pumps were actually more carbon-intensive than gas boilers in North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific due to coal-heavy power grids. By 2021, cleaner electricity grids and improved heat pump technology brought emissions ratios well below the baseline in all three regions, making heat pumps a significantly cleaner option than gas combustion. 

Looking forward, a bar chart of the renewable share of building heat consumption in 2021 versus projections for 2027 shows rising shares globally. The European Union leads, with its renewable share projected to grow from twenty-three percent to thirty percent, followed by China growing from seventeen percent to twenty-four percent, and the United States growing from ten percent to thirteen percent. These International Energy Agency projections reflect both the superior efficiency of heat pumps and the increasing integration of renewable power on the grid. 

However, the author points out a potential offset to these winter carbon savings, particularly in Europe. Since heat pumps also function as air conditioners, their adoption is introducing cooling to homes that previously did not have it. While US homeowners use about eighteen hundred kilowatt-hours per dwelling annually for air conditioning, European homeowners historically use less than one hundred kilowatt-hours. Consequently, rising summer energy use for cooling in Europe could partially offset the emissions benefits gained during the winter.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s annual energy paper provides an update on energy sector investments, arguing that while energy valuations have rebounded from their 2020 historic lows, the sector remains significantly discounted relative to the broader market. Traditional energy has returned to strong profitability after a decade of negative cash flows, the performance gap between clean energy and fossil fuels has narrowed, and US shale operators are showing unprecedented capital discipline.

An analysis of S&P 500 valuations versus return on equity demonstrates that the energy sector occupies an highly favorable position. Plotted on a chart measuring consensus forward 12-month return on equity against consensus forward 12-month price-to-book ratios, the energy sector stands out by offering a high return on equity of approximately 22% while trading at a very low price-to-book ratio of roughly 2x. In comparison, the overall S&P 500 average sits near a 4x price-to-book ratio at a similar 21% ROE level, while premium sectors like Retailing and Info Tech trade at over 8x to 9x price-to-book ratios. 

A historic look at the ratio of energy stocks' price-to-book value divided by the broader market's price-to-book value from 1928 through 2023 further highlights this discount. The relative valuation touched an all-time historic low of nearly 0.35 in 2020, far below the 1928–2022 average of approximately 1.0. While the ratio has since climbed back to about 0.8, it remains historically depressed. This valuation mismatch is also reflected in the S&P 500 energy share of market cap and net income. While the energy sector's share of S&P 500 net income spiked dramatically to around 12% in late 2022, its share of total S&P 500 market cap only recovered to roughly 5%, showing that the sector's profitability has far outstripped its stock market weight.

The underlying driver of this cheapness is a dramatic turnaround in cash generation, as shown in a chart detailing free cash flows from 2013 to 2023. For nearly a decade, both the S&P 1500 Oil and Gas E&P Index and a shale revolution portfolio of 22 companies consistently lost money, with annual free cash flows bottoming out near negative $10 billion in 2015 and 2020. By 2022, however, free cash flows spiked massively, reaching nearly $20 billion for the S&P 1500 E&P index and over $10 billion for the shale portfolio. 

This financial turnaround is closely tied to capital discipline. A chart of US shale reinvestment rates from 2013 to 2022 shows that operators previously reinvested over 100% of their cash flow into capital spending, with reinvestment rates peaking around 180% in 2015. In 2022, however, cash flow from operations skyrocketed to over $24 billion, while capital spending stayed flat at around $10 billion, driving the reinvestment rate down to a decade-low of approximately 40%.

Finally, the publication addresses the performance gap between renewable and traditional energy. An index starting in December 2018 shows that a renewables composite of solar and clean energy indices peaked at an index level near 450 in early 2021 before declining to around 250 by early 2023. Conversely, the MSCI World Energy Index, representing oil, gas, and pipelines, bottomed around 60 in late 2020 but staged a steady recovery to nearly 150 by early 2023, significantly narrowing the premium that clean energy previously held over fossil fuels.

In this publication, Michael Cembalest argues that the Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) is an inadequate metric for evaluating energy systems because it fails to account for the real-world intermittency of renewable energy and the costly backup infrastructure required to manage it. Using real-world events from December 2022, the author illustrates how reliance on averages masks extreme volatility that can threaten grid stability.

In Texas, wind capacity factors averaged 32% in December 2022, yet the actual hourly output fluctuated wildly. This is illustrated in the first chart, "ERCOT wind capacity factors by hour, December 2022," where capacity factors span from a low of 5% to a peak of 70% around the December average. The second chart, "ERCOT baseload and renewable generation vs demand, December 2022, GW," shows that during a severe cold snap on December 23, electricity demand spiked toward 80 GW while wind and solar generation collapsed. To prevent blackouts, natural gas generation had to double. The author notes that even if wind and solar capacity had been five times larger, gas-fired generation would only have been 20% lower, and covering the three-day wind drought with storage would have cost billions of dollars for four-to-six-hour battery capacities. Additionally, a footnote highlights that contiguous US power markets (ERCOT, SPP, MISO, and PJM) share high wind generation correlations of 0.58 to 0.68, meaning geographic diversity offers limited mitigation.

The page then transitions to Germany, which experiences "dunkelflaute," or prolonged periods of low wind and solar output lasting for weeks. This phenomenon is visualized in the third chart, "Germany generation by source, Nov - Dec 2022," where a massive dip in wind generation is labeled "Die dunkelflaute" under a steady electricity demand curve. During this period, the generation gap had to be filled by biomass, nuclear, coal, and imported LNG. The author raises an open question about the vulnerability of next winter's energy supply, given the planned decommissioning of Germany's remaining nuclear plants.

Finally, the author connects high renewable penetration to higher consumer costs in Europe. The fourth chart, "Household electricity prices vs wind and solar penetration in Europe by country," plots electricity prices in EUR per kilowatt-hour against wind and solar generation in Megawatt-hours per capita for the second half of 2021. The chart shows a strong positive correlation, with high-penetration nations like Denmark and Germany facing the highest household electricity prices (exceeding 0.30 EUR/kWh), while nations with low wind and solar generation, such as Hungary, Bulgaria, and Croatia, enjoy much lower electricity prices (around 0.10 to 0.15 EUR/kWh). Ultimately, the author concludes that these rising system-wide costs are clear proof that LCOE math misses the bigger picture of grid integration and backup needs.

This page presents six charts tracking the global energy transition, examining renewable costs, generation shares, electrification end-uses, and coal reliance. 

The first chart illustrates average power purchase agreement (PPA) prices by year of operation in real 2020 dollars per megawatt-hour from 2010 to 2020. It demonstrates a stark decline across all technologies: global solar photovoltaic plummeted from approximately $200 per megawatt-hour to under $50, while US solar photovoltaic dropped from around $140 to $40. Global wind fell from about $80 to $40, and US wind decreased from $80 to approximately $20. These PPA rates reflect the impact of subsidies like the US Investment Tax Credit.

The second chart displays the renewable share of primary energy and electricity generation in percent, including hydropower, across the top nine countries by primary energy use. Brazil leads significantly, with renewables representing nearly 80 percent of its electricity generation and about 45 percent of its primary energy. Canada follows with roughly 65 percent for electricity and 30 percent for primary energy. On a global level, renewables account for roughly 28 percent of electricity generation and 12 percent of primary energy, while South Korea lags at the bottom with around 7 percent of electricity and 3 percent of primary energy from renewables.

The third chart compares global nuclear electricity generation against combined solar and wind generation in terawatt-hours from 1965 to 2020. Nuclear generation plateaued around 2,600 terawatt-hours in the early 2000s, while solar and wind generation experienced an exponential rise starting around 2000. Combined solar and wind generation overtook nuclear power around 2021, reaching nearly 2,800 terawatt-hours.

The fourth chart breaks down US electricity uses, measured in quadrillion BTUs across residential, commercial, and industrial sectors, revealing that electricity is primarily used for HVAC. Residential consumption totals roughly 4.7 quads and commercial consumption is about 4.5 quads, with both heavily dominated by space cooling, lighting, ventilation, refrigeration, computers, and electronics. Conversely, the industrial sector uses about 2.5 quads, primarily for space heating, water heating, motors, and process heat. Transport electricity use is noted as being too small to plot at only 0.06 quads.

The fifth chart traces the coal share of primary energy consumption from 1990 to 2020 across key nations. South Africa remains the most coal-dependent, though its share declined from nearly 80 percent to around 72 percent. China's coal share dropped from over 75 percent to approximately 55 percent, while Vietnam saw a sharp increase from 10 percent to nearly 50 percent. Meanwhile, the United States and Germany both experienced significant declines, with the US coal share dropping below 10 percent and Germany's dropping to around 15 percent.

The final chart details the impact of China on global coal capacity, showing annual capacity additions and retirements in gigawatts from 2000 to 2020. The visual highlights how China’s massive net capacity additions, which peaked near 80 gigawatts in 2006, consistently offset retirements in the US and EU. Even in 2020, China's net additions of approximately 40 gigawatts eclipsed the combined retirements from the US, EU, and other regions, illustrating the ongoing challenge of global coal decommissioning.

This page examines alternative metrics used by grid managers to analyze system reliability and cost in high-renewable grids, specifically focusing on capacity credits and effective load carrying capacity (ELCC) to demonstrate why the Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) metric is insufficient. 

The author begins by discussing capacity credits, which measure the amount of thermal capacity that can be safely retired when new wind and solar are added to the grid. A bar chart titled "How much natural gas capacity can be reduced per MW of new wind and solar power?" shows that across various US regions, adding wind and solar to meet 10% of demand in 2021 only allows for a 10% to 30% reduction in natural gas capacity. Specifically, the displacement percentages are around 18% for NYISO, 20% for CAISO, 15% for ERCOT, 14% for PJM, 21% for SOCO, 16% for SPP, 15% for ISNE, and 16% for MISO. This underscores that backup thermal capacity remains necessary due to renewable intermittency.

The page then introduces the concept of ELCC, a probabilistic metric used by entities like CAISO, PJM, NYISO, MISO, Duke, El Paso Electric, and Nova Scotia Power to evaluate reliability. To illustrate, the author presents a scenario from E3 Energy and Environmental Economics based on California's grid. A column chart titled "California's ELCC: 245 GW of wind/solar/storage only provides 50 GW of load carrying capacity" shows a massive mismatch. On the left, the nameplate renewable capacity totals 245 GW, consisting of 150 GW of solar, 20 GW of wind, and 75 GW of six-hour storage. On the right, this massive footprint yields an ELCC value of only 50 GW, supplemented by a small diversity benefit. 

This discounting effect is detailed in a final line chart titled "The marginal ELCC of California's solar, wind and storage," which plots the percentage of thermal capacity removed per nameplate capacity added (from 0% to 100%) against added capacity (from 0 to 150 GW). The chart shows that the reliability contributions of these resources decline rapidly as more are added. Solar starts with a marginal ELCC of roughly 80% but falls to near 0% by 30 GW of added capacity. Wind begins around 25% and declines to about 10% by 30 GW. Four-hour storage starts near 90% but steadily decreases to around 10% by 75 GW. The author concludes that because LCOE ignores these steep integration and capacity value declines, grid operators must rely on ELCC to ensure long-term resource adequacy.

This page features a collection of essential energy charts detailing global fossil fuel reserves, energy dependence trends, battery metal costs, the shift of energy-intensive manufacturing to developing nations, projected global energy consumption, and the comparative cost of industrial electrification versus natural gas. 

The first chart illustrates the share of global fossil fuel reserves in 2020. It shows that the Middle East holds the largest shares of oil at forty-eight percent and natural gas at forty percent. The United States holds a dominant position in coal reserves with twenty-five percent, alongside fifteen percent of global oil and twenty-eight percent of global gas reserves. Russia also commands substantial reserves across all three categories, holding fifteen percent of coal, nineteen percent of gas, and six percent of oil.

The second chart tracks energy dependence and independence since 1980 by looking at net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal. It highlights the United States' transition from a net importer to a net exporter by 2020. Conversely, Europe remains a major net importer, while China has experienced a steep rise in energy imports, reaching over six hundred million tonnes of oil equivalent. Russia remains a highly dominant net exporter, exporting approximately eight hundred million tonnes.

The third chart depicts estimated metal costs per sixty kilowatt-hour electric vehicle battery from 2020 to early 2023. The data show that Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide and Lithium Nickel Cobalt Aluminum Oxide batteries experienced massive cost spikes, peaking near thirty-four hundred dollars in mid-2022 before retreating to around twenty-five hundred dollars in January 2023. Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries remained a significantly cheaper option, rising from under four hundred dollars to settle near one thousand dollars.

The fourth chart displays the structural shift of energy-intensive manufacturing from developed to emerging economies. Between the late 1990s and the early 2020s, the share of global production in developed economies shrank across all categories. Steel production in developed nations fell from over fifty percent to roughly twenty percent, while cement production fell from thirty percent to less than ten percent.

The fifth chart projects primary energy use changes from 2021 to 2050, showing that anticipated declines in primary energy consumption in developed markets like the European Union, Japan, and the United States, along with a flatlined projection of zero petajoules for China, will be entirely offset by rising consumption in other emerging markets. India and Africa lead this projected growth, with expected increases of roughly thirty and twenty-five petajoules respectively.

The final chart addresses the cost barrier to industrial electrification, showing that electricity is one and a half to four and a half times more expensive than natural gas per megajoule for industrial heat. This price premium is highest in the United Kingdom, where electricity is over four times more expensive, and lowest in China and Japan, where it is approximately one and a half times more expensive.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s annual energy paper explores the slow pace of grid expansion and renewable energy interconnection, arguing that while deep decarbonization plans require massive replacement and expansion of existing grids by 2030 and 2050, actual transformations in the United States and Europe are severely lagging behind China. 

The top-left bar chart, titled Transmission grid development, measures expected kilometers of lines in millions. It highlights that China is projected to build and replace significantly more transmission infrastructure through 2050, exceeding three million kilometers, compared to the European Union and United States, which both hover under one million kilometers. The categories shown include current grid still in use in 2050, current grid replaced from 2022 to 2050, and new lines built during 2022 through 2030 and 2031 through 2050. The top-right stacked bar chart, titled Distribution grid development, shares the same categories and units, indicating that China's distribution network will expand or be replaced on a scale exceeding twenty-two million kilometers by 2050, whereas the United States and European Union are projected to reach only around thirteen million and eleven million kilometers, respectively.

The bottom portion of the page focuses on High Voltage Direct Current, or HVDC, lines of over 400 kilovolts, which are essential for transporting renewable energy from remote areas. A line chart titled High voltage direct current lines by country traces cumulative line distance in kilometers from 2006 to 2020. It demonstrates that China’s total distance surged to nearly 50,000 kilometers by 2020, while active but slower growth occurred in Brazil and India. Meanwhile, lines in Western countries like France, Spain, and Canada remained largely stagnant, with the United States, Denmark, and Italy grouped at the very bottom with minimal infrastructure.

This gap is further detailed in the adjacent table, titled High voltage direct current line outlook, which compares current and projected HVDC line length in kilometers and intensity, measured in kilometers of transmission per gigawatt of generation capacity. The table reveals that China currently leads with 47,990 kilometers of lines with an intensity of 22 km/GW, and projects reaching 65,988 kilometers by 2025. India shows massive planned expansion, with its current 19,087 kilometers projected to reach 165,635 kilometers by 2026, leading to a projected intensity of 197 km/GW. In contrast, the United States is projected to see zero growth in HVDC length, holding flat at 2,462 kilometers by its projection year of 2026, which represents an intensity of just 2 km/GW, the lowest in the entire dataset. European nations like France, Spain, and Italy, along with Brazil, currently hover around 1,500 to 22,000 kilometers and show varying projected expansions through their target years, ranging from 2029 to 2031. Ultimately, the author cites Berkeley Lab data to highlight that underinvestment in regional grid linkages has caused significant opportunity losses for the United States, as evidenced by wide regional electricity price differences.

In J.P. Morgan’s annual energy paper, Michael Cembalest analyzes the critical bottlenecks and slow pace of US electricity transmission expansion, arguing that the current rate of grid additions is dramatically lagging behind what is required to support a deep decarbonization transition. 

To illustrate why clean energy demands more grid infrastructure, the first chart measures the megawatt-weighted average distance in kilometers required for various power generation facilities to reach population clusters of at least two million people. Wind energy sits furthest away, requiring nearly 140 kilometers of transmission, followed by geothermal and hydro at roughly 110 kilometers. Solar is moderately distant at approximately 80 kilometers, while fossil fuels and nuclear are located much closer to major population centers, with bituminous coal requiring about 75 kilometers, natural gas around 55 kilometers, and nuclear power only about 45 kilometers. 

The second chart highlights the growing transmission intensity of a decarbonized grid, displaying data from 1990 with projections out to 2050. Historically, the US operated with roughly 35 to 45 miles of transmission per terawatt-hour of electricity generation. However, as wind and solar are projected to scale from roughly 10% of total generation in 2020 to 90% by 2050, the required transmission intensity is forecast to double, rising sharply to over 80 thousand gigawatt-miles per terawatt-hour. 

The third chart contrasts historical US transmission growth against these targets. While the grid expanded at a modest 1.5% annual growth rate up to 2020, reaching around 200 thousand gigawatt-miles, a successful deep decarbonization plan requires a steep shift to a 5.7% annual growth trajectory, which would target nearly 1,100 thousand gigawatt-miles of transmission by 2048. 

The fourth chart reveals that actual transmission expansion is moving in the wrong direction, showing that annual miles of lines added (for projects over 100 kilovolts) declined from nearly 4,000 miles in 2013 to under 1,000 miles in 2021. This stacked bar chart tracks annual additions across major regional transmission organizations and independent system operators, including CAISO, ERCOT, MISO, PJM, SPP, New England, New York, and non-RTO/ISO regions. Overall, the annual pace of expansion has slowed from 1.5% to 1.0% over the last five years. In 2021, only about 300 miles of higher-voltage transmission were completed across the entire nation, with half of that total coming from a single project, the Western Spirit Transmission line designed to deliver wind power from New Mexico.

This page of the publication focuses on the major bottlenecks facing US clean energy transitions: long transmission completion times and increasingly backlogged regional interconnection queues. 

The first section examines the long timelines required to build physical transmission lines. A scatterplot mapping US transmission lines by distance and completion time reveals that while smaller projects under 150 miles are typically finished in 5 to 10 years, major projects stretching more than 400 miles can take between 15 and 20 years. The text highlights the Transwest Express, a transmission line designed to bring Wyoming wind power to the Nevada and California border, as a prime example of these delays. The project is currently in its eighteenth year due to regulatory and local hurdles, including a sage grouse and elk conservation easement secured by a single family on a 56,000-acre ranch in Northwest Colorado. This easement also blocked the parallel Gateway South transmission project. The author notes that conservation easements in Colorado have risen from 100,000 acres in 1990 to 2.7 million acres, presenting growing barriers to infrastructure. Furthermore, out of seven large transmission projects fast-tracked by the Obama administration in 2011, only two have been completed, four are still pending, and one has been cancelled.

The second half of the page addresses the growing volume of projects waiting in US grid interconnection queues, which are overwhelmed by solar, storage, and wind applications. A stacked area chart of the PJM interconnection queue shows cumulative capacity growing from modest levels in the late 2000s to nearly 300 gigawatts in 2021, with solar, solar-plus-battery, and standalone battery projects representing the vast majority of recent queue growth. A bar chart comparing regional queue growth from 2019 to 2021 reveals that the PJM queue grew 2.4 times, followed closely by CAISO at over 2.0 times, while MISO, NYISO, ISO-NE, and ERCOT also saw substantial queue expansions.

These backlogs have significantly slowed down project timelines. A line chart detailing the median years between an interconnection request and plant commissioning shows that the average wait time for all types of power across all ISOs rose from under three years in 2013 to nearly five years in 2021. For solar PV projects in CAISO, wait times spiked to roughly eight years in 2018 before settling around seven years by 2021. 

Finally, a table quantifies the sheer size of these queues relative to existing grid capacity in 2021. In NYISO, the wind and solar queue capacity is 1,914 percent of currently installed wind and solar capacity, or 705 percent when excluding offshore wind. In PJM, the queue capacity is 1,078 percent of existing capacity (980 percent excluding offshore wind). Other regions also show massive backlogs, with ISO-NE at 628 percent, CAISO at 421 percent, MISO at 415 percent, and SPP at 289 percent of their respective installed capacities.

This page of the J.P. Morgan energy paper discusses the friction and bottleneck of interconnection queues, rising costs, and grid delays for renewable energy projects compared to natural gas and storage. The author advises caution when evaluating projects in the queue, noting that historical completion rates are incredibly low. For projects entering the queue between 2000 and 2017, only 16% of wind projects and 10% of solar projects were completed, while PJM, the largest independent system operator, reports a completion rate of just 5%. 

The visual data begins with a bar chart tracking the average interconnection costs by fuel type for all projects from 2017 to 2022 in US dollars per kW. This chart illustrates that renewable integration costs dwarf those of natural gas. While natural gas costs remain low at around $25 per kW, solar exceeds $250, solar hybrid is over $260, storage is around $330, onshore wind is roughly $130, and offshore wind is the highest at about $375 per kW. 

An adjacent chart monitors interconnection costs over time for completed projects, comparing the years 2000 to 2016 with 2017 to 2022 in US dollars per kW. It highlights that while costs for natural gas fell from $40 to $15 per kW and storage fell from $18 to under $5, the costs for onshore wind tripled from $20 to $60, and solar costs climbed from $58 to $95. 

The author links these rising costs and queue delays directly to rising wind and solar curtailment and transmission congestion. A detailed table lists curtailment and congestion figures from 2019 to 2021 across major US regional transmission systems. In ERCOT, curtailment rose from 2,370 GWh to 6,617 GWh, and congestion costs ballooned from $110 million to $1,400 million, alongside an interconnection queue capacity of 137 GW. MISO saw congestion costs rise from $900 million to $2,800 million, with a queue capacity of 314 GW. In PJM, wind curtailment went from 0.0% to 1.8%, and congestion costs increased from $583 million to $995 million. 

Finally, the text emphasizes that these challenges are not unique to the United States. Wind Europe and the German Wind Association have warned of thousands of projects awaiting regulatory approval, and a final bar chart compares European queue capacities to those in the US. Measuring capacity in kW per customer, the chart demonstrates that European nations face grid pressures similar to the US, with Spain at approximately 3.5 kW, the UK at 3.2 kW, and Italy at 2.8 kW, aligning closely with US regional transmission organizations like SPP, ERCOT, MISO, CAISO, and PJM, which range between 2.8 kW and 4.3 kW of queue capacity per customer.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s annual energy paper explores the rising wave of resource nationalism and the shift away from globalization, focusing on the scramble to reshore the production and processing of minerals needed for the renewable energy transition. Cembalest argues that while thermal power generation requires a continuous supply of fossil fuels, renewable energy requires a massive, one-time upfront investment in construction materials and critical minerals. Because the geographical distribution of these minerals is highly concentrated, securing them poses a unique geopolitical challenge.

The first chart on the page illustrates the construction materials required per terawatt-hour of electricity generated, excluding upstream fuel extraction and transmission, using data from Argonne National Laboratory and the Department of Energy. It shows that renewables are far more materials-intensive than traditional sources. Wind requires nearly ten thousand tonnes of construction materials per TWh, dominated by concrete, with a substantial portion of steel. Solar PV requires around five thousand tonnes of materials per TWh, consisting of concrete, steel, glass, and other materials such as aluminum, copper, iron, lead, and silicon. In contrast, natural gas and nuclear power require negligible amounts of these construction materials, both coming in well under one thousand tonnes per TWh. A brief sidebar clarifies that while the raw materials for cement and concrete are abundant, the primary constraint is the massive amount of energy required to heat and utilize them.

The lower half of the page features two charts sourced from the International Energy Agency that compare the mineral requirements of the energy transition against legacy systems. The first compares vehicles, showing that an electric vehicle requires over 200 kilograms of minerals—including copper, graphite, nickel, manganese, cobalt, and lithium—whereas a conventional internal combustion engine vehicle requires only about 35 kilograms of minerals, almost entirely copper and manganese. 

The second lower chart examines the kilograms of minerals needed per megawatt of electricity generation capacity. Offshore wind is the most mineral-intensive, requiring over 15,000 kilograms per megawatt, driven primarily by large amounts of zinc and copper, alongside manganese, chromium, and rare earths. Onshore wind requires roughly 10,000 kilograms of minerals per megawatt, mainly zinc and copper. Solar PV requires about 7,000 kilograms per megawatt, dominated by silicon and copper. These figures dwarf the mineral requirements of legacy and alternative generation systems; nuclear requires about 2,000 kilograms per megawatt, coal requires roughly 1,500 kilograms, and natural gas requires less than 1,000 kilograms per megawatt.

This page analyzes the long-term challenges of decarbonization, transmission, and grid flexibility, contrasting future global energy assumptions with the current, unresolved regional power issues in New England. 

The first chart, titled "Where will grid flexibility come from in the future?" and sourced from the IEA, compares the percentages of grid flexibility sources in 2021 with the 2050 STEPS projection. While flexibility in 2021 is dominated by fossil fuels like coal, natural gas, and oil, the 2050 scenario projects a massive transition. The IEA assumes future flexibility will rely heavily on demand response (consumers shifting usage patterns to match supply) and battery storage, alongside hydro, nuclear, and a smaller share of natural gas.

The second chart, titled "New England: same electricity prices as Alaska," plots November 2022 electricity prices in cents per kWh across various US regions for residential, commercial, and industrial sectors. The data shows that New England has the highest electricity prices in the continental United States, with residential rates approaching 28 cents per kWh. This matches the elevated rates found in Alaska and far exceeds the prices in regions like the Midwest or South.

The accompanying text explains that despite progressive climate goals, New England is an electricity albatross. The region relies on natural gas for 46% of its generation as of 2022, up from 12% in 2000, yet its five-pipeline network has not expanded. For instance, New York State blocked the Constitution Pipeline project, halting regional gas supply relief. During cold winter spikes, local distribution companies with firm heating contracts take precedence over power plants, causing electricity prices to surge. This lack of adequate gas storage capacity forced the region to rely on fuel oil for 30% of its winter electricity generation. 

Furthermore, high-voltage direct current transmission projects designed to import Canadian hydropower were blocked by Maine and New Hampshire, a situation compounded by a potential policy shift following the resignation of HydroQuebec's CEO. Other clean energy solutions face limitations: rooftop solar does not assist with winter peaks, offshore wind projects face delays as developers like Avangrid renegotiate contracts due to rising costs, and the Jones Act prevents domestic shipping of liquefied natural gas due to a lack of eligible US LNG tankers. The author concludes that these severe structural issues and resulting high electricity costs are likely a major reason why New England has failed to attract new electric vehicle battery factory projects.

This page examines the challenges surrounding transition minerals, arguing that the primary concern is not physical scarcity but rather geopolitical risk, rising resource nationalism, environmental compliance costs, and the difficulty of reshoring processing capacity away from China. A table detailing transition mineral abundance highlights that proven global reserves are highly sufficient relative to current production levels, generally providing over 40 years of supply. For instance, lithium annual production stands at 130 kilotons compared to 26,000 kilotons in global reserves, and copper production is at 22,000 kilotons against 890,000 kilotons in reserves. 

Despite this physical abundance, supply chains are highly vulnerable due to geographic concentration. A horizontal bar chart illustrates how China dominates many renewable energy production and processing stages. China controls nearly 100 percent of solar cell, wafer, and polysilicon production, alongside roughly 70 to 80 percent of lithium-ion battery manufacturing, rare earth production, and electric vehicle mineral processing and cathode/anode production. By comparison, the United States and the European Union hold very small fractions of these supply chains. 

This extreme concentration makes reshoring efforts difficult and costly. Three dual-axis charts plot the annual percentage change in module, turbine, and battery costs against key raw material indices from 2017 to 2022. These charts reveal how inflation in input costs has reversed historical price declines. In solar PV modules, a spike in silicon metal prices to an index level of nearly 180 by 2021 led to positive annual changes in module costs for the first time in years. Similarly, wind turbine costs increased in 2021 as steel prices surged to an index level above 250. For lithium-ion batteries, a dramatic rise in the lithium price index to over 300 by 2022 nearly halted the long-standing annual decline in battery costs. 

The author notes that this inflationary trend is affecting major green energy projects globally, citing the Saudi Neom green hydrogen facility, where the original $5.0 billion budget ballooned to $8.5 billion due to rising costs for spare parts, land, and interest. Additionally, geopolitical risks are underscored by the concentration of platinum group minerals—vital catalysts for polymer electrolyte fuel cells—within South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Russia, while environmental surveillance adds costs and delays in key mining regions like Chile and Peru.

This page explores the global battery supply chain, highlighting China's dominant position, the ongoing shift toward lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, the outlook for lithium reserves, and emerging alternative battery chemistries. The text notes that China’s complete battery supply chain has boosted its automotive sector, helping its passenger car exports match Germany’s at approximately 2.6 million units and positioning it to soon surpass Japan. 

Two visual charts illustrate the underlying data. The first chart, "Battery supply chains: mining, processing and components," breaks down the percentage share of countries involved in various stages of production. While raw material mining is globally distributed—with Australia leading in lithium, the Democratic Republic of the Congo dominating about 70 percent of cobalt mining, and Indonesia and Russia leading in nickel—China heavily controls the subsequent stages. China dominates graphite mining, processes approximately 60 percent of global lithium and the vast majority of graphite, and manufactures the lion's share of cell components, controlling roughly 60 percent of cathode and over 80 percent of anode production. 

The second chart, "Global reserves of lithium by country," tracks lithium reserves in million metric tons from 2018 to 2022. During this period, global reserves doubled from roughly 13 million to 26 million metric tons, driven by substantial reserves in Chile, Australia, Argentina, and China. 

The accompanying commentary explains how rising mineral prices have accelerated a shift toward LFP batteries, which avoid nickel and cobalt altogether. LFP technology was utilized in nearly half of Tesla's 2022 production and is increasingly adopted by companies like BYD. While the International Energy Agency projects lithium demand to reach 320 kilotons by 2030, the global supply remains abundant. This abundance is supported by massive recent discoveries, such as an 8.5 million tonne deposit in Iran and a 6 million tonne deposit in India. However, the author warns of long timelines, noting that Western lithium mines typically require 7 to 19 years to transition from feasibility studies to active production, and recycling is only expected to meet 1 percent to 3 percent of battery demand by 2030. 

Finally, the page reviews alternative battery technologies. Sodium-ion batteries, which feature a modest 20 percent energy density deficit compared to LFP and do not require lithium, are discussed as potential options for urban EVs and grid storage. While the Chinese manufacturer CATL introduced a sodium-ion battery in 2021, the author expects these batteries to hold less than a 10 percent market share by 2030 due to long production lead times. Solid-state lithium-air batteries developed by Argonne National Labs theoretically offer up to four times higher energy density than current liquid-electrolyte batteries, but they remain in the prototype stage. The author counsels caution, suggesting that observers wait for actual production and commercial adoption before making long-term projections.

This page analyzes the sensitivity of electric vehicle battery prices to changing mineral prices, the profitability of various automakers, and the expansion of the US battery supply chain. The author argues that concerns over battery mineral price volatility are often overstated, as battery prices incorporate many other costs like production, labor, and shipping. A study by Schmidt and Staffell indicates that a 100% increase in a single component mineral price would only raise battery prices by 2% to 5% for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and 2% to 10% for lithium nickel manganese (NMC) batteries. A supporting bar chart reveals that NMC batteries are most sensitive to a doubling of nickel (causing an approximately 9.5% price increase) and cobalt (causing an 8% increase), while LFP batteries are far less sensitive to price spikes in their constituent materials like copper, aluminum, lithium hydroxide, and graphite. 

Even when battery costs rise, leading EV manufacturers like Tesla are positioned to absorb these costs or aggressively cut prices to pressure rivals. A chart of 2022 net profit per vehicle shows Tesla leading the industry with nearly $10,000 in net profit per vehicle sold. In contrast, legacy automakers such as Volkswagen, Toyota, Ford, GM, Hyundai, and China's BYD operate on much tighter margins of under $2,000 per vehicle. Startups like XPeng and Nio are unprofitable, with Nio losing roughly $11,000 per vehicle sold, while losses at Rivian, Nikola, and Lucid are noted as too large to plot. 

The text addresses the rapid build-out of the US battery supply chain. Although Rivian’s CEO warned that 90% to 95% of the battery supply chain does not yet exist, substantial investments are projected to scale US battery plant net capacity from 55 GWh in 2021 to 1,000 GWh by 2030. An "Announced battery plant capacity" bar chart illustrates this dramatic growth trajectory, which is overwhelmingly concentrated in the United States, with a small fraction in Canada. Key investment states include Georgia, Tennessee, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, North Carolina, and Nebraska. This 1,000 GWh target would fully supply the estimated 8 million EV passenger cars projected for US sales in 2030, assuming an average battery size of 50 to 70 kWh.

Finally, the page details the geographical origins of the US EV supply chain. A table of 2021 country-of-origin data for lithium-ion cells, battery packs, and electric vehicles sold in the US reveals minimal direct reliance on China. In 2021, the US self-supplied 57% of cells (362,000), 63% of packs (402,000), and 64% of vehicles (406,000). Japan and South Korea provided 26% of cells and 19% of packs, while Europe supplied 15% of cells and 17% of packs. China accounted for only 2% of cells, 1% of packs, and 1% of vehicles sold in the US. However, the author cautions that while the US is successfully expanding its downstream assembly capabilities, it will likely remain highly dependent on global markets for upstream critical mineral mining, processing, and the fabrication of key components like cathodes and anodes.

This page of the J.P. Morgan energy paper discusses the global solar power supply chain, emphasizing China's overwhelming dominance and the growing trend of solar resource nationalism.
