The second chart compares the year-to-date performance of this representative AI ETF against the broader market as of September 20, 2023. It reveals that the AI ETF achieved a staggering year-to-date return of nearly 60%, whereas the overall S&P 500 returned about 16%, and the S&P 500 excluding the AI ETF constituents managed a mere 5% return, highlighting the extreme narrowness of the year's market gains.

To illustrate the technical limitations of current AI models, Cembalest shares three image generation attempts from Bing, Starry AI, and Dall-E. Each model was prompted to depict two workers looking nervously at a robot at their table labeled "Strategy Team Trainee." The resulting images highlight key failures: Bing ignored the label and added a third, horror-stricken person; Starry AI left out one of the human workers; and Dall-E generated gibberish letters spelling "STAAT TRATGY" on the table while failing to have the workers look at the robot. The author frames these visual shortcomings as reflective of the broader state of generative AI, which he further evaluates by grading the performance of GPT 4.0 on seventy-one specific research questions.

Michael Cembalest argues that rising interest rates will take longer to flow through to corporate profit margins and household balance sheets during this economic cycle. Unlike some US banks that mismanaged duration, many US and European companies extended their liability duration to lock in record-low interest rates. Consequently, corporate interest expense is falling for the first time on record even as the Federal Reserve aggressively hikes rates. 

This corporate resilience is illustrated in the first chart, which tracks US nonfinancial corporate net interest costs as a percentage of after-tax NIPA profits alongside the Federal funds rate from 1970 to 2023. It shows net interest payments reaching a 60-year low of under 20% of profits, completely diverging from the rising Fed funds rate. Similarly, the second chart, focusing on US household debt, demonstrates that household debt service as a percentage of disposable income remains historically low at around 9%. This is largely because the average rate on outstanding mortgages remains insulated at approximately 3.5%, even as current market mortgage rates have spiked to around 7%. 

While higher interest rates have cooled the housing market, extremely low inventory has prevented a more severe crash in home prices, permits, and starts. A chart plotting the months' supply of existing single-family homes shows that supply is hovering near historic lows at under three months, which has also caused new homes to sell at roughly the same price as existing homes for the first time since the late 1960s. 

Tight labor markets continue to sustain personal income and consumer spending. The final chart highlights how expectations for a consumer slowdown have shifted. Comparing the Blue Chip Financial forecasts from January 2023 and July 2023 for real personal consumption expenditures, the July report shows a much milder and delayed slowdown. Instead of dipping close to 0% by late 2023 as projected in January, the updated July forecast projects consumer spending growth to bottom out more shallowly at around 0.5% in mid-2024 before recovering. 

Lastly, Cembalest addresses the US banking crisis, noting that deposit outflows have slowed due to perceived FDIC guarantees and new Fed borrowing facilities, despite a major gap between deposit rates at roughly 0.5% and money market rates near 5.0%. He highlights proposed Basel III regulations as the next critical issue to monitor, warning that raising capital requirements at large banks by 1.5% to 2.0% will likely push more lending activity out of traditional banking and into private markets and fintech platforms.

This page contains an appendix exploring the implications of generative artificial intelligence for employment, drawing on economic analysis from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). The author challenges the common axiom that technology-driven productivity gains always create enough new jobs to offset displacement. Citing research by Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo, the text argues that overall labor demand can mask substantial job destruction. 

This argument is supported by three line charts. The first chart, tracking job creation and displacement effects for services and manufacturing from 1947 to 1987, shows a near-perfect symmetrical offset, where job creation effects rose to nearly 18 index points while job displacement fell to about -17 index points. However, this balanced trend did not persist. The second chart, tracking the same sectors from 1987 to 2017, reveals that job creation only reached about 12 index points, while displacement grew to roughly -18 index points. The third chart focuses exclusively on manufacturing from 1987 to 2017, illustrating an even steeper divergence: job creation rose to only about 7 index points, while displacement fell sharply to approximately -32 index points.

The page also features research by David Autor et al. showing how innovation shifted in the 1980s toward worker replacement rather than worker augmentation. Two tables quantify this change in employment and wages. The first table, tracking change in employment as a function of exposure to augmentation and automation, shows that augmentation exposure dropped from 1.85 in the 1940–1980 period to 1.31 in the 1980–2018 period, while automation exposure worsened from -1.52 to -3.99. The second table, measuring change in wages, displays a similar trend: wage augmentation fell from 2.05 to 1.34, while wage displacement worsened from -1.68 to -3.93. The author concludes that after 1980, the pace of employment and wage erosion in automation-exposed occupations accelerated significantly relative to the gains in augmentation-exposed occupations.

This page features an analysis of New York City by Michael Cembalest, comparing its post-COVID economic and structural health to 21 other major U.S. cities. The author highlights New York's enduring strengths, such as its massive size, sector diversification, dominant global financial role, and relatively favorable crime statistics compared to other major cities. Additionally, total employment, airport utilization, and restaurant dining have recovered to pre-pandemic levels. 

However, the city faces critical, unsustainable challenges. Mass transit utilization is stuck at 73% of 2019 levels, office vacancy rates have surged to 18%, and about 35% of workdays are still performed from home, with office-to-residential conversions unlikely to resolve the excess inventory. Furthermore, high tax rates, low housing affordability, and substantial municipal debt have accelerated taxpayer outmigration, leaving New York State ranking next to last in taxpayers and earned income retention from 2011 to 2021. The city's financial outlook is further strained by an influx of asylum seekers and high electricity prices exacerbated by the closure of the Indian Point nuclear plant. Consequently, Cembalest advises boards and investors to manage exposure to New York City as they would a megacap stock—by avoiding an overweight position and diversifying regionally.

To contextualize these issues, the page includes a J.P. Morgan Asset Management heat map comparing 22 cities across four key categories: urban recovery, post-2019 economy and demographics, business conditions, and fiscal health. In urban recovery, New York City performs respectably with a score of 63, far ahead of San Francisco's low score of 26 but trailing top performers like Boise at 82. However, structural problems drag down New York's other scores, with the city receiving a 31 in post-2019 economy and demographics, a 38 in business conditions, and a 39 in fiscal health. Ultimately, New York City's equal-weighted composite score is 43, placing it near the bottom of the group and ahead of only Chicago at 38, Detroit at 36, and San Francisco at 34. In contrast, Boise leads the composite rankings with a score of 73, followed by Austin at 63 and Salt Lake City at 62.

This page serves as the introduction and table of contents for Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan "Eye on the Market" newsletter, where the author argues that geopolitical events rarely act as primary drivers for equity market returns. Citing historical trends, Cembalest notes that out of roughly twenty post-World War II geopolitical events, only the 1973 Arab-Israeli War—which triggered an oil embargo, stagflation, and wage controls—significantly drove equity markets six to nine months later. He points out that the Geopolitical Risk Index has historically shown little correlation with investor returns because conflict zones typically hold a very small share of global economic and financial activity. 

To illustrate this point, a detailed table titled "Conflict zone countries as a % of total world" lists sixteen economic indicators for defined conflict zones (which include nations like Afghanistan, Iraq, Israel, Syria, Ukraine, and Venezuela), comparing their global share with and without Russia. Excluding Russia, these conflict zones account for only 1.3% of global GDP, 1.5% of global trade, 1.0% of gross capital formation, and a mere 0.1% of global equity market capitalization. Even when including Russia, their share of global GDP rises to only 3.6% and equity market capitalization to 0.3%, though energy figures jump significantly: oil production rises from 7.3% to 19.2% and natural gas production increases from 2.3% to 17.5%. 

Cembalest observes that while Russia's invasion of Ukraine temporarily spiked global energy and food prices and led to some de-industrialization in Germany, it has not acted as a primary developed equity market catalyst. He cautions, however, that a dramatic expansion of the conflict in the Middle East, a direct Russia-NATO conflict, or a China-Taiwan conflict could severely alter these market dynamics. 

The remainder of the page outlines six key questions addressed in the report, which cover whether the Middle East war will cause a 1970s-style energy crisis; how Europe’s new international Pillar II tax system connects to NATO, Russia, and Poland; the senescence risks and presidential succession scenarios for Donald Trump and Joe Biden in the 2024 election; Taiwan's defense capabilities against a Chinese invasion; the tax and spending policies required to stabilize the US Federal debt; and reflections on the American experiment at Thanksgiving.

In this section, Michael Cembalest discusses Europe's efforts to spearhead a global initiative involving over one hundred countries to adopt new multinational tax laws, specifically focusing on the controversial aspects of the Pillar II international tax system. While the first two components of Pillar II—a domestic minimum tax on local subsidiaries and a parent country's right to tax subsidiaries in low-tax jurisdictions—are uncontroversial, the third component, known as the Undertaxed Profits Rule, or UTPR, is heavily criticized. The author frames the UTPR as a bounty-hunting rule because it permits a third-party country to intervene in another nation's tax policy and collect taxes from a resident subsidiary to offset perceived underpayment by its parent company or a sister subsidiary in a different nation, despite having no legal nexus to those other entities. The text argues this rule undermines US tax policy and limits Congress's authority to design independent policies, particularly since the Biden administration supports alignment with Pillar II but the US Congress has yet to adopt these rules.

To clarify these concepts, a detailed table outlines the components of Pillar II. The first component, the Qualifying Domestic Minimum Top-Up Tax, or QDMTT, allows a country like Turkey to levy a top-up tax on a local subsidiary of a UK parent to ensure it meets a fifteen percent minimum rate; this is commented on as consistent with existing tax policy. Similarly, the second component, the Income Inclusion Rule, or IIR, allows a parent country like the UK to collect the top-up tax if the host country does not; this is also deemed consistent with existing tax policy. In contrast, two applications of the UTPR are described as bounty hunting with no nexus. In the first scenario, if Turkey lightly taxes a UK subsidiary and the UK does not collect the top-up tax, Italy, where the UK parent has another subsidiary, can collect those underpaid Turkish taxes from the Italian subsidiary. In the second scenario, if a US parent company has an effective tax rate under fifteen percent due to domestic research and development credits and export incentives, France can tax the parent's French subsidiary to recover the underpaid US taxes.

Extensive footnotes elaborate on these contentions. The author points out the tortured logic of Pillar II, noting that under GloBE rules, non-refundable US research and development credits are treated as tax reductions, while refundable European R&D credits are treated as income. The commentary also touches upon President Biden's proposed corporate tax changes, such as a fifteen percent corporate Alternative Minimum Tax and a bank tax, and explains Pillar I's Digital Service Taxes. The author warns that Digital Service Taxes are essentially service sector tariffs that may violate existing tax treaties by ignoring traditional taxable nexus standards, leading some countries to bypass US ratification delays by implementing extraterritorial VAT taxes.

This page argues that discussions about European tax sovereignty, specifically around Pillar II and GloBE tax rules targeting US subsidiaries, should be broadened to include political sovereignty and national defense burdens. The author asserts that US Presidents should not support Pillar II without putting all aspects of national sovereignty on the table, and should consider economic retaliation if Europe proceeds with rules that disadvantage US multinational research and development credits.

This argument is supported by a line chart on the left showing US versus European defense spending as a percentage of GDP from 1968 to 2023. While US defense spending has consistently remained high, fluctuating between roughly 3% and 9% of GDP, spending by NATO members excluding the US fell below the 2% NATO defense spending agreement target in the late 1990s and has remained below it ever since. 

To quantify this gap, a table on the right presents the shortfall in NATO defense spending by individual European countries compared to the 2% of GDP target, measured in billions of 2022 US dollars across three historical intervals. Since the 2006 NATO defense spending agreement, the cumulative shortfall across ten listed European nations is 1.43 trillion dollars. Going back to when Vladimir Putin took power in 1999, the total shortfall rises to 1.785 trillion dollars, and since Ronald Reagan's "Evil Empire" speech in 1983, it reaches 2.041 trillion dollars. 

Germany is by far the largest contributor to this defense gap, with shortfalls of 590 billion dollars since 2006 and 896 billion dollars since 1983. Italy represents the second-largest cumulative shortfall, with 236 billion dollars since 2006. In contrast, countries like the United Kingdom and France have very low cumulative shortfalls of just 5 billion dollars and 53 billion dollars respectively across all three periods, reflecting their relatively consistent defense spending relative to GDP. Footnotes highlight security threats from Russia, such as former President Dmitry Medvedev's hostile statements regarding Polish statehood, to underscore the critical nature of these defense commitments.

This page examines the unprecedented scenario of two elderly candidates, Donald Trump and Joe Biden, potentially running against each other in the 2024 U.S. presidential election, and details the legal processes that would unfold if a candidate withdrew at various stages of the election cycle. 

A prominent line chart titled "2024 election, assuming Biden vs Trump" tracks the average age of both major presidential candidates as a percentage of prevailing non-infant male life expectancy from 1790 to 2030. The vertical axis measures this ratio from 0.4 to 1.1, while the horizontal axis marks time. Historically, only the 1848 matchup of Zachary Taylor versus Lewis Cass exceeded a ratio of 1.0, meaning their average age was higher than male life expectancy at the time. The chart shows that a 2024 matchup between Biden and Trump would mark the second-highest peak in U.S. history, reaching nearly 1.05 and once again exceeding the average male life expectancy. This is a dramatic increase from the historical average, which has mostly hovered between 0.6 and 0.8 for the last century, including matchups like Obama vs. McCain and Clinton vs. Dole.

Given these demographics, the author structures a detailed Q&A exploring what would happen if a candidate dropped out due to health reasons, utilizing Joe Biden as the Democratic nominee and Gavin Newsom as a hypothetical replacement based on betting odds from Vegas Insider and ElectionBettingOdds.com. Under guidance from election law specialist Michael Morley of Florida State University, the text outlines four distinct timelines. First, if a candidate drops out well before the primary ballot eligibility deadline, a replacement would simply gather the required signatures to get on the ballot. Second, if a candidate drops out just before the primary ballot deadline, state delegates would become unbound, and the party could unbind them even if a minor candidate like Marianne Williamson won a plurality of votes. Third, if the candidate drops out after the final primary in June but before the August convention, all delegates would likely become unbound, requiring party officials to use or amend convention rules to nominate a replacement. Finally, if a candidate drops out after the August convention but before the November general election, the Democratic National Committee would name a replacement; however, depending on state laws, the original candidate's name might still appear on the ballot, requiring the party to clarify to voters how their votes will be cast.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest assesses whether the Middle East conflict could trigger an oil and inflation crisis comparable to the 1970s, concluding that energy risks for the United States are generally much lower today, though some critical caveats remain. To support this view, he highlights several structural shifts. First, the United States has transitioned from a net importer to a net energy exporter, with net crude imports down 75% from their 2005 peak and net refined product imports shifting from a deficit of 4 million barrels per day to net exports of the same amount. This shift is depicted in the first chart, "US energy dependence and independence," which plots net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal as a share of total primary energy consumption from 1970 to 2020. The chart illustrates this dependency peaking near 30% in the mid-2000s before sharply declining to below zero percent by 2020, marking the transition to net exporter status.

Second, the oil intensity of US economic growth has fallen substantially, and global demand growth has cooled. The second chart, "Oil intensity and consumption," tracks US oil intensity (measured in megajoules per chained 2017 dollar of GDP on the left axis) alongside global five-year rolling oil demand growth (as a percentage on the right axis) from 1965 to 2015. US oil intensity declined steadily from over 5 megajoules per dollar in the late 1960s to approximately 2 megajoules by 2015, while global demand growth cooled from early 1970s peaks of 8% to 10% down to a range of 0% to 2% in recent years.

Third, geopolitical dynamics have shifted leverage away from OPEC embargoes. Today, 75% of Saudi oil exports are destined for Asia, and China relies on the Middle East for half of its oil, whereas the United States secures most of its imported oil from Canada, Mexico, and other non-OPEC sources. Furthermore, Saudi Arabia retains spare capacity to bring online if needed, as shown in the third chart, "Estimated OPEC spare capacity." This visual displays estimates in million barrels per day from 2000 to 2021 by Bloomberg, J.P. Morgan, and Bridgewater, showing spare capacity fluctuating between 2 and 6 million barrels per day for most of the period, with significant spikes during the 2009 and 2020 downturns.

Finally, the author introduces two major caveats regarding future supply risks. First, current US oil production highs are driven by bringing previously drilled but uncompleted wells online rather than initiating new exploration projects. This capital discipline is highlighted in the fourth chart, "Fossil fuel consumption vs energy capital spending," which covers the years 2006 to 2022. It contrasts global fossil fuel use (in exajoules on the right axis) against the capital spending intensity of S&P Global 1200 Energy companies (expressed as a ratio of operating cash flow on the left axis). While global fossil fuel consumption has steadily risen to nearly 500 exajoules, capital spending intensity has collapsed from nearly 1.0x in 2014 to under 0.4x in 2022, setting the stage for structurally well-supported energy prices outside of recessions. Second, the Biden Administration chose not to refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve before the current Middle East conflict erupted, leaving the reserve down roughly 50% from its peak and at its lowest level since 1983.

This page, written by Michael Cembalest for J.P. Morgan Asset Management, reflects on Thanksgiving by examining immigration to the United States, arguing that despite domestic political, financial, racial, judicial, and social problems, the country remains highly attractive to global migrants. Cembalest emphasizes that the historical process of migration allows newcomers to forge a distinct American identity focused on the success of the nation. 

To support this argument, the author presents three charts. The first bar chart, titled "US remains a beacon that few people leave," illustrates the ratio of migrants to emigrants across nineteen countries using 2022 data from the UN International Migration Stock Database. The United States leads the world by a wide margin, showing a ratio of approximately 17 incoming migrants for every departing emigrant. Australia follows in second place with a ratio of about 13, while Canada is a distant third at roughly 6. Other nations, including Sweden, Spain, Germany, France, Japan, and Argentina, all show much lower ratios, mostly remaining below 4.

The subsequent two stacked area charts, sourced from the 2021 DHS Yearbook of Immigration Statistics, provide historical context on individuals obtaining lawful permanent resident status in the US from 1820 to 2000, broken down by country of origin. The first of these historical charts plots immigration in absolute millions of people. It reveals two massive waves of migration: an early-twentieth-century wave peaking around 1900 to 1910 at over 8 million people—predominantly driven by arrivals from Italy, Russia, and Austria-Hungary—and a larger modern wave peaking in the late 1990s at nearly 10 million people, dominated by migrants from Mexico, Central America, China, India, and other parts of Asia. 

The final chart adjusts these statistics as a percentage of the overall US population, revealing that historical waves had a much more significant relative demographic impact. The mid-nineteenth-century wave, driven by immigration from the United Kingdom, Germany, and Ireland, peaked at around 10% of the population, as did the wave of the early 1900s. In contrast, the absolute surge of the late twentieth century represents a much smaller portion of the total population, peaking at under 2%.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, presents an appendix analyzing the historical behavior of the S&P 500 Index around major geopolitical events and military conflicts from 1950 to the present. The central argument is that equity markets typically recover within six to nine months after a geopolitical crisis begins. The author highlights the 1973 Arab-Israeli War as the main exception to this rule, and clarifies that other prolonged downturns associated with conflicts, specifically the selloffs in 2001 and 2022, were primarily driven by separate macroeconomic factors—the dot-com tech bust and the initiation of Federal Reserve rate hikes following a decade of negative real rates—rather than the military events themselves.

The analysis is illustrated through four charts that track the S&P 500 Index from 12 months before to 24 months after a conflict's inception, with the index level indexed to 100 at the start month. 

The first chart covers the period from 1950 to 1968. It plots the S&P 500 performance around the Korean War in June 1950, the Soviet invasion of Hungary in November 1956, the Six-Day War in June 1967, and the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968. By the 24-month mark, almost all of these events saw the index trend well above the initial level of 100, with the Korean War showing the strongest overall growth.

The second chart focuses on the years 1973 to 1983. It highlights the Arab-Israeli War in October 1973, which stands out as a major exception, with the index declining sharply to near 60. The chart also traces the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, martial law in Poland in December 1981, the Falklands War in April 1982, and the US invasion of Grenada in October 1983, most of which ultimately recovered to or exceeded the 100 level within 24 months.

The third chart spans 1991 to 2010. It maps the index's reaction to the US invasion of Kuwait in February 1991, Serbian operations in Kosovo in February 1998, the September 11 attacks and the US invasion of Afghanistan in 2001, the US invasion of Iraq in March 2003, and North Korea sinking a South Korean navy vessel in March 2010. While the post-September 11 period depicts a prolonged decline down to nearly 70, the other episodes generally display upward or stable trajectories after the initial shock.

The fourth chart illustrates events from 2014 to the present. It tracks the index around Russia's invasion of Crimea in February 2014, the Trump administration abandoning the Iran nuclear deal in May 2018, and Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The 2022 invasion line illustrates a drop to approximately 85 before initiating a recovery, while the other modern crises trended higher after brief disruptions. All data is sourced from Bloomberg and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page analyzes why private equity outperformance improved for recent vintage years, arguing that private equity firms owe their success to public IPO investors. The author explains that an IPO boom in 2020 and 2021, fueled by Federal Reserve and Treasury stimulus that boosted risk appetite, allowed private equity firms to sell off companies at highly inflated valuations. This exit windfall occurred despite the fact that private equity managers were paying higher multiples—with median enterprise value to EBITDA ratios rising from roughly 8x in 2010 to around 11x for 2017-2019 vintages—and leveraging more, with debt to EBITDA ratios rising from about 4.5x to 5.5x over the same period. The author raises an open question: why did private equity managers not sell even more of their holdings during this exceptionally favorable window?

Four charts support this analysis. The first chart, tracking US public listing proceeds by type in billions of dollars from 2010 to 2022, shows a massive spike in 2021 to over $300 billion, heavily driven by a surge in both IPOs and SPACs, which subsequently collapsed to under $50 billion in 2022. 

The second chart shows the average two-year net returns for IPOs and SPACs issued in 2020 and 2021 relative to the S&P Small Cap Growth Index across four sectors: Healthcare, Technology, Consumer, and Diversified. Across all sectors, these public listings significantly underperformed the index, with SPACs performing the worst, lagging the index by roughly 50% to nearly 70%, especially in the Healthcare and Diversified sectors. 

The third chart displays US private equity exit activity from 2012 to 2023. It shows that both the total exit value (measured on the left axis in billions of dollars) and the number of exits (measured on the right axis) spiked dramatically in 2021, with exit values peaking near $300 billion and the exit count rising to around 600, before falling sharply through 2022 and 2023. 

The final chart, illustrating global private equity cash flows by year from 2014 to 2023 year-to-date, highlights that global distributions to investors peaked at nearly $700 billion in 2021, outstripping contributions before both cash flows fell dramatically by 2023. 

The author references previous J.P. Morgan publications warning about the SPAC boom, including "Hydraulic Spacking" and "Spaccine Hesitancy" from 2021, as well as a July 2023 IPO paper titled "Mr. Toad’s Wild Ride." The page utilizes data sourced from Bloomberg, JPMAM, Pitchbook, Burgiss, and Steve Kaplan of the University of Chicago.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication argues that despite recent private equity exits, the gains for investors in vintage years 2016 through 2019 are still mostly unrealized, a phenomenon referred to as a "paper moon." For these specific vintages, more than 50% of the total value in private equity funds remains tied up in existing positions that must still be marked and eventually sold. To illustrate the scale of this issue, the author cites an estimate from Bain & Company showing that buyout firms are sitting on $2.8 trillion of unsold investments. Furthermore, there is very little dry powder left for these vintages, as indicated by paid-in capital to capital committed ratios that are near or at maximum capacity. 

The core data is presented in a table titled "US buyout: average manager stats by vintage year," sourcing median manager data from Burgiss and J.P. Morgan Asset Management as of the second quarter of 2023. The table tracks metrics from vintage years 2005 to 2022, including paid-in capital to capital committed, total value to paid-in capital, distributions to paid-in capital, remaining value to paid-in capital, remaining value as a percentage of fund value plus distributions, and the average Public Market Equivalent (PME) ratio versus the S&P 500. 

For the key vintage years of 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2019, the remaining value as a percentage of total fund value plus distributions is 52%, 58%, 77%, and 84%, respectively. This represents a stark contrast to older, fully realized vintages like 2005 through 2012, where this percentage ranges from just 2% to 13%. While the average PME ratios for the 2016–2019 vintages look strong on paper—ranging from 1.17 to 1.30—the high remaining value percentages demonstrate that these funds are highly sensitive to market conditions. 

In the footnotes, the author addresses data integrity, noting that the Burgiss dataset comprises net-of-fee cash flow data sourced directly from 300 institutional limited partners across 1,400 funds, representing roughly 70% of all private equity funds ever raised. This dataset is contrasted with Venture Economics, which a 2013 paper by Rudiger Stucke at Oxford criticized for severe anomalies, including that over 40% of its funds stopped being updated during their active lifetimes. Finally, the author poses a warning regarding the future realization of these paper gains. Although a remaining fund value of 54% to 65% for vintages that are six and a half years old is historically normal, the critical difference today is the transition to a much higher interest rate regime, which will complicate the liquidation of these unsold assets.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the "paper moon" effects in private markets. The central argument is that recent venture capital vintage years are significantly more sensitive to market conditions than private equity buyouts because a vast majority of their total value remains locked up in unrealized, existing positions. Specifically, for venture capital funds with vintage years from 2013 to 2019, more than 50% of their total value is still reliant on marked positions that have yet to be sold and distributed.

The top table, titled "US venture capital: average manager stats by vintage year," provides a detailed performance breakdown based on Q2 2023 median peer group data from Burgiss and JPMAM. It tracks vintage years from 2005 to 2022 across several performance indicators. Notably, the remaining value as a percentage of total fund value plus distributions starts at 3% for the 2005 vintage and rises to 52% for 2013, 78% for 2015, 90% for 2017, and hits 100% for vintage years 2019 through 2022. This demonstrates that more recent vintages have distributed virtually no capital back to investors. Furthermore, the average Public Market Equivalent ratio against the S&P 500 peaks at 1.61 for the 2011 vintage year and falls to 1.23 for the 2019 vintage, with subsequent years marked as not applicable.

The bottom bar chart, titled "Greater share of VC investments have yet to be monetized," compares venture capital to buyout funds from vintage years 2010 to 2022, measuring remaining value as a percentage of total fund value plus distributions. For every single vintage year shown, the gold bars representing venture capital are visibly higher than the blue bars representing buyouts. For example, for the 2012 vintage, venture capital's remaining value is around 43% compared to buyouts at roughly 10%. For the 2016 vintage, venture capital's remaining value is 85% compared to buyouts at about 50%. This comparison highlights that venture capital investors face much higher ongoing market exposure and valuation risk than buyout investors, as their portfolios remain heavily dominated by paper gains rather than realized cash distributions.

This page examines the challenges and nuances of evaluating hedge fund performance, specifically addressing the issue of using inappropriate benchmarks for low-volatility portfolios. The author notes that a state pension plan recently ended its hedge fund program due to perceived underperformance, but argues that the plan's strict constraints actually produced cash- or bond-like volatility rather than equity-like risk, meaning an equity benchmark was inappropriate. 

To assess how hedge funds have performed since January 2018 from the perspective of an investor building a diversified portfolio, the author analyzes a filtered universe of 644 US-based hedge funds across four core strategies: relative value, equity hedge, event-driven, and macro. The analysis is illustrated in a scatter plot titled Individual hedge funds and 20-fund composites, which plots annualized excess return over T-bills against annualized excess return volatility. 

The chart features two distinct data series. The first, represented by blue dots, displays the 644 individual hedge funds. These individual funds show a massive dispersion, with volatility ranging from nearly 0% to 50% and annualized excess returns spanning from around negative 7% to over 30%. The second series, represented by gold dots, depicts 300 randomly constructed and partially diversified portfolios of 20 hedge funds. These multi-fund composites are tightly clustered, showing dramatically reduced volatility concentrated primarily between 5% and 15%, alongside steady, positive annualized excess returns grouped mostly between 0% and 12%. This comparison highlights the powerful impact of diversification in mitigating the extreme risks of individual fund selection and stabilizing performance.

This analysis focuses on the validity of current private equity valuations, examining two secondary market pricing proxies to determine whether asset marks are realistic. The author observes that while secondary market pricing for buyout funds was only 10% below Net Asset Value (NAV) in the first half of 2023, this was based on late-June pricing when the 10-year Treasury yield remained below 4%. Consequently, the author questions what year-end discounts will look like, noting that because the depth of these pricing estimates is shallow, even modest shifts in supply and demand could alter them significantly.

The first chart, titled "Secondary market pricing" and sourced from Jefferies, illustrates the pricing of buyout, credit, real estate, and venture secondary markets as a percentage of Net Asset Value from 2017 through the first half of 2023. Historically, buyout pricing remained strong, hovering near 97% in 2017, dipping to around 88% in 2020, and spiking near 96% in 2021 before falling to approximately 83% in the second half of 2022, eventually rising back to 90% in the first half of 2023. Meanwhile, credit secondary pricing dropped to roughly 73% in late 2022 before a slight recovery to 76% in mid-2023. Real estate plunged from historical levels above 90% down to approximately 68% in late 2022, recovering slightly to around 72% in early 2023. Venture experienced the most severe drop, plunging from nearly 88% in 2021 to around 70% by late 2022 and early 2023.

As an alternative, albeit imperfect, indicator of valuation discounts, the author points to UK-listed investment companies focused on alternative investments. Through this lens, buyout fund discounts to NAV are closer to 30%, which is the largest discount since 2003, outside of the global financial crisis when they reached 50%. The author also flags massive 50% to 60% discounts to NAV reported for closed-ended growth equity funds in the UK. 

The second chart, titled "UK-listed investment companies discount to NAV," presents the percent discount to NAV for various alternative asset classes as of mid-November 2023, factoring in the number of funds and their current market value in billions of British pounds. It tracks three metrics: market-cap weighted average, median, and equal weighted average. Funds investing in growth capital (5 funds, valued at £2.8 billion) show the deepest discounts, ranging between -50% and -60%. Funds of private equity funds (6 funds, £5.1 billion) show discounts of roughly -38% to -44%. Leasing funds (7 funds, £0.9 billion) demonstrate a wide variance; its market-cap weighted average discount is around -22%—due to a highly concentrated fund with 70% of NAV in a single investment—while its equal-weighted average discount is closer to -30%. Direct property funds (4 funds, £1 billion) have discounts near -36% to -38%. For the largest category, funds investing in private equity (8 funds, £25.9 billion), the discount sits between -26% and -33%. Renewable energy funds (21 funds, £13 billion) exhibit discounts between -20% and -27%, while private credit funds, credit funds investing in CLOs, infrastructure funds, and unquoted real estate debt generally experience discounts spanning from -13% to -24%. Traded credit funds (10 funds, £1.1 billion) show the smallest discounts, sitting close to 0%.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication analyzes how the venture capital landscape is shifting in response to tightening financial conditions, presenting a sharp contrast to the easy funding environment of 2020 and 2021. The author focuses on three main negative trends: the increasing median time between funding rounds, the surge in startup bankruptcies, and the dramatic rise in down rounds alongside steep drops in post-money valuations, particularly for late-stage companies.

A bar chart showing the median time between venture rounds in days compares Q1 2020 to the latest data from Q3 2023. The time required to transition from a priced seed round to a Series A round rose from roughly 530 days to over 700 days. Similarly, the wait between Series A and Series B increased to over 700 days, while the jump from Series B to Series C saw the most dramatic delay, lengthening from around 680 days to approximately 830 days.

Startup failures are visualized in a quarterly stacked bar chart tracking bankruptcies and dissolutions from Q1 2019 through Q3 2023. The total number of shutdowns climbed steadily throughout 2022 and peaked in Q3 2023 at over 200 startups, compared to a baseline of roughly 25 to 75 per quarter in 2019 and 2020. This chart categorizes failures by whether the startup had previously secured a priced round or had no priced round, revealing that a substantial and growing portion of the 2023 failures occurred among companies that had successfully raised priced venture capital in the past.

At the bottom of the page, two related horizontal bar charts break down down-round activity and valuation haircuts from Series A through Series E, comparing full-year 2022 to 2023. The first chart shows that the percentage of down rounds increased significantly across all stages in 2023; Series D was the hardest hit, with down rounds rising from about 11% of all rounds in 2022 to over 30% in 2023. The adjacent chart shows the median decline in post-money valuation for these down rounds, revealing that the valuation penalties worsened dramatically in 2023. For instance, the median post-money valuation decline for Series C down rounds widened from around 25% in 2022 to more than 50% in 2023, while Series E down-round valuations fell by a median of 50%. The charts on this page utilize data sourced from Carta and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market discusses the challenges facing private equity and leveraged buyout markets in a world of higher interest rates. The central argument is that deal activity has troughed because sellers have not yet adjusted their valuation expectations to the reality of higher borrowing costs. As an example, the text points to Carlyle’s failed acquisition of Cotiviti, where 12 percent debt yields spoiled the transaction's economics, and the seller walked away when Carlyle attempted to negotiate a lower valuation. Cembalest criticizes private equity firms that borrow against net asset value or use payment-in-kind financing to artificially sustain distributions to limited partners, arguing these tactics obscure real performance. Furthermore, the 2016 to 2019 vintage years face serious refinancing hurdles, with Triple-C bond and loan issuance down about 80 percent year-over-year and B/B- issuance down 70 percent from 2021 levels.

Four charts illustrate these mounting pressures. The first chart, titled US private equity exit activity, displays quarterly exit values in billions of US dollars on the left axis and the total exit count on the right axis from 2012 through the third quarter of 2023. The data show that both exit values and counts peaked dramatically in 2021 before plunging in 2022 and 2023 to their lowest levels since 2012, with recent exit values dropping well below 100 billion dollars. 

The second chart, titled US LBOs: purchase price multiples, displays the equity and debt contributions to purchase prices relative to trailing EBITDA from 2004 to 2022, compared against the 2004 to 2018 average. Multiples peaked near 12x EBITDA in 2021 and 2022, split nearly evenly between debt and equity, which is significantly higher than the historical average of approximately 9x EBITDA. 

The third chart, Interest coverage for B- rated issuers in the US loan market, tracks the distribution of interest coverage ratios from January 2022 to December 2023. It reveals a severe deterioration in borrower health: the percentage of B- rated issuers with interest coverage below 1.0x—meaning they do not generate enough cash flow to cover debt service—surged from under 20 percent in early 2022 to approximately 50 percent by December 2023. Meanwhile, issuers with comfortable coverage above 1.5x shrank from roughly 60 percent to less than 25 percent. Moody’s predicts that over half of B- borrowers will fail to cover capital expenditures and debt service by the end of the year.

The fourth chart, US leveraged loans amendments and extensions, shows the annual count of loan amendments and extensions from 2009 through year-to-date November 2023. This amend-and-extend activity has spiked to nearly 400 transactions in late 2023, representing the highest level since the global financial crisis peak in 2009. Lenders are increasingly choosing to extend maturities rather than push borrowers into defaults, though pre-emptive selective defaults are rising. 

Notable companies experiencing selective defaults in 2023 include Bausch Health, Community Health, Carvana, AMC Entertainment, Rackspace Technology, Telesat, Shutterfly, Curo Group, and US Renal Care. Finally, the text notes that lenders may become less willing to permit aggressive EBITDA adjustments, which have historically been used to artificially lower reported leverage ratios by 0.5x to 3.0x.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest evaluates how randomly constructed portfolios of hedge funds perform against traditional risk-adjusted stock and bond benchmarks from January 2018 through September 2023. He argues that while hedge fund portfolios generally show strong outperformance against these benchmarks, the success of this strategy relies heavily on diversification. 

The first scatter plot, titled "20-fund composites vs benchmarks [HFR]," compares annualized excess returns against T-bills, shown from 0% to 10% on the vertical axis, with annualized excess return volatility, ranging from 4% to 18% on the horizontal axis. The plot displays 300 randomly constructed portfolios of 20 hedge funds represented by gold dots, plotted against a benchmark curve of black squares representing various S&P 500 and Barclays Aggregate Bond index combinations from 20/80 to 80/20. This visual demonstrates that 78% of the gold hedge fund portfolios generated higher excess returns than their corresponding risk-adjusted benchmarks, sitting above the benchmark curve. 

To highlight the critical role of diversification in achieving these results, a neighboring bar chart titled "Outperformance of hedge fund portfolios declines with the number of funds included" tracks the percentage of outperforming portfolios, shown from 50% to 80% on the vertical axis, against the number of randomly selected hedge funds in the portfolios, shown as 20, 15, 10, and 5 on the horizontal axis. The chart shows a steep decline in performance: while a 20-fund portfolio achieves an outperformance rate of nearly 78%, a portfolio with only 5 hedge funds drops to just a 55% chance of beating the stock and bond benchmark. 

To test these findings, the analysis was repeated using the Pivotal Path database, which is detailed in a secondary scatter plot titled "20-fund composites vs benchmarks [PivotalPath]." Starting with a database of 2,200 funds and filtering down to 470 US-domiciled core strategy funds that reported for the entire period, this plot maps the same excess return and volatility metrics. The results using the Pivotal Path data are even stronger, showing that almost every single one of the 300 gold composite portfolios clustered above the benchmark curve, indicating near-universal outperformance of the risk-adjusted stock and bond benchmarks.

This page addresses the critical issue of survivorship bias in hedge fund performance analysis, which typically inflates reported returns because underperforming funds often stop reporting. To evaluate this impact, the author outlines an iteration of the Pivotal Path analysis that includes 432 partially reporting funds (with at least 24 consecutive months of performance) alongside the original 470 fully reporting funds, assuming a transition to monthly T-bill returns once a fund ceased reporting. 

The primary visual is a scatter plot titled "20-fund composites vs benchmarks [PivotalPath]," which plots annualized return versus T-bills since January 2018 on the y-axis (from 0% to 10%) against annualized excess return volatility on the x-axis (from 4% to 18%). The data series includes 300 random 20-fund hedge fund portfolios containing partially reporting funds, represented as gold dots, and various blended S&P 500 and Barclays Aggregate benchmarks, represented as black squares ranging from a conservative 20/80 mix to an aggressive 80/20 mix. Despite the downward shift of the hedge fund cluster due to the inclusion of partially reporting funds, the vast majority of these composites continue to outperform the risk-adjusted benchmark line. 

To provide broader context, the accompanying table compiles academic estimates of survivorship bias over time, showing the estimated decline in average annual hedge fund returns once dead funds are factored in. The studies span several decades and consistently show positive bias estimates, confirming that excluding defunct funds overstates performance. The estimates range from a low of 0.16% by Ackerman in 1999 and 0.54% by Yuen in 2018, to mid-range estimates like Amin at 2.00% in 2003, Horst at 2.10% in 2007, Liang at 2.24% in 2000, Brown at 3.00% in 1999, Edwards at 3.06% in 2001, and Fung at 3.48% in 1997, up to high estimates of 4.50% by Malkiel in 2005 and 5.00% by Aggarwal in 2010. The author notes a significant caveat: this analysis does not capture the severe real-world liquidations of illiquid assets that occur when a fund winds down, though a shorter five-year analysis window naturally mitigates some of this survivorship impact.

This page analyzes the ongoing structural struggles within the commercial real estate market, focusing specifically on the office sector, persistent work-from-home trends, and the challenging financial economics of office-to-residential conversions. The author begins by highlighting a silver lining: private real estate allocations to the office sector began declining as early as 2015, dropping below 20% well before the onset of the pandemic. 

This trend is illustrated in the first chart, which tracks MSCI commercial real estate core index property type allocations from 2000 to 2023. It reveals that while office and retail allocations have steadily declined, industrial and apartment allocations have climbed, with industrial property allocations surging to become the largest share at over 35% by 2023. The shift away from offices aligns with persistent work-from-home behavior. The second chart, which uses data from Stanford and other institutions, tracks the percentage of paid workdays performed from home across major US metropolitan areas from October 2020 to October 2023. This data shows work-from-home rates stabilizing between 30% and 35% for most cities, representing a massive shift from the pre-pandemic national average of roughly 3%. The San Francisco Bay Area is the clear outlier with a 45.5% work-from-home rate as of October 2023, followed by New York City at 36.8% and Los Angeles at 36.7%, while Chicago represents the lowest of the major cities shown at 25.6%.

The distress in the office sector is further reflected in commercial mortgage-backed securities. The third chart displays CMBS delinquency rates by property type from 2001 to 2023, indicating that while delinquency rates for retail, multifamily, and industrial properties remain low or are improving, office delinquencies are rising sharply, heading toward 5%. The fourth chart compares CMBS special servicing rates for office versus non-office loans, showing a dramatic divergence in 2023. While non-office special servicing rates have plateaued or decreased, office special servicing rates have spiked to nearly 8%, reflecting pending loan modifications and heightened distress.

Finally, the author addresses the viability of converting struggling office buildings into residential spaces, outlining a realistic financial model for a prewar Class B office building in New York City. Assuming monthly office rents of $3.50 per square foot, conversion costs of $320 per square foot, green efficiency upgrades of $40 per square foot, a 15% loss in rentable space, and luxury residential rents at the 90th percentile, a buyer would still need to negotiate a purchase price of just $175 per square foot to achieve a target return of 15% to 18%. Because this price represents a steep 60% decline from pre-pandemic valuations, the author concludes that widespread conversions are unlikely to materialize without massive property price write-downs.

This page, titled "2024 Outlook: Pillow Talk" by Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management, discusses the global macroeconomic and investment outlook for the year 2024. Cembalest argues that falling US inflation and the prospect of easier Federal Reserve monetary policy are fueling expectations of a soft landing rather than a severe recession. Although leading indicators suggest slowing growth and rising real estate and corporate delinquencies, these are characterized as lagging indicators. The text highlights a significant divergence in 2023 equity performance, where S&P 500 earnings were flat overall, but surged 33% for the seven largest megacap stocks while declining 5% for the rest of the index. Looking ahead to 2024, Cembalest forecasts slowing GDP growth, single-digit earnings growth, and single-digit returns for the median S&P 500 stock, recommending a diversified portfolio of cash, long-duration government bonds, high-quality corporate bonds, and equities, with particular interest in US Industrials, Energy, and Japanese markets. 

The analytical point of the page is illustrated in a chart titled "Equities tend to bottom first during recessions." The chart plots the number of months since the beginning of a recession on the horizontal axis, ranging from negative eight to thirty-two months, across seven historical US downturns: Eisenhower, the 1970s stagflation, the 1980s double dip, the 1990s S&L crisis, the DotCom crash, the Great Financial Crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic. Various symbols mark the "time of worst reading" for key economic metrics. Across almost all cycles, equities, represented by red diamonds, bottomed very early in the recession—often within the first five to twelve months—and well before lagging indicators like S&P earnings, high-yield default rates, and real estate delinquencies reached their worst points. The DotCom cycle is explicitly labeled as "the exception" with an arrow pointing to the equity bottom occurring late at month nineteen, long after the official end of the recession at month eight, and after GDP and housing starts had already hit their worst points before the recession even officially began.

This page from the report argues that while many leading economic indicators point to weaker growth in the United States, they do not suggest a sharp recession. The author notes that although their preferred leading indicator—the Institute for Supply Management new orders less inventories—is actually improving marginally, other indicators suggest weakness. These weak indicators include capital spending, construction, and profits, alongside small business expectations. Crucially, the author warns investors that a hard landing in corporate profits is possible even if the broader economy achieves a soft landing, drawing a historical parallel to the market dynamics of 2001.

The argument is supported by six charts. The first chart, titled US new orders less inventories, compares the ISM manufacturing PMI composite index on the left axis to ISM new orders less inventories with a three-month lead on the right axis from 1983 to late 2023. It shows that although both fell significantly, the leading indicator has recently ticked upward from its trough. The second chart, focused on small business expectations, tracks the net percentage of respondents to the NFIB Optimism Survey from 1986 to late 2023. It demonstrates that both sales and profit expectations have deteriorated significantly, with profit expectations hitting deeply negative levels around negative thirty percent.

The third chart relates US bank lending standards to US non-residential capital expenditure. It plots year-over-year non-residential capex against an inverted, nine-month leading measure of bank lending standards from 1992 to 2023, illustrating that the recent, severe net tightening of lending standards points to a coming contraction in capex. Similarly, the fourth chart plots construction activity against the Leading Economic Index with an 18-month lead. It demonstrates that the sharp downward trend in the LEI predicts a substantial deceleration in construction activity.

The fifth chart displays coincident and leading economic indicators from 1970 to 2023, showing that year-over-year leading indicators have dipped sharply below zero, which historically foreshadows a deceleration in coincident indicators. Finally, the sixth chart plots year-over-year corporate profits against a leading indicator model with an 18-month lead that incorporates the federal funds rate, the effective corporate tax rate, unemployment, and productivity growth. This model projects a steep decline in corporate profit growth toward flat or negative territory, emphasizing the risk of a profit contraction.

This page addresses the central question of why rapid increases in the Federal Reserve’s policy rates have not yet triggered a US recession, arguing that recession risks are receding due to structural buffers in the corporate and banking sectors. The author presents several arguments backed by historical data: current real rates remain below the destructive levels of past cycles, corporate cash flows are fundamentally healthier than in previous pre-recession periods, and many firms successfully immunized themselves against rate spikes by locking in long-term debt maturities at lower rates. 

A series of five charts and one historical table support these points. The first chart, showing the real cost of money (calculated as the Fed Funds rate minus Core CPI with a 21-day smoothing), illustrates that despite recent hikes, real rates remain below the peak levels that historically triggered recessions, which often exceeded four to eight percent in the late twentieth century. The second chart, analyzing the US corporate sector financial balance as a percentage of corporate gross value added, shows that companies have maintained positive balances in recent quarters, avoiding the deep deficit spending that typically precedes recessions. 

The third chart illustrates why rising interest rates have had a muted impact on businesses. It compares the Federal funds rate (ranging up to twenty percent historically) against corporate net interest payments as a percentage of after-tax NIPA profits. While interest payments spiked during past tightening cycles, they have remained stable and low, near historical troughs of around four to six percent, even as the Fed funds rate surged post-2020. The fourth chart displays US private non-financial credit creation as a percentage of GDP on a two-quarter annualized change, showing that credit creation remains in line with typical non-recessionary cycles. 

To address the timing of monetary policy impacts, a table details the lag between the first Fed rate hike and the onset of a recession. It shows that recessions historically occur at least seven quarters after the initial rate hike, with examples including an eight-quarter lag starting from Q3 1958, a twelve-quarter lag starting from Q2 1977, and a fourteen-quarter lag starting from Q3 2004. With the current cycle having begun in early 2022, the economy is now entering this typical historical window. However, the final chart, measuring a US liquidity proxy in trillions of dollars, forecasts that liquidity conditions are set to improve in 2024. The liquidity proxy, which hovered around five point five trillion dollars in 2023, is projected to rise toward six point five trillion dollars, driven by the supportive impacts of the Bank Term Funding Facility, the Overnight Reverse Repo Facility, and the Treasury General Account. This expanding liquidity is expected to act as an important cushion against any near-term decline in economic growth.

This page of the publication argues that the battle against inflation in developed economies is mostly won, paving the way for central banks to halt rate hikes. However, the author warns that futures markets may be overestimating the pace of rate cuts, pricing in one point four percent of Federal Reserve easing by the end of 2024. He cautions that too much easing too quickly could reignite inflation, noting that the Fed has enough egg on its face already. Six charts support the thesis that inflation is receding due to easing supply chains, recovering auto inventories, falling used car prices, and a massive wave of residential housing supply.

The first chart shows annualized three-month core inflation declines across Sweden, the United Kingdom, Norway, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, the Euro Area, the United States, and Switzerland. Across all these nations, inflation has fallen dramatically from its cycle peaks; for instance, the United States PCE measure has fallen from over five percent to under three percent. A second chart tracks alternative US consumer price inflation measures since 1985, including the Cleveland Fed median CPI, the Atlanta Fed sticky CPI, and the Cleveland Fed trimmed mean CPI. This visual highlights that while inflation spiked sharply toward eight percent during the pandemic recovery, all three measures have retreated significantly toward three to four percent.

The cooling of supply-side blockages is shown in a chart of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York Global Supply Chain Pressure Index from 2018 to 2023, which shows the index plummeting from a pandemic peak of over four down to negative territory by late 2023. This supply recovery is mirrored in the auto sector, where a dual-axis chart tracks US used vehicle prices and inventory levels. The Manheim US Index of used vehicle values has dropped from a peak of around 260 to near 200, while auto inventories have recovered from less than twenty percent of their 2019 average up toward forty percent.

For the housing sector, the fifth chart compares the Zillow rent index against official CPI Rent on an annualized six-month change basis from 2016 to 2023. The leading Zillow index peaked above fifteen percent in late 2021 before falling below zero, signaling that the lagging official CPI Rent measure, which is currently descending from a nine percent peak, has substantial room to fall further. Finally, a chart of housing supply under construction as a percentage of owner-occupied housing stock shows multi-family construction surging to a multi-decade high of nearly one point four percent, while single-family construction remains steady at around zero point nine percent, indicating that significant multi-family real estate supply is set to online and keep downward pressure on rents.

The author argues that while wage inflation is expected to decline in the short term, long-term inflation risks tilt higher due to structural factors such as US energy and semiconductor industrial policies. In the wage discussion, the author highlights leading indicators of easing labor markets, including declines in temporary help, unit labor costs, and advertised wages, alongside a drop in the voluntary quits rate. Although union negotiated pay raises remain at peak levels, the author notes that union workers represent only seven percent of the workforce, far below the twenty to thirty percent seen in the 1970s.

Two charts support this wage analysis. The first, Wage inflation measures, tracks percent-change trends from 1985 to 2023 across negotiated raises, the Atlanta Fed Wage Tracker, and the Employment Cost Index, showing a post-2020 spike that is beginning to cool. The second, Wages in job postings => Wages, projects the Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker using average growth in wages advertised in job postings, which acts as a four-month leading indicator. This chart shows advertised wage growth sharply falling from a peak near ten percent in 2021-2022 toward three percent in late 2023, signaling that broader wage trackers are poised to follow.

Addressing energy policy, the author observes that transitioning to renewable energy requires a duplication of generation capacity, which increases capital costs and ultimately electricity prices. A chart titled MISO: wind, solar and gas capacity as a function of wind/solar share of load plots megawatts against wind and solar generation as a share of load. As the wind and solar capacity line rises dramatically from under twenty thousand megawatts to about eighty thousand megawatts, the natural gas capacity line shows only a very modest decline, remaining around eighty thousand megawatts. This demonstrates that fossil fuel capacity cannot be decommissioned on a one-to-one basis as renewables increase.

Regarding semiconductor policy, the author discusses Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) building two new fabs in Arizona, costing forty billion dollars. The Chief Financial Officer of TSMC indicates these US fabs are four to five times more expensive than those in Taiwan, coupled with higher domestic labor costs. While renationalizing supply chains mitigates geopolitical risk, it will increase costs for tech-heavy sectors. A final stacked bar chart, Global semiconductor market value, illustrates this expanding sector, showing total market value growing from approximately six hundred billion dollars in 2021 to a projected one trillion dollars by 2030. The largest growth areas within this trillion-dollar projection are computing and data storage, followed by wireless communication, automotive electronics, industrial electronics, consumer electronics, and wired communication.

This page of the J.P. Morgan 2024 Outlook report, written by Michael Cembalest, argues that the exceptional performance and high valuation of market megacaps are largely justified by their superior fundamental strengths, specifically their robust profit margins and free cash flow growth. Cembalest highlights that the "Magnificent 7" stocks—consisting of Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla—have driven the bulk of the equity market's gains, leading to historic levels of index concentration. He observes that in 2023, an extraordinary 72 percent of S&P 500 stocks underperformed the broader index, compared to a historical average of 52 percent. While these megacaps appear expensive on a surface level, he notes that they are reasonably priced once adjusted for their strong long-term earnings growth expectations, though he cautions that the market positioning has become highly crowded.

Six charts support this analysis. The first chart, illustrating the market capitalization of the largest seven companies in the S&P 500 from 1996 to late 2023, shows that these firms represent an all-time high of approximately 28 percent of the total index market cap, surpassing the previous dot-com era peak of roughly 21 percent. The second chart details how the Magnificent 7 stocks led the S&P 500 in 2023, with year-to-date returns reaching about 75 percent for the megacaps, compared to roughly 25 percent for the overall S&P 500 and only about 12 percent for the S&P 500 excluding these seven companies. 

The middle row of charts displays the underlying fundamentals driving this divergence. The growth in free cash flow, indexed to January 2018, shows the Magnificent 7 soaring to an index value of over 210 by late 2023, while the rest of the S&P 500 lagged behind at approximately 150. Meanwhile, the profit margin chart reveals a persistent profitability gap from 2014 to 2024, with the Magnificent 7 ending 2023 with profit margins around 22 percent, whereas the rest of the S&P 500 hovered near 9 percent. 

The bottom row addresses valuation and market positioning. The chart tracking the relative price-to-earnings ratio of the Magnificent 7 versus the median S&P 500 stock from 2013 to 2023 shows a raw relative P/E of 1.7x. However, when adjusted for long-term earnings growth expectations, the relative P/E ratio drops to 0.9x, which is below the historical parity line of 1.0x. Finally, the Nasdaq 100 positioning chart for asset managers and leveraged funds from 2010 to late 2023 shows net long positions surging dramatically to nearly 100,000 contracts by the end of 2023, demonstrating a highly crowded and widely agreed-upon investment theme.

This page from the report analyzes Japan's status as a highly successful "value" investment in 2023 that is regaining attention from international investors. Michael Cembalest argues that while corporate governance reforms and an exit from deflation have boosted the Japanese market, long-term structural headwinds remain. He cautions that Japan is still a very slow-growing economy burdened by unfavorable demographics, negative real wage growth, and flat industrial production growth that mimics Europe. Additionally, China has eclipsed Japan as the world's largest auto exporter, and the Bank of Japan estimates the country's potential growth rate is under one percent. As a result, the positive outlook for Japanese equities is likely a short-term phenomenon driven by a transitional exit from deflation and governance policies rather than a multi-year growth runway. 

Four visuals support this analysis. The first chart, depicting year-to-date cumulative overseas investor inflows into Japan in trillions of JPY, reveals that 2023 saw solid buying from international investors, tracking near six trillion yen by the end of November, though still well below the massive inflow surge of over fourteen trillion yen seen in 2013. 

The accompanying table compares major equity factor returns for 2023 year-to-date across Japan, the United States, and Europe, emphasizing Japan's dominant value factor performance. In Japan, price-to-earnings returned thirty-three percent and price-to-book returned thirty percent. This stands in sharp contrast to the United States, where these factors returned negative eight percent and negative four percent, and Europe, which saw returns of two percent and negative three percent. Conversely, Japan’s actual earnings per share growth was just one percent, compared to fifteen percent in the United States and nine percent in Europe, underscoring that Japan's rally was valuation-driven rather than earnings-driven.

The third chart plots the underweighting of global investors in Japanese stocks from 2003 to 2023, comparing the MSCI All World Global Equity Index's Japan weight to actual global portfolio allocations. While the overall index weight for Japan has declined from around ten percent in the mid-2000s to roughly six percent in 2023, global investors have consistently remained underweight, holding a weight of around five percent in late 2023—representing a modest underweight of roughly one percent. 

Finally, a chart of the Japanese real broad effective exchange rate index from 1994 to 2023 shows a persistent, long-term decline from a peak of nearly two hundred down to historical lows below eighty by late 2023. This dramatic depreciation signals extreme cheapness of the Yen, which the author notes could serve as a continued tailwind for global investors.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2024 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, discusses the divergence between European and Japanese equities. Cembalest expresses skepticism about European equities, noting that despite Europe trading near a record price-to-earnings discount, European stocks underperformed the United States by seven percent in 2023. He advocates for his long-running "barbell" strategy, which overweights the United States and Emerging Markets while underweighting Europe and Japan. 

To support this strategy, the top-left area chart displays the three-year rolling outperformance or underperformance of this barbell strategy against the MSCI All World Index from 1991 through late 2023. The data reveals that this barbell strategy has outperformed in 84 percent of all three-year rolling periods since 1991, with an average positive return of 3.0 percent, compared to an average return of negative 1.2 percent when the strategy does not work. 

The top-right line chart tracks the relative price-to-earnings discount of Europe versus the United States based on forward earnings from 2006 to late 2023, using data from Bloomberg and Datastream. The chart demonstrates that Europe's discount has steadily widened over the years, starting at roughly a 10 percent discount in 2006 and descending to near-record levels of approximately 35 percent to 38 percent by the end of 2023.

Turning to Japan, Cembalest argues that corporate governance reforms and shifting policies are creating a stronger foundation for equity investing. Key catalysts include threats from the Tokyo Stock Exchange to delist companies trading below book value, the emergence of over 50 activist funds proposing governance changes, and an increase in the share of companies with more than 50 percent independent external directors from 30 percent to 60 percent. Additionally, tax incentives and pressure on pension systems to align allocations with the Government Pension Investment Fund are expected to drive more capital into Japanese equities.

This potential is detailed in the bottom-left table, titled "Room for Japan to 'equitize'," which compares various financial metrics between the United States and Japan. The data shows that 50 percent of Japanese companies trade below book value compared to only 4 percent of American companies. Cash represents 21 percent of market capitalization in Japan versus just 7 percent in the United States. Furthermore, Japan's ten-year dividend payout ratio stands at 30 percent compared to 70 percent in the United States, and corporate buybacks as a percentage of market capitalization are only 0.7 percent to 1.4 percent in Japan compared to 2.0 percent to 3.5 percent in the United States. On the retail side, Japanese households allocate 55 percent of their assets to cash and only 11 percent to equities, whereas American households allocate 15 percent to cash and 40 percent to equities. Similarly, Japanese pension equity allocation is lower at 25 percent compared to 40 percent in the United States.

The final line chart in the bottom-right corner, titled "Japan finally exits deflation," plots the year-over-year percentage change in Japan's core Consumer Price Index, excluding fresh food and energy, from 1980 through late 2023. The chart highlights that after decades of deflation or near-zero inflation since the late 1990s, Japan’s core inflation spiked to around 4 percent by late 2023. This exit from deflation has pushed real short-term interest rates to negative 2 percent, making cash holdings significantly less attractive relative to equities for Japanese households and pension funds.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2024 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the current state of US equity markets, focusing on the concentration of megacap stocks, asset yield convergence, and sector opportunities in industrials and energy. The author begins by highlighting a unique macroeconomic juncture where the yields of multiple asset classes have converged to a degree not seen in twenty years. A line chart titled "Convergence of yields across assets" tracks yields from 2000 to late 2023 on a scale of 0% to 12%. It illustrates that the S&P 500 12-month forward earnings yield, US corporate investment-grade bond yields to maturity, the US three-month Treasury rate, and the implied unlevered cap rate of All Equity REITs have all tightly converged around the 5% to 6% range. This convergence suggests that holding cash offers strong risk-adjusted value compared to historical standards. 

The author then addresses equity valuations, referencing a second chart titled "S&P 500 valuations," which plots forward P/E multiples from 1995 to late 2023. The chart compares the market-cap-weighted S&P 500, which has climbed to a high valuation of 19x, with the equal-weighted S&P 500, which sits closer to its historical median at 16x. This gap highlights the heavy influence of megacaps on the index. Cembalest asserts that the valuation peaks of 2020 and 2021 are no longer relevant because the Federal Reserve is expected to maintain a positive real cost of money. Furthermore, underlying corporate fundamentals are weaker than top-line index figures suggest; both real corporate revenues and S&P operating earnings per share have been flat since early 2022, as has free cash flow when excluding the seven largest megacaps. Consequently, the author predicts a soft landing is already priced in, expecting single-digit earnings growth and single-digit returns for the median US stock in 2024, alongside continued outperformance by megacaps.

Beyond technology, the analysis identifies industrials and energy as attractive sectors. A third chart, "Industrial valuations vs the market," tracks the industrial sector's forward P/E relative to the S&P 500 from 1996 to late 2023. Currently hovering between 0.95 and 1.00, industrial valuations are relatively inexpensive compared to prior peaks of 1.15 to 1.20, and the sector is poised to benefit from recent energy, semiconductor, and infrastructure legislation. 

Lastly, the energy sector is analyzed via a table displaying the "Percentile rank of energy sector valuations relative to S&P 1500" from the start of available data to November 2023. It categorizes data by subsectors, including drilling, equipment, integrated oil and gas, exploration, refining, storage, and the total energy sector. On an Enterprise Value to EBITDA basis, the total Energy sector ranks in the extremely cheap 4th percentile for both the last and next 12 months. Meanwhile, its free cash flow yield ranks in the historically high 88th percentile for the last 12 months and 87th percentile for the next 12 months. Subsectors like Oil and Gas Drilling and Equipment show even lower valuation percentiles, ranking in the 2nd percentile for the next 12 months. Although Cembalest cautions that stranded asset concerns may cap valuation upside, he concludes that the energy sector remains a highly compelling source of earnings yield, dividends, and stock buybacks.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2024 Outlook examines the state of fixed income and high-yield bonds, arguing that US corporate credit remains highly resilient despite rising interest rates. The author explains that large-cap companies have insulated themselves from rate hikes because a massive portion of their debt is locked in at fixed rates. This is illustrated by a pie chart of S&P 500 debt composition, which shows that 76% of debt is long-term fixed, compared to less than 50% in 2007, with the remainder split between short-term fixed at 10%, long-term floating at 8%, and short-term floating at 6%. 

Even though leverage metrics are historically high, interest coverage is robust. A table ranking current credit metrics against historical percentiles shows that while US investment-grade corporate net debt-to-EBITDA is in the 92nd percentile and total debt-to-assets is at the 100th percentile, interest coverage is in a healthy 69th percentile and interest expense-to-debt is in the 15th percentile. US high yield exhibits an even stronger interest coverage profile in the 92nd percentile and EBITDA margins in the 73rd percentile.
