Furthermore, an accompanying chart tracking credit rating upgrades and downgrades as a percentage of par from 2010 to 2023 shows that net credit changes have been positive since 2021, meaning upgrades are consistently outpacing downgrades.

However, the high-yield sector is not without risks. A line chart displaying the weighted average maturity of US corporate high yield debt from 1987 to 2023 shows a steady downward trend, reaching an all-time low of just above 5 years in 2023. This short maturity runway increases issuers' exposure to refinancing at today's higher rates. 

Finally, the author celebrates the conclusion of an unprecedented era of negative real interest rates, or "financial repression." A historical bar chart tracks the five-year average of the Treasury bill or Fed Funds rate minus inflation from 1830 to the present. The chart highlights that the post-2010 period of negative real rates was the longest peacetime era of negative rates in US history, matching or exceeding the repression seen during the Civil War, World War I, and World War II. Although the five-year trailing average remains negative, the chart's final "Current" data point indicates that real rates have finally turned positive on a one-year basis, offering a welcome relief to fixed-income investors.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication outlines the primary sources of credit stress in the United States. While delinquency rates remain remarkably low in certain sectors like hotels, retail excluding malls, multifamily, and industrial properties, there are clear pockets of rising distress. These key areas of concern include regional malls, office commercial real estate, subprime auto loans, credit cards, and shrinking interest coverage among leveraged loan issuers.

In the commercial real estate sector, a chart displaying CMBS delinquencies by property type from 2001 to 2023 reveals that regional malls have faced the most severe stress, with delinquency rates spiking to nearly 25% around 2020 and remaining highly elevated near 20% through late 2023. By contrast, other commercial real estate categories have stayed below 5%. This mounting stress in the office sector is further illustrated by a chart tracking special servicing rates for CMBS loans from 2002 to 2023. Special servicing rates for office properties have sharply ticked up to over 8% in late 2023, reflecting a divergent trend compared to non-office properties, which peaked during the 2020 pandemic and stood at approximately 6% in late 2023.

In corporate credit, interest coverage ratios for B- rated issuers in the US loan market have deteriorated drastically between January 2022 and December 2023. At the start of 2022, approximately 60% of these issuers had interest coverage above 1.5x, with only about 20% falling below 1.0x. By December 2023, this distribution completely inverted: over 60% of B- issuers possessed interest coverage below 1.0x, and less than 15% remained above 1.5x. This financial strain has forced corporate borrowers to renegotiate their debts, as demonstrated by a bar chart showing US leveraged loan amendments and extensions from 2009 to late 2023. The count of these transactions reached nearly 450 through year-to-date November 2023, a sharp spike from the roughly 200 to 250 recorded in 2021 and 2022, and nearing the peak of over 500 seen in 2009.

Finally, the publication highlights growing stress within the consumer household sector through a chart tracking US 90+ days loan delinquency transition rates from 2004 to 2023. Subprime auto loans have climbed steadily to exceed 4%, and credit card delinquency transition rates have also experienced a sharp upward trajectory to nearly 4% by late 2023. In contrast, delinquency transition rates for standard auto loans, first mortgages, and second mortgages remain highly stable, hovering at or below 1%. This divergence emphasizes that current consumer distress is heavily concentrated among subprime borrowers.

This page features a fixed income market monitor analyzing various yield curves, spreads, and sovereign bond behaviors leading up to late 2023. Michael Cembalest introduces the monitor by addressing a key question for 10-year US Treasuries: whether their next stop is 3.5% or 5.5%. He predicts that they will fluctuate between 4% and 5% in 2024, with a potential breakout target of 5.5%, and suggests that yields north of 4.5% present decent value for long-term investors.

Nine charts illustrate the current landscape of fixed income. The first chart, showing US Treasury yields from 2000 through late 2023, tracks the 3-month US Treasury bill and the 10-year US Treasury, both of which spiked dramatically toward 5% in late 2023. Beside it, a chart of US Municipal yields tracks long-duration munis of over 20 years alongside municipals of 1 to 17 years, illustrating a sharp rise in 2023 where long-duration municipal yields neared 4.5%. The top-right chart tracks local currency 10-year sovereign bond yields for Europe and China, showing European yields rebounding from negative territory up to approximately 2.5% in late 2023, while Chinese yields steadily declined to a similar level of 2.5%. 

In the middle row, the left chart monitors the spread between 30-year mortgages and the 10-year Treasury in basis points from 2005 to 2023, highlighting a recent spike to over 300 basis points, which matches the historic highs observed during the Great Financial Crisis. The middle chart displays AAA asset-backed securities spreads versus Treasuries for commercial real estate, auto loans, and credit cards from 1998 to 2023. While all three spiked spectacularly during the 2008 crisis, they experienced a smaller uptick in late 2023, with commercial real estate spreads climbing past 100 basis points. The middle-row right chart tracks local currency 10-year sovereign bond yields for South Africa and Mexico from 2006 to 2024, showing South African yields rising toward 12% and Mexican yields reaching nearly 9% to 10% in late 2023.

The bottom row of charts focuses on floating rate instruments and preferred securities. The bottom-left chart tracks USD-denominated floating rate instruments from 2000 to late 2023, showing that both US investment-grade corporate floating rate notes and AA bank commercial paper spiked to around 5.5% in late 2023. The bottom-middle chart measures the preferred option-adjusted spread versus Treasuries using the P0P1 index for US investment-grade preferred stock, which peaked at nearly 800 basis points in 2008 and hovered around 200 to 250 basis points in late 2023. Finally, the bottom-right chart displays US preferred yields from 2010 to late 2023, showcasing that US high-yield preferred yields spiked to nearly 8% to 9%, while US high-grade preferred yields rose to around 7%.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan 2024 Outlook examines the deteriorating state of United States Federal debt, rising interest expenses, and structurally high budget deficits. The author argues that the current fiscal trajectory is highly unusual, particularly because the government is running a massive deficit during a period of full employment. 

To support this argument, the page features five charts. The first chart, titled Debt Held by the Public as a percent of GDP, spans from 1970 to 2030. It illustrates a dramatic spike in federal debt following the COVID-19 stimulus. A comparison of CBO projections from January 2020 and May 2023 shows that the post-pandemic debt trajectory has shifted upward significantly, with debt projected to approach 120% of GDP by 2030, compared to pre-pandemic expectations of around 95%. 

The second chart displays Interest Expense as a percent of GDP from 1962 to 2032, distinguishing between gross and net interest. Both CBO and J.P. Morgan forecasts from late 2023 project net interest expense to rise sharply, potentially reaching a post-war high of nearly 3.5% of GDP by 2032. The author notes this rise could cause net interest expense to exceed defense spending for the first time since the 1990s. 

The third chart shows the Budget Deficit as a percent of GDP from 1970 to 2030. Following the historic deficits of the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic, the May 2023 CBO projection shows the deficit failing to recover, instead remaining stuck around 6% of GDP through 2030. 

The fourth chart compares the US Budget Balance against the Unemployment Rate from 1969 to 2023, utilizing an inverted right-hand axis for unemployment to align the two metrics. Historically, the budget balance and unemployment rate have moved in tandem, with tight labor markets coinciding with smaller deficits or surpluses. The chart highlights the modern anomaly where unemployment is near record lows, yet the deficit is expanding to levels normally seen only during deep recessions. 

The final chart shows the Primary Budget Balance, which excludes interest, as a percentage of GDP from 1985 onwards. While the May 2023 CBO baseline projects this balance to stabilize at roughly a 3% deficit, J.P. Morgan’s November 2023 downside projection shows the primary deficit widening to nearly 6% of GDP. The page attributes this potential downside to three key catalysts: revenues falling below CBO expectations even after the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act expirations, discretionary and defense spending outstripping CBO assumptions by growing faster than inflation, and the rising costs of more frequent federal disaster funding.

This page examines the fiscal position of the United States and the resilience of the US dollar's status as the global reserve currency, specifically challenging the narrative that China is actively divesting from dollar-denominated assets. The author opens by noting that despite past Congressional Budget Office projections of a budget surplus, the US remains a significant fiscal outlier. 

The first chart, titled Government debt / GDP vs average credit rating, is a scatter plot comparing various nations' average credit ratings on the x-axis against their government debt-to-GDP ratios on the y-axis. A dotted trend line shows that higher debt ratios typically correspond to lower credit ratings, such as those of Spain, Portugal, and Italy. The United States is highlighted as a major outlier, maintaining an AA+ rating despite a debt-to-GDP ratio of around 120%, which is far above the trend line for its rating group. Japan is an even more extreme outlier, plotted with an AA-range rating despite a debt-to-GDP ratio of 260%. China is shown with an A+ rating and a debt-to-GDP ratio of roughly 75%. Other AAA-rated nations like Canada, Germany, and Australia are clustered at lower debt levels. 

A sidebar details a timeline of reserve currencies or dominant trade currencies throughout history to put the US dollar's status into perspective. It traces dominance from Rome in the first century BC through the Byzantine Empire, Arabian Dinar, Florence, Portugal, the Iberian Union, the Netherlands, France, and the United Kingdom, leading to the United States, which has held the dominant position since approximately 1920, with its future duration labeled as to be determined.

The second chart, Estimating China's dollar assets in billions of US dollars from 2008 to 2022, addresses fears of China abandoning the dollar. Citing research by Brad Setser of the Council on Foreign Relations, the author shows that China's dollar holdings are actually stable. While China’s direct holdings of US-custodied treasuries, shown by a red line, have steadily declined from over $1.2 trillion in 2013 to around $800 billion in 2022, this is offset by offshore custody. A light blue line tracking Belgian treasuries shows an increase to nearly $300 billion. When adjusting for these offshore holdings and reallocations into US Agency bonds, China’s total estimated dollar assets, represented by a dark blue line, have remained stable since 2015 at around $1.9 trillion. This adjusted metric tracks closely with a green line representing China’s estimated dollar assets calculated using IMF COFER shares, which sits at approximately $2.1 trillion in 2022.

This page revisits J.P. Morgan's April 2023 analysis on the enduring global dominance of the United States dollar across multiple financial metrics, demonstrating that despite ongoing debates over de-dollarization, the greenback remains the undisputed cornerstone of the global financial system. 

The first chart, tracking foreign exchange turnover by currency from 2001 to 2022, displays currency shares in global turnover, which sum to 200% because every transaction involves two currencies. The US dollar consistently claims the lion's share, remaining remarkably stable near the 85% to 90% range over two decades, far outpacing the Euro, Japanese Yen, British Pound, and the Chinese Renminbi, which appears only as a minor fraction. This dominance is further emphasized in a neighboring donut chart showing that US dollar transactions account for a staggering 89% of all global foreign exchange transactions, leaving non-US dollar pairs at just 11%. Broken down by specific pairs, US dollar transactions against all other non-major currencies make up 43% of the total, followed by US dollar to Euro at 23%, US dollar to Yen at 14%, and US dollar to British pound at 10%, whereas Euro transactions against all other currencies account for a mere 8%.

A horizontal bar chart contrasts the physical economic footprint of the United States with its financial hegemony. Although the United States accounts for only about 25% of global GDP and roughly 10% of world trade, the dollar's share in global markets is disproportionately high. It commands over 40% of SWIFT payments, approximately 50% of trade invoicing, nearly 60% of official foreign exchange reserves, roughly 65% of international debt securities (with a significant portion categorized as offshore), around 55% of cross-border loans, and nearly 90% of overall foreign exchange transaction volume. 

Finally, a historical area chart tracks the share of global foreign exchange reserves by currency from 1973 through 2023. While the US dollar's share has fluctuated over the decades—peaking above 80% in the 1970s, hitting a low point near 50% in the early 1990s, and recovering in the 2000s—it has stabilized at just under 60% as of late 2023. The Euro remains the second-largest reserve currency at roughly 20%, while other currencies like the Japanese Yen, British Pound, Canadian dollar, Australian dollar, Swiss Franc, and Chinese Renminbi represent much smaller shares, demonstrating that no rival currency is currently positioned to realistically displace the US dollar's global reserve status.

This page presents a comprehensive visual dashboard of global fixed income and credit markets as of late December 2023, highlighting spreads, yields, and prices across various asset classes to contextualize the credit landscape entering 2024. 

The first several charts illustrate a broad tightening of corporate credit spreads. US investment grade corporate spreads, measured by the JULI index versus US Treasuries, are sitting tight at approximately 100 to 120 basis points, well below previous peaks seen during the 2008 global financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic shutdown. Similarly, US high yield bond spreads have compressed to around 350 to 400 basis points, a significant drop from historic crisis levels of over 1,400 basis points. Emerging markets dollar bond spreads versus US Treasuries show a similar compression, hovering near 300 to 350 basis points. Within high yield, US high yield energy bond spreads have dropped dramatically to around 250 to 300 basis points, a stark contrast to the energy sector crises in 2016 and 2020 when spreads exceeded 1,500 and 2,000 basis points respectively.

In loan and European markets, the US leveraged loan prices index has recovered to around 95 to 96, up from historical crisis lows near 60. Meanwhile, the yield on Pan European high yield debt has moderated to around 7% to 8% after spiking toward 9% in late 2022. For European Contingent Capital preferreds, the page charts yield to worst using two different series: the ICE/Bank of America series, which includes Emerging Market issuers and subordinated Tier 2 issues, and the J.P. Morgan series, which is restricted to European preferreds qualifying as Additional Tier 1 (AT1) capital. Both indices saw yields spike to the 9% to 10% range during banking sector volatility in early 2023 before settling back down to around 7% to 8% by December.

The final two charts look at sovereign debt and real estate credit distress. The local currency yield on Brazil's 10-year sovereign bonds has eased to around 10% to 11% after peaking near 13% in 2022. Lastly, a chart tracking single asset single borrower (SASB) commercial real estate spreads versus Treasury yields highlights severe distress in the office sector. Spreads across all ratings—Office BBB, A, AA, and AAA—have ballooned since 2022. The lowest-tier Office BBB spreads peaked above 700 basis points and remain near 650 basis points, while even senior Office AAA spreads have widened dramatically to approximately 300 basis points, illustrating substantial market concern over office-backed properties.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2024 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the strength of the US consumer and warns that while spending has remained resilient, the financial buffers supporting it are steadily depleting. The commentary begins by noting the strong start to the late-2023 holiday season, with Black Friday online sales growing by 7.5% and Cyber Monday sales rising by 9.5%. This persistent strength throughout 2023 is attributed to tight labor markets, wealth effects from rising home and equity prices, and the ongoing drawdown of pandemic-era excess savings. 

The analysis is supported by four charts comparing economic indicators across the United States, the United Kingdom, the Eurozone (EMU), and Japan. The first chart, depicting real personal consumer spending indexed to the fourth quarter of 2019, shows the US significantly outperforming other major economies. By late 2023, US spending reached nearly 108% of its pre-pandemic level, whereas the Eurozone, Japan, and the United Kingdom lingered close to or below their 2019 baselines, ranging from 97% to 100%. The second chart shows that US household wealth relative to pre-pandemic levels also grew the fastest, rising to over 130% of its late 2019 base. In contrast, the UK and Eurozone hovered near 118% to 120%, and Japan remained the lowest at roughly 110%, demonstrating a stronger wealth effect in the United States. 

The third chart explains how this spending was funded, showing the percentage-point deviation of household saving rates from 2019 averages. The US saving rate fell significantly below its pre-pandemic norm, sitting at a negative 4 percentage point deviation by 2023. Meanwhile, households in the Eurozone and Japan saved more than their pre-pandemic averages, at positive deviations of roughly 1% and 4% respectively. This indicates that US consumers have aggressively drawn down savings to maintain consumption. 

The final chart presents estimates of US household excess savings in billions of dollars, which peaked near $2.5 trillion in mid-2021. Three internal J.P. Morgan divisions project different trajectories for the exhaustion of these funds: J.P. Morgan Investment Bank estimated that excess savings hit zero in late 2023; J.P. Morgan Economics forecasts depletion around mid-2024; and J.P. Morgan Private Bank anticipates a slower decline, with roughly $500 billion in excess savings persisting through late 2024. The author notes that these forecasts align closely with a San Francisco Fed estimate pointing to exhaustion sometime in the first half of 2024, concluding that consumer spending is highly likely to slow down once this financial cushion is fully depleted.

This page from the publication analyzes the state of US consumer credit, delinquency rates, and household debt service, presenting a largely reassuring picture despite some emerging pressure points. The author observes that while delinquency rates are rising for subprime auto loans and credit cards, only subprime auto is currently breaching new all-time highs. Meanwhile, mortgage and prime auto delinquency rates remain remarkably low, and overall household interest costs are rising from very low levels because US consumers locked in historically low mortgage rates below four percent. 

Four charts support these observations using data through late 2023. The first chart, illustrating ninety-plus day loan delinquency transition rates from 2004 to 2024, shows a steep rise in subprime auto loan delinquencies, which have climbed toward five percent, exceeding their previous historical peaks. Credit card delinquencies are also rising but remain well below their financial crisis peaks, while first and second mortgages remain flat and extremely low at under one percent. The second chart presents annualized delinquency transition rates as a percentage of current balances, confirming that credit card delinquencies have rebounded sharply from a low of four percent to nearly six percent, while auto loan delinquencies have ticked up to about three percent, and mortgage delinquencies remain negligible. 

The bottom half of the page focuses on household debt sustainability. A third chart plots household interest costs as a percentage of disposable personal income from 1977 through 2023. It reveals that consumer interest costs have remained relatively stable, hovering between two and three percent, while mortgage interest costs have plummeted from over six percent in the early 1990s to below three percent today. The final chart details US household debt dynamics since 1980, tracking the average rate on outstanding mortgages against overall debt service as a percentage of disposable income. This visual highlights a long-term decline in the average outstanding mortgage rate from over eleven percent in the early 1980s to under four percent by 2021. Because of these locked-in low rates, the household debt service ratio has remained highly manageable, hovering around ten percent of disposable income, which is significantly lower than the thirteen percent peak reached just prior to the 2008 financial crisis. Data on these charts is sourced from Experian, S&P Dow Jones Indices, the Federal Reserve Board of New York, the Bureau of Economic Analysis, Bloomberg, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page serves as an introduction to a section titled The Fats Dominoes, which explores the profound impact of GLP-1 weight-loss and diabetes drugs on equity markets and consumer behavior. The author explains that these drugs have demonstrated significant efficacy in treating diabetes and obesity, alongside early indications that they could help manage related co-morbidities and addictive behaviors like alcoholism. Equity markets are already reacting, impacting the stock prices of insulin manufacturers, snack food companies, and alcoholic or sugary beverage producers. The pharmaceutical sector is heavily investing in this space, with over one hundred weight-loss agents currently under development and global sales projected to exceed one hundred billion dollars by 2030. Roches recent two-point-seven billion dollar acquisition of Carmot highlights this massive interest, which is expected to drive further acquisition activity from major pharmaceutical giants like Pfizer, Bristol, Merck, AstraZeneca, GlaxoSmithKline, Sanofi, and Takeda. Despite this excitement, the author poses critical open questions regarding the long-term durability of weight-loss outcomes, treatment costs, insurance coverage, and the extent to which co-morbidities are reduced. 

The page features a line chart plotting the historical and projected US average monthly total GLP-1 prescriptions in millions from 2008 to 2030. The chart tracks historical drug approvals as vertical dotted lines, including Victoza, Trulicity and Saxenda, Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound for obesity. Starting from 2023, the chart displays divergent projections from J.P. Morgan and TD Cowen for both Type II Diabetes and obesity. For diabetes, J.P. Morgan and Cowen project prescriptions to climb steeply, reaching roughly ten to twelve million by 2030. For obesity, J.P. Morgan projection rises sharply to around ten million prescriptions, whereas Cowens projection presents a more conservative estimate of about four million by 2030. To the right of the chart, a whimsical, AI-generated illustration portrays a round figure made of white dice sitting at a piano in a dimly lit bar, playfully referencing the Fats Dominoes title theme.

This page analyzes the economic challenges facing China, focusing heavily on its weakening domestic activity, collapsing consumer confidence, and a severely overextended housing market. The author argues that China’s core economic struggle stems from misallocated investment in real estate rather than excess industrial capacity. The text notes that China’s homeownership rate peaked at approximately 90%, with 20% of households owning multiple homes, while inbound foreign direct investment has fallen into negative territory for the first time. The author highlights indicators of broad-based disinflation and banking sector weakness, where net interest margins of 1.75% trail the US average of 3.25%. Looking ahead to 2024, JP Morgan China economists project modest policy interventions, including slightly higher budget deficits, small rate cuts, and local government support programs, though the Conference Board still expects GDP growth to decline from 5% in 2023 to 4% in 2024.

Five visual aids support these observations. The first chart, tracking foreign direct investment into China in billions of USD from 1998 to 2023, shows inward FDI, outward FDI, and net FDI. It highlights that net FDI has recently dipped below zero for the first time on record due to a sharp drop in inward investment. 

The second chart, measuring China’s real activity from 2015 to 2023 using a weighted average index of ten monthly indicators—including real estate investment, medicine consumption, various exports, electricity production, and enterprise output—illustrates that economic activity peaked around 2021 but has since steadily weakened, hovering near zero by late 2023.

The third chart illustrates the ongoing housing drag from 2017 to 2023, plotting year-over-year percentage changes for state-owned land use right transfer revenues and the residential floor space of newly started houses. Both series collapsed after 2021 and remain severely depressed in negative territory, contracting by roughly 20% to 40% year-over-year in 2023.

The fourth chart plots China’s consumer confidence index from 1996 to 2023, based on a 1997 baseline of 100. It shows that confidence plummeted from an all-time high of approximately 125 around 2020-2021 to unprecedented historic lows below 90 by late 2022 and 2023.

Finally, a comparative table contrasts the housing sectors of peak-era China and the US, demonstrating the scale of China’s real estate exposure. The peak value of housing stock relative to personal consumption expenditures is 6.0x in China compared to 2.2x in the US. Direct real estate-related activities account for 18% of GDP in China versus 6% in the US. Mid-2023 home price-to-income ratios in major Chinese cities (Shanghai, Shenzhen, Beijing, and Guangzhou) stand at a massive ~40x compared to ~10x in major US cities (New York and San Francisco). Additionally, China's homeownership rate of 90% substantially exceeds the US rate of 66%. A concluding note adds that China's 430 square feet of housing stock per capita is double the levels found in Europe or Japan.

This page evaluates the efficacy and side effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists used for weight loss, comparing various clinical trial results and examining the long-term impact of discontinuing treatment. The author observes that while these drugs facilitate significant weight loss, patients typically regain most of the lost weight—and experience a regression in cardiometabolic markers like blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, and hemoglobin—once treatment ceases. Weight loss from these drugs tends to flatline after about 40 weeks, reaching average reductions of roughly 15% of body weight, which is notable but still below the 25% to 30% reduction typically achieved through bariatric surgery.

The page features two charts illustrating these trends. The first, a bar chart titled "Weight loss observed in clinical trials," measures the percent of body weight lost across a wide variety of GLP drugs color-coded by regulatory status: approved, Phase 3, or Phase 1/2. The data shows that Retatrutide by Eli Lilly (in Phase 3) achieves the highest weight loss at approximately 24%, followed by approved options such as Zepbound by Eli Lilly at about 21% and Wegovy by Novo Nordisk at 15%. Numerous other development-stage therapeutics from manufacturers like Amgen, Pfizer, and AstraZeneca are shown to range from 5% to 15% weight loss. 

The second chart, titled "Change in body weight during and after treatment," plots the percentage change in body weight over 120 weeks for patients on a placebo versus those taking Wegovy. Wegovy patients experience steady weight loss that peaks at approximately -17% around week 68. At this point, indicated by a vertical dashed line, treatment is discontinued. Following discontinuation, the Wegovy cohort experiences rapid weight regain, with their average weight returning to approximately -5% of baseline by week 120, while the placebo group remains relatively flat near a 2% loss throughout.

The lower half of the page details several side effects and clinical concerns surrounding GLP use. The most frequent side effects in Phase II and III trials are nausea, affecting 20% to 45% of participants, and vomiting, affecting 10% to 30%. Rare but serious risks include pancreatitis, loss of muscle mass, and decreased bone density, highlighting a future research need for structured drug-weaning and discontinuation strategies. The author also warns of overdosing risks associated with non-FDA tested compounded GLP alternatives sold in drugstores where patients must manually fill their own syringes, which has led to increased calls to poison control centers. Finally, the text addresses potential psychiatric concerns, noting that while GLPs mitigate dopamine rewards and could theoretically cause a depressive condition called anhedonia, Phase III obesity trials for semaglutide showed no statistically significant difference in psychiatric effects between the treatment and placebo groups.

This page examines how GLP-1 receptor agonists function within the human body and details the ongoing clinical trials that could significantly expand their addressable market. The author explains that while direct Medicare coverage for obesity remains a long-term legislative hurdle, successful trials in other areas could allow GLP drugs to be branded and covered as cardiovascular or other specialty treatments. This potential avenue explains why Goldman Sachs projects twice as many monthly GLP users as estimates from Cowen and JP Morgan.

To illustrate this market expansion, a central matrix chart lists ongoing clinical trials for six molecular compounds across eight medical conditions, alongside their respective manufacturers. The compounds featured are Eli Lilly's Orfoglipron, tirzepatide, and Retatrutide; Boehringer Ingelheim and Zealand Pharma's Survodutide; and Novo Nordisk's CagriSema and semaglutide. The chart shows that all six compounds are currently being trialed for cardiovascular diseases. Other prominent trials mapped include tirzepatide for obstructive sleep apnea, chronic kidney disease, advanced liver disease, knee osteoarthritis, and heart failure; semaglutide for chronic kidney disease, advanced liver disease, peripheral arterial disease, heart failure, and an oral formulation trial for Alzheimer's disease; Survodutide for advanced liver disease; and Retatrutide for knee osteoarthritis. 

The page also details the biological mechanisms of these drugs, highlighting research by Daniel Drucker at the University of Toronto. Drucker's findings indicate that GLPs work via brain pathways to reduce inflammation, which suggests potential future use in treating neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease. Crucially, the reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events occurred before patients lost significant weight, showing that weight loss is not the sole driver of these health benefits. Additionally, the text outlines how GLPs positively impact several organ systems by decreasing gastric emptying in the stomach, decreasing gluconeogenesis and liver fat in the liver, reducing food intake stimuli in the brain, increasing insulin sensitivity in muscle tissue, and enhancing insulin secretion and beta-cell survival in the pancreas.

This page investigates the potential use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, commonly known as GLPs, to treat addictive and compulsive behaviors like alcoholism, smoking, and drug abuse. The core premise is that GLPs mitigate dopamine activity in the brain's reward circuitry. 

In animal trials, researchers found that rodents and primates taking GLPs experienced a reduced dopamine hit from substances like alcohol, cocaine, nicotine, and oxycodone. This relationship is illustrated by a bar chart showing the consumption of sweet alcohol by mice taking various doses of semaglutide. The chart plots grams of alcohol consumed per kilogram of body weight against doses ranging from a placebo up to 0.1 milligrams per kilogram of body weight. The data shows a clear dose-dependent reduction in alcohol consumption: placebo-treated mice consumed over 6 grams of alcohol per kilogram of body weight, which dropped to around 3.8 grams at a 0.001 mg/kg dose, and continued to drop significantly, bottoming out at approximately 0.5 grams at a 0.03 mg/kg dose. Next to this chart is a whimsical illustration of a snowman character playing a piano inside a dimly lit bar.

The page also discusses preliminary human trials, which highlight both potential benefits and current limitations. In a study of 127 patients with alcohol use disorder, GLPs successfully reduced heavy drinking days and total alcohol intake, but this effect was only statistically significant in the subgroup of patients who were also obese. In this obese subgroup, brain scans also revealed reduced activation of reward centers when presented with images of alcohol, though no such reduction in drinking occurred for less overweight cohorts. Additionally, a smoking cessation trial conducted by researchers at the University of Texas showed that 46% of patients who used both nicotine patches and GLP injections successfully stopped smoking, compared to a lower success rate of 27% for those who only used nicotine patches. The author notes that while these preliminary findings are intriguing, more research is required to draw definitive conclusions.

This page examines how glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) weight loss medications impact consumer behavior, specifically household food consumption, which carries long-term implications for equity markets. The author contrasts two analytical approaches: a transactional data study of household spending receipts and a self-reported patient survey, both of which reveal a clear directional shift away from unhealthy foods and beverages.

The first study, featured in a table from J.P. Morgan Global Equity Research, tracks the year-on-year change in projected units of consumption by household. It compares GLP-1 users against the total US average, highlighting a pronounced drop in unhealthy snacks among medication users. The largest differences in consumption trends are seen in meat snacks, where GLP users reduced consumption by 27% compared to a 2% drop in the total US market, representing a 26% difference. Similar declines are shown for snack seeds, nuts, and trail mixes (31% decline for GLP users, a 25% difference), popcorn (27% decline, a 24% difference), crackers (23% decline, a 23% difference), and chips (19% decline, an 18% difference). Packaged portable sweet snacks, baking and cooking ingredients, packaged cookies, soft drinks, canned goods, pasta, noodles, deli prepared foods, and in-store bakery items all registered double-digit negative percentage differences between GLP users and the broader US population. A playful illustration of a round, blue cartoon character wearing a chef's hat and holding a microphone sits adjacent to this table.

The second analysis presents findings from a Morgan Stanley AlphaWise survey of 311 GLP-1 patients with a body mass index over 27 who had been taking the medication for at least two weeks. A stacked horizontal bar chart displays the percentage of patients consuming more, the same, or less of various food categories since starting their medication. The net difference reveals a significant pivot toward healthier eating habits. The only categories with net positive consumption changes are fruits and vegetables at positive 46%, weight-loss management foods at positive 31%, and poultry and fish at positive 23%. Conversely, unhealthy and sugary categories experienced substantial net declines, led by confections at negative 66%, carbonated or sugary drinks at negative 65%, cookies and baked products at negative 65%, alcohol at negative 62%, salty snacks at negative 61%, and preserved meats at negative 53%. Notable net declines were also recorded for frozen meals (negative 45%), instant soups and canned goods (negative 41%), rice, grains, and pasta (negative 35%), red meat (negative 25%), and dairy products (negative 14%).

This page discusses how equity markets reacted to the rising penetration of GLP-1 weight-loss and diabetes drugs in 2023, questioning whether the market's initial sharp selloff in adjacent healthcare and consumer sectors was premature. Following Novo Nordisk’s summer 2023 clinical trials for Wegovy, investors quickly began pricing in winners and losers. While GLP-1 manufacturers saw massive gains, sectors associated with insulin manufacturing, food retail, and alcoholic beverages experienced deep declines, though several of these hard-hit sectors staged partial recoveries late in the year. 

To illustrate these dynamics, the page features two charts and one table. The first line chart, tracking sector equity performance from January to November 2023, shows GLP-1 manufacturers rising near 60% by the end of the year. In contrast, insulin pumps plummeted to nearly negative 50% in the autumn before recovering to around negative 30%. Other segments such as calorie-rich or fast food, beverages (including beer, spirits, and sugary drinks), exposed food retail, and orthopedic devices also experienced notable mid-year dips. The second chart shows the year-to-date relative return of large-cap stocks compared to the S&P 500, illustrating how much adjacent sectors underperformed. Food fell about 37% relative to the index, and pharmaceuticals excluding Eli Lilly fell 35%, followed by managed care down 24%, biotech down 20%, life sciences down 18%, medical devices down 17%, and beverages down 14%.

The author outlines varying predictions on future GLP-1 adoption to explain why these market reactions may have been overdone. While J.P. Morgan Research projects a 15% US obesity penetration rate by 2030, TD Cowen forecasts a much lower 3% obesity penetration rate (alongside 33% for diabetes). According to TD Cowen's model, even if GLPs are perfectly curative, a 3% obesity penetration rate would result in negligible reductions in the overall patient pools for associated co-morbidities. 

This analysis is supported by the final table, which details projected patient pool reductions by 2030. For non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which has a 72% average co-morbidity rate with obesity, the projected total pool size reduction is only 1.0%, representing 2.1 million patients. For obstructive sleep apnea, the reduction is 1.1% (1.8 million patients). Other conditions see even smaller reductions: chronic kidney disease is projected to decrease by 0.5%, osteoarthritis by 0.4%, type 2 diabetes or prediabetes by 0.4%, and cardiovascular disease by 0.5%. Ultimately, these marginal declines suggest that the steep drop in valuation for companies producing treatments for these adjacent conditions was highly premature.

This page of the publication analyzes two key geopolitical and economic forecasts for 2024: the likely failure of Argentine dollarization and the continuation of the Russia-Ukraine war alongside its broader fiscal implications for the United States and Europe.

In the first section, the author argues that Argentine President Javier Milei’s proposals for dollarization are structurally unworkable and destined to revert to de-dollarization. Milei lacks the two-thirds congressional majority needed for constitutional reforms, and the country severely lacks foreign exchange reserves and savings. To illustrate Argentina's weak structural foundation, an institutional index chart ranks countries on a scale of 0 to 100 based on labor market flexibility, business freedom, and economic dynamism. The United States ranks near the top at roughly 83, and successful currency-pegged economies like Hong Kong score high near 78. In contrast, Argentina sits at the very bottom of the chart with a score of approximately 43, far below other pegged countries like the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia. Despite these headwinds, Milei’s aggressive proposal pipeline is noted in an accompanying list, which details initiatives such as cutting $20 billion in public spending, eliminating nine of eighteen government ministries, firing 5,000 employees, and legalizing cryptocurrency for contract payments. 

In the second section, the author predicts that the Russian invasion of Ukraine will drag on through 2024 without a ceasefire. This persistence comes despite staggering Russian losses, including an estimated 315,000 active troops killed or injured (87% of its prewar force) and two-thirds of its tank fleet. The author suggests that continued US aid to Ukraine will hinge on a bipartisan domestic compromise to fund US border security. This political tension is highlighted in a line chart showing Total US Customs and Border Protection Enforcement Actions, which have surged dramatically from roughly 0.5 million actions in 2017 to over 3.0 million actions by 2023. 

Finally, the author notes that the war is pushing Europe to finally meet its 2% GDP defense spending target under the 2006 NATO agreement, having underspent by an estimated $2.0 trillion since 1983 by relying on US defense. A line chart comparing US and European defense spending from 1968 to 2023 shows that non-US NATO members fell below the 2% defense spending target in the early 1990s and have remained below it, averaging roughly 1.5% of GDP. Meanwhile, US defense spending, though down from its late-1960s peak of nearly 10% of GDP, remains significantly higher, hovering between 3% and 4% of GDP in the early 2020s.

This page presents the first three of a predicted top ten list of surprises for 2024, written in honor of the late market strategist Byron Wien. The author, Michael Cembalest, uses these non-consensus forecasts to challenge prevailing market assumptions. 

The first surprise posits that the US dollar will remain stable throughout 2024, ending within seven percent of its starting point and retaining its roughly fifty percent share of global trade invoicing despite concerns over the weaponization of the currency via sanctions. This forecast is accompanied by two charts. The first chart plots the US Fed trade-weighted nominal broad dollar index from 1980 to late 2023, where January 1980 equals 100. The index shows a long-term upward trend, peaking near 200 in the mid-1980s, rising again to nearly 200 in the early 2000s, and hovering between 350 and 400 by late 2023. The second chart illustrates the international role of the US dollar using December 2022 data from the Bank for International Settlements. It shows that while the US share of world trade is under ten percent and its share of global GDP is around twenty-five percent, the US dollar dominates global transactions. Specifically, it commands approximately eighty-five percent of foreign exchange transaction volume, sixty percent of official foreign exchange reserves, fifty percent of trade invoicing, cross-border loans, and international debt securities, and forty percent of SWIFT payments.

The second surprise is that the Department of Justice or the Federal Trade Commission will win a major antitrust case currently underway against tech and telecom giants, specifically naming Google, Amazon, Meta, or T-Mobile. This would mark the first major federal antitrust victory since the landmark Microsoft case of 2001. 

The third surprise predicts that President Joe Biden will withdraw from the presidential election between Super Tuesday and November due to health reasons, with the Democratic National Committee naming a replacement candidate. Cembalest highlights the paradox of Biden’s low approval ratings despite high job growth numbers. This is visualized in a scatter plot comparing presidential approval ratings 1,051 days after inauguration against payroll growth since inauguration for US presidents from Harry Truman to Joe Biden. The plot reveals Biden as a significant outlier, carrying an approval rating of under forty percent despite experiencing roughly nine percent payroll growth. By comparison, Dwight Eisenhower enjoyed a seventy-five percent approval rating with very little job growth, while Lyndon B. Johnson and Jimmy Carter saw higher job growth with approval ratings between forty percent and fifty percent. A final line chart of US nonfarm payrolls from 2018 to late 2023 explains this anomaly. It shows a severe plunge in employment in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, with Biden's inauguration marked on a steep upward recovery trajectory. The author notes that Biden's strong job creation numbers are largely a byproduct of this post-pandemic economic reopening and vaccine rollout rather than typical economic expansion.

This page discusses the historical success of vaccines in reducing preventable diseases globally, alongside rising concerns over declining vaccination rates and subsequent outbreaks in the United States. The author argues that vaccines are among the greatest public health achievements, despite modern skepticism, noting that a single US birth cohort's vaccination prevents 20 million cases of disease and more than 40,000 deaths. 

To support this, the page includes two tables. The first details vaccine-preventable diseases in the United States, comparing pre-vaccine annual data to post-vaccine outcomes. It highlights dramatic case declines of 100% for diphtheria, measles, polio, rubella, and smallpox, alongside a 96% decline for mumps, 92% for pertussis, 87% for hepatitis A, and 93% for tetanus. The second table shows similar post-vaccine declines in China, with case reductions ranging from 65% for encephalitis to 83% for pertussis and rubella across the 1980s and 2010s.

Addressing safety, the author notes that vaccine recalls are exceptionally rare, citing only three major safety-related withdrawals since the 1950s: the 1955 polio vaccine incident, the 1976 swine flu vaccine linked to Guillain-Barre syndrome, and the 1998–1999 rotavirus vaccine linked to infant bowel obstructions. The text also addresses CDC-funded research regarding aluminum adjuvants and childhood asthma, noting that researchers found no strong evidence to question vaccine safety and that research is ongoing. 

Finally, the page sounds an alarm on declining US childhood vaccination rates, which fell from 95% before the COVID-19 pandemic to 93% for the 2021–2022 school year, leaving approximately 250,000 children unprotected against measles. This decline has already led to outbreaks, such as an 85-case outbreak in Columbus, Ohio, in 2022 where 80 of the infected children were unvaccinated, and a 2018–2019 outbreak of 71 cases in Clark County, Washington. Public resistance is growing; a Kaiser survey found that 28% of US adults now oppose mandatory kindergarten vaccination, up from 16% in 2019. With 15 states now allowing non-medical exemptions, 36 states have fallen below the 95% vaccination rate required to maintain herd immunity against measles.

This page argue that multiple complex and uncomfortable realities can exist simultaneously, focusing on the long-term societal damage of COVID-19 lockdowns in the United States and the erosion of public trust in the pharmaceutical industry due to past safety failures and corporate misconduct. 

The author asserts that pandemic lockdowns prioritized the elderly at the expense of the young, noting that school closures displaced 50 million children, set math and reading progress back by two decades, and are projected to cause diminished lifetime earnings. Furthermore, lockdowns sparked rises in domestic violence, mental health issues, alcohol abuse, and chronic school absenteeism, which jumped from a pre-pandemic baseline of 15% to more than 25% nationally in 2021–2022. 

To illustrate why public skepticism of the medical establishment exists, a detailed two-column table highlights historical Food and Drug Administration recalls and severe black box warnings. The drug recall side of the table lists high-profile cases such as Pfizer’s Bextra in 2005 and Merck’s Vioxx in 2004, which were recalled for cardiovascular issues, alongside Bayer’s Baycol in 2001, and Wyeth-Ayerst's Fen-Phen in 1997. The black box warning side lists medications with severe, belatedly discovered risks, such as Merck’s Singulair in 2020 and Eli Lilly and Pfizer’s Prozac and Zoloft in 2004 for mental health side effects, alongside Abbott Labs' Depakote in 2006 for birth defects. 

The author links these regulatory failures to corporate misconduct, noting that illegal drug company activities have severely damaged public perception. Cited examples include Purdue Pharma’s multiple guilty pleas over OxyContin, which led to a $6 billion settlement currently being reviewed by the Supreme Court, alongside massive settlements from GlaxoSmithKline ($3 billion in 2012), Johnson & Johnson ($2.2 billion in 2013), and Pfizer ($2.3 billion in 2009) for off-label marketing and hiding safety data. This corporate track record contributed to the pharmaceutical industry sinking to the bottom of Gallup's industry poll, dropping from a net negative rating of -31 in 2019 to -42, which the author suggests drives contemporary medication non-adherence, trial recruitment difficulties, and vaccine rejection.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication discusses the efficacy and waning protection of original COVID-19 vaccines and Omicron boosters, noting that while they were highly effective in preventing serious illness during 2021 and 2022, protection declined over time as the virus mutated. The author notes that SARS-CoV-2 accumulates mutations 2.5 times faster than the influenza A virus and 7 times faster than other coronaviruses. Consequently, by late 2023, vaccine-derived protection was similar to that of unvaccinated, previously infected individuals. However, because roughly 99 percent of the population has acquired immunity through vaccination, prior infection, or both, overall public health risks remain mitigated, and current hospitalization rates are significantly lower than in earlier waves.

A detailed data table compiles vaccine efficacy studies across various timeframes from May 2021 through April 2023, utilizing sources such as Fisman, Stoliaroff-Pepin, Bermingham, Link-Gelles, Bacon, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC). The data highlights a clear trend of waning protection. For instance, three-dose protection against hospitalization declined from 68 percent to 36 percent after six months in JAMA-published research by Link-Gelles, while Bacon’s research in The Lancet showed booster efficacy against hospitalization falling from 89 percent to 71 percent after four months. Similarly, ECDC data shows second booster protection against hospitalization declining from a range of 76 to 79 percent down to 43 percent after six months. 

To demonstrate how population-wide immunity has lowered severe disease outcomes, the page features two line charts using CDC and JPMAM data tracking weekly US COVID-19 hospitalizations per 100,000 people from March 2020 through early 2024. The first chart focuses on ages 40 and older, divided into four age series: 75 plus, 65 to 74, 50 to 64, and 40 to 49. It shows massive peaks in late 2020 and early 2022, with the 75-plus cohort peaking near 150 hospitalizations per 100,000 before dropping to much lower, flatter peaks below 60 in late 2022 and 2023. The second chart focuses on ages 30 to 64, dividing patients into 50 to 64, 40 to 49, and 30 to 39 cohorts. This chart demonstrates that while the 50-to-64 age group saw a peak of roughly 40 hospitalizations per 100,000 during the early 2022 Omicron wave, hospitalizations for all three younger cohorts remained extremely low throughout 2023, staying well below 10 per 100,000.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, begins with a brief macro update noting that US manufacturing surveys for January improved over December, driven by stronger new orders, though tight labor markets and rising inflation remain concerns. Cembalest also previews an upcoming annual energy paper titled Electravision. 

The primary analysis of the page focuses on the market-dominating Magnificent 7 stocks, arguing that their rally has been fundamentally driven by earnings rather than purely speculative multiple expansion. Since 2019, out of the group’s 28% return, 21% is attributed to sales growth, 6% to margin expansion, and only 1% to multiple expansion, contrasting sharply with the dot-com bubble of 2000 to 2001. A comprehensive table compares the Magnificent 7 against the rest of the S&P 500 (labeled S&P 493). The data shows the Magnificent 7 commanding a 14% sales growth in Q4 2023 compared to 2% for the S&P 493, a 23% margin versus 9%, and a massive 2023 return of 76% compared to the S&P 493’s 14%. The group represents 29% of the S&P market capitalization and 22% of its consensus net income, trading at a 30x price-to-earnings multiple versus 18x for the rest of the index.

Cembalest highlights findings from J.P. Morgan strategists Marko Kolanovic and Dubravko Lakos-Bujas, pointing out that US stock market concentration has reached its highest level since 1972, with the top ten stocks breaking away from the rest of the market. This high concentration is historically linked to recessions and has severely impacted active equity managers, with only 23% of Russell 1000 large-cap managers outperforming in 2023 compared to 66% in 2022. Antitrust enforcement is identified as the chief risk to the continued dominance of these mega-caps.

Two charts at the bottom of the page illustrate these trends. The left chart, titled "Highest stock market concentration since the early 1970s," tracks the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) concentration measure from 1964 to 2024. The HHI has surged past 160 in recent years, nearing levels not seen since the early 1970s and the tech bubble, with shaded vertical bars indicating that previous spikes often preceded or coincided with US recessions. The right chart, titled "Magnificent 7 earnings," shows the annual earnings per share from 2018 projected to 2024 for Meta, NVIDIA, Microsoft, Apple, Google, Amazon, and Tesla. Meta leads the group with EPS climbing toward $20, followed by a surging NVIDIA and Microsoft. In contrast, Tesla’s earnings trend downward toward the bottom of the pack, around $2 to $3. A detailed footnote explains that Tesla's Q4 2023 earnings were artificially boosted by a one-time, non-cash tax valuation allowance adjustment of $5.9 billion.

This commentary page, titled "Armageddonist update," critically examines the track record of prominent financial market bears who consistently predict impending economic disasters. The author argues that following the advice of these "Armageddonists" leads to severe underperformance, illustrating this with historical data and analyzing their highly inaccurate predictions during the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic. To explain why the media continues to feature these figures despite their poor track records, a footnote highlights the human negativity bias, referencing Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman and political scientist Stuart Soroka.

The page features two charts and a supporting table. The first chart, "The consequences of Armageddonism, 2010-2019," measures the negative performance impact of shifting one dollar from the S&P 500 to the Barclay’s Aggregate Bond Index on the specific date of an Armageddonist's bearish comment. The vertical bar chart displays seventeen individual commentators from May 2010 to November 2016, including Nouriel Roubini, David Rosenberg, Jeffrey Gundlach, Marc Faber, George Soros, and Paul Krugman. Every single prediction resulted in significant investment underperformance by the end of 2019, ranging from approximately 30% to nearly 60%.

The second chart, "Timing is everything," tracks the S&P 500 index from 2020 to early 2024, mapping it against extremely bearish comments made during the early days of the pandemic. The index, which plummeted to near 2,200 in March 2020, recovered to nearly 5,000 by early 2024. The chart visually demonstrates that these commentators issued their dire warnings almost exactly at the market bottom, causing followers to miss the subsequent bull run in which the market nearly doubled.

An accompanying table details these specific predictions made between March and May 2020. Among the cited forecasts, David Stockman predicted a further 50% correction to an S&P 500 level of 1600 on March 4, 2020. Later that month, Nouriel Roubini warned of a "Greater Depression" worse than the 1930s, while Peter Schiff anticipated a brutal recession ravaged by inflation. John Hussman expected the S&P 500 to lose two-thirds of its value, and Jeff Gundlach bet that the March lows would be broken. On April 1, 2020, George Soros predicted the worst bear market of his lifetime. In late April and May, Albert Edwards dismissed the idea of central bank liquidity lifting equities, and David Rosenberg claimed the economy was entering a prolonged depression characterized by deflation and bankruptcies. The author concludes by noting that while current investor sentiment is very bullish and a market correction could occur later in the year, investors should expect these same pundits to emerge and predict even worse outcomes when it happens.

This page analyzes China’s ongoing economic struggles, focusing on cheap equity valuations, a massive housing bubble, and systemic risks within its shadow banking sector. 

A bar chart at the top of the page illustrates the world's cheapest equity market valuations measured by forward price-to-earnings ratios, ranging from 0x to 12x. Multiple Chinese equity indices appear near the very bottom of this valuation ranking. While Russia and Pakistan are the cheapest, China H shares are valued at under 4x forward earnings, China Red Chips sit at around 5x, and other Chinese classifications—including China B shares, the Hang Seng Index, and FTSE China—range between 5x and 8x forward earnings. An accompanying text box titled "China’s equity alphabet soup" defines these various segments, explaining the structural differences between A shares, H shares, B shares, Red Chips, P Chips, and ADRs.

To illustrate the underlying cause of these low valuations, a comparison table highlights the extreme scale of China’s housing bubble relative to the United States. According to the data, the value of China's housing stock relative to personal consumption expenditures peaked at 6.0x, compared to 2.2x in the US. Direct real estate activities account for 18% of China's GDP, triple the 6% share seen in the US. Furthermore, mid-2023 home price-to-income ratios in tier-one Chinese cities reached approximately 40x, compared to about 10x in major US cities, while China's homeownership rate stands at 90% compared to 66% in the US.

The commentary explains that this overbuilt real estate sector is generating substantial losses that are reverberating through the financial system, particularly within shadow banking. The author highlights the December 2023 bankruptcy of Zhongzhi Enterprises, which held $141 billion in peak assets but failed with only $30 billion in assets against $60 billion in liabilities. This followed the default of Zhongrong Enterprises, a $138 billion trust. Although shadow banking assets represent only about 5% of China's regular banking assets—totaling around 18 trillion Yuan or 2.5 trillion USD—regular commercial banks provide nearly half of their funding, meaning any crackdown on shadow banking threatens the broader commercial banking sector.

In analyzing potential policy responses, the author draws a parallel to the US response during the 2008 financial crisis. Citing IMF research, the author argues that the historical track record for governments buying bad loans is poor, whereas direct recapitalization of bank liabilities and equities has been far more successful at reviving GDP and markets. While the recent firing of China’s top securities regulator might spark a short-term technical rally, the author asserts that economic conditions are worse today than during previous market interventions in 2016 or 2018. Ultimately, the author states that a long-term bullish stance on China would require the government to directly recapitalize both regular and shadow banks, rather than relying on short-term measures like restricting short sellers. This domestic challenge is further compounded by a bipartisan US political consensus pushing for continued economic conflict, trade restrictions, and tariffs regardless of the outcome of the 2024 US Presidential election.

This commentary highlights several remarkable accomplishments in biomedicine that have been made possible through the latest generation of artificial intelligence. The first major milestone discussed is protein folding and mapping. Prior to AI, using MRI and x-ray crystallography to map enzyme and protein shapes took years and millions of dollars, leaving only twenty percent of proteins mapped by 2021. Today, Google's AI-driven AlphaFold program accomplishes this task in hours, helping map ninety-nine percent of proteins. This is illustrated by an image comparing the actual complex green shape of a DNA replication enzyme to the predicted blue shape generated by AI, showing an almost perfect structural overlap.

The second breakthrough is the discovery of the first new class of antibiotics in decades, aimed at treating MRSA, a staph infection responsible for seventy thousand severe illnesses and seven thousand deaths annually. Researchers Jim Collins at MIT/Harvard and Felix Wong at Integrated Biosciences trained an AI model on thirty-nine thousand compounds to screen a database of twelve million commercially available molecules. A detailed cluster chart visualizes this database, using distance and color to represent antibacterial activity and non-toxicity. On this chart, dark green and black points represent the highest-scoring novel compounds with no unfavorable substructures, while two purple dots mark Compounds 1 and 2, which scored the best in actual lab testing and are currently showing promising results in mice. 

Further advancements include researchers at McMaster University using generative AI to combat antibiotic-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii by screening billions of molecules, leading to the synthesis of thirteen thousand five hundred molecules and the identification of six promising candidates. Finally, the author highlights the use of AI diagnostics paired with retinal cameras to detect diabetic retinopathy, the leading cause of adult blindness, which allows clinicians with minimal training to expand testing coverage and deliver immediate results.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the environmental and economic headwinds facing China, framing these challenges as crucial context for investors considering "bottom fishing" in Chinese markets. 

The commentary begins by highlighting China's severe water quality issues. While coastal seas have seen some improvement since 2015, approximately 70% of China’s rivers and lakes remain unsafe for human use according to a 2021 Nanjing University study. Furthermore, 91% of water bodies supposedly remediated by local governments fail to meet baseline standards, and the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences has linked this surface water pollution to elevated cancer rates. 

To illustrate China's structural economic challenges, the page presents six charts. The first, tracking the credit intensity of GDP from 2004 to 2022, shows that the amount of credit required to generate a single unit of GDP growth has worsened dramatically, rising from around 1.0 in 2004 to nearly 7.0 by 2022 on a three-year moving average. This trend aligns with rising economy-wide debt. A chart comparing total government, household, and corporate debt to the non-financial sector reveals that China’s total debt reached approximately 300% of GDP by 2023. This is significantly higher than the levels seen in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Germany, though still below Japan's leading ratio of over 420%. 

On the structural reform front, a chart of core shadow banking activities shows that these activities are gradually shrinking. From a peak of roughly 24 trillion Yuan in 2019, shadow banking assets—composed of entrusted loans, trust loans, and undiscounted bankers' acceptances—declined to about 18 trillion Yuan by late 2023. Meanwhile, the China Real Activity Monitor index, which tracks ten monthly economic indicators like real estate investment, exports, and energy production, shows that economic activity has stabilized. After a deep plunge in 2020 and a sharp recovery spike in 2021, the index leveled off at a modest positive reading in late 2023. 

However, domestic real estate remains a significant drag. A chart of China's housing drag shows that both state-owned land use right transfer revenues and residential floor space starts have been deeply negative on a year-over-year basis since mid-2021, with both indicators hovering between -20% and -40% throughout 2022 and 2023. Compounding these domestic challenges, the final chart, the China FDI Monitor, shows that net foreign direct investment has plummeted. Historically positive, net FDI dipped deep into negative territory by late 2022 and 2023, indicating that capital is fleeing the country rapidly as outward FDI outpaces inward FDI.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, addresses the rising energy consumption of artificial intelligence and its implications for the power grid and alternative energy sourcing. The author begins by examining the energy cost of AI compute, highlighting that Google’s claim that its Gemini Ultra Large Language Model outperformed GPT-4 comes with a significant caveat: the "32x" methodology means the model ran through prompts 32 times to find the best answer, requiring 32 times more compute and energy than a typical prompt. This is illustrated in the first chart, "Gemini Ultra vs GPT-4," which measures accuracy on Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) tests. In a standard 5-shot approach, GPT-4 outperforms Gemini Ultra, and it is only through Chain of Thought with 32x sampling and greedy sampling that Gemini Ultra achieves its top accuracy of roughly 90%, barely pushing past the human expert performance benchmark of about 89.8%.

This intense computation translates to massive real-world power demands. The second chart shows the progression of power demand forecasts in gigawatts for Dominion Resources, which serves 6 million customers across 15 states. Prior forecasts from 2019 through 2022 projected relatively flat power demand hovering between 20 and 24 gigawatts through 2039. However, the PJM 2023 forecast shows a massive, steep upward departure, projecting demand to reach approximately 40 gigawatts by 2039 solely due to data center expansion. To put this in perspective, McKinsey, BCG, and S&P Global expect total US power demand to grow by 13% to 15% per year until 2030. Sourcing this power is further complicated by supply chain bottlenecks, as shown in the third chart tracking core goods PPI component inflation since 2018. Out of 47 core goods categories, "Transformers & Power Regulators" has experienced the highest inflation, with prices rising by nearly 75%.

The commentary then questions where AI suppliers will secure their energy. While Amazon recently made headlines by purchasing data centers and up to 40% of the output from Talen Energy's Susquehanna nuclear plant at a 50% premium, the author cautions that such deals are not universally feasible. In states with vertically integrated and regulated utilities—which account for about 50% of US nuclear generation—regulators are likely to block the sale of baseload nuclear power that is already included in the consumer rate base. If data centers must develop their own nuclear power, they face severe historical headwinds. The final chart illustrates the levelized cost of four modern Western nuclear plants versus a high-renewable wind-solar-gas system. The nuclear plants—UK's Hinkley Point, Georgia's Vogtle, France's Flamanville, and Finland's Olkiluoto—all show extremely high levelized costs, ranging from about $130 per megawatt-hour to upwards of $230 per megawatt-hour. In contrast, a high-renewable system combining wind, solar, and natural gas backup costs roughly $60 to $65 per megawatt-hour, rendering nuclear power 2 to 4 times more expensive than the renewable-plus-gas alternative.

In this page of Eye on the Market, Michael Cembalest argues that the US economy is showing limited signs of the typical corporate profit or capital spending declines that usually precede recessions. He points out that while an inverted yield curve historically predicts downturns, previous inversions were accompanied by severely negative corporate cash flows and rising interest costs, whereas the corporate sector today remains in surplus with stable interest expenses.

This argument is supported by four charts. The first chart, showing US economy-wide profits and S&P 500 operating profits on a log-scale index from 1995 to 2023, demonstrates that both US national corporate profit after tax and S&P 500 operating profits have remained robust and near peak levels. The second chart, tracking the US corporate sector financial balance as a percentage of corporate gross value added from 1960 to late 2023, shows that the corporate sector is currently in surplus, a stark contrast to the deep negative balances of minus four to minus six percent that triggered prior recessions. The third chart compares the Federal funds rate to corporate net interest payments as a percentage of after-tax NIPA profits from 1970 to 2023. It reveals that despite the aggressive spike in the Fed funds rate, corporate net interest costs have remained remarkably flat and low, at around four percent. The fourth chart displays the ratio of cash yields to S&P 500 dividend yields from 1934 to 2024, showing that the ratio has spiked to its highest level since 2000, explaining why investors are highly incentivized to hold cash.

Looking forward, Cembalest projects high single-digit returns for US equities in 2024, despite potential short-term corrections. However, he warns that the post-election landscape presents significant risks depending on the political outcome. A unified Donald Trump government could introduce a sixty percent tariff on Chinese goods, repeal the corporate AMT and buyback tax, increase defense spending, and extend the TCJA tax cuts, leading to a much wider budget deficit. Conversely, a unified Joe Biden government could pursue two trillion dollars in tax increases to support a safety net expansion, with a risk of wider deficits as spending on initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act continues to outpace initial estimates.

This page analyzes the upcoming US Presidential election by presenting a retrospective "360 performance review" of Donald Trump's presidency and exploring two extreme constitutional contingency scenarios. 

The featured bar chart, titled "Trump 360 review by former Trump Cabinet members and other senior positions," categorizes 43 individuals who served in key administration and congressional leadership roles from 2016 to 2020 for a minimum of nine months. This universe comprises the Vice President, 15 Cabinet department heads, the National Security Advisor, the FBI and CIA directors, the UN Ambassador, White House Chiefs of Staff, the White House Communications Director, the GOP Speaker of the House, and the GOP Senate Majority Leader. The chart organizes these individuals into three distinct categories based on public statements as interpreted by J.P. Morgan. The largest category, representing eighteen individuals, is "Repudiations/disavowals" and includes prominent figures such as Mike Pence, Nikki Haley, John Kelly, John Bolton, William Barr, Rex Tillerson, Jim Mattis, and HR McMaster. The second group, with fourteen individuals, represents "2024 endorsements" and includes Mike Pompeo, Mitch McConnell, Steven Mnuchin, and Ben Carson. The final category, containing eleven individuals, is "No public comment" and includes Chris Wray, Alex Azar, Kirstjen Nielsen, and Sonny Perdue, with a note that some individuals may be restricted from speaking due to their current roles.

The text details two "triple witching hour" scenarios regarding the election outcome. The first scenario, "Insurrection redux," describes a situation where Trump wins the general election, but Democrats gain control of both houses of Congress. At the January 6th Joint Session, the Democratic majority could rule Trump ineligible to serve by citing the insurrection clause of the 14th Amendment. In this scenario, since neither candidate would reach 270 electors, a Contingent Election would be held in the House of Representatives where Joe Biden would be the only eligible candidate. A detailed footnote explains that the 14th Amendment allows for retrospective removal and that Trump’s 2021 Senate acquittal does not prevent this congressional action because the impeachment trial was a civil, not criminal, proceeding. The second scenario outlines a 12th Amendment Contingent Election in which third-party candidates, such as the No Labels movement or Robert F. Kennedy Jr., win enough electors to prevent both Trump and Biden from reaching 270 electors. This would also trigger a Contingent Election in the House of Representatives, where each state delegation gets one vote, meaning the outcome would be decided by whichever party controls the majority of state delegations seated on January 3rd, which currently favors a narrow Republican majority.

Michael Cembalest discusses the residual impacts of rising interest rates on consumers and the broader financial system. Despite expectations that the Federal Reserve will eventually ease rates, credit card holders are already feeling the pinch of tighter monetary policy, with delinquencies rising faster than those for mortgages or prime auto loans. This consumer financial stress is detailed in two charts. 

The first chart, titled "Credit card interest rates and delinquencies," shows data from 2003 through early 2024. It tracks the equal-weighted financing rate on all interest-assessed accounts alongside 90-plus day delinquencies. The financing rate has surged to nearly 23% by early 2024, driven by rising Prime rates and expanding credit card spreads, while delinquencies have rebounded from a pandemic-era low of under 2% to around 5%. The second chart, titled "Consumer financial stress," spans 2012 to 2024 and tracks revolving balances against the percentage of accounts making only the minimum payment. Revolving balances have climbed sharply from approximately $430 billion in 2021 to nearly $650 billion by late 2023, while the share of accounts making only minimum payments has risen toward a multi-year high of roughly 11%. This lingering pressure on household finances poses a distinct risk to economic growth.

Conversely, Cembalest argues that supportive factors should mitigate the duration and magnitude of any potential equity market selloff. Key among these are the stabilization of the banking sector following the March 2023 regional banking crisis and a remarkably tight global net equity supply. The "US commercial bank recovery" chart, indexed to March 13, 2023, demonstrates that relative returns for S&P 500 banks stabilized near an index level of 100 by early 2024 after plunging below 90 in mid-2023. This stabilization is mirrored by US commercial bank deposits, which recovered and leveled off at approximately $17.5 trillion to $17.6 trillion. 

Additionally, the "Net equity supply globally" chart from 1999 to 2023 shows that net equity supply has been negative for three consecutive years through 2023, meaning corporate share buybacks have significantly exceeded new primary and secondary equity issuance, including US and non-US SPACs. In 2023, this supply deficit reached over $100 billion. Such tight supply conditions are historically favorable for equity market returns, as they indicate more investor scrutiny on new issues and support underlying valuations. 

The page concludes with a playful graphic of a band of cicadas performing on stage under the title "In-A-Cicada-Da-Vida," a humorous reference to the classic rock song "In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida" by Iron Butterfly, likely nodding to the rare dual emergence of periodical cicada broods in 2024.

On this page, Michael Cembalest argues that the prospects for a rare US disinflationary boom—similar to those seen in 1982 and 1991—are fading. While US economic growth remains resilient and leading indicators have improved since August 2023, CPI inflation measures have experienced a U-turn since January. This resurgence in inflation has driven 10-year Treasury rates back up to approximately 4.7%. The author highlights that most of the March CPI increase was driven by non-discretionary items rising at 6%, including medical care, child care, car insurance, wireless fees, and expenses linked to the energy transition. As a result, futures markets are now pricing in only one to two Federal Reserve rate cuts by the end of the year, a projection that remains vulnerable to upcoming inflation reports. 

A leading indicators table tracks eighteen different metrics across bankruptcy, capex, construction, economy, employment, lending, production, profits, sales, wages, and equities. Each metric is advanced by a set number of months, ranging from three to eighteen, to predict future shifts in economic behavior. The table compares the pulse in April 2024 to that of August 2023, using color-coded weakness projections where red indicates substantial weakness, orange modest, yellow slight, and green indicates positive momentum.
