This comparison reveals a noticeable improvement across several indicators over the eight-month period, with many moving from orange or yellow to green, particularly those predicting ISM manufacturing index performance, US manufacturing production, and S&P profits.

The shift in inflation is visualized in two charts at the bottom of the page. The first, titled "CPI core services" (measured year-over-year from 2016 to 2024), tracks two series: CPI core services excluding shelter, and CPI core services excluding shelter and transportation. Both metrics show a clear upward trend starting in early 2024, with the ex-shelter line climbing toward 5% and the ex-shelter and transportation line rebounding to nearly 4% after a period of cooling. 

The second chart displays "US consumer price inflation measures" as a three-month annualized percentage change from 1985 through early 2024. This chart plots the Cleveland Fed median CPI, the Atlanta Fed sticky CPI, and the Cleveland Fed trimmed mean CPI. After decades of relative stability below 4%, all three measures show a dramatic spike in 2021 and 2022, a brief deceleration, and a sharp renewed spike in early 2024, with some measures surging back into the 4% to 6% range. 

Finally, a footnote expands on the inflationary impacts of the energy transition, noting that transformer equipment has seen the highest price increase since 2019 among all forty-seven core goods categories in the US PPI report, rising by 71%. The author observes that electricity prices have climbed faster than food, commodity prices, and core CPI since 2019, even though the broader electrification of winter heating and transportation is only beginning.

This page examines the potential negative impact of Elon Musk’s controversial political commentary on Tesla’s stock performance and sales, specifically focusing on how his rhetoric has alienated Democratic buyers who form the backbone of the electric vehicle market. Citing data from Strategic Vision, the author notes that the share of Democrats purchasing Tesla vehicles fell by over 60 percent in the fall of 2023, coinciding with a flurry of contentious tweets from Musk on topics like immigration, religion, and various conspiracy theories. During this period, many of these buyers opted instead for competing electric vehicles from Cadillac, Hyundai, and Mercedes. This political polarization is particularly risky for Tesla because, as UC Berkeley research shows, electric vehicle adoption is highly concentrated in Democratic-leaning areas; from 2012 to 2022, approximately half of all electric vehicles were purchased in the top 10 percent most Democratic counties in the United States. 

To illustrate this demographic reliance, the page features a scatter plot titled "EV adoption vs county-level political ideology," which maps the electric vehicle share of all new vehicles registered from 2012 to 2022 against the Democratic vote share in presidential elections. The chart reveals a clear, positive correlation: in counties with a 20 percent Democratic vote share, electric vehicles make up only about 0.2 percent of registrations, whereas in counties with an 80 percent Democratic vote share, the EV share climbs to over 1.6 percent. This direct relationship remains consistent even after controlling for county income levels. Meanwhile, S&P data cited in the footnotes shows Tesla’s overall electric vehicle market share declining from 80 percent in 2020 to 55 percent in 2023.

The page also details the transformation of Twitter under Musk’s ownership, noting an increase in climate change denialism and disinformation that runs counter to the progressive values of typical electric vehicle buyers. This is supported by a bar chart titled "Misinformation/disinformation hit rate," which displays the percentage of content returned from sensitive searches across major social media platforms, sourced from a September 2023 European Commission report. Twitter recorded the highest misinformation rate at over 40 percent, followed by Facebook at approximately 30 percent, Instagram at roughly 22 percent, TikTok at about 18 percent, LinkedIn at 11 percent, and YouTube at 10 percent. The author concludes by noting that these political alignments and platform trends appear highly inconsistent with the target market for Tesla, raising an open question about the long-term impact on sales that J.P. Morgan will continue to monitor. Extensive footnotes list specific examples of Musk's controversial online remarks, including personal attacks on public figures, conspiracy theories, and inflammatory political statements.

This page discusses two distinct topics: the closing gap between open-source and closed-source artificial intelligence models, and the valuation of the social media platform Truth Social relative to its peers. 

The author begins with a commentary on Meta's impending release of its 400 billion parameter open-source Llama 3 model. This release is expected to make the decision for companies to build their own language models, rather than buy them, more compelling. Open-source models can be fine-tuned for specialized industries, such as finance, while offering greater security compared to sending API calls to external providers like OpenAI. Meta has demonstrated significant efficiency gains, reducing the Llama 3-8B parameter count by 90% compared to Llama 2-70B while matching its performance, which improves accessibility on affordable hardware. Despite training costs reaching into the billions, Meta is funding these open-source models without an explicit revenue model. 

This argument is supported by a scatter plot chart titled "Closed-source vs open-weight model performance," which plots Arena ELO scores against model release dates from March 2023 to March 2024. The chart illustrates a narrowing performance gap between closed-source models, represented by blue dots like GPT-4, Gemini Pro, and Claude 3, and open-weight models, represented by brown dots like Mistral, Command R+, and Qwen. The visual evidence suggests that the lag for open-source models to catch up to closed-source performance has shrunk to just six to ten months, down from years when GPT was first introduced.

The second half of the page addresses the valuation of Truth Social. A bar chart titled "Social media market cap per active user" compares the market capitalization per monthly active user in US dollars across various public and private platforms. The chart demonstrates that Truth Social has an extraordinarily high valuation relative to its user base, sitting at $890 per active user, though it is down from its second-day closing peak of $1,794. In comparison, TikTok's US operations are valued at an estimated $588 per active user, Meta at $408, Discord at an estimated $100, Twitter (X) at an estimated $47, Pinterest at $45, Snap at $24, and Reddit at $8. The chart clearly illustrates how Truth Social's valuation is a significant outlier compared to any other major social media company.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the long-awaited recovery of the Japanese stock market, noting that the Nikkei 225 Index took 34.5 years to regain its 1989 peak. This recovery period is substantially longer than those of the S&P 500 after the 1929 crash, which took 25 years, and the NASDAQ after the dot-com bubble, which took 15 years. He highlights the historic underperformance of Japanese equities, which returned just 1.6 percent annually from 1991 to 2022 compared to 9.6 percent for US equities, meaning compounded US returns were 68 times higher over that span. However, he argues that a fundamental shift is underway, driven by structural reforms, a resurgence in mergers and acquisitions, and improving corporate governance. He notes that the historically low valuations of Japanese equities were not due to a lack of cash generation, as Japan’s free cash flow yield has closely mirrored that of the US over the last two decades. Instead, Japanese companies simply accumulated cash rather than using it to unlock shareholder value.

To illustrate this corporate shift, the page features four charts. The first, titled Corporate finance activity in Japan, tracks the number of deals on the left axis and the aggregate deal value in billions of US dollars on the right axis from 2012 to 2023. This chart shows a dramatic rise in activity, with the number of deals climbing from under 50 in 2012 to over 250 in 2023, and aggregate values increasing toward the 50 billion dollar mark. The second chart, Japanese deal making accelerates, shows Japan's share of deal volumes in Asia from 2005 to 2023. This metric has behaved cyclically but experienced a sharp upward surge to around 34 percent by 2023. 

The third chart, Free cash flow yield, compares MSCI Japan to MSCI US from 2000 to 2024. Both series track each other closely, typically hovering between 3 percent and 6 percent, which reinforces the author's point that Japan's cash-generation capabilities were never the issue. The final chart, Japan performance vs 50/50 Europe and emerging markets, plots Japan's percent excess return from 1988 to 2024. It highlights a massive recent spike, showing that Japan has significantly outperformed this blended benchmark over the last 18 months, even when accounting for a weak Yen. The author cautions, however, that Japanese equities are no longer cheap, as price-to-earnings multiples have expanded from 12.2 times in September 2022 to 17.0 times.

This page focuses on the normalization of global agricultural prices, demonstrating that global food and fertilizer markets have shown significant resilience despite fears of shortages following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. While disruptions occurred, alternative supply sources have mitigated the worst outcomes globally, even though Ukraine's internal agricultural infrastructure has suffered catastrophic environmental damage. 

The first section of the page details the stabilization of the fertilizer market. A line chart depicting global fertilizer prices in U.S. dollars per metric ton from January 2021 to April 2024 reveals that prices for key components—including diammonium phosphate, triple superphosphate, urea (nitrogen), potassium chloride, and phosphate rock—peaked sharply in mid-2022 but have since declined back to early 2021 levels. A companion stacked bar chart shows global fertilizer exports in millions of tons for 2021, 2022, and 2023, broken down by nitrogen, phosphate, and potash. Total exports fell from 100 million tons in 2021 to roughly 88 million tons in 2022 but recovered to approximately 90 million tons in 2023, recovering half of the previous year's decline. This recovery was driven by increased production in other nations alongside falling natural gas prices. 

The second section shifts to crop production, demonstrating how global supply offset Ukrainian losses using two charts that index production relative to a 2008 baseline of 100. The first chart, tracking wheat production from 2008 to 2024, shows that while Ukraine's production index plummeted from around 140 in 2021 to below 80 in 2022, the global production index remained remarkably stable at approximately 115, supported by output increases in Canada, Russia, Brazil, and Kazakhstan. The second chart, tracking corn production over the same period, shows a severe drop in Ukraine's production index from over 350 down to 200. This caused a temporary dip in global corn production in 2022, but by 2024, the global index surged back to about 155, matching pre-war levels due to increased production from China, the United States, Brazil, and Argentina. 

Despite these stable global trends, the author emphasizes that Ukraine’s domestic agricultural base has been severely devastated. The text highlights that approximately one-third of Ukrainian territory is now contaminated with toxic elements like lead, cadmium, arsenic, and mercury. Additionally, 9,300 acres of forests have been burned, rivers have been polluted, wildlife decimated, and landmines scattered across 67,000 square miles. The author notes that these conditions may worsen, citing a report that Ukraine’s air defense interception rate for Russian missiles has dropped from 83% to 30% over the past year.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s financial publication analyzes the ongoing economic and corporate governance transformation in Japan, arguing that despite persistent long-term demographic and structural headwinds, Japan's exit from deflation offers attractive return prospects for global investors. 

To illustrate the room Japan has to "equitize" further, the page includes a comparative table between the United States and Japan. It shows that Japanese corporations hold 21% of their market capitalization in cash compared to just 7% in the US, and 50% of Japanese companies trade below book value versus only 4% in the US. Furthermore, Japan’s 10-year dividend payout ratio stands at 30% compared to 70% in the US, and corporate buybacks represent only 0.7% to 1.4% of market capitalization, compared to 2.0% to 3.5% in the US. On the asset allocation side, Japanese households hold 55% of their wealth in cash and only 11% in equities, while US households allocate 15% to cash and 40% to equities. Japanese pensions also under-allocate to equities at 25% compared to 40% in the US. 

The text highlights that structural reforms are underway to address these disparities. The Tokyo Stock Exchange has threatened to delist companies trading below book value, poison pills in Nikkei 225 companies have plummeted from 65 in 2012 to 8 as of April 2024, and the percentage of companies with majority independent external directors has doubled from 30% to 60%. Tax incentives are encouraging households to shift from cash to equities, and pensions are pressured to raise equity allocations to match the Government Pension Investment Fund, especially as retirees aged 65 and older make up 28% of the population. 

Three charts reinforce these positive trends alongside one comparative table. The first chart, tracking Japan's core Consumer Price Index excluding fresh food and energy from 1980 to 2024, shows that Japan has finally exited its decades-long deflationary cycle, with core inflation recently rising to nearly 4% after hovering near or below 0% since the mid-1990s. The second chart shows Japanese bank loans as a percentage of GDP from 1980 to 2023; bank loans rebounded from a low of around 80% near 2012 to over 110% by late 2023, reflecting rising domestic credit demand. The third chart displays the global investor underweight to Japanese stocks from 2003 to 2023. It reveals that the actual Japan weighting in global investor portfolios has consistently trailed its weighting in the MSCI All World Global Equity Index. While the benchmark index weight fell from around 11% to roughly 6% over two decades, actual global investor allocations stayed lower near 4% to 5%, indicating a persistent, though recently narrowing, underweight position.

The analysis concludes by weighing these structural changes against Japan's ongoing demographic challenges, which include a potential growth rate under 1%, stagnant industrial production relative to Europe, and a falling Yen coupled with a very high debt-to-GDP ratio. Despite these headwinds, the author asserts that the powerful forces of rising aggregate demand and an exit from deflation make Japan an attractive market compared to Europe and Emerging Markets.

This page from the publication analyzes public market equity investments in agriculture, specifically focusing on crop farming and support industries rather than packaged foods. The author examines seven large-cap US agricultural stocks across farm machinery, fertilizer and chemistry, and agricultural products, highlighting that an equal-weighted basket of these industries has outperformed the S&P 500 ex-tech index since 2015, primarily driven by a massive surge in Deere stock in 2021. However, the sector currently faces cyclical pressures, indicated by rising unsold machinery inventories and lower forward price-to-earnings multiples. Over the medium term, positive drivers like biofuel crop demand and US export growth clash with negative pressures such as green fertilizer premiums, costly equipment electrification, and strict ESG compliance. Notably, a February 2024 Buckeye Institute study estimates that net-zero compliance could raise corn farm operating expenses by up to 34 percent, while the rise of weight-loss drugs presents an open question regarding future crop demand.

The analysis is supported by four charts. The first, titled Agriculture returns vs S&P 500 ex-Tech, tracks performance from 2015 to 2024 using an index where January 1, 2015, equals 100. It demonstrates that the equal-weighted agriculture basket and S&P 500 ex-tech hovered near each other until 2021, when farm machinery surged to over 550, dragging the overall equal-weighted agricultural basket above 400, while agricultural products and chemical stocks remained closer to 200. The second chart, displaying forward price-to-earnings ratios from 2015 to 2024, shows that after a brief spike in valuation multiples around 2020 and 2021, agricultural sub-sectors like fertilizers and agricultural products have compressed significantly, trading below the S&P 500 ex-tech multiple, which sits near 15x to 17.5x.

The third chart, showcasing the stock of unsold US farm equipment from 2019 to early 2024, measures monthly inventory of unsold machinery in thousands. Tractors, plotted on the left axis, rose from a low of 16,000 in 2022 to nearly 28,000 by 2024, while combines, plotted on the right axis, rose from under 5,000 to nearly 8,000, underscoring the growing inventory glut. Finally, the fourth chart compares US agriculture returns across different asset classes from 2015 to 2024, with January 1, 2015, indexed to 100. This visual emphasizes that the equal-weighted US agriculture stock basket, which peaked at 479 in 2022, vastly outperformed alternatives. In contrast, global equities represented by the FTSE MFC global agri index, farmland REITs like Gladstone Land Corp and Farmland Partners Inc, and the JPM Agriculture and Livestock futures index all substantially lagged, with the futures index remaining nearly flat near the 100 baseline.

This page introduces a special issue of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market focused on investing in professional sports leagues and related businesses. Author Michael Cembalest explains that sports team ownership has historically been confined to an extremely wealthy cohort, making it inaccessible to typical institutional or individual investors. To demonstrate this, a scatter plot titled "Net worth of major league sports team control owners" maps individual owners in the NBA, NFL, MLB, and NHL on a log scale from $0.1 billion to $100 billion. The vast majority of these control owners have an estimated net worth ranging between $1 billion and $10 billion, with some surpassing $10 billion, illustrating the steep financial barrier to entry.

However, ownership rules are shifting as major North American leagues increasingly permit private equity funds to acquire minority stakes in individual teams and across multiple franchises. A table titled "North American leagues' private equity rules" details these regulatory frameworks. Major League Baseball was the first to allow private equity in 2019, capping total firm ownership of a single team at 30%, single fund ownership at 15%, and allowing funds to own stakes in an unlimited number of teams. The NBA and NHL followed in 2021, both establishing a 30% limit across firms, a 20% limit for a single fund, and capping fund ownership at 5 teams; both leagues also uniquely permit investments from sovereign wealth funds. Major League Soccer set its rules in 2020 with a 30% aggregate cap, 20% single fund cap, and a 4-team limit. Private equity rules for the NFL are still listed as pending. 

The text highlights that minority investments have surged, accounting for 45% of global sports deals in 2023 and approximately 60% of sports deals within the big four US leagues. Footnote data from a Deloitte study notes that there are currently 24 minority owners in the MLB, 138 in the NBA, and 90 in the NFL. Beyond franchise stakes, Cembalest outlines that sports investing now spans adjacent businesses like real estate, media, sports betting, fitness, collectibles, and player management. The special issue aims to analyze franchise valuations, operating margins, broadcast revenues, stadium subsidies, esports, and historical player comparisons.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, explores the burgeoning landscape of private equity investment in the sports industry following the decision of US sports leagues to permit private equity ownership. Cembalest outlines several key constraints and structural dynamics of sports investing. First, regulatory barriers exist; investment firms are generally prohibited from acquiring minority stakes if another fund they control is involved in sports gambling, player management, or athlete representation. Additionally, conflict-of-interest rules prevent a private equity firm from investing in a league if one of its principals is also a control owner in that league due to their access to confidential information. Second, public equity options are highly restricted. While teams like the Atlanta Braves, Manchester United, and the New York Knicks and Rangers are publicly traded, they are tightly controlled via Class B shares that carry ten times the voting power of public Class A shares. For instance, John Malone controls about 50 percent of the voting power over the Braves, the Glazer family controls 69 percent of Manchester United, and the Dolan family controls 71 percent of the Knicks and Rangers through Madison Square Garden Sports. Furthermore, major sports media entities like ESPN, TNT Sports, CBS Sports, FOX Sports, and NBC Sports are nested as subsidiaries of conglomerates like Disney, Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount, Fox Corporation, and Comcast, making them inaccessible as pure-play public investments. Consequently, Cembalest notes that constructing a diversified sports portfolio may be more feasible in private markets, though he poses the open question of whether the typical five-to-seven-year private equity holding period is well-suited for sports investments.

The accompanying table lists the diverse array of sports-related categories that private equity funds are considering for investment and lending. Under the Teams category, funds look at minority ownership as well as majority ownership, though majority ownership is currently restricted to emerging or international leagues and barred from the four largest US leagues. Other investment categories include Collectibles, which covers trading cards, memorabilia, NFTs, and apparel, and Players and Talent, which spans analytics software, sports agencies, contract underwriting, and performance services like training, rehabilitation, and nutrition. The Real Estate category encompasses team and stadium financing, arenas, adjacent property development, and fitness franchises. Under Media, funds target streaming, media rights, fan engagement, and sports-focused media outlets, while Operations includes venue management, ticketing apps, and arena equipment. The remaining segments are Leagues, highlighting emerging leagues, youth academies, and summer camps; Betting, covering fantasy sports, betting apps, and live sportsbooks; and Video Games, which focuses on e-sports and sports video games.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market discusses several structural and financial dynamics of professional sports team ownership. The author begins by addressing franchise valuations, noting that because fifty to seventy percent of NBA and NFL revenues stem from long-term contractual obligations of highly rated counterparties, alternative valuation methods apply lower investment-grade discount rates to these stable cash flows, while applying standard equity multiples to cyclical flows. The commentary also highlights debt caps across major leagues, mentioning that the NFL limits debt to one point four billion dollars for new acquisitions and seven hundred million dollars for existing owners, while the NBA caps debt at three hundred twenty-five million dollars, keeping overall leverage low across the board. 

To illustrate this point, a line chart plots the debt-to-valuation ratios for teams in the NHL, NFL, MLB, and NBA, sorted in descending order. Most teams maintain ratios well below twenty percent, with only three notable high-leverage exceptions highlighted in an accompanying callout box. The Arizona Coyotes hold the highest ratio at sixty-two percent, reflecting a struggling NHL franchise recently sold for relocation to Utah. The Los Angeles Rams stand at forty-six percent due to a special NFL debt waiver granted to finance the construction of SoFi Stadium. The Miami Marlins have a forty-five percent ratio, driven by high debt levels assumed during their 2017 purchase. 

The page further details the growing trend of cross-ownership, citing groups like Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, Harris Blitzer Sports, Monumental, and Fenway Sports Group, alongside eleven Major League Soccer owners who hold stakes in other sports leagues. In addition, real estate development is noted as a major value driver, with modern stadium projects revitalizing surrounding urban areas, as seen with Camden Yards in Baltimore, Truist Park in Atlanta, Wrigley Field, and Capital One Arena. Tax advantages also benefit owners, who can depreciate assets like player contracts, stadium leases, and media rights against active income. Finally, the author cautions against academic studies praising sports assets' risk-adjusted performance, arguing that appraisal-based models mask true risk and that sports investments should instead be measured by excess returns over public markets.

This page analyzes the valuations, transactions, debt levels, and operating margins of the four major US sports leagues—the NFL, NBA, NHL, and MLB. It outlines how franchise values are driven by diversified revenue sources (league revenue-sharing, local brand-building, and ancillary real estate and media assets) and protected by their status as lightly regulated monopolies under the Sherman Act. 

A bar chart titled "NBA, NFL, NHL, and MLB sale values since 2014" displays individual team transactions in billions of US dollars, highlighting that actual transaction prices (represented by colored bars) closely align with pre-sale Forbes valuation appraisals (represented by black dots). Notable high-value transactions include the NFL's Washington Commanders in 2023, which sold for nearly $6 billion, followed by the Denver Broncos in 2022. In the NBA, multiple major transactions occurred in 2023, including the Phoenix Suns, Dallas Mavericks, Charlotte Hornets, and Milwaukee Bucks, with valuations clustering between $3 billion and $4 billion. 

An accompanying table detailing actual sales transactions from 2022 to 2024 lists specific valuation-to-revenue multiples. The highest multiples are found in the NBA, with the Phoenix Suns selling at 13.2 times revenue, the Charlotte Hornets at 11.2 times, and the Milwaukee Bucks at 9.7 times. The NFL's Washington Commanders sold at 11.1 times revenue, and the Denver Broncos sold at 9.4 times. The NHL's Arizona Coyotes sold at 8.3 times revenue in 2024, while the MLB's Baltimore Orioles sold at a lower multiple of 6.5 times revenue in 2024. 

The author explains that sports teams command a massive premium compared to standard public equities, with most teams valued at 5 to 12 times sales compared to approximately 3 times sales for the S&P 500. Valuation dispersion also varies widely by league. The gap between the most and least valuable teams is relatively narrow in the NFL and NHL at approximately 2.5 times, grows to 3.2 times in the NBA, and widens significantly to 7.6 times in MLB. This wide gap in baseball is attributed to a lack of salary caps, less comprehensive revenue sharing, and higher exposure to local media rights.

Two bottom charts reinforce these valuation trends. The first, "Sport team valuations vs equity markets," indexes valuations from 2005 to 2024 (where 2005 equals 100). It demonstrates that all four sports leagues have vastly outperformed the S&P 500. By 2024, the NBA valuation index leads dramatically at nearly 1,300, followed by the NHL and MLB indexes around 800, and the NFL index near 600, while the S&P 500 index trails significantly at around 450. The second chart, "Valuation to revenues for major sports teams vs S&P 500 price to sales," plots individual league teams sorted in descending order of valuation-to-revenues. NBA teams remain the most expensive, spanning from roughly 12 times down to 8 times revenue. NFL teams range from 10 times to 7 times, NHL teams from 8 times to 4.5 times, and MLB teams show the widest variance from 9 times down to 2 times, while the S&P 500 baseline remains flat near 3 times.

This page analyzes the financial operations of major North American sports leagues, specifically the NFL, NHL, NBA, and MLB, focusing on how broadcast revenues, fiscal discipline, and salary cap structures impact team operating margins. The author highlights that NFL, NHL, and NBA teams benefit significantly from these mechanisms, which have led to improved operating margins over the last two decades as player salaries have declined as a percentage of league revenue. In contrast, Major League Baseball, which lacks a salary cap, displays lower and sometimes negative operating margins. A notable case is the NHL, where median operating margins tripled following the signing of seven-year media deals with Disney and Turner Sports in 2021, worth six hundred and thirty-five million dollars annually. Furthermore, the analysis points out a recruiting advantage for NHL teams in tax-free states like Texas, Florida, and Nevada, noting that eleven of the twenty conference finalists since 2020 reside in these states. A footnote illustrates this tax disparity with a three million dollar contract, which faces zero state tax in Texas compared to three hundred and seventy-one thousand dollars in California. The author cautions that operating income excludes interest, taxes, and capital projects, and therefore does not directly equate to net cash flow.

The first chart, titled Operating income margin by team and league, plots individual team operating margins ranked from highest to lowest. The NFL series sits consistently at the top, ranging from roughly fifteen percent to over forty percent. The NHL also shows consistently positive margins. The NBA shows positive margins for most teams but dips into negative territory for franchises like the Nets, Clippers, and Bucks. The MLB shows the most pronounced downward slope, with several teams including the Athletics, Rockies, White Sox, Blue Jays, and Padres posting negative margins, and the New York Mets showing a severe negative margin approaching negative eighty percent.

The second chart, League revenue by type, presents a stacked bar chart illustrating the percentage breakdown of revenue sources for each league. The NFL is highly dependent on national revenue, which accounts for over sixty percent of its total. The NBA and MLB feature a more diversified mix, with national revenue, seating and suites, team sponsorships, and local media each representing significant shares. The NHL is the least dependent on national revenue, which makes up about fifteen percent of its total, relying heavily instead on seating and suites, local media, and team sponsorships.

The third chart, Player expenses as a percentage of revenue, shows historical trends from 2006 to past 2020. Across the NFL, NBA, and NHL, player expenses as a share of revenue have generally trended downwards, falling from levels of fifty-five to over sixty percent in 2006 to levels closer to forty-five to fifty percent in recent years. MLB player expenses have shown more volatility, spiking significantly around 2020 during pandemic disruptions before falling back. The page concludes by previewing upcoming analyses on media rights, specifically mentioning the bankruptcy of Diamond Sports and its impact on MLB, NBA, and NHL, alongside in-person attendance trends and ticket pricing.

This page discusses how team salary caps function as a powerful tool to increase league parity and prevent payroll arms races, comparing the structured payrolls of North American sports leagues to the unchecked spending seen in European soccer. The author explains that hard salary caps in the NFL and NHL keep team spending relatively equal, whereas the NBA's soft cap allows for some slippage due to various veteran and rookie exceptions. Major League Baseball (MLB) has no cap, leading to spending that reflects individual owner willingness to pay, though high payrolls do trigger a luxury tax. 

To illustrate these dynamics, the first chart, titled "Payroll parity in US major sports leagues," plots each team's 2023 payroll divided by the median league payroll on the y-axis against the teams ranked by payroll on the x-axis. The NFL, NHL, and NBA show very flat lines clustered tightly around the 1.0 median mark. In contrast, the MLB curve is quite steep, showing massive disparity. At the top end, the New York Mets payroll is over 2.0 times the league median, with the New York Yankees, San Diego Padres, Philadelphia Phillies, and Los Angeles Dodgers also displaying high relative spending. At the lower end, small-market teams like the Oakland Athletics, Baltimore Orioles, Pittsburgh Pirates, Cincinnati Reds, and Tampa Bay Rays fall well below half the median payroll.

The second chart, "Payroll parity in major sports leagues," expands this comparison to European soccer leagues, showing how much more dramatic the disparities are when no salary caps exist. This chart plots the same ratio of team-to-median payroll but on a much larger y-axis scale from 0 to 9. Spain's La Liga is presented as the ultimate example of an arms-race league: Real Madrid's payroll is nearly 9 times the league median, FC Barcelona is at approximately 7 times the median, and Atletico Madrid is at 5 times, after which the curve plummets. The English Premier League also shows a steeper spending curve than MLB, with top teams spending around 2.5 times the league median, though the author notes that the Premier League plans to introduce a salary cap next year. 

Finally, the author highlights a key structural difference: while MLB spending is independent of league-wide financial health, the NFL, NBA, and NHL tie their salary caps directly to aggregate league revenue, meaning caps would automatically decline if overall revenues were to fall.

This page discusses the massive growth in the value of broadcasting and streaming rights for professional sports, highlighting how live sports have become a dominant force in media. It notes that three of the four major US sports leagues—excluding the National Hockey League, which derives 30%—now receive 50% to 70% of their total revenue from shared national and local media rights. This represents a historic shift from earlier eras when franchise value relied primarily on in-person attendance; in 1946, for example, radio and TV contracts made up only 3% of Major League Baseball revenue. According to the text, global sports media contracts have grown from $24.5 billion in 2011 to over $62.4 billion today. 

A table on the page illustrates the rise in media contract values across different leagues. Major League Baseball secured a 1.3x increase for its 2022–2028 deal, the National Football League achieved a 1.8x increase for its 2023–2033 deal, and the National Hockey League saw a 2.1x increase for its 2021–2028 deal. Meanwhile, the National Basketball Association experienced a 2.9x increase for its 2016–2025 contract and is poised for a 2.6x increase for its projected $76 billion, 11-year deal running from 2025 to 2036.

Several charts support these observations. A line chart showing the real, inflation-adjusted price of a 30-second Super Bowl commercial from 1965 to 2025 indicates that costs have risen from near zero to more than $7 million, doubling since 2005 and also doubling in the two decades prior to that. A bar chart tracking US sports media rights payments shows a steady climb from approximately $15 billion in 2015 to over $20 billion by 2021, with forecasts predicting these payments will exceed $30 billion by 2026. In contrast, a bar chart of the estimated number of adult scripted original series shows a peak of nearly 600 series in 2022 before falling sharply to around 400 in 2023, highlighting a pullback in traditional entertainment production just as sports spending accelerates.

The text presents further evidence of strong consumer demand for sports content. Over 30% of adults in the United States and the United Kingdom have purchased a pay-per-view sports event in the past year, with boxing and Ultimate Fighting Championship events leading this category. Furthermore, the NFL's dominance in live television has grown, accounting for 93 of the 100 most-watched TV broadcasts in 2023, up from 82 in 2022 and 61 in 2018. Within the top 50 most-viewed broadcasts of 2023, 48 were NFL games, with the only non-sports exceptions being the State of the Union address and the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Additionally, eight of the top ten most-watched events in US television history were Super Bowls.

This page analyzed by Michael Cembalest examines the highly debated role of public subsidies in funding sports stadiums and arenas, arguing that these taxpayer contributions represent a substantial transfer of value to franchise owners. While the public's share of construction costs has trended downward, the rapidly escalating complexity and price tags of modern venues mean that total inflation-adjusted public dollars spent continue to rise.

Four charts illustrate these dynamics. The first chart, titled "Stadium and arena median construction costs by decade," displays median costs in millions of 2020 US dollars from the 1970s to the 2020s, dividing costs into total and public expenditures for both arenas and stadiums. Stadium construction costs have grown exponentially, with median totals exceeding $1.8 billion in the 2020s, while arena costs have climbed beyond $800 million. 

The second chart, "Public funding share of total stadium construction costs," maps the number of sports venues built since 1990 against the percentage of their construction funded by the public. While the median public funding share is 61%, the distribution is starkly polarized: a large cohort of nearly 25 venues received 0% public funding, while a substantial number of others received funding levels ranging from 60% to over 90%. A footnote highlights that the most expensive stadium ever built, SoFi Stadium, cost $5.5 billion and was entirely privately financed, and notes that Kansas City voters recently rejected a 40-year sales tax renewal to subsidize a stadium for the Royals.

The third chart, "Stadium costs as a share of team valuation," calculates stadium construction costs as a percentage of 2023 franchise valuations for select facilities opened since 2000 that received over 70% public funding. The Miami Marlins lead this metric, with their stadium cost representing approximately 80% of the team's total valuation, followed closely by the Pittsburgh Penguins, San Diego Padres, Edmonton Oilers, Milwaukee Brewers, and Cincinnati Reds, with the Oklahoma City Thunder at the bottom of the list at around 15%.

The final chart, "Valuation of the Raiders," tracks the NFL franchise's valuation in billions of US dollars from 1997 to 2024 to show how public subsidies boost franchise worth. Following the approval of plans for a new Las Vegas stadium—backed by $750 million in taxpayer funding—the team's valuation surged from $1.4 billion in 2015 to more than $6 billion by 2024.

This page focuses on the financial dynamics of European soccer, emphasizing the high stakes of league relegation, the challenge of soaring player salaries, and the low profitability of clubs compared to the more parity-driven structure of Major League Soccer in the United States. 

To illustrate the revenue disparities across European leagues, a stacked bar chart displays the cumulative revenues of the "Big Five" European leagues for the 2021-2022 season, categorized by matchday, commercial, and broadcasting income. The English Premier League leads by a massive margin, with total revenues exceeding six billion pounds, primarily driven by broadcasting revenues of around three and a half billion pounds and commercial revenues of approximately two billion pounds. In contrast, La Liga and the Bundesliga follow with just over three billion pounds each in total revenue, while Serie A stands at roughly two point three billion pounds, and Ligue 1 trails at about two billion pounds.

The financial risk of relegation from the English Premier League is analyzed in a detailed table of team revenues for the 2019-2020 season. Teams finishing in the top four, qualifying for the UEFA Champions League, generated an average total revenue of four hundred forty-four million pounds, comprising sixty-six million in matchday revenue, one hundred seventy-eight million in broadcast revenue, and two hundred million in commercial revenue. Revenue drops significantly for lower-tier finishes, with mid-table teams (ranked ninth to seventeenth) earning one hundred forty-one million pounds total, and relegated teams (ranked eighteenth to twentieth) bringing in one hundred twelve million pounds. Once relegated to the EFL Championship, teams suffer a steep financial hit, though it can be partially offset by parachute payments. EFL Championship teams receiving these payments generated fifty-two million pounds in total revenue, whereas those without parachute payments generated a mere twenty million pounds, demonstrating a revenue drop of up to eighty percent compared to mid-table English Premier League teams. 

A case study highlights the dramatic financial impact of this system through the story of the Luton Town Hatters. After being relegated from the top flight in 1992, the team fell as low as the third tier. Upon fighting their way back to the English Premier League in 2023, the club's revenue skyrocketed from seventeen point six million pounds in 2021 to over two hundred million pounds in 2023.

Despite rising broadcast revenues, such as a ten-billion-pound English Premier League contract for 2022 through 2025, the author explains that financial success remains elusive due to skyrocketing player salaries. In the absence of salary caps or rookie contracts, player salaries in the English Premier League grew thirty-six-fold between 1992 and 2021, outstripping a twenty-seven-fold growth in league revenues over the same period. Wages consume seventy-three percent of revenue for the average team, rising to eighty-seven percent for clubs outside the top six. Consequently, only seven English Premier League teams—roughly one-third of the league—reported a profit during the 2021-2022 season.

The author contrasts these financial struggles with Major League Soccer in the United States, which utilizes a rigorous revenue-sharing model that pools national broadcast, merchandise, and sponsorship revenues to distribute them equally among team owners. Two-thirds of Major League Soccer team revenue is tied to this pooled national funding. Furthermore, Major League Soccer capped team salary budgets at five point five million dollars in 2024, restricting teams to a maximum of three "designated players" whose compensation can exceed the cap. This emphasis on parity has successfully stabilized the league, with the average team value rising by seventeen percent over the last five years and individual team valuations remaining highly clustered around the league average.

This page discusses the weak economic rationale for subsidizing professional sports facilities, drawing on a 2022 meta-study by Bradbury et al. that analyzed 130 individual studies. The author explains that stadium subsidies typically exceed the local economic benefits they generate because increases in sports-related consumer spending represent shifts from other local spending rather than net-new economic activity. Consequently, these subsidies function primarily as wealth transfers from taxpayers to sports team owners. 

To support this claim, the author includes two horizontal bar charts illustrating expert consensus on the issue. The first chart shows that a significant majority of surveyed American Economic Association members believe state and local governments should eliminate professional sports subsidies, with nearly 60% strongly agreeing and approximately 27% agreeing. The second chart depicts results from a surveyed IGM panel of economic experts, where over 60% agree and around 15% strongly agree that providing subsidies to build professional sports stadiums costs taxpayers more than the generated local economic benefits. 

Despite this economic evidence, the author points out that stadium subsidies remain common, setting the stage for future debates as a major wave of stadium construction approaches. This trend is driven by a typical 30-year stadium replacement cycle and a current median facility age of 24 years across major sports leagues. A line chart at the bottom of the page, titled "Stadium ages by league," plots the age or years since renovation for individual facilities in the MLB, NHL, NBA, and NFL, ranked from oldest to newest. The data reveals that the oldest venues across all leagues currently range from 30 to 35 years of age. Based on this trajectory, the author projects that by the year 2030, 30 facilities—roughly 25% of all stadiums across these four leagues—will be at least 30 years old.

This page analyzes the mechanics, profitability, and regulatory landscape of sports betting in the United States, focusing on the rise of sports parlays and daily fantasy sports (DFS). Michael Cembalest explains that sportsbooks are heavily promoting parlays—combined wagers with higher payout odds—because they carry much higher profit margins than traditional straight bets, boosting customer retention and offsetting smaller average bet sizes. 

To illustrate these trends, the page features three visual graphics. The first line chart, titled "Increase in parlay bets," plots the parlay share of total bets placed from 2020 to 2023. FanDuel leads this trend, with its parlay share rising from approximately 50% in 2020 to roughly 70% in 2023. Other major bookmakers, including DraftKings, PointsBet, BetRivers, BetMGM, Caesars, and Barstool, also saw steady increases, with DraftKings reaching nearly 50% and most others converging between 30% and 40% by 2023. 

The second visual, "Size and profitability: straight bet vs parlay bet," uses data from Illinois to contrast the average bet size against profit margins across seven major platforms. Straight bets are far larger than parlays, exceeding $140 for Caesars and hovering around $40 to $80 for most other sportsbooks. Parlays, by contrast, typically average under $40. However, the profit margins tell a different story: straight bet margins consistently sit near 5% (shown in gray dots), while parlay profit margins (shown in red dots) are much higher, clustering between 15% and 20% across all operators. 

The third chart displays "Sports-gambling app downloads (July 2022-June 2023)" in millions, color-coded by fantasy sports versus sports betting. While FanDuel Sportsbook and DraftKings Sportsbook lead with over 8 million downloads each, the daily fantasy sports provider PrizePicks ranks third with over 4 million downloads, outperforming traditional betting apps like BetMGM, Caesars, and Barstool. 

Finally, the text outlines the "Daily Fantasy Sports loophole," highlighting a regulatory arbitrage where states containing 33% of the US population—such as California, Texas, Alabama, Georgia, Minnesota, Missouri, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Utah, and Texas—do not permit traditional sportsbooks like DraftKings and FanDuel to operate. However, because of permissive legal language, highly populated states like California and Texas allow fantasy companies like PrizePicks to run unregulated, parlay-style games tax-free. Adding to the complexity, some states that allow traditional sportsbooks conversely prohibit DFS operations.

This appendix page focuses on the financial health and valuations of National Football League teams, presenting a detailed breakdown of valuations, revenues, debt, and operating margins. 

The primary visual is a comprehensive table showing the latest team valuations, revenues, debt, and operating income for 31 NFL franchises, sourced from Forbes and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The table reveals that the Dallas Cowboys are the most valuable franchise at $9.0 billion, yielding $1.14 billion in revenue, $504 million in operating income, and an operating margin of 44%. Other highly valued teams include the New England Patriots at $7.0 billion, the Los Angeles Rams at $6.9 billion, and the New York Giants at $6.8 billion. On the lower end of the listed valuations are the Cincinnati Bengals at $3.5 billion and the Detroit Lions at $3.6 billion. The valuation-to-revenue multiples range from a high of 11.3x for the Chicago Bears to a low of 7.0x for the Cincinnati Bengals. Debt-to-valuation ratios also vary widely, led by the Los Angeles Rams at 46%, while several teams, such as the Houston Texans, carry 0% debt relative to their valuation.

Below the table, two historical line charts track league-wide median trends from 1998 to 2022. The first chart, depicting the NFL median valuation to revenue, shows that the median multiple remained relatively stable between 3x and 4x from 1998 through 2012. After 2012, the multiple experienced a steep and continuous rise, climbing past 8x by 2022, illustrating massive valuation growth relative to underlying revenues. The second chart, tracking the NFL median operating margin, reveals a highly cyclical trend. Historically fluctuating between 10% and 25%, the median operating margin suffered a dramatic plunge down close to 5% around 2020, representing pandemic-era disruptions, before staging a sharp recovery to nearly 25% by 2022.

This page examines sports-adjacent business sectors that are increasingly attracting sports-focused investment funds, specifically exploring apparel, image management, and player management. 

In the apparel sector, the author focuses on Fanatics, a company valued at $31 billion during a 2022 funding round. Fanatics has grown from a standard e-commerce brand into an industry heavyweight holding exclusive manufacturing rights, key acquisitions like Topps baseball cards, clothing partnerships with athletes Kevin Durant and LeBron James, and a Nike college apparel agreement. Despite its scale, S&P revised its outlook on Fanatics to negative while affirming a BB- rating, reflecting concerns over elevated leverage, slowing revenue growth from production delays, and a 5.5 percent decline in EBITDA margins during the second quarter of 2023. Key risks facing the firm include high guaranteed minimum royalty payments to intellectual property owners and ongoing antitrust litigation with the NFL.

For image management, the text highlights the rapid growth of Name, Image, and Likeness (NIL) group licensing deals. OneTeam Partners is showcased as an entity that commercializes group licensing rights with major professional unions—including the NFL, MLB, MLS, WNBA, and the US Women's National Soccer Team—and has partnered with Fanatics on college apparel. OneTeam manages NIL rights for over 100 collegiate programs across multiple sports, though the author points out a major operational hurdle: collegiate jersey demand is highly unpredictable, necessitating an on-demand production model. 

The final section addresses the lucrative player management sector, which services a nearly $20 billion annual payroll across the four major US sports leagues. A detailed table lists the top fifteen sports agencies based on 2022 Forbes data and 2024 JPMAM funding data. Creative Artists Agency (CAA) leads the table, representing football, basketball, baseball, soccer, and hockey (FBASH) with $971 million in commissions, $18.0 billion in active contracts, and backing from investors like TPG, CMC, Temasek, Pinault, and Taiwan Mobile. Wasserman ranks second with $733 million in commissions and $9.0 billion in contracts across a broader suite of sports, including golf, rugby, and extreme sports, backed by Providence and Madrone. WME Sports places third, representing football, basketball, tennis, and golf with $588 million in commissions and $6.0 billion in contracts under investors Silver Lake, KKR, and DFO. Excel Sports Management and Octagon follow with commissions of $499 million and $212 million respectively. Other prominent agencies featured include Boras Corporation, Roc Nation Sports, Athletes First, Klutch Sports Group, You First, GSE Worldwide, Newport Sports Management, Rep 1 Sports, Priority Sports & Entertainment, and Independent Sports & Entertainment.

This page analyzes the financial health and historical valuation trends of National Basketball Association franchises, utilizing data from Forbes and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The top portion of the page features a comprehensive table detailing the latest valuations, revenues, debt, and operating statistics for thirty NBA teams. The Golden State Warriors lead the league with a valuation of $7.7 billion and annual revenue of $765 million, alongside a 14% five-year annualized revenue growth rate. The New York Knicks and Los Angeles Lakers follow closely, valued at $6.6 billion and $6.4 billion respectively. At the opposite end of the spectrum, the Memphis Grizzlies represent the lowest-valued franchise on the list at $2.4 billion. While many teams display strong profitability, such as the San Antonio Spurs with a 35% operating margin and the New York Knicks at 34%, others like the Milwaukee Bucks, Los Angeles Clippers, and Brooklyn Nets operate with negative operating income. 

The bottom left line chart traces the historical NBA median valuation-to-revenue multiple from 1998 through 2022. The data shows that the median multiple remained relatively flat, hovering between 2x and 3x from 1998 until around 2011. Following this period, the multiple experienced an aggressive upward trajectory, surging past 10x by 2022. Adjacent to this, the bottom right line chart monitors the NBA median operating margin over the same time frame. Margins hovered near 5% in 1998, spiked to 15% around 2004, and then plummeted to negative territory near the 2010 season. Following this dip, median operating margins rebounded dramatically, climbing to a peak of nearly 30% around 2021 before settling back slightly by 2022.

This page examines the financial health and valuations of Major League Baseball franchises, presenting a comprehensive table of team-by-team metrics alongside historical trends in median valuation multiples and operating margins. The primary table lists thirty MLB teams sorted by valuation, led by the New York Yankees at $7.6 billion and the Los Angeles Dodgers at $5.5 billion, down to the Miami Marlins at $1.0 billion. Despite high valuations, operating profitability varies wildly across the league; for instance, the New York Mets posted a staggering operating loss of $292 million (representing a negative 74% operating margin) and the San Diego Padres lost $116 million, whereas the Baltimore Orioles generated $99 million in operating income with a league-high 30% operating margin. Valuation-to-revenue multiples range from a high of 11.1x for the Yankees to a low of 3.4x for the Marlins. Leverage also varies significantly, with the Miami Marlins carrying the highest debt-to-valuation ratio at 45%, while teams like the Los Angeles Angels and Toronto Blue Jays carry 0% debt.

To put these figures in historical context, two charts trace league-wide median trends from 1998 through 2022. The chart showing the MLB median valuation-to-revenue multiple demonstrates that team valuations remained stable at around 2.5x to 3.0x revenue for over a decade before beginning a steady rise after 2011, culminating in a massive spike to over 12x around 2021 before correcting back down to the 5.5x range. The adjacent chart tracking the MLB median operating margin reveals a highly volatile history. Median operating margins generally fluctuated between 0% and 12%, but experienced a sharp collapse below negative 5% during the pandemic-disrupted 2020 to 2021 period before recovering back to approximately 10% by 2022. Together, these visuals highlight how baseball franchise valuations have soared to historic heights relative to their revenues, even as team-level operating profitability remains highly cyclical and inconsistent.

This page presents a comprehensive financial analysis of National Hockey League franchises, focusing on valuations, revenues, debt, and profitability metrics. The primary visual is a detailed table containing data for thirty-two NHL teams compiled from Forbes and J.P. Morgan Asset Management sources in 2024. The Toronto Maple Leafs lead the league with a valuation of $2.8 billion, generating $281 million in revenue and boasting a league-high operating margin of 45% with a 10.0x valuation-to-revenue multiple. Close behind are the New York Rangers, valued at $2.7 billion with a 10.0x multiple, and the Montreal Canadiens at $2.3 billion. At the other end of the spectrum, the Arizona Coyotes are valued at $0.5 billion, carrying a league-high debt-to-valuation ratio of 62%. The table also includes other prominent franchises such as the Los Angeles Kings, Boston Bruins, Chicago Blackhawks, and Edmonton Oilers, detailing their respective operating incomes, leverage, and five-year annual revenue growth rates. 

Accompanying the table are two historical line charts tracking median league trends from 1998 through 2022. The first chart, depicting the NHL median valuation-to-revenue multiple, shows that team valuations remained relatively stable at around 2.0x to 2.5x revenue from 1998 until approximately 2012. After this period, multiples began to rise, culminating in a dramatic spike to over 8.0x in 2021 before correcting to around 5.5x in 2022. The second chart traces the NHL median operating margin over the same historical period, illustrating the league's historically thin profitability. For much of the two decades prior to 2021, median operating margins fluctuated between negative 5% and positive 8%, with a severe drop below negative 10% during the pandemic era around 2020. This was followed by an unprecedented, sharp rebound in 2022, when median operating margins surged to nearly 22%.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" examines methods for tracking the ideological leanings of United States Supreme Court justices and the broader federal judiciary. The analysis begins with a discussion of Martin-Quinn scores, which continuously evaluate judicial ideology from 1937 to the present on a mathematical spectrum ranging from negative five for most liberal to positive five for most conservative. The underlying model, which is accurate about 75% of the time, relies on overlapping service periods to compare justices across different eras. For example, Hugo Black and William Rehnquist can be placed on the same spectrum because both served alongside Potter Stewart. 

A large line chart maps these ideological leanings over nearly a century, illustrating how individual justices' positions have shifted over time. Highly conservative figures like William Rehnquist, Antonin Scalia, and Clarence Thomas track toward the top of the chart with scores between three and five. In contrast, liberal justices such as William O. Douglas, Thurgood Marshall, and Sonia Sotomayor occupy the bottom of the chart with scores near negative four or negative five. The visualization also captures notable ideological drifts, showing how justices like Harry Blackmun, John Paul Stevens, and David Souter trended significantly more liberal over their tenures on the bench.

A second bar chart focuses on the current court, measuring how frequently conservative justices align with their liberal colleagues in a metric called the "bridging alliance score." The data reveals a wide spectrum of crossing ideological lines. Neil Gorsuch leads the conservative justices with the highest bridging score of approximately 3.5, driven primarily by alignments in cases involving criminal and indigenous law. John Roberts and Brett Kavanaugh follow with scores of 2.5, while Amy Coney Barrett scores roughly 2.25 and Clarence Thomas stands at 1.8. Samuel Alito has the lowest bridging alliance score of 1.0, with the author noting that Alito is the only current conservative justice who has never joined all the liberal justices in a five-to-four decision.

Finally, a third bar chart tracks the percentage of active U.S. Court of Appeals judges appointed by Republican presidents from 1981 to 2024. This trend shows significant cyclical variation corresponding to political shifts. Republican-appointed judges made up just 35% of appellate benches in 1981 before surging to a peak of nearly 65% in 1993. This share fell back to around 40% by 2013, rose again to approximately 53% in 2021, and stands at roughly 51% as of 2024.

This page examines the athletic and financial repercussions of superstar player departures, contrasting the market-driven "Ronaldo effect" in European football with the structurally buffered dynamics of North American sports leagues. The first chart, titled "The 'Ronaldo effect'," tracks Juventus's share price in Euros alongside the Prospect global interest index from 2014 to 2024. The data demonstrates that when Cristiano Ronaldo joined Juventus in late 2018, the club's share price skyrocketed from under three Euros to a peak of nearly ten Euros, while global interest surged from around one percent to approximately three and a half percent. Upon his departure in 2021, both metrics plummeted back to pre-arrival levels, with the share price falling under three Euros and global interest dropping below one and a half percent by 2024. 

The author points out that while player departures in US leagues also trigger massive swings in team performance, revenue-sharing models protect franchise owners from the corresponding financial downside. This performance volatility is illustrated in the second chart, "Major US sports departures," which maps the winning percentages of teams before and after major roster shifts for eight legendary athletes. The data displays significant performance drops for departing teams and corresponding boosts for acquiring teams. For instance, when LeBron James left Cleveland for Miami, Cleveland's winning percentage plunged from around seventy-five percent to nearly twenty percent. Similarly, Michael Jordan’s departure from Chicago after 1997 caused the Bulls' winning percentage to crash from over eighty percent to about twenty percent. The chart tracks similar stark transitions for Julius Erving (Philadelphia and New Jersey), Kareem Abdul-Jabbar (Los Angeles Lakers and a team labeled MIN), Reggie Jackson (New York Yankees and Oakland), Barry Bonds (San Francisco and Pittsburgh), Shaquille O'Neal (Los Angeles Lakers and Orlando), and Manny Ramirez (Boston and Cleveland), highlighting how US leagues successfully decouple team ownership revenue from on-field performance fluctuations.

This page discusses the prolonged underperformance of US small-cap stocks relative to large-caps, framing it alongside two other historically popular but currently out-of-favor strategies: large-cap value versus growth, and non-US stocks versus US equities. Together, Michael Cembalest refers to these three as "the unholy trinity" of underperforming portfolio strategies. While historical data from 1930 to 2010 showed a clear "small cap anomaly" where small caps regularly outperformed large caps, that trend reversed after 2010 due to vastly superior earnings growth in US large-cap growth stocks.

The first chart on the page, titled "Small cap vs large cap index returns," tracks the three-year rolling outperformance or underperformance of small-cap versus large-cap indices from 1930 through mid-2024. It shows six distinct eras of small-cap outperformance prior to 2010, with rolling outperformance frequently spiking above 50% and occasionally exceeding 100%. However, the period after 2010 is characterized by persistent large-cap outperformance, with the rolling metric falling deeply into negative territory.

To illustrate the broader trend, the second chart, "The Big Three: relative underperformance," displays the five-year cumulative performance of these three struggling strategies relative to their dominant counterparts from 1990 to 2024. The lines tracking the Russell 2000 & S&P 600 versus the S&P 500, the MSCI World ex-US versus the S&P 500, and the Russell 1000 value versus growth all show dramatic downward trajectories after 2010, with cumulative underperformance levels plunging toward -75% to -100%. 

The third chart, "The Big Three: relative valuations," displays the relative price-to-earnings premium or discount from 1995 to 2025. It reveals that all three lagging strategies are currently trading at their cheapest levels in 20 years. Specifically, the forward P/E of the S&P 600 relative to the S&P 500, the LTM P/E of the MSCI World ex-US relative to the S&P 500, and the forward P/E of Russell 1000 value versus growth are all hovering at substantial discounts, ranging from 25% to over 50%.

The fundamental driver of this underperformance is depicted in the fourth chart, "Earnings growth," which indexes earnings growth from a baseline of 100 in December 2010 through 2024. The Russell 1000 growth index has dramatically outpaced all other categories, surging to an index value of approximately 325. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 index reached around 280, and both the Russell 2000 and Russell 1000 value lines lagged behind at roughly 240. Crucially, non-US equities have been an earnings wasteland over the last decade, with the MSCI World ex-US developed index sitting around 150 and the index including emerging markets struggling to stay above 125. 

Looking ahead, Cembalest suggests that while all three underperforming strategies are remarkably cheap, they are cheap for a reason due to their weaker earnings. However, he expresses a preference for US small caps, stating he sees better recovery prospects for them than for either non-US equities or US large-cap value. The page concludes with a thematic historical note about the 1968 film *The Lion in Winter*, detailing King Henry II of England's attempts to establish a succession plan with his three sons and his wife, Eleanor of Aquitaine, in 1183 AD.

This page analyzes the structural challenges facing US small-cap stocks, arguing that they exhibit much lower profitability and significantly higher interest rate exposure than US large-cap stocks. To support this view, the author presents six charts comparing key financial metrics across the S&P 500, S&P 600, and Russell 2000 indices.

The first chart displays three-month smoothed free cash flow margins from 1996 to 2023. It reveals that the S&P 500 has consistently maintained superior free cash flow margins, hovering above 10% in recent years, while the S&P 600 has stayed around 4% to 6%, and the Russell 2000 has struggled near 0% to 2%. This lack of profitability is further detailed in the second chart, which plots the percentage of companies with negative last-twelve-month earnings from 1990 to 2020. The gap is stark: over 40% of small-cap companies currently operate with negative earnings, compared to only about 10% of large-cap companies.

Profit efficiency is also addressed in the third chart, which tracks aggregate Return on Invested Capital from 1990 to 2023. Large-cap companies have maintained a solid ROIC above 11%, while small-cap companies have seen their aggregate ROIC decline to around 4%. 

The remaining charts explore debt structures and leverage. The fourth chart illustrates the breakdown of fixed versus floating-rate debt for non-financial companies as of mid-2024. It shows that the S&P 500 ex-Financials carries roughly 90% fixed debt and only 10% floating debt. In contrast, both the Russell 2000 ex-Financials and the S&P 600 ex-Financials carry approximately 40% floating-rate debt, exposing them heavily to higher interest rates. 

Leverage ratios are examined in the final two charts using 90-day trailing moving averages from 2000 to 2024. The fifth chart shows net debt to EBITDA, highlighting that the Russell 2000 and S&P 600 carry higher ratios of roughly 4x and 3x, respectively, compared to the S&P 500, which has steadily remained below 2x. Finally, the sixth chart traces total debt to equity. While the S&P 500 previously spiked to over 2.0x around the 2008 financial crisis, it has since deleveraged, resulting in a convergence where all three indices sit near the 0.9x to 1.0x level by 2024. 

Overall, the data suggests that small caps are heavily burdened by near-term debt maturities, floating-rate interest exposure, and weaker cash generation, making them a challenging area for investors seeking value.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes whether US small-cap stocks are currently cheap, concluding that they are at the very cheap end of their 20-year valuation range across multiple different measures and may represent an interesting entry point for investors. 

The author begins with Method 1, which compares relative forward P/E ratios. A line chart titled "Relative valuation: small vs large cap forward P/E ratio" plots the relative forward P/E premium or discount from 1995 to 2025 for both the Russell 2000 and the S&P 600 against the S&P 500. This chart shows that while the Russell 2000 vs S&P 500 premium has declined from historical peaks of over 75 percent down to roughly 25 percent, the S&P 600 vs S&P 500 relationship sits at a deep discount near negative 35 percent. To address data anomalies in broader indexes, a second chart from Empirical Research tracks the "Small cap vs large cap forward P/E for highest quality stocks" (defined as the top quintile of free cash flow margins) from 1976 to 2024. This ratio has plunged from a peak of around 1.6x in 2009 to nearly 0.6x in 2024, nearing its lowest historical level since the late 1970s.

Next, Method 2 explores relative earnings yields, where a higher relative yield indicates cheaper stocks. To remove outliers, J.P. Morgan's Structured Equity Group winsorizes trailing and forward data from Compustat and Factset. Two charts display these differences from 1990 to 2025. The first, measuring the "Difference in trailing earnings yield" for small versus large cap, shows that the S&P 600 has a trailing earnings yield premium of nearly 3 percent over the S&P 500, signaling extreme relative cheapness, while the Russell 2000 trailing yield difference sits around negative 3 percent. The final chart displays the "Difference in forward earnings yield," showing the S&P 600 vs S&P 500 premium peaking near 4.5 percent and the Russell 2000 vs S&P 500 sitting near negative 1 percent. Overall, both earnings yield charts confirm that small caps are trading near their cheapest valuation levels in 20 years, even if they were slightly cheaper at various points over the prior two to three years.

This publication page analyses US and global small-cap equity performance and valuations relative to large caps, arguing that while US small caps have lagged US large caps, they are historically cheap and have still substantially outperformed international markets. 

The first chart, titled "Small cap valuation measures," plots the premium or discount of the S&P 600 relative to the S&P 500 from 2000 to 2024 using five valuation metrics: Forward P/E, EV/EBITDA, Trailing P/E, price-to-cash flow, and price-to-book. Across all five measures, the S&P 600 is trading at a steep historical discount compared to the S&P 500, with discounts ranging from roughly 20% to nearly 60% in 2024, signaling that small-cap stocks are historically inexpensive.

The second chart, "US small cap performance vs international indices," tracks cumulative dollar returns since December 2010. This visual demonstrates that while US small caps (represented by a blend of the S&P 600 and Russell 2000) disappointed relative to US large caps, they "clobbered" non-US investments. The index for US small caps rose to nearly 350 by 2024, while MSCI Europe, MSCI Japan, and MSCI Emerging Markets lagged far behind, clustered between 150 and 250. 

The third chart, "Small cap vs large cap returns by geography," shows annualized trailing small-cap outperformance or underperformance over 3-year, 5-year, and 7-year periods. The data illustrates that small-cap underperformance is primarily a developed market phenomenon. In developed growth sectors, small caps lagged significantly; for example, US growth small caps (Russell 2000 Growth vs. Russell 1000 Growth) and Japan growth small caps underperformed large caps by roughly 12% to 15% across all periods. Conversely, in emerging markets and India, small caps actually outperformed large caps, with emerging market small caps (MSCI EM Small Cap vs. MSCI Emerging Markets) showing annualized outperformance of 3% to 7% over the measured horizons, and the NSE Nifty Small Cap 250 outperforming the MSCI India index by similar margins. Additional comparisons featured in this geographical breakdown include US core (Russell 2000 vs. S&P 500), US value, MSCI Europe, and MSCI Japan core.

This publication evaluates whether active small-cap managers can generate enough alpha to offset the historical underperformance of small-cap equities relative to large-cap equities. The author notes that for US small-cap core and growth, median manager alpha was positive but generally offset only 30% or less of the small-cap underperformance. This persistent positive alpha may stem from market inefficiencies, as approximately 80% of the small- and mid-cap universe is thinly covered or completely uncovered by analysts. Conversely, US small-cap value managers were much more successful in closing this performance gap, with top-quartile managers closing virtually all of it. In Europe and Japan, median small-cap core manager alpha was negative or only marginally positive, offsetting no more than 15% to 20% of the gap. For India, small-cap stocks generally outperformed large-cap stocks, and median manager alpha was positive, though the analysis is constrained by a small sample size of managers with long-term track records. In Emerging Markets, while median manager alpha was negative, emerging market small-cap equities substantially outperformed their large-cap peers.

A central data table, adjusted for ETF fees and tracking error, details these performance dynamics across 3-year, 5-year, and 7-year horizons. The table tracks the small-cap versus large-cap performance differential alongside manager alpha percentiles for various regions. For US small-cap blend, the 3-year performance gap was negative 12.6%, while the median manager alpha was 3.5% across 233 managers. Over 5 years, this gap narrowed to negative 8.1% with a median alpha of 1.3%, and over 7 years, the gap was negative 7.4% with a median alpha of 0.9%. US small-cap growth showed steeper underperformance, with a 3-year gap of negative 16.2% and a median alpha of 1.4%, which improved over 7 years to a gap of negative 11.4% and a median alpha of 2.0%. US small-cap value showed the smallest performance gaps, with a 3-year gap of negative 6.1% and a median alpha of 3.6%, narrowing to a 5-year gap of negative 1.9% and a median alpha of 2.0%. 

International regions show contrasting results. Europe small-cap experienced a 3-year gap of negative 9.8% with a median manager alpha of negative 2.9%, which improved over 5 years to a gap of negative 3.2% and flat median alpha. Japan small-cap posted a 3-year gap of negative 5.3% with a median alpha of negative 4.4%, while Japan small-cap growth saw a 3-year gap of negative 13.9% and a median alpha of negative 0.6%. India small-cap stood out with positive performance differentials, showing a 3-year small-cap outperformance of 5.1% and a median manager alpha of 5.0%, and a 5-year outperformance of 5.9% with a median alpha of 5.1%. Emerging Markets small-cap also outperformed large-cap by 7.9% over 3 years and 6.9% over 5 years, though the median manager alpha during these periods was negative 1.1% and negative 1.7%, respectively.

The methodology section explains the data constraints and adjustments utilized in the analysis. Drawing from Morningstar data, active managers with more than 35% exposure to large-cap stocks were excluded. The study uses the lowest-fee institutional share classes, noting that higher-fee retail classes would have reduced performance by 75 to 100 basis points. Standardized benchmarks were applied uniformly to each category rather than using each manager's self-reported benchmark. Crucially, the author adjusted benchmarks downward to reflect the real-world tracking errors and fees of investible ETFs. While this adjustment is negligible for US small-caps, it is significant in regions like India, where the Small Cap Index returned 132% over five years but the investible ETF returned only 97%, necessitating an annualized performance adjustment of 3.8%.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the performance and structural characteristics of US small-cap stocks, specifically comparing the S&P 600 and the Russell 2000 as small-cap benchmarks. The overarching observation is that small-cap stocks have dramatically underperformed large-cap equities since late 2010, and their overall share of the US stock market has shrunk from a peak of 4.5% of the S&P 1500 down to just 2.5% today. 

The top-left line chart, titled Large and small cap performance since 2011, tracks cumulative total returns starting with an index value of 100 on January 1, 2011. It shows the market-capitalization-weighted S&P 500 vastly outperforming all other indexes, rising toward a value of nearly 600 by late 2023, with the S&P 500 equal-weighted index also showing solid gains. In contrast, the S&P 600 and the Russell 2000 substantially lagged, remaining well below the 450 level. The adjacent chart, Rolling small cap performance vs large cap, plots the relative three-year rolling return of the two small-cap indexes against the S&P 500. This visual illustrates that small caps have faced prolonged underperformance cycles, with rolling returns dropping deeply into negative territory after 2017, hitting a trough near negative 40% around 2021, and continuing to struggle below zero through 2023.

The text details key differences in how these two small-cap indexes are constructed. The S&P 600 is described as a higher-quality index because it is rebalanced quarterly and requires companies to have positive earnings over their most recent quarter and trailing four quarters to be included. The Russell 2000, by contrast, is rebalanced annually and includes stocks based purely on market capitalization without earnings criteria.
