This difference is stark: 42% of the Russell 2000's constituents had negative net income over the prior twelve months, compared to only 23% for the S&P 600. Additionally, the median market cap of the S&P 600 is twice as large as the Russell 2000 at 1.8 billion dollars versus 925 million dollars. Despite these structural differences, both indexes share similarities, including high annual constituent turnover (around 70%), identical peak annualized volatilities of 84% during the COVID-19 recession, and low levels of analyst coverage relative to large caps.

The bottom-left chart, Earnings growth, plots index earnings starting from December 31, 2010. It shows that the quality filters of the S&P 600 translate to much stronger fundamental performance, with S&P 600 earnings growing to nearly five times their 2010 baseline by late 2023, while Russell 2000 earnings growth hovered below three times its baseline. Lastly, the scatter plot in the bottom right, Analyst coverage vs market capitalization, maps the number of Wall Street analysts covering individual stocks against their market capitalization on a logarithmic scale. The data demonstrates a clear trend: S&P 500 stocks, which are primarily clustered above ten billion dollars in market cap, routinely attract coverage from fifteen to forty analysts. Meanwhile, S&P 600 and Russell 2000 stocks, largely clustered between one hundred million and ten billion dollars, typically have fewer than fifteen analysts tracking them, confirming a consistently lower level of analyst coverage for smaller companies.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the historical performance of US small-cap versus large-cap stocks around recessions, the data sources used to track them, and the changing characteristics of initial public offerings (IPOs) over time. The author notes that while multiple data sources like Ibbotson, Fama-French, Russell 2000, and S&P 600 generally align, they occasionally diverge, such as during the late 1940s. A primary thesis is that small-cap stocks behave as a classic early-cycle asset class. Due to the high cyclical concentration of the S&P 600 compared to the S&P 500, small caps consistently outperform large caps in the immediate aftermath of recessions, though their performance leading up to a recession is highly inconsistent and dispersed.

The first chart on the page tracks the three-year rolling outperformance or underperformance of small-cap versus large-cap index returns from 1930 to 2020. The vertical axis ranges from negative 100 percent to positive 150 percent. Four different data series are plotted: Ibbotson small versus large cap, Fama-French small minus big, Russell 2000 versus S&P 500, and S&P 600 versus S&P 500. The chart visually highlights periods where small caps outperform, such as the late 1930s, late 1970s, and early 2000s, as well as periods of large-cap outperformance, notably in the late 1990s. 

Two subsequent line charts analyze the cumulative performance premium of small caps relative to recessions. The first of these charts covers the twelve months following the end of a recession, with the cumulative percent on the vertical axis ranging from negative 10% to 50%. It shows that across sixteen historical recessions, small caps outperformed in fifteen, yielding a median premium of 16%. A massive outlier is noted for March 1933, which reached a cumulative premium of 198%. The companion chart tracks the twelve months prior to the onset of a recession, showing a wide, directionless dispersion of paths with a median cumulative premium of negative 4%. In both charts, recent recessions are highlighted in dark gray lines.

The bottom-left chart shows the median age of companies going public from 1980 to 2023. The vertical axis represents the median age in years, ranging from 4 to 16. Two series are plotted: all IPOs and technology IPOs. The data shows a clear upward trend in the age of debuting companies. In the early 1980s, the median age for both groups was around 6 to 8 years, whereas by the late 2010s and early 2020s, the median age of companies going public regularly exceeded 10 to 12 years. 

The final chart, a stacked bar chart on the bottom right, displays the share of all tech IPOs by market cap at the time of issuance from 2010 to 2021. The vertical axis measures the percentage share from 0% to 100%, categorized into large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap, and micro-cap. The chart illustrates a significant shift in the composition of tech IPOs. In 2010, small-cap and micro-cap companies dominated, accounting for nearly 80% of all tech issuances. By 2020 and 2021, the share of micro-cap tech IPOs had dwindled to almost nothing, while mid-cap and large-cap issuances grew to represent the vast majority of the market.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" discusses the dramatic unwinding of the global Yen carry trade and its role in triggering a major correction in global stock markets. Michael Cembalest explains that years of negative interest rates in Japan led households, pension plans, state banks, and hedge funds to establish a carry trade estimated by Deutsche Bank to be worth $20 trillion. Under this strategy, investors borrowed cheaply in Yen to purchase higher-yielding overseas assets. This trade accelerated when the Federal Reserve began hiking interest rates in 2022, driving the Yen to its weakest level since 1986. However, rising domestic core inflation and strong spring wage negotiations finally prompted the Bank of Japan to raise rates by a modest 25 basis points. Combined with expectations of Fed rate cuts, this minor policy shift sparked a massive 14% rally in the Yen, prompting a rush of capital repatriation back to Japan and disrupting global markets. Despite the correction, equity markets in the US, Europe, Japan, and emerging markets remain up for the year, though J.P. Morgan FX traders warn that further carry trade unwinds could still lie ahead.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, "Examples of the Yen carry trade," indexes performance from January 2020 to mid-2024. It demonstrates the profitability of borrowing in Yen to buy foreign assets: while Japanese domestic fixed income remained slightly negative, both the S&P 500 and Mexican fixed income priced in Yen surged, with each index climbing past 150 by 2024. 

The second chart, "Yen collapses as Fed tightens in 2022-2023," compares the USD/JPY exchange rate to the Fed Funds rate. It shows that as the Fed aggressively raised its policy rate from 0% to over 5% starting in 2022, the Yen weakened dramatically, climbing from roughly 103 Yen per Dollar in late 2020 to peak at over 160 Yen per Dollar in mid-2024. 

The third chart, "BOJ policy rate, wage growth and inflation," illustrates the economic factors that forced the Bank of Japan to act. Japan's core CPI climbed from negative territory in 2020 to peak above 4% in late 2022, while spring wage negotiation rate increases surged past 5% in 2024. This inflation and wage pressure led the BoJ to finally lift its policy rate out of negative territory to slightly above 0% in 2024. 

The final chart plots the "23-day changes in value of the Yen vs the USD since 1971." A red dot highlights the recent, rapid 14% spike in the Yen's value, marking it as one of the largest short-term moves in the currency over the last 40 years, underscoring the sheer scale of the carry trade unwind.

This page of the publication analyzes the structural shift in the commercial office market caused by work-from-home trends, which have plateaued at roughly 30 percent. Michael Cembalest argues that because of this permanent shift, distressed office properties will require steep valuation discounts of 60 percent or more compared to 2019 levels to attract new investment. While supply-side corrections are underway, such as a collapse in new construction and rising property conversions or demolitions, he notes that a market bottom will depend on how banks and securitized office loan trusts handle a pending wall of loan maturities. He cautions that current office delinquency and foreclosure patterns look very similar to those seen during the 2008 financial crisis.

To prove that work-from-home trends have plateaued and show no signs of dropping to 20 percent, the author evaluates three contemporaneous metrics: mass transit ridership, WFH employment surveys, and building security swipe data. 

A detailed table tracks the post-Covid recovery in mass transit ridership across 22 U.S. cities, comparing Q1 2024 and Q2 2023 ridership against a Q2 2019 baseline. The median recovery across all cities is 70 percent. While some sunbelt cities show significant progress, such as Miami at 111 percent and Houston at 97 percent, major commuter markets remain heavily depressed. New York City transit ridership is flat at 73 percent for both periods, Chicago stands at 58 percent, San Francisco is at 57 percent, and Raleigh sits at the bottom of the list with only 30 percent recovery. 

This plateau is corroborated by a line chart showing the percent of full paid days worked from home for U.S. residents aged 20 to 64 earning over $10,000 to $20,000. Based on research by Stanford's Nicholas Bloom, the chart shows that after peaking near 40 to 45 percent in late 2020, the share of remote workdays across nine major cities, including Atlanta, Los Angeles, Dallas, New York, and Chicago, has flatlined between 25 percent and 35 percent as of mid-2024. 

The final line chart displays commercial property utilization rates based on Kastle security card swipe data compared to February 2020 levels. After plunging to nearly 10 percent in early 2020, office utilization climbed through 2021 and 2022 but flatlined throughout 2023 and 2024. Texas cities like Austin and Houston lead the recovery with utilization rates hovering near 60 percent, while coastal tech hubs like San Francisco and San Jose, along with Philadelphia, remain stuck at the bottom near 40 percent to 45 percent utilization.

This analysis of the commercial real estate market focuses on marginal improvements in office space demand alongside deteriorating credit metrics in the commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) sector. On the fundamental side, the rate of space reduction by major tenants (those occupying 25,000 square feet or more) is moderating. Instead of the 13% to 15% space givebacks seen during 2021 and 2022, firms are now giving back between 10% and 12% of their space. This trend is visualized in a chart plotting the downsizing rate from 2021 to 2024, which shows the percentage of space cut recovering from a low of nearly 17% in late 2021 to around 11% in mid-2024. 

This relative stability is reflected in net absorption, which has hovered near zero in 2024. A line chart tracking office net absorption in millions of square feet from 2015 to 2024 shows that after plunging to a deficit of nearly 50 million square feet during the pandemic, JLL Research registers only a minor negative net absorption while CoStar registers a minor positive value. Furthermore, only 12.5% of buildings experienced a vacancy increase last quarter, the lowest share since late 2017. Driving these supply-side dynamics is a collapsing construction pipeline, with new starts hitting their lowest point since 2000. The pipeline has shrunk 70% since 2019 to just 46 million square feet, 65% of which is already preleased, leaving minimal new supply scheduled for completion in 2025 and 2026.

Despite these physical market improvements on the margin, credit distress in securitized commercial mortgages is worsening in a pattern resembling 2008–2009. The "Office CMBS distress tracker" chart plots various measures of distress—including special servicing, modification, delinquent special servicing, 60-day-plus delinquencies, and foreclosures—from 2002 through 2024. Special servicing has risen sharply from near zero in late 2022 to approximately 9% in 2024, approaching the historic peak of around 12.5% seen in 2011. 

A final stacked bar chart highlights the impending wave of office loan maturities by lender group from 2024 through 2027, totaling $320 billion according to Trepp. The volume peaks in 2024 at over $110 billion, steps down to approximately $95 billion in 2025, declines to about $60 billion in 2026, and rebounds to roughly $85 billion in 2027. Across all four years, commercial banks hold the largest share of these maturing loans, followed by securitized pools (CMBS), insurance companies, and debt funds. To prevent forced, distressed sales, these lenders face a heavy schedule of loan modifications.

Michael Cembalest discusses whether commercial banks will become major sellers of office loans and foreclosed properties, noting that banks currently hold the largest share of outstanding commercial real estate and office loans. While JP Morgan Research indicates bank loan loss reserves of 8% to 12%—implying 20% default rates and 50% recovery rates—Cembalest notes these assumptions might not be far off given historically conservative loan-to-value (LTV) ratios at origination. Specifically, bank-owned office LTVs at origination were 50% to 60%, commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) exposures were 50% to 70%, and life and property and casualty insurer LTVs averaged just 39%. Conversely, a more pessimistic view from distressed office investment firms forecasts that over 90% of office loans maturing by 2025 will have re-underwritten LTVs exceeding 80%, pointing to a potentially high volume of distressed sales. 

Turning to distressed office transactions, Cembalest highlights that many properties are trading at discounts of 60% or more compared to their pre-COVID values, often due to heavy capital requirements or residential conversion costs. A table detailing discounted office sales across major US cities lists properties such as 300 W Adams in Chicago, which shows the steepest discount at 92%, selling at just $16 per square foot compared to its original 2012 purchase price of $202. Similarly, 995 Market in San Francisco traded at a 90% discount ($72 per square foot versus $685 originally in 2016), while 100 SE 2nd Street in Miami recorded the lowest discount on the list at 26%, selling at $257 per square foot versus its original $346 in 2016. 

An accompanying line chart, titled "Bottom fishing during the global financial crisis: real estate delinquencies vs REIT returns," plots data from 2006 to 2011 to argue that the optimal time for distressed investing is well before delinquencies peak. The chart tracks three series: the residential delinquency rate, which peaked at over 11% in late 2009; the commercial delinquency rate, which peaked near 9% in late 2010; and an indicative REIT Index. The REIT Index bottomed sharply in early 2009 near the 300 level, recovering roughly 70% of its gains by the time delinquency rates actually peaked late in 2010. 

In closing, Cembalest mentions recent travels to cities including Tallahassee, Charlotte, Atlanta, Baltimore, and Dallas, and anticipates a late August tarpon fishing trip to Trinidad with clients, while offering a warning that the upcoming autumn financial landscape could be highly turbulent.

This page provides a visual update on the commercial real estate (CRE) sector, focusing on the office market, mortgage debt ownership, vacancy trends, underwriting standards, and metropolitan performance. 

The first chart illustrates that banks hold over half of the overall stock of commercial mortgages. Within this category, a split starting around 2005 reveals that small banks hold a larger portion of CRE debt than large banks. Insurance companies and commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) represent the next largest holding categories, followed by government and agency debt, pension funds, and REITs. This distribution of debt is analyzed alongside rising stress in the sector, as shown in the second chart, where office vacancy rates have climbed steadily to around 17.5% in 2023. This is in sharp contrast to other property types; retail vacancies have stabilized at around 7.5%, apartment vacancies hover around 5.0%, and industrial vacancy rates remain the lowest, at roughly 4.0%.

The next two charts examine the risk profile of CMBS debt. The chart tracking loan-to-value (LTV) ratios by vintage year shows that underwriting has become much more conservative since the 2008 financial crisis. The share of high-risk loans with an LTV ratio greater than 70% has shrunk dramatically, while the share of low-risk loans under 50% LTV has expanded. This safer lending environment is mirrored in the adjacent chart, which displays CMBS credit enhancement through the subordination percent beneath each tranche. Subordination buffers for BBB- rated tranches rose from less than 5% before 2008 to nearly 8% by 2022, while AA and Mezz AAA tranches remained highly insulated, with subordination levels around 17% and 20%, respectively.

The final section connects urban office valuations to physical occupancy and supply dynamics. A scatter plot compares transit ridership recovery (Q2 2019 to Q1 2024) to three-year trailing office price growth per square foot across major U.S. cities. San Francisco is the most severe outlier, experiencing a transit ridership recovery of less than 50% alongside a price-per-square-foot decline of nearly 70%. In contrast, Miami shows robust health, with transit ridership recovery surpassing 100% and positive office price growth of over 20%. Other major hubs like New York and Boston occupy a middle ground with modest price declines and transit recoveries around 60% to 80%. Due to these challenging conditions, new development has ground to a halt; the final bar chart shows that national office groundbreakings collapsed to an all-time low near zero square feet in 2024, down from historical peaks of over 20 million square feet.

This page analyzes NVIDIA’s financial performance, arguing that its phenomenal growth is fundamentally supported by earnings and represents the antithesis of the speculative dot-com bubble. Author Michael Cembalest points out that NVIDIA's operating margins are high and rising, bolstered by a massive step-change in projected revenue growth. The company recently beat expectations and announced a fifty billion dollar stock buyback program. To counter bearish comparisons, the author asserts that NVIDIA bears no resemblance to dot-com leaders like Cisco, whose valuations soared without earnings to match. Consensus analyst reports project that NVIDIA will maintain over ninety percent market share in AI chips for the next two years; despite potential delays in its next-generation Blackwell chip shipments, few competitors are currently positioned to capitalize, though competition is emerging. 

The analysis is supported by six charts. The first, a bar chart comparing the operating margins of the Magnificent Seven in July 2024, shows NVIDIA leading with an operating margin exceeding sixty percent, followed by Microsoft at around forty-five percent, META, Alphabet, Apple, Amazon, and Tesla, which trails at under ten percent. The second chart traces NVIDIA’s net income margins from 2009 through 2023, showing a volatile rise from negative margins in 2009 to a peak approaching sixty percent by late 2023. 

The third chart depicts NVIDIA’s sales growth actuals and estimate revisions from 2017 to 2027. It illustrates a dramatic upward revision between the March 2023 projections and the August 2024 projections. While the March 2023 forecast expected modest growth to around eighty billion dollars by 2026, the August 2024 projections show revenues soaring past two hundred billion dollars, featuring year-over-year growth rates of one hundred and four percent in 2024 and forty-two percent in 2025. 

The fourth chart compares forward P/E ratios from the dot-com era to today, mapping Cisco from 1996 to 2002 against NVIDIA from 2018 to 2024. It shows that Cisco’s forward P/E peaked above one hundred and twenty times in 2000, whereas NVIDIA's forward P/E peaked near eighty times in 2023 and has compressed to around forty times. 

The final two charts contrast share price performance against one-year forward earnings per share (EPS), indexed to one hundred at the start of their respective periods. For NVIDIA from 2018 to 2024, the share price and forward EPS have moved in near lockstep, both surging to an indexed value close to three thousand. In contrast, the chart for Cisco from 1996 to 2002 shows a severe divergence; while Cisco's share price surged past an index value of sixteen hundred in 2000, its forward EPS barely grew, remaining below four hundred, illustrating the lack of fundamental backing during the dot-com peak compared to NVIDIA’s current earnings-driven rise.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication discusses the limits of what standard political polarization metrics can measure, focusing on leadership, governance, and the historically unusual level of opposition to Donald Trump from within his own former administration. The author notes how dramatically political discourse and divisions have intensified over the past decade, warning financial institutions against hosting corporate leaders who make controversial public statements, specifically mentioning Elon Musk. 

The primary visual on the page is a bar chart tracking the stances of forty-three former Trump Cabinet members and senior officials regarding his 2024 presidential bid. To qualify for the chart, individuals must have served at least nine months between 2016 and 2020 in roles such as Vice President, Cabinet department heads, National Security Advisor, FBI or CIA Directors, UN Ambassador, White House Chief of Staff, Communications Director, GOP House Speaker, or GOP Senate Majority Leader. The chart reveals an even split, with sixteen individuals publicly repudiating or disavowing his candidacy, another sixteen endorsing him, and eleven offering no public comment. Among those who have disavowed Trump are high-profile figures like Mike Pence, Rex Tillerson, Jim Mattis, Mark Esper, Paul Ryan, Betsy DeVos, John Kelly, John Bolton, and Mick Mulvaney. The endorsement column features names such as Mike Pompeo, Ben Carson, Mitch McConnell, Nikki Haley, and Bill Barr, while the neutral group includes figures like Sonny Perdue, Eugene Scalia, Kirstjen Nielsen, and Chris Wray. A footnote highlights that this internal opposition is mirrored externally, noting that more than seven hundred former national security and military officials signed an open letter in September 2024 opposing Trump's candidacy.

The lower half of the page lists a comprehensive table of contents for the rest of the report, outlining upcoming sections on fiscal policy, tariffs and trade, energy, immigration, inflation and price controls, NATO, the regulatory state, comments on the Electoral College, and an analysis of the recent China stimulus package as an important turning point for investors.

In this analysis, titled "COVIDIA: GPU orbit now driving equity markets and capital spending," Michael Cembalest discusses how NVIDIA and its major GPU customers are increasingly dominating financial markets and industrial production. He highlights that artificial intelligence spending is reshaping the investment landscape, with the "Magnificent 7" (comprising Amazon, Apple, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla) now spending more on capital expenditures than the entire energy sector combined.

To support this thesis, the page features four illustrative charts. The first chart, "Magnificent 7 domination," tracks these companies' share of the total U.S. large-cap market capitalization from 1990 to 2024. The data shows that the Magnificent 7's share has surged dramatically, rising from around 10% in the mid-2010s to near 30% by mid-2024, far surpassing the previous tech bubble peak of approximately 18% in the year 2000.

The second chart examines S&P 500 performance and earnings estimate revisions by stock tiers, comparing the top 20, 21-100, 101-200, 201-300, and 301-500 cohorts. It reveals that the top quintile of stocks is almost single-handedly driving positive market trends. The S&P 1-20 cohort boasts trailing 12-month returns of over 40% and a positive earnings estimate revision of nearly 18% since June 2023. In stark contrast, all other tiers show much weaker returns and negative earnings estimate revisions, with the S&P 301-500 experiencing a nearly 15% drop in earnings estimates.

The third chart details U.S. industrial production across high-tech industries, indexed to 100 in January 2020. Running from 2015 to mid-2024, it shows that "All industry ex-high tech" has remained completely flat, hovering near 100. Meanwhile, high-tech sectors have soared: semiconductors and computer equipment have reached indices between 120 and 130, while communication equipment has surged past 150, demonstrating a massive divergence in the physical economy driven by technology.

The final chart illustrates Capex plus R&D spending, indexing the Bloomberg Magnificent 7 Index against the Bloomberg US Large Cap ex-Magnificent 7 Index (indexed to 100 in January 2020). It displays a historic divergence: while capital spending for the rest of the market has remained essentially flat, hovering around an index level of 100 through 2024 and projected to stay there through 2026, spending by the Magnificent 7 has exploded past 400 by late 2024. The chart projects this trend forward into 2025 and 2026, with Magnificent 7 spending expected to reach index levels of roughly 500 and 600 respectively, emphasizing the colossal scale of future AI infrastructure investment.

This page discusses the trajectory of corporate generative AI adoption, presenting a nuanced picture of steady growth coupled with some mixed signals. Author Michael Cembalest notes that while US Census Bureau surveys and bullish CEO outlooks show rising adoption and spending priorities—with 50% of CEOs hiring for new AI roles and 40% planning to boost spending—data from Bain suggests that enterprise use remains heavily concentrated in pilot or development stages rather than actual production. Furthermore, Federal Reserve data indicates that AI skill penetration in job listings remains low, tracking the slow adoption curve of 3D printing rather than the rapid, widespread adoption historically seen with smart devices or cloud computing. Cembalest poses the open question of whether a recent decline in technology sector employment, occurring alongside rising overall payrolls, indicates that AI is already reducing labor intensity, though he notes only a modest correlation between job listings and AI disruptability. He observes that historic tech adoptions, like e-commerce or the post-iPhone rise of Uber, took years to mature, suggesting that current expectations might simply be impatient. In the near term, consulting firms are the clear winners, with BCG now generating 20% of its revenue helping companies navigate generative AI.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, "Census: AI adoption rates by sector and date," shows the share of firms using AI (from 0% to 25%) across fifteen sectors in October 2023, August 2024, and projected for the next six months. The Information sector leads all others, with adoption rising from approximately 15% in late 2023 to about 20% by August 2024, and projected to exceed 22% soon after. The Professional, Scientific, and Technical sector is the second highest, while sectors like Construction and Accommodation & Food Services remain near the bottom, though almost all show a positive upward trend over time.

The second chart, "Bain: generative AI adoption rates by stage and sector, Oct 2023 vs Feb 2024," tracks adoption across ten business functions, separating active "Production" use from "Development/pilot" stages. Software and Customer Service are the most active functions, with overall adoption rates between 50% and 55%. However, across all listed functions—including Marketing, Operations, Finance, and Legal—the gold "Development/pilot" bars dominate, while actual "Production" use remains relatively small, illustrating that most corporate AI use remains experimental.

The third chart, "Fed: technology penetration in job openings," tracks the percentage of urban areas with a significant job presence for various technologies from 2007 through 2023. Smart devices saw explosive growth starting around 2011, peaking near 90%, and cloud computing reached over 50% by 2017. In contrast, both 3D printing and AI show nearly flat lines close to 0%, highlighting that AI has yet to make a broad, measurable impact on job postings across geographic regions.

The final chart, "US private employment," compares employment trends from 2021 to 2024 using two axes. Private industries excluding information services (measured in millions on the left axis) have risen steadily from 115 million to over 131 million. In contrast, Information Services employment (measured in millions on the right axis) peaked in late 2022 near 3.1 million and has since steadily declined to around 3.0 million by mid-2024, highlighting the divergence between general hiring and the tech sector.

This appendix, titled "The fate of prior equity market leaders," examines the long-term market share trajectories of companies that have held the largest market capitalization in the S&P 500. This analysis is prompted by Nvidia briefly attaining the largest S&P 500 market cap at $3.33 trillion in June 2024, surpassing Microsoft. The author observes that historical market leaders typically hit an inflection point, after which their share of the total S&P 500 market cap declined significantly. Nine individual charts plot the end-of-quarter share of total market cap for these companies, with gray vertical bars representing periods when each stock was the single largest in the index.

Among the historical leaders whose dominance faded, General Motors represents an early giant, commanding over 10% of the total market cap in the late 1950s and maintaining its leadership until the mid-1970s, after which its share steadily collapsed to near 0% by 2015. IBM held the top spot around 1990 with a market share of 3.0%, but it subsequently embarked on a multi-decade decline to under 0.5% by 2025. Altria briefly led the market in the early 1990s, peaking at around 2.5% market share before experiencing a steady decline to below 0.5%. Cisco Systems represents a dramatic dot-com boom-and-bust cycle, briefly leading the market in 2000 at approximately 4.0% share before rapidly plunging to around 1.0% or less. General Electric held several prolonged periods of market leadership from the mid-1990s through the mid-2000s, peaking at over 4.5% market share, but eventually declined to under 0.5%. Exxon Mobil held the lead for significant stretches between 2005 and 2013, peaking above 4.5% share before a downward trend left it with less than 2.0% share.

In contrast to these declines, Apple and Microsoft have managed to buck the trend and continue thriving. Apple's market share grew from near 0% in the 1990s to nearly 8% by 2024, characterized by frequent periods of market leadership starting around 2012. Microsoft displays a resilient double-peak pattern, commanding leadership around 2000 at nearly 5.0% share, declining, and then climbing back to nearly 8.0% share by 2024 during its renewed periods of market leadership. Finally, Nvidia's chart highlights an exponential, near-vertical climb starting around 2020, rising from negligible share to nearly 6.0% by mid-2024, placing it in the company of these historic market giants and raising open questions about its future trajectory.

In this publication segment on fiscal policy, Michael Cembalest discusses the long-term structural budget challenges facing the United States, emphasizing that neither presidential candidate has addressed the crucial crossover point projected for the early 2030s. At this juncture, entitlement spending plus net interest payments are expected to permanently exceed Federal revenues. Cembalest expresses skepticism about the market implications of marginal fiscal proposals when weighed against this looming structural deficit. 

An accompanying line chart illustrates this issue by plotting entitlements, other mandatory outlays, and net interest payments alongside Federal revenues as a percentage of GDP from 1965 to 2035. The chart demonstrates that while revenues historically fluctuated between roughly 15% and 19% of GDP and are projected to stabilize around 17% to 18%, mandatory outlays and net interest are on a sharp upward trajectory from 2025 onward, projected to cross over and exceed revenues, climbing toward 19% of GDP by 2035.

A side-panel analyzes the expansion of federal debt under the Trump and Biden administrations, referencing data from Marc Goldwein at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. It highlights that if nominal GDP had followed pre-pandemic projections and starting cash balances were netted out, debt-to-GDP would have grown by 15% under Donald Trump and 16% under Joe Biden. However, when looking strictly at debt approved via legislation and executive action and excluding major COVID-19 relief initiatives like the CARES Act and the American Rescue Plan, Trump approved approximately $4.8 trillion of borrowing compared to Biden's approximately $2.2 trillion.

The page then focuses on Kamala Harris's fiscal proposals, framing them as a redistributive policy designed to increase taxes on corporations and wealthy individuals to preserve middle-class tax cuts and boost support for low-income families, homebuyers, and childcare. A detailed table breaks down the 10-year projections for Harris's proposed spending and revenue-raising measures. Total deficit-increasing policies are projected to cost $6,004 billion, led by extending the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 for those earning under $400,000 at a cost of $2,600 billion, making the Child Tax Credit permanent for $1,100 billion, and childcare and early learning initiatives for $600 billion. 

On the revenue side, 10-year deficit-decreasing policies total $4,727 billion. This includes Harris's specific proposals to raise the corporate tax rate from 21% to 28%, bringing in $978 billion, and taxing unrealized capital gains on ultra-high-net-worth individuals, projected at $503 billion. The revenue total also incorporates measures endorsed from Biden's budget, such as increasing the Affordable Care Act net investment income tax to 5% for incomes over $400,000, raising $404 billion, and applying this same tax to active business income for $393 billion. Ultimately, these proposals represent a projected net deficit increase of roughly $1.3 trillion over ten years, which would likely be financed through borrowing.

This page analyzes the history and potential future of US corporate taxes, focusing specifically on the implications of tax increases proposed by Kamala Harris. The author argues that before the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, US corporate tax rates were uncompetitively high, which led to numerous corporate inversions where US companies reincorporated abroad for tax purposes. Since the passage of the act, these inversions have essentially ceased, but the new Harris proposals could raise US corporate taxes to their highest level as a share of GDP since 1980, potentially triggering another wave of inversions.

To support this argument, the page features four charts. The first chart, "Tax rates and inversions out of the US," compares corporate income tax rates from 1981 to 2015. It shows the US corporate tax rate holding steady between 35% and 40% for decades, while the average rate for non-US OECD nations steadily declined from around 45% to below 25%. This growing divergence coincided with a notable rise in US corporate inversions, which peaked at nearly 10 per year in the mid-2010s. 

The second chart displays the "Effective corporate tax rate on new investment," comparing marginal effective tax rates across countries as of September 2024. While the current US rate sits competitively at approximately 23%—roughly on par with the United Kingdom and below the Netherlands—the proposed Harris policies would elevate this rate to 31% by 2025 and roughly 32% by 2028. This increase would push the US rate above Germany and France, trailing only Italy and Japan among the major economies compared. 

The third chart plots "US corporate income tax receipts as a share of GDP" from 1980 to 2030. Historically, this measure has fluctuated dynamically between 1.0% and 2.5%. Under the proposed Harris policies, receipts are projected to rise and stabilize at 2.5% of GDP, which would tie the highest level recorded since 1980. 

Lastly, the fourth chart illustrates "The rise of pass-through entities subject to personal (and not corporate) tax," tracking the number of tax returns in millions from 1980 to 2016. It shows traditional C Corporations declining from a peak of roughly 2.6 million returns in the late 1980s to around 1.6 million in 2016. Meanwhile, S Corporations skyrocketed from about 0.5 million to over 4.0 million, and Partnerships grew from 1.5 million to 3.5 million. The author notes in the footnotes that because these pass-through entities pay personal income tax rather than corporate tax, using the corporate-tax-to-GDP ratio alone underrepresents the true business tax burden in the US and distorts international comparisons.

In this analysis, J.P. Morgan’s Michael Cembalest evaluates the fiscal agendas and projected budget deficit impacts of Donald Trump and Kamala Harris, concluding that budget deficits would likely rise the most under a Trump victory or GOP sweep. The text notes that Trump’s fiscal agenda is highly fluid, proposing broad tax cuts including extending all Tax Cuts and Jobs Act provisions, lifting the state and local tax deduction cap, exempting tips from income tax, cutting the corporate tax rate to fifteen percent for domestic manufacturers, and ending taxation on Social Security benefits. To offset these cuts, Trump proposes cutting green energy spending—with electric vehicle tax credits being most at risk—and introducing a ten percent universal tariff alongside a sixty percent tariff on China. However, the author cautions that tariff revenue estimates are highly uncertain due to unpredictable trade elasticities, potential foreign retaliation, and growth impacts. Citing an op-ed by Jason Furman in the Wall Street Journal, the author aligns with the view that Harris is the safer economic choice, as her primary deficit impacts are projected to be smaller under almost all circumstances. 

To illustrate these outcomes, the page features four charts comparing the candidates' policies against the Congressional Budget Office baseline. The first line chart compares nominal budget deficit estimates for Trump’s proposals as a percentage of gross domestic product from 2024 to 2030. While the CBO baseline deficit hovers between five and five and a half percent of GDP over this period, projections by Bridgewater and Suttle Economics show deficits widening significantly, reaching between negative six and a half percent and negative six point seven percent of GDP by 2030. 

The second line chart presents primary budget deficit estimates under Trump's proposals. Compared to a CBO baseline of under negative two percent of GDP by 2030, assessments by Piper Sandler, Goldman Sachs, and Wharton show deficits reaching negative two point two percent to negative two point five percent of GDP. When factoring in the removal of the SALT cap as modeled by Wharton, the primary deficit worsens to nearly negative three percent of GDP.

The bottom two horizontal bar charts depict the cumulative ten-year budget deficit effects of both candidates' proposed policies in trillions of US dollars. Under Harris's plan, revenue-raising measures like corporate tax hikes of over two trillion dollars and taxes on the wealthy of more than one trillion dollars largely offset proposed spending, which includes nearly two trillion dollars to extend tax cuts for those making under four hundred thousand dollars in adjusted gross income, alongside smaller provisions for childcare, healthcare, and housing. This results in a nearly net-neutral overall deficit effect. In contrast, Trump's plan shows that revenue gains—primarily from a universal ten percent tariff generating one point five trillion dollars, a China tariff generating three hundred billion dollars, and clean energy subsidy repeals generating four hundred billion dollars—are vastly outweighed by tax cuts. These cuts include over three trillion dollars to extend individual tax cuts, over one trillion dollars to eliminate Social Security benefit taxes, and eight hundred billion dollars to repeal the SALT cap, culminating in a substantial net deficit increase of roughly three and a half trillion dollars.

In this analysis of tariffs and trade, the author examines Donald Trump’s proposals for a 60% tariff on Chinese imports and a 10% universal tariff. The text disputes the claim that foreign countries will pay for these tariffs, citing a broad consensus among economists that US consumers ultimately bear the cost. To quantify the impact, the author notes that Goldman Sachs estimates a 10% universal tariff would increase inflation by 1% and reduce GDP growth by 0.5% on a one-time basis, while Barclays projects a larger hit to GDP growth at negative 1.4%. Despite these economic costs, US voters increasingly favor scaling back globalization because of the severe domestic disruption that followed China’s accession to the World Trade Organization in 2001. Both political parties now largely agree on isolating China, with both Kamala Harris and Donald Trump supporting the end of the De Minimis tariff exemption for Chinese imports.

To illustrate the domestic consequences of globalization, the page includes four charts. The first chart plots the ten-year percentage change in US manufacturing job losses against Chinese foreign exchange reserves as an inverted percentage of GDP. Following China's entry into the WTO in 2001, US manufacturing job losses accelerated sharply to a ten-year decline of nearly 40% by the mid-2000s, coinciding with a massive surge in Chinese foreign exchange reserves, which peaked near 40% of GDP on the inverted scale.

The second chart demonstrates how this shift coincided with a sharp decline in US labor's share of corporate profits. It plots the same manufacturing job loss metric against the US labor share of non-financial gross profits. Following 2001, labor's share of gross profits fell from a high of around 64% in the late 1990s to a low of nearly 56% by the mid-2010s. 

The third chart links these economic hardships to a rising social crisis, plotting manufacturing job losses against opioid prescriptions per capita measured in morphine milligram equivalents on an inverted scale. Following China's entry into the WTO, opioid prescriptions spiked from near zero in the 1990s to a peak of nearly 800 to 900 morphine milligram equivalents per capita around 2011.

The final chart characterizes China as the world's most mercantile country, comparing its scores to the rest of the world across a Mercantilism Index where 100 represents the best and 0 represents the worst. The index measures barriers to trade and intellectual property violations, including public ownership of the private sector, protection of trade secrets, IP enforcement, pirated software, barriers to market access, copyright protections, and low receptivity to foreign direct investment. Across all of these categories, China scores poorly, reflecting deep-seated practices of forced local production, export subsidies, intellectual property theft, favoritism toward domestic firms, and currency manipulation.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest addresses common criticisms of the US Electoral College's disproportionate allocation of voting power to smaller states. He notes that while Wyoming has only 144,000 people per electoral vote compared to California's 472,000, the concentration of political power in these less populated states aligns with their massive contribution to the nation's food, energy, and mineral production. Given that the domestic content of US food and energy is roughly 80 percent—far higher than other manufactured goods—and that resource nationalism is rising globally, Cembalest argues that imparting excess political power to these critical states is a reasonable safeguard for national security and resource independence.

To illustrate this point, the page features a cartogram of the United States reconfigured so that state sizes reflect their 2022 production value of energy, food, and non-fuel mining. The map is color-coded by production value relative to population, with green indicating the largest per capita surpluses and red indicating the largest per capita deficits. In this visual, major population centers and coastal states like New York, California, and Florida shrink drastically into red slivers, while Texas, West Virginia, Pennsylvania, and the agricultural heartland swell into massive green and brown shapes. The production metrics factored into this cartogram span fossil fuels, renewable and nuclear electricity generation, agricultural yields, precious and industrial metals, natural aggregates, and non-fuel minerals like cement and clay.

Below this cartogram is a secondary map of Pennsylvania, overlaying its 2020 presidential election results by county with the state's oil and gas fields. Republican-leaning counties are colored red, while Democratic-leaning counties are blue. The map displays the geographic distribution of shallow oil fields, shallow gas fields, deep gas fields, and gas storage areas, highlighting how resource-rich regions, particularly those containing extensive deep gas fields in the western and northern parts of the state, heavily coincide with Republican-voting areas.

This page analyzes the current state of US energy production and the contrasting policies of the presidential candidates, highlighting how the Biden-Harris administration's approach of offering subsidies rather than imposing restrictions has driven US oil and gas production to record highs. The true cost of these clean energy incentives—covering solar, wind, carbon capture, hydrogen, batteries, and electric vehicles—is estimated to reach between $1 trillion and $3 trillion by the end of the decade. The author argues that these high subsidy costs are driving up domestic residential electricity prices, particularly compared to industrial competitors like China and India. This trend is illustrated in a chart tracking residential electricity prices as multiples of the China and India average from 2016 to 2024, where California's prices approach four times the benchmark, New York exceeds three times, Pennsylvania sits around 2.5 times, and Texas remains the lowest at roughly double. 

Additionally, the early stages of electrification have caused severe supply-chain inflation. A scatter plot of core goods producer price index inflation from 2018 to mid-2024 shows that transformers and power regulators have experienced the highest inflation among forty-seven core goods categories, with prices rising by nearly 75%. Despite these efforts, renewables still only represent 8% of final US energy consumption, up from 4% in 2010.

A primary focus of the page is the critical role of hydraulic fracturing, which accounted for 61% of all US primary energy consumption in 2023. A stacked bar chart breaks down this energy consumption, showing that unconventional oil, gas, and natural gas liquids requiring fracking make up the overwhelming majority of the nation's energy mix, far ahead of conventional fossil fuels, coal, nuclear, and renewables like wind and solar. This massive reliance explains Vice President Kamala Harris’s shifting position on fracking, especially given its political importance in swing states. The text notes that Joe Biden won Pennsylvania by a narrow margin of about 70,000 votes in 2020, a victory that could have been reversed by voters in key oil and gas counties like Erie. 

Finally, the page notes a shift in Harris's stance on electric vehicles, moving away from a firm 2035 zero-emission vehicle deadline in favor of a subsidy-based approach. To put the EV transition into context, the author notes that as of the second quarter of 2024, electric vehicles made up only about 9% of US sales and a mere 1% of all vehicles on the road. This transition is framed alongside an initial area chart depicting the substantial, steady increase in the monthly US production of crude oil, natural gas, and natural gas liquids from 2000 through mid-2024, measured in trillions of BTUs.

This page discusses the complex economic and social implications of United States immigration. While immigration is noted to support economic growth, bolster the workforce amidst low birth rates, and reduce the need for aggressive Federal Reserve monetary tightening, the text highlights that unmanaged migrant surges place severe budgetary pressures on major cities, impacting credit ratings and causing municipal budget cuts and housing shortages. 

A series of six charts illustrates these trends. The first chart, tracking net annual immigration in millions of people from 2000 through 2024, reveals a dramatic upward spike starting in late 2020, peaking at over 3.0 million individuals during the period from October 2023 to September 2024. Adjacent to this, a chart on pending immigration cases shows a compounding backlog that has steadily risen from under 500,000 cases in 1998 to more than 2.0 million cases by early 2024.

The middle row of charts explores visa issuances and federal deportations. The chart on permanent immigrant visa issuances shows a sharp drop from an annual rate of about 0.5 million down to near-zero in 2020 due to pandemic-related disruptions, followed by a steady recovery to around 0.7 million by January 2024. Next to this is a timeline of monthly Immigration and Customs Enforcement removals, color-coded by presidential administration from 2002 to 2024. It shows removals rising during the Bush presidency, peaking near 40,000 monthly deportations under Obama around 2012, declining thereafter, spiking and then falling during the Trump administration, and dropping to a low of approximately 5,000 before climbing back to around 20,000 monthly removals under Biden by 2024.

The bottom row details the geographic concentration of new court filings and the overall breakdown of the foreign-born population. A bar chart of new proceedings filed in immigration courts from 2020 to 2023 shows exponential growth in Texas and New York, with Texas filings skyrocketing to over 300,000 cases in 2023 and New York rising to over 200,000, while Illinois and Colorado saw much smaller increases. Finally, a pie chart of the 2022 US foreign-born population estimates shows that unauthorized immigrants made up 23% (11.0 million people) of the total, while naturalized citizens represented 49% (23.4 million), lawful permanent residents represented 24% (11.5 million), and temporary lawful residents represented 4% (2.0 million). In total, lawful immigrants made up 77% (36.9 million) of the foreign-born population in 2022, prior to the major immigration surges of the subsequent years.

This page of the publication analyzes two key political issues: NATO defense spending and the scale of the US regulatory state. 

The section on NATO addresses criticisms regarding European contributions, noting that the defense spending gap between the US and Europe prompted a 2006 agreement requiring NATO members to spend at least 2% of their GDP on defense. To quantify this gap, the author provides a line chart showing US versus European defense spending as a percentage of GDP from 1968 to 2023. The chart illustrates that US spending has consistently remained far above the 2% target, while NATO spending excluding the US fell below the target in the early 1990s and remained there until recently. Accompanying this is a table listing the shortfall in NATO defense spending by country versus the 2% target, measured in billions of 2023 US dollars. The table calculates a total shortfall of $1.54 trillion from 2006 to 2023, driven heavily by Germany at $634 billion, Italy at $255 billion, Spain at $212 billion, and the Netherlands at $141 billion, alongside smaller deficits from Belgium at $112 billion, France at $55 billion, Denmark at $52 billion, Norway at $44 billion, Portugal at $31 billion, and the United Kingdom at $5 billion. This data is used to contextualize voter skepticism regarding the financial burden placed on US citizens.

The second half of the page examines the US regulatory state, highlighting a major policy contrast between Donald Trump and Kamala Harris, with Joe Biden serving as a proxy for Harris. Irrespective of the upcoming election outcome, the author points to four landmark Supreme Court decisions that could usher in a massive pullback of the regulatory state, comparable to the Reagan administration. These decisions include the end of the Chevron deference, the expansion of the Major Questions Doctrine requiring clear Congressional authorization for major agency actions, shifting the start of the statute of limitations to the time of injury rather than the rule's passage, and establishing a right to a jury trial for administrative civil fines. 

This discussion is supported by two charts. The first is a line chart depicting the cumulative number of economically significant rules by month 40 of each US presidency. It shows the Biden administration leading with nearly 270 rules, followed by Barack Obama at around 200, while Donald Trump, Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, and George H.W. Bush cluster closely together between 130 and 140 rules, and Ronald Reagan shows the lowest count at around 60. The final chart presents a regulatory barometer measuring the four-year moving average of new pages added annually to the Federal Register from 1961 to 2021. This barometer tracks a rise from around 10,000 pages in the early 1960s to a peak near 75,000 in the late 1970s, followed by a sharp drop during the Reagan administration's deregulatory push, and a subsequent steady rise back to over 80,000 pages by 2021.

This page analyzes China’s ongoing economic struggles and details the comprehensive policy response package deployed by Chinese authorities. The author highlights several deep-seated issues, including falling commercial and residential property prices, capital flight via fleeing foreign direct investment, historically low consumer confidence, and weak real-time economic tracking indicators. In addition to these visible stressors, the commentary notes that China has experienced five consecutive quarters of deflation alongside its first-ever year-on-year decline in wage growth. 

A series of four charts illustrates these economic challenges. The first chart, tracking China’s commercial and residential property prices on a year-on-year percentage basis from 2010 to mid-2024, shows a steep decline from growth rates near ten percent in late 2016 and late 2019 down into deep negative territory, bottoming out near negative five percent by mid-2024. The second chart, the China FDI Monitor, tracks inward, outward, and net foreign direct investment in billions of US dollars from 1998 to mid-2024. This visual demonstrates that while inward FDI historically peaked near one hundred billion dollars, net FDI has recently plunged into negative territory for the first time in decades, with outflows outpacing inflows by roughly fifty to seventy-five billion dollars. The third chart displays China’s consumer confidence index from 1996 through mid-2024, set to a baseline where one hundred represents 1997 levels. This index shows a dramatic collapse from its pre-pandemic highs of around one hundred and twenty to an unprecedented low of around eighty-five to ninety, where it has languished since 2022. The fourth chart displays Bloomberg's China economic activity monitor from 2022 to mid-2024, which measures year-on-year percentage changes across a variety of sectors, including exports, coal and electricity consumption, steel production, motor vehicle sales, real estate investment, medicine consumption, telecom equipment production, state-owned enterprise output, and private enterprise output. This activity monitor depicts a steady deceleration in growth from over nine percent in early 2022 down to nearly two percent in mid-2024, punctuated only by a brief post-reopening spike in early 2023.

To combat these deflationary and contractionary pressures, the page features a detailed table outlining a major policy package targeting both the real economy and financial markets. To support the economy, monetary policymakers introduced a fifty-basis-point cut to the reserve ratio requirement, a twenty-basis-point cut to the short-term policy rate via the People's Bank of China seven-day repo, and a thirty-basis-point cut to the medium-term lending facility. Fiscal measures include a one-off cash transfer targeted at people living in poverty. On the macroeconomic and housing front, the package provides a roughly fifty-basis-point cut to interest rates on existing mortgages, expands loan guarantees for state-owned enterprises to buy vacant homes for conversion into social housing, lowers the down payment requirement on second-home purchases to fifteen percent from twenty-five percent, and expands the availability of loan extensions to businesses. To support capital markets, monetary authorities established a swap facility for securities, funds, and insurance companies to increase funding for equity purchases, alongside a new relending program designed to fund stock repurchases and holding increases. Finally, market regulation levers are being adjusted to advocate for and refine regulations that direct mid- to long-term capital into the stock market, encourage corporate mergers, acquisitions, and restructuring, and request that listed companies perform active market value management through mechanisms like share buybacks.

This page discusses the historical impact of geopolitical risk on US equity markets, arguing that geopolitics has rarely served as a useful signal for investors. The author critiques a 2017 Eurasia Group prediction of a "Geopolitical Recession," pointing out that global equity markets, measured by the MSCI World Equity Index, actually rose twenty-three percent in 2017 with an annualized daily volatility of just 5.6 percent, the lowest on record since 1972, and have risen one hundred and fifty percent since. 

To demonstrate which signals actually benefit investors, the page presents a table titled "Net predictive return benefit by indicator," analyzing data from December 1998 to June 2023 over a twelve-month investment horizon. The table calculates S&P 500 monthly returns when an indicator is in its top third (percentile greater than 67) versus its bottom third (percentile less than 33), showing the net benefit of perfect foresight in the final column. 

The data reveals that hard economic variables offer the strongest predictive power. Payroll Growth and the Industrial Production diffusion index lead with a 0.5 percent monthly net benefit. They are followed closely at 0.4 percent by the Bureau of Labor Statistics percentage of businesses with rising employment, the Leading Indicator Index, and the National Financial Conditions Index. A footnote highlights that the S&P 500 behaves more like a production index than a consumption index, as two-thirds of its profits stem from manufacturing, while two-thirds of GDP consumption is services. 

Conversely, subjective and sentiment-based indexes show negative net benefits, indicating that trading on them would have been counterproductive. The Geopolitical Risk Index has a net benefit of negative 0.1 percent, followed by the Small Business Optimism Index at negative 0.3 percent, the Economic Policy Uncertainty Index at negative 0.7 percent, and Consumer Confidence at negative 0.8 percent. The author notes that of all postwar geopolitical events, only the 1973 Arab-Israeli war had a lasting impact on global markets, which was primarily due to the OPEC oil embargo during a period of high US energy dependence and Nixon-era wage and price controls.

This page analyzes the immediate impact and long-term viability of China's recent equity market stimulus package. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that while past attempts to stabilize Chinese markets failed, the sheer breadth and commitment of the latest package—which includes RMB 2.4 trillion in potential support from two new People's Bank of China lending facilities—distinguishes this effort. Since the announcement, Chinese equities have surged, but Cembalest poses the critical question of whether China represents a short-term tactical trade or a long-term portfolio investment. He leans toward the former, pointing out that China historically fails to translate its strong nominal GDP growth into corporate earnings and investor returns.

To illustrate the immediate impact of the policy announcements, the page features two bar charts detailing total returns in US dollars. The first chart, titled China equity returns since September 23, 2024, shows that in the days immediately following the package's announcement, returns skyrocketed between 10% and over 30% across various indices and subcomponents. The top performers were the CSI Onshore IT Services, Shenzhen Composite, and Hang Seng Tech, all exceeding 30% returns, while even the lowest-performing subcomponent, MSCI China B Shares, posted a gain of roughly 10%. The second chart, China YTD equity returns, demonstrates how this late-September surge lifted most categories into positive territory for the year. By late September, Hang Seng China Enterprises and MSCI P Chips led year-to-date returns at over 30%, whereas CSI Onshore IT Services remained one of the few negative performers, down roughly 8% year-to-date despite its post-announcement rally.

Despite this sharp rebound, a third chart, titled China equity valuations, shows that forward price-to-earnings ratios remain depressed. Tracking the MSCI China Index and China A Shares from 2014 to 2024, the chart reveals that valuations are hovering near the bottom of their ten-year range. The forward P/E ratios for both series sit between approximately 10x and 12x, a steep decline from their 2015 peaks of over 20x and their 2021 peaks of around 18x.

The fundamental challenge for long-term investors is detailed in a comparative table titled Pass-through from nominal GDP growth to corporate earnings and equity market returns, 2010-2024. This table ranks various global economies based on how effectively their nominal GDP growth translates into corporate performance. China ranks at the very bottom of both categories. Its earnings growth multiple of nominal GDP growth is a mere 0.4, and its market return multiple is only 0.3. This stands in stark contrast to the United States, where the NASDAQ boasts an earnings multiple of 3.0 and a market return multiple of 4.7, and the S&P 500 registers multiples of 1.4 and 2.3, respectively. Other regions like France, Taiwan, and the Eurozone also vastly outperform China in converting economic growth into investor returns. Ultimately, the author concludes that because of this historically poor pass-through, investors cannot rely solely on China's GDP growth to drive long-term portfolio returns.

This page discusses the author's view on Chinese equities, arguing they should be treated as a short-term "trade" rather than a long-term "investment." This cautious stance stems from two main factors: poor corporate earnings pass-through from economic growth, and geopolitical constraints referred to as a "Thucydides Cap." 

To illustrate the first point, a line chart tracks the forward price-to-earnings ratio for China A Shares and MSCI China from 2014 through late 2024. Although Chinese valuations spiked following recent stimulus announcements—with MSCI China and China A Shares both showing clear post-stimulus peaks and subsequent moderate pullbacks—valuations remain historically depressed. This is contextualized by an accompanying table detailing the pass-through from nominal GDP growth to corporate earnings and equity market returns between 2010 and 2024. The table reveals that China has the poorest conversion rate among major global markets, showing an earnings growth multiple of GDP growth of only 0.4 and a market return multiple of GDP growth of 0.3. In comparison, the US NASDAQ leads the group with multiples of 3.0 and 4.7, respectively, while the US S&P 500 stands at 1.4 and 2.3. 

The second part of the argument addresses the geopolitical "Thucydides Cap," referencing Graham Allison's 2017 book, "Destined for War: Can America and China Escape the Thucydides Trap?" which identified 16 historical cases of a rising nation disrupting a dominant power, 12 of which resulted in war. While the author was initially optimistic that deep economic ties would prevent conflict, growing geopolitical tensions have made that outlook less convincing. A stacked bar chart highlights that in 2014, the economic linkages between the US and China—composed of bilateral annual trade, bilateral foreign direct investment stock, and bilateral central bank holdings of each other's government debt—accounted for over 7% of their combined GDP. This level of economic integration is far deeper than other historical or potential adversary pairs of the last century, such as France and Germany in 1930 (roughly 3%), US and Russia in 2014, or the US and Soviet Union in 1983, most of which registered below 2% of combined GDP. Despite these deep economic linkages, the author suggests that ongoing tensions will limit the potential upside of Chinese equities, advising US investors to take profits once short-term targets are met.

This page addresses high-profile Chinese espionage cases against United States entities, arguing that persistent geopolitical tensions and intelligence-gathering efforts will likely cap the upside of any rebound in the Chinese equity market. Michael Cembalest presents data compiled by the Center for Strategic and International Studies based on open-source materials, noting that analysts believe the true volume of espionage is much higher than reported and excludes the smuggling of munitions or controlled technologies. The author advises investors to use any recovery in Chinese equities as an opportunity to take profits and exit, quoting Steve Miller's advice to "take the money and run."

The central visual is a line chart plotting the annual number of publicly reported Chinese espionage incidents from 2000 through 2022, ranging on the vertical axis from zero to thirty cases. The timeline catalogs a series of notable targets over the years. In the early 2000s, incidents hovered near zero, involving targets like Lucent and the Naval Air Weapons Station. By 2008, cases rose to around ten, targeting the Pentagon F-35 program, Oak Ridge Labs, and Boeing. The chart illustrates a sharp dip in cases to around six in 2016, directly following the 2015 agreement between President Obama and President Xi to restrict commercial espionage. However, this decline was quickly reversed, with incidents surging to a peak of over twenty-five cases by 2020. During this peak period, targets expanded widely to include major technology and infrastructure entities such as Microsoft, Verizon, Google, the National Institutes of Health, and the US Navy. 

In addition to espionage, Cembalest highlights broader geopolitical risks in a footnote, pointing to China's October 2024 military drills near Taiwan as reported by major news outlets. These drills simulated a blockade of key ports and employed a record one hundred twenty-five aircraft alongside the Liaoning aircraft carrier, signaling severe potential market implications that further reinforce the author's cautious stance on Chinese equities.

Michael Cembalest discusses the dominant role of the Republican message on inflation in exit polls and critiques the Biden-Harris administration's populist fiscal strategy. He references a 2020 Hewlett Foundation memo that advocated for aggressive government spending under the assumption that there was substantial room to spend without triggering inflation. Cembalest argues this approach instead led to the worst inflation surge since the late 1970s, which was accompanied by record-worst housing affordability. 

To support this, the first pair of charts illustrates these economic pressures. The first chart, detailing year-over-year percentage changes in US core and food inflation from 1970 to 2025, shows a dramatic spike in both Food CPI and Core CPI starting around 2021, mirroring the historic spikes of the late 1970s. The second chart traces the US home-price-to-income ratio from 1974 to 2024, demonstrating that the ratio surged to an all-time high of approximately 10.0 in 2024, surpassing the previous mid-2000s housing bubble peak of about 9.5.

The author then addresses housing affordability directly, critiquing Kamala Harris's campaign proposals to offer homebuyer stimulus, which he argues would worsen inflation. Instead, he links worsening housing affordability to a shortage of starter homes driven by land-use regulations and restrictive zoning. This relationship is illustrated in a chart comparing land-use regulations and starter homes from 1974 to 2024. It shows that as the number of state supreme and appellate land-use cases per million people rose from roughly 1.0 to nearly 3.0, the share of new home sales under 1,400 square feet collapsed from nearly 40% to just around 5%. Finally, the author expresses skepticism that a Harris administration would implement deregulatory solutions, given the administration's regulatory track record. This is highlighted in a final chart tracking the cumulative number of economically significant rules by month 40 of various presidencies. The data reveals that the Biden administration oversaw the steepest rise on record, enacting nearly 300 significant rules by month 40, which vastly outpaces predecessors like Obama, Trump, Clinton, the Bush administrations, and Reagan.

This page addresses the political and financial complexities of immigration in the United States, arguing that many Democrats have underappreciated the associated political risks. While the author notes that immigration is essential to sustain growth in a country with low birth rates, he emphasizes that it cannot proceed on an unmanaged, chaotic basis without causing severe localized fiscal strain. 

To illustrate these financial challenges, the page features two charts focusing on New York. The first chart, showing the NYC Comptroller's estimated revisions for 2023 to 2027 compared to the City’s official budget, highlights a massive underestimate of expenditures. While revenue revisions show a modest increase of about four billion dollars, estimated expenditures are revised upward by roughly twenty billion dollars. The primary driver of this gap is an approximately ten-billion-dollar discrepancy in asylum seeker expenses, followed by substantial underestimates for education and rental assistance. The second chart tracks rising New York State spending on asylum seekers by agency from June 2023 to September 2024. During this brief period, cumulative state spending swelled from around three hundred million dollars to nearly one.four billion dollars, with the vast majority of the budget being allocated to the Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance.

The narrative then shifts to federal enforcement and labor market realities with two additional charts. The first of these charts displays monthly Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) removals by presidential administration from 2002 to 2024. This data reveals that monthly deportations of non-citizens peaked during the Bush and Obama presidencies, often exceeding thirty-five thousand to forty thousand per month. Under the Trump administration, monthly removals hovered between fifteen thousand and twenty-five thousand before dropping sharply to under five thousand at the end of his term and during the first year of the Biden administration. Removals under Biden have since rebounded to approximately twenty thousand per month by mid-2024. 

The final chart contrasts these enforcement challenges with the economic necessity of foreign workers, indexing US labor force growth from December 2009 through 2024. It demonstrates a stark divergence between native-born and foreign-born workers. While the native-born labor force grew very slowly over this fifteen-year period, reaching an index level just above one hundred and five, the foreign-born labor force surged dramatically, indexing at nearly one hundred and forty. This visual emphasizes that the expansion of the US labor pool is overwhelmingly dependent on foreign-born workers, underlining the delicate balance the nation must strike between managed integration and fiscal sustainability.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Thanksgiving Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, discusses the unorthodox nomination of Matt Gaetz for US Attorney General by President-elect Donald Trump. The author argues that Gaetz’s experience is exceptionally limited compared to his predecessors, noting that he has never served in the Department of Justice, a US Attorney’s office, or a State Attorney General’s office. Furthermore, Gaetz lacks federal or state-level prosecutorial experience and executive agency leadership, with his legal career restricted to a small Florida law firm and service on the House Judiciary Committee.

The central visual is a stacked bar chart titled "100 years of US Attorney General appointments: prior years of experience," which maps the years of pre-AG career background for 36 nominees from 1924 to 2024. The vertical axis measures years of experience from zero to 45, while the horizontal axis profiles individual appointees from Harlan Fiske Stone under President Coolidge to Matt Gaetz. The positions are color-coded into sixteen categories, including Department of Justice, US Attorney, and federal judge roles in shades of blue; state-level prosecutors, judges, and attorneys general in shades of green; white house, government, and congressional counsel roles in gold; private law firms in gray; law professors in white; and political offices like Governor, US Senator, or US Representative in shades of red. 

The chart highlights how unusual Gaetz’s profile is relative to a century of precedent. While recent Attorneys General such as Merrick Garland, William Barr, Jeff Sessions, Eric Holder, and Michael Mukasey show decades of experience dominated by deep-blue federal judicial and DOJ backgrounds, Gaetz’s bar is the shortest on the entire chart, representing less than ten years of experience split strictly between private law firm practice and serving in the US House of Representatives. 

The author provides historical context in a footnote regarding the controversial 1961 appointment of Robert F. Kennedy by his brother, John F. Kennedy. At the time, the media criticized RFK as inexperienced because he had never practiced in state or federal courts. The footnote explains that JFK’s father, Joseph Kennedy Sr., insisted on the appointment, and LBJ advisor Bobby Baker had to coordinate a Senate voice vote to secure RFK's confirmation, as a roll-call vote likely would have failed to garner even forty votes.

This page analyzes the potential economic and market consequences of Donald Trump’s proposed fiscal, tariff, and immigration policies, highlighting the skepticism of mainstream economists and tracing the recent, unusual behavior of the bond market. The author questions whether a universal tariff could realistically offset proposed tax cuts and warns of inflationary pressures that could disrupt the Federal Reserve’s rate-cutting plans. 

The first chart, illustrating the ten-year budget deficit effect of Trump's proposed policies in US dollars, demonstrates why many economists are concerned about a rising deficit. While a universal ten-year tariff of ten percent is projected to generate roughly two trillion dollars in revenue, and repealing clean energy subsidies and enacting a sixty percent tariff on China provide smaller offsets, these gains are eclipsed by the deficit-widening impacts of extending individual tax cuts, which would cost more than three trillion dollars. Additional proposals like eliminating Social Security benefit taxes, extending business tax cuts, and repealing the State and Local Tax cap push the net deficit effect deep into negative territory. In tandem with these deficit concerns, a second chart displays a Wall Street Journal and J.P. Morgan survey of forty-four economists regarding the effect of Trump's tariffs on manufacturing employment. A clear majority of fifty-nine percent expect manufacturing employment to decrease, while twenty-five percent believe it will remain level, and only sixteen percent expect an increase.

The commentary points to the ten-year US Treasury note as a critical bellwether, noting that its yield has behaved very strangely following the Federal Reserve’s easing cycle. A chart tracking the ten-year note yield change in the fifty business days following the first Fed rate cut compares the September 2024 cycle to historical precedents like 1989, 1995, 2001, and 2007. While yields typically fall or stay relatively flat after a cut, the September 2024 yield curve has bucked historical trends by rising sharply, climbing about half a percentage point within forty business days. This anomaly is partially explained by a corresponding chart of the US forward five-year breakeven inflation rate, which shows inflation expectations bottoming out in 2020 before peaking in 2022, and recently ticking back up toward two and a quarter percent in late 2024. 

The author also cautions that potential deportation policies could trigger a sharp U-turn in wage growth for lower-income workers. This risk is visualized in the Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker chart, which plots wage growth from 1998 through late 2024. The data shows that wage growth for the lowest quartile of earners consistently outpaces that of the highest quartile, peaking near seven and a half percent in late 2022 before cooling down to approximately four and a half percent in late 2024. Any policy-driven labor shortage could cause these wages to spike again, prompting the Federal Reserve to reconsider its easing path. Consequently, market rate expectations have shifted significantly. The final chart, comparing current and prior market expectations for the Federal funds target rate, shows that back in late December 2023, the market anticipated aggressive rate cuts down to three and a half percent by early 2025. However, as of November 1, 2024, market expectations have shifted to a much slower, shallower path of rate cuts, indicating that interest rates are projected to remain closer to four percent through mid-2025. Ultimately, the author concludes that the ten-year Treasury will serve as the premier indicator to watch, balancing Trump's inflationary tariff and loose fiscal agenda against the supply-side benefits of a less-regulated economy.

This page, titled "Ghost #3: Apparitions," analyzes the growing private credit market and Business Development Corporations (BDCs), warning that paid-in-kind (PIK) income represents "ghost" income where borrowers add principal rather than paying in cash.
