The author notes that the private credit market has tripled in size over the last five years, and the PIK share of BDC income is rising despite tight high-yield credit spreads and benign economic conditions. 

Four visuals support this analysis. The first chart, "PIK income of BDCs," tracks PIK income as a percentage of total investment income from 2019 to 2024. It shows a steady upward trajectory for both the Fitch BDC Universe, which rises from about 4% in late 2020 to over 8% in 2024, and the Moody’s BDC universe, which increases from roughly 5% to over 7% in the same timeframe. 

The second chart, "PIK income of major BDCs, Q2 2024," plots PIK income as a percentage of net investment income net of cash expenses across major firms. Prospect leads with the highest ratio at nearly 40%, followed by Blue Owl Tech Fin I at approximately 28%, and Blue Owl II at roughly 25%. Other major firms listed include FS/KKR, Goldman Sachs, Ares, Blackstone, Golub Cap, and Apollo, showcasing how PIK income has become a substantial share of net investment income across many major players.

The third chart compares outstanding US private debt to commercial and industrial (C&I) loans in billions of dollars from 2010 to 2024. C&I loans have grown steadily from around $1.2 trillion to approximately $2.3 trillion, while private debt has ballooned from near-zero in 2010 to roughly $1.5 trillion by 2024, demonstrating the sector's rapid expansion. 

Finally, a table titled "The economics of bank lending" compares the returns banks receive from lending to middle-market companies versus lending to BDCs. Although middle-market loans offer a much higher spread of 6.25% compared to 2.00% for BDC loans, BDC loans feature a vastly lower expected loss of 0.01% versus 1.60% for middle-market loans. Additionally, BDC loans benefit from lower operating expenses of 0.10% versus 2.00% and a vastly reduced risk weight of 20% versus 100%. Ultimately, this results in a significantly higher return on equity for banks lending to BDCs, at 46% compared to just 18% for direct middle-market company loans.

This page of the publication, titled Ghost #2: Allocations, addresses two primary portfolio allocation topics: the performance impact of active managers being underweight Magnificent Seven stocks, and the diversification benefits of hedge fund portfolios. 

In the first section, the author notes that active US large-cap core equity managers who chose to underweight Magnificent Seven stocks struggled significantly to beat the market. Two scatter plots titled "Active manager Mag 7 weightings vs performance" show data from January 2023 to June 2024. The first plot displays each manager's average aggregate Magnificent Seven overweight or underweight on the x-axis against their excess return versus the S&P 500 on the y-axis. It reveals a strong upward-sloping trend, showing that outperformers were highly clustered among managers holding overweight positions. The second plot shows a nearly identical positive relationship when comparing excess returns against the manager's share of total outperforming periods by stock on the x-axis, demonstrating that managers who consistently overweight each individual Magnificent Seven stock achieved the highest excess returns. 

The second section shifts to hedge fund investing, emphasizing that while hedge funds offer strong diversification benefits, those benefits depend heavily on owning a sufficiently diversified portfolio of funds. A scatter plot on the bottom-left, "20-fund composites vs benchmarks [HFR]," plots annualized excess returns against annualized excess return volatility from September 2019 to August 2024. It compares randomly constructed composites of 20 hedge funds against traditional stock-and-bond benchmarks ranging from 30/70 to 80/20 allocations of the S&P 500 and Bloomberg Aggregate Bond Index. This chart demonstrates that 88% of the 20-fund composites outperformed the benchmark combinations of similar volatility over the five-year period. However, a bar chart on the bottom-right, "Outperformance of hedge fund portfolios declines with the number of funds included [HFR]," illustrates the risk of concentration. The chart shows that as the number of randomly selected funds in a portfolio drops from 20 to 15, 10, 5, and 3, the percentage of outperforming composites steadily declines, falling from 88% for a 20-fund portfolio to approximately 65% for a portfolio containing only five funds.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication analyzes the historical and prospective inflationary impacts of US tariffs, contrasting the experiences of the early twentieth century with modern tariff policies. The central thesis is that while the US tariffs of the 1920s and 1930s were not broadly inflationary, the tariffs implemented in 2018 were, leading many economists to predict that newly proposed tariffs would also drive up inflation.

The first chart illustrates economic trends from 1910 to 1937, tracking the effective tariff rate, the CPI Price Index, and total US trade in billions of dollars. Historically, as the effective tariff rate climbed from a low of around 5% in 1920 to nearly 20% by 1931, both total trade and the CPI Price Index collapsed. Total trade fell from a peak of roughly $14 billion in 1920 to under $3 billion by 1932, while the CPI Price Index dropped from over 20 to approximately 13 during the same period. This trend demonstrates that during the interwar years, rising tariffs coincided with a deflationary contraction in trade and prices rather than an inflationary spike.

The second chart shifts focus to the modern era, examining the impact of the 2018 appliance tariffs on China, where tariffs on appliances were raised from 10% to 25%. Indexed to December 2017, the chart tracks three metrics from 2018 through 2021: appliance import prices from China, appliance producer price inflation (PPI) for US importers, and appliance personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation for US consumers. While the import price of appliances from China remained flat or fell slightly below the baseline of 100, the PPI for US importers climbed to around 108, and the PCE inflation for US consumers rose sharply to over 120 by early 2021. This indicates that Chinese exporters did not lower their prices to absorb the tariffs; instead, US importers and consumers bore the entire cost of the trade barriers.

The final section presents a table compiling GDP and inflation impact estimates for various potential tariff policies from different research organizations, including Piper Sandler/Robinson et al., the Yale Budget Lab, and the Tax Foundation. The projections show consistently negative impacts on economic growth and upward pressure on inflation. For instance, a 60% tariff on China with retaliation is estimated to reduce short-run GDP by 1.4% and long-run GDP by 0.2%. A 10% universal tariff with retaliation is projected to drag short-run GDP down by 2.2% and long-run GDP by 0.1%. Under the most severe scenario of a combined 60% China tariff and a 10% universal tariff with retaliation, short-run GDP is estimated to contract by 3.3%, and long-run GDP could fall by up to 1.2%. Furthermore, the Yale Budget Lab estimates that this combined tariff program would boost PCE inflation by 0.9% to 1.0%, reinforcing the view that modern broad-based tariffs pose a meaningful inflationary threat to the US economy.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s 2025 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the potential economic fallout of proposed US tariffs, arguing that they could reduce domestic manufacturing employment—particularly in Republican-leaning "red" states—and provoke significant Chinese retaliation. 

To support the argument on jobs, the page includes a bar chart detailing a survey of forty-four economists from October 2024. The consensus is largely skeptical of the tariff benefits, with 59% of respondents expecting tariffs to decrease manufacturing employment, 25% expecting employment to remain level, and only 16% predicting an increase. An adjacent bar chart displays the top ten US states by import share of GDP in 2023, revealing that eight of these ten states were won by Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. Kentucky and Michigan lead the list with goods imports representing roughly 26% and 25% of their respective state GDPs, followed by Tennessee and Illinois at around 21%, Indiana at 19%, New Jersey at 18%, South Carolina and Georgia at 17%, Texas at 15%, and Mississippi at 12%. Only Illinois and New Jersey represent states won by Kamala Harris. 

A central table details possible tariff options under consideration by the US. For China, current tariffs of 25.0% on Lists 1 and 2 could rise to 85.0% under Section 301, while List 3 tariffs could rise from 25.0% to 60.0%. It also notes possible hikes on Chinese electric vehicles assembled in Mexico from 2.5% to 100.0%, and European Union auto imports rising from 2.5% to 25.0% under Section 232. Under legislative authority, a blanket tariff on all Chinese imports could reach 53.7%, compared to the current 13.7% rate. 

The analysis notes that China has several pathways for retaliation. These include imposing tariffs on US agriculture, chemicals, and aircraft parts; allowing exchange rate depreciation; selling off US Treasuries; and implementing export bans on critical minerals. The author points out that China has already cut off half of the US supply by banning exports of gallium, germanium, and antimony. China may also impose regulatory or national security penalties on US companies operating locally, or further diversify its trade relationships via the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).

The final section of the page argues that official trade deficits mask the true scale of US business activity in China. While direct trade shows a massive deficit, the bilateral balance is much closer to flat when accounting for sales by local subsidiaries of US companies. A line chart spanning 2003 to 2023 illustrates this discrepancy: while the official reported US-China trade balance sat near negative $280 billion in 2023, the adjusted balance—which includes the in-country sales of foreign subsidiaries—was only slightly negative, ending the period at roughly negative $50 billion.

This J.P. Morgan Executive Summary discusses the economic and fiscal implications of US immigration policies, arguing that the record-setting migrant surge under the Biden administration will negatively impact urban fiscal positions for years to come. The page explores the potential macroeconomic consequences if a future administration implements stricter border controls and deportations, specifically asking if a reduced labor supply will reverse the cooling of low-wage growth and, combined with tariffs, push inflation higher.

To support this discussion, the page presents five distinct charts. The first, a stacked bar chart showing the quarterly inflow of undocumented immigrants to the US in millions from 2018 to late 2024, highlights a massive spike beginning in 2021. The quarterly inflow, driven largely by individuals released between ports of entry and undetected entries, peaked at over one million people per quarter in late 2023 and early 2024. The second chart tracks monthly Immigration and Customs Enforcement removals from 2002 to 2024, spanning the Bush, Obama, Trump, and Biden presidencies. This visual shows that monthly deportations peaked under the Obama administration at nearly 40,000, fell to around 20,000 under Trump before a steep pandemic-era decline, hit historic lows under Biden, and recently rebounded to around 20,000 by late 2024.

The third chart, the Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker, displays wage growth percentages from 1998 to 2025 for both the lowest and highest quartiles. It highlights how wage growth for the lowest quartile surged to over seven percent in 2022 before rolling over to around five percent; the text notes that labor restrictions could reverse this rollover. The fourth chart, a horizontal bar chart sourced from Goldman Sachs and the 2023 Census, displays the share of employees likely to be unauthorized immigrants across various sectors. Landscaping leads at nearly twenty percent, with households, building services, crop production, and animal slaughtering all exceeding fifteen percent, followed by food industries, bakeries, dry cleaning, construction, and rug mills.

Finally, a line chart illustrates US consumer price inflation measures as a three-month annualized change from 1985 to 2025, charting the Cleveland Fed median CPI, the Atlanta Fed sticky CPI, and the Cleveland Fed trimmed mean CPI. This chart highlights the sharp spike in inflation that peaked between seven and eight percent in 2022, poses the critical question of whether the combination of tighter labor markets and tariffs will drive these inflation measures back up, and cites S and P Global Ratings on the budgetary challenges posed by migrants and asylum seekers.

This page examines whether deregulation can deliver a positive productivity shock strong enough to offset the inflationary impacts of tariffs and a tighter labor supply. The author poses the question of whether such a deregulation shock is possible, especially in contrast to the significant regulatory surge that occurred during the Biden administration. 

The first chart, titled Regulation and productivity, plots total factor productivity growth from 2014 to 2025 against an index measuring the burden of government regulation, the ease of starting a new business, and the freedom to compete. A clear upward-sloping trend line across a wide array of countries—including the United States, Germany, the United Arab Emirates, Sweden, India, and others—demonstrates that less regulation is correlated with higher productivity growth. 

The second chart, titled Regulation slows growth in the OECD, helps in non-OECD, illustrates the effect of regulation on annual real GDP growth per capita. For non-OECD nations, moderate regulation actually supports growth, peaking at nearly four percent. However, for OECD countries, any level of regulation drags down growth, with per capita GDP growth falling to nearly negative two percent as the regulation index reaches its highest levels.

A third chart displays the cumulative number of economically significant rules by month forty of each presidency. The Biden administration stands out with the steepest trajectory, enacting more than 250 economically significant rules by month forty. This total far outpaces prior administrations, with Obama coming in second at around 180 rules, followed by Trump, Clinton, GW Bush, and GHW Bush clustered near 110 to 130 rules, and Reagan recording the fewest at under 50 rules. 

A companion bar chart measuring regulatory activity from inauguration day to April 19th of each president's fourth year shows that the total cost of final rules under the Biden administration exceeded 1.2 trillion dollars. This total dwarfs the costs associated with the Obama administration, while the costs under the Trump administration were negligible. In terms of paperwork hours, both the Biden and Obama administrations required roughly 250 million hours, compared to less than 50 million hours under the Trump presidency.

The bottom section of the page, drawing from historical archives, argues that US regulations tend to pass with very little oversight or review. A bar chart focusing on agency use of Regulatory Impact Analysis from 2008 to 2012 shows that over 50 percent of regulations provided no evidence of any such analysis. Only about 15 percent of agencies explained how an analysis affected at least one major decision. Another bar chart details how the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs only reports cost-benefit information on a small fraction of regulations. Out of more than 35,000 federal rules finalized between 2003 and 2012, only 3,203 economically significant rules were reviewed by the office, and a mere 115 rules were ultimately reported with both benefit and cost information.

This page from the report explores key macro-financial questions for the 2025 outlook, focusing on bank regulatory capital relief, energy production targets, and the sticky inflationary pressures in the electricity grid. 

The author first explores whether ending the Basel III regulatory discussions could boost US credit growth. If US banks unwind the excess capital they accumulated in anticipation of these rules, it could release approximately $200 billion in capital, assuming a 10% requirement on an estimated $2 trillion in additional risk-weighted assets. A bar chart illustrates this potential regulatory burden, comparing current risk-weighted asset rules to the Basel III proposal. Under current rules, the standardized approach totals roughly $7.4 trillion and the advanced approach sits near $6.7 trillion, while the Basel III proposal would push Category I and II bank risk-weighted assets up to about $8.5 trillion, primarily driven by a massive expansion in operational risk alongside standard credit risk. 

The discussion then turns to energy, asking whether fossil fuel production can rise enough to lower prices, given that domestic production is already at historic highs. An area chart detailing US monthly production of crude oil, natural gas, and natural gas liquids from 2000 to 2024 shows a steady upward march to nearly 8,000 trillion BTUs per month. The author evaluates the incoming administration's proposed Bessent 3-3-3 target, noting in a footnote that this target of an additional 3 million barrels of oil equivalent per day translates to 529 trillion BTUs per month—a modest 7% increase over 2024 averages. The commentary highlights that the Biden administration did not meaningfully restrict domestic extraction, opting instead to subsidize renewables to the tune of $1 trillion to $3 trillion. Given these dynamics, the author expresses skepticism about whether incremental US drilling can lower domestic prices, particularly if the extra gas is exported and market prices hover near $3.5 per mmbtu.

Finally, the page examines whether the inflationary consequences of recent energy policies are too entrenched to easily reverse. A line chart tracking residential electricity prices by state from 2016 to 2024 reveals a stark upward trajectory in California, where prices skyrocketed to over 30 cents per kWh, while New York and Pennsylvania experienced moderate increases, and Texas remained the lowest and flattest of the four. These rising costs are linked to severe supply chain bottlenecks shown in a final scatter plot of 47 core goods PPI inflation categories since 2018. While most categories have seen minimal long-term price inflation, "Transformers & Power Regulators" stands out as a severe outlier, with prices surging over 70% since 2018, illustrating the steep physical costs of grid modernization and expansion.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2025 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, argues that the US economy is uniquely positioned for a rare soft landing. Cembalest asserts that analysts predicting a recession overlooked the exceptionally strong financial starting position of the corporate sector before the Federal Reserve began raising interest rates in 2022. He highlights supportive macroeconomic trends, including steady consumer and capital spending consistent with roughly 2.5 percent GDP growth, expanding housing supply to curb real estate inflation, tight credit spreads, and low delinquency rates. He also projects a resurgence in merger and acquisition activity, supported by 750 billion dollars in private equity dry powder and the departure of Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan. Cembalest traces the historical benefits of deregulation from the Carter, Reagan, and Clinton administrations, referencing a retrospective study by Peter Orszag to argue that a light-touch regulatory environment combined with a venture capital recovery will bolster business sentiment.

This outlook is supported by four key charts. The first chart shows the US corporate sector financial balance as a percentage of corporate gross value added from 1960 to 2024. It demonstrates that while previous recessions were preceded by deep deficits in this balance, often dropping well below negative two percent, the corporate sector entered the 2022 tightening cycle with a historically strong surplus of nearly two percent.

The second chart, tracking US merger and acquisition deal volume in billions of dollars from 2013 to 2023, displays completed, withdrawn, and pending transactions. It highlights a dramatic drop in completed deals during the Lina Khan FTC regime, falling from a peak of over 500 billion dollars down to around 100 billion dollars by late 2023. 

The third chart traces deregulation and business capital spending from 1987 to 2001. It shows product market regulation indices for telecom and electricity falling sharply following major policies like FERC Order 888 and the Telecommunications Act of 1996, while nonresidential business investment simultaneously rose from 9.0 percent of capital stock to nearly 12.0 percent by 2000. 

The final chart measures small business capital expenditure plans from the NFIB Survey between 2021 and late 2024. It reveals a sharp post-election spike, with the share of respondents planning capital expenditures in the next three to six months rebounding from a low of 19 percent in 2024 to approximately 27 percent by November 2024.

In this executive summary, Michael Cembalest discusses the macroeconomic and market implications of the incoming Trump administration, whose nominees he refers to as the Alchemists. He notes that statements and proposed policies suggest these officials aim to fundamentally disrupt or break various areas, including globalization, the federal bureaucracy, the IRS, the FBI, Medicare, vaccine policy, and border enforcement. Cembalest highlights that because market valuations are exceptionally high and are driving market movements alongside earnings growth, there is little margin for error. He predicts a 10 percent to 15 percent market correction at some point in 2025 due to policy volatility, though he expects US equity markets to ultimately end the year higher. 

The author points to the 10-year Treasury yield as the ultimate barometer for the success of the new administration. If the positive supply-side effects of deregulation and tax cuts successfully counter the inflationary pressures of tariffs, budget deficits, and a shrinking labor supply, the 10-year Treasury yield should remain between 4.5 percent and 5.0 percent. However, if the yield rises and remains significantly above 5.0 percent, it will signal that policies are failing to contain inflationary pressures.

The analysis is supported by a bar chart displaying the global index return decomposition for 2024, illustrating year-to-date return contributions in local currency across various regions. The chart breaks down performance into dividends, earnings growth, and price-to-earnings multiple changes. The S&P 500 led performance with a total return of nearly 27 percent, driven by a P/E multiple contribution of about 14 percent and earnings growth of approximately 11 percent. Other examined indices include the MSCI World, MSCI China, Japan’s TOPIX, MSCI Asia excluding Japan, Europe's STOXX 600, and MSCI Emerging Markets. For most regions, earnings growth and dividends were positive contributors, while P/E multiple contraction held back returns in regions like China and emerging markets.

An accompanying table analyzes the rarity of the S&P 500 achieving consecutive years of 20 percent or greater total returns, showing the ten historical instances this has happened since 1871. Following 2023’s 26 percent return and 2024’s 27 percent return, the table outlines subsequent returns for prior periods. It reveals that only during the Roaring Twenties (1924 to 1927) and the 1990s bull market (1995 to 1998) did the gains persist into a third and fourth consecutive year. Other periods experienced sharp reversals in the third year, such as the 31 percent decline in 1937 and the 3 percent drop in 1929. A footnote emphasizes that intra-year stock market corrections of at least 10 percent occur in 60 percent of all years, while corrections of 15 percent or more occur in 40 percent of all years. Finally, Cembalest notes that this publication marks the 20th anniversary of Eye on the Market, expressing gratitude to Jamie and Mary at J.P. Morgan for their support.

On this page from J.P. Morgan’s 2025 Outlook, Michael Cembalest examines the vulnerability of US financial markets to rising interest rates, noting that falling rates have historically been the primary engine of corporate margin growth. He raises an open question: if long-term interest rates rise past five percent, what will happen to equity price-to-earnings multiples given how expensive markets currently are? 

To support this inquiry, a horizontal stacked bar chart illustrates the largest contributors to S&P 500 margin expansion from 2000 to 2019. It reveals that interest rate declines were the single largest driver, accounting for roughly forty-eight percent of the expansion. Tax rate declines made up the second largest share at approximately thirty percent, while globalization of the supply chain—via wage savings and lower capital intensity—along with domestic wage savings from efficient plants made up the remaining portion. 

Despite these long-term structural risks, the author observes that investors remain highly optimistic, supported by tight supply conditions. A line chart showing the share of US households expecting higher stock prices in twelve months reveals that household optimism, which has fluctuated between fifteen and sixty percent since 1987, is currently hovering near the high end of its historical range at around fifty-five percent. This bullishness is reinforced by a bar chart detailing net global equity supply in billions of US dollars from 1999 to 2023, broken down by US, non-US, US SPAC, and non-US SPAC categories. This chart demonstrates that after a massive peak in net issuance exceeding one point two trillion dollars in 2020 and 2021, global net equity supply collapsed to net negative levels by 2023, primarily driven by US corporations shrinking the outstanding equity pool through massive buybacks.

However, Cembalest cautions that this optimism leaves very little room for error. A comprehensive bar chart at the bottom of the page displays current market valuation percentiles against historical data, where one hundred percent represents the most expensive and zero percent the cheapest. This chart is split into US equities, non-US equities, and fixed income. US equities are shown to be exceptionally expensive, with metrics like the S&P 500 median forward price-to-earnings, trailing price-to-earnings, price-to-sales, and price-to-book ratios all sitting at or near the one hundredth percentile. The only US exceptions are regional banks and small-cap stocks, which sit at more moderate forty to fifty percentiles. Non-US equities generally present more value; notably, Europe's price-to-earnings discount relative to the US is at the one hundredth percentile, representing its largest historical discount, though MSCI India remains an expensive outlier near the ninety-five percent mark. In the fixed income space, credit spreads are remarkably tight and expensive, with US investment-grade and high-yield corporate spreads sitting above the ninetieth percentile, while commercial mortgage-backed securities stand out as a rare pocket of historical cheapness, with AA and BBB CMBS spreads resting below the twentieth percentile.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan report examines a shift in venture capital dynamics following the market corrections of 2021 and 2022, which were characterized by challenges in sectors like the Metaverse, SPACs, and hydrogen. The author argues that 2024 brought stabilization and "second derivative improvements" across several critical venture capital metrics, including cash raised, the frequency of down rounds, pre-money valuations, and overall deal structures.

Six charts illustrate this stabilization. The first chart, showing quarterly VC deal volume and cash raised from 2018 to 2024 based on Carta data, reveals that total quarterly funding rounds peaked at around 2.5 thousand in early 2022 while total cash raised peaked near eighty billion dollars. Both figures plunged through 2023 but stabilized in 2024, with total cash raised leveling out around twenty billion dollars. The second chart details down rounds as a share of quarterly funding rounds. This share rose from under five percent in 2021 to a peak of over twenty percent in early 2024, before declining slightly to around seventeen percent in mid-2024, signaling tentative relief.

The third chart traces VC median pre-money valuations by funding round, measured as a percentage change from the first quarter of 2022. It shows that while Seed valuations held steady, late-stage funding rounds bore the brunt of the correction, with Series D valuations plunging nearly eighty percent by late 2023 before showing signs of a bottoming out or modest recovery in 2024. The fourth chart tracks step-up multiples, defined as the current round's valuation divided by the previous round's valuation. It shows that step-ups fell sharply from their 2021 peaks, where Seed to Series A step-ups exceeded 5x. By 2024, these metrics stabilized at lower levels, with Seed to Series A at roughly 2.5x, Series A to B around 2x, and Series B to C near 1.5x.

The final two charts leverage Pitchbook and JPMAM data. The fifth chart displays the VC demand versus supply index by stage, illustrating a massive demand spike in 2023 where the Later-Stage Index peaked at nearly 3.0x, meaning capital demand vastly outstripped supply. In 2024, this index fell sharply toward 1.5x, indicating a more balanced funding environment. The final chart presents the late-stage VC dealmaking index, measured on a scale of zero to one hundred. It shows that the market shifted from being extremely startup-friendly in late 2021, with the index near ten, to highly investor-friendly in late 2023, peaking near ninety. In 2024, the index receded slightly to around eighty, reflecting a moderate easing of investor-favorable terms, such as dividend catch-up policies, liquidation preferences, anti-dilution terms, and voting rights, as market conditions improved.

This page focuses on the outperformance, profitability, and extreme market concentration of the US technology sector and the Magnificent Seven stocks, noting that their dominance is crucial to understanding US equity market returns. Michael Cembalest highlights that these seven tech giants account for 14 percent of S&P sales, 31 percent of sales growth, and 33 percent of earnings growth, with profitability that surpasses historical market leaders going back to 1950. Meanwhile, S&P 500 ex-Mag 7 earnings growth has been essentially flat for the last year, and only about 30 percent of S&P 500 stocks are outperforming the overall index, which is close to a post-1990 low.

Six charts illustrate these points. The first, detailing regions as a share of MSCI World market capitalization from 1970 to 2025, shows the US share climbing steadily to nearly 70 percent by late 2024, while Europe declines to around 15 percent and Japan dips below 10 percent, marking a significant divergence from the late 1980s when Japan peaked at over 40 percent. The second chart traces the free cash flow margins of the ten largest US stocks by decade from the 1950s through the 2020s. It displays a steady rise from negative and low single-digit margins in the mid-20th century to over 20 percent in the 2020s, citing dominant companies such as Apple, Microsoft, Google parent Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta, Tesla, Berkshire Hathaway, Eli Lilly, and Visa. The third chart compares S&P 500 tech net profit margins against the rest of the market from 1990 to 2025, illustrating a stark divergence where tech margins have expanded to nearly 25 percent, while non-tech margins remain flat between 5 and 10 percent.

The fourth chart shows the cumulative total return of the Mag 7 compared to the broader indices starting in January 2023. By early 2025, the Mag 7 returned nearly 180 percent, dwarfing the S&P 500's return of roughly 60 percent and the S&P 500 ex-Mag 7 return of around 30 percent. The fifth chart examines rolling two-year earnings-per-share growth from 2017 to 2024, demonstrating that Mag 7 growth peaked above 200 percent in 2021 and remains significantly higher than the near-zero growth of the rest of the index. Finally, a chart of the market capitalization of the largest seven companies in the S&P 500 as a percentage of the total index shows concentration blowing past its year 2000 peak of 20 percent to reach over 30 percent by late 2024.

This page, titled "AI adoption" from the J.P. Morgan 2025 Outlook, cautions investors about the risks of excessive capital spending and R&D outlays among major technology "hyperscalers." While companies like Nvidia have experienced blowout earnings—such as a 94 percent year-over-year revenue increase in the third quarter and 73 percent gross margins—the author shifts focus to the sustainability of the capital expenditures funding this growth. The main argument warns that an era of overinvestment can result in long, painful recovery periods, even if the physical infrastructure is eventually fully utilized.

To illustrate the rising costs of AI, the page includes a scatter plot titled "Estimated training cost and compute of select AI models." This chart uses logarithmic scales for both axes, with training compute in millions of petaFLOPS on the horizontal axis and training cost in thousands of US dollars on the vertical axis. It tracks several prominent models, showing an exponential curve where earlier models, such as the Google Transformer and BERT-Large, required minimal compute and cost under ten thousand dollars to train. In contrast, frontier models like OpenAI GPT-4 and Google Gemini Ultra demand vast compute power, pushing training costs toward and beyond one hundred million dollars.

A line chart titled "Hyperscaler capex and R&D as a share of revenues" tracks these expenditures as a percentage of revenue from 2017 to 2025 for Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon. The data shows a notable spike for Meta, which peaked near 65 percent in late 2022, labeled "Metaverse money incineration." While Meta's spending subsequently dipped, it has started creeping back up toward 50 percent. Meanwhile, Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft have also seen their spending trend upward between 2023 and 2025, generally cluster-ranging between 20 percent and 35 percent.

The author draws a historical parallel to the dot-com bubble's fiber optic boom to show what can go wrong during periods of infrastructure overbuilding. This is supported by two charts. The first, "Corning optical communications revenue" from 2000 to 2024, plots nominal and real revenues in billions of dollars. After peaking near 4 billion dollars in 2000, Corning's nominal revenue did not recover to that level until 2018, and its real revenue in year-2000 dollars remains well below its dot-com peak. The second historical chart, "New undersea cables deployed per year," shows a bar graph of cable deployments from 2000 to 2020. Cable installations collapsed after peaking at over 20 cables in the year 2000, and global deployment levels did not exceed that year-2000 peak again until 2020. Through these examples, the author poses an open warning to large-cap US growth managers about the long-term financial hangover that can follow aggressive tech infrastructure buildouts.

Michael Cembalest discusses the rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), noting that while survey data paints a highly optimistic picture of return on investment (ROI) and deployment timelines, actual corporate willingness to pay for ongoing inference-based models remains a critical open question. He warns that investors are likely to become far more sensitive to whether hyperscalers are achieving a real return on their massive capital expenditures, even as adoption levels appear to outpace historical technology curves. 

A central table details various surveys from mid-to-late 2024 regarding the ROI of GenAI applications. A June 2024 Morgan Stanley global survey of about 400 companies shows that roughly 50% of respondents met expectations and 40% exceeded them. An Ernst & Young survey from May 2024 of US decision-makers indicates positive ROI in operational efficiencies (77%), employee productivity (74%), and customer satisfaction (72%). An October 2024 global survey of 1,800 respondents by Enterprise Technology Research reveals that 97% of leading GenAI adopters achieve tangible benefits, and an April 2024 Google Cloud global survey reports that 74% see a positive ROI, with 84% moving projects from idea into production within six months.

Supporting charts illustrate these findings in detail. An estimated production timeline chart, tracking 100 US and EU CIOs across three quarters of 2024, shows that a solid majority of respondents either already have applications in production or expect to by the end of 2024, while those with no plans to utilize AI or large language models in the near future represent less than 10% of the sample. 

Another chart details GenAI project ROI relative to expectations across major industries, including Technology, Consumer, Healthcare, Financials, Manufacturing, and Industrials. Across all sectors, only a tiny sliver of respondents report missed expectations, whereas roughly 40% in Tech, Consumer, Healthcare, and Financials report that projects exceeded expectations, with the rest meeting expectations. 

This success trend is directly correlated with company size, as shown in a chart graphing the share of companies exceeding expectations by revenue. The percentage climbs steadily from approximately 35% for companies with revenues between $751 million and $1 billion to over 50% for those with revenues of $15 billion to $20 billion. 

Finally, a historical comparison chart tracks technology adoption rates relative to years since their first mass-market introduction. A lone data point for AI in 2024 places its adoption rate near 38% within just a few years of introduction, which sits significantly higher than the historical adoption curve for personal computers (1984–2003) and closely aligns with or exceeds the trajectories of the early internet.

This page examines semiconductor supply chains as a critical vulnerability in global AI adoption, focusing on Taiwan's exposure to a potential Chinese naval blockade and the highly concentrated, symbiotic relationship between NVIDIA and TSMC. The author argues that Taiwan has significantly increased its geopolitical vulnerability by phasing out nuclear power, which was its only domestic source of energy independence. 

To illustrate this vulnerability, a bar chart titled "Net imports of fossil fuels as a share of primary energy consumption" shows Taiwan ranking fourth globally, with fossil fuel imports representing nearly 90% of its primary energy consumption, trailing only Singapore, Hong Kong, and Morocco. This reliance is contrasted with a line chart titled "Taiwan nuclear share of electricity generation," which shows nuclear power's contribution peaking at approximately 50% in the mid-1980s before steadily declining to a mere 5% by the early 2020s—a policy decision the author labels as baffling.

The page also details the high level of concentration in the global semiconductor manufacturing sector. A pie chart titled "Global foundry revenue share distribution, 2024" tracks the $131.7 billion total foundry revenue market. Taiwan-based foundries control a dominant 70% share of this revenue, led by TSMC at 62%, with UMC at 6%, and PSMC and VIS at 1% each. South Korea holds an 11% share (led by Samsung at 10%), China accounts for 8% (led by SMIC at 5%), and the remaining 11% is split among other global players, including GlobalFoundries at 6% and Intel Foundry Services (IFS) at 1%.

The commentary concludes with an analysis of the relationship between NVIDIA and TSMC. According to industry data cited on the page, NVIDIA controls 95% of the AI GPU market, while TSMC commands a 92% share of advanced AI chip production, making NVIDIA TSMC's second-largest customer at 10% of revenue, behind Apple. The author notes that NVIDIA is pushing TSMC for annual rather than biennial product refreshes. Additionally, despite thermal redesign issues delaying the rollout of NVIDIA's new Blackwell chip to 2025, it is already sold out for the next 12 months. Compared to the current Hopper GPU, the Blackwell GPU is projected to feature more than double the memory, over ten times the interconnection speed, and 25 times greater energy efficiency.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2025 Outlook by Michael Cembalest analyzes key bottlenecks in AI adoption, focusing on data center energy demands and the rising computational costs of advanced language models. 

Regarding energy, the author argues that market expectations for nuclear power to dominant data center energy consumption by 2030 are premature. Consequently, hyperscalers will likely have to scale back green energy pledges and rely heavily on natural gas. A pie chart showing US data center power consumption by energy source reveals that natural gas currently leads at 43%, followed by nuclear at 19%, coal at 17%, wind at 9%, hydro at 7%, and solar at 6%. 

Although US data center power demand remained flat from 2015 to 2019 due to efficiency gains as workloads shifted to cloud and hyperscale centers—which now represent roughly 95% of compute instances—these efficiency gains have largely run their course. This slowing trend is shown in a bar chart of data center power intensity, which fell from over 1,200 kWh per compute instance in 2015 to approximately 400 kWh in 2023, with improvements flattening out. As a result, future electricity demand is projected to surge. A line chart tracking US data center electricity use shows demand rising from 1.9% of US electricity generation historically to 4.4% in 2022, with projections for 2028 rising to a range of 6.7% to 12.0% of total US electricity generation, or up to nearly 600 TWh.

The second half of the page addresses whether language models are getting better, noting that better performance generally comes at a high compute-time cost. A scatter plot displays OpenAI advanced pattern extrapolation scores on the ARC-AGI-1 evaluation set, plotting accuracy against cost per task on a log scale. The data demonstrates that while basic models like o1-mini have low accuracy and low costs, advanced models like o3 low (tuned) and o3 high (tuned) achieve high accuracy levels of 80% to 85%—approaching a STEM graduate's score of around 90%—but at extreme computational costs ranging from $100 to over $1,000 per task. This reveals that solving complex abstract problems requires customized, longer-running models that may be commercially cost-prohibitive for many applications.

This page, titled "DOGE Quixote: the billionaires quest to reduce US government spending," analyzes the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) led by Vivek Ramaswamy and Elon Musk. The author likens their ambitious goal of cutting federal spending to the quixotic quest of Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, accompanied by a reproduction of Honoré Daumier’s painting of the literary characters. The DOGE effort aims to cut $500 billion in unauthorized congressional spending and slice up to $2 trillion from the $6.75 trillion fiscal year 2024 government budget. The author expresses skepticism that DOGE will come anywhere close to these goals. Other prominent figures mentioned as part of the effort include Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale, investor Marc Andreessen, hedge fund manager Bill Ackman, and former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick.

The page details a potential starting point for spending reductions: reversing executive actions taken by the Biden administration, a process that does not require Congressional approval. Based on data from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, the page presents a table detailing "Savings from Reversing President Biden's Executive Actions," which projects $103 billion in annual savings, or $1.025 trillion in total 10-year savings. The author notes that because these are reductions in planned future spending, they are not equivalent to cutting existing programs. 

The accompanying table breaks down these savings into three categories in billions of US dollars. Under healthcare executive action repeals, the projected savings include $140 billion from Medicaid financing, $75 billion from Medicaid eligibility, $65 billion from Medicare Part D rebates, $40 billion from Affordable Care Act self-only coverage, and $25 billion from Medicaid nursing home staffing. Student debt executive action repeals show potential savings of $275 billion from the SAVE program and $15 billion from closed school rules. Other executive action repeals include $180 billion from the SNAP Thrifty Food Plan, $150 billion from vehicle carbon emissions and EV credits, $20 billion from Social Security Disability Insurance past work period changes, $20 billion from Supplemental Security Income expansion, and $20 billion from reversing IRS enforcement restrictions on incomes under $400,000.

This page of the J.P. Morgan Outlook, titled "Nuclear Renaissance," examines whether new United States regulations will successfully revive the nuclear sector, concluding that it is too soon to tell given the industry's massive hurdles in proving its viability to investors and regulators. The author highlights that nuclear projects are uniquely prone to extreme delays and cost overruns, pointing to the Vogtle 3 plant in Georgia, which was completed in 2023 after extensive delays but was offline for nine and a half of its first forty-eight weeks in 2024 due to technical failures like feedwater pump blockages and failed heat exchangers. Additionally, the author notes that the United States is heavily reliant on imported uranium, lacks enrichment capacity, and possesses virtually no domestic supply of high-assay low-enriched uranium. This shortage has delayed Bill Gates’s Terrapower reactor project in Wyoming to 2030 at the earliest.

Four supporting charts detail these structural challenges. The first chart compares the capital cost of nuclear plants in developed countries versus emerging markets in millions of US dollars per megawatt. It reveals a stark contrast: developed countries see astronomical costs, led by the United Kingdom’s Hinkley Point C at nearly eighteen million dollars per megawatt, the United States’ Vogtle 3 and 4 at fifteen million, France’s Flamanville 3 at thirteen million, and Finland’s Olkiluoto 3 at ten million. Conversely, recently completed emerging market projects in China and Pakistan all hover below five million dollars per megawatt. 

The second chart tracks average nuclear plant completion times in years against their construction start date from 1950 to the 2010s, showing that build times in both developed and emerging nations frequently span six to twelve years, with several extreme outliers taking up to eighteen years. 

The third chart compares average megaproject cost overruns by sector, highlighting that nuclear power has one of the worst historical track records, experiencing average overruns of nearly one hundred twenty percent. This is surpassed only by the Olympic games and nuclear storage, which reaches nearly two hundred fifty percent, while solar, wind, and transmission projects average far lower overruns. 

Lastly, the fourth chart plots United States production versus imports of uranium oxide in million pounds from 1949 to 2019, demonstrating a total structural shift from significant domestic production in the mid-twentieth century to almost exclusive reliance on foreign imports by 2019, with imports peaking near seventy million pounds in both the mid-2000s and around 2010.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, titled "DOGE Quixote," analyzes U.S. military spending, focusing specifically on defense program cost overruns and the massive domestic opportunity cost of unnecessary foreign wars. The author discusses the 1982 Nunn-McCurdy Act, which mandates Congressional notification when major Department of Defense projects exceed baseline costs by 30 percent for a significant overrun or 50 percent for a critical overrun. Despite reports of lower breach rates recently, the author highlights that the Department of Defense continues to fail audits and has seen no reduction in material weaknesses from 2018 to 2024.

Two tables provide evidence of defense budget inefficiencies. The first table, detailing Nunn-McCurdy cost breach rates from 1997 to 2021, shows that out of 215 total programs, 65 suffered breaches, resulting in an overall breach rate of 30 percent. Certain categories had exceptionally high breach rates: chemical demilitarization and space launch both had 100 percent breach rates, while half of all helicopter programs and 34 percent of fixed-wing aircraft programs breached their baselines. The second table lists the top ten projects with the largest cumulative cost growth over baseline from 2010 to 2021. The highest overrun belongs to the C-130J Hercules transport aircraft at 3,267 percent cost growth, followed by the GMLRS/GMLRS AW guided rocket launch system at 1,086 percent, and the MH-60S fleet combat support helicopter at 871 percent. Other notable projects include the F-35 joint strike fighter jet with a 193 percent overrun and the DDG 1000 guided missile program at 191 percent.

The bottom portion of the page features a bar chart originally prepared in 2015, titled "The staggering financial opportunity cost of the Iraq War," which illustrates how the estimated $2.2 trillion in 2014 USD spent on the war could have been redeployed into domestic growth. The first bar, representing the cost of the war, includes personnel, weapons, medical and disability care, homeland security costs, and interest. The second bar demonstrates that the same amount could have completely funded critical components of fixing America's infrastructure, including civil aviation, dams, roads, bridges, electricity, water, levees, railways, schools, and mass transit. Alternatively, a third bar shows that roughly $1.9 trillion could have paid for full tuition, room, and board for every college-bound U.S. high school graduate needing financial aid at a four-year public university from 2003 to 2021. Lastly, a multi-colored stacked bar outlines a variety of concurrent alternative projects that could have been funded for a similar budget, including PEV subsidies for half of the passenger car fleet, burying key residential power lines, building five high-speed train systems, providing protection against a one-meter sea-level rise, funding 30 years of universal pre-K, establishing an HVDC transmission grid, and ensuring mine clean-ups and broadband access for all U.S. households. The author concludes that avoiding unnecessary foreign conflicts is the most effective method to control military outlays and support domestic development.

This page focuses on the economic challenges facing China, specifically its descent into a liquidity trap and structural "Japanification." The author argues that China is experiencing a classic liquidity trap characterized by declining money supply growth, falling loan demand despite aggressive reserve requirement cuts, plummeting interest rates, and a real estate market that has yet to bottom. Highlighting this trend, Barclays reports that China has surpassed Japan on its "Japanification Index," which assesses real growth, natural and nominal interest rates, and deflation. In response to these conditions, China announced a major stimulus program, which Bridgewater estimates will offset only about half of the persistent structural drags on the economy.

Five charts illustrate these economic pressures. The first chart shows China's M2 money supply year-over-year percentage growth from 1996 through late 2024. This metric, which includes cash, checking/savings accounts, CDs, and retail money market funds, has experienced a long-term downward trend, falling from peaks near 30% in the late 1990s and 2009 to a historic low of roughly 5% in late 2024. The second chart compares China's bank loans to its reserve requirements from 2017 to late 2024, visualizing the liquidity trap directly. Even as the central bank slashed reserve ratio requirements from 17% down to around 9.5%, year-over-year total loan growth plummeted from over 13% to nearly 7.5%, demonstrating that monetary easing is failing to revive credit demand.

The third chart illustrates the depth of the property crisis by tracking Chinese residential floor space starts in millions of square meters from 2000 to late 2024. After peaking near 250 million square meters around 2020 to 2021, starts collapsed to under 100 million square meters by late 2024, showing no sign of finding a floor. The fourth chart displays Bloomberg's China economic activity monitor, which tracks year-over-year changes across various sectors, including exports, coal and electricity consumption, steel production, vehicle sales, real estate investment, and private enterprise output. This activity index shows aggregate growth falling from a post-reopening high of nearly 9% in early 2023 to just above 1% by late 2024.

The final chart uses Bridgewater data to analyze the annualized impact on growth from major policies China has announced since September 2024. It shows that while the positive impulse from the September stimulus package, interest savings from debt swaps, local government debt swaps, and expected deficit expansion provides a total current and expected growth boost of about 0.8%, it is severely outweighed by an estimated deleveraging drag of roughly negative 1.8%, leaving a substantial net drag on overall economic expansion.

This page, titled "Dr. Seuss Goes to Europe," uses playful, rhyming subheadings to critically assess the widening economic and structural divergence between Europe and the United States. Michael Cembalest argues that Europe's regulatory burden, high energy costs, lack of business-cycle synchronization, and low labor mobility are severely hampering its competitiveness. 

To demonstrate this disparity, the first two charts compare labor productivity from 2017 to 2024, indexed to late 2016. In terms of labor productivity based on output, the United States has risen steadily to nearly 120, while the European Union has stagnated around 105. Similarly, when measured by employee compensation, US productivity has climbed to nearly 110, while the Euro area peaked around 2020 and has since declined back to its 2016 baseline of 100. 

This productivity gap is compounded by severe energy cost disparities, as illustrated by a chart showing Euro area energy prices relative to the United States from 2018 to 2024. Following a massive spike to over five times US prices in late 2022, European energy prices remain stubbornly elevated at nearly four times the US level in 2024. The adjacent chart shows how this energy crunch has asymmetric impacts on industry; while European low-energy manufacturing output rose to roughly 115 by late 2024 (indexed to December 2019), total manufacturing output flatlined, and Germany's energy-intensive manufacturing plummeted to around 85.

Cembalest also highlights why centralized, "one-size-fits-all" Eurozone monetary policies are fundamentally mismatched to the region's diverse economies. A chart displaying the standard deviation of business cycle proxies from 2004 to 2024 shows that 11 Eurozone countries are poorly synchronized, with an average pairwise correlation of 0.56 and high divergence. In contrast, the 9 US BLS regions are highly synchronized, featuring a 0.94 correlation and a low standard deviation below 3%. This lack of economic integration in Europe is worsened by extremely low labor mobility; a final bar chart shows that while nearly 30% of the US working-age population moves between states, less than 5% of the EU working-age population moves between EU countries. 

Adding to these headwinds, a detailed footnote explains that the new EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive requires large companies to comply with strict carbon emissions and labor standards or face fines as high as 5% of global revenues. Highlighting the potential geopolitical backlash, Cembalest notes that Qatar has already threatened to halt all liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports to the European Union if fined under this law, sarcastically concluding that these aggressive regulations are unlikely to end well for Europe.

This analysis of the cryptocurrency landscape focus on decentralized finance and stablecoins, questioning the sustainability of recent rallies and the independent utility of DeFi. The author posits that Ripple's gains are likely driven by the departure of its critics at the Securities and Exchange Commission rather than transaction execution speed. Additionally, transactions-focused coin volumes are flatlining as stablecoins increasingly dominate crypto trading rather than acting as practical solutions for cross-border remittances, where conversion fees back to local currencies remain high.

The core argument centers on decentralized finance, which the author views as heavily dependent on circular overcollateralized lending rather than real-world applications like leases or mortgages. To illustrate this, four charts are presented. The first chart, titled Decentralized Finance coin values, indexes coin values to one hundred as of January 2022. It shows that while most coins like Binance, Solana, Ethereum, and Cardano hovered near or below their initial 2022 values, TRON experienced a major breakout, rising to over four hundred by late 2024 as it grew to rival Ethereum as a stablecoin platform. 

The second chart, Total value locked in DeFi platforms, illustrates that Ethereum vastly dominates other networks in total value locked, which serves as a proxy for DeFi activity. Ethereum's total value locked plummeted from over eighty billion dollars in early 2022 to around twenty billion dollars in 2023, before recovering to roughly seventy billion dollars in late 2024. The third chart, Ethereum price vs total value locked in, compares Ethereum's total value locked against its price in US dollars. The two lines track each other nearly perfectly, with both bottoming in late 2022 and peaking in 2024 as Ethereum's price neared four thousand dollars, demonstrating that DeFi activity remains entirely coupled with asset price movements. Finally, the fourth chart tracks Ethereum daily verified contracts on a seven-day moving average, showing that daily contracts peaked near nine hundred in mid-2023 but have since declined back to around three hundred, roughly the same level seen in early 2022.

This page presents a highly skeptical outlook on European equities, contrasting them unfavorably with US equities across multiple dimensions of corporate profitability, earnings trends, long-term performance drivers, and the generation of new enterprise value. The author frames the discussion with a play on Dr. Seuss, declaring a persistent dislike for European equities across various global locations, including Trafalgar Square. 

To support this view, a table compares the Return on Assets (ROA) and Return on Equity (ROE) across eight sectors in the US and Europe as of late 2024. Other than healthcare, where Europe leads with an ROA of 6.3% and an ROE of 15.1% compared to the US's 4.4% and 12.7%, the US commands a significant lead in every sector. For example, in technology, the US posts a 12.6% ROA and 28.9% ROE, while European tech lags at 5.8% and 11.4%. In consumer discretionary, US ROE stands at 30.0% compared to Europe's 11.8%.

Short-term trends also disfavor Europe, as illustrated in a line chart tracking three-month earnings revision trends from December 2022 to late 2024. Plotting net earnings per share revisions, the chart shows Europe's revision trend plummeting to nearly negative 25% by October 2024, whereas the US and Japan remain much higher, hovering near flat to positive territory.

A long-term line chart decomposes the cumulative total return index of US equities versus European equities since 2009. While the MSCI US index rose from a base of 100 to approximately 750 by late 2024, the MSCI Europe index in US dollars struggled to reach 250. This performance gap is decomposed into five distinct layers: currency effects favoring the US dollar over the Euro; structural sector weight differences, where the US is overweight tech and Europe is overweight financials, industrials, and staples; and intra-sector outperformance where US technology, consumer discretionary, and financial companies consistently beat their European peers. 

An area chart tracking a three-year rolling portfolio strategy that overweights the US by 10% and underweights Europe by 10% relative to the MSCI All World Index from 1991 to 2024 shows that, despite a period of underperformance in the mid-2000s, this strategy has delivered consistent positive relative returns for over a decade.

Finally, a chart plotting the cumulative market cap of new public companies created in the 21st century reveals a stark divergence in innovation and value creation. The US curve rises steeply to nearly 18 trillion US dollars in cumulative market cap across more than 150 companies, driven by massive market value contributions from enterprises like Alphabet, Meta, Tesla, Visa, Mastercard, Netflix, Salesforce, T-Mobile, ServiceNow, and Accenture. In contrast, Europe's curve remains flat near the bottom of the axis, with only minor contributions from companies like Industria de Diseno Textil, Airbus, Equinor, Porsche, and Adyen.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s 2025 Outlook analyzes the major crypto rally following the November 2024 U.S. presidential election, reflecting on his previous skeptical piece from February 2022 titled "The Maltese Falcoin." Cembalest admits he was wrong regarding Bitcoin's performance as a store of value but argues he was largely correct about decentralized finance and transactions-focused coins up until the post-election surge. He highlights that global crypto adoption has risen, with account holders increasing from approximately 320 million in 2022 to 560 million, and retail ownership of less than one Bitcoin growing from 6.8 percent in 2020 to 9.5 percent. 

Four charts illustrate these performance and usage trends from 2022 through late 2024. The first chart, "Bitcoin: a store of value," tracks Bitcoin's price in U.S. dollars. It highlights a massive decline of 65 percent following the release of "The Maltese Falcoin," followed by a recovery that accelerated rapidly after the SEC approved spot Bitcoin ETFs in early 2024. The price surged past $95,000 shortly after the November 2024 election, driven by significant ETF inflows. 

The second chart, "Crypto coin prices by segment, market cap weighted," indexes prices to 100 as of January 1, 2022. It compares Bitcoin, a transactions-focused basket, and a decentralized finance basket. While the decentralized finance and transactions baskets languished far below their starting index value for nearly three years, the post-election rally caused both Bitcoin and the transactions-focused basket to spike dramatically, with Bitcoin index values exceeding 200 and the transactions basket peaking near 225. 

The third chart, "Transactions-focused coin values," uses the same index base to track individual coins, including Ripple, Stellar, Bitcoin Cash, Monero, and Litecoin. This visual shows that all five assets remained depressed below the 100 index mark for years before experiencing a massive, sudden vertical spike post-election, led by Ripple, which surged past an index value of 300. 

The final chart, "Transactions per day on blockchains, 7 day average," challenges the fundamental justification for this rally. It measures transaction volume in millions, plotting Stellar on the right axis (ranging from 2 million to 8 million daily transactions) and Ripple, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, and Monero on the left axis (ranging from 0 to 3 million daily transactions). The data shows that daily transactions have not increased significantly since 2022; Stellar's volume continues to fluctuate highly between 3 million and 7 million, Ripple averages roughly 1 million to 2 million, and the remaining coins stay flat near zero. Because actual blockchain utilization has not expanded, Cembalest concludes that the recent surge in transactions-focused coin values is highly speculative.

On this page of J.P. Morgan's 2025 Outlook, Michael Cembalest presents items four through seven of his top ten list. 

The first topic argues that high discontinuation rates for weight loss drugs will negatively impact certain GLP-1 stocks. Citing data that 50% to 70% of Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus users stop treatment within a year, the author predicts that Novo Nordisk will finish 2025 below the consensus analyst price target of $127 per share. Two accompanying charts illustrate this trend. The first chart, depicting the probability of therapy persistence over 360 days, shows Rybelsus dropping below a 30% persistence rate, Wegovy ending near 40%, and Ozempic near 45%. The second chart displays consensus analyst sales forecasts in billions of US dollars through 2030, showing Wegovy's sales plateauing near $23 billion, Ozempic leveling off around $20 billion, and Rybelsus flatlining below $5 billion. 

The next forecast focuses on energy, claiming that no small modular nuclear reactors will begin construction in the United States during 2025, despite a pre-development pipeline of 6.5 gigawatts. 

Moving to US federal policy, Cembalest addresses the Department of Government Efficiency, predicting that annualized cost savings from DOGE will amount to $150 billion or less by the end of 2025, which equates to less than 2% of fiscal year 2024 federal spending. 

Finally, the page discusses hedge fund performance, predicting that at least 75% of randomized hedge fund composites with 20 funds will outperform stock-bond benchmarks by the end of 2025. This argument is supported by a scatter plot comparing annualized excess return versus Treasury bills since January 2018 against annualized excess return volatility. The chart displays numerous yellow dots representing randomized 20-fund hedge fund composites, most of which lie above and to the left of the benchmark square markers—defined by varying equity and bond mixes from 30/70 to 80/20—indicating superior returns relative to volatility.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2025 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, presents points eight, nine, and ten of a "Top Ten List" for the upcoming year. The topics cover shelter inflation, interstate migration trends, and potential foreign policy action regarding Mexican drug cartels.

Under point eight, the author predicts that shelter inflation will fall below four percent by the end of 2025, driven by the completion of single-family and multi-family homes currently under construction. This argument is visualized through two line charts. The first chart displays housing supply under construction as a percent of owner-occupied housing stock from 2000 to 2024. It shows that multi-family construction rose steadily from 2012 to peak near one point two percent in late 2023, while single-family construction has stabilized at around zero point six percent, well below its pre-financial crisis peak of one point four percent in 2006. The second chart tracks year-over-year shelter inflation from 1954 to 2024, showing a major historical spike that peaked at twenty-one percent, followed by a recent cyclical surge to around eight percent in 2023, which is now on a downward trajectory.

Point nine forecasts that "blue state out-migration" will persist, with seventy percent or more of all movers relocating to red or purple states in 2025. A table lists the top twenty interstate migrations from January 2018 to October 2024, compiled using Chase credit card change-of-address data. The leading migration corridors are New York to Florida with one hundred forty-eight thousand net moves, New York to New Jersey with one hundred forty-seven thousand, and California to Texas with one hundred ten thousand. The author notes that seventy percent of total movers relocated from blue states to red or purple states. According to the Brennan Center, these demographic shifts will alter the electoral map after the 2030 Census, potentially reducing the electoral college count for a Democratic candidate by twelve votes in the 2032 presidential election compared to the 2024 map won by Kamala Harris.

Finally, point ten predicts that the Trump Administration will deploy targeted military action against drug cartels in Mexico without the Mexican government's authorization. The text supports this prediction by noting that Border Patrol fentanyl seizures rose from four thousand eight hundred pounds in 2020 to twenty-seven thousand pounds in 2023, with the chemical precursors largely sourced from China. The author details growing political support for this measure, citing a 2023 authorization bill drafted by twenty House Republicans and public endorsements from Governor Ron DeSantis, Nikki Haley, Vivek Ramaswamy, Senator Tim Scott, and Trump Advisor Jason Miller. If enacted, this would mark the first unauthorized use of U.S. military force in Mexico in over a century.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2025 Eye on the Market Outlook explores the political and regulatory realities facing US energy infrastructure, wind power, and electric vehicles as the presidential administration transitions. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that streamlining pipeline and transmission permits via executive order will yield limited results without explicit Federal eminent domain legislation. Consequently, infrastructure projects face persistent legal hurdles. Similarly, political targets to halt wind farm leasing on public lands are deemed marginal issues, as only 2% of US wind power is generated on public lands. In response to anticipated funding pauses by the incoming Trump administration, the outgoing Biden administration rushed through late-stage loans, including a $6.5 billion loan to Rivian and a $1.7 billion loan guarantee to Plug Power for a hydrogen project. The author also assesses Trump’s plan to terminate the "electric vehicle mandate," interpreting this as an effort to target Biden's March 2024 rule reducing car and truck greenhouse gas emissions by roughly 50% by 2032. However, the author notes that the $7,500 EV tax subsidy, established under the Inflation Reduction Act, cannot be unilaterally rescinded by executive order. Because EVs still account for less than 3% of the total US fleet, the biggest immediate economic casualties of these policy battles are likely the new EV battery assembly plants being constructed in red states like Georgia and Michigan.

The page features four charts that demonstrate how US energy infrastructure expansion has stalled and trace the path of EV adoption. The first chart, "Annual US liquids pipeline project completions," tracks the number of projects completed annually from 2010 to 2024, broken down by petroleum products, hydrocarbon gas liquids, and crude oil and condensate. This chart shows completions peaking at over 30 projects in 2014 and nearly 30 in 2020, before plummeting to only a few scattered projects per year by 2022, 2023, and 2024. 

The second chart, "Annual US natural gas pipeline capacity additions," measures capacity additions in billion cubic feet per day from 2017 to 2023, categorized by interstate and intrastate pipelines. Additions peaked in 2018 at approximately 24 billion cubic feet per day and have steadily declined to roughly 6 billion cubic feet per day by 2023. 

The third chart, "US transmission line growth," displays miles added per year for transmission lines greater than 100 kV from 2013 to 2023. Growth reached nearly 4,000 miles in 2013 but fell to under 1,000 miles by 2023. This historical trend is juxtaposed against future Department of Energy (DOE) targets, which are shown as dotted horizontal lines: the DOE 2030 target sits at roughly 5,000 miles per year, while the DOE 2035 target is set at nearly 10,000 miles per year, underscoring the vast gap between current deployment rates and policy goals. 

The final chart, "US EV share of passenger vehicle fleet and sales," tracks the percentage share of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) from 2020 to 2024. While the share of sales grew rapidly from approximately 2% in 2020 to over 11% by 2024, the overall share of the total operating passenger fleet grew at a much slower pace, ending 2024 below the 3% threshold.

This page analyzes the potential impact of the "Department of Government Efficiency" (DOGE), led by Elon Musk, on federal spending and employment. The core argument is that targeting federal workforce size or specific regulatory agencies is unlikely to meaningfully reduce overall government spending because federal employment, at three million people, is already at an 85-year low as a share of total US employment at approximately two percent. 

The page features two charts illustrating government employment patterns. The first, an area chart titled "Government employees as share of all employees" spanning 1955 to 2019, reveals that local government employees make up the vast majority of public sector workers, while the share of federal employees has steadily declined since the mid-20th century. The second chart, a treemap titled "Breakdown of Federal workers, 2023," shows that the Department of Defense, excluding active military, is the largest employer at 26 percent, followed by the Postal Service at 20 percent and Veterans Affairs at 15 percent. In contrast, agencies often targeted by DOGE, such as the Environmental Protection Agency, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the Department of Labor, combined account for less than one percent of the federal workforce, while the Department of Education accounts for a mere 0.14 percent.

Consequently, the author asserts that significant spending cuts must instead target entitlement programs, defense procurement, or the reversal of executive orders. A detailed table titled "Savings from Reversing President Biden's Executive Actions" estimates the potential ten-year savings from repealing specific policies, totaling over one trillion dollars, or roughly 103 billion dollars annually. Major sources of potential savings include repealing the SAVE student debt program at 275 billion dollars, restructuring SNAP Thrifty Food Plan rules at 180 billion dollars, rolling back vehicle carbon emissions and electric vehicle credits at 150 billion dollars, and altering Medicaid financing rules at 140 billion dollars. Other notable categories include Medicaid eligibility repeals at 75 billion dollars, Medicare Part D rebates at 65 billion dollars, ACA self-only coverage adjustments at 40 billion dollars, and IRS enforcement restrictions on incomes under 400,000 dollars at 20 billion dollars. The author concludes that while these executive repeals would provide a modest start, DOGE will ultimately have to address entitlement and defense spending—particularly non-competitive weapons procurement contracts—to make a major impact on skyrocketing US debt levels.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2025 Eye on the Market Outlook examines two primary topics: the feasibility and impact of domestic energy production targets and the United States’ stance on international corporate tax frameworks. Author Michael Cembalest argues that the incoming Trump administration has a strong chance of meeting Scott Bessent’s "3-3-3 target" for domestic energy production. This target requires a 7% increase in oil, gas, and natural gas liquids production, which Cembalest views as highly achievable. However, he questions whether this will successfully lower consumer energy prices, noting that price trends will depend on export volumes, state-level transitions away from fossil fuels, and entrenched inflation within the electricity supply chain.

To illustrate the energy landscape, the page features four visual graphics. The first is an area chart showing the "Production of crude oil, natural gas and natural gas liquids" in trillions of BTUs per month from 2000 through mid-2024. The data shows a massive upward trend beginning around 2010, driven by natural gas and crude oil, with production climbing toward 8,000 trillion BTUs per month as it nears the Bessent 3-3-3 target. A second, adjacent stacked bar chart reveals that hydraulic fracturing accounted for a dominant 61% of all US primary energy consumption in 2023. Conventional oil, gas, and natural gas liquids accounted for the next largest share, followed by coal, nuclear power, and small fractions of biomass, hydro, wind, and solar energy.

The page also addresses electricity pricing and supply-chain pressures. A line chart displaying "Residential electricity prices by state" from 2016 to 2024 shows a stark divergence between states. While residential rates in Texas remained relatively flat and low, fluctuating between 10 and 15 cents per kilowatt-hour, rates in California surged dramatically from under 20 cents to approximately 33 cents per kilowatt-hour by 2024. New York also saw significant rate hikes, landing near 23 cents per kilowatt-hour. This utility price inflation is contextualized by a scatter plot of core goods Producer Price Index component inflation, which plots 47 categories by their percentage price increase since 2018. At the very top of this chart, "Transformers & Power Regulators" show a massive price increase of nearly 70% since 2018, demonstrating severe supply-chain bottlenecks for electrical infrastructure.

The second half of the page focuses on international taxation, specifically criticizing European efforts to implement the Pillar II tax system on US companies. Cembalest reiterates his view that Pillar II provisions act as "bounty-hunting rules" that permit foreign nations to collect tax revenues from US companies on income earned within the United States, thereby undermining Congressional authority over domestic tax policy. Although the Biden Administration supported the Pillar II framework, Cembalest notes that tax policy requires Senate treaty approval or Congressional legislation. Consequently, the US has not adopted Pillar II rules, nor has it agreed to the Pillar I Digital Service Taxes, which the author characterizes as European attempts to penalize major US technology firms.

In this edition of Eye on the Market, Michael Cembalest analyzes Donald Trump's tariff policies, noting that the slow rollout of tariffs has been the biggest surprise, despite recent threats of 25 percent tariffs on Mexico and Canada to address border security issues. Although Trump previously made similar threats without implementing them, he has signed executive orders directing federal agencies to examine unfair trade and currency practices.
