The author anticipates future tariff increases on China and EU auto imports, but suggests a universal tariff would likely be limited to critical imports representing only 10 to 20 percent of overall US imports. 

Cembalest highlights a prevailing economic consensus that tariffs actually reduce domestic manufacturing employment, a negative outcome likely to impact Republican-leaning red states the most given their high import-to-GDP ratios. This view is illustrated in a chart displaying a survey of 44 economists by the Wall Street Journal and J.P. Morgan Asset Management in October 2024. The survey reveals that 59 percent of economists expect Trump’s tariffs to decrease manufacturing employment, 25 percent expect employment to remain level, and only 16 percent predict an increase.

The report also visualizes the profound global structural shift in heavy industry through a chart tracking energy-intensive manufacturing. It shows developed economies losing global production share to emerging economies between the late 1990s and 2023. Specifically, developed nations' share of total manufacturing fell from about 80 percent in 1995 to 50 percent in 2023. In specialized energy-intensive sectors, the decline of developed economies is even more stark: ammonia fell from 38 percent in 1998 to 20 percent in 2023; steel dropped from 61 percent in 1998 to 22 percent in 2023; cement fell from 28 percent in 1998 to 10 percent in 2023; and plastics production fell from 51 percent in 2005 to 34 percent in 2023.

To explain the political impetus behind these tariff proposals despite economists' warnings, Cembalest points to a historic lack of trade reciprocity. A scatter plot comparing tariffs applied by the US against tariffs applied to the US by trading partners reveals that nearly every country sits below the "tariff reciprocity line," meaning they charge higher tariffs on US imports than the US charges them. Major nations like India, China, Brazil, Pakistan, and Argentina levy simple average tariffs between 6 percent and 13 percent, whereas the US applies average tariffs under 4 percent to almost all of them.

This lack of reciprocity is tied to the long-term stagnation of American industry, as shown in a chart titled "The Silence of the Plants." This visual indexes US consumer spending, US GDP, and US industrial production to a base of 100 in the year 2000. From 1930 until 2000, all three indicators tracked closely together. However, immediately following China's entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001, US industrial production flatlined, while consumer spending and overall GDP continued to climb significantly, diverging past index levels of 160 by the early 2020s. Cembalest concludes that while economists expect tariffs to be highly problematic, they remain a policy option that can ultimately be adjusted or repealed if they fail.

In this introductory commentary, Michael Cembalest outlines his analytical approach to the second Trump Administration, emphasizing the need for real-time, data-driven tracking over speculative theories regarding policy impacts. To establish this analytical discipline, he introduces a policy tracker and a roadmap detailing the constitutional and statutory challenges that the administration's proposals may face. 

To conceptualize the policy mix of Trump 2.0, Cembalest includes a visual compilation of seven historical U.S. presidents whose past agendas mirror different facets of the current administration. These historical parallels include Calvin Coolidge's focus on small government and pro-business policies; James Polk's pursuit of manifest destiny in the western hemisphere; Andrew Jackson's battles with the deep state to forge a new political order; Woodrow Wilson's pre-war isolationism; Richard Nixon's use of enemies lists and quest for energy independence; Dwight Eisenhower's combination of corporate tax cuts and deportations; and William McKinley's reliance on tariffs and protectionism.

Transitioning to market opportunities, Cembalest previews upcoming research on energy and healthcare, pointing out that biotech, pharma, and healthcare provider stocks currently look cheap relative to their projected profitability. To illustrate this, a scatter plot charts S&P 500 valuations against return on equity, specifically plotting consensus forward twelve-month price-to-book ratios on the vertical axis against consensus forward twelve-month return on equity on the horizontal axis. A diagonal dotted line indicates the market's standard valuation-to-profitability trendline. High-flying sectors like information technology, semiconductors, and retailing sit near the top of the chart with high valuations corresponding to high returns on equity. In contrast, key healthcare subsectors plot significantly to the right of the trendline, signaling undervaluation relative to their projected performance. Specifically, biotech boasts a very high consensus return on equity of nearly forty-four percent but trades at a modest price-to-book ratio of six and a half times. Pharma similarly shows a strong return on equity of thirty-four percent at a valuation of five and a half times, while healthcare providers trade at a low valuation of just over three times book value against a twenty-six percent return on equity.

This page of the publication argues that two years is an eternity in United States politics, emphasizing that initial political climates, policies, and campaign promises can shift dramatically over a short time. To support this thesis, the author provides four historical case studies of rapid political reversals, focusing on deportations, tariffs, foreign policy, and taxation. 

The first example is Dwight D. Eisenhower’s deportation push, which peaked at 1.1 million people in 1954 but collapsed by over 90% to just 90,000 by 1956 due to a loss of funding and political support. An accompanying line chart, titled "Eisenhower deportations," shows the annual volume of deportations from 1945 to 1957, depicting a sharp, symmetrical spike that peaks near 1 million in 1954 before falling back to near-zero levels.

The second example is the McKinley tariffs of 1890, which were initially popular but caused an immediate inflation spike. Consequently, the Republican Party lost 100 seats in the 1890 midterms, marking the third-largest House loss in post-Civil War history. The chart "McKinley tariff aftermath: 1890 midterms" tracks Republican House seats adjusted for the 1890 House size from 1865 to 1910. It shows a severe drop from a peak of around 175 seats down to a trough of around 88 seats immediately following the implementation of the first tariffs in October 1890 and the subsequent November midterms.

The third example highlights Woodrow Wilson’s re-election campaign in 1916, which he won using the slogan "he kept us out of war," despite the German sinking of the Lusitania in 1915. Within six months of the election, Wilson pivoted to deliver a war message to Congress. The chart "Wilson enters WWI" displays military spending as a share of GDP from 1910 to 1925. It shows spending remaining near 1% of GDP through 1916, followed by a sudden spike to nearly 8% of GDP in the years immediately following Wilson's speech to Congress. 

The final example details George H.W. Bush’s pivot to raise taxes in 1990 due to a recession and rising budget deficits, despite his prominent campaign promise of "Read My Lips: No New Taxes." A text box outlines the components of the 1990 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act, which increased the top marginal tax rate from 28% to 31%, raised the individual alternative minimum tax from 21% to 24%, limited itemized deductions, raised the cap on taxable Medicare wages from $53,000 to $125,000, added a 0.2% unemployment insurance surtax, and introduced new excise taxes on luxury goods, alcohol, and tobacco.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the strength of Nvidia's market moats and assesses the future impact of artificial intelligence and policy on United States electricity demand. Cembalest begins by detailing Nvidia's dominant position, explaining that most AI projects rely heavily on its proprietary CUDA software, stable Linux drivers, and optimized open-source libraries like PyTorch. Furthermore, Nvidia's virtual GPU capabilities and advanced interconnect technologies, bolstered by its 2019 acquisition of Mellanox, present a formidable barrier to entry. However, competitors are emerging, including hardware firms like Cerebras and Groq, alongside software initiatives like Apple's MLX, OpenAI's Triton, and Google's JAX, all designed to make code work across varied hardware. 

To illustrate the market's reaction to these dynamics, the author presents a chart tracking the Nvidia forward price-to-earnings ratio from 2020 through early 2025. This ratio has fluctuated significantly, peaking near seventy in late 2021 and close to sixty in mid-2023. By early 2025, the forward P/E ratio had declined sharply toward the bottom of its historical five-year range, settling around thirty. 

The text then shifts to address concerns about energy consumption, arguing that the market should temper fears over extreme increases in electricity demand from data centers. Cembalest points out that innovations such as DeepSeek and strong economic incentives are driving developers to build more energy-efficient chips and software solutions that minimize data movement and training requirements. Furthermore, political shifts under Trump 2.0 may slow growth in electricity demand. A future Congressional reconciliation bill could potentially reduce tax credits for solar, wind, batteries, electric vehicles, and carbon capture to offset tax cuts. 

This argument is supported by a second chart displaying the historical and forecasted US electricity demand by application, measured in terawatt-hours from 1985 to 2030. The historical trend shows demand rising steadily from twenty-five hundred terawatt-hours in 1985 to roughly forty-five hundred terawatt-hours by the early 2020s. For the 2030 outlook, the chart presents two primary forecasts. The high-end scenario represents a nineteen percent increase, driving demand toward fifty-two hundred terawatt-hours when accounting for heat pumps, electric vehicles, and data centers. The low-end scenario projects just a seven percent increase, keeping demand near forty-five hundred terawatt-hours even after factoring in these new electrical loads. Cembalest notes that the competitive analysis of Nvidia and AMD incorporates insights from Jeffrey Emanuel of GLG Insights, and concludes with a lighthearted apology for any potential technical errors given his background as a liberal arts student in the early 1980s.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s annual energy paper introduces the concept of heliocentrism, defined in this context as the belief that rapid growth in solar power and energy storage is the core of the energy transition, rendering new investments in complementary thermal power generation unnecessary. While global solar capacity has more than doubled over the past three years and is projected to double again by 2027, this rapid shift is heavily dependent on China, which controls over eighty percent of the manufacturing supply chain for key solar components like polysilicon and modules. This leaves the United States heavily reliant on imports despite its current efforts to build out a domestic supply chain.

Four charts illustrate these trends. The first chart, depicting global solar capacity in gigawatts from 2011 to 2027, shows actual capacity curving upward to roughly 1,500 gigawatts in 2023 before a steep projected climb to over 4,000 gigawatts by 2027. The second chart shows solar’s share of global electricity generation capacity additions, which rose from under forty percent in 2019 to sixty percent in 2024, and is projected to reach approximately seventy-five percent by 2027. 

The third chart illustrates how the International Energy Agency consistently underestimated solar capacity growth. It compares the actual soaring red line of annual solar additions—which spiked to nearly 350 gigawatts by 2023—against more than a dozen flat, conservative annual forecasts issued by the IEA between 2009 and 2022. The final chart displays global electricity generation in terawatt-hours from 1965 to 2025. It tracks hydropower, which has climbed steadily to over 4,000 terawatt-hours, and nuclear power, which has flattened around 2,700 terawatt-hours since 2000. Meanwhile, the combined generation of wind and solar has experienced exponential growth since the mid-2000s, soaring past nuclear power and positioning itself to overtake hydropower by 2025.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s 2025 Eye on the Market Outlook provides a detailed statistical overview of key economic, regulatory, and demographic indicators in the United States. It tracks crucial themes like domestic energy production, small business sentiment, corporate earnings expectations, mergers and acquisitions, immigration, deportation rates, and the growth of economically significant federal regulations across multiple administrations.

In the top left, a stacked area chart tracks US production of crude oil, natural gas, and natural gas liquids from 2018 through early 2025, measured in trillions of BTUs per month. Total production consistently climbed over this period, hovering between 7,000 and 7,500 trillion BTUs by 2024, with the chart noting the "Bessent 3-3-3 target" aimed at boosting these figures. To the right, a chart based on NFIB survey data depicts small business sales and profits as a net percentage of respondents from 2018 to 2025. Both series collapsed during 2020 and have struggled to recover, with net profits remaining deeply negative at around negative 30% and net sales hovering around negative 10% to negative 15% in late 2024 and early 2025.

The middle section of the page focuses on corporate and market indicators. The middle-left chart tracks the S&P 500 consensus EPS growth rate for 2025 compared to 2024 from February 2023 to February 2025. Consensus projections steadily rose from around 10% in early 2023 to a peak near 20% in late 2024, before settling at roughly 18% in early 2025. Next to it, US proposed M&A and investment deal activity is tracked monthly from 2018 to early 2025. Plotting both deal volume in billions of dollars and total deal count, it reveals a major spike in volume during late 2021 and a sudden, sharp resurgence in both deal count (surging toward 90) and volume (approaching $60 to $80 billion) in late 2024 and early 2025.

The bottom half of the page covers demographic and regulatory trends. A chart on net immigration from 2001 to late 2023 displays monthly and annual rates for both authorized lawful permanent residents and students, and unauthorized illegal entrants and refugees. It highlights a massive post-2020 spike driven largely by unauthorized entrants and refugees, which pushed monthly rates near 400,000, equivalent to an annual rate of nearly 4.8 million. Adjacent to immigration, a chart details deportations—measured as administrative returns and removals—by presidential administration from 2001 to 2025. Deportation rates peaked under George W. Bush and Barack Obama, reaching over 40,000 monthly (an annual rate near 480,000), declined in the late Obama and Donald Trump years, plunged during COVID-19, and rose sharply again under Joe Biden to nearly 40,000 monthly by late 2024. 

Finally, the bottom-left line graph plots the cumulative number of economically significant rules—defined as federal regulations with an annual economic impact of at least $200 million—by month of presidency for administrations from Ronald Reagan to Joe Biden. The chart shows that the Biden administration has tracked closely with Barack Obama’s high regulatory volume, reaching nearly 400 rules by month 48. An accompanying text box explains that Donald Trump was on track to match the lower regulatory footprints of Bill Clinton and both Bush presidents until a COVID-19-induced spike in Department of Health and Human Services rules sharply escalated his regulatory count near the end of his term.

In this executive summary page of the Heliocentrism annual energy paper, the author presents a sobering reality check regarding the global energy transition, arguing that despite the rapid growth of solar power, human prosperity remains deeply dependent on fossil fuels. The main argument posits that because electricity accounts for less than a third of final energy consumption, solar's overall impact on global energy is quite small. The author projects that while solar's share of global electricity generation will double from its current 7% to about 14% or 15% by 2027, its share of final global energy consumption will only rise from roughly 2% today to 4.5% by 2027. 

These trends are illustrated in the first chart, "Solar shares of global electricity and final energy," which plots both metrics from 2011 with projections out to 2027. To emphasize the link between energy use and economic development, the second chart, "Per capita energy consumption and GDP by country," uses log scales for both 2023 per capita GDP and per capita energy consumption in kilowatt-hours. The resulting scatter plot shows a tight, upward-sloping correlation, suggesting that economic prosperity is inherently energy-intensive. 

The author also examines historical energy transitions in the OECD. The line chart "OECD, shares of final energy consumption" tracks energy sources from 1965 to 2025. It reveals that the decline in coal combustion (dropping from 30% to around 10%) has been offset primarily by natural gas additions (which rose to match oil at roughly 35%) and to a lesser extent by wind and solar, while nuclear energy has remained moribund and flat at around 5%. 

Finally, a double-layered visual titled "The fossil fuel intensity of global industrial production" illustrates why heavy industry cannot easily decarbonize. The outer ring shows that global industrial energy demand is dominated by chemicals at 28%, iron and steel at 23%, and cement at 11%. The inner pie chart reveals that the energy powering these sectors remains overwhelmingly fossil-fuel based: coal accounts for 30%, oil for 20%, natural gas for 19%, and fossil-fuel-derived electricity for 14%. By contrast, zero-carbon electricity accounts for only 10% and biomass for 7%. The author concludes that because these essential, energy-intensive products currently rely on fossil fuels for 80% to 85% of their energy, human prosperity—and, as noted in a footnote, national security—will remain inextricably linked to affordable fossil fuels well into the 2030s.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "2025 Eye on the Market Outlook" presents a comprehensive set of six charts focusing on various components of consumer price and wage inflation, tracking their historical trends from 2018 through early 2025. The overall theme is the dramatic rise in inflationary pressures during the post-pandemic period of 2021 to 2022 and the subsequent, though incomplete, cooling of those pressures heading into 2025.

The first chart, located in the top left, displays year-over-year percentage changes in Core CPI and Core PCE inflation. Both indexes show a sharp upward trajectory starting in 2021, with Core CPI peaking near 6.5% and Core PCE peaking around 5.5% in 2022. Since then, both have cooled significantly, with Core CPI settling near 3.5% and Core PCE near 2.5% by early 2025, though they remain slightly elevated relative to their pre-pandemic levels of around 2.0%.

To the right, the second chart tracks CPI shelter inflation measures on a month-over-month basis, specifically breaking down CPI rent for actual rental properties and Owners' Equivalent Rent for imputed rent from owned homes. Both measures rose from roughly 0.2% monthly in 2020 to peaks of nearly 0.8% in late 2022 and early 2023. Since then, shelter inflation has gradually drifted lower to between 0.3% and 0.4% month-over-month by early 2025, showing persistent stickiness.

The middle row of charts explores wholesale and import price pressures. On the left, the chart for key core goods PPI components measures month-over-month percentage changes for Finished Goods, Final Demand Goods, and Processed Materials. This chart illustrates high volatility, particularly for processed materials, which spiked dramatically in 2021 and 2022. By the end of 2024, all three PPI components had stabilized, hovering near 0.0% month-over-month, suggesting that goods-inflation pressures have subsided.

On the middle right, the US import price index of goods, excluding petroleum, displays month-over-month percentage changes. This series was highly volatile, spiking to around 0.75% to 1.00% monthly during 2021 before falling into negative territory, dipping to negative 0.50% or lower, in late 2022 and 2023. By late 2024, import price growth had stabilized to fluctuate within a narrow band around 0.0% to 0.25%.

The bottom row addresses wage inflation and commodity prices. The bottom-left chart shows two wage inflation measures on a year-over-year percentage basis: the Atlanta Fed wage tracker and the Employment cost index. Both trackers rose steeply in 2021, with the Atlanta Fed wage tracker peaking near 6.5% and the Employment cost index peaking above 5.0% in late 2022. By the end of 2024, wage inflation had moderated, with the Atlanta Fed tracker dropping toward 4.5% and the Employment cost index falling to around 3.5% to 4.0%, though both remain higher than their pre-pandemic averages.

Finally, the bottom-right chart reviews energy and food inflation year-over-year, utilizing a dual axis. The left axis, measuring negative 6% to 18%, tracks electricity, meats, poultry, and fish, and dairy, while the right axis, measuring negative 35% to 105%, tracks the highly volatile egg and gasoline categories. Gasoline inflation experienced massive swings, peaking near 60% in 2022 before dropping below zero in late 2023 and stabilizing near 0% by early 2025. Egg inflation also saw extreme spikes in late 2022. Food categories like dairy and meats, poultry, and fish peaked at double-digit levels in 2022 but have since moderated to low single digits, while electricity inflation remains somewhat sticky around 4% to 6% year-over-year.

This page, from J.P. Morgan's 15th Annual Energy Paper, outlines how the global energy transition is being slowed by a mismatch between grid decarbonization and actual end-use electrification. The author argues that cleaning up electricity generation does little to lower emissions until end uses—like industrial plants, furnaces, and vehicles—are electrified. 

One major physical hurdle is the lagging expansion of the US electric grid. The top-left chart, showing US grid decarbonization outpacing electrification of energy use, highlights that while the renewable share of electricity generation has climbed steadily toward twenty percent, the actual electricity share of final US energy consumption has remained stubbornly flat at around twenty to twenty-two percent. This grid expansion is severely hindered by transmission line additions. The top-right chart, tracking annual US transmission line additions of one hundred kilovolts or more, shows that annual additions dropped below one thousand miles in 2023, far below the Department of Energy targets of over five thousand miles per year by 2030 and nearly ten thousand miles per year by 2035. Furthermore, shortages in transformer equipment have seen delivery lead times balloon from four to six weeks in 2019 to two to three years. With half of the seventy million US transformers nearing the end of their useful lives and facing rising threat levels from extreme weather, investment in transformer manufacturing by companies like Schneider Electric and Hitachi North America is highly critical but will take time to deliver results.

Beyond physical grid constraints, the page addresses international trends and economic hurdles. The bottom-left chart tracks the electricity share of final energy consumption for major countries from 1990 to 2025. Over the last decade, China has made the most rapid progress, rising to meet OECD averages of around twenty-seven percent, while progress in the US, Europe, Japan, India, Russia, Brazil, and the United Kingdom remains sluggish. The author notes that small high-renewables countries like Panama, Uganda, Norway, and Iceland are outliers and generally irrelevant to discussions about larger countries. 

The primary economic headwind is the relative price of electricity versus natural gas, particularly in regions lacking a carbon tax. The bottom-right bar chart compares the cost of electricity per megajoule to the cost of natural gas per megajoule, factoring in typical residential and industrial furnace efficiencies. This price premium is steepest for Texas and California industrial users, where electricity is nearly five times more expensive than gas. Across other sectors, such as United Kingdom residential, Louisiana industrial, and Germany residential, electricity costs remain roughly three to four times higher than natural gas. The ratio is lowest but still significant for Florida residential users, where electricity is nearly twice as expensive as gas. This price disparity, combined with the long operating lifespans of existing fossil-fueled industrial plants and heating systems, acts as a powerful brake on global electrification.

This page provides a detailed data-driven overview of global climate indicators and their environmental impacts under the section title focusing on the changing planet. It features six charts tracking indicators of climate change, from ice sheet loss and vegetation shifts to ocean chemistry, atmospheric heat-trapping, biodiversity declines, and extreme weather.

The first chart, tracking Antarctica and Greenland ice sheet mass variations from 2002 to 2023, shows a steady, downward trend in mass. Greenland’s ice sheet has experienced the most severe decline, losing over 5,000 gigatonnes of mass by 2023, while Antarctica's ice sheet mass variation has dropped to nearly negative 3,000 gigatonnes. Directly beside this, a bar chart maps the greening of Antarctica, measuring the square kilometers of green vegetation cover below 300 meters above sea level each March. This index reveals a dramatic surge starting around 2016, with vegetated areas rising from historical levels well below 2 square kilometers to peaks exceeding 10 square kilometers in 2016, 2018, and 2020. An accompanying note cautions that the last time Antarctica was covered with foliage and supported reptilian life, the global climate was not conducive to mammalian life.

The central portion of the page defines ocean acidification as the process by which seawater pH decreases due to atmospheric carbon dioxide absorption. This process threatens marine ecosystems by killing off plankton and preventing calcifying organisms from building shells. The adjacent chart displays Hawaii ocean acidification from 1988 to 2021, showing that the annual average mean seawater pH level has steadily declined from approximately 8.12 to about 8.05, signaling a consistent trend toward higher acidity.

The bottom half of the page covers atmospheric forcing, biodiversity loss, and extreme weather. A area chart illustrating radiative forcing by greenhouse gases from 1979 to 2023 tracks how much heat is trapped in the earth's atmosphere, measured in watts per square meter. Total radiative forcing has increased from roughly 1.5 to nearly 3.5 watts per square meter, driven primarily by carbon dioxide emissions, with smaller contributions from methane, nitrous oxide, and various halocarbons. Concurrently, a chart on the vertebrate biological diversity index shows a steep decline in species diversity globally from 1970 to 2020, using a baseline index of 1.0. The global average has fallen to roughly 0.35, with freshwater species suffering the most extreme collapse to below 0.2, followed by terrestrial and marine species. Finally, a line graph tracks extreme one-day precipitation events in the continental United States from 1910 to 2020 as a percentage of land area. Both the annual variations and the five-year average demonstrate a clear upward trend, with the percentage of affected land area rising from historical averages of around 7% to 10% in the mid-20th century to sustained levels between 12% and 18% in recent decades.

This page compiles essential charts illustrating the challenges facing US electrical grids, specifically regarding capacity credits, transmission, declining reserve margins, low queue completion rates, and the high cost of electricity relative to fossil fuels. The author argues that adding wind and solar does not easily replace natural gas capacity, as high equipment inflation and sluggish grid infrastructure expansion hinder reliability and energy transition goals.

The first chart, focusing on regional capacity displacement, shows that adding new wind and solar capacity does very little to reduce the need for natural gas. Across major regional power markets—such as MISO, ERCOT, SPP, NYISO, ISNE, PJM, CAISO, and SOCO—only about 10% to 25% of natural gas capacity can be displaced per megawatt of new wind and solar, assuming renewables account for 10% of total demand. This grid expansion is further constrained by supply-chain inflation, as shown in the second chart. Comparing price increases for 47 core goods categories since 2018, transformers and power regulators have experienced the second-highest inflation rate, soaring by approximately 70%.

The physical construction of the grid has also decelerated. The third chart shows US transmission line growth from 2013 to 2023, measured in miles added per year for lines greater than 100 kilovolts. Annual expansion has dropped precipitously, falling from nearly 4,000 miles in 2013 to under 500 miles in 2023. This sluggish growth contributes to a projected decline in summer peak reserve margins, illustrated in the fourth chart's forecast from 2025 to 2035. According to NERC projections, generation capacity buffers will steadily shrink, with the anticipated reserve margin in MISO and the Northwest falling to critical single digits by 2035, while regions like PJM, New York, and New England drop to between 10% and 15%.

Meanwhile, very few of the clean energy projects waiting to connect to the grid are expected to materialize. The fifth chart, showing US grid queue completion rates by request year from 2005 to 2023, reveals that completion rates (measured both by the number and capacity of requests) have plummeted from peaks of 25% to 30% down to less than 5% for recent request cohorts, driven by high interconnection costs and financing delays. 

Finally, the sixth chart evaluates the economic friction facing residential building electrification. It compares winter heating fuel prices per megajoule across the top ten electricity-consuming states, as well as the US average, from 2019 to 2024. The ratio of electricity to natural gas prices remains high, ranging from over 4.5x in Illinois to roughly 2.0x in Florida, with a US average of 2.3x. In contrast, the US average price ratio of electricity to heating oil or propane is lower, at roughly 1.3x. The substantial cost premium of electricity over natural gas serves as a key economic barrier to the adoption of residential electric heat pumps.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" energy paper explores the surging power demands of data centers, the growing occurrence of negative electricity prices, and the rapid expansion of global energy storage. The author argues that due to massive electricity demand from data centers, electric vehicles, and heat electrification, technology hyperscalers will likely have to rely primarily on natural gas, potentially walking back their green energy commitments. Wood Mackenzie projects roughly 75 gigawatts of new US gas capacity by 2030 alongside fewer gas plant retirements. While data centers remain heavily concentrated near Washington, D.C., likely due to low-latency military requirements, future centers might relocate to areas like the Texas Panhandle or Southern California, where negative electricity prices are increasingly common. 

The first chart illustrates the US electricity demand forecast in terawatt-hours from 1985 projected to 2030, comparing actual demand to a high-end forecast of a nineteen percent increase and a low-end forecast of a seven percent increase. This expected demand surge is driven by stacked additions of data centers, electric vehicles, and heat pumps. The chart also highlights how the EIA's 2007 projection significantly overpredicted demand for over a decade. A corresponding pie chart detailing US data center power consumption by energy source reveals that as of 2024, natural gas represents the largest share at forty-three percent, followed by nuclear power at nineteen percent, coal at seventeen percent, wind at nine percent, hydro at seven percent, and solar at six percent.

Negative electricity prices are explored across two line charts spanning 2019 to 2024. The first chart shows the percentage of negatively priced hours, with the Texas Panhandle leading at roughly twenty-five percent in 2024, followed by South Australia at around twenty percent, and Germany, Southern California, and Houston trailing at much lower percentages. The second chart monitors the percentage of days with at least one negatively priced hour, where the Texas Panhandle spikes to nearly eighty percent of days in 2024 and South Australia reaches close to seventy percent, demonstrating a growing trend of power gluts. 

The bottom of the page highlights energy storage trends. A bar chart tracking global gross energy storage additions by market in gigawatts from 2016 to 2024 shows explosive growth, climbing from negligible amounts to surpassing sixty gigawatts in 2024, with China and the United States representing the dominant shares of this capacity expansion. This growth is supported by falling costs, as shown in the final bar chart of 4-hour utility-scale energy storage system prices. Total system prices peaked in 2022 near three hundred dollars per kilowatt-hour but fell sharply to around one hundred seventy-five dollars per kilowatt-hour in 2024, driven primarily by cost reductions in battery racks, which comprise the largest share of the system's cost components.

This page focuses on the evolving dynamics of solar costs, supply chains, capacity factors, and the expanding role of renewables in global electricity generation. The author argues that while solar and wind are mature technologies with stable capacity factors, solar generation is rapidly converging with wind due to explosive capacity growth that compensates for its lower capacity factors. The text notes that onshore wind turbine developments are approaching physical limits and highlights how heavily the global renewable supply chain relies on China. 

Six charts illustrate these points. The first chart, "Solar levelized costs vs PPA prices" in US dollars per megawatt-hour from 2011 to 2025, shows Lazard's solar levelized cost of energy declining sharply from around $160 in 2011 to roughly $36 in 2021, before reversing upward to about $60 by 2024 and 2025. LevelTen solar power purchase agreement prices, which account for technology costs, insurance premiums, and supply-demand imbalances, similarly rose from under $30 in 2021 to nearly $60 by 2025. The second chart tracks the "Solar grade polysilicon price" in US dollars per kilogram from 2020 to 2025, demonstrating a dramatic price spike from below $10 in 2020 to a peak of over $35 in 2022, followed by a complete collapse back to around $5 by early 2025. 

The third chart, "Global capacity factors" from 2010 to 2024, reveals stable performance metrics that indicate mature technologies. Offshore wind capacity factors fluctuate between 33 percent and 43 percent, onshore wind remains steady around 33 percent to 35 percent, and solar remains flat at around 15 percent to 16 percent. The fourth chart, "Solar generation converging with wind" in terawatt-hours from 2019 to 2024, shows that China is leading this convergence. China's solar generation skyrocketed from under 200 terawatt-hours to over 800 terawatt-hours, nearly catching up to China's wind generation at nearly 1,000 terawatt-hours. By comparison, EU wind, EU solar, US wind, and US solar exhibit more modest, steady climbs. 

The fifth chart, "Many renewable supply chains go through China, for now," details the market share of China, the US, and the EU across 18 different raw materials and manufacturing steps. It highlights China's overwhelming dominance, capturing over 80 percent to 90 percent of solar cell, module, wafer, and polysilicon production, alongside high concentrations in electric vehicle mineral processing, lithium-ion battery manufacturing, wind turbine order books, and rare earth production. The final chart, "Renewable share of global electricity generation" from 1985 to beyond 2020, shows the total renewable share climbing toward 30 percent of global electricity. While hydroelectric power has historically formed the stable baseline of around 15 percent, the recent sharp upward trajectory is powered by wind and, most rapidly, solar.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 15th Annual Energy Paper explores global trends in fossil fuel consumption, the United States' deep reliance on hydraulic fracturing, future liquefied natural gas capacity, and the shifting dynamics of global coal consumption. The overall argument is that while fossil fuel shares of final energy are falling in key regions like China, Japan, and Europe, global consumption has not yet peaked, largely because rising demand in emerging markets offsets declines in developed nations. 

The first chart tracks fossil fuel shares of final energy consumption as a percentage from 1965 to 2025 across different regions. It demonstrates that fossil fuel shares are falling faster in Europe—dropping toward 80%—as well as in Japan and China, while the United States remains more heavily reliant on fossil fuels at nearly 90%, and Asia excluding China and Japan remains even higher. To contextualize this, a second chart displays global fossil fuel consumption in exajoules from 1965 to 2025, revealing that despite slowing growth, there is no clear sign of a peak. Oil consumption continues to climb above 100 exajoules, while gas and coal consumption hover closely behind, showing ongoing resilience.

A pair of charts highlights the critical role of hydraulic fracturing in the United States. The first of these shows the percentage of US oil and gas production derived from hydraulic fracturing through year-end 2023. Starting from near zero in 1995, the share grew exponentially after 2005; by 2023, natural gas from fracking accounted for roughly 80% of total production, while crude oil and natural gas liquids both exceeded 60%. The second visualizes how these unconventional sources dominate the entire domestic energy landscape, revealing that hydraulic fracturing accounted for 61% of all US primary energy consumption in 2023, while conventional fossil fuels, coal, nuclear, and renewables like wind and solar made up the remaining minority shares.

The document also provides a forecast for global LNG capacity up to 2035, comparing existing capacity, capacity under construction, and demand in billion cubic meters. The chart indicates that global LNG export capacity is set to expand by one-third by 2030, with projects currently under construction pushing total capacity close to 900 billion cubic meters, which comfortably exceeds the projected demand curve that begins to flatten around 600 billion cubic meters. 

Finally, a chart on coal final energy consumption by country from 1965 to the mid-2020s shows that global consumption has remained flat overall at around 100 exajoules. This stability is the result of a geographic shift: steady declines in coal consumption within the United States and Europe have been completely offset by dramatic increases in China, India, and the rest of Asia, with China alone consuming roughly half of the global total.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market energy paper explores energy independence, the global shift in energy-intensive manufacturing, natural gas reserves, and the geopolitical vulnerabilities of China and Taiwan. The central argument is that the United States has achieved energy independence for the first time in forty years, while Europe and China remain locked in a competition for global energy resources. Additionally, the author criticizes Taiwan's decision to phase out its nuclear power sector, which has escalated its energy dependence and left it highly vulnerable to a potential blockade by China.

The page features six charts. The first, titled Energy dependence and independence, tracks net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal in million tonnes of oil equivalent from 1980 to 2023. It reveals a stark divergence: Europe’s net imports remain high near 1,000 million tonnes, and China’s have surged from near zero in 1990 to over 800 million tonnes by 2023, while the US transitioned into a net exporter at around -200 million tonnes alongside Russia, which remains a massive net exporter. The second chart, Net imports of fossil fuels as a percent of primary energy consumption, shows that while China imports a comparable volume of energy to Europe, these imports represent only about 22% of its primary energy consumption compared to Europe's 45%, showing China is relatively less reliant on foreign energy as a share of its total mix. Meanwhile, the US has dropped below zero to around -10%, indicating its net exporter status.

A third chart, A shift in energy intensive manufacturing to the emerging world, illustrates the percentage of global production for key sectors from the late 1990s to 2023. Across manufacturing, ammonia, steel, cement, and plastic, the share of global production has dramatically shifted from developed to emerging economies; for example, developed economies' share of steel fell from roughly 60% in 1998 to 15% in 2023, and cement fell to less than 10%.

The fourth chart compares Natural gas proven reserves vs consumption in 2023. It plots proven reserves in trillion cubic meters against consumption in billion cubic meters for major nations. The United States stands out with extremely high consumption near 900 billion cubic meters but relatively modest reserves around 12 trillion cubic meters, while Russia and Iran hold massive reserves around 37 and 32 trillion cubic meters, respectively, with lower consumption. China is positioned with low reserves around 7 trillion cubic meters and moderate-to-high consumption near 400 billion cubic meters, explaining its ongoing pipeline negotiations with Russia and Turkmenistan. The author notes that China's gas imports are projected to reach 250 billion cubic meters by 2030, up from 170 billion cubic meters in 2023, though almost all of this is already secured by contracts.

The final two charts focus on Taiwan’s energy vulnerability. The Net imports of fossil fuels as a share of primary energy consumption bar chart lists the world’s most import-dependent nations, placing Singapore, Hong Kong, Morocco, and Taiwan at the top, with Taiwan importing roughly 90% of its fossil fuel needs. This vulnerability is linked to the final chart, Taiwan nuclear share of electricity generation, which shows nuclear energy's share of Taiwan's power generation peaking near 50% in the mid-1980s before steadily collapsing to just 5% by 2023. The author questions this strategic decision, noting that it severely exposes Taiwan to economic devastation in the event of a Chinese blockade.

In this analysis of China's energy transition, Michael Cembalest discusses China's status as a renewable energy powerhouse, accounting for fifty to sixty percent of all global new renewable capacity additions. However, he emphasizes that this green expansion is supplementing rather than displacing legacy fossil fuels. China's absolute coal consumption and overall emissions continue to rise, even as coal's relative share of final energy and electricity generation declines. 

This trend is visualized in a chart of China's final energy consumption by type from 2000 to the early 2020s, measured in exajoules. While the coal share of this total fell from 70 percent in 2000 to 57 percent by the end of the period, the absolute volume of coal consumed nearly doubled as other sources like wind, solar, and hydro expanded. Similarly, a chart of China's electricity generation by source, measured in terawatt-hours, shows that although coal's share of total generation dropped from 78 percent in 2000 to 61 percent by the early 2020s, total electricity generation grew so rapidly—surging from around 1,300 to nearly 9,000 terawatt-hours—that absolute coal-fired generation still grew dramatically. 

Two comparative line charts illustrate the divergence in energy pathways between China, the United States, and Europe from 1990 to 2025. The first, detailing fossil fuel final energy consumption in exajoules, highlights China's dramatic rise from under 30 exajoules to over 85, while the United States remains relatively flat around 50 and Europe slowly declines to around 35. The second chart traces greenhouse gas emissions from energy, showing China's emissions soaring from approximately 2 billion tons to over 12 billion tons, far outstripping the stable or declining emissions profiles of the United States and Europe. 

The dominance of coal in China's mix is further emphasized by a bar chart measuring global coal capacity additions and retirements in gigawatts from 2000 to the first half of 2024. This visual highlights how China's net coal capacity additions, represented by large red bars, consistently dwarf the net retirements from the United States and the European Union, which are represented by smaller downward-facing blue bars. 

Finally, a line chart tracking global hydropower generation from 1965 to 2025 in terawatt-hours shows that China has been responsible for 60 percent of global hydropower growth since 1995. During this same period, OECD hydropower generation has remained almost entirely flat at roughly 1,400 terawatt-hours. The text notes that while Oak Ridge Labs identified a potential 9,000 terawatt-hours per year of untapped US hydro capacity in municipal water systems and irrigation canals, this would represent only a modest 4 percent increase in existing US hydro generation.

In this section of the publication, the author evaluates the stark disconnect between the theoretical promise of carbon capture and storage (CCS) and its real-world implementation. The commentary argues that while academic and research interest in CCS is exceptionally high, actual deployment is extremely limited. The fundamental challenge lies in the physics of emissions: the power sectors that generate the vast majority of industrial carbon dioxide emissions, such as coal and natural gas power plants, also produce flue gas streams with some of the lowest concentrations of carbon dioxide, making capture expensive and complex. Real-world projects consistently fall short of the industry-standard 90 percent capture targets, leading the author to note that even cash-rich tech companies like Meta, which is planning a 10 billion dollar Louisiana data center powered by gas and CCS, cannot easily alter the physical and financial realities of carbon capture, potentially establishing a high price point that other, more price-sensitive companies cannot afford.

The first chart on the page, titled "The highest ratio in the history of science," illustrates the disconnect between academic interest and real-world utility by tracking carbon capture research citations per year divided by million tons of annual global operational CCS capacity. This ratio has risen steadily from about 2,400 in 2015 to over 4,100 by 2023, reflecting a massive surge in academic literature without a corresponding rise in operational scale.

A second chart titled "Current vs planned carbon capture capacity by 2030" reveals that even if planned capacity is built, it will represent only a tiny fraction of global emissions. Globally, current capacity is around 50 million tonnes per annum, and planned capacity would bring this to just over 300 million tonnes, representing only 1.0 percent of current global emissions. In the United States, current capacity is roughly 25 million tonnes, with plans to expand to around 120 million tonnes, which would still only account for 2.0 percent of current U.S. emissions. Europe's planned expansions would bring its capacity to about 80 million tonnes, or 1.8 percent of its current emissions, while China's planned capacity remains negligible at roughly 0.1 percent of its current emissions.

The fundamental operational mismatch is highlighted across two middle charts. The first, detailing "Annual US GHG emissions from industrial sector" in million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, shows that coal power plants produce approximately 750 million tonnes and natural gas power plants produce about 600 million tonnes, dwarf-ing all other sectors. In contrast, sectors like ammonia and ethanol produce only about 30 and 20 million tonnes, respectively. However, the adjacent chart, "CO2 concentration in flue gas streams," shows that natural gas power plants and coal-fired plants have extremely low concentrations of carbon dioxide in their flue gas, generally under 15 percent. Meanwhile, sectors with much lower total emissions, such as ammonia processing, ethanol biomass fermentation, and natural gas processing, feature carbon dioxide concentrations near 100 percent, making them far easier and cheaper to target for capture.

The final chart, titled "Real-world CO2 capture," shows that real-world operations capture a far lower percentage of total emissions than the standard 90 percent target assumption. Among coal plants, Petra Nova captures 65 percent of emissions from flue gas, but this drops to around 40 percent when factoring in the power required to run the capture system, while the Boundary Dam project captures about 55 percent. In natural gas processing, capture rates range from 75 percent at the Terrell facility to just 10 percent at the Century plant, with Gorgon capturing roughly 35 percent. Hydrogen production facilities, including Quest and Air Products, capture between 45 percent and 55 percent. Gasification projects like Great Plains and Coffeyville capture 45 percent and 30 percent, respectively. Fertilizer plants like Enid and PCS Nitrogen hover around 30 percent capture. Bonanza Bioenergy, an ethanol project, achieves a higher capture rate of about 70 percent due to its highly concentrated stream, while the Emirates Steel project captures roughly 40 percent.

This page focuses on the market penetration, manufacturing costs, and consumer trends shaping the transition to electric vehicles (EVs). Globally, EVs comprise approximately 20% of new passenger car sales but represent only about 4% of the total vehicle fleet on the road. The transition is highly uneven across regions, with China leading the pack and approaching a tipping point, while other major automotive markets experience significant dispersion. At the same time, declining lithium-ion battery prices and the shift toward cobalt- and nickel-free battery chemistries are helping to manage manufacturing costs, even as the US market remains heavily dominated by larger light-duty vehicle classes like SUVs and pickups.

Several charts support these observations. The first chart, tracking global passenger vehicles from 2015 to 2024, highlights the gap between sales and fleet integration: the EV share of new vehicle sales rose steeply from nearly zero in 2015 to around 20% in 2024, while the EV share of vehicles actually on the road climbed much more gradually to reach just 4% in 2024. 

The regional divergence is detailed in the next two charts, which cover the years 2020 to 2024. Looking at the EV share of passenger vehicle sales, China stands out, surpassing 40% by 2024. European nations like the UK and France follow with sales shares between 25% and 30%, though Germany’s share experienced a decline to around 20% in 2024. The US and South Korea trail at roughly 10%, while Italy, Japan, and India lag near or below 5%. These dynamics translate to very different rates of fleet turnover, as shown in the fleet share chart; by 2024, EVs made up about 10% of the passenger vehicle fleet in China, compared to roughly 7% in Germany, 5% in the UK and France, less than 3% in the US, and under 2% in Japan and India.

The economic drivers of this transition are illustrated in the remaining charts. A chart on lithium-ion battery pack prices shows a dramatic decline in volume-weighted average prices, falling from nearly $800 per kWh in 2013 to just over $100 per kWh in 2024, with only a temporary plateau during the 2022 supply chain disruptions. 

To explain why automakers increasingly prefer Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries over chemistry options like Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide (NMC) or Lithium Nickel Cobalt Aluminum Oxide (NCA), another chart plots the estimated metal costs for a 60 kWh battery from 2020 through early 2025. It shows that because LFP batteries do not require expensive cobalt or nickel, their metal costs have consistently remained much lower, hovering around $500 in 2024 after peaking near $1,200 in 2022. By comparison, NMC and NCA chemistry metal costs peaked above $3,000 in 2022 and settled between $1,000 and $1,200 by early 2025. 

Finally, a chart on US new light-duty vehicles by type from 1975 to 2024 highlights a structural challenge for EV adoption in the United States. Traditional cars have steadily shrunk from about 80% of the market in 1975 to roughly 20% today, while SUVs, pickup trucks, and vans have risen to account for nearly 80% of all US light-duty vehicle sales, necessitating larger, more resource-intensive batteries to power the vehicle types preferred by American consumers.

This page examines real-world research regarding plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV) emissions reductions and electric vehicle (EV) collision repair costs, arguing that actual PHEV emissions are understated and that higher EV repair costs must be factored into lifetime total ownership assessments. 

The first chart, illustrating average carbon dioxide emissions from internal combustion engine (ICE), PHEV, and battery electric vehicle (BEV) cars in grams of CO2 per kilometer, reveals a stark gap between estimates and reality. While the European Union’s official PHEV estimate sits at roughly 70 grams of CO2 per kilometer, real-world data shows PHEV emissions are actually close to 140 grams per kilometer—not far below gasoline ICE emissions at approximately 170 grams per kilometer. In contrast, BEV emissions in Germany and the United Kingdom, which account for local grid mixes, are much lower at approximately 50 and 40 grams of CO2 per kilometer, respectively. 

An accompanying mileage contribution chart for light-duty vehicles explains this discrepancy. It shows that the average PHEV is driven mostly on fuel, consuming about 5.1 liters of fuel per 100 kilometers compared to just 1.1 liters equivalent of electric power. Even among the top 25 percent of PHEV drivers, fuel use still dominates at 3.8 liters versus 1.3 liters equivalent of electric power, demonstrating that these vehicles are largely operated like conventional ICE cars rather than battery-powered ones. 

The bottom half of the page addresses collision repairs. A chart tracking the frequency of repairable claims from 2020 to 2024 shows that while EV repairs are less frequent—with claims for ICE vehicles with small batteries hovering around 4.0 percent while BEVs and PHEVs rise more slowly to about 2.5 percent and 1.25 percent by 2024—they are significantly more expensive. According to Mitchell International data, the average repair cost for BEVs fluctuated between $5,500 and nearly $7,000, ending 2024 near $5,800, which is consistently higher than PHEVs and conventional ICE vehicles, which sit closer to $5,000. 

These findings are corroborated by a November 2023 Solera study comparing the Hyundai Kona EV to its ICE counterpart across 92,000 insurance claims in 20 countries. Solera found that overall EV collision repair costs are on average 29 percent higher than those for ICE vehicles, driven by EV parts costs that are 48 percent higher. The EV battery system represents the single highest parts cost, making up 24 percent of the total EV parts cost, while driver airbag systems, rear bumper absorbers, and rear bumper reinforcements are also replaced more frequently on EVs.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" energy paper explores the unintended consequences of Europe’s transition toward renewable energy, focusing heavily on Germany's grid challenges and their regional spillover effects. The central argument is that Germany's decision to decommission nuclear power in favor of intermittent wind and solar has created severe grid vulnerabilities, increased reliance on imports, and forced a costly duplication of power generation capacity across Europe. These issues have strained political relations, leading to Sweden rejecting a new interconnector project with Germany and contributing to the collapse of the Norwegian government in January over European energy market rules.

The page features four charts that illustrate these dynamics. The first two, situated side-by-side at the top, demonstrate the immediate impact of a "Dunkelflaute"—a period of low wind and solar output—from mid-November to mid-December 2024. The left-hand chart plots German electricity generation and load in thousands of megawatts. While electricity demand consistently fluctuates between approximately 50,000 MW and 75,000 MW, wind power generation collapses to near zero during a period labeled "Die Dunkelflaute," with solar, hydro, and biomass unable to fill the gap. The adjacent right-hand chart shows how this localized supply collapse caused electricity prices to soar across Europe, with wholesale rates in Germany, the Netherlands, Southern Norway, and Eastern Norway/Oslo spiking from baseline levels of around 50 to 100 EUR/MWh to peaks of nearly 350 to 400 EUR/MWh in mid-December.

The bottom-left chart tracks German monthly cross-border physical electricity flows in TWh from 2015 through late 2024. It highlights a structural reversal: between 2015 and late 2022, Germany was a consistent net exporter of electricity, with outward flows regularly peaking near negative 4 to 6 TWh. Following its nuclear shutdowns, Germany became a net importer, with physical net imports rising sharply to peak near 4 TWh in late 2023 and 2024. 

The bottom-right chart illustrates the concept of capacity duplication, which the author identifies as a key driver of higher European electricity prices. Spanning 2010 to 2024, the chart shows that even as electricity generation falls, installed capacity is rising in both the UK and Germany to compensate for renewable intermittency. German generation declined from nearly 600 TWh in 2010 to under 500 TWh by 2024, while its installed capacity climbed from about 170 GW to roughly 270 GW over the same period. A similar trend is evident in the UK, where generation fell from approximately 370 TWh to around 270 TWh, while capacity rose from about 90 GW to 110 GW. The author warns that this costly requirement to build double the capacity for less actual power generation is a structural byproduct of decarbonization that may become increasingly common.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 15th Annual Energy Paper analyzes the adoption dynamics of electric light-duty vehicles, commercial fleets, and heavy trucks, highlighting China's global dominance, battery price advantages, and evolving chemistry trends. It also highlights a critical decoupling of US gasoline demand from vehicle miles traveled, suggesting that US gasoline consumption has structurally peaked. 

The first chart, focusing on global light-duty vehicles under 3.5 tonnes for commercial use, shows that the EV share of new vehicle sales has risen steeply from around 1% in 2020 to approximately 8.5% in 2024. However, the EV share of total vehicles on the road remains very low, crawling from near-zero in 2020 to only about 1.5% in 2024. The second chart illustrates that China is the global leader in electrifying medium and heavy trucks, with its EV share of truck sales surging from about 1% in 2020 to over 5.5% in 2024. In comparison, Europe stands at roughly 2.2% in 2024, the global average is around 1.6%, and the US lags far behind at less than 0.5%.

The third and fourth charts identify the economic and technological drivers behind China's leadership. The third chart shows that lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cell prices in China, averaging roughly $53 per kilowatt-hour in 2024 year-to-date, cost nearly half of the 2023 global average of $95 per kilowatt-hour. Meanwhile, the fourth chart illustrates the unique infrastructure strategy supporting heavy trucks in China; of the more than 30,000 battery-electric heavy-duty trucks sold in 2023 (up from fewer than 5,000 in 2020), roughly half utilize battery swapping instead of charging only. 

The fifth chart shows that LFP has increasingly dominated the battery chemistry for electric and fuel cell medium and heavy-duty trucks, with its share of capacity deployed expanding from around 55% in 2020 to nearly 80% in the first half of 2024, displacing nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) and other chemistries. Despite this, NMC chemistry continues to drive performance improvements. The author notes that since 2017, EV truck ranges have improved from 100 kilometers to 200 kilometers, with energy densities reaching 195 to 250 watt-hours per kilogram, and some producers aim to introduce packs with energy densities of 280 to 300 watt-hours per kilogram in the near future. 

Finally, the sixth chart compares US gasoline consumption with vehicle miles traveled from 1970 through late 2024. Historically, the two metrics moved closely in parallel. However, following the pandemic, vehicle miles traveled fully recovered to reach new peaks near 280 billion miles, whereas gasoline demand peaked in 2018 at over 9,000 thousand barrels per day and has failed to recover, sitting closer to 8,500 thousand barrels per day. This divergence confirms that US gasoline demand has decoupled from driving activity, likely due to fleet fuel efficiency gains and electrification.

This page focuses on the energy landscape and industrial challenges facing Europe, with a particular emphasis on manufacturing declines in the United Kingdom and Germany, rising tensions over European Union environmental regulations, and the progress of renewable electricity integration across the continent. 

The author begins by analyzing the structural economic challenges in the United Kingdom and Germany, which are both seeing sharp declines in manufacturing output and employment. The commentary casts doubt on British Labor Prime Minister Keir Starmer's vision for the UK to become an artificial intelligence hub. This ambition is contrasted against harsh energy realities, including just 12 days of natural gas storage supply, declining dispatchable power, high reliance on energy imports, a 50-year low in offshore gas production, and soaring electricity costs. This vulnerability is further exacerbated by the UK government's plans to shut down aging nuclear plants by 2028, ban fracking in the Lincolnshire shale formations, and rapidly transition to clean power by 2030.

Two line charts support this analysis of industrial decline, indexing seasonally adjusted manufacturing data to a baseline of 100 in January 2021. The first chart, depicting European manufacturing industrial production, shows that by late 2024, the United Kingdom had dropped to an index level of approximately 90, and Germany had fallen below 95. In contrast, France, Italy, and Spain maintained higher levels, hovering between 100 and 105. The second chart, tracking European manufacturing employment, reveals a similar divergence. Germany's employment index fell below 98 by the third quarter of 2024, and the UK remained flat around 100, while Spain and Italy saw their indices rise to roughly 106 and 105, respectively.

The text also details regulatory friction resulting from the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, set to take effect in 2027. Under this directive, large companies operating in the EU could face fines up to 5% of global revenues for non-compliance with carbon emission and human rights standards across their entire global supply chains. In response, Qatar, which supplied 14% of Europe’s imported liquefied natural gas in 2023, has threatened to halt all LNG exports to the EU. The rules would require Qatar to perform due diligence on an estimated 100,000 separate companies in its supply chain. The author notes that a recent Omnibus bill, if approved, could scale back the scope, reporting demands, and enforcement mechanisms of this directive.

The page concludes with a detailed table tracking the renewable shares of electricity generation by country from 2019 to 2024. Overall, the renewable share for Europe grew steadily from 37% in 2019 to 51% in 2024. Performance varied widely by nation. Austria reached 100% renewable generation in 2024, up from 76% in 2019, while Norway consistently exceeded 100% due to its hydro-dominated grid. Spain grew its share from 38% to 64%, Germany increased from 43% to 54%, and the UK rose from 32% to 44%. Conversely, Eastern European countries like Czechia and Hungary started from lower baselines and reached only 16% and 25% renewable shares, respectively, by 2024.

In this section of the J.P. Morgan energy paper, Michael Cembalest assesses whether a true "Nuclear Renaissance" is underway, examining the deep financial, regulatory, and supply chain hurdles facing the United States nuclear sector. The author questions whether new US regulations will make a difference, noting that the industry has much to prove to investors and regulators given that nuclear projects suffer from some of the worst cost overruns of all megaprojects. To illustrate this, the text points to Vogtle 3 in Georgia, which was completed in 2023 after extensive delays and overruns but was offline for 9.5 of its first 48 weeks in 2024 due to equipment failures. Additionally, the US is highly reliant on imported uranium and lacks domestic supply of high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU), which has delayed Bill Gates’ Terrapower project in Wyoming to around 2030 while the Department of Energy attempts to build out a HALEU availability program.

Four charts support these observations. The first, illustrating capital cost and construction time of nuclear plants, compares Western projects with non-Western projects in terms of millions of US dollars per megawatt versus construction years. It demonstrates that Western projects—such as Vogtle 3 & 4 in the US, Hinkley Point C in the UK, Flamanville 3 in France, and Olkiluoto 3 in Finland—suffer from extremely high capital costs ranging from 8 million to nearly 18 million dollars per megawatt and require 10 to nearly 20 years to build. In contrast, non-Western projects like China’s Fang 4, South Korea’s Saeul 1 & 2, and the UAE’s Barakah 1-4 are far cheaper, costing under 5 million dollars per megawatt, and are completed within 5 to 11 years. The second chart shows average nuclear plant completion times by year of construction start, indicating that completion times for developed countries have generally risen since the 1960s, with Vogtle 3 & 4 taking over 12 years. The third chart displays average megaproject cost overruns by sector using the Flyvbjerg database, showing that nuclear power and nuclear storage projects experience average cost overruns of over 100%, trailing only Olympic games and nuclear storage, while solar power projects experience average overruns of just 1%. The final chart tracks US production versus imports of uranium oxide from 1949 to 2019, illustrating that domestic production has dwindled to nearly zero, leaving the US almost entirely reliant on imports to meet its uranium needs.

The second half of the page focuses on nuclear plant reopenings in the US, highlighting Holtec’s plans to reopen the 53-year-old Palisades plant in Michigan, which would be the first plant to begin decommissioning and then restart. Other notable projects include a joint plan by Microsoft and Constellation Energy to reopen the 50-year-old Three Mile Island reactor #1 in 2028 to source power at roughly 100 dollars per megawatt-hour, and NextEra’s efforts to restart the 45-year-old Duane Arnold plant in Iowa, which was shut down in 2020. Despite public interest, the author cautions that the cost and timing of these reopenings are highly uncertain. Many older plants are unlikely to receive modern operating licenses due to evolving safety standards, and skeptics have pointed to Holtec's lack of experience with operational nuclear plants. Ultimately, Cembalest predicts that once decommissioning begins in earnest, restarts become too expensive, meaning these efforts will likely be limited to the Palisades, Three Mile Island, and Duane Arnold sites, alongside uncompleted projects like VC Summer in South Carolina or barely decommissioned sites like San Onofre in California, all of which will likely require massive subsidies to succeed.

This page discusses the environmental debates surrounding crop-based biofuels and the steep thermodynamic challenges of producing synthetic alternatives like e-methane. The author explains that while biofuels are intended to reduce aviation emissions, crop cultivation often displaces food production, driving deforestation and releasing stored carbon. Synthetic fuels avoid these land-use conflicts but suffer from a severe negative energy balance. 

To illustrate this, a column chart shows the energy inputs and outputs required to produce one kilogram of e-methane via the Sabatier reaction. The chart demonstrates that generating 50 megajoules of synthetic methane requires a massive 150 megajoules of energy input. This "Energy in" stack is dominated by electrolysis for green hydrogen, which requires 55 kilowatt-hours of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen. The remaining energy goes toward the Sabatier reaction (operating at 75 percent efficiency) and direct air carbon capture (DACC), which requires 366 kilowatt-hours of electricity and 5.25 gigajoules of thermal heat per ton of carbon dioxide. 

A supporting table outlines the thermodynamic and heat potentials of various molecules to show why reassembling carbon dioxide into fuel is so energy-intensive. Carbon dioxide sits at the very bottom of the thermodynamic hierarchy with an extremely low Gibbs free energy of -394 kilojoules per mole and zero heating value. In contrast, target fuel molecules have much higher energy potentials; methane has a Gibbs free energy of -51 kilojoules per mole and a heating value of 890 kilojoules per mole (56 megajoules per kilogram), while hydrogen boasts a heating value of 142 megajoules per kilogram. Other organic molecules in the table, such as octane, decane, and propane, also have high heating values (44, 44, and 46 megajoules per kilogram, respectively) compared to carbon dioxide's zero. 

The author concludes that any commercial synthetic fuel pathway must overcome this steep thermodynamic deficit. He advises investors to exercise caution and thoroughly understand these thermodynamic realities before backing sustainable aviation fuel pathways. The page references analysis and reports from Spitfire Research, Keith et al., Peter Edwards of Oxford, the Engineering Toolbox, the International Council on Clean Transport, the International Civil Aviation Association, and the Union for Concerned Scientists.

This page from the publication discusses the immense cost, constraint, and chemical hurdles associated with the production of renewable jet fuels and broader biofuels. The core argument is that despite multiple technical pathways for production—such as fermenting plant sugars, anaerobic digestion, or transforming animal and vegetable oils—biofuels remain too expensive and raw-material-constrained to scale. Aside from Brazil and Indonesia, biofuels constitute less than one percent of final energy consumption globally. 

A bar chart titled "Biofuels as a share of final energy consumption" quantifies this, showing Brazil leading at nearly 4.5 percent and Indonesia around 3.5 percent, while the United States sits at roughly 1.3 percent, and all other listed nations (including major European, Asian, and Middle Eastern economies) fall well below the one percent mark. 

For aviation specifically, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) accounted for a mere 0.3 percent of global jet fuel consumption in 2024. The chemical requirements for aviation are more stringent than for ground transit; jet engines demand highly specific molecules with only trace oxygen content. The cost challenge is visualized in the chart "Renewable jet fuel cost estimates," which plots several SAF pathways against the baseline price of fossil jet fuel, represented by a red line at approximately $2 to $3 per gallon. In comparison, NREL and third-party estimates show that HEFA (food oils), alcohol-to-jet, and gasification options mostly cost between $5 and $10 per gallon, while power-to-liquids (synthetic fuels) soar even higher, ranging between $15 and $22 per gallon. 

These severe price premiums are forcing commercial airlines to rethink their voluntary decarbonization commitments. Notably, in July 2024, Air New Zealand became the first major airline to retract its 2030 emissions-cut goal, blaming the lack of affordable SAF. This disconnect is highlighted in the "Global sustainable aviation fuel usage" chart, which contrasts a ambitious straight-line airline target aiming for 10 percent of commercial fuel consumption by 2030 against the flatline of actual usage, which remains stuck near zero percent. 

The financial consequences of these headwinds are detailed in the text and the final chart, "Biofuel company returns." Major energy conglomerates like Chevron, BP, and Shell are scaling back their organic waste biofuel projects, and United Airlines-backed startup Fulcrum BioEnergy has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. The indexed stock returns chart (starting at 100 in January 2022) demonstrates a sector-wide collapse by early 2025. Listed companies such as Neste, Green Plains, Gevo, Aemetis, OPAL, and FutureFuel have all suffered severe declines, with many trading down to index levels of 20 to 40. REX is the single positive outlier, maintaining an index value around 120.

This page from the J.P. Morgan report "Heliocentrism: 15th Annual Energy Paper," written by Michael Cembalest, focuses on the global "Nuclear Renaissance" and presents a detailed collection of charts analyzing historical builds, regional generation trends, plant age distributions, and capacity factors. The author notes that apart from the Georgia Vogtle plants, the United States has seen no new nuclear construction starts since the late 1970s. Internationally, France's nuclear output has been depressed by operational outages and low water levels, Germany's nuclear generation has hit zero, and Japan has reopened only 14 of its 33 operable reactors shut after the Fukushima disaster, with another 11 awaiting approval. In contrast, China's nuclear sector is expanding rapidly, with generation expected to reach 700 Terawatt-hours (TWh) when accounting for projects currently under development.

The first chart, titled "# of US nuclear plants built by year of construction start," shows a massive wave of construction starts beginning in the late 1960s and peaking in the early 1970s at over 25 plants started in a single year, before falling sharply to zero by 1980.

The second chart, "Nuclear generation by country" measured in Terawatt-hours, tracks output from 1965 to 2025. It shows the United States leading globally, peaking above 800 TWh. China shows exponential growth starting in the 2010s, rising toward 400 TWh. France, historically the second largest producer, has declined to around 300 TWh. Japan's generation collapsed to near zero in 2011 and has recovered only slightly, while Germany's output has steadily declined to zero.

The third chart, "Age distribution of existing nuclear reactors" by gigawatts (GW) of capacity, compares the US, Europe, and Emerging Markets by plant age. The US and European fleets are highly mature, with most capacity concentrated in plants that are 35 to 50 years old. Emerging Markets show a starkly different profile, with a young fleet concentrated in the 5 to 10-year-old range.

The fourth chart displays the "Nuclear global average capacity factor" from 1970 to 2020. This metric has risen from a low of around 56% in 1980 to a sustained level of 80% to 85% through the 2010s and 2020s. A 2023 breakdown by reactor type lists boiling water reactors at a 90% capacity factor, pressurized water and heavy-water at 80%, light-water at 75%, and fast neutron & gas-cooled reactors at 70%.

The final chart, "Nuclear global mean capacity factor by age of reactor" from 2019 to 2023, reinforces the author's observation that nuclear capacity factors do not differ much by age. While there is a moderate dip to around 73% for reactors aged 25 years, the capacity factor rebounds, remaining mostly between 75% and 95% and exceeding 90% even for reactors that are 50 to 55 years old.

This page from the publication analyzes the various chemical and industrial pathways currently used or proposed by green aviation fuel start-ups to produce sustainable aviation fuel. While these pathways are functional under laboratory conditions, the author emphasizes that their commercial feasibility is heavily constrained by real-world energy deficits, high all-in costs, and technological scalability challenges. 

The main visual on the page is a flowchart titled "Sustainable jet fuel pathways," sourced from Spitfire Research and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. This diagram maps the production routes starting from feedstocks like food oils, corn, sugarcane, cellulosic biomass, and water combined with electricity. The most direct route shown is the hydrotreating of food oils to create jet fuel. Other pathways transition through intermediate stages, such as fermenting sugarcane or corn into ethanol and butanol, which are dehydrated into olefins and then oligomerized into jet fuel. More complex paths convert cellulosic biomass, water, and electricity into intermediate gases like biogenic carbon dioxide, green hydrogen, and methane. These gases undergo processes like electrolysis, reverse water gas shift, or gasification to create syngas, which is then processed through either Fischer-Tropsch synthesis or methanol-to-olefins synthesis to ultimately yield jet fuel.

The text details five primary pathways and their respective bottlenecks. The first is the hydrotreating of food oils, known as HEFA, which processes triglyceride feedstocks like palm oil, soybean oil, and used cooking oil. Although it is the most mature and commercially deployed pathway, its major challenge is that limited feedstock supply could cause costs to skyrocket under higher utilization.
