The first chart, titled "Municipal bonds, cash and 60 Minutes," displays a total return index from September 2010 to July 2011, indexed to 100 on December 19, 2010. It shows that while a representative intermediate-duration tax-free municipal bond fund dipped to around 99 in January 2011 following Whitney’s interview, it rebounded sharply to over 106 by July 2011, vastly outperforming a representative municipal money market fund which stayed flat at 100.

To prove Detroit’s unique economic vulnerability, the author includes two comparison charts with percentile bands representing other U.S. cities. The first, "Growth in Gross Metropolitan Product" (indexed to 2001=100), shows Detroit’s economic growth line flatlining and dropping below the 5th percentile band around 2005, remaining near 100 by 2011 while the 95th percentile grew to nearly 190. The second, "Labor force growth (employed + unemployed)" (indexed to Jan 2000=100), illustrates Detroit's labor force steadily shrinking to about 85 by 2012, well below the 5th percentile band.

The author concludes that Whitney's dire projections were incorrect, noting that the average five-year municipal default rate since 2012 has been a mere 0.1 percent. Furthermore, an indicative intermediate-duration tax-free municipal bond fund generated 7.5 times the return of a municipal money market fund from 2011 to 2021, proving that credit risk did not harm the performance of longer-duration municipal bonds.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses how equity markets behave during US recessions, presenting the argument that equities tend to bottom well before most other economic indicators. The page features a central chart titled "Equities tend to bottom first during recessions," which plots the timing of the worst readings for various indicators across seven major historical recessions: the Eisenhower recession, the 1970s stagflation, the 1980s double dip, the 1990s S&L crisis, the DotCom crash, the Global Financial Crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic. The horizontal axis measures the number of months since the beginning of each recession, ranging from negative eight to thirty-two months. 

The chart tracks several specific indicators: equities, the ISM manufacturing survey, GDP, industrial production, payrolls, S&P earnings, housing starts, high yield default rates, real estate delinquencies, and the official end of the recession. Across almost all of these historical periods, equities, represented by red diamonds, hit their lowest point earliest, often within the first twelve months of the recession. The indicator most closely aligned with this equity bottom is the ISM manufacturing survey. 

The notable exception to this rule is the 2001–2002 DotCom tech collapse, labeled on the chart as "the exception," where equities bottomed last, nearly twenty months after the recession began and long after other metrics like housing starts and GDP had already bottomed. Ultimately, the author emphasizes that because equities bottom so early in the cycle, investors must expect economic and market news to still be deeply negative when financial assets are at their absolute lowest and most attractive prices.

This page argues that geopolitical events are generally poor signals for equity market performance, advising investors to focus on indicators of growth, jobs, profits, and confidence rather than policy uncertainty or geopolitical risk. 

The top half of the page features a line chart plotting the S&P 500 Index over the twelve months following a variety of military invasions and conflicts since 1950, with the index set to 100 at the start of each conflict. An accompanying table lists twenty of these historical events, ranging from the Korean War in 1950 to the Israel-Gaza War in 2023. The chart highlights that only two major post-WWII conflicts were followed by substantial market declines a year after they began. The first was the September 11, 2001 attacks, which saw the index drop to around 80 points after twelve months, though this decline was largely driven by the dot-com collapse. The second and only conflict that directly caused a lasting US market decline was the 1973 Arab-Israeli War; triggered by an oil embargo and energy crisis, it drove the S&P 500 down to nearly 60 points after twelve months. In contrast, after the 2022 Russia-Ukraine War, the index stood at about 95 points after a year, and after the 2023 Israel-Gaza War, it rose to approximately 130 points.

To identify which market signals actually matter, the bottom table analyzes monthly data from January 1985 to August 2017, comparing average monthly S&P 500 returns when an indicator is above average versus when it is below average to find the monthly excess return. The data shows that indicators tracking economic health and business confidence are the most valuable. The Leading Indicator Index provides the strongest signal with a 1.2% monthly excess return (1.6% return when above average versus 0.4% when below), followed closely by the CEO Confidence Index at 1.1% excess, payroll growth at 0.9% excess, and GDP growth at 0.7% excess. Conversely, policy and geopolitical measures offer the least value. The Economic Policy Uncertainty Index shows a negative excess return of -0.2%, and the Geopolitical Risk Index shows a negative excess return of -0.1%, demonstrating that tracking geopolitical headlines is of little use to long-term investors.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" discusses the critical role of diversification in mitigating the risks of concentrated stock portfolios and highlighting the benefits of hedge fund diversification. The author, Michael Cembalest, references J.P. Morgan’s "Agony & the Ecstasy" study, which analyzed concentrated stock positions and tracked "negative index removals" due to business distress in the S&P 500 since 1980, ignoring benign removals from mergers or acquisitions. The page notes that there were approximately 320 negative removals over this period, mostly occurring in the consumer discretionary, technology, and financial sectors. A review of Russell 3000 business failures since 1980 reveals that many were caused by factors outside management control, such as changes in government policy, commodity price shifts, technological obsolescence, competitor expansion, and intellectual property infringement. 

Two charts at the top of the page illustrate these S&P 500 distress-based removals from 1980 to 2013. The left bar chart, titled "Number of companies removed from the S&P 500 due to distress by year," shows that while removals spike during recessions—such as peaks of over 25 companies in 2001 and 2008—there remains a steady pulse of business failures during non-recession years. The right line chart, "Cumulative number of companies removed from the S&P 500 due to distress," displays a steady, upward-sloping accumulation of distressed company removals, reaching over 300 by 2013. 

The bottom half of the page shifts to the benefits of hedge fund diversification. Cembalest argues that while individual hedge funds can exhibit high volatility, a portfolio approach with even minimal diversification can yield strong outcomes. Two scatter plots analyze the performance of randomly generated portfolios consisting of just four hedge funds from 2012 to 2014, plotting annualized return against annualized volatility. The first scatter plot on the bottom left, titled "Relative value hedge funds," shows most of these four-fund portfolios clustered in a region that outperformed the Barclays Aggregate Index (represented by a red square), boasting an 84% success rate within the main highlighted volatility band and a 97% overall success rate. The second scatter plot on the bottom right, "Market-neutral and other low vol long-short equity HFs," demonstrates a similar trend, showing success rates of 79% and 95% relative to the Barclays Aggregate Index. The text notes that this analysis was repeated in J.P. Morgan's 2023 Alternative Investments Review using HFRI and Pivotal Path data from 2018 to 2023, confirming that 78% to 95% of randomly generated 20-fund hedge fund portfolios outperformed stock-bond benchmarks with the same level of volatility.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market argues that credit markets are highly forward-looking, meaning that credit spreads peak and asset prices bottom out well before defaults and delinquencies actually reach their maximum levels during a crisis. To support this observation, the author presents historical data from two major periods of economic distress: the Savings and Loan crisis of the early 1990s and the Global Financial Crisis of 2008.

The first chart, titled Savings and Loan Crisis, tracks high yield credit spreads and cumulative defaults from 1987 to 1993. The left vertical axis measures the spread-to-worst from 0 to 1,200 basis points, while the right vertical axis shows cumulative defaults represented by the number of issuers from 0 to 300. The blue line for high yield credit spreads shows a sharp climb that peaked in late 1990 at approximately 1,100 basis points. At this peak, marked by a dot on the brown cumulative defaults line, only 55% of eventual corporate defaults had actually taken place, demonstrating that the market anticipated the bulk of the pain before it formally materialized. 

The second chart, titled Financial crisis, displays a similar relationship for high yield credit spreads and cumulative defaults from 2006 to 2013. The left axis measures spread-to-worst from 0 to 2,500 basis points, and the right axis tracks cumulative defaults via issuer counts from 0 to 250. High yield credit spreads spiked dramatically to a peak of roughly 2,200 basis points in late 2008. At this precise turning point, only 30% of the eventual cumulative corporate defaults had occurred, showing an even larger lead time for market pricing relative to actual defaults than in the 1990 crisis.

The third chart, CMBS spreads vs. delinquency rates: 2006 to 2014, plots the AAA Commercial Mortgage-Backed Securities (CMBS) spread on the left axis (from 0 to 1,600 basis points) against the 60+ day delinquency rate on the right axis (from 0% to 9%). The blue line representing AAA CMBS spreads spiked to nearly 1,500 basis points in late 2008, a time when delinquency rates, shown by the brown line, were at a mere 0.5%. While spreads recovered rapidly over the subsequent years, delinquency rates continued to climb, ultimately peaking at 8.5% in late 2011 and early 2012 when spreads had already fallen back to around 200 basis points.

The final chart, Leveraged Loan prices vs. defaults: 2006 to 2011, compares the Leveraged Loan Price Index on the left axis (from 60 to 105) against the default rate on the right axis (from 0% to 9%). The blue price index line plummeted to its lowest level of approximately 62 in late 2008. At this bottom, trailing 12-month defaults (the brown line) stood at 4.5%. By the time defaults peaked at 8.0% in late 2009, the leveraged loan price index had already mounted a massive recovery to over 85. 

Data on this page is sourced from J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, Trepp, Standard and Poor’s, and the S&P/LSTA Leveraged Loan Index. Taken together, these four visual examples reinforce the author's point that waiting for defaults or delinquencies to peak before investing during a downturn means missing the major turning points in market pricing.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the changing economic linkages between the United States and China and how they relate to the historical concept of Thucydides’ Trap, wherein a rising power threatens to displace a dominant power. Political scientist Graham Allison identified sixteen such historical cases over the last 500 years, twelve of which ended in war. Although Cembalest was optimistic in 2018 that deep bilateral economic connections would prevent conflict, those ties have degraded. US-China linkages have fallen from a peak of 7.3% of combined GDP in 2014 to roughly 4% today, driven by a trade war, declining foreign direct investment, and flatlining Chinese holdings of US government debt. 

The analysis is supported by four charts. The first chart, on the top left, compares the combined economic linkages—comprising bilateral foreign direct investment stock, central bank holdings of government debt, and annual trade—of historical and potential rivals over the last 100 years. In 2014, US-China linkages peaked at over 7% of combined GDP, a level of integration vastly higher than other historical adversaries, such as France and Germany in 1930, the UK and Germany in 1930, or the US and Russia in 2014, all of which remained under 3%.

The second chart, on the top right, shows points of dispute in the US-China trade war, ranking China against developed and emerging economies on a scale from 100 (best) to 0 (worst). China ranks poorly across all categories, scoring near 10 on the Mercantilism Index, which tracks forced local production for market access, export subsidies, intellectual property theft, domestic favoritism, and foreign exchange manipulation. It also ranks very low (under 30) on issues like state control of the private sector, protection of trade secrets, intellectual property enforcement, and market barriers.

The third chart, on the bottom left, provides a detailed estimation of China’s US dollar assets in billions from 2008 to 2022. While China’s direct holdings of US-custodied Treasuries (shown in red) peaked near $1.25 trillion in 2011 and have since declined to around $800 billion, actual dollar assets are likely much higher. When factoring in Belgian treasuries (shown in light blue) representing offshore custodians like Euroclear, and reallocations into US agency debt, Brad Setser's adjusted estimate (shown in dark blue) shows China's actual dollar assets have remained relatively stable at over $2 trillion since 2015. This closely matches an alternative estimate using IMF COFER data (shown in green), which hovers around $2.25 trillion.

The fourth chart, on the bottom right, illustrates how the US conducts business in China, charting two versions of the US-China trade balance in billions of dollars from 2003 to 2023. The reported trade balance (shown in blue) shows a deep and worsening deficit, bottoming out near negative $400 billion around 2018. However, when incorporating the in-country sales of US corporate subsidiaries operating within China (shown in gold), the trade balance is significantly less negative, fluctuating between negative $100 billion and negative $150 billion. This indicates that US firms do substantial business in China, but they do so through local subsidiaries rather than direct exports, a structure that exposes them to higher risks of forced intellectual property transfer.

This page explores the rising pressure of entitlement spending on the United States federal budget, illustrating how growing mandatory outlays are crowding out critical non-defense discretionary spending and heading toward a permanent crossover point relative to federal revenues. 

The first chart, titled "What does the Federal government spend money on?", tracks entitlement spending versus non-defense discretionary spending as a percentage of GDP from 1970 through CBO projections to 2025. The data reveals that while non-defense discretionary spending has steadily declined from around 4% of GDP to roughly 3%, entitlement spending has surged from approximately 4% to nearly 12%. As a result, the ratio of entitlement spending to non-defense discretionary spending has expanded from 1.0x in 1970 to 2.0x in 1990, 3.3x in 2015, and is projected to reach 5.1x by 2025. 

The second chart, "Permanent crossover point is coming in the next decade," plots federal revenues against mandatory outlays as a percentage of GDP from 1965 to 2035. While revenues historically fluctuate between 16% and 20% of GDP, the combined total of entitlements, other mandatory outlays, and net interest is rising rapidly. This combined outlay line is projected to permanently cross above the federal revenues line in the early 2030s, highlighting a structural fiscal imbalance. 

The main text explains that when major entitlement programs were created, they lacked calibration mechanisms to align spending with national income. This unconstrained growth now crowds out non-defense discretionary investments that are vital for future economic growth, such as transportation infrastructure, education, disease control, and clean energy development. 

To address this fiscal gap, the page provides a table from Piper Sandler outlining select revenue-raising options and their projected 10-year revenue increases. The most lucrative option listed is increasing the corporate tax rate from 21% to 28%, which is estimated to raise $978 billion. Other high-yielding proposals include taxing unrealized capital gains for ultra-high-net-worth individuals to raise $503 billion, and raising the Affordable Care Act's Net Investment Income Tax to 5% for incomes over $400,000 to raise $404 billion. 

Finally, a dedicated sidebar analyzes the prospect of a national wealth tax. It reviews a March 2021 CBO assessment of Senator Elizabeth Warren’s wealth tax proposal, which was projected to raise $2.1 trillion over ten years by levying a 2% tax on net worth above $50 million and a 3% tax on net worth above $1 billion. The author cautions that wealth taxes in other nations have historically under-delivered due to evasion and avoidance, and notes that a U.S. wealth tax would face significant constitutional hurdles requiring Supreme Court adjudication. Historical footnotes add context, noting that now-popular programs like Social Security and Medicare faced intense opposition and accusations of socialism when they were first introduced by Presidents Roosevelt, Truman, and Johnson.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market addresses the efficacy and positive impacts of the COVID-19 vaccination campaign, analyzing hospitalizations, deaths, long-term cognitive impacts, comparative safety risks, and excess mortality. 

The author argues that vaccines and boosters were highly effective in preventing severe illness, citing a Commonwealth Fund estimate that vaccines prevented more than 18 million hospitalizations by December 2022. Additionally, the XBB booster from the fall of 2023 is noted to have lowered hospitalization risks by 68% compared to unboosted individuals, a figure supported by similar 70% efficacy rates reported in the Netherlands. The text also highlights the threat of "long COVID" cognitive deficits, which can be equivalent to 20 years of aging in hospitalized patients, and points out that vaccination strongly mitigated this risk, with three or more doses reducing long COVID risk by 73%. Addressing safety concerns, the author contrasts the very low risk of vaccine-induced blood clots—about 1.4 per million—with the much higher risk of contracting blood clots from a COVID-19 infection, which occurred at a rate of over 12,000 per million people.

These arguments are supported by two visual charts. The first chart on the left, titled "Vaccinated vs unvaccinated total hospitalizations and deaths from November 2021 to April 2022," displays state-level data for Virginia, Utah, California, and Minnesota. The left side of this visual tracks hospital admissions per million, showing that unvaccinated individuals experienced massive hospitalization rates—peaking near 11,000 to 13,000 in Utah and Minnesota—whereas fully vaccinated and boosted individuals remained under 2,000 admissions per million across all four states. The right side tracks deaths per million, demonstrating a similarly stark contrast: unvaccinated deaths peaked near 3,000 per million in Minnesota, while deaths among fully boosted individuals remained extremely low, near the baseline.

The second chart, on the right, titled "Excess US deaths from all causes," tracks total weekly deaths from 2017 through late 2021 to challenge claims that individuals died "with" rather than "from" COVID-19. The chart compares actual weekly deaths against a normal threshold for excess deaths. Before the pandemic’s onset in early 2020, actual weekly deaths closely tracked the historical threshold, with normal seasonal spikes peaking around 65,000. Following the arrival of COVID-19, actual deaths spiked far above the threshold in multiple waves, peaking above 80,000 weekly deaths in both early 2021 and late 2021, indicating a massive, unprecedented rise in excess mortality.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market twentieth-anniversary edition analyzes the poor performance and structural flaws of Special Purpose Acquisition Companies, or SPACs, which boomed in 2020 and 2021. Michael Cembalest argues that SPACs were primarily structured to enrich sponsors and selling companies at the direct expense of retail and long-term investors. Highlighting this systemic misalignment, a stylized diagram titled SPAC wealth transfers shows how wealth flows away from buy-and-hold post-merger investors, PIPE investors, and SPAC IPO investors, and instead concentrates in the hands of the sponsors and selling companies. 

The fundamental weakness of these transactions is underscored in a bar chart showing the poor profitability of companies brought public via SPACs since 2019. Out of 85 companies studied as of February 2021, only about 15 had positive net income and free cash flow, whereas the vast majority—roughly 70 companies—had negative net income and negative free cash flow. 

The lopsided financial outcomes are detailed in a comprehensive performance table analyzing investor returns for SPACs brought public or liquidated between January 2019 and January 2021. As of March 2021, SPAC sponsors enjoyed an average return of 958% and a median return of 682%, which settled to a still-massive 507% median return by August 2021. In stark contrast, post-merger buy-and-hold investors faced severe underperformance. Their median gross return was only 10% in March 2021 and fell to negative 15% by August 2021. Relative to the IPO index, post-merger buy-and-hold investors suffered median relative returns of negative 53% in March 2021, which deteriorated further to negative 68% by August 2021. 

A final bar chart compares the average IPO and SPAC net returns by sector for vintage years 2020 and 2021 over a two-year holding period, illustrating that SPACs consistently underperformed traditional IPOs across all major industries. In healthcare, SPACs lost approximately 65% compared to a 40% loss for traditional IPOs. In technology, SPACs fell roughly 65% while traditional IPOs fell about 30%. Consumer SPACs declined by around 60% compared to a 40% drop for traditional consumer IPOs, and diversified SPACs dropped about 65% versus a 40% decline for traditional diversified IPOs.

In the commentary, Cembalest recalls his early warnings from February 2021 regarding unprofitable companies, abnormal sponsor incentives, and over-reliance on company projections. He notes that by 2023, the market carnage was undeniable, with SPAC investors suffering two to three times worse returns than traditional IPO investors. Looking forward, he flags a potential, albeit minor, revival of SPACs linked to Howard Lutnick’s prior firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, which may seek to capitalize on a reportedly lighter regulatory environment favored by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

This page argues that the unprecedented scale of fiscal and monetary stimulus deployed globally in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, alongside an exceptional expansion of the money supply, made the subsequent surge in US core inflation highly predictable. The author reflects on the warnings J.P. Morgan published in January 2021, when US core inflation was hovering at a modest 1.5%. These warnings were echoed shortly after by economist Larry Summers, who argued that rapid labor market healing, pent-up savings, and massive deficit-funded stimulus would reignite wage and price inflation. Ultimately, inflation surged to a peak of 6.6% in 2022, creating a major political headwind for the Biden-Harris reelection campaign even after core inflation halved to 3.3% by the 2024 election.

The arguments are supported by four charts. The top-left scatter plot, titled "Stimulus response to COVID sets a new bar," compares fiscal stimulus as a percentage of GDP on the vertical axis against monetary stimulus, measured by central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP, on the horizontal axis. It plots historical precedents against the Global Virus Crisis, showing that the COVID-era responses far outpaced past events. Specifically, during the COVID crisis, Japan pushed monetary stimulus past 30% of GDP, Europe reached roughly 24% monetary and 10% fiscal, the US reached approximately 16% monetary and 13% fiscal, and the UK peaked at about 16% monetary and 15% fiscal. This massive scale dwarfed the Global Financial Crisis, where US fiscal stimulus was around 7% and monetary stimulus was 14%, as well as the 2011 European balance of payments crisis, which featured negative fiscal stimulus.

The top-right chart, "Faster growth in the money supply this time around," indexes the M2 money supply combined with institutional money market fund balances to compare the Global Coronavirus Crisis against the Global Financial Crisis. Starting from a base of 100, the index for the coronavirus crisis rocketed to 120 by mid-2020 and climbed past 125 by late 2021. In contrast, the money supply index during the Global Financial Crisis expanded much more slowly, peaking just above 105 before drifting lower. 

The two bottom charts track year-over-year US core CPI. The bottom-left chart, "US core CPI since 2017," illustrates the short-term trajectory of inflation. A pointer indicates the inflection point in late 2020 and early 2021, showing exactly when J.P. Morgan published its warning on the coming inflation surge. Following this warning, core CPI climbed sharply to its 6.6% peak in 2022 before gradually declining back to 3.3% by 2025. The bottom-right chart, "US core CPI since 1960," places this recent spike in long-term historical context. It demonstrates that while the 6.6% peak was a severe shock—representing a level not seen since 1982—it remained well below the double-digit core inflation peaks of the mid-1970s and early 1980s, which reached as high as 12% to 14%.

This page addresses the troubling decline in public trust in vaccines, which has been exacerbated by social friction over Covid-19 vaccine safety and efficacy. To illustrate the social toll, a bar chart utilizing data from a September 2021 South Dakota State University survey shows the percentage of respondents experiencing relationship strain from COVID-19 disagreements. It shows that thirty-eight percent suffered relationship stress, thirty-five percent stopped socializing, twenty-eight percent experienced damaged family relationships, and twenty-six percent lost their temper. 

To counter this vaccine hesitancy, the author presents a table of vaccine-preventable diseases in the United States, compiled from a 2007 Journal of the American Medical Association study. The table documents the near-total eradication of historically devastating illnesses after vaccine introduction. Vaccines introduced from the 1790s through the 1960s for diphtheria, measles, polio, rubella, and smallpox all achieved a one hundred percent decline in both cases and deaths. Other diseases listed—including mumps, pertussis, hepatitis A, and tetanus—saw case declines between eighty-seven and ninety-six percent, and mortality declines between eighty-seven and ninety-nine percent. The text highlights that for a single US birth cohort, vaccines prevent twenty million cases of disease and more than forty thousand deaths.

The narrative then shifts to the specific threat of a measles outbreak, noting that adults immunized between 1963 and 1967 received an inactivated MMR vaccine that leaves only twenty-five percent of people with detectable antibodies after one year. This poses a unique risk to immunocompromised individuals who cannot receive the live attenuated vaccine. Because measles is highly contagious—with an infectiousness measure of twelve to eighteen, compared to just one to two for COVID-19 and influenza—a ninety-five percent vaccination rate is required for herd immunity. 

Several concerning vaccination trends and forecasts are presented. Nationally, the median US MMR vaccination rate fell from ninety-five percent in 2013 to ninety-two percent in 2023, with Georgia, Colorado, Wisconsin, Alaska, and Idaho dropping below ninety percent. In Gaines County, Texas, where a measles outbreak occurred, vaccination rates sit at eighty-two percent, with one school district below fifty percent and nearly twenty percent of kindergarteners opting out of at least one vaccine. The page concludes with warning perspectives: JB Cantey, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Texas, cautions that measles is the canary in the coal mine for other resurgent diseases, while a Stanford University study models that measles could become endemic in the United States once again within two decades due to these declining vaccination rates.

This page presents a strongly skeptical analysis of the hydrogen economy, arguing that the case for green hydrogen as a transition fuel continues to deteriorate due to poor efficiencies, high costs, and rising project cancellations. To illustrate these issues, the author provides a summary table detailing the poor round-trip energy efficiencies of hydrogen technologies. For instance, conversion losses from natural gas to hydrogen using steam methane reformation stand at 30%, while alkaline and PEM electrolysis suffer 25% to 35% losses. In transportation, fuel cells achieve a round-trip efficiency of only 25%, which drops to a mere 15% to 30% when liquefaction, shipping, and regasification are required. Furthermore, liquefying gaseous hydrogen consumes 30% to 40% of its energy value, and producing liquid ammonia from green hydrogen for shipping yields a dismal round-trip efficiency of 11% to 19%.

The economic viability of green hydrogen is further challenged by a 2024 Harvard study showing carbon abatement costs ranging from $500 to $1,250 per ton of carbon dioxide, which occasionally exceeds the cost of direct air carbon capture. A bar chart breaks down these abatement costs by sector, showing ammonia at approximately $600 per ton, refining at $700, steel at $750, road freight at $800, power at over $1,000, and industrial heat at nearly $1,150, with error bars indicating even higher potential costs for the latter sectors. 

Market performance reflects these fundamental headwinds. A total return line chart comparing hydrogen indices to the broader market shows that since June 2021, while the MSCI World Equity Index climbed to an index value of approximately 130 by mid-2025, hydrogen equities collapsed. Following the publication of the author's critical 2022 paper, the WilderHill Hydrogen Economy Index plummeted to roughly 45, and the Solactive Global Hydrogen Index crashed to nearly 15. This market decline aligns with a dramatic rise in real-world setbacks; a final chart shows that quarterly mentions of hydrogen project delays or cancellations in news and company disclosures skyrocketed from around 200 in 2020 to nearly 1,300 by late 2024 and early 2025.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market addresses the common investor concern that US equities are overvalued compared to international markets. The author argues that while relative price-to-earnings multiples and price-to-book ratios are indeed higher in the US, this valuation premium is justified by the superior profitability of US companies. To illustrate this point, the page features a scatter plot comparing the price-to-book ratio against consensus forward return on equity for various sectors.

The scatter plot, titled "S&P 500 vs developed world ex US," plots price-to-book ratios on the vertical axis from 0 to 12 against consensus forward return on equity on the horizontal axis from 0% to 35%. It maps ten sectors—including consumer discretionary, consumer staples, energy, financials, health care, industrials, information technology, materials, communication services, and utilities—for both the S&P 500, represented by blue circles, and the MSCI World ex US index, represented by red circles. 

The visual distribution reveals a clear upward-sloping trend, showing that the market prices sectors with higher profitability at higher multiples. S&P 500 sectors dominate the upper-right quadrant of high valuation and high returns. Notably, US information technology leads the chart with a consensus forward return on equity of over 30% and a price-to-book ratio exceeding 10. Other US sectors like consumer discretionary, consumer staples, and industrials also show strong returns on equity between 20% and 27%, corresponding to price-to-book ratios between 6 and 9. Conversely, nearly all international sectors from the MSCI World ex US index cluster tightly in the lower-left quadrant, with returns on equity generally remaining below 15% and price-to-book ratios under 4. Ultimately, this comparison demonstrates that the higher price-to-book valuations of US sectors are aligned with a global market that is willing to pay a premium for greater return on earnings.

This page explores the history and shifting dynamics of US bank failures, arguing that while historical failures were almost always driven by poor credit underwriting ahead of recessions, the banking crisis of 2023 introduced a novel catalyst: interest rate risk. Historically, failing banks exhibited clear warning signs like rising non-performing loans, mounting loan loss provisions, and declining net income. In contrast, the 2023 banking panic was driven by sharp increases in long-term interest rates that wiped out bank equity when portfolios were adjusted for unrealized losses on securities and loans, even at institutions with pristine credit quality.

The first chart, titled "Rate of bank failures in the US from 1865-2023," displays failed banks as a percentage of total banks over more than a century and a half. The data series distinguishes between national banks, represented by a blue line, and FDIC-member banks, represented by a yellow line. The chart highlights historical stress periods, showing major spikes during the Panics of 1873, 1884, 1893, and 1907, the Recession of 1920-1921, the Great Depression, the Savings and Loan Crisis, and the Global Financial Crisis. The highest rate of failure occurred during the Great Depression, when national bank failures peaked at nearly 6% of total banks. In comparison, the S&L Crisis peaked at around 2% of FDIC member banks, and the Global Financial Crisis saw failures peak at roughly 1%. 

The second chart, titled "Impact of unrealized securities and loan losses on capital," illustrates how unrealized losses threatened bank solvency leading into the 2023 crisis. Utilizing fourth-quarter 2022 data across thirty-one major financial institutions, the chart plots capital ratios on a vertical axis ranging from negative 5.0% to 15.0%. For each bank ticker, it compares the standard Common Equity Tier 1 Capital Ratio, an adjusted ratio accounting for unrealized losses on securities, and a further adjusted ratio accounting for unrealized losses on both securities and loans. While unadjusted Tier 1 capital ratios for most banks sit comfortably between 8.0% and 13.0%, the adjustments reveal severe capital erosion for several regional lenders. Most notably, Silicon Valley Bank's adjusted ratio drops below zero, indicating its entire equity capital was wiped out by unrealized losses. Significant downward shifts are also visible for other institutions that subsequently faced intense pressure, such as First Republic Bank, Signature Bank, and PacWest Bancorp.

The text provides a detailed post-mortem of Silicon Valley Bank as the prime example of this new failure mode. SIVB experienced extraordinary balance sheet growth from 2019 to 2022, during which its available-for-sale securities book grew from $14 billion to $27 billion, and its hold-to-maturity book surged from $14 billion to $99 billion. Flooded with deposits during the pandemic-era stimulus boom, SIVB purchased long-duration government securities at cyclical interest rate lows. When interest rates subsequently surged, the value of these securities plummeted. This interest rate exposure was compounded by a highly concentrated, unstable deposit base; at the end of 2022, $152 billion of SIVB's $173 billion in customer deposits was uninsured corporate and venture capital funding. A run was triggered when venture capitalists advised founders to withdraw their funds. Looking to the broader banking sector, the author notes that the systemic risk from unrealized losses persists. In mid-2025, US banks still held approximately $500 billion in unrealized losses across available-for-sale and hold-to-maturity portfolios. Although this is down from a peak of nearly $700 billion during the height of the 2022 to 2023 tightening cycle, it remains exceptionally high compared to the period between 2008 and 2021, when unrealized losses rarely exceeded $100 billion.

This page examines the multi-faceted drivers of US equity outperformance relative to Europe since 2009, challenging the simplified view that the gap is merely a result of lower price-to-earnings multiples in Europe. 

The top line chart decomposes this outperformance from late 2009 through 2022 using a total return index where December 2009 equals 100. By the end of 2022, the MSCI US Index reached over 500, while the MSCI Europe Index in US dollars hovered around 200. The decomposition reveals that this gap is built upon five distinct layers: the outperformance of the US dollar over the Euro (currency effects); sector weight differences, where the US is overweight technology and Europe is overweight financials, industrials, and consumer staples; and within-sector outperformance where US technology, consumer discretionary, and financials all beat their European peers.

This fundamental outperformance is supported by superior corporate profitability. A detailed table showing data as of late December 2024 compares Return on Assets and Return on Equity across sectors. In every sector except Healthcare, US companies outperform their European counterparts. For example, in Technology, the US boasts an ROA of 12.6% and an ROE of 28.9%, compared to Europe's 5.8% and 11.4%, respectively. In Consumer Discretionary, US ROE is 30.0% compared to Europe’s 11.8%. Only in Healthcare does Europe lead, with an ROA of 6.3% and an ROE of 15.1% versus the US levels of 4.4% and 12.7%.

The narrative then details how this long-standing trend shifted. The author notes that the onset of the Trump trade wars finally dented US outperformance. The performance gap between the MSCI US and MSCI Europe peaked in November 2024 with the election of Donald Trump. By June 2025, US outperformance since 2010 had retraced to 88% of that peak level. This recent trend is visualized in the bottom right line chart, which plots the two total return indices up to June 2025. While the MSCI US Index ultimately climbs above 700, the gap with the MSCI Europe Index, which sits near 250, shows a slight narrowing towards the very end of the time series.

In this analysis, the author addresses the widespread concern in 2023 over the inverted US yield curve, which historically has had an almost perfect track record of predicting recessions. Using the metaphor of Rasputin's legendary survival, the author explains why the US economy proved resilient to sharp policy rate increases, arguing that the critical context surrounding previous recessions was entirely absent in 2023. This argument is supported by four historical charts covering several decades of US economic data.

The first chart, titled "Yield curve inversion preceded all recessions...", plots the 10-year minus 3-month Treasury yield spread in basis points, using 30-day smoothing from 1967 to 2022. The chart shows that while the yield curve deeply inverted below zero prior to 2023, mimicking the behavior that preceded every US recession since 1960, the underlying macroeconomic conditions were far less hostile than in the past. 

The second chart, titled "...but were caused by a higher real cost of money," clarifies this distinction by plotting real interest rates, defined as the Fed Funds rate minus Core CPI with 21-day smoothing, from 1957 to 2022. While previous yield curve inversions and recessions were triggered by highly restrictive real interest rates ranging from 2% to over 8%, the Federal Reserve in the recent cycle had barely managed to bring real interest rates above zero percent, meaning the actual cost of money remained historically low.

The third chart, "US nonfin. corporate net interest costs at 60 year low," illustrates how the corporate sector was shielded from rising interest rates. It plots the Fed funds rate on the left axis alongside corporate net interest payments as a percentage of after-tax NIPA profits on the right axis from 1970 to 2020. Historically, rising rates drove up corporate interest burdens; however, during the recent rate-hiking cycle, corporate interest payments as a share of profits actually fell to historic lows below 4%. This resilience was a direct result of corporations extending their debt duration during the preceding decade of low interest rates.

The fourth chart, "US corporate sector financial balance," tracks corporate cash flow as a percentage of corporate gross value added on a four-quarter average from 1960 to 2020, factoring in gross savings, capital transfers, capital expenditures, and retained foreign profits. In past recessionary periods, this balance fell deeply into negative territory, hitting levels between -2% and -6%, which forced companies to slash spending when policy rates rose. In 2023, the financial balance remained in surplus, allowing companies to sustain outlays. 

In conclusion, the author highlights that these structural cushions prevented the widely predicted recession in 2023 and 2024. Looking forward, the author notes that recession indicators remained very benign heading into 2025 before the onset of trade wars.

This page from the twentieth-anniversary edition of Eye on the Market evaluates the performance of various artificial intelligence large language models when tasked with answering complex financial, economic, political, and energy questions from the publication's archives. Michael Cembalest discusses the progression of AI capabilities, starting with a baseline test of GPT-4 in September 2023. At that time, GPT-4 was asked 71 questions, resulting in an overall GPA of 2.47, equivalent to a C+ grade. Subject-specific GPAs included 2.62 for economics, 2.31 for markets, 2.70 for energy, and 2.06 for politics. The grade distribution for these initial 71 questions was 26 A grades, 5 A- minus grades, 3 B grades, 3 B- minus grades, 2 C+ plus grades, 7 C grades, 2 C- minus grades, 13 D grades, 2 D- minus grades, and 8 F grades. The author lists common errors observed in GPT-4, including numerical hallucinations, incorrect math execution, misreading files, ignoring subtotals, using wrong energy conversion constants, and claiming questions were too complex.

To track progress, Cembalest re-tested the 23 questions that GPT-4 had flunked—receiving D or F grades—using GPT-4o in May 2025. GPT-4o showed substantial improvement, achieving 8 A grades, 2 A- minus grades, 1 B+ plus grade, 3 B grades, 1 B- minus grade, 1 C+ plus grade, 1 C grade, 1 C- minus grade, 1 D+ plus grade, 2 D grades, and 2 D- minus grades, with no F grades.

As a final step in June 2025, the author used a custom routing tool built by his son Max to test the remaining underperforming questions that received a grade of C+ or worse by GPT-4o across a best-of selection of models, including Gemini 2.5, Claude Opus 4, and OpenAI o3. This collaborative AI approach further improved results on those same 23 original flunked questions, yielding 10 A grades, 2 A- minus grades, 3 B+ plus grades, 3 B grades, 2 B- minus grades, 1 C+ plus grade, 1 C grade, and 1 D grade, with zero grades below D. If this comprehensive multi-model approach had been applied to all 71 original questions, the overall grade would have risen to a B+ with a 3.36 GPA. Despite this improvement, the author concludes that the required workflow of sorting multiple answers and managing files is not yet worth the effort for his line of work, stating that large language models remain most useful for locating sources and defining simple concepts.

This page focuses on two core themes: the immense profitability and market dominance of US technology and interactive media companies relative to Europe, and the ongoing global pre-eminence of the US dollar despite fiscal concerns. 

The first chart, a line graph showing S&P 500 free cash flow margins from 1977 to 2025, compares tech and interactive media against the rest of the S&P 500. It illustrates that free cash flow margins for tech and interactive media have risen dramatically over the last two decades, peaking near 25% recently, while margins for the rest of the S&P 500 have remained largely flat, generally staying below 10%. This high profitability has allowed US tech and interactive media stocks to grow to 35% of market-wide earnings, up from 19% a decade ago. 

This trend of US corporate dominance is further demonstrated by a bubble chart tracking the creation of new public companies in the 21st century by cumulative market cap in trillions of US dollars. Inspired by a report by Mario Draghi on revitalizing European competitiveness, this visual reveals a massive gap between the US and the European Union. The US curve climbs steeply to nearly 18 trillion dollars, driven by corporate giants like Alphabet, Meta, Tesla, Visa, Mastercard, Netflix, Salesforce, T-Mobile, ServiceNow, and Accenture. In contrast, the EU curve remains low and flat, barely reaching past one trillion dollars, represented by much smaller newly public firms such as Adyen, Porsche, Equinor, Airbus, and Industria de Diseño Textil.

The second half of the page addresses the resilience of the US dollar. Despite persistent analyst forecasts of its decline due to deteriorating fiscal dynamics, the author argues there are few signs the dollar is losing its pre-eminent position. A horizontal bar chart tracking the international role of the US dollar highlights that the currency's footprint is vastly disproportionate to the US share of world trade (about 10%) and global GDP (about 25%). 

This point is reinforced by an accompanying data table detailing the US dollar's share of global markets, comparing 2022 figures with the latest data from late 2024 and mid-2025. The data shows that the dollar has actually strengthened in several areas: the dollar's share of cross-border loans rose from 50% in 2022 to 52% in the fourth quarter of 2024, international debt securities increased from 49% to 53% over the same period, and SWIFT payments grew from 42% to 49% by October 2024. Meanwhile, FX transaction volume remained stable at 88% as of April 2022. Slight declines were observed in official FX reserves, which slipped from 60% to 58% by the fourth quarter of 2024, and trade invoicing, which fell from 50% to 42% by June 2025. Taken together, these metrics show that dollar dominance has largely held firm, with certain indicators of strength even intensifying.

This page from the publication focuses on how the policies of Donald Trump draw on historical precedents established by several former United States Presidents. The author notes that they have used these historical connections in client presentations since February 2025 to put current political dynamics into context. 

The page features portraits of seven former Presidents, each annotated with the specific historical policies or themes that align with the Trump administration's modern agenda. Andrew Jackson is associated with establishing a new political order and engaging in deep state battles. James Polk represents Manifest Destiny in the Western Hemisphere, while William McKinley is linked to tariffs and protectionism. Woodrow Wilson represents prewar isolationism, and Calvin Coolidge is cited for championing small-government, pro-business policies. Dwight Eisenhower is shown representing lower corporate taxes, deportation initiatives, and infrastructure investments. Finally, Richard Nixon is associated with keeping enemies lists, pursuing personal vendettas, and striving for energy independence.

On this page, the author reflects on fifteen years of writing J.P. Morgan’s annual energy paper, acknowledging his longtime technical consultant, Vaclav Smil, and argues that modern decarbonization is a slow, linear industrial transition rather than an accelerating revolution. To illustrate this point, the author presents four charts. The first, titled "Decarbonization is a linear industrial transition," plots the renewable share of final energy consumption from 1990 to 2025. It shows that even Europe, the global leader, is rising at a linear rate of just 0.6% per year, reaching about 15% by 2024, while China, the United States, and Asia excluding Japan and China lag further behind, all remaining below 10%. 

This slow progress is contrasted with a historical precedent shown in the second chart, "Rapid energy-saving steel transition of the 1960s/1970s." Tracking global steel production share from 1920 to 2020, it shows open-hearth production plunging from nearly 80% in 1960 to under 10% by 2000, as basic oxygen production soared past 60% and electric arc furnaces climbed to roughly 30%. The author points out that this historical transition succeeded rapidly because basic oxygen and electric arc technology cut production times and energy use by 80% to 90%, paying for itself. In contrast, modern renewables have required nine trillion dollars in global spending since 2010 just to maintain a slow, linear progression, meaning human prosperity will remain reliant on natural gas for many years to come.

The bottom-left chart, "US grid decarbonization outpaces electrification of energy use," displays percentages from 1990 to 2025 to highlight a structural challenge in the United States. While the renewable share of electricity generation has risen from about 10% in the early 2010s to approximately 20% in 2024, the actual share of electricity in final energy consumption has stagnated around 30%. The author notes that until end-uses are successfully electrified, a greener grid cannot effectively decarbonize the economy. Finally, the bottom-right chart, "Share of refined material production by country, 2024," emphasizes China's overwhelming bottleneck control over the transition. The chart shows that China controls over 90% of refined graphite and rare earths, about 75% of cobalt, roughly 65% of lithium, 40% of copper, and over 30% of nickel, leaving the rest of the world with minor shares of these critical mineral supply chains.

This page discusses how the disappearance of political moderates in the United States Congress has led to a decline in GDP growth, less effective legislative problem-solving, and a dramatic rise in highly partisan policymaking. The author argues that a shrinking political center results in one-sided policies that are vulnerable to repeal when power shifts, leaving complex national issues unaddressed while politicians focus on grandstanding. 

A line chart titled "Moderates in Congress and GDP growth that followed" tracks two metrics from 1950 to 2018. The first metric, moderates as a percentage of the House of Representatives (defined by a Voteview score between negative 0.25 and positive 0.25), shows a steady decline from its peak of roughly 45% in the late 1960s to less than 10% by 2010. The second metric, subsequent 10-year cumulative real GDP growth, mirrors this long-term downward trajectory, falling from around 50% in the mid-twentieth century to roughly 20% by the 2010s. 

To illustrate the decline in legislative efficiency, a table titled "The Decline in Congressional problem-solving" compares historical Congressional eras. During the 92nd Congress from 1971 to 1973, hearings averaged 15 witnesses, and 65% of hearings were devoted to discussing proposed solutions. By the 111th Congress from 2009 to 2011, the average number of witnesses fell to 6, and only 20% of hearings focused on finding actual solutions, indicating a self-conscious attempt to limit serious debate on complex issues. 

A large line chart at the bottom, titled "Partisanship of major legislation," traces legislative polarization from 1913 to 2022. Partisanship is measured as the percentage of support from the legislating party minus the support from the opposition party. The chart shows that after highly partisan peaks in the 1910s and 1930s, such as the Revenue Act of 1913 and the 1930 Tariff Act, partisanship dropped to very low levels during the mid-twentieth century. Highly bipartisan legislation during this era included the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, all of which had negligible polarization scores. However, polarization has soared back to near-maximum levels since the late 2000s. Recent major bills, including the Affordable Care Act of 2010, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021, and the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, were passed with partisanship scores near 90%, representing the highest level of legislative polarization in nearly a century.

This page assesses the historic scale of artificial intelligence capital spending, comparing current trends to past technological cycles and examining whether hyperscalers will see adequate financial rewards for their massive investments. 

A chart titled AI Capital Spending in Context shows NVIDIA’s data center revenues as a share of market-wide capital spending from 2020 through projections for 2026. The data illustrates a rapid rise, with NVIDIA’s share projected to reach nearly 15% by 2026, putting it on par with historic tech investment peaks such as Cisco, Lucent, and Nortel’s peak of roughly 13.5% in 2000 during the dot-com boom, and approaching IBM’s peak of over 16% during the mainframe era in 1969. 

The primary drivers of NVIDIA’s revenue are four major hyperscalers—Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon—whose capital expenditure and research and development spending are detailed in a chart titled Hyperscaler Capex and R&D as a Share of Revenues. This visual shows that these companies are dedicating an increasing share of their revenue to capex and R&D, with Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon rising toward 30% to 35% by 2025. Meta’s spending shows a massive peak of over 60% around 2022 to 2023, which is humorously labeled metaverse money incineration, before dipping and then rising back toward 60% by 2025. The text notes that total hyperscaler capex and R&D is projected to rise from $440 billion in 2024 to $596 billion in 2025, representing a 35% increase, with these four companies accounting for more than half of all capex growth in the entire US equity market.

To evaluate the risks of this spending, a third chart details Hyperscaler Free Cash Flow Margins. The lines for Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon display substantial volatility, with Amazon dipping below zero in 2022 before returning to positive territory, and Meta seeing sharp swings. The author argues that tracking these margins is crucial to understanding when these companies will start to show tangible rewards for their capital outlays.

A comparative table titled Magnificent 7 Stocks vs S&P 493 illustrates how the Mag 7 has outperformed the rest of the index over the last five years but faces an impending slowdown. Over the last five years, the Magnificent 7 achieved 31% annual sales growth and 43% annual operating earnings growth, compared to just 6% and 13% for the S&P 493, respectively. However, two-year forward consensus operating earnings growth for the Magnificent 7 is projected to slow dramatically to 11%, which is only slightly ahead of the S&P 493’s projected 9%. The author explains that this slowdown is partly a result of depreciating the immense new AI infrastructure. Although AI adoption surveys from Bain, McKinsey, and the Census Bureau show growing corporate interest, the open question remains whether corporate buyers are willing to pay enough to justify the massive capital outlays made by the hyperscalers.

This page examines the public profile and policy outcomes of the Biden administration, highlighting key areas of regulation, immigration, and media visibility. The author first discusses the prominent role that past Treasury Secretaries, such as Robert Rubin, Donald Regan, James Baker, and Timothy Geithner, played as vocal champions for their respective administrations. In contrast, the author suggests Janet Yellen maintained a much lower public profile. This is supported by a Google Trends chart comparing the search index interest of Treasury Secretaries Steve Mnuchin and Janet Yellen over their first 50 months in office. While Mnuchin saw major spikes in search interest, peaking near 100 in his first few months and rising above 90 around month 43, Yellen’s interest level remained consistently low, rarely surpassing an index level of 20 after her initial appointment. 

The page then transitions to what the author calls the Biden surges, focusing on government regulation and immigration. A chart showing the cumulative number of economically significant rules enacted by modern US presidents over their first 45 months reveals that the Biden administration has been the most active regulator, implementing over 300 rules by month 45. This trajectory is steeper than those of Donald Trump, Barack Obama, Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, George H.W. Bush, and Ronald Reagan, with Reagan’s administration registering the fewest. Adjacent to this, a chart on net immigration from 2001 to 2024 shows monthly and annual rates for both authorized lawful permanent residents/students and unauthorized illegal entrants/refugees. The data illustrates a historic surge in unauthorized immigration starting around 2021, peaking at an annual rate of roughly 4.8 million people (approximately 400,000 monthly) by late 2023, a level far exceeding any prior period in the two-decade timeline. 

Additionally, the page highlights a successful prediction from the author's January 1, 2024, Top Ten Surprises list, which foresaw that President Biden would withdraw from the presidential race between Super Tuesday and the election citing health reasons. A concluding footnote lists several positive economic counter-arguments a Biden advocate could have used in late 2024, including near-record labor force participation, a surge in manufacturing reshoring and construction spending linked to the CHIPS and infrastructure bills, and the strongest year-to-date stock market gains in an election year since 1936.

This page discusses recent medical breakthroughs enabled by machine learning, focusing on protein folding and the discovery of new antibiotics. The first visual demonstrates the accuracy of Google and DeepMind’s AlphaFold program by showing an overlay of the predicted shape of a DNA replication enzyme in blue against its actual shape in green. AlphaFold has revolutionized structural biology, helping increase the share of mapped proteins from just 20% in 2021 to 99% today in a fraction of the time and cost of traditional methods like x-ray crystallography. 

The second visual is a cluster plot illustrating the discovery of a potential new class of antibiotics to treat MRSA, a staph infection responsible for 7,000 deaths annually in the United States. Researchers Jim Collins at MIT/Harvard and Felix Wong at Integrated Biosciences used neural networks to screen 12 million compounds. The cluster map plots these compounds using distance and color to represent antibacterial activity and non-toxicity, where dark green and black values represent the highest-scoring novel compounds without unfavorable substructures. Two purple dots, labeled as Compounds 1 and 2, identify the molecules that performed best in lab tests and are currently being tested in mice. The page concludes by highlighting other AI-driven medical advancements, including efforts at McMaster University that screened billions of molecules to identify six promising candidates to combat Acinetobacter baumannii, as well as AI diagnostics using retinal cameras to screen for diabetic retinopathy.

This page is a visual compilation or collage of twelve colorful, stylized cartoon illustrations depicting various themes related to the global economy, energy transition, finance, and societal trends, serving as a visual transition or gallery of artistic concepts. 

The first row features an island scene where palm trees are laden with signs detailing various economic metrics like debt and stimulus, a black-and-white industrial scene of workers operating a heavy press amongst crates of financial records, and a cartoon of a person bundled up on a snowy bench surrounded by floating red coronavirus spheres resembling snowflakes. 

The second row shows a boat of onlookers gazing at a night sky where the stars are labeled with clean energy technologies like nuclear fusion and quantum glass batteries, a man sitting on a cliff shaped like a dinosaur looking across a dark chasm at a bright city skyline, and a black-and-white noir-style drawing of two men closely inspecting a physical Bitcoin. 

The third row depicts a hot air balloon labeled with the chemical symbol for hydrogen carrying an elephant in its basket, an anthropomorphic wind turbine and solar panel character sitting together on a bench beneath restrictive park rules, and a fast-moving stagecoach labeled "20/2021 IPOs" being driven by a cartoon fox with anxious passengers inside. 

The final row features a Dorothy-like character working on a laptop from her couch with Toto by her side beneath a framed photo of the Wizard of Oz cast, a suburban landscape with solar-powered homes and wind turbines underneath floating bubble spheres, and a dramatic view of the sun rising over the curved horizon of the Earth from space.

This page discusses the intense legal battles surrounding the Trump Administration's executive orders, focusing on the surge of lawsuits, the historical rise of nationwide injunctions, and a significant June 2025 Supreme Court ruling that curtails the ability of lower court judges to grant broad relief. The author observes that the administration's aggressive use of executive orders has met with a corresponding flurry of legal challenges. 

A dual-axis bar chart tracks executive orders and subsequent lawsuits during the first 100 days of recent presidential terms. It shows that the second Trump administration issued approximately 125 executive orders, prompting over 100 lawsuits, a pattern of heavy litigation similar to Trump’s first term, which saw around 45 executive orders but roughly 140 lawsuits. In contrast, administrations like those of Biden and Obama experienced far fewer lawsuits in their opening days.

A secondary horizontal bar chart traces the history of nationwide injunctions by Federal judges, illustrating how this legal tactic, once rare with only 27 instances recorded across the entire 20th century, surged dramatically. During Trump’s first term, nationwide injunctions peaked at 86 according to Congressional Research Service data, while the first 100 days of his second term alone saw 25 such injunctions. The text explains that a June 2025 Supreme Court ruling restricted judges to granting relief only to the specific individuals or groups involved in a lawsuit, making "jurisdiction-shopping" by political parties far more difficult. In response, plaintiffs are trying to convert their challenges into class-action lawsuits, though the author notes the Supreme Court may intervene again if lower courts approve these measures too routinely.

At the bottom, a detailed table highlights the administration's complete legal defeat in attempting to penalize specific law firms through executive orders. Challenged by Jenner & Block, WilmerHale, Susman Godfrey, and Perkins Coie, four executive orders (numbers 14246, 14250, 14263, and 14230) were permanently enjoined across all nine of their sweeping provisions. These provisions included suspending security clearances, ending government representation, and barring firm personnel from federal buildings. Notably, these permanent injunctions were handed down not just by Democratic-appointed judges like AliKhan and Howell, but also by Republican-appointed judges Bates and Leon. The author points out that these rulings, alongside judicial defeats of Trump's reciprocal and fentanyl tariffs, have reportedly led to a public split between the Trump administration and the conservative Federalist Society.

In this page from J.P. Morgan’s Twentieth Anniversary Edition of Eye on the Market, Michael Cembalest reflects on the early years of his career, beginning in 1987, and draws humorous connections between his personal experiences and broader societal and technological shifts. He describes meeting his wife Rachel, who was then a more senior colleague running Latin American Capital Markets, by impressing her with a three-dimensional surface plot made using Lotus 1-2-3 macros. He recounts being forced to transfer to the Asset Management division after a supervisor, Nick Rohatyn, objected to him feeding Rachel candy in the lunchroom—an incident deemed disruptive to the trading floor's equilibrium. Cembalest also shares an anecdote from 1997 when, still a Vice President, he was excluded from an annual Managing Directors' dinner hosted at his own home by Rachel, an experience that fueled his determination to be promoted.

These personal recollections of workplace romance and legacy software are supported by two charts illustrating major structural changes over the same era. The first chart, titled "How heterosexual couples meet, 1940-2019," tracks meeting methods as a percentage of couples from 1940 to 2020. It highlights the dramatic rise of "Online" dating, which went from non-existent in the early 1990s to the single most popular method by 2019, accounting for nearly 40% of meetings. Over the same period, traditional meeting methods experienced steady declines. Meeting "Via friends" peaked around 38% in 1990 before falling to roughly 20% by 2019, while meeting "As coworkers" peaked near 20% in 1990 and declined to about 11% by 2019, mirroring the workplace dating restrictions Cembalest notes in his text. Other categories, such as primary/secondary school, college, church, and neighbors, remained low or continued to decline.

The second chart, titled "Revenue share of spreadsheet market, 1988-1997," visualizes the rapid displacement of early personal computer software. In 1988, Lotus 1-2-3 dominated the spreadsheet market with roughly a 70% revenue share, while Microsoft Excel held less than 10%. However, Excel's share grew steadily, crossing paths with Lotus 1-2-3 in 1992 at approximately 42% each. By 1997, Excel captured nearly 90% of the market share, whereas Lotus 1-2-3 fell below 10%, and Quattro, which peaked at around 15% in 1991, dwindled to near zero.

This page from the publication examines the real-world implications of relaxing capital regulations for the eight US systemically important banks, arguing that the effect of a proposed reduction in the Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR) from five percent to three and a half to four and a half percent would be far more limited than expected. This is because multiple other capital ratios, such as Tier 1 Leverage, Tier 1 Capital-Advanced, and Tier 1 Capital-Standard, sit closely behind the SLR and would immediately act as the new binding constraints.

To illustrate this, two scatter charts compare excess Tier 1 capital as a percentage of current capital under current versus revised SLR rules across JPMorgan, Citi, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, BNY Mellon, and State Street. The plots demonstrate that the SLR, represented by blue dots, is only the binding constraint for Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, BNY Mellon, and State Street under current rules, with other ratio requirements sitting just above it. Under the revised rules, the SLR requirements ease, shifting the blue dots upward, but other constraints immediately bind, leaving the banks with little newly freed capital.

The third chart, a bar graph showing excess Tier 1 capital in billions of US dollars, highlights that total excess capital across these eight institutions would only increase by a marginal six billion dollars, from one hundred twenty-four billion to one hundred thirty billion, with individual bank changes being barely noticeable. For instance, JPMorgan's excess capital remains virtually unchanged at just over fifty billion dollars under both current and revised rules. This minimal increase suggests there is little room for additional stock buybacks or expanded lending for risky assets.

Conversely, the fourth bar chart reveals a dramatic change on paper regarding treasury buying capacity, which is measured in trillions of US dollars. Under current SLR rules, the total capacity of these eight banks to purchase risk-free assets like Treasuries stands at two point seven trillion dollars, but under the relaxed SLR rules, this capacity would skyrocket to approximately eight trillion dollars. For example, Bank of America's capacity would expand from around half a trillion dollars to nearly one point eight trillion dollars. While this could theoretically position banks to act as a crucial safety valve if demand for US Treasuries collapses among domestic or foreign buyers, the author concludes that this remains highly uncertain, as these banks currently hold ample unused capacity to purchase Treasuries but have shown no inclination to utilize it.

This page of the publication addresses three distinct topics: J.P. Morgan's blockchain initiatives, AI voice cloning fraud risks, and the author's upcoming fishing trips. 

First, the author evaluates whether J.P. Morgan’s blockchain projects justify investment positions in Ethereum. He concludes they do not yet, explaining that J.P. Morgan’s Kinexys product, an intraday repo settlement system, was built on a fork of Ethereum and does not generate tolling revenue or direct gains for ETH holders. While daily volumes on Kinexys are only 2 billion dollars compared to the firm's 10 trillion dollars in traditional daily payments, future public blockchain products could theoretically use Ethereum, Layer 2 networks, or Solana. Currently, J.P. Morgan is testing a permissioned deposit token called JPMD on Base, a Layer 2 product by Coinbase built on Ethereum, which may eventually provide minor benefits to ETH holders.

Next, the page examines Sam Altman's warnings about an impending voice cloning fraud crisis, noting that AI tools can create convincing impersonations with just three seconds of audio. To counter this, the author lists several protective tools banks use, such as AI-driven deepfake detection like Reality Defender, in-app push notification authentication, digital payment verification, phone porting and SIM-swap detection services, and automated payment pattern analysis to flag out-of-character transaction history. 

Finally, the author shares details about his upcoming fishing trips, noting he will be fishing from his Hobie Mirage Outback kayak for sturgeon in British Columbia and for tarpon at Bocas del Dragon in Trinidad. Two side-by-side color photographs show the author on a yellow kayak holding up large fish caught on previous trips.

This page analyzes the potential economic implications and unintended consequences of rising United States tariff rates. The author observes that despite a murky US-European Union trade deal, estimated tariff rates are reaching their highest levels since before World War II. While the new tariffs could generate up to 230 billion dollars per year in revenue according to Yale’s Budget Lab, the publication highlights major concerns. These include the impact of protecting a small number of upstream steel and aluminum workers at the expense of about fifty times more downstream workers, and the potential challenges that higher raw material costs pose to building out artificial intelligence and energy infrastructure. 

Several critical questions and forecasts are presented. The author questions how much US trade with Canada and Mexico will become MCA-compliant under new incentives, noting that while 2024 compliance stood at thirty to fifty percent, it could rise to ninety percent. Additionally, the text notes that US imports from China have already fallen by about forty percent this year, prompting questions about where foreign and domestic product substitution will occur. The author also notes outstanding uncertainties regarding pending Section 232 investigations on pharmaceuticals and semiconductors, and the judicial risk if the Administration loses binding appeals in the DC Circuit or the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.

The analysis is supported by four key visuals. A line chart tracking the average tariff rate on all US imports from 1900 to 2025 shows a sharp upward trajectory in 2025 to approximately fifteen percent, approaching the historical peaks of the early twentieth century. This spike is driven by stacked policies including auto tariffs, steel and aluminum tariffs, fentanyl tariffs, and reciprocal tariffs. 

An accompanying table outlines estimated final destination tariff rates as of July 2025 for key exporting countries. For Mexico, representing 506 billion dollars in 2024 imports, the tariff rate is projected to rise from 0.2 percent to 7.7 percent. For China, representing 439 billion dollars, the tariff rate is expected to surge from 10.7 percent to 43.2 percent. Canada's tariff rate is estimated to rise from 0.1 percent to 2.5 percent, while countries like Germany, Japan, Vietnam, and South Korea face projected tariff rates ranging from roughly sixteen percent to over twenty-one percent.

Two bar charts at the bottom of the page illustrate the structural domestic risks. The first chart contrasts the small number of upstream employees in iron, steel, and aluminum manufacturing—including just 3,848 workers in primary aluminum production—with the millions of downstream workers employed in fabricated metals, machinery, and transportation equipment manufacturing who rely on those materials. The second chart illustrates the high effective tariff rates on key capital and intermediate goods imports. It reveals that critical technological components face substantial duties, with pending tariffs on microchips and semiconductor manufacturing machinery reaching between thirty-five and forty percent, while batteries, transformers, and semiconductor devices face duties of twenty-five to thirty percent.

This page addresses the status of the United States dollar as the world's reserve currency and the fiscal impact of the Trump administration's budget legislation, referred to as the OBBBA. 

The author refutes the claim by Charles Gave of Gavekal that the US dollar has lost its reserve status. While acknowledging a recent 5% to 10% decline in the dollar, the author emphasizes that this drop occurred from elevated levels. The page presents a historical line chart tracking the Fed Trade Weighted Real Dollar, Fed Trade Weighted Nominal Dollar, and the Spot Dollar Index from 1973 to 2025, which shows the currency remaining historically strong despite its recent dip. 

To support the argument that the dollar's global role remains intact, a table presents the US dollar's share of global markets, comparing figures from 2022 to the latest available data as of late 2024 or 2025. The data reveals that cross-border loans increased from 50% to 52%, international debt securities rose from 49% to 53%, and SWIFT payments expanded significantly from 42% to 49%. Meanwhile, foreign exchange transaction volume held steady at 88%. Although trade invoicing fell from 50% to 42% and official foreign exchange reserves ticked down slightly from 60% to 58%, the author argues these shifts do not point to any major deterioration or substantial erosion by the Euro, the Chinese Renminbi, or other BRICS currencies.

The discussion then turns to the domestic fiscal outlook, examining the projected impact of the OBBBA with and without tariff revenues and the permanence of certain tax provisions. A line chart modeling federal debt to GDP from 2025 to 2034 shows that under the baseline scenario without OBBBA, debt-to-GDP rises to about 114%. If the OBBBA is enacted with permanent tax provisions, debt-to-GDP climbs to nearly 127%. However, if the legislation includes net incremental tariff revenues—which Yale’s Budget Lab projects could reach $230 billion annually—the debt-to-GDP ratio is mitigated to around 115%. A companion chart for the total budget deficit to GDP shows a similar pattern: the deficit worsens to nearly -7.4% of GDP under the permanent tax provisions scenario but improves to roughly -6.0% when tariff revenues are included, aligning closely with the original pre-OBBBA CBO baseline.

Finally, the author highlights a stark discrepancy in the projected economic growth resulting from the OBBBA. A chart displaying the projected GDP growth impact of the bill from 2024 to 2034 reveals that the White House is a massive outlier, forecasting a peak growth impact of roughly 4.5% in 2028 and ending at nearly 3.0% in 2034. In contrast, estimates from independent institutions—including the CBO, Penn Wharton, Yale Budget Lab, Tax Policy Center, and the Tax Foundation—are tightly clustered near the bottom of the chart, projecting a growth impact of 1.0% or less for the entire decade. The author concludes by criticizing the White House's outlier economic assumptions and political claims regarding price declines.

Michael Cembalest argues that the healthcare sector has experienced a historic valuation collapse relative to the broader market, now trading at a substantial discount despite its strong fundamentals. This trend is first illustrated in a historical line chart tracking large-cap pharma stock valuations from 1976 through mid-2025. This chart plots the forward P/E ratio relative to the 750 largest stocks, revealing that while pharma consistently traded at a premium—often between 1.2x and 1.8x—before the early 2000s, it has since steadily declined and now trades at a substantial discount of approximately 0.8x. 

To demonstrate current sector cheapness, a second chart maps the consensus forward 12-month price-to-book ratio against the consensus forward 12-month return on equity across various industries. Industries situated below the diagonal dotted line are considered inexpensive relative to the market. Healthcare segments appear highly attractive in this framework, with Biotech showcasing an exceptionally high return on equity of over 40% against a modest 7.5x price-to-book ratio, while Pharma, Managed Care, Healthcare Providers, and the collective "All healthcare" index also sit deep in the undervalued territory.

A third chart examines relative forward P/E ratios versus the S&P 500 since 1992, comparing historical ranges against current levels.
