This chart reveals that almost all healthcare subsectors, including Pharma, Biotech, Managed Care, and Life Sciences, are currently priced at or near the absolute bottom of their historical ranges, falling well below the historical market average P/E line of 1.0x. Finally, a breakdown of the S&P 500 healthcare market cap by industry shows that the entire sector represents over $5 trillion in value. Within this aggregate, Pharma and Medical Devices comprise the largest individual shares of market cap, followed closely by Biotech, Managed Care, and Life Sciences, alongside smaller subsegments for healthcare distributors, supplies, services, and facilities.

This page from a J.P. Morgan research report discusses proposals to lower US prescription drug prices to close the substantial gap between the United States and other OECD nations. The analysis establishes that, with the exception of unbranded generic drugs, US prescription drug prices are roughly 2.5 to 3.0 times higher than those in comparable countries such as Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Although this difference drops to about 1.75 times higher when factoring in discounts and rebates, retail-dispensed brand-name drugs remain extremely expensive in the US.

To illustrate these price disparities, the page includes a comprehensive data table comparing US drug prices to OECD counterparts, with 100% representing price parity. On average across all studied nations, overall US prescription drugs are priced at 278% of international levels, while US brand-name originator drugs stand at 422%. Conversely, US unbranded generic drugs are cheaper, averaging 67% of international prices, ranging from a low of 39% in Canada to 56% in Germany. Under the category of retail-dispensed brand-name drugs net of discounts and rebates, the US average is 312% for all drugs, with extreme outliers such as Italy's brand-name retail drugs priced at 569% and Japan's reference biologics priced at 836% of US equivalents. 

Historically, policy proposals such as Medicare and Medicaid price negotiations, commercial import permissions, and inflation rebates would have only reduced US drug prices by an estimated 0% to 3%. However, the report highlights a shift toward discussing a "Most Favored Nation" policy, which would tie prices for government programs like Medicare, Medicaid, and the Veterans Administration to international averages. If adopted, this policy could lower US drug prices by 5% to 10% and depress US large-cap pharmaceutical company earnings by 9% by 2031. 

While some healthcare analysts downplay these risks—noting that price ratios for government-covered drugs are already lower than commercial ones after rebates and that a unilateral agency edict would likely face swift legal challenges—legislative momentum is building. The author notes that at least six bipartisan bills designed to lower drug prices have successfully advanced to the full Senate by voice vote, including the Prescription Pricing for the People Act of 2025, the Drug Competition Enhancement Act, the Affordable Prescriptions for Patients Act, the Interagency Patent Coordination and Improvement Act of 2025, the Stop STALLING Act, and the Preserve Access to Affordable Generics and Biosimilars Act.

This page examines regulatory changes and operational challenges driving projected earnings declines and policy shifts in the United States healthcare and health insurance sectors. The analysis focuses on the proposed Big Beautiful Bill, or OBBBA, and its potential to restructure Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act. The Congressional Budget Office estimates a major federal Medicaid spending cut of 911 billion dollars, representing a 14 percent reduction over the next decade. 

An accompanying stacked bar chart, titled Projected increase in number of uninsured by 2034, illustrates that 16 million people are expected to lose insurance coverage. The chart breaks down this total, showing that the largest driver is the reconciliation bill's Medicaid changes, which account for more than 8 million of the newly uninsured. The remaining portion of the 16 million total is attributed to the reconciliation bill's ACA changes, the expiration of enhanced ACA premium tax credits at the end of 2025, and proposed Trump administration ACA rules. A primary source of the projected Medicaid savings is the introduction of OBBBA work requirements, mandating 80 hours of monthly work for certain adults, which is estimated to reduce spending by 326 billion dollars over ten years. Additionally, the expiration of premium tax credits is projected to cause a one-third decline in ACA marketplace enrollment.

The second half of the page addresses the growing industry challenge of denied claims. A line and scatter plot titled Healthcare claim denial rates tracks historical trends from 2019 through 2023. The average denial rate rose steadily from approximately 9 percent in 2019 to nearly 13 percent in 2022. By 2023, the data is split by coverage type, showing that Medicaid had the highest denial rate at roughly 17 percent, followed closely by Medicare Advantage at around 16.5 percent, Commercial insurance at about 14.5 percent, and traditional Medicare with the lowest denial rate at around 8.5 percent. 

To provide context on these denial rates, the author includes 2022 survey findings from the American Hospital Association. This data highlights significant administrative friction, noting that 78 percent of hospitals reported worsening experiences with commercial payers, 84 percent experienced rising costs to comply with insurer policies, and 95 percent stated their staff spent more time securing prior approvals. Furthermore, the survey indicates that denied claims are more prevalent for high-cost treatments, with the average denial involving charges of 14,000 dollars or more.

This page examines the rapid growth of Chinese drug development and poses critical questions about the reliability of Chinese clinical trial data. While China is aggressively narrowing the gap with the United States in clinical trials and active pipelines, Michael Cembalest points out that partnerships with or acquisitions of Chinese biotech firms have not yet delivered significant value for large-cap US pharmaceutical companies. For example, Merck’s price-to-earnings ratio has lingered near historical lows of 8x to 9x despite securing collaborations with several Chinese drug developers in 2023 and 2024, including Curon, LaNova, Hengrui, Kelun, and Hansoh. Ultimately, China's slice of the global pharmaceutical and biotech market cap is still quite small, standing at around 3.5%.

Three charts illustrate these trends. The first, "Industry-sponsored clinical trials for innovator drugs," plots the annual number of trials from 2010 to 2024 for both China and the US. While US trials remained relatively stable, fluctuating between 1,500 and 2,300, China’s clinical trial activity grew from nearly zero in 2010 to overtake the US in 2021, peaking at over 3,000 trials in 2023 before a minor pullback in 2024. The second chart, "Drugs in development by company headquarters," maps pipeline drugs from 2014 to 2024. It shows the US steadily expanding its pipeline from roughly 5,500 to 9,000 drugs, while China experienced exponential growth, starting from a baseline of under 500 in 2014 and reaching over 6,000 drugs in development by 2024. The final chart, "Country shares of global all-cap pharma & biotech index," tracks market capitalization weights from 2005 to 2025 across major nations including the US, Switzerland, the UK, Japan, Denmark, China, Germany, and France. Throughout this twenty-year period, the US consistently dominates with a market cap share of around 50% to 60%, leaving China with a very minor presence despite its volume-based growth.

The analysis concludes by raising serious doubts about whether Chinese drug trial results published in major Western medical journals, such as the New England Journal of Medicine, JAMA, and The Lancet, can be trusted. The author highlights several worrying statistics regarding research integrity. Until the practice was banned in 2020, Chinese researchers could earn up to $100,000 in cash rewards from domestic institutions for publishing in prominent Western journals. Furthermore, as of August 2025, nearly half of the more than 60,000 retracted papers in Crossref's Retraction Watch database originated in China, and 75% of the roughly 14,000 English-language papers retracted in 2023 featured a Chinese co-author. Lastly, a survey of Chinese scientists and engineers indicated a belief that 40% of Chinese biomedical publications are compromised by research misconduct.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication analyzes the dismal performance of biotechnology IPOs since 2018, framing the search for successful investments as harder than finding a needle in a haystack. The author notes that even before recent regulatory changes at HHS and the FDA, biotech had seen the largest gap between pre- and post-2020 annualized returns among all sectors except Managed Care. Specifically, S&P 500 biotech returns compounded at 17 percent annually during a successful 25-year run before 2020, but have averaged just 6 percent annualized since then. Since 2018, half of all biotech IPOs have lost more than 80 percent of their value, and only 20 percent had positive holding period returns, a trend that persists across all major therapeutic categories.

To support this argument, the author presents a table detailing biotech performance by vintage year. It illustrates a stark contrast between average and median returns. For example, in 2021—the peak year with 104 IPOs—the average return was negative 54 percent, but the median return was a much worse negative 88 percent, with 67 of those companies losing more than 80 percent of their value. Similarly, in 2019, 47 IPOs posted a positive average return of 41 percent, yet the median return was negative 88 percent. 

A second table shows biotech performance by clinical stage at the time of the IPO. Preclinical stage IPOs (88 count) and Phase 1 IPOs (109 count) both registered average returns of negative 46 percent. Phase 2 IPOs (97 count) fared slightly better with an average return of negative 11 percent, while Phase 3 IPOs (44 count) were the only group with positive average returns at 28 percent. Marketed stage IPOs (14 count) fell back to an average return of negative 34 percent. 

The overall distribution of these investments is displayed in a line chart showing the holding period returns since January 2018 across three distinct datasets: the BioPharma universe of 356 IPOs, the Bloomberg universe of 296 IPOs, and the J.P. Morgan Investment Bank universe of 293 IPOs. All three lines track almost identically, showing a massive spike where roughly 35 to 40 percent of all companies fall into the negative 90 percent to negative 100 percent return bin. The chart remains flat and close to zero across all other return buckets, except for a tiny uptick at the far right, where approximately 5 to 8 percent of companies achieved returns greater than 200 percent. The text notes that these datasets exclude makers of generic or over-the-counter drugs, diagnostics, medical devices, and special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs).

This page analyzes the primary market and clinical challenges facing manufacturers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. Michael Cembalest highlights that while these therapies are highly effective, they are plagued by high patient discontinuation rates, rapid weight regain after stopping treatment, and falling insurance-negotiated prices. 

Data on discontinuation rates from a January 2025 JAMA paper reveals that 84.4% of patients without type 2 diabetes discontinue GLP treatment within two years of initiation, and only 46.3% of those who stop eventually reinitiate. For patients with type 2 diabetes, the discontinuation rate is 64.1%, while 57.2% reinitiate. This problem is compounded by rapid post-treatment weight regain, which is illustrated in a chart tracking percentage change in body weight over 120 weeks. Patients on Wegovy experience a weight loss of roughly 16% by week 68, but after treatment is discontinued at that mark, they quickly regain most of it, climbing back to approximately a 7% weight loss by week 120. 

Corporate and public insurance dynamics also present obstacles. The number of companies covering GLPs has plateaued, and drug makers have had to cut prices by 10% to 15% annually to increase penetration. On the regulatory front, the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation is exploring demonstration programs starting in 2026 for Medicaid and 2027 for Medicare. The Congressional Budget Office estimates these coverage expansions would cost the federal government $35 billion for Medicare and $11 billion for Medicaid between 2026 and 2034, which the author suggests will require cost-sharing measures to keep programs affordable. 

The commentary also examines the potential for oral GLPs to revive the sector's growth, though recent Phase 3 clinical data for Eli Lilly’s oral drug, Orforglipron, disappointed the market, causing Lilly stock to fall 14%. A detailed table compares Lilly's 72-week oral Orforglipron trial across several doses to Novo Nordisk's 68-week trial of injected Semaglutide. The data shows that the highest oral dose of Orforglipron (36 mg) yielded a 12% weight loss, compared to a stronger 17% weight loss for the 2.4 mg injected Semaglutide. Additionally, Orforglipron faced high overall discontinuation rates ranging from 22% to 30% across all doses, with up to 10% of patients discontinuing specifically due to adverse events like nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation.

This page analyzes the financial constraints of the US healthcare sector in the face of major scientific breakthroughs, arguing that despite highly anticipated therapies for cancer, Alzheimer's, and longevity, US healthcare spending has likely reached a practical ceiling. 

The first chart, "US healthcare spending as a share of GDP," plots spending percent shares from 1976 to 2022. It reveals that personal consumption health expenditures rose from 5% in 1976 to 11% in 2008 and have flatlined since, with total national health expenditures exhibiting a similar plateau. 

To illustrate the inefficiency of this expenditure, the second chart compares 2023 life expectancy against annual per capita health spending across various countries. The United States stands out as a stark outlier, spending the most of any nation—exceeding $10,000 per capita—while yielding a life expectancy of only about 77 years. In contrast, peer nations like Japan, Switzerland, South Korea, and Australia achieve life expectancies between 83 and 85 years while spending significantly less, generally between $4,000 and $8,000 per capita.

The third chart details federal spending as a percentage of GDP from 1965 with Congressional Budget Office projections through 2035. It highlights the growing imbalance between rising entitlement spending and flatlined non-defense discretionary spending. The ratio of entitlement to non-defense discretionary spending has escalated dramatically over the decades, rising from 1.0x in 1970, to 2.0x in 1990, 2.4x in 2000, 3.1x in 2015, and 3.3x in 2024, with a projected climb to 4.6x by 2035 as entitlements approach 14% of GDP.

The author concludes that while the US healthcare sector is currently pricing in a lot of bad news and represents a compelling long-term value play, investors must remain cautious. Although biotech acquisition targets and potential Medicare coverage for GLP-1 drugs could boost pharmaceutical companies, successful bipartisan efforts toward drug price reduction and patent reform could delay valuation multiple expansion. Finally, the author notes that subsequent sections of the publication cover disputes over publicly funded US scientific research and peer-reviewed mouse studies of longevity drugs.

This introductory page of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, previews the current edition titled Fair Shakes and catalogs prior reports from the year. The current issue focuses on assessing US corporate earnings and broader economic trends during one of the nation's most significant policy shifts since the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration, alongside partisan redistricting, the Supreme Court, the Census, and the balance of power in the US House of Representatives.

A central table lists five notable sector-specific pieces published earlier in the year, humorously paired with national holiday themes. The first entry, from August, covers healthcare, exploring low valuations in pharma and biotech, patent cliffs, tariffs, changes to Medicaid and Medicare Advantage, regulatory changes under a potential RFK-led FDA or HHS, and competition with China. The second, from June, addresses stablecoins, focusing on payment rails versus illicit use cases, the GENIUS Act, tech-issued uninsured stablecoins, and their impact on Treasury bill rates. The third, from May, details artificial intelligence, tracking hyperscaler capital spending, performance benchmarks relative to humans, and model-specific hallucination rates. The fourth, from March, examines energy, evaluating solar capacity, the transition speed, nuclear power, and the status of hydrogen economy visions. The fifth, from July, compiles influential historical publications to celebrate the twentieth anniversary of Eye on the Market.

The main content of the current publication promised to deliver a chart-based look at several key themes. These themes include positive trends in second-quarter S&P 500 earnings, the extent to which US growth is driven by AI capital expenditures, the politicization of economic data, and major shifts in trade, immigration, regulation, and government spending. Additionally, Cembalest intends to analyze how growth, inflation, and employment are reacting to these shifts, alongside the political impacts of mid-decade Congressional redistricting, interstate migration, and relevant Supreme Court cases.

A highly detailed, personal footnote adds a humorous touch to the page, where Cembalest describes a recent visit to a nutritionist following the release of his August healthcare piece. He provides an extensive list of comfort foods now banned from his diet, which includes pizza, French fries, onion rings, cheeseburgers, spare ribs, meatball subs, fried calamari, diet soda, milkshakes, and numerous brand-name treats such as Oreos, Pop-Tarts, and Doritos.

This page features commentary on the historical and modern erosion of trust in science, drawing parallels between contemporary societal trends and past dark ages of human progress. Michael Cembalest argues that the modern decline in public confidence in scientific and medical establishments is part of a recurring historical cycle. He cites the Soviet Union in the 1930s, when Marxist ideology replaced traditional genetics and agricultural science, leading to the persecution of thousands of scientists and long-lasting negative consequences. He then analogizes current trends to Europe's slow descent into the Dark Ages following the fall of the Roman Empire.

The first of two modern trust charts shows whether US adults believe science has had a mostly positive effect on society from March 2016 to May 2024. While the share of Democrats who agree remained relatively high, dipping from a peak of nearly 80% down to 70%, agreement among Republicans plummeted from 70% in late 2018 to just 45% by May 2024. Overall, the average for all US adults dropped from over 70% to around 57% during this period. The second chart tracks US public confidence in healthcare leadership using a three-year rolling average from 1975 to 2025. It reveals that while confidence for both Democrats and Republicans historically fluctuated between 40% and 60%, a sharp political divergence emerged after 2020. By 2025, Republican confidence in healthcare leaders crashed to 25%, while Democratic confidence hovered at approximately 43%.

The lower half of the page uses historical data to demonstrate the depth and duration of the European Dark Ages. A chart tracking European population and health indices from 250 BC to 1250 AD shows the population falling from a peak of about 45 million in 250 AD to a low of approximately 30 million around 750 AD. Concurrently, a health index tracking degenerative joint disease, where lower numbers indicate worse health, collapsed from over 95 in the classical era to its lowest point of 65 around 750 AD, before both population and health rebounded by 1250 AD. 

A final chart illustrates intellectual decline by counting entries in Harold Bloom's Western Literary Canon and the number of notable Western philosophers from 1000 BC to 1800 AD. Both metrics collapsed during the Dark Ages from 500 AD to 1000 AD. The number of notable philosophers plummeted from roughly 40 down to just over 10, and literary canon entries dropped from a peak of over 60 to nearly zero, demonstrating the long-lasting intellectual stagnation of the era before a massive resurgence during the Renaissance and Enlightenment periods.

This J.P. Morgan "Eye on the Market" analysis focuses on the resilient performance of Q2 2025 S&P 500 earnings and evaluates the potential impacts of corporate tax provisions in the OBBBA. The author notes that actual earnings-per-share growth reached 11% compared to expectations of 4%, nearly matching original January targets after consensus estimates fell by 7% earlier in the summer. A significant driver remains the Magnificent 7 stocks, which continue to grow earnings at approximately twice the pace of the rest of the U.S. market—22% versus 12%. Both segments continue to outperform Europe, represented by the Stoxx 600, which posted yet another quarter of flat 0% earnings growth. Furthermore, 58% of S&P 500 companies raised earnings guidance compared to just 29% in the first quarter, exceeding the historical average of 46% since 2007. Looking forward, the author highlights that the OBBBA corporate tax provisions offer time-shifting incentives to invest immediately. By returning to and making permanent the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act policy of 100% bonus depreciation, allowing immediate R&D deduction, and permitting temporary immediate expensing of new factories, these provisions could boost 2026 corporate cash flows by roughly 3% and yield net present value savings of 2% to 4%.

Four charts support these findings. The first, a line chart titled "Year over year earnings growth" tracking March 2024 to June 2025, visualizes the earnings growth gap between the Magnificent 7, the S&P 500 excluding those seven stocks, and the Stoxx 600, illustrating the stark contrast between the Magnificent 7’s peak performance and Europe's stagnant growth. The second chart, "Frequency of earnings beats and misses in the S&P 500" from 2000 to 2025, shows the percentage of companies with earnings surprises greater than one standard deviation of consensus estimates. It demonstrates that beats consistently and substantially outnumber misses, with beats regularly staying above the 50% threshold. 

The third chart, "Trailing 12 month profit margins by S&P 500 sector group" from 2012 to 2025, shows that Info Tech margins lead the market at nearly 27%, while other sectors like Industrials and Consumer Discretionary show recent margin improvements, and Healthcare continues to struggle. The final chart, "Trailing 12 month profit margins by market cap" from 2000 to 2025, compares the S&P 500 large cap, S&P 400 mid cap, and S&P 600 small cap. It illustrates a clear structural divergence where large-cap margins have recovered to approximately 13% to 14%, while mid-cap margins hover around 8% and small-cap margins lag further behind at roughly 6%, showing no recent improvements.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s analysis provides a comprehensive assessment of the US economy amidst some of the most dramatic policy shifts since the New Deal, focusing on tariffs, immigration, executive actions, and deregulation. Cembalest contextually frames these shifts: Trump's tariff initiatives follow decades of non-reciprocal global tariffs, which are linked to a steep decline in US manufacturing jobs after China joined the WTO in 2001. Similarly, current deportation efforts follow a historic wave of unauthorized migration, and Trump's deregulation push counters a massive expansion of regulatory costs under the Biden administration. 

Four charts illustrate these policy areas. The first chart displays the average tariff rate on all US imports from 1900 through 2025, assuming a twenty percent US domestic and twenty percent foreign substitution from China. After hovering around twenty to twenty-five percent in the early twentieth century, average tariff rates steadily declined to near-zero by 2000. In 2025, active tariffs sit near five percent, while contested active tariffs and proposed August 2025 trade deal tariff rates span between roughly eight and fourteen percent. 

The second chart tracks US border encounters and ICE book-ins to detention from 2019 to 2025. Annualized border encounters reached a peak of approximately four million in late 2023 and early 2024 before dropping precipitously to under one million by mid-2025. In contrast, ICE book-ins to detention, which previously hovered around one hundred thousand per year, spiked dramatically to an annualized rate of nearly four hundred thousand in 2025.

The third chart compares Executive Orders and federal lawsuits filed against the president during the first one hundred days of administrations from George W. Bush to Trump’s second term. Trump’s second term represents an unprecedented spike in both categories, reaching over one hundred and twenty Executive Orders and nearly three hundred lawsuits, far outpacing the first terms of Obama, Trump, and Biden. 

The final chart shows the cumulative number of economically significant rules implemented over the months of various presidencies, spanning from Reagan to Biden. The data indicates that the Biden and Obama administrations enacted the highest volume of major regulations, both approaching five hundred cumulative rules near the end of their terms, with Biden’s trajectory representing the steepest path. By comparison, Trump's first term cumulative rule count remained much flatter, ending below two hundred rules.

This page of the Online Trump Tracker analyzes the economic impacts and policy priorities of the administration's major reconciliation bill, the OBBBA, which redistributes $5 trillion in government spending and taxation over ten years. The author describes the bill as a combination of Thatcherite supply-side incentives, Jacksonian nationalism, Clinton-style welfare reform, Reagan-era defense hikes with cuts to safety nets, Coolidge/Eisenhower-style border controls, and Trump's opposition to the green economy. 

A horizontal stacked bar chart, titled "OBBBA sources & uses, Current Policy basis, Senate version (US$, trillions, 2025-2034)," visualizes how these spending cuts and tax changes balance out. The primary "uses" for the roughly $3 trillion in funding include personal taxation changes (such as the standard deduction, child tax credits, and tax exemptions on tips, overtime, and car loan interest) which make up about half of the total, alongside domestic corporate tax adjustments, defense, and border control. These are funded by "sources" that primarily target the social safety net (such as Medicaid, SNAP, and Opportunity Zones) for over $1.0 trillion in cuts, and the green economy (EVs, residential investment, and production/investment tax credits) for roughly $0.6 trillion, alongside cuts to student loans and new taxes on non-US entities and overseas US corporations. The author notes that the Medicaid and SNAP work requirements mirror the 1996 Clinton Welfare Reform Act, which was praised across the political spectrum for reducing caseloads.

Two additional charts illustrate the administration's shift in priorities. The first, "NIH new & competitive renewal grant funding, FY15 - FY25," shows the cumulative percentage of annual grant funding awarded by month. While the historical bands for FY2015–FY2024 steadily rise to between 15% and 18% by July, the line for FY2025 flatlines after the Trump 2.0 inauguration in late January, languishing below 10% by July and indicating a severe slowdown in National Institutes of Health funding. 

The second chart, "New vs cancelled clean energy projects," plots capital investment in billions of dollars from Q1 2018 to Q1 2025. Under the Biden administration, newly announced projects routinely represented tens of billions of dollars per quarter, peaking near $30 billion, with virtually no cancellations. However, upon the transition to Trump 2.0 in early 2025, newly announced projects fell to near-zero, while cancelled, paused, or closed projects spiked to more than $10 billion. The author connects this clean energy slowdown to a August 2025 US Court of International Trade ruling that vacated Biden’s suspension of solar tariffs on Southeast Asia. This decision risks retroactive duties on $50 billion to $70 billion in solar imports from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication by Michael Cembalest explores how massive spending on artificial intelligence and technology is masking the true economic impacts of Donald Trump's policies. The author argues that tech sector capital spending has been driving a remarkable 35 percent to 45 percent of overall US GDP growth over the last three quarters. Without this massive influx of tech spending, US growth likely would have slowed to about 1 percent due to weakening consumer consumption.

The first chart, titled US real GDP growth contribution from tech capex, illustrates the percentage contribution of tech capital expenditure compared to the rest of the economy from the first quarter of 2023 through the second quarter of 2025. It shows that while the contribution from the rest of the economy steadily contracted from nearly 3.0 percent in mid-2023 to around 1.3 percent in 2025, tech capex maintained a steady presence, making up an increasingly critical portion of the remaining growth. 

This trend is reinforced by the bottom-left chart, Contribution to real GDP growth, which tracks a two-quarter rolling average of real GDP contributions from 2022 to mid-2025. It contrasts personal consumption expenditures, which dipped and remained volatile, against information processing equipment and software. While consumption contributions trended downward, the tech equipment and software contribution rebounded from near zero in 2023 to about 0.75 percent by 2025.

The top-right chart, Mag 7 capex & R&D, displays the combined capital and research and development spending in billions of US dollars for Amazon, Tesla, Meta, Apple, Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft from 2022 to an estimated 2026. The chart reveals a massive upward trajectory, starting around $380 billion in 2022, rising by $24 billion in 2023, jumping by $95 billion in 2024, and surging another $158 billion in 2025. It is projected to grow by an additional $110 billion in 2026, reaching nearly $800 billion. The vast majority of this growth is driven by Amazon, Meta, Alphabet, and Microsoft.

Focusing in on these major tech giants, the bottom-right chart tracks Hyperscaler capex and R&D as a share of revenues from 2017 to 2025. Meta shows the most dramatic volatility, with its spending as a share of revenue spiking near 70 percent in late 2022, dropping to about 45 percent in 2023, and climbing back up to approximately 65 percent by late 2025. Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft have also seen their capital intensity rise, converging between 30 percent and 40 percent of their revenues by 2025. 

The author points out that this spending boom is highly concentrated; while the overall S&P 500 showed strong Q2 investment growth, the median stock grew its capex and R&D by only 3 percent to 4 percent. The page concludes with a vital open question for the markets: how long can these hyperscalers continue to spend such an unprecedented share of their revenues on capex and R&D before the trend becomes unsustainable for the broader US economy?

In this analysis of growth indicators, Michael Cembalest evaluates whether coincident and leading economic data signal an impending recession, concluding that the overall outlook remains a mixed bag with no clear warning signs of a downturn. While current economic activity remains steady across coincident trackers, leading indicators and business optimism reveal some underlying vulnerabilities. 

The evaluation is supported by six charts. The first chart, illustrating the Dallas Fed US Weekly Economic Index from 2018 to mid-2025, reflects steady current growth; after a dramatic post-pandemic surge and subsequent correction in 2022, the ten-series index—which includes unemployment claims, retail sales, fuel sales, and electricity output—has stabilized in the 2 to 3 range through 2024 and 2025. The second chart focuses on quarterly annualized real GDP estimates for Q3 2025, showcasing a divergence between the optimistic Atlanta Fed GDPNow estimate, which sits above 3% in late August, and the more conservative Blue Chip consensus, which hovers below 1% within a forecast range spanning from negative 1% to positive 2%. 

Cyclical manufacturing health is represented in the third chart by the ISM new orders less inventories index from 2018 to 2025, showing that after dropping into negative territory in late 2022, the indicator has recovered to hover slightly above zero in 2024 and 2025. In contrast, the fourth chart tracks US business optimism and capital spending from 2006 to 2025, displaying a steep decline in recent years, with the index falling to negative levels near negative 50 by late 2024. 

The fifth chart compares year-over-year changes in the Conference Board's coincident and leading economic indicators from 2018 to 2025. While coincident indicators have remained steadily positive around 1% to 2%, leading indicators fell sharply starting in 2022 and remain negative, albeit recovering slightly to around negative 5% in 2025. Lastly, a survey of the most important problems facing small businesses from 2010 to 2025 tracks NFIB respondents' concerns regarding inflation versus poor sales. This chart highlights that while anxieties over inflation have plummeted from a peak of over 30% in 2022 down to around 10% in 2025, concerns regarding poor sales have steadily ticked upward, approaching the 10% mark.

This page examines whether the Federal Reserve is prematurely easing monetary policy, questioning if a rate cut is appropriate when core inflation stands at 3% and inflation expectations remain above 2%. The author warns that the Fed might be rushed into easing, drawing a comparison to Fed Chair Arthur Burns during the Nixon era. 

To support this argument, the page features six charts analyzing inflation metrics, survey data, historical precedent, and expectations. The first chart displays the annualized three-month percent change in Core PCE and Core goods PCE from 2018 through mid-2025. It reveals that although core goods PCE dipped, it has trended upward in 2025, likely due to tariffs, keeping annualized Core PCE near 3%. The second chart tracks Core PPI and PPI final demand inflation over the same period, showing a corresponding upward tick for both measures in 2025, also approaching 3%. 

The next two charts look at business surveys. A chart plotting US manufacturing PMI input and output prices from 2015 to 2025 reveals that both series have risen since late 2023, with input prices reaching near 70 and output prices climbing well above the neutral 50 threshold. Similarly, a chart of ISM surveys for prices paid in manufacturing and services shows both sectors trending upward in 2025, with both indexes settling near 60. 

A historical bar chart illustrates the trailing six-month change in the ISM manufacturing prices paid index at the time of Fed rate cuts, broken down by decade from 1970 through 2025. It demonstrates that the Fed has rarely cut rates when prices paid were rising, with the 1989–1991 easing cycle during the Savings and Loan crisis serving as the primary exception. 

The final chart tracks US inflation expectations from 2020 to 2025 across four different measures: the University of Michigan one-year household survey, the three-year breakeven rate from TIPS, the Cleveland Fed one-year model, and the Atlanta Fed one-year business expectations. All four metrics remain consistently above the 2% target line, with household expectations near 3.5% and business-focused measures hovering around 2.2% to 2.5% in 2025. The author concludes that because cutting rates under these conditions is historically rare, the Fed must be highly confident that the economy is genuinely weakening.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Online Trump Tracker focuses on analyzing food, energy, and wage inflation, specifically challenging claims made by economist Paul Krugman regarding the impact of farm worker deportations on vegetable prices. The author, Michael Cembalest, begins by noting that while electricity prices are rising due to transition spending, AI demand, transmission equipment costs, and grid projects, other segments like meat, poultry, and fish inflation remain noisy but at a third of their 2022 levels. Egg prices are also falling as the avian flu outbreak subsides. 

Cembalest directly disputes Krugman's claim that a July 2025 spike in "fresh vegetables except potatoes" was caused by farm worker deportations. He points out that this specific price series is historically highly volatile and questions why, if labor shortages were the culprit, similar inflation spikes did not occur for dry vegetables, fresh fruits, or potatoes. The critique is supported by four detailed charts.

The first chart, "CPI energy and food inflation," shows year-over-year percentage changes from 2018 to 2025. It tracks electricity, which has climbed steadily to around 6% to 8%, alongside meats, dairy, and highly volatile egg and gasoline prices, the latter two mapped on the right axis. The second chart, "PPI fruits and vegetables inflation," presents monthly percentage changes from 2022 to 2025. It illustrates that the series for fresh vegetables except potatoes regularly experiences dramatic spikes of 60% or more, similar to the July 2025 spike, while dry vegetables, potatoes, and fresh fruits remain relatively flat. This supports the author's argument that the recent spike is typical volatility rather than a unique policy-driven event.

The page also addresses the broader labor market impact of immigration. Addressing claims by Secretary Noem that 1.6 million undocumented workers left the U.S. in her first 200 days, Cembalest argues that if this were severely constraining the labor force, wages in immigration-sensitive sectors should be rising faster than average. To evaluate this, the third chart compares overall year-over-year wage growth against immigration-sensitive industries—including childcare, cleaning, construction, and food services—from 2019 to 2025. Both series peaked above 10% in late 2021 and have since declined in tandem to approximately 3% to 4% by mid-2025, showing no material divergence. 

Finally, the fourth chart displays the legal status of hired crop farmworkers from 1991 to 2021 using USDA data. It reveals that unauthorized foreign-born workers consistently represent about 40% of the workforce, while US-born workers make up roughly 30%, authorized foreign-born workers account for about 25%, and foreign-born U.S. citizens comprise a tiny sliver. Cembalest concludes with an open observation that while some analysts expect a divergence in immigration-sensitive wages to occur eventually, there is limited evidence of it so far.

This page of the publication provides an analytical appendix on how mid-decade partisan redistricting, interstate migration patterns, and Supreme Court changes to the Voting Rights Act could make control of the House of Representatives incrementally tougher for Democrats. The author discusses how officials in Texas and Florida have sought to justify mid-decade redistricting by citing substantial 2020 census counting mistakes, although the political reality is driven by partisan interests. While federal law and the US Constitution do not prohibit mid-decade redistricting, state constitutions present varying barriers. For instance, California’s legislature is attempting to bypass its independent commission via a public initiative to impose a new congressional map, whereas Florida's state courts could invalidate new districts due to explicit state constitutional bans on political gerrymandering. Texas, however, faces no such barriers. The author notes that among states where one party holds a trifecta, only Illinois and Georgia have as much legislative freedom to operate and redraw districts as Texas.

To support this analysis, a detailed table compares the rules around mid-decade Congressional redistricting in nine trifecta states that have more than two opposing party seats. The table is split into Democratic trifectas—California, Colorado, Illinois, New Jersey, and New York—and Republican trifectas—Florida, Georgia, Ohio, and Texas. It details each state's total House seats, current Republican/Democrat split, constitutional prohibitions on gerrymandering, where redistricting power is vested, constitutional amendment rules, census limitations, and their Princeton gerrymander score. For example, California has 52 seats split 9R to 43D, explicitly prohibits gerrymandering, uses a non-politician commission, and has a Princeton score of B. Illinois has 17 seats split 3R to 14D, does not prohibit gerrymandering, vests power in the legislature, and has a Princeton score of F. Among the Republican trifectas, Texas has 38 seats split 25R to 13D, has no prohibition, vests power in the legislature, does not limit redistricting to only post-census years, and receives an F Princeton score. Georgia, with 14 seats split 9R to 5D, operates under identical rules to Texas and similarly receives an F score. The source note attributes the data to Ballotpedia, NCSL, Book of the States, the University of Pennsylvania, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the ongoing implementation of tariffs by the Trump administration and their broader economic implications on businesses, prices, and the US federal budget deficit. Michael Cembalest argues that despite claims that exporting nations pay for these tariffs, the reality is that US import prices have only fallen slightly, meaning US businesses and consumers bear the burden. He highlights that businesses aggressively front-ran the tariffs by ramping up imports of pharmaceutical and consumer goods in early 2025 and are now working down these inventories. Cembalest also predicts that the Supreme Court will ultimately overrule a lower court's decision against Trump's International Emergency Economic Powers Act tariffs, reinstating them based on a broad definition of presidential regulatory powers. Additionally, he expresses skepticism about foreign direct investment promises, noting that past trade commitments, such as China’s purchase targets under the 2020/2021 Phase One trade deal, were only partially fulfilled at 60 percent to 65 percent of targets.

The page contains four visuals to support these observations. The first chart, showing US pharmaceutical and medicine versus chemical trade from 2002 through 2025 in billions of US dollars, shows a massive, sudden spike in pharmaceutical and medical imports peaking near 300 billion dollars in early 2025, while pharmaceutical exports remained flat around 100 billion dollars. The second chart traces real imports of consumer goods excluding autos using an index where January 2023 equals 100. It depicts a dramatic spike in imports peaking close to 140 in early 2025 before sharply collapsing, validating the narrative of inventory front-running by importers. 

A tabular visual presents tariff rates alongside import price changes from January to July for selected goods categories. It shows that while bauxite, alumina, aluminum, and steel face a 50 percent tariff rate, their import prices only declined by 9.9 percent and 6.0 percent, respectively. Similarly, passenger cars faced a 25 percent tariff with a mere 1.0 percent decline in price, and goods from China saw an average price drop of just 1.9 percent under various tariffs. Overall import prices across all goods fell by only 0.2 percent, proving that foreign exporters are not lowering their prices enough to absorb the tax. 

The final chart presents the US federal government budget balance as a percentage of GDP for fiscal years 2020 through 2025. The fiscal year 2025 curve tracks a deficit that reaches approximately 9 percent of GDP by July, demonstrating that despite 55 billion dollars in year-to-date tariff collections and an estimated 250 billion to 300 billion dollars in annual tariff revenues once fully collected, these inflows are insufficient to dramatically alter the weak overall US fiscal landscape.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the resilience of the US economy, arguing that despite policy disruptions under the Trump administration, the country should narrowly avoid a recession. While the Federal Reserve is expected to ease interest rates to support sensitive sectors like housing, economic growth is forecast to slow to approximately 1% in the second half of the year. This slowdown is attributed to the impact of tariffs on consumers and businesses, a severe decline in labor supply growth as net immigration drops from one million annually to 200,000 or fewer, and the strain on finite power supplies from massive artificial intelligence infrastructure spending. Cembalest suggests that these restrictive tariff and immigration policies may not be permanent, as history shows administrations quickly pivot when policy outcomes turn negative.

To support this view, the author presents two historical charts. The first, titled "McKinley tariff aftermath: 1890 midterms," tracks Republican House seats, adjusted for the 1890 House size, from 1865 to 1910. The chart illustrates how the introduction of the McKinley tariffs on October 1, 1890—which raised average import duties to nearly 50%—triggered severe inflation that decimated the Republican House majority, with seat counts plunging from 171 to 88 in the November 1890 midterms and leading to a Democratic sweep in 1892 that rolled back the tariffs by one-third. The second chart, titled "Eisenhower deportations," measures the annual number of deported individuals from 1945 to 1957. It depicts deportations spiking to a peak of 1.1 million under President Eisenhower in 1954, only to crash by more than 90% to just 80,000 by 1956 once funding and political support for the aggressive deportation program evaporated.

Turning to contemporary immigration enforcement, the page highlights Syracuse University's TRAC database showing that 70% of those held in ICE detention centers as of August 10, 2025, had no criminal convictions, while others had only minor offenses like traffic violations. The text concludes with references to several notable news stories involving controversial ICE detentions of military veterans, firefighters, and families of US service members.

This page serves as the cover and introductory overview for an edition of "Eye on the Market" titled "The Blob: Capital, China, Chips, Chicago and Chilliwack," written by Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The centerpiece of the page is a creative movie poster parody titled "The Data Center Blob!" styled after a retro 1950s science-fiction monster movie. Under the dramatic tagline "Indestructible... Indescribable... It Cannot Be Stopped!", the poster features a retro-style illustration of a monstrous, screaming data center building with cable tentacles emerging from its mouth, chasing terrified citizens through a landscape of power lines. 

The poster lists several major risks and economic impacts of the rapid AI expansion on the surrounding margins. On the left side, yellow text warns of strained power grids, higher nighttime loads, and harmonic distortion damaging equipment and appliances. On the right side, it cautions about higher power prices, soaring PJM capacity payments, and the rapid depreciation of chips and interconnects. 

The poster further satirizes the tech industry by casting major corporations in typical movie production roles. It "stars" Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Meta, and is "produced by" infrastructure and construction firms Equinix, Digital Realty, Turner Construction, and DPR Construction. Artificial intelligence startups OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI are listed as the "directors," while financial heavyweights Blackstone, Digital Bridge, and the Saudi Investment Fund are listed under financing. A final credit notes the "movie" is based on the seminal 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need" by Google Brain Research.

In the introductory text below, Cembalest outlines the key topics covered in this publication. These include the massive AI and data center takeover, the OpenAI-Oracle deal, United States government equity investments in Intel and MP Materials, the origins of TSMC, and how national industrial policies support domestic champions globally. Additionally, the piece addresses China's efforts to curb excess capacity and its impact on equity investors, crime and municipal solvency issues in Chicago and Illinois, how tight net new equity supply has supported US markets since 2011, and concludes with photos from Chilliwack, Canada.

This page, titled "Related issues: the 2030 Census" under J.P. Morgan's "Online Trump Tracker" commentary, discusses how ongoing domestic migration patterns are poised to reshape political representation in the United States following the 2030 Census. The central argument is that interstate migration shifts will likely favor the GOP at the expense of Democrats in congressional apportionment, altering the political landscape and Electoral College representation starting in 2032. The Brennan Center estimates that Democratic-leaning states will lose House seats—specifically, California is projected to lose four seats, New York three, and Illinois, Oregon, Minnesota, and Rhode Island one each. Conversely, Republican-leaning states are projected to gain seats, with Texas and Florida gaining four each, and Arizona, Utah, and Idaho gaining one seat each. 

Supporting these projections, a table sourced from the UVA Cooper Center lists the states with the fastest-growing populations based on cumulative percentage change estimates from 2020 to 2030. Utah leads the list with a cumulative growth rate of 13.1%, followed by Idaho at 12.4%, Texas at 11.4%, North Dakota at 11.3%, Nevada at 10.7%, Colorado at 10.6%, Washington at 10.5%, Florida at 10.5%, Arizona at 8.6%, and South Carolina at 7.7%. 

Adjacent to this table, a stacked horizontal bar chart illustrates congressional districts by region from 1960 through to the 2030 estimate, using data from the Brennan Center. The chart tracks regions including the South, Northeast, Midwest & Plains, Mountain, and West. It visually demonstrates a multi-decade expansion of congressional representation in the South and West, alongside a steady contraction of seats in the Northeast and the Midwest & Plains.

The commentary notes that while Florida has historically been a primary beneficiary of domestic migration, this trend may face headwinds due to a property insurance crisis, repeated landfalls of Category 4 and 5 hurricanes, rising home prices, high property taxes, loss of wetlands, congestion, and increasing utility costs. This potential shift is reflected in two tables showing the top twenty most moved-to and most moved-out-of cities according to the 2025 PODS Moving Trends Report, which compares rankings from 2024 and 2025. 

In the "Most moved-to cities" table, Myrtle Beach, North Carolina, and Ocala, Florida, hold the first and second ranks, respectively, across both years. Raleigh, North Carolina, rose to third in 2025, and Dallas-Fort Worth, Texas, jumped to fifth after being previously unranked in 2024. In the "Most moved-out-of-cities" table, Los Angeles and San Francisco, California, rank first and second, while South Florida/the Miami area ranks third. The author emphasizes that Tampa Bay, Florida, entered the outbound list for the first time in 2025 at rank sixteen, while Orlando dropped off the most moved-to list entirely, indicating that Florida's rapid growth may be starting to cool. Other major outbound regions include Long Island, New York at fourth, San Diego, California at fifth, and Central Jersey at sixth.

This page examines the severity of crime in Chicago and challenges the narrative around the city’s supposedly improving public safety metrics, ultimately linking the issue to broader municipal solvency constraints. The analysis begins by questioning how bad Chicago’s crime is compared to other major cities, noting that while federal intervention has been directed toward Memphis, other metropolitan areas like Baltimore, Philadelphia, and St. Louis are arguably as dangerous as Chicago on a per capita basis. However, among mega-cities with populations over 750,000, Chicago ranks first in aggravated assault, gun assaults, homicide, and robbery, with a homicide rate five times higher than New York City. 

To support these comparisons, a table titled Crime rates per capita, 2024-2025, displays city rankings across nine crime categories based on mid-year 2025 data from the Council on Criminal Justice. Out of thirty-six reporting cities, Chicago ranks twenty-second in larceny, seventeenth in motor vehicle theft, and fifth in robbery. In other categories with fewer reporting cities, Chicago ranks sixth out of twenty-three in aggravated assault, fourth out of nine in carjacking, third out of eleven in gun assaults, and eleventh out of thirty in homicides. The table notes that several key cities, including Los Angeles, Houston, and San Diego, did not report data.

The author thoroughly deconstructs Chicago’s claimed 52% homicide clearance rate, arguing that the term "cleared" is misleading. Of the 319 murders cleared in 2023, only 140 actually occurred that year—some dating back to the Nixon administration—and charges were filed in only 18% of those 140 cases. From 2013 to 2022, Chicago’s actual murder clearance rate by arrest was only about 20%, compared to over 50% in New York City and a national average of 45%. This discrepancy prompted Illinois legislators to introduce a bill requiring law enforcement to disclose arrest and charge numbers rather than general clearance rates. 

Additional statistics highlight systemic policing issues, including the fact that arrests were made in only 6% of the 19,000 non-fatal shootings since 2018, with 80% of those investigations suspended annually. Furthermore, over 70% of arrested and charged individuals are released before trial. Between 2020 and 2024, nearly 400 individuals arrested for murder or attempted murder were already out on bail for a prior felony. Finally, more than half of high-priority 911 calls receive no immediate police response, up from 19% in 2019. The page concludes with an anecdote regarding Governor J.B. Pritzker posing with a community violence worker who was later charged with murder and burglary, suggesting that while Chicago needs to spend more on public safety initiatives, it is severely constrained by municipal solvency issues.

This page of the publication argues that the global economic environment is highly mercantilist, with many foreign countries providing substantial subsidies, tax incentives, loans, and grants to support their domestic manufacturing sectors far more than the United States. In China, which is highlighted as the most mercantilist nation, these industrial subsidies can reach between 15% and 35% of industry profits. In this highly competitive global context, the author suggests that providing a federal government lifeline to US companies like Intel represents a necessary defensive measure. 

Six charts support this analysis of global industrial policy and mercantilism. The first line chart, displaying government expenditures on subsidies as a share of GDP from 2000 to 2020, shows that France’s expenditures rose sharply after 2013 to reach nearly 2.8% of GDP by 2020. Sweden remained relatively flat near 1.5%, while Germany declined to around 0.8%. Throughout this entire period, the United States consistently spent the least on subsidies, flatlining below 0.5% of GDP.

The second chart details industrial policy spending in key economies as a percent of GDP. China leads by a wide margin, with spending exceeding 1.5% of GDP, heavily composed of direct subsidies, below-market credit, and state investment funds. South Korea also exhibits high spending at around 1.0% of GDP, while France, Japan, Germany, Taiwan, the United States, and Brazil all spend less than 0.5%. For the United States, the minimal spending is primarily directed toward R&D tax incentives and direct subsidies.

The third chart illustrates the share of banking system assets held by state-owned banks, dividing nations into emerging and advanced economies. Emerging markets dominate this metric, led by India at approximately 70%, followed by China and Russia at around 60%, and Brazil at nearly 48%. Among advanced economies, state-owned bank asset shares are negligible—typically well below 10%—with the notable exceptions of Taiwan at about 38% and Germany at roughly 34%.

The fourth chart focuses specifically on China, detailing direct subsidies for listed firms by subsector as a share of profits from 2017 to 2020. Software and services lead with subsidies accounting for nearly 38% of profits, followed by technology hardware and automobiles at roughly 33%, transportation at 28%, and semiconductors at 25%. Even the lowest-subsidized sector shown, pharmaceuticals, receives subsidies equivalent to over 10% of profits.

The fifth chart shows the 20 most mercantilist countries based on the 2019 ITIF Global Mercantilist Index score, which measures policies such as forced local production, intellectual property protections, restricted market access, domestic preferences, and currency manipulation. China ranks first with a maximum score of 50, followed by India, Brazil, Indonesia, and Argentina.

The final chart contrasts the cumulative market cap in trillions of US dollars of public companies created in the 21st century between the United States and the European Union. The US has experienced exponential growth, with approximately 200 newly created companies generating nearly $20 trillion in cumulative market cap, led by mega-cap companies such as Alphabet, Meta, Broadcom, Tesla, Visa, Mastercard, Netflix, T-Mobile, Salesforce, and Blackstone. In contrast, the EU's cumulative market cap for 21st-century public companies remains virtually flat, barely reaching $2 trillion for more than 100 companies, which include Industria de Diseno Textil, Airbus, CaixaBank, Equinor, and Siemens.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest argues that the primary driver behind the resilience of the US equity market since 2011 is a shrinking net equity supply. He points out that while supply-demand dynamics are known to dictate prices in goods and labor markets, they also significantly affect financial assets. Specifically, steady inflows from annual defined benefit and defined contribution plans—amounting to approximately 1.5 trillion dollars—provide constant purchasing pressure, even as the overall supply of US equities continues to contract. 

This contraction is illustrated in a bar chart titled Global Net Equity Supply, which measures flows in billions of US dollars from 1999 to 2025. The chart breaks down net equity supply into US, Non-US, US SPAC, and Non-US SPAC categories. The blue bars representing US equities show consistent net negative supply almost every year since 2011, dipping to nearly negative 400 billion dollars in some periods, with only a brief positive spike during the 2021 SPAC boom. 

Next to this, a line chart titled Announced Buybacks as a Share of Equity Market Cap tracks trends from 2001 to 2025. It compares US buybacks as a percentage of the S&P 500 market cap against global buybacks as a percentage of the MSCI All Country World Index market cap. US buybacks consistently outpace global trends, peaking near 4.5 percent in both 2007 and late 2018, and most recently hovering around 3 percent in 2025, while global buybacks run lower, generally remaining between 1 percent and 2.5 percent. 

Below these, a third chart details Defined Benefit and Defined Contribution Plan Household and Employer Contributions as a Share of S&P 500 Market Cap from 2000 to 2022. This ratio peaked near 9 percent during the 2009 market bottom and has since declined to between 3 percent and 4 percent, yet still reflects massive, stable inflows relative to the shrinking pool of available shares. 

At the bottom of the page, the author shares three personal photos from Chilliwack, British Columbia, taken in August 2025, depicting a fisherman in a yellow kayak successfully catching and holding a massive sturgeon, accompanied by an Instagram reel link.

This page from the publication discusses the J.P. Morgan "ARC and the Covenants" project, which tracks the total indebtedness of US states and cities by examining general obligation debt, underfunded pension plans, and retiree healthcare obligations (OPEB). The analysis emphasizes that both Chicago and Illinois continue to struggle with some of the highest ratios of required payments relative to their annual revenues. 

In Chicago, the situation remains highly critical, as the city requires a staggering 35% of its total revenue collections to amortize its underfunded plans over a 30-year period. A primary challenge for Chicago is that its liabilities are predominantly contractually bound pensions rather than more flexible retiree healthcare plans that can be modified. Additionally, the Chicago Police Annuity Benefits Fund is severely underfunded, reporting a funding ratio of just 24%, which may have fallen below the 20% "technically insolvent" mark following pension enhancements in July 2025. The author warns of impending tax increases to address these issues alongside a $1.15 billion municipal budget shortfall. 

On the state level, Illinois faces a similar burden. Although Connecticut slightly edged out Illinois in this update, Illinois remains severely burdened by contractually obligated pensions, a challenge worsened by high outward state migration. 

Four charts illustrate these municipal and state-level burdens using fiscal year 2024 data. The first chart, depicting cities' pension, retiree healthcare, and debt costs as a percentage of city revenues, shows Chicago leading with a recomputed rate of approximately 35%, compared to its reported rate of about 32%. Salt Lake City follows with a recomputed rate of around 27%, and Dallas stands at roughly 23%. The second chart breaks down these city obligations into pension versus retiree healthcare shares. It reveals that Chicago, Salt Lake City, and Dallas have pension shares exceeding 90% of their total annual required contributions, leaving them very little flexibility, whereas New York City has a much larger and more flexible retiree healthcare share of about 45%.

The third chart illustrates state-level costs as a percentage of state revenues. Connecticut leads with a recomputed cost of about 28%, followed closely by Illinois at roughly 27% and New Jersey at approximately 25%. The final chart shows the pension and retiree healthcare split for states. It highlights that Kentucky, West Virginia, and Illinois have the highest proportion of contractually fixed pension obligations, each exceeding 80% of their total liability, while New Jersey has the highest proportion of retiree healthcare obligations at roughly 45%.

This analysis focuses on the potential fallout of China's newly announced critical mineral export controls targeting the United States. The author argues that if these restrictions persist, the consequences for US military, industrial, and renewable energy production could be massive. China has broadened its rare earth export regulations to require licensing for any product containing more than 0.1% of Chinese rare earths by value or manufactured with equipment using them. This acts as an equivalent to the United States' own "foreign direct product rule," specifically restricting military end-uses and high-end semiconductor manufacturing. Affected sectors include automotive, defense, medical imaging, and aerospace, with Dutch lithography giant ASML highlighted as relying heavily on Chinese rare earth magnets.

To illustrate the severity, the page includes a detailed table listing fifteen critical minerals subject to Chinese export restrictions announced in April and October of 2025. It details the high US net import reliance and China's market share for these minerals. For instance, the US relies entirely on imports for Terbium, Holmium, and Erbium, all of which come almost entirely from China and are crucial for applications like night-vision goggles, medical lasers, and fiber optics. Other key minerals like Samarium, Gadolinium, Dysprosium, and Lutetium feature an 80% US import reliance with China supplying approximately 70%, critical for F-35 jets, electric vehicles, and nuclear reactor control rods.

Furthermore, a horizontal bar chart shows that Chinese industries are highly insulated from potential US retaliation. Measuring revenues in billions of US dollars, the chart demonstrates that for nearly thirty Chinese sectors—including consumer electronics, electrical equipment, automobiles, and basic chemicals—domestic revenues and non-US export revenues overwhelmingly dominate, leaving US export revenues as a negligible share of total sales. For example, consumer electronics and electrical equipment generate massive domestic revenues well over one trillion dollars, making US-targeted retaliatory tariffs less threatening to China's broader economy.

Finally, the author presents a comparison table showing how China has constructed direct analogs to the US national security toolkit to wage this trade conflict. This includes matching US lithography and semiconductor controls with Chinese rare earth and magnet controls, countering the US Foreign Direct Product Rule with its own extraterritorial rare earth restrictions, and offsetting Commerce and Treasury sanctions lists with China's "Unreliable entity list." Other equivalent tools include matching US tariff retaliations with port fees on US vessels and matching Treasury rules on outbound investments with Chinese state guidance. The author warns that China possesses far more leverage than the White House realizes, making a negotiated compromise difficult but highly necessary to avoid severe supply disruptions.

This page, titled "Online Trump Tracker: Mad Libs: just fill in the blanks" and authored by Michael Cembalest, discusses historically low presidential approval ratings and introduces several macroeconomic and political topics. Cembalest notes that presidential approval from the opposing party has reached near-zero levels, citing a Pew Research estimate of roughly 6% and an August 2025 Gallup poll showing just 1% approval of the Trump administration among Democrats. 

These trends are visualized in two charts. The first, a line graph titled "Presidential approval ratings from the opposing party," traces the percentage of opposing-party respondents who approve of the sitting president's job performance from 1950 through the mid-2020s. The chart highlights a long-term decline in cross-party approval from the era of Eisenhower, Kennedy, and Johnson down to historically low single-digit troughs under Trump 1.0, Biden, and Trump 2.0. The second chart, "Trump approval ratings by party and policy area," is a horizontal bar chart displaying approval from Independents and Democrats across four categories. The data shows Overall approval at 35% for Independents and 1% for Democrats; Foreign Affairs approval at 33% for Independents and 3% for Democrats; Education approval at 31% for Independents and 5% for Democrats; and Economy approval at 29% for Independents and 4% for Democrats.

Beyond approval ratings, Cembalest outlines key political and economic issues to watch. He raises open questions regarding upcoming midterm elections, including whether the Supreme Court will rule that Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act violates the 14th and 15th Amendments. He forecasts that while 12 to 15 House seats could conceivably switch parties due to redistricting, the actual number is likely to be lower. 

The author introduces a "Mad Libs" exercise designed to cover critical global topics, including tariffs, US immigration policy, Chinese rare earth export controls, Oracle's debt levels, central bank gold holdings, and the gender balance of psychiatric medication. Within this discussion, Cembalest notes he is far more concerned about US labor force growth than tariffs as a risk to economic growth. Looking ahead, he previews J.P. Morgan's upcoming 2026 Outlook, which will examine the strength of the semiconductor manufacturing moat shared by NVIDIA, TSMC, and ASML. This upcoming research will analyze four specific risks: US power constraints, China's ability to scale advanced semiconductor production independently, the geopolitical relationship between China and Taiwan, and the profitability of AI investments relative to capital expenditure. The page concludes with a photograph of Cembalest working on the Mad Libs sheet in his office at the newly completed J.P. Morgan headquarters at 270 Park Avenue.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, argues that while the previous decade was defined by disruption in content distribution, the next decade will be defined by generative AI disrupting content creation, posing severe risks and new opportunities for legacy media companies. Historically, entertainment was protected by moats in content creation and capital-intensive distribution. Once unbundled, the distribution moat dissolved, helping Netflix become a Hollywood powerhouse while video profits of major legacy media companies—including CBS, Disney, NBC Universal, Paramount, and Warner Bros. Discovery—fell 38% from 2018 to 2023 before recovering slightly to a 27% decline through 2024. 

Four charts support this analysis of shifting media dynamics. The first chart, depicting annual streaming earnings in billions of dollars from 2019 to 2023, contrasts Netflix's climbing net income—which rose from around $2 billion in 2019 to nearly $6 billion by 2023—against the massive direct-to-consumer losses of major legacy studios, which peaked at nearly negative $11 billion in 2022 before ending 2023 at around negative $7 billion. 

The second chart breaks down the monthly viewing time of the top 100 streaming titles in 2023. It reveals that although Netflix originals' share of viewing time shrank from 34% in January to 20% in December, Netflix sustained a stable overall share of 50% to 55% because legacy studios remained willing to license their content to Netflix via exclusive and nonexclusive acquisitions. 

The third chart tracks the share of U.S. TV viewing time from January 2023 to July 2025, illustrating a historic shift. Legacy broadcast and cable viewing fell from 57.4% to 42.3%, while Netflix ticked up from 7.5% to 8.6%. Meanwhile, all other streaming platforms—such as YouTube—experienced the fastest expansion, rising from 24.8% to 37.7%, meaning total streaming now exceeds legacy broadcast and cable for the first time.

The fourth chart illustrates traditional versus new U.S. video revenue in billions of dollars from 2011 to 2024. It emphasizes that the total revenue pie is barely growing, remaining stagnant at around $220 billion since 2018. Within this flat total, traditional revenue streams like traditional TV, box office, and home entertainment have steadily contracted, while streaming revenue has grown to fill the gap. 

The page concludes with an announcement for the upcoming December 2 Alternative Investments Review, which will cover buyouts, venture capital, hedge funds, private credit, private real estate, secondary funds, and evergreen funds.

This page examines whether generative AI video models can learn real-world physical laws or merely predict pixels, referencing Google DeepMind’s Physics-IQ benchmark. A bar chart displays physical intelligence scores for various models, showing that all score below 30%, led by VideoPoet (multiframe) at nearly 28%, followed by Lumiere (multiframe) around 25%, and Runway Gen 3 (i2v) near 22%, while OpenAI Sora 1 (i2v) scores around 15%. Accompanying text from DeepMind expresses optimism that scaling video datasets will improve physical understanding, highlighting successes like simulating paint smearing. Below, a visual progression of Midjourney text-to-image generations from February 2022 to July 2024 illustrates the rapid evolution from abstract, low-quality portraits to highly photorealistic depictions over a two-year period.

This page analysis discusses the growing democratization of high-quality content creation, driven by the rise of user-generated content (UGC) and generative AI text-to-video tools like Pika, Runway, Stable Diffusion, and Sora. The author argues that content production is becoming cheaper and easier at the exact same time consumers are lowering their quality standards, drawing a parallel to how lower-bitrate MP3s previously replaced higher-quality CDs. 

Four charts are presented to support these observations. The first chart, titled "Media company share of television screen time, Aug 2025," measures the percentage of TV watch time across broadcast, cable, and streaming. It shows that YouTube has captured the single largest share of TV screen time at over 12%, exceeding major traditional media giants and streaming competitors, including Disney at roughly 9.5%, Netflix at 8%, NBCUniversal at about 7%, and Paramount at approximately 6%. 

The second chart, "US news consumption by source," tracks the percentage of weekly news consumers from 2013 to 2025. It highlights a major structural shift: social and video networks have steadily risen to become the top source for news at over 50% in 2025, officially overtaking traditional television, which fell from over 70% in 2013 to roughly 47% in 2025. Online news sites and apps remain flat around 48%, while print media has steadily declined to under 15%. 

The third chart, "Creator vs corporate global media revenue," compares corporate media economy revenues with creator media economy revenues from 2019 to 2023. While corporate media revenue remains massive at over $1.5 trillion, the creator share of the total media economy has doubled, rising from approximately 7% in 2019 to over 14% by 2023. 

The final chart, "Video gamers vs Roblox users," compares the percentage of the US population who are video gamers to Roblox's daily active users in millions from 2018 to 2025. It shows that while the overall share of US video gamers has plateaued and even declined slightly from peak levels of 80% down to around 72%, Roblox's daily active users have climbed dramatically, rising from roughly 5 million in 2018 to over 20 million by 2025, showcasing the massive growth of lower-fidelity, user-generated virtual platforms.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" discusses the massive expansion of artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure, analyzing its impact on the stock market, energy grids, construction spending, and corporate debt. The author argues that while the AI-driven market run is well-documented, the sheer scale of the shift is reshaping the physical and financial landscape, warning that the capital cycle is moving from self-funded expansion to a debt-fueled arms race.

A table on the page details the performance and contributions of AI-related stocks in the S&P 500 since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, categorized into Direct AI, Utilities, Capital Equipment, and the S&P 500 excluding AI. The performance metrics highlight that Direct AI stocks achieved a 181% price return and 124% earnings growth, whereas the S&P 500 ex-AI managed only a 25% price return and 9% earnings growth. In terms of contributions, Direct AI stocks accounted for 75% of the total S&P 500 price return, 79% of its earnings growth, and 90% of its capital expenditure and R&D growth during this period.

The physical footprint of this expansion is visualized in a line chart of US construction spending from 2014 to 2025, measured in seasonally adjusted annual billions of dollars. The chart illustrates a sharp divergence: while spending on office buildings has steadily declined from a peak near $60 billion to around $50 billion, spending on data centers has climbed dramatically to roughly $40 billion. Meanwhile, construction spending for electric power has risen steeply to over $115 billion. The author notes that data centers are putting substantial pressure on power grids and rising electricity prices, citing that in the PJM region, 70% of the previous year’s increased electricity cost was driven by data center demand. 

The financial structure of this growth is also changing. A bar chart compares the debt-to-equity ratios of 28 Direct AI stocks, demonstrating that most major hyperscalers maintain very low leverage—such as Microsoft at 30%, Amazon at 50%, and Google and Meta even lower. In stark contrast, Oracle’s debt-to-equity ratio approaches 500%. This high leverage is tied to recent news of Oracle's stock jumping 25% on a promised $60 billion annual deal from OpenAI to build cloud computing facilities requiring 4.5 gigawatts of power. 

An included quote by Dan O’Laughlin of *Fabricated Knowledge* expands on this development, arguing that Oracle's willingness to leverage up to fund these ambitions marks the end of a disciplined, cash-flow-funded era. He predicts that tech giants like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google will be forced to defend their turf, turning the AI race into a high-risk, debt-fueled arms race. Finally, Cembalest poses a major medium-term risk to top-heavy US equity markets: the potential for China’s Huawei and SMIC to pierce the $6.3 trillion NVIDIA-TSMC-ASML moat by developing their own competitive supernode computing clusters and deep-ultraviolet lithography machines.

This page highlights the structural and cyclical challenges facing the legacy film and television industries, which are driven by a sharp decline in youth viewership, sluggish post-pandemic recovery, and high production costs. 

The first chart, tracking legacy TV viewing time by age group compared to 2015, shows a stark generational divide. While viewership for the 50+ demographic has remained relatively stable at around 85% to 90% of 2015 levels, younger age brackets have cratered. Viewership for the 18–49 group has fallen to roughly 35%, while the 2–17 age bracket has plummeted to nearly 10% by 2023. 

The struggle extends to the silver screen, as shown by domestic box office results since 1995.
