While annual box office receipts recovered from their 2020 low of around $2 billion to between $8 billion and $9 billion by 2025, actual tickets sold tell a more troubling story. Ticket sales peaked in the early 2000s at over 1.4 billion and have struggled to recover past 800 million in 2025, indicating that rising ticket prices are masking a deeper drop in audience volume. A comparison of post-pandemic recovery rates since 2019 confirms that the film industry is severely lagging behind other sectors. While US restaurant revenues, hotel rates, and North American concert ticket sales have recovered to over 100% of their 2019 baselines, film box office receipts stand at only 75%, and tickets sold hover around 60%, barely outperforming city office occupancy rates.

These pressures have directly impacted stock market valuations. Since January 2022, legacy media companies like Disney, Warner Brothers Discovery, Comcast, and Paramount have significantly underperformed the broader market, with their stock price indexes dropping to between 50 and 80. Conversely, Netflix has thrived, with its stock index surging past 200, while Fox and the S&P 500 equal-weighted indexes have recorded modest gains. 

Despite these distribution headwinds, the traditional content moat remains formidable. A chart of median domestic film budgets shows that producing a top 10 or top 20 grossing movie continues to hover between $100 million and $150 million, while top-tier television series like Wandavision, Hawkeye, The Rings of Power, and Stranger Things routinely cost upwards of $25 million per episode. The author concludes that while this capital-intensive content barrier presents a massive obstacle to traditional competitors, new digital attention platforms are successfully bypassing it by engaging audiences without requiring such heavy financial investments.

This page assesses the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence video generation tools, emphasizing how quickly new models are eclipsing previous leaders. Open-source text-to-video options are drastically lowering barriers to entry; for example, HPC-AI’s Open-Sora 2.0 can train commercial-level video generation models for just two hundred thousand dollars, which is roughly ten percent of the training cost of OpenAI’s Sora 1.0, while delivering comparable quality. Although these open-source videos are currently limited to five seconds in length, the technology is advancing rapidly. As a sign of where the industry is heading, Particle6 recently rolled out Tilly Norwood, an AI-generated digital actress who is actively seeking talent representation. 

The analytical data on the page is presented through two charts and a ranking table. A polar chart details a VBench evaluation comparing the capabilities of OpenAI Sora 1.0 against three Chinese programs—Hunyuan, CogVideoX-1.5, and Kling 1.6—across multiple categories such as human anatomy, multiview consistency, mechanics, camera motion, and composition. 

To the right, a bar chart displays VBench scores ranging from 70 to 86 across three categories: total score, quality score, and semantic score. In the total score category, OpenAI Sora 1 leads with a score of roughly 83.5, followed closely by HPC-AI Open-Sora 2.0 at about 83, HunyuanVideo at 82.5, CogVideo at 81, and HPC-AI Open-Sora 1.2 at 79. While HPC-AI Open-Sora 2.0 performs competitively with OpenAI Sora 1 on the quality score (both scoring around 83.5 to 84), OpenAI Sora 1 maintains a distinct advantage in semantic capabilities, leading with a semantic score of 81 compared to Open-Sora 2.0's score of 76.

Finally, an LMArena text-to-video leaderboard table from October 2025 ranks the top video models by user-determined scores. Google dominates the top of the leaderboard, with veo-3.1-audio holding the first rank with a preliminary score of 1404, and veo-3.1-fast-audio also tied at the top with a score of 1395. OpenAI's sora-2-pro is ranked third with a score of 1365. The table also lists competitive models from other developers, including KlingAI's kling-2.5-turbo-1080p at rank eight with a score of 1223, MiniMax's hailuo-02-pro at rank nine with a score of 1215, and Bytedance's seedance-v1-pro at rank ten with a score of 1193. Other listed models represent technology from Alibaba, Luma AI, Pika, and Genmo AI.

This page examines the potential upside of virtual production and generative artificial intelligence for legacy film studios, arguing that these technologies can significantly streamline workflows and reduce costs. According to research from Bain & Company, shifting to virtual production methods can reduce production times and costs by five to ten percent for fifty-million-dollar films, with even greater efficiencies possible for larger-scale family movies, sci-fi sequels, and animations. The savings are driven by innovations like post-production colorization, markerless motion capture, the automation of repetitive tasks like rotoscoping, and the use of real-time rendered LED volumes. The author frames generative AI as the latest step in a century-long tradition of cinematic innovation, tracing back to stop-motion in King Kong, front projection green screens in 2001: A Space Odyssey, computer-generated imagery in Tron, photorealistic CGI in Lord of the Rings, and underwater motion capture in Avatar II.

An accompanying chart illustrates the estimated range of time and cost savings from adopting virtual production methods across different budget tiers and genres. For a fifty-million-dollar comedy, both time and cost savings are projected to range from five to ten percent. For a one-hundred-million-dollar family movie, time savings rise to between eighteen and twenty percent, while cost savings are estimated at fourteen to twenty percent. The highest savings are seen in two-hundred-million-dollar sci-fi projects, where time savings reach twenty-two to twenty-five percent and cost savings span fourteen to twenty percent.

A detailed table profiles several notable AI animation studios seeking to capture market share. These startups, their prominent backers, and their AI-assisted works are listed to show the commercial traction of AI-generated content. Featured studios include Animaj, backed by HarbourView, which produces Pocoyo; AiMation, backed by private equity; Animated Co, backed by pre-seed funding; and Asteria, backed by Moonvalley. Invisible Universe, backed by prominent names such as SevenSevenSix, SV Angel, Serena Williams, and Jennifer Aniston, is highlighted for its work Qai-Qai. Native Foreign is listed as independent, while Promise is backed by major entities like North Road, Andreessen Horowitz, Google AI, Crossbeam, Saga, and Kivu. Finally, Toonstar, backed by Founders Fund, Snap, and Greycroft, is noted for its work StEvEn & Parker, which has accumulated eight billion views. 

The page also features an illustration depicting King Richard III sitting dejectedly on top of a crumbling stone wall, titled "Richard III sitting on top of a crumbling content moat," which visually represents the threat that these technological disruptions pose to traditional media gatekeepers. Footnotes reference Doug Shapiro’s May 2025 paper on media disruption and offer historical context on Shakespeare’s Richard III.

In this J.P. Morgan report, Michael Cembalest argues that traditional media studios face existential pressure as viewer attention shifts to digital formats, even if studios manage to shave 10% to 15% off their production costs. This migration is fueled by generative AI video and highly engaging social video platforms, which now account for about 25% of daily US video screen time. In addition, major tech companies like Apple and Amazon treat video as a loss leader to bolster their ecosystems—with AppleTV+ originally budgeting for $15 billion to $20 billion in losses over its first five years—while newer digital platforms continue to have a deflationary effect on media monetization.

A bar chart titled "Average time spent per day by US adults" tracks the decline of traditional TV and the rise of digital video from 2021 to 2025. Over this period, digital video consumption grew from 3.0 hours per day to nearly 3.8 hours, overtaking traditional TV, which shrank from roughly 3.4 hours to about 2.8 hours per day. 

Another chart, "Video consumption by type, 2024," tracks total daily viewing hours, showing that out of 8 total hours of daily consumption, legacy TV makes up approximately 3.5 hours. Subscription video on demand and social video each account for about 2.0 hours, while free ad-supported streaming TV accounts for the remaining half-hour. 

A central table compares key metrics for TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts. TikTok leads in user engagement at 8.9% and has 1.2 billion monthly active users, heavily skewed toward Gen Z (42.9%) and female users (57.0%). Instagram Reels features the highest user base at 2.0 billion monthly active users, with a 2.0% engagement rate and a balanced gender split. YouTube Shorts has 1.5 billion monthly active users and the lowest engagement rate at 0.6%, but boasts the largest ad reach at 2.6 billion users, or 32.4% of the population.

A final table, "Monetization rate per hour of video, gaming and music," details how newer digital platforms severely under-monetize compared to legacy media. Linear video monetizes at $0.54 per hour, compared to Netflix at $0.37 and YouTube at $0.19. Music CDs monetize at $0.67 per hour, whereas Spotify brings in just $0.06 per hour. In gaming, consoles monetize at $0.11 per hour, while both PC and mobile bring in $0.06 per hour. A personal footnote from Cembalest illustrates the persuasive power of social media, detailing how highly engaging, emotional TikTok videos of rescue dogs prompt him to donate via Amazon links, despite warnings from his spouse that the videos may be scams.

This page argues that storytelling remains a critical advantage for legacy content creators over user-generated content, with smaller studios increasingly taking the lead. The author highlights the immense financial value of storytelling and content libraries, citing examples such as Amazon’s $3.4 billion acquisition of MGM, Disney’s $87 billion in acquisitions of Pixar, Marvel, LucasFilm, and Fox, and Lionsgate achieving record film library revenues in Q1 2025 despite an overall operating loss. Furthermore, Netflix is reportedly exploring an acquisition of Warner Bros studio and streaming assets (including Harry Potter, DC Comics, and Game of Thrones libraries) to bolster its market position.

The page features four data visualizations supporting these points. The first chart, "Nationwide movie releases by year," tracks the number of released movies from 1995 to 2025, comparing the "Major 6" studios (Warner Bros, Disney, Fox, Paramount, and Universal) against "Other studios." While the major studios historically dominated, peaking at over 120 releases in the mid-2000s, their output has declined to around 70 in 2025. Meanwhile, releases from smaller, independent studios have surged from roughly 20 in 1995 to over 100 in 2025, eclipsing the majors. 

The second chart, "Platform catalog share of industry content," displays the percentage of total industry series and movies held by major streaming services as of Q1 2024. Netflix holds the largest overall share at nearly 27%, dominated heavily by series. Amazon Prime Video holds the second-largest share at approximately 23%, featuring a massive library of movies. Hulu, Max, Peacock, Paramount, and Disney+ follow with progressively smaller content shares.

The third chart, "Movie share of streaming revenue," shows that the demand for feature films is rising across the board between 2022 and 2024. Disney+ leads this metric, with movies making up about 53% of its streaming revenue in 2022 and rising to nearly 70% in 2024. Amazon Prime Video grew from under 30% to over 50%, Netflix increased from roughly 27% to over 40%, and Warner Bros climbed from under 20% to approximately 35%.

The final exhibit highlights the enduring value of television episode libraries through two tables of top streaming programs. For the US in the first half of 2025, "Bluey" leads with 25.1 billion minutes viewed, followed by "Grey's Anatomy" at 22.6 billion and "NCIS" at 19.1 billion, with classic legacy shows like "Gunsmoke" still making the list at 11.0 billion minutes viewed. Globally in the second half of 2024, "Grey's Anatomy" topped viewership with 1,000 million hours viewed, followed by "Prison Break" at 788 million hours and "Lost" at 700 million hours, demonstrating that audiences continue to heavily consume deep library content.

In this section of "Eye on the Market," Michael Cembalest reflects on the survival of traditional film studios and the strength of their creative content. He shares a personal analysis of 21st-century filmmaking based on his Letterboxd account, where he has rated over 400 films. He presents a table listing his top-ranked narrative films from 2000 to 2025 that received either a 4.5 or a maximum 5.0 rating, alongside their producing studios and financial performance.

The table details each film's release year, Cembalest's rating, and the ratio of reported worldwide box office receipts to its production budget. High-performing standouts in terms of budget multiples include "Lost in Translation" from 2003 with a staggering ratio of 29.3, "Three Billboards" from 2017 at 13.4, "Last King of Scotland" from 2006 at 8.2, and "The Artist" from 2011 at 8.0. Conversely, films produced for streaming platforms, such as Netflix's "Mank" in 2020 and A24's "The Tragedy of Macbeth" in 2021, are listed with a ratio of 0.0, highlighting the shifting economics of modern cinema. 

Cembalest cautions that box office multiples are far less accurate today than in the pre-streaming era. Before streaming, theatrical releases, physical media sales, and standardized TV deals provided clear public data. Today, direct-to-streaming deals, alternative screening platforms like Patreon, and other supplemental revenue streams remain opaque. He also notes that these ratios are not direct measures of profitability because distributors typically claim 35% to 50% of box office receipts, though the multiples remain a useful rough indicator of audience success. A concluding footnote highlights some of his favorite documentaries, focusing on subjects like Jeff Buckley, Luther Vandross, Robert Downey Sr., Louis Kahn, Robert Evans, Glen Campbell, Humphrey Bogart, Sam Harkness, and "My Octopus Teacher."

This page introduces Michael Cembalest's 2025 Alternative Investments Review, titled "The Deep End." Cembalest reflects on a decade of writing this review, noting that while top-quartile buyout and venture funds continue to outperform and private credit delivers strong relative returns, risks are escalating. He warns that alternative managers are "swimming in the deep end of the pool" as buyout and venture portfolios remain clogged with unmonetized companies from the mid-2010s, hedge funds face unprecedented concentration and crowding, and private credit underwriting standards have loosened under a deluge of capital. He also notes the significant role banks have played in financing this expansion. Below the text, an alternative cover art image depicts the animated character BoJack Horseman standing in a swimming pool looking out over the ocean, referencing the "deep end" theme.

Three charts support these observations. The first chart, titled "Global alternative assets under management" in trillions of US dollars from 2014 to 2024, shows total assets rising steadily from approximately 7 trillion dollars to nearly 20 trillion dollars. This growth is driven largely by private equity and hedge funds, alongside venture capital, real estate, private debt, infrastructure, and natural resources. The second chart, "Private equity and venture capital assets under management as a share of MSCI World market capitalization," shows this share rising from around 7 percent in 2014 to a peak of approximately 16 percent in 2022, before declining slightly to nearly 13 percent in 2024. 

The final chart, "Bank loan exposure to private credit and private equity intermediaries as a percent of legal entity Tier 1 bank capital" as of March 31, 2025, details the exposure of major financial institutions. First Citizens Bank (FCNCA) has the highest total exposure at 207 percent of its Tier 1 capital, followed by Morgan Stanley at 119 percent, Goldman Sachs at 98 percent, Wells Fargo at 88 percent, Truist at 68 percent, Bank of Montreal at 63 percent, PNC at 60 percent, State Street at 52 percent, US Bancorp at 50 percent, JPMorgan Chase at 35 percent, Capital One at 34 percent, Bank of America at 29 percent, and Citigroup at 18 percent. This exposure is split between private equity exposure and private credit exposure, highlighting how deeply traditional banks are intertwined with alternative market growth.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Alternative Investments Review examines structural shifts in the global private equity landscape, characterized by stagnant distributions, declining exit activity, longer holding periods, and the rise of alternative liquidity mechanisms. 

The first chart, tracking global private equity cash flows in billions of US dollars from 2014 to annualized 2025 estimates, shows that except for the anomalous spike in 2021 when distributions neared $700 billion, distributions have remained relatively flat. Annualized estimates for 2025 show contributions of approximately $400 billion outstripping distributions of roughly $350 billion. This lack of liquidity is reinforced by the second chart, which monitors quarterly US private equity and venture capital exit activity from 2013 to 2025. Both asset classes peaked in late 2021 with 550 to 600 exits per quarter, but private equity exits fell sharply to under 200 by mid-2025, while VC exits hovered near 300. 

The third chart illustrates that global buyout exits as a share of global buyout assets under management (AUM) have steadily declined over the past decade. This metric fell from a high of over 30% in 2014 to a bottom of around 7% in 2023, showing only a slight rebound to approximately 10% in 2024. Consequently, assets are staying in portfolios longer, as demonstrated by the fourth chart showing the global buyout median holding period. The median holding period rose from 3 years in 2000 to over 6 years in 2014, and after a brief dip to around 5.3 years in 2020, surged back to over 6 years in 2024, finishing at approximately 6.1 years in 2025.

To address these distribution challenges, general partners are increasingly utilizing alternative exit routes. The fifth chart shows that the share of global private equity exits executed via continuation vehicles expanded dramatically from a stable 4% in 2020 and 2021 to roughly 18% in 2025. Additionally, the final chart shows that global secondary assets under management have grown significantly to provide liquidity. Secondary AUM grew from about $200 billion in 2014 to nearly $600 billion in 2024. As a share of overall private equity AUM, secondary assets dipped to a low of approximately 3.7% in 2021 before rising sharply to represent over 4.75% of the market in 2024.

This page of the 2025 Alternative Investments Review examines the speed of buyout and venture fund monetization, demonstrating that the cycle ending in 2025 exhibits the slowest pace of monetization on record. The author addresses the question of whether the current pace is unusually slow, noting that buyout funds from the 2016–2019 vintage years still have 35% to 68% of their total value to be monetized. 

The first chart, titled "The speed of monetization in buyout funds," plots the median remaining value as a percentage of total value against fund age in years, ranging from six to nine years. The horizontal axis is reversed, with age nine on the far left and age four on the far right. The current 2016–2019 vintage cohort (measured in 2025) represents the slowest monetization path among all periods analyzed, showing remaining values of approximately 68% at six years, 60% at seven years, 45% at eight years, and 35% at nine years. This trajectory is consistently higher than prior cycles, which include the 2005–2008 cohort in 2014, the 2010–2013 cohort in 2019, the 1995–1998 cohort in 2004, the 2000–2003 cohort in 2009, and the 1990–1993 cohort in 1999.

The second chart, titled "The speed of monetization in venture funds," uses the same axes and vintage cohorts to show that the slow monetization trend is even more severe for venture capital, resulting in exceptionally high unsold amounts. For the 2016–2019 vintage in 2025, the median remaining value is roughly 82% at six years and only declines to about 63% by nine years. This is dramatically higher than historical benchmarks; for example, the 1995–1998 vintage (measured in 2004) had only about 10% of its value remaining at nine years, and the 1990–1993 cohort had under 20%. To illustrate the current gap between the two asset classes, the text highlights that for the 2017 vintage at eight years of age, the median buyout fund has an unsold portion of 45% compared to over 60% for the median venture fund. Both charts rely on data from Steve Kaplan of the University of Chicago, MSCI/Burgiss, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2025 Alternative Investments Review argues that the current recovery in initial public offerings, secondary issuances, and merger and acquisition volumes provides a timely exit window and capital-raising environment for private equity and venture capital managers. To support this observation, the author presents six charts detailing liquidity, pricing, and funding conditions through late 2025.

The first chart tracks US IPO activity on a three-month rolling average from 2018 to September 2025, using data from Bloomberg and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. It shows that both deal value, in billions of US dollars, and the offering count peaked extraordinarily high in late 2020 and 2021 before bottoming out in 2022 and 2023. By 2024 and 2025, a modest recovery emerged, with three-month rolling deal values climbing back toward five billion dollars. 

The second chart, based on Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research, displays the US average IPO return on the first trading day for deals larger than twenty-five million dollars from 1995 to September 2025. While average first-day returns reached heights of sixty to seventy percent during the dot-com era of 1999 and 2000, they have maintained a long-term median of roughly fifteen percent. In 2025, first-day returns rebounded to nearly thirty percent, indicating renewed investor appetite.

The third chart illustrates US secondary IPO activity on a three-month rolling average from 2018 to September 2025, using Bloomberg and J.P. Morgan Asset Management data. Secondary deal values and offering counts peaked in late 2021, fell sharply in 2022, and have steadily recovered through 2024 and 2025, with monthly deal values stabilizing between fifteen and twenty billion dollars and offering counts rising back toward one hundred. 

The fourth chart presents total announced M&A volumes by quarter from the first quarter of 2018 to the third quarter of 2025, drawing from Morgan Stanley Research. It divides quarterly volumes, which peaked at over one point four trillion dollars in late 2021, into strategic acquisitions and financial sponsor acquisitions. Following a severe contraction in late 2022 and 2023, quarterly M&A volumes have trended upward, reaching over one point two trillion dollars in the third quarter of 2025, driven by a resurgence in both strategic and sponsor-backed transactions.

The final two charts focus on funding and sponsor liquidity. The fifth chart, with data from J.P. Morgan, tracks leveraged loan and high-yield bond issuance for M&A use of proceeds from 2020 through an annualized estimate for 2025. Debt funding peaked at nearly three hundred and eighty billion dollars in 2021, fell to around one hundred and ten billion dollars in 2023, and recovered to an annualized run rate of nearly two hundred billion dollars in 2025. The sixth chart, also using J.P. Morgan data, shows registered block trade volumes linked to financial sponsors from 2015 to an annualized estimate for 2025. Sponsor block trades peaked at thirty-six billion dollars in 2015 and plummeted to just four billion dollars in 2022. However, sponsor block trades rebounded significantly to twenty-eight billion dollars in 2024, with 2025 tracking at an annualized pace of twenty-three billion dollars, demonstrating that financial sponsors are increasingly able to monetize their equity positions.

This page from the 2025 Alternative Investments Review evaluates the performance of buyout funds relative to public equity markets, specifically the S&P 500, from the early 1990s to 2020. The primary argument is that median buyout funds historically outperformed public markets consistently, with very little divergence between average and median fund performances. However, performance is highly dependent on manager selection: top-quartile managers significantly outperformed, while fourth-quartile managers underperformed the public equity markets in nearly every vintage year. The author notes that relative buyout performance has declined for post-2020 vintages, but cautions that this drop is not yet conclusive due to a soaring, megacap-driven US stock market and the standard J-curve lag in private equity reporting.

Two line charts at the top of the page illustrate US buyout performance using the Public Market Equivalent ratio against the S&P 500 from 1992 to 2020. Both charts are sourced from Steve Kaplan at the University of Chicago, MSCI/Burgiss, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The first chart, plotting average and median PME ratios, shows the two metrics tracking each other closely over time, staying mostly above the 1.0 baseline before dropping below it after 2020. The second chart presents percentiles, plotting the 75th percentile, the median, and the 25th percentile. It shows that the 75th percentile consistently remained well above 1.0, peaking near 1.7, while the 25th percentile remained almost entirely below the 1.0 line, demonstrating that bottom-tier managers consistently failed to beat the public benchmark.

The bottom half of the page explains that the PME ratio compares private equity cash flows to public market equivalents, which can be converted into direct alpha to measure annual outperformance in percentage terms. A scatter plot titled PME vs Direct Alpha for a hypothetical fund by fund inception year models this relationship. The hypothetical fund assumes LP commitments of 25 million dollars in periods 1, 5, 9, 13, and 17, and LP distributions of 40 million dollars in periods 21, 25, 29, 33, 37, and 41. The vertical axis measures Direct Alpha versus the S&P 500 from negative 4 percent to 14 percent, while the horizontal axis measures the PME ratio from 0.75 to 2.00. The plot, sourced from J.P. Morgan Asset Management, shows that inception years in the late 1990s and early 2000s, such as 1998, 1999, and 2004, delivered the highest performance, with PME ratios above 1.75 and direct alpha near 10 percent to 12 percent. In contrast, funds established in the early 2010s, such as 2012 and 2013, as well as 1993 and 2009, are clustered in the lower-left quadrant with PME ratios around 1.0 or lower and direct alpha hovering near or below 0 percent, reflecting how strong subsequent public equity returns lower relative buyout outperformance.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, "Eye on the Market," evaluates the absolute performance of private equity and venture capital by examining multiples of invested capital (MOIC) and internal rates of return (IRR) for median, 75th, and 25th percentile managers across vintage years from 1999 to 2022. A footnote clarifies that MOIC is very close to Total Value Paid In (TVPI) for median managers, suggesting that the temporary use of credit lines to delay capital calls has a negligible impact on these figures.

The author argues that buyout performance was remarkably steady from 1999 to 2019, with the median manager achieving a MOIC of approximately 2.0x and IRRs between 15% and 20%. While recent 2021 and 2022 vintages show a sharp performance decline, the author notes that it is still too early to tell if this is a genuine performance issue or a standard J-curve effect, as many of these funds are still in their commitment periods and holding assets at cost. 

Two charts illustrate these buyout trends. The first, tracking US buyout MOIC, plots vintage years against multiples ranging from 0.8x to 2.8x. The 75th percentile manager peaks near 2.6x in the late 2010s, the median stays very close to 2.0x, and the 25th percentile hovers between 1.4x and 1.6x, before all three series drop sharply for the most recent vintages. The second chart, displaying North American median buyout IRR with a scale from -5% to 30%, shows the median manager consistently landing between 15% and 20% before falling to around 8% recently, while the 25th percentile drops below 0% for the earliest and latest vintages on record.

In contrast, venture capital performance has been far less consistent. Following the dot-com bust, median venture funds struggled to achieve positive absolute returns. Vintages from 2009 to 2018 improved, with median MOICs ranging from 2.0x to 2.5x and IRRs between 13% and 15%. However, performance declined again starting in 2019. The author asserts that this recent decline is not merely a J-curve issue but rather reflects capital destruction from the Metaverse and SPAC investment cycles. An open concern is that the median 2019 vintage venture fund still holds 80% of its assets, meaning future write-downs and asset dispositions could push performance numbers even lower.

Two venture capital charts highlight these dynamics and reveal substantial performance dispersion. The US venture capital MOIC chart, which has a vertical axis from 0.5x to 5.0x, shows that the 75th percentile manager spiked to nearly 5.0x for the 2010 vintage before collapsing to about 1.3x for recent vintages. The median venture manager peaked near 2.5x and has fallen to around 1.2x, while the 25th percentile manager rarely exceeded 1.5x over the entire period. Finally, the North American venture capital IRR chart, ranging from -15% to 30%, shows the 75th percentile manager peaking near 25% for 2010 vintages. The median venture manager's IRR peaked around 15% before falling to just above 0%, while the 25th percentile spent much of the early 2000s in negative territory and has recently slipped back below 0%. Data across these charts is sourced from Steve Kaplan at the University of Chicago, MSCI/Burgiss, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Alternative Investments Review examine performance benchmarking for private equity buyouts, focusing on the role of leverage and addressing whether buyout funds are overleveraged. The author, Michael Cembalest, discusses how leveraged buyout funds utilize significant debt, creating a wide gap in leverage ratios compared to public companies. He references academic arguments that private equity performance benchmarks should be adjusted using leverage, such as a leveraged S&P 500 or Russell 2000, to compensate for this risk discrepancy.

The first chart on the page, titled US buyout vs comparable public equity debt ratios, illustrates this leverage gap by plotting net debt to EBITDA ratios from 2008 to 2020. The US buyout series, shown in blue, starts at approximately 5x in 2008, dips slightly, and then steadily climbs to nearly 7x by 2020. In contrast, the Russell 3000 series, shown in brown, starts at roughly 4x in 2008 but drops sharply to under 2x by 2011, fluctuating between 1.5x and 2.5x for the remainder of the decade and ending near 1.5x in 2020. This chart, using data from Lietz and Chvanov at Harvard Business School and Bloomberg, highlights the wide and expanding divergence in debt levels between private buyouts and public equities.

To evaluate how leveraging a public benchmark affects measured outperformance, the author presents a second chart titled Pro-forma excess returns on a sample private equity fund based on start year. This chart tracks the Public Market Equivalent ratio on the vertical axis, from 0.0 to 3.0, against fund start years from 1993 to 2014. It compares a pro-forma private equity fund with a 12.7 percent internal rate of return and a 1.9x multiple on invested capital against two benchmarks: the standard S&P 500 and a 2.5x leveraged S&P 500. For most vintage years, such as those starting around 2008, comparing the fund to a 2.5x leveraged S&P 500 reduces the PME ratio from about 1.0 to roughly 0.5, indicating lower relative outperformance. However, during certain periods like the 1999 start year, the leveraged benchmark actually results in a higher PME of about 2.5 compared to the standard benchmark's 1.8. The author notes that because buyout leverage is deal-specific and not cross-defaulted, it carries less risk than leveraging an entire public portfolio.

The final section of the page addresses the question of whether buyouts are overleveraged by citing a Federal Reserve analysis. The Fed researchers estimated theoretically optimal levels of debt for buyout transactions and concluded that the LBO industry is currently utilizing leverage levels in line with these optimal figures. The authors justify this higher buyout debt by pointing out that private equity ownership lowers expected distress costs because sponsors can contribute capital during downturns, buyout companies exhibit lower sales volatility than public counterparts, and the asset values of value buyout companies are inherently less volatile than public equities.

This page from the J.P. Morgan report examines buyout multiples, global and domestic dry powder, and venture capital demand-to-supply ratios, arguing that buyout multiples are unlikely to decline significantly because of the massive amount of dry powder waiting to be deployed. The author also notes that venture capital dry powder remains very high in dollar terms, which has driven down the VC demand-to-supply ratio since 2023. 

Five charts support these points. The first two line charts illustrate median total enterprise value to EBITDA multiples from 2004 to 2024 for North American and Western European buyouts, using Bain data. In North America, buyout multiples bottomed near 7x in 2009, peaked around 12.5x in 2021, and remained elevated near 12x in 2024. Western European multiples followed a similar trajectory, rising from a 2009 low near 6.5x to peak around 11.5x in 2021, finishing close to 11.5x-12x in 2024.

The third chart displays global buyout dry powder in trillions of US dollars from 2017 to 2024, categorized by years since the capital was raised. Total dry powder climbed steadily from roughly $0.75 trillion in 2017 to a peak of nearly $1.3 trillion in 2023, before settling near $1.2 trillion in 2024. The overwhelming majority of this capital is "young," having been raised less than three years prior. 

The fourth chart tracks US venture capital dry powder from 2014 to 2024 using Pitchbook data. Dry powder rose from below $100 billion in 2014 to over $300 billion in 2023, with a slight dip to approximately $280 billion in 2024. An inset pie chart breaks down this 2024 dry powder by vintage year, showing roughly equal distribution across pre-2021, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024 vintages. 

The final chart shows the US venture capital demand-to-supply ratio from 2020 through early 2025 across three indices: late stage, venture growth stage, and early stage. All three indices spiked dramatically starting in late 2021 and peaked in 2023, with the venture growth stage index reaching over 3.5x, the late stage index peaking above 3.0x, and the early stage index topping out near 2.8x. Since those peaks, all three ratios have fallen sharply through 2024 and into 2025, though they remain higher than their 2020 levels, with late stage ending near 2.8x, venture growth around 2.3x, and early stage around 1.6x.

This page of the J.P. Morgan Alternative Investments Review argues that using "risk-adjusted returns" for private equity, venture capital, and real estate is fundamentally flawed due to "volatility laundering" and return smoothing. Author Michael Cembalest points out that stale private valuations lead to extremely high autocorrelation, making quarterly returns appear artificially stable. Citing a 2022 academic paper, he notes that while the headline volatility of private equity is reported at 10%, its true economic volatility is closer to 30%, which translates to a true 30% drawdown probability of 15% to 16% over three years, compared to an engineered 0% probability under smoothed valuation methodologies.

To illustrate this lack of variability, the page features two line charts and a statistical table. The first chart, "Lincoln Private Market Index vs public markets, 3Q21-1Q25," plots index values where Q3 2021 equals 10,000. It shows the Lincoln Private Market Index rising in a smooth, nearly straight diagonal line to roughly 13,000 by early 2025. In stark contrast, the S&P 500 enterprise value and S&P 500 ex Magnificent 7 enterprise value reflect significant real-world market volatility, plunging below 9,000 in late 2022 before recovering to roughly 12,500 and 11,500, respectively. 

The second chart, "Lincoln Private Market Index by company size, 1Q14-1Q25," indexes performance from Q1 2014 to Q1 2025, demonstrating that larger private companies have outperformed smaller ones. Private companies with EBITDA of $50 million to $250 million grew to an index value of approximately 23,000, followed by mid-sized companies with EBITDA of $20 million to $50 million at roughly 21,000, and small companies with EBITDA of negative $5 million to $20 million ending around 19,000. 

Finally, a table of "Autocorrelation rates by index, quarterly data, 2001 to 2025, using a one period lag" highlights the statistical disconnect between private and public markets. Alternative asset classes show exceptionally high positive autocorrelation, led by Venture capital at 0.76, Real estate at 0.70, Buyout at 0.64, Secondaries at 0.60, and Private debt at 0.39. Public market indices show virtually no autocorrelation, with the S&P 500 at negative 0.01, Russell 3000 at negative 0.02, Russell 2000 at negative 0.08, REITs at 0.06, and Leveraged loans at 0.13. This statistical disparity underscores why reported private market risks are severely understated.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Alternative Investments Review addresses the subjectivity of evaluating hedge fund performance, highlighting how inappropriate benchmarking can lead investors to make poor termination decisions. To analyze hedge fund performance over a five-year period from September 2020 to August 2025, J.P. Morgan examined 695 US-based hedge funds reporting to HFR, focusing on relative value, equity hedge, event-driven, and macro strategies. 

The first scatter plot, "Individual hedge funds and 20-fund composites," compares annualized excess return over T-bills (ranging from negative 10% to positive 40%) against annualized excess return volatility (ranging from 0% to 50%). Blue dots represent the 695 individual hedge funds, showing a wide dispersion of returns and high volatilities. Gold dots represent randomized portfolios of 20 hedge funds constructed to ensure diversification across the four core strategies. The visual comparison clearly illustrates how diversification benefits collapse the gold cluster into a tighter, lower-volatility area, supported by an average fund correlation of 0.25 over the five-year period.

The second scatter plot, "20-fund composites vs 70/30 benchmark," focuses on these randomized 20-fund portfolios against a common hedge fund benchmark consisting of 70% S&P 500 and 30% Barclays US Agg 1-5, represented by a black square. This chart plots annualized excess returns against volatility ranging from 4% to 14%. While only about one-third of the randomized portfolios outperformed the 70/30 benchmark on an absolute return basis, the benchmark's volatility was nearly 12%, which is higher than almost all of the randomized hedge fund composites. Based on this volatility differential, the author questions the suitability of using a 70/30 stock-bond mix as a fair hedge fund benchmark.

This page, titled Wrapping up, discusses the potential litigation risks associated with the democratization of alternative assets. The author, Michael Cembalest, warns that while retail access to alternatives may benefit portfolios over the long run, a severe recession or liquidity crunch could trigger a massive wave of litigation that tests the legal documentation firewalls of alternative asset fund managers. He points to several historical litigation waves as precedent, including 401k excessive fee litigation, the 2008 collapse of the auction rate security market, structured notes issues, and the SPAC boom-and-bust cycle. 

Four charts on the page illustrate these past and ongoing litigation waves. The first chart, 401k excessive fee litigation settlements, is a dual-axis chart covering 2020 through 2023. It shows that the number of annual settlements rose from approximately 11 in 2020 to 41 in 2023. Meanwhile, the total value of these settlements rose from about $150 million in 2020 to nearly $350 million in 2023, peaking after a brief dip to around $180 million in 2022. The second chart, 401k excessive fee and performance lawsuits by year, is a bar chart tracking annual lawsuits from 2016 to 2023. Lawsuits peaked in 2020 at 100 before declining to roughly 60 in 2021, rising to around 90 in 2022, and dropping back to around 45 in 2023. Footnotes clarify that these 401k claims often target plan sponsors for failing to offer the cheapest share classes or focusing on underperforming, high-fee funds.

The third chart, Percentage of failed auction rate security auctions in 2008, is a line graph tracking the sudden collapse of this market between September 2007 and July 2008. It tracks two definitions of failed auctions: one where the total buy orders from new investors were less than sell orders from existing bondholders, which spiked to nearly 60% in February 2008; and another where the auction reset rate equaled the maximum auction rate, spiking to over 40% during the same month. A footnote details that this collapse led to over 1,000 SEC complaints in 2008 and a subsequent $50 billion settlement by large financial institutions by 2009.

The final chart, Summary of trend cases, is a grouped bar chart displaying the number of core federal filings from 2019 through the first half of 2023 across six categories: Cybersecurity, Crypto, Cannabis, COVID-19, SPAC, and 2023 banking turbulence. The chart shows that SPAC-related filings saw a massive wave peaking at over 30 filings in 2021 and remaining high in 2022, with a footnote highlighting that roughly two-thirds of these lawsuits named directors and officers of the SPAC entities. Crypto-related filings also surged significantly, peaking in 2022 with over 20 filings, while COVID-19-related federal filings remained steady at around 17 per year in both 2021 and 2022.

This page from the 2025 Alternative Investments Review, authored by Michael Cembalest, argues for evaluating hedge fund performance using a calibrated, risk-adjusted benchmark rather than a pre-selected fixed one. Instead of choosing a benchmark in advance, Cembalest proposes matching each fund or composite with a customized stock-bond mix—composed of the S&P 500 and the Barclays US Aggregate 1-5 Index—that exhibited the exact same ex-post volatility over the period from September 2020 to August 2025. 

To support this argument, the page features four scatter plots tracking annualized excess returns versus T-bills on the vertical axis against annualized excess return volatility on the horizontal axis. The top-left chart, titled "20-fund composites vs benchmarks [HFR]," shows that 98% of randomized 20-fund hedge fund composites (represented by gold dots) outperformed the interpolated benchmark curve formed by the black squares, which range from a 30/70 to an 80/20 stock-bond mix. The top-right chart, "10-fund composites vs benchmarks [HFR]," demonstrates that when the analysis is repeated with smaller 10-fund portfolios, the outperformance rate remains high at 91%, even with slightly wider dispersion in the data.

The bottom two charts replicate this analysis using the Pivotal Path hedge fund universe to prove the findings are not unique to HFR data. The bottom-left chart, "20-fund composites vs 70/30 benchmark [PivPath]," shows that when compared to a single fixed 70/30 stock-bond benchmark, only 30% of the hedge fund composites outperform on an absolute return basis. However, as shown in the bottom-right chart, "20-fund composites vs benchmarks [PivPath]," when the analysis shifts to the calibrated risk-adjusted benchmark curve, practically all of the hedge fund composites show outperformance. This shift is due to the strong correlation benefits of hedge funds, which lower their overall volatility relative to their returns. 

Ultimately, Cembalest concludes that this outperformance is highly compelling, but notes that to accept these findings, investors must prioritize risk-adjusted returns over absolute returns and be willing to use an ex-post benchmark rather than an ex-ante one to evaluate portfolio performance.

This page discusses the rapid rise of private credit, which has grown globally from $250 billion in 2007 to $2.5 trillion. The author argues that while the asset class has seen strong returns and minimal distress over the last decade, a future recession will separate high-quality underwriters from low-quality ones, leading to wider performance dispersion. Rather than representing a net expansion of risky credit in the United States, private credit has largely gained market share at the expense of other credit types.

This structural shift is illustrated in several visual aids. First, a chart titled US risky credit market shares shows total outstanding risky credit as a percentage of US GDP from 2000 to 2025. While total risky credit has remained relatively stable at around 15 percent to 18 percent of GDP, private credit has steadily expanded, taking share from high-yield bonds, leveraged loans, and especially bank loans to small and medium enterprises. A second chart, tracking US middle-market leveraged buyout loan issuance from 2014 to 2024, shows that direct lending expanded from under 40 percent to 90 percent of the market, effectively squeezing out syndicated bank debt. 

The author explains that this trend is driven by regulatory incentives. A comparative table titled The RoE on bank lending to small companies shows that banks have a massive risk-based capital incentive to lend to Business Development Companies rather than directly to middle-market companies. Although bank loans to middle-market companies offer a higher spread of 6.25 percent compared to a 2.00 percent spread for loans to BDCs, the risk weight for BDCs is only 20 percent compared to 100 percent for middle-market companies. Consequently, lending to BDCs requires far less capital (2.40 percent of assets versus 12.00 percent) and yields a much higher return on equity of 46 percent compared to 18 percent.

Finally, the page addresses potential systemic risks. A chart of the revolving-credit liabilities of BDCs, indexed to Q1 2015, shows a dramatic increase in total liabilities to an index level of nearly 9 by 2024, with undrawn revolving amounts making up roughly half of the total. While this raises concerns about sudden drawdowns, the author highlights a May 2025 Federal Reserve analysis indicating that US banks are adequately capitalized to absorb these risks. Systemic comfort is also supported by the fact that the average BDC has a stressed capital ratio of 30 percent, significantly higher than the 10 percent average for US banks.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Alternative Investments Review, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the risk, yield, and performance of private credit relative to broadly syndicated loans and high yield bonds. The author notes that while private credit offers a yield premium over broadly syndicated leveraged loans, it carries higher credit risk. For instance, while thirty percent of broadly syndicated loans are rated B-minus or below, eighty-five percent or more of private credit loans to small and medium-sized enterprises fall into this low-rated category. Additionally, the International Monetary Fund estimated in 2025 that about forty percent of companies borrowing from direct lenders experienced negative free operating cash flow after accounting for capital expenditures.

The first visual is a line chart tracking yields to maturity from 2020 through 2025 for private credit, syndicated loans, and high yield bonds. It features the Houlihan Lokey Private Performing Credit Index, JPM Securities private credit at transaction close, JPM Loan Index, and the BAML High Yield Bond Index. The chart shows that private credit yields peaked near twelve percent in late 2023 and early 2024 before declining toward ten percent in 2025, consistently maintaining a yield premium over the JPM Loan Index and the BAML High Yield Bond Index, the latter of which fell below eight percent by late 2025.

To further compare credit quality, a collateralized loan obligation table presents data from August 2024 comparing broadly syndicated loans to small and medium-sized enterprise private credit. It shows that private credit has significantly higher risk exposures, with S&P B-minus or below exposure at eighty-seven percent compared to thirty percent for syndicated loans, S&P CCC exposure at thirteen percent versus six percent, and Moody's Caa exposure at twelve percent versus five percent. The weighted average rating factor is notably higher and riskier for private credit at 3734 compared to 2804 for syndicated loans, while Moody's weighted average recovery rate estimate is slightly lower for private credit at forty-four percent versus forty-seven percent.

Performance-wise, the text notes that a composite of three private credit indexes outperformed a leveraged loan index by an annualized three and a half percent since 2014, though private credit spreads versus loans narrowed from 200 to 250 basis points in early 2023 down to 150 to 175 basis points in September 2025 due to a major influx of new capital. Two bar charts illustrate these performance trends in annual total returns from 2014 through 2025. The first bar chart compares a private credit composite—incorporating Cliffwater Direct Lending, Preqin Private Debt, and PitchBook Private Debt indexes—against the JPM Leveraged Loan Index. It highlights that the composite outperformed in nearly every year, leading to an annualized return of around nine and a half percent for the 2014-2025 period compared to roughly six percent for the leveraged loan index. The second bar chart breaks down the performance of the three constituent private credit indexes, demonstrating that Cliffwater, Preqin, and PitchBook indexes performed similarly over the decade, with annualized returns for each closely matching around the nine to ten percent range. Ultimately, the author cautions that this outperformance may not be an apples-to-apples comparison, citing research indicating that approximately twenty percent of private credit holdings on a value-weighted basis have equity-like exposure, and adjusting for this exposure would reduce the outperformance of private credit to nearly zero.

This page analyzes the health of the private credit market, arguing that there are currently few signs of distress and that the market's aggregate health remains consistent with an economic expansion. The author notes that downgrade-to-upgrade ratios have generally declined despite a minor uptick in the third quarter of 2025, and default rates remain low. The text highlights that financial sponsors provide strong implied support to less profitable companies, as sponsor-backed loans represent approximately 80 percent of middle market loans when measured in dollars, despite making up only 10 percent of total loans. Additionally, the author addresses concerns regarding Payment-in-Kind (PIK) allowances, demonstrating that the PIK share of gross Business Development Company (BDC) investment income barely rose between 2023 and the second quarter of 2025.

Several charts support this positive assessment. The first chart displays the ratio of downgrades-to-upgrades from 2021 through 2025 for direct lending, private credit, and broadly syndicated loans. It reveals that direct lending and private credit ratios spiked to nearly 5x in early 2024 before falling sharply, ending 2025 with a slight upward tick. The second chart tracks default rates with and without selective defaults from 2017 to 2024. It shows that while private credit default rates including selective defaults peaked near 8 percent in 2020 and around 5.5 percent in 2024, they have since trended downward, while default rates excluding selective defaults remained consistently below 2 percent. The third chart outlines nonperforming loans as a share of total loans from 2020 to 2025, showing that both broadly syndicated and middle market loans have remained safely below 1.0 percent since peaking near 1.5 percent in late 2020. 

The stable trend in PIK interest is illustrated through a bar chart and two comprehensive tables tracking the PIK interest share of gross investment income from 2023 to the second quarter of 2025. The data, asset-weighted for eight large BDCs, shows that publicly traded BDCs carry a higher PIK share—averaging 11.9 percent in 2023, rising to 12.8 percent in 2024, and settling at 12.5 percent in the second quarter of 2025—compared to non-traded perpetual BDCs, which averaged 4.9 percent, 5.4 percent, and 5.1 percent over the same periods. 

Individual company data is provided in the final two tables. Among publicly traded BDCs, Blue Owl Technology Finance Corp reported the highest PIK share at 17.6 percent in the second quarter of 2025, while Ares Capital Corp stood at 16.3 percent, and Main Street Capital Corp recorded the lowest at 4.4 percent. Among non-traded perpetual BDCs, Blue Owl Capital Corp II posted the highest PIK share at 13.5 percent in the second quarter of 2025, followed by Blue Owl Credit Income Corp at 6.2 percent and Sixth Street Lending Partners at 6.1 percent, while Apollo Debt Solutions BDC registered the lowest share at just 1.5 percent.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Alternative Investments Review analyzes private cash flow and credit default trends, highlighting how borrower size and industry sector impact financial performance. The central argument is that while larger private credit borrowers are experiencing robust cash flow growth, smaller companies remain financially challenged, leading to elevated covenant defaults among the smallest firms and higher actual default rates in the middle-market segment. 

The first chart, sourced from Lincoln International, illustrates year-over-year EBITDA growth for private companies from Q3 2024 through Q2 2025. It reveals a clear divergence based on company size: smaller companies with less than $50 million in EBITDA saw stagnant growth hovering between 2% and 4%, while the largest companies with over $100 million in EBITDA saw strong growth that climbed to approximately 11% by Q2 2025. 

The second chart, also from Lincoln International, tracks covenant default rates by EBITDA size. Consistent with the weak cash flow growth of smaller firms, covenant default rates are heavily concentrated in the smallest tier (under $10 million EBITDA), where defaults spiked to roughly 30% in Q1 2025 before settling near 27% in Q2 2025. In comparison, covenant defaults for companies with over $100 million in EBITDA remained negligible, staying well below 2% across all quarters.

The third chart, utilizing Proskauer data through Q3 2025, shows that actual private credit default rates do not perfectly mirror covenant defaults. Instead, actual defaults peaked in the middle-market segment, defined as companies with $25 million to $50 million in EBITDA. This segment's actual default rate peaked at about 4.5% in Q4 2024 before declining to approximately 3.2% in Q3 2025, whereas both the smallest (under $25 million EBITDA) and largest (over $50 million EBITDA) cohorts maintained actual default rates below 2%.

The final chart details private credit default rates across five key industries. The data shows pronounced periodic stress in the manufacturing and consumer sectors, both of which peaked in Q1 2025 at around 8% and 7% respectively. Healthcare and software & technology experienced moderate distress, with software & tech peaking near 4.5% in Q1 2025 and healthcare topping out around 4.0% in Q4 2024. Business services was the most resilient sector, keeping default rates around 1% or lower across the entire period.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, titled Alternative Investments Review, argues that real estate fundamentals across commercial, residential, and industrial sectors remain weak. The author notes that office delinquencies are rising sharply, leading to elevated special servicing rates. Additionally, multifamily delinquencies now exceed ten percent in several Texas and Florida cities, and industrial vacancy rates have doubled since 2022. For the hotel sector, revenue per available room, or revpar, grew by only 0.4 percent in 2024, and CBRE projects a negative 0.1 percent contraction for 2025. This hotel slowdown is attributed to reduced inbound travel, less business travel, government layoffs, and a five percent growth in competing short-term rentals. Hotel profit margins are expected to face pressure throughout 2025 from rising labor costs, increased operating expenses, and weaker demand relative to the hurricane recovery and election year bump of 2024.

The page includes six charts to support these observations. The first chart displays commercial mortgage-backed securities, or CMBS, delinquencies by property type from 2001 to 2025. It reveals that regional malls experienced a massive spike in delinquencies during the pandemic, peaking above 20 percent, while office delinquencies have skyrocketed recently, climbing past 15 percent by late 2025. Delinquency rates for multifamily, hotel, and industrial properties remain comparatively low but are ticking upward. The second chart illustrates special servicing rates for office and non-office CMBS loans from 2002 to 2026. Office special servicing rates are surging toward 15 percent, surpassing their Global Financial Crisis peak, while non-office servicing rates have leveled off to around 7 or 8 percent after a brief spike in 2020.

The third chart plots the overall United States residential vacancy rate from 1965 to 2025. Vacancies peaked at approximately 11 percent around 2009, dropped to a historic low below 6 percent in 2021, and have since rebounded to roughly 7 percent. A corresponding bar chart details residential vacancy rates for the twenty-five largest metropolitan statistical areas as of the second quarter of 2025. This chart shows high vacancy concentrations in the Sunbelt and Florida, with Orlando exceeding 12 percent, followed closely by Austin, Houston, Dallas, Tampa, and Phoenix, while Riverside and Boston record the lowest vacancy rates at under 4 percent.

The fifth chart tracks the national industrial vacancy rate from 2001 to 2025. The rate reached a peak near 10 percent in 2010, bottomed out at approximately 4 percent in 2022, and has since climbed sharply back to about 7.5 percent. The final bar chart breaks down industrial vacancy rates for select United States cities in the third quarter of 2025. Austin leads the nation with an industrial vacancy rate approaching 14 percent, with San Francisco, Phoenix, and San Antonio also showing elevated vacancy levels, while Detroit, Washington D.C., and Chicago report the lowest rates at under 5 percent.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Alternative Investments Review examines valuation practices and credit issues in middle-market private debt, focusing on pricing staleness in Business Development Companies and recent high-profile defaults. The author argues that many middle-market loans are held at par valuations as long as possible, leaving private credit investors unaware of deteriorating positions until they become too large to ignore. 

The first chart, titled Price Declines on Select Middle Market Securities, tracks prices in cents on the dollar from January to September 2025. It shows that both the Tricolor 2025-2A E asset-backed security and the First Brands TLB 2027 loan fell off a cliff, plummeting from near-par values to between ten and thirty cents on the dollar by September 2025 due to reported collateral fraud. During the same period, the NFE 12% 2029 and Saks 11% 2029 senior secured bonds declined more gradually, ending between thirty and fifty cents on the dollar.

This valuation delay is supported by the second chart, Accounting Fair Value of BDC First-Lien Loans, which indexes valuations from 2014 to 2024. The chart compares BB-rated and B-rated leveraged market loans against the accounting price of BDC loans. While the market-traded BB and B-rated loans experienced deep, V-shaped drops during market stress events—most notably plunging to an index level of 85 during the 2020 downturn—the BDC accounting valuation remained remarkably flat, dipping only slightly to 95 before recovering, which illustrates the staleness of private credit marks.

The table, Fair Value Assigned to Medallia's Private Credit Loan, provides a real-world example of inconsistent valuations for the same underlying asset across different BDCs from Q2 2024 to Q3 2025. By the third quarter of 2025, the fair value assigned to Medallia varied significantly: Apollo marked the loan lowest at 77 cents on the dollar, Blackstone marked it at 82, Monroe marked it at 84, and both FS KKR and Onex held it higher at 91 cents on the dollar.

The final chart, BlackRock TCP BDC Loans to Renovo, tracks the cost and fair value of loans to a direct-to-consumer home remodeling platform from Q4 2022 to Q4 2025. The position started with a cost of around 13 million dollars, marked near par at 98 cents. In Q1 2024, the loans went into payment-in-kind mode, and the fair value mark subsequently dropped to 53 cents by Q4 2024. Following a debt write-off and partial recapitalization in Q1 2025, the remaining debt was marked back up to 97 cents in Q2 2025. However, this was followed by a sudden, complete write-off in Q4 2025 down to zero dollars due to a Chapter 7 liquidation. The author notes this case demonstrates how asset-light borrowers of BDCs can quickly see their salvage values wiped out entirely. 

Additionally, the author references investor Howard Marks, who identified several overlooked red flags at First Brands. These included permitting the company to receive factored receivables directly rather than remitting them to banks, utilizing opaque financing structures that hid debt that was double the disclosed amount, boasting five billion dollars in sales despite the CEO having no online profile and a history of litigation, and maintaining above-average profit margins across a confusing web of corporate entities.

This page analyzes the state of the commercial real estate (CRE) capital markets, highlighting tentative signs of recovery alongside substantial brewing challenges, particularly concerning looming loan maturities through 2027. The author observes that while debt origination volumes are picking up across multiple lending types and regions—particularly Manhattan office lending—a significant share of maturing debt faces insolvency or severe debt service stress.

A series of five charts supports this analysis. The first chart, illustrating quarterly commercial real estate debt origination volume in billions of U.S. dollars from 2015 to early 2025, shows that activity peaked near $275 billion in late 2021 before dropping sharply through 2023 and 2024 to around $100 billion. However, by the first half of 2025, volumes show a clear rebound, rising back toward $200 billion. 

The second chart displays the rolling 12-month total origination value from 2002 to mid-2025 across five primary lending types: banks, government agencies, financial institutions, CMBS, and other sources. Banks remain the dominant capital source, peaking above $400 billion in 2022, bottoming near $200 billion, and showing a strong upward turn in 2025. Government agency lending represents the second-largest portion, maintaining steady volume, while CMBS and financial originations remain much lower but are also beginning to tick upward.

Geographical and property-type concentrations are explored in a chart detailing loan volume in the top 15 U.S. markets. Manhattan leads by a wide margin, approaching $28 billion in volume, which is uniquely dominated by office lending. Other major markets like Los Angeles and outer New York City boroughs follow at much lower volumes, roughly $15 billion or less, with their activity heavily concentrated in apartment and multifamily sectors rather than office space.

The fourth chart tracks the distressed share of total CRE volume as a percentage from 2005 to 2025. Following a peak of roughly 18% around 2010, the distressed share remained below 2% for most of the last decade but has recently begun a gradual, slow climb back toward 4% in 2025, a trend the author characterizes as a healthy sign of market-clearing.

The final chart presents a major upcoming challenge, breaking down the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) of outstanding securitized CRE debt maturing before 2027. It classifies debt into four risk tiers: insolvent with a DSCR under 1.0, higher risk with a DSCR under 1.25x, medium risk with a DSCR under 2.0x, and lower risk with a DSCR over 2.0x. Across all sectors, the share of insolvent loans is remarkably high. In multifamily housing, nearly 50% of the maturing debt is classified as insolvent. The office sector is similarly distressed, with approximately 40% of maturing debt categorized as insolvent and another 30% deemed higher risk. Industrial, retail, and hotel properties show relatively lower distress, with retail exhibiting the smallest insolvent share at approximately 10%.

This page of the alternative investments review argues that performance dispersion is coming to private credit, much like it has for other alternative asset classes. Michael Cembalest explains that private credit managers have seen tightly clustered performance since 2014 because there has not been a lasting recession to test their underwriting. 

To support this context, a line chart titled "COVID was not a typical recession" tracks high-yield credit spreads and high-yield default rates from 1987 through November 2025. It shows that although there was a recession during the COVID-19 pandemic, credit spreads peaked around 10% and default rates peaked near 8%. These peaks were much lower and shorter-lived than those seen in the recessions of 1991, 2001, and 2008, largely due to supportive fiscal and monetary policies. 

The author posits that the next recession will drive manager dispersion in private credit, mirroring the historical patterns of other alternative assets. Four charts illustrate this typical dispersion. First, a line chart showing US buyout performance from 1999 to 2020 via Multiple on Invested Capital (MOIC) illustrates a consistent gap between performance tiers; for the 2014 vintage, the 75th percentile MOIC reached approximately 2.6x, compared to a median of 2.0x and a 25th percentile of roughly 1.6x. Second, a line chart of US venture capital MOIC over the same period reveals even wider dispersion, with the 75th percentile peaking over 4.5x for 2010 vintages while the 25th percentile remained near 1.5x. Third, a scatter plot tracking top and bottom quartile hedge fund performance from September 2020 to August 2025 shows top-quartile annualized excess returns over Treasury bills ranging from 5% to 35% across various volatility levels, while bottom-quartile returns clustered near or below 0%. Fourth, a distribution curve of absolute returns from activist hedge fund campaigns between 1994 and 2014 reveals a very long positive tail; while the median return was near 0%, the average was pulled higher by dozens of outlier campaigns that returned well over 200%, with 11 campaigns exceeding an 800% return.

Cembalest suggests that in private credit, manager success during the next downturn will depend heavily on underwriting discipline and document covenants. A final horizontal bar chart, drawing on October 2023 data from Moody's Investor Services, compares key covenant features between broadly syndicated loans (BSL) and private credit. The chart demonstrates that BSL deals are far less protective. For example, about 75% of BSL deals allow inside maturities compared to only 15% of private credit deals. Furthermore, roughly 65% of BSL deals allow the conversion of unused restricted payments into debt and allow automatic debt increases per dollar of new equity, whereas private credit allows these features in only 12% and 0% of deals, respectively. Finally, while approximately 35% of BSL deals lack a "J Crew" intellectual property blocker, no private credit deals in the sample lacked this protection. This stronger underwriting discipline is projected to be the defining factor for private credit managers when the credit cycle turns.

This page explores the structural shifts in work habits driving the deterioration of commercial office real estate fundamentals. The author argues that work-from-home employment remains stubbornly high, hovering between 30% and 35% compared to less than 5% before the COVID-19 pandemic. To substantiate this claim, the analysis triangulates findings from three primary sources: Nicholas Bloom’s Work-From-Home survey, Kastle Systems key fob swipe data, and post-pandemic mass transit ridership recovery trends.

The first line chart, titled "Work from home: large metropolitan cities," tracks the percentage of full paid days worked from home from October 2020 to October 2025. Focusing on U.S. residents aged 20 to 64 with annual earnings above $10,000 to $20,000, the chart shows that while work-from-home rates peaked near 40% to 45% in late 2020, they have since plateaued, remaining elevated between 25% and 35% across major metropolitan areas such as Los Angeles, Miami, Washington D.C., Chicago, New York, Atlanta, San Francisco, Houston, and Dallas.

The second line chart, "Commercial property utilization rates based on security card (key fob) swipes vs Feb 2020 levels," illustrates physical office attendance trends from 2020 through October 2025. After plunging to near 10% in early 2020, key fob swipes across major cities gradually recovered but have mostly leveled off between 40% and 65% of pre-pandemic levels. Austin and Dallas lead the recovery, approaching the 60% to 70% range, while cities like San Francisco, Philadelphia, and Los Angeles lag behind, plateauing closer to 40% to 45%.

Supporting this physical vacancy data is a detailed table on "Post-Covid recovery in mass transit ridership," comparing Q1 2025 ridership levels against a pre-pandemic Q2 2019 baseline. The median transit recovery across 22 major North American transit authorities stands at 71%, representing a meager 4% increase over the past two years. Miami is the sole city to completely surpass its pre-pandemic levels with a 105% recovery rate, followed by Salt Lake City at 97%. Several major transit hubs have plateaued at an 80% recovery level, including New York City, Washington D.C., and Los Angeles. On the weaker end of the spectrum, transit systems in San Francisco, Detroit, and Chicago report only 60% recovery, Atlanta sits at 52%, Raleigh is at 46%, and Boise trails at the bottom with a 22% recovery rate. Data for the page is sourced from Bloom, Barrero, and Davis, Kastle, Bloomberg, J.P. Morgan Asset Management, and the American Public Transportation Association.

This page from the 2025 Alternative Investments Review analyzes the dramatic, historic shift in institutional investor portfolios away from office real estate and toward industrial assets, while presenting evidence that the downturn in the office sector is beginning to stabilize. The author notes that since 2015, NCREIF returns on industrial real estate reached 250% compared to just 20% for offices. Despite this divergence, several metrics suggest the worst of the office downturn is over: net absorption is approaching zero, construction pipelines are drying up, and sublease availability is declining. Pointing to JLL data, the author highlights that future office deliveries are projected to fall to just about one million square feet annually between 2027 and 2030, with 70% of that supply already preleased. 

The first chart illustrates MSCI commercial real estate property type allocations within the US All Core Open-Ended Property Fund Index from 2000 to 2025. It shows office allocations declining from a peak of nearly 30% down to approximately 15% by 2025, while industrial allocations surged from around 10% to over 30%, overtaking apartments as the dominant property type. 

The physical stabilization of the office market is detailed across several charts using data from Colliers, CoStar, JLL, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. A chart of US office net absorption and deliveries from 2020 to 2025 shows that net absorption, which plummeted to nearly negative 40 million square feet during the pandemic, has steadily clawed its way back toward zero in 2025, while quarterly deliveries have consistently shrunk. This is mirrored in the US office construction pipeline chart, which depicts total space under construction falling precipitously from over 150 million square feet in 2020 to around 50 million square feet in 2025. 

Another chart compares the US office vacancy rate against sublease availability. While the headline vacancy rate has climbed from roughly 10% in 2019 to over 14% in 2025, sublease availability peaked in 2023 at nearly 240 million square feet and has since dropped below 200 million square feet, indicating that shadow space is being digested. 

The final two charts explain why headline vacancy rates do not tell the whole story, revealing a deep divergence in asset quality. A chart of cumulative net absorption by building vintage since Q2 2020 shows that only buildings constructed from 2015 to the present have positive net absorption, gaining nearly 150 million square feet. In contrast, older vintages have all experienced negative absorption, led by 1980s-built properties which lost over 120 million square feet. Lastly, the office vacancy concentration chart shows that vacancy is highly unequal; a tiny fraction of underperforming "zombie" buildings accounts for the vast majority of vacant space, whereas 40% of all office assets have almost no vacant space.

This page of the J.P. Morgan Alternative Investments Review evaluates the structural shifts and outlook for commercial real estate, specifically focusing on the financial viability of office-to-residential conversions, the recovery in retail re-leasing spreads, and the massive expansion of AI-driven data centers. 

The author begins by analyzing the challenging economics of office-to-residential conversions. Using a hypothetical prewar Class B office building, the text explains that even with new residential rents at the 90th percentile, high conversion costs of $320 per square foot plus $40 per square foot for green efficiency mean that a buyer would need to purchase the office building at a massive 60% discount from pre-pandemic levels to achieve a 15% to 18% return. Physical hurdles like HVAC retrofitting, floor plate mismatches, and zoning issues further limit these projects. While about 100 to 150 million square feet of office space are slated for conversion across the United States, this is small compared to the 430 million square feet of vacant office space added since 2019. 

Two charts illustrate these office supply dynamics. The first, titled "Office conversions by status & estimated completion year," tracks the number of projects and total square feet from 2018 to 2027 and beyond. It shows that completed and underway projects remained low through 2025, but a massive spike in planned and announced projects is expected by 2027 and beyond, pushing total square feet under conversion to over 60 million. The second chart, "Office conversions & demolitions vs new supply deliveries," shows that new supply deliveries have historically dwarfed demolitions and conversions. However, in the 2025 projection, combined demolitions and conversions are expected to exceed new supply deliveries for the first time since 2018 as new supply falls sharply.

The bottom portion of the page transitions to positive developments in retail and data centers. Strip center retail is experiencing a strong recovery in re-leasing spreads. Meanwhile, data centers are seeing unprecedented demand, growing from just 2% of fundraising to 31% in 2025, with artificial intelligence workloads estimated to consume half of all data center square footage. 

These trends are depicted in two final charts. The first, "Strip center REIT blended re-leasing spreads," tracks the weighted average spread by gross leasable area from 2006 to 2024. The line shows that spreads plummeted to near 0% in 2010, rose to 11% in 2016, fell to 4% during the pandemic in 2020, and have since surged back to nearly 13% by 2024. The final chart, "US data center vacancy rates and pre-leasing," highlights a booming sector from 2020 to 2025. The pre-leased share of megawatts under construction, shown as gold bars, has risen steadily from 50% to nearly 80%. Concurrently, the colocation vacancy rate, shown as a blue line, has plummeted from 10% in 2020 to less than 3% in 2025.

This page is a professional biography of Michael Cembalest, the Chairman of Market and Investment Strategy for J.P. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management. It features a portrait photograph of Mr. Cembalest alongside a summary of his career at the firm, which he joined in 1987. The text highlights his leadership in strategic market and investment insights for a division supervising six trillion dollars of client assets as of 2025. It details his previous roles within J.P. Morgan, including serving as the Chief Investment Officer for the Global Private Bank for eight years, heading a fixed income division, and acting as Head Strategist for Emerging Markets Fixed Income. Additionally, the biography notes his academic credentials, including a Master of Arts from the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs in 1986 and a Bachelor of Arts from Tufts University in 1984.

This page from the Alternative Investments Review provides updates on the US multifamily housing sector, hotel performance dynamics, and investor redemptions within the Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust, known as BREIT. 

The author first attributes rising US multifamily vacancy rates to a substantial supply surge over the past few years.
