This trend is illustrated in a line chart tracking housing supply under construction as a percentage of owner-occupied housing stock from 2000 to 2024. The data shows that while single-family supply under construction peaked in 2006 at about 1.5% and hovered around 0.8% in 2024, multifamily supply under construction experienced an unprecedented post-2020 surge, peaking at nearly 1.4% of the existing stock in late 2023. An adjacent chart on historical and projected US multifamily supply from 2014 through 2028 shows that new multifamily completions peaked in 2024 at nearly 600,000 units, representing almost 3.0% of existing inventory. However, the author highlights a projected decline in new supply once these current units are fully absorbed, with completions forecasted to fall back to around 200,000 units, or just 1.0% of inventory, by 2028.

Regarding the lodging sector, the commentary highlights a stark divergence in performance between luxury accommodations and the rest of the market. A bar chart tracking US hotel performance by class year-to-date through the second quarter of 2025 illustrates this polarization, comparing Average Daily Rate (ADR) and Revenue Per Available Room (RevPAR). Only the Luxury and Upper Upscale segments achieved positive growth, with Luxury leading at nearly 3.0% growth for both metrics. Conversely, Upscale, Upper Midscale, Midscale, and Economy classes all recorded contraction, with Economy experiencing the deepest decline at roughly negative 1.8% in RevPAR. The author suggests this performance gap is consistent with a strong stock market benefiting wealthy consumers alongside a sluggish broader economy impacting average travelers. A lighthearted footnote also critiques the common hotel practice of leaving in-room televisions turned on for arriving guests.

The final section provides a liquidity and performance update on BREIT. The author recalls that in 2023, investor redemption requests had surged to approximately 8% of Net Asset Value (NAV), causing fulfillment rates to collapse to just 5%. A dual-axis line chart detailing monthly requests as a percentage of NAV alongside the percentage of requests fulfilled from late 2022 through mid-2025 illustrates how this situation stabilized. While monthly redemption requests peaked near 8% of NAV in late 2022 and early 2023, they steadily declined to around 1.0% to 2.0% of NAV by mid-2025. Concurrently, the monthly fulfillment rate recovered from its low points in 2023 to reach 100% of requests by early 2024, maintaining full liquidity fulfillment through mid-2025. The author notes that this stabilization is unsurprising given BREIT's minimal office exposure, which stood at just 3% of NAV.

This appendix page from J.P. Morgan's Alternative Investments Review analyzes the dynamics and performance of LP-led versus GP-led secondary funds compared to primary buyout funds. The author explains that in LP-led secondary transactions, limited partners sell their positions to new investors, typically at discounts of five to fifteen percent for buyouts, private credit, and infrastructure, though discounts are much wider for venture capital and real estate. In contrast, GP-led transactions involve a general partner rolling assets into a new fund near the end of the original fund's life, typically resulting in smaller discounts. Over the last decade, GP-led transactions have expanded to represent a much larger share of the overall secondary market. 

Four distinct charts support these observations. The first chart, depicting LP-led secondary transaction prices as a percentage of reference date net asset value from 2013 to the first half of 2025, shows that buyout, infrastructure, and private credit secondary pricing has generally hovered between eighty-five percent and ninety-five percent of NAV. Meanwhile, real estate and venture/growth secondaries saw steep declines starting in 2022, with venture bottoming out around sixty-five percent of NAV in 2023 before recovering to seventy-five percent by early 2025. 

The second chart displays secondary market transaction volume in billions of US dollars from 2014 through the first half of 2025, breaking down volume by LP-led and GP-led structures. Total secondary market volume grew from around forty billion dollars in 2014 to a peak of nearly one hundred and forty billion dollars in 2024, with GP-led transactions consistently making up a substantial portion of the volume over the latter half of the decade.

The final two charts compare the performance of global buyouts and global secondaries by vintage year from 2010 to 2022. The chart for median TVPI, or total value to paid-in capital, illustrates that global buyouts have consistently outperformed global secondaries across every vintage year, with buyouts regularly exceeding 1.8x TVPI for mid-2010s vintages while secondaries remained closer to 1.5x or 1.6x. Despite this lower return profile, the final chart on IRR dispersion—measuring the difference between top and bottom quartile IRR—reveals why secondaries remain attractive. While buyout dispersion remains volatile and high, ranging from nine percent to fifteen percent, secondary fund IRR dispersion is much lower, typically fluctuating between four percent and nine percent. This tighter dispersion reflects the lower risk and uncertainty inherent in purchasing shorter-duration, already-established buyout portfolios, which is the primary value proposition for secondary fund investors.

This page analyzes the characteristics and performance of evergreen funds, which are hybrid investment structures with no end date that continuously accept new capital, unlike traditional closed-end drawdown funds. The analysis compares a sample of the three largest evergreen funds and the three largest closed-end drawdown funds across three categories: private credit, private equity, and real estate. The introductory text notes that while evergreen funds offer quicker access to a diversified portfolio, they also carry limited liquidity subject to redemption caps and gates. These funds typically utilize higher vehicle-level leverage in private credit and real estate than drawdown funds, though deal-specific leverage is slightly lower. Additionally, evergreen managers maintain significant cash plus credit facilities of around twenty to twenty-five percent due to their open-ended nature, resulting in more diversified portfolios with a higher number of investments.

Several charts support these observations. The first chart, showing the number of evergreen funds by asset class from 2015 to 2025, illustrates rapid growth in the sector, with the total number of funds rising from approximately one hundred in 2015 to nearly six hundred by 2025. Private debt and private equity make up the vast majority of these funds, with real estate and a small sliver of infrastructure completing the mix. An adjacent pie chart displays the breakdown of evergreen launches by type in 2024, showing a diverse range of vehicles, including European long-term investment funds, interval funds, listed business development companies (BDCs), long-term asset funds, non-traded BDCs, non-traded real estate investment trusts (REITs), private BDCs, and tender offer funds.

Two leverage charts compare the structural profiles of the fund types. The vehicle leverage proxy chart—measured as total vehicle assets minus net asset value, divided by total vehicle assets—reveals that evergreen funds are significantly more leveraged at the vehicle level in private credit (around forty percent) and private real estate (about fifty-three percent) compared to drawdown funds, which stand at roughly twenty-two percent and thirteen percent, respectively. In private equity, drawdown funds show higher vehicle leverage at twenty percent compared to just five percent for evergreens. Conversely, the deal leverage chart, which measures the loan-to-value ratio, shows that drawdown funds carry slightly higher deal-level leverage in private credit (about fifty-two percent versus forty-five percent for evergreens) and private real estate (about fifty-eight percent versus forty-seven percent for evergreens), with private equity data noted as not applicable.

The final two charts detail cash holdings and investment diversification. The cash levels chart shows that evergreen funds carry substantial liquidity buffers, with cash and credit facilities combined totaling approximately nineteen percent in private equity and twenty-five percent in both private credit and private real estate. Credit facilities make up the bulk of this evergreen liquidity, whereas traditional drawdown funds hold very little cash, typically between zero and five percent. Lastly, the chart comparing the number of investments highlights that evergreen funds are far more diversified than drawdown funds. In private equity and private credit, evergreen funds hold upwards of five hundred investments compared to fewer than one hundred for drawdown funds. In private real estate, evergreens hold about one hundred sixty investments, while drawdown funds hold around ninety.

This page of the private credit research section presents a study by Chernenko et al. titled "Bank capital and the growth of private credit," which analyzes the capitalization of Business Development Companies (BDCs) and the economics of bank lending. The author notes that BDCs are highly capitalized private credit funds with median risk-based capital ratios around 36%, comfortably exceeding the Federal Reserve’s stress-testing requirements. 

Two line charts illustrate these distributions. The first shows the distribution of BDC risk-weighted capital ratios, highlighting a peak around 30% to 35% and comparing it to the Federal Reserve's stress testing requirement for banks at 10%. The second chart shows the distribution of BDC stressed capital ratios, pointing out that the average BDC stressed capital ratio is 30.4%, with only one fund falling below 4.5%. This is contrasted against the average bank stressed capital ratio of 9.9% in the 2024 stress tests.

The text argues that banks find lending to private credit funds like BDCs more lucrative than lending directly to middle-market companies due to over-collateralization and favorable capital treatment. To support this, a detailed table compares the return on equity (ROE) for these two lending channels. While lending directly to a middle-market company offers a higher spread of 6.25% compared to 2.00% for BDC loans, the BDC option features a vastly lower assumed default rate of 0.25% versus 4.00% and a high assumed recovery rate of 95% versus 60%, resulting in an expected loss of just 0.01% compared to 1.60%. Furthermore, BDC lending has lower operating expenses of 0.10% versus 2.00% and a much lighter risk weight of 20% versus 100%. Consequently, the capital required as a percentage of assets is only 2.40% for BDC lending compared to 12.00% for middle-market lending, ultimately generating a far superior return on equity of 46% for bank loans to BDCs compared to 18% for bank loans to middle-market companies.

In the JP Morgan Asset Management 2026 Outlook, Michael Cembalest presents an analysis titled "Smothering Heights: is the largest moat in market history indestructible?" arguing that the generative AI investment theme has dominated the US equity market since late 2022. He observes that 42 AI-linked companies have driven 65% to 75% of S&P 500 returns, profits, and capital spending since the launch of ChatGPT. Without these 42 stocks, the S&P 500 would have underperformed equity markets in Europe, Japan, and China. Furthermore, tech sector capital spending contributed 40% to 45% of US GDP growth over the last three quarters of 2025, up significantly from under 5% in early 2023.

This market concentration is detailed in a table tracking S&P 500 performance metrics from November 2022 to late December 2025. The 42 "Total AI" stocks, which include direct AI, AI utilities, and AI capital equipment, achieved a 190% price return, 153% earnings growth, and 68% capex/R&D growth. These 42 stocks accounted for 78% of total S&P 500 price returns, 66% of earnings growth, and 71% of capex/R&D growth. In comparison, the S&P 500 excluding these AI stocks generated a modest 26% price return and 19% earnings growth, underperforming the broader MSCI Europe, MSCI Japan, and MSCI China indices, which posted price returns of 33%, 59%, and 50% respectively. 

To illustrate the historic scale of current technology investments, a bar chart compares peak annual tech capital spending in 2025 against major historical US infrastructure projects as a percentage of GDP. While major national efforts such as the 1930s public works, the Manhattan Project in 1944, rural electrification in 1949, the Apollo Project in 1964, and the Interstate highway system in 1966 each peaked at around 0.3% to 0.4% of GDP, and the broadband capex wave in 2000 reached approximately 1.1%, tech capex in 2025 soared to nearly 1.8% of GDP. This scale of spending is shown to be nearly as large as all of those historic projects combined, which stack up to just over 2.1% of GDP.

Looking forward, Cembalest outlines a forecast for 2026, predicting a 10% to 15% market correction at some point during the year due to profit-taking and a growth scare, though he expects equity markets to ultimately finish the year higher than they began. He raises four critical open questions regarding the stability of the tech moat: the adequacy of US power generation, China's capacity to build its own technology moat, geopolitical risks involving China and Taiwan, and whether hyperscalers can generate sufficient profits to justify the $1.3 trillion spent on capital expenditures and R&D since 2022.

This page of the J.P. Morgan 2026 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, argues that while analysts worry about high valuations during the current AI cycle, these valuations are internally consistent with high corporate profitability. Cembalest points out that looking at high valuations in isolation ignores the extraordinarily high profit margins of the technology sector compared to the rest of the market. Supporting this, he notes that in 2025, the forward P/E of the S&P 500 rose by only about 3%, meaning the rest of the market's 18% year-to-date gain was driven by actual earnings growth.

The first chart, "S&P 500 price to book and ROE," plots consensus forward price to book ratio on the y-axis (from 0 to 14) against consensus forward return on equity (ROE) on the x-axis (from 0% to 35%). It illustrates a clear upward-sloping trend where lower-ROE sectors like utilities, energy, and financials cluster at the bottom-left with low price-to-book ratios, while the Information Technology sector sits far to the top-right with a forward ROE of over 30% and a price-to-book ratio around 13.

The second chart, "S&P 500 vs Hyperscalers & Semiscalers," scales the x-axis up to 100% ROE and the y-axis up to a price-to-book ratio of 35 to map individual mega-cap technology firms alongside general S&P 500 sectors. This chart demonstrates that massive valuations are tied to exceptional profitability, highlighting NVIDIA with a consensus forward ROE of approximately 85% and a price-to-book ratio of about 30. Other individual firms shown along this valuation-to-profitability curve include ASML, Microsoft, Alphabet, Taiwan Semiconductor, Meta, Amazon, and Advanced Micro Devices.

The third chart, "S&P 500 free cash flow margins: tech & interactive media vs the rest," tracks free cash flow margins from 1976 to 2025. It reveals a stark divergence between the two series: while the rest of the S&P 500 (excluding financials and REITs) has hovered flatly between 5% and 10% for decades, the tech and interactive media sector has seen a major secular increase, rising from under 10% in the late 1970s to peak near 25% by 2025.

The fourth chart, "PEG ratios for global tech stocks vs the market," measures the forward P/E ratio divided by year-two forward EPS growth from 1995 to 2025. It compares the MSCI All World Equity Index for information technology against the overall MSCI All World Equity Index. The chart shows that global tech PEG ratios have historically tracked the broader market closely and ended 2025 in a very similar position, with both ratios hovering around 1.35, indicating that tech valuations relative to projected growth are not detached from broader market realities.

This page analyzes the rapid advancement of generative AI models across data science benchmarks, while highlighting that many performance metrics can be gamed and that key weaknesses, such as hallucinations, persist. On the positive side, AI models now match or exceed human abilities in fields like image recognition and visual reasoning. Notable milestones include OpenAI's o3 achieving a performance rating better than 99% of human competitors in Codeforces coding challenges, and Otto-SR reproducing a medical research review in two days that would have taken humans twelve work-years to complete. 

Four charts illustrate these trends. The first chart, the AI Model Performance Tracker, plots the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v3.0—which aggregates ten different benchmarks—from September 2022 to September 2025. It shows US AI performance, led by models like Gemini 3 Pro Preview, rising from a score of approximately 10 to nearly 80. China’s AI performance, led by Kimi K2 Thinking, climbed from around 10 in late 2023 to over 60 by late 2025.

The second chart displays the ability of models to solve real-world GitHub issues from Q2 2024 to Q4 2025, using the SWE-bench database. The percentage of issues resolved by the top-scoring models per developer rose dramatically from around 30% to about 70%. Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI lead this metric, while competitors like Alibaba, DeepSeek, xAI, and Meta AI also show upward trajectories.

The third chart examines AI model hallucination rates, measuring incorrect answers as a percentage of total questions. Anthropic models like Claude 4.5 Haiku, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude 4.5 Sonnet demonstrate the lowest hallucination rates, sitting between 10% and 15%. On the opposite end of the spectrum, open-source models like gpt-oss-120B and gpt-oss-20B show shockingly high hallucination rates approaching 50%.

The final chart measures "opaque reasoning ability," plotting the time in minutes it takes a human to solve math problems that AI models can solve in a single pass without using a chain-of-thought. Tracking model releases from January 2023 to July 2025, this proxy for pretraining-based intelligence has risen from under one minute for GPT-4 to nearly four minutes for top-tier models like Gemini 3 Pro and Opus 4.5. The author notes that only a select few models, primarily from Google Gemini and Anthropic Opus, are experiencing real improvements in this opaque reasoning capability, while other models rely heavily on increased inference-time compute to pad their test scores.

In this executive summary page, Michael Cembalest explores the historic market concentration and dominance of key technology and semiconductor firms, questioning whether this massive "moat" is indestructible. The foundation of this market position relies on Nvidia's chip designs, TSMC's manufacturing, and ASML's lithography machines. Cembalest highlights how the market capitalization of just four semiconductor companies ("semiscalers") and four "hyperscalers" has surged from $3 trillion seven years ago to $18 trillion today, now accounting for about 20% of developed world equity markets and 16% of global equity markets.

Two charts at the top of the page illustrate this trend. The top-left stacked area chart tracks the eight largest hyperscaler and semiscaler market caps in trillions of US dollars from 2018 through late 2025. It details the individual contributions of Nvidia, TSMC, ASML, AMD, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta, showing their collective value rising from roughly $3 trillion to nearly $18 trillion, with Nvidia experiencing the most dramatic expansion in the latter years. The top-right line chart shows these same eight firms as a percentage of global market cap from 2018 to late 2025. Their share of the MSCI World Index climbed from approximately 7% to nearly 20%, while their share of the MSCI ACWI (which includes emerging markets) rose from around 5% to approximately 16%.

The page then transitions to the topic of trade policy, arguing that "the revolution will be imported" because the US semiconductor ecosystem relies heavily on foreign manufacturing. Thus far, this ecosystem has been largely spared from Donald Trump’s tariffs. Cembalest notes that while a Section 232 investigation on semiconductors is ongoing, it may ultimately provide exemptions for companies that commit to domestic US production. 

Two charts at the bottom of the page detail these import and tariff dynamics. The bottom-left line chart plots annualized monthly US imports of semiconductors, large computers, and computer parts in billions of US dollars from 2015 to late 2025. It shows that imports of large computers (which include GPU and CPU rack servers but exclude laptops) skyrocketed beginning in 2024, peaking near $230 billion in late 2025. In contrast, imports of standalone semiconductors and manufacturing equipment remained relatively steady, hovering between $60 billion and $80 billion, while other computer parts sat between $30 billion and $50 billion. The bottom-right horizontal bar chart shows Trump tariff exclusions by product category as a percentage of 2024 US imports. It reveals that the "semiconductor ecosystem" (highlighted in red) enjoys exceptionally high exclusion rates, with computer parts at roughly 85% excluded, computers at 80%, and semiconductors at 78%. These high exemption rates are rivaled only by energy and pharma, while consumer goods like apparel, textiles, and footwear receive almost no exclusions.

To categorize this market, the page defines J.P. Morgan's S&P 500 AI universe, which is composed of 42 stocks across three distinct categories. The "Direct AI" category comprises 28 stocks, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Broadcom, Tesla, Oracle, Palantir, AMD, Salesforce, IBM, Uber, ServiceNow, Qualcomm, Arista, Adobe, Micron, Palo Alto, Intel, Crowdstrike, Cadence Design, Dell, NXP, Fortinet, HP, and Super Micro Computer. The "AI utilities" category contains eight companies, including NRG, Vistra, NextEra, Southern, Constellation, Public Service Enterprise, Entergy, and NiSource. Finally, the "AI capital equipment" category includes six stocks: Eaton, Trane, Johnson Controls, Quanta, GE Vernova, and EMCOR. 

A closing footnote provides technical context on ASML, Europe's largest technology company with a market cap over $300 billion. It notes that ASML’s extreme ultraviolet light (EUV) lithography machines—which are the size of large buses and use high-frequency lasers and microscopic mirrors to etch features smaller than 10 nanometers onto silicon wafers—remain absolutely essential to the production of artificial intelligence technology.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2026 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the capital expenditures, research and development spending, and debt profiles of the primary artificial intelligence and technology hyperscalers. The central argument is that while hyperscalers are spending historically unprecedented shares of their revenue on capex and R&D to compete in the AI race, this investment cycle has been overwhelmingly funded by internally generated cash flow rather than debt, setting it apart from previous infrastructure bubbles. However, very recent data from late 2025 shows initial signs of a shift toward debt financing. 

Four charts illustrate these financial dynamics. The first chart, located at the top left, is a line chart titled Hyperscaler capex and R&D as a share of revenues, mapping percent of revenue from 2017 to 2025. It shows Meta aggressively scaling its spending to hit a record high of 70% by late 2025. Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft also show elevated spending, clustering between 30% and 40% of revenue, which dwarfs both the S&P 500 Info Tech median of roughly 20% and the overall S&P 500 median of 10%. 

The top-right chart, Capex financing vs capex cycle, looks at US tech and communications companies in the Russell 3000 from 1996 through 2026. It compares capex to sales against the share of capex and dividends financed with debt. During the dot-com bubble peak around 2000, debt-financed capex spiked to nearly 14% of the total, alongside a capex-to-sales ratio that reached over 40%. In comparison, despite capex-to-sales climbing toward 9% in 2025 and 2026, the debt-financed portion remains very low at approximately 5% to 6%, though it has begun a slight upward turn.

The bottom-left chart, Net debt to EBITDA ratios of Direct AI stocks, presents a bar chart comparison of 28 key AI firms using data from Q3 2025 and Q4 2025. The chart demonstrates that the vast majority of direct AI companies—such as Palantir, Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, and NVIDIA—have net debt ratios of zero, meaning their cash and marketable securities exceed their total debt. A small group of companies show positive net debt ratios, led by TSMC at over 6.5x EBITDA, Oracle at approximately 3.5x, and HP and Dell at around 2x. Several of these indebted firms show a noticeable increase in their multiples from Q3 to Q4 2025, reflecting a recent surge in AI-related debt.

The bottom-right chart, Free cash flow to revenue ratios of Direct AI stocks, highlights how cash-generative these businesses remain. Aside from Intel, which sits at roughly negative 20% free cash flow to revenue, and Oracle, which is slightly negative, almost every other direct AI company significantly exceeds the S&P 500 median of 10% and the S&P 500 info tech median of 18%. Leading companies such as TSMC, ASML, Arista, NVIDIA, Broadcom, and Adobe boast exceptional free cash flow to revenue ratios ranging from 30% to over 50%.

Additionally, the author includes a critical footnote targeted at Meta. Cembalest urges Meta to utilize its substantial cash flow to police fraudulent WhatsApp stock scams that illegally use his name. He references a November 2025 press release from Senators Hawley and Blumenthal alleging that Meta generates up to $16 billion annually from hosting fraudulent, high-risk, or banned advertisements.

This page focuses on the rising adoption rates of generative AI, presenting data on how quickly the technology is being integrated into businesses and personal workflows. The author introduces the topic by noting that while surveys point to rapid adoption, they fail to reveal how much companies or individuals are willing to pay for these models, or how much revenue can be generated through advertising. To illustrate the scaling intensity of enterprise usage, the author cites a December 2025 OpenAI report showing that ChatGPT message volume grew eight times and API reasoning token consumption per organization increased 320 times year-over-year.

The analysis is supported by four charts. The first, sourced from Ramp in November 2025, tracks the share of US businesses with paid subscriptions to AI models, platforms, and tools by sector from January 2023 to September 2025. It shows steady upward trends across all areas, led by Information Technology, which reached approximately 70% adoption by late 2025, followed closely by Finance & Insurance at around 60%. In contrast, US government estimates for AI adoption remained low, hovering under 10%. 

The second chart, utilizing US Census Bureau data from October 2025 across 200,000 businesses, displays AI adoption rates by sector for August 2024, October 2025, and projections for the next six months. The Information sector shows the highest usage, approaching 35% in the near-term projections, followed by Professional, Scientific, and Technical services, and Finance and Insurance. Traditional sectors like Transportation/Warehousing and Accommodation & Food Services show the lowest adoption rates. 

The third chart presents a St. Louis Fed survey from November 2025 of 25,000 respondents, showing the percentage of adults using generative AI between August 2024 and August 2025. Overall usage rose from 45% to nearly 55% over the period, with personal or "nonwork" usage consistently outperforming and rising faster than usage strictly for "work," which only increased from 34% to about 38%. 

The final chart, sourced from Anthropic and the Stanford AI Index Report 2025, examines the depth of AI usage across organizations based on one million Claude conversations. It plots the fraction of occupations against the minimum fraction of tasks executed with AI, highlighting a key finding that 36% of occupations use AI on at least 25% of their tasks. The curve slopes downward, showing that very few occupations currently use AI for the vast majority of their tasks.

In this section of J.P. Morgan's 2026 Outlook, Michael Cembalest evaluates how close artificial intelligence models are to matching the capabilities of expert human workers. Drawing on OpenAI’s September 2025 "GDPval" benchmark, which uses tasks from 44 professions designed by industry experts with 14 years of experience, the author notes that while human work is still preferred overall, AI tools are making significant headway, particularly in software development. 

The first chart, "AI model overall performance on realistic work tasks," displays the percentage of time an AI model's work product is preferred over a human expert's. It reveals a clear upward progression in model quality, starting with GPT-4o at roughly 12% preference, scaling up through Grok 4 at 20%, Gemini 2.5 Pro at 22%, o4-mini high at 26%, o3 high at 28%, GPT-5 high at 36%, and Claude Opus 4.1 at approximately 41%. 

The second chart, "AI model performance on software developer work," shows that in the coding domain, several advanced models have already surpassed the 50% preference threshold. GPT-4o sits at 26%, Grok 4 at 41%, and Gemini 2.5 Pro at 42%. However, newer models like o4-mini high, GPT-5 high, o3 high, and Claude Opus 4.1 dominate, being preferred over human experts at rates of 64%, 65%, 67%, and 67% respectively.

The third visual, "Efficiency gains from AI assistance to human experts," plots cost improvement against speed improvement, demonstrating the productivity boost when experts collaborate with AI. Compared to an unassisted human baseline of 1.00x, using GPT-4o actually results in poorer relative efficiency at roughly 0.6x speed and cost improvement, likely due to the need for extensive human correction. In contrast, o4-mini yields 1.1x speed and 1.3x cost improvements, o3 provides 1.3x speed and 1.45x cost improvements, and GPT-5 leads with approximately 1.5x speed and 1.6x cost improvements. 

The fourth chart, "AI software engineering task complexity," tracks the rising complexity of tasks that AI models can complete with 50% accuracy, measured by the hours it would take a human to finish them. Between 2019 and late 2025, this complexity measure climbed from near zero for GPT-2 and GPT-3 to 0.5 hours for GPT-4o, 1.2 hours for o4-mini, 1.5 hours for Claude Opus 4.1, and 2.3 hours for GPT-5. 

Finally, the author addresses the open question of whether AI models will run out of training data. Referencing Stanford's 2025 AI Index Report, the page concludes that a data shortage is unlikely before 2030. This conclusion is supported by massive token estimates across different digital repositories, noting that Common Crawl contains a median of 130 trillion tokens, the indexed web holds 510 trillion, and the entire web spans roughly 3,100 trillion tokens, which is further bolstered by an estimated 300 trillion tokens in images and 1,350 trillion in video.

This page, titled "Metaverse moment," discusses the impact of artificial intelligence on labor productivity, using research and data compiled by Goldman Sachs. The text explains that overall non-farm and technology-focused productivity have risen since the launch of ChatGPT compared to pre-COVID levels. While these current gains are concentrated in coding, customer service, and consulting, Goldman Sachs projects that AI adoption will spread across other industries, ultimately delivering a 15% boost to US productivity and an $8 trillion net present value gain. Author Michael Cembalest notes that such a large AI productivity boost may be necessary to sustain US GDP growth and keep inflation low, given macroeconomic headwinds like an aging population, low birth rates, Trump immigration policies, tariff pressures, a weaker dollar, and high budget deficits.

Two bar charts at the top of the page display the estimated percentage increases in labor productivity from AI. The left chart shows company-level estimates across twenty organizations. Anthropic leads with an estimated productivity gain of approximately 80%, followed by Autodesk at over 60%, UC San Diego at around 60%, and Adobe at 50%. This scaling list concludes with companies like Bank of America, Ernst & Young, and Klarna showing smaller estimated gains. The right chart displays academic estimates of AI's productivity impact across nineteen papers, with a study by Ju Aral (2025) showing the highest estimate at over 70%, followed by Peng et al (2023) at over 50%, with others like Brynjolfsson et al (2023) and Korinek (2023) scaling down to under 5%.

The bottom of the page features two tables comparing annualized productivity gains from the pre-COVID period (Q1 2016 to Q1 2020) against two post-GPT periods (Q4 2022 to Q2 2025, and Q3 2023 to Q2 2025). The left table, which uses the Real GDP method, shows that non-financial corporate productivity rose from 1.1% pre-COVID to 3.1% and 3.9% in the respective post-GPT periods. Under this same method, the information sector rose from 5.0% to 8.9% and then settled at 6.0%, while data processing rose from 8.0% to 12.1% and then 9.9%. The right table uses the Real gross output method, showing that non-financial corporate productivity followed the same path (from 1.1% to 3.1% and 3.9%). The information sector under this second method rose from 3.7% pre-COVID to 7.3% and 5.7% post-GPT, and data processing rose from 7.8% pre-COVID to 10.2% and 10.6% in the two post-GPT periods.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s outlook focuses on the difficulty of tracking generative AI profitability among major tech hyperscalers, arguing that a clearer path to profitability is necessary in 2026 to sustain current market valuations. To make this point, the author highlights that Microsoft is the only hyperscaler disclosing AI-specific revenue, while also detailing earnings call commentary, rising cloud revenues, falling free cash flow margins, declining cash balances, and estimated annualized revenues for various public and private AI entities. 

A summary of earnings call comments shows strong growth, with Microsoft reporting its inference business as the fastest in company history to reach a ten-billion-dollar annualized run rate, while Amazon’s AWS AI business is labeled a massive opportunity that requires heavy upfront infrastructure investments. Additionally, Google reports that revenue from products built on its generative AI models grew by more than 200% year-over-year.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, tracking hyperscaler quarterly revenue from cloud services between 2021 and late 2025, shows Amazon Web Services leading the industry with revenues climbing toward $35 billion. Microsoft Azure follows at roughly $23 billion, while Google Cloud is near $15 billion, Oracle cloud approaches $10 billion, and IBM cloud remains under $10 billion. 

The second chart displays hyperscaler free cash flow margins net of capital expenditures over a trailing 12-month period. It reveals downward pressure, with Microsoft’s margin sliding from its peaks down to about 28%, and Meta’s margin dropping from a mid-2024 peak down toward 30% by early 2026. Alphabet’s margin declined from over 25% down to under 20%, while Amazon recovered from negative margins in 2022 to sit slightly below 10% by early 2026, which is lower than the S&P 500 median of roughly 12%.

The third chart illustrates the decline in hyperscaler cash and cash equivalents as a share of total assets from 2019 to 2026. Alphabet's share dropped from above 50% in 2019 to under 20% in late 2025, while Microsoft and Meta dropped from around 45% and 40% respectively to around 15%. Amazon's cash share fluctuated, ending near 12%. 

The fourth chart tracks the dramatic rise in annualized revenue from AI between January 2024 and late 2025. Microsoft Azure leads the pack, climbing to an annualized run rate of approximately $18 billion, followed by OpenAI which grew to over $12 billion by mid-2025. Anthropic and CoreWeave also show strong upward trajectories, reaching annualized rates of around $8 billion and $6 billion respectively, while xAI and Nebius remain much lower, hovering below $2 billion.

Finally, a footnote addresses questions regarding vendor financing by highlighting details from an Nvidia note. It points out that in 2025, Nvidia invested $4.7 billion in private companies, representing just 3% of its revenues, and emphasizes that these private companies generate their revenues from third-party customers and raise capital from third-party sources rather than from Nvidia itself.

This page of the J.P. Morgan 2026 Outlook, titled "Metaverse moment," addresses emerging concerns regarding GPU and networking equipment depreciation assumptions by major technology hyperscalers. Since 2020, these companies have steadily extended the depreciation lifetimes of their assets under the assumption that older hardware, such as NVIDIA's A100 chips, remains highly utilized and profitable for several years, often being repurposed for AI inference or resold. However, the author cautions that GPU hourly rental rates have recently fallen by 20% to 25%, a shift that likely contributed to a substantial correction in CoreWeave's stock price after its peak in mid-2025. 

To document these shifting pricing dynamics, a table of NVIDIA GPU hourly rental rates displays changes from November 2024 to December 2025. It shows that A100 rates for neoclouds dropped 22% to $1.4 per hour, while H100 rates on AWS fell 24% to $3.4 per hour. In contrast, H200 AWS rates, which began tracking in early 2025, increased by 11% to reach $3.3 per hour by late 2025. 

A second table details the historical rise in GPU and networking depreciation lifetimes in years from 2020 to 2025 across major tech firms. Meta's estimated depreciation lifespan grew from 3.0 to 5.5 years, Google and Microsoft moved from 3.0 to 6.0 years, and Oracle expanded from 5.0 to 6.0 years, while Amazon adjusted its assumption to 5.0 years in 2025. 

The core of the author's analysis explores the severe financial consequences if these companies are forced to return to a standard 3-year depreciation lifetime on AI capex deployed since January 2023. A comprehensive income statement impact table models this scenario for Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Google, and Oracle. Reverting to a 3-year timeline would double estimated depreciation charges for many of these firms; for instance, Microsoft's estimated depreciation would surge from $8,365 million to $16,731 million, and Google's would rise from $8,667 million to $17,335 million. This acceleration would reduce pro-forma EPS by 6% to 7% for Google, Meta, and Microsoft, and by 7% for Amazon. Oracle would face the steepest consequences, with its operating margin dropping by 14% and pro-forma EPS falling by 17%. 

In terms of future outlook and open questions, the author notes that shorter depreciation lifespans could be triggered by high physical failure rates of around 9% annually, rapid customer transition to next-generation Blackwell chips, or data center refurbishments. Conversely, the policy decision by the Trump administration to allow NVIDIA H200 chips to be exported to China is highlighted as a factor that could bolster the residual value of older hardware and support current extended depreciation schedules.

This page of the J.P. Morgan 2026 Outlook, titled "Metaverse moment," evaluates the massive potential deficit in AI workload compute relative to future consumer inference demand. The author highlights that SemiAnalysis estimates Western AI workload compute will reach approximately 36,000 exaflops at FP8 precision in 2026, a steep rise from 11,500 exaflops in 2025. Assuming a 50% utilization rate, this translates to roughly 1.7 billion exaflops per day, which is far below the estimated 7.2 billion exaflops required for consumer inference demand. A footnote notes that out of 125 gigawatts of data center capacity globally, only 10 to 13 gigawatts are currently set up to handle AI workloads rather than traditional enterprise tasks. 

An included table shows current hyperscaler compute as a share of future consumer inference demand for 5 billion users across different GPU utilization rates (75%, 50%, and 33%) and token intensity levels. At a moderate 1.2 million cloud tokens per day of future inference demand, current compute would only cover 44% of demand at 75% GPU utilization, 29% at 50% utilization, and 19% at 33% utilization. Across all scenarios, current compute would only meet 14% to 66% of future demand just for consumer inference, completely excluding additional demand from enterprises, sovereigns, defense, or low-latency applications like robotics, self-driving cars, and commercial drones.

To explore what might shift these dynamics, the author presents a detailed breakdown compiled with J.P. Morgan AI professionals outlining drivers of future demand. Factors expected to increase demand for cloud compute include the rise of reasoning models (which use 20 to 40 times more tokens than non-reasoning models), the early adoption phase of domain-specific models, token-intensive creative and agentic monitoring tasks, AI-driven drug discovery, and the transition of fraud detection to transformer-based architectures. Conversely, factors that could decrease demand include model optimization techniques (such as mixture of experts and specialized accelerators), a shift toward smaller, post-trained, purpose-built models, and moving AI workloads to cheaper edge devices and PCs.

In a humorous sidebar titled "On flops and floppers," the page defines computational flops (floating point operations per second) before comparing them to soccer "floppers" or players who dive. It references a 2018 Bleacher Report ranking of the sport's worst divers, highlighting Angel di Maria, Sergio Busquets, Cristiano Ronaldo, Arjen Robben, and Neymar, with an honorable mention for Jurgen Klinsmann.

This page from the 2026 Outlook discusses the growing power constraints facing the utility sector, particularly driven by the rapid expansion of data centers. The primary argument is that while utilities are applying higher tariffs to data centers, these rates are still insufficient to cover the capital costs of building new generation capacity. Compounding this issue is a severe shortage of electrical equipment and gas turbines, alongside high tariffs on power generation equipment imports, which contrasts with the significant tariff exemptions granted to the semiconductor industry.

The first chart compares specialized data center power rates against the cost of new generation in US dollars per megawatt-hour. It shows that electricity rates across various utilities—such as Idaho Power, Duke Energy, and Dominion—range from roughly $35 to $65 per megawatt-hour even with specialized tariffs included. These rates remain well below the benchmark cost of a new combined cycle gas turbine, which sits near $95 per megawatt-hour, and are often barely enough to cover unsubsidized solar and storage costs of around $70 per megawatt-hour.

An accompanying text box highlights a competitive scramble for gas turbines, noting that over the last 24 months, the cost of a new combined cycle turbine has doubled from approximately $1,200 per kilowatt to $2,500 per kilowatt, with delivery lead times stretching to three to seven years. Single-cycle turbine costs have similarly risen from $800 to $1,500 per kilowatt. This supply logjam is visualized in a chart of global gas turbine orders, where demand is projected to spike well beyond the current production limit of roughly 60 gigawatts, peaking above 100 gigawatts in the late 2020s. 

This supply deficit is occurring just as interconnection requests are surging. A chart detailing ERCOT large load interconnection requests shows a massive projected increase from negligible levels in 2022 to over 200 gigawatts by 2030, with a significant portion of these requests remaining in the "under review" or "planning study approved" stages rather than being operational.

Finally, the page analyzes the impact of trade policy on the energy transition. A chart on tariff exclusions reveals a stark disparity: while the semiconductor ecosystem enjoys high tariff exclusions—with computer parts, computers, and semiconductors seeing 70% to 90% of their 2024 imports excluded from Trump tariffs—the power generation ecosystem faces heavy taxation. Key components like transformers, electrical switches, solar panels, and batteries have tariff exclusion rates below 30%, and in some cases, under 10%. Despite these trade barriers, US power generation imports have steadily climbed from under $100 billion annualized in 2015 to over $200 billion by late 2025, underlining the country's growing reliance on foreign-sourced electrical equipment to meet rising grid demands.

In this section of the outlook, the author analyzes the bull case for artificial intelligence by examining OpenAI’s highly aggressive growth forecasts while simultaneously warning of severe physical power constraints and corporate risks. OpenAI is estimated to be six to twelve months ahead of its competitors—including DeepSeek, Gemini, Perplexity, Grok, Claude, Kimi, and Tencent—in terms of user engagement, monetization, and model capabilities. However, sustaining this trajectory requires unprecedented levels of energy infrastructure and capital expenditure.

To illustrate how quickly OpenAI’s expectations are scaling, the first table, titled OpenAI forecasts keep rising, compares the company’s 2027 projections made in mid-2025 to revised forecasts made just three months later on October 31, 2025. Over this brief period, the projected 2027 revenue was revised upward by 50 percent, from $60 billion to $90 billion, and projected weekly average users rose from 1.4 billion to 1.8 billion. Paid subscribers were adjusted up by 31 percent to 76 million, and estimated 2027 inference compute costs climbed from $21 billion to $30 billion. 

The physical demands of this growth are detailed in the second table, which outlines current and future GPU and power requirements. In 2024, OpenAI added 72,098 B200 GPU equivalents for inference and 120,163 for training, requiring 0.5 gigawatts of cumulative power capacity. By 2030, these numbers are projected to balloon to nearly 1.97 million GPUs for inference and over 2.23 million for training. Assuming 400,000 B200 equivalent GPUs per gigawatt, this would require OpenAI's cumulative power capacity to reach 30.2 gigawatts by 2030. The author notes this 30-gigawatt hurdle is exceptionally high, considering the entire United States added only 25 gigawatts of net reliable generation capacity in 2024. Grid interconnection bottlenecks, turbine delays, and unrealistic timelines for small modular nuclear reactors present massive roadblocks to meeting this demand.

The final chart, showing OpenAI’s projected compute budget in billions of dollars from 2024 to 2030, highlights that training costs are expected to exceed inference costs for the remainder of the decade. Training costs are projected to peak in 2028 at $81 billion compared to $30 billion for inference, before tapering to $56 billion in 2030 while inference rises to $49 billion. 

Beyond energy constraints, the author highlights OpenAI as the single largest corporate risk to the broader AI sector. Despite being a private company, OpenAI has committed $1.4 trillion to corporate partners while remaining heavily reliant on subscription and developer fees with minimal search, cloud, or hardware revenue. Compounding this risk, OpenAI's own chief economist disclosed that 72 percent of GPT queries are non-business related, raising questions about sustainable commercial monetization over the next 12 to 18 months.

This page explores US power generation constraints as a key market wildcard, focusing on how the massive energy demands of artificial intelligence and data centers are colliding with grid capacity. The author highlights testimony from Sam Altman in May 2025 predicting that the cost of AI will eventually converge with the cost of energy, as well as an October 2025 report from the PJM Independent Market Monitor stating that peak load forecast increases for 2026 and 2027 are almost entirely due to data centers. Although data centers currently represent only 4% to 8% of US power demand, they are projected to account for two-thirds of future load growth. To illustrate the severity of these constraints, the author points to Microsoft and Constellation Energy's decision to restart a decommissioned nuclear reactor at Three Mile Island at a costly premium of $110 to $130 per megawatt-hour. 

Four charts illustrate these growing pressures on the US power grid. The first chart shows the power used to train frontier AI models in megawatts from 2018 to 2026. Plotted on a logarithmic scale, it demonstrates that training power requirements have grown 2.2 times per year, rising from under 1 megawatt for early models to roughly 100 megawatts for frontier models like Llama 3.1-405 and Grok-3 by 2025 and 2026. 

The second chart tracks US construction spending in billions of seasonally adjusted dollars from 2014 to 2025. It shows a dramatic surge in spending on electric power, which rose to over $110 billion by 2025, and a steady climb in data center construction to over $40 billion, while spending on traditional office buildings fell to around $45 billion. 

The third chart illustrates soaring capacity prices within the PJM market, looking at the Base Residual Auction rate in US dollars per megawatt by delivery year from 2007 through the 2027/2028 cycle. Prices for both the Mid-Atlantic Area Council and the Regional Transmission Organization have spiked dramatically from historical levels under $50 to nearly $350 per megawatt, with a note indicating that uncapped rates would have reached $530. The author details that PJM leads the nation with 67 gigawatts of existing and planned data center capacity, compared to 20 gigawatts for ERCOT in Texas and 8 gigawatts for CAISO in California. 

The fourth and most critical chart compares annual US electricity generation and storage capacity additions from 1950 to the mid-2020s. While raw nameplate capacity has spiked to over 60 gigawatts in recent years, the capacity weighted by Effective Load Carrying Capability factors—which adjusts for the reliability and intermittency of solar, wind, and hydro—shows a much more gradual and limited increase of under 30 gigawatts. This highlights that reliable, firm power additions are growing much slower than nominal capacity figures suggest.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2026 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, discusses the severe power constraints facing the rapid expansion of data centers and the growing trend toward onsite power generation, often referred to as Bring Your Own Generation, or BYOG. 

The author begins by illustrating the massive impact of data centers on natural gas markets. A bar chart showing data center natural gas demand by 2030 estimates that total demand will reach nearly 5 billion cubic feet per day, driven primarily by about 3.0 billion cubic feet per day of new grid-based demand and around 0.6 billion cubic feet per day of new behind-the-meter demand. This projected increase of 3 to 4 billion cubic feet per day is significant against the backdrop of total US dry natural gas production, which stood at approximately 107 billion cubic feet per day in 2025. This heavy reliance is further emphasized in an area chart tracking incremental grid-connected data center fuel mix from 2025 to 2030. The chart indicates that new data center additions will remain roughly 60% reliant on natural gas throughout the rest of the decade, with coal, wind, and solar making up the minor remaining shares.

As a solution to these power constraints, many operators are turning to onsite generation. While only 1% of data centers currently generate their own power, a Bloom Energy survey reveals that 38% expect to do so partially by 2030, and 27% plan to rely entirely on onsite power. The primary driver for this shift is illustrated in a line chart showing the time elapsed from an interconnection request to the commercial operation date. Between 2000 and 2024, wait times have ballooned dramatically, with the median time rising to over 50 months and the 75th percentile climbing to over 70 months. 

To bypass these delays, notable current and proposed onsite power projects are underway, including xAI Colossus 1 and 2, OpenAI/Oracle Stargate, Microsoft Three Mile Island, Equinix, CoreWeave, and Meta Socrates South. Although GE Vernova, Mitsubishi, and Siemens dominate gas-fired power generation, new entrants are emerging, such as Doosan Enerbility of South Korea with H-class turbines, Wartsila of Finland with modified ship engines, Boom Supersonic of the US with modified jet engines, and Caterpillar with gas turbines and reciprocating engines. 

A detailed technical table outlines the various onsite generation options available to operators. Fuel cells offer the shortest lead times at just 3 to 4 months, though they have high all-in capital expenditures of $3,000 to $4,000 per kilowatt and small unit capacities of 0.325 megawatts. On the other end of the spectrum, massive H-Class combined-cycle gas turbines ranging from 600 to 1,000 megawatts offer high efficiency of 50% to 60% but require 36 to 60 months of lead time and incur estimated levelized costs of energy between $100 and $200 per megawatt-hour. Other options balanced in between include industrial gas turbines, which boast the lowest estimated levelized costs of energy at $65 to $110 per megawatt-hour with a 12 to 36-month lead time, as well as aeroderivative gas turbines and various reciprocating engines that offer rapid ramp rates of 5 to 10 minutes.

This page, titled China scales the moat, examines China's aggressive expansion of electricity generation and heavy state-backed industrial policies compared to those of the United States. The author argues that China's competitiveness relies on a combination of massive brute-force power capacity and highly mercantilist state subsidies. 

The first chart, an area chart titled China electricity generation by source, tracks power generation from 2000 to 2024, showing total capacity soaring toward nearly 10,000 terawatt-hours. While coal remains the dominant source, there are growing contributions from wind, solar, hydro, and nuclear energy. To illustrate this rapid scale, the text notes that since 2019, China's power generation increased by 2,500 terawatt-hours, compared to a modest increase of 221 terawatt-hours in the United States and a decline of 110 terawatt-hours in Europe. Accompanying this is a line chart titled Electrification: China and Japan power ahead, measuring the electricity share of useful final energy from 1990 to 2025. It shows China and Japan leading global peers, with China’s share rising sharply over the last three decades to nearly 38 percent by 2025, while the United States remains flat below 24 percent.

The analysis then transitions to national champion industries and state subsidies, noting that China ranks first on the ITIF Mercantilist Index. A stacked bar chart titled Industrial policy spending in key economies shows China’s spending at over 1.5 percent of GDP, which is significantly higher than other major nations like South Korea, France, Germany, and the United States, the latter of which spends less than 0.5 percent of GDP. This Chinese spending is highly diversified, consisting of state investment funds, below-market credit, direct subsidies, and R&D support. On the right, a horizontal bar chart titled China direct subsidies for listed firms by subsector shows that from 2017 to 2020, direct subsidies represented over 35 percent of profits for the software and services subsector, and roughly 30 percent of profits for technology hardware and automobiles. Other sectors, such as transportation, semiconductors, and professional services, also heavily rely on these direct subsidies for their profitability.

At the bottom of the page, a detailed commentary compares two contrasting approaches to US industrial policy using MP Materials and Intel. The US government support for MP Materials, a critical minerals company, features an anchor of demand, including 10 years of price support for neodymium and praseodymium at 110 dollars per kilogram and a commitment by the Department of Defense to purchase 100 percent of the output from its second magnet facility. Conversely, the US government's support for Intel via the Chips Act lacks a demand anchor. Of the 12 billion dollars in grants and subsidies, only 3 billion dollars were deployed, with the remaining 9 billion dollars converted by the Trump Administration into a cash investment. Because companies like NVIDIA and Softbank have pledged capital without committing to use Intel manufacturing due to prior defect issues in 13th and 14th Gen Core CPUs, the author poses an open question: will the US government eventually take the next step and compel major US companies like Apple, NVIDIA, Qualcomm, and Broadcom to use Intel manufacturing?

This page argues that China is rapidly closing the technology and innovation gap with the United States and Europe, making it a matter of "when, not if" before China successfully scales the technological moat surrounding advanced semiconductor lithography. To support this premise, the page presents several charts documenting China's upward trajectory across global innovation rankings, export complexity, clean energy, artificial intelligence, and nuclear research. 

A chart tracking the Global Innovation Index from 2012 to 2026 illustrates that China has steadily climbed from a rank of roughly 34th to break into the top ten by 2024, while the United States has remained relatively stable near the very top of the ranking. Similarly, a chart depicting US and China export complexity from 1998 to 2023 shows the two nations converging; the US rank drifted from 5th down to approximately 15th, while China's rank rose from around 31st to meet the US at the same level by 2023. 

The divergence is even more pronounced in patent applications and scientific research. A chart on annual clean energy patent applications shows China's submissions skyrocketing from near zero in 2010 to over 250,000 by 2022, while applications from the US, European Union, and the rest of the world remained flat and under 50,000. For artificial intelligence patents, another chart shows China's share of the world total surging from around 12% in 2010 to more than 60% by 2022, while the US share fell from about 40% to 15% and Europe's share declined from 35% to roughly 12%. In nuclear science and engineering research, a chart measuring highly-cited publications from 2008 to 2022 shows China rising from about 100 to 350 publications, closing in on the EU's 450 publications and the US's 400 publications, while France and South Korea remain below 100.

Finally, a detailed commentary sidebar argues that US and European antitrust regulators are inadvertently assisting China's rise. The text highlights how EU regulators and the Biden Administration's Federal Trade Commission, led by Lina Khan, blocked Amazon's acquisition of iRobot. Following the termination of the deal, iRobot laid off half its staff and filed for bankruptcy, leaving the company vulnerable to a takeover by a Chinese supplier. The author points out that while Western companies face regulatory headwinds, Chinese robotics hubs receive 20 to 40 times more government funding than their US counterparts, positioned to directly benefit heavily subsidized Chinese competitors like Ecovacs and Roborock.

In this section of J.P. Morgan’s 2026 Outlook, Michael Cembalest addresses the critical power constraints facing data centers, evaluating natural gas, behind-the-meter solar and battery configurations, nuclear energy, and quantum computing. BNEF projections suggest that data center gas demand alone could flip the United States from a supply surplus to a supply deficit by 2030. However, Cembalest argues that a looming supply glut in the global LNG market could instead leave more gas available for domestic consumption. This is supported by a chart showing global LNG capacity utilization from 2005 to 2035. The chart illustrates that while global LNG export capacity is projected to rise to approximately 1,000 billion cubic meters and LNG imports to 800 billion cubic meters by 2035, the overall utilization rate is forecast to drop sharply from its mid-2020s peak of nearly 98% down to roughly 84% by 2030 before slightly recovering. 

Cembalest then evaluates whether behind-the-meter solar and battery storage can replace gas turbines for data center baseload power. He asserts that even with a 40% Investment Tax Credit (ITC), solar and battery systems are far more expensive per megawatt-hour than combined-cycle gas turbines. A chart mapping data center configurations for a 1-gigawatt utility-scale facility in Las Vegas shows that electricity costs rise from approximately $50 per megawatt-hour for a pure natural gas turbine setup to over $180 per megawatt-hour unsubsidized (or $150 per megawatt-hour with a 40% ITC) as the configuration scales up to include 6.0 gigawatts of photovoltaics and 17 gigawatt-hours of battery storage. Despite these high costs, Cembalest notes that speed-to-market is crucial for AI infrastructure developers who may lose billions from delays; thus, Google’s December 2025 acquisition of Intersect Power (which includes 6 gigawatts of solar and 12 gigawatt-hours of storage) is a key development to watch.

The discussion then turns to nuclear energy. Cembalest observes that only two to three decommissioned US nuclear plants—specifically Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania, Palisades in Michigan, and Duane Arnold in Iowa—remain intact enough to potentially restart. He expresses deep skepticism regarding small modular reactors (SMRs), describing them as a "reverse learning curve." To illustrate this, a chart tracks the average capacity of global nuclear plants by construction start year from 1950 to 2020. The average gross capacity rose from under 200 megawatts in the 1950s to over 1,000 megawatts by 1980 to spread high fixed capital costs over more megawatt-hours, with a temporary dip to 400 megawatts during India's self-reliance era. Cembalest argues that SMRs are not yet cost-effective, stating they must achieve costs of $4 to $6 million per megawatt or electricity costs less than twice the grid power rate to be viable. Finally, he briefly addresses quantum computing as a potential long-term solution to reduce data center power demand by replacing GPUs for complex calculations, though he concludes this technology remains several years away at the earliest.

This page analyzes how China is scaling its domestic technology moat to reduce its reliance on Western semiconductor suppliers. The commentary explains that China has now blocked major domestic firms like ByteDance from using NVIDIA chips in new state-funded data centers for AI inference. This restriction, combined with extensive stockpiling of foreign hardware and rapid local technological advancement, has created a significant oversupply of inference chips in China. For instance, a line chart illustrating China's large surplus of inference chips forecasts that domestic supply will skyrocket from roughly 1,000 exaflops in 2025 to over 11,000 exaflops by 2030, while local demand is only expected to reach approximately 5,000 exaflops by that same year. 

The performance of these chips is detailed in a scatter plot mapping AI chip performance by total processing performance score, which assesses training capability, against memory bandwidth, which assesses inference capability. The chart shows that local Chinese options like Huawei’s Ascend 910B and Ascend 910C outperform NVIDIA’s H20 chip, which is one of the few models the United States allows to be sold in China. While high-end restricted NVIDIA models like the B100, B200, and B300 score much higher in both metrics, domestic Chinese alternatives are proving to be competitive options for local use. 

Declining reliance on Western technologies is further evidenced by a line chart showing ASML’s revenue share by country. China’s share of ASML's net sales peaked dramatically at nearly 35 percent around 2024 and 2025 but is projected to plummet to 20 percent in 2026, while the United States' share remains lower, fluctuating between 10 percent and 15 percent. 

Finally, the page highlights domestic financial enthusiasm for local alternatives. A comparative line chart indexes the market capitalizations of NVIDIA and its Chinese competitor, Cambricon, which is backed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Starting from an index of 100 in January 2023, Cambricon's valuation skyrocketed to a volatile peak of over 2,500 by mid-2025, vastly outperforming NVIDIA's steady growth to an index of roughly 1,000 over the same period. The author poses the key milestone to watch of how quickly Chinese companies will transition to adopting Cambricon-made chips.

This page examines how China's tech giant, Huawei, is attempting to scale the technology "moat" built by NVIDIA in the AI chip and hardware space. On a per-chip basis, NVIDIA continues to hold a clear lead. A direct comparison of the Huawei 910C NPU and the NVIDIA B300 GPU reveals that NVIDIA dominates in computing power, offering 2,250 dense BF16 teraflops compared to Huawei’s 780, while also maintaining a 2.3x advantage in high bandwidth memory capacity and a 2.5x lead in HBM bandwidth speed. Crucially, NVIDIA's all-in power efficiency is more than twice as good, drawing 0.90 watts per teraflop compared to Huawei's 1.87. This gap is expected to widen further when comparing Huawei’s 910C to NVIDIA’s upcoming R100 GPU.

To bypass this individual chip disadvantage, Huawei is aiming to compete at the cluster level rather than the chip level, as detailed in a comprehensive cluster roadmap comparison spanning 2025 to 2027. This comparative table pitches Huawei's Atlas SuperPods against NVIDIA's Blackwell and Rubin NVL architectures. Huawei claims its Atlas 950 SuperPod, slated for release in late 2026 with 8,192 Ascend 950DT chips, will deliver 8 FP8 exaflops of dense computing power, 1,152 terabytes of high bandwidth memory, and 16.3 petabytes per second of intranode bandwidth. If achieved, this would theoretically represent 6.7 times more computing power, 15 times more memory, and 62 times more intranode bandwidth than NVIDIA's planned 2026 NVL144 Vera Rubin cluster.

However, the analysis presents several critical caveats to Huawei's claim of cluster-level parity. First, achieving this performance requires a flawless low-latency interconnect, HBM capacity, and training software ecosystem across thousands of connected chips. Huawei relies on an entirely optics-driven scale-up mechanism rather than the copper wiring typical of Western servers, a method that is prohibitively expensive. Second, the physical space requirements are immense, with seven racks of Ascend 910C NPUs required to match the power of a single rack of NVIDIA B300 GPUs. 

Third, and most importantly, this massive hardware scaling is extremely power-inefficient. Huawei’s 2026 cluster is projected to require 8 to 12 times more power per teraflop than NVIDIA's comparable systems, demanding 1.50 watts per teraflop at FP8 precision compared to NVIDIA's highly efficient 0.19 watts. For further context, Google's rival Ironwood Pod delivers 42 FP8 exaflops across 9,216 TPUs with an efficiency of just 0.23 watts per teraflop. Because of these prohibitive hardware costs, immense spatial footprints, and extreme energy demands, the author concludes that Huawei's compute clusters will likely only find adoption among subsidized Chinese state-owned enterprises or domestic companies under direct government pressure to buy local.

This page from the report focuses on the significant geopolitical risks surrounding China and Taiwan, specifically analyzing the global and American reliance on Taiwanese semiconductor chips and high-tech components. Michael Cembalest argues that global and US reliance on Taiwan's semiconductor industry dwarfs the reliance Europe had on Russian energy prior to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. 

To illustrate this scale of dependence, the first chart compares regional reliance for critical goods by percentage. It shows that in 2021, Russian energy imports made up under twenty percent of European primary energy consumption. By comparison, global semiconductor reliance on Taiwan is close to seventy percent, and global reliance on Taiwan for advanced chips reaches approximately ninety percent. The second chart details US semiconductor reliance on Taiwan, demonstrating how direct import figures fail to capture the full picture. While the direct Taiwanese share of US semiconductor imports by value sits at around eighteen percent, the US exposure rises to twenty-four percent for memory chips and reaches forty percent for logic chips once indirect flows through third-party intermediaries are factored in.

The next two charts present monthly annualized US import data in billions of US dollars from 2021 through mid-2025. The third chart, tracking US semiconductor-related imports, shows "All other" countries dominating at around thirty-five billion dollars, while individual nations like Taiwan, Malaysia, Vietnam, China, South Korea, Thailand, and Mexico remain clustered below fifteen billion dollars. Cembalest explains that the Taiwan figure in this chart is artificially low because international trade databases do not track Taiwanese chips routed to other countries for assembly and packaging. In contrast, the fourth chart, which tracks US AI-related computer imports including graphics processing units, parts, and large computers, reveals an extraordinary surge in imports from Taiwan. Taiwanese AI imports skyrocketed from roughly twenty billion dollars in 2021 to peak at over one hundred and sixty billion dollars by mid-2025. US imports from Mexico in this category also saw a substantial rise to nearly one hundred billion dollars over the same period, while imports from China, South Korea, Thailand, Malaysia, and Vietnam remained flat and well under twenty billion dollars.

The page concludes with a historical and political commentary regarding US-Taiwan relations and the doctrine of strategic ambiguity, which was established in 1979 when the US recognized the People's Republic of China and ended formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan. Cembalest compares historical precedents, pointing out that when George W. Bush broke from strategic ambiguity in 2001 by stating the US would defend Taiwan, his administration quickly walked back the comments to reaffirm the One-China policy. Conversely, Joe Biden repeatedly and explicitly stated the US would militarily defend Taiwan, leaving National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan to manage the diplomatic fallout. Cembalest connects these repeated rhetorical shifts to his own political predictions, noting that these departures from established strategic ambiguity formed part of the rationale for his January 2024 Outlook prediction that Biden would withdraw from the presidential race before the Democratic convention due to health reasons.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2026 Outlook analyzes the escalating military and economic tensions between China and Taiwan, highlighting Taiwan's acute geographic and supply-chain vulnerabilities alongside China's increasingly aggressive military posture. 

The first of two maps illustrates the value of imports into Taiwan’s major ports in 2022, measured in billions of US dollars, to demonstrate how heavily concentrated Taiwan's trade flow is. The port of Kaohsiung alone accounts for $159.0 billion, or 57% of all imports, including vital containerized goods, oil, and liquefied natural gas. The remaining major ports handle significantly less traffic, with Keelung at $67.8 billion, Taichung at $21.7 billion, the Port of Taipei at $20.0 billion, Mailiao at $9.5 billion, and Hualien at a marginal $0.2 billion. The second map depicts the spatial layout of China’s "Joint Sword-2024A" military exercises, which were launched following the inauguration of Taiwanese President William Lai. This map shows red-shaded exclusion zones closely encircling Taiwan, encroaching upon its contiguous zone and territorial waters, and surrounding critical outlying islands such as Kinmen, Wuqiu, Matsu, and Dongyin.

In the accompanying text, titled "Heating up," the author examines the broader geopolitical implications of these maneuvers, quoting President Xi Jinping’s statements on the historical inevitability of reunification. The text notes that China’s maritime probing of Taiwanese boundaries surged by 60% in 2024 compared to 2023. Additionally, intelligence from September 2025 indicates that Russia has been actively training Chinese airborne units using its own battlefield experience—including high-altitude parachute drops of armored vehicles—and selling China military hardware such as heavy-lift transport aircraft, light amphibious vehicles, and anti-tank guns. In a conflict scenario, Russia's exports of oil and gas could serve as a vital strategic backup for China. 

Author Michael Cembalest raises several open questions, noting that while President Xi's exact timeline remains unknown, it is highly risky to assume a Chinese takeover would not disrupt Western access to TSMC semiconductor chips. Furthermore, he speculates that Beijing might view Donald Trump’s second term as a window of US non-intervention in East Asia, pointing to a December 2025 US National Security Strategy document outlining a "Trump Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine" that prioritizes Western Hemisphere defense. Under this framework, Cembalest suggests that a record $11 billion US arms package to Taiwan announced in December 2025 might function more as a commercial transaction than a committed military alliance.

This analysis focuses on the global semiconductor supply chain, highlighting the extreme uniqueness of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and the challenges confronting US efforts to onshore advanced microchip manufacturing. The author emphasizes that eight of the ten largest companies by market capitalization rely heavily on TSMC, with more than one-third of their combined two trillion dollars in revenue derived from hardware using its products. TSMC’s deep-seated efficiency in Taiwan is driven by a highly concentrated cluster of science parks, close physical proximity between fabrication facilities, and robust state subsidies. In contrast, TSMC founder Morris Chang’s warnings about the inefficiency of US-based fabs are supported by the data, and US-manufactured chips must currently be sent back to Taiwan for packaging, dicing, and testing until domestic packaging facilities are built around 2028.

To illustrate the stark cost disparities, a detailed table compares the 2025 economics of a five-nanometer wafer between TSMC’s Taiwan Fab 18 (Phases 1-3) and its US Fab 21 (Phase 1). While Taiwan's fab has an installed capacity of 90,000 wafer starts per month, the US fab has only 24,000. On a per-wafer basis, the US faces double the costs for raw materials ($3,040 versus $1,520) and labor ($3,600 versus $1,800). Due to lower production volume and high capital expenditures, US depreciation per wafer skyrockets to $7,289 compared to Taiwan’s $1,500, driving the total cost per wafer in the US to $16,123—well over double Taiwan's cost of $6,681. Consequently, the gross margin per wafer drops from an exceptionally high 62 percent in Taiwan to a meager 8 percent in the United States. 

The text addresses the policy goal set by US Commerce Secretary Lutnick to onshore 40 percent of semiconductor demand by 2028. With global advanced node demand expected to reach 1.4 million wafer starts per month (wspm) by 2028, and US customers representing roughly 75 percent of TSMC's leading-edge revenue, US advanced node demand is projected at approximately 1 million wspm. 

An accompanying stacked bar chart projects how the US might achieve 30 to 35 percent self-sufficiency in advanced node (under five-nanometer) production by the 2028–2030 timeframe, totaling roughly 320,000 wspm. This output is broken down by key contributors: 145,000 wspm from existing Intel production (representing the 50 percent US-based portion of its global output); 50,000 wspm from estimated future Intel production in Arizona and Oregon; 27,200 wspm from future Samsung production in Texas; and three phases of TSMC Arizona development, comprising 24,000 wspm from Phase 1, 24,000 wspm from Phase 2, and 50,000 wspm from Phase 3. 

Finally, the author poses an open question regarding whether Taiwan's government will transition its technology export policy from an "N-1" rule to an "N-2" rule. Under the current N-1 rule, TSMC is permitted to export fabrication processes that are only one generation behind its domestic leading-edge. A shift to an N-2 rule would force overseas US facilities to remain two generations behind, meaning that as Taiwan transitions to cutting-edge two-nanometer production, its Arizona Phase 2 fab would be restricted to producing three-nanometer chips.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s 2026 Outlook focuses on the massive impact of AI-driven technology capital spending on the United States economy. The author argues that without a once-in-a-generation surge in tech-related capital expenditure during the first half of 2025, the US economy would have been in a noticeably worse state. Specifically, annual real GDP growth from the third quarter of 2024 to the third quarter of 2025 was 2.3%; without above-trend tech capital spending, this growth figure would have dropped to just 1.8%. 

To illustrate this point, the page features three charts. The first two line charts show quarterly contributions to real GDP growth from the third quarter of 2021 through the third quarter of 2025. The top-left chart measures this contribution in billions of US dollars, contrasting the contribution of information processing equipment and software against the rest of the economy. It highlights a sharp drop in the rest of the economy's contribution to negative territory in early 2025, while tech spending remained positive. The top-right chart shows this in percentages, comparing personal consumption expenditures to information processing equipment and software. This chart demonstrates a rare occurrence in the first quarter of 2025, when the contribution of personal consumption fell below 0.5%, dipping below the rising contribution of tech equipment and software.
