The bottom bar chart provides a historical comparison of this tech capital spending surge, evaluating tech capital spending in 2025 against several of the largest US infrastructure and capital outlays of the 20th century, measured by peak annual project spending as a percentage of GDP. The 2025 tech capex alone is shown as a massive black bar peaking at approximately 2.0% of GDP. For context, individual historic projects had much lower peak annual shares: the 1930s public works—which included the Hoover Dam, Golden Gate Bridge, Triborough Bridge, Midtown Tunnel, and LaGuardia Airport—peaked at about 0.6%; the Manhattan Project in 1944 peaked at 0.6%; farm electrification in 1949 peaked at 0.6%; the Apollo Project in 1964 peaked at 0.5%; the Interstate Highway system in 1966 peaked at 0.5%; and the year 2000 broadband capex peaked at 1.0%. A final "Combined" bar stacks the historical peaks of the 1930s public works, the Manhattan Project, electrification, the Apollo Project, and the Interstate Highway system, showing that their combined peak share of GDP, totaling just over 2.1%, was roughly equal to the tech spending boom of 2025.

This page from the publication assesses the growing military power imbalance between China and Taiwan, framed by a New Year’s Day speech from Chinese President Xi Jinping asserting that reunification is unstoppable. The text details China’s recent "Justice Mission" military exercises, which simulated a blockade of Taiwan using long-range artillery, destroyers, bombers, and fighter jets. The overall narrative of China's rapid military modernization and regional dominance is supported by five distinct data exhibits covering naval forces, air power, and satellite capabilities.

A detailed table compares the balance of naval and air power in the Taiwan Strait using CSIS data. It reveals a stark disparity between total Chinese forces, those deployed near Taiwan, and Taiwan’s own assets. For instance, while Taiwan has no aircraft carriers or amphibious assault ships, China has two carriers (with one deployed near Taiwan) and three amphibious assault ships (all three deployed near Taiwan). Of China’s forty-two destroyers, thirty are positioned near Taiwan, vastly outnumbering Taiwan's four destroyers. Similarly, of China’s 1,900 fighter jets, 750 are deployed near Taiwan, more than double Taiwan's entire fleet of 300. China also holds a massive advantage in bombers, with 300 of its 500 bombers stationed near Taiwan, whereas Taiwan possesses none.

The rapid growth of the Chinese military relative to the United States is illustrated in a line chart comparing navy size by the number of battle force ships. The data shows that the size of China’s navy surpassed that of the United States around 2016. Looking forward, the chart projects that China’s battle force fleet will expand to approximately 430 ships by 2030, while the United States fleet is expected to remain relatively flat, plateauing around 310 to 320 ships. 

An area chart tracking Chinese fighter aircraft by generation from 2009 to 2024 highlights a significant technological upgrade. Over this period, total fighter counts grew from roughly 1,500 to over 2,000. This growth was accompanied by the phase-out of older second- and third-generation aircraft, which have been largely replaced by advanced fourth-generation, 4.5-generation, and cutting-edge fifth-generation fighters. 

The high concentration of Chinese forces near Taiwan is further explored in a bar chart showing the percentage of military assets deployed in the Taiwan Strait. It shows that 100% of China's amphibious assault ships, coastal patrol craft, medium landing ships, and nuclear ballistic submarines are deployed in the Taiwan Strait. Additionally, more than 70% of its destroyers, 60% of its frigates, and 60% of its bombers and special mission aircraft are concentrated in this narrow corridor.

Finally, a stacked bar chart illustrates the exponential increase in China’s military and dual-use satellite launches between 2014 and 2024. The total number of annual launches grew from under 100 in 2014 to approximately 120 in 2019, before surging to nearly 270 by 2024. This massive space-based expansion is heavily dominated by intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) satellites, alongside significant increases in electronic intelligence, signals intelligence, and navigation satellites, underscoring China’s enhanced targeting and battlefield awareness capabilities.

This page of J.P. Morgan's 2026 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest and titled "A run for their money," compares historical, highly controversial presidential cabinet members to contemporary public health policy concerns surrounding Robert F. Kennedy Jr. 

The author first highlights the legacies of JFK and LBJ's Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, a primary architect of the Vietnam War who later issued a notable 1995 mea culpa, and Nixon's Attorney General John Mitchell, who was jailed for actions including expansion of warrantless wiretapping, approving the Watergate break-in, and the suppression of anti-war protesters. Two small portrait photographs of McNamara and Mitchell are featured alongside these descriptions.

Cembalest then draws a parallel to modern controversies, referencing an October 7, 2025 Washington Post Op-Ed signed by six former U.S. Surgeons General—Antonia Novello, Joycelyn Elders, David Satcher, Richard Carmona, Vivek Murthy, and Jerome Adams. These officials collectively warned that RFK Jr. represents an unprecedented threat to public health, arguing that ideology and misinformation are taking precedence over science. The page details their specific policy concerns, which include RFK Jr.'s unsubstantiated claims regarding autism and vaccines, his promotion of vitamins over vaccines during a severe measles outbreak where U.S. vaccination rates dropped below 93% (under the 95% threshold needed to prevent contagion), his dismissal of all 17 members of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, and his warnings about prenatal acetaminophen that pediatric and obstetric groups have advised doctors and patients to ignore. Additionally, the Op-Ed accuses RFK Jr. of silencing hundreds of scientific experts and fostering an atmosphere of intimidation and censorship. Cembalest concludes by suggesting that, given these developments, RFK Jr. may ultimately rival McNamara and Mitchell in the scale of his controversial policy decisions.

This page of the 2026 Outlook analyzes the Federal Reserve's current strategy, termed the "pig-in-the-python" bet, where the central bank is easing monetary policy on the assumption that any tariff-driven inflation spike will quickly subside. The author highlights that the Fed faces a challenging divergence where labor market indicators are weakening even as prices-paid surveys remain in expansionary territory. This employment-inflation divergence currently sits in the 70th percentile for manufacturing and the 83rd percentile for services.

To illustrate these trends, the page features four charts and a comprehensive table of labor market indicators. The first chart displays the monthly net change in nonfarm payrolls as a three-month seasonally adjusted average from 2018 through late 2025, showing a sharp downward trend in both total and private payrolls toward the end of the period. The second chart tracks the ISM prices paid surveys, revealing that both manufacturing and services indices remain elevated well above the neutral 50 level, indicating expanding prices. In contrast, the third chart shows the ISM employment surveys trending downward, with manufacturing dipping below the neutral 50 threshold into contraction territory. The fourth chart subtracts the ISM employment index from the prices paid index to highlight the Fed's dilemma, illustrating a stark historical spike into the "rising inflation, falling employment" quadrant for both sectors in late 2025.

A detailed labor market indicators table compares metrics from December 2022, December 2024, and the latest late-2025 data. Notable shifts indicating a cooling labor market include the three-month average for nonfarm payroll growth collapsing from 209,000 in December 2024 to just 22,000 in the latest reading. Over the same period, Challenger monthly announced job cuts surged from 38,792 to 71,321, while the consumer confidence spread of "jobs plentiful minus jobs hard to get" fell to 10%. Furthermore, the U3 unemployment rate climbed from 4.1% to 4.6%, and the U6 underemployment rate rose from 7.5% to 8.7%. 

In a concluding footnote, the author addresses the open question of Fed independence. While noting that it is too early to evaluate a new Fed chair's performance over an entire business cycle, the text details the long history of presidential pressure on central bank policy, referencing President Nixon's efforts to influence Fed Chair Arthur Burns. The author also highlights a critique by Wharton professor Peter Conti-Brown regarding President Biden's Fed appointments, which Conti-Brown characterized as having a "stunning anonymity within central bank circles" and lacking traditional academic or institutional central banking backgrounds.

This page features a professional biographical profile of Michael Cembalest, the Chairman of Market and Investment Strategy for J.P. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management, accompanied by a photographic portrait of him. The text outlines his responsibilities leading strategic market and investment insights for a firm supervising six trillion dollars in client assets as of 2025. It details his extensive history at the company, which he joined in 1987 in the Corporate Finance division. His prior leadership positions include serving as the Chief Investment Officer for the Global Private Bank for eight years, head of a fixed income division, and Head Strategist for Emerging Markets Fixed Income at J.P. Morgan Securities. Additionally, his committee involvements are noted, such as serving on the Investment Committee for the J.P. Morgan Retirement Plan for the firm's more than 256,000 employees. The biography concludes with his educational credentials, noting an M.A. from the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs in 1986 and a B.A. from Tufts University in 1984.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2026 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, discusses three key financial themes: the stability of the US dollar, a rebound in healthcare stocks relative to technology, and the enduring strength of the US-Emerging Markets barbell strategy. 

Addressing the first theme, the author argues that the US dollar should remain stable in 2026. Although the dollar fell approximately 10% in 2025 from its post-financial crisis high, sparking fears among dollar skeptics, key indicators of the dollar's global status remain robust despite worsening US debt and deficit projections. This point is supported by a long-term historical chart from 1973 to 2025 depicting the Spot Dollar Index alongside the Federal Reserve's trade-weighted real and nominal dollar indices, highlighting the recent drop from elevated levels. An accompanying table tracks the US dollar's share in global debt, foreign exchange, reserves, and trade, comparing 2022 to the latest available data from 2024 and 2025. According to the table, the dollar's share of cross-border loans rose from 50% to 52%, international debt securities rose from 49% to 53%, foreign exchange transaction volume increased from 88% to 89%, and SWIFT payments grew from 42% to 47%. In contrast, official foreign exchange reserves declined from 60% to 56%, and trade invoicing fell from 50% to 42%.

The second section focuses on US healthcare stocks, which severely underperformed technology stocks leading up to mid-2025. Following the publication of J.P. Morgan's August 12, 2025 piece titled "Sick as a Dog," healthcare stocks experienced a strong rebound. Cembalest expects healthcare performance to continue improving in 2026, driven by low valuations. This trend is visualized in a chart comparing S&P 500 Healthcare and S&P 500 Information Technology total returns from 2023 through late 2025, indexed to 100 on the August publication date. The chart shows technology returns soaring far above healthcare for most of 2023 and 2024 before a dramatic convergence in late 2025 following the report's release.

Lastly, the author highlights the performance of an asset allocation strategy that overweights US equities by 10% and Emerging Markets by 5%, while underweighting Europe by 10% and Japan by 5%. Cembalest calls this US-Emerging Markets barbell one of the most consistently beneficial strategies since 1987. A chart tracking the rolling three-year excess return of this barbell against the MSCI All World Index from 1992 to 2025 reveals that the strategy has spent nearly the entire period in positive territory. Although the strategy briefly dipped into negative returns during 2025, it rebounded to end the year in positive territory, maintaining a track record whose only major period of underperformance occurred around 2006 to 2007.

This page of J.P. Morgan's outlook commentary focuses on the recovery of capital markets, which Michael Cembalest argues will act as an important barometer of new administration policies. Pointing to signs of recovery in primary and secondary initial public offerings as well as mergers and acquisitions at the end of 2025, he predicts that buyout and venture capital managers will capitalize on these improved conditions to monetize an enormous backlog of unsold positions. This argument is supported by five charts analyzing activity trends. 

The first chart, illustrating US IPO activity on a three-month rolling average from 2018 to early 2026, details how monthly deal values approached twenty billion dollars and offering counts neared one hundred during the 2021 peak before crashing in 2022 and staging a gradual recovery throughout 2025. 

The second chart presents the average first-day return for US IPOs larger than twenty-five million dollars from 1995 to 2025, revealing that while the historical median sits around fifteen percent, the first-day return spiked to nearly thirty percent in 2025 after a post-2020 lull. 

The third chart shows a similar three-month rolling average for US secondary offerings, which mirrors the primary IPO market's trajectory of a 2021 peak, a deep 2022 trough, and a steady rise in both deal count and volume through late 2025. 

The fourth chart displays quarterly announced M&A volumes from 2018 to late 2025, split between strategic and sponsor acquisitions; total volumes peaked at over one point four trillion dollars in 2021, fell sharply in 2023, and rebounded to over one point two trillion dollars by late 2025. 

Finally, a chart titled "Waiting for Godot" highlights the median remaining value of unmonetized venture capital and buyout shares as a percentage of total fund value plus distributions across vintage years from 2010 to 2024. It emphasizes the pressure on fund managers, showing that more recent vintages, particularly those from 2020 onward, still hold eighty percent to nearly one hundred percent of their value in unmonetized assets.

This page analyzes whether the long-running era of US stock market outperformance is finally over. While the S&P 500 generated 3.6 times the return of the MSCI World ex-US Index from 2009 to 2024, the US underperformed most global markets in 2025, which lowered the cumulative relative return multiple to 3.0 times. The author argues that despite incoming policies under the Donald Trump administration regarding trade, the dollar, and the national deficit—which support a less US-centric portfolio—investors should not expect valuation parity between US and international equities because US companies continue to deliver far superior fundamental growth and profitability.

To illustrate historical performance, a bar chart titled "Investors reaped large gains by sticking with US stocks" tracks cumulative total returns from January 2009 to December 2025 based on the year an investor decided to switch from the S&P 500 to the MSCI World ex-US Index. The data shows that sticking with the S&P 500 yielded the highest cumulative return of over 900%, and bailing out in any year prior to 2025 left money on the table. The year 2025 was the very first time in fifteen years when switching out of the S&P 500 would have yielded higher cumulative returns. At the same time, a line chart titled "Non-US P/E discount vs US" tracks the forward P/E of the MSCI World ex-US divided by the US forward P/E from 2005 to 2025. This ratio dropped from roughly 115% in 2005 to around 70% by late 2025, demonstrating that international equities still trade at a substantial valuation discount.

Looking at recent performance, a bar chart detailing "2025 ytd total returns for major equity markets" shows US dollar returns across various regions. Korea led all markets with returns exceeding 90%, followed by Latin America at over 50%. In contrast, US Large Cap, US Small Cap, and the Nasdaq underperformed most other global regions, while India sat at the bottom of the list.

Despite the recent underperformance, US corporate fundamentals remain stronger than global competitors, as highlighted in three distinct tables. The first table, "2025 year over year EBIT growth by sector and country," reveals that total US EBIT grew by 12%, compared to negative 1% in Europe, 0% in China, and 8% in Japan. US growth was strongest in Information Technology at 27%, Financials at 23%, and Communication Services at 19%. 

The structural advantages of US corporations are further demonstrated in two valuation tables comparing key sectors across the US, Europe, Japan, and China. The table "Return on Assets: Higher in the US" shows that the US leads across nearly all sectors, notably in Tech at 13.1% (compared to Europe's 8.8% and China's 9.1%) and Communication Services at 10.4% (compared to Europe's 2.1%). Similarly, the table "Return on Equity: Higher in the US" showcases dominant US profitability, with a US Tech RoE of 29.3% (versus 17.1% in Europe and 10.7% in China) and US Consumer Discretionary RoE at 26.0% (versus 5.5% in Europe). Based on these superior profitability metrics, the author forecasts that the MSCI World ex-US Index P/E is unlikely to exceed 80% of US levels.

This J.P. Morgan publication examines the geopolitical significance of Venezuela, focusing on how its oil production and critical mineral reserves align with United States strategic interests. The author argues that the United States has a strong interest in Venezuela because its heavier oil grades are a natural fit for US refining gaps. 

To support this, the first chart, "US oil production & refining vs Venezuela production," plots volume in millions of barrels per day across three categories: US production, US refinery inputs, and Venezuela's normalized pre-Maduro production. The data shows that while US oil production is high at around 13 million barrels per day, it is overwhelmingly composed of light oil. Meanwhile, US refinery inputs exceed 15 million barrels per day and require a much more balanced mix of light, medium, and heavy grades. Venezuela's normalized pre-Maduro production of roughly 2.5 million barrels per day is dominated by heavy and medium grades, which would perfectly complement the deficit in US domestic production. 

The second chart, "Oil production vs proven reserves," is a scatter plot comparing 2024 production in millions of barrels per day against proven reserves in billions of barrels for major global oil producers. This visualization underscores a stark imbalance: Venezuela possesses the largest proven reserves in the world, exceeding 300 billion barrels, yet its production remains extremely low, under 2 million barrels per day. In contrast, the United States has high production approaching 20 million barrels per day but relatively low proven reserves, well under 100 billion barrels. Other major players shown include Saudi Arabia, which has high reserves (around 260 billion barrels) and high production (around 10 million barrels per day), alongside Canada, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, and the Russian Federation. The text notes that among the top reserve nations, many face severe geopolitical headwinds: Russia is under heavy sanctions, Saudi Arabia and the UAE are clashing in Yemen, Iran is experiencing internal riots, and the US has previously intervened in Venezuela. 

The final section of the page addresses the debate over Venezuela’s critical minerals, such as coltan, rare earth elements, nickel, bauxite, iron ore, and cassiterite, which are vital for military technology, missile guidance, and aerospace manufacturing. Although the official 2025 USGS Mineral Commodity Surveys do not list Venezuela as a major reserve holder for these materials, the author highlights reports of illicit supply chains. Specifically, Chinese buyers are reportedly working with Colombian guerrilla groups and the Venezuelan military to extract these minerals from the Orinoco Mining Arc. The author concludes that while Venezuela's official and black-market economies remain highly opaque, the active presence of China—which dominates global critical mineral processing—signals that Venezuela's untapped mineral wealth represents a major geopolitical battleground.

This page analyzes the United States' ongoing dependence on petroleum for transportation and industrial sectors, alongside a broader global comparison of the oil intensity of economic growth. The author argues that despite the long-term potential for vehicle electrification to reduce this reliance, near-term transition prospects are limited. This outlook is driven by the policy priorities of the Trump Administration, the September 2025 expiration of US electric vehicle subsidies, and corporate pullbacks such as Ford scaling back plans for the F150 Lightning.

A Sankey diagram from the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory illustrates US energy consumption in 2023, which totaled 93.6 quads. The diagram traces energy sources—including petroleum (35.4 quads), natural gas (33.4 quads), coal (8.17 quads), nuclear (8.1 quads), and various renewables—into intermediate generation and end-use sectors. Petroleum flows, represented by the dark green bands, heavily dominate the transportation sector, supplying 24.8 of the sector's total 28 quads, or approximately 90%. Within transportation, passenger vehicles, SUVs, and light trucks account for about 60% of consumption, with the remainder split among class 8 heavy trucks, aviation, and maritime transport. Petroleum also fuels roughly 33% of industrial sector energy (8.53 of 26.1 quads), primarily for high-temperature heat and feedstocks, while its use in residential and commercial heating remains negligible at under 10%. Ultimately, the diagram shows that a significant portion of US energy is lost, with 61.5 quads classified as rejected energy compared to only 32.1 quads realized as energy services.

A second line chart tracks the oil intensity of GDP from 1990 to 2025, measured in tonnes of oil consumption per trillion dollars of 2022 real GDP. The chart displays data for the US, Brazil, Spain, Japan, China, India, Germany, and France. Although every country listed exhibits a gradual decline in oil intensity over this period, the United States consistently records the highest intensity. The US intensity level started at roughly 65 in 1990 and fell to just above 30 by 2025. China experienced a sharp decline from around 55 in 1990 to the high 20s by 2025, while European nations like France and Germany ended the period with the lowest oil intensities, near 15 to 20. The author notes that while falling intensity globally makes economies more resilient to oil supply shocks, the US's higher baseline and slowing transport electrification make it highly unlikely to converge with its international peers in the near future.

This report page details recent regulatory and zoning changes in New York City, contrasting the potential significance of the "City of Yes" zoning reform plan with the relatively marginal impact of recent Floor Area Ratio (FAR) changes. Passed in December 2024, the "City of Yes" plan aims to produce 80,000 new homes over 15 years by easing permitting for low-rise apartment buildings near transit and commercial hubs, allowing accessory dwelling units, facilitating office-to-housing conversions, and reducing parking mandates. Additionally, the author notes the August 2025 approval of the "Midtown South Mixed-Use" plan, which could yield 9.7 thousand units across 42 blocks, and the November 2025 "OneLIC Neighborhood Plan" in Long Island City, which aims for 14.7 thousand new units, including 4.3 thousand affordable ones, supported by $2 billion in public investments. 

In contrast, the author argues that the FAR changes are "much ado about very little," with minimal impact in Manhattan and waterfront areas of Brooklyn and Queens, and limited density impact on Staten Island due to existing single- and two-family rules. This marginal shift is shown in a line chart plotting the NYC average allowable residential Floor Area Ratio against the distance from the Empire State Building in miles (ranging from 0 to 25). The data series for the 2024 average FAR and the 2025 post-zoning average FAR run almost entirely on top of each other, demonstrating very little change.

An accompanying table, "Impact of Floor Area Ratio changes by borough," further breaks down these figures, weighted by lot size. It shows that between 2024 and 2025, the average FAR in the Bronx went from 1.9 to 2.1 (a 7% increase on 0.5 billion square feet of residential floor area), Brooklyn increased from 1.7 to 1.9 (an 8% change on 1.1 billion square feet), and Manhattan edged up from 5.8 to 5.9 (a 2% change on 0.9 billion square feet). Larger percentage changes occurred in Queens, which rose 25% from 1.0 to 1.2, and Staten Island, which jumped 38% from 0.6 to 0.9. Overall, the total city-wide average FAR moved from 1.5 to 1.7, representing a 13% change across 3.6 billion square feet of total residential floor area.

The page concludes with a localized "YIMBY" anecdote concerning a vacant Brooklyn multiplex on Court Street designed by Hardy Holzman Pfeiffer and developed by Forest City Ratner. Despite losing 88% of its appraised value since closing in 2022, the parcel's current C6-2A zoning limits—specifically a 120-foot height limit and a 6.0 FAR—have failed to attract redevelopment capital. The author suggests that for a conversion to be financially viable, the site would require a building height limit twice as high as currently allowed.

This page of the publication analyzes New York City’s severe housing supply shortage and examines how the newly elected Democratic Socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani, might address it. Mamdani campaigned on high-profile proposals including a seventy-billion-dollar city-funded capital investment in affordable housing, fast-tracked land use approvals, rent freezes for rent-stabilized apartments, and increased taxes on wealthy residents and corporations. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that this ambitious plan faces major hurdles due to the city's historical borrowing constraints, which stem from the 1970s financial crisis. Cembalest attributes the root of that crisis to the debt-financed spending and ballooning municipal payrolls under former Mayor John Lindsay's administration from 1966 to 1973, which ultimately triggered the Financial Emergency Act. Footnotes elaborate that between fiscal 1970 and 1975, city spending grew by eighty percent while tax receipts rose by only fifty-four percent, leading to a loss of over five hundred thousand jobs and a severe population decline.

Two charts illustrate the scale of the current crisis. The first chart, titled "Payroll employment and housing units in NYC," plots both metrics in millions from 1980 through 2023. It reveals that while housing units climbed at a slow, linear pace, employment grew rapidly, climbing from around 3.3 million in 1980 to roughly 4.7 million by 2023. Consequently, the housing-to-employment ratio fell from eighty-nine percent in 1980 to seventy-nine percent in 2023, highlighting a severe structural deficit in housing construction relative to job growth. 

The second chart, titled "NYC rental vacancy rate," displays the city's historically tight rental market from 1945 to 2025. The overall vacancy rate has fluctuated but shows a sharp downward plunge in recent years to below two percent. To detail this tightness, the chart plots specific dots representing the 2023 vacancy rates across different rental price brackets. It reveals that the vacancy rate for affordable apartments under eleven hundred dollars and those between eleven hundred and twenty-four hundred dollars is virtually zero percent, while apartments renting for twenty-four hundred dollars or more have a slightly higher vacancy rate of approximately three percent. 

The author concludes that if Mamdani’s seventy-billion-dollar housing plan cannot be funded due to NYC's tight borrowing limits, the city will have to rely on alternative paths. These include dismantling restrictive zoning laws that block new developments, fostering public-private partnerships to boost affordable housing supply, and restructuring the rules around rent-stabilized renovation cost recoveries to make building maintenance and upgrades economically viable.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Online Trump Tracker evaluates the validity of drug smuggling as a primary rationale for a potential military invasion of Venezuela and the arrest of President Nicolás Maduro, while analyzing global fentanyl trafficking routes. 

The author begins by exploring the Maduro regime's deep economic reliance on illicit activities, noting that these operations collectively represent between 15% and 20% of Venezuela's gross domestic product. Citing research from Ecoanalítica, a Venezuelan economic consulting firm, the text highlights that profits from these illicit activities constitute 56% of Venezuelan exports, 56% of total government income, and 78% of all imports. 

An accompanying stacked bar chart, titled "Illicit activities as a percent of Venezuela GDP," illustrates the shifting composition of these illegal revenues for the years 2018, 2020, 2021, and 2022. The tracked categories include gasoline smuggling, drug trafficking, gold smuggling, currency exchange subsidies, port smuggling, and rhodium and coltan trafficking. The data shows that illicit activities peaked at approximately 20% of GDP in 2021, driven primarily by a massive spike in drug trafficking, which was the single largest illicit segment from 2020 through 2022. By 2022, the total illicit share of GDP dropped back to around 16%, with currency exchange subsidies, gold smuggling, and drug trafficking remaining the primary contributors, while gasoline smuggling shrunk significantly compared to its 2018 levels.

Despite the prominence of drug trafficking in Venezuela's broader economy, the author clarifies that the nation is not heavily involved in the fentanyl trade. To support this, the analysis references a 2020 U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration report on fentanyl flows into the United States, which does not mention Venezuela at all. Instead, China and Mexico are identified as the primary source countries for fentanyl, with India emerging as a key supplier of finished fentanyl powder and chemical precursors. 

A detailed DEA map included on the page illustrates these global trafficking patterns. The map shows that fentanyl powder, unregistered pill presses, and manufacturing precursors (labeled as items 1, 5, and 6) originate in China and India and are shipped via mail services directly to Canada, the United States, and Mexico. In Canada, powder fentanyls are processed and mixed with heroin (labeled as item 2) and smuggled into the United States on a smaller scale. In Mexico, cartels use Chinese and Indian precursor chemicals to clandestinely manufacture fentanyl, which is then cut, diluted, pressed into counterfeit prescription pills (labeled as item 4), or mixed with heroin (labeled as item 3) before being smuggled across the southwestern border into the United States.

This appendix page focuses on the City of Yes zoning changes proposed for New York City, outlining six key policy initiatives accompanied by geographic maps of the five boroughs to illustrate where these changes apply. The author notes that while the City of Yes represents a significant step change in New York City zoning policy, last-minute political carveouts are expected to reduce the potential impact on new housing units by roughly 25 percent. Specific limitations cited include retaining parking mandates in the mass transit deserts of Southeast Queens and cutting the transit-oriented development zoning radius in half, from a half-mile to a quarter-mile, near the thirteen easternmost Long Island Rail Road stations and four northern Metro-North stations.

The page includes six maps detailing the geographic reach of these policies. First, the Transit Oriented Development map shows the areas where modest apartment buildings will be relegalized near rail and subways in low-density districts. Second, the Town Center Zoning map highlights commercial overlays in low-density areas where housing can be built above businesses along commercial streets. Third, the Accessory Dwelling Units map displays where homeowners can add basement or detached units up to 800 square feet, highlighting restrictions in coastal flood zones, historic districts, and specific low-density outer districts. Fourth, the Universal Affordability Preferences map shows medium- and high-density districts where buildings can add 20 percent or more density if the housing is permanently affordable to households earning 60 percent of the Area Median Income. Fifth, the Parking Mandates map illustrates three distinct zones, showing where parking requirements are eliminated in Zone 1, which covers Manhattan and waterfront Brooklyn and Queens, relaxed in Zone 2, or largely maintained in Zone 3, which covers the remaining outer-borough areas. Finally, the Residential Conversions map demonstrates a vast expansion from the old eligible geography to a new, much larger eligible geography for converting non-residential buildings to residential use across the outer boroughs.

This page from the report discusses the warehousing of vacant rent-stabilized apartments in New York City, explaining how the 2019 New York Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act has rendered renovations economically unfeasible and led to the dilapidation of the city's housing stock. Landlords are currently holding an estimated 25,000 to 50,000 units vacant because post-renovation rent increases are capped at $320 to $347 per month, resulting in prohibitive 27-year payback periods for a typical $111,000 renovation. Releasing these units back into the market would push New York City's rental vacancy rate from 1.4% up to between 2.5% and 3.5%.

Two charts support this analysis. The first, titled Apartment and building improvement filings at rent stabilized properties, tracks the number of filings for individual apartment improvements and major capital investments from 2014 to 2022. It visually demonstrates that following the passage of the 2019 Act, individual apartment improvement filings plummeted from over 4,000 to below 1,000, while major capital investments dropped from roughly 250 to near 50. The second chart, Operating cost vs rent stabilized rent increases, uses indexed values where 2012 equals 1.0. It shows that by 2024, operating costs soared to nearly 1.8, while permitted rent increases—including one-year and both odd- and even-year two-year increases—lagged significantly behind, ranging between 1.1 and 1.3. This disparity has resulted in approximately 200,000 rent-stabilized units operating with negative net operating income.

The text also notes that the median discount for rent-stabilized units compared to market rates is 25% overall, though it reaches 50% in Manhattan and stays around 10% in outer boroughs. Policy interventions have failed to correct these imbalances. Mayor Adams’s 2023 Unlocking Doors initiative sought to reimburse landlords up to $50,000 for renovating units leased to low-income voucher holders, but the program saw near-zero uptake due to rigid rent limits of $1,200 for one-bedroom and $1,400 for three-bedroom units. Lastly, the author highlights a pending piece of state legislation, Senate Bill S6904, also known as the Local Regulated Housing Restoration Adjustment, which would allow landlords to raise post-renovation rents to Section 8 voucher levels for long-term units vacant after tenures of ten or more years.

This page examines New York City's tax burden, focusing on personal, corporate, and property tax rates. The author highlights that while the NYC mayor has proposed a 2% surtax on personal incomes exceeding $1 million, such changes require New York State legislative approval. He points out that New York State already represents the highest tax jurisdiction in the United States based on per capita collections, and that the city lacks the unilateral power to raise these rates.

The first chart, titled "Top 15 marginal personal income tax rates," shows that New York City has the highest combined state and local marginal personal income tax rate in the country, approaching 15%. This rate is driven by a combination of state taxes and a local NYC tax component. It sits above major California cities like Los Angeles, San Jose, San Francisco, and San Diego, which lack local-level personal income taxes but have high state rates near 13%, and far surpasses cities like Washington D.C., Boston, and Philadelphia.

The second chart, titled "Top marginal corporate income tax rates," displays corporate tax percentages across various states and cities, identifying NYC as the highest at 17.4%. This total is comprised of three segments: a state tax, a city tax, and an MTA surcharge. The New York State rate within the MTA region is also high at nearly 14%, while New Jersey follows at around 11.5%, and Florida registers the lowest rate shown at just under 6%.

Turning to real estate, the author argues that NYC property taxes disproportionately burden rental and commercial properties. A table detailing "Effective property tax rates per square foot" compares NYC against nine other major US cities—including Atlanta, Chicago, Dallas, Houston, Los Angeles, Nashville, Miami, San Francisco, and Washington D.C.—across four property classes: Industrial, Office, Retail, and Multifamily. NYC leads almost every category, with industrial rates at $10.69 per square foot, office rates at $15.96, retail at $16.24, and multifamily at $13.53. In comparison, Atlanta's industrial rate is only $0.85, and Dallas's multifamily rate is $5.07.

Finally, a table titled "Market value and property tax shares by class" demonstrates the structural disparity in tax burdens within NYC. Class 1 properties (residential with three or fewer units) make up 49% of citywide market value but contribute only 15% of tax revenues, resulting in an effective tax rate of 0.67%. In contrast, Class 2 (larger rental buildings) represents 24% of market value but contributes 36% of revenues with a 3.31% effective rate. Class 4 (commercial and industrial) represents 24% of market value while carrying a massive 42% share of tax revenues at a 3.85% effective tax rate. This data underscores how rental buildings and commercial spaces shoulder a disproportionate tax burden relative to small owner-occupied homes.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s report examines the rising backlash against data centers regarding their impact on US electricity prices, arguing that the public narrative is disconnected from actual data. The author points out that US power prices have only increased by 2 cents per kWh in real terms since 2022—rising from 13 to 15 cents—and make up a minor 1.4% of average household expenditures. Instead of blaming data center demand, the analysis shows that rising power costs are primarily driven by massive utility grid investments aimed at system hardening against wildfires, floods, and hurricanes, rather than generation capacity additions. 

Supporting this argument, a bar chart depicts US investor-owned utility grid investments from 2015 to 2024, showing a steady rise from just under $100 billion in 2015 to $178 billion in 2024, culminating in a total investment of $1.3 trillion over the ten-year period. To further exonerate data centers, a second chart displays a scatter plot analyzing the correlation between end-use customer load growth and retail electricity price increases by state from 2019 to 2024. The data demonstrates that load growth is actually inversely correlated with price hikes. For instance, California experienced minimal load growth but the highest price increase of nearly 12 cents per kWh, whereas North Dakota recorded load growth approaching 80% alongside a real price decline of about 3 cents per kWh. 

At the bottom of the page, a three-panel area chart tracks annual US electric investor-owned utility expenditures in real 2024 dollars from 2005 to 2023 across generation, transmission, and distribution, each broken down by operating and capital expenditures. While generation expenditures have steadily declined—driven largely by falling natural gas prices rather than renewable energy—both transmission and distribution expenditures have risen significantly over the period. This visual evidence reinforces the author's conclusion that rising transmission and distribution grid reinforcement costs, rather than new generation demand from data centers, are the primary upward drivers of US retail electricity prices.

This page analyzes the potential economic disruptions that would result from a closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20% of global oil consumption and 3% of global natural gas consumption flow. The author notes that while LNG is heavily discussed, it only represents 14% of global gas consumption, though certain nations like Japan, Korea, Taiwan, France, and Portugal rely on imported LNG for 90% to 100% of their gas needs. Footnote data adds that 75% of global oil trade is maritime, of which 27% passes through the Strait, while 14% of gas trade is maritime, of which 22% of LNG passes through the Strait.

To evaluate vulnerability to energy shocks, the author presents two scatter plots comparing energy sensitivity on the X-axis (the share of oil or gas in useful final energy consumption) against import sensitivity on the Y-axis (the import share of that consumption). The most vulnerable nations occupy the upper-right quadrant of these charts. 

The first chart, focusing on sensitivity to oil price spikes, shows that highly exposed nations include Belgium, Korea, the Netherlands, Taiwan, Japan, and Germany, which all import nearly 100% of their oil, with oil representing 35% to 45% of their final energy consumption. China is less exposed, with oil accounting for under 20% of final energy, even though its import share is over 70%. India has a higher import share of nearly 90% with oil making up roughly 26% of final energy.

The second chart maps sensitivity to gas price spikes. Here, Italy, Germany, and Turkey are highly vulnerable, with gas representing 35% to 50% of final energy and import shares exceeding 90%. Conversely, Pakistan has a high gas reliance of over 55% but a low import share of under 30%. Mexico is also a major consumer of gas at over 50% of final energy, with an import share of around 62%, though the author notes most of this is piped from the United States rather than sourced from the Persian Gulf.

The commentary highlights several key country takeaways. China remains relatively insulated on both charts due to its heavy reliance on domestic coal and its own gas production. Taiwan, Korea, Italy, Germany, and the Netherlands remain highly exposed. Spain serves as an example of energy transition complexity; while its electrical grid is only 20% reliant on fossil fuels, its overall final energy consumption is 70% reliant on fossil fuels, all of which are imported. In contrast, Sweden has successfully lowered its vulnerability; despite importing 100% of its oil and gas, fossil fuels make up only 35% of its total final energy due to high electrification powered by wind, hydro, and nuclear energy.

This page from the report analyzed the impact of data centers on power prices and electricity grid loads, focusing on recent empirical studies and regional grid data from Virginia and Texas. 

The author first highlighted a study on Virginia’s power market showing that new data center connections increase local marginal electricity prices by $2.58 per megawatt-hour (MWh), which is a 7.3% increase driven primarily by grid congestion. This congestion price increase is notably higher in census tracts with larger shares of renewable energy capacity compared to fossil fuel capacity, indicating that data centers in renewable-heavy tracts require power to be transmitted from more distant generation sources. 

This dynamic is visualized in the first chart, titled "Data center impact on locational marginal electricity prices," which shows the percentage change in prices from one year prior to interconnection over a timeline of six years before to six years after the connection. The chart utilizes point estimates with 95% confidence intervals, illustrating that price impacts transition from neutral or slightly negative before interconnection to consistently positive afterwards, peaking around 3% to 4% higher a few years post-connection. An accompanying note explains that sustainability frameworks rarely require physical matching between local data center consumption and local renewable generation, as renewables are typically credited at the system level.

The discussion then turned to the consistent rise in nighttime electricity loads between 2023 and 2025 in data-center-heavy regions, specifically the Northern Virginia Dominion Zone and the ERCOT grid in Texas. Because nighttime loads are less influenced by industrial shifts or population changes, and because the increase is evident at moderate temperatures of 50 to 60 degrees Fahrenheit where heating or cooling demand is minimal, the author attributed this growth directly to data centers and battery price arbitrage. 

This trend is illustrated in two subsequent scatter-plot charts showing average nighttime load in gigawatts (GW) from 11 PM to 7 AM against temperature in Fahrenheit for 2023, 2024, and 2025. The chart for the Dominion Zone shows a clear upward shift in its U-shaped load curve over the three-year period; at a mild temperature of 55 degrees Fahrenheit, the average nighttime load grew from approximately 10 GW in 2023 to about 12 GW in 2025. Similarly, the ERCOT chart reveals an upward-shifting curve, where the nighttime load at 55 degrees Fahrenheit climbed from roughly 38 GW in 2023 to about 44 GW in 2025. 

The author concluded that while these data points provide strong circumstantial evidence of data centers driving up power demand and prices, the most critical forward-looking issue is an emerging political and social backlash against data centers, which the report intends to outline following a detailed look at the PJM interconnection grid.

This page from the publication discusses the soaring capacity prices within the PJM grid region and the political push to allocate these incremental costs to data centers. The PJM region, spanning Virginia, Pennsylvania, Maryland, and Ohio, boasts 67 gigawatts of existing and planned data center capacity, making it the largest cluster in the United States, far outstripping ERCOT in Texas at 20 gigawatts and CAISO in California and Nevada at 8 gigawatts. Spikes in capacity payments, which serve as insurance premiums for future supply, are driving up retail power prices. In response, the White House and thirteen PJM governors have urged a one-time emergency auction to force large loads like data centers to bear these costs. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that data centers will likely participate in these auctions rather than migrate out of PJM, as power accounts for only 10% to 15% of their lifetime costs. He notes that the new rules favor large hyperscalers over smaller companies and aligns with utilities like Exelon, First Energy, PPL, and PSEG in questioning whether industry re-regulation is a better option.

A line chart titled "PJM capacity prices are soaring" tracks the Base Residual Auction rate in US dollars per megawatt per day by delivery year from 2007/2008 to 2027/2028. The data shows historically volatile but generally low rates, mostly under $150, for both the Mid-Atlantic Area Council and the broader Regional Transmission Organization. However, rates spike dramatically starting around 2024/2025, climbing close to $300 by 2027/2028, with a note indicating that uncapped rates would have cleared at $530. 

Two tables illustrate the retail bill impacts of the 2025/2026 PJM capacity auction. In Maryland, customer bill increases range from 2% for Delmarva Power & Light and 10% for Potomac Electric Power, up to 14% for Baltimore Gas & Electric and 24% for Allegheny Power Systems. In New Jersey, the impact on residential and small commercial bills is even higher, showing a 33% increase for Public Service Electric & Gas, 34% for Jersey Central Power & Light, and 36% for both Atlantic City Electric and Rockland Electric Company.

A final table details the declines in PJM’s effective load carrying capability for solar and storage from the 2023/2024 delivery year to 2027/2028, which has contributed to the rising capacity payments. The data shows tracking solar’s capability plummeting from 54% to just 8%, while 4-hour storage drops from 83% to 58%, and 8-hour storage falls from 100% to 70%. Onshore wind capability rises slightly from 15% to 41%. For the later years shown, traditional generation resources remain highly rated, with nuclear at 95%, coal at 83%, gas combined cycle at 74%, and gas combustion turbines at 61% by 2027/2028.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Energy Paper examines the growing conflict between rising artificial intelligence power requirements and localized opposition to data centers, alongside the question of whether rapid chip design and efficiency gains can mitigate this soaring electricity demand. The author notes that in 2025, local opposition led to the cancellation of at least 25 US data center projects, representing at least 4.7 gigawatts of projected capacity. This was four times the cancellations seen in 2024, with the highest cancellation rates occurring in Virginia and Indiana, followed by Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Michigan, and Georgia.

The fundamental driver of this demand is the massive compute scaling required for frontier AI models. In 2020, models like GPT-3 required only 3.1 times ten to the twenty-third power FLOPs and 4 to 10 megawatts of power. By 2025, Grok-3 is estimated to need up to 5.0 times ten to the twenty-sixth power FLOPs and 150 to 200 megawatts. By 2030, a frontier training run could require ten to the twenty-ninth power FLOPs and 4 to 16 gigawatts of power. While chip energy efficiency per watt has increased by 40% annually and training run durations have extended, computational intensity still outpaces these gains. Citing research from Epoch AI, the author states that without mitigating factors, training power demand would grow by four times per year. With longer training runs and improved chip efficiency, this growth rate drops to 2.2 times per year, which matches the observed historical trend but still implies an aggressive upward trajectory.

The page features three key charts illustrating these trends. The first, "Power used to train frontier AI models," plots megawatt usage on a logarithmic scale from 2018 to 2026. It maps individual models like GPT-3, Gopher, GPT-4, Llama 3.1-405, and Grok-3 along a dotted trend line showing 2.2-times growth per year, climbing from under 1 megawatt to nearly 200 megawatts. The second chart, "Leading AI hardware energy efficiency," measures FLOPs per watt on a logarithmic scale from 2016 to 2026, plotting the upward efficiency curve of prominent hardware. This includes early hardware like the NVIDIA P100 and Google TPU v2 near the ten to the eleventh power level, up to the NVIDIA H100, Google TPU v5e, and NVIDIA B100 approaching or exceeding ten to the thirteenth power FLOPs per watt.

The third chart, "Energy efficiency of chips over time," plots the declining energy consumption per token in Joules on a logarithmic scale from 2014 to 2026. This chart visualizes a massive plunge in energy intensity across NVIDIA architectures, falling from Kepler at 42,000 joules per token, to Pascal at 17,460, Volta at 1,200, Ampere at 150, Hopper at 10, Blackwell at 0.4, Blackwell Ultra at 0.2, and finally to Rubin at 0.1 joules per token. 

Additionally, a sidebar cites estimates for average data center utilization rates, noting that official agencies do not aggregate this data. Citing sources from MIT/NBER, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and Innovation Endeavors, the page notes that typical industry utilization rates range from 40% for inference up to 80% for training. The author’s ultimate conclusion is that the sheer scale of modern AI workloads is outpacing even these dramatic, order-of-magnitude improvements in hardware efficiency, ensuring that overall power demand will continue to rise.

This analysis examines the massive electricity demands triggered by the expansion of artificial intelligence and data centers, questioning whether the technological shift from AI model training to lower-intensity inference will mitigate this power crunch. While Brookfield Asset Management projects that the global power absorption for AI compute will rise to roughly eight gigawatts by 2035—with inference growing to dominate the vast majority of that total as training needs decline after 2028—OpenAI contends that training will continue to demand more capital than inference through 2030. Regardless of this debate, power grid queues and turbine orders are already surging to unprecedented levels to accommodate the expected load.

A chart detailing ERCOT large load interconnection requests illustrates this dramatic rise, showing total requests skyrocketing from negligible levels in 2022 to over 200 gigawatts by 2030, with the vast majority of these requests currently classified as having no studies submitted or being under review. ERCOT reports that seventy percent of this demand is driven by new data centers, while the midwestern grid operator SPP similarly reports 110 gigawatts of projects in its interconnection queue. 

To meet this looming demand, global orders for gas turbines are soaring far beyond manufacturing capacities. A chart on global gas turbine orders reveals that historical demand historically hovered between thirty and ninety gigawatts, remaining mostly below a global production limit of roughly 58 gigawatts. However, projected orders for 2025 through 2028 are expected to spike to over 100 gigawatts, creating a severe supply bottleneck. The market is highly consolidated, with GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, and Mitsubishi each commanding twenty to twenty-five percent of the global market. To address the backlogs, Mitsubishi is planning to double its production capacity, Siemens is investing one billion dollars to raise its US capacity by twenty percent, and GE Vernova is ramping its output from 16 gigawatts to 26 gigawatts by mid-2028. This turbine land grab is global, with Germany, Japan, Saudi Arabia, and China all planning massive new gas-fired capacity expansions. 

The consequences of this demand spike are illustrated in a final chart projecting a widening US power supply-demand gap between 2024 and 2033. While the peak supply anticipated by NERC and Schneider Electric is expected to crest at around 1,160 gigawatts in 2027 before declining back toward 1,120 gigawatts, the actual peak supply needed is projected to march steadily upward from 1,080 gigawatts to over 1,230 gigawatts. This divergence threatens to create a massive structural power deficit in the United States over the coming decade.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s energy paper examines the sheer scale of China’s energy consumption, which now exceeds that of the United States and Europe combined. Author Michael Cembalest highlights that China has accounted for half of the entire increase in global power generation since 2010, adopting an "all-of-the-above" expansion strategy that spans coal, nuclear, hydro, gas, wind, and solar, alongside industries like electric vehicles, battery storage, and critical minerals processing. 

Two charts tracking China's useful final energy by type from 2000 to 2024 in exajoules illustrate this growth. The first categorizes energy into fossil fuels, renewables, and nuclear, showing fossil fuels rising from around 20 exajoules to roughly 70 exajoules. The second provides a detailed breakout, revealing that coal remains the massive, dominant foundation of China's energy mix, despite visible growth at the top from wind, solar, and nuclear power. Similarly, a chart on China's electricity generation from 2000 to 2024 shows total output skyrocketing from 1,000 terawatt-hours to nearly 10,000 terawatt-hours, with coal serving as the dominant source, followed by hydro, wind, and solar.

The rapid modernization of China's energy grid is captured in an electrification chart comparing the electricity share of useful final energy in China and the US from 1990 to 2025. China’s share surged from just 12% in 1990 to nearly 40% by 2025, overtaking the US, which saw a more gradual rise from about 27% to 35% over the same period. 

Finally, the page addresses whether China's rising energy use and environmental impact are primarily due to Western outsourcing. A chart plotting annual territorial versus consumption-based emissions from 1990 to 2025 in gigatonnes of CO2 compares standard in-country emissions with those adjusted for where goods are consumed. For China, standard emissions rose to over 12 gigatonnes, while consumption-based emissions are only about 10% lower. Similarly, India’s emissions drop by only about 10% when adjusted for consumption. While the US and EU27 are net importers of emissions, with consumption-based figures tracking higher than standard in-country emissions, the author concludes that Western outsourcing is only a minor contributor to China’s massive emissions footprint, which is driven primarily by domestic consumption and infrastructure.

This page from the report explores the growing trend of "Bring Your Own Behind the Meter Generation" (BYOG) for data centers, driven primarily by rising wait times for grid interconnection. Currently, less than one percent of data center power demand in 2025 is met by onsite power, but surveys suggest that 38 percent expect to rely on it partially and 27 percent fully by 2030. Furthermore, 30 percent of planned US data center capacity, representing 56 gigawatts out of 190 gigawatts, now intends to build onsite generation. This planned behind-the-meter generation relies heavily on fossil fuels and nuclear, with 75 percent using natural gas and 21 percent relying on nuclear. The author notes that most facilities will opt for "grid-adjacent" setups to maintain a grid connection for redundancy rather than being completely stranded. However, the author predicts that this behind-the-meter trend will face headwinds because data centers must compete for equipment with utilities, independent power producers, and each other.

To illustrate the grid delays motivating this shift, a line chart shows the time elapsed from interconnection requests to commercial operation dates in years from 2000 to 2024. The data reveals a significant upward trend in wait times. The median wait time has risen from under two years in 2000 to approximately four and a half years in 2024. Over the same timeframe, the 75th percentile has grown from roughly three years to nearly six years, and the 25th percentile has climbed to about three and a half years. 

A detailed table compares seven behind-the-meter generation alternatives across various metrics. Aeroderivative gas turbines provide 30 to 60 megawatts per unit, with an all-in capex of 1,500 to 1,800 dollars per kilowatt, an 18 to 36 month lead time, a fast 10-minute ramp rate, 30 to 50 megawatts per acre of land use, and 35 to 40 percent efficiency. Industrial gas turbines offer 5 to 50 megawatts per unit, with a lower capex of 1,000 to 1,300 dollars per kilowatt and a 12 to 36 month lead time. Small combined-cycle gas turbines supply 40 to 100 megawatts per unit, requiring 1,800 to 2,500 dollars per kilowatt and 18 to 36 months of lead time, but achieving 40 to 55 percent efficiency. Medium-speed and high-speed reciprocating engines provide smaller capacities (7 to 20 megawatts and 3 to 5 megawatts, respectively) with lead times of 15 to 24 months and 5 to 10 minute ramp rates. Fuel cells represent a highly localized option at 0.325 megawatts per unit, carrying the highest capex at 3,000 to 4,000 dollars per kilowatt, but they offer baseload ramp rates and high efficiencies of 50 to 55 percent. Finally, H-Class combined-cycle gas turbines provide massive utility-scale capacities of 600 to 1,000 megawatts per unit, with 36 to 60 months of lead time, a capex of 2,200 to 2,800 dollars per kilowatt, and the highest efficiency range at 50 to 60 percent. 

The footnotes detail the specific corporate entities involved in these energy transitions. Mentioned data centers with current or proposed onsite power include xAI Colossus 1 and 2, OpenAI/Oracle Stargate, Microsoft Three Mile Island, Equinix, CoreWeave, and Meta Socrates South. While established giants like GE Vernova, Mitsubishi, and Siemens dominate the gas-fired power industry, the text highlights new entrants providing alternative equipment options, such as Doosan Enerbility, Wartsila, Boom Supersonic, and Caterpillar.

This analysis explores whether China is approaching an energy emissions plateau, noting conflicting signals in its industrial and forestry sectors. While Carbon Brief reported a 1.6 percent decline in China's coal-fired power generation in 2025—the country's first such decline since the 1970s—electricity accounts for only 55 percent of Chinese coal consumption. The rest is consumed for thermal heat, and China continues to construct new coal plants rapidly. This makes the overall trajectory of China's carbon dioxide emissions for 2025 uncertain. While a plateau seems possible, predicting its duration is difficult, especially given the expansion of China's coal-to-liquids facilities for producing synthetic natural gas. On the positive side, reforestation has turned China into the world's largest carbon remover from land-use change, reversing its status from fifty years ago when it was the second-largest land-use emitter. However, these land-use removals of 0.25 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide per year are minor compared to China's massive energy-related emissions of 12.3 gigatonnes per year.

The accompanying charts illustrate these dynamics in detail. The first chart, tracking fossil fuel useful final energy in exajoules from 1990 to 2025, shows China's consumption rising dramatically from around 10 exajoules in 1990 to roughly 75 exajoules by 2025. In contrast, consumption in the United States peaked and leveled off near 45 exajoules, while Europe's energy use steadily declined from 40 to just over 20 exajoules. 

The second chart, depicting global carbon dioxide equivalent emissions from energy, process emissions, methane, and flaring in billions of tons from 1990 to 2025, underscores China's dominance. China’s emissions escalated from under 4 billion tons in 1990 to approximately 12 billion tons by 2025, vastly exceeding emissions from the United States (around 5 billion tons), Total Europe (under 4 billion tons), and India (around 3 billion tons), while the Rest of the World collectively reached about 16 billion tons. 

The third chart, a China coal tracker indexed to the year 2000, shows that by 2024 both coal capacity and coal-fired electricity had indexed to over 500 percent of their 2000 levels, while coal thermal heat leveled off near 200 percent after 2010. Projections including coal capacity under construction and in pre-construction stages indicate that total capacity is poised to rise even further toward 2030. 

Finally, the fourth chart displays annual carbon dioxide emissions from land-use change in gigatonnes from 1960 to 2020. It highlights China's transition from a net emitter peaking near 1.0 gigatonne in the late 1980s to a net negative emitter (carbon sink) at roughly -0.25 gigatonnes by 2020. This trajectory contrasts sharply with countries like Brazil and Indonesia, which have remained major net emitters, with Brazil fluctuating between 1.0 and nearly 3.0 gigatonnes over the decades.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market explores the primary drivers of China’s massive renewable energy expansion, illustrating how the nation has scaled up its manufacturing, grid infrastructure, and domestic adoption to lead the global energy transition. 

The first chart tracks China’s energy storage capacity from 2016 to 2024. Historically dominated by pumped hydro, the capacity surged from under 30 GW in 2016 to nearly 150 GW in 2024, with the expansion after 2021 driven almost entirely by the rapid rollout of lithium-ion battery storage. This growth in storage capacity has directly contributed to the trend shown in the adjacent chart: a substantial decline in China's solar and wind curtailment rates since 2015. Solar curtailment plummeted from over 14% in 2015 to roughly 1% in 2021, before ticking up slightly to around 3% in 2024. Similarly, wind curtailment dropped from approximately 15% in 2015 to 3% in 2021, ending at around 5% in 2024.

Domestic adoption is further highlighted by a chart on heat pump sales in 2024, where China leads the world with approximately 37 GW of capacity sold, followed by the United States at roughly 31 GW, Europe at 24 GW, the rest of the world at 12 GW, and Japan at 8 GW. 

China’s industrial dominance is illustrated in the cumulative production of solar modules since 2010. By 2024, total cumulative global production approached 2,700 GW, with China accounting for roughly 75% of this output, cementing its role as the world's primary solar manufacturer.

The page also details the rapid electrification of transport in China, showing the electric vehicle share of vehicle sales from 2010 to 2024. EV sales shares for passenger cars began a steep upward trajectory around 2020, climbing to over 40% by 2024, while EV vans followed a similar rapid rise to reach over 30% of sales in 2024. 

In terms of offshore wind power, cumulative global installed capacity expanded exponentially between 2000 and 2022. While European nations like the United Kingdom, Germany, the Netherlands, and Denmark initially built up most of the capacity, China’s installations exploded after 2018. By 2022, China accounted for nearly half of the global offshore wind capacity, representing roughly 30 GW out of a total global capacity of approximately 65 GW. 

Finally, grid transmission infrastructure is illustrated in a bar chart of installed high-voltage direct current (HVDC) lines in gigawatts. China dramatically leads the world with 218 GW of HVDC lines, compared to 90 GW for the rest of the world, 53 GW for Europe, and just 15 GW for the United States, demonstrating China's unmatched capacity to transmit renewable energy across vast distances.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Annual Eye on the Market Energy Paper, titled "Exporting the transition," analyzes the global impact of China’s massive expansion in green technology manufacturing and exports, alongside the potential cybersecurity risks of importing these technologies. Michael Cembalest notes that Chinese firms have pledged between $225 billion and $250 billion to overseas green manufacturing projects, an amount surpassing the inflation-adjusted value of the post-WWII US Marshall Plan aid. The page contrasts the positive environmental impacts of cheap Chinese exports for global decarbonization with the severe competitive threats they present to foreign corporations. Additionally, it raises security warnings, citing the "Volt Typhoon" hacking group that infiltrated US critical infrastructure and referencing former FBI Director Chris Wray's warnings about Chinese hackers positioning themselves to disrupt US infrastructure.

Five charts illustrate these manufacturing, export, and investment dynamics. The first is a stacked bar chart titled "China overseas green project pledges," which tracks Chinese commitments from 2013 to 2025 in billions of US dollars. Pledges remained below $10 billion annually until 2022, when they jumped to over $30 billion, eventually peaking near $70 billion in 2024. This growth was driven primarily by massive investments in batteries, battery materials, and solar energy.

The second visual, a horizontal bar chart titled "China manufacturing capacity vs production, 2024," highlights China's substantial industrial overcapacity. In 2024, solar PV module production reached 587 GW against 1,045 GW of capacity; wind power nacelle production was 96 GW against 204 GW of capacity; battery cell production was 890 GWh against a massive 2,830 GWh of capacity; and electric car production was 12 million units against a capacity of 22 million units.

The bottom three line charts track China’s clean-tech exports by destination in billions of US dollars from 2015 to 2025. The chart for solar PV exports shows a massive surge to emerging markets, peaking near $50 billion in 2023 before dropping slightly, while exports to Europe peaked near $28 billion, and exports to the US remained near zero. The battery exports chart shows a sharp upward trajectory to Europe, reaching over $30 billion by 2024, and to the US, rising to about $20 billion. The EV exports chart demonstrates a rapid rise to emerging markets, reaching roughly $17 billion by 2024, followed by Europe, which peaked near $14 billion in 2023 before declining, while EV exports to the US remained negligible. 

Footnotes on the page provide additional political and source context, detailing the replacement of FBI Director Christopher Wray with Kash Patel, the defense of Wray by Senator Mike Rounds in late 2024, and citing data sources including the Net Zero Industrial Policy Lab, the International Energy Agency, and EMBER.

This page of J.P. Morgan's 16th Annual Eye on the Market Energy Paper, written by Michael Cembalest, focuses on the high environmental and human health costs of China's dominance in critical minerals and green energy supply chains. Cembalest argues that global advocates of renewable energy and electric vehicles often overlook the severe pollution linked to these supply chains. He notes that mining and processing have left severe environmental scars, including a four-mile toxic sludge lake in Northern China containing lead, cadmium, and thorium, and points to a 2012 statement from China’s cabinet acknowledging that excessive rare earth mining has led to landslides, clogged rivers, and major health crises. 

To support this argument, the page presents two scatter plots of Environmental Performance Index scores from Yale University, the CIA Factbook, and JPMAM. Both plots compare national performance scores on the vertical axis against per capita GDP in thousands of dollars on the horizontal axis, marking China in red. The first plot, showing China's environmental health score (a measure of how well nations protect their populations from environmental health risks), highlights China as a severe outlier. At its per capita GDP level of around twenty thousand dollars, China’s score sits near the bottom of the distribution at approximately 32. The second plot shows heavy metals exposure scores, which track the direct human health impacts of heavy metal pollution. China is again positioned near the bottom with a score of about 42, reflecting high exposure to toxic metallic elements and metalloids like mercury, lead, and arsenic.

The geographic footprint of this contamination is detailed in a map of cadmium cropland concentrations based on 2021 data from Sichuan University. The map shows that five provinces—Guangxi, Guizhou, Hubei, Henan, and Gansu—have soil cadmium levels well above the standard agriculture safety limit of 0.5 milligrams per kilogram. 

Finally, a table of Chinese crop heavy metal concentrations quantifies how this soil contamination affects food supplies. It compares cadmium and lead levels in rice and wheat against a safe standard limit of 0.20 milligrams per crop kilogram, bolding levels that exceed the limit. The data shows elevated lead levels in rice and wheat from Zhengzhou, Henan, at 0.53 and 0.99 milligrams per kilogram respectively. It also lists cadmium in Anhui rice at 0.21 milligrams per kilogram. The most extreme contamination is found in wheat from Balyin, Gansu, where two samples show cadmium levels of 0.61 and 0.75 milligrams per kilogram, and lead levels reaching 1.29 and an extremely high 9.96 milligrams per kilogram, nearly fifty times the standard safety limit.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s March 2026 Energy Paper examines China's extensive dominance over the supply chains for renewable energy technologies and critical minerals, detailing the geopolitical leverage this control provides. The author discusses how China has weaponized its dominant position through aggressive export controls, such as a temporary April 2025 cutoff of rare earth exports to the United States and subsequent October 2025 regulations. These regulations require licenses for any product containing more than 0.1% of Chinese rare earths by value or manufactured with equipment containing them, mimicking the reach of the United States' own "foreign direct product rule." Although China paused some of these controls in late October 2025 in exchange for a reduction in U.S. fentanyl tariffs and eased chip controls, it continues to issue only short-term, six-month licenses. The author notes that China's ongoing goals likely include further easing of U.S. chip restrictions and securing safeguards for Chinese foreign investments. As an alternative, a footnote highlights demonstration projects at Sandia Labs and the Department of Energy using supercritical carbon dioxide and mild acids to extract rare earth minerals from coal fly ash.

The page features four charts that quantify China’s supply-chain dominance. The first chart, showing China's share of manufacturing capacity by product, illustrates that the country controls roughly 95% of PV wafer manufacturing, 90% of permanent magnets, 85% of PV cells, 80% of batteries, 75% of PV polysilicon, and over 70% of PV modules. 

The second chart details the top producer's share of refined strategic mineral output. China produces nearly 100% of refined gallium and graphite, about 95% of manganese, 90% of rare earths, and more than 80% of magnesium and silicon. China also holds a majority share in refining molybdenum, cobalt, tellurium, antimony, germanium, indium, lithium, titanium, and vanadium. The single exception highlighted in this chart is Indonesia, which dominates refined nickel production with a share of nearly 40%.

The third chart illustrates the elemental composition of major global rare earth deposits. It reveals a key geological advantage for China: while deposits in the United States (Mountain Pass) and Russia (Revda) are dominated by light rare earths like Lanthanum and Cerium, China’s laterite and xenotime basins (such as Xunwu, Xinfeng, Longnan, and Southeast Guangdong) contain a much broader and more valuable mix of heavy rare earth elements, including Yttrium, Dysprosium, and Terbium.

The final chart tracks China's monthly rare earth exports to the United States from 2018 through late 2025, broken down by rare-earth metals, compounds, and magnets. Historically, monthly exports hovered between $20 million and $55 million. The chart vividly displays the dramatic impact of the April 2025 controls, when exports plunged to nearly zero, followed by a volatile and partial recovery in the latter half of the year as negotiated pauses took effect.

This page focuses on China’s emergence as the global leader in nuclear power development, detailing how state support, cost advantages, and technology acquisition have accelerated its nuclear sector. The author notes that China has thirty-two reactors under construction and plans to build six to eight new plants annually, putting it on track to surpass the United States in nuclear-generated electricity by 2030. Chinese nuclear projects benefit from being built in seven years or less at only fifteen to thirty-five percent of Western costs. While China successfully commercialized the world's first fourth-generation reactor—the gas-cooled Shidaowan-1 in Shandong province—the author emphasizes that much of its reactor fleet relies on US Westinghouse technology obtained through a 2008 transfer contract as well as alleged military-backed hacking of Westinghouse systems in 2010. This rapid buildout is further propelled by domestic subsidies, low-interest financing, and fast-tracked regulatory approvals.

Four charts illustrate these points. The first, a bar chart detailing new nuclear plants under development with estimated grid connection dates between 2025 and 2030, shows China leading the world with over thirty-five gigawatts of capacity, categorized as developing market capacity. This dramatically outpaces Russia, the next closest developer, which has around seven gigawatts, followed by smaller pipelines in India, Turkey, Egypt, the United Kingdom, Korea, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Iran, Slovakia, and Argentina. 

A second line chart tracks historical nuclear generation by country in terawatt-hours from 1965 to 2025. It shows the United States leading at roughly eight hundred terawatt-hours, while China’s generation has risen exponentially since 2010, approaching four hundred terawatt-hours and surpassing France, South Korea, Canada, Japan, and Germany, the latter of which has completely phased out its nuclear generation.

A scatter plot compares the capital cost and construction time of nuclear plants in US dollars per megawatt versus years of construction. It contrasts expensive, protracted Western projects with cheaper, faster non-Western ones. For example, the United Kingdom's Hinkley Point C and the United States' Vogtle 3 and 4 in Georgia cost between fifteen and eighteen million dollars per megawatt and took eleven to thirteen years to complete, while France’s Flamanville 3 and Finland’s Olkiluoto 3 took fifteen to eighteen years. Conversely, non-Western projects such as China’s Fang 4, Pakistan's Kanupp 3, and South Korea's Saeul 1 and 2 cost less than four million dollars per megawatt and were completed in under eight years. 

The final line chart compares China's wind and solar generation to its nuclear generation from 2005 to 2030. It reveals that despite the massive nuclear push, nuclear power will remain a fraction of wind and solar.
