Even assuming all thirty-seven gigawatts of nuclear capacity currently under construction are completed by 2030, nuclear generation is projected to reach approximately four hundred terawatt-hours, whereas wind and solar generation is on track to surpass eighteen hundred terawatt-hours.

This page argues that the energy transitions of small countries are often overemphasized in public discourse, despite having limited relevance for large nations. The author coins two terms to describe these nations: PUNIs, which are countries with high renewable shares that represent only a small portion of global power demand, and PIEs, or Parasitically Irrelevant Examples, which are small countries that boast high renewable shares but rely heavily on importing electricity from neighboring grids. 

The first chart, titled PUNI update, uses a dual-axis format to plot the number of countries against percentages to show that countries with high renewable shares make up a very small part of global demand. Point A on the chart shows that while 76 countries have renewable energy shares over 50%, they represent only 14% of global electricity generation. Point B narrows this focus, showing that countries with renewable shares above 75% represent a mere 5% of global generation. An adjacent stacked bar chart, titled PUNI countries get 75% of power from hydro, shows that out of nearly 1,300 TWh of power generated by these high-renewable nations, the vast majority—roughly 1,000 TWh—comes from hydropower, with only minor contributions from solar, wind, and geothermal or biomass sources. This indicates that their energy models rely on geographic advantages that other countries cannot easily replicate.

Below these charts, two tables contrast the import reliance of small renewable nations against the world’s largest electricity producers. The table on the left, titled The PIEs: Parasitically Irrelevant Examples, lists countries with over 50% renewable power and more than 25% import reliance in 2024. Notable examples include Denmark, which has an 83% renewable share but relies on imports for 77% of its electricity consumption, and Luxembourg, which has an 87% renewable share alongside a 105% import reliance. Other highly import-dependent nations listed include Montenegro at 199% import reliance, Estonia at 86%, and Lithuania at 83%. 

The table on the right displays the fifteen largest electricity-generating countries, demonstrating that large power grids cannot rely on the grids of neighboring nations. The world's top generators have minimal import and export reliance, averaging just 1% to 2%. For instance, China generates 10,341 TWh of electricity with 0% imports and exports, the United States generates 4,486 TWh with 1% imports and 0% exports, and India generates 1,821 TWh with 0% imports and 1% exports. Germany is the only significant outlier among the large nations, generating 481 TWh while maintaining a 17% import share and a 12% export share. The author concludes that while the green achievements of PUNIs and PIEs are noteworthy, larger nations must find independent, scalable solutions since they cannot rely on neighbors to balance their electricity grids.

This page from the publication explores the growth trajectory of renewable energy and whether the global transition is reaching a tipping point. The author poses the question of how quickly the renewable share of useful final energy might rise over the next decade. On the top left, a chart detailing Europe’s annual year-on-year growth from 1990 to 2025 reveals that renewable energy growth has consistently and significantly outpaced growth in useful final energy. Consequently, the adjacent top-right chart projects that if the average growth rates from 2020 to 2024 continue, Europe’s renewable share of useful final energy will double from 20% in 2025 to 40% by 2035. Under the same assumptions, China is projected to reach a 30% share, the United States 20%, and Asia excluding Japan and China around 14% by 2035.

The text questions whether the world is at a tipping point for a faster transition, noting that over 90% of global power capacity additions in 2024 and 2025 have been renewable. However, the author cautions that rapid energy transitions historically require drastic improvements in cost, time, and energy. For instance, the 20-year transition in steel production during the 1970s was catalyzed by basic oxygen and electric arc furnaces, which cut production times to less than a tenth of open-hearth furnaces and yielded 80% to 90% energy savings. Because current green technologies lack these massive, natural cost and time savings, the transition relies heavily on trillions of dollars in subsidies, especially since the global emissions-weighted carbon price stands at a low $19 per tonne.

Two bottom charts illustrate these dynamics. The bottom-left chart highlights China's massive industrial overcapacity in 2024, comparing production to capacity across four sectors: solar PV modules (587 GW produced versus 1,045 GW capacity), wind power nacelles (96 GW produced versus 204 GW capacity), battery cells (890 GWh produced versus 2,830 GWh capacity), and electric cars (12 million units produced versus 22 million units capacity). This excess capacity allows China to export transition technology worldwide. Finally, the bottom-right chart tracks the annual power capacity expansion from 2004 to 2024, showing that the renewable share of new electricity generating capacity has soared from roughly 20% in 2004 to over 90% in 2024, with renewable additions in 2024 exceeding 500 GW while non-renewable additions remained minimal.

This page of the report, titled "Heliocentrism update: solar adoption continues to rise, courtesy of unprofitable Chinese solar companies," highlights the rapid global growth of solar energy, driven primarily by ultra-cheap Chinese supply chains. It contrasts international solar capital costs, breaks down pre-subsidy module production costs, tracks the crash of polysilicon prices, and details the growing trend of pairing utility-scale solar with battery storage in the United States.

A chart tracking global solar capacity from 2011 to 2027 shows an exponential climb, rising from near-zero levels to a forecasted total of approximately 4,500 gigawatts by 2027. Concurrently, a second chart displays solar shares of global electricity and final energy consumption. By 2027, the solar share of electricity generation is projected to reach nearly 15 percent, while its share of useful final energy consumption rises to about 6 percent. 

The report underscores steep regional disparities in solar capital costs. A chart tracking residential solar capital costs from 2009 to 2025 reveals that while costs have plummeted globally, the United States remains the most expensive market, hovering near four dollars per watt in 2025. This is significantly higher than Germany, Australia, and the United Kingdom, and vastly higher than the baseline cost of a Chinese standard module, which sits at less than one dollar per watt. Another chart details estimated pre-subsidy costs for solar modules at the end of 2025, illustrating that domestic US production is the most expensive at nearly 50 cents per watt. In contrast, global free-trade markets utilizing China-integrated module costs sit under 15 cents per watt. These cheap module costs are underpinned by a dramatic drop in solar-grade polysilicon prices, which peaked at nearly 40 dollars per kilogram in late 2022 before collapsing to under ten dollars per kilogram by 2024 and remaining depressed through early 2026.

Lastly, the final chart illustrates how US utility-scale photovoltaic capacity is increasingly paired with battery storage. Comparing 2019 to 2025, the share of cumulative solar capacity paired with a battery surged dramatically in western regions. In California, this share jumped from roughly 8 percent in 2019 to nearly 38 percent in 2025, with the Southwest seeing a similar rise to about 36 percent. Other regions like Texas, MISO, and PJM experienced much more modest growth in battery pairing over the same period.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market Energy Paper analyzes the global solar power industry, focusing on the impacts of massive Chinese manufacturing overcapacity, the collapse of profitability among solar hardware manufacturers, and the structural dependencies of the United States solar supply chain. The main argument is that while Chinese overcapacity ensures the continuation of the global solar installation surge, the current economic model is unsustainable for most manufacturers, which may prompt the Chinese government to enact capacity controls. 

The first chart, titled Global solar manufacturing capacity vs installations, compares historical and projected capacity in gigawatts from 2015 to 2030 against actual global installations. The data shows that global manufacturing capacity, overwhelmingly dominated by China, is set to approach 1,600 gigawatts by 2030, whereas actual global installations in 2024 lagged far behind at roughly 600 gigawatts, illustrating a massive supply-demand gap. 

This extreme overcapacity is shown to have devastated corporate profitability in the second chart, Net profit margin of select listed solar companies. Based on trailing twelve-month data from the third quarter of 2025, almost every major Chinese solar company is operating in the red. Daqo faces the worst losses with profit margins approaching negative 50 percent, while other major players like Jinko, Longi, Tongwei, and Trina are also deeply unprofitable. The only profitable entities in this select group are First Solar, which boasts a positive net profit margin of approximately 25 percent, followed by DMEGC, CSI Solar, and Canadian Solar. 

The distress in the Chinese solar sector is also reflected in the third chart, China CSI photovoltaic stock index, which tracks the index from 2013 to early 2026. The index peaked above 5,000 in late 2021 before experiencing a sharp downward trend. However, a notable rebound occurred in October 2025, bringing the index back up toward 3,000 amid market discussions that Chinese authorities might intervene with capacity controls to rescue the struggling industry.

The final two charts shift focus to the United States. The chart titled United States net solar capacity additions by type shows that total additions peaked in 2024 at nearly 50 gigawatts, with utility-scale solar accounting for the vast majority. In 2025, utility-scale additions dipped slightly to 35 gigawatts. Despite these substantial domestic installations, the final chart, US solar manufacturing capacity, reveals severe structural imbalances across the domestic supply chain. While operational capacity for finished modules (around 45 gigawatts) and raw polysilicon (over 30 gigawatts) exceeds the 2025 solar PV demand forecast of approximately 43 gigawatts, the US possesses zero operational capacity for critical intermediate components like ingots, wafers, and cells. Consequently, the US remains heavily dependent on cell imports manufactured at Chinese-owned factories located in Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand, and Cambodia to sustain its domestic module assembly and deployment goals.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Energy Paper analyzes the structural, political, and economic drivers of residential electricity prices across US states and global countries. The author argues that power prices are heavily influenced by five key factors: state-level utility regulation, the share of low-marginal-cost generation sources like nuclear and hydro, per capita wealth, political orientation, and the cost of doing business. 

The first chart, comparing percent changes in residential electricity prices since 2020, shows that deregulated US states have experienced much sharper price increases than regulated states, with deregulated prices climbing by over 35% by late 2025 compared to a more modest 25% increase in regulated states. The second chart focuses on the energy mix across 211 countries, demonstrating a clear downward trend in residential prices as the combined share of hydro, nuclear, and geothermal generation increases. 

Economic and political factors are detailed in the remaining three scatter plots. One chart illustrates that higher wealth—measured by per capita GDP in US dollars or Euros—correlates with higher residential power prices for both US states and European countries. Another chart uses the Cook Partisan Voting Index to show that more Democratic-leaning states face higher power prices than more Republican-leaning ones, with prices trending downward from around 30 cents per kilowatt-hour in highly Democratic areas to under 15 cents in strongly Republican areas. Finally, the page addresses business friendliness and tax policy, plotting electricity rates against a combined ranking of tax competitiveness and the cost of doing business. This chart reveals that states ranked as the most expensive and least competitive to operate in—specifically California, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York, and New Jersey—also pay the highest residential electricity rates, ranging between 24 and 32 cents per kilowatt-hour, while other states like Michigan are highlighted closer to the middle of the spectrum.

This page of the energy paper discusses how distributed rooftop solar power is keeping pace with utility-scale applications, while also evaluating the technological advancements and hurdles of high-efficiency perovskite-silicon solar cells. 

The first chart, titled Global solar capacity by type, tracks capacity in gigawatts from 2014 to 2025. It shows an exponential rise in total capacity toward 3,000 gigawatts, with distributed solar PV consistently matching the growth trajectory of utility-scale solar PV.

The second chart displays the 2025 solar capacity by the top ten solar capacity countries in gigawatts, indicating the percentage share of distributed solar PV for each. China dwarfs other nations with capacity plotted on a separate scale up to 1,400 gigawatts and a 42 percent distributed share. For the other nine countries plotted on a scale up to 300 gigawatts, the distributed solar shares are 29 percent for the United States, 21 percent for India, 59 percent for Japan, 66 percent for Germany, 63 percent for Brazil, 23 percent for Spain, 62 percent for Australia, 72 percent for Italy, and 14 percent for Korea.

The third chart, showcasing global investment in solar projects in billions of US dollars, tracks half-year intervals from the first half of 2020 through the first half of 2025. Total half-yearly investment has climbed from around 100 billion dollars to approximately 250 billion dollars, with small-scale solar investment expanding significantly alongside utility-scale solar, while solar thermal remains a minimal sliver of total spending.

The fourth chart illustrates best-in-class solar research-cell efficiency from 2000 to 2025. Perovskite-silicon tandem cells have seen a dramatic rise in efficiency, reaching approximately 34 percent to 35 percent by 2025. This compares favorably to silicon heterostructures, which have steadily improved to around 27 percent efficiency, and older multi-crystalline cells that plateaued near 23 percent around 2021. 

Despite the high efficiency of perovskite-silicon cells, the author highlights a significant commercialization hurdle: durability. Perovskite cells degrade rapidly due to photo-bleaching, heat, and humidity, falling to 80 percent of their starting efficiency in less than a year. By contrast, traditional silicon cells maintain their efficiency for an industry-standard lifespan of about 20 years. This short lifespan creates high replacement costs, preventing widespread commercial adoption. Finally, a concluding note distinguishes cell efficiency from capacity factors, citing data from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory indicating median capacity factors for tracking panels of 23 percent in third-quartile irradiance locations and 29 percent in top-quartile locations.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication "Eye on the Market" by Michael Cembalest evaluates whether utility-scale solar combined with battery storage is truly cost-competitive with natural gas in the United States. The discussion focuses on a report by the organization EMBER, which claims that a solar-plus-storage configuration can meet a constant 1 GW hourly load in sunny locations like Las Vegas for 97% of the year. EMBER asserts that this system, consisting of 6 GW of solar capacity and 17 GWh of battery storage, would cost $104 per megawatt-hour, a price only 38% higher than a natural gas system. While EMBER describes this premium as affordable and cost-effective, the author notes that achieving this would represent a massive paradigm shift, given that high-solar areas like Hawaii currently get only 20% to 30% of their power from solar. 

To evaluate these claims, the author presents a comprehensive table outlining the detailed assumptions for a Las Vegas utility-scale grid configuration analysis. The parameters are color-coded to denote their sources, which include EMBER, NREL, Lazard, EIA, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management, using a system-wide discount rate of 7.7%. 

For the solar component, the model assumes a 20-year useful life, a DC-to-AC ratio of 1.35, and capital costs of $436 per kilowatt. Operating costs are set at $12.50 per kilowatt-year, with a solar degradation rate of 0.50% per year and grid connection costs of $76.00 per kilowatt of solar. The solar generation profile assumes single-axis bifacial panels with backtracking, system losses of 10.06%, and inverter DC-to-AC losses of 2.00% over a 20-year useful life. 

The battery storage assumptions include a capital cost of $165 per kilowatt-hour, operating costs of $5.51 per kilowatt-year, a 20-year useful life, and an annual degradation rate of 2.60%. Although the round-trip efficiency is noted as 100% because EMBER embeds losses elsewhere, the model applies a peak and minimum buffer size of 5% and DC-to-DC conversion losses of 1.80%. 

For the natural gas alternative, the capital cost is modeled at $1,400 per kilowatt with a 40-year useful life. Fixed operating costs are $13.73 per kilowatt-year, and variable costs are $0.0021 per kilowatt-hour. The fuel cost is assumed to be $3.50 per million British thermal units (mmbtu) with a heat rate of 6,370 btu per kilowatt-hour. J.P. Morgan notes some methodological differences from EMBER, such as sourcing local solar data from NREL’s PVWATTS database rather than a European Commission database, and deriving gas capital costs from Lazard's updated 2025 figures. 

The page concludes with a critical commentary on why mainstream media outlets accept clean energy claims uncritically. The author cites a January 2026 study by Nick Deiuliis analyzing the Wall Street Journal’s 70-person energy reporting pool. The study revealed that none of the reporters had degrees in core STEM fields like chemical, electrical, petroleum, or mechanical engineering, physics, or chemistry, with the only exceptions being two reporters with degrees in computer science. Furthermore, not a single reporter in the pool had ever worked in the oil, power, pipeline, auto manufacturing, solar, battery, or aviation sectors.

This page analyzes the accelerating growth and real-world deployment of Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) in North America, while noting that the rising energy demand from data centers may stall the retirement of traditional peaker plants. 

The author begins by highlighting VPP market growth with data from Wood Mackenzie. A comparison of 2024 and 2025 figures shows active company deployments rising 33% (from 1,459 to 1,940), monetized programs increasing 35% (from 321 to 433), unique offtakers growing 38% (from 139 to 192), and total VPP capacity expanding 14% (from 33 GW to 37.5 GW). The US Department of Energy projects that scaling VPP capacity to 80–160 GW could handle 10% to 20% of peak loads, saving $10 billion in annual grid costs.

To illustrate VPPs in action, the page details a July 29, 2025, test event in California where the state's Demand Side Grid Support and Emergency Load Reduction programs mobilized approximately 100,000 residential batteries. This test produced 535 MW of dispatchable power between 7:00 PM and 9:00 PM, lowering the California Independent System Operator's (CAISO) system peak net load by 1.7%. Two accompanying charts from the Brattle Group illustrate this event. The first chart, showing system net load in MW against hours of the day (18 to 24), illustrates a clear gap between the base CAISO net load and the reduced net load resulting from the VPP contribution. The second chart tracks battery charge and discharge in MW from 24 hours before the event to 24 hours after. It contrasts the typical battery operations on July 28th—which show standard charging behavior—with a dramatic, sharp discharge spike on the evening of July 29th during the 7:00 PM to 9:00 PM test window.

Other real-world examples are cited, including the VPP aggregator Leap, which dispatched 546 MWh across New York, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island during a June 2025 heatwave using 12,125 distributed energy resources like commercial batteries, industrial HVAC, and EV chargers. Additionally, on June 24, Tesla's California VPP utilized thousands of Powerwall batteries to deliver 345 MW to the grid for two hours during evening peak hours.

The author concludes with a forward-looking cautionary note regarding the ultimate goal of VPPs, which is to phase out fossil-fuel peaker plants. Although VPPs should theoretically reduce peaker plant utilization, surging energy demand from artificial intelligence and data centers is complicating this transition. For instance, NRG Energy reversed plans to retire a profitable peaker plant in Chicago due to data center demand, and the PJM interconnection has reportedly postponed or canceled retirement plans for 60% of its oil, gas, and coal plants—many of which operate as peakers.

This page presents a comprehensive collection of climate charts that document rising carbon dioxide levels, climbing temperatures, ocean warming, ice sheet loss, vegetation changes in Antarctica, and accelerating ocean acidification. To introduce these trends, the author shares a personal observation of a saltwater lagoon in the southern Mexican Yucatan that he first visited in 1991; once teeming with vibrant marine life such as fish, crabs, sea urchins, and coral, it is now nearly barren. 

The first chart on the page tracks atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations alongside global temperature anomalies from 1750 to 2020. The left axis, measuring carbon dioxide in parts per million, shows concentrations rising sharply from a historical baseline near 275 parts per million to over 400 parts per million by 2020. Simultaneously, the right axis, tracking temperature anomalies in degrees Celsius relative to the 1901–2000 average, reveals a closely correlated spike that pushes anomalies past 1.0 degree Celsius in the 21st century.

The second chart focuses on ocean heat content and sea levels from 1955 to 2025. Ocean heat content, measured on the left axis in Zettajoules relative to a 1957 baseline, has surged to over 350 Zettajoules. This corresponds with rising sea levels, plotted on the right axis in millimeters against a 1993 baseline, which have climbed to approximately 100 millimeters. The author notes that this increasing ocean heat content directly contributes to sea level rise, marine heat waves, fishery collapses, dead zones, and widespread coral bleaching.

The third chart illustrates the shrinking mass of the Greenland and Antarctica ice sheets from 2002 to 2026. Measured in gigatonnes of mass variation on a descending scale from zero, Greenland shows a steady decline, losing approximately 5,000 gigatonnes by 2026. Antarctica follows a similar downward trend, losing around 2,500 gigatonnes over the same period. 

The fourth chart illustrates the greening of Antarctica, measuring square kilometers of green vegetation cover in March of each year below 300 meters above sea level from 1986 to 2020. The chart reveals a dramatic increase in vegetation cover over the last decade, peaking near 11 square kilometers. A historical note cautions that the last time Antarctica was covered with foliage and supported reptilian life, the rest of the planet was not conducive to supporting mammalian life.

The lower left of the page explains that ocean acidification occurs as the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide, lowering the water's pH and destroying the building blocks of marine life. This is supported by a chart detailing Hawaii ocean acidification from 1988 to 2024. The mean seawater pH level, shown on both a monthly and annual average, has steadily declined from around 8.12 in 1988 to approximately 8.04 by 2024, signaling a continuous increase in acidity.

The final chart measures the greenhouse effect through radiative forcing by greenhouse gases from 1979 to 2023, measured in watts per square meter. Total radiative forcing has increased from under 1.5 watts per square meter in 1979 to nearly 3.5 watts per square meter by 2023. The stacked area chart indicates that carbon dioxide is the dominant contributor to this forcing, followed by methane, nitrous oxide, chlorofluorocarbons, hydrochlorofluorocarbons, and hydrofluorocarbons. An explanatory note defines radiative forcing as the degree to which greenhouse gases trap solar radiation inside the Earth's atmosphere, warming the planet.

This page analyzes the operational, geopolitical, and economic characteristics of Bloom Energy’s solid oxide fuel cells, accompanied by a performance comparison of turbine and fuel cell manufacturers. 

The author outlines several critical technical and supply chain challenges for Bloom Energy. First, while Bloom’s fuel cells offer a higher carbon dioxide concentration that makes carbon capture and storage (CCS) more cost-effective than capturing gas plant flue gas, the minimum practical scale for CCS projects is 300 megawatts, meaning smaller installations will likely never capture their emissions. Furthermore, the technology is not entirely carbon-neutral, as carbon monoxide is burned and its carbon dioxide is vented. The report highlights Crusoe’s data center in Wyoming as an attempt to leverage the nearby Tallgrass sequestration hub for long-term carbon capture. Geopolitically, Bloom is highly dependent on China, which supplies 70 percent of the rare earth metals used in its components. Operationally, Bloom’s fuel cell stacks have a lifespan of roughly five years, with stack replacement representing about 65 percent of anticipated service costs, and the low-pressure steam produced as waste heat is insufficient for further electricity generation. Finally, while Bloom claims its cells can operate in a "load-following" mode without external storage systems, it has not publicly disclosed figures regarding how this thermal cycling affects performance or stack durability.

To contextualize these findings within the broader energy sector, the page includes a table showing the cumulative total returns of gas turbine and solid oxide fuel cell manufacturers from January 2022 through late February 2026, comparing each against a regional benchmark index. Bloom Energy, the sole solid oxide fuel cell player, posted a cumulative return of 697 percent, far outpacing the Russell 2000’s return of 26 percent. This strong performance aligns with stellar gains across traditional combined-cycle turbine manufacturers: GE Vernova returned 570 percent since its March 2024 listing (compared to 36 percent for the S&P 500), Siemens Energy grew 657 percent (compared to 58 percent for the DAX), and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries posted an exceptional return of 1,818 percent (compared to 120 percent for the Nikkei 225). Other major engine and turbine manufacturers also outpaced their benchmarks, including Caterpillar with a 300 percent return (versus S&P 500's 55 percent), Doosan with a 408 percent return (versus MSCI Korea's 146 percent), Rolls Royce with a 980 percent return (versus MSCI UK's loss of 41 percent), and Wartsila with a 237 percent return (versus Stoxx 600's 49 percent).

This page from the J.P. Morgan Energy Paper focuses on the global role of geothermal energy, arguing that it is a comparatively small low-carbon source whose primary real-world utility is heat rather than electricity generation. The author notes that geothermal is often lumped into catch-all categories in energy databases because of its minor scale. 

A bar chart titled "Shares of global useful final energy" compares geothermal to other low-carbon resources, showing geothermal at slightly over one percent, lagging behind hydropower at nearly five percent, nuclear at around three percent, and both wind and solar. The geothermal share is color-coded to show that the vast majority of its useful final energy is consumed as heat rather than electricity.

A second bar chart, "Geothermal energy use by country" in petajoules, reveals that China, the United States, and Turkey account for about 65 percent of global geothermal energy production. China is by far the largest user, approaching 600 petajoules, driven overwhelmingly by geothermal heat pumps and district heating. The United States is the second-largest user at around 200 petajoules, split between heat pumps and electricity generation, followed by Turkey at around 120 petajoules. Other featured nations include Sweden, Indonesia, Iceland, Japan, New Zealand, Germany, the Philippines, France, Canada, and Norway.

The preference for heating over power is reinforced by a pie chart titled "Global geothermal energy use by type," which shows that approximately 80 percent of geothermal energy is dedicated to thermal applications—such as heat pumps, district heating, and direct commercial or residential heating—while electricity generation makes up only a minor slice. The accompanying text explains that conventional geothermal electricity production requires high-temperature gradients found only at tectonic hotspots like Iceland, Indonesia, and Nevada. Outside of these hotspots, the most practical, low-risk, and cost-effective applications are ground-source heat pumps operating at depths of 50 to 200 meters to supply ambient building climate control or low-temperature industrial heat.

Finally, a line chart comparing global wind, solar, and geothermal electricity generation in terawatt-hours from 1990 to 2025 highlights the stark difference in growth trajectories. While wind and solar have grown exponentially over the last two decades, reaching approximately 2,400 and 2,100 terawatt-hours respectively by 2025, geothermal electricity generation has remained virtually flat and extremely low, barely registering above the zero line.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s energy paper explores the mechanics and economic questions surrounding Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) and unconventional geothermal developments. The text details how thermal recovery factors, which are typically well below 100 percent in real-world applications, measure the efficiency of recovering heat from a geothermal operating zone. Factors such as uninitiated fractures, disconnected pathways, and rapid heat depletion limit recovery efficiency. The author highlights Fervo Energy, which uses cased and cemented wellbores to mitigate these inefficiencies; however, due to Rankine cycle thermodynamic limits, the projected thermal-to-electric conversion efficiency for Fervo's Project Cape remains at just 19 percent. Ultimately, the author raises the critical open question of cost, suggesting that the industry will have a clearer understanding of the economic feasibility of unconventional EGS within two to three years.

To illustrate these concepts, the page displays two comprehensive technical diagrams sourced from a 2024 study by Khodayar and Bjornsson in the Open Journal of Geology. The left diagram, titled "Unconventional Geothermal Developments: Enhanced Geothermal System or Engineered Geothermal System (EGS) in Hot Dry Rock," maps various fracking-based designs against depth and temperature scales down to seven kilometers. It displays specific configurations from Eden Geothermal, which utilizes single-well and closed-loop hybrid systems down to five kilometers at temperatures between 85 and 200 degrees Celsius; Geo-Energie Suisse, which employs multistage reservoir fracking; Sage Geosystems, showing its hybrid "HeatRoot" and "HeatCycle" systems operating at three to six kilometers and temperatures between 100 and 250 degrees Celsius; and Fervo Energy, which uses multistage reservoir fracking with long horizontal fractures and monitoring wells down to 3.4 kilometers. 

The right diagram, titled "Unconventional Geothermal Developments: Deep Closed-Loops: Advanced Closed-Loops (ACL) / Advanced Geothermal System (AGS)," showcases closed-loop well designs that do not rely on fracking to create pathways. This panel details Greenfire's GreenLoop, which utilizes a tube-in-tube borehole heat exchanger going down to six kilometers at temperatures between 70 and 250 degrees Celsius. It also illustrates Eavor Loops, showing a sedimentary formation design (Eavor Loop 1) reaching down to 4.5 kilometers at 270 degrees Celsius, and an igneous rock design (Eavor Loop 2) reaching down to 6.8 kilometers at 408 degrees Celsius. Finally, the diagram outlines Chevron and Mitsui ACL's closed-loop heat exchangers deployed in hot dry layers. Both diagrams visually emphasize how these unconventional designs dramatically increase the surface-area-to-volume ratio of geothermal wells compared to conventional vertical wells.

This page of the report examines the levelized costs and temperature requirements of geothermal energy applications, evaluating both direct heat uses and electricity generation. The author argues that because geothermal remains a relatively undeveloped resource, its real-world costs are highly variable and uncertain. 

A horizontal bar chart, sourced from the IEA in December 2024, maps the temperature requirements in degrees Celsius for different applications. Direct heat uses range from low-temperature geothermal heat pumps requiring under 50°C, up to wood, paper, and metal surface processing that require temperatures between 100°C and 200°C. Electrical power generation requires much higher temperatures, with binary plants requiring 100°C to 250°C and flash or dry steam plants requiring 220°C to over 400°C. 

To evaluate geothermal heat competitiveness, a table presents levelized cost of closed-loop geothermal heat (LCOH) in dollars per MMBtu from various sources. Estimates from Cornell (2021) at $9.30, Stanford (2022) at $15.62, NREL (2023) ranging from $3.7 to $17.5, and the Energy Journal (2025) ranging from $5.8 to $7.0 are compared to wholesale natural gas costs. The comparison shows that while geothermal is generally uncompetitive with low US wholesale natural gas heat costs of $2 to $4 per MMBtu, it can be highly competitive with European wholesale natural gas heat costs of $9 to $12 per MMBtu depending on the location.

For power generation, which typically converts thermal heat to electricity at a low efficiency rate of 10% to 20%, a bar chart displays the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) in US dollars per MWh from 2021 to 2024. The data, sourced from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (formerly NREL), shows that conventional hydrothermal flash and binary LCOEs remained steady, with 2024 costs sitting at roughly $70 and $103 per MWh respectively. Meanwhile, Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) saw massive cost declines in 2024; near-field EGS binary plummeted from around $400/MWh in preceding years to just over $100/MWh, while deep EGS binary fell from over $400/MWh to around $150-$180/MWh. 

A sidebar defines hydrothermal flash as extracting hot water and flashing it to steam to spin a turbine, and hydrothermal binary as using hot geothermal water to heat a secondary, low-boiling-point working fluid like isobutane or pentane to drive a turbine. While geothermal power costs are higher than the LCOE of wind at $62/MWh and solar at $58/MWh, the author notes that geothermal offers valuable baseload power, highlighted by an 88% capacity factor in 2024. Ultimately, the author advises treating these geothermal cost estimates with caution due to the scarcity of real-world utility-scale applications.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Energy Paper focuses on greenhouse gas and methane emissions footprints, presenting findings from MethaneSAT and research on liquefied natural gas supply chains. The text explains that prior to losing contact due to a power failure, MethaneSAT gathered critical data showing that greenhouse gas emissions from major oil and gas basins generally exceed inventories like EDGAR and the EPA by approximately 50 percent. While methane intensity is typically higher in oil basins, gas basins recorded emissions three times higher than reported levels, and none fell below the 0.2 percent target agreed to under the United Nations Oil and Gas Decarbonization Charter.

The first chart on the page shows gas-normalized methane intensity compared to this 0.2 percent UN target, plotting emissions divided by marketed gas production across dozens of global basins from May 2024 to June 2025. Basins like Widyan in Iraq, Zagros Foldbelt in Iran and Iraq, and Russia's Central Sub-Basin East exceed 10 percent intensity, while major United States basins like the San Joaquin, Powder River, Permian, Haynesville, and Appalachian range from roughly 0.5 percent to 5 percent intensity. Crucially, every single tracked basin sits well above the 0.2 percent target line at the bottom of the chart.

The second chart compares MethaneSAT total emissions with reported emissions in tonnes of greenhouse gases per hour across US basins. The data highlights a stark discrepancy: in the Permian basin, MethaneSAT observed emissions of roughly 420 tonnes per hour, compared to reported emissions of only about 80 tonnes per hour. Significant gaps also exist in the Eagle Ford, Haynesville, and Appalachian basins, where measured emissions hover around 100 to 120 tonnes per hour, while reported figures remain near 30 to 40 tonnes per hour.

The discussion then turns to LNG supply chains, noting that the United States has become the global leader in LNG exports. This trend is illustrated in a chart tracking select countries' LNG exports from 2017 to 2025 in billion cubic feet per day. The US line rises steeply over the period, peaking above 14 billion cubic feet per day in 2025, surpassing Australia and Qatar, which both sit between 10 and 11 billion cubic feet per day, as well as Russia and Malaysia, which remain below 5 billion cubic feet per day.

Aerial LIDAR surveys conducted over three years by scientists at the University of Texas at Austin revealed that actual LNG supply chain greenhouse gas measurements were 20 percent to 40 percent higher than activity-based inventory assessments provided by operators. The final chart on the page displays the life cycle greenhouse gas emissions of three specific supply chains—Marcellus-SPL, Haynesville-SPL, and Permian-CCL—in grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule. For each supply chain, side-by-side stacked bar charts compare measured emissions to operator estimates across six stages: liquefaction, storage, transmission, processing, gathering/boosting, and production. In all three cases, measured emissions are higher than operator estimates, with Permian-CCL showing the highest measured emissions at over 18 grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule compared to an operator estimate of about 14 grams, with the largest discrepancies concentrated in the production and gathering/boosting stages.

This page features an analysis by Michael Cembalest evaluating the economics of local gasoline versus electricity options for his plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV), a Jeep Wrangler 4xe. The author explains that the vehicle features a 17 kWh battery that provides a 22-mile electric-only range, translating to 1.29 miles per kWh, and gets 20 miles per gallon of gasoline once the battery is depleted. He argues that whether charging is cheaper than gasoline depends heavily on the specific utility plan selected and how diligently the vehicle is charged overnight. 

A central table titled "Jeep charging options on Long Island (PSEG)" breaks down three hypothetical charging scenarios under PSEG Long Island’s rate structures, which include a flat daily charge of 56 cents. The first scenario, the Standard Plan, features a peak rate of 47.5 cents per kWh between 3:00 PM and 7:00 PM and an off-peak rate of 21.5 cents per kWh between 7:00 PM and 3:00 PM. This scenario assumes the driver charges 90% of the time during off-peak hours and 10% during peak hours. The Optional Plan, designed to incentivize overnight charging, features a super off-peak rate of 13.3 cents per kWh from 10:00 PM to 6:00 AM, an off-peak rate of 24.0 cents per kWh during day and evening shoulder hours, and a peak rate of 50.0 cents per kWh between 3:00 PM and 7:00 PM. This plan is analyzed under Scenario 1, where the driver is only mildly focused on off-peak benefits (charging 50% super off-peak, 40% off-peak, and 10% peak), and Scenario 2, which maximizes economic benefit by conducting 100% of charging during super off-peak hours. 

To the right of the table, a photograph shows a person standing in the open back of a black Jeep Wrangler parked on a gravel beach next to a body of water, with a kayak loaded inside and a fishing rod set up nearby. The caption reads, "Getting ready to hunt for striped bass on Peconic Bay in early May." 

Footnotes on the page provide additional context. One detail highlights the extensive recall history of the Wrangler 4xe, including issues with motor power loss, coolant leaks, and high-voltage battery defects that carry fire risks. Another footnote outlines the plug-in hybrid share of the overall EV fleet in major global markets, noting shares of 51% in Japan, 47% in Italy, 40% in Germany, 35% in France, 34% in the UK, 28% in China and Canada, 24% in the US, 17% in Australia, and 10% in South Korea.

This page from the annual energy paper addresses the economics of plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV) charging compared to using gasoline, focusing primarily on the impact of Long Island's high utility rates. The author argues that unless a driver utilizes an optional time-of-use plan and charges exclusively during overnight off-peak hours, gasoline is often more economical than electricity. To illustrate how regional rates affect this trade-off, the text mentions energy consultant Paul Martin in Ontario, where extremely low overnight electricity rates of approximately 4 cents per kilowatt-hour combined with higher gasoline costs of $3.45 per gallon yield a substantial $13.82 charging benefit for a Jeep Wrangler over 100 miles of driving. This is compared to a maximum benefit of only $4.07 under Long Island’s local utility, PSEG, under its Optional Plan Scenario 2.

The analysis features four detailed tables comparing the costs of gas versus electricity over 100 miles of driving across three pricing tiers: the Standard Plan, Optional Plan Scenario 1, and Optional Plan Scenario 2. 

The first table examines a Jeep Wrangler 4xe, which has a gas efficiency of 20 miles per gallon and an electric efficiency of 1.29 miles per kilowatt-hour. For this vehicle, gas costs are a constant $15.50. Under the Standard Plan, the EV cost is $20.68, resulting in a net loss of $5.18 compared to gas. Under Scenario 1, the EV cost is $18.25, a loss of $2.75. Only Scenario 2 shows a positive return, with an EV cost of $11.43, saving the driver $4.07.

The second table looks at a Lexus NX 450h+, which achieves a superior 36 miles per gallon on gas and 2.06 miles per kilowatt-hour on electricity. Because of its excellent gas mileage, the gas cost is low at $8.61. Consequently, EV charging is less attractive here, with a Standard Plan EV cost of $13.02 (a loss of $4.41), a Scenario 1 cost of $11.49 (a loss of $2.88), and a Scenario 2 cost of $7.20 (a modest gain of $1.41).

The third table analyzes the BMW X5 xDrive 45e, which represents a consistently positive scenario due to high electric efficiency of 1.82 miles per kilowatt-hour relative to a lower gas efficiency of 20 miles per gallon. With gas costs fixed at $15.50, electric charging saves money across all pricing tiers, showing a savings of $0.82 under the Standard Plan (EV cost of $14.68), $2.55 under Scenario 1 (EV cost of $12.95), and $7.39 under Scenario 2 (EV cost of $8.11).

The fourth table presents the Volvo XC90 T8, which is the worst-performing vehicle in the study due to poor electric mileage of 0.95 miles per kilowatt-hour relative to its 27 miles per gallon gas efficiency. With gas costing $11.48, EV costs are extremely high: $28.25 under the Standard Plan (a loss of $16.77), $24.93 under Scenario 1 (a loss of $13.44), and $15.62 under Scenario 2 (a loss of $4.14). 

Adjacent to the tables is a photograph showing the back of an off-road vehicle parked near a grassy coastline, rigged with fishing rods and a blue kayak holding a large caught bluefish. A caption under the photo notes that bluefish tastes best as ceviche or smoked into fish jerky or pâté, adding a personal anecdote to the author's vehicle comparisons. Ultimately, the author concludes that blanket statements cannot be made about PHEV charging versus fuel costs, as the financial benefit depends heavily on local utility rates and the specific efficiency metrics of individual vehicles.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Energy Paper argues that electric vehicle manufacturing is structurally unprofitable for almost all global automakers, with positive operating margins achieved by only four Chinese companies and Tesla. Future profitability, especially in the United States, is highly uncertain due to headwinds such as the expiration of the seventy-five hundred dollar consumer tax subsidy, relaxed environmental mandates like Zero Emission Vehicle and CAFE mileage standards, and tariffs on Chinese battery parts. Highlighting this distress, several major legacy automakers have recorded massive asset writeoffs, including twenty-six billion dollars by Stellantis, nineteen point five billion dollars by Ford, and six billion dollars by General Motors, reflecting a shift toward consumer demand over regulatory mandates.

An extensive EV operating margins table tracks twenty-four global brands in 2024, displaying their production volume, operating margins from 2023 to 2025, and trailing two-year equity returns. Xiaomi leads the positive performers with an eleven percent margin on over one hundred thirty-six thousand vehicles sold, followed by BYD at six percent on over four point two million vehicles, Li Auto and Tesla both at five percent, and Seres at three percent. The remaining legacy and pure-play EV manufacturers operate in the red; BMW, Mercedes, and Volvo suffer negative ten percent margins, Ford sits at negative seventy-two percent despite selling one hundred five thousand EVs, and Toyota exhibits a negative sixty percent margin on over four point three million vehicles. The steepest operating losses are recorded by Vinfast at negative one hundred twenty-six percent and Lucid at negative two hundred fifty-nine percent.

The financial market’s reaction to these struggles is illustrated in a bottom line chart displaying the total returns of auto and EV equity indices from 2020 to early 2026, reindexed to one hundred in January 2021. The chart shows that while the S&P 500 Auto Industry Index and the MSCI World Auto and Components Index recovered strongly to end above one hundred fifty by 2026, the Bloomberg EV Index consistently underperformed after peaking in 2021, languishing near seventy by early 2026. This trend demonstrates that EV investing has been a money-loser compared to traditional automotive stocks since April 2023.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 16th Annual Eye on the Market Energy Paper by Michael Cembalest presents a comprehensive country-level dataset under the section titled "Useful final energy, electrification and related statistics by country." The included table lists thirty-three countries that collectively represent eighty-six percent of global useful final energy consumption. The dataset, sourced from the Energy Institute, the International Energy Agency (IEA), and J.P. Morgan Asset Management (JPMAM) as of 2025, details various metrics divided into four main categories: useful final energy, electricity, biofuels, and import reliance.

Under the useful final energy category, the table details total consumption in exajoules alongside percentage shares for nuclear, renewables, wind and solar, fossil fuels, oil, gas, and coal. The electricity section provides the overall electricity share of useful final energy, as well as the power generation shares from renewables, wind and solar, hydro, nuclear, biomass or geothermal, fossil fuels, and coal. The final columns show the biofuel share of transport energy and the percentage import reliance for oil, gas, and coal. 

China leads the list with eighty-seven point seven exajoules of useful final energy. China’s profile reveals a heavy dependence on fossil fuels, which account for eighty-five percent of its useful final energy, largely driven by coal at fifty-four percent. Coal also makes up fifty-eight percent of China's electricity generation, while its oil import reliance sits at seventy-two percent. The United States follows as the second-largest energy consumer with forty-four point five exajoules of useful final energy. Fossil fuels also represent eighty-five percent of the U.S. total, though natural gas is the dominant fuel source at forty-seven percent. Reflecting its domestic production boom, the United States has negative import reliance figures for gas at negative fourteen percent and coal at negative thirty-four percent, indicating it is a net exporter of these fuels.

India ranks third with twenty point zero exajoules of useful final energy, exhibiting a ninety-two percent fossil fuel share of useful final energy, with coal representing fifty-six percent. Coal accounts for seventy-five percent of India's electricity generation, and the country has high import dependencies, particularly eighty-seven percent for oil and fifty-four percent for gas. 

The dataset highlights significant global variation in decarbonization and energy trade. France stands out for its high nuclear integration, where nuclear power comprises thirty-two percent of its useful final energy and sixty-eight percent of its electricity generation. Sweden and Norway demonstrate high electricity and renewable shares; Sweden has a sixty-six percent electricity share of useful final energy, while Norway has a ninety-eight percent renewable share of electricity generation, heavily supported by hydro power at eighty-eight percent. Furthermore, Norway exhibits massive net exporter statistics, with an oil import reliance of negative eight hundred twenty-eight percent and a gas import reliance of negative three thousand two hundred sixty-one percent. Other major net energy exporters include Canada, with negative import reliance metrics across oil at negative one hundred seventy-nine percent, gas at negative fifty-one percent, and coal at negative two hundred ninety-one percent. Denmark leads in wind and solar integration, with these sources providing sixty-nine percent of its total electricity generation.

This page focuses on renewable and clean electricity generation trends, illustrating how different regions compare in transitioning to low-carbon power. The overall analysis highlights Europe as the global leader in clean energy transition. Specific clean energy shares for leading European countries show Sweden at 99%, France at 95%, Switzerland at 94%, Denmark at 85%, Spain at 75%, Germany at 57%, Netherlands at 53%, and Italy at 49%. On average, Europe's 70% clean energy share is composed of 25% wind and solar, 20% nuclear, 18% hydro, and 6% biomass. 

Six supporting charts present different cuts of this data. The first chart, tracking the renewable share of electricity consumption from 1990 to 2025, shows Europe leading with a steep rise toward nearly 50% by 2025. China follows with a sharp upward trajectory to around 35%, while emerging markets excluding China have remained relatively flat around 25%, and the United States tracks upwards to just over 20%. When nuclear power is added to the renewable share in the second chart, Europe's dominant lead becomes even more pronounced, approaching 70% by 2025. In this combined metric, the US rises to nearly 40%, while emerging markets excluding China and China itself cluster lower, between 20% and 30%.

The third chart isolates wind and solar as a share of electricity consumption, showing a dramatic, exponential increase for all regions starting around 2005. Europe leads this trend, reaching roughly 24% by 2025, while the United States and China have converged at about 18% to 20%. Emerging markets excluding China lag far behind, sitting below 5%. The fourth chart compares global legacy clean power (nuclear and hydro) against new clean power (wind and solar) in terawatt-hours. While legacy generation remains the largest slice—climbing steadily from 4,000 TWh in 1990 to over 7,000 TWh by 2025—new wind and solar generation has surged from virtually zero in 2000 to approximately 4,500 TWh in 2025. 

The final two charts detail global generation dynamics. A stacked area chart of the renewable share of global electricity generation from 1985 to post-2020 shows the total renewable share climbing above 30%, with wind and solar driving almost all of the growth in the last decade, supplementing a stable base of hydro and a small sliver of biomass. The final line chart compares global electricity generation in terawatt-hours from 1965 to 2025 across individual sources. Hydro has risen steadily to around 4,500 TWh, nuclear power has flattened out at approximately 2,700 TWh, and the combined wind and solar category has risen exponentially since the mid-2000s, overtaking nuclear and nearly matching hydro generation at roughly 4,500 TWh by 2025.

This page focuses on key trends in global renewable and clean power, examining the convergence of solar and wind generation, the stability of capacity factors, regional disparities in hydropower growth, and the factors driving up clean energy costs in North America. 

First, solar generation is rapidly converging with wind generation in major regions. A line chart tracking generation from 2019 to 2024 shows China leading this surge, with wind generation nearing 1,000 Terawatt-hours (TWh) and solar generation climbing steeply to around 900 TWh by 2024. Over the same period, Europe’s wind generation reached approximately 600 TWh while its solar generation grew to about 350 TWh. In the United States, wind generation sat near 450 TWh, with solar generation rising to roughly 300 TWh. 

Meanwhile, global capacity-weighted capacity factors have remained relatively stable. A chart spanning 2010 to 2024 illustrates that offshore wind capacity factors are the highest but show significant volatility, fluctuating between roughly 35% and 45% before ending near 42%. Onshore wind capacity factors have experienced a steady upward climb, rising from around 28% in 2010 to approximately 35% in 2024, while solar capacity factors have remained stable and low, hovering around 12% to 15%.

For hydropower, the capacity-weighted capacity factor for the top 15 nations—including Austria, Brazil, Canada, China, India, Norway, Russia, and the United States—rebounded to approximately 41% in 2024 after a three-year decline that bottomed out near 39% in 2023. This trend is accompanied by a massive geographic shift in capacity. A chart from 1965 to 2025 highlights that OECD hydropower generation has remained flat at around 1,300 to 1,400 TWh for decades. In contrast, China accounts for 60% of global hydropower growth since 1995, skyrocketing from near zero to more than 1,200 TWh by 2025, while Latin America and Asia (excluding China) have seen only modest increases, remaining below 600 TWh.

Finally, the page addresses rising clean energy costs in North America. A chart mapping market-averaged continental Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) prices from 2019 to 2026 shows wind PPA prices ascending from under $30/MWh to nearly $70/MWh, while solar prices rose from below $30/MWh to nearly $60/MWh. Data from LevelTen Energy attribute this rise to a development frenzy in 2025 spurred by the OBBBA, as developers rushed to meet milestones before the expiration of tax credits. Other compounding pressures include Section 232 50% tariffs on steel, aluminum, and copper; more rigorous federal reviews and permitting; pending Foreign Entity of Concern rules; and a new AD/CVD investigation targeting solar component producers. General global inflation also drove PPA price increases between 2021 and 2023.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 16th Annual Eye on the Market Energy Paper analyzes the steady adoption progress of electric vehicles (EVs) globally and in the United States, evaluating sales trends, regional market shares, regulatory impacts, and battery chemistry transitions.

The page features four charts tracking passenger vehicle trends through 2025. The first chart shows the EV share of global passenger vehicles from 2015 to 2025, highlighting a stark divergence: while the EV share of new vehicle sales surged to approximately 25% by 2025, the EV share of the cumulative vehicle fleet on the road reached only about 6%. 

The second and third charts contrast the EV share of passenger vehicle sales against the EV share of the total vehicle fleet across the largest global car markets from 2020 to 2025. In sales share, China leads dramatically, with EVs exceeding 50% of new vehicle sales by 2025. The UK, France, and Germany follow in the 25% to 35% range, while the US lags at roughly 12%, and Italy, Japan, and India remain under 10%. Fleet share transitions are significantly slower; by 2025, China's total fleet EV share reached about 14%, while Germany, the UK, France, South Korea, and the US all remained under 8%. 

The fourth chart focuses on US EV and Tesla market shares from 2021 to 2025. It reveals that the BEV share of total vehicle sales grew to nearly 10% by late 2025, while Tesla’s share of those BEV sales steadily declined from about 70% in 2021 to a low of roughly 40% in 2025 before surging back to 55% at the end of the year. The commentary explains that the September 2025 expiration of the US EV tax subsidy triggered a pre-expiration buying spike followed by a sharp sales decline in the fourth quarter, during which Tesla reclaimed market share in a cooling overall market.

Finally, the text details a shift by US automakers toward cheaper, safer, and more durable Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries over traditional Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) cells. While LFP batteries have lower energy density, the author notes that average daily travel in the US is only 33 miles, making the nominal range trade-off highly acceptable. Furthermore, because LFP batteries can regularly be charged to 100% capacity whereas NMC batteries are restricted to a recommended 80% to 90% limit, the effective range penalty is modest. Assuming an 85% NMC limit, the actual midpoint range difference is only 10%, translating to an effective range of 285 miles for LFP compared to 315 miles for NMC.

This page from the publication addresses the adoption of zero-emission commercial vehicles, making the core argument that this transition is currently a phenomenon concentrated in China, though Scandinavian nations are keeping pace with adoption rates of around 15%. The primary driver of this discrepancy is identified as the substantially lower unit cost of electric vehicle batteries within China compared to the rest of the world. 

The first chart on the page tracks global quarterly sales of zero-emission medium and heavy-duty trucks from 2019 to 2025, measured in thousands of units. It demonstrates a rapid rise in sales, growing from nearly zero in 2019 to approximately 50,000 units per quarter in 2025, with China making up the vast majority of the volume. Other regions, including Europe, the United States, and other global markets, represent only a tiny fraction of global sales. 

The second chart displays the sales share percentage of zero-emission medium and heavy-duty trucks over the same 2019 to 2025 period. China's curve spikes sharply starting in 2023, surpassing a 14% market share by late 2025. In contrast, the global average and Europe hover around 3% to 4%, while the United States remains flat near 0%. 

The third chart zeroes in on Europe, displaying the sales share of zero-emission medium and heavy-duty trucks in select European countries during the first half of 2025. Switzerland and the Netherlands lead the pack with shares near 19% and 18% respectively, followed closely by Sweden and Norway at approximately 15% and 13%. Despite these high-performing leaders, the overall European average sits around 3% to 4% due to lower adoption rates in major economies like Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Austria, and Belgium. 

The fourth chart highlights the cost gap driving these trends, comparing average lithium-ion battery pack prices for commercial vehicles and buses in China versus areas outside of China from 2018 to 2024, measured in 2024 US dollars per kilowatt-hour. While battery prices have fallen across the board, China has maintained a massive cost advantage; in 2024, battery pack prices in China fell to under $100 per kilowatt-hour, while prices outside of China remained significantly higher at approximately $200 per kilowatt-hour. 

The final chart at the bottom of the page shows the rapid expansion of product choices, charting the number of zero-emission commercial vehicle models available globally from 2020 to 2025. The total number of available models surged from roughly 400 in 2020 to more than 3,000 by 2025. This expansion is overwhelmingly driven by battery electric vehicles, which vastly outnumber plug-in hybrid electric vehicles and fuel cell models.

This page from the publication focuses on the current state and future vulnerabilities of the US electricity grid, highlighting sluggish transmission line expansion, shrinking reserve margins, and aging infrastructure. 

The first section examines transmission line growth using two charts covering the period from 2013 to 2024. The chart titled "US transmission line growth by ISO" tracks the miles of transmission lines (at or above 100 kV) added each year across various grid operators, including CAISO, ERCOT, MISO, PJM, SPP, New England, New York, and non-RTO/ISO regions. It reveals a steep decline in annual installations, falling from nearly 4,000 miles added in 2013 to consistently under 1,000 miles annually between 2022 and 2024. The neighboring chart, "US transmission line growth by voltage," reinforces this trend by breaking down annual mileage additions by voltage thresholds. While additions of lines of at least 100 kV dropped from a peak of 4,000 miles in 2013 to around 1,000 miles in 2023, additions of high-voltage lines of at least 345 kV and at least 500 kV have languished at very low levels, with the highest-voltage lines (>= 500 kV) rarely exceeding 500 miles added in any given year.

The middle section of the page details the projected generation capacity buffers, or anticipated reserve margins, from 2025 through 2037 during peak summer and winter demand. Both charts illustrate a worrying downward trend across most US regions due to the retirement of thermal power capacity. In the summer peak demand chart, MISO (Midwest) is projected to fall below a 0% reserve margin by roughly 2028 and remain negative, while PJM (Mid-Atlantic) is forecast to cross below 0% around 2031. Other regions like California, the Carolinas, ERCOT (Texas), Georgia/Alabama, New England, and SPP (Plains) also show steady declines. The winter peak demand chart shows similar vulnerabilities: MISO and PJM are projected to decline toward or below 0% by the mid-2030s, and the Carolinas, which starts with a high winter buffer of 80% in 2025, is projected to fall sharply to approximately 15% by 2037. 

Finally, a horizontal stacked bar chart at the bottom of the page displays the age of the existing US transmission and distribution infrastructure as of early 2025. It reveals that 30% of transmission infrastructure is near or at the end of its useful life, with 70% within its useful life, 5% near the end, and 25% at the end. The distribution infrastructure is in worse condition, with 45% near or at the end of its useful life, broken down as 55% within its useful life, 5% near the end, and 40% already at the end of its useful life.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Energy Paper, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the challenges facing the US electricity grid, focusing on backlogs in the interconnection queue and regional grid vulnerability during extreme weather events. The primary argument is that although there is a massive volume of proposed energy capacity waiting to join the US grid, very little of it actually becomes operational, and wait times have grown dramatically. Furthermore, regional reliance on imported clean energy, such as Canadian hydropower, can fail during extreme winter storms, forcing a temporary reliance on carbon-intensive peaker plants.

The first section of the page details the queue backlog through four charts based on data from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL). The first chart, a stacked bar graph titled "US capacity in the queue by type," tracks capacity in gigawatts from 2014 to 2024. It shows that total queued capacity has surged to nearly 2,500 gigawatts in 2024, which is significantly larger than the actual US installed capacity of 1,300 gigawatts. This queue is overwhelmingly dominated by solar, wind, and storage projects, while natural gas and other sources have shrunk to a tiny fraction of the total. 

To demonstrate why this queue is a poor proxy for actual future operational capacity, the second chart, "Generation completion rates by interconnection request year," plots the percentage of total capacity or number of requests that actually get connected from 2000 to 2024. Both lines—by number of requests and by capacity—show a steep decline from their peaks of around 30 percent in the mid-2000s down to nearly zero percent in recent years, as projects remain backlogged or are withdrawn. 

The third chart, "Completion rates for projects with signed interconnection agreements by interconnection request year," measures the completion percentage of projects by count. Even among projects that successfully sign interconnection agreements, completion rates have fallen from a peak of nearly 80 percent in 2015 to below 10 percent for projects requested in 2024. 

The fourth chart, "Time elapsed from interconnection request to commercial operation date," tracks the duration in months from 2000 to 2024 across the 25th, median, and 75th percentiles. The median duration has more than doubled, rising from 22 months in the early 2000s to 54 months by 2024, while the 75th percentile has climbed to nearly 70 months.

The second half of the page provides a case study of regional energy dependency titled "Oh Canada! Storm-related hydropower export issues." It discusses the newly completed 1.6 billion dollar New England Clean Energy Connect power line, which was built to import cheap Canadian hydropower from Quebec to Massachusetts. During a severe winter storm in January 2026, temperatures plummeted in Quebec, driving up local electric heating demand and forcing the utility to halt power exports to New England. This sudden disruption forced the New England grid operator to activate oil-fired peaker plants under a Department of Energy Emergency Order. For a 72-hour period before imports resumed, New England's fuel mix shifted dramatically to 33 percent fuel oil, 30 percent natural gas, 18 percent nuclear, 6 percent wind and solar, and 6 percent hydro. 

This crisis is visualized in the final chart, "Winter storm cuts off Canadian hydropower, requires oil peaker plants," which plots New England ISO hourly generation in megawatts during late January 2026. The stacked area chart, based on data from the EIA and JPMAM, displays generation sources including natural gas, oil, hydro, solar, wind, batteries, nuclear, and other. It features a prominent, massive red spike representing the rapid surge in oil-fired generation needed to offset the loss of imported Canadian hydropower during the storm.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Energy Paper explores global battery energy storage, highlighting rising adoption fueled by falling costs, while noting China's overwhelming dominance in battery manufacturing. 

The first chart tracks global gross energy storage additions by market in gigawatts from 2016 to an estimated 2025. It shows exponential growth from virtually zero in 2016 to over 80 gigawatts expected in 2025, with China representing the vast majority of this expansion, followed by the United States and various European and Asian nations. To the right, a chart detailing the price of a four-hour utility-scale energy storage system from 2019 to 2025 illustrates how costs spiked slightly to roughly $370 per kilowatt-hour in 2022 before collapsing to approximately $125 per kilowatt-hour in 2025. The battery rack represents the largest share of this cost, alongside other components like power conversion, system integration, and battery optimization.

A middle-left chart displays volume-weighted average lithium-ion battery pack prices for e-buses and commercial uses from 2018 to 2024 in real 2024 US dollars per kilowatt-hour. It contrasts China with the rest of the world, showing that China's prices fell from roughly $175 to under $100 per kilowatt-hour, while the rest of the world saw a steeper drop from nearly $475 to around $200 per kilowatt-hour. The middle-right chart compares various 2024 cost estimates for lithium-ion utility-scale battery systems, showing a wide variance among organizations. For instance, the Energy Information Administration estimates costs near $450 per kilowatt-hour, whereas WoodMac and BloombergNEF sit around $280, and the National Renewable Energy Laboratory's bottom-up estimate, which incorporates extensive component, permitting, and installation overheads, places costs near $325.

The bottom-left bar chart details battery-pack energy density in watt-hours per kilogram for 2025, comparing lithium iron phosphate at around 160, sodium-ion at around 170, and nickel manganese cobalt 8:1:1 at around 240. Although lithium iron phosphate has a lower density, the text notes it dominates stationary storage in the United States with a 90% market share, up from 25% in 2020. Finally, the bottom-right chart highlights China's dramatic dominance in global battery manufacturing capacity across all major supply chain segments. China controls over 60% of processed lithium capacity, nearly 95% of battery anodes, and over 80% of battery cell, cathode, and separator production, leaving the rest of the world with minor shares in comparison.

This page from the report argues that the primary impediment to electrification in the United States is cost. This barrier manifests in three ways: the soaring costs of essential electrical equipment like transformers, the high cost of electricity relative to fossil fuels for residential heating, and the steep premium of electricity over natural gas for industrial heat, which makes electrifying high-temperature processes economically unviable. 

The first chart illustrates the electricity share of useful final energy from 1990 to 2025. While China's electricity share has surged rapidly over the last two decades to reach nearly 38% by 2025, the US and Europe have seen much flatter trajectories, hovering around 32% to 33% in 2025. A key contributor to the slow expansion of electrical infrastructure is highlighted in the adjacent chart on producer price inflation for core goods, which tracks percent increases versus 2018 across 47 categories. Out of all categories, transformers and power regulators experienced the highest inflation, with prices rising by roughly 80% to 85% by the end of 2025.

Residential electrification faces similar economic headwinds. A chart comparing the ratio of electricity to fossil fuel prices per megajoule (MJ) across the top 10 US states shows that the US average price ratio of electricity to natural gas is approximately 3.6x, with states like Illinois and New York exceeding 4.5x. The author notes that an electricity-to-gas price ratio above 3.0x effectively erases the operating cost benefits of a highly efficient heat pump with a coefficient of performance (COP) of 3.0. In contrast, the electricity-to-heating-oil/propane ratio is much lower, generally between 1.5x and 2.5x. Although US air-source heat pump sales have risen to 4.1 million units by 2025, surpassing gas furnace sales which fell to 3.1 million, the transition of the total heating stock remains slow because annual new home construction represents only about 1% of the existing housing stock in both the US and Europe.

Industrial electrification is similarly stalled by high operational costs. A bar chart reveals that electricity is 2.0x to 5.5x more expensive than gas for industrial heat, assuming 85% furnace efficiency. The ratio is particularly punitive in California and the UK, where it exceeds 4.5x, while it is lower but still substantial in Texas at over 3.0x and China at just above 2.0x. Because of these cost dynamics, a final line chart shows that the electricity share of US industrial final energy consumption has remained completely stagnant at around 22% for nearly 35 years (from 1989 to 2024), while natural gas and petroleum have consistently dominated the industrial sector at roughly 35% and 32% of final energy consumption, respectively.

This page from the report focuses on the persistent rise of global fossil fuel consumption and emissions, identifying a looming liquefied natural gas glut and the enduring dominance of coal, particularly in China. The author argues that tracking primary fossil fuel energy is crucial for understanding why global greenhouse gas emissions continue to climb. While China represents about half of the increase in emissions since 2010, the rest is driven by other emerging nations. Oil, coal, and natural gas consumption are all rising, albeit slightly slower than during the 2018–2019 period.

The first chart, depicting global fossil fuel primary energy consumption from 1965 to 2025 in exajoules, illustrates a steady long-term upward trajectory for all three main fossil fuel types. Oil remains the largest source of primary energy, approaching 210 exajoules, followed by coal at approximately 160 exajoules, and natural gas, which has grown to about 145 exajoules. This relentless consumption is mirrored in the adjacent chart tracking global carbon dioxide equivalent emissions from energy, process emissions, methane, and flaring. Emissions have climbed from around 24 billion tons in 1990 to roughly 40 billion tons by 2025, with only a brief contraction around the 2020 pandemic before returning to growth.

The report also forecasts a substantial global liquefied natural gas glut. In a chart analyzing global LNG capacity utilization from 2005 to 2035, export capacity is projected to expand much faster than imports starting after 2025. Consequently, capacity utilization is forecast to plunge from historical levels above 90% down to around 84% by 2031, marking the first time utilization is projected to drop below the 90% threshold on record. A stacked bar chart detailing the cumulative change in LNG export capacity from 2025 to 2031 highlights that North America is the dominant driver of this new supply, contributing to a total cumulative increase of nearly 400 billion cubic meters by 2031, with further additions from the Middle East, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Russia. 

The final section of the page addresses global coal dynamics. A chart tracking coal useful final energy by country from 1965 to the mid-2020s shows that while coal use has steadily declined in the United States and Europe, it has exploded in China and is rising in India, driving total global coal final energy to over 60 exajoules. The accompanying China coal tracker from 2000 to 2025 highlights a striking paradox: even though coal’s share of Chinese power generation fell below 60% for the first time in 2024 and its share of useful final energy dropped to roughly 55%, absolute coal-fired power and coal useful final energy have continued to rise. This indicates that despite clean energy additions, absolute coal consumption for power and heat in China is still climbing.

This page from the publication focuses on US fossil fuels, specifically highlighting the dominant role of natural gas and hydraulic fracturing in the domestic energy supply. The central argument is that hydraulic fracturing has become the backbone of US energy production, accounting for 68% to 87% of crude oil, natural gas liquids, and natural gas in 2024, and representing 62% of all US primary energy consumption. Furthermore, estimates of US gas reserves continue to rise due to resources in the Haynesville/Deep Bossier Shale, updated assessments in Alaska, and offshore additions in Alaska and the Atlantic East Coast. Despite some analyst expectations of a rapid peak, US oil consumption remained stable through 2025, while liquefied natural gas exports reached 10% of total US production.

The first line chart, titled "Percentage of US oil and gas production derived from hydraulic fracturing through year-end 2024," plots the rise of fracking from 1995 to 2024. It shows natural gas leading the trend, rising from about 30% to over 85%, followed by natural gas liquids (ethane, propane, and butane) rising to around 75%, and crude oil climbing from near zero to roughly 68%. 

An adjacent stacked bar chart, "Hydraulic fracturing accounted for 62% of all US primary energy consumption in 2024," illustrates the total US primary energy mix. Unconventional oil, gas, and NGLs requiring hydraulic fracturing make up the largest block at 62%, followed by conventional oil, gas, and NGLs. Coal, nuclear, and renewables (biomass/geothermal, hydro, wind, and solar) make up the remaining top portions of the energy stack.

In the middle row, the bar chart "Estimates of US natural gas supply" measured in trillion cubic feet from 1988 to 2024 demonstrates a major expansion of resources. The total supply grew from roughly 1,000 trillion cubic feet in 1988 to more than 4,000 trillion cubic feet by 2024. The vast majority of this increase is categorized as total potential resources, while proved commercially viable reserves make up a smaller, stable slice at the top of each year's bar. 

To its right, the stacked area chart "US natural gas resources by component" categorizes these resources from 1988 to 2023, totaling over 6,000 trillion cubic feet by the end of the period. This chart details cumulative production, proved reserves, and traditional potential resources split into probable, possible, and speculative resources, alongside coalbed gas.
