A total of 36 Republican House members have opted not to seek re-election, which is the highest retirement figure recorded since the data series began in 1930. Historically, as illustrated in a scatter plot comparing GOP retirements to seat changes, whenever more than 20 members retire—a zone labeled "Get Out of Dodge"—the party experiences at best marginal gains or, more frequently, severe seat losses of up to 80 to 100 seats. Consequently, betting markets place the probability of the GOP maintaining House control after the midterms at just 15%. Additionally, congressional redistricting efforts remain highly uncertain, with the GOP projected to net anywhere from a loss of one seat to a gain of nine seats depending on upcoming state-level legal challenges, referendums, and Supreme Court Voting Rights Act decisions.

The author attributes the shift in midterm voter sentiment to three main economic factors: declining blue-collar employment, surging commodity prices, and rising inflation expectations. A stacked bar chart of year-over-year changes in US blue-collar employment shows a sharp decline from peak growth of nearly 900,000 jobs in early 2023 to net job losses, approaching negative 200,000 jobs by early 2026. This downward trend is driven primarily by contractions in manufacturing, transportation, and warehousing.

Compounding this job slowdown is a massive spike in commodity prices, detailed in a chart showing absolute year-to-date price changes. The largest increases are seen in energy and chemical inputs, led by naphtha (up 178%), wholesale gasoline (up 121%), sulfur (up 111%), methanol (up 111%), shipping fuel (up 109%), and jet fuel (up 102%). While natural gas fell 25%, most other commodities surged, including WTI crude (up 77%), urea (up 73%), and fertilizer (up 51%). This price surge has intensified a farm solvency crisis, with US farm bankruptcies rising approximately 50% year-over-year in 2025 due to tariffs raising input costs, retaliatory trade measures, and immigration policies reducing undocumented farm labor. Additionally, the doubling of jet fuel prices contributed to the collapse of Spirit Airlines, prompting the author to criticize the Biden administration—specifically naming Merrick Garland, Pete Buttigieg, and Jonathan Kanter, with backing from Senator Elizabeth Warren—for blocking the JetBlue-Spirit merger.

Finally, a line chart tracking US short-term inflation expectations across three major consumer surveys (the Conference Board, University of Michigan, and New York Fed) reveals a modest upturn in early 2026. After declining from their 2022 peaks, household inflation expectations are ticking back up, with the Conference Board 1-year measure hovering near 6% and the New York Fed and University of Michigan surveys rising toward the 3.5% to 4% range, further dampening consumer sentiment ahead of the elections.

This page analyzes the resilience of US equity markets despite a major war-driven commodity shock, attributing the market’s V-shaped recovery to rising 2026 S&P 500 earnings expectations and a historic decline in the US economy's oil intensity. Although the geopolitical crisis poses substantial headwinds, offsetting forces like corporate and individual tax cuts and lower tariffs are providing a stimulus of roughly 2% of GDP in 2026. Q1 2026 corporate earnings reports have been strong, with 11% sales growth and 26% earnings growth, though the earnings figure is artificially inflated by Google and Amazon revaluing their stakes in AI startup Anthropic. Excluding these revaluations, S&P 500 Q1 earnings growth sits closer to 16%, compared to a meager 5% in Europe. However, this US market strength is exceptionally narrow; only 28% of S&P 500 stocks are currently outperforming the index on a trailing two-month basis—a steep decline from 65% before the war, placing market breadth in its second percentile since 2010. 

To visually explain the US economy's reduced vulnerability to energy shocks, the author presents three historical charts. The first, "S&P 500 change in forward earnings vs price," plots the percent change from January 1, 2025, through April 2026, showing that the index's price has closely tracked its rising 12-month forward earnings per share, with both measures rebounding from early 2025 lows to register gains of over 20% by spring 2026. The second chart, "Energy intensity of GDP, US," measures exajoules of consumption per trillion dollars of real GDP from 1935 to 2025. It highlights how oil intensity peaked near 5.5 exajoules in the 1970s before dropping below 2 exajoules by 2025, alongside long-term declines in coal and natural gas. The third chart, "Oil intensity of the US economy," indexes 1990 levels at 100 to show that by 2025, the oil intensity of GDP and S&P 500 profits had both fallen by roughly 50%, while the oil intensity of National Income and Product Accounts (NIPA) profits plummeted by about 80%.

Despite these positive structural shifts, the author warns that the global economy faces a severe oil inventory crisis. Because the last tankers to leave the Strait before the conflict have finished delivering their cargo, global oil inventories are now shrinking at a rapid pace of 8 million barrels per day. The final chart, "Global oil and refined product inventories," plots monthly inventory levels in millions of barrels for each year from 2017 through 2026. The data series for 2026 is depicted as a steep, red-dashed line projecting a sharp drop from roughly 7,900 million barrels in the spring down to a critical operational stress floor of 6.7 to 6.8 billion barrels by September. The author warns that if the Strait is not reopened by September, global inventories will hit this hard operational floor, triggering rapid, forced demand destruction that will primarily impact consumers in Asia and Europe.

This page analyzes how artificial intelligence continues to drive the US equity market even as technology stock valuations undergo a significant correction. The author, Michael Cembalest, emphasizes that a group of 42 AI-related stocks has dominated S&P 500 performance. 

A table titled "Contribution of 42 AI stocks to S&P 500 returns, earnings and capex/R&D growth" highlights this dominance across various periods. Since November 2022, these 42 stocks contributed 76% of price returns, 87% of earnings growth, and 75% of capex/R&D growth. When narrowing the focus to the more intense phase starting in November 2024, their contribution rises to 81% of price returns, 99% of earnings growth, and 88% of capex/R&D growth. Even since November 2025, they accounted for 42% of price returns, 84% of capex/R&D growth, and an outsized 193% of earnings growth.

Despite this market dominance, tech P/E multiples have experienced a massive correction. The line chart "S&P 500 tech forward PE drawdown" plots the percentage drawdown from previous highs from 2016 through 2026. It reveals that the recent correction, labeled "Software/Iran," reached a drawdown of nearly 40%, which is larger than the drawdowns observed during the 2022 bear market (around 33%), the onset of COVID-19 (about 25%), or the interest rate hike cycle (around 28%). 

An adjacent bar chart titled "The price investors pay for earnings growth" measures the PEG ratio (P/E ratio divided by projected 2-year consensus earnings growth) across multiple sectors and indices. Surprisingly, Tech has the lowest PEG ratio at roughly 0.5, while Staples has the highest at over 3.5. This low tech ratio is driven by semiconductors, which sit at a very low PEG ratio (around 0.25) due to an expected 62% earnings growth, whereas software stocks trade at a higher PEG ratio of approximately 1.5 on 16% expected earnings growth.

The commentary then shifts to "hyperscalers" (Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft), noting strong Q1 earnings (up 61%) and sales (up 20%), but highlighting a diverging outlook based on capital spending. The line chart "Hyperscaler capex and R&D as a share of revenues" traces historical and projected consensus estimates from 2017 to 2027. Meta's capex and R&D share is projected to spike dramatically to over 80% of revenues by 2026, while Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon also show projected increases to between 30% and 55%, compared to a stable S&P 500 median of roughly 10%. 

Consequently, the final chart, "Hyperscaler free cash flow margins (net of capex)," projects a sharp decline in free cash flow margins from 2025 through 2027. Meta's margin is forecast to drop from a peak of over 30% down toward 0% by 2027, Microsoft and Alphabet decline to the 15%–20% range, and Amazon remains near 0%, as massive capital spending weighs heavily on cash generation.

This page of the publication analyzes the current state of the United States data center buildout, highlighting emerging supply chain bottlenecks and legislative hurdles that signal a potential construction slowdown. The author notes that while data center construction and power generation spending continue to rise, satellite imagery reveals that over 60% of data center capacity planned for completion in 2027 has not yet begun construction, with another 7% delayed. The primary culprits for these delays are permitting issues and supply constraints in gas turbines, transformers, and skilled labor.

The page includes four supporting charts. The first, a line graph of US construction spending from 2014 through early 2026, shows that seasonally adjusted annual spending on electric power has surged dramatically to nearly $120 billion, while spending on data centers has risen steadily to around $45 billion. In contrast, office building spending has fallen from its peak of $75 billion to around $45 billion. 

The second chart is a horizontal bar graph illustrating US data center capacity by status and completion year in gigawatts. While the planned capacity for 2025 is around 12 gigawatts and 2026 is around 22 gigawatts, the planned capacity for 2027 jumps to approximately 45 gigawatts. Crucially, the visual highlights that the vast majority of this 2027 capacity is marked as having no construction observed, underscoring the potential for a near-term bottleneck.

The third and fourth charts focus on supply chain inflation and delivery delays. A scatter plot of producer price inflation since 2020 across 47 core goods categories reveals that transformers and power regulators have seen the second-highest inflation rate, spiking nearly 80%. A line graph tracking transformer delivery times shows that wait times for generation step-up transformers roughly tripled, rising from 50 weeks in early 2022 to nearly 160 weeks by late 2024. Power transformer lead times also climbed significantly, peaking near 130 weeks before settling around 110 weeks by mid-2025. This equipment shortage is mirrored in gas turbines, where GE Vernova bookings have risen from $103 billion three years prior to a projected $200 billion by 2028.

Finally, the text refutes misleading online commentary regarding a widespread legislative backlash against data centers. The author clarifies that no state-level bans have actually passed. Proposed state-level bans have either failed or been vetoed by governors in Maine, New Hampshire, South Dakota, and Wisconsin, while remaining proposed but unpassed in several other states. Instead, bans remain strictly localized at the county level, with examples including Larimer County in Colorado, Champaign County in Illinois, and Chatham County in North Carolina. Meanwhile, many states—including Texas, Tennessee, Utah, and West Virginia—actively continue to attract data centers using tax and financial incentives.

This page explores the feasibility of the "Gulf Super Express," a theoretical pipeline project proposed in a Rice University Baker Institute paper by Gabriel Collins. The project addresses the geopolitical risks posed by Iran by constructing a massive pipeline stretching from Southern Iraq to Oman, thereby bypassing high-risk maritime chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. 

Geographically, a map on the left illustrates the proposed route, starting at the Basra pipeline intake in Southern Iraq, traversing Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, and concluding in Oman with terminals at Duqm and Salalah Port, the latter reached via a dedicated spur pipeline. Physically, the project would feature twin 56-inch pipelines with a combined capacity of 10 million barrels per day, a 2 million barrel per day spur to Salalah, and 150 million barrels of storage capacity. Financially, the estimated capital cost is $55 billion, built over five years. This total includes $15.7 billion for pipelines and pumping stations, $11.9 billion for soft costs and interest, $10.1 billion for defense and hardening (including Patriot PAC-3 and Mantis C-RAM systems), $7.2 billion for contingencies, and billions more for terminals and spurs. 

An accompanying bar chart on the right displays the capital expenditure of oil pipelines longer than 500 kilometers completed since the year 2000, measured in 2024 US dollars per barrel per day of capacity. The chart shows that at 100% capacity utilization, the Gulf Super Express's cost of $5,500 per barrel per day sits at the lower end of the global cost spectrum. At 50% capacity utilization, the capital cost rises to a moderate $11,000 per barrel per day, which is still lower than historical projects in countries like Canada, China, India, and the highly expensive Chad-Cameroon pipeline, which approaches $35,000 per barrel per day. 

Despite these competitive capital costs, the project introduces a substantial operational "security premium." Shipping oil to East Asia using a very large crude carrier (VLCC) alone from Southern Iraq costs approximately $1.94 per barrel. In comparison, utilizing the pipeline-VLCC combination would cost $3.27 per barrel at 100% pipeline utilization and rise to $4.92 per barrel at 50% utilization. Ultimately, the author raises open questions regarding whether Gulf states can successfully cooperate to share these costs—especially given tensions such as the United Arab Emirates withdrawing from OPEC—and whether they are willing to pay this premium to mitigate the threat of future strait shutdowns.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication features an analysis of congressional redistricting, state-level referendums, and Supreme Court Voting Rights Act decisions, and how they could collectively shift the balance of power in the U.S. House of Representatives. Cembalest argues that the net impact of these changes for the Republican Party could range from losing one seat to gaining nine seats, depending on court rulings, election outcomes, and the survival of a contested Virginia referendum.

A central chart illustrates the potential distribution of new House seats resulting from these state redistricting efforts and legal rulings. The chart shows a potential total of fourteen seats for Republicans and ten for Democrats, categorized by their legal status. For the Republicans, five seats in Texas, two in Ohio, and one in North Carolina are shown as secure gains from enacted state legislation with no further challenges expected. Another group of Republican seats remains subject to state supreme court challenges, including four seats in Florida and one in Missouri. Additionally, single seats in Louisiana and Tennessee are highlighted as possible gains resulting from the Supreme Court decision in Louisiana v. Callais. On the Democratic side, five seats in California and one in Utah are from enacted legislation or court-ordered maps. The remaining four potential Democratic seats are in Virginia, though these are currently subject to state supreme court challenges. 

The text provides critical context for these figures. On the Republican side, Texas could secure its five new seats under a map signed into law in August 2025. The Supreme Court's ruling in Louisiana v. Callais determined that the Voting Rights Act did not necessitate a second majority-minority district in Louisiana, which may eliminate a Democratic district there, while Tennessee may also convene a session to eliminate a Democratic seat. However, fast-approaching 2026 primary deadlines and mail-in voting mean the impact of these changes might not be realized until 2028. In Florida, Governor Ron DeSantis’s proposed map is expected to face judicial challenges in the state supreme court, despite all seven judges being Republicans, six of whom were appointed by DeSantis himself. This is because Florida’s constitution explicitly disallows partisan redistricting, a rule DeSantis reportedly believes is unconstitutional. 

On the Democratic side, California could secure five seats following its redistricting referendum, while Utah could add one seat. The most contested situation is in Virginia, where Democrats stand to gain four seats. Cembalest details what he describes as an unforced error by Virginia on redistricting. To alter its current balance of six Democrats and five Republicans to a heavily partisan ten Democrats and one Republican, the state legislature held a referendum to temporarily suspend its own constitutional protections against partisan gerrymandering. The referendum was presented to voters with the biased rationale "to restore fairness." A state trial court has since enjoined officials from certifying the results, ruling that amendments must be presented neutrally and noting that the legislature committed several procedural and timing violations. Consequently, the fate of these four seats rests with the Virginia Supreme Court.

This page examines the financial dynamics of the artificial intelligence boom, focusing on hyperscaler debt issuance, credit metrics, and the valuation of domain-specific AI startups. The central argument is that while hyperscalers have recently begun using debt financing to fund data centers instead of relying solely on internal cash flow, their leverage remains modest relative to cash-flow capacity. A major exception to this trend is Oracle, which stands out as a leveraged outlier compared to its peers. Additionally, the author notes that unlike the dot-com era, the current expansion in technology capital expenditures is not being driven by aggressive, aggregate debt financing.

The page features four charts that support these observations. The first chart, located in the top left, tracks the annual change in hyperscaler long-term debt, including bonds, loans, and leases, in billions of US dollars from 2015 through early 2026. This visual shows a dramatic shift starting in the fourth quarter of 2024, with total annual issuance surging from historical levels of under $50 billion to nearly $140 billion in 2025 and 2026, driven by major issuances from Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle. 

To the right, the second chart plots the net debt to trailing twelve-month EBITDA ratio of direct AI stocks. It highlights that the median S&P 500 company has a leverage ratio of just under 2x, and most AI companies, including Nvidia, Google, Apple, Meta, and Microsoft, register near 0x, indicating they hold an excess of cash and marketable securities over debt. Oracle is the stark exception, with its leverage multiple standing around 7x in the third quarter of 2025 and rising toward 8x in the first quarter of 2026. 

This divergence is further illustrated in the bottom-left chart, which compares five-year credit default swap spreads for select AI stocks from 2022 to 2026. While spreads for Alphabet, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft remain tightly bunched together at very low levels of under 60 basis points, Oracle's credit default swap spread spiked significantly in early 2026, approaching 180 basis points. 

The bottom-right chart compares the capital expenditure cycle against capex financing for US technology and telecommunications companies in the Russell 3000 from 1996 to 2026. It reveals that while the capex-to-sales ratio has ticked up to around 9% in 2026, the share of capex and dividends financed with debt rather than operating cash flow remains extremely low, hovering under 5%. This contrasts sharply with the dot-com bubble peak around 2000, when capex-to-sales hit 12% and the debt-financed share of capex and dividends reached approximately 40%.

The page concludes with a discussion on the impact of agentic AI on domain-specific startups, focusing on the legal AI company Harvey. Harvey raised over $1 billion from investors, reaching an $11 billion valuation, but admitted that general frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, and Google outperformed its proprietary model on its own "BigLaw Bench" benchmark. Consequently, Harvey pivoted to a workflow model that routes tasks to these external frontier models. The author poses critical questions about whether a company functioning primarily as a wrapper for other models can maintain its high valuation and what long-term competitive moats it can establish, beyond providing superior security and client confidentiality. The text notes that the BigLaw Bench includes complex transactional tasks, such as drafting board consents regarding lawyer conflicts of interest, and litigation tasks, such as analyzing trial documents to build detailed chronological timelines.
